input: Sea visibility 0 statute mile and vertical visibility 100 feet/foot in fog. No runway visual range was given in automatic terminal information service simultaneous approaches to runways 16l and 16r were in use. Fdc notice to airmen / of air missions 7/2249: instrument landing system runway(s) 16l clear air turbulence ii and clear air turbulence iii amdt 3b. Procedures na. Temporary crane 562 feet/foot mean sea level 868 feet/foot east of runway(s) 16l/34r. (i have saved original fdc notams from this flight.) we briefed a clear air turbulence iiib autoland to runway 16r and were later told by approach to 'expect runway 16r.' then after handoff to the next approach controller we were assigned runway 16l; just prior to turning base. I immediately asked for the runway visual range and was told 1800 feet/foot i then reprogrammed the box for a clear air turbulence i approach to runway 16l. The captain was pilot flying and at decision height did not have the runway environment in sight and we executed a missed approach. Approach asked intermediate fix we would like vectors back to try it again. I stated we wanted vectors to runway 16r second officer we could conduct at clear air turbulence iii approach. I also told them there was an fdc notice to airmen / of air missions prohibiting clear air turbulence ii and clear air turbulence iii approaches to runway 16l. The controller appeared surprised by this information. While being vectored to runway 16r approach control asked for the number of the fdc notice to airmen / of air missions i gave it to him. We successfully accomplished a clear air turbulence iii autoland on runway 16r. At the completion of the flight; the captain called dispatch and they could not find that notice to airmen / of air missions -- i suspect approach control deleted it with the information i gave them. It was in the packet for our return flight but only because it was probably printed out as we were landing. I ante meridiem filing this because we were aware of the notice to airmen / of air missions and therefore flew a clear air turbulence i. We saw (tcas) and heard numerous flights making successful approaches and landings to runway 16l prior to us. Arrivals were being evenly split between both runways. It is obvious to me from the weather reported and observed that no one was able to land clear air turbulence i on runway 16l. I believe everyone was utilizing clear air turbulence ii or clear air turbulence iii -- they just didn't read the fdc notams. I faithfully do and ante meridiem penalized for it. The fdc notice to airmen / of air missions system is broken. Every listing is repeated at least twice and often four times; at every airport; which increases the amount of data i have to wade through every leg.
output: AN A319 FIRST OFFICER COMPLAINED ABOUT FDC NOTAM PROCEDURES; NOTING LISTINGS ARE OFTEN OUT OF DATE AND REPEATED MULTIPLE TIMES; MAKING IT DIFFICULT TO EFFICIENTLY READ AND COMPLY WITH NOTAMS. ON THIS PARTICULAR FLIGHT THEY MISSED THE APPROACH AT SEA BECAUSE OF A NOTAM THAT WAS OUT OF DATE BUT INCLUDED IN THEIR PACKET.

input: While working south departure we requested the tower to stop using area navigation dual departures due to weather obstructing the south departure lane. The tower launched aircraft x on a braves departure and then aircraft y on a non-rnav 250 heading inside of aircraft x. I have not reviewed the tape nor do i recall aircraft y advising me that he was on a heading. I stopped aircraft y off at 8;000 on initial contact (climbing out of 3;000) and got a good read back. I then went back to aircraft x and issued 'leaving 8;000 cleared direct braves.' i assumed that aircraft y was still on the area navigation and would turn parallel to aircraft x. When i noticed aircraft y pass ftball without turning i issued a turn to the south. Aircraft were approximately 2 miles apart and aircraft y was level at 8;000 and aircraft x was out of 8;600. When transitioning from area navigation to vector the pilot phraseology may or not convey the fact that the aircraft is on a vector or climbing via the standard instrument departure while working departure with numerous requests for deviations and outside coordination happening rapidly it is very easy to miss when the tower transitions. I find day-in and day-out i have to question pilots as to their area navigation status.an easy fix to this problem is for local control to key the landline and advise departure an time they transition from area navigation to headings (example 'aircraft y non-rnav; heading 250' or 'aircraft x is the last area navigation departure.'i really can't believe we don't do this already as a matter of procedure.
output: A80 Departure Controller reported that two aircraft came off on different departures that were a conflict of each other. One was on a RNAV departure and the other was assigned a heading; but inside of the RNAV departure. Reporter wants some type of standardization to let the Departure Controller know if the aircraft is on a RNAV departure or a heading.

input: On feb/thu/97 at approximately xg30 post meridiem i took off from stuart airport in florida to travel to nassau; visual flight rules i had done a thorough preflt and runup before takeoff with all indications of a normal flight i use noise-canceling headsets and have attuned myself to the normal sounds of my engine when i ante meridiem wearing them. My takeoff was normal until i reached 300-400 feet/foot above ground level when my engine started missing. I did my normal routine for a rough-sounding engine (that i learned as a student) but the engine continued to miss. My passenber could also hear the change in the sound of the engine my other indicators were normal (oil pressure; temperature etc). I asked stuart tower intermediate fix i could make an emergency landing which i did without incident. A local repair station checkeded out the plane and found a broken baffle in the muffler which had blocked 3/4 of the exhaust. They replaced the muffler.
output: PVT PLT OF AN SMA SEL MADE AN EMER LNDG AFTER CLBING TO 400 FT AGL WITH THE ENG MISFIRING AND LOSING PWR.

input: Outside air temperature was one hundred plus degrees. Carrying on an exchange with another technician while performing work; i was tasked with servicing the crew oxygen bottle since it was below the minimum value for the service check limit. Referencing m/m 12-15-21 for the servicing limits; i proceeded to the forward pit of the b737-800 to gain access to the o2 panel. As i have done for years; i removed the bottle from the airplane and brought it to the servicing station where it was filled to the specifications as outlined by the manual. After returning to the aircraft with the serviced o2 bottle; i began reinstalling the bottle. During the final steps of the crew o2 bottle installation; i had started a discussion with a fellow technician at the open (cargo) pit door. After fastening the blow-out line and regulator to the bottle; in my mind; i recall opening the valve to the full open position and then; back in a quarter turn; before installing the break-away wire. I don't recall removing my hand from the valve after beginning to open it. I performed the leak check after securing all connections and all checked out good. Our conversation had carried through to completion of the bottle install.as we were walking away from the aircraft; i asked my fellow technician to perform the functional test while i proceeded to the office to address the paperwork. He acknowledged that he would perform the test and i went to the office. I filled out the log page with the appropriate information about the crew o2 reading and the applicable servicing that was accomplished. The functional test was performed and signed by a separate technician and i finished the log page by signing-off the resolution box.
output: Two Mechanics describe their involvement with the servicing of a B737-800 Crew Oxygen Bottle.

input: We were forced by [operations] to work a duty day of more than the federal aviation regulation duty max of 20 hours.we were informed by the flight deck that we were going to remain at the gate due to weather in the area. That delay lasted until [late that night] when we finally departed. While holding at the gate with passengers onboard for 7 hours 13 minutes; we were contacted by the crew desk that we were going to be going over the international on duty max of 16 hours 30 minutes. The crew desk informed us that if we extended our duty and continued with our assignment that we would receive [premium pay]. However; if we didn't accept the [premium] pay that the crew desk was prepared to reassign us each new trips no matter our present duty since they were short staffed flight attendants. We decided to stay on our present trip.upon our arrival; we were aware that our duty was now going to be over the extended duty max federal aviation regulation of 20 hours. We contacted [company] and spoke to crew scheduling. He instructed us that they was no such federal aviation regulation duty max and that if we didn't continue on that our previous agreement of [premium] pay would be removed as penalty. We felt that we had no choice but to continue on and go over 20 hours of duty. With that; our cabin crew had been up for 23 hours upon our arrival.
output: Air carrier flight attendants reported they feel they were coerced to work beyond the FAA mandated 20 hour duty day maximum.

input: During routine flight ord - ric; air traffic control issued crossing restriction 40 westbound of ric at 9000 feet/foot perhaps i was distracted; but i promptly forget about the crossing restriction; i even wrote it down! At approximately 42 westbound of ric and descending 290 knots indicated airspeed at approximately 13 - 14;000 feet/foot air traffic control inquired as to whether or not we would make the crossing restriction. I immediately remembered; apologized; and asked for relief. A quick checked of traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii showed no traffic conflict. I pushed the nose down to barber pole; approximately 350 knots indicated airspeed and leveled off 9250 feet/foot to bleed off airspd; now well inside 40 mile restriction (approx 35 deg.) my reasoning was that intermediate fix there was non- transponder equipped instrument flight rules traffic it would be better to be at altitude and 100 knots indicated airspeed too fast at 9000 feet/foot than be at 250 knots indicated airspeed and collide with somebody at 10000. About the time we leveled off; air traffic control provided relief from the crossing restriction and handed us off to approach control this was nobody's fault but mine. (fo was busy with new automatic terminal information service etc. At my request.' it was the end of a longitude day: (late pm.) cure - eternal vigilance?
output: ACR CAPT WRITES DOWN CLRNC WITH XING RESTRICTION. TOTALLY FORGETS; MAKES RAPID DSCNT WHEN REMINDED BY ATC.

input: I was conducting a multi-engine flight test. Automatic weather observing/reporting system indicated wind was calm. Applicant decided to taxi to runway 06 for departure. Unknown to us aircraft y with no radio taxied to runway 24 for departure. The ramp and taxiway to 24 were behind us as we taxied toward runway 06.after completing runup; the applicant made the normal common traffic advisory frequency announcements indicating we intended to depart runway 06. Neither the applicant nor i observed any traffic during takeoff or climb.we were later informed that aircraft y was departing at the same time on runway 24 and that we almost collided over the runway. I do not know if aircraft y saw us or took evasive action. Because of the slope of the runway; it would not have been possible for either plane to see the other until after takeoff. This could have been a very serious accident and could have been avoided if aircraft y had been radio equipped.while a calm wind is good for flying; it was a set up for this close call.
output: Check pilot reported a NMAC during takeoff from a non-towered airport.

input: Night visual meteorological conditions on an instrument flight rules flight plan; with 8 passenber on board. We were at 13000 feet/foot mean sea level on the arrival, arrive into zzz when the cabin pressurization failed in the automatic mode and allowed the cabin pressure to drop; activating the emergency pressurization. We complied with the appropriate chklist and requested a lower altitude we notified approach that we would be unable to comply with the arrival, arrive altitudes and needed a reroute to avoid mountainous terrain. Approach was unable to reroute us; thus we exercised command authority/authorized and declared an emergency and asked for direct to zzz airport at that time the airport was in sight; and we were cleared down to 10000 feet/foot the cabin pressure stabilized at the lower altitude and a landing was made visually without further incident. The inability to receive an immediate reroute from zzz controllers prompted the declaration of an emergency in order to deviate from the standard terminal arrival route restrs for altitude clearance over mountainous terrain at night. (as information this arrival, arrive routing is over mountainous terrain; where our current direct routing at that time was direct to the airport and not over mountainous terrain.)
output: LEAR 35 PRESSURIZATION CONTROL FAILED. FLT CREW DECLARED EMER; APCH AND LNDG COMPLETED UNEVENTFULLY.

input: After landing on runway(s) 15l at jan; turned off runway(s) onto high speed taxiway ramp construction barriers were sighted ahead. Stopped aircraft and requested taxi instructions from ground control ground control directed a sharp left/right (directions) turn onto intersecting taxiway while making this turn; left/right (directions) main gear xed edge of grass divider strip. When parked at the gate; i checkeded left/right (directions) main gear and found mud on left/right (directions) gear tires. Made an entry in aircraft maintenance log requesting inspection at left/right (directions) main gear for possible damage. Contacted ground control on radio; telling them what had happened and requested a checked of taxiway for possible taxiway light damage. Left/right (directions) main gear was washed and inspected. No damage found. Results of taxiway inspection is unknown. Cause of problem was unfamiliar airport at night with construction barriers obstructing normal taxi patterns; pilots inability to see clrly taxiway that he was cleared to turn onto; and being unaware of the close proximitypa of grass divider strip. Situation could be corrected by posting clrly marked alternate taxi rtes while construction is in progress or by receiving less demanding sharp turn instructions to comply with alternate taxi rtes. Supplemental information from 171702. The lack of lights on taxiway for night operation; light emitting diode directly to this mishap. No lighted signs telling you where any txwys are. Also no lights on the construction area; where it blocked the ramp; were visible.
output: TXWY EXCURSION IN A NIGHT OPERATION.

input: I departed heading to john wayne airport (sna). Prior to departure; i contacted ground control to arrange for an air traffic control flight following to john wayne airport. I was issued a squawk by ground control and were told to contact socal approach at after departure.i departed and established two-way communication with the socal departure. I was acknowledged by the air traffic control controller and we were told by him to correct our squawk. I found our squawk to be correct as assigned therefore i simply recycled the transponder. The controller appeared to be very busy and was rushed to accommodate not only the incoming and outgoing visual flight rules aircrafts; but also aircraft requesting instrument flight rules approaches at the time.the busy controller never advised me to contact the next frequency nor did he ever advised me to stay clear from class celsius airspace. If he did he must have been stepped on by other busy transmissions as i never heard any instructions from him. As such; and since i had established two way communication with the air traffic control and since i did not get any instructions from him not to enter class celsius we proceeded on course to our destination; john wayne airport.however; since i did not get a hand off where i usually get such hand offs; i became uncomfortable and attempted to get the air traffic control controller attention by performing two 'radio checks'. Each time the busy controller ignored me and did not reply. At that point i decided to contact john wayne airport tower directly. I explained to the tower that i was on flight following with the air traffic control but unable to get the controller's attention. John wayne tower did not comment at all and routinely accommodated me to land.upon landing the sna ground control advised me to contact a supervisor regarding a pilot 'violation'!few minutes later i called a number and spoke with an federal aviation administration employee who did not identify himself. He appeared to be upset and accused me of entering john wayne class celsius airspace 'without talking to anyone'!! It was obvious that the gentleman was totally clueless and unaware of the following facts: i had obtained air traffic control flight following for a visual flight rules flight from to john wayne airport directly from ground before even getting airborne. I established two way communications with the air traffic control after departure and after being released by tower; and when i entered john wanye class celsius airspace i was utilizing air traffic control flight following! And; the air traffic control controller's apparent busy and overwhelming work load.i calmly and politely explained the above facts to the unidentified federal aviation administration employee on the phone. His attitude changed somewhat as he stated he will have the above information checked out. He added i will have no violations if federal aviation administration verifies the above facts. He then demanded my phone number and the pilot certificate number which i provided to him right away.at the end he added that the verification process has to be done by another 'team' and not him. He will refer all the information to the other team who will contact me. I requested that he preserves all [departure] airport; john wayne airport; and enroute air traffic control radar and communication tapes and any other evidence regarding the flight and the alleged incident whatsoever available to him.i explained to him that i will need these evidence should this matter escalates to a point that i will have to further explain or defend myself. He indicated that had 'already' done so.after finishing the phone call with the federal aviation administration employee; i remain puzzled that if the gentleman had indeed examined and preserved the radar and communication tapes; why was he so clueless as to the true facts of the alleged incident and why he accused me of entering into the class celsius airspace 'without talking to anyone'?it is clear the overwhelmed and busy air traffic control controller dropped the ball and failed to timely communicate with me or to provide me with further instructions. In absence of clear instructions such as 'stay outside of class celsius airspace' my obligation as a pilot was to establish a two-way communication with the air traffic control before entering class celsius airspace which i did.there was no violations on my part. After all i exercised due caution by taking my time to request and obtain air traffic control flight following and a squawk before even leaving the ground in my departure point. I then complied with the rest of the requirements to establish a two-way communication with the air traffic control upon getting airborne. If the controller was busy why was i not given an instruction to stay clear from sna class celsius airspace until he catches up with his work load and get back to me? Why even i have to be placed in a position by air traffic control failure to defend myself and why i was falsely accused by the unidentified federal aviation administration employee of entering the class celsius airspace 'without talking to someone'?as pilot and a flight instructor my aim has always been to fully comply with all federal aviation administration regulations and to promote safety at all times. However; even the most experienced pilots can make a mistake and i am no exception. If i do make a mistake; i will be the first to fully acknowledge and to fully take responsibility for it. This was not the case! I did not make a mistake rather i was set up for this incident through the failure of the system that is designed to prevent and avoid exactly this type of situations; that is visual flight rules flight following to help and assist pilots to utilize and to avoid air space violations.
output: General aviation pilot reported they may have entered Class C airspace without clearance.

input: We were cruising at fl280 after departing london; england; bound for washington; dc. The capt said he was going to be off the radio #1 and on #2 to receive the oceanic clearance from shannon. I took over the communicationss with london and made several voice communications with london as we were being vectored. At some point the capt said 'tell them you want fl310.' i got the clearance to climb and began to climb to fl310. I could see that the capt was re-inserting waypoints on the inertial navigation system and asked intermediate fix we had gotten a different routing. He replied yes we now have track 'h.' the capt had the track message in his hand as he was loading the new waypoints. This is nothing that doesn't happen from time to time and many times we can't get the requested altitude second officer i figured fl310 was the crossing altitude since the capt had told me to ask for it with london. A few minute(s) later london cleared us direct to 54n 15w and i asked the capt where he had loaded 5415. He said in 6 second officer i went present position to waypoint 6. The capt said he was 'back' second officer i assumed he was on the radio #1 again. There was some discussion with the engineer about an oven door that was stuck closed and intermediate fix he should go back and help open it. This could have distracted the capt and me because i never heard a handoff from london to shannon control approaching 15w; the selective calling went off and it was shanwick telling us to contact shannon on 127.9 very high frequency we attempted several times but the frequency was second officer congested we could not make contact. By that time we had arrived at 15w which was our new oceanic control point at fl310. In reality we had been cleared to make the crossing at fl350. Since we had not gotten the handoff to shannon from frequency 133.6 to 127.9 we were not cleared to climb to fl350. We called shanwick back on high frequency and gave our position rpt for 15w told them we were at fl310 and were unable shannon on very high frequency 127.9 we crossed 15w at xa39z. At xa47z shanwick called back and said shannon control request to know why we did not work shannon air traffic control on 132.15. The capt replied that we never got the frequency change. For the next few minute(s) the capt tried to contact shannon on the frequency 127.9 but could not establish contact for a climb clearance we could hear other people talking but could not make contact ourselves. Now we were approaching 20w at fl310 and realized that we were not going to get through. Shanwick called again on high frequency and cleared us to climb to fl350 and be level fl350 by 30w. 4 minute(s) later; shanwick called back on high frequency and asked why we had not complied with our oceanic clearance to which the capt replied that we were never cleared out of fl310. 5 minute(s) later; shanwick called back with a message that shannon control had been trying to contact us on very high frequency including 121.5 and that some sort of rpting action will be taken. Lesson: make sure that all of the crew know the oceanic clearance my policy in the future will be to have the clearance read back aloud by the crew member receiving the clearance to all the crew second officer that all the crew are aware of the clearance also; on 3-man aircraft the third pilot will monitor the receiving of the clearance with the pilot actually calling for the clearance i should have made inquiry into the clearance and who we were talking to. As soon as you receive the oceanic clearance ask for the crossing altitude from the controling agency. Supplemental information from acn 251470: after receiving the oceanic clearance the capt asked me intermediate fix we could make fl350. I said we were too heavy at that time and would be able in a few minute(s) then; air traffic control cleared the first officer direct to our oceanic entry point. A few minute(s) later; a cabin crew member called with a galley oven problem i was concerned about the oven overheating second officer notified the capt and requested to go take a look at the oven in the lower aft galley. Consequently; i was absent from the cockpit during most of the time of this event.
output: ALTDEV ALT UNDERSHOT IN ACR WDB FAILURE TO MAKE ALT XING RESTRICTION.

input: Data for wet runway(s) the data is based on a dry runway(s) no correction is available until a contamination threshold of 1/8 inch or greater of standing water is applied. However; we operate daily on wet runway(s) where the aircraft takeoff weight is equal or nearly equal to the runway(s) limited weight ie; lga on most summer days with no adjustment intermediate fix the runway(s) is rpted wet. When i asked 3 different checked airmen during my last checked about this; none were even aware of the fact that the numbers were not adjusted for a wet runway(s) when i submitted this question to air carrier they replied; 'there is no regulation for the manufacturer to provide or the operator to use wet runway(s) data. Contaminated runway(s) data is provided but unless the runway(s) is considered contaminated; only dry runway(s) data is used for takeoff performance.' do we need a federal rule to ensure we operate as safely as possible? It is my belief that we are betting our airline on the hope we will not lose an engine within 10 knot(s) of v1 every time we take off on a wet runway(s) where our takeoff weight is nearly equal to the runway(s) limited weight with many takeoffs per day; i do not think we have the luxury of feeling lucky. I believe we are taking an unnecessary risk by not providing our pilots with accurate data for wet runway(s) conditions and we are operating with a false sense of security just because a problem hasn't happened yet. However; intermediate fix we as an airline have decided that we cannot afford to take a wet runway(s) correction every time a weight limited runway(s) is rpted as wet; then pilots need to know that fact. And while we are being concerned intermediate fix a 140000 pound aircraft takeoff weight is 100 pounds over the planned takeoff weight on a maximum power i think we ought to also share the fact that the numbers we are betting on are not even valid for a wet runway(s) i hope there is something i ante meridiem missing here; but i fear i ante meridiem not. I hope marketing and financial planning have not eroded a ctlable margin of safety.
output: ACR PLT IS CONCERNED HIS ACR DOES NOT PROVIDE WT PENALTIES FOR WET RWY TKOFS.

input: Entering the terminal area after an overnight oceanic flight from the united states. The flight planned route terminated with a standard terminal arrival route based upon our experience from previous trips; we were expecting the area navigation transition following the standard terminal arrival route to end up with an instrument landing system to runway 26r. During the standard terminal arrival route approach cleared us to zzzzz and zzzzz1. We were not cleared for the area navigation transition. We entered the waypoints and continued. We were then handed over to the final controller. Passing zzzzz1 we were told to expect the instrument landing system runway 26l approach (we previously were expecting the instrument landing system 26r). At that point the pilot in command (pilot not flying) was focused on changing the approach in the flight management system as the aircraft passed zzzzz1; the aircraft began a right turn based on the instrument landing system being loaded into the flight management system we immediately asked the controller for a heading and were given a turn back to 070. We then took vectors for an instrument landing system 26l and completed an uneventful landing. At no time did we come near any other aircraft (noted both visually and on tcas).the area navigation transition notes that at zzzzz1 the aircraft should maintain track and expect radar vectors to the final approach.in our minds; this event developed due to a combination of a bad clearance from approach and our failure to confirm what actions would be required following zzzzz1. If approach had cleared us for the entire area navigation transition; the procedure loaded in the flight management system would have prevented us from turning towards the runway at zzzzz1. Further complicating the issue; upon initial contact with the final controller; aircraft are expected to state only their call sign; again; a full check in might have increased situational awareness for both our crew and air traffic control given the long oceanic flight and our operations within a circadian low; we believe that fatigue was a factor in this event. We intend to share our experience with our entire pilot group to ensure that as a team we learn from this situation.
output: A corporate flight crew on an international arrival started a turn to the initial approach fix before asking for further clearance.

input: We were assigned the dotss 1 area navigation departure. We departed 25l; somewhere between docker and weiler we were given direct pevee. We were also given 280 knots when able. input: While on takeoff at bos runway(s) 9; just after v1; we ingested seagulls into the #2 (r) engine there was a bang and smell of smoke in the aircraft we declared an emergency and returned to bos without incident. (eng remained running and operated normally.)
output: AN ACR FLC FLYING B737-200 AT BOS INGESTS SEAGULL INTO #2 ENG DURING TKOF ROLL.

input: Prior to push back from zzz we simultaneously received 3 unusual messages from the aircraft. We got an xpdr fail message annunciated on the transponder; ads-b fail light on the panel; and on our flight management system we had a global positioning system not available message. Initially i thought that similar to our electronic flight instrument system comp mon messages; this may have been due to interference from the airport infrastructure; so the captain and i decided to continue our push off the gate and see if the problem fixed itself as we taxied away from the gate. Just in case there was a global positioning system outage; i updated the flight management system position with the current position for the gate. We asked ground control if they were receiving our transponder; and they confirmed that they were receiving our transponder normally. We received a taxi clearance to a hold pad short of the runway to troubleshoot the issues. The problems did not resolve during taxi. We sent a message to dispatch; and the captain called maintenance [mx] control. Mx control knew that the xpdr fail message was due to a nationwide ads-b outage; and told us that the xpdr should still function normally; and there were no airworthiness issues; with our transponder; but simply that without an appropriate ads-b signal the transponder would give us that message. They said specifically not to write up the transponder since the issues was associated with the nationwide ads-b outage and not with any faulty aircraft equipment; and then that we were still airworthy and legal to depart normally. The captain and i discussed the global positioning system not available message on the flight management system and determined after conversing with dispatch that it was also related to the system failures. Our dispatcher sent us an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message that 'it's an air traffic control system issues. As far as we know we are still good to depart and land'. We told him that since we were no longer area navigation 1 capable (fom 5-65 & sopm 4-16.21); we would need to be refilled on non area navigation sid's & star's. Our dispatcher said; 'i was told to file flights normally...since the issue is with the gnss system and not our aircraft'. He then sent us an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message saying 'atc command center is reporting the outage was due to 'geomagnetic activity' as reported by norad'. At this point i contacted clearance to try and receive a reroute and they told us to re file the flight plan with our company; so we told our dispatcher again to re file us and change the equipment code since we were no longer capable of global positioning system or the area navigation 1. He told us 'i'm sure air traffic control will be able to give you what you need but on our end we are required to just file normally.' about a minute later he sent us another message saying; 'you are complying with everything - it is not our issue it is atc's issue.' we talked again to clearance and they were able to rework our departure to the only non-rnav departure out. We were under the impression that he also changed our equipment capabilities in our flight plan. The captain and i re-briefed our departure; and double-checked to make sure we were doing everything by our procedures. After referencing the fom we felt that we had satisfied all of the requirements to legally and safely depart. We also discussed the equipment anomalies and determined that after discussing with mx and dispatch that all three messages were due to the 'geomagnetic activity' and not any aircraft specific problems. We felt that we were airworthy and legal; however just with degraded navigation capabilities due to the ads-b & gnss system outage; which had nothing to do with inoperative equipment on the airplane. We departed using dme/dme area navigation in the flight management system on the sole non-rnav departure. Prior to takeoff the flight management system radio tuning page was selected to automatic and the runway update was performed per using the toga buttons once lined up with the departure runway. The fom stated that we were authorized to use the flight management system for enroute area navigation navigation as long as it was not on q or t routes. We flew without issue enroute and had center switch us to a non-rnav since we still had a global positioning system not available message. We transitioned onto the instrument landing system with green needles. The flight management system had about a 0.35nm drift that had developed during the flight. On the descent we received a message from dispatch saying 'we are holding flights that have xpder fail on the ground. Flight ops doesn't want those planes flying'. After landing; the ramp was an absolute disaster and all the gates were occupied due to our aircraft and other carriers having these same issues. We called and spoke directly with our dispatcher and he didn't seem to have any issues with how we operated; and said that flight ops made the decision just because these types of operations were irregular and it was becoming problematic trying to dispatch aircraft that had these issues to certain airports that we operated into. The cause of this event was geomagnetic activity according to air traffic control and our dispatcher. We did not have an actual ads-b transponder or global positioning system failure; it was a failure of the ads-b and gnss network outside of our aircraft. While our manual does provide guidance on how to operate without global positioning system it was hard to find and took well over 15 minutes. It would maybe be appropriate to put this information in a quarterly cbt for review since it isn't often that we are having to fly without gps...however occasionally it does happen; and a refresher course for our pilots on the capabilities/limitations of our navigation equipment would be good. I did not know until i referenced the manuals last night that our flight management system was certified for dme/dme area navigation but does not meet the pbn requirements of area navigation 1 for sid's star's and approaches. Additionally; since the three messages we got were not engine indicating and crew alerting system messages; there is no guidance in the quick reference handbook or our procedures on how to deal with them. Since our system is becoming more highly reliant on ads-b; it might be appropriate to address these holes in our operations with some updated procedures on how to deal with this type of an issue. After refiling with air traffic control we were able to operate fairly normally to zzz1 without any issues.
output: A CRJ-700 First Officer reported flight plan filing issues related to a nationwide GPS outage.

input: I was inbound to boise; approach control asked 'where do you park?' i said fixed-base operator i was told to enter left/right (directions) downwind for runway(s) 10r. I was downwind ; asked to switch to tower contacted tower they said continue i will call your base then changed me to runway(s) 10l. I called it back and i was doing my before landing chklist and runway(s) 10r was just stuck in my head; second officer i landed on runway(s) 10r causing another aircraft to go around as soon as i heard the radio and my tail number i knew i made a mistake. Corrective action: write down changes like that on my knee board and try not to do to many things at once and be a better listener. I can say i won't let this happen again.
output: BEECH 60 PLT MISTAKENLY APCHED AND LANDED ON THE WRONG RWY CAUSING ANOTHER ACFT TO GAR.

input: We departed ptk at xa15 for a 3 hour flight to mlb. We decided to try an approach into leesburg; flight level gp3 13. We went missed. We went to mco who had rpted 15 minute(s) earlier 700 feet/foot overcast visibility 7 mile mist; dewpoint and temperature were 1 degree apart. After missed approach at lee; we went to mco instrument landing system runway(s) 36r. Tower said new special weather 100 feet/foot 1/4 mile visibility. We were now into a fuel consideration. We had missed at leesburg; mco weather had changed to worse. We had 40 minute(s) of fuel and 15-17 minute(s) flight to mco then 12-15 minute(s) flight to mlb. We elected to shoot mco runway(s) 36r instrument landing system ceiling 100 feet/foot 1/4 mile plan to divert to mlb upon missed approach at 200 feet/foot we had the runway end identifier lights rabbit; in sight. We descended to 100 feet/foot saw runway(s) and landed. However; tower called visibility 1/4 mile the view was in our eyes hard to say; but the approach was for 200 feet/foot 3/8 mile we were ok on altitude but maybe the 3/8 mile was not there. In our situation we saw the runway(s) and decided to land. The distance runway visual range was not considered after runway(s) was in sight. Our first plan of action was to land mco. Weather was 700 feet/foot overcast 6-7 mile visibility. We should have ignored lee and flew directly to mco; then mlb intermediate fix needed. Lee was our boss's second choice; second officer we tried for him -- not again.
output: C500 PLT GOT TRAPPED IN LOW WX AND HAD MINIMUM FUEL.

input: During the pushback from gate xz; the tow bar became disconnected from either the tug or the nose gear. I had just started the left/right (directions) engine during the push out and the tug was turning us and pulling forward at the same time. It is not clear from ground man communicationss whether the tow bar came off accidentally or was unhooked by the other ground man accompanying the tug driver on headset. The only signal i received was 'parking brakes; parked' from the headset man. I noticed we were still moving forward slightly and waited a second to see intermediate fix he was still in a stopping mode; second officer as not to jerk the aircraft to a stop. He again said 'parking brakes; parked' and i then said; 'we are still rolling.' he then told me we were not hooked up any longer; second officer i immediately applied brakes. The tug was moving such that he was matched in speed to our speed while moving forward at the top of the alley and without a call saying we were not hooked up. I had no idea that the problem even existed until after his second call. Damage and injury were averted; but only by luck; i'm afraid. A callout or procedure needs to be addressed for this type of situation -- such as 'emer stop' or 'tow bar has disconnected; stop and park brakes.' i find no such guidance listed in part 1 or in the operating manual under pushbacks. More careful communicationss need to be designed and this incident should be briefed to all affected personnel -- both ground and flight -- to avoid a more dangerous outcome.
output: AN MD SUPER 80 ON PUSHBACK FROM A GATE HAD THE TOW BAR INADVERTENTLY DISCONNECT FROM THE ACFT PUTTING THE RAMP GUIDEMAN AND TUG DRIVER AT RISK OF INJURY.

input: I was flying on an instrument flight rules 'round robin' training flight from alb to 1b1 to sch and then back to alb. A series of practice approaches had been mapped and requested to each of the above listed airports. On the approach into 1b1 we requested the global positioning system 21 approach; was given the approach; cleared for the approach but then was not turned over to the common traffic advisory frequency and given climb out instructions until we were 3 miles from runway 21 at 1b1. It was at that time (after discussing with my instructor whether i should request to be 'handed off' for the approach so that i could communicate on the ctaf); i requested the hand off and the controller apologized for not doing so earlier. We realized at that time that we were working with a newer controller or a controller in training. After conducting a 'touch and go' at 1b1 we then came back to the alb controller and indicated that our next request was the global positioning system 4 at sch. We were given vectors to fosra intersection and an altitude of 3500 to fly at. When we reached fosra we assumed we should proceed to the next leg and that we were being vectored to bumps intersection. The controller indicated that we had not yet been cleared for the approach and that we should maintain 5500 until cleared for the approach. The global positioning system 4 for sch shows a procedure turn that is to be completed at an altitude no lower than 3700' mean sea level we had been assigned an altitude of 5500. We made an assumption that we were being vectored to the final approach course and proceeded to turn to the bumbs intersection when apparently the controller had expected us to fly the procedure turn (as published). For my very experienced instructor and i we were surprised since we assumed we did not have to fly the procedure turn since a) we believed we were being vectored; b) we had been assigned an altitude lower than the minimum for the initial approach fix; and c) in the areas around albany we are always vectored unless we request the full approach from a specific fix. While there were no questions raised by the controller; except that he indicated we had not yet been cleared for the approach; (and then cleared us for the approach quickly afterwards); when my instructor and i debriefed we both agreed that we should have a) asked the controller if he wanted us to fly the procedure turn; and b) flown the procedure turn unless specifically instructed not to do so. The lesson learned from this experience is a) communication is the key -- when in doubt ask questions; b) fly the approach as published unless directed to do otherwise.
output: A Pilot approaching SCH IFR at 3;500' assumed that because he was on vectors the GPS 4 procedure turn was not required but the TRACON Controller expected him to execute the turn because he was not instructed not to do so.

input: While conducting the area navigation (gps) or instrument landing system rwy 05r approach to mmmx in visual meteorological conditions conditions; i noticed as we flew over mavek (smo vor) intersection the flight management computer alerted 'gps invalid left/right (directions) r'. This occurred perhaps one mile from mavek. As we were in visual meteorological conditions we continued a stable approach to an uneventful landing. I strongly suspect global positioning system jamming is once again occurring in the vicinity of the mateo vor.
output: A B737-NG pilot reported possible GPS jamming in the vicinity of SMO while flying the MMMX RNAV (GPS) or ILS Runway 5R in VMC. The FMC alerted 'GPS INVALID L; R.'

input: I was working a panel backlighting minimum equipment list all three instrument panels affected drew power through a common fuse; f0401. As the dimming controller had already been changed; i suspected the fuse. In order to get access to the fuse; a number of instrument panels must be removed -- including the number 2 fire handle panel on the flight deck. Fuse f0401 was indeed blown; and upon installing a new fuse from stock; the panels' backlighting worked again. When i reinstalled the fire handle panel; i installed it upside-down in its mount and failed to notice. I did not double-check my work upon completion; and no other mechanics involved in work on the aircraft noticed the improper orientation. In addition; the aircraft made 3 legs before the problem was reported. Operation of the fire handle would not have been affected with this orientation.more cockpit familiarization training for mechanics is required; as well as a company culture of having other technicians check work performed.
output: Maintenance Technician reported installing cockpit panel upside down without noticing.

input: We were cleared to back taxi from taxiway hotel into position on runway(s) 36. On making the 180 degree turn at the end of the runway(s) the nosewheel went off into the grass. I backed the aircraft up and continued the turn to line up on the runway(s) i saw no evidence of damage and the aircraft turned and taxied normally. My first officer asked intermediate fix i thought we should go back to the gate. I told him it appeared normal and we would continue. Flight to pit was normal. Upon arrival, arrive pit we had maintenance checked the nose gear. There was a lower piece of the spray deflector broken off. Maintenance advised it was secure and okay for service we also advised the crew receiving the aircraft as to what had happened. Note: runway(s) 36 at sbn is 100 feet/foot wide; and area to back taxi for full length appears to be somewhat smaller.
output: CAPT OF MLG ACFT DAMAGED ACFT NOSE GEAR SPRAY DEFLECTOR DURING TAXI FOR TKOF.

input: On nov/sat/03 at approximately xa15 hours flight zzz to ewr encountered a bird strike at 2500 feet/foot 2 mile westbound of the teb vor and dme (co-located) the flight was just given the turn to final approach course and clearance for the instrument landing system runway(s) 22l at ewr when a loud explosion was heard. An emergency was declared and a request was made for the crash fire rescue equipment equipment with the landing chklist complete; a normal visual approach was completed and the aircraft landed without further incident. After visual inspection of the aircraft by the crash fire rescue equipment crew; the airplane was taxied to the gate. The passenber exited the aircraft via the jetbridge. Most passenber were calm and showed no signs of distress. As we were about to intercept the final approach course; i heard a loud explosion and noted the aircraft interior trim of the clear view window had been pushed toward my left/right (directions) shoulder. I heard a rush of air. I originally suspected a rapid depressurization and was looking for a cracked or broken window. I asked the capt intermediate fix he wanted me to declare an emergency and he said yes. I called approach to declare the emergency and requested the crash fire rescue equipment crew. The capt said he was having a hard time controling the aircraft but later it was suspected that it was the turbulence and initial yaw of the bird strike. We configured the aircraft further and then spoke to the flight attendants to ascertain the situation of the passenber compartment. They rpted no smoke; damage; or additional noises from the rear of the plane. I instructed them to prepare for an emergency landing and that we did not now the nature of the emergency but they had 1 minute(s) 30 seconds to prepare. The aircraft landed without further incident. After landing i called to the back and asked intermediate fix the situation had changed and they stated that a flight attendant (suspect a commuter or deadheader) in the back of the plane saw a bright flash from the left/right (directions) side of the plane. The capt then elected to shut down the left/right (directions) engine we told them there would not be an emergency evacuate/evacuation and that we would go to the gate. The crash fire rescue equipment crew did not see any engine damage second officer the capt decided to taxi to the gate with the crash fire rescue equipment crew in trail.
output: MD80 BIRD STRIKE IN AREA OF R SIDE COCKPIT WINDOW ON ILS RWY 22L APCH TO EWR. FLT CREW DECLARES AN EMER AND MAKES AN UNEVENTFUL LNDG.

input: We departed ord runway(s) 32l at intersection t10. The takeoff was normal. It was performed using flaps 2 with a flex temperature of 61 degrees. Shortly after takeoff we received a new final weight manifest which had an increased zfw of approximately 1600 pounds. The passenber count on the new manifest was 8/79 vice 6/73 on the old manifest. An actual count was requested and the new count proved to be correct. Our takeoff weight with the new manifest was approximately 800 pounds over the maximum weight for the flex temperature selected. Load planning was notified and we continued on without incident.
output: REVISED TKOF WT MANIFEST RECEIVED AFTER TKOF REVEALS TKOF WAS MADE WITH REDUCED THRUST INAPPROPRIATE FOR ACTUAL ACFT WT.

input: Acft had just reached fl350. Power set. Felt slight airframe vibration. Notice fluctuating fuel flow. Then noticed (#1 eng) fluctuations in other engine instruments on #1 engine heard a muffled bang. Reduced power to approximately 70 percent n2 on #1 engine #1 stabilized. Elected to shut down #1 and proceed to denver. Flight to denver uneventful. Descended to fl280. Supplemental information from acn 191947. Consultation with company flight ctl/dispatch resulted in an encouragement to 'press on' to den. The capt agreed that it could be done safely and asked for our input. (the weather was clear and fuel adequate). The second officer recommended going back. I agreed that we could make denver safely but dfw was right there and iah was closer than den. I also told him to go on in a similar situation and they were not praised for their decision.
output: ACR AT FL390 HAS #1 ENG PROBLEM. SHUT DOWN. ELECT TO CONTINUE TO DEST.

input: While shooting photos of a construction site; inadvertently descended to approximately 500 feet/foot over a populated area due to concentration on getting a good photo. Should have had a safety pilot to monitor terrain clearance and required alts.
output: PLT OF A SMT TWIN FLEW BELOW THE MINIMUM REQUIRED ALT OVER CONGESTED AREAS DURING PHOTO FLT.

input: Tug driver failed to stay on guide-in lines on pushback from gate. As soon as i saw that we were digressing excessively; i estimate 15 feet/foot to the east of ctrline; i instructed the tug driver to correct immediately or stop the aircraft there is little room for error in that area. The rest of the pushback was uneventful except that the tug driver used non-standard calls for the disconnect. I had maintenance come out to inspect our left/right (directions) wing for any possible damage (there was none luckily) as i had almost no confidence in the pushback crew. The company needs to hire and train the ground personnel properly or it is going to continue to damage aircraft and endanger personnel and passenber and my crew. When will this be corrected?
output: B737 PUSHBACK WAS NOT BEING CONDUCTED WITH ANY PRECISION. THE CAPT BECAME CONCERNED AND INSTRUCTED THE TUG DRIVER TO CORRECT COURSE OR STOP TO PREVENT DAMAGE TO THE ACFT.

input: After a normal profile approach and at a 1/4 to 1/2 mile final to runway(s) 33; a windshear alert was received from the egpws. After an 'analyzation' of the acft's new position with respect to the short runway(s) 33; a go around was elected. After notifying air traffic control of the go around a '060 degree heading and climb to 2000 ft' clearance was given and was accomplished precisely. This maneuver did place the aircraft close to p56. After being assigned 3000 feet/foot then 4000 feet/foot and being vectored east of dca and andrews air force base then back towards andrews; we received a traffic advisory from potomac approach of an f18 from andrews climbing up from 1300 feet/foot to 3000 feet/foot 'off our r.' after further vectoring; we rejoined the mt vernon visual for runway(s) 1. The visual approach and landing were completed uneventfully. My perception of the crew's performance and decision making were that actions taken were timely and accurate following a joint decision not to continue the approach to a short runway(s) after experiencing a windshear which placed the aircraft into a situation where continuing the approach potentially; could have been unsafe.
output: AFTER RECEIVING A WINDSHEAR ALERT WARNING ON SHORT FINAL TO RWY 33 AT DCA; FLT CREW OF CL65 FOLLOW ATC GAR INSTRUCTIONS AND TRIGGER LAUNCH OF F18 INTERCEPTOR DUE TO CLOSE PROX TO P56.

input: On approach to lga; automatic terminal information service was giving vor and dme (co-located) 'c' to runway(s) 22 and we set up accordingly. Approaching ny harbor we were advised runway(s) 13 was available. We replied that would be acceptable and were given a heading and told to maintain 3000' and to rpt the statue in sight. I replied we had the statue and river in sight. Approach then clrd us direct to the statue and cleared us for a river visual approach to runway(s) 13 to maintain 2000' until north of central park. We read back the clearance and descended to 2000' which concurred with the only altitude given on commercial plate 19-2 for the river visual approach to runway(s) 13. Approach then queried our altitude and said we should be at 3000'. We climbed back to 3000'. The river visual approach plate does not depict a 3000' limitation. Intermediate fix air traffic control requires an altitude to a certain position it should be on the approach and defined by a radial off lga. Clearance for an approach includes clearance to the next altitude once established on course. In this instance; established on the hudson river the plate says 'maintain 2000' or above as longitude as possible.' the approach plate is ambiguous and should be redesigned to satisfy any altitude and geographical requirements of air traffic control with reference to navigate, navigation aids and radials to eliminate confusion. Since there was no traffic rpted or sighted by us no evasive actions were required. However; by having to maintain 3000' instead of 2000' as depicted on the approach plate; an uncomfortably steep approach was required to land. These ambiguities should be eliminated by redesigning the approach plate to reflect any air traffic control requirements in definitive terms.
output: ACR WDB DESCENDED TO NEXT ALT AFTER RECEIVING VISUAL APCH CLRNC. APCH CTL INSTRUCTED THEM TO MAINTAIN THE HIGHER ALT.

input: Were on a charter mwc to eau. I checkeded weather and notams and found that restrict, restricted, restriction area 6900 a & b; r6901; and the moa's falls 1; volk westbound a; b & celsius were hot above 8000' mean sea level with the use of current sectionals i proceeded to eau at 2000' mean sea level the route to be between r6904 a & b and r6901 a; and underneath the moa's. At a point 65 nautical mile se of eau i was approached by an fgt from head on. The fgt proceeded to descend to my altitude and i could see that he was slowing (flaps and gear out) when he passed along my left side. The passage made my passenber very uncomfortable and they did not understand why a military aircraft should pass us second officer closely. I feel this passage was very unnecessary for it was apparent i was a civilian and was not at any time in a restrict, restricted, restriction area or in hot military operating area passages; such as this might make a pilot and passenber feel as though they are being put upon by unfriendly aircraft and might make an irrational decision. I do not feel this should be done to a plane that is making a point to stay out of special use airspace.
output: AIRBORNE CONFLICT; DELIBERATE.

input: In cruise at fl360 the lead flight attendant informed us of a foul odor in the forward cabin. She said the smelled was like that of dirty socks. At this point; we did not smell it. We ran the quick reference handbook procedure; elimination of foul odors in flight deck and cabin. We decided to turn off pack 1. At that point the smell came forward and it was the dirty sock smell. Within 5 minutes the smell dissipated; in both the cabin and flight deck. We left pack 1 off and the crossbleed shut. After communicating with the cabin crew and determining the smell was gone we decided to continue to zzz. We sent a message to dispatch about our situation but did not get a reply until i queried them about our first message. Then the reply was an affirmative that they got the first message. No guidance was offered. We landed uneventfully; but had to wait 19 minutes for a gate. During this period we requested paramedics and maintenance to meet the aircraft. I wanted my crew and myself to be checked for any adverse effects from the odor. We were checked and cleared. When maintenance boarded the aircraft they stated that they could smell the dirty sock smell.
output: A320 Captain reported they were notified by the Lead Flight Attendant of a 'dirty socks' smell during cruise.  The flight crew turned off Pack 1 per QRH and the smell dissipated allowing the flight to continue to its destination.

input: Paragraph 2 section 80 of the operations(s) manual in warning alert section page 31 needs to be revised for clarify to read 'override 'on' disables terrain display on both navigate, navigation display system or weather radar and cancels aural alerting functions.' this correction will prevent potential go around action when the egpws system has failed and the white lights in the override button have burned out making it impossible to determine that the switch is in fact in the override position until aural alerts sound at the critical stage of flight upon lndg/entry into the terrain clearance floor regime. A caution note in the operations(s) manual volume i; warning page 1 under obvious false warnings that says; 'note: checked egpws switch in override position intermediate fix warnings continued; pull circuit breaker epc -f20.'
output: AN MD80 CAPT SUGGESTS REVISING THE MD80 FOM DEALING WITH EGPWS OVERRIDE MODE.

input: I was visual flight rules on an approach to pne. Approaching from the north i contacted pne tower abeam the ard vor and dme (co-located) with information hotel. I was told to call abeam the race track for landing straight in on runway(s) 24. I was also in a hurry to pick up my friend and return to princeton because i also had a business appointment to go to.
output: GA SMA WRONG ARPT APCH LNDG.

input: I received a briefing for my duty times and flights for the next morning; which were a positioning flight mfi then a part 91 flight with 2 passengers. While planning the flights that evening i noticed a ficon (field condition report) notice to airmen / of air missions for mfi that listed both runways being contaminated with ptchy thn sn ba fair; and the same report for all taxiways and the airport apron; a total of four notam's in all. The longest runway at mfi is 5;002 feet/foot and that is not long enough for either wet or contaminated landing distance numbers. As per company procedure i contacted dispatch that night; notified them of the issue that could affect the flight; suggested cwa as an alternative; and was told it would be passed down and looked at in the morning. The next morning; i received my crew itinerary listing the flights for the day; which were the same as i was briefed the evening prior. I checked in for duty slightly early and spoke to dispatch and once again informed him the latest notice to airmen / of air missions i had showed the same unsuitable field conditions at mfi and again suggested cwa as an alternative. I asked him to run landing numbers based on the conditions at mfi and get back to me; however this was only an exercise as i already had run the numbers and i did not have the runway length for the current conditions to legally land at mfi. A little over an hour later i called dispatch and asked if they had informed the customer of the notice to airmen / of air missions airport conditions and changed my destination airport to cwa. He told me they spoke to the customer and the customer said it had not snowed the day before and thought the airport would be ok to land there. The dispatcher then asked me to dispatch to mfi and 'do a flyover' and 'take a look'. I asked him what 'take a look' meant; and he responded if the runway looked ok then i could 'give it a try'; disregard the notice to airmen / of air missions and land anyway. I told him i believed that would be illegal; and i base that on both cfar 91.103 and 135.69; among others as well. Over the next hour and a half; i received five more calls from the dispatcher. On every call he again asked me if i would be willing to go 'do a flyover' and 'take a look'. On one call he told me he spoke to the airport manager and tried to coerce him to remove the notice to airmen / of air missions but the manager refused; saying the notice to airmen / of air missions was accurate. The dispatcher called me five times trying to get me to take off for mfi and 'take a look.' there was literally nothing i could do make him understand that i could not legally land at mfi. I felt like the dispatcher; in his role in dispatch; which is to represent the wishes of our carrier; was trying to make me do something both illegal and unsafe. On every contact i had with dispatch; i professionally and steadfastly declined to depart to an airport i could not legally land at. Our chief pilots and flight duty officer do not have authority over scheduling. Our pilots do not have authority over dispatch.
output: A fractional airline Captain reported that his Dispatcher attempted to coerce him to depart for an airport where braking action was reported as fair and his performance calculation indicating insufficient runway available for the conditions.

input: At fl360 and rerouting toward a gap in a line of radar returns. Several aircraft had used the gap with success. Before i got near the gap i entered in instrument meteorological conditions conditions and experienced light to moderate chop. Suddenly my electronic flight instrument system displays (two) and the multifunction display went blank. Attitude and dg information were displayed on these tubes. The multifunction display can be used after channeling information with a toggle switch. However; it was dead also. I felt the circuit breakers for a popped one but couldn't find one out. I also reset both inverters to try to bring them back on line. Then i noticed my altimeter was descending. I transitioned to a tiny peanut gyro standby display for attitude information. By then my attitude was in a steep descending turn probably from the turbulence initiating the unusual attitude while i was troubleshooting. I throttled back and gently tried to regain a safe descent rate and attitude. The standby gyro was difficult to use because of its size and location. Air traffic control inquired about the descent and i told them i lost my displays and needed to land. They asked if i wanted to go to the nearest airport. I picked zzz as it was the most appropriate. I entered visual flight rules conditions and landed without incident at zzz. I left it there to have a mechanic look it over first. I had one passenger and he was ok. If i were to do this over again i would have skipped the troubleshooting and gone straight to the standby gyro. If there were two pilots; then the second pilot could have troubleshot the problem while the first was concentrating on attitude of the plane.
output: A Piaggio P180 took an apparent lightning strike on a propeller while IMC at FL360 and subsequently all EFIS data was lost. While troubleshooting; the aircraft entered a descending turn which the pilot arrested using his Standby Gyro; then diverted to a nearby airport.

input: We were on a scheduled air carrier flight # xx between san and slc. Flight had been cruising at fl370 with zlc in lateral navigation and vertical navigation mode. Slc gave clearance from 370 to 310. F/o was flying and selected 310 in mode control panel and vertical speed 1000' descent the 1000' altitude alert sounded at 32000 and callout made. Capt noticed altitude acquire annunciate then altitude hold in green on mode annunciator panel. Aircraft cruised at fl310 for several minute(s) all normal; in altitude hold at 310. Slc gave xx clearance to cross 5 south of ffu; at 15000'; 250 knots indicated airspeed altimeter 29.99. 15000' was selected in mode control panel altitude window. F/o then proceeded to make a waypoint in flight management system consisting of the ffu/188/5. While in the process of making the waypoint and discussing with capt; slc requested altitude of xx aircraft was noted climbing through 31500' at approximately 1300 feet per minute climb. Aircraft was stopped at 31700' and immediately returned to 31000'. Mode control panel window was still at 15000'; altitude hold and vertical speed armed. At no time was vertical navigation used; and at no time was anything on flight management system scratch pad placed in the flight management system or executed. Waypoint was being built on scratch pad; but not brought up to flight management system used or executed. In addition scratch pad was for descent and vertical navigation not in use. Autoplt was in 'b' mode use by f/o. Lateral navigation was disconnected and lateral navigation vertical navigation modes not used remainder of flight on arrival, arrive slc; maintenance found 'b' autoplt failed byte test; wrote up and placed on mco and downed 'b' autoplt for maintenance on subsequent leg (slc-jac) with 'a' autoplt in use; we were unable to engage vertical navigation mode and discontinued all autoplt lateral navigation and vertical navigation operations. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: reporter states that both crew members were discussing the control display unit inputs and that neither was watching the aircraft second officer the altitude excursion went unnoticed as there was no aural warning because of the fact that the altitude alerter was set for descent the autoplt experienced some system failure as it failed the maintenance test upon arrival, arrive there is no normal condition where an input to the control display unit will affect the autoplt in the altitude hold mode.
output: ALT DEVIATION. EXCURSION FROM ASSIGNED.

input: During climb out from vidp we received a green hydraulic system reservoir overheat electronic centralized aircraft monitoring the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring procedures were accomplished including turning off both green system pumps. We declared an emergency and decided to return to vidp. All associated procedures from the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring message including quick reference handbook and normal checklist were run and completed. The aircraft was overweight for the return to vidp by approximately 10;800 pounds and the vertical speed at touchdown was around 200 feet per minute we were then towed off runway and back to the gate without further complications. Air traffic control ramp; and the flight crew communicated clearly; concisely; and effectively to resolve the issue.
output: An A310 flight crew returned to their departure airport after receiving a Green Hydraulic System Overheat alert.

input: We were told by approach control to follow traffic for runway(s) 17c but not cleared for visual approach we were high and fast due to approach control keeping us high. Saw traffic and started turning to follow because passing through localizer course. Tower cleared us to land runway(s) 17r with no conflict.
output: MD80S FLC SEQUENCED FOR VISUAL APCH WAS HIGH AND FAST ON FINAL FOR DFW RWY 17C. DUE TO ACFT CONFIGN AND POS; ACFT OVERSHOT RWY 17C FINAL. APCH CTL RECOGNIZED CHANGING TFC CONDITION AND CHANGED MD80S TO RWY 17R. ACR LANDED WITHOUT FURTHER INCIDENT.

input: On soldo 2 area navigation departure aircraft began turn from mechl to mavvs before reaching mechl. Because mechl is not a compulsory flyover point; aircraft will lead turn this point to stay in the depicted track. Controller was alarmed because aircraft did not overfly mechl but during subsequent conversation with controller was advised that departure expects aircraft to overfly mechl on soldo 2. Suggest that mechl be changed to a compulsory flyover point intermediate fix indeed departure expects overflt of this point. Controller also advised there was no danger of aircraft separation in this incident.
output: A300 ON SOLDO RNAV SID FROM DFW TURNS INSIDE MECHL.

input: Acr x; a dc9; was cleared to taxi to runway(s) 11l. As x approached the approach end; i cleared x for takeoff i then noticed x passing the approach end; and continuing toward runway(s) 21 at taxiway a. I advised x that he had passed the approach end and had him turn left/right (directions) at taxiway d and reclred him for takeoff callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information facility supervisor stated airport signage is in compliance with federal aviation administration standards. Charts show where approach end of runway(s) is.
output: ACR NON COMPLIANCE WITH ATC INSTRUCTION TAXIED BEYOND END OF RWY.

input: An elderly friend; mr x; owns a c303 aircraft the airplane sustained damage to its tail empennage in a hangar collapse at the zzz airpark during hurricane wilma. There being no repair facility at this airport mr x hired an aircraft mechanic mr y; to repair the aircraft in mr y's hangar. Mr y also agreed to perform an annual inspection of the aircraft on or about nov/fri/06; mr x called to say the airplane was fixed and he wanted me to give him instruction in the airport traffic pattern. During our preflt inspection of the aircraft i noticed fasteners missing on an improperly installed tail cone fairing which was rubbing on and interfering with the rudder. The master warning panel was also inoperative and the electric trim switch rotated the elevator trim wheel in what appeared to be reverse rotation. I asked mr y intermediate fix i could look at the log entries and confirm that the annual inspection had been accomplished. Mr y replied that the airplane would have to be test flown before the annual could be 'signed off.' i replied that the annual inspection must be accomplished and signed before the aircraft is operated. He told mr x to come back in a couple of days and he would have 'it' taken care of. On nov/tue/06; we met again at mr y's hangar and i observed the electric trim switch operating in reverse motion as before. An annual inspection had been signed in the maintenance record by an ia who was at the hangar at this time; but whose name i do not remember. I asked this person about the electric trim problem and he and mr y both said that it was working properly and that i was probably not familiar with the c303 airplane. Having been told by an ia that the airplane was airworthy; mr x decided it be flown in the traffic pattern. I observed the elevator trim wheel indicator in the takeoff position prior to the takeoff roll. At rotation however; the airplane pitched up violently with a force that required the efforts of both mr x and i to prevent the airplane from stalling. Rotating the elevator trim wheel forward made the problem worse. A determination was made that the elevator trim system was reversed and acted accordingly. The plane was landed immediately without further incident. Back at the hangar; i explained to mr y what happened and he said he would checked it out and contact mr x after he had looked at it. Mr x called me on nov/thu/06; and asked me to meet him at the airport to again fly with him. At the airport i questioned mr y about what problem he found with the trim system he replied that he found a problem with a corroded cannon plug. I asked him how an electrical cannon plug could affect a mechanical trim system at that point; and with key in hand; he locked the cabin door and stated 'there would be no more test flts until mr x paid up.' i called the local flight standards district office office on nov/fri/06; to ask intermediate fix the federal aviation administration could help mr x in some way. The 2 inspectors on the phone said their issue was with the pilot flying the airplane 'knowing' it was defective. At this point i had the feeling they were interested only in violating the pilot second officer i stopped my conversation with them. I believe this spirit which pervades the federal aviation administration is a contributing factor to aviation's safety problems my hope is that the aviation safety rpting system will bring some change in the future.
output: A CESSNA 303 ON TKOF PITCHED UP VIOLENTLY AND REQUIRED 2 PERSONS TO PREVENT STALLING. ELEVATOR TRIM WAS RPTED AND WORKED ON TWICE PRIOR TO FLT. THIS TECHNICIAN ALSO PERFORMED AN ANNUAL INSPECTION PRIOR TO FLT.

input: Just prior to landing flare; experienced wind shear requiring rejected landing approach was being hand flown; autothrust was engaged. Aircraft type a320. Aircraft contacted runway(s) surface during reject. No damage to aircraft but we did experience a brake sys/fault and #2 rmp failure. The next apch/lndg was uneventful. We rpted wind shear to tower after the go around and 1 minute(s) later another aircraft landing rpted the shear. Autothrust did not increase at all during the shear. It would have been better to have been manually flying the thrust also during these gusty conditions (wind 300 degrees 16 knot(s) gusts 26 kts).
output: WIND SHEAR ON LNDG WITH GAR.

input: During approach to lga; gear lowered. The left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) main gear indicated down and locked; with no nose gear indication -- the light was not red or green. Executed a missed approach and declared an emergency the gear was cycled and the gear indicated down and locked. The nose gear took longer than normal; but the green light was illuminated with no landing gear pin extended on the center console. The emergency was canceled with the 3 green down and locked indications in the cockpit. The landing was uneventful; taxied to the gate.
output: AN S80 MAKES A MISSED APCH WHEN THE NOSE LNDG GEAR FAILS TO INDICATE A DOWN AND LOCKED CONDITION 5 MI NE OF LGA; NY.

input: I was in an incident where i lost control of my tractor and it ran into a lav truck. I was running a trip as a luggage distributor and i had dropped off all my bags except those for the hub airports. I went into the makeup area with all the hub stations to drop off the bags for two of the stations but; to my surprise; it said that one of the flights was already at its gate but wouldn't leave until almost three hours later. [however;] my scanner wasn't set right so the time on it was not accurate. As a result i had no way of telling what time it really was and when i saw the flight was already on the ground it made me think i was falling really behind on time; so i got into a kind of hurry mode. I drove out to the gate where that trip was and dropped off the three bags on the orange carts and drove off in a hurry. Right around the corner was a turn that i decided to take because; that way; it would be a straight shot to drop off one of the other flights' bags if the plane wasn't at its gate and get back to the assignment room as soon as i could. Right when i took that turn i tried pressing the brake but ended up pressing both the brake and gas pedal at the same time and when i tried to readjust i was already mid-turn and my body had started to slide from the inertia. I ended up falling off the tractor but was able to land on my feet; running to prevent myself from falling; however the tractor kept turning and ran into a parked lav truck and then bounced into another lav truck and ran into some dollies which slowed it down enough for me to catch up and firmly press the brake down with my hand. I had been in the middle of grabbing and pulling the seatbelt across my body [while already] in motion; until i got to the turn where i had to release the belt so; at the time of the incident; i was not wearing a seatbelt--a major mistake on my part.
output: A baggage tractor driver; hurrying because he had no accurate way to determine the time relative to the scheduled departure time of flights to which he was delivering bags; attempted to take a turn at too high a speed and was ejected from the vehicle. The unmanned baggage vehicle continued uncontrolled and struck two lavatory trucks and several baggage carts.

input: After landing on runway(s) 13 at greg county airport (ggg); longview; we turned nwbound on the taxiway. It was a dark night! Ground told us to hold short of runway(s) 22. As we approached runway(s) 22 ground cleared us to cross 22 and hold short of runway(s) 17. Runway(s) 22 did have a red runway(s) sign at the taxiway; but runway(s) 17 does not (maybe it was burned out). I almost taxied too federal aviation regulation and would have been onto the runway(s) 17 which had landing traffic on it. I stopped in time and stayed clear of runway(s) 17; because our pwrful landing lights illuminating the taxiway and the landing aircraft gave me a clue where runway(s) 17 was. I told ground about the very unsafe situation! It scared me getting that close to an active runway(s) that intersection needs a runway(s) hold short sign!
output: FLC OF LTT TAXIING AT GGG UNABLE TO SEE RWY TO HOLD SHORT -- NO SIGN.

input: We were given a crossing restrict, restricted, restriction to cross cutta intersection at 10000 -- however approaching cutta we received a resolution advisory on our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii causing us to adjust our descent and were high at cutta (basically the resolution advisory prohibited us from crossing cutta at 10000 ft) we rpted this to approach -- and were advised there was no traffic conflict and the traffic causing the resolution advisory was at 9000 ft.
output: MLG UNABLE TO MAKE XING RESTR DUE TO TCASII RA.

input: Our tlr [takeoff/landing report] was based on landing on runway 23r at our destination. 23r was notamed closed but disregarded as 23l/5r was open. I did not associate the tlr runway and the notice to airmen / of air missions until reviewing the release for the next flight which was a departure out of the airport. When i verified the tlr runway for departure was the open runway i sensed that i had not made that verification on our previous arrival.
