We continued in with the assumption we were under tower control; the ramp was safe and all ramp control was closed for the evening. The activity in the surrounding ramp area supported that belief. Concerned we possibly made an error; an attempt to contact ramp was made after setting the parking brake. The ramp controller responded advising that particular ramp was indeed open.
output: Air carrier First Officer reported they taxied to the ramp as cleared by EWR Tower and did not contact Ramp Control because it appeared to be closed. First Officer stated that due to the changing responsibilities of controllers; it was difficult to know what the correct procedures were.

input: During approach to runway 22 at rdm at approximately 7 miles from the airport on a right base; setting up for a 2 mile final we got a 'terrain; pull up' ground proximity warning. It only sounded once and was gone. The altitude at the time was 5;000 feet/foot mean sea level i immediately responded with the ground proximity warning system recovery procedure and climbed to approximately 5;500 feet/foot the display on the mfd was set to 10 mile scale. At no time did i see any terrain on our flight path that was at an altitude above us. The rest of the flight (5 minutes) was uneventful. Looking back at the flight perhaps our descent was closer to the higher terrain northwest of the airport. The smith rock area. Neither the first officer nor myself felt that we were close enough to the higher terrain. We both had the airport in sight from beyond 50 miles. At 30 miles from the airport; we were cleared for the visual approach. I maintained a course direct to the airport until about 7-10 miles out when i maneuvered to the base leg. Looking back; i would have continued to the airport and entered on the downwind.
output: An air carrier pilot on a seven mile final to RDM Runway 22 at 5;000 FT responded to an EGPW 'TERRAIN-PULL UP' warning. Terrain in the area is approximately 3;000 FT.

input: While starting the right engine; the gpu went offline aborting the start. I followed the qrc for abnormal start and secured the engine. I had the ground crew remove the gpu and started the left engine on battery power. After limitation wait time; i started the right engine using generator assist. The right engine started; but the starter would not disengage. I again followed the abnormal start qrc; but while the engine shut down; the starter would not disengage. I used the right engine fire switch to secure the engine.the encore+ qrc does not have; nor points to the more expanded abnormal start procedure that exists in the quick reference handbook that procedure would have most likely resolved the stuck starter without having to use the engine fire switch. I did not think of this procedure as i was concerned about major damage or even an engine fire with passengers on-board. I suggest that the full engine start malfunction procedure be incorporated in the qrc; or at the very least; the qrc point to the appropriate section in the quick reference handbook should the qrc actions not resolve the abnormal start.
output: CE-560EP Captain reported the right engine starter failed to disengage and the procedure to resolve the issue was not in the QRC.

input: On the robinsville 1 arrival, arrive into ewr; we were on autoplt and given a descent to 8000 feet/foot mean sea level over rbv; altitude alert sounded. I looked up and noticed altitude descending through 7600 feet/foot mean sea level told the capt our clearance was to 8000 feet/foot he disengaged the autoplt and climbed back to 8000 feet/foot the lowest altitude i saw as 7500 ft.
output: B727 PIC OVERSHOOTS HIS ASSIGNED ALT WHILE ON AUTOPLT DSCNT OVER RBV; NJ.

input: While attempting an auxiliary power unity start to power up the aircraft for its first flight of the day the first officer noted the auxiliary power unity hung start at 24% revolutions per minute after aborting the start the auxiliary power unity fire indication illuminated on the engine indicating and crew alerting system the first officer then completed the auxiliary power unity fire epc. As i entered the aircraft from the jetbridge i noted black smoke coming from the auxiliary power unity compartment. I then entered the cockpit and observed the first officer complete the auxiliary power unity fire epc. Pit fire/rescue was called as a precautionary measure and they responded in a timely manner. I then contacted moc/soc for further guidance. Moc contacted contract maintenance in pit and a mechanic rpted to the aircraft within 10 minute(s) i observed the mechanic open the auxiliary power unity service panel and begin a visual inspection. At that point i left the aircraft for approximately 20 minute(s) when i returned the mechanic was gone but the minimum equipment list entry i made had not been signed off or cleared i contacted moc and was informed the contract mechanic had finished with the inspection and communicated to moc that he could find no evidence of a fire. Moc instructed me to enter into the logbook a crew placard and continue my flight sequence to mia in the aircraft when i questioned why the mechanic did not make the appropriate maintenance entry i was xferred to a moc supervisor named xxxx. Xxxx insisted the mechanic did not need to sign the aml and a crew placard was appropriate for the aml entry i had made. Xxxx also reaffirmed the mechanic was satisfied the auxiliary power unity or auxiliary power unity compartment showed no evidence of a fire. He then issued me an aml crew placard authority/authorized number for the placard.
output: AN EMJ PIC IS BOTHERED BY THE FACT THAT HE WAS ADVISED BY MAINT CTLR TO ENTER A CREW PLACARD NOTATION FOR AN MEL OF THE APU AFTER IT HAD BEEN INSPECTED; BUT NOT SIGNED OFF FOR A GND FIRE INDICATION AT THE RAMP IN PIT; PA.

input: Long night; complications with transportation to the airport; fuel spill; late departure from origin; late arrival at destination; continual late stairs to the airplane at destination; habitual late automatic communications addressing & reporting system not closing because of main cabin door not being 'cracked' enough. Upon block-in; stairs had been late getting to the airplane during the week (as late as 13 minutes); automatic communications addressing & reporting system was not closing out unless doors were 'cracked' open more than normal; etc. Shutdown was normal and checklists accomplished. While waiting for stairs; captain cracked the door to initiate automatic communications addressing & reporting system closing process; but door was not disarmed. Door starting initiating process of opening and inflating slide. Slide never deployed completely nor door opened all the way. Slide and door remained partially deployed and open. No injuries; no damage except for need of slide replacement. Log book entry made. Normal checklist flow and normal procedures dictate that after block-in; the first officer or crew insure that the slides are disarmed. Because of aforementioned distractions with late stairs; etc.; the doors were not double checked via normal procedures. Thus; any crewmember must insure that the door is disarmed completely before opening the door for any reason.
output: An A310 Captain opened the main cabin door before disarming the slide because he was impatient about ground crew delays and ACARS close-out message sending; and so partially inflated the slide.

input: We were en route from houston to msp and had leveled off at fl350. One of our company engineers wanted to ride up front for a while; second officer he and the coplt changed seats. The boss requested to let engineer fly the plane. I explained the controls turned off the autoplt and leg him fly. I was coaching him on heading and altitude control and he was doing ok. His wife came forward with a camera and wanted me to take his picture. I took the camera and she went back to her seat. I checkeded the aircraft attitude and heading and they looked good. I leaned back against my side window and took his picture. The next thing i heard the altitude alert go off. By the time i got back on the controls the altimeter showed 400 feet/foot above cruise altitude and climbing i shoved the nose down and simultaneously pulled the throttles back. We were shortly back on altitude center never said anything; but it sure shook me up. I learned to never let an unqualified person take the controls while in positive control airspace. Things can get out of hand way too fast.
output: CPR ACFT HAS ALTDEV IN PCA.

input: Sfo changed 28r to 19l short notice. Vectors for 19l instrument landing system on base leg told to intercept 020 radial and follow to airport. I put sfo 020 in fix page and raw data sfo vor and dme (co-located) while first officer flying built intercept leg 200 to sfo. Intercepted 020 radial in lateral navigation 10 miles called airport in sight. Advised traffic for 19r as emb170. Traffic in sight. Landing check completed at 1000 ft stable approach; first officer hand flying with auto throttle on. Traffic appeared very close exactly parallel even while we were offset from 19l centerline. 900 ft got traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory fly up indication. Told first officer to follow commands. Re-verified visual separation ok with emb170 and turned traffic alert and collision avoidance system to traffic advisory mode cancelling resolution advisory immediately following was low glideslope warning. Told first officer fly up and capture glideslope. Distracted by false traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory and fixation on very close parallel traffic. Back on glideslope at 700 feet and stable. Uneventful landing. Note: we were not on the localizer yet (flipping 020 sfo radial) and approaching at an angle to 19l so validity of glideslope may have been suspect as well as possibility of glideslope distortion for our runway due very close parallel traffic. I chose to accept that we were close enough to centerline that it was valid warning.
output: B757 flight crew reported a TCAS RA and low glide slope warning while on a visual approach to SFO Runway 19L with parallel traffic for 19R.

input: Prior to departure; the push back driver came to the cockpit and asked to see me outside. He had found some aircraft damage that he wanted to report. The auxiliary power unity access door had become mangled and then forced closed. The seal of the door is noticeably deformed. I called maintenance and a mechanic responded. When he came to the cockpit i asked if he had inspected the door on the way up. He had. Mechanic then asked if i had written up the damaged door. I had. I gave him the logbook. He signed off the door 'as is'. He then left. A few minutes later i noticed that he and the push back driver were having an 'animated' discussion in front of the plane. When they were done the push back driver returned to the tug. I asked the driver if the mechanic had been giving him a hard time about reporting the damage to the aircraft. The mechanic had disciplined the push back driver for reporting the damage and told the driver that finding damage was not his job. I believe that safety is everyone's responsibility. I think i read that somewhere..... The damaged door is not a safety of flight item. It is damaged and may or may not need to be replaced. But there is no way to tell if the damage; any damage; is already a known issue or not. The only way to find out is to write-up the damage and see what the responding mechanic says. That is exactly what happened. The push back driver was absolutely correct to report something he was unsure about. The mechanic was absolutely wrong to disciplining him for reporting a potential safety violation.
output: A Captain reported that when he wrote up an access door that was reported damaged by his pushback driver.  The responding mechanic chastised the driver for reporting the damage.

input: We were climbing at mach .84 to fl390. The entire climb had been in smooth air with a 70 knot(s) tailwind as we passed fl360. Approximately fl361; the wind changed 180 degrees to a 40 knot(s) headwind. That was an almost instantaneous change of wind component of 100 knot(s) the autoplt and autothrottles could not react fast enough to prevent a 20 knot(s) increase in indicated airspd; which gave us a 5 knot(s) overspd that lasted about 5 seconds. It looked and felt like the classic microburst windshear that we practice in the simulator. The flight continued normally the rest of the way to sfo. A logbook entry was made and maintenance was notified.
output: A B777 FLT CREW EXPERIENCED A SIGNIFICANT WIND DIRECTION SHIFT; RESULTING IN A SPD BEING EXCEEDED.

input: This was a horrible experience. We were trying to avoid thunderstorm heads and i advised air traffic control of heading and altitude that was needed to avoid a cell. Air traffic control said no go heading 360 if you can't descend to 12;000 feet. We advised we were unable 12;000 feet due to a thunderstorm and needed a 010 heading. Air traffic control argued with us. The pilot in command wanted one thing and air traffic control wanted another. Then air traffic control said if you're not going to descend then traffic alert head on course with 737 that air traffic control did not move either. Finally we stayed our course and maintained 16;000 feet and eventually turned on to our flight plan route. This was very dangerous for air traffic control to argue with us and we did hit moderate border line severe turbulence and scared our passengers trying to comply with air traffic control instructions. Air traffic control should not have argued and the pilot in command should have talked to air traffic control directly rather than have me relay it. He should have transferred controls since i did not know what the pilot in command wanted.
output: Fractional First Officer reported ATC would not approve a deviation for weather resulted in an airborne conflict and severe turbulence encounter.

input: Cruising at 5500 feet/foot mean sea level saw aircraft at approximately 1230 o'clock and same altitude turned left/right (directions) and saw c172 approximately 200 feet/foot to my left/right (directions) no advisories were given by cha apch.
output: M-5 PLT AND A C172 HAD AN NMAC ABOVE CHA CLASS C AIRSPACE.

input: Ny approach was giving us radar vectors for isp instrument landing system runway(s) 6 from the south we were given a heading of 360 (i think) to intercept the 058 degree course inbound at 1800'. I mistakenly never reset my horizontal situation indicator course to 058 degree second officer it was left/right (directions) at 036 degree from a previous clearance second officer when the localizer came alive with the autoplt on; it started to intercept but the course went left/right (directions) through and the autoplt flew a heading of 020 degree i reset the heading bug to a 055 degree heading thinking it would intercept. Then ny approach told us to fly heading 090 degree to intercept. I noticed at this time that 090 degree put me direct to the compass locator at ils outer marker once the course came alive again (hdg 090 degree thinking i had to turn to 036 deg) i quickly turned back to 035 degree and lost the course again. Then i realized i had the course set wrong and also noticed i was at 1600' (assigned 1800' until established) even though i was on g/s. I fixed my course to 058 degree and turned to correct while at the same time the ny approach controller yelled/asked intermediate fix we had the airport we saw it and called it in sight. He cleared us for the visibility and we proceeded w/o incident to land. I feel the main cause was that i did not set the inbound course on the localizer properly. Contributing factors was that my f/o was brand new. This was his first line flight i was distraction watching him and making sure he was doing his duties at the time; lowering approach flaps; lowering gear and doing the before landing checked also his inexperience putting all his concentration on doing pilot not flying duties and not keeping an eye on what was going on to catch my mistake contributed. I think he may have also completely trusted me to intercept the localizer and didn't monitor it. He had the proper course twisted in but may have felt he was not to touch/set my course in.
output: INEXPERIENCED COMMUTER FLT CREW COMMITS HEADING AND ALT DEVIATIONS ON APCH TO ISP.

input: At cruise altitude of fl320 the coplt noticed that the flow light had illuminated. As the coplt was initiating the flow light chklist; i noticed that the cabin climb indicator was pegged at above 1500/fpm climb rate; and cabin altitude was climbing we received clearance to descend but had no inoperative lights illuminated on the pressurization panel. The left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) pneumatic supply pressure appeared to be normal. As i continued our descent the coplt started to initiate the automatic pressurization inop/manual pressurization chklist. The coplt selected automatic #2 at approximately fl310 and the cabin rate of climb decreased with a momentary bump and the flow light extinguished; but then the cabin climb rate quickly increased again to greater than 1500/fpm. As we continued our descent it became apparent that the cabin altitude was out of control at which time the coplt initiated the rapid decompressions/cabin altitude warning chklist as i initiated an emergency descent we donned our oxygen masks and at 10000 feet/foot cabin altitude the red cabin altitude light illuminated and the warning horn/vocal sounded. The cabin altitude appeared to go above 14000 feet/foot momentarily but the passenber oxygen masks did not deploy and since the cabin altitude was rapidly descending with the acft's altitude toward 9000 feet/foot i elected not to manually deploy the passenber oxygen masks. During all this i was coordinating with the flight attendants who stated that none of the passenber seemed to notice the descent nor did anyone complain about the pressurization. The only apparently noticeable event was that the rear galley door was making a slightly loud noise during descent all of the dscnts were coordination with air traffic control who was able to keep our clrncs below our desired altitude until we reached 11000 feet/foot where a momentary delay was encountered. At this time i declared an emergency and received an immediate clearance to 9000 feet/foot at no time was it necessary to violate any air traffic control clrncs. The coplt was starting to make some progress with the manual control of the pressurization but he stated that it was difficult to move the cabin control wheel and was unable to get the position indicator beyond the flaps 28 degree setting. At this time we were initiating our leveloff and i asked the coplt to discontinue his attempts to regain control of the cabin manually. After landing i made a public address notifying the passenber that our aircraft had encountered some pressurization difficulties and apologized for any discomfort. No passenber said anything to me concerning the pressurization except for one lady near the very rear of the airplane who said she was having some difficulty clearing her left/right (directions) ear.
output: AN MD80 LOW FLOW LIGHT ILLUMINATED AT FL320. AN EMER DSCNT WAS COMPLETED BECAUSE THE CABIN COULD NOT BE CONTROLLED. THE PAX O2 MASKS DID NOT DEPLOY.

input: During climb out at aprox. 18;000ft; hyd 1 lo qyt message on engine indicating and crew alerting system followed by hydraulic system 1 fail w/ associated messages. Electric pump fail message; the electric pump cycled on and off twice as observed. Then we declared the emergency with center and diverted. Informed air traffic control flight attendant and pax. Followed checklist for hyd fail and abnormal landing gear extension. Confirmed on the engine indicating and crew alerting system and rmu that the gear was down and locked. Followed appropriate power settings. Once on the ground we stopped on the runway and shut down the engines; and were towed in by maintenance. Loss of all hydraulic pressure and pumps on system 1.
output: EMB145 First Officer experiences hydraulic system 1 failure at FL180 during climb. An emergency is declared and flight diverts to nearest suitable airport after complying with checklist procedures.

input: Aircraft x was on the localizer approach to hhr. The waiver requires radar coverage to be adequate; which it was not. The aircraft's target disappeared outside of demon; the final approach fix for one or two sweeps; and then i lost all radar coverage on about a 2 mile final. I am unable to separate an la arrival from that hhr arrival by terms of the waiver sct la area has; if i do not have adequate radar coverage. This has been brought up countless times in the past. The controllers have been informed that maintenance says the radar is operating within tolerance. However; we routinely lose radar coverage between 2 and 1 mile final on the hhr arrivals. The usual course of action is to verify with hhr that the aircraft is in sight or has landed. Recommendation; change the waiver to allow for this known radar inadequacy; fix the radar system or cancel the waiver. When the hhr approach occurs; you do not know when you will lose radar coverage; only that it will probably happen. Consequently; the controller cannot take action until it is too late. Additionally; if an hhr aircraft were to stray north of its final; bear in mind that in my many years at la; this has never happened; the controller could not tell due to lack of radar coverage.
output: SCT controller voiced concern regarding the current waiver requirement for HHR approach procedures and the limited RADAR coverage in the subject area; either RADAR coverage should be improved and/or waiver requirements changed.

input: I was flying the instrument landing system to 27l at ord via the flight director and autoplt when we encountered windshear. Our first indication in smooth air on the glideslope was a 40 knot(s) increase in airspd at about 3000 feet/foot mean sea level immediately i noticed our sink rate go to 1500 feet per minute down followed by light chop to moderate almost severe turbulence i disconnected the autoplt and initiated a go around following our windshear procedures the first officer told air traffic control we were going around and of our condition. The aircraft was initially slow to respond to inputs and approximately 500 feet/foot was lost. At first the air traffic control controller told us to level at 4000 feet/foot and we were at 4500 when he immediately cleared us to 5000 feet/foot on level off we drifted to 5300 feet/foot as we were still in pretty choppy air; the controller cleared us to 6000 feet/foot at which time we were through the shear and were able to maintain aircraft control i feel the controllers did an outstanding job in assisting us in altitude and maneuvering around the cells to the north of the airport i feel the situation was an insidious set up in that the thunderstorms were 5-10 mile north of the field and no other aircraft were rpting any problems and the ride was smooth until we hit the shear. I feel that the windshear simulator training we go through on recognition and recovery was invaluable in our maneuvering once we encountered the shear. The lesson learned here is that even though everyone else is landing it doesn't mean that you are assured a landing in other words i have a much healthier respect for thunderstorms and their effect in a terminal area.
output: ACR MLG ENCOUNTERED WIND SHEAR ON APCH TO ORD 27L. ALT AND AIRSPD FLUCTUATIONS CAUSED FLC TO GAR.

input: During non stop flight from sfo to ewr got a major rerte from air traffic control due to weather in the chicago/cleveland airspace. It added 45 minute(s) to flight time and dropped our planned landing fuel from 11800 pounds to 6400 pounds when still about 1 hour from ewr; zbw cleared us to maintain 33000 feet/foot and expect 27000 feet/foot by art. This premature descent would have dropped our landing fuel to about 5000 pounds or less; which would have given us less than 45 minute(s) fuel reserves at ewr. At this time the capt declared a 'fuel advisory' or 'minimum fuel advisory.' our 'fom' states that this is not an emergency situation and it does not imply the need for traffic priority. However; we think that we were given traffic priority by air traffic control and also were asked 2 or 3 times about our fuel remaining in minute(s) since the weather at ewr and at other area airports was good; i feel that we were never in a dangerous situation because of having stayed at altitude until close to ewr; our fuel at the gate was 7300 pounds which gave us more than the legal reserves required for the conditions. I think that declaring a minimum fuel advisory was the correct judgement given the circumstances; even though it was borderline. I should add that most of us like to land this airplane with no less than 9000 pounds of fuel even though the minimum landing fuel is 1800 pounds (just enough for a visual flight rules go around close pattern and lndg).
output: ACR FO EXHIBITS A MOD LEVEL OF CONCERN REGARDING THE FLC'S MINIMUM FUEL ADVISORY THEY GAVE ATC. LANDED WITH ADEQUATE FUEL. SINCE THE CTLR ASKED FOR FUEL IN MINS FLC THOUGHT CTLR INTERPRETED ADVISORY AS A DECLARATION OF AN EMER.

input: While on approach into atl; we were blocked at least 5 times from receiving our clearance from the final controller the controller was extremely busy and in my opinion; was handling too many aircraft and was overloaded for a final controller he was second officer busy and impatient that he would block the aircraft reading back their clrncs; thus reblocking his newly issued clrncs. I was told to maintain 5000 feet/foot and look for air carrier y. I saw the aircraft and informed the controller he responded second officer fast that the clearance wasn't clear to me. I didn't even have a chance to respond to the controller because he was off doing something else. Since i wasn't about to fly through the localizer for runway(s) 26r; we intercepted the localizer for runway(s) 26r second officer as not to create a conflict to traffic inbound to atl on the south side. I asked 3 or 4 more times to make sure i was cleared for the visual and the controller was blocked each time. But i did hear my call sign and i did hear approach in the readback. I assumed we were cleared for the visual for runway(s) 27r. We were about 2 mile from ajaay intersection at 5000 feet/foot given that location; we should be around 2800 feet/foot to be on the glideslope we descended to around 4800 feet/foot when i noticed a plane on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii descending to our left/right (directions) confused as to what was going on; i told the first officer to climb back up to 5000 feet/foot i called the controller for the fifth or second officer time intermediate fix we were cleared and he responded with annoyance; 'acft x; cleared for the visual approach to runway(s) 26r.' we descended and landed without incident. In retrospect; i shouldn't have descended at all -- regardless of the pressure from the controller unless i ante meridiem absolutely sure of my clearance although i put some blame on myself; i feel that the controller should have done something like; 'everybody be quiet; i need to talk to aircraft x.' almost every pilot on that frequency was confused because the controller was blocking his own clrncs because of his impatience.
output: ATL APCH CTLR OVERLOADED WITH TFC AND TALKING TOO FAST; CONCERNS FLC ON APCH TO RWY 26R.

input: The chief certified flight instructor was administering a proficiency check to a certified flight instructor while doing 'simulated emergency operations the pilot in command and acting certified flight instructor pulled the engine to 'simulate' an emergency engine failure. We were approximately at 5;000 feet/foot mean sea level the examinee went through his normal emergency checklist. The examiner was clearing the engine every 15 seconds and maintained about 1500 revolutions per minute throughout this practice maneuver. After cycling the engine for the 3rd time; the examiner went to apply power (clearing the engine) to maintain engine temperature when she noticed that the throttle was jammed approximately 1/4 inch in the open throttle position. Examiner then tried to push and pull the throttle lever and checked the throttle lock and friction. At that point she asked the examinee for his assistance; as he was the flying pilot at this time. He then also tried to push and pull the throttle lever and checked the throttle friction; which was taut. He then loosened it. At this time; the examiner took control of the plane as the pilot in command and while the examinee continued to attempt to move the throttle lever. The examiner told the examinee to continued attempting to troubleshoot the throttle until the examiner made the decision at about 200 feet/foot above ground level at which time he could pull the mixture; as they were unsuccessful in unjamming the throttle. We were committed to land. At this point in time; the examiner told the examinee that we had an 'actual emergency; real world.' the examiner picked the field to land heading towards the north. The winds were light. The examiner flew the plane and due to the fact that we had in partial power (stuck lever) was concerned about not overshooting the field and wanted to slow the plane down. The examiner requested the flaps and gear extended. At 200 feet/foot above ground level we were committed to land and pull the mixture; shut off the fuel; the mags; and the master switch. The examiner held the plane off and we came to a quick stop. Landed safely with no injuries or apparent damage to plane. Both pilots double-checked that all systems were shut down and evacuated the plane. During all phases of flight; the throttle was operating normally. Weather conditions were visual flight rules conditions.
output: A M20 throttle stuck while power was reduced during a simulated engine failure. An emergency was subsequently declared followed by an uneventful off airport landing.

input: On final approach to lnk airport we were on the instrument landing system 18 under visual conditions; it was dusk; the first officer was flying and as we came about 100 feet above touchdown i noticed birds (geese); i verbally communicated birds and it was too late; we hit about two of the geese and i could tell there was about a flock of 6 or so. During out decent we briefed the possibility of birds and we had our eyes open; however; with the dusk situation; we didn't see them till it was too late. After hitting the birds i looked at the engine indications and they were all in the green; the first officer did a fantastic job flying the aircraft till we landed. We notified the air traffic control about our bird strike; they gave us a phone number to call; we called and talked to them and they wanted to know what kind of damage it was; and if it was considered aircraft accident. I told them; that maintenance had been notified and i wasn't able to answer that question; the police came and took our names down. I called the manager on duty and he said we hand the situation well. Also; talked with controller and filled the paperwork with them.
output: EMB-175 flight crew reported a bird strike on final approach that resulted in damage to the aircraft.

input: The nos approach plate books have the sids with the approach plates and the stars in the front of the book with the takeoff procedures this seems backwards to me adding a bunch of paper shuffling during high workload times. I believe the sids should be in front with the takeoff procedures and the stars back with the apchs.
output: THIS RPTR FEELS THAT THE NEW NOAA APCH CHART BOOKS SHOULD HAVE THE STARS LOCATED WITH THE APCH PLATES AS THE SIDS ARE.

input: Copy clearance for flight. Air traffic control changed the first part of routing to read our first fix to a vor and dme (co-located) down the same airway. The first fix was on the start of the airway and the last fix was still on the same airway. Checked flight plan and confirmed both fixes on our flight plan. I started checking plane book and could not find the airway. Plane book was showing q routes. Reviewed paper charts and did find the airway we were cleared on and again confirmed both fixes on airway. The problem was our flight plan started on the first fix then took off the airway then back on to the same airway. I did not take the time to review all the waypoints on the paper chart to the flight management system because of time restraints. Air traffic control report off airway and ask us our routing and to turn 30 to the right. We were then cleared direct to the vor and dme (co-located) next time i will reload the flight plan with the new clearance and confirm all waypoints.factors: plane book did not show the airway cleared. While writing this report i still could not find the airway on commercial chart view. Looks like the high alt charts in the north east have change.
output: A time constrained Corporate pilot identified airway fixes; but could not identify the connecting airway on either his paper chart or commercial view; but departed anyway and was given vectors by ATC.

input: Checked in with lga at 1.5 north on hudson for a tour; lga informed pilot of traffic ahead helicopter 1.5 northbound and traffic behind 1 mile 1.5 northbound. Pilot informed lga that he has traffic ahead insight and would maintain visual; also informed lga that he would look for traffic behind in the upcoming turn. Shortly later pilot checked out from lga. Immediately after checking out pilot looks left just before initiating turn and sees fixed wing fly by... Same alt 20 feet off left hand side.
output: A helicopter pilot and a small aircraft pilot reported a NMAC over the Hudson River.

input: Lgt was heading 090 degrees level at fl370. Mlg was heading 160 degrees at fl350. Lgt approximately 10 mile westbound of mlg was issued right turn to heading 180 degrees descend and maintain fl240. Aircraft appeared to be slow turning and was getting close to mlg. Lgt had not rpted leaving altitude and mode celsius indicated still level second officer i re-restr lgt to maintain fl370. Pilot said aircraft would return to fl370 and mode celsius then update. I believe intermediate fix the pilot had rpted leaving fl370; the other aircraft could have been issued a lower altitude and sep maintained.
output: STANDARD SEPARATION WAS NOT MAINTAINED BETWEEN 2 ACFT UNDER THE CONTROL OF ATC CTLR.

input: On rotation from we encountered the same problem we had earlier that day. I was the pilot flying for this leg. Gear up the left main amber light stay on the nose gear amber stay on the right main gear unsafe red light stayed on. We informed air traffic control of the situation; that we needed vectors. The first officer brought the checklist out; we contacted operations which in turn contacted dispatch and for some reason they came back to us saying they couldn't talk to maintenance. We had difficulty understanding them because we were only at 3;000 feet. We climbed to 4;000 and we had better reception. The checklist was followed. Maintenance told us to return to departure airport and we landed with no further complications. The event occurred because the plane was not fixed when it had been written up three times prior.
output: A Dash 8-100 flight crew encountered two instances of failed gear retraction on two back to back legs.  The crew stated that other flight crews had identical anomalies a few days before.

input: We took off from weatherford airport at xx20 ante meridiem and a friend was visual flight rules private pilot and was also pilot in command at the time of takeoff as we are reaching towards okc we saw some fog building up. My friend requested me; since i ante meridiem instrument pilot that i should get clearance and be pilot in command from now on. I called okc control 40 nautical mile westbound of okc in visual flight rules condition; okc approach gave me the clearance and i was cleared for instrument landing system approach at okc. I did through instrument landing system approachs at okc and i have to go miss approach controller cleared me to proceed to tinker air force base since there is precision approach radar available. I was vectored by okc approach control to tinker air force base and i did precision approach radar and landed safely.
output: PVT INST RATED PLT ATTEMPTED 3 APCHS RESULTING IN MAPS. ATC INTERVENED AND VECTORED ACFT TO NEARBY AFB FOR A PAR APCH.

input: We were on approach to runway(s) 22r in ohare international we were being vectored to the final approach course. Our heading was 310 degrees at an altitude of 3000 feet/foot the controller told us to turn to a heading of 250 degrees and intercept the final approach course to runway(s) 22r. He was immediately answered by an air carrier y aircraft that acknowledged the approach clearance he did not correct the air carrier y flight we turned inbound to intercept the course and could not ask about the clearance because of the heavy volume on the radio. When we finally told the controller that we thought someone else had answered our call; air carrier y answered again and said 'yes; we did; what do you want us to do about it?' before the controller could respond and blocking the controller finally the controller answered and asked us intermediate fix we were 'turning back now?' we thought he meant back to the 310 degree heading second officer we started to turn on the localizer course to that heading. He then said 'oh; i see what you are doing now; turn left/right (directions) to 210 degrees maintain 2000 feet/foot cleared for the apch?' after we were again established on the localizer he told us we were too close to the heavy behind us and vectored us around again for another approach federal aviation regulation too much congestion on radio. Too many aircraft being controled on 1 frequency 1 controller controling too many aircraft on 1 frequency 3 runway(s) for approach supplemental information from acn 540322: on the evening of 03/fri/02; i was first officer on flight xxx operating to chicago o'hare (ord). We were on a heading of 310 degrees at 3000 feet/foot and being vectored by approach for the instrument landing system runway(s) 22r. We then heard the controller issue the following clearance '...turn left/right (directions) heading 250 degrees to intercept the localizer runway(s) 22r.' the capt who was flying began turning to 250 degrees to intercept. Before i could answer with the readback; an air carrier y aircraft mistakenly read back our clearance the controller never corrected the air carrier y pilot therefore; i called for confirmation that the clearance really was for us. The first call was blocked; however; on the second call; i stated that another aircraft answered our clearance and to confirm that 250 degree heading was for us. Before the controller could answer; air carrier y stated; 'that was us; what would you like us to do now?' the next thing the controller said was to ask us intermediate fix we were 'turning back now.' by this time; we had just intercepted the localizer second officer we assumed he meant 'turning back' to the 310 degree heading and that the original clearance hadn't been for us. We initiated a turn to the left/right (directions) to go back to 310 degrees and the controller said; 'i see what you're doing now; go back left/right (directions) to 210 degrees to intercept; 2000 feet/foot until established and cleared for the instrument landing system runway(s) 22r. As we neared the localizer again; and started our descent from 3000 feet/foot to 2000 feet/foot the controller stated that our separation was not adequate now for the heavy behind us; and turned us left/right (directions) to a north heading and maintain 3000 feet/foot he then sequenced us behind the heavy and we landed without further incident. I believe a contributing factor in this situation was frequency congestion since it was very difficult to confirm our clearance also; i believe the controller's workload was excessive for second officer many aircraft he was the only approach controller we talked to from the arrival, arrive through the approach at some airports such as laguardia (lga); the approach controller working arrs switches you to a final approach controller working only approachs i believe that solution would help intermediate fix used in ord.
output: MD80 HAD CLRNC CONFUSION IN ORD CLASS B BECAUSE OF TFC DENSITY AND APCH CTLR STAFFING.

input: On climb out passing through approximately 7;000 feet/foot we received an 'efis comp mon' caution message immediately followed by an ap trim is nd (autopilot trim is nose down) caution message. I instinctively looked at the elevator trim display and observed the trim running nose down. I immediately pushed the stab trim disconnect and instructed the first officer to do the same. I assumed control of the aircraft and told the first officer to request a level off at 10;000 feet/foot from air traffic control as he was doing that i disconnected the autopilot and found it to be excessively out of trim to the point that it was very difficult to control. I instructed him to run the stab trim runaway checklist. Although we never heard the trim clacker; it seemed at the time the more prudent checklist to run.i had the first officer request a turn back towards [departure airport] as a precaution although we had not committed yet to a return. During this turn i lost some altitude due to the excessive nose down trim as the primary cause but was able to gain it back. Upon further reflection; i decided to run the ap trim is nd checklist because i felt that the autopilot was the more probable cause. I reengaged the trim and trimmed the aircraft for level flight. We did not experience any trim runaway.after briefing the first officer about the autopilot possibly driving the trim nose down; a reengaged the autopilot per the checklist. Immediately the trim started moving nose down so i once again disconnected the trim and the autopilot. I reengaged the trim and left the autopilot off. I determined the autopilot had malfunctioned and since at this time we had full control of the aircraft; i elected to not [get priority handling]. I had the first officer request a return to [departure airport] and instructed him to notify the flight attendants and to automatic communications addressing & reporting system dispatch. We returned and landed uneventfully.
output: CRJ-700 Captain reported returning to departure airport after experiencing an autopilot malfunction that drove the stabilizer trim to a nose-down position.

input: On [date] we were turning final just outside teb to join final to 22l at ewr. There is a building in jersey city; nj; that is a new construction recently completed that has white hazard lights atop the building that appear to be high intensity light emitting diode type that have an irregular flash pattern. While turning final on this evening they appear to be reils for a runway. At other times they appear to be rails for a runway. They are misleading and could be very confusing to somebody not familiar to the airport area. I subsequently queried ewr tower and they stated that they have reported these lights as a problem and i was told by them that they were informed that these lights are stuck in the day mode. These lights are still stuck in bright mode 24 hours a day. I did some sleuthing and have found that this is a newly constructed building located at approximately the intersection of york and hudson streets in jersey city; nj. While i understand the requirements for these lights to be installed they are exceptionally bright and a distraction when vectoring for an approach to ewr. In addition these lights could be plainly be seen from crank intersection at night on another flight. This is a general report as it did not involve any incident or error for my flights.
output: Air carrier pilot reported that a building nearby EWR airport has high intensity; flashing LED type lights that sometimes appear to be REIL or RAIL lights and could be confusing to pilots.

input: Taxied through a hold short line; causing air traffic control to issue go around to another aircraft i did not taxi onto the runway(s) but did go past the hold line. Air traffic control corrected me and asked that i call the tower at engine shutdown. I called tower and discussed the error with them; and on their suggestion; talked with a safety counselor at hgr. Each phase of flight deserves absolute attention not allowing distrs to hamper safety. After noticing the error i should have immediately contacted the tower to clarify the situation and to obtain corrective instructions.
output: PLT RPTR TAXIED ACROSS RWY HOLD LINE CAUSING LNDG TFC TO GAR.

input: I entered the pattern on a 45 for right downwind and was flying a normal pattern for landing at arlington on 16. When i was on short final approx 500' from the threshold and 300' above ground level [aircraft y] crossed the hold short line and rolled onto runway 16. As he crossed the hold short line i made a radio call announcing go around; said aircraft on the runway don't take off and applied full power. [aircraft y] continued onto the runway and began his takeoff roll. I deviated right of center so i could keep him in sight and he climbed out and turned right crosswind approximately 500' below me without making any radio call. I was talking to other planes in the pattern so my radios were working. I was in full power climb so went well above traffic pattern altitude to make sure i was clear of the other pilot that clearly wasn't looking or listening.this event was entirely human failure on the other pilot. I was short final with my landing lights on and was making appropriate radio calls. I suspect his radio was not working. Additionally he was not adsb out equipped; i got his tail number visually.
output: GA Pilot reported a NMAC after another aircraft entered the runway and took off as the reporter was landing.

input: At arrival, arrive gate; ground crew noticed broken nose taxi light when hooking up towbar. Outbound crew was made aware of this prior to their walkaround and outbound capt advised us he would write up the problem and call out contract maintenance found out later that the #2 engine had suffered foreign object damage; most likely from the shattered nose taxi light; which was loose and probably damaged in its holding bracket. Possibly our crews could be made aware of the potential foreign object damage possibility from a loose or damaged nose taxi light.
output: FLT CREW OF B733 ADVISED BY RAMP PERSONNEL OF A BROKEN NOSE GEAR LIGHT ON ARR. LATER LEARNED ENG HAD SUFFERED FOREIGN OBJECT DAMAGE AND SURMISE THE TWO ARE RELATED.

input: Per build up team at the company cargo warehouse; they received a pilot manipulating controls [large pallet] containing 2 boxes of non dg (dangerous goods); 6 boxes of excepted quantities and 131 total individual boxes of dangerous goods in limited quantities (totaling 139 boxes) was loaded on board the aircraft in one ld7 in one compartment in zzz over-exceeding pit limit for dg.
output: Airline Ground Personnel reported Dangerous Goods quantities loaded in cargo compartment exceeded compartment Dangerous Goods limit.

input: [i was] working 3 arrivals into sequence for lih and two departures outbound; also working the oceanic arrivals/departures unassisted. I rated the complexity a little higher because i had to closely monitor the arrival and departures. The traffic was fairly average but required pretty steady work to manage. As my first two arrivals were transitioning onto the approach into lih a piper navajo; called requesting flight following about 6 miles from lih eastbound. I gave him a code and the altimeter and held onto my arrivals instead of switching them to tower right away to ensure they would clear the navajo. After radar identifying the navajo i issued him traffic for the b717 inbound and also for a b757 about 20 miles away to alert him to the inbound b757. I also called traffic to the b757 at least twice. After at least one more traffic advisory the navajo reported he had the b757 in sight. I issued a cautionary wake turbulence advisory. At this time he had climbed to 5;500 feet/foot and i had advised the b757 that the navajo had reported he was climbing visual flight rules to 5;500. I think the navajo reported the b757 at 7 miles. I advised the b757 i would keep him at 6;000 until he cleared the navajo. The navajo then advised me he would climb above the b757. I recommended that he stay below the b757 and subsequently advised he turn northbound if he wanted to avoid the b757's wake but he climbed as i was giving the b757 another traffic advisory and was already leaving 6;300 when the b757 reported he had descended due to traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory it was all but over when i was making the transmission so i never got a chance to issue the safety alert; just a broken advisory. Clearly; i'm not happy with the navajo's decision and i believe he was unaware that by climbing in such close proximity to the b757 he would cause an resolution advisory however; i rated the event as 'minor' because the navajo reported having the b757 in sight and was able to; at least in his judgment; safely avoid the b757. Recommendation; at hcf we are a terminal facility but the area i work in is enroute. There is a common perception here that we should issue hard altitudes and headings to visual flight rules aircraft; not recommended or suggested as is done at my former facility and as i was taught at the federal aviation administration academy. 'hcf approach' confuses the heck out of pilots. They expect certain services from artcc's; tower's; and approach controls. We are provided them with center services while calling ourselves 'approach'. This wasn't a factor as far in this event as far as i know but it's been a recurring problem here that nobody seems to want to address.
output: HCF Controller described a TCAS RA event between an Air Carrier and a VFR aircraft applying see and avoid

input: After making several practice short field lndgs; i failed to extend landing gear and landed wheels up on runway(s) 35. To prevent any other similar occurrence; i plan to install an aural gear warning horn and a bigger; more centrally located gear up/down light.
output: PLT OF SMA ACFT LANDED GEAR UP.

input: I had the flight into rno night of 10/thu/05. During preflt planning received the company notice to airmen / of air missions sheet that listed the closure of runway(s) 16r/34l and associated instrument landing system navigational aid shutdowns. No txwys were listed as being closed. On arrival, arrive the automatic terminal information service verified the runway(s) was closed. We were given the visual approach to runway(s) 34r. We anticipated clearing the runway(s) at taxiway fahrenheit after landing we turned onto taxiway fahrenheit and the tower said; 'if able; turn back onto the runway(s) and clear at the end.' it was then that i noticed that there was a big hole in the middle of the closed runway(s) we were able to turn back onto the runway(s) my concern is that there were a significant number of taxiway closures on the airport (txwys j and b were also closed); and we were never advised of such. Not on the company notice to airmen / of air missions sheet or the airport atis.
output: B737 CAPT RPTS NOTAMS AND ATIS FOR RNO FAILED TO ADVISE ABOUT CLOSED TXWYS.

input: We were on a flight to zzz. Upon reaching fl370; we lost communications the capt told me to squawk 7500; i agreed. After 15-20 minute(s) we realized that we needed to put 7600; not 7500; second officer we did. My communicationss did not work at all. The capt got one of his to partly work getting clearance to land at zzz. After landing we were surrounded by 20+ cop cars and guns drawn. We made a huge mistake and will never happen again.
output: NORDO FLT CREW OF FA10 SQUAWK 7500 VICE 7600. MET BY LEOS UPON LANDING.

input: The fahrenheit flight attendant called the cockpit and advised that lavatory celsius had a faint 'rubbery' smell that appeared to originate from the overhead vent in the lavatory. The captain instructed me to go to the lavatory and examine. The lavatory had a strong smell of what smelled like electrical and or plastic origin; i tried to locate the source but no heat was apparent and the smell could possibly be from the vent. I returned to the flight deck and advised the captain of my findings. He instructed me to obtain a clearance for mach .83. He instructed a flight attendant to monitor the lavatory for any developments. He contacted maintenance over the satellite phone to get further information about the lavatory ceiling electrical components. A flight attendant then called us back and advised that the source of the smell appeared to come from the bright lavatory light that illuminates when the laboratory door is locked. Maintenance agreed that this could be the source of the smell. The captain instructed the flight attendant to close off the lavatory; but not to lock it. He also instructed the flight attendant to monitor the lavatory for any changes. We looked at our options and decided that [diverting] would be the best option. We sent a message to dispatch [who] concurred with our plan. We got a re-analysis of the remainder of the flight at the new cruise speed of .83. The flight attendant monitored the lavatory and gave us continuous updates - nothing really changed. The smell lingered but wasn't getting any worse. No smoke was present. We were assigned a [distant] gate and discussed getting a better one but; ultimately; decided the original one would suffice since the issue was identified; isolated and mitigated. On arriving at the gate and deplaning we got a call from the galley flight attendant that the light fixture was arcing and smoke was present. He asked us to turn off the lights in the lavatory. The captain instructed me to pull the lavatory lights circuit breakers. I called maintenance on the radio to see if they could assist further with shutting down the light in the lavatory. The galley flight attendant removed the light and the arcing stopped. The captain asked maintenance about removing the light and fixture in flight but maintenance advised against it; since the light was off while the door was unlocked. The captain asked what circuit breakers controlled the lights in the lavatory; but maintenance did not respond. After the passengers deplaned i asked the mechanics about why the lights were on; and they told me that the aircraft had a 'ground mode' where all lavatory lights came on. Had we known this; we would have asked for a different gate and also had the light bulb removed; and or continued to ask for the appropriate circuit breaker to pull.
output: A B767-300ER diverted to a closer airport when a flight attendant reported a strong odor associated with lighting in a lavatory.

input: During landing rollout at high altitude airport as we turned off the runway(s) at the high-spd taxiway we blew both tires on the left/right (directions) landing gear side; we stopped on the high-spd; called tower dispatcher and maintenance buses came out to remove passenber ground crew came with bag carts to remove bags. Maintenance and airport personnel helped tow the aircraft to the ramp. This was a tire failure.
output: AN EMB-145 FLT CREW EXPERIENCED TWO FLAT TIRES WHILE EXITING THE RUNWAY AT A HIGH ELEVATION AIRPORT.

input: There are many risks associated with this airport and also non-standard items and practices that need to be put out to the pilots operating in and out of sps. The airport is an air force base first and foremost. The civilian sector in my opinion is merely an add-on. It is completely controlled by military controllers and they are not all that used to controlling civilian flights.we were scheduled out in night conditions with thunderstorms in the area of sps. The first officer and i talked extensively before departure about the weather and our plan of action and alternatives if they needed to be used. We initially planned a descent and left downwind entry for a visual to runway 17; but we also briefed about possible instrument landing system to 15c. We deviated throughout most of the flight to sps for thunderstorms along the route. We ended up well east of the airport and finally turned west while we were ne of the field. Due to the weather we planned at that point to shoot the instrument landing system to 15c instead of the visual to 17. Air traffic control vectored us close enough that during the descent we were able to fully see the runway and proceeded to join the localizer for 15c several miles outside of the final approach fix. We were visual flight rules at this time and while there were thunderstorms in the area; the immediate vicinity around sps was in the clear. We joined to the localizer and proceeded to do a visual backed up with the instrument landing system as we approached the runway i noted that we had a dot deviation off the localizer that increased as we closed to the runway. After looking at the chart closely; we realized that we were lined up for 15r which was the lighted runway. There were no lights on 15c. We verified that we were indeed lined up for sps and proceeded to land on 15r. Taxied [to parking] and the flight ended successfully. Here are where my notes come in.i do not know why; but the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) had been turned off from transmitting and we had to get the weather from the center. Perhaps the air force turns off the broadcast feature when the tower is closed as part of an air force practice. Crews need to know that current weather is unavailable over the radio when the tower is closed. Either obtain on the ground prior to departure (from sps when local tower is closed) over the phone or inflight with center prior to arrival. While the instrument landing system to 15c is on and usable when the tower is closed it will guide pilots to an unlit runway. We attempted to turn on the runway lights several times with no success. Major threat. There appears to be no pilot controlled lighting at sps. As mentioned above we attempted to turn on the lights for 15c several times with no luck. Additionally; even in perfect visual flight rules conditions at night and with a preferred visual approach to 17; the 17 lights are set on dim and we are unable to adjust the setting. Runway 17 can be lost quite easily during a downwind approach and not having the ability to turn up the lights to a higher intensity can complicate the approach. This can lead to pilots flying an instrument landing system simply because it has better guidance; but threat wise now we are flying an approach to an unlit runway that if pilots are not aware of may cause confusion and a last minute sidestep to the lit runway. Fortunately in this case we were visual quite early and easily made the adjustment in a timely and safe fashion. But if under low approaches during low ceilings; this could be a major problem especially if unprepared for this situation. Also note; that runway 17 has no guidance at all; no approaches; and no visual guidance such as a precision approach path indicator or visual approach slope indicator to a prepared crew; not a problem; but it is a threat.day time operations at sps are also a challenge. The controllers sometimes use non-standard communication for civil use and there is a high possibility of ta's or ra's due to high intensity military training. My one day time operation (arrival) to sps we were following a commercial aircraft and they received an resolution advisory resulting in a go around for them. The local controller asked us if we were familiar with sps and noted there is a high frequency of ta's/ra's. We landed without incident. Crews need to be aware that they are operating into an air force base that does things differently.
output: Pilot reported several non-standard issues at SPS mostly related to runway lighting and weather reporting.

input: I was pilot flying flight scheduled service from sps to dfw. We had deviated north of course as we worked ourselves around a line of thunderstorms between sps and dfw. Cruising at 7000 feet/foot we encountered a strong downdraft. We had maximum climb power and were descending at about 200 feet per minute we leveled off at 6500 feet/foot mean sea level and advised air traffic control of the problem we returned to 7000 feet/foot as soon as possible. At time of downdraft we were in an area of visual meteorological conditions with the nearest thunderstorm cell about 13 mile south of us. We had cells at 20 mile to the north of our position also. As we entered the downdraft no turbulence was noticed.
output: TEMPORARY LOSS OF ACFT CTL IN AN ACR SMT. DOWNDRAFT ENCOUNTER BTWN TSTM ACTIVITY.

input: Dsnding to vny for the vor-a approach from the ne. We cross over a mountain range (oat mountain) approximately 5 mile north and running parallel to our approach course. We are turned sse to cross mountains and be on base leg for the approach the ground proximity warning system sounds terrain and pull up just as we receive the intercept vector. We initiated an immediate climb to approximately 4500 feet/foot where the ground proximity warning system stopped alarming. Socal approach advised us that the minimum vector altitude for the area was 3500 feet/foot mean sea level we advised them that instrument meteorological conditions when the voice says pull up we do what he says. We continued our approach from there and landed. While i was pretty sure the alert was false; when you are in the clouds it can be very disconcerting. This approximately position has been the site of at least 3 other false ground proximity warning system warnings in the past in this aircraft i think it is possible that there is a fault in our ground proximity warning system or that the mountain range that we flew over may contain some radio equipment that interferes with the radar altimeter for the ground proximity warning system callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that his company does not choose to checked out their equipment second officer he has no idea intermediate fix that is the problem the mountain over which they fly on this approach has a great amount of radio facilities on it and he feels this may be the problem both pilots have had such warnings in the past but always in visual flight rules this one shook up rptr because it was instrument meteorological conditions in the visual flight rules conditions they did not respond but continued flight and it was a longitude time before the warning stopped; quite a distance from where they cleared the terrain. The terrain does rise rather fast up to 4000 feet/foot in fairly close proximitypa to the airport both pilots had just completed school and had been given several ground proximity warning system sits due to the accident in south america. This was just like the simulated experiences; only real.
output: CORP MLG HAS GPWS ALERT WHEN DSNDING ON RADAR VECTORS IN IMC.

input: Apch cleared for visual runway(s) 5; call tower 5 mile final. At 5 mile final called tower rpted inbound. Called tower second time at 3 mile final. A male voice stated; 'clred to land runway(s) 5.' called in 'clred to land runway(s) 5.' landed; turned off runway(s) called tower and a female voice told us to contact ground called ground for taxi instructions. Male controller on ground cleared us to taxi to ramp then asked intermediate fix we had received a landing clearance we stated we had; from a male voice; and were surprised at hearing a female voice on tower frequency after landing ground stated no problem had occurred; clear to cross runway(s) 13/31 and taxi to ramp. Also; he had our departure clearance when we were ready. Taxied to ramp.
output: TWR CTLR QUESTIONED A FLC'S HAVING OBTAINED A LNDG CLRNC.

input: We had one flight attendant stay with our crew and one called in sick in the middle of the duty day. We pen and inked the change that occurred with the new flight attendant joining the crew. However; the second flight attendant was supposed to swap as well and the new flight attendant was on the release; a fact that was missed by the flight crew on the release. The second flight attendant whom had been flying with us all along was 'x;' but the release had him listed as 'y.'  'y' never joined the crew. The paperwork was double checked enroute and the error was noticed. The fact that both flight attendants were in error was missed by the flight crew in trying to achieve an on time departure. The captain showed up as i was calling scheduling 10 mins prior to departure; leaving me little time to review the release in his possession. Dispatch was notified of the error via automatic communications addressing & reporting system  dispatch and crew scheduling should be in better communication as to whom is working the flight.
output: A CRJ700 First Officer discovered enroute that names of both the flight attendants listed on the dispatch release were incorrect.

input: On an emergency medical service mission; i had departed the accident site and was taking the patient to hospital in xyz. The visibility in flight was 2-3 mile due to haze. That part of the country is nothing but woods. Flying the heading to take me up to zzz and then over to xyz; i noticed a familiar landmark. I checkeded the directional gyro with the mlg compass and saw that the directional gyro had precessed about 30 degrees thus flying what i thought was the correct heading (as shown from the loran); it put me into rxxx. I immediately turned north checkeding the magnetic compass; and proceeded to exit the restrict, restricted, restriction area and continue to the hospital with the patient. As i flew along i checkeded and saw that the slaved; free toggle switch was in the free position i feel that on final approach to the accident site; my paramedic hit the slave-free switch by mistake; thus allowing the directional gyro to precess. On this helicopter the intercom-xmit switch (which is a toggle switch also) is about 2' above the slave-free switch. I think that on final he must have hit the slave-free switch when he went to transmit that we were landing to our dispatcher at the hospital.
output: EMS HELICOPTER INADVERTENTLY PENETRATES RXXX; AIDED AND ASSISTED BY DIRECTIONAL GYRO INDICATION ERROR.

input: Our flight was cleared to descend from 24000 feet/foot second officer as to cross ccc (calverton vor) at 12000 feet/foot and 250 knot(s) the controller gave the ccc altimeter setting as 29.21. We noted the low altimeter and requested verification; then set the standby altimeter to this setting. We then became preoccupied with programming the vertical descent mode of the flight management computer second officer as to make the ccc restriction. The descent had to be manually controled to make the crossing and in doing second officer we passed 18000 feet/foot without resetting our altimeters to 29.21. Thus the aircraft leveled off at 12000 feet/foot (or 600 feet/foot low 11400 msl). The zbw controller asked us to checked our altitude and we then reset the altimeters to 29.21 and climbed back to 12000 feet/foot contributing to this incident was that the crew had spent the last 6 days flying in europe; where altimeters are reset at low altitudes (ie; transition levels 3000-5000 ft) second officer a readjustment to united states rules had to be made. Also; the preoccupation of programming the vertical navigation computer was a large factor. Recommendations: change united states rules to allow altimeters to be set in advance to local settings intermediate fix descending to a level below fl180; from a level above fl180; and stress that 1 pilot flies; the other pilot talks on the radio; programs the computer; and watches for traffic supplemental information from acn 204745: discovered rapidly falling altimeter pressure had put us at an actual altimeter reading of 11500 feet/foot as discovered from latest pvd automatic terminal information service immediately went back to 12000 indicated. No altitude comment from either zbw or pvd approach cannot remember getting altimeter update from zbw.
output: ALTDEV ALT OVERSHOT IN DSCNT. ALT XING RESTRICTION NOT ADHERED TO.

input: Our destination was runway(s) 27 localizer san center had kept us high despite a request for lower. A timely descent was initiated when received but we were still high. At 20 mile out my suggestion to request a '360' was ignored. Then approach asked us intermediate fix we were going to be able to get down in time. Closer in i suggested a request for s-turns which was accepted by the capt and approved by approach we were still too high and informed the tower we were unable to complete the approach instead of following the missed approach procedure we continued in a 90 degree turn to the right (our last s-turn direction). Clearance was given to turn left to 270 degree (missed approach proc) and climb. Despite reading back the clearance and confirming the flight director was commanding the left turn it was not accomplished until the 3rd request by tower factors: in cruise i was mentally preparing for an upcoming 6 month check instead of preparing for the descent and approach the approach brief didn't cover the missed approach procedure (lulled by excellent wx). The crew was not familiar with aircraft missed approach procedure to the point where they were comfortably followed. I was not totally familiar with the descent capabilities of the aircraft otherwise i would have been more positive with my suggestions. Corrections: planning ahead and admitting early that there was a problem would have averted a stressful and confused last second decision. Assisting the capt more with the missed approach and aircraft procs.
output: NON ADHERENCE TO PUBLISHED MISSED APCH PROC EVEN AFTER RECEIVING SPECIFIC CLRNC FROM ATC.

input: During cruise at fl320 electronic centralized aircraft monitoring showed hydraulic y sys lo and quantity indicated zero. Accomplished electronic centralized aircraft monitoring actions in accordance with checklists and advised dispatch and maintenance control. Elected to continue to zzz. During descent on autopilot aircraft abruptly pitched down; autopilot disconnected and electronic centralized aircraft monitoring momentarily showed hydb + y sys lo pr.recovered aircraft from pitch down and [requested priority handling] with mayday call. The electronic centralized aircraft monitoring hydraulic b 'self-healed' and disappeared from electronic centralized aircraft monitoring display. We used the 7700 automatic communications addressing & reporting system feature to notify dispatch. Apparently; it did not work according to our dispatcher. Accomplished non-routine landing considerations checklist; coordinating with cabin crew and air traffic control did not re-engage autopilot for the remainder of the flight and hand flew the approach. There is a discrepancy between electronic centralized aircraft monitoring and the manual on turning on y system engine pump during approach. We chose the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring guidance and turned on the pump after configuring.we expected only one reverse on rollout; but had indications of normal reverse on both engines. Taxied to gate with [crash fire rescue equipment] following. Terminated emergency with ground after shutdown. On post flight; first officer found fluid covering the bottom of the airplane; in the left wheel well and on the left main landing gear. During the van ride to our layover hotel; the flight attendants told us a burning mechanical smell in mid cabin occurred soon after the pitch down.
output: A319 First Officer reported loss of hydraulic fluid and an associated pitch down resulted in a priority landing.

input: I filed a flight plan to zzz1; with a required alternate of zzz2. I departed with 3;100 pounds of fuel; requiring only 2;900 to make my alternate and 45 minute cruising time. Upon arrival in zzz1 class celsius airspace; i was informed that the runway visual range had dropped to 1;200. I asked to hold; and was told to hold at [navigational aid]; which i did. After 2 turns in holding at 5;000 mean sea level i asked to climb to 12;000 for fuel conservation. I elected not to divert to my alternate of zzz2 because zzz3 (which i was holding over) has an lpv approach; and was reporting 6 statute mile visibility. I was able to see the runway lights and beacon at zzz3 with each turn in holding. After approximately 30 minutes of holding; i noticed that there was a reduction in visibility at zzz3 (i could still see the beacon and runway lights; but with less clarity); and checked the automatic weather observing/reporting system there. It was reporting 2 statute mile visibility.i then decided to attempt to land at zzz3 before the weather deteriorated any further. I attempted the area navigation runway xx there; but had to go missed. I then requested vectors to zzz4; and began to set up for the approach there; however; their automatic weather observing/reporting system showed 1/4 statute mile visibility. With approximately 30 minutes of fuel left; i realized i had boxed myself into a very bad situation. I am very familiar with the instrument landing system xx at zzz1; and elected to [advise air traffic control of minimum fuel] and attempt the instrument landing system there. The runway visual range was reported to be 1;600; but i was essentially out of options. I landed successfully; and was escorted to the ramp by airport operations.i will never hold for more than 2 turns before diverting again. I believed that the weather would clear (the runway visual range would bounce from 1;000 to 1;600 at zzz1); but should have erred on the side of caution and proceeded to zzz2. I was emboldened to stay in holding because of the weather at zzz3.
output: A Cessna Citation pilot reported having to advise ATC of minimum fuel due to deteriorating weather conditions at the destination airport; which necessitated several holding patterns and a missed approach at an alternate airport.

input: During the instrument landing system runway(s) 23 approach into cak we noticed small intermittent lateral movements of the localizer needle on both sides but always returning to center (not a loss of signal; nor full scale deflection). The capt had already turned off the autoplt approximately 2 mile outside the final approach fix but was using the flight director for the approach at approximately 1800 feet/foot mean sea level (550 feet/foot hat); the needle snapped to a full scale deflection; the capt then called for a missed approach we set the missed approach power retracted flaps to 12 degrees and retracted the gear as per the company's standardizations manual. After leveling at 3000 feet/foot on the runway(s) heading as directed by air traffic control the airspd exceeded 200 knot(s) (vfe flaps 12 degs). Immediately the capt called for and the first officer retracted the flaps to 0 degrees the airspd reached approximately 206 knot(s) for about 2-4 seconds. Contributing factors include the sudden full scale deflection of the localizer which caused us to go missed approach at an unusually high altitude (ie; short climb to missed approach alt). A combination of this and air traffic control communicationss caused the first officer to overlook the standard '500 ft' above ground level callout (at which the flaps are retracted to 0 degs) until already leveling at 3000 feet/foot once leveling; the aircraft quickly accelerated and the flap speed was exceeded briefly. Additional factors were that the crew was on their 14th hour of duty that day; and the fo's low time in type (2nd day online). Supplemental information from acn 564611: i called 'select heading' and then called 'select vertical spd.' this activated the flight director at 2700 feet/foot and we were beginning to leveloff. I called for after takeoff checkeds and was concentrating on leveling the aircraft when we got a single chime and a flap overspd cas message. I called flaps up and pulled the throttles back immediately. The '500 ft' call was never made because the missed approach was commenced from an altitude above 500 feet/foot under normal circumstances; the '500 ft' call prompts the pilot flying to call 'flaps up.' also under normal circumstances; the after takeoff checkeds would be accomplished while still climbing and used as a backup to verify the flaps were retracted. There wasn't enough time to accomplish the after takeoff checkeds before leveloff. After the flap overspd; we set up for the instrument landing system runway(s) 23 at cak again. On our second attempt at the instrument landing system we had similar problems with the course deviation indicator and had to do another missed approach we decided not to attempt the approach again and diverted to cle where the weather was rpted visual meteorological conditions we landed in cle uneventfully.
output: A LOC NEEDLE DEFLECTION PROB DISTRACTS A DO328 FLC TO THE POINT THAT; DURING THE MISSED APCH; THE CREW FORGETS OR FAILS TO RETRACT THE FLAPS FROM THE 12 DEG POS BEFORE EXCEEDING THE VFE SPD DURING LEVELOFF NEAR CAK; OH.

input: Hypoxia due to air leak in l1 door the entire flight:just after 10;000 feet; i heard loud; sharp alarm sounding screech on a 737. After looking for source of alarm; checking lavatory; circuit breakers; switches on phone panel; feeling walls for heat (thinking it might be a fire alarm; though lavatory alarm not going off) was unable to locate anything other than loud; high pitch alarm sound near the forward l1 door. All rows in first class also heard and inquired what it was.i then called the captain immediately advising of the sound and that i was not able to immediately determine. He asked to come out; called to the back and flight attendant celsius came forward and guarded door; stating she felt dizzy and nauseous. After calling flight deck again to confirm flight deck door was guarded; i stood up and felt dizzy and woozy.captain came out; i went into the flight deck and i grabbed the spare oxygen mask in the flight deck. I felt anxious; woozy; and light headed. The captain examined and said it was a door leak and to stay away from the door; all would be okay. While i was in the flight deck the first officer told me everything up their looked fine and there shouldn't be an issue as they were breathing the same air and no lights were indicating a loss in cabin pressure. I stated to the first officer i didn't feel okay. He asked if i had ever heard the door whistle; i said yes; but this is a high pitched screeching alarm sound. Stated again i didn't feel well. I felt as though my concern for my safety was being a bit dismissed by the first officer.after 10 minutes; captain called and said he went a bit lower and i advised it was still screeching and would call if it stops. He advised to stay away from standing next to the door; i was in the galley continuing service. I am not sure being less than 5 feet away makes a difference.l1 door continued to screech the high pitched sound the entire flight (for an hour) while i continued service feeling what i describe as loopy; but filled with adrenalin. My entire first row of very large men were asleep with drinks in their hands on their tray tables; i noted. It was a very busy flight and the b and celsius flight attendants barely finished service.
