I was making a point to stay focused to keep my operations and responsibilities as the a safe; it did feel like it took extra focus.captain soon advised us we would have turbulence coming in to land; so to be cleaned up and seated soon after 18;000; which we did. The loud alarm sounding screeching from the door continued until about 10;000 feet when i noted it had finally stopped.upon door opening; a ground crew member was there and i noted he was eying the door as our passengers deplaned. Ground crew said he saw the problem; ice chunk in the door and the plane would have to meled.on the ground i felt 'high'; loopy; detached. I was scheduled to fly another turn and called crew scheduling immediately calling sick online as i did not feel safe to fly and conduct my operational duties safely; then called my supervisor and was put on workers comp. I then had a friend drive me to urgent care as i did not feel competent to drive. Doctor determined 'altitude sickness.'
output: B737 Flight Attendant experienced a loud screeching noise coming from the L1 door and informs the Captain. The Captain determined that the L1 door seal was leaking; but that pressurization was normal and the flight continued to destination. The Flight Attendant felt light headed and asked to be removed from the trip to see a doctor.

input: Departed bos logan airport handed off to departure instructed to fly 270 degree heading and climb to 5000 feet/foot as we approached 4000 feet/foot air traffic control advised traffic at 2 o'clock position 4 mile 5000 feet/foot swbound. Climbing through 4500 feet/foot we spotted the traffic a b757 at 2 o'clock position and about 4 mile air traffic control called and ordered an immediate descent to 4000 feet/foot and advised we were assigned only 4000 feet/foot we still had the traffic in sight and the capt and i were sure we had been given 5000 feet/foot we passed below and behind the traffic with no conflict.
output: SMT TURBOPROP BUSINESS CREW AND A B757 HAD A CONFLICT IN BOS CLASS B. THE SMT CREW CLAIMS THEY WERE CLRED TO 5000 FT; THE DEP CTLR SAID THEY WERE CLRED TO 4000 FT.

input: I was relieving a controller at the final position and to my memory i believe i had plugged in to watch for a satisfactory amount of time in order to become comfortable with what was happening. During the briefing; aircraft x on a visual approach to 16r was eventually 600 ft below aircraft y who was also on a visual approach; but to 16l. Aircraft y went through his localizer but was already on tower frequency. When i assumed the position and noticed aircraft y on the wrong localizer; i gave my brain a chance to assess the situation and i think i noticed the aircraft y making a correction back to 16l. I didn't say anything to aircraft x because of the correction that aircraft y was making back to the 16l localizer and after aircraft y was no longer a factor for aircraft x; i shipped aircraft x to the tower.i think calling traffic 'again' would be good but i'm not sure that aircraft x would have been able to see him. Both aircraft were issued traffic prior to this happening and both reported the other in sight. The timing of this event was unfortunate because it happened during a relief briefing.
output: Denver TRACON Final controllers reported a loss of separation when the leading aircraft went through the other aircraft's final.

input: I received this trip at xa00 with a chk-in of xn05. I have to wake up at xj00 to arrive on time. This trip starts with the flight attendant having to drive in the dark due to early chk-in and on this day also in heavy rains. It ends with the flight attendant having to drive home at the end of a 14+ hour duty day in the dark. More than 1/2 of the flight attendants sleep in their cars or in the domicile before starting out on their drive home. Most of us who live more than 1 hour away end up pulling over and sleeping in our cars during the drive home. I believe that intermediate fix i don't feel that i ante meridiem safe enough to be driving on the road then i was not safe enough to be on the aircraft being responsible for saving people's lives. During the trip over and part of the leg back home; we encountered turbulence that was in the moderate range that required the capt to make the announcement for flight attendants to take their seats. After each episode; flight attendants spoke of being tired and struggling to hold off fatigue (this was on first leg). Most of the crew tried to get some type of rest on the bright; loud; and noisy aircraft as we are not provided a crew rest area anytime during this 14+ hour duty day. The only time that rest can be attempted is during the turn time; but it is a losing battle due to catering; cleaners; and mechs all trying to get their jobs done. I knew i was tired but not enough to satisfy the fatigue requirements. The deadheading crew that was traveling with us commented on both mine and my galley's obvious signs of fatigue. I had flown with 4 of the flight attendants and one of the pilots previously second officer that had previous experiences with me to compare my actions to. By the last hour my fatigue was obvious to everyone. For the first time; i felt weak to my knees. My galley was a ready reserve who was woken at xh00 to be told that she had this xn05 chk-in turn. She was zombie-like -- not aware of her own fatigue. No situational awareness the last 1/2 of the flight back. Deadheaders voiced their concerns about her.
output: FLT ATTENDANT DESCRIBES THE FATIGUE INDUCED BY 14 HOUR DUTY DAY WITH A TWO HOUR COMMUTE ON EACH END.

input: At cruise at 12000 feet/foot on the majic 9 arrival, arrive into clt; we were advised of a b737 climbing to 10000 feet/foot by gso approach the b737 was to our left/right (directions) (n) and heading south we advised gso approach that we did not have the traffic in sight; as there was an undercast below us. We entered instrument meteorological conditions and shortly after this we received a ta/ra from our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii looking down at the target; it was 200 feet/foot below us; just off our left/right (directions) rear and climbing by the time the target traffic was at our altitude it was at its closest to our aircraft and still climbing the resolution advisory told us to 'dsnd;' second officer the capt initiated a descent and told me to advise gso. I did second officer and gso told us that the conflict aircraft was given the climb and had us in sight. Neither the capt nor i ever heard the b737's climb clearance nor did we hear the b737 rpt us in sight. Neither of us understood how the b737 crew could have us in sight when we clrly were in instrument meteorological conditions we both estimate that the b737 passed about 1 mile behind us. This is too close without further advisement from air traffic control the ta/ra caught us both by surprise and we acted accordingly to protocol and safety.
output: DHC-8 FLC DSND IN RESPONSE TO TCASII RA DURING ARR SID DUE TO A B737 CLBING THROUGH THEIR ALT.

input: We were asked to slow as much as possible for delays into ewr on sunday evening. I had just come back from the bathroom and one of our jump seaters was in my seat (he was a company crew member). The capt probably asked him to situation there while i went back. I sat in the jump seat for about 10 minute(s) as the capt and the jump seater talked. When zdc or maybe ztl asked us to slow as much as practicable; the capt slowed back past top bug from takeoff i asked him what top bug was at our current weight and he said about where we were at 230 knots indicated airspeed without actually referring to the chart. The jump seater remarked it didn't really matter as longitude as we didn't exceed 15 degrees bank. Center then asked us to climb from fl330 to fl350 for traffic the capt checkeded the gw/alt chart and began a climb we then began a shallow climb and the airspd began to bleed off even though the engs were at climb power as stall buffet began; the capt directed the jump seater out of my seat second officer i could return. Then center asked us to turn left/right (directions) about 90 degrees to heading 350 degrees as the capt did this; the plane went back into stall buffet and began to descend center asked us why we were not turning and we said we had gotten behind the power curve and had to descend to pick up speed before we could turn. We did this and it took about 10 minute(s) to finally get to fl350. We delayed the left/right (directions) turn for about 3 minute(s) to pick up speed recommend this be demonstrated in the simulator during initial training.
output: FLC OF DC10-10 REQUESTED TO MAINTAIN SPD AS SLOW AS POSSIBLE. THEY SLOW BELOW TOP BUG SPD. WHEN ASKED TO CLB AND CHANGE HDG THEY GET A STALL BUFFET AND BEGIN TO DSND.

input: I landed uneventfully. I switched to ground and asked to taxi to a flight service station specialist on the ground i was told to taxi via taxiway b. Within seconds i was notified by ground that i was not on taxiway b; but in a 'restr area' on the field. I replied that i; too; had just took note of this; but it was too late to turn off at this point. Ground reminded me this was a restrict, restricted, restriction area used for commercial transports; but allowed me to continue to taxi through it to my dest.
output: A PIPER PA28 PLT TAXIED IN AN AREA RESERVED FOR AIRLINE PARKING AT SBA.

input: Ecam notified crew of low yellow system hydraulic fluid. System was shut down per procedures consulted with dispatch and maintenance in regards to condition. Notified station and flight service station specialist of our situation dispatch coordinated with air traffic control for runway(s) 32l. Landed into the wind; used runway(s) 32l due to limited potential braking and loss of thrust reverser on left/right (directions) engine upon uneventful landing heavy vibration was felt in nose gear and air frame. Fearful of additional safety issues; cleared runway(s) and had fire crews look over aircraft for additional problems and fire risks associated with hydraulic leak. Shut down aircraft on taxiway until communications with ground crews confirmed safe operations(s) of aircraft was assured. Taxied to the international gates without additional problems with fire watch trailing the aircraft landed with minimum brakes but still had hot brakes on left/right (directions) side of aircraft (330 degs). Hydraulic fluid and smoke was rpted initially by ground fire crew coming from left/right (directions) main brakes. Maintenance cleared us to taxi to the gate once they looked over the aircraft on taxiway a. Air traffic control provided excellent service with no delays. Landed as soon as possible given the location and time remaining from the initial site of the event.
output: AN A320 LOST YELLOW HYD SYS FLUID RESULTING IN A PROCEDURAL SECURING OF THE AFFECTED SYS. EMER DECLARED; HOT BRAKES ON LNDG.

input: After calling rotation speed we experienced violent compressor stalls; engine indicating and crew alerting system indications showed #3 engine egt rising rapidly; exceeding takeoff maximum instrument marking line and bold in red; i elected to shut down the engine declared emergency standard emergency procedures followed with a climb to 6000 feet/foot fuel was dumped to landing weight all chklists performed in accordance to standard operating procedure landed without further incident.
output: B747-400 LOSES AN ENG ON TKOF; EMER DECLARED; FUEL DUMPED; RETURN LAND.

input: On the morning of 01/xx/90; i was conducting a flight lesson at 2500' mean sea level (note: prior to flight i conducted a normal preflt inspection [demonstrated for student's first flight including draining each wing sump twice and draining fuel sump/eng twice. Fuel level indicated half tanks each side. No water or contamination.) executing medium turns; turns to a heading and climbing turns and dscnts; approximately 50 minute(s) into the flight i had my student performing a descending turn to an assigned heading power was reduced to 2000 revolutions per minute and a cruise descent was made to an altitude of 2000' mean sea level i then instructed my student to increase power to full power and climb back up to 2500'. As he applied full throttle i noticed no increase in engine power and the engine began to run rough. (note: at the full power setting i was only able to maintain 2000 rpm.) i immediately applied carburetor heat and took command of the aircraft and leveled out at approximately 2300' (radio contact with columbus approach was initiated 14 mile ne of practice area). As i applied carburetor heat i noticed a normal reduction in rpm's; indicating that heat was being applied to the carburetor inlet. The engine can't run rough and i noticed i was slowly losing rpm's. Now was down to 1500-1600 rpm's and altitude approximately 1800' mean sea level and descending (note: throttles position was still at full pwr.) engine roughness now became more acute and i reduced the throttle/power setting (approx 1') and an increase of 300 revolutions per minute was indicated. Rpm's now stabilized at 1800 revolutions per minute any increase i made in the throttle setting brought back acute engine roughness and further loss in rpm's. I then proceeded to execute the emergency procedures chklist. As i proceeded through the chklist i pushed the carburetor heat back in and gained an additional 75-100 rpm's. (eng now running slightly rough; and rpm's fluctuating between 1800 and 1950.) my altitude was now down to approximately 1500' and i was working with columbus approach on obtaining a landing site when the engine suddenly began to run acutely rough again and rpm's fell to approximately 1100'. Unable to gain any power over 1100 rpm's; i executed the emergency landing chklist told columbus approach i was unable to make the field and selected a suitable field and set the aircraft down with no damage to the aircraft or persons aboard. Conclusion: after landing a fuel sample was taken from the left wing sump and a small amount of water was found. Investigators assumed due to the intense cold weather in the area; water in the left tank had frozen; sow when a fuel sample was taken prior to flight no water contamination had shown. While in flight the ice in the left tank broke up/crystals and was able to work its way into the fuel line; partially blocking fuel flow and crystal/water that was in the line melted; contaminating fuel flow.
output: INSTRUCTOR AND STUDENT ON FIRST FLT LESSON EXPERIENCE ENGINE ROUGHNESS AND POWER LOSS ON SMA; FORCED LNDG RESULTS.

input: Air return back to [departure airport]. Leveled off cruise altitude; 'r oil strainer clog' light illuminated on oap. Complied with quick reference handbook procedures. Light did not extinguish. Engine oil temp reached 129 and fuel temp peaked at 38. Contacted company; spoke with both dispatch and maintenance control; and returned without incident. Both oil temp and fuel temp decreased during descent. As a note; [this aircraft] had the same issue 3 days prior. The aircraft had been flown only about 10 hours until we got the light again. When these issues occur; replacing a part or 'ops check normal' is not the best course action. Many times there is more than meets the eye. We need to stop fixing the symptoms and fix the real problems. If you ask me; [this aircraft] does not just need a new oil filter; but needs to be looked at much closer. Also; i believe the right engine is the one on the mto program. As the technicians were finishing up putting on the new oil filter; scheduling was informing me that they were thinking of launching us back to [destination]. (note: they informed us that hotel rooms were very hard to find.) i shared my concerns and proceeded to talk with maintenance control. Flight was finally cancelled.
output: MD-83 Captain reported 'R OIL STRAINER CLOG' light after takeoff. He returned to departure airport and noted this was a recurring problem.

input: Shortly after takeoff the capt called for gear up; and upon completion; the smoke master warning panel went on; and the bell chimed. The second officer silenced the bell and declared that there was smoke in the left/right (directions) portion of the main cargo deck. Shortly after that; the capt and i argued that we smelled smoke. I switched over to departure control as the capt called for smoke on the flight deck; and we donned air masks and goggles and established communicationss we then declared an emergency and began a left/right (directions) turn for a left/right (directions) downwind for runway(s) 28r at sfo. While the capt flew the approach to a level off height; i gave the controller our souls on board and fuel; the second officer worked on the completion of the emergency checklist; and the smoke began to clear. We continued the traffic pattern and landed on runway(s) 28r without further incident. We taxied to parking and were followed by local fire auths. No further events occurred. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the cause of the smoke was an internal and external engine oil leak; allowing oil to enter the engine bleed ducts direct to the air conditioning packs. The rptr stated the engine was a general electric cfm56-502c and was replaced. The rptr said the national transportation safety board requested and removed the cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder.
output: AN AIRBUS 300 ON CLBOUT AT FL200 DECLARED AN EMER AND DIVERTED DUE TO SMOKE AND FUMES IN THE COCKPIT AND CARGO MAIN DECK CAUSED BY #1 ENG INTERNAL AND EXTERNAL OIL LEAK.

input: My first officer and i arrived at the aircraft and upon an inspection of the logbook i noticed that the aircraft had just received an airworthiness inspection. Before the first officer went to do the walk around i informed him to please make sure there are no gear pins in the aircraft as there has been an issue lately with them not being removed. He came back from the inspection and continued his normal duties.the flight operated normally to our first destination. After arrival i informed the first officer that i would conduct the preflight walk around for the return flight. Upon arrival at the left main gear well i noticed the inspection lights were left on. I did a normal look over and noticed something red i had never seen before in the very center of the top of the gear well and out of reach. I got as close to the object as possible and i realized it was some sort of pin. The flag attached to the pin was red but did not say anything on it.i then asked the first officer what it was and asked if he had seen it on his initial preflight. We determined it was some sort of pin and should not be there. We then asked the ramp agent for a stool or steps to take a closer look. I then pulled the flag down from its position and noticed on the backside it said 'remove before flight'.i called the maintenance controller and informed him of what i had found and asked him what it could be? He stated; 'i don't know.'  i said; 'what do you mean you don't know. It's in the center of the main gear well and it says remove before flight.'  he said he would need to call contract maintenance to remove it. The contract maintenance technician had no idea what the item was either. He went inside; called maintenance control and came back out to the plane. He said they told him it was the 'bypass solenoid lockout pin'. He spent the next 15 minutes or so removing the pin. He then came back with a signed off logbook. I again asked him what was the pin supposed to be locking out? He said it was something for the leading edge slats. I recalled actually looking at the leading edge position lights on approach and everything was in the normal range. We finally left about 40 minutes late.how to keep this event from happening again is difficult to determine; but what i will say is if the captain of an aircraft asks maintenance control to explain what an item is and what it does or affects i expect a response. If the flag had been installed with the flag hanging down in line of sight it might have been more visible to the first officer on his initial walk around.
output: A B737-700 flight crew; during an enroute walkaround; discovered a flagged pin of undetermined function in the left main gear well.  The aircraft had undergone an intensive maintenance inspection prior to their initial departure.

input: About 12 minutes prior to departure; approximately one minute after switching from external power to auxiliary power unity power; auxiliary power unity auto shutdown. Auxiliary power unity fire light illuminated with engine indicating and crew alerting system auxiliary power unity fire warning; fire bell and fire bottle auto discharge. Ground control was contacted for crash fire rescue equipment to respond and passenger deplaned right away via jet bridge. No fire (per cfr). Maintenance performed inspection; meled auxiliary power unity and we departed. Upon switching to external power [after arrival]; auxiliary power unity fire light illuminated with engine indicating and crew alerting system auxiliary power unity fire warning and fire bell. Ground control contacted to inform of situation and for crash fire rescue equipment to respond. Operations and maintenance also contacted. No fire. Maintenance then took aircraft. There is nothing that we could do to change this. Maintenance [at the departure airport] said that a spike in a power card (or something like that) was the cause. We would not assume anything after arrival and it was absolutely required to call crash fire rescue equipment we also had no fire bottle at that time.
output: Widebody First Officer experiences an APU fire warning with auto shut down and fire bottle discharge during preflight. The passengers are evacuated through the jet bridge; but CFR finds no evidence of fire. The APU is MEL'ed and the flight departs for North America. Upon gate arrival; with the APU off and switching to ground power; the scenario repeats.

input: We were departing teb (teterboro; nj;) assigned to fly a teb five departure for runway 24. We selected the departure from the flight management system database and set up the flight management system so the aircraft autopilot would fly the procedure. At approximately 1200 feet/foot above ground level i attempted to engage the autopilot; i was experiencing difficulty getting the autopilot to engage. At this point we were in continual light with occasional moderated turbulence. After several attempts the autopilot engaged and flew the aircraft. We contacted ny departure control as instructed. The controller informed us of the 1500 feet/foot until 4.5 vor and dme (co-located) restriction. We both acknowledged the standard instrument departure requirement to each other. With the delay in getting the autopilot engaged i can't be sure just when we departed 1500 feet/foot for 2000 feet/foot in summation; the compressed workload (speed restrictions; noise abatement procedure; turbulence) combined with autopilot issue all contributed significantly to the occurrence.
output: A Falcon 2000 flight crew flew through an altitude restriction on the TEB departure; in part because of autopilot problems.

input: On the return from the designated se practice area; an initial call by me was placed to tulsa approach for stage ii back into tulsa left/right (directions) left/right (directions) jones airport we were; in my opinion 500 feet/foot below the clouds; indicating 1600 feet/foot mean sea level airspd of 95 knots indicated airspeed and approximately 3-5 mile sw of bixby heading 300 degrees a second call was placed to tulsa approach as a result of no answer to initial call up. We changed heading 270 degrees and were located 2 1/2-3 mile se of the tank farm and 1/8-1/4 mile south of power plant. Tulsa received the second transmission and advised that an smt was on the approach at 2100 mean sea level above us. I then brought back the throttle and initiated a 500 feet per minute descent and leveled off at 1300 feet/foot mean sea level the smt was in instrument meteorological conditions and we were in visual meteorological conditions the request made by me to proceed over the tank farm then straight in to 1l was approved by tulsa. The rest of the flight was uneventful. In my opinion both parties have to be very vigilant in their facet of operations(s) the sma is of a high wing confign which gives limited upward visibility and the smt is of a low wing confign. We can see the possible conflict that may arise. Note: i didn't realize there was a problem until the pilot of the smt approached me. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that smt pilot indicated they missed by 150 feet/foot as smt descended into visual flight rules federal aviation administration did follow up investigation and found both parties in compliance. The matter has been dropped. Apparently this particular smt pilot has been an ongoing complainer reference the flight school operating in area with larger; faster acft.
output: INSTRUCTOR WITH SPI HAS CLOSE PROX WITH SMT DSNDING THROUGH CLOUDS; IFR.

input: On the departure; climbing through approximately 3000 feet; both fmc's flashed momentarily with resulting failure of both flight directors; route and performance data. Route 2 (blue line was displayed) was activated. Crew was distracted with these events and subsequently ended up being slightly left of course. Departure control questioned our course. We let him know we had an aircraft navigation problem and asked for vectors. Departure provided an initial heading and subsequent direct routing. Aircraft was loaded with new flight management computer software.while i believe that the entire crew did a great job of handling the situation (fairly complex considering area navigation departure; international ops; etc); we certainly could have done a better job of transitioning back to a lower level of automation as well as delegating who's talking; flying; and working the issue.
output: The B787 crew experienced an FMC malfunction which dumped the route and performance data while climbing out of 3;000 feet. They were able to activate Route 2 and proceed after getting vectors from ATC.

input: On nov/thu/03; at approximately xa30 i was sent out to aircraft x to inspect fan blade damage to the #1 engine my crew chief pulled up maintenance manual for and limits for repair. He instructed me how to blend the repair. After finishing repair; crew chief inspected the repair and signed off aircraft logbook. I personally did not read maintenance manual due to time constraints on departure of acft.
output: A B737-800 L ENG FAN BLADE WAS REPAIRED OFF LINE AND RETURNED TO SVC IN NON COMPLIANCE. REQUIRED DYE PENETRATE INSPECTION NOT DONE.

input: While turning to fix; leveling off with throttles coming back; aircraft hit wake turbulence rolled to right; aircraft buffeted; autoplt did its best to control it and i didn't turn it off. Aircraft settled 200-300 feet/foot low and corrected back to altitude did not get any stall warning during event; but was shown (by this event) that md88 is not a solid performer at high altitude our policy now is to fly slow to save gas; ie; .74 mach instead of .76 mach; which gives a lot less margin in wake turbulence at alt.
output: AN MD88 ENCOUNTERS WAKE TURB AT FL340 THAT INDUCED A BUFFET; ROLL AND LOSS OF ALTITUDE.

input: While operating under visual flight rules and using the area navigation (gps) 31 lpv guidance for reference; all global positioning system reception was lost. On about a 2 mile final there was an aural annunciation that stated: 'terrain system not available.' that was accompanied by a 'ter n/a' on the pfd and 'no global positioning system position' on the mfd. The aircraft was equipped with synthetic vision and that reverted back to the blue/brown attitude indicator. Since i was in visual meteorological conditions and visual flight rules i continued the landing visually and taxied to the ramp. Once on the ramp i pulled up the 'alerts' window on the g1000 pfd. There were multiple messages including 'gps navigate, navigation lost - loss of global positioning system navigation. Insufficient satellites;' 'abort apr - loss of global positioning system navigation.' 'abort approach.' 'ahrs1 global positioning system - ahrs1 not receiving any global positioning system information.' the pilot of another aircraft which was equipped with a garmin glass panel said that he experienced the same failure while taxing to the ramp. My concern is the fact that this was a waas approach on a robust system with redundant global positioning system receivers in a brand new aircraft. If i had been in instrument meteorological conditions i would have been above the minimum descent altitude prior to the vdp. The missed approach segment is global positioning system based so i would have been unable to execute the published missed approach. The fact that a failure like this occurred; while hopefully very rare; exposes some potential problems with widely utilized and heavily relied upon global positioning system navigation for critical phases of flight.
output: C172 pilot experiences a loss of GPS reception during a VMC RNAV 31 LPV approach to HIO and continues to a landing. Had the weather been IMC the missed approach procedure would have required an operational GPS.

input: I was switched from zhu center to kingsville approach and i requested direct to the initial approach fix celiv for the copter area navigation 22 into the alice hospital. Kingsville approach stated that they could not clear me for the approach; because they did not have the procedures; yet in the past we have had other controllers clear us. This has been an on-going issue with this particular facility. The approaches are certified and have been established for this hospital for some time. A short time later kingsville came back and told me to maintain altitude until reaching celiv and established; switch to advisory and report instrument flight rules (instrument flight rules) cancellation on the frequency; or call their number when i'm on the ground. In hindsight; i'm not sure if they were finally able to locate their copy of the procedure; and i may have confused their last set of instructions as the clearance. When i contacted kingsville terminal radar approach control facility by phone to coordinate my departure from the hospital; i was given the designated obstacle departure procedure (odp) for that particular location; adding further confusion; because there must be a copy of the procedure.
output: Helicopter pilot reports Air Traffic Control did not have proper procedure.

input: We were told to expect landing runway(s) 4r at ewr and not being real familiar with the honeywell flight management system we set it up and briefed the approach beforehand. We were given a descent from 5000 feet/foot to 4000 feet/foot and told of traffic off to our left/right (directions) at 3000 feet/foot that would not be a factor. During the descent we were told to head direct to the final approach fix for runway(s) 11 and that the traffic was still there. The capt/pnf was looking for the traffic as they showed up on traffic alert and collision avoidance system as blue while i/pf began setting up the approach for runway(s) 11; the autoplt was on at this time. Approaching 4000 feet/foot the traffic on traffic alert and collision avoidance system turned yellow and said they were climbing into our altitude somewhere in here the autoplt was accidentally turned off; with no aural 'autoplt; autoplt' sounding. We were both trying to find the traffic to avoid an resolution advisory and the next thing we hear is zny telling us we were 300 feet/foot below our altitude we noticed the autoplt was disconnected and began a climb back up to 4000 feet/foot which was the assigned altitude at approximately 3800 feet/foot we were told again that we were deviating from our assigned altitude and the capt/pnf informed the controller that we were aware of that and we were correcting and were busy trying to stay away from the traffic advisory on our traffic alert and collision avoidance system the controller proceeded to tell us again that he needed us at 4000 feet/foot and by that time we were back at the assigned altitude neither one of us knew how the autoplt was disconnected as we would have taken immediate corrective action had we heard the aural warning. The traffic advisory coupled with trying to load an unfamiliar flight management system may have caused some difficulties in situational awareness that caused us to miss the aircraft capturing the 4000 feet/foot altitude a possible fix on this problem would be to ensure every aircraft on the 145 fleet's aural warnings are working properly as some autoplt disconnects and trim warnings do not sound every time. Another fix would be to ensure that crews flying an unfamiliar flight management system in high traffic congestion areas are familiar on how to accurately load various functions in a brisk manner second officer that their time may be more closely spent on monitoring the aircraft and autoplt. This can be accomplished through brief classroom sessions during recurrent ground school.
output: EMB145 CREW ON ARR TO EWR HAS AUTOPLT DISCONNECT; WITHOUT AURAL WARNING; WHILE BOTH PLTS ARE BUSY WITH TFC AND FMS RWY CHANGES. DISCONNECT GOES UNDETECTED UNTIL TCAS TA AND A CALL FROM APCH.

input: No very high frequency due to precipitation static. We were at fl370 in a stratus layer going around several storm cells and started to hear static on the radios. The static grew so intense that we could hear nothing other than the static. Then the automatic communications addressing & reporting system went to no comm/standby. This probably lasted 2-3 minutes when we began to hear other aircraft but not air traffic control  i broadcast in the blind for maybe 30 seconds for a radio check with air traffic control  we finally made contact and were handed off to the next sector. It seemed they had been waiting for us for a few minutes. This has happened before with the airbus; but this lasted for a long time and i don't recall loosing automatic communications addressing & reporting system  the speed brakes don't work to dissipate the charge like on the 727.
output: A319 temporarily lost contact with ATC due to static associated with convective activity.

input: Performed rudder free-play checked (engineering document) on aircraft xxx. All 3 rudders; pcs's failed free-play checked generated n/r xxx to cover remove and replace of pca's. I missed step 34 of engineering document thinking by generating n/r's i had complied with step. I later realized that i did not comply with the whole step. In the future; i will take my time reading the paperwork and make sure i comply with all steps.
output: A B757-200 MECHANIC REPORTS ON GENERATING MAINT WRITE-UPS TO REPLACE THREE RUDDER POWER CONTROL UNITS THAT FAILED FREE PLAY CHECK. MECHANIC DID NOT COMPLY WITH THE WHOLE STEP IN THE ENGINEERING ORDER.

input: Atc had assigned 250 knot(s) on clbout from dtw due to traffic ahead of us. Passing through fl180 (we were assigned fl280) we passed through a cold front and encountered a windshear with severe turbulence resulting in a sudden increase of airspd (to plus or minus 300 kts) and rate of climb while on the autoplt. I disconnected the autoplt; increased pitch and reduced power trying to maintain turbulent airspd va (285 kts); hoping to find smooth air at a higher altitude air traffic control voiced some concern of our airspd and conflict with traffic ahead while being very upset with our airspd increase; claimed we had a 100 knot(s) closure. Passing 22300 feet/foot air traffic control demanded that we level off at fl230 and do a tight 90 degree turn off course. It took everything we had to just control the aircraft in the turbulence while trying to level off and turn and slow down. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii never did go off; second officer we never did know just how close we came to traffic ahead. Later we were told that the winds were 180 degrees out across front and winds rpted at 135 knot(s) at that altitude later; after being reassigned to climb to fl310; we encountered shortly after breaking out (fl250?) on top the reverse wind shear with loss of airspd and rate of climb dropping to '0.' the front was visible later on climb and had a sharp line of definition with clouds looking like a 25000 feet/foot wall on one side; clear on the other side. I never did find out how much of a temperature and pressure difference there was across the front to cause such an upset. (i.e.; our dc9-30 was pwred with big engs; -15's; and we had only a medium wt/load. I guess i never gave wind shear at altitude much thought before; until now.
output: SPD RESTR NOT ADHERED TO IN FLC DEV. SPD DEV.

input: While working the local north position i cleared a b737 for takeoff too soon behind a b757 off a parallel runway(s) separated by 3565 feet/foot i was advised by another position of the b757 departing and my sequence was to follow. Since i had an arrival, arrive i was not able to taxi my aircraft into position and hold. I observed the b757 in position on runway(s) 7l while waiting for the arrival, arrive on runway(s) 8 to land. After the arrival, arrive landed; i put my b737 into position i also had an airbus on a 4 mile final for runway(s) 8. Once the landing aircraft exited the runway(s) i cleared aircraft x for an immediate takeoff to ensure appropriate arr/dep separation. As aircraft x began takeoff roll; i scanned upwind and observed the b757 upwind off runway(s) 7l. The initial departure routing of the 2 aircraft initially were to converge second officer i gave aircraft x a runway(s) heading vector to avoid a path that would not put it directly behind the b757. I also restrict, restricted, restriction the clbout speed to 210 knot(s) to try and meet the 4 mile separation standard. I issued the b757 traffic to aircraft x. Aircraft x rpted the b757 in sight. I asked aircraft x intermediate fix they could maintain visual and they replied affirmative. At approximately 4 mile east of the airport aircraft x was on a converging course less than 4 mile behind a b757 with visual separation. At this point; the aircraft was switched to departure ctl.
output: PHX CTLR ALLOWED A B737 TO DEP FROM PARALLEL RWY AND LOST SEPARATION WITH PRECEDING B757.

input: After landing the right brake failed when i tried to apply brakes. Eventually got the aircraft slowed; but to exit the runway to the right; i had to make a left-hand 270 turn. There were aircraft landing in trail behind me and when i initiated the left-hand 270 turn the tower sent the king air around although i had exited the runway. Ground control gave me a number to call the tower. I spoke with the tower controller; who wanted to know why i had turned left instead of right to exit. I explained the brake situation; told him it was the only way for me to immediately exit the runway and that i was sorry that the king air had to go around. The controller said he understood and that there was no problem. I suppose i could have warned the controller of the issue and my intentions; but i really was trying to exit the runway as quickly as possible to avoid slowing down the incoming aircraft. All three runways at the airport were extremely busy.
output: A right main gear brake failure on a C210 required extra time for the pilot to exit the runway; forcing a following aircraft to make a go around.

input: [we were] descending for the approach into zzz in visual meteorological conditions [when] we got a ground proximity warning system (ground proximity warning system) warning to climb for terrain. We got a ground proximity warning system warning from the plane. There was a ridge in between us and the airport and we decided to descend to final approach fix altitude slowly so we wouldn't trigger the warning to go off. The captain disconnected the auto pilot and started a climb; once we were on the other side of the ridge and deemed that a normal approach can be continued; we started a descent and landed as planned. We should have stayed at the minimum safe altitude (minimum safe altitude) and started the descent on the other side of the ridge since we were coming from that direction.
output: ERJ First Officer reported receiving a Ground Proximity Warning while conducting a visual approach with the terrain in sight.

input: [we] lined up for takeoff. After setting power at 43 psi torque; a standard takeoff occurred. At approximately 300 ft. Above ground level the master caution illuminated and i saw the torque gauge surging back and forth from 35-51 psi (above max limitations); without anyone touching the throttle. I tried adjusting the throttle lower; to no avail. I did not feel the engine itself surge; but being so close to the ground and concentrating on flying; i could not check all the other gauges and diagnose the problem properly. I asked the copilot (who had just switched to departure frequency) to advise we needed to remain in the pattern and return to land immediately. The copilot relayed that to air traffic control who asked if we were [requesting] for priority (they were busy at the time). We remained left closed traffic and ran the appropriate check lists. Once the power was pulled back to about 30 psi; the torque surging stopped. Two aircraft on final were given go around/vectors as a result of our [situation]. We made an uneventful landing and taxied in. No emergency services were used or ever seen.
output: PC-12 Captain reported returning to departure airport after noticing the torque gauge surging shortly after takeoff.

input: Was on visual flight rules flight following. Given instruction to contact tower and was cleared to land on runway(s) 27l. Runway(s) 27r was clrly visible; but i could not see runway(s) 27l. Runway(s) 9l is a bit obscured. After re-vectoring; was able to see runway(s) 27l; but was asked to give the tower a call. Aircraft were held until situation resolved. There were no incidents. Also was some distraction in cockpit from passenber with intense earache while descending from altitude made cockpit very busy. This pilot thinks that runway(s) 27l needs better markings. The tower when phoned as requested; indicated they were concerned and wanted to know what the problems were. I explained that runway(s) 27l was just not visible from the point that i was cleared to land. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr advised that it was his first time into pbi; that he received vectors to the airport and that weather conditions; runway(s) location; passenber illness; and the afternoon sun position 'conspired' to cause his problem in finding the runway(s) the rptr's problem is that he did not recognize runway(s) 27l because of its position reference other runway(s) and its much narrower width. The rptr advised that bigger; more prominent numbering might help in runway(s) recognition.
output: M20E PLT HAS DIFFICULTY WITH PBI RWY 27L RECOGNITION WHILE DISTR BY PAX CONDITION AND WX FACTORS; CAUSING DEP DELAYS AFTER EXECUTING A GAR.

input: Prior to takeoff on runway(s) 12r i had indicated i wanted to go south over the downtown area of the city and was second officer cleared after climbing to 2000' mean sea level i realized the bases of a very thin layer of clouds were lower than the 3500' indicated by automatic terminal information service although i was squawking in mode celsius the controller quizzed me a couple times about my altitude after making a circle of downtown area i could see that the clouds were lowering and that proceeding westbound as i had indicated to air traffic control that i wanted would soon not be possible at 2000' and still maintain visual flight rules in visual meteorological conditions i then asked to proceed se at that altitude it soon became apparent that to continue around to westbound would necessitate going instrument flight rules and i requested an instrument flight rules clearance i had been asked about my altitude again. At no time prior to being given an instrument flight rules clearance did i penetrate a cloud. After being cleared to climb to 4000'; i entered a very thin layer (maybe 30-50'); second officer was in actual instrument meteorological conditions a mere few seconds. I continued on the instrument flight rules clearance until landing including being cleared to make a 360 degree turn around sea world at 4000' (clear below on westbound side of city. I went back through that very thin broken layer) on final approach again; it took only a few seconds to clear it. The cloud conditions around the city were very variable at the time and changing fairly rapidly. The quizzing about altitude made me suspicious that air traffic control may have thought that i was not maintaining visual flight rules before obtaining the instrument flight rules clearance not so! Route of flight (as filed) was direct c5n direct dca direct w00. I intruded into davidson aaf (near dca) at 1500' without contacting the tower i possibly slightly incurred into washington; dc terminal control area (near davidson) at 3000'. I was supposed to get an instrument flight rules clearance from iad air traffic control but they never gave me my clearance (ifr clearance filed with leesburg afss). Conditions were visual meteorological conditions but a line of thunderstorms were moving into my flight path. I was all set up in cockpit for an instrument flight rules flight but when air traffic control refused to read me my instrument flight rules clearance i was getting close to the air traffic area and the terminal control area by the time i got my visual flight rules chart out; i noticed i was above davidson air traffic area i ante meridiem not sure intermediate fix i incurred into the terminal control area also but intermediate fix i did it wasn't by much. The turbulence associated with the approaching thunderstorms (they were 10 mile north of me; flight was vmc) made it hard to get everything organized quickly. Air traffic control was absolutely no help; they never gave me my instrument flight rules clearance and i had to continue to destination visual meteorological conditions circumnaving thunderstorms next time i will have visual flight rules charts handy because even though you file instrument flight rules air traffic control can refuse to read you your clearance and you might have to continue vfr.
output: PLT OF SMA DEPARTING SAT IS QUERIED BY CTLR ABOUT HIS ALT ON TWO SEPARATE OCCASIONS. REPORTER BELIEVES CTLR WAS CONCERNED THAT FLT WAS VFR IN IMC.

input: First approach attempt was to mandan (y19). Reported weather was 300 ft ceiling with 2.5 miles visibility. I was established on the approach (rnav 31) and shortly after the final approach fix the approach downgraded to lateral navigation the weather was below minimums for the lateral navigation so i declared a missed approach and requested the area navigation 31 into bis. After the initial approach fix approximately at the final approach fix the approach downgraded to an lateral navigation approach. I was high on final and declared missed approach. By this time; i was lower on fuel than i expected and advised air traffic control of the situation. Air traffic control advised they would provide instrument landing system 13 to save time. The receiver did not provide accurate glide slope; but air traffic control advised altitudes at the fixes and landing was made without incident.after landing; two other pilots indicated they had experienced similar problems with area navigation approaches degrading at the same airports at approximately the same time frame. One pilot also reported he had been advised of difficulties with the localizer; but it may have been an incorrect configuration in the g530w on my part. I intend to practice more instrument landing system approaches and also lateral navigation approaches. Overconfidence due to a [previous] near flawless approach may have led to being unprepared to fly the lateral navigation global positioning system approach to low minimums.
output: Mooney K pilot reported difficulty with RNAV approaches degrading to LNAV on approaches to Y19 and BIS.

input: During climb approximately 5500 feet/foot the purser entered the cockpit and informed me that some overhead panels in the middle of the coach cabin were coming down. I told him we would attend to it when we were clear of the weather and above 10000 feet/foot he then returned to inform me that there was a crackling sound from the overhead panels; a loud air noise; and more panels coming down. I told him that we were diverting to miami. On final approach he returned again to inform me of excessive condensation in the cabin. We turned off packs. I declared an emergency due to overwt landing (2000 lbs). Mechs found large crack in the main overhead air conditioning duct. Aircraft removed from svc.
output: B757-200 CREW HAD AIR CONDITIONING DUCT FAILURE IN FLL CLASS E AIRSPACE.

input: We began flying; remaining in the pattern at eky. We made a fuel run to eet; shelby county later. On returning to bessemer eky; we entered a standard left/right (directions) downwind pattern for runway(s) 23. There was no wind and we saw no traffic in the pattern and it was the easiest entry from our position i and my rear seat passenber both noted that we saw no traffic on downwind; base; or the runway(s) on final approach we saw the king air off to our left/right (directions) that had just completed a low approach the king air had apparently seen us as well and was veering off to our left/right (directions) and was 1500-2000 feet/foot away from us and a little above us. We continued on to a normal landing the problem arose from a relatively fast kingair doing a low approach from the opposite runway(s) 5. Our plane has no radio or electrical system thus we were not in contact with the other aircraft both i and my passenber were on the lookout while in the pattern for other aircraft once on final approach my attention was focused on the landing i made a call to the birmingham control tower just to checked in. I was asked to make better use of the radio. I explained that we had no radio. I don't believe any rules were broken and the system actually worked in that neither plane was in any serious peril as both planes saw one another and avoided trouble. There are no known issues affecting human performance in this case.
output: J3 ON APCH TO EKY EXPERIENCES CONFLICT WITH OPPOSITE DIRECTION B350.

input: We were allowed to leave the deice pad with snow on the aircraft. We were at the beginning of the takeoff roll i was increasing n1 to 40%. I heard over the tower frequency; someone say something unintelligible about our company. Later; in flight; i asked the first officer intermediate fix he had heard something. He said that he heard what he assumed was the air carrier jet on the taxiway (leaving their remote deice area); say; 'doesn't our company have to take snow off their roof.' the assumption here is that we were the company the air carrier pilot was referring to; and that intermediate fix he was able to see 'snow on our roof' it would seem we were not adequately de-iced; even though we had left the remote de ice pad with a fresh application of type-1 and type-4. We did receive the required communication from the ground personnel; including the post de-ice confirmation that the aircraft was clean. To my knowledge this was not a non adhering snow day.
output: B737 CREW DEPARTS AFTER DE-ICING UNAWARE THAT THE DEICE CREW MAY HAVE FAILED TO REMOVE SNOW ADHERING TO THE TOP OF THE FUSELAGE.

input: Mel 36-21-06 for left bleed loop rather then minimum equipment list 36-11-02 for the prsov. Both mels state 1 pack inoperative; bleeds open [takeoff at landing performance correction] applied. I called flight operations about a huffer for the next crew; i was told we did not need one per minimum equipment list but item #10 of 36-21-06- states cross bleed start is not used for engine start. Paragraph b section 2 states both engines started prior to taxi. I should have pushed for a better answer since something was not right. It was written wrong from maintenance.
output: A flight crew was notified after the fact that they flew a CRJ700 with an incorrect MEL applied to the HPSOV so that the valve was not secured closed and penalties taken. The MEL for the bleed loop was correctly applied but was not applicable to the problem.

input: "this flight started the night prior when my normal first officer had flown someone a few days earlier who contracted covid-19. That night; i was left trying to find a new first officer for the next morning's flight at xa:00am. I found an first officer who has not flown in a while. Our flight to zzz was uneventful. On climbout from zzz the tower controller had issued a speed of 230 kts and a climb to and maintain 10;000 feet. I asked the first officer to run the climb checklist. While doing so; the controller issued us instructions. My first officer was caught off guard and looked at me as if to say; 'i didn't hear that.'  i thought i heard and understood the instructions to be 'normal speed and climb 12;000 feet and i read back 'normal speed; climb 12;000 aircraft x'. I then began to climb. This put me into conflict with aircraft y that was in the downwind for zzz; i never got a traffic alert and collision avoidance system or ta/ra alert from my traffic alert and collision avoidance system system.i know that after the instruction to proceed with normal speed; there was another instruction after that statement. I just cannot remember what it was. The crew change and heavy workload contributed to the misunderstanding. I do not know what could have been done differently to avoid this in the future. I do wonder why air traffic control would have pilots turn left towards another aircraft even if they were planning to keep the aircraft separated by 2;000 feet. I have flown this departure from zzz many times in the past and the point where we were issued normal speed was completely normal from past experience. I really wish that air traffic control would issue a climb straight ahead until the departing aircraft is no longer in a position to potentially interfere with other aircraft."""
output: Corporate Captain reported an incorrect read back for altitude which caused their aircraft to climb an additional 2;000 feet resulting in an airborne conflict with another aircraft.

input: Navigating inertial navigation system dir to federal air marshal vor and dme (co-located) from east of buffi. A line of thunderstorms were indicated on the weather radar in the msy area in a sw to ne line. Detoured to a north heading to pass over the east end of line. After passing over line; with no echos on the weather radar; encountered moderate chop/light turbulence requested lower altitude clrd to 33000'; then to 31000'; 28000'; 14000' and 10000'. Out of 34500-34000'; we encountered severe turbulence with large variations in airspd and altitude capt's airspd indicator fluctuating between 150-350 knot(s) 2; 3 times during des. F/o's varied also; but 180 degrees out of phase with capt's. Observed v/s pegged 6000' down once. I was unable to attempt a level off prior to reaching 28000-30000' with the indications i was receiving from my flight instruments. Entire des in instrument flight rules conditions. I did level off at 28000'; but was still encountering moderate chop; second officer continued to 18000' which was smooth. Was in constant communications with hou center during this time. Broke out into the clear soon after level off assessed situation. No structural; personnel or passenber injury was evident; second officer ascended back to 37000' crs altitude and continued to destination supplemental information from acn 81603: the capt elected to fly on the dir routing as no returns were along this path and only slight course changes were needed to fly between the scattered areas. There were no contours and no dappler returns. As the airplane approached the area of rain; the capt turned on the fasten seatbelt sign and the s/o made an announcement. The air was smooth with occasional light chop. The radar showed 2 small areas of light rain using the 40 mile range and 3.50 degree nd. The one left was 12 mile westbound the one east was 10 mile east another yet smaller area appeared at 12 o'clock and 18-20 mile as the turbulence became steady and at moderate intensity the capt requested a lower altitude air traffic control indicated a traffic conflict ahead and would call back. The turbulence continued and the capt requested heading information from the f/o. Again a slight left turn; about 10 degrees was initiated. Suddenly the airspd indicators fell to 160k; f/o mach below .70 with a loss of 1000' in altitude immediately; the f/o transmitted 'heavy; severe turbulence we're coming down.' air traffic control issued des clearance to fl310. The capt lowered the nose to 8-10 degrees nose down in an attempt to regain airspd. The ivsi pegged at 6000 feet per minute down; the f/o airspd at 160k; but then the capt airspd went to the barber's pole. With the nose attitude still at 8 degrees nose down and increasing wind noise; the f/o pulled the power to idle. The capt's airspd indicated an airspd condition the f/o indicated below 160k turbulence and downdrafts still a factor. A lower altitude was requested. Air traffic control assigned fl240. The capt attempted to reduce the rate of des and airspd at around 28000'. F/o airspd returned to normal and an overspd warning sounded. At slightly below fl240 the first officer requested still lower and received clearance to fl180 and at 21000-22000' the ivsi stabilized at 1000 feet per minute down; airspd at 320k. As rpts from the cabin came in; it was apparent the galleys had emptied and everyone was upset; but no one was injured. All systems were normal and the airplane was flying and responding normally. There had been some g loading on the airplane during the des; but not to the extent any crewmember felt the integrity of the airplane was damaged. Supplemental information from acn 81666: a plane flying behind us told air traffic control that he encountered heavy (may have said severe) turbulence and had no warning of it on his radar. Callback conversation revealed the following: rptr stated that although on instruments; according to the radar; they were past the storm front line; and as stated in narrative; no storms within 15 mile at the very closest. He did state on that day there was a jet stream to the south of msy over the gulf and another to the north over the mem area and strong winds in the immediate area. But; no real knowledge as to whether these could have been the cause. Stated was able to keep wings level with no trouble; but that no way to stop the rapid airspd fluctuation. Afterincident he inquired of company personnel why the difference in the 2 indicated airspds. No one could give real answer to cause except to surmise may have been enough yaw to cause large pressure differences on the static ports. The company did take aircraft out of service for inspection later because of request from federal aviation administration which apparently initiated by an federal aviation administration maintenance inspector who had been riding in the coach section of aircraft but never made himself known to pilot in command rptr has heard nothing from company on results of inspection second officer assumes nothing was found and has had no further follow-up from faa.
output: ACR HVT ENCOUNTERED SEVERE TURBULENCE AND UNABLE TO MAINTAIN ALT.

input: We were approximately 50 nautical mile westbound of fnt vor and dme (co-located) at fl330 when zob gave us a crossing restrict, restricted, restriction to cross 15 nautical mile westbound of fnt vor and dme (co-located) at a particular altitude the capt; who had prior radio problems read the altitude portion of the clearance as 15000 feet/foot and the controller did not respond by saying 'negative;' but repeated the same clearance again. Fearing that he was again experiencing radio problems he had me respond to the controller instead. Zob said that i indeed read back the correct altitude of fl290; not the 15000 feet/foot that we had in the altitude alerter. I believe what happened is that i indeed read back fl290 and had not set this in the altitude alerter because the capt told me after the fact that he actually remembered setting the alerter from fl290 to 15000 feet/foot of course; i did not see him do this and therein lies the problem i ante meridiem still bewildered that center did not catch our mistake sooner. We were at fl189 before anything was mentioned. And the only thing said at that time was 'stand by for possible pltdev.'
output: AN EMB145 FLC FAILS TO CROSS THEIR ASSIGNED XING POINT AT THE CORRECT ALT SOME MI W OF FNT; MI.

input: Upon taxi out at oakland; i inadvertently ran over a taxi light. As i departed the ramp area; i was instructed to keep to the federal aviation regulation left/right (directions) of the ramp to allow incoming taxi access to the gate area. This position required a 60-70 degree left/right (directions) turn to enter taxiway u. The taxiway u has 3-4 green ctrline lights to aid entering the taxiway then only a ctrline marking. As i entered the taxiway i instructed the first officer to contact tower and determine intermediate fix a 'u' intersection takeoff would expedite our departure as the first officer was changing the radio frequency i inadvertently steered toward the blue edge lights thinking that they were ctrline lights. Since the first officer was heads down changing the radio frequency i taxied the aircraft to approximately 3-4 feet/foot of the txwy's double stripped edge marking when i realized that the lights i thought were ctrline lights were actually taxiway edge lights. I immediately corrected to the txwy's ctrline. At the time; i was unaware of striking one of the edge lights and did not find out about it until the next day. It was very dark the night of this occurrence and i believe intermediate fix additional green ctrline lights (in addition to the 3 or 4 heading lights on ramp entering to taxiway u) were installed on the taxiway it would have prevented me from mistaking edge lights for ctrline lights. Supplemental information from acn 591777: i looked down to change to tower frequency hoping to depart runway(s) 29 from intersection u. When i looked up; i saw that we were well left/right (directions) of the taxiway ctrline; near the blue edge lights. Before i could say anything; the capt was already correcting back to the left/right (directions) we did not think we had been federal aviation regulation enough left/right (directions) to hit any lights and we had no indication (bump; noise; etc) that we had struck anything. The flight was normal and post-flt of the tires revealed no cuts; scrapes; etc. I believe that the angle from which we approached taxiway u; the limited number of green ctrline lights on that taxiway the darkness; and the fact that i was heads down at the time probably all contributed to this event.
output: DURING A NIGHT OP; A B737-300 FLT RUNS OVER A TXWY EDGE LIGHT ON TAXI OUT FROM THE RAMP AS THE PIC MISTAKENLY IDENTS THE EDGE LIGHTS AS CTRLINE TAXI LIGHTS ON TXWY U AT OAK; CA.

input: During preflt; the cargo load was reduced from 96600 pounds to 93363 pounds by the crew for anticipated conditions at the scheduled departure time. Upon taxi out; automatic terminal information service was rechked at 31 degrees celsius and all other parameters remained unchanged for anticipated takeoff on runway(s) 6. Takeoff thrust for 620000 pounds was calculated to be 1.64 epr. Actual takeoff thrust obtained was 1.605 epr at maximum power the power levers were against the breaker bar. All engs indicated identical power a rejected takeoff was initiated at 80 knot(s) the aircraft was decelerated gently. The company was contacted by telephone and everyone agreed that the high outside air temperature appeared to have caused the problem the crew recalculated the takeoff for 35 degrees celsius with a 5 knot(s) headwind. 11333 pounds of cargo was removed. A new flight plan was obtained. The takeoff was accomplished at 34 degrees celsius with winds of 120 degrees at 14 knot(s) or 7 knot(s) of headwind. All parameters were normal. During flight individual toilets began to fail. Within 5 hours after takeoff all lavatories were inoperative waste tanks indicated full. Sewage backed up to the very brim. Upon shutdown; the #2 aircraft generator did not accept the load from generators #1 and #3. The auxiliary power unity would not accept a load. Ground power was unreliable. Aircraft doors were not able to be opened as the aircraft was on emergency power only from the battery; with the #2 engine running; auxiliary power unity running and ground power connected. Finally the aircraft accepted ground power longitude enough to allow for the passenber doors to be opened electrically. Both electrical controllers and manual back up were employed but to no avail. Multiple electrical problems were noted. The total number of write- ups for this leg was twelve. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr described the engine low power situation as a 'non event.' he is convinced that the problem was caused by an automatic terminal information service that was not updated. The takeoff performance was calculated on 31 degrees celsius while the actual temperature was 35 degrees celsius the rptr has not documented any faulty load manifests; but has had many trips with much higher than predicted fuel burn and longer takeoff roll. The rptr does not know exactly why his air carrier would not give him an incident rpt form. The total air temperature gauge on the md11; as on most aircraft cannot be used on the ground because it is not shaded and can give erroneously high readings. It needs moving air to give a proper reading. The rptr wonders how the cargo weight decreased intermediate fix the cargo door wasn't opened.
output: AN MD11 CAPT ABORTED HIS TKOF BECAUSE OF LOW ENG PWR. HE ALSO SUSPECTS THAT HIS WT MANIFEST MAY HAVE BEEN DELIBERATELY FAULTY.

input: I arrived at the airport at xx30 for my morning run to monroe. I received my weather brief from nashville automated flight service station the forecast for monroe was to be 5 broken 5f until 1600z. I then selected jackson as my alternate. At xx45 i started my walk around inspection of be-18. Twilight was just beginning. I started inside the cockpit; releasing the controls checkeding fuel level (full mains; full aft auxiliary tanks); extending flaps and checkeding battery power the rest of the walk around was routine and by the chklist. After checkeding the gasolator on the left/right (directions) engine i drained the left/right (directions) main. Nothing seemed abnormal; second officer i continued the preflt. After loading in which i had 390 pounds in zone b; and 302 pounds in zone celsius i secured the load with the net; and gave a copy of my manifest to mr x; the supervisor on the morning shift. I started the left/right (directions) engine then the left/right (directions) and proceeded to engage the generators and electrical equipment i listened to the automatic terminal information service broadcast which was calling 2 overcast 1/2f. I received taxi and instrument flight rules clearance from ground control and proceeded to runway(s) 15r for departure at the departure end of runway(s) 15r i then proceeded to do the pretkof chklist and runup. Again nothing seemed abnormal. Upon departure i was given a heading of 180 degrees and contact departure control after switching to departure i was given a heading of 270 degrees and cleared to 3000 feet/foot mean sea level climbing through 1300 feet/foot i turned off the electric fuel pumps and it was then the left/right (directions) engine lost power i contacted departure control and rpted the power loss on the left/right (directions) engine and that i was attempting to restart. Departure asked how much fuel and number of persons aboard; and my intentions. I said that i wanted to get some al then make some decisions. I was never able to gain altitude with power set at 32 inches missed approach point and 2100 revolutions per minute i was asked intermediate fix i wanted the airport surveillance radar approach or an instrument landing system to runway(s) 15l. I elected to do the instrument landing system because i never would have had chance to see the runway(s) with the airport surveillance radar approach the controller vectored me for a 5 mile final to runway(s) 15l and i knew that i was going to intercept the localizer inside the final approach fix. I started down the glideslope but a little too quickly. I got below the glideslope but was never able to get back on the glideslope and i rpted this to the controller as i got down to decision ht i was below the glideslope and rpted that i couldn't hold it; meaning i couldn't hold the altitude it was then that i saw the runway(s) and rpted such and made an uneventful landing it was later when i found out that there had been sufficient water to fill the gasolator and carburetor bowl to cause fuel starvation. Although i followed normal preflt procedure and was not remiss in my duties; i had no reason to believe the liquid coming out of the left/right (directions) main tank was water and not fuel.
output: ATX BE-18 RETURN LAND MANDATED BY AN INFLT ENG SHUTDOWN. FUEL CONTAMINATION.

input: I entered flight plan into flight management system it was verified and compared to departure page -- triss2/txk trans -- flight plan legs and clearance on taxi out; responded to dfw queue with correct information i was pilot flying. At 500 feet/foot engaged navigate, navigation initial dfw departure control cleared us direct triss and normal speed capt entered clearance into flight management system i failed to verify entry. After passing triss; we continued along magenta flight path towards what we thought was our next fix. Zfw said that we were drifting left/right (directions) of course. They asked intermediate fix we were proceeding toward shero or txk. We were heading towards txk -- incorrectly. We should have been going to shero. As pilot flying; i failed to verify next fix in flight management system with published route not certain how shero was dropped from navigate, navigation rte.
output: AN MD80 CREW ON THE DFW TRISS2/TXK WAS FLYING DIRECT TXK AFTER A DIRECT TRISS CLRNC BECAUSE THE INTERVENING WAYPOINTS WERE DROPPED FROM THE FMS. ATC REDIRECTED ON RTE.

input: Upon approach into zzz the gear would not go down. Tried numerous times to cycle gear and hand pumped it numerous times with no luck. Gear would not go down.
output: PA31 pilot reported landing gear extension failure.

input: Aircraft 1 was in the downwind. I decided i was going to turn my traffic on to base leg above my traffic to the parallel runway. Aircraft 2 was downwind ahead of aircraft 1 descending to 7000 feet. I vectored them to join final; no clearance to use altitude leaving. Aircraft 3 was straight in to the parallel runway. I based aircraft 1 the first time with the wrong call sign xxx ; no response. Aircraft 3 and aircraft 1 were head to head at same altitude with 8 miles of separation. I transmitted three additional times for aircraft 1 feet twice no response before 'say again' and finally got a read back. Aircraft 1 had divergence with aircraft 3 by about 1/2 mile. I shipped aircraft 2 to turn heading 050; more panicked each time; finally got a response. Told aircraft 3 to expedite with a speed restriction; not realizing i had not cleared them for an approach. They said nothing because [of] my near miss seconds before. Local control called and asked if they were landing; i said i thought they were cleared. Aircraft 2 went around because of this mistake.this was a tight hole to get into. I pushed to get in it because without; aircraft 1 would have flown 10 more miles. If pilots would have listened; this would be a non-event; but i instead was panicked and forgot to clear aircraft 2 i feel terrible for the go around; and scared that i barely had separation; head to head; between two aircraft. I think i will be much more hesitant to attempt to get general aviation aircraft their preferred runway. Just a few minutes before this; i made another general aviation land on a different runway because i deemed it not worth the risk. It's not that i don't have cutoffs; in fact; i'm less aggressive than a lot of my coworkers. This exact situation has been completed without incident numerous times by myself and others. Plain and simple; this happened because the pilots didn't hear and then i allowed a distraction to make me forget to clear aircraft 2. That being said; at least for a while i won't be accommodating general aviation aircraft quite as much. That situation could have been much; much worse and that's going to be playing in my head for quite some time.
output: A TRACON Controller reported two aircraft were not complying with assigned headings and altitudes for final approach sequencing resulting in a NMAC. While attempting to resolve the situation the reporter shipped another aircraft to the Tower without issuing an approach clearance causing that aircraft to go around.

input: While we were level at 5;000 mean sea level in cavu conditions; an air carrier flight in front of us was given traffic; a cirrus; visual flight rules 4;500 mean sea level 12 o'clock. The air carrier reported traffic alerts and claims cirrus is not at 4;500 msl...much closer. Approach gave us the same traffic; 12 o'clock; 4;500 mean sea level and visual flight rules we did not have visual contact; but the cirrus reported us in sight (said he had our lights). As we closed; we got simultaneous 'traffic' and 'climb; climb' resolution advisory alerts. Cirrus showed 400 below moving to 300 below. The first officer who was pilot flying began a climb away from traffic in response to the resolution advisory i advised approach who replied that the cirrus 'said he was at 4;500 feet/foot and radar confirms'. We climbed to approximately 5;400 feet/foot and the resolution advisory ended as traffic passed below us and slightly right of the nose. I caught a glimpse of the cirrus passing to the right and he indeed did not look to be anywhere near 500 feet/foot below us (or in this case it should have been 900 feet/foot with our climb). I could see the occupants clearly. I advised approach we were returning to our assigned altitude and in response got a frequency change and 'that was that'.
output: While in terminal airspace two air carrier aircraft sequentially followed TCAS Resolution Advisories with respect to a Cirrus aircraft apparently well above his assigned altitude and conflicting with that of the air carriers.

input: I own a small aerial photo business. My business partner and i (he's the photographer; i'm the plt) were on our first photo flight after the september attacks. We were photographing residences near the towns of turners falls and greenfield; in areas we were familiar with; and at the legal limit of 1000 feet/foot above ground level the nature of aerial photography is to orbit the target; which we were doing. This made some people on the ground concerned. They called the police; who met us at the airport when we landed. Apparently; a state police helicopter was also called into action; although we didn't see him till after landing i was cooperative with the policeman; giving him the names of my clients and other pertinent information nevertheless; i received a summons in the mail charging me with violating state law 90/46 'flying aircraft too low/as to endanger.' i feel the major factor in this incident was the heightened state of alert since september attacks. A suggested solution (and i mentioned this to the policeman on the ramp) is to call police in jurisdictions in which we'll be photographing before we make the flt.
output: LOCAL LAW ENFORCEMENT BRINGS CHARGES AGAINST AN AERIAL PHOTOGRAPHER UNDER A LOCAL REG REFING LOW FLT WHEN THE OP WAS FLOWN IN ACCORDANCE WITH FARS. THE TIME PERIOD WAS JUST AFTER SEP-TUE-01.

input: Ltt x inbound at 6000 feet/foot to pdk. Smt y pdk departure to bhm at 5000 feet/foot turned smt y to 240 degrees and climbed to 7000 feet/foot about 1 1/2 minute(s) later; ltt x lost separation with smt y. I had ltt x turn immediately to a 290 degree heading and descend to 4000 feet/foot smt y was only at 6500 feet/foot problem was caused because i was not watching rate of climb on smt y. I had 10-13 aircraft on frequency at time and was working on a couple other sits.
output: DEP CTLR CLBED SMT THROUGH LTT ALT WITH LTSS.

input: While on routine patrol approximately 20 mile ssw of dulles airport at an zlt of 500' above ground level i experienced what i first perceived as a high side governor failure. I immediately climbed to an altitude of approximately 1000' above ground level in an attempt to keep the n2 power turbine down to within limits the engine out light and audio came on along with engine reignition; both repeatedly. After further investigation of the problem i determined it was an electrical malfunction and elected to proceed back to baltimore for maintenance at this point i tuned mtn airport in the long range navigation turned to the desired heading and climbed to 1500' mean sea level i then contacted dulles approach on the designated frequency i was then given a squawk on the transponder and after radar contact was established i was informed i was in the quantico restrict, restricted, restriction area 6608a and was informed that on my present heading would exit said area in four mile at this time i turned to a westerly heading to expedite my exit; feeling i was just barely on the edge. After informing me i was clear of the restrict, restricted, restriction area; approach then asked for my last name; home base of aircraft and gave me a number to call upon reaching my destination of which i did all the above. I patrolled down the westbound side of that restrict, restricted, restriction area twice a week know where it is; and remain clear at all times; however; in lieu of the preceeding chain of events; i was preoccupied with my own safety and the well being of the aircraft and accidentally penetrated restrict, restricted, restriction area 6608a.
output: PLT OF HELICOPTER CRUISING ON PATROL AT 500' AGL HAD ENGINE PROBLEM. DISTR OF COPING WITH PROBLEM AND CLIMBING TO SAFER ALT CAUSE PLT TO ENTER R6608A. WAS ADVISED WHEN CONTACT WITH IAD APCH CTL; EXITED AREA PROMPTLY; RETURNED TO MARTIN ARPT; BAL; MD; FOR MAINTENANCE.

input: Clred for jawbn 3 arrival, arrive we xed victoria and began descent to 15000'. When switched to sea center frequency 125.10; we were cleared to cross lofal intersection (sea 307 degree r/29 mi) at 10000'/250 knot(s) we asked about the ride and center had no rpts. We continued normal descent to cross lofal on schedule. Descending through 28000' entered clouds and icing. Aircraft limitations require 55% north with anti-ice on; therefore increased thrust from idle descent to 55% north and extended speed braked to make crossing restriction. Descending through 21000' we entered turbulence and had to slow to 280 knot(s) (airplane limitation).
