I concurred; he communicated this to air traffic control with crash truck request; and we were cleared direct to zzz. We discussed which pilot would land; capt asked me my opinion; and i stated that i felt capable of a safe landing considering the relatively normal approach speed (vref 137); the longitude runway(s) lack of runway(s) slope; instrument landing system availability; visual conditions; light winds and also stated that i didn't feel any kind of nervousness; tension; adrenalin; or discomfort. Capt got automatic terminal information service i briefed; we readied charts; completed a preliminary landing chklist; and with some more time en route to zzz; the capt reviewed a flaps 20 degree approach and landing technique; reading from the quick reference handbook as well as advising from his experience. I described this back to him; as i understood it; a normal approach to landing normal profile; smooth touchdown less than 400 feet per minute rollout longitude use thrust reversers first; brakes as necessary; but try not to use them. Cleared to land on a visual approach to runway(s) we flew a normal instrument landing system profile; intercepted the glideslope and landed with a 200 feet per minute touchdown; nose high; about 1000 feet/foot past the 1000 feet/foot aiming markers. Thrust reversers only were used to slow; brakes were used less than 40 knots indicated airspeed after reversers were stowed. After turning off the runway(s) the 'ops' personnel in fire trucks asked ground to have us hold just off the runway(s) to inspect our brakes. When they gave to go-ahead to ground we were cleared to the gate with no further incidents. During my walkaround i spent 15 minute(s) inspecting the wing flaps and could not find any evidence of physical damage; foreign debris or other cause of malfunction. Maintenance at zzz was called; and after 2 attempts to reset the circuit breakers; the flaps would still not move out of 20 degs.
output: CRJ DIVERTS TO A NEARBY ARPT WITH A LONGER RWY WHEN THEY RECEIVE A FLAPS FAIL MSG ON APCH TO ZZZ.

input: Sometime in early may; i filed a rpt concerning confusion with a particular taxi clearance and txwys at lax. While the depiction of the txwys was correct on the chart; the clearance created confusion. It appears from the latest revision; and the new lax pages; that the remedy was to simply redraw the taxi chart second officer that the 2 txwys in question now line up. The new chart is in error and does not accurately reflect the location of txwys 'an' and 'mike.' due to the angles of the respective txwys; i believe it is not possible to clear runway(s) 25l on taxiway 'an' and then transition to taxiway mach number to cross runway(s) 25r and stay within the boundaries that define taxiway 'ac;' taxiway celsius and taxiway mach number i was told earlier that tower should not be giving the clearance to join taxiway mach number but they continue to do second officer an issue that could cause greater confusion; and in my opinion creates a dangerous situation; is that the taxi routing in question is presented as a low visibility taxi route on an smgcs chart. Once again; the 2 txwys in question simply do not come even close to being aligned as the chart indicates.
output: ACR PLT REPORTS THAT NEITHER THE COMMERCIAL OR GOVERNMENT ARPT PAGES FOR LAX SHOW THE ACTUAL ALIGNMENT OF TXWYS 'AN' AND 'M' AS THEY CROSS TXWY 'AC' BETWEEN THE SOUTH COMPLEX RWYS AT LAX.

input: Weather and thunderstorms were in the zzz area on our approach. We briefed and flew the instrument landing system to xxr. On the approach; my first officer (first officer) got a little behind in configuring and i was late to prompt him to take different actions resulting in an unstable approach with the conditions we faced. I called for the go-around and my first officer executed it appropriately. Tower gave us a left turn and climb to 2000 feet. As we leveled off; there was a bit of confusion with the mcp/autopilot as it wouldn't engage. As we discussed what was going on with the automation; the airspeed started an insidious decay. My first officer started adding power to correct the decaying speed; but not quite fast enough. Then; very rapidly we apparently hit the outflow of one of the cells around us. We almost instantly lost 30 knots total around [recovery] speed. I took control of the aircraft when i saw 186 knots and falling; applied emergency thrust; and lowered the nose to get airspeed back. We kept the aircraft out of a stall; but as i got back to [recovery] speed and started to apply aft pressure on the yoke to level off/climb; tailwinds continued to increase and the stick shaker activated. Lessened the pressure on the yoke and gained more speed. We were able to initiate a climb at that time in heavy moderate turbulence. There was a cell in front of us and approach gave us a 060 heading to avoid weather. With the turbulence and 50 knots or so tailwind it was a bit of a struggle to get the airplane to turn. Eventually; i started to reduce climb passing 7000 feet mean sea level we leveled at 8000 feet after we got out of the rough air.
output: B737-700 flight crew reported a loss of airspeed due to wind shear resulting in a momentary stick shaker activation.

input: Flt was a repos to ont. At 6000 feet/foot en route on v8 almost over pdz vor and dme (co-located) crew received an resolution advisory to descend we began an immediate descend and called socal to rpt the resolution advisory with no response. Capt continued descent to about 5200 feet/foot with aircraft passing overhead with 700 feet/foot separation according to traffic alert and collision avoidance system no visual was ever obtained. Continued calls to socal were not answered using very high frequency #2 and resetting the frequency tried guard on very high frequency #1 several times with no response either. Eventually; we recycled the very high frequency #2 circuit breaker and switched to ont tower frequency on very high frequency #2. Tower responded immediately. No one ever responded on guard inflt using very high frequency #1. Very high frequency #1 worked first time on the ground after lndg.
output: DC8 FLT CREW COMPLIES WITH A 'DSND' TCAS RA WHILE FLYING A REPOS FLT. TEMPORARY LOSS OF COM WITH ATC MAY HAVE CONTRIBUTED.

input: While flying the tulsas 1a department from mex; we found that the gfms route differed from raw data on one leg. The sec segment of the procedure intercepting the positive control area r194 into positive control area was depicted several miles east of the actual vor and dme (co-located) radial. We flew the raw data which subsequently rejoined the gfms route after the positive control area radial. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr revealed; a subsequent trip into mmmx; with a different aircraft same type; produced the same results. Company's vague response to his rpt implied the gfms routing was correct while the chart depiction is wrong. Rptr is expecting more information to be forthcoming as company continues to investigate the matter.
output: AN MD80 CREW; DEPARTING MEXICO CITY; (MMMX) OBSERVED THAT THE 'GFMS' RTE AS FLOWN DEVIATED FROM THE RTE AS DEPICTED ON THE PUBLISHED DEP CHART.

input: Arriving into gate; with engine 2 shut down; aircraft was moving toward the gate normally under minimal power on engine 1 when; just a couple feet from the spot; the nose gear rolled down into a depression (felt almost like a hole) and the aircraft immediately stopped. Tried taxiing out of it under increased thrust from #1; but using a safe amount of thrust; we were unable to move. First officer asked if i wanted to restart #2; which i said yes to (we were already late and i knew this was the quicker option than having the ramp crew connect the tug to tow us in). I gave the ramper the visual signal that we were restarting #2; which he acknowledged. With number 2 restarted; it still took both engines at approx. 40% n1 to move; at which time the nose wheel practically jumped out of the depression. Fortunately; i was prepared for it and was immediately on the brakes after exiting and was able to stop normally on the parking spot. I immediately contacted [airport] ops and informed them what happened and they did send someone out to look at 'the hole'. After exiting the plane; the jet bridge operator/gate agent told the first officer that this was a normal occurrence on that gate and many aircraft just have the ramp tow them in.
output: 737 Captain reported the nose gear rolled into a depression approaching the assigned gate and came to an immediate stop.

input: Flt was on clbout from ewr airport given a climb to 10000 feet/foot it was the fo's leg. We passed 9000 feet/foot for 10000 feet/foot with normal 1000 feet/foot to go call. We had a good climb rate; quickly approaching 10000 feet/foot the first officer was slow to initiate the leveloff. I gently nudged the yoke forward. As this was happening; the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii began to say 'reduce clb' then 'dsnd.' we leveled at close to 10000 feet/foot also; air traffic control said 'maintain 10000 ft.' we repeated back 'maintaining 10000 ft.' the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii at one point showed altitude of traffic plus 300 feet/foot we; however; were never off at a supposed 200 feet/foot off the other aircraft may have been off of their altitude we believe the traffic was general aviation aircraft visual flight rules at 10500-ish feet/foot the rest of flight was uneventful. Air traffic control did not further question us as to any details.
output: AN E145 CREW OVERSHOT ASSIGNED LEVELOFF ALT DEPARTING EWR.

input: Enclosed is a graphic description of an incident that occurred during landing involving my aircraft (sma) and a 2-engine turboprop commuter; both cleared to land on a controled field (ksav) at the same time period. The sma came relatively close to the runway(s) intersection this was completely unintentional. I was instructed to land on runway(s) 27 and hold short of runway(s) 18; 36 by the control tower a normal procedure when landing according to this clearance is to land and taxi off the runway(s) on bravo taxiway this is what i expected and planned to do. However; i did not compensate enough for the additional ground speed due to landing 'downwind' and with a relatively active field; my final approach speed was higher than usual for spacing. The ground roll stopping point was anywhere from 100-200' past where i had expected the stopping point was just after the bravo taxiway but short of the runway(s) intersection as instructed.
output: RWY TURNOFF OVERSHOT WHEN SMA GIVEN A HOLD SHORT OF INTERSECTING RWY ACCOUNT LNDG TRAFFIC. TAILWIND PRESENT. RWY NOT ENTERED BUT POTENTIAL CONFLICT OCCURRED.

input: Old unreliable displays continue to malfunction at my facility. During a 30 minute(s) period my display went blank on 3 different occasions. The outage lasted for about 5 seconds each time. I was working up to 10 aircraft at the times this scope was replaced and the old one worked on. Bad displays continue to be a major prob.
output: A RADAR CTLR CLAIMS THAT THE RADAR SCOPE DISPLAY WENT BLANK 3 DIFFERENT TIMES DURING A 30 MIN PERIOD. THE CTLR FURTHER CLAIMS THAT BAD RADAR DISPLAYS CONTINUE TO BE A PROB AT THE FACILITY.

input: Aircraft x was inbound instrument flight rules on a visual approach to runway 16r on a right base. Aircraft y was on roughly a three mile final for runway 16r. Aircraft x entered pae class delta at high speed on a right base visual approach to runway 16r. Aircraft x was not in communication with pae until well within the class delta surface area and aircraft x heading and altitude put him in conflict with aircraft y. Traffic was issued to both aircraft; aircraft x reported traffic in sight. However; after reporting traffic in sight aircraft x continued to fly directly toward aircraft y within 200 feet of aircraft y's altitude. The two aircraft appeared to merge on the radar screen; but out the window it was obvious that aircraft x was taking evasive action to avoid aircraft y by descending below aircraft y's altitude and continuing eastbound. Around the time the targets merged on the radar screen lc1 instructed aircraft y to climb to avoid conflict. Lc1 judged that aircraft x was executing an resolution advisory and once aircraft x was clear of traffic lc1 instructed aircraft x to fly heading 360 and maintain 3;000 feet. Once aircraft x was stabilized and climbing to the north lc1 instructed aircraft x to contact seattle departure. I believe it was the late communication transfer of aircraft x from s46 on the visual approach and the lack of coordination from s46 that led to this conflict. Aircraft x's approach to runway 16r was very unexpected.it states in the pae/s46 letter of agreement that s46 must transfer communication of jet aircraft eight miles out. Had s46 adhered to this requirement the conflict would have been avoided. Also; had s46 coordinated that they were going to bring aircraft x in on a tight right base visual approach to runway 16r; pae would have been able to prepare for it. The traffic that conflicted with aircraft x on final for runway 16r at pae was clearly depicted on the radar screen at the time of the event.
output: PAE Tower controllers reported Approach Control gave them an aircraft on a base leg in conflict with straight in traffic which resulted in an NMAC.

input: While departing out of zzz on the climb we encountered moderate turbulence and heavy precipitation on the clbout. About 20000 feet/foot we heard a thud and received excessive aircraft vibration. Air traffic control cleared us to fl450. At 21000-22000 feet/foot we level off and slowed the aircraft we did not declare an emergency and diverted. We had a normal approach and landing upon arrival, arrive we had numerous fire equipment standing by at the airport we noticed the fuel panel access door was bent back against the side of the aircraft both pilots observe the fueler properly close the fuel door.
output: LEAR 31 FLT CREW HAS AIRFRAME VIBRATION DURING CLB AND DIVERTS FOR LNDG.

input: New coplt was having trouble with radio communications button versus pitch sync button. This is caused some confusion in the cockpit. As we were approaching the hold short line; the coplt's chair went to full down; causing me to turn my head. When i looked up; i saw the hold short line and stopped with the front of the aircraft past the line.
output: BEECH 200 PLT BECAME DISTR WITH ACTING COPLT AND CROSSED RWY HOLD SHORT LINE WITH NOSE OF ACFT.

input: Company b767-300 had [eicas] oil filter message. Contract maintenance replaced filter and housing packing next day (no parts at station); [because they] had to be flown in. Aircraft maintenance manual (amm) 79-21-05 page xxa says to remove drain plug (16) and [o-ring] packing (13). [i] believe this is an amm error; because item (13) is for oil filter housing. Amm never states to remove drain plug [o-ring] packing (15). Contacted company engineering and they wrote an engineering order (e/o) to inspect current drain plug (15) [o-ring] packing and reuse if no defects found. Amm 79-21-10 page xxb; item 'e' was reviewed for same issue.
output: A Maintenance Controller reports a discrepancy found in their Aircraft Maintenance Manual (AMM) 79-21-05 during an oil filter change on a PW-4000 engine for a B767-300 with an EICAS oil filter message. The AMM illustration mistakenly associates the oil filter housing O-ring packing with the oil filter housing drain plug.

input: Dfw approach control 3000 feet/foot dfw terminal radar approach control facility location: denton airport transmitter on vectors for runway(s) 18r instrument landing system we were descended to 3000 feet/foot mean sea level at 3000 feet/foot we were approximately 1/2 mile east of the denton airport after review of the airspace chart; i noticed that in that area 4000 feet/foot mean sea level is the floor of the airspace. After landing i called dfw terminal radar approach control facility and asked about being vectored below class b airspace and the supervisor replied that this was normal while running triple instrument landing system approachs this could be a threat to safety -- especially on a sunday with numerous general aviation traffic in the area. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that since he also flies small aircraft he is very familiar with the denton and dfw class b airspace. He is also aware that the controller is required to tell the flight crew when being vectored outside class b and again when entering class b airspace. In the rpted incident; this notification never took place.
output: S80 ON APCH FOR DFW IS VECTORED OUTSIDE OF CLASS B AIRSPACE.

input: During cockpit prep; first officer (fo) loaded winds into flight management computer i verified this before loading departure and arrival info into flight management computer once pre departure clearance received; i put in new standard instrument departure transition and verified all standard instrument departure and standard terminal arrival route crossings; with fo's input. At gate; we received well over 15 final weight messages across printer; followed by almost as many messages from load planning invalidating weights (for cargo change and then waiting for ramp to finalize weights.) after about ten minutes of this; i called operations to tell them we were waiting for correct weights. They checked with ramp and said final weights should be forthcoming. The weights that came were different by only about 300 pounds (not significant; in my mind). We pushed. The first officer kept waiting for the weights to upload into the flight management computer but they would not. We tried referencing the flight manual but there was no guidance about how to proceed. Fired a message to dispatch; who could not provide assistance. Asked federal aviation administration jumpseater; a maintenance inspector familiar with our aircraft. He said he'd seen this once before and it required a complete re-initialization. We tried manually entering weights; but vertical navigation wouldn't arm; so we were stuck. I thought about wind requests filling the buffer and blocking further action; and we discussed that; but agreed winds had only been requested once and already executed. Still; first officer checked route data page and noticed an erase prompt. He selected it and immediately; the final weights uploaded. We got takeoff data; and off we went. Once airborne; air traffic control gave us headings followed by clearance direct to fix on standard instrument departure that is when i realized our cleared standard instrument departure and transition were gone and the original standard instrument departure was in flight management computer i quickly reloaded correct standard instrument departure and checked rest of route. The standard terminal arrival route with runway(s) and transition were also missing! We all had seen these entries confirmed and executed at the gate; even the federal aviation administration guy confirmed this; so how they went missing is a mystery. The federal aviation administration guy encouraged me to write this report; because the whole thing was so screwy; and set us up for a potential navigation deviation. I referenced the quick reference handbook and sent a miscellaneous report using the nd (navigation display) code; typing 4 pages of explanation. What i got back was a message saying that quick reference handbook code was not supported by this automatic communications addressing & reporting system or something like that. So the quick reference handbook codes are useless on this fleet (who knew?) this entire debacle with a [faa employee] onboard was stressful; and pointed out the lack of guidance in our manuals dealing with such anomalies. The flight management computer shouldn't be so quirky; or 'inaccessible' for pilot intervention during malfunctions.
output: B737 Captain reports being unable to upload weight and balance information into the FMC until an erase prompt is noticed on the route page and pressed. Once airborne it is determined that the erase prompt has removed all the route changes made at the gate. The SID is quickly reentered.

input: I was under pressure from management and the zzz1 federal aviation administration flight standards district office to perform a special ferry flight for maintenance from zzz2-zzz3. I later discovered the flight was performed illegally because the paperwork (special ferry permit) did not properly document the carriage of 2 passenber on the flight i also believe that; based on facsimile control number on special ferry permit; that management may have illegally altered the ferry permit without federal aviation administration approval.
output: THE CAPT QUESTIONS FERRY PERMIT AUTH WITH DEADHEAD CREW MEMBERS ON BOARD. THE COMPANY'S DISPATCH AND FSDO AUTH WERE QUESTIONED BY THE RPTR.

input: Ground advised me to contact socal on 135.05. After leaving smo airspace i tuned to socal and i announced my call sign; altitude passing and final altitude to socal before entering burbank class celsius the controller responded (clearly irritated) and said; 'whoever is transmitting on 135.05 you're stepping over everyone; come to my frequency on 124.6.'i dialed in 124.6 and could not get a word in as the frequency was 100% busy. The controller was way too busy. Even announced; 'i can't call everyone twice....' shows you how overworked controller was. I assumed that meant i had established communication as required by 91.130 but then when i was on 124.6 i heard controller giving a traffic warning to this twin above me and told the twin that; 'i'm not speaking to that pilot' which was referring to me.the frequency was 100% busy and by the time i was out of burbank class celsius airspace and in the zone that 125.5 looks after so i tuned to 125.5 and got a code for flight following without any further communication with the controller on 124.6.i've noticed these frequencies are very busy at times and why is the facility having one controller covering both frequencies when is clear to a lay person that the workload is too much. It's a crunch zone for smo arrivals; bur [and] vny approach and departures.the last thing you want is departing smo traffic circling around that area before burbank class celsius as they will conflict with smo arrivals.
output: Small aircraft pilot reports frequency congestion when trying to obtain flight following with SCT while departing enroute to Burbank. Pilot offers concern as to why one Controller is responsible for two different frequencies.

input: At fl410 we were beginning our descent to land at hnl. As the power was reduced; #4 engine stalled and egt; n1; n2; went to red line. Engine was shut down and landing was made with #4 engine out.
output: INFLT ENG SHUTDOWN ON A B747 DURING AN OVERWATER OP.

input: Had flown from pit to san. Was told by approach to turn to a heading to intercept localizer slow to approximately 180 knot(s) and descend to 5000 feet/foot capt turned to the heading but did not intercept localizer until i drew it to his attention after announcing localizer alive. He then turned off autoplt and flight director and flew raw data as he continued to slow and descend capt kept asking me intermediate fix i saw the traffic we were slowing for and to keep looking for it. At 4700 feet/foot altitude alerter went off (i'm still looking outside for traffic per capt's request) and we descended to 4550 feet/foot before capt arrested descent and climbed back to 5000 feet/foot assigned altitude capt was more concerned on what controller was doing than what plane was doing!
output: ACR GIVEN SPD; ALT AND HDG CHANGES AND TOLD INTERCEPT LOC. OVERSHOOTS LOC.

input: On approach to runway 4r; we were told to hold 170 knots to final approach fix just like the aircraft in front of us. We slowed to 170 and were approaching the final approach fix when we noticed we could see the aircraft in front of us and the traffic alert and collision avoidance system showed them slowing down before they reached the final approach fix we were very close and i was going to tell approach we needed to slow when we were suddenly rocked hard to the right about 60 degrees. I grabbed the controls and shut off autopilot and we were rocked to the left very hard. We initiated a go around and landed 10 minutes later. We definitely were hit by wake turbulence.suggest pilots in front wait to slow at the fix and not before.
output: CRJ-200 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to EWR.

input: I was working local control and the airspace was moderately busy. I had been on position about 20 minutes already; so not too long. I first talked to an aircraft that was on the gps-a approach into mri. I directed him to circle south direct west high and then enter left downwind for 25. I cleared an aircraft for a touch and go clearance on runway 25. Traffic continues and in my scan i notice he is about a mile south of west high in lake hood's airspace so i call lake hood and point him out. In the gps-a aircraft correction; he is due straight north towards ship creek. I correct him to make left traffic and so he makes a circle 360 and enter left downwind. I get a call that aircraft y is ready to cross runway 25 at taxiway delta. I tell aircraft y to hold short of runway 25 for traffic on short final (aircraft on touch/go clearance). He reads back correctly. Aircraft x calls ready to depart 25. I tell him to hold short of runway 25 traffic is on short final. He reads back 'hold short 25 at kilo; aircraft x'. After the touch and go passes the threshold for runway 25; i clear aircraft x to 'runway 2-5 line up and wait' and he reads back 'line up and wait 25; aircraft x.' i transmit to aircraft x; 'and aircraft x; traffic will be crossing downfield'. After the touch and go aircraft is done and airborne again; i clear them to make right traffic (to remain clear of the 'lost' gps-a aircraft in the left pattern). My next transmission to aircraft y; 'aircraft y; cross runway 25 at delta; traffic holding in position full length.' aircraft y reads back 'crossing 25 at delta; aircraft y; expediting.' i was scanning between and watching the aircraft cross the runway when i hear my controller in charge 'he's rolling; he's rolling!' at this point; i observed aircraft x in departure roll nearing taxiway hotel without a takeoff clearance and i transmitted 'aircraft x; hold position.' he reads back; 'hold position; aircraft x.' we estimate he was as little as 1850 feet from the taxiway aircraft y was crossing at. I advised aircraft x to 'turn left at hotel and contact ground unless you can take departure from current position.' he opted to depart from where he was at on the runway; which was between taxiway juliet and taxiway hotel; definitely closer to hotel though because that's the intersection i departed him from. I told him 'aircraft x; from current position runway 25 at hotel cleared for takeoff; unable altitude deviation' and then he departed. I cleared the gps-a aircraft to land; and worked a couple other aircraft before giving aircraft x a brasher warning. The brasher warning was given before switching him to departure.there was never any imminent danger of the two aircraft involved hitting or any damage caused. It was just a mere fact that there was two aircraft on runway 25 at the same time and one wasn't doing what he was cleared to do. I think the pilot of aircraft x had an expectation bias because often they are just cleared for takeoff and don't have to wait to depart. He read back the lineup and wait clearance like he should have and i think he just had a brain [lapse]. I would just recommend that he be prudent when listening for clearances. On my part; i was scanning; but not in the right place at the right time. I was watching aircraft y as he crossed to the other side of the runway; verifying he was clear of the runway; so i then i could clear aircraft x for takeoff. I would also recommend a controller in charge (and other tower team members) be as attentive as possible; because if mine hadn't been at the time; it would have been a few seconds later and the departing aircraft could have been airborne. I would have noticed a few seconds later after observing aircraft y clear of runway 25 upon my takeoff clearance to aircraft x. This is a good example of 'see something; say something' coming into play to. Because of this mentality; i knew as soon as i could that aircraft x was rolling.
output: MRI Tower Controllers reported an aircraft attempted to depart when it had been instructed to line up and wait. Traffic was crossing the runway downfield.

input: We were scheduled to fly a phenom 300; on an empty leg. After starting both engines the ventral rud fail - cas message illuminated and we shut the aircraft down and notified maintenance control. They immediately directed us to a procedure found in section 5 of the poh that is intended to reset the malfunctioning ventral rudder system by tripping and resetting a circuit breaker. Since the poh does not contain faa-approved procedures i did not comply with his recommendation. I indicated that i would be amenable to working with maintenance control for troubleshooting purposes only and to provide information for maintenance personnel to use in diagnosing the problem. He argued that i am authorized to reset circuit breakers when directed to do so by maintenance control. Again; i reiterated that i would assist in troubleshooting only; and that i would not attempt to reset the malfunctioning system for the purposes of flying the aircraft without properly documenting the discrepancy.this is the second time i have been directed to complete one of the non-approved poh procedures by maintenance control in the last 3 weeks. There is absolutely no reason the maintenance controllers should be recommending we attempt to reset a malfunctioning system without first properly documenting the discrepancy. Properly training the maintenance controllers that pilots may only complete approved afm and aom procedures and that the pilot in command (pic) has the ultimate authority for determining the airworthiness of the aircraft and will not participate in performing undocumented or unapproved maintenance procedures under any circumstances.
output: Phenom 300 Captain reports receiving a VENTRAL RUD FAIL - CAS message after engine start and shuts down to contact Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control wants to do a circuit breaker reset which the Captain refuses to accomplish; believing it should be written up in the Logbook and corrected by a licensed Maintenance Technician.

input: Severe mountain wave. Aircraft accelerated to mach maximum operating in just a few seconds and started to climb at up to 1500 feet per minute aircraft is an a320 and was coupled up to autoplt 2 and autothrust. Had to disconnect autoplt to get control and descended back to cruise fl370. Maximum altitude reached was fl383.
output: A320 ACFT IN CRUISE ENCOUNTERED MOUNTAIN WAVE ACTION. ACFT ACCELERATED TO MACH MAX OPERATING AND; DUE TO PROTECTION MODES IN THE ACFT; IT PITCHED UP AND CLBED 1400 FT BEFORE THE RPTR WAS ABLE TO DISCONNECT THE AUTOPLT AND DSND BACK TO ASSIGNED.

input: The common traffic advisory frequency used at myv is listed at 123.05 in the current airport/facility directory the current united states terminal procedures sw; and on the sfo sectional aeronautical chart dated mar/xa/01. There is a notice to airmen / of air missions with flight service station specialist that 119.3 is in use at this time. This poses as a hazard for aircraft using the common traffic advisory frequency listed without knowledge of the notice to airmen / of air missions and aircraft using the notice to airmen / of air missions freq!
output: RPTR STATES THE CTAF AT MYV IS LISTED IN THE AFD AND ON THE CURRENT SFO SECTIONAL CHART AS 123 PT 05 BUT ON AN FSS NOTAM AS 119 PT 3.

input: I departed lga (dest is frg) with a clearance through class b airspace. The last ny approach control navigate, navigation instructions: ny approach 'cherokee identify proceed direct to republic.' the final ny approach controller instructions were: ny approach '12 mile nw of republic. Radar services terminated. Squawk 1200. Contact republic twr.' prior to the handoff i listened to frg automatic terminal information service the automatic terminal information service said: '...when number one; contact the tower on 125.2' on the ny 'tca' chart; it says 118.8 and 125.2. I contacted frg tower on 125.2: pilot 'republic tower cherokee (id); 12 mile nw; information xxx; landing republic.' frg tower 'contact the tower on 118.8.' i immediately announced on 118.8: pilot 'republic tower cherokee identification 12 mile nw; information xxx; landing republic.' i got no response. The frequency was somewhat busy and may people were talking over each other. After about 30-40 seconds; i tried again. I got no response. After about 1 minute(s) i tried again. Then i heard a controller say there was a stuck microphone on the frequency for a couple of minute(s) i was finally able to get it: pilot 'republic tower cherokee identification over the microphone information xxx; landing republic.' actually; i was about 1 mile nw of the microwave; but in my rush to get 'a word in edgewise;' i rpted 'over microwave' (about 6 mile nw of frg). The controller said: frg tower 'remain clear of the class b airspace.' at that moment i was descending from the ny class b airspace. I thought the controller was confused. I thought the controller thought i was near class b airspace (which i was because i had just exited it) and warning me to stay away from it. However; i 'came' from class b airspace (with a clrnc) second officer this wasn't an issue. The controller said: frg tower 'remain clear of the class b airspace. Exit either laterally or vertly.' that is when i realized that the controller must have been saying 'class d;' not 'class b.' i immediately turned north i was over the walt whitman mall and the controller said: frg tower 'remain clear of the class b airspace.' (said with some urgency.) i looked at my 'tca' chart at that moment. The walt whitman mall is 'definitely' outside the class d airspace (this was confirmed by an instructor at frg). The tower gave the instructions: frg tower 'proceed to dpk vor and dme (co-located) suggested heading xxx. Proceed south to the shoreline.' about 2 mile vor and dme (co-located) nw of dpk; i got the next instruction: frg tower 'suggested heading xxx.' i entered the pattern and landed without any further problems later that day; the frg tower called the fixed-base operator to find out what went wrong. The fixed-base operator explained that i thought i had a handoff; but the tower was unaware of this. The tower said that they had several problems before with ny approach not handing off properly. Frg tower was looking to document the problem to get ny approach to work with them better. What went wrong: i thought i was handed off from ny approach to frg tower because they said 'contact the twr.' to be precise; i thought i had clearance into the class d airspace; but not yet clearance to land. The automatic terminal information service said use frequency 125.2. This was the wrong frequency for the tower the keyed microphone which prevented communications aggravated the problem the controller said 'class d' which sounded like 'class b.' this caused confusion. The controller thought i was within the class d airspace over walt whitman -- this is wrong. The vectors from the tower caused me to circumscribe about 270 degrees of the class d airspace. This was very much out of my way and possibly in the way of the inbound/outbound traffic of frg. How to improve things: the reason for using the international civil aviation organization alphabet is to eliminate confusion when saying letters. Controllers should say 'class bravo'; 'class charlie'; 'class delta.' previously; there was no confusion with 'tca;' 'arsa'; 'ata.' controllers should make it clear when no handoff was made. The phrase 'radar services terminated' doesn't necessarily mean you've reached your clearance limit. See air traffic control phraseology: 5-53a note: after an instrument flight rules aircraft receives the statement 'radar contact' from air traffic control it discontinues rpting over compulsary rpting points. It resumes normal position rpting when air traffic control informs it 'radar contact lost' or 'radar service terminated.' (atc phraseology; section 5-53; page 5-8; attached.) intermediate fix 'radar services terminated' meant also 'clrnc limit is reached;' then instrument flight rules aircraft would be operating without a clearance when they heard 'radar services terminated;' thus a contradiction. Intermediate fix i were going from class b to class celsius and got a 1200 squawk; i might have suspected something was wrong; but not from class b to class d where i don't need a non-vfr squawk. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that clearance through multiple airspace areas has become a problem he feels that since he had to have an appointment and clearance to departure lga with destination frg; that his clearance would be to frg. Instrument flight rules clrncs have a stated clearance limit and he feels such a limit is implied in a case such as his. He expected a hand off to frg tower and did not receive it. He feels he was abandoned in a very unsafe situation he was counselled that 'radar service terminated; squawk 1200' indicates he is visual flight rules with no further clearance another concern is the confusion of airspace identify when b; celsius and d may sound alike over the radio as happened to him. He feels we have been taught to use the phonetic alphabet and should do second officer a third concern has come up in discussions with several flight instructors and at pilot meetings regarding special procedure for noise abatement and unique pattern procedures at an airport the handouts given at airports are great but that is after arrival, arrive how is a pilot new to the area supposed to be aware of these special procedures prior to arr? The group feels such procedures should be published in the airport facilities directory.
output: SMA UNABLE TO CONTACT TWR MAY HAVE ENTERED CLASS D AIRSPACE.

input: During initial clbout; at approximately fl355; electronic centralized aircraft monitoring displayed cabin altitude flashing green at a cabin altitude 8800 feet/foot while attempting to contact air traffic control to request a descent the aircraft continued to climb towards the assigned altitude of fl390. At fl365; contact was made and clearance received from air traffic control to descend to and maintain fl310. Air traffic control was advised we had a cabin pressurization problem and we may need lower. The flight control unit heading and altitude was reset for a heading of 120 degrees magnetic (due to tfc) and a descent to fl310. An autoplt descent was initiated. At this point; the aircraft had reached fl370. Electronic centralized aircraft monitoring then displayed cabin altitude in red at a cabin altitude of 9950 feet/foot electronic centralized aircraft monitoring then displayed the emergency descent chklist and the fault message 'cabin alt' fault along with the master warning. Oxygen masks were donned and crew communicationss established and the emergency descent initiated per the chklist. An emergency was declared with air traffic control and clearance to 10000 feet/foot mean sea level and a turn to 140 degrees magnetic was received. At approximately fl280; the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring emergency chklist and fault message were removed from view. Due to the lengthy maintenance history of the pressurization system descent to 10000 feet/foot mean sea level was continued. Air traffic control was advised of our desire to maintain present heading which was almost direct zzz at this time. Via automatic communications addressing & reporting system dispatch was notified of our descent due to cabin pressurization problems and our change of destination from zzz1 to zzz. Air traffic control was also advised of our desire to continue to zzz. At 10000 feet/foot mean sea level oxygen masks were removed. The passenber emergency oxygen system had not been activated. Voice contact was made with dispatch; flight attendants were advised and passenber notified of our descent and change of destination emergency fire equipment was refused with both air traffic control and dispatch. Air traffic control asked and received 'souls on board' and fuel remaining. Air traffic control asked intermediate fix the aircraft could accept normal handling and we responded that we could accept normal handling. The flight continued to zzz uneventfully.
output: A320 CREW RPTS PRESSURIZATION PROBS PASSING FL355 ON CLBOUT. AT FL370 CREW DECLARES AN EMER AND BEGINS AN EMER DSCNT.

input: We crossed the field at 9000 feet/foot for a left/right (directions) downwind to runway(s) 22r. We were vectored to intercept the runway(s) 22r localizer at 5000 feet/foot just inside of fnuch intersection there was another aircraft 3 vor and dme (co-located) ahead of us -- also level at 5000 feet/foot i do not know what type. The wind read 210 degrees at 43 knot(s) just as we rolled level on the localizer we encountered the wake turbulence of the aircraft ahead of us. The first effect was a roll of about 30 degrees bank followed by pitch oscillations. At one point the controls felt next to useless. I then put the nose down and the gear down and told the pilot not flying to set 4000 feet/foot level change; flaps 15 degrees speed 150 knot(s) call the tower and advise of our deviations he did all of this and at about 4500 feet/foot we were clear of the turbulence with 4 mile separation after our speed change we had no future encounters with preceding airplane's wake. This situation was very difficult to control and it must have been very uncomfortable for the passenber as a side note; this was the end of my 6th consecutive day of duty at the end of a month.
output: FLT CREW OF B737-500 ENCOUNTER SEVERE WAKE TURB ON ARR TO ORD; RWY 22R.

input: During takeoff at the 80 knot(s) airspeed indicator check; my (first officer) airspeed indicator was not indicating any airspeed. The captain rejected the takeoff at approximately 90 knot(s) we let maintenance troubleshoot the problem. They found a relatively large bug in the first officer pitot tube. Once they cleared the pitot tube; we were able to takeoff on the next flight without incident.
output: A B757-200 flight crew reported rejecting their takeoff because First Officer airspeed indicator read zero at the 80 KT check. They returned to the ramp where a bug was found in the First Officer pitot.

input: After holding for gate at lga we were cleared to gate by ground control after turning into ramp we noticed other aircraft were pushing off their gate. We stopped and contacted gate control and were told we should have contacted them first. I feel ground should tell you to contact gate control prior to clearing you to a gate and the gate control frequency should be published on the airport chart.
output: AN ACR FLC FLYING B727 AT LGA RPTS CONFUSION WITH CLRNC FROM GND CTL TO TAXI TO GATE THEN BEING ADVISED BY GATE CTL THAT THEY SHOULD HAVE BEEN CONTACTED BEFORE TAXIING TO THE GATE.

input: When we are number 2 for departure; and at the runway hold short line in las vegas; the las vegas tower frequently requests as to whether we have the aircraft in sight that is directly in front of us; holding in position on the runway; fifty yards away. When we say we do; then they state that we need to keep them in sight after they takeoff; and during our takeoff. This is virtually impossible; and should not be a stipulation of departure. We can not say we do not see them at 50 yards; but that should not tie us to the departure responsibility for separation; or relieve air traffic control of their obligations.
output: LAS air carrier departure expressed concern regarding ATC's application of visual separation with successive departures and the transfer of responsibility to the flight crew.

input: We were on radar vectors to intercept localizer to runway(s) 6 at cks airport taipei. I was pilot not flying and had my approach chart in book on top of flight bag. After paging through several times; i located instrument landing system runway(s) 5l; turned page over and saw what i wanted to see -- runway(s) 6. Unfortunately it was runway(s) 5l clear air turbulence ii. Tuned wrong instrument landing system frequency in; set inbound course -- same for runway(s) 5l and runway(s) 6. Capt set his frequency to mine and the controller took us through localizer she gave a reintercept of heading 030 degrees which seemed good to us. We flew back and intercepted nicely! Broke out at 2000 feet/foot and saw we were lined up for wrong runway(s) at same time; tower asked intermediate fix we wanted; or needed to land runway(s) 5l. We were able to sidestep to runway(s) 6 in normal apch/lndg confign. During approach phase; we had been monitoring traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and were only aircraft in area for approach controller seemed to be in training; and the late turn to intercept all seemed to be in place. Moral of the story is always put your chart in front of you and verify proper chart selected during approach briefing.
output: WRONG ILS FREQ SELECTED SINCE WRONG CHART USED. ACR LGT ENDS UP WITH WRONG RWY APCH IN FOREIGN AIRSPACE. UPON VISUAL; SIDESTEPS TO INTENDED RWY.

input: Aircraft x was released out of zzz airport. Aircraft y was in the run down list at zzz1. When aircraft x was abeam the departure end of runway xx at zzz; aircraft y was cleared for takeoff without a release. Aircraft y called me out of 1;800 feet and i turned him right to a 270 degree heading to avoid aircraft x. The 270 at 2;000 feet put aircraft y into a 2;300 feet minimum vector altitude after coordinating with zzz1 and calling for a supervisor; i climbed aircraft y out of the minimum vector altitude i could not turn aircraft x because there was a 3;500 feet minimum vector altitude just to the left of him. The two aircraft were 1.2 miles apart at the same altitude. If proper procedure would have been followed this would not have happened.
output: D10 Controller reported IFR traffic departed without a release; resulting in a traffic conflict.

input: Received and acknowledged initial approach clearance to 'expect visual approach 27l.' rpted runway(s) in sight and received clearance for the visual approach upon lining up for 27l; noticed an lgt 1000 feet/foot above also lined up for 27 left/right (directions) immediately instructed the first officer (pf) to turn left/right (directions) several seconds later; received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning; and received another call from approach control informing us that we were cleared for the visual to 27r. Acknowledged and stated that this was the first time we had heard and confirmed 27r. In this situation; the system worked as designed: this was a visual approach and the other aircraft was sighted in plenty of time to avoid a conflict. The traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii system provided a reliable backup; and approach control issued further instructions in a timely manner.
output: ACR HAS CLOSE PROX WITH ACR LINED UP FOR SAME RWY. LCL CTLR INDICATES CLRNC TO PARALLEL RWY.

input: I was conducting radar ojti. W174 and w465 had been active all day. Aircraft x was climbing southwest bound with crossing traffic. We were advised that w465 was no longer active. When the status board was updated; i observed w174c was not being shown active. I questioned this and it was confirmed that it was cold. With this information separation techniques were discussed with my trainee that would allow aircraft x to safely climb above traffic. It was decided to place aircraft x on a heading that would remain clear of traffic. This became possible with w174c being inactive as the vector would put the aircraft in the warning area. When vertical separation was established; aircraft x was cleared on course. We were offered a break and during the relief briefing it was stated w174c was cold. The d-side heard this and stated it was going active. The time of activation was questioned and it was very close to the current time. Aircraft x was issued a vector to expedite clearing the area and the d-side called the mru to cap the airspace below aircraft x. I believe this was done timely but i am not positive. Recommend zma have procedures in place for sua activation. When correctly followed this should be sufficient.
output: A possible airspace incursion event when coordination regarding activation of a restricted area was not timely.

input: I was the capt on air carrier flight inbound to tulsa. We were talking to tulsa approach and inbound to tulsa vor and dme (co-located) at 3000 feet/foot heading almost due westbound the approach controller asked us to rpt the airport in sight which we did at 5 mile he then cleared us for a visual approach we turned downwind for a visual approach to 17l. We tuned in the outer compass locator and were turning crosswind inside the locator at about 2600 feet/foot when a supervisor came on and said we weren't cleared to 'widen out' like that. He gave us vectors behind 2 fgts inbound for the overhead pattern. Unless he wanted us to land on a runway(s) 7000 feet/foot wide and 150 feet/foot longitude we had to 'widen out' exactly as we did. We were turning inside the marker which the approach chart shows as 5 nautical mile from touchdown. We are limited to 200 knot(s) in the control zone. The fgts were much faster. My coplt had less than 100 hours in the aircraft and we were not informed of any other traffic i feel the controllers were blaming us for their control shortcomings.
output: ACR MLG ACCUSED OF DEVIATING FROM A DIRECT TRACK TO THE ARPT AFTER BEING CLRED FOR A VISUAL APCH.

input: After announcing on common traffic advisory frequency that i was 9 miles south of airport and inbound; i smelled something burning. I started to shut some non-important items off like lights; when i started to see smoke come up from under the dash. As i turned off the master switch; i could see a small flame from near my left foot. I turned the fuel switch to the off position and searched for a landing area. The flame went out almost immediately. I noticed a paved county road below me and i landed into the small amount of wind that was present that day. A mechanic came to the scene and found one power wire had fallen from the wiring harness somehow and landed on a small fuel pressure hose (metal) and created an arc. Some wires burned and a pitot-static tube was damaged; since the airspeed indicator went dead sometime after i took off from the road and returned to the airport. Due to training; i knew to immediately shut off fuel for a fire; shut down electricity and find a place to land. This plane has a 28 volt electric system; so no circuits tripped.
output: A C185 pilot noticed open flame under the dash; turned off electrical and fuel; and landed on a county road.

input: I was parked on special course for helicopter championships -- when given visual signal to enter start area. I was again motioned to stop and land aircraft at 1/3 the distance to start point. The judges were forward of my position audience to my left/right (directions) when i looked to my rear left/right (directions) i then saw aircraft y passing by my aircraft in rear left/right (directions) hover. Missing my aircraft by 18 feet/foot i was on his blind side. Coordination of events and proper safety briefing of ground personnel would prevent future problems. After near miss; when aircraft y crew was asked intermediate fix i was in sight; they stated that they never saw me. Judges told to stay away from aircraft paths. This pilot expressed his displeasure about 2 aircraft positioned to each other's blind sides in windy conditions -- 18 knot(s) gusts to 40 knot(s) plus.
output: NMAC AT SPECIAL INTEREST ACTIVITY AIRSHOW CONTEST WITH ROTARY WING TFC.

input: In and out of clouds; the capt illuminated the seat belt sign and made appropriate public address the only returns on radar were approximately 60 mile north light chop developed; which rapidly escalated to moderate to severe and culminated in one especially severe jolt. Just before the severe jolt; in and out of cirrus; i saw a build-up slightly off to the left/right (directions) this was not showing on radar. We rpted severe turbulence to air traffic control and diverted to okc after cabin crew rpted injuries. Descent approach and landing were normal with aircraft handling normal. 4 flight attendants injured. There was just light chop being rpted in the general area. There were no returns within 60 degrees of the nose. Every tool and cues didn't give us any indication that we could expect anything more than light chop. Supplemental information from acn 403022: the seatbelt sign was on and all passenber were seated and strapped. The flight attendants were not seated at the time. We were en route to lax from pit and diverted to okc.
output: CABIN ATTENDANTS ON B757-200 INJURED WHEN ACFT ENCOUNTERED SEVERE JOLT OF TURB.

input: Bird strike at v1; no initial indications of airframe; engine damage; as flight progressed left/right (directions) engine became erratic. We diverted to dtw with company concurrence. My carrier has no guidance for erratic engine probs.
output: DC9-50 BIRD STRIKE AT V1 DEVELOPS ERRATIC ENG INDICATIONS AS FLT PROGRESSES AND DIVERTS TO DTW.

input: Shortly after arriving at the aircraft a mechanic came to the cockpit and stated they needed to do some work because the fueler couldn't get the correct amounts in the tanks due to fuel shutoff valves closing. This isn't unheard of so i was not concerned. After stepping back to say hi to the flight attendants i saw the mechanics had opened the equipment access hatch in first class. This i have never seen before to work a fuel transfer issue; but again i wasn't concerned.shortly afterwards the fuel issue was resolved and the fuel sheet was brought to the cockpit. At this point i noticed the fuel load of left 63.1 center 118.0 right 63.1. I took note of it because it was exact (left and right) this is unusual but good; i thought to myself the mechanics did a perfect job!about 45 minutes later when preparing for the before push checklist i noticed the fuel was now 2000 lbs lower in the left tank and 2000 lbs higher in the center tank. Also after my before push flow the center right fuel pump should have load shed but this time it didn't. Right away i thought something in the fuel system is still set to transfer fuel or was left 'connected' between the left main and the center tank.after having maintenance come back out to the aircraft they looked the plane over made some adjustments (i am not sure what exactly they did) the fuel was again balanced and the center right fuel pump now load shed like it should.at this point we believed the issue was corrected. We then taxied for takeoff. After takeoff when passing 10;000 an international relief officer (international relief officer) asked what was happening with the fuel. We brought the fuel synoptic up and shockingly the left tank was now 3000 lbs higher than it was at the gate.we decided the best course of action was to get up to altitude before an in-depth discussion. After getting close to cruise the captain called dispatch and [maintenance] on the satellite phone and i was in charge of flying and talking to air traffic control the captain; with input from the iros; dispatch; and [maintenance] attempted to understand and remedy the situation. After quite a while it became apparent that none of the crew was comfortable taking the aircraft over the pacific ocean like it was.we elected to return to [departure airport] for further maintenance work. The crew was also not comfortable jettisoning fuel which would open more valves and further complicate what we considered an 'unknown' fuel system. By now we had the system burning out of the center tank and decided to use delaying vectors altitude and landing gear to increase our burn to a weight we were comfortable with.after arriving at that weight we conducted the arrival and made an uneventful overweight landing.
output: B777 First Officer reported returning to departure airport after experiencing fuel system anomalies.

input: I was as 6;000 mean sea level flying heading 360; requested n27 area navigation (gps) runway(s) 23 approach into airport n27; initial approach fix domvy; under instrument flight rules  visual meteorological conditions prevailed. High terrain south of airport. The published miss turns right; north; away from the high terrain. Approach controller overrode the published miss. Gave us this missed approach instruction instead:  'upon entering controlled airspace; turn left heading 060.'  n27 is class g on the ground; has elevation 730 mean sea level and has overlying class east starting 700 feet above the surface. Mean sea level elevation of the class east floor is therefore 700+730 = 1;430 mean sea level  terrain south of airport has a peak at 1;476 mean sea level a peak at 1;327 mean sea level a peak at 1;304 mean sea level and a peak at 2;696 mean sea level  we flew the published miss. If it had been instrument meteorological conditions and we had followed the controller's instruction; we could have been killed.
output: A pilot on the N27 RNAV GPS RWY 23 was issued custom missed approach instructions by BGM TRACON. If followed; the instructions would have led to a terrain impact versus the charted missed approach procedure which accounted for nearby high terrain.

input: Acr x began takeoff roll after both capt and myself heard 'clred for immediate tkof'. We noticed that air carrier y was an mlg just beginning to clear the runway(s) by the time our aircraft was spooled up and indicating 60 knot(s) air carrier y had cleared runway(s) 36. The controller called us twice but never issued a new clearance or instructions to alert. There was absolutely no conflict. It seems that there should be less emphasis on clearing aircraft for anything and everything as fast as possible. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: reporter stated air carrier x had been instructed to 'taxi into position and hold; be prepared for immediately dep'. Air carrier y had landed and was about 5000' down the runway(s) and about to clear when the capt started takeoff roll. The reporter stated he advised the capt the tower had not cleared them for takeoff reporter stated he felt the tower saw they were taking off without a clearance saw that air carrier y was clearing downfield and just let it go. Analyst agrees with reporter. Supplemental information from acn 142810: tower cleared air carrier x into position and be ready for immediately takeoff as we began to spool-up for position movement tower advised cleared for immediate takeoff was in process of clearing runway(s) and spooled-up and had in fact cleared the runway(s) prior to us reaching even 60'. Tower called us twice but never said anything to us. A safe takeoff was initiated and completed.
output: ACR X UNAUTH TKOF OCCUPIED RWY. ACR X HAD LESS THAN STANDARD SEPARATION FROM ACR Y. PLT DEVIATION.

input: Ecl non-normal fuel imbalance checklist appears to be able to lead a pilot to turn off all main fuel pumps in the low quantity fuel tank with all cross-feed valves closed.we were dispatched and fueled with no center tank fuel and less than full main tanks. About three hours into the flight we got a fuel in center advisory engine indicating and crew alerting system message.we turned on both center tank fuel pumps to the burn the center tank fuel. We noted that the right main tank had approximately 1;600 lbs less fuel than the left main tank. We determined the engines were burning evenly and suspected that fuel had transferred from the right tank to the center tank.we did not have a fuel imbalance advisory engine indicating and crew alerting system message but we went to the ecl fuel imbalance checklist to attempt to balance the fuel. We determined; per the checklist; there was no fuel leak and commenced the checklist.page 3 of the checklist: there is a box that says'there is no indication of an engine fuel leak and the fuel imbalance message shows' we checked the no box as we did not have the fuel imbalance engine indicating and crew alerting system message. Upon checking no; that step blued out showing we completed that step and the very next step; fuel crossfeed switch (either): on; blued out as well. In other words; upon the fuel crossfeed step bluing out there was no switching to occur per the checklist.page 4 of the checklist: asks if the left main tank quantity is low. We checked 'no' which blued the rest of that page out.page 5 of the checklist: asks if the right main tank quantity is low. We checked 'yes'the next step directed and stated 'r fuel pumps fwd and aft switches(both): offthis allows fuel from the higher quantity tank to feed both engines. The next and final step of page 5 is to check when fuel balancing is complete. At no point does the ecl in our configuration direct us to open the crossfeed valves. We did not turn off the left/right (directions) main fuel pumps and elected to leave the imbalance as it was as we were not at the fuel imbalance limit. We did contact maintenance control and wrote up the fuel transfer issue.guidance from our training is to follow the ecl without second guessing it. I completely understand the rational as some of the checklists are complicated but in this case had we follow the checklist verbatim we would have had the left tank fuel pumps supplying the left engine and the right engine being fed by no fuel pumps at all. Furthermore; i looked at the 777 flight manual non-normal fuel imbalance checklist. It is different from the ecl. Following that checklist would have led to proper fuel balancing.in conclusion: the ecl fuel imbalance checklist; under certain circumstances; can lead to an engine being fed by no fuel pumps. The 777 flight manual illustrates a discrepancy with the ecl. The 777 flight manual leads to configuration so the engine will be supplied with fuel pump pressure.
output: B777 Captain reported a discrepancy between checklists and the flight manual while attempting to correct a fuel imbalance.

input: Jetbridges and portable ground power units used do not include a proper 'ground power cord support device' or strap that is to be utilized on aircraft when connecting ground power. This can be a serious hazard for ramp personnel and can cause damage if the cord ever becomes disconnected while in use. This has been brought up many times in local safety meetings with nobody taking responsibility to correct.
output: Air carrier ramp employee reported a possible safety issue regarding portable ground power units that were not equipped with the proper power cord support device.

input: During takeoff upon application of takeoff n1; the master caution illuminated along with the fuel indication on the left/right (directions) 6 pack. The throttles were immediately retarded to idle and a low speed abort was initiated. Master caution and fuel lights went out and would not recall. We examined all engine and fuel indications and discussed possible causes. We felt it was likely a fuel filter bypass since the wing tanks were nearly full and center was empty; second officer there was no reason for a nuisance 'low pressure light' we agreed to taxi out after running all chklists and do a static runup to see intermediate fix the problem reappears. All indications were normal. Upon application of takeoff power master caution reappeared and this time we all saw the fuel filter bypass light. Another low speed abort was accomplished and we cleared the runway(s) to contact dispatch and maintenance at that time we returned to the gate for investigation by maint.
output: B737-500 FLT CREW ABORTS TKOF TWICE FOR THE SAME MASTER CAUTION; FUEL FILTER BYPASS; RETURN TO GATE.

input: This is to rpt what i see as an issue with regard to an excessive time between opportunity for nutrition for our cabin crew. It also seems to be a trend with regard to reassignment of cabin crews on hawaiian island 1-day trips. In this particular case; the flight attendants arrived at hnl from lax and were reassigned to fly to sfo. These flts do not include meals for the cabin crew because there usually is time between flts on the ground at hnl to expected approach time in this case; however; flight x arrived at the gate in hnl at xa53z and blocked out for the outbound flight at xb49z. That is less than 1 hour to offload and board the next flight obviously not enough time for the crew to get a bite to expected approach time much less a break. Intermediate fix you look at this closely; you can see that they hadn't had a chance to expected approach time in quite some time. That works out to about 11 hours without the opportunity for a meal. And this only because the purser demanded that meals be boarded on the outbound flight even intermediate fix they had eaten before the meal service on flight y; it still would have been about 9 hours between meals. Still; a very longitude time. The issue here is that the cabin crew has safety responsibilities on these flts. We make sure the flight deck crew has adequate chance for nutrition; and we should also do the same for the cabin crews. 11+ hours without eating is not what most would describe as providing for such. It puts people in a low blood sugar state; and reduces their capacity to make decisions; and react in the case of an emer.
output: RPTR ADVISES THAT CABIN ATTENDANTS ON HAWAIIAN ISLAND TURNAROUNDS FROM THE US WEST COAST ARE OFTEN FORCED TO GO FOR LONG PERIODS OF TIME WITHOUT PROPER NUTRITION.

input: Dc9 on visual approach to runway(s) 6. Passenber (2) noticed flares exploding near left/right (directions) side of aircraft as they passed over a golf course on 3 mile final. They told capt; who told tower twr called a local country club to discover they had shot off 2 flares to signify the start of a shotgun start golf tournament. No notification was given to the tower of this planned activity. Neither the flight crew nor tower controller saw the flares explode. Tower controller advised he noticed a small area of smoke behind aircraft as it was on short final; could not determine distance or altitude callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr had been made aware of the situation by other controllers and submitted an event rpt. Rptr advised that management effected coordination with event manager and obtained a change of practice -- to discontinue the flare gun use and return to a shotgun to announce the event start.
output: ERI CTLR RPTS OF DC9 FLC NOTIFICATION OF FLARE SHOT IN VICINITY OF ACFT WHEN OVERFLYING GOLF COURSE.

input: Dtw ground control crossing runway(s) 22l. We landed on runway(s) 22r; taxied to hold short of runway(s) 22l on taxiway v. We were changed to a ground control frequency to cross runway(s) 22l.
