input: Departure clearances consistently read 'cleared xxxxxx departure xxx transition maintain 230 knots climb via standard instrument departure exp fl370 10 minute(s) aft dp;dp frq xxx.x' they read the same via cpdlc or pre departure clearance confusion comes from improper phraseology. Should read 'climb via standard instrument departure except maintain 230 knots'. Sometimes an altitude restriction is also included and this is normally phrased correctly. Many of the area navigation sids have a speed restriction of 230 knots; which leaves pilots wondering if the 230 knot restriction is a reminder not to exceed the first crossing restriction or if air traffic control wants us to maintain 230 until otherwise advised since climb via comes directly after the speed restriction (it is the latter). Approximately six months ago i requested clarification from air traffic control on this exact point and the controller sounded irritated that i was even asking the question; as if they had answered this exact question many times before. I suggested over the radio that they change the text to reflect verbal phraseology which seemed to induce further irritation in the controller. After multiple trips in and out of slc; phraseology has not changed and several captains i have flown with have asked me to clarify with air traffic control most of these have occurred without the controller sounding irritated. But bottom line; the verbiage remains confusing and should be corrected before an incident occurs.as a short term fix send notice to clearance delivery to change verbiage phraseology on takeoff clearance to match expected/standardized phraseology. 'climb via standard instrument departure except maintain 230 knots and 10;000 feet' (i used a dual restriction since it is fairly common as well). As a long term fix i recommend changing area navigation sids to reflect standard clearance from air traffic control only the wevic5 does not have a 230 knot speed restriction. Air traffic control could submit a change to incorporate a 230 knot restriction at a point of their choice and include 230 knot crossing restrictions later on the other sids and just have air traffic control cancel airborne if not needed. Ultimately; if air traffic control needs to implement a 230 knot climb restriction on every departure; it should change the sids to reflect this need and eliminate the 'exceptions.'
output: Air carrier First Officer reported the speed restriction verbiage used in their clearance received via CPDLC/PDC is confusing to pilots due to its non-standard nature.

input: Ils approach; zzz tower closed. Dark night with overcast. Active cell with heavy precipitation. Wind reported 350@12. Coming from the southwest; we requested and were given direct zzzzz; descend to 7000. The active cell over zzzzz had us divert left. After clearing the cell; we were instructed to turn right heading 070; then turn left 350 to intercept the localizer; descend and maintain 5300 until established; cleared for the approach. We verified the 5300 altitude with air traffic control level at 5300; course alive between zzzzz and zzzzz1; we got a terrain caution followed by a terrain pull up alert. Pilot [flying] (first officer) immediately disconnected the autopilot; climbed and pilot monitoring (captain) advised air traffic control we leveled-off at 6500 and re-engaged the auto-pilot in altitude and heading modes. Air traffic control vectored us to the west. After discussing the incident with air traffic control they indicated the minimum vectoring altitude in the area is 5300. Captain checked sufficient fuel on board for a second attempt. Not sure if the terrain warning was erroneous after the minimum vectoring altitude discussion and reviewing the terrain information on the approach chart; we requested and got vectors back to final. We were instructed to descend and maintain 5300 once again. On a heading of 150 while being vectored and descending to 5300 we had another terrain pull up alert. Pilot flying disconnected the autopilot and immediately initiated a climb to a safe altitude and pilot monitoring advised air traffic control after re-engaging the auto-pilot in altitude and heading modes at about 6300 ft. We had another discussion with air traffic control regarding minimum vectoring altitude. We were then vectored to intercept the localizer and capture the glide slope between zzzzz and zzzzz1 but closer to zzzzz this time (the cell over zzzzz was still active). We asked air traffic control to maintain our altitude until established. We intercepted the localizer and glide slope at 6300 ft. And performed a visual approach backed-up with the instrument landing system to an uneventful landing. Landed with > 4000lbs of fuel on board (tankering). At no time was any aircraft limitation exceeded. This report is erroneously indicating it was a non-revenue flight when it was a revenue flight. After further review on a sectional chart; highest terrain in the area is at 3;457 ft.; left of localizer between zzzzz and zzzzz1. A minimum vectoring altitude of 5300 ft. Put us 1843 ft. Above the terrain. Had the cell not be present over zzzzz; we would have intercepted the localizer further out and at a higher altitude and probably would not have received any terrain warnings. Minimum crossing altitude is 5500 at zzzzz and 5000 at zzzzz1. Add more detailed terrain information on the approach chart. The 3;457 ft. Terrain depicted on the sectional is not depicted on the approach chart. Increase minimum vectoring altitude to match the [terminal arrival altitude] for the area (5500 ft. Msl).
output: CRJ-200 Captain reported the flight crew received Caution Terrain and Terrain Pull Up warnings while on radar vectors from ATC for the same approach during two separate approach attempts.

input: I was flying a traffic watch c172 in the vicinity of moffett field when my engine began to run very rough. I could feel an abnormal vibration through the yoke and could see that the instrument panel was shaking much more than normal. I initiated emergency procedures with my chklist. Already in contact with moffett tower i requested a precautionary landing after being cleared to do second officer i landed without incident at moffett federal. I requested a precautionary landing instead of declaring an emergency because i was unsure of the severity of my problem thinking about it afterwards; i find that the term precautionary landing is somewhat ambiguous. Intermediate fix faced with a similar situation in the future; i will declare an emer.
output: A C172 PLT EXPERIENCES A ROUGH RUNNING ENG AND DECIDES TO LAND AS A PRECAUTION.

input: This is a follow up for your information rpt filed on this incident 12/x/91. Lgt came out of 'c' checked locking pin not removed from left/right (directions) ground spoilers. Ground spoilers locked in full extended position (should have had red flag attached to pin; none attached). Not detected on preflt as company procedure is to deploy all spoilers prior to outside walk around; second officer all spoilers were up during flight engineer checked which is normal. There is no requirement to checked spoiler retraction once speed brake handle returned to stowed position so! We took off with spoiler up. It caused roll and yaw plus caused #3 engine to violently compressor stall continuously until shut down. Roll problem quite severe. 5 units rudder 50 degree left/right (directions) aileron -- to fly straight -- very little ability to turn left/right (directions) (thrust from #1 plus spoiler). Landed uneventfully. Fortunately i ante meridiem an lgt checked capt and we experimented around with this stuff in the simulator all the time; second officer it wasn't a big deal; but coupled with bad weather or mexico city; etc. It could have been a disaster. Supplemental information from acn 195898. After takeoff (capt flying) aircraft flight controls had a problem and #3 engine started compressor stalling. A precautionary shutdown was accomplished and fuel was dumped. Flight controls still had a major problem. An emergency was declared and fire trucks were standing by for us. We found our inboard left/right (directions) ground spoilers were fully deployed. At this time maintenance thinks that a lock out was forgotten by maintenance after a heavy 'c' checked and the disrupted air after takeoff flamed-out our #3 engine and caused the obvious flight control problems.
output: FLC OF LGT TOOK OFF WITH R GND SPOILERS EXTENDED.

input: After taking off from byron i monitored the local airport from frequency until climbing through 3000 feet/foot then i called norcal approach to get a squawk code and traffic advisories up to the skydivers jump altitude of 13;000 feet/foot on the flight climbing out i was not informed of the traffic an aircraft crossing my path from left to right that i turned left to avoid and then back right as the aircraft went by. Then over the top of us from left to right another aircraft that i heard and saw after it went by. I saw it was red and white in color. I advised norcal approach that we had just missed 2 aircraft. I got very little help from them. Lack of air traffic control advising me of this traffic.
output: A sky diver drop aircraft departed C83 (Byron; CA) climbing through 5;000' for 13;000 and talking to NCT for traffic. The aircraft had two NMAC's within seconds of one another with no conflict reports from ATC.

input: Inbound from se of airport being vectored to final; we could tell approach controller was being overwhelmed from the tone of voice and his rapid instructions. The supervisor (we guess) was coming on and giving instructions too. Initially we were 3000 feet/foot heading westbound (lndg north runway(s) 36l/r and runway(s) 27). Center had us maximum speed inbound and when turned over to approach were slowed to 210 knots indicated airspeed then 190 knots indicated airspeed about 3 mile from final we were told to slow to 160 knot(s) and given a nw heading to intercept localizer for runway(s) 36r. About 30 seconds later; i'm not sure but might have been supervisor told us to turn back westbound for vectors to runway(s) 36l. We did and i was worried that even at 15 degree flaps; at 160 knot(s) the autoplt would not make the turn to final; second officer i disengaged the autoplt. We were getting set for runway(s) 36l; i was busy trying to maintain 160 knot(s) i then noticed i was sinking below 3000 feet/foot (approx 100 feet/foot low) second officer added power and pitched up. The capt said watch hard altitude we were then about 200 feet/foot low; i pitched up more; and did not add power we were above 160 knot(s) i remember seeing 12 degree pitch up several times but the aircraft continued to sink to maybe 250-300 feet/foot low (2700-2850 ft). The capt then took control of the aircraft and brought us up to 3000 feet/foot the controller then turned us to a north nw heading to intercept the runway(s) 36l localizer we overshot final; because of the sluggish airplane or late turn; the controller gave us. Heading 010 degrees to recapture localizer we intercepted localizer were given approach clearance and when everything was settled down the capt gave me back the aircraft and we landed safely. Looking back; i was too concerned about flying 160 knot(s) and the overwhelmed controller vectoring us into other aircraft i should have not let altitude drop from xchk. Supplemental information from acn 529345: first officer disconnected the autoplt just as we were intercepting the runway(s) 36r localizer because the autoplt was not turning quickly enough and the first officer did not want to overshoot the localizer approach control gave us a turn to 250 degrees and apologized and said we could expect runway(s) 36l. After we turned i could see traffic passing under us to runway(s) 36r. A short while later the first officer stated that we should be at 3000 feet/foot we were at 2800 feet/foot and descending at 2700 feet/foot i took the aircraft and returned to 3000 feet/foot during this time approach gave us clearance for the runway(s) 36l instrument landing system the rest of the approach and landing was normal. Contributing factors: marginal weather air traffic control was behind and we were getting multiple heading and speed changes. Inability of the autoplt to respond fast enough. We were distracted from flying by looking outside for conflicting tfc.
output: EXCURSION FROM ALT DURING A NIGHT APCH IN WX AT A MAJOR ARPT.

input: High desert terminal radar approach control facility had released airspace back to the center because it was a holiday and not normally used. The controller at high desert forgot the airspace had been released and climbed military x into my airspace.
output: MIL X UNCOORD PENETRATION OF AIRSPACE. OPDEV.

input: Approach phase; receiving radar vectors for visual approach; i was pilot not flying. Parking brake on light illuminated and subsequent engine indicating and crew alerting system warning prkg brk not released. Quick reference handbook procedure complied with (called for cycling of parking brake lever). Radioed maintenance to advise and asked for suggestions to resolve. Maintenance had no further advice. Decided to land on the longest runway; flaps full. [i] assumed pilot flying duties for landing. Advised tower of aircraft situation; declared emergency and requested emergency vehicles for precaution. Upon touchdown; found braking was normal. Parking brake on light extinguished and engine indicating and crew alerting system message changed to prkg brk fault. Upon shutdown at gate; engine indicating and crew alerting system had no abnormal messages.
output: An ERJ190 EICAS alerted PRKG BRK NOT RELEASED prior to approach but the QRH procedure failed to remedy the fault so an emergency was declared followed by a normal landing where the alert changed to PRKG BRK FAULT; then subsequently extinguished at the gate.

input: Cruising at fl320; first officer flying; when aft cargo fire warning alerted. Cargo fire annunciator; master warning; and aft cargo indicator on the cargo fire control panel all illuminated and the cargo fire horn sounded. I declared an emergency with air traffic control and requested immediate vectors to the nearest airport. First officer began an emergency descent and i performed the quick reference handbook procedure for aft cargo fire; including firing the first extinguisher. I briefed the flight attendant's of the situation and told them to prepare for an immediate landing including a possible evacuation. I then made a public address to the passengers. I asked air traffic control for a single frequency approach and got the crash fire rescue equipment crews on frequency. I let them know we will stop on the runway and we need an inspection of the aft cargo bay. During this; the first officer has been doing the emergency descent. He had exercised the captain's emergency authority and kept the speed above 250 knots below 10;000 feet/foot to expedite the descent. I rejoined him at about 5;000 feet/foot on final for the vor and dme (co-located) approach. I run a quick before landing checklist and he configures and continues the approach; breaking through a thin overcast at about 2;500 feet/foot we land and stop on the runway; i make a public address for the passengers to remain seated; but we prepare to the aircraft to possibly evacuate. The fire crews approach and inspect the aft cargo bay with infrared and visually and tell me there is no indication of fire. I let the passengers know the situation is over; and we taxied to the ramp. It took about 16 minutes from first warning to landing; the first officer did a super job. I think overall we handled the situation well; except i could not find the button to silence the horn. We listened to the horn all the way down.
output: MD83 flight crew experiences an aft cargo fire warning at FL320 and diverts to the nearest suitable airport. An emergency descent is initiated; the QRH is complied with and a normal landing ensues 16 minutes after the initial warning. No actual fire existed.

input: Forgot to checked on with center after given frequency change. We were given a frequency change from center to call toronto center on 119.77. I switched to that frequency and then was distracted and forgot to checked on. About a minute(s) later he called us.

input: Acr x changed to zhu frequency 128.1. That is also houston clearance delivery frequency (iah cpt). The iah cpt was second officer much stronger than the center that communicationss were almost impossible! No alternate frequency was available! We had been deviating around thunderstorms but fortunately were on a safe heading at the time. The rptr has not flown route again; second officer he does not know intermediate fix the problem is ongoing. The specialist stated frequency 128.1 has been changed.
output: ACR X DEVIATION FROM CLRNC ROUTE BECAUSE OF WX FACTORS ENCOUNTERED RADIO COM PROBLEM OVERLAPPING FREQ.

input: I recently made a part 91 visual flight rules pleasure flight in my personal aircraft to an unctled airport as i approached the field; automatic weather observing/reporting system was rpting winds at 18 knot(s) gusting to 31 knot(s) and i had been experiencing enough turbulence that the ride was not pleasant. On 1 occasion during the flight about 10 minute(s) from landing the autoplt automatically disengaged via the g-switch acceleration sensor. Although i did not lose control of the aircraft during this event; maintaining aircraft control was a primary focus during my approach to landing this aircraft is equipped with a landing gear warning system to help prevent an inadvertent gear-up landing retarding the throttle from cruise setting normally produces a loud; intermittent tone through the aircraft speakers. 1 week prior to the incident flight i made a local flight to practice flight procedures and verify aircraft system operations(s) during this practice flight the landing gear warning system performed as intended during each of several lndgs; sounding loudly as the throttle was retarded. On approach during the incident flight as i retarded the throttle; the gear warning system did not sound and i did not notice the failure of this important warning system instead; i continued slowing the plane; adding flaps; and minding aircraft control right down to a gear-up landing my attention to aircraft control apparently allowed for a (relatively) soft impact; and the damage to the aircraft was confined to the propeller and aircraft skin. In a typical approach as i lower the gear; i checked for a green indicator light and visually verify gear down only after the warning horn is silent and the mechanical sound and motion of the gear extension mechanism stops. (i wouldn't the recreational uas safety test an attempted verification before then.) in this case; the first did not occur; and neither did the second. After clearing the plane from the runway(s) an a&p lowered the gear (it functioned normally); but discovered a broken solder connection on the landing gear warning system (it did not function). Would i have lowered the gear intermediate fix the gear warning system had been screaming in my ears as usual? I'd like to think i would; but the incident certainly would not have happened intermediate fix i had independently verified gear extension as i approached landing a number of if-only scenarios could have saved me from this incident: in an instrument flight rules approach i lower the gear at a predetermined point in the approach same with a standard pattern approach but this was a straight-in approach i'll revise or restrict my straight-in approachs even with the retractable gear; this is a relatively simple airplane to land. Does it justify reading through a written pre-lndg chklist? My answer today would be yes; but at least 1 authority/authorized has said that using a written or mnemonic chklist should be taught but any type of chklist can be interrupted by distrs. However; even that is taught and practiced by instructors. Will i ever make another landing without thinking about this one? No; but that's one very expensive lesson. For me; it will be more written chklists; a more reliable mnemonic procedure for gear down verification; more practice with distrs; and more vigilance.
output: C182 PILOT REPORTS MAKING GEAR UP LANDING AFTER LANDING GEAR WARNING HORN FAILS TO SOUND WHEN THROTTLE IS RETARDED DURING THE APPROACH.

input: On the hobtt arrival into atl; we encountered wake turbulence from [a] b747 twice. Subsequently; the first atl approach controller slowed us down to 210 knots due to the b747 in front of us. I slowed down; and shallowed out the descent rate to avoid any more encounters. On downwind; we were experiencing quartering tailwinds. Abeam the airport; the next controller's supervisor or monitor position broke into approach's transmissions and told us that our descent rate was unacceptable and warned that if we didn't get down that we would have to do a 25-mile final. She seemed very upset. I felt; at that point; we would not get into the wake upset anymore since [the other] aircraft got cleared a few minutes prior. I then increased the descent rate. I am very familiar with the downwind descent rates needed in atl. The captain and i have both experienced wake turbulence in the past. I felt it was safe to do a shallow descent to avoid further encounter. Even the prior controller cautioned us of the b747 in front of us. I felt that the monitor/supervisor that got upset with us should have communicated this to us. It's great for air traffic control to get numerous aircraft into a large terminal facility very quickly. But more importantly it is better to avoid a wake turbulence encounter.
output: B737-700 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence from a preceding B747 on arrival into ATL.

input: An a321 was at fl240 and on the ivane1 arrival to clt. The a321 was cleared to descend via the ivane1 arrival landing north. The a321 almost immediately descended to fl220 and violated the south boston (22) sector's airspace. I believe the ivane1 arrival was put into place without proper education of both the controllers and pilots. I was under the impression that if the aircraft was below the mstrd altitude window; that he wouldn't start to descend until he hit the next window (which would be mayos); just like the pilots do when they intercept a glideslope. This misunderstanding and/or lack of education created an unsafe situation where the aircraft descended into the south boston (sector 22) sector's airspace without them being informed or made aware of the traffic. Fortunately; there was no aircraft in the way; so there was no incident. However; there have been many questions and confusion on both the controller and the pilot's part that deem this ivane1 arrival a very unsafe situation. Pilots are constantly asking for clarification when the descend via clearance is given. Part of the problem contributing to the confusion is the fact that; on a daily basis; the ivane1 arrival is run; then suspended; then run again; then suspended again. When the descend via is suspended; then we get all of the frequency congestion of the pilots asking if they should descend via when we just give regular clearances. If the ivane1 was consistently running (24/7) it would be a whole lot easier to learn and apply all of the rules pertaining to it (through repetition). Therefore; my recommendation would be to either run the ivane1 arrival 24/7; or suspend it until a time at which it could be run 24/7. On a separate note; our 'official' training on the ivane1 arrival was done more than 6 months ago. Since then; it was tested for a few days; suspended indefinitely; used for a few days; suspended again and now is on and off during the day and then suspended for the midnight shift. This 'lack of education' may not be from me not learning it initially. It may simply be from me not retaining the information for over 6 months before i have a chance to apply it. We (both pilots and controllers) need to have refresher training on the ivane1 arrival along with the consistency of using it on a daily basis.
output: ZDC Controller voiced concern regarding the misunderstanding of a 'Descend via' clearance with specific applications to the IVANE 1 STAR; one event resulted in an airspace incursion and unsafe condition.

input: Departed mci; climbed to 10000 feet/foot on a departure vector heading westbound traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alerted us to a descending aircraft heading east at our 2 o'clock position through 11000 feet/foot we visually acquired the aircraft and watched it pass down our left/right (directions) wing within 3 nautical mile of our aircraft descending through 10000 feet/foot shortly thereafter; we believed to have received a climb to 15000 feet/foot and to contact zkc on 123.8. At approximately 13000 feet/foot we received an resolution advisory at approximately 10 o'clock position and a little high; heading ne and 15000 feet/foot estimated. The first officer and i visually acquired the aircraft and first officer complied with the resolution advisory to the extent necessary to deconflict. I checkeded in with zkc and told them we were given a climb to 15000 feet/foot from kansas city departure received an resolution advisory during the climb and the whole picture seemed 'a little weird.' center remarked 'no harm; no foul' and said he would checked into it. Zkc came back and said something to the effect that the climb clearance was not for us. I replied rather assuredly that we both heard climb to 15000 feet/foot and contact zkc on 123.8. I then told center that intermediate fix it was a mistake on our part; that we apologize for any confusion. A couple of frequencies down the road; high sector air traffic control gave us a phone number to contact departure upon arrival, arrive to pdx. Looking back at this situation both the first officer and i were well rested. It had not been a longitude duty day; the weather was clear and kansas city departure frequency did not sound unusually saturated; nor did we hear or get the impression that we stepped on someone else during our readback and took their clearance we did not hear a correction from departure nor the intended aircraft whose clearance we supposedly mistook for our own; prior to us switching to 123.8. We still believe we heard air carrier xxx. Having said that; the lesson here is for increased diligence in all areas of the flight intermediate fix unsure of a clearance or an air traffic control transmission is a little weak in reception; verify it again. This incident has made me more aware of just what can happen during an otherwise routine flight intermediate fix just 1 facet of a series between point a and point b is not executed properly. As professionals; we strive for that perfect flight i will use this incident to become better at my trade and to strive to listen more closely to air traffic control xmissions. Supplemental information from acn 498130: we departed mci on the wildcat departure climbed to 10000 feet/foot on a departure vector heading 270 degrees to intercept the departure radial. Then the capt and i both believe we heard instructions from kansas city departure to 'clb to 15000 feet/foot and contact zkc on 123.8.' at approximately 13000 feet/foot we got a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory to descend and the other aircraft was displayed on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii at 10 o'clock position slightly high; and descending the first officer (me) initiated the initial descent maneuver and visually picked up the other aircraft at approximately 10 o'clock; approximately 1 mile heading the opposite direction. The capt then checkeded in with zkc and stated we had just received an resolution advisory and center said he would checked into it. Zkc later informed us that we had mistakenly taken the clearance for another company aircraft the capt politely replied that we both believed that the call was for us; but intermediate fix it was a mistake on our part; we sincerely apologize. Approximately 15 minute(s) later; zkc gave us a phone number to call when we landed in portland in order to discuss a possible pilot violation. Looking back on the situation the capt and i were both well rested. The departure frequency was not saturated. We both were listening attentively to the radio. We did not get any sort of corrective call from kansas city departure nor did we step on another aircraft trying to answer the clearance call. Having said that; the lesson here is for increased diligence on the radios and intermediate fix any question remains regarding an assigned clearance get a clarification! This situation has made me even more aware that there is no phase of flight that will allow even the slightest bit of complacency. In the future; i will ensure that i monitor all air traffic control radio xmissions even more carefully. Supplemental information from acn 497831: multiple aircraft on frequency both air carrier y and air carrier x were restrict, restricted, restriction to 10000 feet/foot for crossing arrival, arrive traffic (acr zulu time (utc/gmt) at 12000 ft). I climbed air carrier y to 15000 feet/foot and told him to contact zkc on frequency 123.8. Multiple xmissions occurred; and i observed air carrier xx 5 nautical mile south mci; a departure i contacted air carrier xx and he acknowledged. I then observed air carrier x climbing into the altitude of air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) and immediately attempted to contact him and remind him of his altitude restrict, restricted, restriction of 10000 feet/foot air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) was on the arrival, arrive freq.
output: B737-700 AND A B737-300 HAD LESS THAN LEGAL SPACING IN MCI CLASS E AIRSPACE.

input: Just after passing kessel vor and dme (co-located) the new automatic terminal information service came up indicating that rather than runway(s) 1l; which we had expected; that we would now get runway(s) 19r or runway(s) 12. The capt reprogrammed for runway(s) 12. Upon execution; the box dumped our arrival, arrive we had been told to cross 5 west of druzz at 11000 feet/foot and 250 knot(s) i mentioned that we had lost our arrival, arrive the capt attempted to go to raw data while i attempted to reinsert the arrival, arrive the arrival, arrive plate no longer gives a frequency for the kessel vor! Thus no raw data could be used. I had not yet finished entry for the arrival, arrive but realized that runway(s) 12 is not available on that arrival, arrive at that point; the capt had started trying to get the box updated with our current arrival, arrive we decided to ask for direct druzz; which the controller wouldn't give us. During this process; i erased what the capt was entering using the number 2 box. Oops. We managed to keep the aircraft on a reasonably accurate track using heading select until we had gotten the flight management computer reconfigured. The descent was made on profile; but the entire situation was laughable. After we landed; we discussed what had happened; what we could have done better; and finally just laughed at the state of confusion that this flight management computer issue caused. I do not want to see anyone else go through this when dulles is instrument flight rules and the controllers are not prepared for an aircraft deviation from the area navigation arrival, arrive i hope that this issue will be addressed.
output: A B757 FLT CREW DEVIATED SLIGHTLY FROM ARR COURSE WHEN THEY LOST NAV INFO FROM THEIR FMC DURING REPROGRAMMING.

input: As a precautionary measure i am filing this report. I do not believe we did anything wrong or caused a violation. I was the first officer on flight from den to zzz. We pushed off gate xxx and were told to taxi to; 'x east; call ground 121.85.'  ground issued taxi instructions to; 'taxi lima to 17l.'  so we complied. While we were still on taxiway lima; i heard ground tell the other carrier in front of us to; 'taxi on ed; monitor tower 132.35.'  almost immediately after that; while still on taxiway lima; we were told; 'taxi ed; follow the traffic ahead; and monitor tower 132.35.' (identical instructions as the traffic ahead). I also commented to the captain at this point; 'we were going to runway 8 now;' because that was the frequency for runway 8 not 17l. We continued the taxi onto ed and toward runway 17l. As we crossed the approach end of 17r; a landing aircraft passed immediately overhead. And; the captain and i both commented on it. (this is a known 'hot spot' but we had not been issued hold short instructions.)  as i was listening to the tower frequency; i realized this was the frequency for runway 8 tower not runway 17l tower. At that same moment; i heard the traffic in front of us ask for 'the correct frequency for 17l.'  he was told the frequency was 133.3. I also switched to that frequency because we were on ed in line for 17l. As we were climbing out; air traffic control gave us a phone number to call for a 'possible violation.'
output: Pilot reports of a runway incursion that was caused by possible miscommunication and a frequency that was not issued.

input: Extended landing gear on approach left/right (directions) main gear did not indicate down (no green light); red 'unlock light' was not on -- conflicting indications. Went through abnormal procedures recycled gear with no change. Observed main gear through viewer in floor; down lock indicated normal. We landed uneventfully. Gear position switch on strut found to be defective.
output: AN ACR DC9-30 FLC DID NOT GET A GREEN LNDG GEAR (DOWN AND LOCKED) INDICATION ON THE L-HAND MAIN LNDG GEAR. THE FLC USED THE MID CABIN LNDG GEAR VIEWER TO CONFIRM THAT THE L GEAR WAS SAFE AND THEN MADE A NORMAL LNDG.

input: I landed on runway(s) 23 with a thunderstorm approaching and windshear warning in effect; cleared on taxiway left/right (directions) stopped and contacted ground control i was cleared to cross runway(s) 18l on taxiway left/right (directions) and taxi which i proceeded to do after reading back my taxi clearance by the time i reached the hold line the storm was almost over the airport with gusty winds and what looked like smoke blowing across the northern part of the airport i had to work at just keeping the aircraft straight. Then i heard ground control telling me to hold position repeated 3 or 4 times. I stopped with the entire aircraft over the hold line on the runway(s) side and informed ground control that i was over the hold line. When i looked to my left/right (directions) i saw a b737 on its takeoff run on runway(s) 18l no more than 100 yards from the taxiway intersection it rotated just past the taxiway i was on. There was no way it could have missed me had i not stopped. I always make a point of checkeding the runway(s) both ways when cleared to cross; and when instructing would emphasize that point to my students and show them the federal aviation administration runway(s) incursion dvd which i have in my possession but perhaps due to the unusual weather conditions on the airport this one time i hadn't done second officer i can only assume the problem was caused by lack of communications between the tower and ground controllers but since i wasn't monitoring the tower frequency i have no way of knowing for sure. It was made worse by my brief distraction by the 'smoke' blowing over the ramp and txwys to my left/right (directions) -- i thought there was a fire somewhere. The solution is simply to follow my own rules; and the advice given in the federal aviation administration dvd -- checked both ways!
output: C402 PLT LNDG CLT WAS CLRED TO CROSS RWY 18L BY GND CTL; BUT THEN TOLD TO HOLD SHORT FOR DEP TFC ON RWY 18L AFTER XING HOLD LINES.

input: A second time; upon arrival, arrive of flight on apr/xa/01 in sfo from mia; i noticed the agent removing 2 portable bottles of oxygen from a first class closet. I was not aware these bottles of hazmat were on the flight the departing agent in mia never gave me the paperwork or informed me that these oxygen bottles were on board the aircraft before departing mia; i; as the capt of the flight had stopped by the podium to introduce myself to the agent and offered my services as capt of this flight and wanted to be made aware of any problems according to air carrier manual and far's these oxygen bottles were boarded illegally without my knowledge and proper paperwork delivered to me as capt. This is not my first rpt/dangerous goods manifest concerning this same situation in mia. It would appear there is a total disregard for the importance of hazmat procedures and/or training -- especially in delivering the dangerous goods manifest to the capt of a flt.
output: B767 CREW HAS HAD MIA GATE AGENTS VIOLATE COMPANY DANGEROUS GOODS PROCS ON MORE THAN 1 OCCASION.

input: After takeoff during initial climb out we received a automatic communications addressing & reporting system message. The message informed us of dangerous goods being carried and to expect a notoc (notification to captain) prior to gate departure.reporter suggests it would be preferable to have a system in place that would ensure a notoc was presented to the flight crew prior to closing the boarding door.
output: A-321 Captain reported uneventful flight completion after receiving airborne ACARS notification of undocumented Hazmat cargo cargo on board.

input: This is a repeat situation on denton tower frequency 119.95; dto. Inbound to dto at approximately xa46; the tower frequency 119.95 was monitored from 20 nautical mile westbound through landing it was noted that the tower controller was speaking continuously for at least 2 minute(s) in several bursts. The controller chastised a foreign student for 'not answering quickly' and berated another pilot for blocking the frequency (exactly what the controller was doing). It appeared that the controller was thinking aloud (mike switch depressed) when not otherwise directing traffic aside from being distracting; this made necessary radio calls almost impossible. Perhaps this was a new tower ctlr.
output: SMA PLT EXPRESSED CONCERN REGARDING ATC SERVICE AT DTO; LISTING ATC FREQ DISCIPLINE AND UNPROFESSIONAL TECHNIQUES AS DISTRACTIONS.

input: [there were] two cards. One i requested for runway xx using flaps 5. I looked at the reduced speeds and thought it was high for a 210;000 pounds b757. The [other] card was sent by request from dispatch. The only environmental difference between the two is the new one is for 209;400 pounds vs. My 210;800 pounds card on the left. Vr and v2 are 13 and 12 knots less on the dispatch message. Something is screwed up in some database or in the programming. When i tried to bug the first speeds; the v2 bug was within 13 knots of f5 maneuvering speed. I have never seen v2 that close to f5 maneuver speed. I know there can be differences between reduced and max power numbers; but look at the max numbers at the left card versus the reduced numbers. The fact that dispatch generated more reasonable numbers means the cockpit was accessing something else. Even after getting airborne; i was able to consistently generate unreasonably high reduced v-speeds at all sorts of weights. It shouldn't be 13 or 15 knots high. I'd hate to think of someone doing a high-speed reject at those unusually high numbers.
output: B757 First Officer questions takeoff V speeds generated by the FMC and asks Dispatch to send new numbers; which are significantly lower. The Dispatch numbers are used for takeoff.

input: Climbing to flight level 310 as cleared. Noticed traffic alert and collision avoidance system target closing climbing through fl26.5. Air traffic control told us to 'go back down and level off' at flight level 260. Received an resolution advisory to 'descend; descend' and we acted accordingly. Descending aircraft came within 400 feet vertical clearance.
output: CRJ-200 Captain reported NMAC in climb at FL265.

input: I used to fly for a commuter in atl. In atl; airport rules state that 'all aircraft shall readback all runway(s) holding instructions including aircraft ident.' this rule is a great safety device for airports with parallel runway(s) and it is printed on the atl airport diagram and spoken on the arrival, arrive and departure automatic terminal information service i now fly for a commuter in dfw and although their taxi procedures are much more complex there is no requirement to readback all runway(s) holding instructions. Why? Runway(s) incursions are the #2 violation in the united states army behind altitude busts; and with their parallel runway(s) operations(s) and super complex taxiway layout they should have a rule making runway(s) holding readbacks mandatory. I do it anyway but it should be a rule.
output: RPTR SUGGESTS ALL ARPTS OPERATING PARALLEL RWYS HAVE ARPT REQUIREMENT THAT ALL RWY HOLD INSTRUCTIONS BE READ BACK WITH FULL IDENT OF ACFT AND RWY.

input: I was working local one and two combined. Runway 17r departure windshear alerts off and on. Air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) waited in position for windshear with aircraft x on final. Windshear no longer indicated with aircraft x on a 10 mile final. Air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) and air carrier westbound depart. Air carrier y was given takeoff clearance with aircraft x on a 4 mile final. Then a runway 17r departure windshear alert goes off and air carrier y refuses takeoff. I try to get air carrier y off the runway and i messed up the call sign. I again try to get air carrier y and ultimately have to send aircraft x around.recommendations to prevent reoccurrence would be to not use a runway with windshear for mixed operations. I would like to use this space on the form to write a narrative for contributing factors. I have witnessed numerous wind shear alerts in the tower cab that pilots do not concur with more often then not. I have notified numerous supervisors and they have made phone calls about it and nothing has happened. A common phrase in the tower cab is runway 26 windshear alert 25 knot gain 2 mile final previous 15 arrivals did not experience it. Or runway 17r departure windshear alert 20 knot gain on the runway the airbus on climb out did not experience it. While the event with aircraft x could have been handled a lot better; i would like to take this opportunity to report this equipment's problems to someone outside of the facility so we will not continue business as usual; and with the equipment contributing to a go around with an air carrier on the runway hopefully it becomes a priority. In the hour on position not one pilot encountered the report on the llwas.
output: DEN Tower Controller described a go around event resulting from a departure delaying takeoff due to a windsheer alert. The reporter recommended limited use of 'mixed operations' when windshears are active.

input: Acft was launched from the airport on mar/xa/02. The torque link was disconnected for pushback. Upon disconnecting the tug and towbar from the aircraft the torque link was reconnected utilizing the torque link lock pin. Both mechs checkeded that the lock pin was installed correctly with the latch in the detent position the aircraft was then taxied out making 2 left/right (directions) turns to taxiway b; proceeding onto the active runway(s) eventually making a total of 5 turns. After lining up on the active runway(s) the aircraft made a normal takeoff with no gear problems during landing the pilot experienced severe nosewheel shimmy at 80 knot(s) utilizing alternate braking methods the pilot was able to keep the aircraft straight and then realized he had no steering. After coming to a stop he called tower and company came to tow aircraft off the runway(s) upon maintenance inspection of the aircraft they found a bushing missing from lower torque link assembly where lock pin is installed. The ground sense tube was bent; but lock pin was still attached to conduit in nosewheel. Both tires (nose) and the ground sense tube; conduit bracket as well as bushings on lower torque link were replaced. Inspection of the lock pin revealed no apparent damage but it was also replaced.
output: A B727-200 ON LNDG HAD SEVERE NOSE GEAR SHIMMY AND LOSS OF STEERING. CAUSED BY A MISSING LOWER TORQUE LINK BUSHING.

input: This procedure for takeoff is too complex when other problems arise on takeoff such as power or navigate, navigation problems on our takeoff that morning; the lateral navigation was slow to respond. The pilot flying was slow to turn; thus getting our flight close to the prohibited area. At about 4000 feet/foot the pilot flying trying to put the autoplt on; was unsuccessful; thus letting the aircraft get slow for the flap confign. Capt was distraction by air traffic control changing frequency pilot flying was a new hire and new to the aircraft he had a hard time flying the aircraft with no automation. There should be more basic hand flying in ioe.
output: LGT CAPT THINKS THE COMPLEXITY OF THE DCA DEP PROC IS OVERLY COMPLEX.

input: I was on the last leg of an instrument flight rules cross country with my student. I ante meridiem an instructor and have approximately 150 hours of dual given. The occurrence took place on the last leg of the cross country while returning to gfk. My student is very competent and had performed flawlessly throughout the flight after completing our approach at gaf (in imc) we received vectors from gfk approach control for the instrument landing system to runway(s) 35l for a full stop landing while receiving vectors for the approach i pulled my student's electric directional gyro/hsi unit. I asked the student what he planned to do to deal with the situation the student then decided to request 'no gyro vectors' from gfk approach for the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l. Gfk approach initiated the no gyro vectors at that time. My student and i discussed how we would commence with the approach (apch briefing). I pulled the compass circuit breaker to disable the directional gyro. We were heading south from gaf to gfk. After tuning and identing gfk; we were given our final no-gyro vector and approach clearance we were cleared for the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l. We intercepted the final approach course and my student started to track inbound and initially things were going well; then the course deviation indicator began to deviate and eventually went full scale. The deviations were most likely the result of the student overcorrecting on the approach course. When the course deviation indicator went full scale i told the student to execute a missed approach i also decided to reset the compass circuit breaker to reset the directional gyro. Gfk tower told us to track inbound on the localizer course which we proceeded to do. While this was occurring; the directional gyro did not begin to align itself with our magnetic heading and it simply froze. I was preoccupied with resetting the directional gyro and for that instant i let my student fly me around the sky. Our directional gyro was inoperative at that moment and i decided to take control of the aircraft tower assigned us a 270 degree heading and to my bet estimate we were heading roughly 250 degrees using the compass for heading information i executed a left/right (directions) turn to put us back on course. I then asked to be switched back to approach once i was back with approach i asked to maintain my current heading of 270 degrees while we troubleshot the problem after manually aligning the directional gyro to the compass we received vectors for the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l; did the approach without incident and landed the aircraft after landing my student and i debriefed on the occurrence and i explained what had happened. We both discussed the chain of events that took place and realized that instrument meteorological conditions was not the time or place to be 'pulling' instruments on the date of the incident i was not told by any air traffic control authority/authorized that action was being taken against me. However; today i was told that air traffic control had to file a separation violation because our aircraft came within 1 mile of another aircraft on the instrument landing system i feel the actions and decisions made on that day were for the most part acceptable. However; as i said before; i will not fail instruments under instrument meteorological conditions again. I also believe the best way to prevent such an occurrence from happening again is to fly under actual instrument meteorological conditions with all instrument operating!
output: FLT INSTRUCTOR; WITH STUDENT; DISABLED DIRECTIONAL GYRO IN IMC. OTHER TFC INVOLVED.

input: Missed altimeter setting. After leveling at fl310; fwc asked us to verify our altitude we responded with fl310. He then asked us to verify altimeter 29.92. We then realized we had not reset at fl180 and were 500 feet/foot off. We corrected immediately.
output: F100 CREW DID NOT SET QNE AT THE TRANSITION LEVEL IN ZFW CLASS A AIRSPACE.

input: Pages 10-2 through 10-2 celsius for toronto/pearson international airport are very poorly designed. The crossing restrictions seem to point at radial/dme arc's instead of given points. Example approach control expects ricki at a given altitude and speed but the arrow seems to point at a radial (unlabeled)/26 vor and dme (co-located) arc. It is a violation waiting to happen. This needs redesigning.
output: ACR FLT CREW'S COMPLAINT ABOUT THE DESIGN OF THE PROFILE DESCENT CHARTS FOR CYYZ.

input: On final approach and extending the landing gear; there was a gear warning light and horn activated as well as no green gear indicator lights illuminated. We called the tower to advise about the landing gear problem and requested a go around and visual inspection by the tower while we worked on the problem i was close to the runway(s) and high as i went by the tower with enough speed to make it difficult for the tower to confirm the gear status. However; the tower rpted that they thought the gear was not down. On this first approach to land i tried to recycle the landing gear several times with no results. The red gear warning light remained lit and indicated to me that the gear was not extending or retracting. I continued downwind on the first go around and checkeded the circuit breaker and found the gear circuit breaker tripped. We reset the breaker and tried to recycle the gear both up and down -- gear warning still lit. I tried to activate the emergency gear extension procedure several times and got the 2 main gear indicated green lights but not any green light for the nose gear. I checkeded the green gear indicator lights to make sure all light bulbs were operational; they were. We referred to the poh in the cockpit to make sure that i was following the emergency gear extension procedures precisely and i was with the exception of my 100 knot(s) airspd. The recommended gear extension speed is 80 knot(s) i was cleared to land a second time and elected to do another go around and slow pass by the tower for another visual inspection of the landing gear. The tower advised that the main gear looked down and normal but the nose gear was not fully extended. I elected to land on the next approach i attempted to perform the emergency gear extension procedure another 4 times at 80 knot(s) with no apparent effect on the nose gear extension problem i also tried to cycle the gear with the electric lever and the breaker popped out. I pulled out the emergency gear activation knob and we tried bouncing the nose up and down at under 80 knot(s) and tail walking with the rudder pedals to no avail. We never got any nose gear green light. The tower asked intermediate fix i wanted to land on runway(s) xxl as they were calling out emergency equipment we declined runway(s) xxl and requested runway(s) xxr to avoid congesting the main runway(s) as i felt comfortable to land runway(s) xxr. The tower handed me over to approach and i proceeded south on vectors while the emergency equipment was assembled. The tower finally cleared me for the third and last approach to land. Visibility was more than 10 mile visual meteorological conditions and few clouds at 3000 feet/foot weather was no factor. I touched down at 75 knot(s) cut off the engine fuel and electric; and rolled out in about 800 ft.
output: PA32 NOSE GEAR FAILED TO EXTEND. AFTER NUMEROUS ATTEMPTS TO EXTEND GEAR WERE UNSUCCESSFUL; EMER LNDG WAS CONDUCTED.

input: Prob was faulty wiring; resulting in 'false alert' in cockpit. Per procedures engine was shutdown and we landed elp. Indicator light (faulty) showed oil leak left/right (directions) engine found out after landing aircraft had been parked in desert for 1 1/2 yrs before being cleared to return to service only 1 month ago. 3 hours later; and after many calls to maintenance we finally were cleared to leave for lgb. My opinion: these 'old' aircraft have not been maintained; and are not up to my company's standards.
output: AN MD80 FLT ATTENDANT RPTED THAT AN ACFT RETRIEVED FROM DESERT STORAGE BY HER COMPANY EXPERIENCED AN ENG PROB DURING A FLT FROM DFW TO LGB; CAUSING THE CAPT TO DIVERT TO ELP.

input: First officer flying through fl200 on way to fl270; in instrument flight rules conditions. First officer and captain's airspeed indicators [were] unreliable. Standby airspeed indicator correct. Captain's airspeed indicator came back; but first officer's out for 5 minutes and eec (electronic engine control) systems went to standby. Qrc and quick reference handbook procedures accomplished as well as followup procedures. Anti-icing systems working; engine and wing heat on. Stayed as much out of weather; zzz closed; zzz1 still in visual flight rules weather and location of heavy maintenance for the b-737. Briefed flight attendants and passengers. Captain flew to zzz1; safety vehicles checked out aircraft.good crew coordination of verification of the unreliable airspeed indicators.don't fly into clouds with icing conditions. May have been multiple problems that happened at the same time. Eec systems went to standby while in heavy thick clouds; on climb out; through the freezing level.
output: Captain reported diverting after airspeed indications became unreliable in IMC conditions and the destination airport closed.

input: On the way to tvc; we listened to the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) (tower was closed) and the weather was 200/8g13 10 statute mile once we were stable on the approach we realized that the crosswinds were a lot higher than the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) had reported; we experienced turbulence and as we continued getting close to the runway the crosswinds were still stronger than expected; i decided to go around for the safety of the flight. On the way up to 3;000 feet we picked up a lot of ice; later the controller cleared us to climb to 4;000 feet and we were still picking up ice. I called to get a higher altitude to stay clear of ice. We were very busy. I determined that if vectored for another approach the ice accretion might exceed the deice capabilities of our ice protection system. As a result i decided to return for my alternate. I sent a message to the dispatcher informing that we were going back to [departure airport]; unfortunately i did not have enough time to relay more information to dispatch due to the short duration of flight. I think it was the safest and best thing to do; get more fuel and try again.asos weather report a crosswind completely different than actual wind.
output: EMB-145 Captain reported executing a go-around after encountering high winds and inflight icing during the approach to TVC.

input: On final; passing over the numbers on xxr [and] preparing to touch down probably no more than 10 ft. Above the runway; i experienced a wind shear which i think was a dust devil as i noticed swirling dust off my left wing. I lost all lift and hit the runway and subsequently veered off to the left-hand side. I was unable to control the direction of my aircraft.
output: Vans RV-3 Pilot reported encountering a dust devil on landing resulting in runway excursion.

input: My flight crew and i received our aircraft from the inbound crew with approximately 25 minute(s) until our scheduled departure time. As i did my preflt inspection i noted a mechanical irregularity that would have certainly light emitting diode to a delay in departure time or possibly the cancellation of the flight the irregularity was a faulty oil pressure gauge that would cause erroneous and unreliable readings. I chose to ignore the discrepancy and made every effort for an on time departure recent letters to the air carrier pilots from our president/ceo wzzxx has intimidated pilots to the point of ignoring mechanical irregularities. It is the position of the company that pilots who are making maintenance write-ups are participating in a work slowdown. It is believed by the pilots that we face possible reprimand from the company intermediate fix we are considered part of a slowdown. In fact; rumor has it as many as 20 capts are on a list and face suspension. My prior 2 flts had been canceled due to a maintenance write up i had made. I had an uncomfortable feeling after those 2 cancellations; now feeling like a target. Oddly enough; it was the same irregularity that i was again facing. I believed that had i made another write-up second officer soon after 2 cancellations; i would have certainly faced scrutiny by the company. At the same time; i believed that i would face scrutiny intermediate fix they knew about the discrepancy and i didn't write it up. It was a 'catch 22.' i made the decision to not rpt the irregularity based on my thought that it was less likely they knew the aircraft had the same discrepancy.
output: A FOKKER 28 WAS DISPATCHED IN NON COMPLIANCE WITH A KNOWN ENG OIL PRESSURE INDICATOR MALFUNCTION BUT NOT ENTERED IN LOGBOOK.

input: Acft descending bdf-plano heading 052 degrees (see chicago area) to dpa. Automatic terminal information service 1100' overcast 5f-wind 2815; land and depart runway(s) 28.' out of 4000' approach turned us right to 070 degrees left to 010 degrees 350; descend (in steps) to 2600'. He said he could clear us for the vor and dme (co-located) 28 circle to land immediately; but the instrument landing system would result in 'considerable delay.' we took the vor and dme (co-located) he vectored us nearly on top of dpa; then 'turn left to 068 inbound clearance for the approach contact tower now!' all at once the following occurred: we called tower broke out at about 1900' mean sea level (1100' agl) and watched an sma pass from 11 to 5 o'clock about 150 yds ahead; 150' below. Were only terrified for 2.65 secs--long enough. Tower replied; 'rpt fox river.' we replied; 'well past fox river on departure end of active 1900'.' controller turned us right to left downwind. No further problems no one complained. I doubt anyone else recognized anything was wrong; but we do. How do we prevent this? 1) obviously; the sma did not have visual flight rules sep; but i much prefer not having to rely on the other fellow for safety. 2) we knew before plano from automatic terminal information service that we would be approaching toward visual flight rules traffic departing; yet we proceeded as intermediate fix we had guaranteed sep all the way to the restroom. 3) approach turned us loose almost over the federal aviation administration a little more time might have helped. 4) tower didn't know where we were; exactly. By the time we all agreed on our position our problem had passed under us. 5) circling approachs are not even for the birds. I do not use them in restrict, restricted, restriction visibility; or much below 800' above ground level i now think they are even more dangers in barely vfr.
output: SMA PLT ON IFR APCH VECTORS DESCENDED THROUGH CLOUDS; HAD NMAC WITH SMA.

input: On nov/xa/99; i was first officer of air carrier x flight from bhm to phl. I was handling radio communicationss while capt was pilot flying also aboard was a jump seating employee. Ztl cleared us to climb to fl330. Shortly afterwards; we were handed off to another controller i advised air traffic control of our current altitude and climbing to fl330. Center instructed us to expedite to fl270. I repeated to expedite to fl270 and climbing to fl330. At approximately fl275; air traffic control asked intermediate fix we were leveling at fl270. The capt got on the radio and told center we were cleared to fl330 and expedite through fl270. At about this time; traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alerted us with a descend resolution advisory which we complied with. We descended below fl270 and after the resolution advisory climbed back to fl270. The capt advised air traffic control we were complying with a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory moments later we were cleared to climb to fl330. The capt acknowledged and apologized for any misunderstanding. The controller responded and did not imply there were any probs.
output: FLC OF A CANADAIR CL65 REGIONAL JET OVERSHOT ASSIGNED ALT DURING CLB RESULTING IN A TCASII RA TO WHICH THEY RESPONDED BY DSNDING BACK THROUGH ASSIGNED ALT.

input: The lear landed and was rolling out. The b350 was put in position for takeoff the lear appeared to be taxiing off the runway(s) the b350 was cleared for takeoff after clearing a jetstar to land; i looked back on the runway(s) and saw the lear had turned back onto the runway(s) and was taxiing to the next exit point. I looked at the b350 and he had rotated already. I told the b350 to offset to the left/right (directions) and he did. The aircraft never got within 5000 feet/foot of each other. Supplemental information from acn 505301: phx airport lands on runway(s) 7r and departs aircraft on runway(s) 7l during east traffic flow. A king air taxied out for departure from an fixed-base operator located south of runway(s) 7r. Arrs were landing runway(s) 7r. The tower local controller cleared a learjet to land on runway(s) 7r. As this happened; another controller came to the handoff position to give me a break. input: We were holding short of runway(s) 16 at xna. [an aircraft] had just been cleared for take off on a runway heading. Additionally; there was an aircraft inbound about 7 miles out on the instrument landing system 16. We were then cleared for take off via the highfill 8 turn heading 180.metar at the time: xna 08005kt 4sm -ra br sct005 ovc040 17/16 a3017 i was the non flying pilot and during the take roll; i noticed radar showed moderate rain (yellow) at the 180 heading. Once airborne and before the 400 feet heading call; i asked the tower for runway heading to avoid the weather. Tower approved the runway heading and at approximately 2;500 feet to 3;000 feet we received a terrain terrain alert. I looked first at my radar altimeter which was reading and flickering between 0 and - 5; our altitude was now over 3;000 feet; and we were climbing over 1500 feet per minute i stated i thought it was a spurious error; but due to the marginal weather conditions the first officerfollowed his instincts and went to max thrust. At about 4;000 feet i pulled up the instrument landing system 34 jepp chart and noted a tower 1;855 feet se of the localizer and about 8 km se of the airport. I also noted that our global positioning system position was showing on this chart and we were on the outbound localizer course. Additionally; there is no obstacle dp for runway(s) 16 on the 20-9 page. I still believe this was a spurious radar atl error but while troubleshooting i may have distracted the first officerfrom making the terrain max thrust call. Considering the marginal visual conditions i should have stated terrain instead of troubleshooting.
output: E175 flight crew reported ATC approved weather avoidance clearance where crew received a terrain alert that the Captain doubted resulted in failure to call and allow First Officer proper escape and recover maneuver.

input: I ante meridiem reporting a poorly flown course into runway(s) 19l; at wichita mid continent airport i filed my instrument flight rules flight plan in the air en route to wichita; i was under radar vectors to the back course instrument landing system and on the back course instrument landing system when i was a mile off course on final approach to the best of my knowledge i did not bust any altitudes i was under radar surveillance at all times; was descending to visual flight rules visibility and ceilings below me. To the best of my knowledge did not come close to any other aircraft or endanger any property. However i did fly very poorly an unacceptable back course instrument landing system due to the fact i was off course both to the left and to the right back course instrument landing system i believe the reasons to be for such a poorly flown instrument landing system are twofold. My area of blame is that i started this flight visual flight rules i was flying down on business and my mind was on the business; not tuned to fly instrument flight rules and with visual flight rules ceilings and visibility below the clouds i was not concerned about making a precision approach therefore i was lax in my flying. I was flying an aircraft that was different than the one i had been flying in previous months; different radios; in different arrangements; and different flying characteristics; an sma x versus an sma y. Therefore i was not as comfortable in flying this aircraft as i was in flying the sma x. I had a directional gyro that was precessing more than what i was used to; however; it was acceptable for instrument flight rules flight but my xchk had become lax due to the fact that the sma x had a better dg and it did not have any precessing. In my defense the approach control into mid west continent were not always clear as to at which point i was given clearance to fly the approach mid continent approach control told me to expect a back course instrument landing system for 19l and for some reason due to either poor radio transmission or my inattentiveness or their language and i don't know which one is to blame. I never felt throughout the flight until the very end that i had been cleared for a back course instrument landing system at one time on the radio and had crossed the instrument landing system and was heading westbound of it and i asked intermediate fix i was to turn on the instrument landing system or maintain heading they then had me turn to a heading to intercept the instrument landing system and i was on a zigzag pattern heading coming back down the ils.
output: GA SMA TRACK HEADING DEVIATION WHILE MAKING AN ILS BC APCH TO ICT.

input: Captain was pilot flying. We had been cleared on the flight management system bridge visual approach to runway 28r. Air traffic control informed us that an rj aircraft was on visual approach to 28l with our aircraft in sight and would follow us in. We initially saw him abeam of us before he turned onto final. Approaching samul i observed the rj close to us but above and behind. Just prior to samul air traffic control advised be that the aircraft we were following to 28r had slowed to 110 knot(s) and advised us to slow to slowest practical speed. Vref for flaps 25 was 131. At 180 knot(s) flaps 15 i called for gear down flaps 20 and began to slow to approach speed. Wind was reported at 17 knot(s) i called for flaps 25 when the gear was down and slowed to 137. Inside samul approaching f101d approximately 1;300 feet/foot above ground level we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory alert to climb. The vsi arc showed red from about 10 o'clock to 6 o'clock on the dial with no green guidance. Knowing that the rj at last view was just above me and to my left i chose not to follow the resolution advisory climb command since any climb would place me in the rj's flight path. I decided to accelerate the aircraft to 150 knots to gain lateral separation from the rj since i could not see him. I turned the traffic alert and collision avoidance system to traffic advisory and continued the visual meteorological conditions approach to a stabilized approach and landing. After landing and shutdown i called sfo tower supervisor to advise him of the resolution advisory alert and that i thought the rj had not provided enough visual separation as they had been instructed to do. Sfo air traffic control continually pushes the limits on separation when visual approaches are in use. Sfo air traffic control relies on flight crews to provide aggressive separation distances to make their arrival rates work. It's almost akin to formation flying doing visual approaches to sfo.
output: B767 Captain on visual approach to Runway 28R reports a TCAS RA caused by the aircraft on the visual to Runway 28L. The reporter speeds up and continues the approach to landing.

input: Fire alarm went off due to smoke at 4l we all smelled electrical; like a hairdryer burning up x10. Used a halon but water came out of it. input: Level at 6000 feet/foot mean sea level we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii advisory. input: Apching slc in receipt of automatic terminal information service information the rpted airport visibility was 4 mile from 8-10 mile north the airport was in sight; as were numerous other inbound aircraft the approach was briefed for clear air turbulence i/visual possibilities. On downwind vector approach controller requested we rpt the airport in sight. Since the first officer was the pilot flying i informed him i had the airport in sight. By agreement we did not call the airport in sight to air traffic control until on left/right (directions) base; outside flagg when we both could see runway(s) other traffic and terrain in distance. Approach control then cleared us for visual approach to runway(s) 34l which we had insight. As the pilot flying (fo); called 'gear down; flaps 15 degrees set spd.' tower cleared us to land on runway(s) 34l; then added 'rwy 34l runway visual range greater than 6000 feet/foot mid field 400 ft.' since we were always clear of clouds; inflt visibility greater than 3 mile with our most recent automatic terminal information service rpting 4 mile airport visibility; i accepted landing clearance the final approach and landing were conducted in visual conditions. Only taxiing to clear the runway(s) did we encounter a brief area of ground based obscuration that reduced visibility briefly. In retrospect; i question approach control giving us a visual clearance intermediate fix ground fog was a known factor. It was not apparent to us at any point until taxi speed should this occur again; i would call for a go around to clarify weather intermediate fix the automatic terminal information service had in fact changed and airport visibility was below 3 mile that should have been broadcast by either approach or tower -- not just runway visual range greater than 6000 feet/foot clearing the runway(s) it was easy to miss the turn on taxiway a and continue to taxiway b; the unlit parallel taxiway since ground ctl's only instructions were 'taxi east to gate.'
