input: I departed my home base late afternoon and flew to oxc; arriving at approximately about a half hour later. I was flying solo (the sole occupant of the plane). Upon arriving at oxc; i requested taxi to the east side of field as i was meeting somebody there. The tower gave me taxi instructions and i proceeded. As i went to make a 180 degree turn to park the plane into the tie down; i misjudged my clearance on the left hand side; causing the plastic wing tip to strike a chain-link fence at an angle of about 10 degrees. Immediately upon realizing what happened; i shut down the aircraft; and a line crew member in the area helped me push the plane off the fence and to a more suitable location. Inspection of the damage revealed broken strobe and nav lights; some paint damage; and a small dent on the front left corner of the plastic wing tip. I immediately called our operations officer and we decided to have the plane towed to the maintenance shop to get a disposition on the plane. When the plane was towed; the fixed-base operator staff were all in consensus that the damage was very minor and cosmetic; and that as long as we unscrewed the bracket for one of the lights and taped over the dangling wiring harness from the lights; the plane could be flown back. With help from the fixed-base operator the bracket was unscrewed; the area taped over; and the aircraft was flown back to its home base without incident; arriving back still during daylight hours.it is noteworthy that multiple people noted to me that i was far from the first person to strike a fence in that area. I was shown other places where planes struck; and have been told that some planes have even practically taken the fence out. While i accept fault for misjudging my clearance on my left side; it appears as though this spot for some reason poses a problem for pilots. Perhaps further action should be taken in the future to make the parking in this area more pilot-friendly.
output: A single engine pilot taxiing and turning to a tie down spot reported striking the wingtip on a chain link fence at OXC. The plastic wingtip; nav light; and strobe were damaged. Maintenance secured the damaged area which allowed the pilot to return to his home base.

input: We departed runway(s) 24 on runway(s) heading; climbed to 1500 feet/foot and then turned to heading 280 degrees at 4.5 vor and dme (co-located) we climbed to 2000 feet/foot at some point during numerous hand-offs and radio transmissions; air traffic control commented that we needed to 'check your compliance with the sid.' to the best knowledge our teb 5 departure had been completed correctly. Air traffic control implied that there was a discrepancy between our altitude and the altitude specified on the departure the departure occurs very quickly once airborne and is complicated by several radio frequency changes. Normally altitude changes are directed by air traffic control rather than left up to the crew of the aircraft this greatly reduces the work-load of the crew especially when they are concentrating on directional changes dictated by a sid.
output: CAPT OF LJ35 DISPUTES DEP CTLR'S IMPLICATION OF AN ALT DISCREPANCY ON THE TEB SID FROM RWY 24.

input: Climbing in instrument meteorological conditions from fl270 to fl280 we had an abrupt loss of all systems related to the avnx mau 1a failure including autopilot; autothrust; stick shaker; mcdu 1; automatic communications addressing & reporting system etc. We leveled off and started the quick reference handbook procedure and during the process we were able to recover the failed mau. I contacted dispatcher to advise that another subsequent failure would require an emergency declaration and to prepare for a landing with half our brakes; half the spoilers; no nose wheel steering and a required tow from the runway. We didn't have another subsequent failure and landed normally where the aircraft was taken to the hangar. We tried contacting multiple arinc frequencies while enroute and were unable to connect with either sfo or ny radio. After regaining the automatic communications addressing & reporting system we were able to maintain contact with dispatch. Hats off to my first officer for being vigilant and of great help.failure in the modular avionics unit taking out numerous crucial systems.my main issue was with the failure taking out the automatic communications addressing & reporting system and my inability to contact arinc on multiple frequencies. I called both sfo radio and ny radio.
output: ERJ-190 Captain reported loss of an MAU (Modular Avionics Unit) that caused multiple systems failures. They regained use of the MAU after running the QRH procedure.

input: With auxiliary power unity running and in the blocks at gate preparing for pushback; cockpit filled up with heavy; acrid smoke. Turned off packs and closed bleed valves; smoke slowly dissipated. Smoke emanated from the vent areas on the lower left side of the flight deck. First officer got up and opened l1 door; stairs were in place. Contacted ramp tower; who notified fire department; and then we contacted maintenance. Conferred with both maintenance and fire crew; wrote up discrepancy.possible de-icing of the tail area without notification to flight crew. When leaving the aircraft; noticed de-ice fluid on the ground. There was also snow in the courier area and main cargo deck upon arrival at the aircraft. Called maintenance; who removed the snow and water; but moisture may have gotten into certain systems.
output: A B757-200 filled with smoke while at the gate with the APU running. The smoke dissipated with the packs off and bleeds closed. Apparently the de-ice crew allowed fluid to enter the APU intake.

input: This report is an example of how i believe the anti-ice checklist item would be more effective in the taxi check than in the second half of the starting engines check. First flight of the day; the aircraft had frost on the upper fuselage and left wing. [weather was] three degrees celsius and visual meteorological conditions after pushback; while finishing up the starting engines checklist; anti-ice is one of the items we must evaluate. In this case; the weather/ramp conditions were normal; so cowls weren't needed for taxi. Wings weren't called for either; since it wasn't final taxi. We taxied to de-ice for type i. Upon completion; we then complete the taxi checklist; but anti-ice isn't on this checklist. It's left to the crew to remember an item called for ten to twenty minutes ago (or more; in jfk) and to use 'common sense' as a chief pilot told me when i discussed the issue with him. Consider this situation if light snow were falling but type i offered an adequate holdover time. Procedures would require us to have the wing anti-ice on in this situation (as opposed to type iv; when it isn't needed until just before takeoff thrust). Cowls would be needed if the taxiways were contaminated. But the checklist item was called for at the gate; not after de-ice. What would it hurt to have de-ice in the taxi check vs. Starting engines? If you're deicing and therefore not performing the taxi check until later; it wouldn't be a problem to not turn on the anti-ice just after push; because the deicing process would eliminate any accumulation. The same is not true in the reverse scenario. Now; perhaps because the type i holdover times are shorter; it's not a factor in forgetting to turn it on for taxi because the checklist calls for it again prior to takeoff. But it certainly wouldn't hurt having the checklist item in a more advantageous position on the checklist.
output: A CRJ50 Pilot suggested placement of the ANTI-ICE Checklist on the Taxi Checklist is more appropriate than its present location on the Starting Engines Checklist.

input: This rpt focuses on the current fuel conservation program utilized by our air carrier and i ante meridiem using as an example a flight that i flew in jul/08 in an airbus 319. The weather was good; the arrival, arrive rate into zzz1 was not heavy during our scheduled arrival, arrive time and the operations(s) of the flight was about as perfect as can be expected in today's world. It took only 14 minute(s) from pushback to takeoff we got right up to altitude and we landed straight-in to the south which also placed us close to the gate. We were vectored twice; 10-15 degrees left/right (directions) of course; for traffic for about 3 minute(s) each. Release fuel allowed 1.4 for taxi out of zzz2; no alternate; no contingency fuel and only 15 minute(s) of hold fuel. Our mandatory reserve was 3.5 and the flight plan showed a shutdown fuel of 5.0. This is outside of safe boundaries in my opinion because it had no margins for the unexpected. For this to go as planned; everything had to work perfectly which is the exception and not the rule. Also; as a flight travels further westbound there are fewer locations available to divert into and there are usually greater distances to travel to get to them. I added 1.7 in fuel. This increased our actual ramp weight only 357 pounds over our planned ramp weight we took a 17 minute(s) delay past departure time to get the fuel because we received the release only 20 minute(s) prior to departure time and it took that longitude to evaluate the fuel; coordination and get it on board. We still arrived 17 minute(s) early at zzz1. Our shutdown fuel was 6.7 second officer a dispatcher or bureaucratic supervisory pilot federal aviation regulation removed from the real world of operations(s) might argue that intermediate fix the 1.7 hadn't been added; we would've shut down with our scheduled 5.0 fuel. However; intermediate fix we had burned all of our 1.4 taxi fuel; which would not be unusual leaving; our shutdown would've been 4.0 which is 500 pounds above our reserve. I would also point out that since the shutdown; fuel was the equivalent of 5.0; the cost of adding the additional fuel was negligible in this case. Second officer what do i mean by no margins for the unexpected? First; the software utilized for fuel planning has a built-in negative bias. On many rtes it falls apart on the arrival, arrive portion of the flight on our flight we flew the standard terminal arrival route and the flight plan reflected no standard terminal arrival route waypoints instead showing us going direct to zzz2 and landing within 10 minute(s) our actual time was 13 minute(s) and would've been federal aviation regulation worse intermediate fix we had landed to the north the flight plan showed us at fl220 over abc with a ground speed of 341 knot(s) when our actual altitude was 12000 feet/foot slowing to 250 knots indicated airspeed another example is arriving in zzz2 from the south typically the flight plan shows us at fl280 over xxxx when we will always be at 15000 feet/foot over xxxx as directed by air traffic control a flight cancels and fills up another flight increasing its payload and; therefore; its fuel burn over what is planned. Insufficient fuel allowed for taxi and no fuel available to xfer down below the takeoff minimum line. Flight is caught in a runway(s) change either departing or arriving. An arrival, arrive runway(s) is closed because of a disabled aircraft or other reason. Major vectors off course and/or speed changes for inbound sequencing by air traffic control not an unusual occurrence. Forced to depart early from altitude or not allowed up to planned cruise altitude by air traffic control weather crumps in spite of the forecast. Pulled off an instrument landing system approach by approach control due to insufficient spacing. Handoff refused by the next air traffic control sector requiring a 360 degree turn by the current controller a missed approach or even multiple missed approachs for various reasons. The fueler shorts the fuel load by a couple hundred pounds happens all the time. And; finally; ship x has an engine intermix. I have no data available to me on engine fuel flows and i do not know intermediate fix they burn at the same rate. I doubt very much that the fuel software reflects any differences. All i'm trying to say with all of this is that we're cutting things just a little too skinny with our current fuel philosophy. I recommend a minimum 30 minute(s) of holding fuel on all flts. That would automatically cover many of these contingencies and the added cost would be minimal. It is money well spent for safety and to minimize diversions.
output: A319 CAPT LAMENTS THE LACK OF CONTINGENCY FUEL FOR FLIGHTS WITH NO ALTERNATE REQUIRED.

input: We were dispatched with #1 generator inoperative second officer we were running the auxiliary power unity continuously for our second generator. The #2 generator was written up for having high rise temperature coming into sfo. The mechs drained some constant speed driven oil out and we ran the engine at the gate and the generator was within all limits. In cruise; we noticed the rise temperature was in the yellow band and climbing it stabilized at 29 degrees celsius we tried calling dispatch through comrdo but dispatch could not hear me speaking (i could hear him but it was weak). Second officer i had comrdo tell him i would automatic communications addressing & reporting system him and maintenance controller we sent 2 messages to maintenance controller requesting information on how longitude you can run in the yellow band. Maintenance controller never responded to any of our queries. We tried to shed as much electrical load that we could (recirculation fan; galley power and one fuel pump on #2). No help. We looked at the chklist regarding high constant speed driven oil temperature the chklist did not offer any guidance for operating in the yellow band; it only provided a solution for the high oil temperature light on (which we did not have). We also referred to the electrical chapter to determine operating limits. We had no high oil temperature light second officer we left the generator running. We were about midway between rno and slc when the generator dropped off line. We switched the autoplt to 'a' and the capt took over as the pilot flying we declared an emergency and looked at the chklist for loss of 1 bus. We then checkeded our options of airfields. We decided to continue to slc due to good weather familiarity with the field; and suitable runway(s) we then notified dispatch. We gave a cabin advisory to the flight attendants (we did this before we declared the emer). We then flew an uneventful visual approach using the auxiliary power unity generator to supply all electrical needs to runway(s) 34r at slc. No equipment or other services were needed. We taxied to the gate.
output: B737-300 CREW HAD THE #1 GENERATOR MEL'ED INOP. THE #2 GENERATOR TRIPPED OFF WITH A HIGH RISE TEMP. ONLY THE APU GENERATOR WAS OPERATING.

input: Location: bwi 230 degree radial; 20 vor and dme (co-located) was climbing out of bwi; assigned a heading of 230 degrees with clearance to climb to; i believe; 17000 feet/foot when handed off to dca departure new vector of 270 degrees was issued with climb clearance to fl230. We told dca departure that there was severe thunderstorms to the westbound and sw and the overhang was directly above us and that we were unable to turn to a heading of 270 degrees and climb rapidly to fl230. His response was 'ok; just fly heading 270 degrees and i need a good rate of climb to fl230.' we told him again we were unable to climb to fl230 and that we needed to fly present heading for about another 10 mile or second officer his response was again the same. We finally decided to continue a slow climb about 1000 feet per minute and maintained our heading of about ssw to avoid level 6 thunderstorms controller mentioned that we could not turn any further left/right (directions) because of p56 prohibited area and he couldn't hand us off to zdc until we climbed to fl230. He then gave us another turn into the weather and we again told him we were unable to turn into that weather he was silent for a couple of minute(s) then asked intermediate fix we could turn to the westbound this time we were past the biggest cell and turned to the westbound and continued a good rate of climb to fl230. He then handed us off to zdc and we were given clearance to continue our climb and intercept our file route supplemental information from acn 407061: as all of this was going on; we were also dealing with an abnormal procedure of a left/right (directions) high temperature pack light. We were held on the ground in bwi for 1 hour for weather to the westbound and when we were released; the spacing was 25 mile in trail. We were the first departure out of bwi after they released aircraft wbound.
output: A CLBING; DEPARTING S80 PIC HAS A PROB WHEN THE DEP CTLR REPEATEDLY ISSUES A HDG AND CLB CLRNC THAT WILL STEER THEM INTO A TSTM SW OF BWI. IF CLRNC NOT ACCEPTED THE FLT WILL PENETRATE THE P56 PROHIBITED AREA IN DCA. CAPT ELECTS TO PENETRATE P56.

input: We were taxiing in to gate x at lax. As we rounded the corner into the alley; i was initially distraction trying to find gate x at terminal x. This is complicated by the numbers on the terminal itself -- well to the left/right (directions) of the actual jetway. I shut down the #2 engine and was further distraction by the lack of a marshaller and a lavatory truck; which was parked on the left/right (directions) side of the safety zone. I gave a quick look at the left/right (directions) side of the safety zone; and it appeared clear prior to being obscured by the left/right (directions) wing as i lined up the aircraft perpendicular to the j line. I turned onto the jetway run in line and virtually came to a complete stop; as we still had no marshaller. My first officer and i again were distraction to the left/right (directions) of the aircraft by a group of about 6 individuals just standing around at gate x immediately to the left/right (directions) of our gate. Just then; as i had almost come to a complete stop; a female ramper stepped out from the left/right (directions) of the jetway and began marshalling us in. I added power to the #1 and followed her directions. She hesitated just slightly and looked a little nervous; second officer i wondered to myself intermediate fix she was qualified to marshal; but she seemed sure of her marshalling commands. My first officer commented at that time that it 'looked a little tight' and i disregarded his comment thinking that the alleyway in lax is always congested. I had to add a little more power just prior to her 'stop' command. Almost simultaneously with that; my first officer commented that a ramper on the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft was signaling for us to stop. We then saw a group of people gathered at the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft and a ramp supervisor came to the fo's side. After opening the window; he informed us that we had made contact with a baggage loaded. We informed him that we did have a marshaller and went downstairs to inspect the damage. There was a group of dents on the lower left/right (directions) side of the nose cowl -- approximately 1/2 inch deep and 6-8 inches in length. There was also a puncture on the outboard fan cowl. I immediately called dispatch; maintenance control and the chief pilot on duty. Both my first officer and i failed to adequately clear the safety zone on the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft and missed the baggage loader protruding into the safety zone on the left/right (directions) we had numerous distrs to the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft which should have been our first warning flag. In hindsight; i should have stopped the aircraft on the j-line until an adequate number of personnel wre present to continue marshalling operations(s) to the gate. I also feel strongly about the level of ramp congestion in the alleys at lax. This has been an extremely congested and dangerous place to taxi for as longitude as i have worked here. There is absolutely no valid reason to have anything parked in an aircraft safety zone when an aircraft is not parked at the gate. Ramp supervisors should be training personnel to high standards and enforcing them as longitude as this congested ramp area continues to exist. Furthermore; the lack of attention and motivation of ramp personnel at lax continues to be disappointing. Supplemental information from acn 532023: both of us were looking outside and were very alert and attentive to the parking of the aircraft we were distraction as the circumstances detailed above illustrate which caused our attention to focus ahead and toward the l-hand side of the aircraft causing us to miss seeing the belt loader on the r-hand side of the aircraft the distrs caused my attention to focus on the 10-12 o'clock position as opposed to scanning the entire area of the safety zone. Had i performed my normal scan; i would have possibly seen the belt loader and had the capt stop the aircraft in retrospect; i realize i was federal aviation regulation more distraction than i realized at that time. In the future; i will try not to allow myself to focus on any one specific area. In addition; i think that procedures and training for ground personnel should be looked at. As a minimum; i feel that aircraft being pushed back or marshalled in at lax should be under a minimum of a 3-person watch due to all of the ramp congestion.
output: A B737-300 CREW; WHILE APCHING JETWAY AT LAX; MADE CONTACT WITH A BELT LOADER DAMAGING #2 ENG.

input: Acft arrived at the gate from the maintenance hangar after a terminal checked aircraft was visually inspected by maintenance after arrival, arrive i then completed a visual walkaround and found everything normal. After arrival, arrive at abc; [during] my walkaround of the aircraft i found the trailing edge of the left/right (directions) elevator damaged. Further inspection found considerable damage on the top of the elevator. No damage was visible at xxx during preflt by both myself and maintenance aircraft was grounded until elevator was replaced. Maintenance at zzz said the plane was struck by a stair truck; but didn't know when. The area of damage would not be visible from the ground from any position the missing chunk of elevator apparently came off after air pressure was applied during flight no control indications of vibration were noted.
output: A B757-200 DURING PREFLT CHK FO DISCOVERED THE TRAILING EDGE OF THE R ELEVATOR DAMAGED. MAINT IN ZZZ RPTED DAMAGE CAUSED BY A STAIR TRUCK; BUT DON'T KNOW DATE OR TIME.

input: On maintenance task job card #x; procedure was performed on #1 engine of aircraft this included removal and installation of the fan blades and associated components. All work was performed per air carrier maintenance task job card #x and maintenance manual. I was notified that aircraft experienced a problem with #1 engine during departure from zzz. Upon returning; it was discovered that a fan blade platform had liberated from the fan blade section. I reviewed the maintenance task job card and maintenance manual referred to above and ante meridiem confident all parts were installed correctly. Intermediate fix the platform in question had not been installed properly; the next step in the installation process could not have been completed. The fan blade retaining ring can only be installed intermediate fix all platforms are correctly installed.
output: AN INSPECTOR AND MECHANIC ARE INFORMED THE B737-700 #1 ENG THEY HAD WORKED ON TEN MONTHS EARLIER HAD LIBERATED A FIRST STAGE FAN BLADE PLATFORM FROM THE SAME ENGINE.

input: I was on final for runway(s) 26 and cleared to land approximately 4 mile out. Tower told me to be #3 to land. I repeated (confirmed) that i was cleared to land as #4. I proceeded on final and saw 2 aircraft landing and getting off active runway(s) (to txwy). When i came closer to the threshold; i noticed a high wing white cessna in the takeoff position as i had landed that morning 3 times previously; the white cessna at first looked like remnants of snow on the runway(s) but when i realized that the snow was also the cessna; i sidestepped my approach glide to my left/right (directions) second officer that i could observe the cessna staying in a hold position at that time the tower said 'acft on final; go around.' since there were 1 or 2 other aircraft behind me; i understood that someone else was meant! Next; i started to flare out on the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) since i kept an eye on the cessna. I think just when i touched down the tower said 'acft go around.' this was too late for me.
output: RV6A PLT HAS A RWY INCURSION AND LANDS WITHOUT CLRNC AT FTG.

input: About 1/2 way into flight from lax-ord; there was light to moderate chop. Having finished service i was sitting on the forward jump seat with another flight attendant. Suddenly (without warning) the plane jolted 4 or 5 times. I was not hurt due to the fact i was sitting; and did not realize how bad it was in the back of the plane. No passenber were hurt; they were all fastened in. The remainder of the flight there was moderate turbulence we landed without further probs.
output: CABIN ATTENDANT ON A B767-200 RPT OF TURB DURING HIGH ALT CRUISE RESULTING IN NO INJURY TO HERSELF; BUT TO ANOTHER CABIN ATTENDANT IN THE BACK OF THE CABIN.

input: Shortly after takeoff; had bird strike at about 1;500 feet/foot very loud strike; stayed at pattern altitude while we communicated with dispatch and maintenance control. Flew for about 25 minutes to burn some fuel and conduct overweight checklist. After consultation with maintenance; we conducted an uneventful landing. Emergency was declared not knowing if nosecone was damaged. After landing; discovered point of impact was below first officer's front windshield. No apparent damage and overweight inspection conducted. Fueled and continued to destination.
output: A320 Captain reports bird strike at 1500 FT on departure. Emergency is declared and flight returns to departure airport for inspection.

input: Reported 10 west of dwh with [current atis] and was told to report right downwind for 17r about one mile later further instructions continue for right base 17r number two following an aircraft on short final. Three miles out made contact with aircraft on short final and was told cleared to land keep my speed up and head for the numbers of 17r aircraft following. Turning final with the #1 aircraft still in sight and on the runway i started preparing for a go around. Tower told him twice to expedite. Desending through 200-100 over the threshold that aircraft got airborne after a touch and go. After touchdown tower said thanks for the help and asked where i was parking. After my speed was under control and assured taxiway echo i replied. Instructed to contact ground on echo. Exited the runway on echo ensured my tail was cleared (concern about aircraft #3) came to a stop and contacted ground. Was instructed by ground to taxi to the ramp via echo cross 17l a minute later was contacted to called the tower with a phone number. Spoke to the controller. At that time i was made aware by him there was a possibility of a incursion on 17l. To my knowledge i complied with all signs and markings. The controller mentioned a light identifying the hold short line at echo and 17l but it was not visible or illuminated. I'm aware of the hot spot and operated cautiously and safely in that area.as a pilot for the last 25 years; in retrospect don't understand why that spot is not controlled by the tower.
output: After landing on DWH Runway 17R then clearing at Taxiway E; a Pilot held short of Runway 17L but was informed by Tower that he may have incurred the Runway at the hotspot. The pilot disagreed.

input: I was approaching the airport from the northwest for the purpose of landing. The tower instructed me to enter left traffic on tunway 36 and report mid field. The tower had not yet spotted me. I was still about 5 miles out at this point. The tower then cleared a bonanza for takeoff on 36 and approved a right turn out. The bonanza pilot then requested a left turn out which the tower approved and told the bonanza to be on the lookout for my cessna. The tower then called me and asked me my altitude; which was 2;500 i had not yet started my decent to the pattern altitude of 1;800. The tower did not tell me to hold this altitude. The tower then advised me they had cleared a bonanza for left turn out. I told the tower i would be looking for the traffic which i never had in sight. I was about 3 miles northwest at this point and was about to start my decent. Then suddenly the bonanza passed right underneath my cessna with no time for me to take evasive action. The bonanza pilot immediately told the tower what had happened and nothing else was said. I have flown into this airport several times and this was the first time i ever had a problem. The tower always seems to know what they are doing. As a pilot i know how difficult it can some times be to spot traffic and even more so for a controller with no radar at a class d airport. I think it would improve safety if class d towers assigned altitudes and had some type of radar to help them spot traffic.
output: A C180 pilot reports a near miss with a Bonanza aircraft while the reporter was approaching a Class D airport from which the Bonanza departed. ATC called the traffic but did not provide controlling instructions to prevent a conflict.

input: Had a plane swap in xxx. After the first officer's preflight; he mentioned to me that the number 2 main tire had a puncture and should be checked by maintenance. We called maintenance out and; after looking at it; they stated that the tire was within the puncture limits of 3/8 of an inch or less in depth and that we were good to go. My first officer had gone into the terminal to take care of some personal business and; upon his return; i told him what maintenance had told me. My first officer stated to me that this did not sound right to him and that i should go look at it with him so i could see it for myself. We went outside to see the puncture and determined that it was much deeper then 3/8 of an inch and went as deep as the tire cord. I returned to the cockpit and called maintenance back out for a second opinion on this tire. A maintenance supervisor came out and confirmed that yes the tire was damaged and needed to be changed. The tire was changed and logbook completed. We left xxx 45 minutes late. Upon my return to the cockpit prior to our departure; i was both somewhat upset and shocked that a company mechanic would release an aircraft for flight with an unsafe tire. I thanked my first officer for his persistence in pursuing this matter to its safe conclusion. As a result of having to call out maintenance twice; i did not follow my standard cockpit flow in preparing for departure and missed the notice to airmen / of air missions for runway closure. We encountered scattered thunderstorms on our way to our destination and requested numerous vectors to circumnavigate our way there. Needless to say this required our utmost attention on the short flight and there was no time to reflect on our departure from xxx and the fact that i had not reviewed the notams. Upon arrival into the approach environment; we requested runway 18 since the winds were 170/07 knots. Air traffic control then cleared us for the rnav/gps 08 and handed us off to the common traffic advisory frequency upon stating our intentions over the common traffic advisory frequency we were informed by airport operations that runway 08 was closed and we then entered a right downwind for runway 27 and landed uneventfully. This airport does not have digital automatic terminal information service so my first officer received it over comm 2 and did not recall anything about a runway closure nor did air traffic control mention anything about a closed runway.letting my emotions get to me in xxx after the tire change and having my pre-departure flow interrupted. Taking a minute to take a couple deep breaths and relax could have prevented this.
output: A crew departed for an airport with a NOTAM for a closed runway which was requested for landing but advised on CTAF it was closed. The Captain was upset with himself for missing the NOTAM closure; but during the flight's preflight was distracted by maintenance's failing to identify and change a damaged tire until notified twice by the crew.

input: Maintenance in zzzz found the cannon plug broken on the first officer's stick shaker. We applied minimum equipment list 27-32-02 which has you pull and collar the circuit breaker for the affected system isolating the stick shaker motor. The cannon plug was secured and capped per the aircraft maintenance manual (amm) chapter-20; since it could not be re-connected to the broken receptacle on the motor. Initially; an engineering authorization was pursued until we realized that we could deactivate the system by pulling and collaring the circuit breaker per the minimum equipment list and that would isolate the broken connector. At that point; with engineering management's concurrence; we did not pursue an engineering authorization. The system was deactivated by pulling and collaring the circuit breaker for the stick shaker per the minimum equipment list  the cannon plug on the motor was broken; it was not removed for isolation of the motor; and it could not be connected to the receptacle on the motor. I felt that the intent of the minimum equipment list was met and that we were not further isolating the system with the broken cannon plug being disconnected as the maintenance alert states. [recommend] clarifying the intent of maintenance alert xx-000. What is the exact communication from the federal aviation administration on this? When an item of equipment is inoperative (stick shaker motor cannon plug circuit breaker) and maintenance is deferred under the guidance of the minimum equipment list (pull and collar circuit breaker); the airplane must be operated under all applicable conditions and limitations contained in the minimum equipment list (pull and collar circuit breaker). Until further notice; if an additional isolation procedure is deemed to be necessary at any time during the deferral period of an minimum equipment list item; contact maintenance control and submit an engineering request. Engineering may issue an engineering authorization on a case by case basis to permit these procedures if appropriate. If engineering does not issue an engineering authorization; or the conditions of the minimum equipment list cannot be met; the item must be repaired prior to further flight. Additional isolation needs to be defined. This was a broken cannon plug on the stick shaker motor. Is this an additional isolation; or an inoperative system addressed by the mel? Aircraft maintenance manager.
output: An Aircraft Maintenance Manager reports about the need for clarification of a company Maintenance Alert that describes the importance of requesting an Engineering Authorization (E/A) when an additional isolation procedure is applied during a deferral process. Cannon plug for the first officer's Stick Shaker motor was broken and was capped-off; but was not part of the MEL procedure for deferral of the Stick Shaker System on a B757-200.

input: We experienced a recurring taxiway incursion problem the aggravating thing is that i had already seen a rpt of it before our event. There are some mitigating circumstances i believe contributed to us missing the gate. One of the big problems is getting out to the aircraft with enough time to preflt without being rushed. The crew van situation in sdf can make this very difficult; especially when they are svcing multiple ramps. This is an ongoing source of frustration and i would like to advocate that vans only service 1 ramp. There were problems with the computer/printer interface; which necessitated a call to technical support. It took 5 extra minute(s) second officer 15-20 minute(s) total. Headed for the back door and looked up our ramp. At ramp; a van pulled up shortly and a full load of crew members ahead of us boarded. We had to wait another 5 minute(s) for the next van. Boarded van and now it's probably 30-35 minute(s) to block-out time. Van dropped crew on federal aviation regulation end of ramp x first; stopping to wait for an aircraft that was blocking out; then reversed route through complex to head for federal aviation regulation end of ramp and dropped us next. Another 10-12 minute(s) elapsed. Started lugging our bags up the stairs at approximately 20-25 minute(s) prior to block time. This is not enough time to do a preflt/flt deck security checked manually load flight plan in flight management computer do cockpit flows; obtain automatic terminal information service complete runway(s) analysis; obtain pre departure clearance modify flight management computer routing since the filed flight plan and pre departure clearance are always slightly different; close doors; call rcc with load complete time; and release brakes for an on-time block-out. On top of everything else; when power was xferred; automatic communications addressing & reporting system froze up; which took another 3-4 minute(s) of fiddling before it functioned again. Weight and balance paperwork arrived with load complete time of xa38z and capt signed at xa40z. Scheduled block was xa52. See above text to understand what all was going on during this time. Finally blocked out 1 minute(s) late; but it was very rushed. Just like above rpt; we also failed to brief the taxi route not because we were complacent; but because things had been second officer rushed. We should have taxied to the hold point for the ramp; set the parking brake; and briefed it there; but once you have the aircraft rolling; there's a tendency to want to maintain the inertia; especially with a crowded ramp behind you. Also; this was the first time either of us had taxied to runway(s) 35l since the runway(s) threshold had been relocated to gate. I ante meridiem a firm believer in briefing the taxi route and can honestly say this is the first time in memory that i failed to do second officer there was also no page which might have allowed us to trap this error. Called ground for taxi and told to 'taxi to runway(s) 35l via taxiway b.' capt repeated clearance it is a very short taxi. I did not start my takeoff briefing until we were on a straightaway and the flaps were at 15 degrees as is one of my error-trapping habits. As i was briefing the seo pink page and looking at the 10-7 chart; ground called us to ask intermediate fix we realized that gate was the last remaining intersection for runway(s) 35l. Of course; at this time we had a pretty good head of steam and there was no way we could have stopped; second officer i sheepishly told air traffic control we would have to go down to end of taxiway b and do the loop through ramp. Received further clearance to do second officer and proceeded through ramp to gate. Remainder of flight uneventful. We discussed this scenario in cruise; and all of us (including our jumpseater) agreed that intermediate fix air traffic control were to change their phraseology to 'taxi to runway(s) 35l at gate via bravo;' this probably would have given us a heads-up and allowed us to trap the error. I hope this can be discussed with air traffic control also; what about temporarily painting something on taxiway b; or putting up temporary wig-wag lights; etc -- something to get one's attn? I know that ultimately it is the crew's responsibility; but there sure could have been some better error traps built in; starting with improved van service that doesn't 'chew up' our allotted preflt time; a construction page; making sure we either brief the taxi route while in the blocks or stop at the ramp spot; set the parking brake; and brief it before calling for taxi; and air traffic control phraseology which could specify the intersection unambiguously.
output: FORGETTING THAT TXWY B1 WAS CLOSED; B767 FLT CREW FAILS TO STOP AT TXWY B2 FOR TKOF AT SDF.

input: Twr cleared us for takeoff on runway(s) 8r in atl. There was no turn given with the takeoff clearance we maintained runway(s) heading until switching to departure dep turned us immediately to a 020 degree heading telling us that we should've been given a turn by tower second officer as not to conflict with 'straight out' traffic taking off from runway(s) 9l. We had the traffic from runway(s) 9l in sight at all times. There was no conflict; either visually or on tcasii.
output: DC9 CREW WAS NOT GIVEN A DEP TURN BY THE TWR AS EXPECTED BY THE DEP CTLR.

input: I arrived at fixed-base operator a located at msy around xa40 ante meridiem the msy metar read as follows: msy 10sm bkn041 12/11 a2986 rmk a02 slp113 to 20106. Having received my aircraft assignment from operations(s) i proceeded to preflt a be58. Completed my walkaround; and entered the aircraft noticing that the windscreen had a considerable amount of condensation on it; i got out and wiped the water off the outside with my hand; returned to the cockpit and set up my working environment. I checkeded the hobbs against our maintenance for airworthiness directives; inspections due; squawks; and vor and dme (co-located) checkeds all was satisfactory. I started both engs to warm them to an acceptable operating level. My aircraft was located on fixed-base operator a's ramp where a white line divides the areas between fixed-base operator a and fixed-base operator b. I was facing se towards the fixed-base operator a building and parking lot where the glare from lights on poles restrict, restricted, restriction my vision. These lights are pointed in the ramp's direction and limit anyone's vision who would enter the ramp from the runway(s) and darken the ramp when leaving towards the runway(s) condensation continued to fog up the inside and outside of the windscreen. The left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) pilot windows were no better. I did my run-up while parked there and taxied closer to the fixed-base operator a building slowly and cautiously. The lineman waved me closer but due to my limited visibility; i could only see his light sticks. I shut down and went to get paper towels to wipe both sides of the windscreen down. After loading my freight; i noticed again that my windscreen had more mist and condensation in and outside of it. I again wiped the condensation off. I quickly got into the aircraft started both engs and started to taxi after talking to ground at about xb08 ante meridiem by the time i taxied out; the window was fogged again second officer i proceeded slowly; being guided off my left/right (directions) wing by a lineman. I could barely see him except for his lighted waving wands. As i headed for what i thought was taxiway b; i searched for a taxi line; looking to my left/right (directions) where my landing light showed. I found no taxi line second officer i continued in the direction i thought was correct. I was cleared to taxi to taxiway b and then left/right (directions) on taxiway east to runway(s) 28 at taxiway celsius taxiway b exits runway(s) 28 and 10 into the westbound ramp where the fixed-base operator a building; intermediate fix entering the ramp to the south would be straight ahead. I saw ahead of me in the distance a red runway(s) 28/10/b sign on the left/right (directions) and an e/b/e sign to the left/right (directions) and proceeded directly between them. I decided to go slowly and cautiously towards the gap. I saw blue taxi lights in that direction thinking they indicated the taxiway b and intermediate fix not i would parallel the lights intermediate fix needed to exit the ramp via taxiway b. I never got close to the lights before i felt the airplane roll off the ramp onto the grass. There were no taxiway lights on the ramp edge at all. The taxi lights i had mistaken for the taxiway b were taxiway edge lights for taxiway east which paralleled the ramp's edge. I missed taxiway b's ctrline by approximately 70 feet/foot to the left/right (directions) while exiting. Taxiway b only has edge lights which lead you in and out of the general aviation ramp. The ramp itself is not lined with lights. When i returned later that afternoon; i examined the ramp and what i had done. There were a lot of factors which light emitting diode to my mistake. 1) i noticed that fixed-base operator a does have a taxi line to taxiway b but i did not see it because i could not see out my left/right (directions) window due to glare from lights that are pointed from the fixed-base operator a building north towards taxiway b. These lights make it difficult to see; especially intermediate fix any precipitation or condensation is a factor. 2) i didn't taxi federal aviation regulation enough to the left/right (directions) to see the taxi line. 3) i looked ahead more and not to the left/right (directions) or left/right (directions) where my lights shined and got disoriented due to illusions created by taxiway e's lights which i had mistaken for ramp edge lights. Looking ahead and not to my left/right (directions) caused me to miss the taxiway line out of fixed-base operator b and also a helipad marking which i taxied over. Ultimately; i made a mistake that luckily hurt no one and caused no damage to property or the aircraft itself. I ante meridiem a very cautious person as it is; especially with my career. I have learned a great dealfrom this experience and will work to ensure that sits like this never happen again. The following are some hazards i feel would help the new orleans ramp area intermediate fix implemented: 1) line the edge of the general aviation ramp with taxi lights. It is difficult enough to see at night in that area and is one of the factors which light emitting diode to my problem 2) find some other way to light the ramp besides shining lights in the direction of oncoming txwys or traffic the large amber and white lights that point towards the taxiway b limit all acft's vision especially in bad weather or when the ground is wet. 3) repaint the taxi lines. The taxi lines are second officer old; they don't reflect any light.
output: PLT OF AIR TAXI FREIGHT OP TAXIING AT NIGHT ROLLS OFF THE RAMP AREA INTO THE GRASS.

input: I was training at the bearz d. Aircraft x was on frequency (don't remember where he departed) at 14;000 to bmi. He stated '14;000 is right in the tops; requesting a climb to vfr-on-top.' the radar trainee was unfamiliar with the procedures and her instructor directed her to use the edst [en-route decision support tool]. Vfr-on-top procedures are indexed on the zau reference page; my trainee located the paragraph in the 7110.65 (kudos to whomever compiled the reference page. In this instance; it worked flawlessly and was a great help) and the four of us were able to discuss the vfr-on-top clearance. The trainee fumbled through the phraseology the first time; then i corrected her and showed her the phraseology example listed in the 7110. We had no other traffic and she issued the appropriate clearance. The pilot reported reaching visual flight rules conditions on top; and after corrections from her instructor and me; she issued the appropriate response. 'roger; maintain vfr.' aircraft x leveled at 14;500.we initiated a handoff to eon (sector 44) and the r-side transferred communications thusly 'for further visual flight rules flight following; contact chicago center 120.12.' my trainee and i discussed visual flight rules on top and its applications. I explained that it's an instrument flight rules clearance and the appropriate computer entries. Later the eon controller called and questioned aircraft x's clearance. Based on her explanation; i believe aircraft x did not fully understand his clearance that after reporting reaching visual flight rules on top and the r-side's clearance 'maintain vfr;' he was visual flight rules i don't believe it's clear that while vfr-on-top is an instrument flight rules clearance; once the pilot reports on top and is instructed to maintain visual flight rules whose responsibilities are what? I don't think i've seen phraseology 'cancellation of instrument flight rules received.' i thought it was odd an instrument flight rules aircraft requested an otp clearance; climbed to a visual flight rules altitude; was told to maintain vfr.
output: ZAU Controller reported issuing a VFR on top clearance and confusion ensued as to what the pilot and Controller responsibilities were.

input: In the traffic pattern at zzz; my certified flight instructor and i were on the right downwind for runway xxr when we were told to continue for runway xxr. We then continued and a few moments later was told to turn right base for xxr. When turning right base we noted traffic; but i didn't think it was a factor at first because we assumed it was for the parallel because we still were told to turn right base. As we got established on base we saw the traffic was close and my certified flight instructor took controls to avoid a mid-air collison. We got no warning from the tower and later found out that the tower told the other aircraft to continue for runway xxr. Shortly after the tower told them to continue for xxr that's when the tower said to turn base. I didn't think that traffic that was on final would be a factor for us and thought it was for runway xxl. In the future; i think the tower should be more clear and understand the traffic spacing better because if he did then he could've told us to extend a couple of miles so we could've passed behind the traffic instead of passing in front and coming within 1;000 feet horizontally of each other. I believe the talking between me and my certified flight instructor also contributed because maybe we would've heard the call for the other aircraft to continue and could've challenged that with the tower but even then we still were told to turn base. I believe the tower should've noted the other aircraft and looked at the spacing; and told us this isn't going to work and this near-miss could've been avoided altogether instead we got turned directly into the path of another aircraft.
output: Flight instructor and student reported an NMAC occurred in the traffic pattern when Tower Controller cleared them to turn in front of another aircraft on short final to the same runway.

input: I received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from a company b757-200 on a flight stating the windshield lower power feed plastic cap looks burnt and is hot to the touch. Seems ok but definitely hotter than the others [caps]. I then received a second automatic communications addressing & reporting system stating i mention this since this aircraft diverted yesterday.
output: A Maintenance Controller reports about receiving two ACARS messages from a company B757-200 aircraft about a forward windshield lower power feed plastic cap looking deformed; burnt and 'hot' to touch. Item was deferred. Two flights later the window heat electrical harness at the forward window began smoking after take-off and crew diverted. No circuit breakers popped to cut-off electrical power.

input: The passenger in 13b approximately turned on her assistance light. We had been sitting in this hot and getting hotter; aircraft for over 40 minutes with the door closed and no auxiliary power unity when i got to her i knew she was in distress. She was able to get out the words 'diabetic'. I told her i would call a medical. I called the flight crew and said we have a medical; i'll get back to you. Now i ask for a doctor on board. The passenger in 1a quickly said 'yes what's the problem.' me '13b diabetic.' he went immediately to her.another passenger closer to her had gotten up to help and he came back to me relaying the doctor's orders. Orange juice and water. I sent this by him and called the flight crew back to give all the information. Flight crew relayed info to operations. Within minutes the passenger had come back around and after an additional 10-15 minutes was given the ok; by the doctor; to fly. I asked her if she wanted to continue to zzz and she said yes. I could see she was in full possession of her faculties and with the doctor's ok only if we take off immediately.the doctor confirmed that this episode was a direct result of sitting in an overly hot aircraft for an extended amount of time with no air conditioning. I relayed the information to the flight crew and the captain said he would relay the information to operations because we were in a very long line for take-off and would see if we could get a medical clearance to go ahead. This was obtained and we did move out in front of the long line and took off. I checked on my passenger in 13b many times during the very turbulent flight and she was doing well. I passed out can drinks to everyone on board to help with the thirst and overheating that we all had gone through. I used the can drinks because of the turbulence and this was safer than having an open bottle of water in my arms that could have gone awry. The full cause of this incident was a deferred auxiliary power unity on a crj200. This happens way too often with no thought for the passengers and crew on board. This has to stop; and these aircraft must be repaired and not deferred. This has been a problem for way too long. This practice must stop for the safety of the crew and passengers.
output: CRJ200 Flight Attendant reported lack of air conditioning caused by a deferred APU resulted in a passenger medical emergency.

input: I left feet/foot lauderdale executive airport at approximately afternoon local time en route to tampa's peter o'knight airport on business. The flight was visual flight rules and on entering the feet/foot lauderdale arsa; flight following was requested. The flight across the state was uneventful until i was handed off from 1 tpa approach controller to another and a frequency change to 134.25 was performed. My altitude was 1600' mean sea level and my vor and dme (co-located) location was approximately 14 mile out on the 090 degree left/right (directions) from the st petersburg vor and dme (co-located) by vor and dme (co-located) on contacting the controller on 134.25 i was asked intermediate fix i was asked intermediate fix i were headed for peter o'knight. I answered yes and was told to turn 10 degrees right. I asked him twice and he replied that the airport was 10 degrees right of my present heading and 4 mile i turned to this heading and visualized an airport with traffic on final. I entered a left base for this runway(s) but on examining my commercial chart airguide found the runway(s) did not correlate with that for peter o'knight. I initiated a go around over the approach end of the runway(s) and a climbing left turn and switched from 122.8 unicom frequency to 134.25 and contacted o'knight airfield. He stated he had not handled me before; but gave me a heading of 160 degrees and told me the airfield was at approximately my 12 o'clock position he stated the airfield was 3-4 mile i visualized an airfield with a runway(s) heading of 21 on a peninsula and checkeded this with the sectional and felt this to be peter o'knight. By this time; the sun was setting in the westbound and detail on departure end of the runway(s) was difficult to determine. I asked for a frequency change and rpted my intentions to peter o'knight unicom and traffic and maintained unicom traffic advisory through my longitude final. Just prior to t/d i noted the tails of 2 military jets against the horizon on the departure end of the runway(s) and initiated a go around simultaneous to the realization that this was not peter o'knight but mac dill air force base runway(s) 21. I recontacted approach on 134.25 and received additional guidance at locating peter o'knight airfield and the remainder of the approach and landing was uneventful. At the tpa approach controllers request; i contacted both tpa tower and mac dill air force base tower by phone after landing the above incident arose when i was vectored 10 degrees right while at 1600' on the 090 degree left/right (directions) from the st petersburg vor and dme (co-located) due to the setting sun and the location of peter o'knight beneath the nose of the aircraft i mistakenly took tpa for peter o'knight. On realizing my mistake; my exasperation on having made this mistake may have added to my anxiousness at finding peter o'knight and caused my second misident of mac dill air force base runway(s) 21 for peter o'knight. Realizing that there were several airports in a small radius; i had purposely identified peter o'knight by vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) from the st petersburg vor and dme (co-located) in my flight planning prior to flight when air traffic control vectored me 10 degrees right; i followed his lead and lost following of the vor-dme setting which would have light emitting diode me to peter o'knight. The perception of unfamiliar airfields with similar runway(s) headings in close proximitypa to one another light emitting diode to my confusion mac dill air force base for peter o'knight; especially with the low light present at dusk. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr had not been issued vectors within an arsa before. Felt he was right on target according to vor and dme (co-located) and vor and dme (co-located) indications. Controllers 10 degree correction confused him. Off he went to tpa. On return; runway(s) alignment of mac dill and o'knight airports is identical and both located on peninsula; second officer more confusion. Tpa said no interference with traffic recognized it was wrong airport did not land; second officer no violation would be filed. Mac dill controller said he was student pilot at o'knight field. Confessed he had almost done same thing twice due to runway(s) alignment. Federal aviation administration had contacted and will violate rptr. Knows as pilot in command he is responsible. Stated he has certainly learned from experience.
output: APCH TO WRONG ARPT TWICE PENETRATION OF ATA.

input: I was returning to zzz airport on date; flight following with terminal radar approach control facility 15;500 ft. Altitude; began a decent for zzz and in an attempt to decrease power for the decent realized i no longer had control of my variable pitch prop. The prop lever would not change the pitch in either direction. I was concerned about a prop run away situation so after talking with zzz1 control; i decided to request priority handling so as not to delay landing at zzz. I did not encounter any problem with the landing and called my mechanic upon shutdown. The next day he found that the 'propeller bracket arm had broken and allowed the propeller control cable to disconnect itself from the governor control bracket.' he repaired it and returned the aircraft to service.
output: Pilot reported a broken bracket cause the propeller control cable to detach; causing loss of prop control and a precautionary landing.

input: Rptr states: cylinder baked for 6 hours instead of the 12 hours it required. Supervisor instructed the crew to bake part for 6 hours the authority/authorized requires a 12 hour bake. Confusion in shop due to re-write of the work sheets utilized for process authority/authorized engineering is currently merging sheet information into the program.
output: A SHOP TECHNICIAN RPTS A CYLINDER WAS REQUIRED PER THE SHOP WORK SHEET TO HAVE 12 HRS HEAT TREATMENT. SUPVR DIRECTED HEAT FOR 6 HRS.

input: Acft (ce421c xyz) departed apa at approximately xa45. Instrument flight rules flight plan to ril. Clearance from air traffic control resume own navigate, navigation to intercept (rockies 3 departure dbl transition) climb and maintain fl200. At approximately 15 nautical mile westbound of apa; climbing through 10000 feet/foot mean sea level the left/right (directions) engine made a 'pop' sound and smoke appeared through vents in top of cowling. No immediate indication of oil pressure loss or high temperature on engine pilot decided to feather engine and secure due to impending failure. At approximately xb00; pilot advised air traffic control of left/right (directions) engine failure/feather and declared an emergency pilot advised air traffic control he wanted to return to apa. At approximately xb10; aircraft landed on runway(s) 17l and taxied off runway(s) no injuries or substantial damage occurred to airframe. 5 passenber on board; 1 pilot crew. Preliminary inspection of engine indicates catastrophic internal engine failure. Hole in top of engine case; left/right (directions) magneto sheared from mount and intercooler dented from ejecting parts. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the engine was a continental gtsio-520-n with only 500 hours and the preliminary rpt was a thrown connecting rod. The rptr said the engine was sent to the manufacturer for teardown and the final rpt was not complete.
output: A C421C IN CLB AT 10000 FT DECLARED AN EMER AND DIVERTED DUE TO THE R ENG FAILURE CAUSED BY A THROWN CONNECTING ROD.

input: As pilot of flight i took off from tlh visual flight rules destined to pfn; which was instrument flight rules at the time. My intention was to pick up instrument flight rules clearance from pam approach as i neared pfn. When i received my clearance i did not specify an alternate. In the course of the approach i lost communicationss and navigate, navigation due to double alternator failure. I performed a missed approach and initiated the missed approach proc's turn and climb instructions to the best i was able; considering that i had only magnetic compass for navigate, navigation at that point upon reaching 500' mean sea level as i arrived at the missed approach point; i announced my go around and did not receive a reply. That's when i noticed my electrical failure. At 500' mean sea level i was in visual flight rules conditions; but could not notify anybody; and with no alternate; no one but me knew what i was going to do. I was able to subsequently restore left alternator power and regained sufficient electrical power enabling navigate, navigation and communications capability. I completed my flight w/o incident. My concern was forgetting to specify an alternate on a canned flight plan which became required.
output: PRIMARY ELECTRICAL SUPPLY PROBLEM EXACERBATES FACT THAT PLT DID NOT FILE AN ALTERNATE ARPT FOR AN IFR DESTINATION AND ON MISSED APCH HE WAS WITHOUT COM.

input: Descending on the anthm standard terminal arrival route under washington center control; we were cleared to descend 'via the anthm' arrival. We had the automatic terminal information service but because washington does not assign the runway transition; we set 11;000 in the mode control panel which is the lowest we can go without a runway assignment. When we were switched over to potomac approach; reporting altitude passing; descending via to 11;000; and the automatic terminal information service the response we got was '33 left'. No 'continue descent via 33 left transition'; or 'maintain 11;000 ; expect 33 left'; or 'continue descent to x thousand; expect 33 left'(or some variation thereof). After a few moments; i queried the controller if we were cleared to continue descent via the 33 left transition; at which point he responded; 'continue via the 33 left transition'. We continued without further incident. To me this exchange was confusing and could lead to a misinterpretation of the approach clearance. This is the second time this has happened to me and on advice from the chiefs i am filing this report because this confusion needs to be addressed. Standardized phraseology needs to be used. I think the controllers are assuming that we will fly the transition because the automatic terminal information service has the active runway information. But i don't think this is correct. The controllers need to be specific.
output: B737-800 Captain experiences confusion during the ANTHM RNAV to BWI due to the late runway transition assignment by PCT Approach; and their reluctance to issue the transition on the initial check in.

input: I received a briefing before the flight with pilot reports rpting icing 6000-9000 feet/foot on clbout (mlg acr) from stp. I filed for 5000 feet/foot to avoid ice. After takeoff from stp i received vectors through the terminal control area upon reaching 5000 feet/foot i noticed ice forming on the wing struts. I asked for lower; air traffic control gave me 4000 feet/foot having just been through 4000 feet/foot i thought this would solve problem it did not. Rime continued to form at a fairly fast rate. I again asked for lower. I was cleared to 3000 feet/foot ice continued to form. I tried to climb only to find the plane was unable. I asked center to advise on an airport close with better conditions. I knew that maintaining airspd was becoming critical; as the plane had stalled once. Air traffic control gave me vectors to mankato. I was unable to maintain the last assigned altitude (3000 ft). At about 2600 feet/foot mean sea level i noticed ground contact. I cancelled instrument flight rules and continued to mankato and landed without event. The only prevention of these incidents are more frequent pilot reports by more pilots intermediate fix general aviation pilots are going to fly instrument flight rules we need help from the big boys. The air traffic control facilities did their job flawlessly and prevented a catastrophe.
output: PLT OF PVT SMA SEL ACFT LOST CTL OF THE ACFT DUE TO ACFT ICING AND DSNDED BELOW ASSIGNED ALT.

input: On the flight from zzzz to zzz; i picked up the clearance on ground and we were ready early. Passengers were early and after loading and starting; we couldn't contact anyone on ground; tower or departure frequencies! Aircraft y told us the tower just closed. We switched to update the automatic terminal information service and sure enough info q said the tower was shut down due to staffing issues. We talked with aircraft y landing on runway x; he gave us the frequency for zzzz center; while we self broadcast on tower frequency that we were taxiing to runway y. Prior to takeoff; we again tried ground; tower and departure frequencies! No answer! After aircraft y landed and cleared all runways; we broadcast in the blind on frequency and departed. Once airborne; we tried to contact departure on frequency. No luck. We were visual meteorological conditions and maintained that until establishing contact with zzzz center. After radio and radar contact was established; we were cleared to fl230. After about 30 miles; zzzz center told us zzzz tower called and reported we had an unauthorized departure!we tried again to contact them on the assigned frequency; no luck. We continued to zzz with normal radio contact the whole way. Unusual circumstances with the virus affecting operations. Tower shutdown after giving us our instrument flight rules clearance. There were only two airplanes flying at that time. Very strange circumstance.
output: Pilots reported departing without clearance in what they thought was an uncontrolled airport resulting in runway incursion and airspace violations.

input: After contacting ground control; we were instructed to taxi south on taxiway left/right (directions) and wait for departure time at pad x in cleveland. The wait would be about 30 minutes. Because of this delay i decided to taxi extra slow since there was no other airplanes behind us. Approaching pad y on the taxiway i noticed the close proximity between my left wing tip and the nose of a regional jet parked in pad y. I slowed down even further and thought that being on the taxiway center line and the other airplane behind the edge of his pad that we would be clear but i proceeded with caution until we heard on the ground frequency 'stop; stop.' i immediately assumed it came from the pilots of the regional jet and pressed firmly on the brakes for an instantaneous stop. After this i started a short communication with the other pilot who asked me to swing a bit to the right before moving forward. I did and he said it was all clear and we continued to pad x without any issues. Upon arriving at the pad; a flight attendant called asking what had happened because she was standing in the galley and she hit a galley door. I asked her if she wanted to return to the gate to have her arm checked out and she said it was not serious enough and she was ok to continue her duties. After 20 minutes; we departed to our destination uneventfully.
output: Air carrier Captain reported coming to an abrupt stop to avoid a collision while taxiing at CLE.

input: On approach to mroc; given expect instrument landing system runway(s) 7 circle to land runway(s) 25. Winds were 240 degrees at 14 knot(s) at arrival, arrive time. When handed off to final approach we were established on runway(s) 7 localizer and given instructions to rpt tio vor and dme (co-located) we asked whether to circle for left/right (directions) traffic to runway(s) 25; and were told affirmative. Commercial chart page says visual expect a left/right (directions) pattern; however; instrument landing system runway(s) 7 conflicts and says circle to land use belen visual. The belen visual is a teardrop pattern with an initial turn to the left/right (directions) then a left/right (directions) teadrop to the runway(s) commercial chart page arrival, arrive note 3 states to request left/right (directions) pattern with approach to runway(s) 25 (conflicting with 11-1). Since approach confirmed circle to left/right (directions) we commenced a left/right (directions) pattern visual approach and landed on runway(s) 25. Tower informed us after landing that normal circle is to the left/right (directions) 10-7 arrival, arrive 3 should be updated to include normal circle to land runway(s) 19-1 from the instrument landing system vor and dme (co-located) runway(s) 7 11-1 page (as well as 13-1). These use a quasi left/right (directions) pattern. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that at the mroc airport english is the second language. Therefore; it is a strong possibility that the controller did not understand the crew's question and because of that misunderstanding; the controller's response light emitting diode them to believe a l-hand turn to a left/right (directions) traffic pattern was correct instead of a r-hand turn to a left/right (directions) traffic pattern. The airport approach charts correctly depict the approach to runway(s) 7 with a circle to runway(s) 25. Their company 10-7 chart verbiage is what initially caused them to question a left/right (directions) turn to a left/right (directions) pattern. The rptr now understands the confusion and is working with his company to have the 10-7 more clrly describe the circling proc.
output: AN A320 PLT CIRCLED IN A R LNDG PATTERN VERSUS THE CORRECT L PATTERN AT MROC.

input: Being vectored for the instrument landing system runway(s) 19r sna; heading 090 degrees we were advised of traffic pilot not flying (r seat) responded 'we'll be looking.' however; we were instrument meteorological conditions -- solid. Seconds later pilot not flying pointed to the left/right (directions) saying; 'look at that airplane!' i glanced l-hand side and spotted a cessna 150 passing off our l-hand side from front to rear; approximately heading 240 degrees 200 feet/foot horizontal our altitude (exactly 3000 ft) in the clouds. We rpted this event to air traffic control just a few seconds later; pilot not flying called 'loc alive.' at about this time as we were intercepting the localizer i told the approach controller i would like to file a near miss rpt. We were given a phone number for the supervisor on duty at socal approach and i spoke with him approximately 45 minute(s) later. I was told they had followed the other aircraft to lgb; spoke with the pilot who said she; a 30 yr federal aviation administration pilot examiner; had us in sight and there was no prob! The supervisor said they had lost radar contact with this airplane momentarily; second officer maybe they followed the wrong airplane to lgb. Question intermediate fix it was the wrong airplane; why did she say she saw us? Supplemental information from acn 304248: socal approach called me after landing mr. X at socal said a citation on an approach to sna complained about a near miss with my aircraft i saw the citation from the time he broke out until he intercepted the instrument landing system for sna north of snake and outside the class celsius airspace. No evasive action was needed. I estimated my distance more than 2 mile from him. Socal gave me as traffic to the citation as 11 o'clock and 2 mile this class east airspace north of sna is congested.
output: POSSIBLE NMAC.

input: The pilot flying of helicopter xxx made a precautionary landing on the side of the freeway. Highway patrol called a tow truck to transport the aircraft to a recovery yard. I went to the recovery yard; talked to the pilot about his landing i determined that he had made the landing due to fluctuating tachometer indication. I called the a&p that maintains the aircraft he told me to checked a plug on the l-hand magneto. This i did. I found no problem i then started the engine and performed all of the power checkeds all indications normal. I picked the aircraft up to a hover for power checkeds all indications normal. I then stopped the aircraft and did another visual inspection; all normal. I restarted the aircraft and performed a takeoff and climbed to 700 feet/foot above ground level and flew 5-7 minute(s) at various power settings; all normal. I then flew the aircraft to its base at lgb. During this flight all indications normal. During all of the preflt and inspections; i did not find any discrepancies or make any alterations. I determined that the aircraft was airworthy and safe to fly. At the scene of the original landing the federal aviation administration and national transportation safety board were notified. It was not indicated that the aircraft could not be moved. I believe the original pilot had some electrical interference on the tachometer. He stated the power was stable. He made a good decision to make a precautionary landing the repositioning flight was not an issue.
output: R22 PLT MADE A PRECAUTIONARY LNDG AFTER EXPERIENCING POSSIBLE ENG PROBS IN ZLA CLASS G.

input: First snowfall day of year. 2 snowplows were operating on runway(s) 28 told to hold short of runway(s) 4 intersection snowplows acknowledged transmission in the meantime; commuter aircraft was cleared for takeoff on runway(s) 4. Observed snowplows cross runway(s) 4 intersection and asked operators their position they answered they were on the other side of the runway(s) and seemed confused. Weather at the time was instrument flight rules with visibility 3/4 mile snowplows were operated by county personnel who are very familiar with procedures at this airport it seems there was a problem with effective listening on the part of the plow operators.
output: SNOW REMOVAL EQUIPMENT TOLD TO HOLD SHORT OF RWY 4; THE ACTIVE RWY; ON RWY 28. PLOWS CROSSED WITHOUT CLRNC AS SMT TOOK OFF.

input: While on a north heading for a 90 degree intercept to the final approach course for runway(s) 8l in hnl; we got a left/right (directions) hydraulic quantity message on engine indicating and crew alerting system status page showed zero hydraulic quantity. We told approach we need a left/right (directions) turn out over the water and i started a left/right (directions) turn. Controller told us to turn left/right (directions) to intercept the localizer we told controller we were turning left/right (directions) controller told us there was terrain and to turn left/right (directions) to 180 degrees immediately. We answered that terrain was in sight and not a factor. Controller modified our heading to 230 degrees and said we should have told him earlier. Controller then immediately started talking to other aircraft before we could get a word in to declare an emergency the engine indicating and crew alerting system message went away and the status page showed good quantity for the left/right (directions) hyds. We told controller we were ready for the approach and he vectored us for approach and landing i turned left/right (directions) over the water to take terrain out of our situation. Also; i wanted to stay out of the hnl traffic area. Good plan; poor execution. I should have followed controller's instructions; intercepted the localizer and then asked for vectors over the water. Instead of reducing the controller's workload; i added to it. It was the wrong decision and it will not happen again.
output: A B767-300 ON APCH TO HNL EXPERIENCED A HYD PROB AND TURNED OFF COURSE WITHOUT COORDINATING WITH ATC.

input: Shift manager was informed of the [control center] being overstaffed and was told to send people home by upper management. The manager made the decision to leave because there was another shift manager that was working in dispatch that could fill in. That; somehow; became my problem when the shift manager; working dispatch at the time; was pulled to the podium to work as shift manager and the flights on their dispatch desk (mountain desk) were added to my desk; both sent and unsent flights. The flights i had sent on my dispatch desk were left on my desk; but my flights that were not due yet were sent to the irop desk. This created a few issues. I do not feel properly trained for the mountain desk having never worked it. I also had 18 flights in the air while trying to work up a full bank load of flights; making it impossible to flight follow with any level of detail. At one point; i had 32 active flights on my desk and another bank needing to be worked up. This is a major safety issue and should not be taken lightly. If this had happened during busier banks; there could have easily been closer to 40 flights in the air at a time.the [control center] was overstaffed and the company sacrificed safety of flight to save paying an additional person. I am sure someone could have been sent home without affecting dispatcher work load if better procedures were followed.this cannot happen again; mountain desk especially. If the [control center] is overstaffed; a plan needs to be in place before the shifts begin. I started my shift at 2pm. There was plenty of time to spread flights and increase each desk by 1 or 2 flights before they started; rather than increase my work load; and the work load of the irop desk by 20 plus flights.the company cannot allow a couple hundred dollars in payroll to affect the workloads so much that it becomes unsafe.
output: Dispatch Supervisor sent staff home and dispatchers were over worked and understaffed.

input: Tcasii gave traffic advisory then resolution advisory we followed resolution advisory and climbed to 8500 feet/foot target leveled at 7000 feet/foot we advised air traffic control when clear of conflict we returned to 8000 feet/foot we had not received an acknowledgement from air traffic control second officer we advised him again. He had not heard our first call.
output: FLC OF AN MLG ACR ACFT CLBED ABOVE ASSIGNED APCH VECTORING ALT IN RESPONSE TO A TCASII RA.

input: On aug/xa/98 i was doing an overnight checked on aircraft xyz; an f100. I found the left/right (directions) main landing gear downlock actuator leaking. I went to our (acr) rotable book. These books are for us to find the part number easier and faster. I looked up the fleet type which is 'y'. Then i looked for the air traffic area chapter which is bb. Looking down through the numbers; i came to a left/right (directions) main landing gear downlock actuator. The number was yxyx.
