Then i verified the effectivity; the effectivity was a number 'y' telling me the actuator is good to use on a fokker f100. We installed the actuator; swung the gear; leak checkeded -- everything checkeded good per the maintenance manual. The aircraft left zzz; was stopped in www. The actuator had to be changed because it was for a fokker f28 1000 and 4000 series aircraft i ante meridiem concerned why the rotable books were not updated with a revision date of may/xa/98; why the svcable tag (xx) did not specify f28 only; and why air carrier still has svcable f28 parts in stock when air carrier retired its f28 fleet.
output: A FOKKER 100 WAS DISPATCHED WITH THE INCORRECT PART INSTALLED IN THE R MAIN LNDG GEAR DOWNLOCK ACTUATOR POS CAUSED BY A PARTS CATALOG DEFICIENCY.

input: I was entering the dvt traffic pattern with inoperative communications (ref aeronautical information manual paragraph 205). From point a; i overflew the traffic pattern by 500' (1500' agl) and determined that runway(s) s7 were in use by noting the only other aircraft in the pattern on upwind leg). I planned to follow him when he turned downwind; apparently in closed traffic starting at point a; i rocked my wings frequently; while flying the path shown; in an attempt to gain the twr's attention i followed the other aircraft (sma y) maintaining 1+ mile sep. The sma y flew the normal right-hand pattern and made a full stop landing after i turned final; i received a steady green light from the tower and landed. I did not see the sma zulu time (utc/gmt) who had been cleared to land on 7r from a left base. He saw me at point b on 3/4 mile final and took evasive action; landing on runway(s) 7l. The following factors may have been involved: distraction of tower operators; relative to their failure to see my aircraft with only 2 other aft in the air traffic area until point b. Lack of specific no radio procedure in aeronautical information manual including light signals. My concentration on the preceding aircraft and tower detracted from normal (wider) scan pattern. Presumption by sma zulu time (utc/gmt) pilot who had landing clearance that no other traffic existed (impaired scan). Color of my aircraft (gray) is difficult to see.
output: CLOSE PROX 2 GA SMA IN OPPOSITE DIRECTOR TRAFFIC PATTERN INTO DVT.

input: While holding; zdc advised we had gone beyond the holding fix limits. We advised center we had not. Zdc had said the same thing to another flight a few minutes previously. Sequence: 1) cleared to the gso-058/60; left turns; 20 mile legs; maintain fl330; efc 2306. 2) cleared to the gso-038/50; right turns; 20 mile legs; fl330; efc 2331 make a left turn to 360 degree and intercept. 3) this vector actually made an intercept of the gso-038 degree radial at the 70 mile fix. 4) entered holding. 5) at the outbnd end of the holding pattern zdc advised we were 15 mile ne of gso and had exceeded holding limits (actual position was 25 mile ne of gso). 6) advised zdc we had not gone outside of holding airspace. 7) reclred by zdc to same holding pattern with 10 mile legs. 8) at the fix end of the holding pattern (50 mi) i requested zdc to confirm our position at that point. I told center the reason for the request was that our position at the outbnd end of the fix was 10 mile different than where he said we were. Zdc then said something to the effect that 'you do admit that you had overflown the holding pattern by 5 mi'. I said negative. It is possible that the mapping feature was incorrect on his radar but it is my real feeling that i was talking to a controller that did not understand the construction of a holding pattern.
output: DEVIATION NOTED FROM LIMITS OF HOLDING PATTERN.

input: We were assigned the visual approach to runway 34 into avl. As per our poh we briefed the instrument landing system to 34 and had the localizer frequency selected for the instrument landing system 34. If you follow the glideslope to runway 34 the visual approach slope indicator shows all white. It can be confusing coming in to land with the visual approach slope indicator showing such a huge discrepancy. I believe (just by looking visually) that the glideslope is way too high. I would say that the glideslope touchdown crossing height would be around 150-200 feet/foot it is my understanding that my takeoff landing report is predicated at having a touchdown crossing altitude of 50 feet/foot and touching down in the touch down zone.up until the last few months the glideslope and visual approach slope indicator have always coincided. I believe that the visual approach slope indicator is the correct approach path. However the glideslope has you landing long.i questioned the tower about the glideslope and visual approach slope indicator not coinciding. The tower said they have had numerous complaints over the last 6 months; however the federal aviation administration says that it is normal.the federal aviation administration needs to check the instrument landing system to 34 and correct the problem. The approach plate for instrument landing system 34 should at least say that the visual approach slope indicator and glideslope don't coincide (however i think there is such a huge discrepancy that it needs to be fixed).
output: A CRJ-700 Captain reported discrepancies between the ILS glideslope signal and the VASI for Runway 34 at AVL; advising the ILS glideslope signal commands an excessively steep descent and a threshold crossing well above the charted TCH.

input: This flight was running late and we had already worked three legs. The aircraft had two mels: one for the 'b' autopilot and one for the hgs (hud). I was the pilot flying. At the gate; i briefed the departure standard instrument departure off of the commercial chart page with the captain. I was familiar with the standard instrument departure and waypoints. We got to the end of the runway. I did a runway update and we had the flight management system on the takeoff page. At 400' i called for lateral navigation  at 1000' i called; 'set speed flaps 1; climb thrust.'  the aircraft accelerated rapidly as we were very light. The flight director was trying to give me a hard turn to the right which i knew was not correct as per the standard instrument departure  i asked the captain to verify the standard instrument departure  i also called for flaps up at this time but it may have gone unheard since we had red lights flashing on the panel for hgs fail. I engaged the 'b' autopilot at this point to allow me to better assess the departure. The autopilot almost immediately kicked off because it was mel'ed. We momentarily had the autopilot disengage horn which added to the confusion. This added to the brief task saturation of both of us. Air traffic control then asked if we were going to rejoin the standard instrument departure and i believe i answered him and said yes. I clicked on the 'a' autopilot and saw we were in heading mode. At this point; air traffic control gave us a clearance to a fix and the captain entered it in the box. This is when the captain realized we still had the flaps set at 1. We exceeded the flap limitation speed. The captain notified maintenance upon our arrival of the flap overspeed. The hgs flashing on the panel was an immediate distraction for both of us on departure. If the circuit breaker would have been pulled; we would not have had a red flashing light at an important phase of flight distracting us. Anytime you see a red light your eyes are immediately drawn to it. I also selected an inoperative autopilot. I knew it was mel'ed; but it is not normal to be mel'ed and it was part of my habit pattern to reach for the 'b' autopilot. Better monitoring did play a role. We did; however; follow all company procedures; including briefings. I should have concentrated on my primary duty of flying and let the captain deal with the monitoring and then i would not have oversped the flaps.
output: A B737 Crew departed without the FMC programmed for the SID which resulted in a track deviation; a flap overspeed while troubleshooting an inoperative autopilot and a flashing red HUD inoperative annunciation.

input: Apch runway(s) 22 instrument landing system eau position (11 mile arc) eau. Localizer did not come in (indicate passage). Noticed compass locator passage; turned towards locator. Requested missed approach because of navigate, navigation problem zmp asked position switched to #1 navigate, navigation gave position all frequencies were tuned and identified there was no navigate, navigation flag. Navigate, navigation difficulty (cdi no sensing) was discovered. Switched to #2 navigate, navigation at this time center lectured about potential problem because of error in position rpt. Minimums approach was made using #2 navigate, navigation and g/s. I feel that center; as soon as it was made known that there was a navigate, navigation problem on the final approach should have given a vector away from any other aircraft in the approach airspace. Asking to give a position rpt when on a minimums approach with malfunctioning navigate, navigation equipment is time ill spent intermediate fix there is a known navigate, navigation problem note: navigate, navigation flag did not show until the beginning of the second approach it was later found that water leaked in on #1 navigate, navigation on the top of the radio stack. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: the aircraft was transponder equipped but that they are sometimes lost by air route traffic control center when at low altitude the weather was at minimums. There was a jet smt to the se to follow him. He was on a vor and dme (co-located) arc transition to the approach he wanted air route traffic control center to give him a specific heading a hard altitude was issued by air route traffic control center sometime later.
output: SMT HAS NAVIGATION PROBLEM AND SHOOTS MISSED APCH.

input: Please review the tailwind limitation for aug; along with the company bulletin and the new commercial chart. Because of the limitation and current winds; we did the vor and dme (co-located) approach to runway 35; which resulted in a missed approach. While holding; the duty flight manager told operations that we should land runway 17 because the memo and the operations bulletin had been rescinded. He then quoted the bulletin to sound more official. I can't stress how unsafe this practice is. I flew to augusta the day that a light transport overran the runway and saw the mess myself. Our situation was set up the same way. I could see the accident chain forming; so i made the call to continue to boston; where i was met with more flack. We had held for more than one hour; and fuel was a major concern. The weather in boston was also near minimums and the instrument landing system to runway 4r; the favored runway; was out of service. On the way to boston we held over scupp; and any more holding would have been unsafe. I'm filing this report in lieu of contacting the federal aviation administration but the event needs to be addressed; as pilots are accountable for every action whereas it seems most other departments are not.
output: Captain of a light transport responds to management criticism of his decision to divert to an alternate in lieu of flying an ILS approach to a short runway with what he considered to be excessive tailwinds.

input: Our facility was involved in a truly unbelievable hearback/readback incident. Aircraft x was nebound at fl390 over southern indiana. His destination was zzz. Aircraft y was ebound at fl410 landing yyy. Both aircraft were in the super high sector. The sector was quite busy; thus the similar call signs went unnoticed by both the radar controller and the associate controller (d-side); meaning the pilots were thus not warned. Aircraft y was the first aircraft switched to sector 92. The aircraft y pilot took the frequency change and this went unnoticed by both controllers and both sets of flight crews. The aircraft x then checkeds on frequency with the r92 controller they initially thought something was not quite right; as the controller started to call the flight aircraft x; but then after looking at the aircraft y data block corrected themselves and called the flight aircraft y. Being called aircraft y again went unnoticed by the aircraft x flight crew. It should be noted that the aircraft also checkeded on level at fl390; whereas the data block showed fl410. This again should have caught the attention of the r92 controller (a seasoned veteran) but it did not. Later; this aircraft y flight was handed off and switched to the next in-house sector; r70; and again called aircraft y. Aircraft x again answered and away he went. Aircraft x then checkeded on the r70 level at fl390. Again the controller did not catch the call sign or the altitude to recap; the aircraft y data block at fl410 has now been handed off twice and both times the flight crew of aircraft x answered. Both times this aircraft x flight crew checkeded on at fl390 and both times the receiving controller acknowledged the chk-on by calling the flight aircraft y. Again the aircraft x crew did not catch this either. To call this entire mix-up simply a hearback/readback incident is an understatement. It is utterly astounding that all the controllers involved and both sets of flight crews repeatedly answered for the other flt.
output: RADAR CTLR DESCRIBED READBACK HEARBACK ERROR INVOLVING SIMILAR ACFT NUMBERS; THAT INCLUDED SEVERAL CTLRS AND SECTORS; REPEATEDLY MISSED BY EVERYONE.

input: I was the first officer and pilot flying on a scheduled airline flight out of zzz. After departure the capt performed the after takeoff chklist and we noticed that the nose gear unsafe light was illuminated. All other gear indications were normal for gear retracted; and there was no unusual noise or vibration. We coordinated with center to level off and slow down; and then the capt performed the chklist for unsafe gear indication - gear handle up. At this point the capt had xferred responsibility for air traffic control communications to me and the autoplt was engaged. Per the chklist; the capt lowered the landing gear; and all indications were normal for gear extended; except we still had the nose gear unsafe red light illuminated. The md88 has a mechanical indicator in the cockpit for nose gear position and it was in the nose gear down and locked position since we had conflicting indications of the nose gear position the capt contacted dispatch and maintenance over the radio and discussed the problem with them. They decided that leaving the gear extended and not recycling it was best; and that we should return to zzz. We coordinated with air traffic control for a return and the capt declared an emergency since we were not sure of the status of the nose landing gear. We completed the chklist for unsafe gear indication -- gear handle down. The capt briefed the passenber and flight attendants on our landing we coordinated with tower and emergency personnel to overfly runway(s) with the approach lights turned up to high; second officer they could try and see the position of our nose gear. Several observers on the ground said our nose gear appeared to be down and locked. Tower requested we land on runway x for traffic considerations. We flew an uneventful visual approach and landed safely. We exited on taxiway where we were met by emergency personnel. We still had a nose gear unsafe indication; second officer we had maintenance come out and install the gear pins before we taxied to the gate.
output: MD88 FLT CREW REPORTS UNSAFE NOSE GEAR INDICATION AFTER GEAR RETRACTION. ACFT IS RETURNED TO DEPARTURE ARPT WITH UNSAFE WARNING; BUT WITH THE MECHANICAL PIN INDICATING SAFE.

input: During visual runway(s) 18r approach clt approach control kept us high and fast on base leg. Turning final at final approach fix we were still high. Several unanswered calls to tower were made requesting an s-turn to westbound in order to get down. On my own; i finally made an s-turn on final to the westbound this collapsed spacing behind us and the aircraft following us was directed to go around by tower we continued to a stabilized uneventful landing on runway(s) 18r. Tower issued no comment and appeared busy with other traffic both approach and tower were busy on radio frequencies their instructions keep us high and fast.
output: CAPT OF AN AIRBUS A320 S-TURNED ON A VISUAL APCH IN ORDER TO LOSE ALT AND AIRSPD DUE TO ATC INSTRUCTED HIGH AND FAST FINAL APCH.

input: Upon my arrival, arrive at the gate for an originating flight the aircraft was in the process of being towed from a remote parking spot. I reviewed the release and noticed an minimum equipment list auxiliary power unity inoperative however; when the aircraft arrived at the gate; the auxiliary power unity was running. It had been started in error by the ramper riding the brakes. I reviewed the logbook and the auxiliary power unity write-up was 2 days old. It indicated that the oil low pressure light remained illuminated and frequency and voltage readings read zero. Additionally; there was a sticker at the switch and a sticker inside the front cover of the logbook. However; at this time; the auxiliary power unity was performing as it was supposed to; the low oil pressure light was out and the frequency and voltage readings were correct. The ramper had xferred power to the generator busses. Bottom-line; the auxiliary power unity was not inoperative i did not notice any historical write-ups in the logbook that concerned the auxiliary power unity (there may have been some; i did a fairly quick scan). I called dispatch to inform them that it appeared the write-up may be in error. I was told that it would cost too much to correct it in zzz and he would pass the information to maintenance and it would be addressed when we arrived at our first destination the dispatcher indicated that the auxiliary power unity should not have been started. I agreed but since it had been and was working appropriately; i elected to use it. In retrospect; i probably should have just shut it down and pressed on without it. Inflt i messaged maintenance requesting someone meet me at the gate to address the situation. Upon arrival, arrive i was met by a mechanic who said that; 'maint was a bit up in arms that we had used the auxiliary power unity it had a history of low oil pressure probs.' he pulled a circuit breaker to ensure it could not be started and made an addition to the sp portion of the write-up. We continued on. A. My part (2 things): 1) i did a fairly quick scan of the logbook after i found the original write-up. It's possible there may have been history. I did not notice any; but neither can i say with absolute certainty that there wasn't any. I need to be more thorough in my review. 2) a more conservative approach by me may be warranted next time. I'll just return the aircraft to its mel'ed status until the write-up is actually cleared b. Ramp personnel: the person that started the auxiliary power unity in the first place needs to be refreshed on the need for logbook review and sticker observance (there was a sticker by the auxiliary power unity switch). Celsius maintenance -- 2 things: 1) maybe a better write-up would have helped prevent this type of event. Auxiliary power unity inoperative didn't really tell the correct story; it wasn't inoperative it just had some problems that required it to not be used. 2) since maintenance was riled up that i used the auxiliary power unity my guess is that the dispatcher passed the word to them concerning our conversation. Intermediate fix the problem was such that it excited them; maybe they or dispatch could have let me know about their concerns before i reached the maintenance base (i'm thinking the auxiliary power unity is good -- intermediate fix some type of event had required its use; i would have used it). Further; since it was important enough an issue that they eventually pulled a circuit breaker to prevent future starts; maybe that should be an initial precautionary measure in auxiliary power unity problems like this. Sum: i ante meridiem not aware of any significant problem that resulted from this event. However; it is a good example of how contributions from different entities can lead to a potentially bad situation. Intermediate fix the ramper hadn't started the auxiliary power unity there would have been no problem intermediate fix the logbook entry had provided some more enlightening information or maintenance concerns had been relayed; i'd have shut it down without reservation and there would have been no subsequent problems intermediate fix i'd have taken a more conservative approach and shut it down; again there would have been no subsequent problems intermediate fix the circuit breaker had been pulled in the first place; there would have been no problem in my case -- lesson learned.
output: B737 CAPT REPORTS ACFT WITH MEL'ED APU IS TOWED TO GATE WITH APU RUNNING. APU IS USED TO START ENGINES.

input: After [takeoff] zzz tower notified me on negative transponder signal. I acknowledged and attempted to reset. The tower then gave me a frequency change to [tracon]. Right after contacting [tracon] i noticed my back up radio went black. Air traffic control cleared me to climb to 6500 feet and verified my location. Within 30 seconds of conversation with air traffic control my aspen primary flight instrument went black. I immediately requested to return back to zzz and checked and cycled fuses and avionics power after verifying proper volts on the jpi engine monitor. [tracon] handed me off to zzz tower who asked if everything was ok and i responded with instrument failure. They immediately cleared me to enter left pattern for xxl cleared to land number 2. Within seconds of that call my garmin 650 primary radio went black and 30 seconds later i lost my jpi engine monitor. I landed safely on xxl at zzz but was unable to transmit 7600 or communicate with tower or ground.
output: Bonanza pilot reported a series of equipment malfunctions and returned to departure airport.

input: On climb out our air driven generator deployed while the captain (pilot monitoring) completed the after takeoff checklist flow. This occurred as we were climbing through 8000 feet/foot to our assigned altitude of 10000 feet/foot with departure. When the air driven generator deployed; we were around 8600 feet/foot below a sct layer of clouds; which appeared to be around 10;000 mean sea level when the air driven generator deployed and took over powering the primary air conditioning / alternating current electrics; i lost my primary indicators on the pfd and the autopilot disconnected as a result of losing yd2. At this point i announced i was on standby instruments; with the autopilot inoperative. At this point we received a handoff to center and the captain requested we stay with departure; get vectors clear of traffic and permission to level at 9000 feet/foot to stay clear of the clouds while we addressed the issue; to which we were granted. The captain asked if i could handle the aircraft while he runs the checklist; to which i replied by asking him to take control of the aircraft while i revert my pfd to indicate those indications of pfd 1. We did this; and i took control of the aircraft hand flying; maintaining 9000 feet/foot and following air traffic control assigned vectors. The captain completed bnormal checklist from the manual and the air conditioning / alternating current power was restored to normal; with both engine generators providing the primary air conditioning / alternating current electrical power; with the exception of my inertial reference system/unit still inoperative (as it could not realign in flight) and the yd inoperative; rendering the autopilot inoperative. Around this time the captain communicated with the flight attendant regarding our situation; and tentative plan of action. He advised them that the aircraft is flying normally; we had an abnormal electrical malfunction; which we needed time to address; and asked them to remain seated and give us some time to address the issue. He would be getting back to them; and making an announcement to the passengers once he knew more. At this point; the captain asked what i thought about returning to our departure airport; and we decided that based on our situation and current position; returning visual flight rules would be a better choice than continuing to destination where they were advertising instrument landing system approaches; with thunderstorms in the forecast. The captain sent dispatch an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message advising them that we were returning; and would communicate more on the ground...no emergency necessary. Dispatch returned with an acknowledgment message and advice to watch our landing weight. (we were predicting a landing around 71000 pounds so this was not a concern). We set up for the visual approach; and briefed it accordingly. The captain then advised approach that we would be returning for landing; and asked that the equipment be standing by simply as a precaution. Once we got our final vector; we called the airport in sight and began our final approach. The aircraft handled normally; through descent; approach; and landed without further incident. The trucks followed us during the landing roll and taxi but were not utilized. Once we came to a stop at the gate; we completed all checklists and began the required communications with operations; ramp personnel; dispatch; operations; arff; flight attendants; passengers; etc. At this point; i do not know exactly why this incident occurred. The captain (pilot monitoring) was advised by personnel in operations today that it is possible the reason the air driven generator deployed yesterday was because he switched the generators to the off position; while in-flight. I suspect this could have been the cause; because it happened right as he ran the after takeoff flow/checklist. It is also possible this was not the cause of the incident; and if this is the case; i am not sure why it happened. If this was a case of improper checklist usage; i think continued emphasis on the importance of knowing the checklist flows; proper and diligent completion of the checklists is extremely important; because things like this can happen if we rely too heavily on memory and do not slow down and take the time to completethem properly. Ideally; the pilot flying should back up the pilot monitoring and vise-versa in all stages of flight. However; in this example; during the initial climb out; the pilot flying cannot watch the piot monitoring complete the checklist flow items. These are items expected to be completed properly without specific confirmation by the pilot flying (examples of these items can be found in emergency checklists as those; which require a; 'confirm?' probe followed by the response 'confirmed.' by the pilot flying. Because normal checklist items are normally completed with out specific supervision by the other pilot; there is a loss of redundancy in the cockpit; and because of this specific emphasis needs to be placed on the safe; accurate completion of these checklists.
output: A CRJ-900 flight crew experienced loss of electrical power on departure; possibly due to the Captain shutting down the generators.

input: I was working the radar position at the beginning of the session. Two aircraft were instrument flight rules inbound to an airport. Aircraft y was slightly behind and at 5;000 feet and direct to the airport. Aircraft x was slightly closer and at 6;000 feet setup to execute the area navigation approach into the airport. When aircraft x checked in i informed him that i would have to issue holding instructions as the approach would make him later to the airport but if he wanted to execute a visual approach we could get him inbound first. Aircraft x said he would take the visual so i cleared him inbound direct; cleared him to descend to 4;100 feet which is the minimum instrument flight rules altitude (mia). I told them to report the field in sight for a visual approach.aircraft y was informed that he was number 2 and would have to climb to 5;100 feet to provide separation between him and his friend both inbound at the same time. Aircraft y then turned 90 degrees to the north (right at aircraft x) and asked if he should go direct to the initial approach fix for the area navigation approach. I told him no and that i saw his turn and that he needed to continue westbound for the moment until we had altitude separation before i could issue a turn to the north. While this is happening aircraft x crosses my boundary and i issue 3;900 feet which is my mia and i inform him if he is unable to get the field in sight we may have to go to plan b as there were no lower altitudes i could provide. Aircraft x then proceeds to descend below 3;900 feet all the way to 2;100 feet and i asked him 'do you have the airport in sight?' aircraft x responds 'i have the ground in sight.' i am then getting my supervisor's attention to let her know what is going on (now about both aircraft) and that i need to have the brasher warning so i could provide it to them. While i am getting her attention aircraft x says field in sight cancel ifr... I accept his cancellation and then clear aircraft y inbound on the area navigation as it was obvious to me that 3;900 feet was not able to provide visual conditions to the field. I then give a briefing to the relieving controller and came here to report what had happened.both pilots need a refresher as to what instrument flight rules means and maybe take a break for a bit. One pilot almost had an instrument flight rules to instrument flight rules conflict by turning without instruction; the other could have had collision with terrain as he descended below his assigned altitude... Ridiculous!
output: An aircraft was descended to 3;900 feet for a Visual Approach. The aircraft descended on its own to 2;100 feet which is below the Minimum IFR Altitude before cancelling IFR. Another aircraft was climbed to 5;100 feet for separation. Instead the aircraft turned 90 degrees to the right on its own.

input: While on the rodio2 area navigation arrival into san antonio (ksat); the automatic terminal information service informed us runway 4 was in use. The pilot flying entered the runway and instrument landing system 04 in the flight management system while i checked the chart. While comparing the waypoints he mentioned that the flight management system had us going over troop and criss intersections. At first glance i thought runway 4 would take us over the southern arrival gate using poyig and berne; then saw the note at criss that listed runways 4; 12r; 30l so i agreed we would be using criss. Shortly; the approach controller asked if we were on the runway(s) 4 arrival course and i confirmed we were and expecting runway(s) 4. He came back in a minute and gave us a heading. I thought that might mean we were on the wrong one so i checked again and noticed that the note at criss stated 'landing other than san antonio int'l runway(s) 4; 12r; 30l'. I asked if we should rejoin and we were cleared to.then we had to resolve why the flight management system had kept the wrong transition points. We don't know exactly but i found that to get the correct ones i not only had to enter the runway(s) and approach but if i selected the standard terminal arrival route that it changed the waypoints to the correct transition. It is now my conclusion that when the flight plan was filed; the rodio2 was filed without a runway; but the criss arrival transition was in the flight plan. We were cleared as filed so these remained in the flight plan as it was loaded in the flight management system  the waypoints were correct but the rodio2 was not in the flight management system as a standard terminal arrival route merely as waypoints that were chosen from the flight planning software for filing.my mistake was obvious (misreading the note) but aggravated and allowed by the flight management system issue which caused me to believe my mistake. I would think that avoiding words like 'other than' would avoid missing this negative reference to the runways that are not intended.
output: A flight crew discovered that their FMS had kept the wrong transition points for their arrival runway. The arrival STAR was not loaded in the FMS. A confusing note over an expected transition point added to the confusion.

input: During cruise flight at 6000 feet/foot mean sea level our ground proximity warning system warning system sounded 'terrain; terrain; pull up; pull up.' i reacted to the warning because we were in instrument meteorological conditions conditions. We immediately initiated climb to 7000 feet/foot during this climb the ground proximity warning system stopped. Air traffic control was advised of this action immediately. There was agreement and coordinated action between the crew members. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr first officer upon looking back; knew that there was no high terrain in the area of the ground proximity warning system the flight crew says they were in heavy rain and icing conditions which could have caused the false warning. Aircraft was a fairchild f27.
output: GPWS 'TERRAIN; PULL UP' WARNING WHILE IN CRUISE. FLC FOLLOWED THE RA COMMAND AND CLBED. FALSE WARNING ATTRIBUTED TO HVY RAIN AND ICING.

input: An airbus on vectors to the instrument landing system runway 30 approach lgb heading north bound 030. A king air departed sna opposite direction on a local visual flight rules code with sba in his scratch pad. Initial call i ask if he wants flight following to sba? [it] seemed weird to me that he would come off on a local code to sba which is out of sct airspace. He then advised he wanted to pick up his instrument flight rules flight plan to sba. I looked over at the departure controller and asked if he would get me his instrument flight rules strip to sba. Since there was no prior coordination; as there usually is when they depart instrument flight rules i had no idea what he wanted. I then realized the airbus was approaching the final approach course and turned and descended/cleared him for the instrument landing system approach. The king air was then level at 2;400 feet/foot 2 miles north of the final; i then climbed the king air and told him to expedite his climb for airbus traffic 11 o'clock and 3 miles. While i was instructing the king air to climb; unannounced to me the airbus started a climb in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory from the king air. The king air; while reading back his climb instructions; advised me that the he had the airbus in sight and that the airbus appeared to be climbing. The airbus then advised that he was responding to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory and was climbing. The king air advised that he was turning right in response to the climbing airbus. While this was happening; the towers were opening; the line was ringing from ful and toa tower was calling over the shout line. A heads up would have been nice. It would have saved me coordinating with the king air.
output: SCT Controller described a conflict event between a LGB Air Carrier arrival and a VFR King Air departing SNA seeking an IFR clearance; the reporter indicting a heads-up from SNA Tower would have eased the situation.

input: I was working cd/cic combined in the tower. The local controller had traffic landing runway 1 and runway 10. A md82 was landing roll on runway 10; and an e170 was on final behind him. I told the local controller several times that i didn't think it was going to work; meaning that we would not have the runway separation we would need. He replied that if he had to send him around he would. I trusted that he would do this; i had no reason to doubt him. When the e170 was short final for runway 10; i stood up to see where the md82 was and he did not appear to be clear of the runway. I told the local controller that it looked like he (the e170) needed to go around. He said that he thought it was going work. I gave it a few more seconds; and then told him; 'you need send the e170 around.' he did not. The md82 was not yet clear of the runway and therefore separation was not ensured. It is extremely rare that we have any supervisors in the tower as they generally stay in terminal radar approach control facility or their office during their shift. I am not the only controller that has had these problems with other controllers not listening to the controller in charge in the tower; and i feel as though it makes the operation unsafe. I do not believe the local controller would have refused to do what i told him to do if a supervisor would have been present. I also feel as though we should be able to refuse the duty of controller in charge if we do not feel comfortable. I feel as though putting 'co-workers' in charge of each other throughout the day sets us up for failure in many different ways.
output: Tower CIC voiced concern regarding the lack of response to his direction to a controller reference runway separation; noting shift supervisor rarely reside in the Tower but spend time in the TRACON and their offices during the shift.

input: Normal climb to fl350; bwi direct atl. After being level at fl350 for some time; the ztl controller asked us our altitude replied level fl350. She then asked altimeter setting. Replied 29.92. She said she had us below fl350 (forget the exact altitude she said). We confirmed again we were level at fl350 with 29.92. We then switched modes on the mode celsius rpting; went to standby on the transponder and checkeded all system -- to no avail. She now had us level at fl310; yet we were still at fl350. She tried for quite some time to get another aircraft (acr y; b737) to see intermediate fix they could see us; but we had no other aircraft on our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii close to us. In addition; we had a normal climb to fl350 and were on top of a cloud system about 1000 feet/foot below us. An additional confusing problem was the fact that the controller kept calling us by the #xxxa instead of #xxxb. We tried several times to correct her. After quite a while of her talking to others; we lost her voice coverage and called in the blind for another frequency -- which we got; but we were never xferred. We don't know intermediate fix she mixed up aircraft with call signs that were similar or not. On our descent we got accurate mode celsius rpts from every controller after her -- no indication of failure of degradation in the mode celsius at all; nor on the succeeding flight where we had repeated checkeds done all the way up to fl330.
output: B737-200 CREW HAD THE ZTL CTLR TELL THEM THAT THE RADAR ALT READOUT ON THE RADAR SCOPE SHOWED AN INCORRECT ACFT ALT.

input: Clbing through 9100 feet/foot after handoff from msn departure to chi center 133.3. Told by center to level at 9000 feet/foot -- instantly told that was impossible; and took over control of aircraft stopped climb at 9600 feet/foot and hand flown back to 9000 feet/foot confirmed instrument flight rules status with chi center and saw another aircraft evading us in a left/right (directions) turn. No resolution advisory chi center recommended a turn for us but we were too busy stopping a climb and looking for conflicting traffic loss of coordination seemed to happen on handoff between departure and center clearance was given to 10000 feet/foot on initial contact (as best i can remember) with chi center climb clearance was confirmed when issued.
output: A G5 FLT CREW CLBING OUT OF 9000 FT WAS TOLD BY CHI ARTCC TO MAINTAIN 9000 FT FOR TFC. THE G5 CLBED TO 9600 FT BEFORE DSNDING TO 9000 FT.

input: Enrte from lihue; hi; to honolulu we were cleared to 15000 feet/foot we were following slower traffic which we had on our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii as we approached our cruise altitude we were told to expect to slow up to 250 knot(s) at booke intersection i was looking outside for the traffic and flew through 15000 feet/foot to 15600 feet/foot at about the same time we were given 8000 feet/foot and were asked by the controller to say our altitude second officer that he could verify his equipment by now we were at 14600 feet/foot on our dscnt.
output: RPTED 600 FT ALTDEV BY DC9 CLBING TO 15000 FT.

input: Additional paper was inserted into the release. It was a copy of a government chart for tpa. On this chart; it indicated that the current commercial chart for tpa was incorrect. This government chart indicated by a caution note on the bottom to inform pilots that the taxiway signage changes the commercial chart were not yet changed on the airport surface area making the commercial chart inaccurate as to airport taxiway signage. The government chart received had an effective timeframe as to the effective change of when the airport signage on the surface area was to be completed. Intermediate fix tpa operations(s) did not take the time to make photo copies of this page and insert it into releases; this information would not have been disseminated. The signage that has not been changed are a taxiway on the east side of the airport and certain taxiway intxns. Even though you are legal with the current commercial updates; you may not have all the correct information to taxi on the surface area at tpa. I feel the chart manufacturer should be notified; or a copy of this government chart should be attained from tpa operations(s) or the tpa commercial charts themselves and distribute it via an operations(s) memo for those pilots have not been to tpa. The problem and safety issue could arise when visibility is reduced and the taxi instructions given can be different from those on the commercial page itself.
output: EMB135 PLT IS CONCERNED WITH THE COMMERCIAL CHART FOR TPA.

input: Given clearance to cross 40 mile se of atl (on the sinca arr) at 11000 feet/foot first officer was pilot flying and i was working the radios. I had taken the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction from center and had repeated it aloud (i thought) to the first officer as per company procedures however; he did not hear what i said and did not note our new clearance we flew at 15000 feet/foot until we were within 5 nautical mile of our assigned crossing altitude before zjx called and asked us what we were doing. We were then told to switch to ztl who informed us that we could descend basically at our discretion. Fortunately there was no traffic conflict. First officer had been tired and absentminded the previous day and had not slept well the previous evening. I should have done a better job of making sure my message had been received and understood by the other crew member.
output: AN ACR LTT MISSED ITS XING RESTR BECAUSE THE FO FAILED TO LISTEN TO; OR HEAR; THE CLRNC AND THE CAPT'S REPEAT OF THE CLRNC. ALTDEV. NON ADHERENCE TO ATC CLRNC. ERROR ADMITTED.

input: This unsafe condition is the result of lights blinding and/or disorienting pilots on short final to touch down. This condition was created with a private airpark adjacent to an indian reservation. The airpark has 50 plus aircraft the yavapai-apache built a casino on the reservation with no ill affects to the nation or the airpark. In 2001 the nation installed a rotating beacon of lights on the roof of the casino. These approximately twelve beacons are in the shape of a cone that rotate and are directed over the runway(s) of the airpark. The lights are directed at a highway on a hill approximately five miles away. Due to the dry air of arizona the beacons viewed from the side are virtually invisible. The rotating beams of light are not seen until turning from base to final then are viewed directly into the beam. Conversation with the casino manager met with little cooperation in redirecting or extinguishing the lights. The lights are on from the onset of darkness until around 3:00 ante meridiem it is recognized that the reservation is a sovereign nation and not subject to the laws of the united states or the state of arizona. But; once these light beams cross the property line they are no longer on the sovereign nation but in federal aviation airspace.
output: AMATEUR BUILT SMA PRIVATE PLT IS TEMPORARILY BLINDED DURING A NIGHT APCH AND LNDG AT A PRIVATE ARPT DUE TO FLOODS LIGHTS SHINING INTO HIS EYES FROM AN INDIAN OWNED CASINO ADJACENT TO THE AIRFIELD.

input: The problem arose due to out of date charts. The pilot crew had no reason to suspect that the company issued flight kit was out of date. The company had declared this flight kit was brand new. We received the 'new' flight kit on nov/fri/89 for a new upstart flight operation out of erie; public address beginning on nov/mon/89. Our normal run is from erie; public address to cleveland; oh. On nov/thu/89 our flight was dispatched to detroit; mile on a pop-up unscheduled run which light emitting diode to our discovery that our charts for the area were out of date. We suspected out of date chart when unable to find spica intersection (a clearance routing received from erie dep) on our low en route chart (#22). The actual discovery was made when given a heading to intercept airway; which we already indicated we were on. Air traffic control then made mention that our chart was out of date. Corrective actions included picking up sufficient; up to date chart coverage before leaving detroit; mile and immediately notifying company to this issue. The kit was obviously not brand new. Revisions number 28 and 29 were missing. The crew has no way of knowing this and it is not considered frugal to question your company's integrity to this. A possible solution to deter the recurrence of such a problem would be for chart publisher to stamp the 'record of revision sheet' with the next revision due date or put the date by the last revision stamped since all pilots know that revisions come out every 2 weeks.
output: COMMUTER SMT FLEW FOR A WEEK WITH OUTDATED ROUTE CHARTS. ARTCC RADAR CTLR FINALLY DETECTED THE PROBLEM WHEN ACFT REPORTED ON TRACK BUT WAS NOT.

input: Departing cmi; received lavatory smoke indication on engine indicating and crew alerting system shortly after takeoff completed chklist; and engine indicating and crew alerting system message extinguished. Approximately 3 minute(s) later; lavatory smoke engine indicating and crew alerting system message reappeared and cycled on and off continuously. Decision to return to cmi made; and diversion successfully completed without incident.
output: EMB145 FLT CREW HAS EICAS MESSAGE 'LAVATORY SMOKE;' DIVERTS AND LANDS.

input: At approximately yy15 local my student and i were instructed to hold over the mlb vor and dme (co-located) at 3500 feet/foot south on the 180 degree radial with left/right (directions) turns. As we were holding; i heard another aircraft approach the area with a vector of 270 degrees to fly around an aircraft holding over the vor and dme (co-located) at 3500 feet/foot which was us. I cannot recall patrick approach notifying us of this traffic approximately 5 minute(s) later as we were turning inbound to the vor and dme (co-located) i saw the other aircraft at our 12:30 o'clock position and lower; approximately 100 feet/foot flying away. At that time patrick approach tried to reach us. The controller told us he tried to reach us twice without response. My student and i cannot recall approach calling us. I believe the controller forgot us because he was handling a passenber jet that was inbound to mlb. Upon the near midair; i requested to terminate holding. As the safety pilot i did not see the traffic nor did i hear the aircraft approach the protected area of the holding pattern. Since he was lower; i think the low wing design contributed to the inability to see the other traffic supplemental information from acn 359742: fully occupied in the cockpit with my training; my instructor was watching visual for traffic just entering a left/right (directions) turn for 180 degrees i heard patrick approach call out to another pa28-161 that i was holding on 180 degree radial at 3500 feet/foot after completing my 1 minute(s) leg in the 180 degree radial; i made my left/right (directions) turn inbound on the 360 degree radial. Turning left/right (directions) i completed my 180 degree turn to 360 degrees and when i rolled out of the turn; i noticed out my left/right (directions) front window there was a pa28-161 approximately 25 feet/foot below my holding pattern. He was aiming straight at me with no intention to avoid a situation or traffic whatsoever. Approach warned the traffic of our position and flight pattern. He was to avoid us and pay attention which he failed to do. We then got a call from approach and they knew nothing about the close encounter. This situation could have been avoided intermediate fix the other party paid attention and listened to our position and avoided it. I honestly cannot think of anything wrong that we did or could have done to avoid this sit.
output: A PA28-161 HAS AN NMAC WITH ANOTHER PA28-161 IN THE HOLDING PATTERN OVER MLB; FL. ACFT MISS EACH OTHER BY 100 FT; BUT NO EVASIVE ACTION IS TAKEN.

input: I was working the rober radar position about xa00 when i lost my radar and my radios at the same time. I had 5 aircraft on vectors to jfk airport at the time that i lost all of my tools. Other position in the jfk approach area also lost radar and their radios. For about 5 minute(s) the airplanes were not under air traffic control control in a very busy and congested terminal area.
output: N90 CTLR DESCRIBED A FIVE MIN RADAR AND RADIO FAILURE WHILE WORKING ARR'S TO JFK.

input: I was working in hangar and was told to help move aircraft x and aircraft y into [another] hangar. I was told there were no leads nor mechanics working in that hangar. Aircraft x was towed to the hangar first at around xa30hrs. Aircraft y followed at around xb30hrs. While waiting for aircraft y to arrive; i noticed a large area of prior lightning strikes; on the aircraft's right side; that had been repaired. While looking at the repairs; i was walking towards the right ram air door and pushed in on it. There's a prior fleet engineering directive on them and i knew we've been having many planes come into hangar with them bad. When i pushed on it; it moved inward; which meant it was bad. I checked the left side and it was good. A short while later aircraft y was pulling up; so while we (the move team i was on) was waiting to receive the aircraft; i took a look at the ram air doors and found the right one bad on it too. After the aircraft was in the hangar; the move team [and i] all went back to our hangar. I waited a short time for a computer to become available so i could look up to see if the ram air doors on the two aircraft weren't already written up. Once i learned that there wasn't any open log pages on them; i decided to write them up. After i wrote them up; i went back to my work assignments. I was waiting for an eec (electronic engine controller) to arrive to install it on the aircraft in hangar. About an hour later; i was approached by my supervisor and asked about my write-ups. I told him about them and he walked away. About 15 minutes later; he comes back up to me and tells me to go get started on my write-ups and so i got my tools and walked over to [other] hangar. I started working on aircraft x by filling out tags and removing panels. By this time it was shift change and the graveyard shift had come onto the floor and i gave my turnover to the mechanics working my write up. I went back to hangar to update my work i had just performed. A few minutes later supervisor came into the computer room telling me to go to [other] hangar to fill out a fact finding sheet. I told him that i was still signing my work off. He persisted for a few minutes to tell me to go. By this time it is getting close to the end of my shift so i told him i am not staying over; i will fill one out when i come back in to work. A few more minutes go by and shift manager comes blasting through the computer room door where i'm still updating my work performed and he starts yelling and badgering me to go next door and fill out that fact finding sheet! This went on for another minute until he tells me to give him my badges and he is going to punch me out. After another minute; i finish my updates and i am escorted by shift manager to [other[ hangar supervisor's office. Just prior to entering the office; union steward meets me and i briefly explain the situation to him. Union steward and i enter the office where shift manager then leaves and i am met with a barrage of questions and allegations from supervisor and [another] supervisor ([other] hangar supervisor) about my write-ups. After the fact finding sheet was completed; i walked over to hangar and washed up and went home.
output: Technician reported that after checking several aircraft; he found them to have malfunctioning RH ram air door actuators requiring replacement and made logbook entries; after which Company Management berated him for doing so.

input: Vectored off of zzzzz 4 standard terminal arrival route and directed to descend to 5;000 feet and proceed direct to zzzzz and intercept the runway xxl localizer loaded zzzzz in flight management system selected lateral navigation and armed localizer while on a roughly southwest heading and proceeding direct to zzzzz in lnav/vnav; but still well east of runway xxl we experienced a false localizer capture and the autopilot and flight director system turned the aircraft to a heading of 176 degrees. Disconnected autopilot and flight director system and de-armed the localizer and then used heading select to turn back to zzzzz. While in the process of turning back to zzzzz; approach control called us and said 'flight aaab i need you direct to zzzzz; turn right heading xxx.' we proceeded direct to zzzzz and landed uneventfully.pf and post meridiem both recently returned to flying after long layoffs and that may have contributed. I knew for sure not to arm the approach (app) mode too early due to the aircraft either climbing to join the glide slope or descending on the glide slope before being established on the localizer; and was aware of the possibility of false localizer capture; but had never experienced a false localizer capture before.using lateral navigation to intercept the localizer is a normal procedure; but possibly don't arm not only the app mode; but also the localizer until within a few degrees of the instrument landing system final approach course. However this procedure could cause its own set of problems/conflicts by setting you up for flying through the localizer if you forget to arm the loc.
output: Air Carrier flight crew reported a false localizer capture; they were slow to react to the event and a track deviation occurred. The pilots stated an extended period of time off was a factor in their reaction time.

input: Company engineering started the practice of making available pdf versions of the component maintenance manual (cmm) engineering orders (eo) for field use; instead of putting the information in the boeing illustrated parts catalog (ipc). These engineering orders are generally used for cabin furnishings/galleys/seats and the like. The web page that is used to deliver this information to the mechanic contains aircraft effectivity and links to the effective engineering orders.some of these are for obsolete equipment that has been long removed. The overall layout of the site is very confusing and has erroneous links/labels; and within it; is a link to another eo site with a different presentation; different labels and erroneous labels/links for those engineering order manuals. I fear that someone is going to mistakenly put the wrong part on the wrong seat/component. The chances of an actual unsafe condition are low; but there is greater probability of an federal aviation administration violation. The mistakes seem to be only with the presentation [display] of the component engineering orders. The data contained within seems to be ok. The trick is getting to the correct eo to begin with. The problems i am aware of are in the b767 and b777 index of the web page.i have tried for over a year to get someone to update the information with engineering requests; no luck. I hope that someone can convince engineering and [technical] publications to get together and correct how this information is presented and correct the effectivity problems. The new b777s are on the way with all new cabin interior; it would be nice to have a solid foundation to deliver this new data.
output: A Technician describes a practice started by Engineering of making available a PDF version of their Component Engineering Orders (EO) for field use; instead of putting the EO information for their B767/B777 aircraft in the aircraft Manufacturer's Illustrated Parts Catalog (IPC). The web page presentation has been very confusing with erroneous links.

input: The aircraft was instructed by edmonton center to descend to fl290. On further investigation; the original flight plan was found to have used both an incorrect cardinal altitude and rvsm altitude data when the flight plan was compiled. The actual flight plan reflected fl310 from departure through n6000.00 w08600.00. After this fix it incorrectly showed fl320 through n7500.00 through w08500.00. When the aircraft reached edmonton center they immediately recognized the aircraft was not on the correct rvsm altitude and issued a descent instruction to the correct fl290 altitude it was at this time that dispatch became aware of the flight plan error. Because of the assigned fl290 would have necessitated a fuel stop; discussion began with edmonton to enable the continuance of the flight until the aircraft could climb to the appropriate rvsm altitude when this problem was investigated we found the following: the incorrect altitude issue is a problem when our minimum time tracks zigzags through canadian airspace. Unfortunately this known flaw with the flight planning system is manually corrected by the use of overrides by dispatch support when they message the route into the flight plan computer. Unfortunately the flaw was not found in the time track until edmonton center informed us of the wrong altitude the current flight planning system is severely challenged when changing from conventional airspace into rvsm airspace and particularly when the flight is starting out on a westerly heading then changing to an easterly heading and then finally back to a westerly heading. The airspace into which this aircraft was flying is some of the most challenging; not only from an air traffic control perspective; but also from an operational rules perspective and our current flight planning infrastructure is being stretched beyond its fixed fte origins/capabilities. The maintenance of a manual navigate, navigation database augmented by data supplied by the time track process is of serious concern. They require too many manual 'user-work-arounds' to many patches with the minimum of automation in terms of quality control checkeds built into the system to support this type of advanced flight planning.
output: B747-400 CREW WAS NOT AT THE CORRECT ALT IN CANADIAN RVSM AIRSPACE. THE COMPANY DID NOT FILE THE CORRECT ALT.

input: On final approach smoke appeared in cabin. A bluish smoke. I continued flying aircraft capt communicated with flight attendants. Capt turned off suspected air-conditioning pack. Smoke stopped. Landing uneventful. Taxied to gate.
output: MD88 ACFT ON APCH HAD SMOKE IN CABIN. CAPT TURNED OFF SUSPECTED AIR-CONDITIONING PACK AND SMOKE STOPPED. RPTR FO CONTINUED THE APCH; LANDED AND TAXIED NORMALLY WITHOUT FURTHER SMOKE.

input: Aircraft x departed lex assigned 050 for crossing traffic that was pointed out to tower. Crossing traffic was aircraft y. Traffic was issued to both aircraft by radar east. Shortly after; aircraft y reported the aircraft x in sight. As legal class celsius separation of 500 feet vertical was being maintained; aircraft y was not instructed to maintain visual separation as it was not required. Aircraft x was advised aircraft y had him in sight but aircraft x immediately reported he was responding to resolution advisory and descending. The pilot of aircraft x stated that even he was confused why his traffic alert and collision avoidance system was commanding an resolution advisory in this situation. No loss of separation occurred.this is all too common an occurrence in class celsius radar environments. It's getting so that we either have to provide 3 miles or 1;000 feet between ifr/vfr aircraft or else the instrument flight rules will report they're responding to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory for a non-event. I honestly have no idea what could be done to fix the issue. It's not like we want to go back to the days of giving the pilots an option to follow or not follow traffic alert and collision avoidance system ras; but perhaps there needs to be a system setting for class c/d airspace and class a/b airspace environments. Given that the pilot of the aircraft x sounded perplexed as to why he was getting an resolution advisory and the frequency at which this type of event occurs; it doesn't seem too farfetched to consider that maybe pilots are getting tired of such 'the boy yelled wolf!' scenarios. At what point do such nuisance/unwarranted ras cause pilots to lose faith in the resolution advisory system; or induce a false sense of complacency when responding to them?
output: A LEX Tower Controller reports of an airborne conflict that traffic has been issued to. One of the two aircraft sees the other. The other aircraft gets an RA and descends. Legal separation was continued but the Controller is reporting that this type of conflict happens all the time in the Class C environment. The Controller is concerned about the 'boy yelling wolf' scenario that pilots might lose faith in the RA System.

input: On final approach into ord the nose gear red warning light illuminated when the landing gear lever was lowered indicating that the nose gear was not down and locked. I executed a missed approach and advised air traffic control a visibility fly-by rpted by another airline crew advised us that the nose gear was only partially lowered. After consultation with company maintenance and advising dispatch; we exhausted all flight manual corrective procedures we then declared an emergency with air traffic control accomplished all required chklists and briefed the passenber and f/a's who accomplished the required emergency landing preparations. We then landed w/o incident.
output: EMERGENCY DECLARED AS GEAR INDICATION FOR NOSE WHEEL INDICATES UNSAFE.

input: In 1997 aircraft x sustained damage to nose area of fuselage. Damage at the time was determined minor. No further action taken and damage entered on aircraft damage file. On feb/mon/00; aircraft was in heavy maintenance for quality checked i performed an inspection of aircraft and accomplished job card x (adf). Step 3 of card asks to rechk damage for further progression; none was noted. It also asks for you to xfer items to x discrepancy cards. My interpretation was for any new damage items which there were none at the time. Recently; air carrier x accomplished a self audit and found that the damage that occurred in 1997 should have had repetitive inspections and not just signed off onto the damage file of the aircraft they also noted that in feb/00 during quality checked no items were written. They feel that should i have written all damage items that were listed on the aircraft damage file; that the original oversight would have been picked up and corrected. It was brought to my attention that i did not accomplish the intent of the job card. I explained to the chief inspector for air carrier x the reason i did not accomplish this and we both agreed that further clarification was needed to correct any future discrepancies; not only by me but any inspector. At present; the inspection department is looking into clarifying the sit.
output: A B737-300 INCURRED NOSE GEAR DAMAGE IN 1997 BUT FOLLOW-UP INSPECTIONS DID NOT CARRY FORWARD OLD DAMAGE AS WELL AS NEW DAMAGE FOUND DUE TO JOB CARD INTERP.

input: My first indication that we might have crossed a runway(s) without clearance was when we advised tower that we were ready for takeoff and the tower controller seemed somewhat surprised that we were on the east side of runway(s) 3 on celsius taxiway and asked us which runway(s) we were using for takeoff we thought (may have assumed) runway(s) 36. In retrospect we were unsure which runway(s) we had been cleared to originally; but had been apparently confused (unaware) by some of the instruction we received from ground control we received taxi instructions to depart the ramp and follow the ltt ahead of us to the runway(s) when the ltt was approaching the intersection of taxiways a and celsius it was directed to follow the air carrier lgt on taxiway celsius to runway(s) 36 and another air carrier mlg holding on celsius taxiway was directed to follow the ltt to runway(s) 36 and we were told to give way to the mlg and follow it to runway(s) 36 or was it 3 (we thought or assumed 36). It was when we called the tower ready for takeoff while on taxiway celsius east of runway(s) 3 when we got our first indication that we may have crossed runway(s) 3 without clearance to do second officer i suspect that there was no close call as we crossed runway(s) 3 right behind the mlg and were not asked by the tower controller why had we crossed runway(s) 3 without clearance human factors: there was some sense of urgency for the crew; as we were trying to arrive at jfk prior to 1500 (l) after which aro's are required and we didn't have one. This may have caused some distraction for us. The taxi sequencing and instructions tend to make us think that we were cleared to runway(s) 36 instead of 3. Also at that time no other aircraft in front of us had been clear for a runway(s) 3 departure and seeing all the other turbojet aircraft departing runway(s) 36 we may have wrongly assumed that we were departing from runway(s) 36 also. I also suspect that there was some confusion on the part of the ground controllers for intermediate fix in fact they had intended a runway(s) 3 departure for us they should have (as logic would seem to dictate) instructed us to turn left/right (directions) on taxiway b from a (instead of following the mlg on celsius taxiway) in order utilize the full length of runway(s) 3. Additionally as runway(s) 3 is only 4905 feet/foot and runway(s) 36 is 6869 feet/foot it would seem that in most cases runway(s) 36 is the preferred runway(s) foremost turbojets. This fact in conjunction with our company policy of not normally using runway(s) shorter than 5000 feet/foot may have influenced our perception that we had been cleared to runway(s) 36 and not runway(s) 3.
output: CHARTER FLT CONFUSED REF TAXI CLRNC.

input: As we were cleared to taxi off gate and turned on my taxi light for a left/right (directions) turn out of the gate. As i added power and began moving; i noticed a truck off my left/right (directions) not slowing down approaching me. I had to jump on the brakes as the driver of the truck did not slow down. He sped in front of me. It appears that the contracted companies are not trained to allow aircraft the right of way. Intermediate fix i had not stopped; i ante meridiem convinced i would have hit him.
output: AN A320 PLT WAS FORCED TO RAPIDLY STOP THE ACFT IN ORDER TO PREVENT A GND COLLISION WITH A CONTRACTOR'S VEHICLE IN THE RAMP AREA.

input: After takeoff with positive rate of climb; the gear was selected up. The gear handle stopped only halfway. I left the gear selected in the down position and figured that we would gain altitude and check it out. I looked out the front and saw a flock of geese. I said it out loud to make sure the pilot flying had seen them; however there was nowhere to go. We then heard and felt geese hit the plane. The left engine indications became erratic and we decided to return for landing. I informed the tower of what had happened and our intentions. We were cleared to enter downwind and land. I then heard someone say that our left engine was smoking. We had gained enough altitude to make the decision to shut the left engine off; especially with the indications we were getting and the fact that it was reported smoking. We landed cautiously with the knowledge that the gear was down during the bird strike and could potentially be damaged. The landing was normal and we taxied to parking.
output: Distracted by a landing gear that failed to retract; the flight crew of a BAE-125-850XP noted a gaggle of geese too close ahead to avoid; and felt one or more strike the aircraft. The impact was followed by erratic indications and a report of smoke from the left engine heard over the radio. They performed an inflight shut down; and returned to their departure airport for an uneventful landing.

input: The plane departed the fixed-base operator maintenance ramp for a post maintenance and pre-buy flight with myself and the buyers agent in the aircraft. The planned flight (ifr plan) was round robin out and back. The takeoff and climb out and all checks during the flight were normal with only a few minor squawks discovered. The tests were concluded and we returned to the departure airport from a couple instrument landing system to runway 11. The approach and touchdown were normal and as i tapped the brakes and applied thrust reverse; it became obvious there was a problem. The brakes were locked and both main tires were blown as a result. Maintenance is inspecting the plane for a fault determination; anti-skid is a suspect. There were no injuries.
output: A C550 returned from a test flight and upon landing a suspected antiskid malfunction locked the brakes locked causing flat tires.

input: We experienced very high frequency data packet bursts interfering with primary communications during landing. We were in the last stages of a night visual approach into den on final for 35r. Our altitude was between 200 and 300 feet above ground level transitioning to the landing phase. The aircraft was fully configured for landing. Very high frequency comm 1 was selected for both receiving and transmitting and was tuned to denver tower on 133.3. Very high frequency comm 2 was tuned to arinc and deselected. Very high frequency comm 3 was in its normal data mode and deselected. All other settings were per standard operating procedure the data bursts were easily heard on the active comm 1. There were three bursts total; similar in sound; each lasting less than two seconds and occurring successively. One burst blocked a portion of denver tower's transmission; however; the transmission was not intended for our flight. The other two bursts occurred during radio silence between transmissions. The bursts were consistent with the sound of automatic communications addressing & reporting system transmissions or other very high frequency packet bursts. We didn't experience any other radio anomalies during our two legs that day on that specific aircraft. This is not the first experience i've had with these bursts; merely the first that i tracked data for. Previous experiences occurred in nearly identical positioning of the aircraft on final approach into denver.
output: A319 pilot reported VHF communications were interrupted by data packet bursts on short final at DEN.

input: Prior to taking runway(s) 31 at mli for takeoff adjusted pilot seat closer to instrument panel 1 stop. Tried to scoot seat both ways as a checked that the locking pin was seated and seat was apparently locked in place as there was no significant motion. However; upon advancing the throttle for takeoff the seat slid back too federal aviation regulation for the pilot to reach the rudder pedals. The throttle was partly withdrawn (or maybe fully) in an attempt to abort the takeoff but the airplane was heading too fast off the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) at a runway(s) light and no braking was within reach. The airplane was lifted off in ground effect to avoid the runway(s) light; successfully; and possibly some throttle was added; but probably not much; because of the lack of rudder control next the airplane which was in a positive rate of climb by this time; had to be banked to the left/right (directions) to avoid a pole with a windsock on it. Once the maneuver was completed; with no other obstacles in sight; the pilot was able to return his seat to the proper position and regain full control and continue the climb he rpted what had happened to the tower and told them he wanted to continue the flight to mgy. However; when they asked him to call the tower when he reached his destination he offered to return immediately. He also assured them that he had felt no jar as intermediate fix the airplane had contacted anything and that it was running fine. At mgy; he called the mli tower at the number they had given him. He again assured them that there was no damage to his airplane. Upon his inquiry; they said they had found no damage at mli. Upon their request; he gave them his name; address; and telephone number. A cessna secondary seat stop kit is installed in the airplane; which should have prevented the seat from coming second officer federal aviation regulation back in event of lack of locking in place. The pilot plans to take the airplane to the certified repair station when he has the annuals done on the airplane; to have the seat rails and locking mechanism checkeded and also the action of the secondary seat stop. On the ground the stop appeared to work ok when tested by the pilot at mgy. In the air at mli; the normal locking mechanism appeared to function properly; as it did later at mgy.
output: PLT LOST DIRECTIONAL CTL OF HIS SMA SEL DURING TKOF DUE TO HIS SEAT SLIDING BACK AND REMOVING HIM FROM THE ACFT RUDDERS AND BRAKES. HOWEVER; HE WAS ABLE TO CTL ACFT SUFFICIENTLY TO AVOID HITTING A RWY LIGHT AND A WIND SOCK POLE.

input: In late july the #3 cylinder exhaust valve broke. Today; 11/fri/01; was a clear beautiful visual flight rules day second officer i decided to fly an hour to help break in the new cylinder. I flew from my home airport and since i fish in the river near yyy; i decided to follow highways to yyy and observe my fishing grounds from the air. I returned along the same route; somewhat more north of us highway being very cautious to avoid the zzz controlled airspace. I had not yet flown an hour second officer i flew to zzz1 for a practice instrument landing system approach i monitored advisory frequency the entire flight since that is the advisory frequency for two other airports i announced my maneuvering while near second airport when i landed the zzz2 airport manager asked me to call the zzz tower which i did. They asked me to call a supervisor at center. I don't recall which of these informed me that a restricted 10 mile airspace had been placed around a power plant; and as i had followed along us highway route i had violated that airspace. Center said i would be contacted in the next few days. I was following a current sectional which had no restrict, restricted, restriction airspace. The recorded flight service station specialist weather for the route had no mention of additional restrict, restricted, restriction airspace near that route. Because the weather was cavu and i thought i was on just a local flight i did not talk to a briefer nor did i file a flight plan. Although i don't usually talk to a briefer prior to a local warm-up flight the zzz2 airport manger suggested to me afterwards that due to 09/tue/01 events it would be a good idea to always talk to a briefer prior to any flight even intermediate fix only in the local pattern. I will adopt that policy to avoid flying in restrict, restricted, restriction airspace. I did not intentionally violate any airspace.
output: A COMMERCIAL PLT ENTERS THE NEWLY ESTABLISHED NO FLY ZONE/TEMPORARY FLT RESTR AREA NEAR A NUCLEAR PWR PLANT NW OF ZZZ VOR; US.

input: After gdl approach control changed our approach 3 times we finally flew the vor and dme (co-located) to runway 10 to intercept the instrument landing system to runway 10. This was a very confusing clearance seeing as the controller could have just cleared us to the vor and dme (co-located) to start the instrument landing system procedure turn. Our original clearance was vectors to the instrument landing system 10. Also; my ipad did not have a single vor and dme (co-located) approach in it. Only the fo's ipad had the vor and dme (co-located) approach. We confirmed that the radials and altitudes on the approach were the same; so we continued the approach. After crossing the 12 vor and dme (co-located) fix outbound on the procedure turn we could descend to 8400 feet until crossing the 12 vor and dme (co-located) fix inbound on the instrument landing system during the turn inbound to intercept the instrument landing system at approximately 8500 feet we got a caution terrain on the ground proximity warning system we were both somewhat confused about the warning as we could see the top of the hill and per procedure cleared to 8400 feet on the turn inbound. I turned off the autopilot and stopped the descent rate and climbed a few hundred feet. As soon as i stopped the descent the warning went away. We could only assume that it was the descent rate with open descent selected on the mode control panel that caused the warning. In any case; that certainly was a very confusing warning as per procedure you are cleared to 8400 feet on the turn inbound to the instrument landing system we continued to land without incident and discussed the warning after the parking checklist was finished. We both concluded that we flew the procedure correctly and that the only issue that could have caused the ground proximity warning system warning was our descent rate closure to the hills below us.
output: As an A320 approached a known 7;840 foot obstacle on the MMGL ILS 10 approach; the EGPWS alerted CAUTION; TERRAIN nearing the 8;400 foot descent constraint.

input: Ozark area had weather from the start of the shift. We started with 11 cpc's however our flm left for a class so we needed to utilize a controller in charge by the time i started working on sector 31 we had 20 miles in trail (mit) for dfw and a line of weather running through the middle of our area. On multiple occasions; every cpc on the shift was working; no one on break. Ozark was required to get 20 mit by the zme boundary; however we were getting dfw arrivals from every direction and many aircraft were deviating around the weather. It was extremely difficult for us to meet all of our requirements at that time and keep everyone safe. There were occasions where we were told to reroute a/c for the weather; for tmu restrictions and for other sectors that have been alerted. I called zme at one point and told them that we were having a difficult time getting out 20 mit and asked for relief. They were more than willing to accommodate us. This is a phone call that tmu should have been making. Every sector at the time in ozark was very busy. We shouldn't have to override tmu and do sector to sector coordination in these situations. Later; i spoke with other controllers from other areas and they said that they were having similar problems.
