This is an unsafe and inefficient situation that shouldn't have happened in the first place. Also; we had another supervisor that was assigned to rivers area across the aisle. They were not as busy and had the same staffing. A controller from rivers actually recommended that the flm go back to our area to help and to put a controller in charge in charge because ozark was swamped and he said; 'no; they'll be fine.' this is unacceptable.tmu needs to be held more accountable. Saying; 'we need 20 mit' isn't an acceptable answer when we have weather and a high volume of traffic. Tmu needs to be more proactive in helping its fellow controllers at zkc. Problems like this happen more often than not with our tmu. Also; the outer marker should have had more of a hand in the situation. He even came in to the area at one point and just stood behind the controllers. Either come in to offer help or don't come in. This only makes the controllers uncomfortable and diverts their attention. I recommend that the outer marker be more involved. He should have told the flm to put a controller in charge in at rivers and go work in ozark until the traffic died down. Or; pull the other supervisor from training and have him work the desk. Tmu should have realized that ozark was over their heads and helped by getting us relief on our in trail requirements or told our surrounding sectors to start in trail or moved a/c out of ozark. Ot should have been called. We need tmu/om to 'have our backs' and they didn't.
output: ZKC ARTCC controller's sectors experienced numerous weather deviations and an excessive amount of complex traffic. The supervisors were out of the area doing administrative duties and the Traffic Management Unit was not taking any action to restrict the traffic into the affected sectors.

input: We were instrument flight rules level at 10;000 ft. We received an alert on the avidyne traffic system; and also on foreflight which was running on an ipad. I advised the controller that we had traffic showing at 9 o'clock near our altitude. She advised us that they were going to pass 1;000 ft below us at 9;000 ft. We showed the aircraft was still at 10;000 ft and getting very close (less than 1/2 mile). At that time we received an alert that showed the other aircraft was at our location and less than 100 ft below. We made an immediate 90 degree turn to the right (north) and climbed. As we were talking; another controller came on and said that the other aircraft was descending. We advised air traffic control of the diversion and returned to our assigned course when the traffic was past us.upon landing; we were still not sure how close we were. We downloaded the ads-b data from both aircraft and plotted them in excel (we had the call sign from the traffic system and hearing air traffic control talk to them after). We were chilled to see just how close we had come. The adsb data shows that the cj2 began a descent; but then briefly leveled off at 10;000 ft (our altitude). Unfortunately this happened just as they were passing our location.
output: C182 pilot reported an NMAC with a CJ2.

input: I was observing the operation on the south side of the tower. Aircraft x landed runway 25l; exited to join taxiway h westbound; and was now being taxied across runway 25r at taxiway t by the lc1 controller. Aircraft y was in position on runway 25r. When aircraft x had crossed the majority of runway 25r; lc1 cleared aircraft y for take off. Aircraft x had stopped and not turned onto taxiway b; aircraft x still had a good portion of their tail over the runway 25r hold bars when aircraft y was cleared for take off. Aircraft x was just fully clearing runway 25r when aircraft y had rotated; and was passing taxiway p. I believe that the lc1 controller knew that aircraft x was still partially on the runway; but cleared aircraft y for take off anyway. Recommendation; i recommend a change in the safety culture at lax airport traffic control tower because it doesn't appear that they got the memo about the federal aviation administration being safety focused. Quite simply; it appears that lax management is willing to 'play the odds' that if they bend/break the rules; the odds say; nothing will happen.
output: LAX Controller described a potential ground conflict event.  Local Controller cleared an aircraft for take off; prior to crossing traffic being clear of the departure runway.

input: Level 11000 feet/foot on trake arrival, arrive to stl. Cleared to 7000 feet/foot slowed 250 knot(s) and extended speed brakes. Passing 7300 feet/foot traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory sounded with climb command. Approach had not previously issued traffic climb commenced; traffic acquired visually and conflict resolved by 7700 feet/foot aircraft was cleared to 6000 feet/foot (other aircraft y) on the departure air traffic control was notified of the deviation and we were cleared back to 7000 feet/foot aircraft did not level at 7000 feet/foot and descended below 7000 feet/foot before recovery was initiated. Aircraft x descended to about 6700 feet/foot before reversal was accomplished. Aircraft flown to 7000 feet/foot promptly. Air traffic control asked for altitude confirmation. We confirmed 7000 feet/foot and were cleared to 4000 feet/foot and the rest of the arrival, arrive was uneventful.
output: 2 ALTDEVS ALT EXCURSION ALT OVERSHOT IN DSCNT AFTER TCASII RA.

input: We were hearing drone reports by air traffic control we were eventually given a traffic advisory for the drones ourselves. We kept a look out and the first officer spotted 2 drones flying about a half mile laterally to the right of us; and 500-1000 feet below us when we were 2 miles prior to greko on the approach for runway 22 in la guardia. He kept them in sight and we were clear of them; continuing without having to take evasive action. The sun was setting and he wasn't sure if the light was reflecting off of red paint; or if the drones were emitting a red light on each of them. We reported the drones to air traffic control and made a phone call to them after we parked at the gate.
output: Air carrier Captain reported sighting 2 UAVs while conducting an approach at LGA. The event was reported to ATC; however no evasive action was taken.

input: I was assigned as pilot in command to fly a trip to lft and then back to rdu. The day prior to the trip i was teaching a learjet recurrent ground school and the two students in the class happened to be the director of operations and the chief pilot of the company. During the class i received a text from my dispatch asking; 'will you be able to do 8 passengers on tomorrow's flight?' i knew that lafayette only had one long runway and that it was going to be a hot day (100 degrees f) so i replied; 'checking notams' because i knew that if the long runway was for some reason closed then the trip would not be possible. At the time i was teaching a class so i thought it would be a good idea to use this as a training exercise for aircraft performance. I went and got the weight and balance and performance charts out of the aircraft that i would be flying. We pulled up the notams in class and found that there was a partial closure for runway 4r/22l -- lft 0/006 lft runway 4r/22l northeast 1;433 clsd wef (effective from) 12xxxxxxxx. I showed the notice to airmen / of air missions to our director of operations and told him that i interpreted that as saying that 1;433 feet/foot of the northeast end of runway 4r/22l: was closed and he agreed. He also suggested that we call flight service station and try to get more information on the notams. We called flight service station specialist on speaker phone and identified ourselves and we spoke to a briefer and queried him about the notice to airmen / of air missions for runway 4r/22l and we also asked him for an abbreviated briefing concerning the temperature for the following day. I asked if he could tell us what the actual takeoff distance available was for runway 4r/22l and he told me that he could not tell us that but he could gave us a number to the lft tower and he said that the high for the next day would be around 100 degrees fahrenheit we were concerned about the actual takeoff distance because the runway length on the airport diagram is showing that the runway 4r/22l runway length is 7;651 feet/foot and the notice to airmen / of air missions is saying that 1;433 feet/foot of that is closed; which would only leave you with 6;218 feet/foot remaining. After we got off of phone we then called lft control tower and identified ourselves again and i told him that we would be flying in the next day and that i needed to know the actual takeoff distance available for runway 4r/22l. He said that it was 6;600 feet/foot that was good news to me. I asked him if it was 6;600 feet/foot available for 4r and 22l and he said yes but you would have to back taxi from taxiway left/right (directions) to get the full 6;600 feet/foot on runway 22l. I told him that was great that i would see them tomorrow. After we got off the phone i was kind of scratching my head because we had come up with 6;218 feet/foot and the tower was saying that they had 6;600 feet/foot available. If you have 6;600 feet/foot available and 1;433 feet/foot closed you would have an 8;033 feet/foot runway which is not the case when you look at the airport diagram and the notams. It led me to believe that they must have reopened a portion of the closed section and not changed the notice to airmen / of air missions my airport diagram was very recent and it still said 4r/22l was 7;651 feet/foot so they obviously haven't added runway to it; right? There us no notice to airmen / of air missions stating that the new runway length for 4r/22l had been increased. The next day when we arrived we landed on runway 4r so we really didn't have a good picture of what was going on at the approach end of runway 22l. While we were there; the winds turned around and the airport started landing and departing runway 22l. When we taxied out we taxied straight out on taxiway left/right (directions) and held short of runway 22l. From here we can see the threshold of the runway and we can see that the barricades have been moved back about 500 feet/foot at this point it is making sense to me that they reopened this 500 feet/foot of runway and that is where they are getting 6;600 feet/foot takeoff distance available from. I am the non flying pilot so i am sitting on the right side and we have to make a left turn and back taxi and i remembered the tower telling us that we would have to back taxiso everything seemed normal. While sitting on taxiway left/right (directions) we can see the barricades but really can't tell anything about runway markings painted on the runway. All we know is that the runway is notamed as partially closed and we can see the barricades and we both consider that is where the closure starts and we need every bit of the 6;600 feet/foot available. It wasn't terribly tight but we were going to do flaps 20 takeoff and utilize the entire runway available to us. The tower comes on the radio and says; 'turn right heading 040 you are cleared for takeoff runway 22l shortened.' we acknowledged and we back taxi and turn and do a 180 and then the tower cancels our takeoff clearance and asks us to exit at taxiway left/right (directions) we comply. I asked if the controller would like us to do another 180. We were told to do a 180 and hold short of the runway and to standby for a 'possible pilot deviation.' we queried what the deviation was for and the controller stated that we had taxied onto a closed portion of the runway. I told the controller that we understood that they had 6;600 feet/foot available and that we need all of it and wanted to make sure that if we departed from the threshold line that we would have that and the controller said that we would. The controller gave us a number to call and then we were re-cleared and this time were told 'remain south of the threshold line.' why didn't the controller say that the first time? Apparently we had taxied onto a blast pad/stop way that they had painted on the runway. There were no notams that there was a temporary blast pad/ stop way installed and there was nothing elevated on the runway. The whole thing looked non-standard in my opinion. Most blast pads/stop ways are inaccessible to aircraft. There are normally threshold lights elevated on the runway. Threshold lights not being present are more common with a displaced threshold. After we arrived at our destination we called the number we had been given and spoke to the tower manager. We told them we were in the wrong but we felt like we were misinformed. I told him that if the airport is 7;651 feet/foot and you have 1;433 feet/foot closed; and then you can't possible have 6;600 feet/foot available for takeoff. He told me that our charts were old and that they had added and extra 500 feet/foot to the runway and that if we had up-to-date charts; it would show 8;000 feet/foot i told him that my airport diagram for lft is dated for june of this year and it shows 7;651 feet/foot i asked him if many other aircraft had done the same thing and he said; 'yes; that is a hot spot.' i told him my point of view on the whole thing and asked for his mercy and he stated that it had been turned over to the airport and that they would decide if we would be given a 'pilot deviation.' i asked him when i would find out and he stated a week and a half to two weeks but they would not call if they decided not to pursue it. He stated that it was up to the airport because we had to run over a cable to access that part of the runway. My co-captain and i neither recall running over any cables. I do recall seeing some cables rolled up on the side of the runway. I know there was a notice to airmen / of air missions that the runway would be fully closed that night and i think they might have already taken them up. He says we could have damaged them. In conclusion; we as pilots were wrong to taxi onto a stop way/blast pad. In our defense i feel that we were misinformed of all the runway changes. How do i believe thuds cold have been avoided? 1) we should have been informed of the runway addition (notam) which would have helped us better understand the available takeoff distance. 2) there should have been a notice to airmen / of air missions for the blast pad they installed. 3) i believe that if that portion of the runway is notamed as 'closed' it should be marked as closed. 4) the tower should inform all aircraft that are having to back taxi to remain south of the white threshold line.
output: A pilot back taxied on the closed section of LFT Runway 22L because of confusion about the actual runway length and the lack of runway closure barriers.

input: On clbout; the 'a' flight attendant rpted the smell of smoke in the cabin. Shortly thereafter both the forward and aft lavatory smoke alarms went off. We were visual flight rules and the airport was about 5 mile away second officer we received clearance to return to the airport expeditiously. After landing we pulled off the runway(s) and stopped; configuring the aircraft for a possible evacuate/evacuation i walked through the cabin to confirm no presence of fire. We elected to taxi to the gate and spoke directly with the fire crews to confirm no indications of fire outside the aircraft we deplaned in a normal fashion and to my knowledge the source of smoke is still unaccounted for. I'd like to make a few comments. 1) i commend the capt for taking quick and decisive action to return to the field. 2) the flight attendants were prompt and thorough in informing us of the status of the cabin. 3) i think it was wise that we ascertained the condition of the airplane before risking the possibility of injuring somebody in an evacuate/evacuation unnecessarily.
output: CABIN ATTENDANT NOTIFIES COCKPIT OF SMELL OF SMOKE IN CABIN. BOTH LAVATORY FIRE ALARMS SOUND.

input: I received a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory as a result of an emergency descent which i initiated. We were initially level at fl430 when we began to experience occasional moderate turbulence and increasing outside air temperature. This caused significant airspeed deviations and eventual loss of airspeed to nearly stall speed. We attempted contact with air traffic control numerous times; but were unable to establish contact due to frequency congestion. When we eventually did contact air traffic control we requested an immediate descent which i initiated simultaneously. At that time air traffic control directed an immediate right turn and declared an emergency. He also called out conflicting traffic which we were able to observe visually. We subsequently received a resolution advisory which i complied with by leveling the aircraft until clear of conflict. Air traffic control then cleared us to fl400 and direct to our next flight planned fix. I contacted the air traffic control controller via telephone after landing per his instructions. He indicated that he would submit a loss of separation report.
output: G200  experienced decreasing airspeed at FL430 due to turbulence and increasing OAT. A descent initiated prior to receiving clearance results in a TCAS RA.

input: [maintenance technicians were] dispatched to aircraft to evaluate damage to the sidewall liners in the aft pit r/h side. We found unserviceable liners based on amm 25-52-01 (holes larger than 1.5'). This is not the first aircraft in the last two weeks that had to have minimum equipment list applied due to excessive damage to the sidewall liners. The damage appears to be frame by frame progressive over time. The question is; when is it now unserviceable and when does the ramp decide it's time to call it in? It seems these holes are out of limits long before the call is made. That would be an unsatisfactory condition for flight based on amm 25-52-01; federal aviation regulation 25.855 and federal aviation regulation 25.853. Two more aircraft come to mind that i was involved with in the last two weeks. These also required minimum equipment list in order to release the aircraft. Both had damaged r/h sidewall liner damage that appears to be progressive. Normal wear with lack of aggressive inspection intervalsincrease inspection intervals by mechanics. Educate ramp. Apply a strip of 'pile velco' (sticky back) to the rivets on each frame where wear occurs. This acts as a barrier between the liner and frame button head rivets. It's these rivets that are wearing through the liner.
output: Line Aircraft Technician reported finding excessive damage to cargo pit sidewalls in a B737-900 due to wear from rivet heads on the frame. He found holes larger than 1.5 inches which exceeded the limit in the FARs.

input: Clearance was obtained before departing and i was in contact through all phases of flight. During the flight some icing was encountered. Center was made aware. Center asked if i had the weather at [destination]. I told them yes; but i asked center to provide me what they had for weather. They provided winds light and variable and 700 ft ceilings. They also provided the notams. This aircraft is equipped with both xm weather and adsb weather. The onboard equipment reported light and variable on the windows with a 700 ft ceiling. Center provided the same weather. I requested and was cleared by center for [the approach] so i proceed to the initial approach. More ice was encountered so i requested lower and then higher. Center asked about the ice and if i wanted a different direction of flight. I indicated that if cleared i would fly the approach. The approach proceeded without incident and i touched down. While on the rollout the aircraft was spun to the right and exited the runway. The plane came to rest with its tail back towards the runway. I exited the plane. As soon as i opened the door (facing north) i was hit with gusts of wind that made it difficult to open the door. When i got on the ground it was apparent that the field conditions were 0/0 (solid ice). Talking with the fixed-base operator manager and the city manager it was determined the weather reporting equipment on the field was reporting inaccurate information.
output: BE36 pilot reported loss of directional control after landing due to strong winds and ice on the runway. Reporter stated the controlling Center and his onboard XM and ADSB weather gave him inaccurate field condition and weather information.

input: Ifr was canceled 5 mile east and the aircraft proceeded in a left/right (directions) traffic pattern and a stabilized visual approach with winds 12 knot(s) 20 degrees left/right (directions) crosswind no other traffic in the pattern. Upon touchdown; power was reduced to idle. A porpoising action was noted with the left/right (directions) wing low due to crosswind while the aircraft drifted towards the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) full power was applied and an uneventful go around was executed with an uneventful subsequent landing postflt inspection of the left/right (directions) propeller showed the distal approximately 2 inches of the tips curled posterior. No audible or tactile indication of propeller strike was noted during the initial landing or go around no loss of aircraft control or engine power was noted during the go around or subsequent lndg.
output: PA34 PILOT REPORTS LEFT PROP STRIKE DURING CROSSWIND LANDING ATTEMPT AND GAR.

input: Canada (drummond sector) called with a non-automated hand off on a flight of 3/f15's on a vector. I asked for the equipment qualifier and the drummond controller said 'tango uniform;' which is not a qualifier. When i questioned him; he said it might be different from canada to the us. I accepted radar contact; started a track on the 3 f15s. I told the radar controller to verify the equipment qualifier. An f15 said he was 'slant india'. I entered the code into the flight plan. A few minutes later the f15s and a b737 were flashing conflict alert about 30 miles apart. The radar controller and myself both evaluated it. We spoke about the flashing. I stated that it may be from three in the flight. The radar controller issued traffic. I don't recall a coral box that indicated non-rvsm. Recommendation; i recommend that the same equipment qualifiers be used between canada and the us. I also believe that it would be helpful if the drummond controller would have coordinated a non-rvsm aircraft.
output: Enroute Controller described a Conflict Alert event involving a flight of military aircraft being transfered from the Canadian ATC system to the US; noting the confused 'qualifier' (slant) designators between the two ATC systems should be corrected.

input: Acr flight xx outbound flight was on assigned heading 010 degrees at 13000 feet/foot center advised us of a c130 opposite direction at 14000 feet/foot we had just leveled at 13000 feet/foot when we got a conflict alert. A few seconds later our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii gave us an resolution advisory to descend which we did. We descended to 12500 feet/foot and saw the unknown aircraft that looked like a twin engine king air cross less than 1/2 mile in front and 500 feet/foot above us. Center did not see the unknown until we received the ra.
output: A WDB CRUISING AT 13000 FT IN ZOB AIRSPACE IS LOOKING FOR AN APCHING C130 WHEN THE FLC HAS TCASII RA COMMANDING THEM TO DSND BECAUSE OF AN APCHING KING AIR.

input: Upon entering the ron airbus; i went in the cockpit to perform safety and power on checklist; and i heard the lead flight attendant exclaim there was a noxious odor in first class cabin and she asked me to come quickly. Aft of the main entry door the smell was extremely foul; i told the flight attendants to leave the aircraft. I exited and started to dry heave from the smell; and went to the podium and advised the agent that i needed to call maintenance. I entered the write up in the logbook and advised maintenance. I returned to the plane and tried turning off ground air; turning on packs; open doors to air it out. The odor dissipated about 50% but changed to a chemical smell. I noted that there was the hot air valve on minimum equipment list i filled out the air quality form and we were dead headed out leaving it for maintenance to discover the reason for the noxious fume and odor. More training is needed for handling fumes/odors of unknown source. We all were exposed only for seconds but we were all concerned about health ramifications. The lead felt she had a headache; but no medical attention was required; and i had a slight headache and metallic taste but probably was from dry heaving after smelling the stench.
output: A noxious odor on an A319 prevented a flight crew from preflighting the aircraft so the flight was canceled. The Lead Flight Attendant discovered the odor in first class and the Captain became ill after smelling it while verifying the Leads opinion.

input: Obtained clearance (ifr) kpbi-kdet and started engines on ramp. Called ground control for taxi; 'dep runway(s) 09l; hold short of runway(s) on taxiway juliet.' then received clearance to cross runway(s) 09l and taxi to departure end on taxiway 'charlie.' after arriving at departure end of runway(s) 09l we switched to tower frequency 119.1. Our performance numbers for takeoff were v1-103kts v2-115kts with a balance field length of 3200 feet/foot after kpbi tower cleared us into position on runway(s) 09l we turned on our landing lights along with our taxi light. Cleared to takeoff we advanced power for takeoff the co-plt called v1 and just at that time i noticed an aircraft starting to cross runway(s) 09l at taxiway 'foxtrot' (looked like a lear jet) (txwy foxtrot is approximately 4350 ft? From departure end of 09l). I rotated and crossed foxtrot at 200-250 feet/foot estimated. At the same time someone called clear on the tower frequency i glanced left/right (directions) and saw the aircraft had cleared the runway(s) corrective action suggestions. 1) we always takeoff with all lights on. Crossing aircraft should visually checked for landing or departing aircraft before crossing. 2) coordination between ground control and tower improve. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information capt had no further contact with air traffic control he did not rpt this as a 'near miss.' the pilot has heard nothing from the federal aviation administration nor has he talked to anyone about the incident.
output: F900 CREW HAD A LJ TAXI ONTO THEIR TKOF RWY ON RWY 09L AT PBI.

input: I had complete electrical failure in the aircraft outside class d for zzz. I followed procedures by climbing to 500 feet/foot above pattern altitude of 800 feet/foot above ground level i entered class d of zzz at 1;300 feet/foot mean sea level squawking 7600 on the transponder. I approached over the tower at 1;300 feet/foot mean sea level rocking my wings waiting for the light gun signal. The tower controller did not see or hear me passing over the top and did not proceed with the light signals. I circled over the top for two more times. I did not get light signal from the tower yet. On the fourth time around; i cleared the final approach path for the active runway according to the last automatic terminal information service information. I landed and cleared the runway at the end. I stopped aircraft after clearing the runway waiting for the light signals from the tower for taxi clearance. No light signals from the tower were provided. I proceeded to taxi to the parking area. I held short enroute to the parking for runway xxl. No light signals were provided by the tower. I proceeded taxiing for hold-short line. I got red light stop taxi from the control tower this time. I stopped and held short. After a while; i got flashing green taxi light from the control tower. I proceeded to taxi and crossed runway enroute to parking. I explained the situation to the control tower personnel and the airport operation after parking and engine shut-down.
output: C172 pilot reported a complete electrical failure; stating he then followed proper procedures for airspace entry and landing but Tower apparently did not notice him until after he landed.

input: It was brought to my attention that the md80a aircraft are filing illegally on x rtes. I went through all of the releases i had for my day and came across several instances of service volume issues just on my desk just on this shift. The worst thing was on a flight that made several calls to our commercial supplier to alert them to the problem once we were aware it was happening. They only seemed to fix the specific rtes we mentioned. All the y rtes need to be carefully reviewed for compliance.
output: AN ACR DISPATCHER RPTED THAT THE VENDOR FOR HIS ACR'S NAV DATABASE OVERLOOKED A NUMBER OF INACCURACIES; CAUSING THE ACFT TO FLY WITH INADEQUATE NAVAID SVC COVERAGE.

input: Ewr to btv #2 engine oil pressure/filter bypass light came on during approach descent phase of flight approach control was notified and company procs/checklists were followed requiring a precautionary engine shutdown. The crew did not declare an emergency however; approach control initiated emergency procedures the flight continued to an uneventful lndg.
output: FLT CREW OF ACR LGT EXPERIENCES ENGINE FAILURE DURING DESCENT INTO BTV. ENGINE IS SHUT DOWN AND APCH AND LNDG ARE COMPLETED WITHOUT FURTHER PROBLEM.

input: I was working the non radar position at zid; ne love. There was sma x on approach at zzv. Sma y called from zzv; visual flight rules requesting an instrument flight rules clearance sma y was advised that there was an aircraft on approach sma y departed visual flight rules but could not continue to climb visual flight rules to get above the protected airspace for the zzv approach (acft types used in narrative due to similar call signs.) when sma x called; he didn't say missed approach or cancel instrument flight rules either. He requested an instrument flight rules clearance to hlg to practice approachs then landed at 2g2. When asked intermediate fix sma x could hold at zzv (so we could get sma y a clrnc); he stated that he would circle the field and maintain 3500 feet/foot (the instrument flight rules missed approach altitude is 3000 ft). When i attempted to remove the inland flight plan (fp) on sma x i mistakenly removed an sma zulu time (utc/gmt) at 7000 on westbound side of area. At that time; hlg sector called because they saw sma y code approaching them; climbing and they had traffic at 8000. They called radar contact (we did not see a target) and approved instrument flight rules climbing to 7000. When i tried to depart the outbound flight plan on sma x it would not start (because correct inbound still active). The radar controller looked up the flight plan by call sign and started a track on the number of the flight plan that was displayed. At this time; the left/right (directions) controller and i believed there were 2 computer numbers on the inbound for this aircraft and that he had tagged the second. In reality; the inbound track had just moved over. Since the pilot requested practice approachs the left/right (directions) controller suggested that i amend the flight plan to land at hlg and add 'dest 2g2' to the 'practice approachs at hlg' that was in the remarks section. I did this and verbally coordinated with hlg sector to make sure they understood. In retrospect; i removed the wrong flight plan. No excuses. I didn't realize the error because the 'practice apchs' amendment served to change the inbound flight plan to reflect the outbound destination in my mind; i had removed 1 flight plan and started one as normal. Though not causative; the question of sma x thinking he was visual flight rules and sma y stuck under the clouds visual flight rules requesting instrument flight rules captured my attention the error was brought to my attention when the investigation began later that day.
output: CTLR REMOVED ACTIVE FLT PLAN ON SMA Z BY MISTAKE.

input: I was acting as pilot not flying while receiving my initial operating experience on the md11. The checked capt was flying in the left/right (directions) seat and was the pilot flying after departing cvg for europe; we were at cruise altitude of 33000 feet/foot mean sea level near syracuse; ny. The weather was deteriorating rapidly with multiple thunderstorms extreme turbulence strong winds; and according to the center tornadic activity. It was necessary to make many lateral deviations to avoid the weather and we were both concentrating on the weather radar while being given several changes to our clearance by zny. I was very busy talking on the radio and attempting to checked our route on the charts and maps. Center called and asked our altitude at which point we both realized that the airplane (which was on autoplt at all times) was level at 32000 feet/foot the pilot flying immediately climbed back to 33000 feet/foot there was never an altitude warning from the autoplt or altimeter system and neither of us can explain how the altitude changed. It is possible that in all the confusion taking place; that the pilot flying turned the altitude control knob instead of the heading knob to attempt a weather deviation the 2 knobs are next to each other and are almost identical on this airplane. The controller said that there was no conflict and 'no prob.'
output: ALT EXCURSION DURING HIGH ALT CRUISE BY FLC OF AN MD11.

input: This was a flight from tampa; flight level to cancun; mexico. When navigate, navigationing on b646 from fish hook (fis) to robin intersection the navigate, navigation is accurate only to vinka intersection after that; fis takes you north of the airway; even though fis shows you still on course. This has been verified by cancun (cun) vor and dme (co-located) and havana center. Upon reaching the cun 011 degree radial; the cun vor and dme (co-located) is 122 mile 36 mile north of course. All the time; fis shows us on course. At no time could we receive merida (mio); the other end of the airway. Also; starting about 150 mile out from fis; there is another station identifier on the frequency making it difficult to hear the fis identify the second identify sounded like w-z-m. This is the second trip i've made to cancun and i've had this problem both times. This is my second national aeronautics and space administration rpt on the subject. Perhaps this route needs to be checkeded callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information analyst and rptr discussed a normal error in reading butt end of needle flying out from automatic direction finder station as much as 200 mile his company had not offered any information on variation error passing through 2 or 3 degrees of variation change. Rptr plans to discuss with his chief plt.
output: FLC OF LGT NAVING BY ADF WAS ADVISED BY MUHA CENTER THEY WERE 15 MI N OF COURSE.

input: I requested ppe; a face mask; from operating manager on duty. Immediately he asked;'what for?'  i explained i would like a face mask during the covid-19 pandemic while working over 15+ aircraft for the day. He then asked me 'what amm task are you doing that requires a face mask?'  i stated again; that i would like a face mask regarding my health and safety since i will be aboard so many aircraft. He then told me he needed to make phone call. That phone call ended and he made another phone call regarding my request. Once the second phone call was over he reluctantly gave me a mask from a stack of at best; 20 face masks. We do not have an adequate amount of ppe face masks during this covid-19 pandemic and when requested ppe we are challenged.provide adequate ppe for all mechanics and do not challenge the technicians when requested. There are no masks readily available for us. We are not being supplied ppe during covid-19 pandemic.
output: Technician reported a Supervisor made two calls before reluctantly providing him with a mask. Technician stated they are not adequately being supplied with PPE equipment during the COVID-19 pandemic.

input: Normal taxi and initial takeoff at 700' above ground level heard and felt loud bang coming from rear of aircraft engine failure light came on simultaneously and we continued to climb to 6900' mean sea level proceeded cleaning up the aircraft along with the engine failure chklist. Noticed 0 revolutions per minute and pegged egt. Continued to feel constant rumbling; even after engine was shut down. Requested den weather and decided to continue to den where weather was much better then cos. Cos weather was rapidly deteriorating with snow and visibility less than 3/4-1/2 mile emergency initially declared and we were expeditiously handed off to zdv with uneventful landing followed. Taxied off active runway(s) 35r and requested emergency vehs to inspect rear of aircraft particularly left #1 engine they rpted a large hole and other damage to engine but no fire. Continued on to gate assignment for deplaning. Good crew coordination within cockpit; as well as f/a's. Chain of events was hectic due to contact interruption by air traffic control and the concern of constant rumbling; even after engine shutdown. F/o did a fine job of flying; but i decided to make the landing due to snow on ground don't particularly like transitioning on rollout from f/o to capt with any irregularities or runway(s) cover.
output: ACR LGT ENGINE FAILURE AFTER TKOF FROM COS. CONTINUED TO DEN DUE COS WX.

input: I was returning visual flight rules from vyx to my home airport of pwk. I had just cleared nw of dpa class d with no incident and good communicationss with dpa tower in order to remain well clear of ord class b and simplify navigate, navigation i planned to fly at 2000 feet/foot mean sea level from dpa vor and dme (co-located) to obk vor and dme (co-located) and then to pwk. I tuned in pwk automatic terminal information service on the communications #2 radio and wrote down the pertinent information i tuned the communications #1 radio to pwk tower and flew on for a few minute(s) until i got closer to obk. I called pwk tower on communications #1 with my position intended route of arrival, arrive from obk; and intent to land. I heard no reply from the tower second officer i waited a moment and then called again stating my position as 'over northbrook vor' and again that i was inbound for landing again i heard no reply; second officer i verified the twr's frequency from my (current) sectional and checkeded that the radio made noise in its 'test' position which it did. I thought to checked pwk's hours of operations(s) second officer i looked in the (current) airport/facility directory and didn't immediately find the twr's hours not wanting to spend too much time 'head down' in a busy visual flight rules environment; i looked at the guide sheet for pwk which i had attached to my kneeboard and saw the tower closing time listed as 'xa00.' i looked at my watch; which was set to zulu time; and saw that it was several minute(s) after xa00. I also looked at and around the airport which was now in sight; and saw no traffic believing that the tower had just closed and i was now dealing with a nontwred airport i made my next call to 'palwaukee tfc' on the ctaf/twr frequency of 119.9 per nontwred self-announce procedure i gave my distance from the vor and dme (co-located) and rpted inbound with intent to land. I called again shortly; giving position as 5 mile out; 'lndg runway(s) 12; correction 16.' on short final; i called short final landing runway(s) 16. I looked up from my visual checked of the glideslope to see a light single engine low wing aircraft blue and white; making a climbing left/right (directions) turn above and to the left/right (directions) of me. The other aircraft was clear of me and our flight paths were divergent at the time second officer no evasive was necessary. I remember being very startled and thinking that the other aircraft had made a serious error by a) not announcing his/her actions over the common traffic advisory frequency and b) departing on the opposite runway(s) from the one i had twice announced my intent to land on. Somewhat rattled; i made my landing on runway(s) 16 and turned off runway(s) 16 to taxiway east and announced 'clr of runway(s) 16 on taxiway b' (the 2 signs were close to each other). I later correctly announced that i was 'on taxiway east headed to area x;' then parked and announced clear of all txwys. After i stopped the engine and was collecting my belongings; the other acft's silence on the radio and the loss of separation began to concern me. A truck from one of the fbo's on the field arrived and informed me that i was to call the tower postevent: i called the tower and the person who replied asked me intermediate fix i 'knew that we had a tower here.' i said that i did; but believed them to be closed at xa00z. He indicated that the tower was active until yy00 (xa00 lcl) and that 'this is a very busy arpt.' he further indicated that my xmissions had been received; as someone (either a controller or another plt) had joked about my announcing my radio calls to 'palwaukee tfc.' he also asked intermediate fix i had heard his instructions to me and i replied that i had not. Anxious; wanting to solve the problem and recalling some odd behavior with the frequency selector on communications #1 (see below). I speculated on the possibility of there being some trouble with the radio. He reminded me of no radio procedures which i know; and said that he was going to have to rpt this event 'in case anyone ever asks what i did about it...' because it was 'his job on the line; too.' the next day; i tested the communications #1 radio on the ground with the aid of a cellular phone and an employee at the fixed-base operator the radio made its appropriate noise in 'test' mode; and picked up automatic terminal information service just fine. When i called the fixed-base operator on their private frequency the employee heard me and i heard her reply. I twice had her monitor the tower frequency while i called for a radio checked the fixed-base operator employee said that she did not hear my transmission and the tower did not reply. Whilei'm not an avionics technician; the radio obviously was operating in an intermittent manner: the mechanical frequency indicator seemed to be 'slipping' on its gears in some fashion; and only for a certain range of frequencies this was probably why i had no difficulty communicating with the other facilities previously; and was a difficult situation to detect and diagnose on the ground let alone inflt. Backgnd; contributing factors; prevention: the aircraft i operated was a rental; with older mechanical-indicator radios. While i'm not a very high-time pilot i have the majority of my time in a more modern aircraft with bendix/king digital- display radios and have always believed that a certified radio will 'do what it says' and either work or not work. I ante meridiem familiar with the class d requirements for 2-way communications and with no radio procedures intermediate fix i had suspected radio difficulties; i would have circled and looked for the light gun; or just tried calling the tower with communications #2.
output: PLT OF A PA28-180 IS UNAWARE OF RADIO PROB; BELIEVES TWR IS CLOSED AND ENTERS CLASS D AIRSPACE WITHOUT CLRNC. HE HAS AN NMAC WITH ACFT DEPARTING OPPOSITE DIRECTION.

input: Saturday night; an aircraft was turned over to me from swing shift maintenance with a lightning strike. Damage was found on the rudder; vertical stabilizer and below the forward service door. All items were temporarily repaired or deferred as required. The mv-1 checked was also required and performed on the aircraft the following morning during the crew preflt walkaround; burn; low on the left engine outboard thrust reverser was found. The item was addressed before push but took a 44 minute(s) delay. Factors for the error were it was dark and item was low on the engine to prevent this from happening in the future; 2 mechs should be required to perform and sign off the inspection. An extra set of eyes should prevent items from getting missed.
output: B737-700 WAS INSPECTED FOR LIGHTNING STRIKE DAMAGE. DAMAGE FOUND WAS REPAIRED OR DEFERRED. PREFLT INSPECTION BY CREW FOUND BURN SPOT LOW ON #1 ENG OUTBOARD THRUST REVERSER.

input: Gps jamming: global positioning system position unavailable and ads-b out left/right (directions) cause: global positioning system jamming.
output: Air Carrier Captain reported GPS position unavailable and ADS-B OUT L. Possible GPS jamming.

input: Flt was given cruise dsnt clearance to 16000' from 20000'. Upon level off in instrument meteorological conditions with all anti-ice equipment systems in use we started picking up mostly severe occasional moderate rime ice. We immediately informed bos center of ice and asked for lower. We were given 14000' and continued to pick up moderate rime. Upon level off at 14000' ice accumulation continued and aircraft became incapable of maintaining altitude with almost maximum power we requested lower due to ice however center did not respond quickly enough and we then advised center we were descending to lower altitude and please clear other aircraft from our area. At 9000' ice accumulation stopped and we were able to maintain altitude center told us during dsnt; intermediate fix we had told him of icing he would have responded sooner. Both f/o and myself were astonished; we had in fact told this center controller several times. Also there were no rpts of or sigmets regarding icing. We did contact syr approach bos center and dispatch with a pilot report 1 hour later we checkeded local rpts still no published pireps? Suggest less controller workload and more timely dissemination of met condition on air carrier freqs.
output: ENCOUNTERED HEAVY RIME ICING UNABLE TO MAINTAIN ALT. DESCENDED WITHOUT CLRNC.

input: During approach to landing at hutchinson municipal airport i was cleared for the visual approach to runway(s) 17 by wichita approach control and advised to change to hutchinson tower frequency after checkeding in with the tower i was approaching the airport from the se and circled in very hazy conditions to the north of the airport for downwind and base to runway(s) 17 but in that high wing aircraft i lost sight of the runway(s) in the turn. My directional gyroscope was also off by 15 degrees when i rolled out; i was on base then final; but it wasn't until i was over the numbers that i realized that i had come in on the wrong runway(s) paying more attention to position as well as traffic watch would have prevented this from happening.
output: AN AC50 CARGO FLT ON VISUAL APCH TO RWY 17 LAND ON THE WRONG RWY. THE RPTR DID NOT REALIZE THAT HE WAS LINED UP ON THE WRONG RWY UNTIL HE WAS OVER THE NUMBERS.

input: I was on the ramp at the fixed-base operator which is located at the end of the taxiway. I had received my instrument flight rules clearance for departure on runway 7 on the clearance frequency. I then switched to the ground frequency and requested taxi clearance. (it was now well after sunset) i was told to taxi to runway 7 via foxtrot. I left the ramp and made an immediate left. Upon reaching foxtrot 2; i realized that i wasn't actually on taxiway foxtrot; but was on a parallel road which was intended for vehicle traffic; not aircraft. I stopped at foxtrot 2 and notified ground control what had happened. I informed them that i could make a right onto foxtrot 2 to get on the foxtrot taxiway. The controller notified me to hold my position and that he would send an ops (airport operations) vehicle out. About 5 minutes later the ops vehicle arrived behind me. The ground controller notified the ops vehicle that i had stated that i could make the turn onto foxtrot 2. The ops vehicle approved that which i did and i made the right onto foxtrot 2 and then left onto taxiway foxtrot and proceeded to the hold line for runway 7 without further incident.after making the wrong turn on what i thought was taxiway foxtrot i did see a sign with an fahrenheit on it with a black background on my right which is why i thought i was on taxiway fahrenheit as i proceeded towards runway 7. I commented to my passenger that there were several dips in the pavement which was unusual. As i approached f2; i saw a red sign past f2 indicating no entry. That's what was literally the red flag. Fortunately; i was in a high wing aircraft which cleared all lights and signs. This may not have been the case in a low wing aircraft. This second road was not shown on my airport taxi diagram which might have helped. I don't know if anyone else had ever made this same mistake; but i think better signage would have helped. Perhaps a sign coming out of the ramp on f1 indicating 2nd left to foxtrot or a red no enter sign like the one at f2 might have might have also helped. I had not flown into this airport in over 15 years. I did not request progressive taxi instructions because the route appeared to be very simple. I will be more vigilant during night operations at unfamiliar airports.
output: GA pilot reported unknowingly taxiing on a vehicle roadway at ROC airport; thinking it was the taxiway.

input: Apching ind; i got the automatic terminal information service weather was marginal visual flight rules (3 mile visibility). Approachs were being made to runway(s) 23l/r. We briefed an approach to runway(s) 23r. Coplt was flying. At midfield; we were at 4000 feet/foot and 220 knot(s) i noticed we had a 27 knot(s) left/right (directions) quartering tailwind. At about 10 mile the controller gave us a left/right (directions) turn to 140 degrees and a descent to 3000 feet/foot he asked us intermediate fix we had traffic at 12 - 1 o'clock position or the field. I saw the traffic and immediately knew we had problems he was 12 - 1 o'clock position and slightly below us. I said to the coplt; 'i have the acft.' we got an resolution advisory i banked the aircraft hard left/right (directions) for traffic avoidance. We got a 'bank angle' alert. I threw the throttles up and tried to maintain altitude i saw the aircraft going under the nose and lost sight of him. When i leveled the wings on runway(s) heading i saw we were left/right (directions) of the ctrline for runway(s) 23l. I usually picked up on the other aircraft and the field and landed the aircraft on runway(s) 23r. At the gate; i called approach control summary: in my opinion; the weather at the field was changing to visual flight rules and we were anticipating an instrument landing system approach the controller was anticipating a visual approach that piece of information along with the wind factor was what caused the breakdown. On the radar vector; we complied with the instructions; but the controller lost sight of wind factor.
output: B732 FLC INITIATE EVASIVE TCASII RA MANEUVER DUE TO ANOTHER B737. WX A FACTOR.

input: L engine oil pressure dropped to zero and oil light illumiated. Shut down left/right (directions) engine normal weight landing callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the airplane was a b757-200 with rolls royce rb211-535e4 engs. The rptr said the loss of oil pressure occurred 170 mile nw of sju at fl330. The rptr stated the engine was shut down per the manual and the plan was to continue to sju due to airport familiarity and visual flight rules wx.
output: A B757-200 FLC AT FL330 SHUT DOWN THE L ENG DUE TO LOSS OF ENG OIL PRESSURE CAUSED BY A SHEARED INPUT SHAFT ON THE MAIN OIL PUMP.

input: I was scheduled to fly atl-fll and fll-lga. Due to weather in atl; we blocked 2 hours 15 minute(s) to fll. As we departed fll for lga; a ne [wind] started dumping snow at lga. We held at 3 places before finally diverting to bwi. We blocked 4 hours 42 minute(s) for a total of 6 hours and 57 minute(s) the ground people at bwi said they needed the gate and that we were to take the aircraft back to fll. Due to the weather the capt and i thought we were operating under irregular operations(s) which made us legal to fly over 8 hours in addition; the company hadn't updated our rotation (trip); second officer the system didn't (flag) catch the problem until we were airborne en route to fll. Somewhere near columbia; sc; we were notified to divert to atl because we were no longer legal to fly. My mistake was my misconception that we could fly over 8 hours during irregular operations(s) even once we had departed our scheduled trip. I now know this isn't the case.
output: AN ACR CREW IS SCHEDULED TO FLY OVER 8 HRS IN NON COMPLIANCE WITH THE REG WHEN A REPOS OF THE ACFT IS TACKED ONTO THEIR SCHEDULE.

input: Arriving dkx runway 26 at dark; full flaps deployed on final; approximately 75 knots. Nothing seemed out of the ordinary; although the plane seemed a little light and floated more than usual before settling to the runway. Upon applying the brakes; i did not feel any significant braking action. I applied full elevator back to help with braking action and intended to retract the flaps. Since the plane did not seem to be slowing i pushed still harder on the brake pedals; but with only minimal slowing of the plane. I also tried to swerve the plane some to slow the roll or stretch the distance. I finally exited the runway at a favorable spot between the lights; stopping nose down about 5 feet of water. Minor damage to the lower cowling; nose gear and main wheel pants; along with any possible water damage to engine.the plane had no passengers or luggage and very little fuel. There were skipping skid marks on the runway that appeared to be mine. In hindsight; it is my belief that full flaps along with a very light aircraft caused plane wheels to skip along instead of 'biting' the asphalt. I usually pull flaps up upon landing; as advised and i reached to do so this time. However; in the dark; i likely did not reach the lever and then concentrated on slowing the plane. Although winds were reported to be calm; a slight intermittent tail gust may have contributed to this as well. It is also possible that speed had something to do with it; although unlikely. I remember being close to the preferred approach speed prior to landing.
output: SR22 pilot reported that during landing rollout brakes were applied and the aircraft failed to stop; resulting in a runway excursion and damage to the aircraft.

input: I was given an assignment to complete when i arrived for my work shift. My lead asked me to look into [a specific] non-routine.i looked up the paperwork to repair the conduit as requested by my lead; and went out to inspect the extent of the damage. After i inspected the extent of the damage; i let my lead know that the conduit required replacement in accordance with (iaw) the boeing standard wiring practices manual (bswpm). He told me it's okay just repair it; to which i refused to do because the manuals says that any damage more than 25 percent of the circumference requires replacement. He told me i just need to do it because the line maintenance manager told him to get it repaired. At this point i handed my lead the paperwork and said i would not repair it; so i was put on another task. My lead proceeded to instruct one of our unlicensed mechanics to repair it by placing teflon tape inside the conduit and filling it with red silicone and taping the outside of the conduit up. My lead annotated on the paperwork the following:1) assessed damage to l/h body gear conduit; found to meet conditions for repair as described per bswpm 2) no damage exists to wires or convoluted tube as described in accordance with bswpm 3) repaired metal overbraid with no defects in accordance with bswpm
output: A Maintenance Technician disagreed with a Lead Technician on the use of an electrical conduit repair based upon the extent of the damage.

input: During descent into sea on the chins arrival, arrive we were slowed to 250 knot(s) and given holding instructions to hold at raddy fl240 east expect further clearance at xx43. Later on; we were cleared to fl190. I repeated the clearance to descend and hold at fl190. Flight management computer told us that we would arrive at the holding fix after our expect further clearance the holding fix was entered into the flight management computer with fl190 expect further clearance xx43. Later; we were cleared to a lower altitude i repeated the clearance and asked intermediate fix this 'eliminates the hold' and the controller said (roger/yes?). This gave both of us the impression that the holding was cancelled and we were to continue on the arrival, arrive at a reduced speed 4-5 mile past the fix we were asked intermediate fix we had entered holding; i said 'negative; you had cancelled the holding.' the controller said turn left/right (directions) 170 degree maintain fl170; which we did. After 1 turn we were cleared on the arrival, arrive to sea.
output: FLC OF AN LGT ACR ACFT FAILED TO 'HOLD' DURING AN ARR DSCNT DUE TO A MISUNDERSTANDING OF ATC INSTRUCTIONS.

input: Plt was on a training/proficiency soaring flight from hinckley airport to sky soaring airport and return; a distance of 59.6 nautical mile pilot had proceeded about 15 mile from his departure when he encountered poorer soaring conditions than forecasted. Abandoning his task he attempted to return to hinckley airport but encountered continued sink making it impossible to reach hinckley from the altitude he was at. His course line was 5 mile east of de kalb airport where he knew the airport was closed due to an airshow taking place. Finding an area of zero sink ne of the airport the pilot was able to maintain an altitude of 1700 feet/foot mean sea level for close to 15 minute(s) while attempting to determine intermediate fix there was better lift in the area in order to gain enough altitude to make it back to hinckley. None was found and additional altitude was lost forcing a landing decision. Because the farm crops were of sufficient ht to make an off-arpt landing extremely hazardous it was decided to land at de kalb airport pilot landed to the westbound on the grass south of the arpt's e- westbound hard surface runway(s) touchdown; rollout and stop consumed less than 200 feet/foot he had the higher airshow traffic in sight and was not in conflict with that traffic as he was very low and able to maintain a shallow glide angle. Pilot and glider were aero-retrieved from the airport after the airshow concluded.
output: COMMERCIAL PLT RETURNS TO LAND GLIDER AT DEP ARPT EVEN THOUGH THE ARPT WAS CLOSED FOR AN AIRSHOW DUE TO RUNNING OUT OF SOARING LIFT ON AN ATTEMPTED CROSS-COUNTRY FLT.

input: I cleared seneca for takeoff on runway(s) 7r. His gear collapsed on takeoff roll; coming to a stop on the south side of the runway(s) just past taxiway c-3. Emergency equipment was dispatched. Flight standards district office to inspect nature of occurrence.
output: THE LNDG GEAR FOULED ON TKOF ROLL OF AN SMA.

input: As a reserve i was assigned to standby at the airport starting in the early afternoon. After an hour sit i was assigned an east coast turn that later canceled. I was then assigned a non-stop to the west coast departing about six hours after my standby began. When i arrived i was informed by crew scheduling my trip schedule hadn't been updated. When i arrived at the layover hotel--and initially my room wasn't ready and i had to wait--i called crew scheduling again and i was advised i'd have a 14 hour and 50 minute layover and then fly an east coast non-stop with a 19 hour layover. Then i'd be surface transported to another airport the next day and work a flight back to my domicile and that would close out my id.i didn't sleep well at my layover because of bug bites through the night. The layover hotel only has a coffee bistro so there were limited food options during my 19 hour layover. Exhausted from not being able to sleep the night before i drank a couple cups of coffee hoping it would help me stay alert to work the flight. My fifth straight day working and last day of a three day identification (i'd worked a two day turn prior to this sequence); i felt if i could just stay alert this last flight i'd be ok. So i drank more coffee onboard...the coffee helped a bit at first but i had to struggle to stay alert. At some point unknown to me crew scheduling added two other flights to my identification without advising me as the contract requires; another two day east coast turn. Sleep deprived and fatigued i felt i had the responsibility to myself; my flying partners; my company and the passengers we serve to inform the crew desk i didn't feel safe to be the one standing there to arm and disarm an airplane door or respond in an emergency situation. I spoke with a scheduling supervisor and explained that not only had i not been advised of the additional segments i was too fatigued to work them. She had a few questions for me and then she took me off the added segments and placed 'fatigue' in my flight record and told me i needed to speak with an onboard supervisor. That supervisor suggested i go to a local hospital to be checked out. I said i'd prefer to see my own doctor. She responded that i was not being denied the right to see my own doctor but the crew desk would provide a cab for me to go to the company's selected medical facility. She further stated this type of situation doesn't come up often and she wasn't totally sure how to handle it and had to research some protocol. I said i understood. I then filled out a report and left.
output: A Flight Attendant reported cumulative fatigue from arduous rescheduling over a five day period. When her fatigue reached an unacceptable level her airline took measures to coerce her to complete the last reassignment by ordering to undergo medical assessment at a hospital of the airline's choice.

input: It was the end of my duty day and the workload all day was very busy with delays. With 2 different aircraft types and 11 lines of flts. The minimum equipment list for deferring the ground spoilers and anti-skid is very vague. I made a mistake and missed the connection.
output: BA41 DISPATCHER HAD TROUBLE INTERPRETING CONFUSING MEL ITEMS.

input: During the preparation of the load manifest; critical numerical information was transposed from the load information sheet to the load manifest. This data is manually xferred to the load manifest; and then manually converted into an index number that is placed on the load manifest. The process is conducted in a high workload environment with many interruptions and distrs. On the day of the incident we were operating as an international 2 pilot crew. This is very unusual for operations(s) at this airline and increases the workload normally encountered by the flight deck crews. As the load manifest was being prepared; many people came and went from the flight deck. These workers included maintenance personnel; flight attendants; ground service agent; the local handler and others each with an inquiry or need from either myself or the capt. During a 3 pilot operations(s) much of this traffic to and from the flight deck is avoided or intercepted by third pilot on this day it fell to whichever of the 2 pilots least engaged to hand the inquires. Although i have not yet reviewed the documentation from this flight i ante meridiem told that load figures were transposed resulting in an 8800 kilogram weight discrepancy. This could have only resulted from the amount of traffic moving on and off the flight deck creating many distrs. At times during the preflt perpetrations as many as 5 people at once were on the flight deck of the b757; all trying to accomplish task necessary for our departure prevention of a possible recurrence could be achieved by limiting the traffic to and from the flight deck. Additionally; adding a protocol that requires a person entering the flight deck to wait for acknowledgement by the flight crew before presenting information or making inquiries could also help in reducing distrs at critical points. Distrs in a high workload environment cannot completely be avoided. However; adding the suggested protocol to the company procedures might reduce the number of critical point distraction encounters on the flight deck.
output: B757 FLT CREW REPORTS 19000 POUND LOAD MANIFEST ERROR INTRODUCED DURING MANUAL CALCULATIONS BY FO. ERROR DISCOVERED POST FLIGHT.

input: While picking up a new plane and taxiing to the hangar ramp the brakes failed; and at very slow speed i rolled into the horizontal stabilizer of another plane. The mixture was in idle-cutout but the propeller was still turning; damaging the left/right (directions) horizontal stabilizer. I had full pressure on the brakes. They had worked fine when tested; pulling out of the parking spot; pulled the emergency brake and pulled throttles and mixtures back. After this i learned that the plane had been written up before and was involved sometime before in a braking failure which resulted in the plane running off the end of the runway(s) at another arpt.
output: A PART 135 CARGO PLT COLLIDES WITH ANOTHER ACFT PARKED AT THE RAMP WHEN HIS BRAKES FAIL NEAR THE RAMP AT BHM; AL.

input: Due to fatigue and distraction in the cockpit; all three crew members omitted the 'pushback/start' chklist. Resulting in no brake pressure to set the parking brake after pushback. The aircraft rolled a few feet/foot after the tug disconnected; before we realized that the hydraulic pumps were not on. Luckily; no injuries or damages incurred. This occurred on the sixth day of a six day international trip; including three 24 hour layovers. Paris; mumbai; paris. All the crew's body clocks were confused; since with each 24 hour break we must sleep twice. Also; the time zone changes of 6 hours for paris and 9.5 hours for mumbai are a factor. The pushback start chklist is to be completed before the push and includes the doors; fuel pumps; hydraulic pumps; and rotating beacon. Since the federal aviation administration and the company are very specific about not turning the beacon on until pushback clearance is received; many pilots do not start the chklist until they receive the clearance in many cases; this results in the chklist being completed during the pushback instead of before. On this day; we were distracted by a last minute fuel slip needing to be thrown in the window after the doors were closed; and by a three minute delay for pushback clearance after calling ground control ready for push; thus breaking the flow of the chklist. The capt didn't call for the chklist and neither myself nor the relief pilot realized the omission. After the push was complete; the ramp agent communicated over the headset to set the parking brake. The b767 parking brake handle will pull up and lock even without hydraulic pressure. The tug disconnected and the ramp agent again told the capt to set the brakes; since he could clearly see the plane was rolling. The capt; thinking they were set; informed him of that. Since the cockpit is second officer much higher than the ramp; it is very difficult for us to see when the plane is moving. Once the capt realized we were rolling; he attempted to apply the brake pedals to no avail. He then directed me to apply the pedals. Being involved in the engine start process; my head was down and totally out of the loop with what was happening on the ramp. As i applied the pedals the relief pilot announced that the hydraulic pumps were off. The capt turned on the pumps and the aircraft came to a stop; thankfully; some distance before striking the tug or ramp agent. While the ramp agent did not cause or contribute to this at all; i feel that intermediate fix he had said; 'you are rolling!'; instead of 'set the brakes'; we would have realized our error sooner. Five things affected this situation fatigue; aircraft design; company procedure communication; and complacency. An improvement in any one of these areas may have prevented this from happening.
output: INT'L FLT CREW OF B767-300; FATIGUED BY 6 DAYS OF CIRCADIAN RHYTHM CHALLENGED FLYING AND DISTRACTED BY OTHER DUTIES; FAIL TO COMPLETE PUSHBACK/START CHKLIST AND; WHEN ADVISED TO SET BRAKES BY THE PUSH CREW; ARE UNABLE TO DO SO DUE TO FAILURE TO TURN HYDRAULIC PUMPS ON.

input: [engineering department] originally wrote an ea (engineering authorization) for replacement of numerous damaged airbag seatbelt covers to be replaced nlt (no later than) 2902 fc (flight cycles). When the twd came; and the seat-belts could not be replaced; [engineering department] wrote a revision to the original ea allowing additional time provided no airbag material extrudes outside the covers. Per that ea; if there was any material found outside of the cover; the seat needed to be placed on minimum equipment list (they also mentioned a specific minimum equipment list which is not their determination). After that ea was written; and during the accomplishment of repair instruction ii of the ea; maintenance found airbag material extruding outside of the cover. At that point ; and due to the amount of seats that would have been unusable; [engineering department] wrote another ea against the previous ea allowing the seats to continue in-service (useable) with subsequent inspections to be accomplished. This is in direct violation of the mel's; [procedures manual] ([maintenance control] determines which minimum equipment list is to be used)in an effort to mitigate a delay and ensure all seats were available; regardless of the safety of the passengers; [engineering department] issued a 3rd ea against previous ea's. The use of ea's by engineering has been out of control and getting worse. All to ensure an on-time performance disregarding the safety of passengers and crew. There needs to be a limited availability for the use of engineering authorizations. In the past; every ea ([engineering] and [line engineering order]) came through maintenance control to be issued. The controller had to approve its use and their name was on the authorization prior to its issuance. We were the checks and balances. Now; there aren't any. There was also extremely limited [procedures manual] and guidelines for issuance of an authorization. I believe; in order to ensure safety and compliance; the use of the carte blanche ea process needs to be reined in and check and balances re-established as before.
output: Air Carrier Maintenance Technician reports improper use of Engineering Authorization to defer maintenance action.

input: Was on a vector to visual approach at lax. Socal gave us a 220 heading to a visual approach. Upon reaching turn to final we experienced wake turbulence that rolled the aircraft about 40 degrees. Since we were cleared for visual approach we chose to widen out to the left to avoid the wake turbulence. There was a corporate jet for the south complex (25l); we were 24r. We advised air traffic control we had the corporate jet in sight when beginning visual approach. We saw that we were getting a little to close to the corporate jet and then turned towards end of our runway. Air traffic control asked 'do you have 24r in sight?'  we said 'yes; turning for numbers now'. I know that air traffic control was a little worried; however we had aircraft in sight at all times. I think in the future this could have been avoided if we immediately advised that we were avoiding the wake turbulence. This would have let the controller know that we were in control and still had traffic in sight.
output: A corporate jet Captain reported encountering wake turbulence from a preceding corporate jet on approach to LAX and made adjustments to prevent further wake experiences without advising tower.

input: Departed anchorage international visual flight rules en route to kenai. Kenai was visual flight rules weather at time of departure flight is 25 minute(s) longitude kenai went instrument flight rules while en route we came in close proximitypa to an sma while awaiting clearance at the ne boundary of kenai control zone extension. We may have also entered the extension briefly while holding for clearance next time i'll depart instrument flight rules and save the hassle.
output: COMMUTER ENCOUNTERS IFR WX AT DEST. WHILE HOLDING OUTSIDE CTL ZONE HAS CONFLICT WITH SMA; POSSIBLE CTL ZONE ENTRY.

input: Our local management in an effort to decrease coordination errors; has implemented a requirement to record all coordination between local ctl/twr and ground ctl/flt data. Unfortunately; this recording of coordination is cumbersome; awkward; time-consuming; and distracting -- particularly for local control our busiest and most demanding position. We are using an override function to accomplish this and this can be very disruptive. It also often requires local control to return to the console to push a button; when a better use of local ctl's time might be looking out a window on the federal aviation regulation side of the cabin attendant to spot an aircraft of course; when traffic in light; this coordination is easily accomplished and offers some limited benefits. However; as both local controllers and ground ctl's/flt data's workload increases; the limited benefits are quickly outweighed by the decrease in safety and awareness that the recording process involves. Funny thing is; the federal aviation administration considers an frequency modulation radio playing softly in the backgnd completely unacceptable; but an override in your ear is perfectly acceptable. As federal aviation regulation as i know; there is no national requirement to record all this; only to the extent practical! And it is not practical to record these coords during busy traffic to require this; results in unnecessary distrs decreasing safety!
output: STS CONTROLLERS EXPRESS CONCERN REGARDING NEW PROCEDURE REQUIRING CONTROLLERS TO RECORD RELIEF BRIEFINGS; ALLEGING PROCEDURE IS NOT PRACTICAL AND AN UNNECESSARY DISTRACTION.

input: There still seems to be confusion on the flight director (flight deck) door entry/exit procedures on the airbus. Fa's (flight attendants) received a bulletin stating that the procedure matches the boeing procedure fleet wide. That information isn't aligning with airbus procedure. I was the a and was told to stay in there during the times the captain and first officer (first officer) were stepping out.please align procedures with both work groups and clarify whether there are in fact fleet wide procedures.
output: Flight Attendant reported that the cockpit security procedure for the Boeing and Airbus aircraft does not match.

input: While replacing the borrowed part which generated a log page; i noticed the maintenance manual reference i was working from (b737-400 31-26-41/401) was not the same as was used while installing it (b737-ng 31-51-04/401). I read through the ng reference and found no flight deck discrepancies (ie; pulled breakers) that may have come from using those procs.
output: A B737-400 TECHNICIAN REPLACING A BORROWED AURAL WARNING UNIT NOTED THE MAINT MANUAL REF NUMBER WAS DIFFERENT FROM THE MANUAL REF USED TO INSTALL THE BORROWED UNIT. THE PROCS AND TEST WERE THE SAME.

input: Gnd had repositioned us via hover taxi from our location at the helipad to taxiway intxns of taxiway b and taxiway h. History has shown that tower normally clears us across the airport direct nne to the helicopter training area. Tower cleared us to depart north on taxiway b and would call our turn ebound. The error was a complete result of my mindset. Being accustomed to direct air taxi i perceived our clearance to be nebound on taxiway h. Tower asked intermediate fix i had the approaching aircraft on final in sight and gave me the clearance as stated above. What i thought i heard light emitting diode me to believe i was to cross the runway(s) nbound. I asked the tower intermediate fix he wanted me to wait and cross behind the landing aircraft or proceed. Tower responded quickly saying that i was cleared north on taxiway b. With my mindset of a direct air taxi to the north side of the airport i heard my clearance expressed with an urgency to proceed now! Without delay; i executed my air taxi across the runway(s) down taxiway h. Air traffic control was very clear on the clearance but i heard what i expected to hear as a north departure subsequently; i crossed the active runway(s) and crossed in front of the landing aircraft this incursion did not result in any deviation required by the landing aircraft fortunately! This incident has been a very good lesson on listening to and understanding your clearance each time. I set myself up with certain expectations and had already made my mind up. Listen; listen; listen. Understand -- and only then depart as cleared had i done second officer this would not have been an incident.
output: HELI PLT INADVERTENTLY MISINTERP ATC GND CTLR WHEN MAKING A HOVER TAXI ACROSS AN ACTIVE RWY WHEN ANOTHER ACFT WAS ON FINAL.

input: Prior to takeoff clearance delivery provided a full route reroute. The first officer loaded new route and i verified the new route was loaded correctly. After departure; flight was given direct las. The first officer inserted direct las; which i verified; and engaged with 'abeam points'. The first officer loaded en route winds into flight plan. During loading; the first officer remembers seeing the route with j100 from las to sny while loading bce winds. Shortly after passing las; center asked if we were on j100. We responded we were supposed to be and checked the flight management guidance computer route. The route now showed las direct to sny with no 'abeam points'. We corrected it and got back on course. We do not know how the route got changed. Less than two minutes later; the same thing happened to another air carrier flight behind us. The most likely explanation would be that one of us mistakenly inputted a 'direct sny'. However; the first officer's technique would be to program such a change including 'abeam pts'. They were not there. The first officer does not remember making that input and i did not verify any such input. This makes that mistaken input somewhat less likely. I did not make any inputs. We are at a loss to explain what actually happened. Since the same thing happened to the next flight; at the same point; on the same route; on the same day; at almost the same time; there is a small possibility that there is a database or other flight management guidance computer glitch. This is worthy of further investigation.
output: An A320 flight crew received a reroute clearance prior to takeoff and programmed the FMGC accordingly. Inexplicably; after takeoff when ATC inquired as to their deviation from that route they found the programmed 'airways' route between LAS and SNY had vanished and was now showing a 'direct' route. Strangely enough; another air carrier A320 flight crew flying the same route shortly behind them reported what appeared to be an identical anomaly.

input: Approximately 30 minutes into the flight; the low voltage light and discharge light illuminated. I completed the checklist items and the lights did not extinguish. I elected to return to zzz to have maintenance look at the issue. Upon arrival at zzz my aircraft was met by the fire brigade and i was asked to provide my name and telephone number.
output: C206 pilot reported low voltage and discharge lights illuminated 30 minutes into the flight and resulted in a return to departure airport.
