How could things have gone better; i'm not sure. We did the best we could but it became task saturated for them and us. They told us that it wasn't a problem; however; i'm still filling out this report to enlighten the team on how screwball things got with 4 different arrival changes in such a short period of time. I don't have any thoughts on how this could have been avoided.
output: Corporate jet pilot reported receiving several revised clearances in a short amount of time from a very busy ZLC Center Controller due to GPS jamming occurring in the area.

input: #2 reverser was deactivated due to faulty reverser light. Minimum equipment list requires 2 of 3 reverser system for dispatch. During preflt maintenance found a cracked reverser blocker door on the #1 engine and removed blocker door. Cdl (confign deviation list) allows 1 blocker door to be removed but instructs flight crew to use no more than 65% n1 during reverse operations(s) we accepted the aircraft after questioning maintenance as to whether this less than fully functional reverser met the minimum equipment list requirement of 2 reverser system and received their assurances that it did. We felt that there was no compromise of safety in this particular flight as the aircraft was relatively light; and both departure and arrival, arrive runway(s) were longitude and dry.
output: A FLC ON A COMMERCIAL FIXED WING WDB ACFT QUESTIONED THE MEL DISPATCH REQUIREMENTS ON INOP ENG REVERSERS. #2 ENG REVERSER DEFERRED AS INOP AND #1 ENG BLOCKER DOOR REMOVED. STILL MEETS MEL REQUIREMENTS FOR DISPATCH.

input: On arrival, arrive to runway(s) 174 at dfw; i was pilot flying and called flaps to 25 degrees the flap indicator stopped between 20-25 degrees i called for the flaps to be retracted to 20 degrees flaps did not move and the trailing edge flap disagreement light illuminated. We went around and performed the abnormal chklist. I elected to declare an emergency and have crash fire rescue equipment standing by. Briefed flight attendants and made a public address landing was uneventful.
output: B757 FLAP DISAGREEMENT WARNING CAUSES FLC TO DECLARE AN EMER AND LAND WITH CFR EQUIP STANDING BY.

input: When on an east flow (lndg runway(s) 8/12 at cxy; and runway(s) 13 at mdt) with a departure off runway(s) 12 at cxy and an inbound coming from the se on an extended downwind for left/right (directions) traffic runway(s) 8; due to the close proximitypa of the 2 airports automated radar terminal systems data tags often overlap making it difficult to distinguish one's inbound traffic near the airports normal traffic pattern for runway(s) 8 is l- hand traffic with the above situation several times separation minima was lost. This became an issue between mountain daylight time and cxy facilities. Cxy tower requested that mountain daylight time approach provide a manual verbal handoff for the inbound traffic mountain daylight time approach has refused saying that the conflicts don't happen frequently enough. Does an accident have to take place before our requests are met? This is also a reason why cxy tower should be an l-rac. Cxy tower already has a letter of agreement to allow its controllers to use the d-brite for separation. However; the federal aviation administration refuses to delegate airspace to cxy citing economic instead of safety reasons for their refusal. Callback conversation with mountain daylight time terminal radar approach control facility supervisor revealed the following information unable to connect with the rptr but was able to speak to a supervisor at mountain daylight time terminal radar approach control facility regarding airspace. The supervisor stated that cxy tower is a level 1 facility with d- bright radar indicator tower equipment radar and has an automated radar terminal systems data keyboard for flight plan information regarding the terminal radar service area the tower is located 3.5 mile from mountain daylight time and the only airspace cxy has is the ata/ctl zone up to 2000 feet/foot he disputes the rptr's claim of airspace violations without coordination by terminal radar approach control facility the tower is scheduled to go contract in the near future.
output: RPTR AT LEVEL 1 ATCT CONTENDS THAT CERTAIN E FLOW AIRSPACE CONFIGNS BY THE PARENT APCH CTL CONFLICT WITH THEIR CLASS D VFR TFC. LEVEL 1 TWR IS EQUIPPED WITH D- BRITE RADAR AND HAS ARTS KEYBOARD FOR INPUT OF VFR TRSA TFC. TWR HAS CLASS D AIRSPACE 2000 FT AND BELOW.

input: Acft departing runway(s) 22l encountered bird strike on rotation approximately 5000 feet/foot down runway(s) flight crew heard loud noise with bird strike. The noise continued; and crew also noticed partial loss of power on left/right (directions) engine (type b737-500). Aircraft yaw was also noticed. Left/right (directions) engine power was lower by approximately 4% n1 and n2. Crew decided that return to airport was safest course of action. After briefing cabin crew; the aircraft was given air traffic control instructions for a return visual approach runway(s) 27l. Landing was uneventful using normal sop's. Upon arrival, arrive at gate; it became evident that the bird had been ingested partially into the left/right (directions) engine distorting several fan blades. Dispatch notified. Supplemental information from acn 574545: large bird struck left/right (directions) side of nose just after liftoff. Loud noise begun shortly after; and continued until end of flight -- indicative of engine damage. #1 engine indications were relatively normal; although numbers slightly less than #2's readings (as intermediate fix at slightly less pwr). Vibrations normal. Landed as soon as possible runway(s) 27l. Post-lndg inspection showed strike left/right (directions) side of radome; bird splatter between aircraft body and #1 engine and bird impact inside #1 engine wall forward of fan blades. Extensive fan blade damage.
output: B737-500 CREW HAD A BIRD STRIKE ON TKOF THAT DAMAGED #1 ENG FAN BLADES.

input: I had a lear jet level at fl320 and he was looking for higher. There was an air carrier directly above the lear at fl340. It was a busy sector with aircraft deviating for weather and i was trying to climb and descend aircraft at the same time. All of a  sudden the lear jet showed an altitude of fl335 and i thought the aircraft was climbing; so i asked him to say altitude and he did not respond. I then tried to turn the air carrier aircraft 50 degrees to the right but he would not turn due to weather so i climbed him to fl360. I then went back to the lear jet and asked if he was level at fl320 and he reported level. It ended up being a mode-c swap. I thought i was going to have a mid air collision. It was a terrible time for a mode-c swap to happen considering the traffic volume and unusual situations going on at the sector. I strongly believe that mode-c's transposing is a huge factor especially in my situation. I feel this problem somehow needs to be addressed. This situation could have escalated and made a worse problem.
output: ZJX Controller described a stressful event when traffic at FL340 and traffic immediately below at FL320 swapped Mode-C information; indicating a climb initiated by the aircraft at FL320; the reporter indicating Mode-C swaps are problem.

input: The chief pilot contends that i went against/violated federal aviation regulations by not shutting the engine down the moment i got a red light (oil pressure) and a fluctuating oil pressure gauge. I have combed the afm. On pgs 2 and 3 it states; 'oil pressure light on and oil pressure gauge less than 40 psi = monitor engine instruments.' also; i called fairchild and they backed me up stating; 'they could not find it in the afm or maintenance manual where it states; shut engine down.' around santa barbara; the oil pressure needle began to oscillate slightly. The oil temperature remained cool. As a precautionary measure; i tuned in local automatic terminal information service stations and then had my f/o contact flight service station specialist to get additional weather rpts. I overheard on the frequency that someone had missed the approach at oxnard and; according to sbp station manager no one had made it into san luis obispo. As the weather rpts started to come in; the oil pressure light started to flash on intermittently. I told sbp station manager to get maintenance control on the phone and to advise them of the oil pressure fluctuation; oil pressure light beginning to flicker; cool normal oil temperature and acquire any additional information they may be able to add to this situation. The entire coast and local company stations were rpting unfavorable conditions; aircraft missing the approach down around minimums; or closed. Because paso robles had previously been an approved airport and 2 yrs before that paso robles was the chosen alternate when the coast was down; i contacted flight service station specialist for their current weather as well. Paso robles weather came back as being clear and 25 mile visibility based on all the circumstances and available information i determined that paso robles was the closest suitable airport the oil pressure gauge appeared to become more inaccurate. The light eventually came on; while the oil temperature remained stable with no increase whatsoever. I notified maintenance of this situation. The maintenance control rep said he discussed it with the director of maintenance who was there with him by the phone. About that time; the sound of the revolutions per minute appeared to momentarily flicker and then continue to be normal. I contacted sgu maintenance and told him to inform them of what i heard. They in turn said; 'if the rpm's begin fluctuating; then it may be advisable to shut the engine down.' with that information i turned toward paso robles and ran our chklists. All chklists and procedures were completed properly. The rpm's began fluctuating; the engine was caged and we landed on runway(s) 19. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following. Conversation revealed that the scavenger pump failed and before the engine shutdown; the rear turbine bearing had seized. Rptr admits that he misread the operating manual and thought he had only one indication when; in fact; the oil pressure light and oil pressure gauge are activated off of two different sources second officer did; in fact; have two indications which call for immediate engine shutdown. Irony is that he was talking to maintenance for some time and they had the information and never suggested he should shut down immediately. End result is that after 4 yrs with company with no other problems they have reacted by terminating his employment. He's not denying he was wrong but feels company has overreacted by terminating him.
output: ACR SMT INFLT ENGINE SHUTDOWN ACCOUNT OIL PRESSURE.

input: While performing an upset [recovery] flight in training area alpha i had a traffic conflict with a caravan at 7000 feet. We started spin training at 7;500 feet and while the student was performing a spin maneuver we had a tcad alert; i immediately instructed the student to recover. At the same time [another] grob who was also maneuvering in the area alerted me to traffic. Passing 7;000 feet i noticed the traffic and immediately started an extreme dive to avoid the traffic at which point i noticed the caravan pilot started to maneuver away from me. Tcad alert was 0.3 at same altitude. The alpha aerobatic area was opened with terminal radar approach control facility that morning.i believe when we open an aerobatic box that terminal radar approach control facility should not route traffic right through it.
output: Aerobatic instructor reported Cessna Caravan traffic was routed through his training area resulting in a conflict.

input: We were flying to iad via the gibbz2 arrival. Tail wind was 160 kts which we made sure was in the descent planning page. Washington center held us at altitude past the top of descent due to crossing traffic. When clear of the conflict they told us to descend via the gibbz2 arrival. I stated that we were unable to make the altitude restrictions on the arrival as we were already 5;000 feet above path. The controller then told us to go direct kilmr and comply with the restrictions and contact washington on 133.2. The captain flew the plane using idle thrust and speed brake and programmed in direct kilmr. I changed frequency and checked in with washington center and said we had a request; as it was obvious we were still unable to make any restrictions. The controller told us to stand by. I made repeated attempts to get a reasonable clearance from air traffic control but was ignored. Finally i broke in and stated that the clearance was impossible and we needed a new clearance and i requested a phone number to center. The controller told me they had a lot going on and he would get back to me. They never issued any altitude relief in spite of our repeated statements that we could not comply. We crossed every restriction over 5;000 feet high. Finally they told us to contact approach control. When i checked in with approach i simply told them we were descending to 6;000 feet (bottom altitude of the star). He told us to descend to 5;000 and we continued to a normal approach and landing. I have serious concerns about washington centers total disregard of our concerns and failure to resolve the clearance issues.
output: Pilot reports of being left high and advising ATC that they could not make the assigned restrictions. ATC never advised the crew on what to do. Aircraft crossed every restriction high. Pilot was concerned about the center and their disregard for the flights clearance issues.

input: We departed a station with an open write-up. The write-up stated 'eng #2/#3 needs oil svcing.' i talked with maintenance control earlier about another minimum equipment list write-up and missed the open write-up. The aircraft had above the required minimum oil quantities for departure per the limitations on the aircraft talked with maintenance control about this after the fact and they stated this was the third time this has happened at this out station where open maintenance items were not addressed. Supplemental information from acn 397230: i inadvertently overlooked the open write-up during preflt. Discovered it upon landing i normally checked the logbook status as the first item upon entering the cockpit. In this instance; another crew member preceded me to the cockpit and took the logbook to operations(s) to call maintenance control about a deferred item. When the logbook was returned to the cockpit; i failed to checked it; except to note the inbound oil quantities noted there.
output: A B727 WAS DISPATCHED WITH AN OPEN UNANSWERED LOGBOOK WRITE-UP.

input: We were cleared for the instrument landing system runway 05 at cyyz. We broke out just inside the outer marker and had the approach lights and runway in sight. There was rain over the north half of runway 05 extending to the west. As we got over the approach lights and i began to reduce power to slow and begin the transition; we hit heavy rain and our forward visibility was greatly reduced. We were able to land but the rain intensified to where we could not see out the forward windows. We struggled to find the runway exit (h3) and were able to exit; but then continued slightly right onto an access road. We soon realized our mistake; notified air traffic control and were cleared for a 180 degree turn and hold short of runway 05. Just as i was turning back onto the taxiway; i noticed what appeared to be a light that had the glass top knocked off. I was not sure if this was done by us or not; but we mentioned this to toronto air traffic control and they sent a crash fire rescue equipment truck out to check. We never heard of the findings of their investigation whether it was us or not. We thought it was possibly done by us as we had our flaps in the 'ground' position as we taxied off. We checked out our aircraft thoroughly once we cleared customs. I gave my name and phone number to crash fire rescue equipment and secured the a/c for the evening. The next morning we inspected the aircraft again more thoroughly and again found no evidence of any impact with a light.
output: CE525 Captain reports landing in a rain storm reducing forward visibility to near zero. Once off the runway on the desired taxiway an inadvertent turn onto a service road is made; requiring 180 turn back to the taxiway. No damage to the aircraft is reported.

input: Departed iad for jfk. 34 passenber approximately 500 pounds under gross weight aircraft at aft center of gravity limits. Cleared for visual approach to runway(s) 13l at jfk by new york approach called tower approximately 10 mile out. Told to 'continue.' at approximately 2 mile final; still no landing clearance tower controller very busy; in process of telling all aircraft monitoring one frequency to change to another. Told 747 on final to runway(s) 22l to go around at approximately 50 feet/foot above ground level still no landing clearance even though i have requested at least 3 times with no response. At this time capt becomes extremely irate; almost shouting on tower frequency for our landing clearance he tells me later that at this point he was preparing for go around i asked again for landing clearance it is given at approximately 20 feet/foot above ground level airspd drops about 10 knot(s) below vref. Touchdown is fairly hard; causing bounce. Due to aft center of gravity nose comes way up; stick shaker actuates. Second touchdown is very nose high causing tail strike. Aircraft control is regained and capt taxies normally to gate. I believe the primary cause of this incident was an aft center of gravity condition; compounded by allowing the aircraft to slow below vref. The speed reduction was allowed due to the distrs of air traffic control and also due to loss of concentration; due to loss of temper by the capt.
output: CAPT LOSES CTL OF HIMSELF AND AIRSPD AND MAKES HARD LNDG.

input: Flt was assigned a crossing restriction of 35 sw of bld vor and tacan (co-located) at 15000'. I programmed the flight management computer (flt management computer) for this crossing restriction and verified this information on the flight management computer cdv. The coplt also confirmed the correct data entry. At approximately 35.5 vor and dme (co-located) sw of bld vor and tacan (co-located) lax center asked us our vor and dme (co-located) from bld. (note: the flight management computer indicated 42 mile sw of bld; ie; 6 mile from the fix.) we told the controller to standby second officer we could verify the vor and dme (co-located) distance with raw data directly from the navigation receiver. Upon accomplishing this; the vor and dme (co-located) indicated was actually 35.5 mile a discrepancy of 6.5 mile from what the flight management computer was indicating. We told the controller we were 35.5 vor and dme (co-located) from bld. The controller then asked us our altitude we responded; 'we are passing through 18000' (the controller then handed us off to las vegas apch). The coplt and i believe the problem was caused by the computer malfunctioning. The trip had originated in ontario; ca. It took the coplt and i 1 hour to align the inertial reference system/unit system we believe that this difficulty could have had an effect on the erroneous vor and dme (co-located) information the computer was generating. In summary; the coplt and i believe that computer malfunction was responsible for the missed crossing restriction. However; we have learned that backing up the computer with raw data from the navigate, navigation receiver could prevent an occurrence of this sort in the future. Incidentally; flight did not pose any conflict to other aircraft as a result of this error and we were not asked to contact anyone with regard to this incident.
output: ACR MLG ALT DEVIATION UNDERSHOT ALT CROSSING RESTRICTION DURING DESCENT.

input: At 95 knots indicated airspeed takeoff warning horn sounded. Takeoff was aborted. We could not determine cause of horn. We returned to gate; wrote it up for maintenance they inspected aircraft and could find no cause. On next takeoff everything was normal. Trim was set at top of green arc but why did it not go off until 95 kias?
output: ABORT TKOF ACCOUNT TKOF WARNING HORN SOUNDED AT 95 KTS.

input: At xa00 local time on jan/xx/97; i executed a landing at the anv; ak; airport and had to nearly overfly a grader performing snow removal on the field. I was flying a c207 on a regularly scheduled flight and was carrying 1 passenber as i approached the runway(s) i made all the standard traffic calls; including 2 announcing that i was on final for runway(s) 35 at anv. The weather conditions were poor with a 500 feet/foot overcast 2 mile visibility; and a 20 knot(s) headwind component on short final. A grader was performing snow removal just outside the lights along the westbound side of the runway(s) about 150 feet/foot past the approach threshold. I made a higher than normal approach and landed 1/2 way down the runway(s) after electing to overfly the grader. Unknown to me; the airport had been notamed closed earlier that morning. The company calls for a briefing every morning and requests notams. Another pilot obtained the briefing that morning; requested the notams; but received none pertaining to the airport being closed. There was no 'x' at the approach end of the runway(s) either. I believe 2 problems occurred with this incident. First; i landed on a runway(s) that had been notamed closed. The company received no information about the closure either through flight service station specialist or from its local agent regarding the runway(s) closure. It is not normal for a runway(s) to be closed simply for snow removal unless the snow is excessively deep which this was not. Second; i landed longitude over the grader without buzzing the grader to announce my presence. Given the windy conditions and turbulence caused by terrain around the airport i elected to make an extra high approach and land past the grader on the sufficient runway(s) remaining. The grader was not equipped with a radio and thus short of buzzing the grader i could not notify him of my presence.
output: ATX PLT LANDS ON CLOSED RWY AT ANV; AK. OVERFLIES A WORKING GRADER IN THE PROCESS OF SNOW REMOVAL.

input: During the last few weeks in bwi; i have noticed an increased amount of foreign object debris on the ramp; flight line; near the terminal; on the taxiways; grassy areas adjacent to the taxiways; runway; etc. The question was 'where is all this foreign object debris coming from?' i have reported the foreign object debris to bwi ground operations; and it seems as if the foreign object debris is never picked up (look at the abundance of foreign object debris in the grassy areas next to the taxiways and runways). During the preflight today; we noticed massive amounts of foreign object debris in and around the bwi gate area. Specifically; it appeared that a trash dumpster had been emptied in the vehicle storage area under the terminal. There were a large number of plastic bags; cans; cups; etc. Which had collected in this area. It looked as if the foreign object debris had collected over a period of several weeks.it looked as if nobody noticed the foreign object debris and nobody was picking it up. In fact; while we sat at the gate; a bwi ramp supervisor was standing amongst the pile of trash and foreign object debris smoking a cigarette. He did not pick up any of the foreign object debris the wind was blowing hard; and foreign object debris was being blown from this area onto the flight line. A coffee cup was approaching the aircraft as we taxied into the gate. I called bwi operations several times to have the foreign object debris removed with no response. Finally; the manager of operations showed up. His response to the foreign object debris problem was 'it's windy today; and that is why the foreign object debris is there.' i answered; 'the wind did not create the foreign object debris the wind is only blowing the foreign object debris back onto the flight line.' i asked him who was responsible for ensuring that the flight line is foreign object debris free.he reluctantly responded that he was the one responsible. He gave me the usual answers as to why it the foreign object debris was still there. 'i just started my shift; the wind is blowing; etc.' there was a large grey trash bag blowing around in the area (one similar to the one i recently ingested in my #1 engine just before takeoff causing us to shut down the engine; return to the gate; and have maintenance remove the pieces of bag from the engine). Bwi is not taking the foreign object debris program seriously. Ramp agents; ramp supervisors; etc. Walk right by foreign object debris without picking it up. The answer i get to this is that the 'vacuum' is deployed every once in a while; and the 'vacuum' is responsible for retrieving foreign object debris not the individuals who work on the ramp.vice president of ground operations needs to re-emphasize the importance of foreign object debris awareness in bwi (and system-wide). Bwi station manager needs to 'tour' the bwi flight line daily to ensure that the managers of ramp and operations (mros) are enforcing the foreign object debris awareness program. There are several dumpsters on the bwi flight line which are often left open; are often overflowing with trash; and nobody seems to notice. Dumpster doors need to be secured when not in use; and dumpsters need to be emptied more often. Mros; ramp supervisors; and ramp agents need to act more responsibly. If you see foreign object debris take immediate action. Pick it up and dispose of it properly. Don't wait for someone else (the 'vacuum') to pick up the foreign object debris take personal initiative and pick up the foreign object debris without waiting to be told to do so. The leadership on this issue starts from the top. Foreign object debris can be picked up between flights. Rather than going to the break room; get out to the ramp; and pick up the foreign object debris the wind does blow the foreign object debris around; but it does not create the foreign object debris when it is windy; it is even more important to retrieve the foreign object debris to prevent foreign object debris from being ingested in the aircraft engines. I sent photos of the bwi foreign object debris issue to [name]; ground operations; at headquarters.
output: Air carrier Captain reported that a trend of excessive FOD on the ramp and airport environment resulted in a hazardous situation to taxiing aircraft.

input: When i arrived at our jet i found an minimum equipment list on the log book relating to a write up we had made on this aircraft when we brought it in the night before. That write up described an indication on the hydraulic electronic centralized aircraft monitoring page that indicated a failed or faulty pressure switch or related cannon plug downstream from the blue electric hydraulic pump. My past experiences with this specific write up has caused me numerous disagreements with maintenance control with regards to whether or not a suitable minimum equipment list exists for this condition. Those past experiences only reinforced my interpretation that the minimum equipment list does not address this specific condition; and it is therefore not 'mel'able. When the condition was discovered the night before; i entered it and another discrepancy into the logbook and called maintenance control and relayed the info regarding both. I made clear to him that it was my interpretation of the mels that the hydraulic issue must be fixed; as it was not 'mel'able. I assumed; wrongly; that with the aircraft overnighting with ample maintenance staff on duty the issue would be correctly addressed. Unfortunately; upon arriving the next morning i found the inappropriate minimum equipment list applied to the write-up.i called maintenance control and explained that their minimum equipment list did not address the indication; instead it addressed the label; an entirely different indication. We went back and forth; with him stating that airbus had put out some kind of an engineering statement years ago that supposedly addressed this indication and that we were 'good to go'. I replied that i had; in fact; read such a report years before and it was determined to not address this condition. I acknowledged that there may in fact be another report and i would be very eager to read it as i was looking for some way to legally fly this airplane with its passengers to their destination. After considerable discussion he acknowledged that the applied minimum equipment list was in fact incorrect; and he now wanted to apply the same minimum equipment list number; but with a new condition. The new proposed condition was for the electric pump indication. I pointed out that too was incorrect; as the pump indicated properly and the failed switch was downstream of the pump. I repeatedly stressed that i did not consider this a safety issue; but rather a legal one; as it was simply a poorly written minimum equipment list that did not adequately address all the potential electronic centralized aircraft monitoring indications.after significant additional dialog back and forth without a mutually agreeable solution i had no choice but to call maintenance control and refuse the minimum equipment list and; if it remained on the logbook; refuse the aircraft as well. I called dispatch and explained the situation and was transferred to the maintenance representative there. I relayed to him the disagreement with maintenance control and explained my pained position. He listened and said he'd get back to me. A short time later i learned that the flight had been put on an extended delay and a repair would be made. The delay extended into late afternoon when we finally departed. Simply put; this specific failure provides only 2 options. The first; fix the aircraft and proceed with schedule. Second; if fix isn't possible at current station within a reasonable period of time; as determined by maintenance control and dispatch; then maintenance ferry the aircraft to a station where repairs can be accomplished. The third option maintenance control tried to apply is not acceptable. One cannot twist an existing minimum equipment list to fit a scenario where it doesn't properly apply; as i believe was the case here. The fix is very simple; modify the mels to address this specific situation. Until this occurs; maintenance will not be able to avail itself of the very simple and reasonable process of applying a legal and safe minimum equipment list to this relatively innocuous situation. Oh; and ensure moc understands and respects the limits of the mels; and proceeds accordingly.
output: An A319 Captain refused an aircraft due to a deferred hydrualic system MEL item which he felt was inappropriately applied to the anomalous condition.

input: Acft proceeded direct to dvc after oveto intersection instead of published turn to waypoint reference n3652.8 w11346.3. Caused by failure of pilots to enter transition in flight management computer failure reinforced by instrument flight rules clearance routing which does not show this turn in the wording. Pilots verified routing but failed to note this turn. Air traffic control noted mistake. No conflict.
output: AN ACR MLG CREW FAILED TO ENTER A WAYPOINT IN THEIR FMC. THIS CAUSED THEM TO FLY 'OVETO' DIRECT DVC VICE VIA THE PRESCRIBED ROUTING. ERROR ADMITTED.

input: Approximately 1 hour and 25 minutes into flight; crew sent automatic communications addressing & reporting system advising that both transponders had failed. Flight was near zzzzz intersection. I contacted maintenance control to see if there was any advice they could provide; but there was not. Due to security concerns; i did not want to attempt overfly and if air traffic control would allow; a return back to zzzz would be best option. Crew concurred and flight turned around. I contacted zzzz and they approved the aircraft to re-enter airspace with no transponder.[the cause was] transponder failure.
output: A Dispatcher reported an aircraft had both of their transponders fail enroute.  After discussing with flight crew; they decided to turn around and return to the departure airport.

input: Arrived in n.y. Approach area for approach into ewr. Weather was well below forecast weather for our arrival, arrive company notams received in chicago made no mention of runway(s) 22l approach lighting system being out of service ewr automatic terminal information service at 50z also did not mention the approach lighting system notice to airmen / of air missions weather was 600/1. Approach informed us runway visual range was 2600'. We briefed the approach with minimums of 1800' runway visual range with capt landing from monitored approach intermediate fix runway visual range fell below 2400' runway visual range at g/s intercept; runway visual range was rpted as 3000'. We picked up the runway(s) environment at 350' above ground level and noticed the approach lighting system was not on. A quick checked showed runway(s) 22l requires runway visual range 4000' for approach lighting system inoperative we started on illegal approach due to lack of information on the notice to airmen / of air missions landing was made w/o incident.
output: ACR PIC REPORTS AN ILLEGAL APCH PERFORMED DUE TO APCH LIGHT SYSTEM BEING OUT OF SERVICE.

input: I ante meridiem submitting this rpt to get to the bottom of the smoke and fume incidents on b757 aircraft xxx. I was advised earlier today that there have been three individual events over the past two flts. Background: i was the first officer on flight xxxx; zzz to zzz1 last night. Prior to my exterior preflt inspection i noticed an extended history of erratic left/right (directions) engine oil consumption; possibly suggesting an intermittent; yet potentially large; oil leak. A few minute(s) later during my exterior preflt inspection i noted that the left acm/pack exhaust had a stream of oil running down the fuselage; while the right side acm exhaust duct was completely dry -- as they should probably all be. I advised the capt of this anomaly; noted the left/right (directions) engine oil consumption history; and requested we have maintenance look at it; he concurred. The amt's effectively dismissed my concerns re: oil leaking from the engine into the bleed air supply and signed it off. Flight attendant rpted light smoke in the center cabin and a sulfur odor occurring at takeoff +-5 minute(s) and at takeoff +-20 minute(s) we advised and discussed this with our dispatcher/maint control via multiple automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages and via a phone patch later in the flight during our flight to zzz the left/right (directions) engine consumed 2 quarts of oil; the left/right (directions) used zero. The capt allowed me to make an 'info to maint' entry in the log book regarding the smoke and fume events. Today i spoke with maintenance control for more than 30 minute(s) to follow up on last night's events. Despite extensive inspection by zzz1 amt's; i was told that the aircraft had another (third) fume event on the return flight from zzz1 to zzz; a 'sour milk odor' for several minute(s) after takeoff; as rpted by a flight attendant and a passenber zzz maintenance had removed power from one or more of the eight over-wing exit door heaters per minimum equipment list please address the following questions? 1) why do we have no reference to these electric heaters in our b757 manuals (with the minimum equipment list exception; this volume is usually review after-the-fact)? Why are they not addressed in initial or recurrent training? 2) where exactly are these 8 heaters located? What are the possible failures modes and do they manifest themselves via smoke in the cabin? 3) why do only some of our b757 aircraft have these heaters? 4) while i ante meridiem not an a&p; i have nearly 40 years of experience in aviation. I remain uncertain that the over-wing exit heaters are the source of odors and smoke in this b757. I was advised that ship yyy (b757 smoke and fume ground evacuation at zzz2 a few days ago) had engine oil residue found on the recirculation fan filters. Have thos filters been checkeded on b757 aircraft xxx? 5) i only recently learned of the b757 aft cargo 'false' overheat indication/smoke/fire event in a recurrent training class. May i please urge that we have important information such as this event shared more promptly among all b767/757 plts? I was disappointed to learn about this event in a regular recurrent training class -- all our b767/757 pilots should have been informed as soon as the initial results were available; given the potentially catastrophic nature of an inflt electrical fire.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated the lack of concern by maintenance was troubling. He does not believe the cabin sidewall electric resistant heaters are the source of the light smoke or the cause of the smell of sulfur or sour milk odors in the cabin rpted by the flight attendants; especially since the problems seem to be noticeable during takeoff and climb out. Rptr stated when he saw the stream of oil running down the fuselage from the left acm pack exhaust and also noted the #1 engine oil consumption; he thought maintenance would have been interested; but they were not. Rptr stated this same aircraft had at least three situations of smoke and strong fumes in the cabin.
output: PLT OF A B757-200 RPTS FLT ATTENDANTS NOTED LIGHT SMOKE IN THE CENTER CABIN AND A SULFUR ODOR OCCURRING AT TKOF+5 MINUTES AND AGAIN AT TKOF+20 MINUTES. PLT BELIEVES OIL LEAKING FROM ENG INTO BLEED AIR SUPPLY.

input: Cruising at fl350 we were given a descent clearance to cross fredy intersection at 10000 feet/foot moments later one of our flight attendants entered the cockpit and explained that we had a clear liquid coming from our left/right (directions) wing root; aft section of the wing; and that it was spraying onto the window just forward of our left/right (directions) engine i asked her to enlist one of our deadhdg pilots in the cabin to survey the situation and return. I quickly calculated that it would take 65 mile to descend to 10000 feet/foot looked at the arrival, arrive plate and decided that we would start down approximately at nickl intxn.??? 23+39=62. Our flight attendant returned and stated that the deadhdg pilot was not familiar enough with the aircraft to make a fair judgement of the situation at that time i decided to send my first officer back to the cabin for his opinion. While he was gone i went back into the aircraft logbooks looking for a past history of fuel seepage; recalculated the flight plan fuel burn; tested the fuel gauges; and looked over the circuit breaker panels for popped breakers. Everything was normal up to this point. My first officer returned and indicated that he thought that the liquid was residue deicing fluid from deicing that must had taken place earlier that day. About that time zmp asked intermediate fix we had started our descent yet. We had just arrived at nickl intersection and to myself; i questioned why they were asking intermediate fix we had started down yet. Since this was my planned spot to start descent we did and answered that we were in fact starting descent after initiating descent i recalculated the required mileage to descend to 10000 feet/foot and revisited the arrival, arrive plate one more time. This is when we discovered that i mistakenly used 39 mile instead of 7 mile distance between fredy and biltr intxns for my calculations. I deployed the spoilers and made a maximum effort descent notified air traffic control that we were not going to be able to make fredy at 10000 feet/foot and was in fact 10 mile short of the restrict, restricted, restriction intermediate fix i had not flown this arrival, arrive 100 times in the past; i have not flown it once. I believe the leaking liquid; hasty descent planning; familiarity with the arrival, arrive coupled with the absence of a crew member to double checked me were all contributing factors in this missed restrict, restricted, restriction always remember rule #1 'fly the aircraft first.'
output: ALT CROSSING RESTR NOT MET.

input: I was operating a cessna caravan from corvalis; or. The flight was filed under instrument flight rules and initially proceeded north from cvo on v-23. I obtained a clearance from cascade departure while on the ground in corvalis and advised them i would be departing on runway(s) 17. While obtaining the clearance i observed an aircraft preparing to depart on runway(s) 27; and also heard (on ctaf) an aircraft inbound from the se intending a left/right (directions) downwind entry for runway(s) 27. Cascade cleared me 'as filed' and told me to rpt airborne. I waited for the aircraft to depart on runway(s) 27 and then announced on common traffic advisory frequency that i would be departing runway(s) 17. After departure i notified cascade departure and they advised me of traffic inbound to corvalis as well as the traffic that had just departed. I advised cascade that i had the traffic in sight. Since the inbound aircraft was about to turn downwind for runway(s) 27; i continued sbound on a 170 degree heading until well clear of that traffic at which point i queried cascade approach to confirm that i was cleared to turn on course. As i was approximately 4-5 mile south of cvo at this point cascade questioned why i had not already turned on course. I responded that i had continued south to make sure i was well clear of the traffic into and out of corvalis. I then turned on course and the flight was completed without incident. I bring up this incident because of the confusion on my part and on that of the controller (cascade dep). Evidently cascade expected me to turn sooner than i did; and in hindsight; i realize i should have advised air traffic control that i was continuing south to be clear of the traffic that they pointed out. As i would not have turned on course sooner than i did in order to avoid the traffic and since i was not that federal aviation regulation from the departure airport i did not consider my flight path to be unusual for a departure from runway(s) 17. I was mistaken; however; to assume that air traffic control would expect me to give the traffic pattern wide berth. In the future; i can see i will need to be more vigilant in informing air traffic control any time my flight path may need to deviate even a small amount from my expected and cleared rte.
output: PLT OF C208 DEPARTING CVO FAILED TO TURN NORTH ON COURSE PRIOR TO CONTACT WITH CASCADE DEP CTL. DELAYED TURN DUE TO INBOUND AND DEP TRAFFIC FOR OTHER RWYS.

input: I was assigned pilot in command on a flight carrying three passengers on a lr 40. The preflight was conducted in accordance with the checklist. Engine start and subsequent cockpit checks did not yield any abnormalities that would cause the flight to be cancelled/delayed. Takeoff; departure; and cruise were uneventful. During our descent we got an amber engine indicating and crew alerting system message 'rudder boost inop'. We ran the appropriate checklist which called for pulling a circuit breaker that tripped off both yaw dampers (yd) and autopilot. The airplane started a roll to the left which i counteracted. The circuit breaker was set in accordance with the checklist. Yd and ap were re-engaged and everything seemed to work normal again. No engine indicating and crew alerting system message at that time. A short time thereafter we got the same message again. Simultaneously we received a prim pitch trim fault (white) and indicated air speed (amber; pfd) message. The airspeed indications were unreliable; differing between both pilot's pfds up to 60 knots indicated airspeed the indicated air speed on the pf/left side dropped at some point by about 130 knots indicated airspeed before returning to a 'normal' value. At this point; as the indications seemed more 'reliable' the controls were transferred to that side. Air traffic control was advised of our situation. While the sic was flying i monitored the systems available as well as requesting speed and altitude read outs from air traffic control (difference between cockpit and air traffic control was up to 80 kias). We were assigned block altitude 5500-7000. As we had no reliable indications with regards to speed i told the sic to fly by power settings and don't rely on the airspeed tape. To avoid any further distractions i requested to be taken off the arrival and being vectored straight to the instrument landing system air traffic control accommodated immediately. We flew the instrument landing system when handed off to tower we were advised of our airspeed which was reported to be 110 knots indicated airspeed while our cockpit instruments indicated 130 knots indicated airspeed to be safe pilot flying added a little more power. From what i remember we landed a little faster than vref but did not exceed any limitations.i am glad that we landed safely. As we had multiple issues to deal with; multiple engine indicating and crew alerting system messages at the same time; instrument meteorological conditions icing; it became apparent that we had to prioritize. Possible air data computer (air data computer) failure took precedent over everything else. No doubt; the decision to [advise atc]was the best course of action. We were able to focus on the tasks at hand while air traffic control kept other planes 'away' from us. We made it safely on the ground. That's all that matters. No injuries; no damage. The fact that the pilot flying cut off the engines after touchdown instead of engaging the thrust reversers is/was the least of our problems. Clear of the runway we waited for transportation for our passengers who didn't seem to be phased by the events as well as a tug to pull the plane to the facility. After the plane was parked i called maintenance and the chief pilot and advised them of our experience. Consequent maintenance write ups were filed and submitted. In our case proper training and great cockpit resource management made all the difference.
output: LR40 Captain reported 'Rudder Boost INOP' light illuminated followed by pitch trim and IAS faults; as well as unreliable airspeed indications.

input: During the approach briefing for area navigation global positioning system 35 at avl; i had pointed out to the captain that due to obstacles and terrain characteristics in the vicinity of avl; air traffic control would keep us high until very close to the station. As anticipated; atlanta center kept us at a high altitude (i do not remember exactly; but well above 15;000) until about 12-15 miles from the station. Upon being handed to asheville approach; and considering the terrain; night time; and the need for sufficient airspace to descend to a reasonable altitude in order to execute an effective and stable approach; i requested radar vectors for the area navigation global positioning system 35 (glideslope for the instrument landing system was out of service). Approach instructed us to descend to 6;000 and to a heading that would put the aircraft on a downwind to runway 35. Subsequently; the approach controller gave us a heading that put the aircraft on a left base leg to runway 35; and instructed us to descend from 6;000 to 5;100. During this descent; the ground proximity warning system issued an aural terrain caution. We immediately initiated a climb; advised air traffic control of the situation; and stopped the climb at 6;000; at which point the ground proximity warning system silenced. In addition; we advised we had the field in sight; and were cleared for a visual approach to runway 35. The minimum sector altitude corresponding to the left base leg to runway 35 stated 6;200 ft. We should have queried air traffic control of the validity of the instruction to descend from 6;000 to 5;100. From a cockpit resource management standpoint; the jeppessen avl airport reference page alludes to the fact that a high rate of descent in the vicinity of the airport may cause a ground proximity warning system activation due to mountainous terrain in the vicinity (we did not exceed 1500 fpm); hence an emphasis on this matter during the approach briefing; in conjunction to minimizing the rate of descent to; perhaps; no more than 700 fpm; more than likely would have avoided the situation.
output: Air carrier First Officer reported a CFIT event during approach under Approach Control which was followed by an uneventful visual landing.

input: Pnf. Arrival, arrive changed to wilber 2. Cross addvl at 11000 feet/foot 250 knot(s) first officer attempting to comply. Approaching fix; conflict with jumpers and aircraft at 10000 feet/foot 2 mile we both looked for traffic first officer missed turn to 240 degrees at addvl by 2/3 mile no comment by approach nor traffic conflict noted.
output: F100 CREW HAD A TRACK DEV ON THE WILBER 2 ARR TO DFW WHEN DISTR BY SKYDIVERS JUMPING DIRECTLY BELOW.

input: Due to deteriorating weather in new england; ground instructed us to notify them 5 minute(s) prior to pushback for air traffic control release time. Approximately 1 minute(s) prior to push; we called them to notify them per previous instructions. We were then instructed to notify them when ready to taxi. After pushing back we were told to call them in the future before pushing back for pushback clearance it appears they are assuming that 'call prior to taxi' means call prior to push; for push and taxi clearance additionally; they gave us taxi instructions to a new taxiway fahrenheit which is not depicted on the commercial plates nor was it in the company messages. This is part of the air traffic control mentality that air crews know the layout of their own personal airfields which of course is not the case as has been proved at places like detroit and tenerife. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the latest commercial chart has taxiway fahrenheit depicted. The rptr was more upset about the air traffic control attitude in general about pilots and flcs than by this incident and said he did receive instructions from the ground controller to taxiway f.
output: ACR CAPT COMPLAINT ABOUT BEING CLRED TO TAXI TO A TAXIWAY NOT SHOWN ON THE COMMERCIAL ARPT PLATE.

input: After touchdown during rollout; heavy rain was encountered. Air traffic control gave us clearance to exit the runway at a specified taxiway; i could not discern which taxiway was the correct taxiway; or even exactly where the taxiways were. I had my windshield wipers on high/fast. While slowing and identified where i was supposed to exit; air traffic control cleared a flight for takeoff. We had not even started our exit off the runway; nor did i know where exactly i was exiting. After the takeoff clearance issued; i tried to alert air traffic control we were on the runway; [departing aircraft] was simultaneously reading back their clearance. After [departing aircraft] read back their takeoff clearance; i told them to 'cancel their takeoff clearance; [we are] is still on the runway'. Air traffic control then asked [departing aircraft] to taxi down the runway and make the first available exit.
output: B737 Captain reported that after landing; they were still taxiing on the runway when another aircraft was given clearance for takeoff.

input: We departed san runway 27. Normal take off to a heading of 290 for noise abatement. Upon reaching 7000 ft mean sea level we received the instructions to fly direct to pgy vor and dme (co-located) via the left turn (almost a 180 degree turn). We set pgy vor and dme (co-located) on top in the flight management computer and upon reaching 90 degree intercept executed and confirmed that navigate, navigation function is 'tracking' inbound direct to pgy vor and dme (co-located) in both navigate, navigation and vor and dme (co-located) function. At approximately 2.9 vor and dme (co-located) to pgy vor and dme (co-located) aircraft made a slight left turn at about 10 degrees off course indicated; which from what we were seeing on our mfd's didn't make any sense. At the same time the controller said 'i see you in a left turn direct to pgy vor'. This caused confusion on the flight deck; as well as prompted the controller to ask us if our equipment is operational. There was no abnormal or caution messages displayed. As soon as we situated ourselves; we started troubleshooting and couldn't find the issue. We also checked with center controller and as it was a clear night confirmed we are on the cleared route. We continued flying now in vor and dme (co-located) mode as when the problem occurred it happened in nav.upon descent to [our destination] our flight management system displayed 'fms navigate, navigation dr' 'nav bus fail' and 'xfeed inop'.upon landing we recycled power to the flight management computer and the fault messages cleared. I made an entry in the logbook describing the erroneous indication as well as the annunciators observed. I believe that we have experienced navigate, navigation failure without any indications which caused us to deviate slightly right of the pgy vor and dme (co-located) either way vor and dme (co-located) indicated 2.9 nautical mile to pgy vor and dme (co-located) when the turn started. Paying closer attention and flying in both navigate, navigation and vor and dme (co-located) modes simultaneously monitoring both 'pictures' --not only selecting it--would of prevented the initial confusion and possible deviation.
output: An MD-83 flight crew got confusing NAV information between their FMS and VOR based systems. They opted to continue to destination utilizing the VOR. Approaching their destination they received CAS messages reflecting FMS and NAV buss problems. Upon recycling power to the FMC post landing the fault messages cleared. They wrote up the event in the logbook.

input: Company charts and notam's did not reflect an operational control tower/ground control/atis. We canceled instrument flight rules with miami center around 5;000 feet when we had the field in sight. I was making position reports on common traffic advisory frequency (common traffic advisory frequency) and was contacted by tower over common traffic advisory frequency with a frequency for tower. We were approximately 15 miles out and performing a left 360 for separation at the time. Tower ask us to report established on final. When we were back on final they cleared us to land. On short final i noticed that the rotating beacon was on. After landing and taxiing in; i discovered that the tower had been operational for the past two weeks. On flight after departing visual flight rules and getting back into automatic communications addressing & reporting system range we received the missing notice to airmen / of air missions for the first time; which reflected the information about the new tower and that the arff (aircraft rescue and firefighting) had been downgraded. At this time we realized that the fire department on the field may not have been able to handle the amount of passengers our aircraft is able to carry.lack of communication between the company and air traffic control previous [company] pilots not reporting changes over the past few weeks of flying into the airport.
output: First Officer reported not knowing the airport had an operational Control Tower until Tower Controller called the crew on CTAF and advised them of the correct frequency to be on.

input: The capt of flight xyz contacted dispatch at departure time requesting information about minimum equipment list fuel for minimum equipment list xx-yy. The logbook did not reflect minimum equipment list xx-yy as open minimum equipment list item. Capt replied it had been open minimum equipment list item for 2 previous flight legs. Dispatch contacted technician and confirmed the item was still on placard. The release and logbook showed no open mel's. Dispatch is requesting information on how open minimum equipment list items requiring dispatch action can be omitted from release and logbook.
output: AT DEP TIME THE CAPT NOTED NO EXTRA FUEL BOARDED FOR AN OPEN DEFERRED ITEM REQUIREMENT. DEFERRED ITEM WAS MISSING FROM THE MAINT RELEASE AND THE DISPATCH RELEASE.

input: Acft green hyds safety valve leaking hydraulic fluid from its pilot valve. I replaced pilot valve without a maintenance manual reference maintenance ferried aircraft to maintenance hub to do a full functional test of the safety valve (tooling nis). Maintenance ferry authority/authorized per duty mgr.
output: AN AIRBUS 319 HAD GREEN SYS HYD FLUID LEAKING FROM THE PILOT VALVE. PILOT VALVE WAS REPLACED WITH NO MAINT MANUAL REF.

input: The first officer made a routine takeoff from runway(s) 28r. Shortly after gear retraction an engine indicating and crew alerting system message 'antiskid' annunciated. Due to a high air traffic control and pending class ii workload environment we elected to defer analyzing the message until level at cruise altitude and established in class ii operations(s) we were unable to recall the message and there were no associated status messages. We did not look at cmc status. We decided to familiarize ourselves with the associated irregular procedure in the flight manual. The balance of the flight was routine. For the approach briefing we elected to set autobrake ii and land flaps 25 degrees as recommended in b747 flight manual standard operating procedure the air traffic control environment workload was high and the approach controller became distraction and forgot to give us a visual approach clearance to runway(s) 8r. I was able to finally effect an approach clearance this was only a distraction and did not preclude the first officer from executing a stabilized approach the weather conditions were typical with steady winds at approximately 060 degrees at 15 knot(s) there was no windshear rpted. Descending through 200 feet/foot above ground level the 'antiskid' engine indicating and crew alerting system message reappeared. The autobrake selector released to the disarm position there was no associated or additional autobrake engine indicating and crew alerting system message which i had expected to see. I then physically moved the autobrake selector to 'off' and advise the first officer to continue and land. I briefed that there would be no autobrakes and to use minimal manual braking which he acknowledged and did. Immediately; on touchdown; the tower advised that they observed a blown tire on our left/right (directions) main gear. We did not hear or feel any indications of a tire failure. The aircraft tracked and decelerated normally. We exited the runway(s) and observed the brake temperatures on the left/right (directions) main and body gear were acceptable; approximately 100/200 on an approximately 80 degree fahrenheit day and a landing weight of approximately 530.0 pounds the tower had already dispatched equipment before we could request it. The emergency crew confirmed to us that there was 1 tire (deflated) on the left/right (directions) main gear and no subsequent fire or smoke. We informed the station to have personnel stay clear the left/right (directions) main landing gear and to inform maintenance of the problem our assigned gate was approximately 100 yards straight ahead we elected to taxi the aircraft in to the gate. Flight attendants and passenber were unaware of any problem the entire sequence of events was 2 minute(s) from touchdown to gate arrival, arrive i debriefed the purser after the flight i briefed a maintenance technician and he informed that he had seen this before on the b747. The next day i talked to maintenance person and he confirmed that it was indeed an antiskid malfunction. All airport and station personnel involved in the incident did an excellent job.
output: B747 CREW REPORTS AN ANTI-SKID MALFUNCTION ON LANDING THAT CAUSES A SINGLE WHEEL TO LOCK UP AND CAUSE TIRE FAILURE.

input: I contacted midway clearance delivery on the ground and was given a full route clearance with routing that was 'cleared to cincinatti; lunken field via the midway four departure; lewke; gipper; gipper 97 degree radial; 36 vor and dme (co-located) fix; direct fort wayne...' i asked tower intermediate fix i could pull off to the side for a minute at the end of the runway to load the routing; which was approved. This is where the confusion started. I have received many clearances from midway airport that included the lukey intersection; second officer i was familiar with the spelling of that nearby intersection. In previous flights i have always been given direct destination before actually flying to lukey. As i punched lukey into the flight plan; it seemed a little odd to be headed south then east; but the whole routing seemed strange second officer i didn't really question it. After takeoff we were given heading 090; then direct lewke. I punched the navigate, navigation mode; which was set for lukey. As we turned toward the southeast; the other pilot questioned the heading to me. I asked departure for a heading while we straighten it all out; which the controller did. We found lewke on the chart; reset the flight plan; and the rest of the flight was uneventful. Our flight didn't really deviate from the assigned routing; it was just a moment of confusion. The pilot in the right seat had found lewke on the chart before takeoff; and even spelled it to me. But at that point i had already entered it incorrectly; and didn't notice that he spelled it differently than i had. This could have all been avoided by more careful study of the flight plan; but it didn't occur to me that there would be two lukey's in close proximity to midway. Lukey is 72 miles south-west of midway; and lewke is 31 miles east. In my opinion having two fixes that sound identical in the same area is setting the stage for confusion; which could be a safety issue in the busy airspace surrounding chicago.
output: A LR35 PILOT REPORTS DEPARTING MDW WITH A CLRNC THAT INCLUDED LEWKE INTXN. A SIMILAR SOUNDING NEARBY INTXN LUKEY WAS ENTERED IN THE FMS; AND THE FLIGHT EXPERIENCED A TRACK DEVIATION.

input: After establishing communication with the tug driver i released the brakes and was cleared to start engine 2. Roughly 4 seconds after beginning the engine start sequence; the tug driver requested we abort the engine start. I conducted the engine start abort memory items and then called for the checklist. After completing the checklist i asked what the reason for the abort was. The tug driver mentioned that the wrong 'plate' was attached to the tug and was too small for the q400. The tug driver didn't want us to have an engine spinning as they tried to correct the issue. I thanked the tug driver for making the right call and keeping our operation safe.i've noticed a large pressure across our system; at all levels of the operation; to turn planes as quick as possible to have no delays; and if we do have a delay then to start pointing fingers at whomever is to fault. After such a challenging season with our performance; i understand the push to get our operation back on track; but i think that pressure is being applied in the wrong places and safety is starting to be sacrificed for the zero delay metric. This tug driver noticed something was wrong and spoke up; potentially saving us from another safety event; but the plate being used should be verified before we get to that point. We can focus on hitting zero delay or we can focus on doing things right; usually one parameter will bow to the other. My recommendation would be to make safety the uncompromising priority again.
output: Q400 flight crew reported that the ground crew asked them to abort engine start due to an incorrect tow bar attached.

input: Due to inadequate sleep; i experienced fatigue related symptoms during my scheduled flight. Weather was below category i minimums; so i took control of the aircraft from the first officer and we set up for a clear air turbulence iii approach.during the first approach attempt; i had begun the descent too late; resulting in the aircraft not being properly configured prior to the final approach fix. We asked air traffic control for vectors so we could go around and try the approach again. On the second approach attempt; we had the aircraft configured appropriately prior to the final approach fix; but we failed to get the aiii arm message. We elected to perform another missed approach and discovered that the flight path angle was not properly set in the heads-up control panel. We were finally able to perform a successful clear air turbulence iii approach and land safely on the third approach attempt. I believe i operated the aircraft at a degraded level of safety due to a severe lack of sleep caused by long duty days; minimum rest two nights in a row; and the resulting upset of my natural circadian sleep cycle.the 'it is legal' attitude in scheduling is a tremendous safety hazard! I felt like i was simply expected to accept the assigned schedule. The recent letter from our chief pilot concerning excessive sick time usage made me fearful of using our fatigue policy or calling in sick from this trip until after a major safety issue had manifested itself! I'm not sure of [the chief pilot's] intent; but his letter caused a severe degradation of safety in my case.in retrospect; i should never have left the hotel that morning without getting more sleep. Day 2 of the 4 day trip was almost 13 hours on duty due to several maintenance issues; followed by a 9 hour overnight. We were also somewhat late on day 3 which resulted in a 9:35 hour overnight. I did not get to sleep until 0230 on the first day. Yet i was somehow supposed to fly my schedule later that day; then wake up at 0330 on the second day and be expected to fly safely!! I don't care if it was a 'bid packet trip' or not; this trip was 100% at risk of having a fatigue issue even if we ran on time. Inadequate staffing is running all pilots ragged. Improving trips will help; but there is a much bigger problem in that safety is taking second place to completing the flight at all costs.
output: An air carrier Captain related multiple missed approaches due to inappropriate configuration and/or approach stabilization while attempting a CATIII approach.  Believes the go arounds were the result of reduced personal performance resulting from fatigue inducing scheduling practices at his airline.

input: There is a continuing problem with loss of automated radar terminal systems tracking with ebound traffic flying at 4000 feet/foot 7000 feet/foot departing dfw or dal. The sma type aircraft are especially affected by this. During the morning departure rush this is especially hazardous because the automated radar terminal systems tracks stop and other tracks cover them up; making trying to find the primary target almost impossible. This situation is always brought up to supervisory personnel. They relay this to maintenance and there it dies; only to have to deal with it the next morning. I firmly believe this will cause loss of separation or worse a midair collision; because these aircraft are all at the same altitude with varying speeds this problem will not be fixed unless someone with more influence than a controller complains! Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: rptr states that the radar system was recently changed to an asr-9 and the previous no radar problem has been fixed.
output: CTLR CLAIMS THAT CERTAIN TYPES OF SMA'S WILL DROP TRACK AT LOW ALTS EBOUND.

input: Approximately 11-13 miles on downwind; approach cleared us to follow aircraft abeam us for the visual. We turned base at 4000 feet/foot in heading mode; approach said to 'make room for traffic following as well as departing on runway.' a little confusing (non-standard); but no issue. I took it off autopilot and hand flew while still looking for traffic. Overshot the final as a result and the darkness. We maintained 4000 feet/foot until we got back on runway c/l. Glideslope was out of service on automatic terminal information service so we were backing up visual with rnav/papi and fix page. We started down on runway(s) c/l while configuring. Got the 'too low terrain' caution. I briefly strained to look outside while leveling with power. Couldn't make out terrain; and immediately called for a go-around. We told tower the reason for the go-around. They cleared us to 3000 feet/foot we couldn't figure out the reason for the ground proximity warning system but briefed the extra precaution we would take on the next approach. Again we turned right base and remained at last assigned 3000 feet/foot (msa 3100 ft) till assured on c/l. First officer backed me up that we were inside the vor and dme (co-located) to start down. I looked at the visual approach slope indicator showing all white. We configured and i told him i would stay a one red/three white and high as a precaution. We got a partial call briefly and again we ensured visually that we were safe. We both continued on the high side but stable at 1000 feet/foot and landing checklist complete. On landing we debriefed everything; still unable to find the reason for the caution. This runway should not be made 'visual' approach at night time. The terrain on final could easily get a caution ground proximity warning system warning. Strict step-down procedure is required.
output: B737 flight crew experienced a GPWS terrain warning during a night visual approach to Runway 28R at PIT and goes around. On the second approach more care was taken to remain on profile and a second GPWS warning was annunciated while showing three white over one red on the PAPI. The approach was continued to landing.

input: We were scheduled to deadhead. After the flight was completely boarded and ready for departure the captain asked over the p.a. That everyone deplane due to a current tornado warning in the area. As we were waiting in the terminal everyone's phones received another tornado warning. This time it was accompanied with 2 additional messages asking people to call 911 for life threatening emergencies only. After the agent started boarding the aircraft for the second time everyone's phones received another tornado warning. The agent stopped boarding and disappeared down the jetway for several minutes. Once back he said everything was ok and continued to board. Since my phone showed the warning lasting for 30 more minutes i decided to dig a little bit deeper. The warning stated that thunderstorms nearby have the possibility to cause tornadoes. The radar showed rotation and zzz was in the predicted path for 30 minutes. Take cover now! Yet we couldn't because we were on the aircraft. Prior to boarding the second time many people were commenting on the fact that faa.gov showed that zzz was closed for weather. Also; if one were to log onto the company portal; there was a message on the bottom of the homepage stating that zzz has suspended operations until tomorrow. After seeing this message i tried to call operations manager for clarification but was unable to get through and my voicemail was not returned. Against my better judgement i decided to get on the plane at the end of the boarding process. Just prior to departure we received our final tornado alert stating that zzz was in fact in the path of a possible tornado for an additional 30 minutes. I was later told that all arrivals and departures were halted with the exception of aircraft that had received special permission.as of now; of the 11 flights scheduled to fly to zzz1 today only 2 took off. I was not operating this flight so i cannot say for sure; but it did seem like airport operations was pushing for these special authorized flights to go. After looking at weather and the tornado reports; all i could do was tighten my seat belt and pray for the best. This time it ended up working out. However; it could have easily been a very different outcome.
output: Air carrier deadheading First Officer reported that flights were canceled due to tornadoes reported in the area.

input: Flight departing sent an automatic communications addressing & reporting system saying they needed their weight and balance. I contacted loads and the reply was the now have their closeout. 20 or so minutes later the ca (captain) called to say that tower told them not to leave; without any explanation. I said; 'everything looks good on the closeout so if you're happy i'm happy.' [the captain] called back and then said that  ops had called and told air traffic control to not let them depart. I tried contacting ramp; turn coordinator; and finally the gate planner answered. He said that ramp had physically loaded ballast in the wrong compartment and the flight would need to come back so that it could be moved to the correct position. I asked him why he did not advise ca (via radio) or myself (via phone call). I told him that contacting air traffic control for the purpose of delaying a flight is not operations concern or responsibility. Ramp loaded physical ballast in the wrong compartment; but said they put it in the right compartment when closing out; and then; with most likely best of intentions infringed on operational control by contacting air traffic control operations in any facet outside the scope of pilot/dispatcher must contact either or and not act outside their responsibilities. Simply telling the pilot they need to come back without information why; and not telling the dispatcher takes us outside confines of the regulations. If ops needs training on what operational control is defined by 14cfr part 121 then the company needs to provide it.
output: EMB-190 Captain and Dispatcher reported communication breakdown between them and Company ramp and operations personnel concerning the placement of cargo compartment ballast.

input: With oak approach 5000 feet/foot given; 270 degree heading for left/right (directions) downwind leg; deviated for weather between 270-290 degree heading noticed oak hills below while navigate, navigationing in and out of weather while in weather ground proximity warning system sounded' terrain; pull up; terrain; pull up.' first officer was keeping close eye on resolution advisory prior to encounter; due to our proximitypa we initiated toga power (a320); pitched up; cleared conflict at 5500 feet/foot airspd increased to 275 knot(s) no full recovery. Since we had arrs into runway(s) 19 into sfo area above and fully aware of terrain; resolution advisory went from 2400 feet/foot to 1800 at lowest when recovery began; and warnings concluded after approximately 5300 feet/foot after warnings; informed tower and proceeded to land runway(s) 11.
output: A320 CREW EXECUTED A GPWS ESCAPE MANEUVER WITH AN EMER MAX RATE CLB UNTIL THE WARNING STOPPED. ACFT WAS AT THE MVA AT THE TIME OF OCCURRENCE.

input: The flight management system was evidently not programmed correctly or it dropped out on departure when given the first fix; it was not in the flight management system as well as the next. Checked the history page and it was not there. By the time we got the first fix in the flight management system we had past it by a couple of mile when questioned by air traffic control we were given a heading second officer we could get the flight management system reprogrammed. No further incident noted.
output: CL65 FLT CREW FAIL TO PROGRAM DEP INTO FMS. MINOR TRACK DEV RESULTS.

input: Upon arrival, arrive at the airport we noted a ground fog condition which i estimated visibility to be approximately 1/2 to 1/4 mile after flight planning and arrival, arrive at the aircraft i checkeded the commercial charts and determined that austin; transmitter takeoff capability was 600/600/600 runway visual range on the most capable runway(s) (actually runway(s) 17l). At that time i noticed 2 aircraft (b737's) taxiing to takeoff on runway(s) 17r. We were subsequently given taxi instructions to runway(s) 17r. At this time i was thinking that runway(s) 17r must be the most capable runway(s) and it didn't dawn on me that i had looked at the chart for the wrong runway(s) (rwy 17l). When switching to tower they advised 1200 feet/foot runway visual range touchdown and 1400 feet/foot runway visual range mid-point. I was thinking -- no problem the runway(s) capability has 600/600/600 runway visual range capability. We were then given takeoff clearance and upon lining up i noticed that there were no ctrline lights but that there were full runway(s) markings visible. I also noted that i could see runway(s) 8 edge lights and it looked to be 1600 feet/foot runway visual range my mind then assumed that for the 1200 feet/foot runway visual range rpted that the runway(s) markings must be an adequate substitute for the ctrline lights (which they are not) but that the prevailing visibility would allow for a legal and safe takeoff second officer the takeoff was continued uneventfully. As we continued down the runway(s) the visibility improved even further to 10+ lights (rwy edge). After takeoff i heard another air carrier state to the tower that he needed 1600 feet/foot runway visual range for takeoff at cruise i had another look at the takeoff page and noticed that i had in fact looked at the wrong chart; for runway(s) 17l; and that 1600 feet/foot runway visual range was required for takeoff on runway(s) 17r. I felt that we in fact had 1600 feet/foot runway visual range even though it was not rpted as such by the tower i feel that this was an error compounded by the fact that other aircraft were using the same runway(s) for takeoff (they may have had better visibility than when we arrived at the takeoff pos); which lulled me into a sense of security in my assessment of the situation i will take more time to read the takeoff pages in future sits.
output: CAPT OF A B727 TOOK OFF WHEN THE WX WAS RPTED BELOW TKOF MINIMUMS FOR THE RWY USED.

input: The first officer and i arrived late at our aircraft due to late arrival on previous aircraft and changing aircraft and gates. While in the middle of our preflight procedures our load closeout came up on the automatic communications addressing & reporting system (xa:47 for a xa:55 push). This was a surprise to us since we hadn't even had time to send in our fuel yet!after calling operations to ask if we didn't have to send in our fuel load any longer they said we still did but they would check why we received our closeout and also asked us for our fuel quantity at this time. This is a clear violation. We are always asked for our fuel quantity prior to getting load closeout if it has not been sent. The correct load closeout was sent a few minutes later showing the correct fuel.this event occurred because most people are concerned with on time departures and not safety! Since we were late someone took it upon themselves to make up the fuel quantity and then send it to us! After receiving the false load closeout information i told operations we would be pushing late and not to try to push us into closing the door to show an on time departure. We would close the door when we had finished our duties on the flight deck. We closed the door only 4 minutes late!the need to show and close the door on time or earlier precludes all safety to the flight and as a captain i am seeing this culture being driven from the top on down! Slow down!!!! Stop trying to push the plane 10 minutes early and think about safety; not on time departures.
