We immediately informed tower on 126.7 we had crossed the runway(s) 12r hold short line. Tower asked us to verify we were clear of the runway(s) 12r threshold. We did and we were. Msp tower 126.7 landed a company dc9 and b727 with our aircraft positioned beyond the runway(s) 12r hold short line. We were then cleared for departure at xa11z.
output: ON TAXI OUT; MSP RETRACTED A POS AND HOLD CLRNC WITH A HOLD SHORT TO A DC9 FLC. AFTER NOTIFICATION OF NOSEWHEEL OVER HOLD SHORT LINE; FLC ADVISED CLR OF THRESHOLD; ALLOWING 2 ADDITIONAL LNDGS.

input: We were enroute at fl360; deviating around thunderstorms and in light turbulence at about .76 mach when number two engine exceeded normal limits in n1 vibration. Our limits are 5.0 and the engine lower display electronic centralized aircraft monitoring was flashing at 6.0. Over the next five minutes the vibration number increased to a high of 8.3 and noticable vibration was felt throughout the airplane and controls. No other adverse indications from any other engine indications. We referred to the flight manual and contacted maintenance through dispatch. As the captain tried to communicate problem to maintenance we reduced the bad engine power to idle. I coordinated a slow descent with air traffic control since we could not hold altitude with one engine at idle. The n1 vibration at idle initially indicated 3.5 which was below the 5.0 limit. We decided it best to keep the engine at idle. We did try one increase and the vibration increased again. We did not try again. After discussions with dispatch and maintenance we made the decision to divert to the closest suitable airport. We made an uneventful descent and landing using the good engine and keeping the vibrating one in idle. I did note the n1 vibration was almost zero once we were with approach and at about 10;000 feet. After landing we shut the engine down as soon as we cleared the runway. Our checklist in the flight manual provided very little guidance. It did direct us to land at the nearest suitable airport and that's the only statement that really provided any useful guidance in this situation. It should be also noted that our maintenance did not have access to engine data while we were airborne as is provided by other modern aircraft. This resulted in us having to spend time to accurately report the condition of the engine to maintenance. I think zzz logistically would have been a better divert airfield but would not have met our requirement to land at the nearest suitable airfield.
output: An A320 flight crew diverted to the nearest suitable airport when the vibration level of the right engine suddenly increased beyond limits.

input: A b737 called up on the shead7 departure climbing to 7;000. The departure itself states to climb to fl190 with clearly stated restrictions along the way. The first restriction being roppr at 7;000; approaching mddog the b737 asked for higher and i said negative expect higher in 8-9 miles because he should have crossed mddog at 9;000. Once i saw he was still at 7;000 i climbed him to 11;000 to get him climbing above the minimum vector altitude which is 10;000 and keep him below the inbound traffic descending to 12;000 and gave him a traffic alert. I informed the pilot via the departure he should have been climbing to fl190 via the departure and he stated he was issued 7;000 and no higher. Recommendation; since the new procedures of climbing all aircraft to fl190 on departure with restrictions has been implemented a couple months ago many pilots have made this mistake. Many different altitudes have been stated on departure. An effort needs to be made on the controllers and pilots part to get a uniform altitude report on initial call up.
output: L30 Controller and commercial flight crew voiced concern regarding continued confusion reference the altitude assignments and crossing restrictions on several LAS RNAV SIDs.

input: I was working all locals combined and i launched the second aircraft a bit too close. I ended up having to give the 2nd guy a couple of turns to get 3 miles. As soon as i had it i shipped them both. The first guy didn't take the switch and then the 2nd guy sped up a little about 10 knots and the terminal radar approach control facility controller wasn't able to talk to the first guy and i'm pretty sure we lost the 3. It was all around a bad call on my part and i should have just waited on the second guy or run him out on a different heading for longer or stopped his climb or anything like that.in my defense; i was working all locals combined which i'm not super proficient with because while we were on covid schedules. I will also note the following:1. I was working lcw combined with other locals which is supposedly not safe per the district because we can't see the runway.2. No ot used and we are operating with 3 cpcs and an flm when normal numbers are 8 and an flm due to quarantine from a covid positive. 3. The atm will not use tmi [traffic management initiative] for staffing because of political pressure not because it isn't needed. Tmi for staffing have been definitely needed especially this week with 15 ish controllers out of 25 on quarantine.
output: Tower Controller working 3 Local positions reported an airborne conflict between two departures.

input: It had been a cold day for texas; and i'd already canceled my first lesson for frost that had frozen on the planes overnight. Our school's deicing equipment consists of moving planes in/out of a heated hangar and/or waiting for the sun to melt any ice. While waiting at the flight school for my next lesson to start; i'd started working on homework. I'd gotten a standard weather briefing prior to the start of my first lesson; and didn't think much of the weather as the show-time for my next lesson approached. The email from flight service station specialist for the standard briefing. I spent more time than anticipated working on the school work; and barely finished the assignment i'd been doing right before my lesson time. The student and i had been trying to get in a review flight (unsuccessfully -- weather cancels) for an upcoming stage check several times. We had walked through the brief for the flight a number of times prior; so i rushed the preflight discussion and summed it up to something like 'we're going to do what we'd planned last time.'the student went to the plane to start the preflight; and i followed after using the restroom. I did not double-check the weather prior to walking to the plane. The briefing i'd received earlier that day had an airmet zulu time (utc/gmt) for higher altitudes; with a forecasted end time that aligned with my scheduled departure time for that lesson. This was obviously my first mistake. Upon return to the airport; i checked awc and found several key indicators that would have warned me of the conditions i was about to subject myself and the student to. I am confident in saying i would not have flown had i updated my initial brief. This was my first huge mistake and lapse in judgment. Once in the plane; we begin to experience some light drizzle. My student opted to turn on the pitot heat. I checked the outside air temperature and we were about 5 degrees celsius. As we climbed; the temperature stayed about the same. We climbed to 3500 ft.; leveled off; and i noted the temperature to be a few degrees above freezing. We were still getting the drizzle. I asked my student to descend back down to 3000 ft. In an attempt to get to warmer temperatures. Once we did so; the temperature was right at/above freezing instead; so we climbed back up to 3500 ft. At this point; i had started to monitor the automatic weather observing/reporting system of nearby airports (pez/cvb); in an attempt to find somewhere to work outside of the precipitation. Both airports were reporting drizzle and near-freezing temperatures. Around this same time; i heard another one of our training aircraft on frequency call san antonio approach and state they were returning to the airport. I told my student that we needed to do the same thing. We had pitot heat; cabin heat; and carburetor heat on; but at this point; we had acquired a decent amount of rime ice on the windshield. I could not see any on ice the wings but was worried that we might have a trace amount. We asked to return to stinson; were shortly directed to switch to the tower; and instructed to enter left downwind for runway 14. I let my student enter the pattern; then took the controls. I made a no flap landing with a target approach speed of 70 kts. I came in much faster though (about 80) and ended up high on final. I opted to forward slip the airplane down with the extra speed; then floated about 1/2 down the runway bleeding it all off in the flare. We landed without incident and turned off at the end of the runway. After clearing the runway; tower asked if we had encountered icing. I answered that we had in the practice area; and gave them a report on the drizzle and temperatures at various altitudes. There was no further communication between the tower and us during the taxi to park/shutdown. After stepping out of the plane; i immediately checked the wings and elevator. I did not see any ice; but at this point; most of what had built up on the windshield had already melted. I took responsibility for my error and explained to my student why i did what i did during the approach/landing. I did not fly for the remainder of the day; although conditions improved sufficiently.
output: C172 Instructor reported multiple errors precipitated by not thoroughly considering the weather prior to flight; then encountering icing conditions during flight.

input: Descending from flight level 300 to flight level 270. Voice/aural 'airspeed low' warning; accompanied by indicated air speed disagree and altitude disagree cautions. Captain airspeed tape shot down to approx. 170 knots indicated airspeed captain altitude indication climbed rapidly; autopilot commenced nose down pitch and auto throttles increased to gain airspeed. Autopilot/autothrottles disconnected; crosscheck with flight path vector; aoa indication and standby instruments quickly confirmed cautions. [advised atc]; qrc procedure and follow-up quick reference handbook procedure performed; cleared by air traffic control to descend and proceed direct zzz. Captain gave aircraft to first officer once stable and insured all procedures completed and correct. First officer indications returned to normal much more quickly (passing approximately fl210. Captain indications returned to normal more slowly; but were correct approaching approx. 15;000 [feet]. Entire evolution took place in solid instrument meteorological conditions with all pitot heat and engine anti-ice switches in correct places and appearing to be functioning normally. Opted to remain [a priority] aircraft due to uncertainty of actual malfunction; and because of intermittently poor ceiling/visibility conditions at zzz. Uneventful descent/approach/landing in zzz. Logbook write-up completed; avionics tech personally debriefed post flight in zzz. Suspect some form of pitot tube ice up or blockage; despite pitot heat on and appearing to be functioning. Ice crystals maybe? Just an unlucky combination of outside air temperature moisture content; winds aloft; etc?
output: B737-800 pilot reported encountering erroneous inflight airspeed indications; possibly due to ice contamination of the pitot-static system.

input: Aircraft x was ready to push out of gate xx; leaving zzz going to zzz1. Departure equipment check includes checking the towbar to ensure it is fully connected to aircraft airbus 320.push driver; entered the pushtractor and instructed wingwalker to remove the nose landing gear chalks. Push driver started the pushtractor and engine roar and everything turned on. As the push driver scanned; the runway and neighboring gates for push clearance; he communicated to flight deck 'ready for push out and break release.'flight deck responded 'stand by'. Push driver stood by; monitoring his area and his equipment and informed his wingwalkers to stand by for push. Seconds later; flight deck called 'ready for push' and push driver replied 'copy that. Pushing out' push driver flashed his wingwalkers with his headlights and told them 'pushing out' push driver set the pushtractor to gear 'f3' and waited for the equipment to roll forward. Push driver gently tapped on the gas to gain movement with the aircraft. Pushtractor and aircraft moved synchronously and sluggishly. Push driver pressed on the gas a little harder to gain more momentum but all of a sudden; the pushtractor acted up and jumped and the towbar followed the jump. During that jump; push driver was shocked but readied himself for a possible breakaway. Push driver let go of the gas to stop the pushtractor's misbehavior; but seconds later; towbar gave way. Push driver immediately pressed on the break while watching the plane breakaway slowly. With quick reflex; push driver contacted the flight deck; yelling 'breakaway! Breakaway! Breakaway!' before the communication cable was about to break off. Communication cable stretched but never broke off and flight deck'replied brake set' everything was stopped and supervisor who was watching the dispatch came to inspect everything. Push driver set the brake and turned off the pushtractor. Dispatcher came out to inspect the damage with supervisors and others who saw the breakaway. Towbar had several bolts break off and the part where the towbar connects to the nose landing gear got bent but the latch that locks in the plane remained in the lock position. After supervisor did their investigative duty; i was instructed to move the pushtractor out of the way for the plane to return to the gate. Another dispatch guided the plane to the correct stop mark so that maintenance can inspect the damage on the nose landing gear. Maintenance informed us that the towbar connection piece was damaged and so the plane had to go out of service. Plane was offloaded and a new plane was used for aircraft x.
output: Pushout Driver reported the tow bar pins broke and the tow bar damaged the aircraft's nose gear.

input: Someone needs to look into our air carrier deeply before someone gets hurt. This is a serious safety issue.
output: An Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) describes a maintenance work environment where overhauls are not accomplished; engine failures not reported; incorrect fuel used; aircraft discrepancies not written-up; all combined with a fear of retribution.

input: This is an automation issue. Both of these aircraft tagged up on the wrong scope. They tagged up on an 'e' tag which is radar departure east (high sector) instead of a 'd' tag which is satellite disney (low sector). The clearance delivery specialist check and modified both aircraft to the 'd' tab list but they both still tagged up on the wrong scope. Low level aircraft automating to the wrong scope has been an ongoing issue for many years at mco and has been on the backs of the controller workforce to fix. Fix the automation so aircraft tag up on the correct scope.
output: F11 Controller reports of an automation problem with aircraft tagging up on the wrong scopes; even after clearance delivery modified both aircraft to the correct tab list.

input: Flt from boston logan to new york laguardia was cleared for takeoff on runway(s) 22r. At approximately 95 knot(s) the f/o observed an aircraft enter runway(s) 22r about 1500-2000' ahead. The captain applied firewall thrust (full forward limit of throttle travel) and steered slightly right as it appeared that the other aircraft was slightly left of the centerline. The computer vfr military training routes was 125 knot(s) but the f/o initiated an early rotation at about 110 knot(s) to avoid hitting the other aircraft the aircraft became airborne at about 120 knot(s) after striking both the tail skid and #2 engine lower reverser housing on the runway(s) about 2-3 seconds after liftoff; the stick shaker activated for several seconds--pitch was around 25 degree and the airspeed was 120 knot(s) once clear of the aircraft on the runway(s) the nose was lowered to accelerate and the gear was retracted. Climb to a visual downwind was initiated and an immediate landing was accomplished. No contact occurred between the two aircraft and the vertical miss distance was estimated at 20'. The aircraft that entered the runway(s) in front of us was y airlines flight--smt. Apparently the tower cleared this flight into position to hold; thinking that they were in line behind us for tkof--when they actually had requested an intersection takeoff from taxiway tango. Two factors contributed to this extremely close call. First; and of primary importance; was the failure of the tower controller to notice the request for an intersection departure mixed in with the heavy flow of normal traffic departing at the time. This may be as much a design flaw in the traffic control system being used as it was pure human error on the part of the controller second; the crew of flight y failed to adequately check the runway(s) for traffic before entering it. We were less than 2000' away with all lights on and still were not noticed. Supplemental information from acn 98222: a few seconds later the f/o called out an aircraft crossing the runway(s) the aircraft appeared to be about 1500' ahead of us as we accelerated down the runway(s) i called for firewall thrust and shoved the throttles full forward at the same time. At approximately 110 knot(s) i called rotate and at that same time the f/o began the rotation. Vfr military training routes should have been 123 knot(s) for our weight of 143; 000 pounds we were now almost upon the smt. The f/o made a rapid rotation to 20 degree nose up and the aircraft leapt into the air. The rotation continued to about 23 degree nose up and the airspeed began to decrease followed by the stick shaker which lasted only two to three seconds as the f/o had already initiated recovery action. At about the same time the flight engineer said; 'ok guys; fly the acft' which lowered my fright level from a high 5 to about a 2. We raised the landing gear and tower advised us to turn to a heading of 140. I replied 'turning to 140 to return and land due to severe overboost of our engines avoiding an aircraft on the rwy.' the tower had cleared aircraft to cross the takeoff runway(s) prior to our takeoff clearance but i never heard the tower clear the smt to position and hold on runway(s) 22r. I will now pay a lot more attention to the call signs of the aircraft just ahead of me and just behind me in line for takeoff i think my ears are conditioned to hear instructions passed with my call sign and with total disregard for instructions passed for other aircraft in this case; however; i don't think it would have clicked that the aircraft was at the midfield intersection. Perhaps another case for full length takeoffs for all aircraft lights at night. Several months ago i read a letter to the editor in a magazine about turning off your landing lights while on the runway(s) until takeoff clearance is received. By waiting to turn on those big illuminators until one has received takeoff clearance a very bright and valuable non-verbal signal is sent to anyone approaching that runway(s) that you are underway. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: all parties involved have talked to each other. Tower supervisor reported that incident was caused when air traffic control tower local missed the notation on the flight progress slip passed from the ground controller that the smt was making takeoff from down field intersection and cleared the smt into position and hold under the impression the smt was behind the lgt at runway(s) end. Pilot flying of smt knew lgt was going onto runway(s) but had missed takeoff clearance and thought lgt was to position and hold and would be taking off behind the smt. Smt also thought lgt landing lights on just because he was maneuvering onto runway(s) otherwise would not have taken runway(s) without clarification regards lgt intentions. Supplemental information from acn 99066: our aircraft was cleared into position and hold 22r at tango intersection. An lgt was cleared for takeoff from 22r full length. The pilot of the lgt pulled up abruptly dragging the lgt tail skid for 200'. The number two engines' exhaust fairing dragged for another 100'. The drag marks from the number two engines exhaust ended 100' from tango intersection where our aircraft was sitting in position. The pilot of the lgt veered right and climbed at an excessive angle of attack to avoid hitting our aircraft the local controller assumed our aircraft was waiting for takeoff clearance from the full length of 22r not from the tango intersection. The controller did not realize that he cleared our aircraft into position and hold front of the departing lgt.
output: GND CONFLICT CRITICAL. ACR-LGT TKOF OVER ACR-SMT IN POSITION AT MIDFIELD.

input: The inflt crew of 15 flight attendants knew at briefing that the jumpseat at door 5l was inoperable. No provision was made by crew desk to save a passenber seat for flight attendant position #10; as instructed in the operations(s) manual. The purser agreed with crew desk. The reasons behind this decision were the minimum crew complement for the b747-400 is 8 flight attendants; second officer position #10 at 5l could be ignored in this case; and that company could use the revenue; as the economy section was planned to be full. Position #7 at door 5r was assigned as required by the operations(s) manual but position #10 was left open; and the now 'extra' flight attendant was assigned position #17 at 3r inboard.
output: B747-400 CABIN CREW RPTS THAT DOOR 5L IS NOT MANNED PROPERLY.

input: The wdb was deviating north around thunderstorms prior to the incident. Wdb had turned south and was descending to 6000'. Traffic was called at 12 o'clock and 4 mile opposite direction; type and altitude unknown. Wdb pilot reported the traffic was a twin (acft a) and that aircraft a took evasive action.
output: ACFT A SAW WDB AND MADE A TURN TO AVOID CONFLICT.

input: While approaching ewr on the philbo3 from the south at 6;000 at the metropolitan intersection; ny controller gave us an instruction to fly present heading. I responded to that call as it was our call sign. My first officer was pilot flying and followed the instructions as he heard it too.about two minutes later; the controller asked what procedure we were flying and what our routing was. I informed him of the present heading that he gave us. He said something to the effect that he meant another flight. We were following aircraft y. Our call sign was aircraft x. He then gave us several other vectors and handed us off to another frequency. Nothing else was said about this confusion of aircraft; as it was on the controller and not us.
output: Air carrier Captain reported a track deviation on the PHILBO3 arrival to EWR as the result of ATC Controller confusing similar call signs and issuing clearance to the wrong aircraft.

input: Final approach phase of landing at the point of gear extension; capt extended gear; followed by loud bang. Gear fell; nose failed to lock down. Able to recycle gear same consequences. This was confirmed by a gear horn flaps 30 degrees and the failure of nose gear light to illuminate. Request go around indicated to tower (dtw) we needed to dump. They (atc) gave us a left/right (directions) turn (lndg runway(s) 21r); climb to 3100 feet/foot we were then given 5000 feet/foot for dump altitude followed all company emergency procedures and chklist. Third attempt to extend with down and lock was successful. Emergency vehicles were standing by. Landing was uneventful. Possible frozen landing gear; -20 degrees i realized during descent into dtw.
output: THE NOSE LNDG GEAR OF AN LGT FAILED TO EXTEND IN THE LOCKED DOWN POS DURING FINAL APCH UNTIL AFTER THE LNDG GEAR EXTENSION WAS CYCLED FOR A THIRD TIME AFTER A GAR.

input: While climbing through fl230 heading ne approximately 75 nautical mile ne las; left/right (directions) oil pressure low annunciator illuminated associated with a master caution light. First officer was pilot flying and retained control of the aircraft while the capt analyzed the problem left/right (directions) engine oil qty was 17 quarts on previous flight and during initial climb oil qty now at 16 qts. Left/right (directions) oil temperature generally 15 degrees cooler than left/right (directions) oil temperature on previous flight left/right (directions) oil temperature remained normal. Left/right (directions) oil pressure now at 35 psi. Advised zla and leveled at fl250. Reduced left/right (directions) engine power to flight idle. Utilized oil pressure low quick reference handbook chklist. Left/right (directions) oil pressure stabilized at 32 psi. Oil qty very slowly dropping. With reduction in left/right (directions) engine fuel flow; left/right (directions) oil temperature initially rose to 120 degrees but reduced and stabilized at 80 degrees as expected. Requested vector to las runway(s) 25l. Runway(s) selection based on wider runway(s) in consideration of crosswind component. Advised #1 flight attendant of problem and that we were diverting to las. Estimated time to land at approximately 15 minute(s) elected to keep left/right (directions) engine operating at flight idle due to high landing weight and high density altitude discussed parameters for shutting down engine should oil qty drop significantly or oil temperature increase and continued to monitor engine indications for duration of flight made cabin public address announcement advising passenber of problem and decision to return to las. Contacted dispatch via commercial radio. Communicationss were broken due to frequency coverage in area and aircraft altitude advised dispatch of problem and decision to return to las. Dispatch advised that the computer was unable to generate numbers from our position due to projected overwt landing advised dispatch that i was exercising capt's authority/authorized in not continuing with the release amendment process due to workload as we were entering into las approach airspace approximately 40 nautical mile from las. Advised dispatch of fuel onboard and las estimated time of arrival transitioned control of aircraft to capt for landing at approximately 35 nautical mile from las. Reviewed single engine landing procedures since left/right (directions) engine was operated at flight idle. Discussed potential for partial use of left/right (directions) engine power should a go around be necessary. Normal visual landing las runway(s) 25l utilizing instrument landing system guidance flaps 28 degrees exited runway(s) and shutdown left/right (directions) engine oil qty now at 6 quarts. Landing weight was 131000 pounds (3000 pounds over mglw). Smooth landing noted with descent rate less than 360 feet per minute (6fps). Oil noted on left/right (directions) engine nacelle during postflt inspection.
output: MD81 FLTCREW HAS LOW OIL PRESSURE INDICATION ON R ENG AND ELECTS TO DIVERT TO LAS.

input: While being vectored for a visual approach; we were cleared to follow a falcon three miles outside of the final approach fix we established visual contact with the falcon and when spacing looked good we turned on base. I asked for flaps 15. Immediately after selecting flaps 15 the stabilizer miscompare and hydraulic press on annunciators illuminated.the hydraulic press on checklist calls for the hydraulic control circuit breaker to be pulled; but [it] must then be reset prior to approach; we elected not to touch it since we were on approach already and we did not want to worsen the situation or compromise other hydraulic sub-systems. The landing gear was extended using normal procedures; and the before landing checks were completed.we then ran the stabilizer miscompare checklist which states: - intermediate fix landing 1. Flaps: check in desired position; 2. Use normal procedures; 3. Touch and go landings prohibited; procedure complete. So we did; we continued using normal procedures. At about 200 feet/foot and approximately 120 knots indicated airspeed the horizontal stabilizer started to move to its originally commanded position; causing the airplane to pitch up smoothly but unexpectedly. It felt like a runaway trim initially; but we realized what was happening after we noticed the stabilizer miscompare annunciator extinguish. The aircraft was under positive control at all times and it only required a relatively small change of power; a higher than normal forward pressure on the controls; and a pitch trim adjustment to maintain the desired flight path.
output: A C560XL flight crew overcame STAB MISCOMPARE and HYD PRESS ON annunciations and landed safely.

input: As we descended through 24;300 feet/foot for fl200; center stated; 'there is moderate turbulence in your 12 o'clock position from 240 down to 210.' i turned the seatbelt sign on immediately and at the same time stated; 'flight attendants be seated immediately. We need everyone seated now.' the word immediately had just left my mouth when we hit severe clear air turbulence. Our altitude was 240 and it was less than 10 seconds from warning until encounter. We climbed back up to 24;300 feet/foot with no improvement; however; that allowed our airspeed to decrease from mach .72 (280 knots) down to .67 mach (245 knots). At the lower speed; we continued the descent to fl200. The severe intensity continued down to fl200 with no relief. We requested to keep descending and found relief below fl200. I checked on the flight attendants and was told of possible passenger and flight attendant injury. We told air traffic control about the severe turbulence encounter seconds after it started. We soon after told air traffic control that we had 'possible flight attendant and passenger injuries.' we were asked by air traffic control if we were declaring an emergency. I said; 'yes; we are; due to precaution after severe turbulence and possible injuries onboard.' air traffic control asked if we needed assistance for aircraft or passengers. I responded; 'aircraft controls and systems all appear normal; so no aircraft assistance needed on ground; however; we do need paramedics for possible injuries in the cabin.' on final approach to runway 27r; in instrument meteorological conditions snow; ice and weather at minimums; the controller advised us that braking reported 'nil' by aircraft in front of us. We executed a go-around and shot the approach for 27l with fair to poor braking. Very slow taxi to gate due to ice on taxiways. Passengers and flight attendant were bumped around pretty badly in the cabin; however; no passengers were injured other than one man who hit the floor a couple times in aft galley. After the flight; he told me he was okay and felt good. Then he added; but i don't know how i will feel tomorrow. One flight attendant was cleared by paramedics; but wanted to go to hospital for x-rays of her arm. All tests and x-rays normal and she was released with no injuries. The passengers and crew were extremely lucky with this outcome. The flight attendants did an excellent job.as far as flight deviations; our airspeed was plus and minus 60 knots and our altitude was plus and minus 300 feet/foot to 400 feet/foot we also deviated off course slightly left due to coming off lnav/vnav. This turbulence occurred in beautiful weather with a cloud layer below us about 10;000 feet/foot or more.the biggest problem in this entire event; in my opinion; is the late heads up from the controller about moderate turbulence. By receiving this alert at the time of the encounter; due to being at the exact altitude being warned about; no one onboard had any time to prepare. That was information of extreme importance.
output: Minor to moderate injuries were reported by flight attendants and a passenger when their B737 encountered 'severe' turbulence during descent for landing.

input: Arrived over ia5 at xx15. Clear everywhere except thin cloud layer over east end of airport descended to investigate. Top of layer at 1200 feet/foot above ground level since approach to runway(s) 7 was clear i decided i could legally land. Unfortunately; due to hills in the approach area i ended up too high to land on final; second officer i elected to go around i thought i could do this without entering the cloud layer; but was unable to avoid going instrument meteorological conditions on the go around for a few moments (15-20 seconds). Landed uneventfully on second attempt. Although a technical violation occurred; the decision to land was made after careful thought and evaluation of the circumstances (ie; this was not careless or reckless). The alternative was to circle for some time waiting for cloud layer to burn off or go elsewhere to land. Under the same circumstances i'd probably do it again; being more careful to avoid the thin cloud layer on the gar.
output: RPTR PLT WAS TOO HIGH ON INITIAL APCH AND DID A GAR; BUT ENTERED CLOUDS IN THE GAR. AND; RPTR HAD NO FLT PLAN. RPTR SAYS THAT ALTHOUGH IT WAS A TECHNICAL VIOLATION. HE CONSIDERED HIS ACTION CORRECT.

input: We were given instructions to taxi via taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) to y12 for runway(s) 30 at iad. While traveling down taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) we noticed an aircraft to our left/right (directions) that appeared to be departing in front of us. It was actually a maintenance aircraft and not in line for takeoff to get behind this aircraft the capt taxied into a large holding area instead of continuing down taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) this part of the taxiway is very confusing because there are no marks on the commercial chart page showing the track of taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) through this area. Dfw has a similar area near runway(s) 17r; but the commercial chart actually shows taxi lines unlike the chart for iad. This situation could be greatly improved by providing more detail on either the taxiway or the commercial chart page. This entire area is a huge piece of concrete and the markings are not very clear especially at night.
output: ACR FLT CREW BECOMES CONFUSED DURING TAXI TO RWY 30 VIA TXWY Z AND TXWY Y11 WHILE PASSING THROUGH HOLDING BLOCK.

input: While operating under part 91; we were being vectored for the instrument landing system runway(s) 27r at ord. Simultaneous instrument landing system approachs were being conducted to runway(s) 27l and runway(s) 27r. Chicago approach issued us a clearance to descend to 4000 feet/foot mean sea level my first officer was the pilot flying and i was performing pilot not flying duties. The first officer was not utilizing the autoplt at the time of this event. During the descent i asked the first officer to briefly arrest the descent second officer that the indicated airspd would decay enough to facilitate flap deployment of 20 degrees at the time of my request; our altimeter indicated 4200 feet/foot mean sea level very shortly thereafter; we were given an intercept heading for the localizer i replied to the clearance and reset the heading bug to the intercept heading a few moments later; we received another radio call from the controller questioning our altitude at that point; i looked up and our altimeter indicated 5000 feet/foot mean sea level i then looked at the altitude alerter; and it indicated 4000 feet/foot i realized that we were 1000 feet/foot high; and i replied to the controller that 'we are level at 5000 feet/foot i'm not sure why we stopped the dscnt.' the controller replied with some urgency; 'it appears that you have been climbing i have traffic at 5000 feet/foot i need you at 4000 feet/foot now.' i immediately retarded the power levers and applied forward pressure to the control yoke while simultaneously verbally directing the first officer to descend i then remembered that we had been at 4200 feet/foot only a few seconds earlier. I realized at that point that the pilot flying instead of resuming the descent to 4000 feet/foot had actually climbed back to 5000 feet/foot mean sea level moments after beginning the descent the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii provided a basic traffic advisory alert at an altitude of approximately 4500 feet/foot an aural alert of 'tfc' was heard. There was no resolution advisory issued by our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii nor was there an audio warning to descend the instrument approach was continued. My lack of supervision over the pf's altitude control was a contributing factor. My desire to reduce our airspd and subsequently deploy 20 degrees of flaps was premature; and could have waited until the pilot flying had stabilized the descent my pilot not flying duties of replying to the intercept clearance and setting the heading bug contributed to a reduced performance of my supervisory duties. A lack of experience in ord's extremely high density traffic environment was a contributing factor to the lack of situational awareness for both pilots the pilot flying had never flown into ord; and although i have limited experience at high density airports prior to this day i had very little intermediate fix no experience at ord while simultaneous approachs were being conducted to parallel runway(s) the use of the autoplt during this event could have played a significant role in decreasing our workload and could have prevented our reduction in situational awareness.
output: NON COMPLIANCE WITH ALT CLRNC; ALT UNDERSHOT BY THE CREW OF A LEAR 45 ON APCH TO ORD; IL.

input: Everything was normal until on climb out we were struck by lightning while flying through a small rain shower. None of the crew; myself included; thought the rain shower posed any threat to the aircraft and we were all surprised when it happened. Of the 4 main display panels 3 of them went blank. We leveled off at 6000 feet and evaluated the situation. I was the second international relief officer so from my seat i couldn't see the one remaining panel very well. I was told later that the panel had not auto switched into a combined mode and the captain had to manually switch to inbd du in order to restore his attitude display. We looked at the checklists that were presented and there was none about restoring a lost display. I looked through my ipad to see if the manual had a checklist for a lost display and couldn't find one. The captain had us use the loss of all displays checklist to see if that would be of some use since it was the closest we could find. That checklist had us reset the left/right (directions) ccr which caused a loss of the lower display unit for around 40 seconds and did not restore the left display panels. At that point the decision was made to return. We climbed to 9000 feet and i was tasked with running the fuel jettison checklist with the captain. The 'fuel to remain' was blank so we watched it manually and turned it off at the correct time. The rest of the flight was uneventful. Surprisingly the aircraft even showed land 3 on final approach as if nothing was wrong. Crew worked exceptionally well together.
output: First Officer reports being struck by lightning during initial climb; resulting in three of the four main display panels going blank. Attempts to restore the lost panels are not successful and the flight returns to the departure airport after dumping fuel.

input: We cleared runway(s) 19l in las at taxiway westbound ground directed us to taxi via taxiway d; taxiway g to the ramp. On taxiway d; we followed the lighted signage onto what i thought to be taxiway g. It was lighted with green ctrline and blue edge lights and was open. It was also at what appeared to be the reverse 45 degree angle on our 10-9 page. However; it was not taxiway g; it was taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) -- a taxiway not on our 10-9's as of this date. I called ground and told them where we were; on taxiway zulu time (utc/gmt) heading back towards taxiway westbound ground said no problem and directed us to taxi straight ahead; go left/right (directions) on taxiway westbound and contact ramp control as i turned left/right (directions) (e) on taxiway westbound we dialed in ramp control i was proceeding slowly (less than 10 kts) on taxiway westbound toward taxiway g and spot x. The ramp control frequency was very busy and it took us time to break in for instructions. In the meantime; i was proceeding. I saw another carrier aircraft under tow to the north of spot x by an estimated 300 feet/foot and i also saw a dc9/md80 type aircraft to our left/right (directions) about 2000 feet/foot away on taxiway g pointed nw towards us but not really moving. As intermediate fix they were waiting to move through taxiway g. I was just westbound of spot x. Ramp's first transmission to us was 'yelling' 'company number; you should have held short of taxiway g!' i stopped us smoothly at spot x about 200 feet/foot from the other carrier under tow and still about 2000 feet/foot from the dc9 type. Now no one was moving and i was blocking taxiway g and did not have clearance into the ramp. Ramp then told us to continue and gave them our 'numbers.' i then queried him as to what exactly he meant by our 'numbers;' our call sign; our flight number; a phone number; what? I gave him our call sign and gate assignment and he cleared us to the gate. I called ramp control and talked to them about the event. I thought the ground control had coordinated with ramp and we were going through spot x to the gate. This was not the case; i guess they do not talk. The ramp controller i spoke to said aircraft coming from where we were usually hold short of taxiway g on taxiway westbound the fact that we had just come off of a taxiway that is not on any maps and that ground was handling both runway(s) 25 and runway(s) 19 arrs complicated this situation ground never gave us hold short instructions and passed us to ramp while we were still out of ramp's domain. I did disagree with his accusation that i just 'cut off the dc9' as we operated safely through everyone. I assumed that since no one was moving; they were waiting for us to move through spot x; second officer they could too. My assumption was a factor here also. To prevent recurrence; i will operate even more cautiously around transition areas between las ground and ramp control and not assume that they are coordinating actions. Up-to-date 10-9's are not always possible; but this new taxiway we discovered at las needs to be on the missed approach point and included in the signage on the gnd.
output: B737-700. THE FAA ATCT GND CTLR AND THE COMPANY RAMP CTLR HAD NO INTERFAC COORD WITH ACFT GOING TO THE GATE.

input: Upon departure of runway(s) 23 at lsgg; climbing on the konil 2 juliett standard instrument departure air traffic control informed flight crew of terrain in vicinity of position questioned intermediate fix terrain was in sight; and issued a climb to 7000 feet/foot initial flight conditions were intermittent instrument meteorological conditions at time of air traffic control question of whether terrain was in sight; with a negative response from the flight crew. Immediately following the negative response; terrain became visible. Flight crew did not inform air traffic control of visual contact with visible terrain. At no time did ground proximity warning system indicate conflicting terrain or threat. Air traffic control issued a command to climb to 7000 feet/foot to avoid terrain which was performed at a maximum rate of climb air traffic control advised the flight crew that the maximum speed for the konil 2 juliett standard instrument departure was 190 knots indicated airspeed with a bank of 25 degrees the aircraft flight management system was programmed to follow the konil 2 juliett standard instrument departure which included the 190 knots indicated airspeed speed restrict, restricted, restriction and bank angle. The aircraft was being manually flown with guidance from the flight director and flight management system lateral navigation source. Autothrottles were utilized and operating properly. Contributing factors: 1) encountering a tailwind during the initial climb and turn pushed the aircraft outside of the protected region of the standard instrument departure 2) moderate to severe turbulence during the initial climb and turn limited climb rate and bank angle. Future flight crew actions: 1) strict adherence to standard instrument departure departure instructions with increased awareness of contributing factors such as a tailwind component which would modify the normal flight path. Supplemental information from acn 698515: closer attention should have been monitored to actual flight path of the aircraft with respect to strong wind conditions.
output: A GV DEPARTING LSGG RECEIVED A TERRAIN ALERT FROM THE DEP CTLR. CREW CLBED THE ACFT TO SAFE ALT.

input: Was told to hold short of runway(s) 6-24; but was not sure that was the instructions given by the tower the movement area was snow-covered and not plowed. It might have been impossible to stop before crossing 6-24 because of the 3' of snow on the taxiway but; what it boiled down to was a miscom between the crew members themselves and the control tower (if unsure which runway(s) we should hold short of; we should have asked the tower again. And intermediate fix we were unable to stop because of snow or ice; we should notify the tower of that before xing.)
output: FLT CREW OF CPR JET ACFT TAXIED ACROSS ACTIVE RWY WITHOUT AUTH.

input: The weather was clear with calm wind in lebanon; nh. While briefing the arrival; i elected to choose lateral navigation global positioning system to runway 7 because of the surrounding mountainous terrain and night time. During the descent; air traffic control offered the visual which i declined and i continued with flying the full approach. While inside the final approach fix at akhom; the pilot not flying asked me to offset visually from the approach in order to line up with the runway. I replied that i will remain on the lateral navigation approach until short final because of the elevated terrain on the north side.i then realized that he was looking at downtown lebanon which was very bright and had two crossing main boulevards that looked like runways with yellow light. Then the lebanon airport appeared at 12:30; very faint with red edge light. The bottom line of this incident; if i had listened to the pilot not flying by leaving the approach path and lining up with a city boulevard at night; it could have caused a missed approach or even worse.two points to remember: 1) never accept a visual approach on a mountainous or unusual airport at night; and 2) request and follow the full approach until minimums; and then positively identify the runway in sight before switching to visual cues.
output: CE750 First Officer reports being cleared for the RNAV RWY 7 at LEB during night VMC. Inside AKHOM the Captain asks the pilot flying (PF) to offset from the approach to line up with the runway and the PF declines due to terrain. Upon descending further it is determined that what appeared to be the airport is actually the lights of downtown Lebanon.

input: 1 hour 30 minute(s) into a 2 hour 15 minute(s) flight the #1 engine low oil pressure light illuminated. The oil pressure gauge on the flight engineer's panel confirmed the low oil pressure. Since the oil pressure was below limits i completed the phase #1 items and shut down the engine the first officer and engineer completed the appropriate chklists for the engine failure. I notified the senior flight attendant and had the cabin prepared for an emergency landing air traffic control was notified after chklists completed. We were being vectored to pxt for the arrival, arrive to ewr. We continued on to ewr and landed with no further complications. Upon inspection; mechs found the engine required 17 quarts of oil to fill it. I called our maintenance control and found out the #1 engine was on an 'oil watch.' this was not in the logbook. I debriefed the flight engineer and found the following facts: 1) the incoming crew advised him they put 2 quarts of oil in the #1 engine 2) they did not mention any write-ups and none were in the book. The following day after investigating the incident i found the following facts: 1) #1 and #2 oil quantity indicators inoperative (status not in log). They would test when checkeded but gave false full indication. 2) inbound crew knew oil level was low but did not brief my crew. They have false impression #1 oil was topped by the 2 quarts of oil they added. 3) maintenance control did not advise flcs of 'oil watch' status of engine company pilots appear afraid to put proper write-ups in logbook. Had proper log entries been put in logbook this would not have happened. Crew communications was very poor between inbound/outbound crew. They knew oil was low and failed to inform my crew. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the aircraft was as b727-200 with p&w jt8d engs and before departure 2 quarts of oil were added to #1 engine and later the rptr found out it needed 10 quarts but only 2 quarts were available in the pit oil supply. The rptr said the #1 and #2 engine oil quantity indicators were inoperative and no logbook or deferred item placards were present. The rptr said in 1 hour and 30 minute(s) this engine used 8 quarts of oil and when checkeded at termination needed 17 quarts to fill a 16 quart tank. The rptr said the oil consumption was 5.33 quarts per hour which puts this engine way beyond the manufacturer's maximum limits of 2 quarts per hour the rptr stated the maintenance controller was advised and rpted the engine was on an 'oil watch' for high oil consumption but no external leaks were found in previous checkeds the rptr stated there was no logbook write-ups or oil added numbers in the logbook and that the crew was not advised of the oil quantity indicators being inoperative the rptr stated most crews seem to go along with this idea of no logbook write-ups which can cause delays and schedule interruptions but the practice is now out of hand. The rptr stated this company has displayed a lack of understanding and utter disregard for aircraft maintenance procedures the rptr requested and was given the federal aviation administration 'hotline' phone number as the rptr's only remedy to alter or correct the maintenance sit.
output: A B727-200 IN CRUISE AT FL290 DECLARED AN EMER AND SHUT DOWN #1 ENG DUE TO LOSS OF OIL PRESSURE AND LOW OIL PRESSURE WARNING LIGHT ILLUMINATED CAUSED BY A HIGH OIL CONSUMPTION ENG.

input: Pushback onto active taxiway were cleared to push from the gate at jfk onto taxi lane. This was passed to the push crew and acknowledged. During engine start; push crew moved the aircraft onto active taxiway a. We did not realize the mistake until too late to get the crew to stop or call jfk ground jfk ground was notified and said they would contact company. We contacted ramp to relay the error to company. Were informed company would debrief the push crew.
output: B767 CREW HAD TXWY INCURSION WHEN THE PUSHBACK CREW PUSHED ACFT ONTO AN ACTIVE TXWY AT JFK.

input: While flying the quabn3 standard terminal arrival route air traffic control gave us a hold at ondec intersection (intersection on the quabn3 bos star) due to the fact that a snow plow had gotten stuck on the runway in bos during the snow removal process. When we left the hold; air traffic control cleared us direct to urowt and the quabn3; and we continued on to bos. Nothing happened during the flight; no far's or sop's were broken; and no speed or altitudes were busted. The flight was uneventful.however; my issue is with the name of the urowt intersection and possible hear back/read back issues. When spoken; this intersection; urowt; can be also be heard as 'your route'; as in cleared direct xyz; the rest of your route is unchanged.....instead of urowt; (spoken as 'your out).....particularly with a boston controller's accent. So; urowt and your route; are very similar; in fact; so similar that it could create hear back/read back issues. Since neither ondec nor urowt were not on our original flight plan; we did have a little misunderstanding between pilots as to the air traffic control clearance. However; we did rectify the situation and the flight continued uneventfully to boston. Therefore; to prevent any hear back/read back errors; may i suggest that the name of this intersection; urowt; be changed to prevent any possible hear back/read back errors.
output: B757 First Officer reports being cleared direct to UROWT on the QUABN3 arrival to BOS which causes confusion in the cockpit due to the way UROWT is pronounced by the ZBW Controller (your route) and believes it should be changed.

input: On final approach to runway 20 at icl there are grain bins in the flight path with the red obstacle [light] burned out. I have requested for weeks that it be fixed; but has not as of today. On a night landing training flight; student was making adjustment for a wind change and drifted too close to the bins because he could not see them without the red light. I as the instructor had to take immediate action to avoid collision with them when i noticed that the wind had drifted us too close to them. I will continue to request that the light be fixed and have students fly an above glide slope on runway 20 in the future.
output: Flight instructor reported the aircraft flew close to an obstacle at night that did not have a red obstacle warning light during approach to ICL airport.

input: Crossed sli at 4000 feet/foot vectors to visual 19r at sna. New heading 090 degree 'field in sight' and cleared for a 'visual 19r.' moderate radio congestion. To complete chklist; first officer left communications #1. I continued descent to clear clouds (broken layer at 3300 ft) above. Then spotted an sma at 1 o'clock at 1/4 nautical mile traveling north at 3000 feet/foot sma maintain course and altitude i pushed nose down to clear under by 150 feet/foot ask coast intermediate fix they saw traffic response was 'just coming up now. Was over radar site which has a 2 nautical mile radius blind spot!' called coast by phone from sna and rpted near midair collision was informed that the radar site was 5 nautical mile north of my pos! As i recall; there were 2 controllers working the frequency at the time. Was 1 a trainee? With all the computer ability at terminal radar approach control facility why can't a different radar site (el toro?) cover that small (6 square mi) area above the sli radar site and eliminate the blind spot in what has to be the densest traffic area around! Copy of this rpt to company and alpa to request review of radar tape.
output: CLOSE PROX COMMUTER-LTT GA-SMA NEAR SLI VOR.

input: On takeoff; right engine developed compressor stall at rotation. Takeoff continued normally and aircraft air returned to zzz with an overweight landing.
output: A B767 right engine developed a compressor stall at rotation but continued to operate normally; so the flight returned to the departure airport for an overweight landing.

input: At den tower we have a continuing procedure problem with area navigation departures. The area navigation procedures off of parallel runways will actually turn aircraft into each other. Management has implemented local procedures to try and mitigate the risk. But time and time again; the mitigations do not work. The newest mitigation procedure is to add the phrase 'for traffic' when issuing a heading to a pilot expecting to depart on the area navigation  which is what i did and it is still not enough to jar the pilot into not flying the area navigation procedure that will fly them into another airplane. I instructed aircraft x; 'for traffic; fly heading 335; rwy34l cleared for takeoff.'  i also instructed aircraft y 'rnav to nuggs; rwy34r; cleared for takeoff.'  aircraft x engaged the area navigation to fly to caazz; which turned him close to aircraft y. I don't know how close they got; but i estimate between 1.5-2.5 miles laterally. I cannot remember how close they got in altitude. Later when aircraft x called the tower; the pilot said he was thinking area navigation all the way. This pilot is not the first and won't be the last to fly the area navigation procedure when issued a heading. They have an expectation bias and even the extra phrase 'for traffic' will never ensure they fly the assigned heading rather than the area navigation procedure. After listening to the tapes; i found that i did not ensure a readback of the heading assigned as our local procedure requires. The pilot only readback rwy34l cleared for takeoff. This is another mitigation required here at den due to the flawed area navigation procedures. The area navigation procedures must be fixed.the area navigation departure procedures at den must be stopped in their current form. We have had very very close calls of aircraft almost hitting each other due to the design of the area navigation procedure. Den tower has been trying to work with den terminal radar approach control facility on an interim vectors off the ground procedures until metroplex can redesign the departure area navigation procedures into vectors off the ground. Both are taking too long to fix. It seems to me that terminal radar approach control facility considers this a den tower problem and is unwilling to work with tower in any way. This is a huge safety issue that everyone needs to work towards eliminating. No more mitigations. Stop area navigation departures at den. Don't let two airplanes collide for the agency to make the necessary change. Do it now. Pull all the previous incident reports. This has happened before and will continue to happen.
output: DEN Tower Controller describes a situation relating to RNAV departure procedures that have aircraft turning into each other.

input: I was working 4 positions combined; arrival east; arrival west; boeing arrivals sector; and pae sector. I had 4 frequencies with aircraft checking in and blocking each other. Because i was working multiple sectors i was zoomed out much farther than normal to see all the airspace; so about a 80 mile range. Therefore it was difficult to see all the vfrs; and there were a lot of vfrs out. My scope was cluttered with visual flight rules targets that no one was talking to. I was vectoring aircraft x for a visual approach into rnt. I was also working multiple other aircraft and trying to look up an identifier for a destination. After i cleared aircraft x; he was straight in to runway(s) 15. I saw a visual flight rules aircraft at 2;000 feet to aircraft x 10:00 3 miles converging. I called traffic; he didn't see him. He got closer. I called it again; he didn't see him. Now i couldn't turn left and cancel his clearance because that's where the visual flight rules was. If i were to try to turn right; i would hit a higher minimum vector altitude (minimum vectoring altitude) and have to climb into finals airspace where aircraft are descending into sea; which would involve breaking out sea arrivals and getting a point out which i didn't have time for. I can't remember if i called traffic two or three times; but the last time aircraft x saw him and responded to an resolution advisory unfortunately i didn't see him earlier as data tags were overlapping; although i don't know if i could have avoided the aircraft anyway; as i am not talking to him and have no idea what he's doing. Rnt airport; sea airport; and bfi airport are all within 3 miles of each other; surrounded by mvas so there's not a lot of wiggle room. We have to push the rnt and bfi aircraft down really low below the bravo airspace to stay out of sea finals way; and this forces aircraft to be tangled up with vfrs. After this; the supervisor split sectors into a high/ low configuration which was better and allowed to see vfrs easier. The best solution to these ifr/vfr traffic alert and collision avoidance system ra's which occur daily here is to somehow have protected airspace around bfi and rnt. Either class celsius or lower the bravo to 2;000 feet. After this i split and worked only bfi and pae sectors and i had another traffic alert and collision avoidance system with an ifr/vfr  even though the instrument flight rules was delay vectored and altitude stopped 500 feet above. There's too much visual flight rules traffic within that area that we aren't talking to and that makes things very dangerous; especially since a lot of them are at instrument flight rules altitudes. The workload becomes intense because you are staring so hard at vfrs; trying to anticipate what they are going to do; and it takes your focus off of your other traffic.
output: A TRACON Controller reported a conflict with an aircraft they were vectoring for an approach and an unidentified VFR aircraft in airspace that routinely has situations such as this occur.

input: On jun/xa/99 i was flying to xxx in anderson for a static display. En route altitude was 600 feet/foot above ground level 1400 feet/foot mean sea level prior to arrival, arrive at location; descended to approximately 300-400 feet/foot above ground level over parking lot; turned left/right (directions) then immediate left/right (directions) when coplt advised landing zone was in sight. A high reconnaissance was performed at 300-400 feet/foot above ground level while in orbit. I descended to approximately 200 feet/foot to perform low reconnaissance and do a final checked for wires or other obstructions in the landing zone. Sheriff's office personnel on the ground had cleared landing zone and helicopter in all phases of flight was greater than 500 feet/foot from any person on the ground when turning base to final; coplt called 'wires.' i took evasive action by turning hard left/right (directions) and climbing once out of situation coplt was speaking of same wires i had visual contact with. A normal stabilized approach was completed after an additional orbit. During landing we were at least 100-150 yards away from any person on the ground upon landing we were informed of complaint being filed. Coplt and i had misunderstanding of wires; that i felt required evasive action. Since the area to my left/right (directions) i knew to be clear i turned left/right (directions) no damage was sustained. Better intercockpit communications will be implemented.
output: FLC OF A GOV HELI APCHING; SURVEYING FOR WIRES AND LNDG AT A SHOPPING MALL FOR PUBLIC STATIC DISPLAY; RECEIVED A PUBLIC CITIZEN COMPLAINT FOR LOW FLYING. LCL LAW ENFORCEMENT OFFICERS WERE ON THE GND FOR CROWD CTL.

input: Due to our heavy weight we requested authorization to use runway(s) 14l at ord. We taxied to the 14l hold short line as instructed by the tower and then held our position as instructed. We remained in our position holding short for about 10-15 minutes awaiting takeoff clearance as we waited; we were instructed to prepare for an immediate departure as the tower was trying to build a slot. We acknowledged that we could accept an immediate takeoff tower then instructed us to continue holding short as they would be unable to get us a departure on 14l in a reasonable time. (acft were departing 14l and left/right (directions) 9l and r.) after a few minutes of waiting; tower called to inform us that takeoff sequencing would be better intermediate fix we used 14r instead. We told him we could accept 14r. He then said '...turn right and head for the scenic to hangar alley.' since we were holding position at the 14l hold short line; we could only turn right and head down the runway(s) 14l and exit to the runway(s) via the scenic in compliance with his instructions. We followed his directions and cleared final before starting our right turn onto 14l. Just as we exited the runway(s) onto the scenic we heard an aircraft going around. Supplemental information from acn 141235: we heard a pilot announce his intention of executing a go around. I believe that the tower operator; being primarily occupied with the 9 departures he lost track of our position at the hold line and assumed we were in the run-up pad. This due to the high departure and arrival, arrive workload.
output: ACR WDB UNAUTHORIZED RWY ENTRY AT ORD.

input: Clbing through 34000 feet/foot cabin altitude warning horn sounded. Cabin altitude indicated 10000 feet/foot followed qrc and quick reference handbook procedures and descended to 10000 feet/foot cabin altitude never exceeded 12000 feet/foot declared emergency for descent once level at 10000 feet/foot all system indicated normal. Terminated the emergency and made normal approach and landing in zzz. Passenber oxygen masks did not deploy. No passenber mentioned anything about the event while deplaning in zzz. Maintenance found popped aft cargo door seal on aft cargo door.
output: B737-400 FLT CREW HAS LOSS OF PRESSURIZATION; DECLARES EMER; AND DESCENDS.

input: The military is filing a flight plan from npa to the eagle a working area above pensacola terminal radar approach control facility airspace. This flight plan does not automate to zjx; who owns eagle a (eag-a) area. Also; there are no written air traffic control procedures governing ingress or egress from this area. Second officer for each flight departing npa to eag-a; there are at least 2 lengthy phone calls generated between the pensacola terminal radar approach control facility controller and the zjx controller to xfer radar identify of; and coordination handling of each flight while these calls are occurring; all of the other traffic the controllers are working can be going to hell in a hand basket. This problem has been ongoing for months. I have advised pensacola terminal radar approach control facility management of this problem no less than 5 times. And nothing has been done.
output: A CTLR AT P31 TRACON STATES THAT EXCESSIVE COORD FOR MIL ACFT ENTERING AND DEPARTING RESTR AIRSPACE WITH ZJX ARTCC INCREASES CTLR WORKLOAD AND RECOMMENDS THAT HDOF PROCS BE ESTABLISHED BTWN THE 2 FACILITIES.

input: After taking off we retracted the landing gear and noticed the 'gear door open' light was still on. After consulting the quick reference handbook we continued the flight to our destination at the required reduced airspeed of .70 mach or 300 knots indicated airspeed approaching destination; center asked us to maintain a speed of .76 mach. After telling center that we were unable; we realized that we had failed to notify center of our [qrh required] reduced airspeed. During approach; we were anticipating the gear door light to extinguish upon gear extension. However; when we put the gear down the door light remained on. We declared an emergency and did a missed approach. While holding we talked with dispatch; ramp and maintenance and briefed the flight attendants and passengers. After reducing fuel and accomplishing checklists; we requested the runway which maximized the headwind component and gust factors (220@18g26).on base leg; we were told to follow a b747 for a visual approach. After contemplating the ramifications of this request; i told approach control we were heading directly to the runway. Due to the vectoring; our fuel was at its optimum amount. However; when asked to follow the b747; our fuel would have been much lower; wake turbulence was a definite factor and the most prudent decision was to head directly to the runway thus making the b747 land on a different runway. Upon landing; the gear doors were hanging down (procedure calls for this) and dragging on the runway. Arff equipment was on the scene and verified all was okay. Company maintenance arrived secured the doors and we taxied to the gate.
output: When their landing gear doors failed to retract after takeoff the flight crew of an MD82 elected to continue to ORD at reduced mach per their QRH procedure. When the doors failed to close as they had expected after gear extension for landing they performed a missed approach; declared an emergency and landed with the doors open and dragging on the runway.

input: As capt on flight en route from kansas city international airport to charlotte; nc; the senior f/a notified me of a lady passenber with a lot of bleeding and cramping. Luckily there was a medical doctor on board. After the doctor examined her the f/a advised me she was in serious condition and was probably having a miscarriage. The doctor said she needed emergency care. We notified memphis air route traffic control center and squawked 7700 on transponder we were given priority handling into nashville; tn. I landed straight in on runway(s) 13 and turned off midfield. I could see flts taxiing out of taxiway t1 for runway(s) 20r. Second officer as to give right hand traffic flow and expedite ramp arrival, arrive i headed for taxiway t2 and nashville ground control cleared me to turn into taxiway t2. After clearing t2 and entering the ramp i was blocked adjacent the concourse by an air carrier mlg. I then pulled off to the left/right (directions) second officer he could taxi on by and open up the taxiway for us. For a while he would not move his lgt. I finally told him to move his lgt that we had an emergency problem and he was in the way. The lgt replied back that we were in our own way and overly excited about the problem i told him i pulled off to the left/right (directions) second officer he could continue to taxi and we could then taxi into our gate. After he moved on i parked at the gate and emergency medical service was there to help the lady. I was surprised that after all the good air traffic control handling that there would be any problem on the ground what type of coordination does federal aviation administration ground control have with company controled ramps in a case like this? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information advised the rptr no coordination between ramp control and the ground control is made; one controls one area and the other his. Feels this should be looked into when an emergency is in progress. Is much concerned since his company is deactivating the loading stairs on he aircraft account of high maintenance costs. Feels the slides are not the best way to get people off in an emer.
output: DIVERT BNA; EMERGENCY DECLARED ACCOUNT ILL PASSENGER.

input: Miami center handed us off at joses intersection and we were told to contact port au prince center on 124.5. After several attempts we were told to descend from fl330 to fl290 and to fly a315 to ganiv intersection where we would expect to hold. After passing joses; we turned on all our exterior lights. Prior to entering the hold we made several more attempts to contact center to let them know we were fuel critical and would not be able to hold for more than one turn. Communication with center was very sporadic. At times we could hear talking to other aircraft with no response back and other aircraft trying to contact center with no response back which made it very difficult to keep track of where other aircraft were. We were able to talk to tower on 118.3 while in the hold to let them know we were fuel critical and requested a landing sequence. They told us there was an airplane on a six mile final and we could be next but they could not clear us to descend. After several more attempts with center explaining our landing sequence and fuel situation they cleared us to fl240 and then told us to fly the pap vor and dme (co-located) after prompting them for a clearance after we reached the vor and dme (co-located) (which was only six miles away) we were told to fly the 108 degree radial and they would take us outbound for a descent. After the vor and dme (co-located) we were cleared to fl170 and soon after to fl150. At the time the flaps were up and the airspeed was 220 knot(s) at the start of the descent we received an resolution advisory with an indication to climb at a minimum rate of about 1900 feet/foot per minute. Prior to the resolution advisory there was never an indication of an aircraft in our location on the traffic alert and collision avoidance system and we never received a traffic advisory indication. We never had a visual on the aircraft. We initiated an immediate climb with maximum thrust and the airplane started to buffet. As the back pressure on the yoke was released the buffeting stopped and again we continued to increase our pitch attitude to comply with the resolution advisory the resolution advisory ceased after passing fl170 and we leveled off at fl180. We informed air traffic control of what happened; what our present altitude was and requested an immediate turn and clearance back to zma airspace. They cleared us to the vor and dme (co-located) and to fly the 340 degree radial outbound. Approaching the vor and dme (co-located) we received a traffic advisory alert indicating an aircraft 300 feet/foot below us approximately on the 340 radial. We did not turn and the aircraft passed off or right side; we never saw the actual aircraft. We informed center of the traffic advisory and were told now to fly the 012 radial without further instructions. After a few miles we requested a climb and a turn toward joses intersection. They told us later after the 35 vor and dme (co-located) fix we were cleared to joses and to climb to fl280. We contacted mia center prior to joses and got our clearance to our diversion airport and a climb to fl340 after joses.
output: A B737 crew reported a near miss with an unidentified aircraft as they approached MTPP in a night time non radar environment. The fuel critical flight diverted to a domestic airport.

input: Air carrier x on visual approach runway 26l. Helicopter y maneuvering near 4 mile final. Local control issued traffic to both and both said they had each other in sight. Air carrier x got a tcas/ra and went around. Then air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) was issued traffic about the helicopter y; and helicopter y was also issued the traffic of the air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) and to maintain visual. Air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) got an resolution advisory and went around. Air carrier westbound was then cleared for takeoff runway 26r (in due time for wake turbulence) and then local control canceled takeoff clearance and told to line up and wait. Local control had to say something and that is what came to mind; instead of continue holding in position. If the aircraft has the other in sight; why would they have to respond to an ra? Why do they not trust their eyes but listen to a computer? I would have liked the aircraft to either let us know that they lost contact with the helicopter or said that they never saw it.
output: ONT Controller described multiple TCAS RA events; resulting in two go arounds during police helicopter operations near the landing runway.

input: Right at v1 we got the le flap transit light. Rotation was initiated and we got the configuration warning horn and a stick shaker for five seconds. Flaps 1 was retracted on schedule. Looking at the light emitting diode annunciator showed all le devices in amber transit. The view from flight deck showed le devices extended both sides. Started reviewing quick reference handbook flaps; leading edge: le flaps transit. Aircraft was flown at 230 knots. Above 10;000'; we advised air traffic control of warning light and that no emergency was being declared. Called and asked operations for a patch to dispatch. Started talking to flight attendants; passengers; and company pilot riding in cabin; who told me le devices were extended. Went back to the quick reference handbook and now was talking to dispatch. Were going through about flight level 200 and heard pop sound. (later we found out it was le actuator #4 failing.)  dispatch got back to us and told us to go back to the departure airport for passenger consideration. We ask for vectors back. Called flight attendants and pilot in cabin for any more information. Pilot told me of hydraulic fluid flowing over wing. Hydraulic quantities were good. The plane was flying well. Advised passengers of return to the departure airport and estimated time of arrival. Went back to quick reference handbook  reviewed landing configuration and we talked about it; but now i had to get automatic terminal information service and landing performance information. Got all that out of the way but forget to execute it in fmc! On final visual xxl; flaps 15+5 not 15+15. Speed was in minimum maneuvering band. Still didn't realize our mistake. I went to the performance reference and selected flaps more than 1 less than 15 speeds and selected flaps 10 with max autobrake. Rest of approach and landing were uneventful. Checked brake cooling time of 30 minutes. At gate; met with maintenance and called chief pilot on call. Logbook writeup was made. Went on to next flight to our destination.
output: A B737-700 leading edge flap actuator failed at V1 so the takeoff continued. After trouble shooting; the flight returned to the departure airport where an incorrect V speed was flown; putting the aircraft in the min maneuver range.

input: We were leveled at 13000 feet/foot due to rpted traffic at 14000 feet/foot at about 10 o'clock position center asked the airline transport rating intermediate fix they had us in sight and could remain clear when they responded that they could; we were issued a climb clearance to fl230. We had the airline transport rating on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and visually acquired the airline transport rating as we started our climb shortly after starting climb with a good rate; we got an resolution advisory to descend since we could see that the airline transport rating was going to pass below and behind and they also were expecting us to climb we continued to climb i'm not sure intermediate fix center knew we would get an resolution advisory but it was disconcerting.
output: AN A320 CAPT RPTED THAT ZBW ISSUED A CLRNC TO CLB WHICH CAUSED AN RA WITH ANOTHER ACFT.

input: I was giving training at r-41. Sector 40 was open. We were working approximately 4 oak arrivals that were descending via the windsr (opd) arrival. I was looking up the arrival chart to discuss published speeds; phraseology options and techniques for assigning speeds. As i was discussing this with the developmental; aircraft x reported that they were responding to an resolution advisory we then saw the visual flight rules traffic and acknowledged the resolution advisory and issued the traffic advisory. The developmental advised the conflict alert had previously gone off but he evaluated and suppressed it. At the time the 1200 code was at approximately 7;000 feet and the aircraft x was descending from 21000 feet on the wndsr arrival. When aircraft x responded to the resolution advisory their altitude was approximately 16;000 feet and the visual flight rules target was approximately 15;000 feet descending.tcas ra's happen daily at sectors 40/41. There is a high volume of visual flight rules sightseeing traffic; visual flight rules flight training; skydiving aircraft; and many uncontrolled airports. I had an resolution advisory last year because i was busy issuing traffic advisories to a visual flight rules aircraft in conflict with an oak arrival. During this time a 1200 code departed dvo and climbed into a jet at 5000 feet between sgd and sts. My recommendation at that time was to create an alert area for the sonoma valley. Alert areas are clearly depicted on sectional charts and as a pilot and flight instructor i would definitely avoid flying through one; especially if i was not talking to air traffic control the 1200 code in this event was a [business jet].
