As we were descending to 1;500 feet; somewhere around 1;700 feet or so we got a ground proximity warning system 'terrain; pull up'. At that same time the approach controller came on and told us that the minimum vectoring altitude in that area was 2;000 feet; of which we had no idea; and that we should climb back up to 2;000 feet. I had already begun climbing as the captain was resetting 2;000 feet. As soon as i began initiating a climb the ground proximity warning system terrain warning went away. I leveled the aircraft off at 2;000 feet; for a total climb of approximately 300 feet. After we returned to 2;000 feet we continued with the visual approach to a normal landing on runway 22l without incident.
output: A320 flight crew reported triggering a terrain warning from the GPWS when they descended below MVA on a night visual approach to RWY 22L at EWR.

input: While flying southwest just east of the hpw vor and dme (co-located) at approximate 900 feet/foot the non-flying pilot noticed something red and immediately looked up to see a small tailwheel aircraft heading directly toward us. He immediately began a descent away from the other aircraft. The oncoming aircraft appeared to be at or below 1;000 feet/foot we estimate that we passed within 100 feet/foot of the other aircraft. I; the flying pilot; had been looking at something out the left window at the time. The aircrew person did not see the oncoming traffic. Approach had just terminated flight following with us and we had not yet contacted the next approach. The traffic had not been called to us by approach prior to discontinuing service. The oncoming aircraft took no evasive action. It would appear that he never saw us. This incident was discussed at length amongst all on board the aircraft in an effort to learn from the incident. None of us saw the aircraft coming. All on board the aircraft were engaged with the flight and discussing observations in the area at the time.
output: A pilot reported taking evasive action during a near miss with a single engine aircraft at 900 FT near HPW VOR.

input: The airline station manager placed passenber on the courier seats of the aircraft against company policy to facilitate an overbooked situation. I was only partially aware of the situation and did not give a great deal of concern due to the necessity of preparing for the next leg of the trip. I did not object based on my feeling that it was not inherently unsafe. (the courier seats are in the aft portion of the cargo area of the cargo convertable aircraft when the forward cabin has 2 pallet locations and the aft cabin has less than 8 seats. The courier seats are isolated by a bulkhead; but equipped with all normal emergency equipment and evacuate/evacuation routes are available. It is permissible for company employees to occupy the seats in all phases of flt.) i believed that any use of the courier seats by revenue passenber was a company policy that could be waived by appropriate mgrs. After the incident i was surprised to learn that my license could be revoked by the action and that it was against the far's. I ante meridiem not aware of any such regulation that is published. The courier seats are not within the cockpit nor is access to the cockpit permitted more easily from them. However; i will monitor the boarding of revenue passenber more carefully in the future. I will recommend a more suitable published policy on the subject.
output: FLT CREW IS CONCERNED ABOUT USING COURIER SEATS IN CARGO AREA FOR REVENUE PASSENGERS.

input: While being vectored by santa barbara approach for the instrument landing system runway(s) 07 our final vector was 'turn right to heading 040 descend to and maintain 2000 until established cleared for the apch'. This vector took us through the localizer to the north and the f/o who was flying the approach corrected to recapture the localizer once on the localizer we descended to minimum glide slope altitude of 1774 mean sea level it appeared the glide slope was alive and the landing gear was extended. I began the before landing checklist and then noticed that the glide slope indication was premature. While still outside the minimum glide slope altitude of 1774 mean sea level i elected to continue the before landing check. The controller called us and told us to check our altitude because he had gotten a low altitude warning showing the aircraft at 1300 mean sea level i responded that we showed 1500 mean sea level and that we were correcting. The controller asked intermediate fix we had the field in sight and i replied negative. Approximately 5 seconds later i told the controller that we did have the field in sight at which time he cleared us for the visual approach to runway(s) 07. No further incident and visual meteorological conditions conditions were maintained during the entire approach i believe that the poor final approach vector to the localizer was a contributing factor due to the fact that we had to recapture the localizer close to the minimum glide slope altitude at the same time that we were getting reestablished on the localizer we were configuring the aircraft for landing be extending gear; flaps; and performing the landing checklist. The late final approach vector added to the high workload and in my opinion was a contributing factor to the inadvertent loss of 274' of alt.
output: ACR LTT DESCENDED BELOW FAF ALT ACTIVATING MSAW.

input: Fo; flight attendant; and capt smelled acrid burning odor in cockpit emanating from overhead panel and possibly from gasper vents. Consulted with dispatch; declared an emergency at dispatch's urging; cabin alert given to flight attendants to review information in case situation worsened. Considered diversion to zzz; but it was shut down with thunderstorms and electrical outage. Continued to zzz1 and landed uneventfully. Per flight manual; crew donned oxygen masks. In the actual operations(s) this became very cumbersome and distracting to cockpit communicationss it was almost impossible to really understand what the other crew member was saying and air traffic control seemed to have a problem understanding us.
output: FLC DECLARED EMER DUE TO FUMES AND SMOKE.

input: During taxi out on ramp we attempted to follow ground controls instructions. However the taxiways have recently been renamed. Additionally the jepp 10-9 has the old info and 10-9b has the new taxiway info. Ground control appeared to be working off old taxiway info. Assigned us l1 exit. Captain stopped aircraft to verify exit and ground sent follow me [vehicle] out to assist turn back to new l2 (old l1).issue pilot alert message warning of jepp chart needs to be updated. Contact jepp to alert them of need for update.
output: B777 flight crew reported being unable to comply with taxi instructions at Rio De Janeiro Airport (SBGL) because the airport taxiway depiction; provided on the current Jeppesen charts; did not agree with the actual signage on the field. A 'follow me' vehicle was required to assist the crew with the taxi clearance.

input: I was the front line manager (flm) in the terminal radar approach control facility when this event happened. We were on a west flow; all radar positions were combined; which is our normal configuration; traffic was light until about five minutes prior to the event. I was at the desk in the back of the terminal radar approach control facility monitoring radar and going through web scheduler. As traffic picked up; i started paying more attention to what the radar controller had going on. I noticed aircraft x and aircraft y on parallel courses east of the field; both descending; aircraft y was south of aircraft x. Aircraft y was an instrument flight rules arrival to e98; a very small satellite airport that seldom has any instrument flight rules traffic.it appeared to me that the radar controller would have a difficult time swapping out the altitudes of these two aircraft as aircraft x could only descend to 9200 feet and aircraft y was descending to 10000 feet. It was obvious to me that the radar controller recognized the situation and would control it. Aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) was inbound to runway(s) 26 on the lzzrd area navigation standard terminal arrival route on a course that would cross with aircraft y. The floor of the standard terminal arrival route is 10000 feet; i ran the minimum lines on the scope and it showed aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) would have .45 miles of separation with aircraft y. I heard the radar controller clear aircraft x for the area navigation visual approach to runway(s) 26 and subsequently descend aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) to 9000 feet. I walked over to the radar scope and sat next to the controller and brought his attention to the converging courses.he stated he was concerned with aircraft x and aircraft y. Aircraft x made a sharp left turn to join the approach at tacoh. Although he had been cleared to 9200 feet; the altitude over tacoh is 10000 feet which put him in immediate conflict with aircraft y. I reminded the controller to issue traffic to both aircraft; hoping we would be able to establish visual separation; but neither had the other in sight.the radar controller turned aircraft y to a 180 heading in an attempt to maintain separation. This put aircraft y on a heading at 10000 feet into an area where the minimum vectoring altitude (mva) was 11300 feet. I reminded the controller about the minimum vector altitude the radar controller also turned aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) off the arrival toward the northwest; away from aircraft y. Subsequently; aircraft y was turned back to the west; but had already entered the area of higher terrain. None of the pilots reported a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory i was surprised that aircraft x made such a large left turn for the approach; i don't think either of us expected that. It would have been more prudent to leave aircraft y at 12000 feet or 11000 feet until aircraft x was below him as aircraft y was still 20 miles from his destination. I will be much more cautious in the future and display the approach track on the radar map so there is no question as to what the pilot is going to do.
output: ABQ TRACON Supervisor reported observing a Controller vector an aircraft away from conflicting traffic. The vector was insufficient to maintain separation and placed the aircraft in an area where it was below the Minimum Vectoring Altitude.

input: The flights were to adjust autorotation revolutions per minute i departed eastbound then asked for a climbing southeast heading to 2500 (class b 3000) where i would enter a power off 60kt glide (2000 fpm). This procedure was done 4 times (3 different aircraft) in less than an hour with each flight lasting 6 to 12 minutes. The airport has a split frequency most of the time with all helicopters and traffic north of the field on 134.6 and traffic south of the field on 118.9. The second flight was a different controller who asked me to contact approach above 2000ft for b airspace. I responded that b started at 3000 so declined to comply. On the forth flight on a east south east heading; on the helicopter frequency descending through 1500ft; a piper cherokee passed directly underneath (300 or less) westbound on the south frequency of 118.9. I inquired to the controller of the traffic who told me to switch to 118.9 for that info. Doing as directed i then had a lengthy discussion with the tower chief over the phone after landing. The piper may have had his vision blinded by the position of the sun. I do not believe he saw us. The n/helicopter controllers sometimes point out traffic to us helicopters when they are not busy with north traffic. I think the procedure should insist that helicopters operate on the south frequency whenever we are approaching or turning that direction especially when climbing above 500 ft. I calculate at my rate of descent i was about 10 to 15 seconds within impact.
output: Helicopter Pilot reported that while conducting maintenance checks of autorotation a NMAC with another aircraft occurred.

input: Metal ring of crew logbook came in contact with windshield heat electrical terminals. Logbook heated up and caused fumes in aircraft logbook was then removed from windshield and problem was corrected. Lesson: never put anything up on the dashboard near the windshield.
output: SMOKE FUMES IN COCKPIT AND CABIN.

input: We were following a 757 on the tynee2 into rsw. The 757 was approximately 12-15 miles in front of us. We were both given to cross ogger at fl270. We were given a max speed of 300 kts. We started our descent before the 757. As we were coming through fl280 we started to feel some light turbulence; then all of a sudden the plane banked hard to the right; i'm approximating at least 30 degrees. The autopilot kicked off and [the other pilot] grabbed the yoke and brought the aircraft back to level/descent flight. We leveled off at fl270; turned the autopilot back on & notified air traffic control of the wake turbulence.
output: Air carrier flight crew member reported encountering wake turbulence descending into RSW 12-15 miles in trail of a B757.

input: During the initial climb of the flight we experience 9 events of strong radio interference due to automatic communications addressing & reporting system transmissions/crosstalk. These events caused both discomfort due to the very loud volume of the interfering transmissions and difficulty in understanding air traffic control communication. We followed the temporary procedure issued recently by the company and switched the comm 3 radio from 'data' to 'voice' disabling automatic communications addressing & reporting system communications. Above fl180 we reactivated automatic communications addressing & reporting system communications and there was right away 2 more events of interference. During the last eight weeks many crews have been experiencing frequent events of radio interference due to automatic communications addressing & reporting system transmissions/crosstalk. These interference events should be a safety concern. They caused in more than one occasion to miss/misunderstand critical air traffic control communications and instructions during the departure phase of the flight. Last week the company has finally made available a temporary mitigation procedure but did not notify the pilot group about it. Some of the airplanes in our fleet do not have the comm 3 voice/data button which allow to disable the automatic communications addressing & reporting system system as recommended by the temporary procedure.root cause: something changed since december 2013. The interference could be caused by changes in the automatic communications addressing & reporting system communication software; protocols; procedures; equipment. Usually after weight off wheel both the flight management system and the engine indicating and crew alerting system show an 'acars no comm' message; shortly after that a very loud burst of digital communication is heard into the pilot headsets. In the worst cases the interfering signal is repeated multiple times during the first few minutes after takeoff. There should be an investigation of these events. Only last week; 8 weeks after the beginning of the interference problems the airline has finally provided pilots with a mitigation procedure for the interference problems. The procedure is not applicable on some of the airplanes in our fleet because they do not have a comm 3 voice/data button which allows to disable automatic communications addressing & reporting system system communications. It is also true that they never notified the pilots about the issue nor of the availability of the mitigation procedure.
output: CRJ900 First Officer reports strong VHF radio interference when the ACARS transmits data on VHF 3 after takeoff. Switching VHF3 to voice will stop the data transmission but not all aircraft have this switch.

input: Acft was being flown on a ferry flight to reposition the aircraft for the next day's flts. Only a crew of 2 were on board. The weather at jhw was rpted as 600' overcast 3/4 mile visibility in snow and blowing snow; wind 280/15 with gusts of 30 knot(s) runway(s) was snow and ice covered. The aircraft was landed on the centerline of runway(s) 25; aligned on runway(s) heading moments after t/d a wind gust from the right blew the aircraft to the left side of the runway(s) striking 2 runway(s) lights with the left propeller the aircraft was steered back onto the runway(s) and stopped. Due to the ice on the runway(s) the rapid deployment of right aileron could not stop the left-ward drift of the aircraft there was insufficient time to use differential pwr/reverse to try to correct the drifting. (i truly believe that due to the momentum; it only would have caused the aircraft to leave the runway(s) at a different angle.) the wind was blowing second officer hard that sand would probably not stay on the rwy! A better system to rpt runway(s) conditions and to allow the flight crew to better assess current conditions is needed. More importantly; ground crews need a method to assess conditions as well. Should the airport be closed?
output: RWY CONDITION ICE SNOW IN A NIGHT OPERATING CROSSWIND LNDG RESULTS IN PROPELLER STRIKE ON RWY LIGHTS AS LOSS OF ACFT CTL IS ENCOUNTERED.

input: Aircraft nxxx: right engine failure about 30 minutes away from zzz our destination.
output: A CRJ-700 air crew experienced an engine failure about 30 minutes away from their destination.

input: In april 2016 we were operating a scheduled flight. Upon vacating the runway after landing we received a call from the flight attendant advising us that there was a passenger who appeared to be having a seizure. At this point [priority handling was requested] on the ground. We were then given clearance to cross a runway and were advised that everyone would be notified. We entered the ramp; but it appeared that the ramp controller was unaware of our emergency status since a new spot clearance and frequency was given. My crewmember advised once again of our emergency situation. Afterwards; we were advised to contact ground; as we contacted ground; they were able to bring us back towards the main taxiways and utilize a runway as a means to help us expedite our taxi to the gate. During this emergency my fellow crew members and i worked together to the best of our training and experience to ensure no regulations; limitations or sops were ever exceeded or violated at any point during the emergency to attain immediate medical attention to the passenger.in the wake of the events; there are a few items that were debriefed that as a crew we felt needed some addressing to better enhance the outcome of similar; future scenarios.some aspects that made the event challenging to manage was the swapping of multiple frequencies in order to receive our clearances to get to the gate due to ramp and ground controls handling. Had there been awareness throughout the entities; i believe that one controller could have sufficed in expediting our taxi in a complex; frequency congested airport; especially as an emergency aircraft. Also; operationally the gate was essentially on the other side of the terminal. An arrangement could have been made by operations to get us the nearest available gate to give the passenger the medical attention that was needed. To our surprise also; emergency medical service was not waiting for us at the gate. There was a delay between our arrival and their presence on board. Considering our distance to position the aircraft; i feel that responders should have been there. The flight was completed and a debrief was made with the mangers without further event.
output: Flight crew reported that after landing with an ill passenger and obtaining emergency status; the crew still had difficulty expediting a direct route to the gate to get medical attention.

input: During predep briefing; first officer advised that aircraft were departing runway(s) 22r/l. Ground control cleared us to taxi to runway(s) 22r via taxiway a and taxiway north as we passed taxiway n1; tower advised us that we were on a closed taxiway and that we needed to stop. We did second officer and then tower told us to turn left/right (directions) and taxi into position and hold runway(s) 22r. We used taxiway n2 and departed normally on runway(s) 22r. I asked first officer intermediate fix he knew that taxiway north was closed north of taxiway n1. He then stated that automatic terminal information service said the departures were using runway(s) 22r and taxiway n1; but he did not remember anything about a taxiway closure north of taxiway n1. Since we were cleared to taxi to runway(s) 22r via taxiway north (no mention of using taxiway n1); the first officer assumed that we were to use the full length. Hence; when i asked him (fo) what runway(s) were in use; he replied 'rwy 22r.' perhaps the pilot getting automatic terminal information service should brief the other pilot on all items and not make any assumptions. Also; ground control issued a clearance that was not entirely correct and light emitting diode us to a closed taxiway he (gnd ctlr) should have cleared us to runway(s) 22r via taxiway north and taxiway n1. Also no closure marking (flashing light; etc) indicated a closed taxiway i found out later that taxiway was closed due to a weak spot in the taxiway that cracked earlier in the day.
output: CLOSED TXWY AT BOSTON IS NOT MARKED. TAXI CLRNC MADE NO REF TO CLOSURE. CREW ASSUMES CLRNC TO THE RWY IS TO THE END.

input: I was called in to do an annual inspection on a turbocharged c310 that had been involved in an accident and the repairs were completed. When i saw the airplane; both engs; propellers and turbochargers had already been overhauled and re-installed. The mechs that did the work have extensive experience with turbocharged navajos. I asked about airworthiness directive 2000-01-16 concerning the exhaust system and was assured that it had been thoroughly inspected; was found in good condition; and that the 'v' band clamps had been replaced with new. After an extensive inspection of the installation; repairs; and overall condition of the aircraft i signed it off as airworthy; including compliance with airworthiness directive 2000-01-16. We got a call on dec/mon/04 from the owner's mechanic stating that he felt we had not completely complied with the airworthiness directive. I agreed that on item g of figure 1 it couldn't be proved that the exhaust components in question were overhauled within the preceding 12 yrs. He is removing the components to be sent out for overhaul and we will pay for the removal and replacement. I recommend that figure 1; item g be reworded to: 'remove the exhaust system from the slip joints aft to all turbocharger attached components; and send to any federal aviation administration approved exhaust repair facility;' at whichever occurs later; etc. That should eliminate any confusion on this matter.
output: A T310R HAD BOTH ENGS AND TURBOCHARGERS OVERHAULED WITH AIRWORTHINESS DIRECTIVE 2000-01-16 ACCOMPLISHED. NO METHOD OF PROVING EXHAUST COMPONENTS WERE OVERHAULED WITHIN PRECEDING 12 YRS.

input: After day 2; trial attempt of high speed taxi above 60 mph at taunton; ma; i overshot the end of runway(s) 30. I caused minimal damage to the experimental bd-5b and damaged a runway end identifier lights with the left/right (directions) wing. No one was hurt. Loss of brakes contributed to the overshoot. To correct this action; a paved strip of no less than 5000 feet/foot should have been used.
output: PLT OF HOMEBUILT SMA RUNS OFF END OF RWY DURING HIGH SPD TAXI TEST. STRIKES RWY LIGHTS.

input: Tkof and clbout appeared normal through 10000 feet/foot when we received a 'cabin alt' caution message. I selected for the autoplt to level out instead of continuing the climb to 15000 feet/foot as assigned. The aircraft was climbing quickly and leveled at 11400 feet/foot we were in the process of notifying air traffic control and running our quick reference handbook procedures when a cabin altitude warning appeared on the engine indicating and crew alerting system we did the emergency memory item chklist and began our descent to 10000 feet/foot we notified air traffic control and continued down to 5000 feet/foot which was below the cloud layer which was from 7000-9000 feet/foot and put us in good visual flight rules conditions. Air traffic control also gave us direct routing to cvg. We accomplished all required and company recommended procedures and had a normal landing in cvg. At the gate; the ground crew came up to the cockpit to notify us of the cargo door situation the capt and i looked at it while waiting for maintenance personnel to arrive. The cargo door was closed and latched; but out of position in the upper l-hand corner. It appeared to be out of position in its track a small amount which had created our pressurization prob.
output: A CL65 FLT CREW HAS TO DIVERT FOR A PRESSURIZATION PROB CAUSED BY A CARGO DOOR NOT BEING ON ITS TRACKS.

input: Weather was clear; light winds; no turbulence. Xm weather on 530w and portable garmin 696 indicated no precipitation at all. Ads-b system showed a line of magenta with red and yellow levels of intensity at our location. This indication was completely inaccurate; as there was no precipitation. Two other aircraft in our group reported the same inaccurate display. We were midway between jwn and m93 in cavu conditions.was the ads-b system hacked? How can the system present such misinformation? I now have no confidence in ads-b weather depiction. If it can report significant fronts that do not exist; can it report clear conditions when there is bad weather?also; hours after the flight; i called the flight up on flightaware and it showed weather that did not exist. I presume that flightaware uses the same data that ads-b is using.
output: BE-55 pilot reported that while flying in clear weather conditions; the ADS-B display showed a line of heavy precipitation that did not exist at the current aircraft position.

input: I got a duats briefing; cross-checked with national oceanic and atmospheric administration data and was satisfied that i had a handle on the weather. I saw that the coastal areas of the northern panhandle were bad; but likely would move north so i had to be alert for flight plan alteration in flight. I also have a garmin 496 with weather. I contacted miami center for flight following at 8500 and to my surprise i was cleared direct to 82j. I queried the controller and was assured that i was cleared direct. I was turned over to tampa and they warned me that my present heading would take me through w470 (a fact that i was aware of; but thought the center clearance was sufficient. I quickly altered my route to navigate directly to hevvn intersection and then to pfn and 82j) i noted severe weather after hevvn on my path; tallahassee apc also warned me and i noted that there was a defined area of no apparent activity south of my route that i could use; i visually confirmed that deviation to the left (south) would be the correct move. I was not informed about 'hot' areas as i indicated my route and was cleared; however i was now informed that i could not alter left because of artillery firing! My planned route was closed to me; but i decided to descend and try to 'skirt' the indicated areas of bad weather (note that i could still see the ground occasionally and that aided my decision). However; before i could get around an go down i was 'in it and inadvertently ifr' i immediately told the controller and was asked if i wanted an instrument flight rules clearance and that i should try to contact tyndall approach. I replied that 'i was very busy flying the aircraft and i'll get back to you.' the controller persisted and i told him that i was very busy controlling the aircraft and getting bounced around severely. I got the distinct impression that he did not appreciate the situation i was in. I did not declare an emergency because i was able to control the aircraft and did not feel that i was in danger of losing it! I finally got on to tyndall approach and the first controller asked me if i was aware that i had excessive rates of heading changes and altitude-i did; again mention that i was busy and a controller got on the line and asked the correct questions about my qualifications to fly instrument flight rules (before assuming the lsa status; i was a rated instrument pilot and in this situation i took the clearance. It took a while before i could get relatively stable on the 260 heading and 6000 feet/foot she requested; i then said i preferred aaf airport and requested a lower altitude; she said okay but that 2100 feet/foot was the lowest she could offer i acknowledged and started down. Soon i saw a hole that was large enough to maneuver into; visual to the ground; and i canceled descended to visual flight rules at 1000-1300. From this point i decided; again using my in-flight weather and the excellent advisories from tyndall; to fly around the weather and head for destin and then home. The above reflects several disturbing things to me: first i admit that i tested the weather a bit farther than was wise. However; i did think that i had an adequate plan; until it was taken away from me by the late notification of 'hot' areas. Had i known that; i would have gone north just prior to hevvn intersection and miss the bulk of the nasty weather. What concerned me was the apparent lack of controller understanding that i was (potentially) in a serious; if not deadly; situation. There were no offers of 'the fastest way out' 'did i need help such as heading to nearest suitable airfield etc.' i was pelted with unnecessary communications that frankly were not helpful. The second tyndall controller was first-rate; we quickly got together and all was well. Lessons learned: i should not have accepted a 'direct' clearance from miami as i had a good plan and knew that direct was improbable given the complexities of tampa class b and the eglin defense areas. When i had my escape route eliminated i should; at that point said no; reversed course and deviated to get better weather--i could see the better way. I should realize the many controllers are not pilots and have no idea what it is like trying to control an aircraft in a storm with vertical and lateral vectors affecting control. They could be more sensitive to obvious stress situations and tailor information to help. In this instance; i learned that my lsa aircraft is controllable through a wide range of external inputs. As soon i saw i was in for a tough ride i thought to reverse course; but i found it impossible to do so because i felt that attempting the turn could possibly be an unsafe maneuver. At this point i concentrated on aircraft control; but i did not cinch my shoulder straps sufficiently; i got a bloody nose. Point here is that i could have been rendered unconscious-stupid mistake! I recognize that i did everything correctly to have a safe flight but failed to follow through. Instrument training is a life saver!
output: A Light Sport Aircraft pilot took off in marginal conditions and subsequently flew in to IMC and turbulence.

input: On a scheduled part 135 flight between white plains; ny; and syracuse; ny; we shut the left/right (directions) engine down due to a fire light in the t-handle (fuel shutoff valve). We were being radar vectored for an approach and descending through 6000 feet/foot when we encountered light chop and at the same we got a left/right (directions) engine fire light. I looked out the window at the left/right (directions) engine and did not see any indications of a fire but the light stayed on. The capt was flying and; therefore; he did the memory action items for an engine fire inflt. We shut the left/right (directions) engine down and after pulling the t-handle; there were no indications of a fire and the fire extinguish did not illuminate second officer we did not need to extinguish the fire. After completing the engine fire inflt memory chklist we advised air traffic control we had a precautionary shutdown; told them there were 3 souls on board and 2 1/2 hours fuel and did not ask for priority and i also told the passenber what was happening. Air traffic control gave us vectors for another approach which was quicker to the airport and cleared us for the approach we reviewed the approach completed one engine inoperative approach and landing chklist and reviewed one engine go around we were cleared to land and had the emergency trucks waiting at the runway(s) the capt landed safely and taxied to the gate with the trucks following us. The passenber got off and we taxied to a maintenance hangar where they found a broken fire loop on the left/right (directions) eng.
output: A BE02-D MODEL FLC RECEIVED A FIRE WARNING LIGHT IN THE T-HANDLE. A PRECAUTIONARY ENG SHUTDOWN WAS PERFORMED AND ATC ADVISED. WHEN THE FLC LANDED THEY WERE MET BY EMER CREWS IN TRUCKS WHO FOLLOWED THEM TO THE GATE.

input: I was on climb to 1500 feet/foot mean sea level just after takeoff at zzz for a 2 hour island tour. Unicom informed a transitioning helicopter of my departure then informed me that the helicopter was ne of the fields transitioning to the nw. Then the helicopter rpted 'chieftain in sight;' and that his intentions were to 'pass over the bay.' i spotted the helicopter about 2.5 mile away and rpted him in sight to unicom; when i was .5 mile from the end of the runway(s) climbing through 800 feet/foot mean sea level i had broadcasted on unicom frequency before my takeoff roll; that i was making a left/right (directions) downwind departure i could see that the helicopter and my aircraft were converging and headed for the bay. I started my upwind turn approximately .5 mile early (ie; before the bay) to avoid the helicopter when i leveled the 30 degree bank turn-out and i was 90 degrees of original heading on my upwind leg; there i saw the helicopter about 100 feet/foot directly above me. I couldn't believe this guy; i'm taking evasive action to miss him and he just keeps coming at me all the time he's saying on frequency 'do you have me in sight;' while he is coming at me. The helicopter company agreed with me that the helicopter pilot was not on his subscribed rte.
output: AN ISLAND TOUR PA32 PLT TOOK EVASIVE ACTION TO AVOID AN ISLAND TOUR HELI DEPARTING ZZZ; UNITED STATES.

input: After airborne we received a message stating there had been a damage incident at msp. After landing at dfw i spoke with the dispatcher. He stated a fuel truck refueling an aircraft at an adjacent gate had a ladder blown off the top of it and it struck the aircraft it was refueling. My taxiout involved a 180+ degree turn. My use of thrust was normal. The wind at msp was rpted on the automatic terminal information service as 320/22g26. The dispatcher also stated the refueler had not secured the the ladder to the fuel truck. Perhaps a combination of strong winds and my normal jet blast may have caused the unsecured ladder to depart the fuel truck and strike the acft.
output: MLG DEPARTING GATE AREA MAKING 180 DEGREE TURN. JET BLAST DISLODGED LADDER FROM TOP OF FUELING TRUCK. LADDER STRUCK THE ACFT BEING REFUELED.

input: Possible near midair collision in owens valley near olancha; ca. F/a-18f operating low level; heading northbound. Approximately 450 kcas (knots calibrated airspeed). Object observed close over canopy. Not identifiable. Possible large bird or small aircraft. No onboard radar tracks or advisory calls noted.
output: F/A 18 pilot experiences a NMAC with a large bird or small aircraft over the Owens Valley in California; during a low level training exercise.

input: I relieved a controller that had cleared aircraft x off of dro airport and had rerouted that aircraft direct hct. The aircraft was not in radar when i assumed the radar position. I asked aircraft x numerous times to reset his transponder; make sure the transponder was turned on. I continually asked aircraft x his position from dro and his altitude. I updated the data block when i could. I entered a point out to sector 41 and told the resolution advisory (radar assistant) controller; to point aircraft x out. Aircraft y came over descending to fl270. The transmissions were hard to hear because of the radio congestion (diversity algorithms) and the aircraft's radio. I continued to try and radar aircraft x. I asked my resolution advisory controller if he did point out the data block to sector 41; he said yes. I finally got aircraft x in radar when he changed to his backup transponder about 65 miles northeast of dro at fl250-fl260. I noticed aircraft y at fl262 and i told aircraft y to maintain fl270. I was informed that aircraft x had an resolution advisory i did not hear the pilot mention this on the frequency. There are frequency problems on this sector with diversity algorithms. Depending on the location of the aircraft; you do not hear any transmissions from the aircraft but you can see the receiver light up. You sometimes have to turn off some of you receivers in order to hear the aircraft. A fix to this problem would help out many situations.
output: ZDV controller described possible loss of separation event; noting ATC and aircraft equipment problems as possible causal factors.

input: Acft was approaching the lead-in line for parking at gate at zzz. Initially the guide man was not visible until the aircraft approached the 70-80 degree position reference the lead-in line. The capt began the 90 degree turn onto the lead-in line and was following guide man directions. Nothing appeared out of the ordinary except for the fact that the jetway appeared to be in a much lower position than normal. It did not; however; appear to be an obstruction to the aircraft the capt continued to taxi toward the stop bar following guide man signals and was ctred on the lead-in line throughout the entire event. I checkeded the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft as we rolled out on the lead-in line for any obstructions and then also monitored the guide man visual signals as the aircraft approached the stop bar. Approximately 5 seconds before reaching the stop bar; both the capt and i heard a grinding noise from the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft i immediately looked to the left/right (directions) and saw the jetway moving. As the aircraft stopped; and the brakes were set; the capt commented that he hoped that the noise was not us hitting something. I commented that i thought it might have been the gears or drive motor of the moving jetway that we heard. It took several minute(s) to get external power after which we completed engine shutdown and parking chklists. At no time during or after parking did the flight attendants or any passenber mention anything unusual. There were also no communicationss with ground personnel to indicate anything unusual. After passenber and flight attendants had left; both the capt and i went down to the ramp and noticed a dent on the outside lip of #1 engine cowling. It was approximately 1.5 inches deep and 10-12 inches top to bottom. We proceeded to operations(s) where ground personnel confirmed that the jetway had come in contact with the aircraft maintenance was contacted. The next morning when we came back to the airport we were told by several air carrier employees that this was a new jetway and the previous night was the first time that it had been used. We were also told; and our visual observations confirmed; that the jetway parking envelope markings and limit markings had not yet been painted on the ramp. As a result the ground personnel did not have a clear indication that the jetway was parked in a position that would be clear of the arriving aircraft supplemental information from acn 649476: the jetway was new; not approved for use by the airport or acr.
output: DURING A NIGHTTIME JETWAY PARKING OP; AN A329 ENG COWLING STRUCK A JETWAY NOT AUTH FOR THAT TYPE OF ACFT.

input: There are currently no notams published for n40.upon landing i see that the runway is not plowed full width; and there are large snow piles on either side of the runway that could result in an impact with low wing aircraft. The taxi way snow piles are high enough that low wing aircraft will strike their wing on them.also the awos-3 has been inoperative for at least a year and i've never seen a notam.someone could easily strike a wing or flap on the snow piles during takeoff or landing and end up in an accident. The problem is caused by the airport management's ongoing failure to publish notams. N40 has forty (40) separate owners. Which may lead to a 'if everyone is in charge; no one is in charge' situation. To prevent this in the future someone needs to tell n40 airport management to keep their notams up to date. If there are no plans to fix the automatic weather observing/reporting system then it needs to be removed from the chart.
output: Pilot reported concerns with the lack of NOTAM publications at N40 airport for known issues. Pilot stated the AWOS-3 has been inoperable for at least a year and has never been NOTAMed.

input: After a position rpt to company; capt initiated a fuel xfeed from left/right (directions) tank to left/right (directions) engine for the second time during flight crew noticed a discrepancy between current fuel quantity and estimated fuel quantity remaining. Crew contacted company dispatcher and maintenance for their input. Aircraft had no history of any fuel gauge problems crew calculated fuel burn to atl and received preferential handling by air traffic control crew elected to have fire trucks dispatched. Landing was uneventful. At the gate; maintenance confirmed a fuel leak on the #1 engine as a side note; crew's attention was distraction by a sick passenber and numerous advisories by flight attendants as to her status. Several automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages were subsequently sent to company by the crew regarding this sick passenber prior to noticing possible fuel leak. Supplemental information from acn 371699: we requested a direct routing to atl from air traffic control (who had been advised of our situation via our dispatcher). Lesson learned: checked your fuel at each position rpt! That is what we did; which light emitting diode us to the discovery of the fuel discrepancy.
output: B737-200 CREW NOTICED A FUEL IMBAL DURING FLT. CONFERRED WITH ACR MAINT AND DISPATCHER. FLEW DIRECT TO ATL; PREFERENTIAL HANDLING FROM THE CTR. POSTFLT INSPECTION SHOWED A FUEL LEAK ON #1 ENG. OBSERVATION OF LEAK DELAYED BY PAX PROBS.

input: Were reported 17.8 miles north off course at 49/50 enroute from shannon to gander. By gander control was using 2 flight management system each with 2 very low frequency omega; 2 inertial reference system/unit 2 vpu followed all procedures established by company. First both irs' drifted off course by 17 miles then came back. Vlf's were drifting as well to as much as 22 miles. All of them together not being able to deselect per company procedures we continued on our blended position as described in company flight management system flight manual. At gander airport both flight management system were off by 12 miles after using the vpu's for 150 miles. This problem was escalated to the top level of management of mfg and company. Presently awaiting answers. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: the inertial reference system/unit units were in fact correct and the vlf/omega sets were in fact drifting and since company procedure is to fly the very low frequency since it can direct the a/p by lock on and the inertial cannot. Since this incident the aircraft mfr has flown their test aircraft on the route and found their omega had the same drift problem. Now believe it is an installation problem and the omegas are being affected by the aircraft equipment. In this aircraft they did find occilators in omegas were overheating and causing drift second officer manufacturer is looking for solution; possibly relocating the omega units which are now located under the middle engine and being affected by engine radio frequency noise. In interim company has changed procedure and using the two inertial sets for primary longitude range overwater navigate, navigation and omega for backup.
output: CORP MDT TRACK DEVIATION NORTH ATLANTIC.

input: It was day #3 of a 5-day trip; which had us flying between ind and fnt. The morning prior instead of our scheduled 1 leg from ind to fnt (dep at xa40) the company revised our trip to fly ind-fnt-ind. Arriving at the hotel later the next evening; we were rescheduled to go ind-fnt-ind with a 5 hour turn and back to fnt. This sequence had a local show time of xy00. Having been disrupted from our normal routine for the week none of us slept well during the day. I personally got only 3 1/2 hours of sleep. En route to fnt from ind; this flight routinely receives multiple intermediate leveloffs and rarely attains planned cruise altitude followed by many leveloffs during descent this night was no exception. During our descent zob had given us a couple of descent altitudes and then a rerte clearance followed by another descent clearance and a local altimeter setting. As we were descending through 14500 feet/foot mean sea level zob asked why we had not leveled at 16000 feet/foot then issued us a turn and cleared us to 12000 feet/foot which is what i had set in the altitude select window. We all were pretty sure we had been cleared to 12000 feet/foot as that is what was set in the altitude alerter and what i had read back. Intermediate fix this was an altitude deviation fatigue would seem to be the largest contributor. As hard as i try to get adequate rest prior to flying; when the company keeps changing trip sequences and disrupts my sleep routine; it is hard. We really need more regulation to protect those of us who fly the back side of the clock. Another concern i have that may have been a contributor is the requirement of air traffic control to verify the readback of clrncs no longer required.
output: B727 FLT CREW FAILS TO LEVEL AT 16000 FT MSL AS CLRED. CITES FATIGUE FROM BACK SIDE OF THE CLOCK SCHEDULES AND REST DISRUPTION BY ACR.

input: I was going to fly from o04 to lar to accompany my mother to an eye operations(s) i have made this trip many times before and felt confident that i cold make it in nearly any situation i called flight service station specialist the night before to checked weather and was told that the front that had passed through carson that day would present some problems with mountain obscuration; low ceilings; and a freezing level just above the minimum enroute altitude they also told me to expect icing in clouds. I was told that due to a strong dry air flow; the freezing levels would be getting higher and that system was breaking up and getting warmer as it progressed eastward. I called flight service station specialist the next morning to file an instrument flight rules flight plan and update weather route of flight was to be visual flight rules from o04 to hzn then instrument flight rules hzn- v32-bam-v6 ogd. I was told to expect instrument flight rules at my altitude east of bam; icing in clouds; turbulence and light headwinds. We checkeded weather at various airports along route of flight and the weather was literally getting better as he was giving me the rpts. The freezing level at the time was 12000-13000 feet/foot i figured that i would go and turn back intermediate fix it got too bad. My experience with flight service station specialist weather is that it is pretty pessimistic and i could spend the night in ogd intermediate fix the weather did not improve. I filed an altitude of 11000 feet/foot (mea). I figured that intermediate fix i was below freezing level; i would not be in the forecast area of icing and thereby ok by the federal aviation regulations i was intermittent instrument meteorological conditions east of bam; temperature was +2 degrees celsius and there was no turbulence just east of dobys intersection i encountered clear ice that cause a temporary loss of pitot instruments but no degradation of flight performance. I told center of my problem and asked for a vector to elko; nv. Once out of the icing; i thought it would be better to go back to bam due to better weather further westbound rest of flight was uneventful. My familiarity with route of flight confidence in my abilities; and disregarding an federal aviation regulation were causal.
output: PLT OF SMA ENCOUNTERS ICING INFLT IN MOUNTAINOUS TERRAIN. DIVERTS WITH VECTORS THEN TURNS BACK TO BETTER WX TO THE W.

input: After shutdown and after calling controller supervisor about another unrelated event; supervisor accused flight crew of crossing an active runway(s) (rwy 4/22) after clearing our landing runway(s) (rwy 9r). First officer called ground after clearing runway(s) 9r at taxiway left/right (directions) and was issued clearance to the gate prior to crossing runway(s) 4/22. At no time did tower or ground control tell us to hold short of runway(s) 4/22. It was felt by the crew that the mlb control facility was reacting to an earlier situation while flight was on final to runway(s) 9r. When we questioned the controller later via telephone about the incident on final and us asking for them to pull the tapes about the unrelated incident; we were then informed of the alleged runway(s) incursion. The controller told us intermediate fix we were going to pull the tapes then they would have an incident about us to rpt.
output: PERSONAL CONFLICT BTWN LCL CTLR AND FLC. FLC CONTACTED TWR AFTER SHUTDOWN AND REQUESTED INFO REGARDING THEIR NMAC ON FINAL (SEE ACN #325630). TWR INFORMED FLC THAT IF THEY WANTED THE TAPES PULLED FOR REVIEW; THEN THE TWR WOULD FILE AN INCIDENT RPT THAT FLC CROSSED A RWY WITHOUT CLRNC. FLC DENIES THAT ALLEGATION.

input: Arriving to the gate that morning we found our aircraft just taxing in from the maintenance hangar. We were doing preflt checkeds as the passenber were boarding and maintenance was still onboard but had already signed the aml for return to service. However; the emergency lights would not test (they would not even come on; well maybe they did; but by the time i unbuckled and rose up to look over the flight attendant; mechanic and the boarding passenber they were out); and we placed an entry in the aml reflecting the discrepancy. Our maintenance tech made some calls and after 15 minute(s) ran a functional checked on the system. The lights came on for 15 seconds and then died. He stated that the batteries had been replaced overnight and since they had been in a freezer; they needed to 'thaw' out. He also stated that they had been installed 6 hours previous. (hmmmm... A rump roast will thaw out in two hours.) and intermediate fix they needed thawing out; why was the aircraft signed off? We waited almost 30 minute(s) and another test was done. Their test requires that the lights remain on for 60 seconds. However; the lights died in 45 seconds. We waited almost one more hour and he did another test; this time the lights did last 60 seconds; but were starting to dim fast. He quickly turned the lights off and declared the system ready for service and made an airworthy sign off in the aml (i have a photo copy). To make a longitude story short; we received heavy pressure from maintenance control to take the aircraft later our base manager was called to attempt to pressure us into taking this aircraft with the emergency lighting system in an unairworthy state. Having witnessed the whole event; we knew the batteries were dead when the aircraft arrived at the gate. We knew that they were charged just enough to pass the 60 second test and that they could not be depended upon to last even one minute more. The local mechanic told us that there were maybe two more batteries in the entire maintenance system (each aircraft needs four) and that they had been complaining about it for weeks. Our question to maintenance control was; 'how longitude does it take to charge the emergency lights?' in the aircraft from a cold dead state? The reply was that no one knew. I; for one; find that impossible to believe. What should have been a simple battery swap at the gate turned into a lengthy delay and cancelled flts depriving our passenber of the service they deserve and paid for. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr indicated that during the four hours the airplane was delayed for charging and testing; the capt was subjected to heavy pressure from maintenance control to take this inoperative emergency lighting system. Reportedly; no one had any answers on how longitude it would take to replace the batteries and no battery change available; nor how longitude to charge the existing batteries. The rptr indicated that this company needs a complete shake up top to bottom. He stated he took the airplane only after the lights passed the 60 second test; adding the pressure to fly an unairworthy airplane was great from maintenance control maintenance manager check airmen; and other upper concerned managers.
output: A CRJ-200 CAPT RPTS AN AIRPLANE JUST OUT OF MAINT HAD EMER LIGHTING FAIL TESTS. FLT CREW INCURRED A 4 HOUR DELAY BEFORE FLT DEPARTED.

input: There were two other amt's and a qa inspector on or at the aircraft. I took the task of being the monitor amt and the other two amt's were the task amt's. We were assigned the task of putting the left over wing exit hatch back into a serviceable condition. This included re-arming the emergency escape system. Initially [the] steps were confusing to me. I had to re-read them several times; eventually i became frustrated with what i interpreted them to be. Having said that i now know that i made a mistake by not continuing to be the monitor of the task. At the time of the incident i felt that i had interpreted the point the paperwork was trying to convey to me. I then let my mechanical experience take over and proceeded to do what i felt should have been done to complete the task within the intent of our assigned referenced task.
output: B737 Maintenance crew reported that they installed an over-wing slide and it deployed when they connected the electrical connector.

input: Departing mco we had a pressurization problem. We advised zjx of the nature of our problem and requested an altitude of 10000 feet/foot mean sea level to see intermediate fix we could resolve it. We had been instructed previously to intercept the orl 355 degree radial; which we did. 5 minute(s) later; about 28 vor and dme (co-located) on the 355 degree radial we requested a return to mco. After several calls and no reply from air traffic control a cargo aircraft tried to assist us in communicating with zjx. We were also unable to reach orlando approach i asked cargo aircraft to advise air traffic control we were returning to mco. We turned back to mco. I started to display 7700 in the transponder for 1 minute(s) then 7600. After 30-40 seconds; zjx responded to our call and vectored us around restrict, restricted, restriction airspace. I told zjx we were presently displaying 7700 and asked what we should squawk. He replied with another vector. I returned transponder to our original code. We returned to mco without further incident.
output: CARGO FLT HAS PRESSURIZATION PROBLEM ON CLBOUT. WHILE TROUBLESHOOTING; LOSES RADIO CONTACT. ANOTHER FLT RELAYS MESSAGES THAT FLT RETURNING.

input: I was cleared for a practice instrument landing system 24 approach. During the approach; my horizontal situation indicator (horizontal situation indicator) directional gyro failed; distracting me from the approach and making it difficult to complete the approach. Additionally; the controller kept me very high (3000 ft) when the approach normally would start at 1700 feet/foot for a transiting aircraft at 2000 feet/foot the missed procedure was simply given as 'fly east.' the actual published missed is 'climb to 600; then climbing right turn to 2000 direct to the vor and dme (co-located) and hold.' due to the distractions of the horizontal situation indicator failure and the high approach; i called missed before getting to the decision altitude; and executed a right turn; ending it at an easterly direction; at 2000 feet/foot the controller questioned what my clearance was; and i said i was told to go east. At no time was i told which direction to turn; so i assumed that he wanted me to fly the missed to the right as the plate shows. He stated that by turning right and then going east i would fly through final. However; since i was at 2000 feet/foot i was well above pattern altitude and therefore there was no conflict with traffic in the landing pattern. I apologized and requested a return to my home base because of the failed gyro. I should have clarified the missed because the controller didn't fully describe it; or could have assumed to turn left because that would be the shortest turn.
output: Distracted by instrument problems and being given a non-standard missed approach procedure during a practice ILS; a light aircraft pilot turned the wrong way after beginning the procedure before the missed approach point.

input: Target jumps and gndspd variations up to 80 knot(s) occur regularly in an approximately area defined as a 60 mile radius from the bum 240 degree radial at 60 mile this impacts control actions by increasing workload and distracting the controller a naval air station problem rpt filed in regard to this situation resulted in no change. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated the facility response to the naval air station problem rpt was a sort box between 2 radar system and that the controller should not rely on the airspd shown for separation purposes. Rptr has filed a ucr.
output: ATC EQUIP PROB RADAR TARGET JUMP AND 80 KT GNDSPD VARIATION.

input: While in cruise flight at fl410 [we] received left/right (directions) pack temperature engine indicating and crew alerting system caution message. Reduced outflow temperature from 77 to 35 degrees and caution message remained. Received a bleed duct warning message. Started running quick reference handbook procedures for warning. Crew donned oxygen masks and established crew communications. [advised] air traffic control and initiated an emergency descent to 10;000 feet. During descent; cabin pressure altitude increased to approximately 15;000 feet and passenger oxygen masks were automatically deployed. Leveled off at 10;000 feet. Completed all emergency and abnormal checklists. Sent automatic communications addressing & reporting system message to dispatcher listing events and plan. Diverted to [an alternate]. Flight attendants reported no undue reaction from any of the passengers. Requested emts to meet us at the gate. No passenger(s) requested medical attention and all the passengers were rebooked on the next flight.
output: CRJ-700 flight crew reported diverting to an alternate after loss of cabin pressure related to a pack overheat and bleed duct leak messages.

input: Atis active runway(s) was instrument landing system 15. Winds were 330 degree at 14 knot(s) the runway(s) conditions were given as snow and ice patches with braking action as good by an airport vehicle. Maximum tailwind for our approach and landing is 10 knot(s) we held until the winds were rpted at 8 knot(s) on final at approximately 800'; the tower gave wind as 14 to 22 knot(s) and advised a circle to land to runway(s) 33 was approved as circling weather minima was now rpted. We circled and landed on runway(s) 33 and found braking action as poor. Two problems circling weather (1000/3 mi) with strong/gusty winds and braking action rpt of good. In snow squalls; visibility and ceiling change rapidly. Braking action (as rpted) by ground vehicles is highly unreliable.
output: ACR MLG FLT CREW COMPLAINS OF VARIABLE CEILING AND VISIBILITY DURING CIRCLING APCH TO RWY 33 AT BTV; AS WELL AN INACCURATE BRAKING REPORT.

input: I had requested permission from the microphone (crystal) control tower to transition their air traffic area at 2600 feet/foot from nw to se. Permission was granted and i was asked to identify once and the tower confirmed my altitude as per my altimeter. As i was transitioning; the tower kept me and other traffic advised once referring to an 'unknown' aircraft that was probably not aircraft #2. The controller asked me to stay south of runway(s) 32. As i was just abeam of the center (on a n/s line) of the airport the controller advised me of a float plane at 2200 feet/foot at approximately my 10 o'clock position i responded that i had that aircraft in sight and at that time i also noticed a single engine piper type propeller aircraft approaching my aircraft from about 11 o'clock position and at what appeared to be my altitude it seemed to be approaching from slightly east of north i dived sharply as i considered the very strong possibility that we would soon collide. I advised the controller that i had just 'almost been hit' by another aircraft and the controller responded that 'that acft' was controled by (the) minneapolis or international controller or being 'worked' by 'minneapolis.' i returned to 2600 feet/foot mean sea level and continued my course. No other description of aircraft #2.
output: AN ACR COUPE PVT PLT DSNDS TO AVOID XING TFC NEAR MIC ARPT; MN.

input: I was doing aerial photography at 500 feet/foot above ground level and about 2 hours 50 minute(s) into the flight when my engine quit. During the cross country phase of the flight i had switched to the left/right (directions) tank to even out the weight but didn't switch back to both when i descended down to 500 feet/foot above ground level after the engine quit; i pitched for best glide and then picked my landing area. Just before touchdown i was able to do an emergency checked and found i was still on the left/right (directions) tank. After switching over to the left/right (directions) tank; i had power but no room to climb out; second officer i continued the landing in a field. After checkeding the aircraft for damage i found none. After taxiing off of the field; i was able to takeoff from a nearby road. After reviewing what happened in this situation i have identified several errors in my decision making process and procedures the biggest error was made in not using my chklists. I did my pretkof; takeoff and cruise checkeds but didn't do a descent checked since this incident; i have made a 500 feet/foot checked before i start the photography; which is very similar to a premaneuver checked i now use this at all times before starting photography and consider it as important as my pretkof checkeds in closing; i would like to add that i have always considered myself as a careful and conscientious pilot but upon reviewing this incident i have identified several errors in my procedures and decision making process and has forced me to review other aspects of my flying that could be improved. Hopefully this incident has caused me to become a better plt.
output: SMA PHOTO PLT RAN A FUEL TANK DRY WHILE TAKING PHOTOS AT 500 FT AGL.

input: On the release; the flight from las to dtw was scheduled to depart at xa40z. We received our pre departure clearance via the automatic communications addressing & reporting system we were busy with preflt duties. We had a passenber that had to be removed (pax brought to the attention of a flight attendant that a 70 yr old passenber lost control of his bodily functions and had an unbearable odor); and we were trying to find out from las operations(s) why we were being further delayed for announcements to passenber it turned out that the ground agents were attempting to get a pax's large electric wheelchair into the cargo bin. Brake release was at xc45z. It did not feel like we were that late; and i didn't checked the times. We taxied to the runway(s) and were cleared for takeoff after takeoff we were handed over to departure control departure control cleared us to fl190. During the climb departure control after attempting the coordination of our handoff to zla; told us that apparently our clearance had timed out and he had no routing for us. Departure control then told us to switch to zla and give them our routing. We called center and they had nothing on us. Zla asked us for type of aircraft requested routing; and requested altitude after we complied; zla then gave us a clearance to dtw. I will not forget this event. Now whenever i ante meridiem delayed; this incident will remind me to checked the time second officer that i will ask clearance delivery to keep our clearance active.
output: B757 FLT CREW DEPART LAS WITHOUT AN ENRTE CLRNC.

input: I was operating aircraft x departing zzz. Departure time was approximately xa25 ante meridiem local time. At the gate; i listened to automatic terminal information service and called clearance delivery for our clearance to the best of my knowledge i used our correct call sign; 'acft x.' after reviewing our clearance both the capt and myself verified the correct transponder code input. When it was time to push back i called ramp; again to the best of my knowledge; using our correct call sign. Once pushed back and the engs started; i asked ramp to taxi. Ramp cleared us to taxi to taxiway 'p' where we then call ground for further taxi instructions. Once near point papa; i then called ground identing us as; 'acft x point papa ready to taxi.' we were told to 'taxi to xxr via charlie and romeo behind the 757' off our nose. I read back the clearance and we proceeded to xxr. Once near xxr we switched frequencies to monitor tower we were the only company aircraft waiting for takeoff unless one was behind us that we could not see. Once our turn came we were cleared for takeoff behind another air carrier airbus. To the best of my knowledge i read back the appropriate call sign; 'acft x cleared for tkof.' the capt taxied onto runway(s) xxr and xferred the controls to me. Everything up to this point was uneventful. We were handed over to departure by the tower around 1000 feet/foot above ground level the capt called departure to checked in. From this point on there was confusion on our call sign. I believe the capt used our correct flight number and the departure controller asked us to identify we did second officer and the departure controller asked about our squawk as well as gave us a new one. We then changed our squawk per his request. There may have been confusion with another air carrier flight y in the vicinity. Departure assigned us a higher altitude than we normally fly to zzz2 from zzz1 and we questioned it requesting a lower altitude 17000 feet/foot versus fl210. We continued flying the standard instrument departure leveling off at 7000 feet/foot mean sea level for traffic at some point during all of this i believe air traffic control issued our original squawk back and the capt changed the transponder to reflect that. We were handed to the next controling agency and advised to call zzz1 approach once on the ground at zzz2. Supplemental information from acn 804686: i was working ground aircraft x called for taxi while i was correcting another aircraft of a bad readback of the runway(s) assignment. I then issued a clearance to aircraft y to taxi to runway(s) xxr. I thought i heard aircraft y read back the instructions. Aircraft x accepted the clearance for aircraft y. Aircraft x then accepted multiple clrncs for aircraft y and got airborne and caused a dev.
output: AN AIR CARRIER FLIGHT CREW ACCEPTED A GROUND TAXI CLEARANCE FOR A COMPANY AIRCRAFT WITH A SIMILAR SOUNDING CALL SIGN. SUBSEQUENT CONTROLLERS THEN ATTEMPTED TO CONTROL THE FLIGHT TO AN INCORRECT DESTINATION.

input: Captured the glide slope from above in visual conditions. Had higher than normal sink rate and touchdown point appeared to be in the water about 1.5 miles out from runway. Left engaged to see what would happen; and took over manually at 800 feet/foot would have made a big splash. Duplicated this again on same flight on the several days later.

input: Had scheduled 9 hour reduced rest overnight in hou on sunday and instead of receiving rest of 12 hours in dfw on monday; was reduced again. Capt verified with crew coordinator who said it was ok. I ante meridiem sure this was not ok; because we were scheduled for more than 9 hours flying in 24 hours that requires 11; reducible to 9; payback 12; we did not get payback. On sunday need 11 hours reduced to 9; payback 12 on monday. On monday got another 9 hours rest overnight. I talked it over with capt who was sure it must be legal since crew coordinator was sure it was legal. I ante meridiem new with company and was the only one who was questioning the sit.
output: PLT QUESTIONS LEGALITY OF REST PERIOD.

input: Inbound crew wrote up #1 engine as having large oil temperature fluctuations (ecam) during the flight maintenance was at the plane when we arrived. They decided to change the sensor at the engine 3 hours later; after the work and a test run at the gate; we departed. All was normal during start; taxi and takeoff during clbout; we noticed the oil temperature starting to fluctuate again. After a few minute(s) of monitoring; i decided to return to jfk. We notified air traffic control of our intentions and received a clearance back to jfk. All other indications on the engine appeared normal; second officer i decided to keep the engine running for our approach and overwt landing i briefed the flight attendants of the situation and what to expect. We were planning a normal approach and landing with the normal parade of emergency vehicles surrounding us on the trip to the gate. The new first officer did an excellent job of flying the airplane and working with air traffic control as i completed all my tasks. I decided to land the plane since this was his first flight on the new equipment the approach and landing went smooth. We taxied to the gate. I completed the required paperwork and advised dispatch of the details. After all was said and done; i realized i notified air traffic control of the situation and requested the emergency equipment to be standing by; but i never did actually declare an emergency or state i was exercising capt's emergency authority/authorized with zny. This is required per flight manual and most of all; it is the best way to handle it.
output: A300 CREW RETURNED TO THEIR DEP ARPT AFTER EXPERIENCING FLUCTUATING OIL TEMP INDICATIONS. THE ACFT WAS WRITTEN UP FOR THE SAME PROB THE LAST FLT.

input: I am in the zzz pilot crew room lounge area. There are greater than 12 pilots not wearing masks. Approximately 8-9 at the table area and another 5 at the recliners/lounge area. I thought wearing a mask is required. I just heard a public address announcement upstairs in the terminal that says masks are required inside the terminal. Don't you have cameras down here? This is a blatant disregard for the face mask and social distancing policy!! I guess i have to leave because i don't want to be down here.
output: Air Carrier First Officer reported pilots are not adhering to face mask policy in the crew lounge area.

input: Were operating flight into jfk; were sequenced on jfk vor and dme (co-located) runway(s) 13l behind unknown aircraft which we could see but not well enough to make out type -- traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii showed traffic about 4-5 mile ahead -- air traffic control told us to keep the speed up; cleared us for the approach and turned us over to tower after passing canarsy vor and dme (co-located) started descent to minimum descent altitude at approximately 2 vor and dme (co-located) ne off canarsy; noticed capt becoming uneasy. He then made comment about the preceding acft's wake and (on cue) we started encountering wake turbulence short; choppy bumps; left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) rolls which required some positive control inputs to keep (returned wings level; pushed power up and climbed out of it). Asked tower what we were following; turned out to be a b757. Completed approach uneventfully and above visual approach slope indicator we must have inadvertently descended into the b757's wake; but flying out of it was not a problem compared notes with capt a week later and we both agreed that we were amazed at how much wake we encountered considering the b757 was a good 4 mile ahead of us. Lesson learned: from now on; i will treat b757's with the same precautions as any 'hvy.' callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: the rptr stated the aircraft was a dehaviland dash 8. The rptr was not on autoplt. There was ground proximity warning system but it did not activate. The traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii indicated the b757 was 4-5 mile ahead. The wings rolled about 20 degrees left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) there was about 7 seconds duration before managing to escape the wake. Intermediate fix there were advisories of following a b757 ahead and or caution wake turbulence the flight path would have been flown higher and perhaps more offset. The rptr wishes the controllers would ride more in the flight station of airplanes to gain first hand education on the violence associated with wake encounters.
output: FLC ENCOUNTERS BOEING B757 WAKE TURB ARRIVING JFK.

input: Landed at ord on runway(s) 4r. Near end of runway(s) deceleration was not normal. Stopped near end of runway(s) notified tower and maintenance no damage to aircraft gear or tires. Contacted dispatcher. Recommendation: use more autobrakes in inclement weather conditions to get more braking action sooner. Supplemental information from acn 361719: at 1000 feet/foot remaining (60 kts); the capt applied full braking and the anti-skid began to cycle. Even though the anti-skid was cycling; the aircraft did not appear to be decelerating. At about 200 feet/foot remaining; it felt as intermediate fix the brakes finally began to grab and the plane began to decelerate rapidly. We came to a full stop about 6-10 feet/foot in the paved overrun. After notifying the tower we taxied to the gate. Maintenance inspected the aircraft and found no damage to the aircraft we should have rpted the poor braking action to the tower sooner to preclude the possibility of this happening to another crew.
output: B737 OVERSHOT RWY AFTER BEING UNABLE TO STOP DUE TO POOR BRAKING ACTION. FULL BRAKING WAS APPLIED TOO LATE TO STOP WITHIN THE CONFINES OF THE RWY.

input: Acft departed runway(s) 7 (25 optimum) due to weight restrictions. After takeoff we received no xmissions from tower or departure control although they later said they heard and acknowledged all of our xmissions. We attempted contact on 119.9; 133.95; 127.15; our company heard us on 129.2 and we heard them. As we were in a heavy aircraft in mountainous terrain; we flew the departure procedure and commenced a climb to 15000' mean sea level as per our pre-dep air traffic control clearance approximately 5 minute(s) after takeoff we finally were able to establish contact with las departure control no evasive action was required. I ante meridiem not sure why we heard no xmissions from air traffic control facility possible due to receiver failure (but company heard us immediately); or possibly due to a delay in controller response. Suggest checked area of xmitter coverage east of las and request controllers respond in a timely manner.
output: ACR MLG UNABLE TO ESTABLISH COM AFTER TKOF INSTITUTED LOST COM PROC.

input: On flight dfw to mco scheduled to arrive at mco with 7500 pounds of fuel onboard. Due to moderate chop above fl290 we remained at fl290 and burned about 800 pounds more fuel. Just prior to lal we turned ne to parallel a line of weather at lal we had 7200 pounds and had been slowed for arrival, arrive traffic we were slowed to 210 knot(s) and given lower at this time. Our runway(s) was changed from runway(s) 18r to runway(s) 17 for weather we were slowed to 180 knot(s) and given vectors to follow an l1011 on final. When we turned final at 27 mile there was a line of level 2 storms between us and the airport i elected to discontinue the approach and was given a left/right (directions) turn and climb to fl040. We were given vectors for holding at which time called dispatch using mco operations(s) as relay and requested a fuel burn to tpa. While talking to dispatch air traffic control advised that the storms were level 4 and the airport was experiencing windshear. I got the burn and immediately advised operations(s) and then approach that we were going to tpa. When switched to departure i advised them of minimum fuel and wanted vectors to tpa. Tpa automatic terminal information service advised that they were landing runway(s) 36l and because we were hitting headwinds and were going to be low on fuel i declared an emergency for priority handling. Due to gusty wind 310 degrees 11 knot(s) gusting 22 knot(s) we could not land on runway(s) 18 and elected to land on runway(s) 27. We briefed the low fuel procedures from part 1 and shot a visual approach we made an uneventful landing with 2800 pounds fuel onboard. During this whole time we kept getting conflicting rpts from mco tower how aircraft were landing and it was visual flight rules but then we were getting rpts of windshear and wind 90-180 knot(s) difference. I think a little better coordination needs to be achieved between approach and the tower the automatic communications addressing & reporting system automatic terminal information service feature was extremely helpful; it allowed one pilot to fly and talk to approach and the other pilot talk to dispatch while getting the current automatic terminal information service it also permitted listening to tower frequency while getting updated information another feature that would be extremely helpful would be the ability to pull a sls*city/all out of the automatic communications addressing & reporting system this would give weather and field conditions as well as the airport notams. When trying to find a divert field this would really aid the decision making process. Also another after note on the event; when going to the last automatic terminal information service pulled up just prior to divert; wind had shifted 180 degrees and was gusting to 22 knot(s) preventing us to land on the in use runway(s) supplemental information from acn 384505: we were 27 vor and dme (co-located) north of mco. Other aircraft were getting in and when we were given a 100 degree heading to join the runway(s) 18r localizer we got a good look at the thunderstorms which were about 12 vor and dme (co-located) north of the field; solid red level 4 thunderstorms at this point we had 6500 pounds fuel remaining and air traffic control said they were going to give us runway(s) 17 from runway(s) 18r. They said it was due to the weather on the field. Now they were calling windshear north boundary. At that point; they cleared us for the approach we elected to get off of the approach for vectors for holding. Air traffic control said the weather was moving through very fast and should be east of the airport in about 10 mins.
output: AN S80 FLC DIVERTS TO TPA WHEN THEY ENCOUNTER TSTM ACTIVITY N OF MCO; THEIR DEST ARPT. THEIR PLANNED DIVERSION PLUS PREVIOUS ENRTE DIVERSIONS AND DELAYS HAD BY THEN CREATED AN EMER FUEL SIT. CAPT USED HIS EMER AUTH TO STATE THAT CONDITION.
