This would have been a bad situation considering the weather and our weight after i returned the aircraft to stl; i wrote down on the log page the reason why we returned to stl. At this point the mechs and i talked about the problem and i gave them the logbook and proceeded to a different aircraft to continue the trip. In the wake of all this; i apparently didn't make the proper write-up on the log page.
output: LNDG GEAR WILL NOT EXTEND NORMALLY FOR COMMUTER LTT AT SPI.

input: Xing runway(s) 23 at wdr. On taxi out; came to runway(s) crossing point. No observed traffic visual or radio; and no response to crossing announced. Other pilot was taxiing while i did radio calls and settings. As we turned into the crossing i noticed that flip-flop was on wrong frequency and reselected it to unicom. We entered the runway(s) area with no visible traffic but then i heard a sudden announcement of an aircraft on 'short final!' i looked again (with full view of the area due to our being in a low wing) and saw no traffic on final -- we are crossing i ante meridiem looking. As we began to clear the runway(s) a twin (baron) 'appeared' at the runway(s) end (about 1900 feet/foot away) about wingspan high. He had been invisible against the tree-line backgnd in a head-on profile. Surprise! As we cleared the runway(s) other aircraft then initiated a go around from beginning of flare. It seemed to be a 2-plts mind change; rather than a delayed response by same individual who had made the 'short final' announcement as they continued the approach i made a radio apology for the event and the baron landed with no comment or further announcements i could hear. As we prepared for takeoff he remained stopped on taxiway at midfield and we departed. Human factor: limits of vision to see aircraft against a mottled backgnd. Pilot's reliance on radio xmissions to 'ensure' no traffic or that their presence is known. (i have dubbed this 'the radio cloak of collision immunity' and lots of pilots are wearing it.) the fault was mine; technically; but a landing light 'on' the baron would have made it visible at all times on final. I won't be caught dead without mine on in the future.
output: PLT TAXIING ACROSS MAIN RWY AT AN UNCTLED ARPT DID NOT SEE ANOTHER ACFT APCHING TO LAND UNTIL STARTING ACROSS THE RWY. UNICOM RADIO CALLS MISSED BECAUSE RPTR DID NOT HAVE THE COM SELECTOR ON THE UNICOM FREQ.

input: Holding number one for takeoff runway 13l at skbo we were given the clearance 'after the departing airbus line up and wait runway 13l' the first officer read the clearance back exactly as stated above. Tower said 'affirmative.' while waiting for takeoff clearance i saw our traffic alert and collision avoidance system alert turn yellow with traffic 200 feet/foot above us. We watched that traffic go around. A few minutes later we were given takeoff clearance.
output: B757-200 flight crew reported they were holding in position at SKBO when they noticed an aircraft 200 FT above them on approach to the same runway.

input: It was the start of a 6 leg day. And it was the first time i had flown with the capt. It was determined that i would fly the first 2 legs to twin falls; identification and the return leg to salt lake city. For reasons i could not determine; the capt seemed rushed and missed multiple radio calls. After landing at twin falls; the controls were xferred to the capt and he asked for the after landing checked i no sooner looked down to perform the checked when the capt realized we were about to go off the taxiway and applied full left/right (directions) tiller steering to avoid going off. Once i realized what was happening; i could tell the capt had been preoccupied with the fuel gauges rather than looking outside. This certainly flustered me; and should have acted as a red flag. However; the reason for this rpt occurred during takeoff from twin falls. The wind was calm and the capt wanted to depart runway(s) 7. Using this runway(s) requires a back taxi for full length. The taxi out was normal with all the appropriate checkeds completed. Back taxiing on the runway(s) the capt asked me to perform the before takeoff checked which entails using the cockpit to cabin interphone to talk to the flight attendant to see intermediate fix they are ready. Just before leaving communications #1 to talk to the flight attendant; i heard the capt tell tower we were ready to go. I then heard tower clear us for takeoff at the end. After talking with the flight attendant; she told me she was not ready; which i then told the capt. I told tower we would pull off at the end in the turn-around area. Tower then cleared us to remain in position and hold on the runway(s) and advise when ready to go. I acknowledged the twr's instructions and the capt again asked me to call the flight attendant; which i did; to find her ready to go. I told the capt she was ready and he said something to the effect of 'let's get going; you have the flight ctls.' i advanced the power and departed. Once airborne; tower informed us we had not been cleared for takeoff i attribute this breakdown in cockpit resource management to being rushed and assuming the capt had received a takeoff clearance when he said 'let's get going; you have the flight ctls.' the capt told me he took full responsibility for the situation however; i feel i share the blame; since i knew i was off frequency at a crucial time and could have simply have asked 'are we cleared for tkof?'
output: UNAUTH TKOF BY AN EMB120 FLC AT TWF; ID.

input: I worked on a b777 aircraft all day. It was scheduled for extended range twin operations flight on a trip early in the day and then pushed back to two other trips later in the day. The primary problem with this airplane was a popped delta-p [red indicator] on the center hydraulic system return filter in the right wheel well. There are two packing [o-rings] in the illustrated parts catalog (ipc) chapter 29-11-45 with invalid part numbers (p/n). The first packing is for the [hydraulic return] filter bowl. In ipc 29-11-45; it can be found in item 30. The packing is identified as nas1601-430; which doesn't break to any company [stores] p/n. There are no alternate parts listed.i consulted with domestic maintenance control support and they found the wing hydraulic return filters in ipc chapter 29-11-44 have a comparable o-ring with the p/n nas1611-430; which is stocked by our air carrier. I used this packing on the [center hydraulic system] filter bowl. The second o-ring packing with an invalid p/n belongs to the delta-p indicator. The delta-p indicator wouldn't reset. It is sealed with two packing's (found in ipc 29-11-45 items #55 and #60). Item #60 is p/n nas1601-014; which again; doesn't break to our stores p/n. Maintenance control support crossed-referenced that p/n in the ipc and found nas1601-014 was an alternate part for nas1611-014 in ipc 27-31-09. This packing was stocked locally and i used it as a substitute for nas1601-014.one of the items i generated [and wrote-up]; was for the popped delta-p indicator on the center hydraulic system return filter. This [red indicator] would not reset. The delta-p can be found in ipc 29-11-45; item 135. Initially; our company stores parts computer showed it as being in-stock locally. I removed the delta-p indicator [body] based on this information. It was later learned the delta-p indicator body part was not in stock. Supervisor suggested i defer the reset of the popped delta-p [red indicator] using a non-essential function (nef) deferral. Myself; my coworker; and the two lead mechanics involved declined to use this [type of] deferral. Management then agreed to call and sign for the nef deferral.i made two [write-up] items in the logbook to cover this scenario. The first [write-up] for the delta-p [red indicator] not resetting (log report x). The second [write-up] was for reinstalling the malfunctioning delta-p [red pin indicator] with new [o-ring] packing's (log report y). I signed for [log report y]; while supervisor signed for the nef deferral of log report x. The plane was released and departed for an international destination. There the nef deferral [log report x] was cleared without any maintenance being accomplished. Instead; international maintenance control used my log report y; the re-installation of the delta-p [indicator body]; as the authority to clear the log x nef deferral [for the popped indicator].
output: A Line Mechanic reported making two logbook write-ups for a popped Delta-P indicator pin on the center hydraulic system return filter of a B-777 ETOPS aircraft. First write-up for popped indicator was deferred by a Maintenance Supervisor as Non-Essential Function (NEF). The second write-up signed-off by Mechanic. Later; Maintenance Control cleared the NEF deferral using the Line Mechanic's sign-off as authority.

input: Ztl advised a single f/a-18 was at our 12 o'clock position visual flight rules at 15 mile at 15500 feet/foot we were on the arrival, arrive into atlanta to cross husky at 14000 feet/foot when we were descending through 15500 feet/foot i could see on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii that the traffic was now 7 mile and co-alt still off the nose; we got no further advisories from air traffic control and i'm not sure the controller was talking to the f/a-18. Then we got an resolution advisory to monitor vertical speed and i still had no visual. I finally saw the traffic off my left/right (directions) side. Both appeared to be in a left/right (directions) turn to avoid us. When we told air traffic control that that was a little close; i heard laughter. I'm not sure of the full call sign of the f/a-18's but xyz was the first part. I believe they are the reserve squadron out of zzz. I'm not sure that departing atlanta second officer near to an arrival, arrive corridor was a smart thing to do; especially at altitudes second officer near the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction altitudes of the arrs. I had these passenber comment to me about the proximitypa of the aircraft and one passenber identified them as the correct acft.
output: NMAC BTWN AN MD88 DSNDING AND A PAIR OF MIL F18'S IN LEVEL FLT AT 15500 FT MSL. THE MD88 FLC INCREASED THEIR RATE OF DSCNT IN RESPONSE TO TCASII RA AND THE F18'S WERE OBSERVED IN A R TURN AS IF TO ASSURE SEPARATION.

input: Coming out of 16000' we experienced a #1 constant speed driven high oil temperature we followed procedures and disconnected the constant speed driven we then started the auxiliary power unity and used it to power the #1 buss. Being that we were second officer close to phx; and the weather in chicago; we elected to go back to phx to have the system looked at. This was a very conservative measure; but since it was snowing at our destination and we had minimum fuel for trip; second officer auxiliary power unity running for 3 hours would dent our contingency fuel. Therefore; we thought it best to have system looked at; since we were second officer close to a maintenance facility and the temperature had jumped second officer fast. In order to go back to phx we would have to make an overweight landing we weighed 110000 pounds aircraft limit 105000#. Conditions were favorable: very light winds; longitude runway(s) longitude final to stabilize and capt's recent streak of very smooth lndgs. I notified company--alerted maintenance for inspection. We did not declare an emergency we contemplated burning off the excess; but did not feel the 1 hour burn time was warranted under conditions. The landing was picture perfect. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr stated that aircraft did not have fuel dump capability; therefore the election to land overwt. Further stated that a proper log book write up was made in that it was stated that an overwt landing had been made and that write-up was signed off as being inspected. As further events unfold; it appears that the company had taken punitive action on this capt; using marginal judgement and financial loss as a basis. (someone had cancelled the flight and revenue was lost--no one knows who cancelled the flt.) it was rpted that the capt involved was also in some form of contestant mode with the company; having made several unscheduled lndgs prior to this event. Pilot group generally thought company was making an example of this pilot by suspending him for 7 days and sending him back for training. The flight re-originated to destination 2 hours later. Rptr also brought up the information that he felt that morale was at an all-time low as contract negotiations were still in progress and that the pilot group felt disenchanted with the management group.
output: MLG FLT CREW ELECTED TO RETURN TO ARPT OF DEP AFTER DISCONNECTING #1 GENERATOR.

input: At approximately xx00pm local today; oc3/4 had to be moved to oc9. Oc9 had to be moved to oc5. The reason for this was due to pvd outages at oc3/4. It is my understanding that this outage occurred because the oc3/4 pvds were unplugged on the midshift during new carpet installation.
output: ATC EQUIP PROB RADAR SCOPE OUTAGE CAUSED COMBINED POS OF OP.

input: Flight was released with stl as alternate. Flight was given reroute which burned some fuel; and held about fifty miles southwest of ord. Captain failed to coordinate with me on fuel status but i noticed flight holding on our flight display. I changed his alternate to pia about the same time as i noticed a flight display reroute to ind. I advised flight via automatic communications addressing & reporting system i would be filing this report due to this federal aviation regulation violation and bad technique of not calling dispatch while in range of the company frequency and then diverting to an alternate which was not on his release and further than pia from his present position.
output: An air carrier Dispatcher reports one of his flights diverted to an airport not on the flight plan; without informing Dispatch.

input: I was conducting primary flight training in the traffic pattern at zzz. While on left downwind to runway xx; i thought i heard another aircraft on frequency announce; '...opposite direction.' but didn't hear the specific airport and didn't ask for a second transmission because i didn't think it came from zzz because i didn't see any runway activity and my experience at this airport is there is relatively little traffic. I proceeded with the normal traffic pattern with my student and made my 'base' call and then was late making my 'final' traffic pattern call because i got involved in instructional direction. My traffic pattern call was probably made about 1/4 mile on short final and that specific call was '...on short final.' all of the sudden out of my peripheral view i saw a single-engine turboprop aircraft (might have been a pc-12 or tbm) flying the opposite direction off runway xy (opposite direction runway) and turning to the right to avoid me. The pilot of the aircraft asked if i saw him and i stated that i did. The se turboprop continued with its departure and we finished our landing and continued our pattern work. Clearly during an instructional traffic pattern ride there is quite a bit of concentrated discourse between the instructor and the student; and that was the case here. My preconceived notions about the traffic density at the airport lured me into thinking i didn't need to ask for a retransmission of the partial radio call i heard regarding the 'opposite direction.' that most assuredly was a mistake. Furthermore; i didn't see the oncoming aircraft on the runway because the paint livery on the aircraft allowed the oncoming aircraft to blend in well into the background color of the runway itself and that's even with my eyes refocusing towards the end of the runway as i continued to evaluate the student's descent to the runway. Additionally the aircraft did not display on my ipad from my stratus input and i didn't see it on the mfd from any tis input. Lastly; today's flight was the end of an intense 2-week training period during which i was flying twice a day with two different students with pre-and-post briefings and debriefings and simulator instruction in the evening with the two different students as well. Last week was physically taxing with intense heat throughout the day for the entire week. I believe that fatigue did play a role; however; my nature is i don't necessarily feel the fatigue while engaged in flying-related activities because the adrenaline is pumping and artificially masks the full effects of the fatigue. Corrective actions include my not disregarding an 'opposite direction' call regardless of any preconceptions or specific circumstances. Second is realizing a thorough search of an uncontrolled runway on final is warranted in all circumstances because of the potential impacts of paint livery on the aircraft permitting the aircraft to be easily overlooked on a runway of similar coloring. Also i now am facing my evaluating my habit patterns regarding aircraft traffic. I realize that with the expanding availability of reliable traffic information transmitted to me onin different ways; my disciplined approach to scanning the horizon for other aircraft is declining because of increased reliance of ads-b inputs pushed to me; complete with aural traffic conflict alerts.
output: C182 Instructor reported an airborne conflict with opposite direction traffic due to failure of understanding radio transmission at a non-towered airport.

input: During walkaround; noticed #2 nose landing gear tire axle washer missing. Installed a new axle washer on #2 nose landing gear tire assembly as per amm 32-45-02. All the procedures were complied with amm 32-45-02. Refer for inspection on bearings and tires.
output: DURING A WALKAROUND; MECHANIC NOTICES THE RIGHT (#2) NOSE LANDING GEAR TIRE AXLE WASHER WAS MISSING ON A B767 AIRCRAFT.

input: A cold front was forecast to move through arizona and colorado during our flight from gjt to phx. The first leg of this scheduled trip (phx-gjt) was completely free of inclement weather en route our flight was on the ground approximately 10 minute(s) in gjt and it took approximately 25 minute(s) to go from gjt to the 80 nautical mile north of tbc. Therefore; from the time we first passed the area of freezing rain on our way to gjt to the time we actually encountered it was only about 1 hour we first encountered what seemed to be light to moderate mixed icing at fl220. (our aircraft is approved for flight into known icing; complete with heated windshield; leading edge boots; heated propellers and pneumatically heated pt6-a engine inlet lip heat.) however; after a short time; the heated windshield began icing up; as well as the engine inlet lip area! The inlet lip heat is heated to approximately 720 degrees celsius by ducting exhaust air through ducting under the lip. We noted the outside air temperature of 0 degrees celsius and were cleared to 15000 feet/foot mean sea level the temperature (0 degrees c) and icing continued all the way down to 11000 feet/foot mean sea level moderate turbulence occurred throughout the flight which lasted 2 hours 25 minute(s) with a diversion to prc for fuel. A postflt inspection of the aircraft revealed large pits in the fuselage paint adjacent the propellers and propeller paint nicked off from the ice. All the literature on freezing rain is true -- it's dangerous! The b1900d is a fantastic aircraft in icing conditions. However; not even this aircraft comes anywhere close to being able to deal with freezing rain. My best advice -- be aware of and avoid freezing rain at all costs; plts!
output: AN ACR BE02 FLC RPTS ON THEIR ENCOUNTER WITH FREEZING RAIN. THEY WERE CORRECTLY QUITE IMPRESSED BY ITS RAPID EFFECT ON THE ACFT'S PERFORMANCE.

input: 10 minute(s) prior to pushback; white dense smoke in cabin. Evacuated people out of doors 1l and 2l. Suspect auxiliary power unity shut auxiliary power unity down via evacuate/evacuation chklist and smoke cleared no injuries or damage. Deployed 1 slide at door 2l.
output: A320 WAS EVACED DURING BOARDING; WHILE ACFT WAS PARKED AT THE GATE. DENSE; WHITE SMOKE IN CABIN CLRED WHEN SUSPECT APU WAS SHUT DOWN.

input: Apparent aircraft database error: las tyssn1; prino intersection listed on standard terminal arrival route as 8000 feet/foot mean sea level hard altitude while aircraft database shows 8000a. Standard terminal arrival route was coupled with instrument landing system runway(s) 25l. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the reporter advised that company standard operating procedure is to always load the runway(s) first; then any associated arrival procedure. Reporter noted the apparent discrepancy when the instrument landing system was programmed and it remained that way when the standard terminal arrival route was entered and activated.
output: B757-200 FO NOTES ALT AT PRINO INTERSECTION ON TYSSN STAR TO RWY 25L AT LAS SHOWS 'AT 8000' ON THE AERO CHART BUT THE ACFT DATABASE INDICATES 'AT OR ABOVE 8000 FT.

input: Our flight was climbing to 15000 feet/foot mean sea level after takeoff from ues. En route to luk; we began picking up moderate ice at 7600 feet/foot mean sea level ice accumulation continued through 11000 feet/foot in the climb we requested descent to 9000 feet/foot for ice and were approved. After a short time at 9000 feet/foot the situation began to worsen. The aircraft deice anti-ice system were functioning properly; but because of 'non shedable' ice on the airframe; we began losing airspd at the rate of approximately 1 knot(s) every 10 seconds. Because of very heavy traffic on the frequency we were unable to contact the controller to request lower altitude right away. After approximately 90 seconds we got an opening on the frequency and requested an immediate descent to 7000 feet/foot because of icing. There was no reply. Airspd now at 160 knot(s) down from 200 knots indicated airspeed i forcefully xmitted that we were 'vacating 9000 feet/foot for 7000 feet/foot because of heavy icing.' the controller responded; 'well; intermediate fix you're going to do that; turn left/right (directions) to 220 degrees you have traffic at 11 o'clock at 8 mile at 8000 ft.' problem extremely heavy radio frequency traffic hampering effective air-to-gnd communications indifferent attitude of controller zau frequency not recorded.
output: FLC OF A BEECH 1900 AIRLINER (BE02) FAILED TO MAINTAIN ASSIGNED ALT WHEN ENCOUNTERING UNFORECASTED SEVERE ICING CONDITIONS AND FREQ CONGESTION PREVENTED THEM FROM OBTAINING IMMEDIATE DSCNT APPROVAL FROM ATC. AS THEY DSNDED ATC FINALLY REPLIED TO THEIR EMER AND PROVIDED A VECTOR HDG TO AVOID OTHER TFC.

input: On apr/xa/01 i was told by my immediate supervisor mr x to checked on the bird strike repairs on aircraft upon doing second officer i was told by mechanic ms y that she was instructed to pound out a dent on the fuselage skin above the flight deck window. She was to cut out the cockpit drip shield to do second officer i then noted that she should stop because per b767 srm 51-70-01-0 dent rework procedures that dent could not be reworked. I was then told by technical crew chief mr zulu time (utc/gmt) that there was a change in the repair documentation that allowed this. When i could not find this; i questioned mr zulu time (utc/gmt) and he asked me to come to his office where he showed me an engineering change order dated mar/xa/01. Mr zulu time (utc/gmt) assured me this would cover it. When i questioned this with my supervisor mr x because of a section of the engineering change order he said i should then checked with the engineer mr a. When i did second officer he informed me that it indeed did not cover the damage in question. When i informed mr zulu time (utc/gmt) of this; he became upset and asked me to go with him back to see mr a. He again told us it did not apply. At this time mr zulu time (utc/gmt) became very upset and left. On apr/xa/01 i was told there would be something done for this damage. I then inspected and evaluated the area of bird strike after entering this information on form. Mr zulu time (utc/gmt) later asked ms y to change one of my measurements. Upon further investigation; i discovered that a repair approval request was sent to boeing with a different description of damage than i had evaluated. The repair approval request was to leave out of limits dent as is with no further action/inspection required. This deviates from our repair procedures per b767 srm 51-70-01/53-00-01-1 figure 101 sheet 2 note 1; for the damage in question is adjacent to primary structure which was not inspected. I feel there has been an attempt to deceive both the mechanic and inspector on this repair. And that boeing was not given enough information about this damage in the repair approval request; ie; damage adjacent to frame and with crease. Also; that no inspection of internal structure is planned. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the federal aviation administration requires a clear delineation between the production part of maintenance and quality control (inspection) of maintenance the rptr said this did not happen in this incident as management submitted a proposed repair to the manufacturer with smaller damage dimensions. The rptr stated the proposed repair did not require adjacent structure inspection. The rptr said this information has been submitted to the company and no answer has been received.
output: AN ACFT WITH FUSELAGE BIRD STRIKE DAMAGE OUT OF STRUCTURAL REPAIR MANUAL LIMITS HAS MGMNT SUBMIT ALTERED DAMAGE DIMENSIONS TO THE MANUFACTURER FOR REPAIR APPROVAL.

input: While en route; air traffic control informed us that there had been a stuck microphone for about three minutes. We were unsure if it was us or not. We had no prior or later events in the aircraft that would indicate a problem.
output: A B737-700 flight crew was advised of a stuck microphone on their frequency; but were unable to determine if they were the cause.

input: I cleared an aircraft for takeoff. Right after the aircraft had started its takeoff roll; i noticed vehicles on the runway and canceled takeoff clearance. The aircraft departed anyway. Once airborne the aircraft mentioned the vehicle and said he thought i had tried to amend his departure clearance.
output: Local Controller described observing a vehicle on the runway after takeoff clearance had been issued. Reporter cancelled takeoff clearance; aircraft failed to comply; and departed.

input: I was on the instrument landing system runway(s) 9; mli. It was dark and snowing. I was cleared to land. I touched down with a lot of runway(s) remaining (in touchdown zone) and decided to take it easy on the reverse. Approximately half way down the runway(s) the plowing stopped and the snow approximately 1 inch thick concealed the lines. I reversed harder and tower then told me to make a left/right (directions) turn on runway(s) 5/23. I thought i was going to miss the turn but then realized; as did the tower that i turned on the wrong runway(s) (rwy 13/31). I taxied down runway(s) 13 and exited to the left/right (directions) i was now confused. I had asked to taxi to 'cargo;' but that was a different place on the field. I was not extremely familiar with the airport and probably would have been all right except for: 1) snow covered runway(s) and 2) tower giving me a taxi clearance while still moving at approximately 40-50 knot(s) down the runway(s) i could not concentrate on what he was saying because i was still trying to maintain aircraft control in loud reverse and in the snow. I taxied to parking and nothing further was said.
output: PLT OF AN SA277 METROLINER CARGO FLT ENCOUNTERS 1 INCH THICK SNOW PART WAY DOWN THE LNDG RWY AND CANNOT SEE THE TURNOFF LINES. HE EXITS ON THE WRONG RWY.

input: We pushed back at oak. Shortly after pushback the ground crew advised the capt that we were cleared to start. While the capt accomplished the start; i copied the weight and balance numbers from operations(s) i noticed that the takeoff weight seemed low. It was 20000 pounds below our maximum release weight however; when i added the zero fuel weight and fuel together it was the same takeoff weight that i had been given. I consulted the quick reference performance manual and determined that we could use 20 knot(s) reduced power with the maximum allowable reduction for assumed temperature i entered the takeoff speeds into the flight management computer and i completed the takeoff briefing. We then completed the taxi and takeoff checked it was my leg and i began what seemed at first to be a normal takeoff as we accelerated through v1 and vfr military training routes everything was normal. As i began to rotate; the nose felt heavy as the rotation continued through 9 degrees i began to have to push instead of pull to slow down the rotation. As the aircraft lifted off; we felt and heard a thud. The tail had struck the ground we continued the takeoff and clbout but returned immediately to oak. The approach and landing were normal. Upon our return examination of the aircraft showed 2 antennas on the aft belly broken off and 3 scraped areas on the aft belly skin ahead of the tailskid. All of the damage turned out to be superficial. After checkeding the aircraft i went to operations(s) where i learned that the takeoff weights we had been given were 18000 pounds less than the actual takeoff weight operations(s) had made a mistake in the weight and balance computations. In retrospect; i believe the following to be contributing factors: 1) we use manual computations for our weight and balance this leads to possible mistakes such as this incident. 2) we currently have no procedure for the flight crew to xchk the zero fuel weight against our load -- we merely add the zero fuel weight we are given to the fuel as a xchk. 3) from pushback to takeoff was only 6 minute(s) perhaps intermediate fix we had taken more time we might have noticed the large difference between our release weight and actual takeoff weight and investigated further.
output: B737-400 ACFT FLC NOTICED PRIOR TO TAXI THAT FINAL TKOF WT WAS LOW; BUT WHEN RPTR FO ADDED THE FUEL TO THE ZERO FUEL WT; IT CAME OUT THE SAME. NEW WT AND SPDS WERE ENTERED INTO THE FMC. ON ROTATION IN TKOF ROLL; RPTR FO PF NOTED THE NOSE SEEMED HVY; THEN HAD TO PUSH BECAUSE OF THE RAPID ROTATION. TAIL STRIKE OCCURRED AND FLC RETURN LAND; AND FOUND DAMAGE TO UNDERSIDE OF ACFT.

input: Taxiing in to gate at abe; a fuel truck was parked beside a jet on next gate. We slowed and waited for a wing walker. The wing walker gave us a thumbs up. I then followed the marshaller on the ctrline in to the gate; and set the brakes. The wing walker ran up to the marshaller showing him the stop signal; and shortly thereafter i was called out to the jetway. Our left/right (directions) wingtip was on the fuel truck. We did not feel any impact. The wing walker stated that when our wing was 10 feet/foot from the truck; she realized it wouldn't clear she began signaling to stop; but the marshaller never saw it; and waved us in to the chocks.
output: ACFT CONTACTS FUEL TRUCK WHILE BEING GUIDED TO PARKING SPOT.

input: Tkof was successful; but during climb at 100' above ground level the engine quit abruptly (prop continued to windmill; but there was no sputtering or coughing). Followed emergency procedures and landed in an open field slightly to left of departure path. Shut down all systems and quickly exited aircraft there were no injuries or property damage. Damage to aircraft appeared to be limited to gear; propeller and dents. I do not know why the engine quit; but the wet field may somehow have contributed. It was a grass strip with some standing water and mud. I intend to study thoroughly the sma x aircraft inlet system and fuel supply system to see intermediate fix somehow mud or water in the inlet that subsequently got sucked into the engine on climb could be the cause.
output: LIGHT ACFT EXPERIENCES ENGINE FAILURE AFTER TKOF; MAKES FORCED LNDG.

input: At the end of 20 hours of training in the repair and overhaul of this valve; i made 3 valves svcable and returned them to stock. At that time; i reviewed the joint document and realized that some of the testing required to make a unit svcable after overhaul had not been accomplished. I asked my trainer about it and was told that we did not have the equipment to perform all the tests. I then went to my lead wxvx and he and i informed our team leader xxxz of the situation she ordered us to hold all the other units i was working on out of service pending a review by the engineering dept.
output: AN OVERHAUL SHOP RPTS P&W 2000 ENGS DURING #4 BEARING SCAVENGE VALVE OVERHAULS ARE NOT TESTED PER VENDOR'S MANUAL DUE LACK OF TEST EQUIP.

input: Triple inertial navigation system unreliability at time of transition to otw. Under radar contact requested return to base and fuel dump area. Approved. Dumped to below maximum landing weight. Replaced two ins'. Continued flight again when cleared by ground personnel and air traffic control sec flight uneventful met by flight manager at arrival, arrive problem explained and released aircraft had had previous write up affecting ins.
output: WDB DUMPS FUEL AND RETURN LAND NRT BECAUSE OF DUAL INS FAILURE. WERE THE INS'S LOADED PROPERLY?

input: I was returning to my home airport today on a visual flight rules flight. Clear skies; visual flight rules i passed over my normal inbound reporting point but because frequency was saturated; i was unable to report my arrival at zzz until i was about 1 mile past it. I was told to return there and hold due to busy airspace. As i headed there; i got traffic alert from zzz tower controller. I had heard previous warning to another aircraft and i identified that aircraft and their relative position to mine using foreflight/stratux display. I was told to turn 20 degrees right; but that would have put me into conflict with the other aircraft. I initiated immediate descent and lost 300-400 ft. And passed close under the conflicting traffic. This was a close call and loss of separation between two aircraft; both of which were in contact with air traffic control i was given a vector (turn 20 right) which would have put me on a direct collision course with conflicting traffic at same altitude.i do not believe i have done anything wrong here; i have not committed any violation. I did not adhere to air traffic control instructions because it would have resulted in a midair collision; destruction of my aircraft; and killed me.so; i think somebody better listen to the tapes; look at the radar data; and maybe go over this with tower controllers. The tower was dealing with an overloaded situation; they did the right thing by telling me to turn back; hold; and give them some relief. No problem. Vectoring me directly towards another aircraft at same altitude? Sorry; they do not get a free pass on that one.
output: Single pilot reported taking evasive action to avoid a collision with another aircraft.

input: Prior to pushback; as is normal procedure; the clearance for our flight was obtained from clearance delivery. Our initial clearance was to expect our filed altitude of fl300. During taxi out; newark ground control asked us to contact clearance delivery for a new routing. We were on taxiway bravo holding short of golf with brakes set. The first officer contacted clearance delivery and i; the pilot in command monitored as well as copied the new routing as did the first officer. There was no mention of any altitude changes for our new route of flight mentioned. Once the clearance was confirmed; the first officer and i worked together to verify the route and input into the flight management system the new route was checked for accuracy; time; distance and fuel. The new route appeared to slightly improve our time; distance and fuel performance upon arrival at destination as compared to the original routing. The first officer and i agreed on the new routing and advised ground control. Once we departed; we were cleared to level off at 6000 ft. After a few minutes time; we began to inquire with air traffic control about when we could expect higher. Air traffic control advised us that 6000 ft would be our final altitude. We further inquired and were informed that we had accepted clearance for a 'sermon south' route and would not be given higher. They also informed us that our company had agreed to use 'sermon south' routes which is why we were assigned the clearance. The first officer nor i had ever heard of 'sermon south' routes and were perplexed by this. Newark clearance delivery had never made and mention of a 'sermon south' route nor the fact that we would be required to maintain 6000 ft for the majority of the cleared route. Prior to takeoff and up until we were notified of the 'sermon south' routes; both the first officer and i believed we would be cleared to our filed flight plan altitude of fl300 (as per the initial clearance) and had no indication from anyone that our final altitude would be limited to 6000 ft. I immediately began making fuel calculations and communicating with dispatch about our situation. I also advised air traffic control of the fact that if we were limited to 6000 ft; we would not have enough fuel to legally make it to the destination and we would be diverting. Air traffic control did attempt to make some concessions and eventually cleared us to 16000 feet; then to fl200. Even with the higher altitudes; the calculations revealed that we had consumed too much fuel at the lower altitudes for us to safely proceed to destination. Dispatch and i agreed to divert the flight to refuel.newark clearance delivery was under high pressure to re-route numerous aircraft and may have inadvertently omitted the fact that they were clearing us for a route at 6000 ft. It is imperative to advise the crew of a turbojet aircraft that they are being re-routed to a significantly lower altitude than originally cleared for as fuel consumption rates at 6000 ft are significantly different than at fl300. Additionally; if those routed are to be used; there should be some sort of education granted to pilots who will be operating them prior to assigning the routes. Lastly; in the future; when i receive such a large re-route; i will also confer with dispatch prior to departure to ensure an incident like this is not repeated.
output: ERJ Captain reported receiving a reroute prior to departure from EWR which appeared shorter than the original route. Once airborne the crew learned of an altitude restriction that consumed additional fuel; resulting in a diversion.

input: The standard terminal arrival route placed us on downwind at 12000 feet/foot mean sea level (11000 feet/foot agl) heading 010 degrees approach gave the calls 'spd your discretion' and 'dsnd to 7000 feet/foot msl.' (the standard terminal arrival route calls for 210 knot(s) as the 'expected' speed second officer we had to nudge air traffic control for this airspd and dscnt.) passing approximately 8500 feet/foot mean sea level on downwind just past the abeam for the touchdown point of mci runway(s) 19l; we were told to descend to 5000 feet/foot this call was followed less than a minute(s) later with a call to descend to 3000 feet/foot and turn left/right (directions) to 270 degrees cleared for a visual approach to runway(s) 19l. Upon rollout from my left/right (directions) turn; i could see that the aircraft was high and close to the runway(s) approach control had vectored us for a visual approach to mci runway(s) 19l. The turn to final had placed us well above the instrument landing system glideslope and in close to the runway(s) we corrected for the high situation and crossed the threshold on speed and on glideslope touchdown was in the center of the touchdown zone -- firm; but not hard. After touchdown; i felt as though we had become slightly airborne second officer i attempted to hold up the nose as we settled back down to the runway(s) (apparently we had not gone airborne again because there was no second touchdown.) on rollout the second officer noted a tailskid light illuminated. Postflt inspection revealed damage to the tailskid; second officer we contacted ground control to sweep the runway(s) for foreign object debris i believe the tailskid was struck after touchdown as i was holding the nose up anticipating a second touchdown. Human factors: 1) perception -- decelerating all the way to touchdown; followed by speed brake (spoiler) and thrust reverser deployment may have contributed to the feeling that aircraft had gone back into the air. 2) visual -- night time with upsloping runway(s) and runway(s) lights as only visual cue; may have added to feeling that aircraft was becoming airborne again.
output: HIGH; CLOSE IN APCH; DECELERATING TO TOUCHDOWN; ACFT NOT STABILIZED. PF (FO) THOUGHT ACFT BOUNCED (IT DIDN'T); SO WAS HOLDING NOSE UP AND HIT TAILSKID.

input: This is a follow-up report similar to one i filed four months ago. This pertained to door window fogging on b767s and the absence of language in the minimum equipment list to identify this condition as unserviceable. The same scenario played out again at zzz in august 2013. A b-767 aircraft arrived with the forward right cabin door window completely covered in condensation. Supervisor x explained to me that the technical manager approved the condition and issued minimum equipment list 56-xx. I told supervisor x that i would not be a party to the deferral. Our air carrier is not taking seriously the [need for] visibility [out] of the door window. This is why minimum equipment list 56-xx must be revised to explain fogging and condensation are not permissible.
output: A Line Aircraft Maintenance Technician (AMT) reports about his Air Carrier's continued practice of releasing B767-300 aircraft with Main Cabin Door window viewports completely obscured by moisture condensation due to window heater panel failure. No Cabin Door window visibility requirements exists when deferring heat panels under B767 MEL 56-XX.

input: Upon receiving our air traffic control clearance there was a fair amount of confusion on how we were cleared due to the language transition from the mexican controller and the flight crew we; therefore; had the clearance reread 3 times to verify what air traffic control wanted us to do on our departure our understanding for our clearance was 'depart runway(s) 33 at mmto; intercept the 314 degree radial to 8 nautical mile then left/right (directions) turn back to the toluca vor and dme (co-located) cross at or above 14000 feet/foot cleared to fl250; then continue on the conto 1 departure to mexico city transition fpr.' however; as we were passing 16400 feet/foot at 8 nautical mile on the 314 degree radial; the departure controller (toluca) asked us to verify our altitude when we did; he informed us that we should be at 14000 feet/foot until the toluca vor and dme (co-located) to prevent conflicts with arriving and departing aircraft to mexico city. I told him that the clearance we had received on the ground was to climb unrestr to fl200 and to cross the toluca vor and dme (co-located) at or above 14000 feet/foot at no time was there any conflict with other aircraft to correct this situation the clearance received on the ground should read 'clb to cross the tlc vor and dme (co-located) at 14000 feet/foot and then climb unrestr to fl200.' supplemental information from acn 504390: this could have been avoided intermediate fix mmto tower controller had used standard phraseology; or intermediate fix mmto had automatic communications addressing & reporting system capability. Company should also issue a 'fly safe' notice to airmen / of air missions to alert crews to nonstandard climb clrncs.
output: AN A300 CARGO CREW CLBS ABOVE THE ALT THAT DEP CTLR THOUGHT THEY HAD BEEN CLRED TO BY TWR CTLR AT MMTO; FO.

input: Upon arrival, arrive at the airplane; i noticed a dangerous goods manifest in the cockpit. It identified our hazardous cargo as class 8 corrosive. 8 liters of sulfuric acid and 8 liters of hydrochloric acid. I was uncomfortable with this type of cargo on the airplane. I decided to checked the customs declaration documents to verify that the dangerous goods manifest was correct. It was not. What i found was that the shipment actually contained 38 liters of sulfuric acid (15.6 liters of hydrochloric acid); 9.04 liters of acidic acid; and 4 liters of isopropanol alcohol. This is well in excess of the maximum 25 liters of dangerous goods limit specified in the manual. Also; the isopropanol alcohol and acidic acid were not identified on the dangerous goods manifest. I had the entire shipment removed from the airplane. All supporting documents are available upon request.
output: MD80 CAPT DISCOVERED THE ACTUAL DANGEROUS GOODS BEING SHIPPED WAS IN EXCESS OF THAT SHOWN ON THE DANGEROUS GOODS MANIFEST. IN ADDITION; THE DANGEROUS GOODS MANIFEST DID NOT LIST ADDITIONAL DANGEROUS GOODS THAT WERE LOADED ON THE ACFT.

input: While flying an emergency medical service helicopter i contacted approach control and was granted permission to enter the active stadium tfr to land to pick up a patient at the hospital rooftop helipad. The hospital helipad is about 3 nautical mile from the stadium and the tfr must be entered in order to conduct a safe approach into the wind and land. Upon my departure i was unable to contact approach control from the hospital rooftop (which is quite normal); second officer i lifted off the helipad in lifeguard status and attempted to contact them in the air to inform them that i was departing the tfr. After several attempts; i was finally able to make positive communications with approach when i reached an altitude of approximately 1500 feet/foot mean sea level the air traffic control controller was very nice and apologized for the delayed communicationss and explained that radio communicationss are many times unreadable at those lower altitudes later that evening i was returning to the hospital with another patient on board and once again in lifeguard status. My flight was extremely short; only 8 minute(s) of en route flight time and i remained at altitudes of 800-1000 feet/foot mean sea level for the entire route in regard to the safety of the patient on board; who was sensitive to pressure and oxygen changes. After about 3 attempts; i was unable to contact approach to enter and land within the stadium tfr. Climbing to altitude would delay my flight and also add pressure to my patient's lungs; making the flight not only longer; but also making it more difficult for the patient to breathe. I continued on my flight path for the safety of my patient; made a blind radio call of my intentions to enter the tfr and land at the hospital within the tfr; then descended for my approach to the helipad. I entered and landed within the stadium tfr without making positive communicationss with approach i was in lifeguard status. The safety and survival of my patient depended on a quick arrival, arrive i do know of many other occasions that other lifeguard flts have had difficulty making radio communicationss at those low altitudes especially when weather is involved and the helicopters are visual flight rules and remaining beneath the cloud ceiling. This is definitely an issue being that there are several hospitals within the stadium tfr. The only fix to this dilemma might be to give lifeguard status aircraft an automatic clearance through this particular stadium tfr while talking on the common air-to-air frequency or; to allow emergency medical service or emergency helicopters at these low altitudes to call approach from cell or satellite phones while inflt to gain permission to enter the tfr (if this were a legal option while in low flight many would utilize it). Cell phones have good reception in areas where radios do not.
output: EMS HELI PLT FORCED TO ENTER STADIUM TFR WITHOUT CONTACTING APPROPRIATE ATC CTL.

input: End of late duty day preceded by a late duty day with short layover. Automatic terminal information service called for runway(s) 24 or runway(s) 33 approach with calm winds. Set up and briefed instrument landing system runway(s) 24. Initial contact with approach told to expect runway(s) 6 approach rush to set up runway(s) 6 approach in flight management system tune radios and brief. Next or following transmission was told to expect runway(s) 24. Asked for winds and approach rpted calm. Asked about runway(s) 6. Told runway(s) 24 or runway(s) 33. Took runway(s) 24. On short final; told about aircraft on approach for runway(s) 33 who was s-turning because approach botched sequencing. On rollout; told to go to taxiway we couldn't make it and then told to roll quickly through intersection of runway(s) as we passed runway(s) 33; saw aircraft less than 50 feet/foot above the ground not sure what was going on; but approach and tower did not have a handle on ops.
output: B757 CREW LNDG BDL RWY 24 WAS UNABLE TO MAKE AN ASSIGNED TURN OFF; INSTRUCTED TO ROLL QUICKLY THROUGH RWY 33 INTXN. WHILE XING RWY 33; OBSERVED TFC -- MOST LIKELY LNDG; ABOUT 50 FT HIGH.

input: After receiving a lengthy departure clearance from the sdl ground controller (which both capt and f/o were familiar with) we were cleared for takeoff by sdl tower and departed runway(s) 03. According to our clearance we began a left climbing turn to heading 260 degrees and 5000' mean sea level all the while prepared to intercept the srp 325 degree left/right (directions) nwbnd. After a longer period of time than we normally experienced prior to being handed off to departure we prompted the sdl tower controller and were advised to switch to the phx departure frequency 120.7. We rpted to phx departure that we were heading 260 degrees level at 5000'. Departure acknowledged our transmission and from what the capt and i recall; we were instructed to maintain our original 260 degree heading and climb to 6000'. In retrospect; both the capt and i then felt this new clearance negated our previous clearance and we continued on our 260 degree heading shortly thereafter we were further instructed to contact phx approach frequency 120.9. This new departure frequency was very busy. After 2 or 3 attempts we finally contacted phx approach with possibly a somewhat abbreviated message; 'clbing to 6000'.' we were then instructed by this second departure controller to climb and maintain 7000'; turn right heading 070 degrees which we acknowledged and were further instructed to 'expedite turn to 070 degs.' this same controller a short time later; queried us as to why we had overflow the srp 325 degree left/right (directions) (which was part of our first departure clrnc). This question took both the capt and myself by surprise because we had felt that we were given a new clearance 'maintain heading 260 degs;' which had precedence over our previous clearance there was obviously some miscom between ourselves and the departure controllers or between the controllers themselves. Only the recorded communicationss may lead to the answer. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: there was no loss of sep and rptr does not think the tapes were ever played. Stated the controller was very busy and thinks controller just neglected to state to intercept radial after giving maintain heading rptr suggested that since this radial off or srp (both a victor and high altitude arwy) is heavily used for nw departures it be incorporated in a standard instrument departure to cut down communications time on clearance delivery.
output: DEP CTLR GAVE INCOMPLETE INSTRUCTIONS CAUSING TRACK DEVIATION BY CORP MDT. OPERATIONAL DEVIATION.

input: Preflt was normal with engine oil levels in the normal ranges. From the cockpit; the takeoff appeared normal; however; personnel in the hangar next to the runway(s) rpted hearing a sound like 'a playing card against bicycle spokes.' about 15 minute(s) into the flight while climbing through 16000 feet/foot we heard an aural 'oil' warning. We were unable to maintain the oil pressure/nh within acceptable limits; second officer the decision was made to shut down the engine i flew the airplane and handled communications while the capt ran the chklists. An emergency was declared and we diverted to dayton. The landing was uneventful. This emergency was handled exactly as we were trained in ground and simulator. Our reaction was instinctive and without excessive excitement. I also feel that excellent cockpit resource management training made this event a 'non event.' it was determined an oil line had ruptured; dumping 14 quarts (non-pre flightable item).
output: FLC OF AN LTT DIVERTED TO LAND WHEN ONE OF THE ENGS LOST OIL PRESSURE AND THE ENG WAS SHUT DOWN. THE MALFUNCTION WAS CAUSED BY A BROKEN ENG OIL LINE. DIVERSION TO ALTERNATE.

input: First controller gave us runway(s) 35r. We did not hear the second controller give us runway(s) 34r. The frequency was busy and we may have missed it. All she said was we were to be taken through the final. As we approached the runway(s) 35r localizer we were given turn left/right (directions) to 320 degrees and intercept the localizer the localizer captured almost immediately and as we rolled out we were told to turn to 320 degrees and intercept runway(s) 34r. We had to reload the box and there was a slight overshoot with no further problems.
output: AN A320 PLT RPTS RECEIVING INITIAL CLRNC FOR DEN RWY 35R AND MISSED CLRNC FOR RWY 34R IN HEAVY RADIO TFC. LOC CAPTURE RWY 35R BUT CREW VECTORED TO RWY 34R WITH FMGC CHANGES.

input: At the departure end of runway(s) 34r at slc; tower advised runway(s) 34r; cleared for takeoff we completed the below the line chklist and began to set takeoff thrust. At approximately 40% north we heard the tower clear an aircraft to cross runway(s) 34r. I remember thinking this was strange because we were just beginning our takeoff roll on that runway(s) i did not advance the power levers because of a potential collision hazard. I could not immediately verify the runway(s) would be clear of this potential traffic aircraft were landing and departing runway(s) 34l; runway(s) 34r; and runway(s) 35. Approximately 1 second later; i retarded the power levers to idle and requested the first officer advise the tower we were aborting the takeoff the tower asked why and we told her we were concerned about the crossing clearance of the other aircraft the aircraft attained a speed of approximately 40 knot(s) no reverse or brakes were used because of the slow aircraft speed we rolled to the best of my recollection to taxiway h3 and exited the runway(s) i advised the passenber and the flight attendants what had happened and that we would taxi back for takeoff no brake cooling procedures were required. The tower advised us the other aircraft was at taxiway h2. I don't remember hearing this during the transmission all i heard was cross runway(s) 34r. I think aborting the takeoff in this situation was the best course of action. We proceeded to runway(s) 34r and departed. I don't know what can be done to prevent this problem from recurring except not to clear an aircraft to cross a runway(s) that is being used by another aircraft for tkof.
output: A B737 PIC ABORTS HIS TKOF ROLL PRIOR TO 40 KTS WHEN HEARING ANOTHER ACFT BEING CLRED ACROSS HIS TKOF RWY 34R AT SLC; UT.

input: We were on an instrument flight rules flight plan; part 121 scheduled flight to sav. We were estimated to arrive sav at xa30. At this late hour the tower was closed and it was necessary to get the field weather observation from zjx. The weather (rpted by awos) was a 20 minute(s) old observation and was visual meteorological conditions conditions rpted were: winds variable at 5 knot(s) sky clear visibility 10 mile temperature 18 degrees celsius dewpoint 17 degrees celsius altimeter 29.65. When we departed cvg; a line of thunderstorms was rpted to have just passed over the airport at sav. When we arrived at sav; they had moved approximately 20 mile east when we were 10 mile from the airport we rpted the airport in sight; as we could see the rotating beacon. Zjx cleared us for the visual approach to runway(s) 9 and gave us a frequency change. The capt was the pilot flying and he flew a downwind; base and final pattern. He flew a visual approach backed up with the instrument landing system to runway(s) 9. As we lined up with the runway(s) and began descending it became apparent that there was a low-lying scattered to broken layer with bases at 500-600 feet/foot above ground level and we were unable to remain clear of the clouds. This inadvertent entry into instrument meteorological conditions while on a visual approach was caused mostly by the extreme darkness of this area (no moonlight and this area westbound of the airport is undeveloped and extremely dark). A contributing factor was the lack of a human weather observer on the field. The automatic weather observing/reporting system was rpting visual meteorological conditions which may have been the case directly over the sensor platform; but was definitely in error. After landing uneventfully; we closed our instrument flight rules flight plan with zjx and issued a pilot report that conditions were marginal visual flight rules at the airport at best; for the benefit of later arriving acft.
output: CL65 CREW ON A VISUAL APCH TO SAV AFTER THE TWR IS CLOSED ENCOUNTERS WX BUT ELECTS TO CONTINUE.

input: During takeoff at v1 experienced an unusual vibration. The vibration ceased after rotation. After chklists were complete during clbout contacted maintenance control the decision was made to continue. Just to be on the safe side an emergency was declared and fire rescue was notified. Landed uneventfully. Experienced vibration after touchdown as nosewheel touched the runway(s) vibration diminished to none as ground speed reduced. Upon further inspection it was determined that part of the tread on the left/right (directions) front tire was missing. (12 inches by 2 inches by 1/2 inch deep.) the tire remained inflated. No damage to the aircraft was noted.
output: A DHC8 NOSE TIRE BEGAN SHREDDING ON TKOF. OTHERWISE UNEVENTFUL TKOF AND LNDG.

input: I was cleared for a visual flight rules 'standard dep' from hawthorne airport (ca) runway(s) 25. After takeoff flew straight in maximum performance climb to hawthorne blvd (noise abatement proc); then turned left/right (directions) heading approximately 200 degrees to intercept shoreline 1-2 mile north of king harbor. About 3 mile from king harbor was advised by tower operator i had entered lax class b airspace. I advised tower i was not aware of that. My altitude was approximately 2000 feet/foot mean sea level overlying class b is charted at 5000-12500 feet/foot mean sea level tower advised 'lax class b surface area' is 'trw and w.' hawthorne class d airspace is depicted on the chart in this area. Later telecon with a different hhr tower operator confirmed the airspace is hhr class d but there is a letter of sub-delegation for the airspace westbound of 405 freeway to lax tower this agreement is unknown to most local pilots except for banner tow and helicopter which operate in the immediate area. I recommend that lax/hhr towers publish a local 'letter to airmen' and post on the airport prominently instructions for visual flight rules departures to remain clear of the sub- delegated lax airspace. The addition of phraseology such as 'remain east of 405 freeway until past trw sbound' to takeoff clrncs (vfr) would help; intermediate fix that is what is desired. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr states there has been no follow up regarding this incident; except on his part. He voluntarily called the tower though not requested to do second officer hawthorne blvd is the first road westbound of the runway(s) and highway 405 is the second road off the end of the runway(s) trw is a building which is a prominent landmark in the area. Rptr spoke with a local pilot examiner who is active in local airspace problems he too felt the chart does not show any controled airspace aside from the class d in this area. Rptr feels a line on the chart indicating where the delegation of airspace occurs; to segregate the two areas; would allow pilots to be aware that this airspace change exists.
output: C172 PLT ON DEP FROM HHR IS TOLD HE IS IN CLASS B AIRSPACE. THE CHART DOES NOT INDICATE THAT THIS IS SO. RPTR IS TOLD THERE IS A DELEGATION OF AIRSPACE TO LAX. AIRSPACE CHANGE NOT SHOWN ON CHART.

input: We continually find ourselves understaffed. Desks continue to be split; trainers taken off training desks to cover sick calls/open desks without overtime list being run with people on the list wanting overtime. In effort to save money we are beating the dispatchers badly to fatigue. Anything deviating from a smooth day creates workload issues. Screen printer becomes a monster....some dispatchers don't even bring it up. Fellow dispatchers are unable or unwilling to help since they were pounded the day before and still exhausted. Podium usually unaware of workload; and often times not very helpful. A time or two after asking them a weather question floater was brought in although it was a little late...and weather was forecast the day before. Lots of fatigue building up with dispatchers. Calling fatigued not an option during a shift...just compounds the problem on the floor. New dispatchers continue to be put on the floor well before they are fully trained. Seems as if they are pushed through training to avoid paying for overtime/open shifts. It used to be okay to learn a lot on the floor after signed off...does not work well these days and hasn't for a while. Weak dispatchers are now training improper or incorrect techniques. Increases workload when take over for new dispatchers (with already a year's experience) who miss alternates; etc....needing extra help from fellow dispatchers who are already busy on the floor.... Latest new dispatcher got a diversion and didn't know what to do. Most new dispatchers do not know how and when to update; unaware of a lot of air traffic control procedures; reroutes; amending releases when taf changes; unaware of r/i r/f u/f entries on jr mask...how and when air traffic control strips sent to air traffic control guess at alternate minimums.... Taught to work as fast as they can to avoid being pummeled not checking winds/altitude minimums/notams. Fahrenheit shift turnovers difficult when everyone else is up to their eyeballs in work. As if we need a dispatcher on call for each shift.
output: A Dispatcher reported he is concerned about training; fatigue; and general work environment issues.

input: During preflight; i tried to retrieve the clearance via controller pilot data link communication (cpdlc) on the aircraft during preflight. The dispatch paperwork stated the aircraft was cpdlc capable. We could not establish air traffic control comm link. Shortly thereafter; i attempted to retrieve the clearance via pre-departure clearance (pdc). The clearance came back via pre departure clearance and was matched up with what had been manually input in to the route page on the flight management computer during our preflight briefing; the flight plan was verified between the dispatch paperwork and the route programmed in the flight management computer as the aircraft was being pushed back from the gate; a clearance was received from the cpdlc even while there was no indication on the engine instrument display screen of an air traffic control data link with the letters 'atc'. The clearance was as filed and it was accepted. While in cruise at 34;000 with indianapolis center; a controller queried as to where we were going? We stated that we were proceeding direct to butler vor and dme (co-located) (bum). The controller responded by asking who had cleared us to butler instead of centralia (enl). We stated that bum was the next fix on our flight plan. The controller asked who had cleared us to bum and we again stated it was the next fix on clearance. He then issued the clearance to proceed direct to bum. We queried if there was an issue that we should be concerned about and the controller stated that he was only trying to determine if a prior controller had issued the clearance to proceed to bum and not enl. The controller then stated that if there was an issue; we would be advised by the next controller; and then handed us off to the next sector controller. We never heard anything regarding the incident upon being handed off to the next sector.
output: B737 First Officer reported a track deviation occurred when there was apparently a routing change that was not reflected in the Pre-Departure Clearance or Controller Pilot Data Link Communication.

input: We received a message from navigate, navigation data that a tape load was being performed. After the tape load was completed; we received another navigate, navigation data message stating the load is complete and that if any flight plans required to be refilled the dispatcher needed to enter frc in the remarks line of the release. Due to schedule disruptions flights were operating 60 to 75 minutes late and 6 to 8 flight plans calculated after the tape load ended. I started to receive reject messages from the air traffic control computer on several fights due to the fact that the host computer did not recognize some of the new sid's that had been filed on these flights. Apparently our tape load was premature and did not coincide with the host computer navigate, navigation update. Therefore the flight plans were rejected. This occurred for three flights i was working. I called navigate, navigation data to find out what they could do to fix the problem. My attempts to build temporary routes were unsuccessful since our computer did not recognize our old sid's. Dispatch desk worked real hard to get new routes built for me and i was able to refile correct flight plans. All this upheaval occurred during a schedule disruption and a nationwide security threat with all my flights needing information and instruction with regard to threat levels and required responses. I certainly didn't need added confusion that easily could have caused improper flight plan filings; possible gross navigation errors or worse. When i asked one of the navigate, navigation data specialists why the tape load was done so early; his response was; 'we always do tape loads at this time.' i recall that this same situation occurred several years ago and the procedure was to have navigate, navigation data check with the center manager prior to initiating a tape load to avoid additional confusion during schedule disruption. Also; why do we prematurely change our navigate, navigation database so much earlier than the air traffic control computer and not expect to have these kinds of problems? I reviewed my flights for navigate, navigation errors and did not find any on the flight plans but a repeat of this situation is unacceptable.
output: Air Carrier Dispatcher reports the company NAV data base being updated prior to the effective time causing many flight plans to be rejected by the ATC computer.

input: Acr x arriving at sfo and needing to taxi to the air carrier y ramp via taxiway left/right (directions) ground cleared us to 'taxi to the ramp.' having a wing span of 148 feet/foot 6 inches; and having read the airport diagram note 'acft with wing spans of 140-156 feet/foot must be under tow with wing walkers on taxiway left/right (directions) east of taxiway left/right (directions) chkpoint;' confusion surfaced as to the location of the chkpoint and direction of tow requirement. Asking for clarification; i requested that company call sfo airport for instructions. Company called sfo operations(s) and faxed me an airport diagram with 'e' changed to 'w' with the notation 'stated wrong; should be w.' leaving the ramp that evening; we were towed with wing walkers to the chkpoint; released to taxi westbound of the chkpoint. Ground informed us that it was prohibited to taxi on taxiway left/right (directions) or to even have the engs running. Having already been towed and taxied to the 'r/s' throat; there was no way to remedy the situation not wanting to argue with ground we thanked them for the clarification and they issued further taxi instructions. Airport diagram needs to be corrected.
output: FLC OF A DC8 CARGO ACFT FAILED TO HAVE THE ACFT TOWED; WITH WING WALKERS; AND ENGS NOT RUNNING; DURING TAXI ON TXWY R AT SFO. ARPT DIAGRAM DID NOT CLARIFY THE CHKPOINT IN THE NOTE REF AND INDICATED THE DIRECTION OPPOSITE TO THE SUBSEQUENT NOTATION ON ANOTHER COPY OF THE ARPT DIAGRAM.

input: We were descending on the panoche 2 arrival, arrive from san to oak. Center handed us off to approach control (134.5). Bay approach gave us a descent to 7000 feet/foot i noticed on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii that we had a target approaching us from 1 o'clock that appeared to be at 7000 feet/foot i told the first officer (pf) to shallow his rate of descent we visually acquired the air carrier y b727 belly up to us in a turn. We stopped the descent about 500 feet/foot above him to ensure he could slide under us intermediate fix necessary. Approach control then called out the traffic we acknowledged traffic in sight; and were told to maintain visual separation. Approach then descended the air carrier y to 6000 feet/foot approach then proceeded to give us paralleling vectors to oak runway(s) 29 that never produced much lateral separation. We began to slow. Approach cleared us visual approach behind the air carrier y b727. We immediately put the gear and full flaps down as we were about 2000 feet/foot higher than normal and almost on top of the air carrier y laterally. This created a ground speed difference and lateral separation. At this point a new voice gave us a 90 degree turn off course for separation and then turned us back for the approach we did our best to comply with all the controller's instructions. I usually keep the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii on 10 mile range in the terminal area on the ivsi and 20 mile range on the radar. This allowed us to spot the conflict before a traffic advisory or resolution advisory was produced and to adjust our flight path accordingly. A traffic advisory did show up at the b727 closest point of approach by this time we were easily maintaining visual separation. I love tcasii.
output: CAPT OF A B737-300 INSTRUCTED THE FO TO SLOW DSCNT FOR A TCASII TARGET THAT WAS INDICATED IN CLOSE PROX TO THEIR FLT PATH ON A STAR ARR. THE TARGET WAS SUBSEQUENTLY SIGHTED; AND A TA ISSUED; OF A B727 ON THE SAME ARR.

input: During initial climb segment (less than 100 feet/foot agl) on departure from rdu; both screens on my side failed (eadi/ehsi) simultaneously. I xferred the flight controls to the acting first officer (chk airman); whose electronic flight instrument system screens were functioning correctly. In order to maintain visual meteorological conditions we decided to level off about 1200 feet/foot above ground level the checked airman recommended we declare an emergency and return to rdu. I agreed and assumed the role of the pilot not flying declared the emergency and asked for left/right (directions) traffic we maintained visual with the ground and the airport however; were unable to execute any troubleshooting through our quick reference handbook a normal visual approach and landing were made by the checked airman from the left/right (directions) seat. All descent and approach and landing chklists were completed.
output: JETSTREAM 41 FLC DECLARED AN EMER AND RETURN LAND AFTER EXPERIENCING THE EFIS PRIMARY ACFT CTL SCREEN FAILURE ON THE CAPT'S SIDE WHO WAS FLYING AND HAD JUST LIFTED OFF ON INITIAL CLB. THE CHK AIRMAN WHO WAS ACTING AS FO TOOK CTL AND RETURNED TO LAND.

input: Flt was released to altitude with bhm as alternate and 2172 pounds of hold fuel. Flight sent efc message at about xb35z. Efc xb00 at sinca. Correction: efc sent message about xa35z. Shortly before xb00z atl operations(s) called dispatch. Flight called atl operations(s) to say they were diverting to jax. Dispatch told atl operations(s) to tell flight to divert to listed alternate of bhm; not jax. Capt said there were strong headwinds to bhm and fuel wise jax was better. Dispatch told flight that jax was not an alternate and fuel burn to jax was higher than to bhm. Then atl operations(s) told flight that air traffic control would clear the flight straight into alternate. Flight said fine. Dispatch hung up with atl operations(s) a few minute(s) later; atl operations(s) called dispatch to say flight had been called back and was going to jax. Dispatch sent flight fuel burn to jax and jax weather notams and flow rpt via automatic communications addressing & reporting system flight landed in jax and aircraft was taken out of service account of crew logbook write-up on a recent item. Please note that federal aviation administration inspector was in the jump seat on this flight and new capt was on his federal aviation administration capt checked ride. Checked capt did not stop new capt from violating federal aviation regulations by diverting to an alternate not specified on the flight release. Flight crew never attempted to contact dispatch to discuss changing alternate or trying to get help being released from holding. This capt violated federal aviation regulations and exercised very poor judgement.
output: CREW DIVERTED TO AN ARPT WITHOUT COORDINATING WITH THE DISPATCHER OR HAVING THE DIVERSION ARPT NAMED AS AN ALTERNATE.

input: Maintenance was servicing the nosewheel strut. In an attempt to get the flight out on time; or at least not take the hit for the delay; they issued a maintenance release prior to the service being completed. In other words; they cleared a maintenance item while they were still working on it. They requested that we push back with an invalid maintenance release. We did not push back until a new legal maintenance release was issued. Supplemental information from acn 820395: while performing the walkaround; i observed that the nose strut appeared to be under serviced due to the fact that no silver was showing on the inner strut cylinder. I found a mechanic who told me he would check the limits. I asked him to let me know what he found out; and completed my walkaround. I got back to the cockpit and made the necessary maintenance release report on automatic communications addressing & reporting system to alert maintenance. Meanwhile; the #3 hydraulic system fault light needed to be re-lamped; but when the mechanic came up to fix the indicator; he found that the contacts were broken and the repair was then deferred. The mechanic who i spoke with about the strut also appeared and reported that a nitrogen service bottle had been requested from 'somewhere on the airfield;' and it would be here soon to service the strut. I inquired as to how long; and he did not know. We noticed the gear door engine indicating and crew alerting system message come on but we never heard when the servicing was begun or completed. We received our maintenance release over the printer with the time stamp. The gear door engine indicating and crew alerting system was still illuminated and we had not been told that the service was complete; and we did not have a deferred sticker on the #3 hydraulic system fault light indicator. In fact; the indicator lamp had been completely removed from the space and placed in one of the compartments above the first officer's table. Captain was very uncomfortable with this situation saying that the dispatch was not legal with the discrepancies noted above incomplete. He initiated several calls to dispatch and we also requested that operations have maintenance send a maintenance release with the correct time stamp for when the work was complete in order to make the release legal. We finally got everything resolved and pushed back; over 30 minutes later than scheduled. The illegal dispatch with maintenance signed off as complete and not actually completed was the main complaint; not to mention the safety aspect of essentially saying the aircraft was ready for 'push' when gear doors were not closed and the potential for personnel still in the wheel well was possible. Supplemental information from acn 820400: i was acting as the first relief pilot. The doors were closed prior to departure and the mechanic still had not put the deferred sticker near the fault light for the deferral. We ended up putting the deferred sticker on the overhead panel to make us legal.
output: B747-400 flight crew reported on the maintenance practices of an international contracted maintenance provider; trying to get them to accept a Maintenance Release; prior to completing the nose strut servicing and the gear doors being closed.

input: After landing in slc; an autospoiler fault light illuminated on the overhead annunciator panel. The fault was written up and maintenance then elected to defer the item. After looking up the problem in the minimum equipment list a performance penalty was noted. The dispatcher was then contacted and asked about the legality of operating into sna with this problem the dispatcher said aircraft could be operated into sna. Plane then departed for sna. A message was received inflt to return to slc; because there was apparently a misunderstanding between maintenance and the dispatcher as to what the real problem was and the proper performance penalty was not applied initially. Therefore; the aircraft was overwt for landing in sna. The problem was a repeat write-up; and could be corrected by following the procedures in the book; which consisted of resetting circuit breakers for the system the problem was fixed in slc and redispatched for sna. Supplemental information from acn 379437: problem returned after clearing runway(s) was ok for landing fixed with box change. We couldn't find sna in airport section of aircraft restrs manual. Return decided because of legalities and safety considerations.
output: MD90 INCORRECTLY DISPATCHED WITH AN AUTO SPOILER PROB DEFERRED BY MAINT CTL. THE EQUIP PROB WAS NOT ASSESSED PROPERLY. ACFT RECALLED FOR MAINT ACTION. 'BOX' WAS CHANGED AND CIRCUIT BREAKERS RESET. PROB STILL EXISTED AFTER LNDG AT DEST ARPT. ACFT NEW TO AIRLINE.

input: As the flight was slowing and configuring for the landing; the crew (double augmented) was attempting to utilize the new standard operating procedure guidance of not selecting a mode control panel airspeed in the mode control panel window that is below the actual minimum flap maneuvering speed for the flaps selected at that time. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot not flying as the aircraft approached the final approach fix with flaps 5 and the speed set to 180 knot(s) the captain called for; 'gear down; landing checklist.' with the gear coming down; the captain then called for; 'flaps 15; speed.' the first officer set the new flap setting and adjusted the mode control panel speed to the flap 15 minimum maneuvering value. By the time he had the speed set; the captain was calling for; 'flaps 20; speed.' setting the flaps to 20 and resetting the mode control panel speed to flaps 20 minimum maneuvering; the aircraft was approaching 1;000 feet/foot above ground level and the captain asked for; 'flaps 25; set target speed.' then came the 1;000 feet/foot call with the captain asking for the missed approach altitude of 2;000 feet/foot to be set as the tower was clearing the flight to land.
