The controllers did not ask him to declare an emergency in order to enter class a airspace and appeared willing to assist.
output: A BE33 PLT CLBED ABOVE 17500 FT IN SEA AIRSPACE IN ORDER TO REMAIN VMC AND ABOVE THE ICING LAYER. ATC ASSISTED VMC DSCNT PLANNING.

input: Working b position; sitting aft aircraft left. At 10;000 feet turned on galley lights and noticed r2 door handle in a compromised position. Called flight deck; captain (ca) asked me to push down on handle; it bounced back up to compromised position. All indicators upfront reading ok. Confirmed with celsius flight attendant that door handle had not been like that on the ground; she also tried to reset it and it bounced back up. Called ca again to express handle did not look right and had not been like that before takeoff. Ca said he would call maintenance. While he was calling; their door indicator light came on in the flight deck. Ca called back and said we were turning around and heading back. When we were asked to take our seats for landing by the ca i elected to take 28c. There was also a pilot jumpseater in 28d who i introduced myself to and showed the r2 door so he understood the issue with it. After we landed safely i returned to my jumpseat to be near doors. We deplaned as usual and commenced delay.
output: In a climb out of 10;000 feet; a B737 Flight Attendant notices that the R2 door handle is in a compromised position. Attempts to return the handle to the normal closed position are unsuccessful and the flight returns to the departure airport.

input: After crossing final approach fix inbound to thv; gear selector was placed down. Only the nose and left/right (directions) main gear green lights illuminated and the red unlocked light was on. We recycled the gear but the indications were the same. We terminated the approach and orbited ne of the field and executed the appropriate emergency chklist per the flight manual. After executing the chklist; we contacted harrisburg approach to get vectors to mountain daylight time while en route we called local fixed-base operator to relay message to our home base. We executed an instrument landing system at mountain daylight time with low approach to verify that the landing gear was down. According to the tower the landing gear appeared to be down. We made a left/right (directions) traffic pattern and landed uneventfully. Upon touching down the left/right (directions) main gear light came on; indicating that the gear light switch was stuck. A mechanic replaced the switch. We requested to have emergency vehicles standing by; however; we never verbally declared an emer.
output: SMT ACFT HAD UNSAFE GEAR INDICATION FOR R MAIN; BROKE OFF APCH; ORBITED ARPT DOING EMER CHKLIST. UNABLE TO OBTAIN A SAFE INDICATION; PLT DIVERTED TO ANOTHER ARPT. AFTER LNDG THE GEAR LIGHT CAME ON INDICATIVE OF A STUCK SWITCH.

input: An unexpected change of runway(s) and approach caused us to continue something that we had not done; nor briefed. We were 1000 feet/foot high on 2 mandatory xings for the approach and light emitting diode to an unstabilized situation on final. We should never have accepted the assignment. A proper briefing should have been made. We were in excess of 1500 feet per minute on final below 500 feet/foot upon roundout for landing we got the ground proximity warning system 'terrain; terrain; pull up.' we also got 'gs; pull up' (as the first officer still had the original runway(s) 22l instrument landing system dialed on slide). The landing was made in the touchdown zone uneventfully. I can assure you that this situation will never happen to me again; as i now notice all of the events overlooked that would have flagged the problem supplemental information from acn 618754: we had briefed and set up our flight management system system for the instrument landing system to runway(s) 4r which was being given to other aircraft in addition to the ils's to runway(s) 22s at jfk. On what we thought was a base turn for instrument landing system to runway(s) 4r; approach cleared us for the vor and dme (co-located) to runway(s) 13l. The capt elected to accept the clearance despite the fact that we had not briefed nor set up the approach at this point; and for the remainder of the flight we were visual meteorological conditions with the field in sight. I was uncomfortable with accepting the clearance but because of my low time in this aircraft and the fact that i had never encountered such a situation before in my experiences; i relied on the capt's decision making skills. Passing canarsie; the mandatory altitude is 1500 feet/foot we were more than 3000 feet/foot i felt executing a missed approach would result in further deviations because it had not been briefed. At this point we were following the lead-in lights; on short final. We also earlier received the 'gs' aural warning because my electronic flight instrument system system was still programmed for the instrument landing system approach during the vor and dme (co-located) approach i was answering the capt's questions and setting up his side for the approach this problem happened because we had fully set up for an approach we were never told specifically to expect. Hindsight being 20/20; we could have asked approach what to expect; requested delay vectors to set up for the vor and dme (co-located) or requested a specific approach my lack of experience in this acft/operating environment did not adequately 'back up' the needs of the capt. The only thing that kept us from scraping metal; or causing damage; was the capt's finesse during the flare. There was no doubt in either of our minds having landed that we were wrong -- after all; hindsight is 20/20.
output: A CL-65 FLT CREW FAIL TO BRIEF A CHANGED APCH RESULTING IN A NON STABILIZED APCH; MISSING REQUIRED APCH XING RESTRS.

input: Controller pilot data link communications (cpdlc) not yet ready for prime time. Dangerous.1. This system must be modified to allow the current clearance to be printed out on the cockpit printer.2. When a complete reroute is sent via this system; the new route must be allowed to be printed and reviewed prior to auto-loading it in the fms.the current system of having an air traffic control clearance; current and /or revised; stored on multiple; disjointed pages of the automatic communications addressing & reporting system / flight management system display is confusing; causes excessive heads down time while taxiing; will cause a gross navigation error (i would wager multiple errors have already occurred) and is just plain stupid.we were taxiing out of a very congested; weather-impacted; jfk airport the other day. Ground freq was non-stop due to long taxi routes because of 20-mile in-trail spacing for departing aircraft in all directions. A cpdlc message for 'this is a revised clearance' appeared with no other information (no revised route included).spent next 5-10 minutes heads down; while taxiing; trying to figure out what was happening; in addition to eventually calling clearance delivery on the radio; and dispatch. No place to pull out of way due to long taxiways with no exits. And; we were getting automatic automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages about must be airborne in 15 minutes due to 9 hour flight time restriction. A simple printout of the revised clearance would have resolved the issue in a few moments and been much more intuitive. This is a defective system and it is going to harm someone.
output: B737-800 pilot reported that he does not believe that Controller Pilot Data Link Communications is 'ready for prime time' yet. He stated that being able to print both the original and revised clearance would be a great improvement and would enhance understanding of the revision; rather than blindly uploading the information into the FMC.

input: While en route from ocl to azo; i decided to divert to sbn in order to purchase additional fuel. I had filled the aircraft with enough fuel (30 gallons) in kansas to give me 50 gallons of fuel for the anticipated 4 hour trip at a rate of 10 gph; compensating for necessary reserves. During cruise; i noticed the fuel gauges registering lower than i was comfortable with; and when i decided i had about 15 gallons remaining (i was approximately 3.5 hours into the flt) between both tanks made the decision to refuel. I called up sbn about 13 mile se of the airport to request to land '...to purchase fuel...that i was low....' they gave me permission to descend from my cruise altitude of 7000 feet/foot cleared to 3000 feet/foot about that time i switched tanks to the left/right (directions) from the left/right (directions) as i passed through 5500 feet/foot the engine became rough and sputtered; still maintaining some rpm's but not enough to maintain safe descent i called sbn; indicated i had a problem the engine was out; i had no fuel (so i thought) and needed to land immediately. They cleared me for any runway(s) i switched back to the left/right (directions) tank and the engine ran normally for about 1 minute(s) having been cleared to land on any runway(s) i attempted to line up for runway(s) 36l; runway(s) 9l; runway(s) 18; but was federal aviation regulation too high in all instances. As i lined up for runway(s) 18; i was 1800 feet/foot high; and dropped the landing gear. I decided i was still federal aviation regulation too high to make a safe landing second officer continued to circle around for runway(s) 27r. I landed on runway(s) 27r without incident; or damage to either the aircraft the airport or injury to my passenber 1 passenber did sustain a broken eyeglass band when she inadvertently hit herself in the temple after landing she was holding onto her brother. The airplane rolled out onto the runway(s) i shut it down and promptly evacuated the plane. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that the fuel pump had been changed during the acft's annual inspection. He had just received the sierra from maintenance prior to leaving home base for his flight to kansas city. He faithfully checkeds the travel and detent position of his fuel selector during his preflt inspection. He said that the be24 has a known problem with the retaining screws on the fuel selector 'working' their way out due to aircraft vibration. This is what happened on the way back to home base when he went from left/right (directions) tank to the left/right (directions) tank. He thought that the detent had been entered but failed to checked visually (night time) that it was seated properly. Second officer the engine stopped due to fuel starvation. The aircraft holds 58 gallons of fuel. He only took 50 gallons out of ocl for his return flight when asked why not the 58 gallons; he said that the aircraft was near maximum gross weight he was slightly behind in his flight plan and simply had second thoughts about fuel reserves at destination airport and felt that instead of the 1 hour reserve; he might have about 50 minute(s) rather than 'sweat it out' regarding the required 45 minute(s) reserve he decided to land at sbn. The federal aviation administration sent him a form to fill out regarding this incident second officer he feels that they may be asking him questions about possible fuel mismgmnt. He feels this was an aircraft maintenance discrepancy or design prob.
output: CB A BE24 (SIERRA) PVT PLT MAKES AN EMER LNDG AT SBN WHEN HIS ENG STARTS TO RUN ROUGHLY AND FINALLY FAILS.

input: On flight to grk after deviating around weather we were cleared to descend to 2;000 feet for vectors instrument landing system 15. When [we] were at 2;000 myself and the first officer (fo) remarked that this seems very low at that time we got a too low gear warning at that time we asked air traffic control if he wanted us at 2;000 since that is what we were cleared to. He said i was going to tell you to climb up to 3;000 for vectors for the instrument landing system 15. So we did and completed the approach. We were approximately about 5 miles from okest fix for the ils.i believe the controller said 2;000 feet and that is what we said back and verified with each other it was 2;000 feet. It also was a long delay in zzz due to severe weather along the route.make sure both crewmembers verify the minimum safe altitude and landing elevation to maybe prevent this from happening again.
output: An air carrier crew on vectors for GRK ILS Runway 15 was given a descent to 3;000 feet but read back and descended to 2;000 feet. The crew felt low and when asking about the cleared altitude received an EGPWS 'TOO LOW GEAR' aural warning.

input: I participated in a 'fly-by' at 800 feet/foot above ground level at the bkd airport on may/sun/93. Several type aircraft operating at altitudes from 200 feet/foot above ground level through 800 above ground level airspds varied from 60 mph to 160 mph. Due to the amount of traffic (40 plus acft) most pilots (9 out of 17) brought a 'tfc observer' in the back seat as is done at most air shows (usually with the 'blessings' of the faa). After landing all of the pilots that had observers were advised by the federal aviation administration representatives that we had 'violated' the air show waiver by exceeding the 'minimum crew' that was required. At previous air shows an 'observer' was considered to be additional safety factor. The air show waiver was for low level aerobatics; high speed passes (250 knot(s) plus); aerobatics on an airway; etc. None of these things were done on my 'fly-by.' while i don't agree that i was in violation of the waiver i do believe that flying with an observer was safer than flying without one. P.s. The 'formation' was thoroughly planned and briefed prior to takeoff as required by federal aviation regulation 91.
output: PLT OF A PVT MTR ACFT EXCEEDED THE MINIMUM CREW AIR SHOW WAIVER PROVISION BY CARRYING AN OBSERVER.

input: I had gotten just wet runway(s) rpts from 3 flts and the field condition rpt stated runway(s) 17l/35r wet with braking action good. Both runway(s) 17l/35r and runway(s) 12/30 are grooved and runway(s) 17r/35l has porous friction overlay second officer i released flight dfw-cos with #2 thrust reverser inoperative though there was still precipitation i felt that the runway(s) would be good. When flight landed; capt had trouble stopping aircraft and put flat spot on all tires. Supplemental information from acn 400013: aircraft landed and rpted runway(s) slippery that he could barely keep aircraft on the runway(s) he blew 1 tire and balded the other 3.
output: DISPATCHER RPTR'S ACR MLG RELEASED FLT WITH INOP #2 REVERSER. BRAKING ACTION WAS CHANGING AND WHEN THEIR ACFT LANDED; RWY WAS FAIR BRAKING; RESULTING IN 1 BLOWN TIRE AND FLAT SPOTS ON THE OTHERS.

input: Ctlr stated that airplane climbed from 1500 feet/foot to assigned altitude of 2000 feet/foot before plane reached the teb 4.5 vor and dme (co-located) fix. Pilot feels he followed the standard instrument departure and did not start climb from 1500 feet/foot to 2000 feet/foot until the 4 vor and dme (co-located) fix and controller was incorrect.
output: C525 PLT DISPUTES ATC CLAIM OF FAILURE TO MEET TEB 5 DEP CLB RESTRS.

input: Clbing out of las; encountered moderate turbulence at 26500 feet/foot (wind shift from 216 degs/18 knot(s) to 260 degs/30 kts). Pitch increased to 13 degrees exceeded cleared altitude of 27000 feet/foot leveloff at 27000 feet/foot would have resulted in negative g's. Seat belt sign was off and flight attendants were up and about. Leveled at 27700 feet/foot and notified air traffic control of deviation and turbulence air traffic control cleared us to 29000 feet/foot and we continued clb.
output: A WDB ACR FO DESCRIBED A MODERATE TURB ENCOUNTER WHILE CLBING OUT OF LAS; WHICH CAUSED THE ACFT TO OVERSHOOT THE ASSIGNED ALT.

input: Ifr flight plan filed for published departure. Washington center was then called to give a heads up for coordination; with anticipated off time. Washington center gave new squawk code and frequency. Pilot lifted on schedule and finally got radio contact over first fix at 1;200 feet/foot controller wanted to know who had given me permission to fly that departure; when told clearance had come from washington center while on ground; pilot was told to continue as they did not have radar contact at that time. When radar contact was finally established controller verified pilot was flying published departure toward ridge line; and was told to continue. Controller then told pilot to come to heading of 275 and continue until controller figured out how to vector pilot to initial approach fix at destination airport; which was in new york center's airspace. When pilot verified he was shooting a published approach to the york airport and not a helicopter point in approaches airspace; controller said she was aware of that but she did not have the plates for that area since it was not in her airspace. She eventually told me to contact harrisburg approach for vectors and clearance for the approach to york. By this time our flight to york airport was delayed by approximately 10-20 minutes. This approach has been unsatisfactory since its inception. The missed approach procedure turns the aircraft back toward the ridge line and p-40. If the president is at camp david; this approach will not be approved under actual conditions since the missed goes into the expanded p-40. Whoever designed this approach should have been aware of this and placed the missed in another direction. This approach also utilizes two different centers to complete; mandating coordination between centers to start and end the approach. On the initial approach; though the approach went rather smoothly; the controller at harrisburg approach which had the initial part of the procedure was not aware that the frequency switch should go to washington center. He thought the switch went to potomac approach. Had the pilot been from out of the area and not known the procedure; it could have caused unnecessary delay getting the confusion worked out and the correct contacts identified. This would result in unnecessary vectoring and fuel consumption while things were being worked out. This approach should be redesigned with emphasis being placed on keeping it in the same airspace and having the missed procedures turn away from and not toward camp david.
output: A helicopter pilot noted the confusion caused by working between both ZDC and ZNY Controllers during a THV IFR approach. The interaction caused an extensive in flight delay. As a separate issue; the Runway 17 Missed Approach reportedly may take an aircraft into the P-40 expanded airspace when the President is at Camp David; although this statement could not be verified on the commercial chart.

input: On approach into msp at xa00 local prior to final approach fix approach control told us that the runway visual range for runway(s) 30r was 4000 feet/foot automatic terminal information service at that time said the visibility was 1 1/2 mile the approach controller then said that tower might be calling some other visibility; calling into question the runway visual range value. We continued for the instrument landing system runway(s) 30r because we were 1-2 mile from the final approach fix and we were assuming that tower was calling the higher value. After we passed the final approach fix tower called the visibility below clear air turbulence 1 instrument landing system minimums. We continued the approach and went missed.
output: B757 MISSES APCH IN IMC CONDITIONS IN MSP AIRSPACE.

input: I was on flight following and talking to las vegas approach control. During decent for final approach to khnd i noticed a small amount of fluid on the windscreen that i took to be condensation on the interior of the window. It was not. When the defroster had no effect i tried to wipe it off and realized it was on the outside of the glass. It was only a small spot and i could look around it so i continued descent. When i reduced power the spot grew larger and began to obstruct my forward view. I reduced decent rate to buy time to investigate the problem. By this time the windscreen was 70% obscured with oil. Air traffic control informed me i had entered bravo without being cleared and then cleared me for bravo and asked me to expedite descend. I apologized and complied. I was able to see the airport though the side window and told air traffic control i had the airport in sight. They switched me to khnd tower who cleared me for straight in 35l.i was unable to see out most of the front window but i could see the blurry but bright runway lights through it. I was able to land the aircraft by looking out the side window for vertical guidance and tracking the runway left edge during touchdown.though the entire event i could hear my instructor's voice in my head 'aviate; navigate and then communicate'. I managed to keep the plane right side up and find the airport. However; i did not communicate well enough with atc.in hindsight i should have asked for help.
output: A Bonanza pilot reported that he entered Class Bravo Airspace after he discovered that oil was obscuring 70% of his windscreen. He landed successfully; but he laments not reporting his condition to ATC.

input: On arrival, arrive iah gland seven; aircraft encountered light/moderate turbulence abeam airport in scattered/broken layer approximately 7000 feet/foot mean sea level flight attendant was preparing to situation in aft flight attendant jump seat for landing when turbulence occurred. Movement of aircraft caused her to bump her head on bar cart next to jump seat. #1 flight attendant notified me on arrival, arrive at gate that incident occurred. Flight attendant was ambulatory and conscious and proceeded to company clinic for evaluation. Flight attendant schedules notified and capt irregularity rpt filed.
output: WHILE PREPARING FOR LNDG LIGHT TO MODERATE TURB WAS ENCOUNTERED IN A B737. 1 FLT ATTENDANT'S HEAD BUMPED A SERVING CART NEXT TO THE JUMP SEAT.

input: I was under the hood in left/right (directions) seat making practice localizer 21 approach to ckb. Tower had already cleared us to land. At about 8.6 vor and dme (co-located) from vor and dme (co-located) (or about 5 mile from rwy) tower asked how federal aviation regulation we were from airport i answered that we were about 8 vor and dme (co-located) from the vor and tacan (co-located) tower cleared the cessna to enter pattern in front of us. At about 3 mile and 2000 feet/foot my safety pilot in left/right (directions) seat saw the cessna below and to our left/right (directions) on base leg. We called out traffic to tower and asked what they wished us to do. The tower didn't respond; second officer we called again. Finally the tower told us to s-turn and land #2. I was too close and fast for that; second officer i asked to do a 360 degree turn. Tower told us to do a 360 degree turn to left/right (directions) which involved a lot of climbing to clear hills near airport contributing factors: both local radars were out; and in spite of '10 mile visibility' haze was very thick; second officer tower couldn't see traffic it was trying to control my answer to twr's question was not what she expected. She wanted distance from airport but i gave distance from vor and tacan (co-located) (more precise; but not what asked).
output: A COMMERCIAL RATED PLT FLYING A PA28 NEAR CKB EXECUTED A MISSED APCH AFTER REALIZING A CONFLICT WITH ANOTHER ACFT CLRED TO LAND BEFORE HIM.

input: The area was short staffed. We only had 8 controllers to start the shift. The supervisor left on leave so a controller in charge was stood up. As the evening went on every time i plugged in i would almost reach two hours on position. Other controllers did reach two hours or more. At one point sectors 20; 63; and 78 were combined up to give relief to a controller that was there on overtime and had been on position for more than 2 hours [without] a break. This resulted in the combined sector being red for well over an hour straight. The controller working the sector was given a trainee that was not certified on one of the sectors that were combined as a d-side. The controller working the red sectors ended up on position for over two hours by himself. On top of that we were given reroutes for aircraft from tmu; but the points [where] the reroute took place were well inside zfw center and there was no reason for us to give the change especially with the current workload. The new policy in the building during the day is that controllers are not allowed to work red sectors so we continually split sectors and we are told that tmu is doing something. Now we have controllers who are not used to working this volume of traffic and i feel as if tmu did nothing because they were still asking us to do more and they were going home anyway. This was probably one of the worst situations i have seen of not caring about the controllers from management. It repeatedly happens on the mid. Management is always acting concerned about volume when upper management is there during the day but not on the mid when they are at home.the fix to this would be to staff to 10 on a swing as this is not the first time that we had to hold people over because we are short staffed on the swing.
output: ZAB Controller reported of short staffing and management's policy related to working traffic when the sector is in the red (Monitor Alert Parameter).  Controller would like to see shift staffing up to what the requested numbers are.

input: After modeling a slip for my student with the airplane in its proper configuration; we experienced engine roughness at 3;000 feet mean sea level we were on a 4 mile 45 entry for the downwind for runway 18. I established best glide; called our position; situation and intentions to the two aircraft in the area (which was to proceed inbound for a short approach landing due to engine roughness) then began to troubleshoot. I confirmed that the carb heat was full on; mixture full rich; fuel tanks on both with both being nearly full and fuel gauges checked normal. When we departed; both tanks were full at 26 gallons total and our flight according to the hobbs was 1.1. The mags also checked okay. Despite full throttle; we were in a steady descent with minimal engine power and unable to climb. Approximately 1 mile east of our downwind entry; it was evident we would not make the runway; and with housing between us; i opted to remain to the east; and aim for a field east of the housing. I continued my descent and prepared for a forced landing; while continuing to attempt to regain power. The two aircraft that were in the pattern had visual on our position. At approximately 100 feet above ground level i attempted the throttle one last time. The engine regained full power; was smooth; and i was able to establish a climb. I continued my climb and was able to establish an altitude to safely proceed over the housing which would allow me the option; should it occur again; to glide to either side of the development; at about 800 feet above ground level i was able to enter a short base and land without incident. The engine remained normal.
output: C150 instructor reported engine roughness and loss of power after demonstrating a slip at 3;000 feet with a recovery at about 100 feet AGL with a climb to pattern altitude and a successful landing. Instructor reported probable carb icing.

input: While on final to runway(s) 18r at dfw; we had trouble establishing communications with dfw tower we thought we heard the controller issue a landing clearance to us but the #1 communications radio was intermittent and some xmissions were garbled. The weather conditions were visual flight rules and air traffic was light; second officer we made the decision to land. We made an entry for the #1 very high frequency communications radio second officer it could be checkeded upon landing we re-established communications with tower and there was no indication of a conflict.
output: AN MD80 FO RPTED THAT THEY LANDED AT DFW; EVEN THOUGH THEIR RADIO PROBS MADE THEM UNSURE IF THEY HAD ACTUALLY BEEN CLRED TO LAND.

input: I was the pilot flying on a delayed flight to lga. The weather in lga was marginal all day with low ceilings; rain and gusty winds. The two prior flights to ours had cancelled and the two flights after us cancelled as well. Our aircraft arrived late and we spent close to an hour in the awaiting our edct. We held for close 40 minutes just 5 minutes shy of diverting to avp or jfk. We were vectored for instrument landing system 13 to lga and were informed of pireps reporting speed gains and losses of up to 15 knots on final. With the speed fluctuations; i instructed the first officer (pilot monitoring) to watch my speed. At 1000 feet mean sea level we experienced the reported speed gains and losses of 15kts a couple times. We were in instrument meteorological conditions it was raining heavily and the wipers were on high - cockpit noise was high. I kept the ap and at's on as i transitioned from 'inside the cockpit' to 'outside - flying visually' as the first officer called the runway -'in sight!' [at] 600-700 feet [agl] i got visual of the runway. Prior to the '500 foot call out' we got the wind shear warning. The warning lasted just a few seconds and my speed fluctuated only 10-12kts. By the time i realized what had happened the warning went away; we were still on glide path; localizer and the speed was under control. I continued the approach and landed safely. We discussed what had happened after the flight and both agreed that i should have initiated the wind shear recovery procedure. The first officer said he prompted me to initiate the recovery procedure but i didn't hear it at the time. I realized what had happened too late and it was over so quick. I never actually heard the 3 wind shear audible warnings. This was my first wind shear warning on landing; outside the simulator.be more proactive and vigilant when it comes to wind shear events. Brief recovery procedures prior to takeoff and landing; when wind shear warnings/pireps exist.
output: ERJ-170 flight crew reported receiving a wind shear warning on approach to LGA but nevertheless continued to landing.

input: At night; cleared to land. Below 500 feet; after selecting 20 degrees of flaps; and bringing the nose up to slow down; a total loss of engine power occurred. An attempt to restart the engine failed. Gliding down i landed on the extended runoff area prior to the threshold of the runway. The aircraft continued rolling and was unable to stop before contact with plastic barriers placed across the pavement. The nose gear wheel pant was damaged with the fiberglass cracked.after the incident i found the two electronic ignition power switches in the off position. The only explanation is that during the run-up; these were turned off to check the internal power from the emag ignition; and they were never turned back on. The ignition supplies its own power; unless the engine revolutions per minute drops below approximately 1400 revolutions per minute once the engine revolutions per minute got too low; both ignition emag devices stopped supplying the spark plugs.
output: Vans RV-9 pilot reported the engine quit on short final; leading to slight damage to a wheel pant after a runway excursion. Reporter stated after landing he found the ignition power switches in the wrong position; causing the engine to shut down.

input: I was doing an 'a' checked on aircraft xyz; and per the paperwork i was supposed to lower the flaps. I looked around to make sure there was no equipment under the flaps and went up and turned on hydraulic then i lowered the flaps. My partner came up and told me that the reverser cowls were open on #2 engine i had forgotten that you could not lower flaps with reverser cowl open. Second officer i raised the flaps back up and went down and found the damage. Second officer the first thing i did was to go to axax; the crew chief; and told him what happened and then i went to azyx; the supervisor and told him what happened. Azyx called a sheet metal man over to see what they could do with it. He told azyx that he thought it was out of limits; but that he would go back to the shop and make sure. I didn't hear any more about it from the sheet metal man. Azyx pulled me aside later in the morning and told me that he had taken care of it; that it was within limits and he had put it in the damage log. He gave me a silver department of transportation to put on damaged area. The next day i found out that azyx had used my name and employee number on the rpt in the damage log and that the damage was out of limits. I did not sign anything; nor did i know that it was out of limits.
output: A B757-200 WAS DISPATCHED WITH OUT OF LIMITS SKIN DAMAGE TO THE R INBOARD THRUST REVERSER CAUSED BY EXTENDING SLATS AND FLAPS WITH OPEN THRUST REVERSER COWLING.

input: Our flight plan was direct wleee3 aus. During climb we were cleared direct bocck (named after the style of beer; i suspect) which we complied with. When i opened the wleee arrival on my ipad i saw that on the arrival there is a 'bbach' intersection; presumably named for the composer. I figured we were correct in going to bocck; but i queried the controller to confirm (and yes; we were correct).i question the wisdom of having two intersections with identical pronunciations in such close proximity. To reduce the potential for confusion; how about renaming bbach to batvn (beethoven)?
output: Air Carrier Captain reported of similar sounding intersections that caused confusion for their flight to AUS.

input: Both first officer and i thought we were cleared to 4000 feet/foot approach control said we were cleared to 5000 feet/foot controller stated there was no problem and to have a nice day. We believe the cause to either be: we did not listen correctly; or the controller misstated the cleared alt.
output: ALTDEV POSSIBLE OVERSHOOT ON DSCNT.

input: While on an instrument flight rules time building flight to gain instrument flight rules proficiency; was being vectored through and around class b airspace which put me about 15 mile from the nearest solid ground had just leveled off after descending from 7000 feet/foot to 2000 feet/foot when engine quit. My first thought was to turn to the nearest airport as i was simultaneously pushing the mixture to full rich and turning on the fuel pump. As soon as i got airtime i xmitted a mayday and requested vectors to the nearest airport what i did not do was fly the airplane. By the time i finished talking to the controller i was descending through 800 feet/foot at 1000 feet per minute i pulled the nose up for best glide and finally remembered to switch tanks. At 300 feet/foot above ground level the engine restarted and i was able to climb back to 2000 feet/foot my inattention to fuel management was the single cause. I had set my timer for 15 minute(s) as a reminder to switch tanks which i had done twice on this flight but opted not to change at the last interval since the gauge appeared to show 1/4 to 1/2 tank remaining. I neglected to checked again since i had become engrossed in the navigate, navigation instruments i was trying to get the most from my experience by checkeding my position with vor's and vor and dme (co-located) in addition to using the global positioning system in the future i will stick to my fuel management plan and not rely solely on the fuel gauges. When confronted by an engine failure my first priority will forever be to 'fly the airplane.' the extra weight forward of the pa32 really drops the nose when power is lost and it must be trimmed for best glide.
output: PA32 PLT EXPERIENCED ENG FAILURE DUE TO FUEL MISMANAGEMENT. ENG WAS SUCCESSFULLY RESTARTED.

input: Flying at [cruise] altitude we received an engine indicating and crew alerting system message celsius hydraulic qty. After checking our status page we realized we were down [to] 49 percent. Realizing we had a leak in the center system we elected to depressurize the system by turning off both electric pumps and the center demand pump and switching autopilot from center to left. This stopped the loss of fluid. We now had one hour and 20 minutes to plan for a total loss of the center system and our plan of action. Since we had 49 percent left in the center system and this was holding we decided we would turn the pumps on when on approach and see if gear and flaps would extend normally. We discussed our option if they did not and we both were well versed on hydraulic system pressure (c only) checklist. On approach flaps and gear did extend; however fluid loss was increasing. We had discussed that the loss of all center fluid down to the standpipe was a possibility; so we could use reserve brakes and steering if needed. Approach and landing were normal and we had 11 percent fluid left with steering commands normal. We taxied in leaving the flaps down and had enough fluid to steer to parking. The cause of the leak was determined to be an o-ring the size of a dime that had deteriorated.
output: B767 pilot reported landing safely with a leak in the C hydraulic system that ultimately reduced quantity to 11%.

input: At flight level 350 the right engine rolled back. The appropriate enroute emergency procedures and quick reference handbook (qrh) procedures were conducted. The engine responded to throttle movement at fl245 and i leveled at fl240. An uneventful; overweight; 2 engine landing ensued.
output: At FL350; Engine anti-ice turned off; Right Engine parameters rolled back; turned Engine anti-ice on; descended to FL250 and regained engine control.

input: I was working as a radar controller at zdc air route traffic control center on sector 19; 3/mon/88. I took the handoff on lgt x at fl240 and descended him to fl210; i accepted the handoff on mlg y climbing to fl210. I thought the mlg y was turning ne bound over ood. I briefed the next controller and walked away. He called me back and showed me what happened. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: separation was lost between the lgt and the mlg. Aircraft were on crossing courses and rptr had thought they would be parallel. Aircraft got within 1.4 mile and 400' by odep readout. The controller that relieved the rptr had been plugged in for about 2-3 minute(s) and then was given the sector as the rptr took a break. Rptr was still in the area when the relieving controller said to come back and see what was happening. Relieving controller was very experienced and had trained the rptr. Traffic vol was light; 6 aircraft and weather was not a factor. Controller working sector at time of less than standard separation was working alone in combined position confign. Rptr admits that relief briefing was not thorough and that is why the rptr was classified as controller (a) in this incident. Reliever was controller (b). Action taken by reliever was incomplete to maintain legal sep. Not known intermediate fix traffic was given or sighted.
output: LESS THAN STANDARD SEPARATION BETWEEN CLIMBING AND DESCENDING ACFT ON CROSSING COURSES. INCIDENT JUST AFTER POSITION RELIEF HAD TAKEN PLACE.

input: Atc queried at urnuw why we hadn't turned to cdc. Pre departure clearance initial clearance read wevic 1 bce ksino. Amended line showed wevic 1 ksino. No mention of cdc. Zlc was also confused with this clearance and understood the confusion. No factor. Within 4 mile for correction. Flight continued uneventfully to ksino and grndpa 1. Amended clearance should read: wevic 1.cdc.ksino. That would clarify departure for both air crew and center supplemental information from acn 802289: we noted that we were flying as cleared with bce as our transition; ie; wevic 1 ksino bce gndpa1. We then noticed the amended portion of the pre departure clearance was different. Wevic1 ksino grndpa1. The amended clearance when we researched showed that we should pass over cdc rather than bce. The controller said he was also confused by the pre departure clearance clearance and it wasn't clear to him what our filed route should be. No problem though; and he cleared us to ksino and the rest of the filed route we advised him that we could see our error and that he was right about cdc. We continued without further incident. The amended clearance was confusing. It would have helped intermediate fix the clearance would have noted cdc rather than no transition as the identify for the fork in the road (so to speak). Often an amended clearance shows a little difference from the filed route but when we research the routing there is no difference. We need the transition to show up; ie; cdc to help hindsight a different route example: filed as wevic1 ksino bce grnpa1. Amended as: wevic1 ksino grnpa1.
output: FLIGHT CREW OF B737-700 SUFFERS TRACK DEVIATION WHEN FILED ROUTE AND REVISED SEGMENT PORTIONS OF PDC CLEARANCE ARE MISUNDERSTOOD.

input: Often flight attendants will stop allowing carry-on baggage when the bins are full and then require the passenger to leave their bag at the aircraft door. The passenger is then allowed to continue boarding after the bag is left; the flight attendant will then put a note with their seat number on the bag so the agent can then tag the bag correctly or sometimes a hand written tag is filled out and given to the flight attendant to pass back to the customer. The issue is that in all the haste to get the door closed at the end of boarding the customer service agent has not asked the customer about hazardous materials; smart bags; e-cig; etc.
output: Ramp employee reported passenger carry-on baggage that is gate checked to cargo due to lack of space in over-head bins; is frequently not checked for hazmat items.

input: Zzz landing south. Heavy arrivals. I sent aircraft x around due to inadequate separation on final. Atpa (air traffic spacing tool) triggered to red and proceeded to go below legal spacing for arrivals. The runway is a reduced spacing arrival runway of 2.5 miles. I sent aircraft x around as soon as the atpa showed less than the legal separation to avoid the go around inside of a half mile and while still at an altitude to provide safe operation of the aircraft.the lack of real adequate spacing on the finals at this airport has been an issue for years. While the terminal radar approach control facility controllers at fancy that tower 'shall' provide visual separation if the lateral separation drops below the allowed legal separation to avoid having an operation loss; the runway spacing separation as allowed in the 7210.3 is commonly broken forcing the flight crews to be required to brake hard; change landing points; change landing speeds; or somehow maneuver the aircraft to exit the runway for aircraft close behind. I personally have heard the users express concern about being required at the last minute to hurry off of the runways or being required to overly brake the aircraft.tracon has for a long time failed to provide adequate legal spacing to all arriving runways.i have done everything in my power to try and convince management to do something about this issue. Every manager since my arrival has vowed to fix this issue. All have failed. This is an ongoing systemic issue here. Zzz has the highest rate of 'go-arounds' in the naval air station a good portion contributed to inadequate spacing on final. It will someday result in a catastrophic accident.
output: Tower Controller reported that a loss of spacing on final resulted in a go around.

input: We were instrument meteorological conditions being vectored for the instrument landing system the autopilot and autothrottles were engaged; and plane was descending out of 5000 for 4000 feet when we felt something hit the plane with a whump. Almost immediately; we smelled something burnt (not electrical); and the f/as called to report burnt smell and smoke in the cabin. All engine and system indications appeared normal at this time. Within moments; the plane began to level at 4000 feet; and the engines began to spool up. An increasing vibration/shaking of the plane was felt. I looked at the engine gauges and saw that the right engine was spooling up past 65% n1; but the left engine was stagnant at approx. 54% n1; with the trend arc indicating more thrust was being demanded. I realized we had an issue with the left engine; and immediately disconnected the autothrottles and retarded the left throttle. With the left throttle retarded to near idle; the vibration/shaking ceased. I attempted to spool up the left engine once again; but near 50% n1; the vibration/shaking would ensue. All other indications were normal. I retarded the throttle enough to prevent the vibration and left it there. Realizing we most likely had substantial damage to the left engine; i instructed the f/o to '[advise atc]. I want to land immediately.' about this time; we had emerged from instrument meteorological conditions into visual meteorological conditions conditions; and i acquired the airport visually off our right side. I disconnected the autopilot and began turning towards the airport; and transmitted to air traffic control that i had the field in sight and wanted visual approach clearance now. They immediately cleared us for the visual. The final approach and landing were otherwise uneventful. Since i didn't know the status of the left engine; i elected to use idle reverse and max autobrakes on landing. Emergency equipment visually inspected our aircraft; and then we taxied to the gate.
output: B737 Captain reported a bird strike that damaged the #1 engine while on approach in IMC .

input: As we approached our destination; which is a non-tower/uncontrolled airport - we heard on the unicom frequency a single engine aircraft in closed traffic; report on left downwind for runway xx. The instrument landing system at this airport was on runway xy; a 5000 feet/foot runway with a 1 degree upslope. For these reasons; the captain had expressed his preference to use runway xy. I reported our position 10 mile out and then later on the midfield overhead for runway xy. As we approached the airport we heard an air carrier announce its position northeast of the field and that it would use whatever runway became the commonly used runway; in fact they mentioned they didn't care which. As we entered the pattern at approximately 1500 feet/foot above ground level the air carrier (5 miles out) announced it would use runway xx. At this point the flying pilot (captain) declared he would accommodate the prevailing traffic (with a sense of frustration). He directed me to report entering a right downwind to runway xx. I queried him twice as to this choice stating my understanding that we should make left traffic - not right. He declared his intention to continue in right traffic. As i didn't think the time was appropriate to argue the point; i reported us turning onto the right downwind to runway xx; at which point an unknown person (i expect from the fixed-base operator on the field) stated on the unicom frequency that left traffic was the accepted pattern on this runway. With greater frustration the captain told me to report an extended left base for xx. At this point in time we were still east of the field. We turned southwest and made a 270 degree turn to enter the left base to final. There was no direct conflict that involved avoidance maneuvers with other aircraft and the sequencing worked out between us and the light aircraft and the air carrier. It became apparent later; the light aircraft was a student pilot in closed traffic. I expect the captain thought the light aircraft would give way to a larger jet. Upon landing and while discussing this with the personnel at the fixed-base operator i learned that the airport strictly adhered to the left traffic pattern guideline. I have always adhered to this practice in my career. At those times upon departure; when a turn contrary to the preferred traffic pattern direction was most efficient; i have always climbed above pattern altitude before making the turn. On this flight; it was clear that anywhere in close proximity to the destination was not the place to brief the arrival including traffic patterns. Briefings were very short for the entire duration of this contract; something i've noticed previously among the 'old school' pilots. On my part; i hadn't considered traffic patterns in much detail; assuming; incorrectly; that we would use the correct pattern. That and the fact that i felt to some extent i was along for the ride and not in a real position to contribute to the flight. Although i have been in aviation for 20 years of which; for the last 12 years; as a captain leading flights to all parts of the world and considered myself a qualified crewmember. This pilot complained a lot to me and the passengers; that he disliked uncontrolled airports and smaller fields such as this; before and after this flight. Even though the aircraft was well able to land on a runway of this size; (landing distance was 2400' and landing field length 4000'). This attitude may have contributed to his predetermined conviction to land on the upslope runway; regardless of prevailing traffic. A better alternative on this flight would have been to simply enter the left downwind to runway xx; a practical and more efficient entry as we arrived from the southwest. We also should have briefed the pattern prior to arriving in the vicinity.
output: First Officer aboard a corporate CL604 expressed concern the Captain was insufficiently schooled in traffic patterns at non-towered airports.

input: Tcas aural warnings are too loud and inappropriate. They are second officer loud as to be extremely and totally distraction i jumped when i first heard it; the (during approach in la basin with numerous acft) found myself spending time and attention figuring out when i was going to get an aural warning just second officer i could steal myself mentally to endure the startle reflex (all of this while i was flying an apch). Someone is going to die because of this severe distraction we also receive numerous inappropriate warnings at cruise; received warning of aircraft 10 mile away and 1900' above or below. Apparently traffic alert and collision avoidance system sensed altitude moving from 2000' to 1900'; projected trend for entire 2000' and saw conflict but 100' deviation sensed could be 10' movement across threshold and inappropriate. Need different tolerances. On apch(es) at 1200' above ground level in la basin; received full down vui command on resolution advisory from visual flight rules traffic 500' above; called by approach and visly acquired by me. At 1200' above ground level i chose not to follow resolution advisory because of terrain; what intermediate fix i had been in weather low visibility; or no visibility contact with vfr? Again inappropriate responses to high traffic congestion environment.
output: ACR REPORTER COMPLAINS ABOUT THE LOUDNESS OF THE TCAS AND THE NUANCE ALERTS WHILE APCHING LAX.

input: I was training my developmental. The aircraft was requesting fl360 and zny center said they were unable so was recoordinated at fl350. It was properly strip marked. We moved on to our training. Later after the radar controller had terminated the aircraft and the aircraft was passed the fix zny called and said the aircraft checked in at the wrong altitude and needed to be descended for traffic. We had the radar controller check and he was still on frequency and we were able to issue the descent.i recommend that zma take airspace from zny now that we have increased radar separation; and believe aircraft are being over restricted by having to adhere to non-radar rules and separation when they are well within radar airspace.
output: A radar sector reported coordinating an altitude for an aircraft to enter another sector's non-radar airspace. The sector failed to assign the coordinated altitude.

input: Prior to approach at runway(s) 23 in buf; i discussed with my first officer that many times i have received a false glideslope on the instrument landing system runway(s) 23. He said he was aware of the problem the weather was foggy and the runway visual range was going up and down between 1800 feet/foot and 2000 feet/foot we were vectored for the approach and given 2300 feet/foot and a heading to intercept the localizer cleared for the approach it was kind of a late turn for the localizer but the approach was armed and captured the localizer and glideslope almost at the same time. Immediately the glideslope started moving up and the aircraft began a climb my first officer disconnected the autoplt and made the corrections to descend back down to 2300 feet/foot we were still outside the outer marker and decided we would try to get re-established on a stabilized approach intermediate fix we could not; prior to the outer marker we could go missed. We got back to our assigned altitude and we were able to make a stabilized approach to landing i informed the approach controller of our deviation and the reason. I also talked to the tower controller about the problem i called the supervisor and she told me that there is a notice to airmen / of air missions about the glideslope she faxed it to me. It has been like this for yrs! I have had this problem many times. This glideslope needs to be fixed! Or maybe they should not use a left/right (directions) downwind; since it only happens on the left/right (directions) downwind for runway(s) 23.
output: CARJ FLT CREW LNDG BUF EXPERIENCED ERRATIC GS RECEPTION DURING INTERCEPT FOR ILS RWY 23.

input: The #2 inertial reference system/unit [inertial reference unit] would not align so we replaced the adiru [air data inertial reference unit] and adiru battery. Which fixed the problem. Referenced the maintenance manual procedure after we replaced the parts. Closed the circuit breaker. The paperwork tell you to perform ops test   the inertial reference system/unit and ops test of air data system. The next steps are to close up the area. It does not tell me to do the auto land test. I found out that i was supposed to do this the next day when we had an inertial reference system/unit problem on [another aircraft]. I questioned why we had to do it on [the other aircraft model] but not a 717. According to  the maintenance manual. I should have done the auto land test on the 717. The b717 maintenance manual never told me perform the test. If the test is required; it should be part of the b717 procedure when i remove and replaced the adiru; or at least have a reference to go to the manual for more tests procedures. If i did not encounter the [other aircraft model] issue the next day i would not have known about the b717 issue. If the auto land test is required it should be part of the b717 maintenance manual procedure.
output: B717 Maintenance Technician reported conflicting procedures resulted in autoland test not being performed prior to aircraft departure.

input: Alt excursion. Ferry flight departed afw on runway(s) 16 for dfw. Cleared to 2000 feet/foot heading 020 degrees takeoff weight was 156700 pounds first officer was flying aircraft after takeoff attempted to contact departure control but was unable. While looking on chart to verify frequency i heard the altitude warning go off and saw we had overshot to 2500 feet/foot by this time we were in contact with departure who questioned our altitude we rpted 2500 feet/foot and returned to 2000 feet/foot situation may not have occurred intermediate fix after gear was retracted; autothrottles were disengaged and power set for a climb rate commensurate with the 2000 feet/foot restrict, restricted, restriction also be wary of looking away from flight instruments during busy periods. Supplemental information from acn 364691: since it was a ferry flight aircraft was very light. It was the first time capt and myself have flown out of afw. On departure capt busy with air traffic control while i flew aircraft at 800 feet/foot above ground level i disconnected autothrottles and pulled throttles back due to low leveloff and rapid airspd acceleration; but i still received a slat overspd warning on attitude direction indicator i focused my attention to slowing aircraft and lost awareness to altitude i used my altimeter still set to afl to leveloff at 2000 feet/foot we were actually at 2500 feet/foot mean sea level when air traffic control and the capt confirmed i leveled off 500 feet/foot high.
output: FO OF A B757 OVERSHOT INITIAL CLB ALT DUE TO HIGH RATE OF CLB OF A LIGHT FERRY ACFT AND NOT DISCONNECTING THE AUTOTHROTTLES SOON AFTER TKOF TO REDUCE THE PWR SETTING FOR THE CLB.

input: Acft drifted back hitting belt loader. Brake not properly set. Ramp agent had not chocked the aircraft before offloading bags. Aircraft drifted back and put a puncture hole next to access panel. Damage area measured approximately 1 1/2 inches by 2 inches in diameter. I was notified after passenber and bags were off the aircraft that we had drifted back and damage occurred to aircraft noted damage in aircraft log. Notified maintenance of what had happened and of write-ups in logbook. Corrective action. Absolutely make sure that brakes are set. Never assume that the aircraft is chked.
output: THE ACFT WAS NOT CHOCKED AND IT ROLLED INTO GND EQUIP CAUSING DAMAGE.

input: We had been cleared for takeoff on runway(s) 35 in aus; transmitter as i applied full power the coplt door (which had been hard to close in the past) swung open and my jacket was sucked out. I aborted the takeoff and exited the runway(s) while informing the tower i was; therefore; cleared to taxi back and allowed to retrieve the jacket. As i approached the spot where the garment was; i shut down the left/right (directions) engine and after applying the parking brake (and testing it under higher pwr); i exited the aircraft for about 15 seconds and retrieved the jacket. In the meantime; my passenber was still strapped in the furthermost back seat. I restarted the left/right (directions) engine and after being cleared i continued the takeoff and trip. Later on my duty officer informed me that my failure of shutting down both engs was careless that for that reason i was terminated. Please note that my company operates 13 ltts under federal aviation regulation 135 commuter; and i ante meridiem airline transport pilot certificate and type-rated on them; and the one smt is federal aviation regulation 91 for company trips. My reason as pilot in command to leave 1 engine running in that circumstance was that i was getting erratic voltage responses on the gauges and i did not want to shut both engs down sitting on a runway(s) to perhaps finding out of not being able to restart them due to a weak or dead battery. I still believe my course of action was the safest under the circumstances.
output: SMT ACFT HAS DOOR POP OPEN ON TKOF ROLL. ABORT. STOP ON RWY TO RETRIEVE JACKET SUCKED OUT.

input: Departing runway(s) 1l at sfo. Clearance to 15000; at 3 vor and dme (co-located) air traffic control assigned a 230 degree heading in the left/right (directions) turn at about 2600 mean sea level traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory sounded. At about 3000 mean sea level traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii gave the command to descend which we complied. Once clear of traffic we continued our climb to 15000; with a 2000 feet per minute climb air traffic control then called traffic and assigned 4000 for traffic this was about 3600 mean sea level when assigned. Approaching 4000 mean sea level the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii again sounded with a traffic advisory (3 targets) were on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii screen. My attention was diverted from the assigned altitude of 4000 mean sea level by the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning; and an overshoot of 280 feet/foot occurred above the assigned 4000 altitude the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii seems to be a good system on numerous times the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii system sounded at the most critical portion of the flight (i.e.; approaching runway(s) with parallel runway(s) at 500 feet/foot traffic advisory with commands to climb or descend on the sna (19r) deep cutback (noise abatement) on departure less than 1000 feet/foot in air traffic area where visual contact is made; for visual separation; etc...). The warnings are very distracting at the critical portion of flight where compliance is required. Pilot experience has to locate targets; and take the best action; with the least amount of possible violations; with safety being first.
output: ACR MLG ALTDEV OVERSHOT CLRNC ALT. RPTR SAYS DISTR BY TCASII TA.

input: Our company has been doing regular maintenance on majority of our airplanes. During this week i have got every morning different airplane for use as an add hock airplane for that morning and different airplane for afternoon. On friday i have got airplane that just come back from maintenance previous day. During the flight left fuel gauge indicator was start showing erratic indications indicating full tank and shortly it would return to normal indication; and normal quantity. This kind of erratic indication continued few more times through the flight. On the way back to point of origin; fuel indications on left side did show normal quantities without any erratic movement. I have research the minimum equipment list and planning to defer the instrument gauge; however the fuel gauge was not one of items for deferral. Same airplane had w/b and poh removed out of airplane. Flight had been completed without any further any further incidents. In background after this incident; previous pilot reported that during drop/pick up airplane from corporate maintenance facility; he did reported mechanic problem with gauge but mechanic ask him not to put that item on logbooks (as that grounds airplane immediately) as gauge is showing only intermittent erratic indications.
output: A C208 pilot reported a corporate maintenance facility mechanic asked that an intermittent fuel gauge not be entered into the maintenance log because it immediately grounds the aircraft.

input: This flight was day #4 for me and day #2 for the capt. The day before we had an 18 hour duty day. I went to the hotel and i had a very good rest. Up to this flight i was very fatigued. I told the capt intermediate fix we had an early morning flight that i would call in sick. He did advise the chief pilot what i had said without my permission second officer more conflict; and fatigue. Also; the night before this flight he did not brief me on the clearance out of another airport as i was acting as capt that day and air traffic control had to correct my direction of flight i knew the area a little bit and i was able to get the standard instrument departure together by memory. Back to dc area; we were cleared for the barin 1 arrival, arrive and told to descend per the marin 1 arrival, arrive we were in moderate weather and icing conditions. I had automatic terminal information service and approach was set up for runway(s) 19l both green source and in the fms's. Next they told me to expect runway(s) 19r for landing all vertical navigation information was in the flight management system and i told the capt to descend per the arrival, arrive that it was in the flight management system he said 'ok i understand.' normally at this point i would arm the vertical navigation button second officer the jet will fly the arrival, arrive on its own; but this capt doesn't believe in using this function of the jet; also you do have to monitor the system because it doesn't always capture the dscnts but it does tell you how many feet/foot per minute(s) you need to use to get down. Second officer i proceeded to set up the other runway(s) in the fms's and green source for the instrument landing system system the next thing i heard was air traffic control asking intermediate fix we were going to get down by barin and i said yes. The capt was for sure late; and i told him to start down. We needed around 4500 feet per minute to make the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction which is no problem in the lear 60. I was still not totally focused on what was going on until air traffic control started yelling and traffic alert and collision avoidance system was going off. For some reason the flight was off course and i told air traffic control it was the computer; but come to find out the capt was trying to hand fly a jet that is really an autoplt aircraft we were headed about 60 degrees off course and we were pointed toward dc and oncoming traffic and the jet was saying bank angle with a steep descent angle. I dropped the approach plates and this is the point that i had to take over the airplane and started making yelling commands to the capt; plus taking an immediate turn from air traffic control to turn to heading 270 degrees to rejoin the arrival, arrive and avoid the traffic there is only a 4 degree turn after barin; i still don't know where he was trying to go. I never heard the autoplt tone when he turned it off due to the noise and everything that was going on. Also at this point due to fatigue and me stopping the approach set-up and review; we missed an altitude before the initial approach and started to descend too early. Second officer the mistake was not the computer; but probably pilot error due to spatial disorientation leading from fatigue. This capt will do anything it takes to get the job done and i do refuse to operate that way. I believe in being safe and following the rules. I should have had air traffic control put us into a hold somewhere until we were ready to do the approach there was just too much going on at once. Also; somehow i need to refuse to fly with a capt like this who does not respect safety and procedures at all. I haven't had to do a rpt in a very longitude time; until i started flying here. I ante meridiem currently seeking employment with the airlines where it will be safe again.
output: FLT CREW OF LJ60 EXPERIENCE LOSS OF CTL; TCAS RA; TRACK DEV AND ALT BUST WHILE ATTEMPTING TO HAND FLY THE BARIN STAR AND ILS RWY 19R TO IAD.

input: Descending into roa for a visual approach to runway 34; the ground proximity warning system provided an aural warning of terrain. To accommodate air traffic control and terrain to the south of the airport we remained high initially; but began a descent once cleared for the visual approach. The use of electronic means of glideslope for the instrument landing system to 34 were used to back up the visual approach. About 7 vor and dme (co-located) the ground proximity warning system advised the terrain and the flight crew adjusted its flight path.
output: Air carrier flight crew experienced a GPWS warning in visual conditions while executing a steep visual approach to the airport. Nearby high terrain was a factor.

input: During climb; we had a rudder ratio engine indicating and crew alerting system message and a rudder ratio light on the overhead panel. Simultaneously complying with the quick reference handbook procedures; changing configuration; radio calls; and navigation to join the star; we were at our planned cruise altitude of 9000' for our very short flight. The 15kt crosswind limitation per quick reference handbook dictated careful analysis of existing wind for particular runways at [destination] and our alternate. [ops] was consulted several times. We received updated winds which made [the selected runway] the only runway we could use to stay within our x/wind limitation. Air traffic control informed us about a 30 minute delay since the flow was for [a different runway]. We could accept this delay since we had adequate fuel though we discussed the alternate and its fuel requirements with possible x/wind scenarios accompanied with gusty winds. After 10 minutes of vectoring air traffic control informed us that [the] runway was closing soon. We had no assurance that the winds in [our alternate] would not shift to an unfavorable direction exceeding limitations with unknown runway closures with snow removal. We [requested] priority handling with flight control malfunctions and landed uneventfully.
output: B757-200 flight crew reported landing safely after receiving a Rudder Ratio EICAS and warning light.

input: This was a charter flight to gunnison from denver. The weather at guc was rpted by automatic weather observing/reporting system to be clear below 12000 10 mile visibility and wind from the sw at 10-15 knot(s) in order for any of our pilots to fly into guc at night they must sign a waiver required by the guc airport normally the gunnison airport does not allow night lndgs except for select operators who have complied with the arpt's requirements. The approach plate for guc specifies that the instrument flight rules approachs are not authorized at night. I believed however; that being approved to fly to the airport at night also allowed us to fly the instrument approach second officer longitude as we had the latest weather and it was approved weather in addition 2 other operators were also flying the instrument flight rules approach at approximately the same time i was. This restriction is confusing as to who it applies. Also the restriction should be placed on both the instrument landing system 6 chart and vor and dme (co-located) a chart in the same respective position in bold type. As it is now printed the restriction is easy to miss on the vor and dme (co-located) a approach plate because of the small print and because it's in a different location as compared to the instrument landing system 6 approach plate. Finally; although i was cleared for the approach it was conducted primarily visual flight rules and i in fact cancelled my instrument flight rules clearance before i reached the final approach fix because we had the runway(s) in sight and were talking to the unicom at the arpt.
output: CHARTER PLT FLIES IFR APCH NOT AUTHORIZED AT NIGHT.

input: Xa30z; 1000 feet/foot bda tower instrument landing system runway(s) 30 bda. On short final to bda; at about 1500 feet/foot and selecting flaps 25 degrees from 20 degrees engine indicating and crew alerting system displayed 'trailing edge flaps disagree.' flaps indicated 20 degrees at about 1000 feet/foot a go around was initiated with concurrence of tower on downwind; the trailing edge flap disagree chklist was accomplished and an emergency was declared. Reference 20 speed was 140 knot(s) and winds were 270 degrees at 14 knot(s) landing was in touchdown zone with autobrakes at 4. Taxi speed attained 1/2 way down runway(s) emergency vehicles were released and we taxied to gate uneventfully.
output: ON FINAL APCH A B757 EXECUTED A GAR DUE TO A FLAP DISAGREEMENT INDICATION AT BDA.

input: I'm going to first describe events that occurred on the evening of feb xa when i was attempting to depart zzz. Although not the subject of this particular rpt; it has direct bearing on decisions i made 11 days later. We were in the process of boarding passenber in zzz. The automatic terminal information service changed to indicate that light freezing rain was beginning to fall. I recalled a warning in the dornier 328 flight manual regarding operations(s) in freezing rain. It reads as follows: 'warning: severe icing may result from environmental conditions outside of those for which the airplane is certificated. Flight in freezing rain; freezing drizzle; or mixed icing conditions (super-cooled liquid water and ice crystals) may result in ice build-up on protected surfaces exceeding the capability of the ice protection system or may result in ice forming aft of the protected surfaces. This ice may not be shed using the ice protection system and may seriously degrade the performance and ctlability of the airplane.' based on this warning; i decided that it was unsafe to depart and i informed dispatch of my decision. Dispatch disagreed; stating that i was 'absolutely incorrect' (even after i read him the warning). I was convinced that i was right; second officer dispatch called the director of operations(s) who also tried to convince me that it was safe to depart. I read the warning to him but he remained convinced that the flight could safely depart. I was not convinced by the arguments presented by dispatch and the director of operations(s) second officer i canceled the flight the following morning i was called in to the chief pilot's office. He tried to convince me that the warning in the afm did not constitute a prohibition against taking off into light freezing rain. His reasoning (and the reasoning of director of operations(s) director of safety and security; and manager of flight standards and training) was that the flight could be safely conducted for the following reasons: 1) the warning doesn't specify 'light' freezing rain; only 'freezing rain.' 2) there was a holdover time for type 4 anti-icing fluid for the conditions present at the time of departure 3) the warning didn't specifically state that anything bad would happen; only that they may happen. 4) the national aeronautics and space administration icing video which presented the danger of flight into sld was based on flts of a dehavilland twin otter and were; therefore; not applicable to a dornier 328 because the wings of the 2 aircraft were different. In order to obtain clarification i contacted dornier 328 support services they sent me the following response: 'take off into freezing rain including light freezing rain is not permitted. Icing fluids protect the aircraft only on ground until brake release against ice accretion. By design most of the fluid is shed away from the airframe before liftoff. Freezing rain consists of large water droplets hitting the airframe aft of the boots with the result of lowering the stall angle of attack dramatically. A safe escape from those conditions; when entered unintentionally during flight is defined in the manual requiring high minimum speeds to avoid stalling the aircraft takeoff is only permitted into normal icing conditions. The manual contains all information -- takeoff speeds climb gradients; etc; for those conditions.' i shared this information with those present. They essentially ignored it; stating that they weren't convinced that dornier support services had the authority/authorized to interpretation the warning. They said they were going to try to get them to retract this statement. I will now describe the events of today. When i departed; freezing rain was in the current metar. Before i left; i contacted dispatch and told them that there was a chance that i would encounter freezing rain on the approach i gave them copies of the e-mail from dornier support services second officer they would know what i was basing my decision on. Sure enough; when we were about 30 minute(s) out; the automatic terminal information service was rpting light freezing rain. The automatic terminal information service was about to change second officer i decided to wait and see what the new automatic terminal information service had to say. When it came out; the new automatic terminal information service also rpted light freezing rain. I contacted dispatch and told them that there was light freezing rain and; based on the explanation i received by dornier support services i considered an approach unsafe. We decided that the flight should return to origination. When i landed; i was called in to see the director of operations(s) he told me that i made an extremely poor decision by choosing not to fly into light freezing rain; that i had no right to contact dornier support services to obtain clarification on the pertinent warning; and that i had no right to share this information with dispatch. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the reporter stated that dornier was quite clear that this aircraft should not be operated in any kind of freezing rain. This aircraft is equipped with deicing boots which may be the reason for this prohibition.
output: DO328 CAPT REPORTS REFUSAL TO OPERATE HIS ACFT IN LIGHT FREEZING RAIN.

input: Cruise at fl350; clear with white cloud deck on horizon. Got traffic alert; aircraft same altitude rapidly followed by resolution advisory 'dsnd.' capt immediately began response to resolution advisory and well into response controller said 'acft x; make an immediate left/right (directions) turn.' i saw the white jet about my 3 o'clock position about belly up. After clear of conflict we climbed from fl340 back to fl350 and advised controller no explanation was offered. We did hear controller talk to an air carrier and said he had 'strayed from his holding pattern.' i ante meridiem reasonably convinced the traffic alert and collision avoidance system saved us on this day. A white aircraft against a white cloud horizon would have been very difficult to detect with enough time to take evasive action. Closure rate was super fast. I think of the times we flew with traffic alert and collision avoidance system inoperative and i'm sure glad today was not one of those days. Supplemental information from acn 676165: at cruise altitude fl350 passing agard intersection on j222; received traffic advisory followed almost immediately by a 'dsnd' resolution advisory i descended aircraft to fl340. First officer noticed an aircraft belly passing from the nose down the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft slightly high. Zdc called for an 'immediate left/right (directions) turn to 320 degs' and we complied. After starting to return to the assigned altitude and course; center controller told an air carrier to tighten up his holding pattern as he was straying from holding airspace. Weather was visual flight rules with a brilliant white undercast and very bright sunlight. We could not see the aircraft at the traffic advisory and only picked him up when we were below the flight level.
output: B737 FLT CREW RESPONDED TO TCAS RA WHILE CRUISING AT FL350. ACFT IN HOLDING PATTERN HAD STRAYED FROM ITS ASSIGNED AIRSPACE.

input: Enrte to ravine vor and dme (co-located) on 340 degree to the station; what looked like 2 military jets came within 100' of my aircraft and disappeared behind me.
output: NMAC BETWEEN REPORTER ACFT AND 2 UNIDENTIFIED MILITARY JETS.

input: This report concerns acceptance of extensions to federal aviation regulation 117 duty time limits. On a recent flight; as a crew we decided that we would hold to the federal aviation regulation 117 limit as found in table celsius since this flight was a window of circadian low (wocl) flight; we believed it not in the interest of safety to extend our duty day beyond the normal limit. After we were unable to make it off the ground before our max off time had expired; we returned to the gate. Dispatch was notified of our reason for returning. On my drive home; i received what can only be described as an irate call from crew tracking; scolding me for not calling them with my 'fatigue notice.' i explained to the crew tracker that i was not fatigued nor making a declaration of fatigue; but simply illegal to continue the flight duty period under federal aviation regulation 117 limits without an extension. She told me that if i did not negotiate an extension that i was in fact declaring myself fatigued. I again told her that i was not fatigued; but at this point decided to take it up with my base chief pilot in the morning. It appears that the cart and the horse have been reversed here by my air carrier concerning extensions to federal aviation regulation 117 duty time limits.
