Aborted approach and had to 'scud run' to minute man airport probably at 500 feet/foot above ground level or less. Probably violated a bunch of federal aviation regulations but had to exercise my authority/authorized to do second officer as pilot in command for safety of flight as compression on 1 cylinder was a little low when pulling propeller through on preflt; i thought i might have a broken ring; or possibly a bird's nest. Turns out; it was just a faulty cylinder head temperature probe that failed by indicating high temperature before going totally ots.
output: ATP PLT OF GLASAIR HAS INDICATION OF A HIGH CYLINDER HEAD TEMP. WAS ON AN IFR CLB WITH BOS DEP CTL. SAW HOLE OVER 9B1 ARPT AND SPIRALED THROUGH. PLT HAD ELECTED THAT ACTION. 9B1 RWY TOO SHORT TO USE; HE SCUD RUNS UNDER A 500 FT CEILING TO 6B6 ARPT FOR LNDG. DEFECTIVE PROBE IN #2 CYLINDER.

input: On a vector to final on runway(s) 36l at dfw; i transitioned from autoplt to hand flying for the visual approach i got distracted during frequency change from approach to tower and overshot final. Tower didn't mention anything and no other traffic was involved.
output: AN SF340 FO WAS THE PF DURING APCH TO DFW. HE BECAME DISTRACTED BY THE FREQ CHANGE AND OVERSHOT APCH.

input: Since the aeronautical information manual went to a revision system the revisions to the aeronautical information manual arrive some time after the effective date of the revision. For example; change 3 to the aeronautical information manual (effective dec/xx/94) arrived at my home on dec/yy/94). One cause of the problem may be the use of third class bulk mail. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he was a member of the atpac committee when it was first formed and he has a very special interest in aviation safety. He feels pilots should receive the revisions ahead of the effective date to be able to study and learn what those changes are. Since they are sent bulk mail; they are received often 2 weeks late. It is his belief that controllers receive their copies with first class postage. Since this is a 4-times per yr revision service it can cause problems with controllers working with 1 set of information and pilots another. Intermediate fix the cost of first class mail is the problem he believes that cost should be added to the subscription second officer revisions arrive prior to the effective date. Rptr has tried the address in front of aeronautical information manual with no response to his queries.
output: PROBS WITH AIM REVISIONS ARRIVING AFTER THE EFFECTIVE DATE.

input: During discretionary descent to 11000 feet/foot company called (through atc). We contacted company and were informed of possible reroute. We advised center that we would like to stop at fl200 for a few minute(s) air traffic control approved. As we continued toward ind; i monitored second officer communications with company. It was decided to continue to ind. At this time; first officer began a descent to 11000 feet/foot center asked what we were doing and we rpted out of fl200 for 11000 feet/foot we weren't sure intermediate fix center wanted to know of our divert plans or intermediate fix the discretion to 11000 feet/foot was forgotten; or no longer valid. We thought we still had discretion; but should have queried center to be sure.
output: B727 CARGO CREW DSNDING TO 11000 FT; LEVELED OFF AT FL200 TO TALK WITH COMPANY ABOUT A REROUTE. AFTER TALKING WITH COMPANY; THEY CONTINUED DSCNT.

input: While deviating around some thunderstorms zdv asked us intermediate fix we were proceeding direct oma as previously cleared i responded 'no; deviating around wx.' he said we needed to ask permission to deviate and i advised him we were cleared to deviate from the previous ctlr/freq. He then told me we should have gotten a clearance from him; even intermediate fix the previous controller issued the clearance to deviate. I politely told him the previous controller should have advised him we were deviating. Better coordination between air traffic control ctlrs.
output: ACR AT FL350 IS QUESTIONED BY ZDV CTLR REGARDING RTE; PLT ADVISED RTE/WX DEVIATION APPROVED BY PREVIOUS CTLR.

input: Enroute from zzz to apf; we were cleared direct to ugyow to descend to 2;100 feet; and we were cleared for the area navigation 23 approach at apf. About 4 nautical mile from ugyow; the flight management system dropped ugyow from our route completely; and the final approach course with a line to infinity was redrawn on our mfd with ofdoy still in view. The flight management system commanded a turn to intercept the final approach course at a 45 degree angle; inside ofdoy.here's what's so strange about this. We had the same anomaly happen to us on the same routing several months ago. I was ready for it today; but the airplane still turned and there was a minute of confusion and discussion because our next fix ugyow was no longer in view; and dropped from the flight management system we had no guidance anymore to ugyow. Having had this happen twice now; i have to say with confidence; there is an issue with the universal uns-1e flight management system we have on board to provide this guidance. I realize the turns necessary to get us on the final approach course are significant in this procedure; but the flight management system should not drop the initial approach fix fix from view and redraw the final approach course as it is doing. Someone at universal and the federal aviation administration need to look into this; and they need to publish that this procedure can't be used when coming from the sw so that others don't have this bad experience. There was no conflict with traffic; but the controller got a little excited when we first made the turn; and he canceled our approach clearance; and turned out back out to the ne and he gave us radar vectors to the final approach course; which worked out perfectly. My copilot on this flight had been an instructor on the aircraft x at [the] simulator training center for years; and he agreed the flight management system shouldn't have done that and its guidance is wrong when this happens. I will contact universal to discuss it with them; and i plan to try this approach in the simulator when i go back for recurrent training.
output: Corporate pilot reported that while on an RNAV approach; the Universal UNS-1E FMA dropped the IAF and redrew the final approach course. Reporter stated this had happened previously on the same routing.

input: After the flight had been pushed out ramp lead called inquiring why he was getting a weight message wanting to know if the flight was overweight; because [load plan application] would not let him finalize. After looking at the [load plan]; i noticed the hazmat in pit 4; told the ramp he had hazmat in pit 4 with only 10 bags. His response was first there is no hazmat onboard the flight. I then told him there was; and item 2 was hazmat. The ramp lead thought i was referring to the aog (aircraft on ground parts); he said the aog is not hazmat. I then asked him to look at his paperwork and questioned him if he did in fact load item 2; a 100 pound quick pack; he said yes he loaded the quick pack but he didn't know the quick pack was dangerous goods. The ramp lead who is now in charge of planning out the flight again failed to properly identify dangerous goods while they were planning the flight. The ramp lead did not have a paper copy of the [load plan] and was totally dependent on the scanner.
output: Air carrier Load Planner reported a communications breakdown with Ramp Lead regarding Hazmat shipment incorrectly configured for air shipment. Hazmat shipment was corrected.

input: Aircraft x was inside of a quarter mile final on the instrument landing system runway 31c approach. I turned around for a second to tell the supervisor about the visibility getting better on final when the supervisor noticed an airport vehicle going onto runway 31c. At that point i issued a go around to the aircraft and to climb and maintain 3;000 ft. Mean sea level and turn right to a heading of 110. I also let the aircraft know the reason of the go around. They were able to respond in time and were re-sequenced for another approach and landed without incident. I understand it was snowing and airport markers are difficult to see. I suggest airport vehicles be more vigilant of their position on the airport before moving anywhere. Driver refresher course recommended.
output: ATC approach controller reported issuing a go-around clearance to an aircraft on short final due to a vehicle reported on the runway.

input: Filed and cleared valdi ul621 roe un983 elpol un195 adlar (polish airspace). On available en route charts there is no un195. Also; the flight management computer legs un983 from roe 129 degrees for 16 nautical mile to amror 130 degrees 25 nautical mile to elpol. The en route chart from roe 119 degrees 16 nautical mile to kolob 135 degrees 25 nautical mile to elpol. Dispatch was notified en route callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the reporter stated that he has not been back on this routing since he recorded this event. However; there have been several navigate, navigation database cycles since this experience and he would assume a correction has been made since the route is a frequently traveled. He did note additionally that there seems to be an increase in database errors particularly in europe.
output: A B777 PILOT REPORTS THAT FMC LEGS VALDI UL621 ROE UN983 ELPOL UN195 ADLAR DIFFER FROM PAPER CHARTS. NO UN195 AIRWAY EXISTS.

input: I was working the local controller position the aircraft departed runway(s) 23 with a right turn on course. Approximately 1/4 mile off the departure end; the pilot rpted smoke in the cockpit due to an electrical fire. I cleared him to land on any runway(s) and reclred the one other aircraft in the air traffic area to prevent a conflict. I then picked up the phone to the crash station and advised them of an aircraft on final for runway(s) 12 with smoke in the cockpit. The crash station is clearly visible from the tower and there was no sense of urgency at all as the firefighters walked to the trucks. By the time the first truck exited the crash station and established radio contact; the aircraft had cleared the runway(s) and advised that he would not need assistance. When the second truck established radio contact with me; he inquired as to which the runway(s) the aircraft was inbound for. At this pint; i was able to advise him that the first truck was already returning to the station. Had this become any type of real emergency valuable time would have been lost. I don't know how to instill a sense of urgency in firefighters; but i would think that frequent surprise practices would help. In 2 yrs; i have not seen a practice session although i have heard of one.
output: FIRE EQUIPMENT SLOW TO RESPOND TO AN EMERGENCY.

input: Tkof was from runway(s) 19r at sna with an initial altitude assigned of 5000 feet/foot mean sea level while using noise abatement clbout procedures tower changed our leveloff altitude to 2000 feet/foot mean sea level this occurred while using maximum takeoff power passing 1100 feet/foot mean sea level and climbing at 4000 feet per minute we reset the altitude alerter to 2000 feet/foot but the flight computer had already passed its capture point and rendered the command bars useless. We overshot our altitude by 200 feet/foot (2200 feet/foot msl). The reason for the change was a visual flight rules aircraft at 2500 feet/foot mean sea level we realize the change was for our safety. However; a 30 second delay in our takeoff clearance or better coordination with socal would have saved this occurrence. Sna wants noise abatement to work and they are serious with their fines and operating suspensions. However; the tower and approach control folks need to ride through a couple of these takeoffs in a high performance aircraft to see what a sudden leveloff does to the crew and passenber a better realization might space the takeoffs a little to help out. We'll do our best not to have this happen again.
output: DA90 CREW WAS FLYING THE SNA NOISE ABATEMENT PROC AND WAS GIVEN A LOWER LEVELOFF ALT.

input: While on final approach to zzz on the practice instrument landing system xx approach we made the decision to shut down our left/right (directions) engine due to low fuel. The wind was calm and there was only 1 airplane in the pattern that i was aware of. I asked the tower as we made this decision; intermediate fix we could land on runway(s) xx instead of the active runway(s) yy. No emergency was declared and i told them that no assistance was needed. Priority was granted and we landed straight-in to runway(s) xx with no problem after landing we exited on taxiway x and then tried to turn left/right (directions) onto taxiway y. Because the left/right (directions) engine was the only one running; we could not make the turn; second officer we shut the engine down; manually towed it to an open area; refueled and taxied back to the flight school. There was no damage to the aircraft no one was hurt and no regulations were broken. As i review this situation; i know that more attention to detail is needed as it pertains to fuel levels and situational awareness. We left the airport with tanks 1/2 full and believed that would be enough to complete the training that was planned. In the future; much better planning will take place in these situations. In cases like this; we will always leave with full tanks to avoid this situation from ever taking place again.
output: A PA44 INSTRUCTOR PILOT REPORTED SHUTTING DOWN THE RIGHT ENGINE ON FINAL APPROACH BECAUSE OF LOW FUEL QUANTITY.

input: While performing an 'a' maintenance checked i replaced halon fire extinguisher due to an expired date of manufacture. I installed a new serviceable unit out of stock per checked instructions (note: serviceable unit from stock came with serviceable yellow tag from stock). Due to high workload i did not checked new unit's date of manufacture and misinterp inadvertently the serviceable tag's date to be the same as the manufacture's date. (it was only after i spoke with another mechanic did i realize these dates could be different). I spoke with my supervisor and notified him of the problem because the paperwork ('a' checked detailed instructions doesn't tell or specify to checked the manufacturer's date); and just installing a new serviceable unit per instruction sheet could be wrong. He said there is a committee trying to clarify this problem with different dates; in relation to tracking units; in relation to paperwork; and until it's clarified; or rectified we'll have to double-chk all dates as to avoid this type of confusion.
output: ACR MECH RPT ON AIRLINE MAINT POLICY PROCEDURAL PROBS IN REPLACING UNSERVICEABLE ITEMS ON THE ACFT DURING A CHK 'A' SVC.

input: While sitting at a jfk gate; we noted a jolt of the aircraft the passenber were on board and the paperwork had been completed and given to the ramp agent. The jolt occurred while the door was closed waiting pushback permission. I went outside to determine what happened and intermediate fix any damage could be seen. The ramp personnel didn't see anything. During the walkaround inspection; i could not see any visible damage. Earlier; the ramp had removed the tow bar for another pushback. I then wondered intermediate fix during tow bar re-attachment; that was possibly the jolt that we felt. The flight proceeded to destination upon post flight inspection; the first officer noted a missing static wick at the base of the left/right (directions) winglet. I called ramp and informed them that it appeared the aircraft had been possibly hit by a belt loader. A discrepancy was entered into the maintenance log.
output: WINGLET DAMAGE TO A CRJ700 AT JFK WAS NOT DISCOVERED UNTIL 2 DESTS LATER EVEN AFTER AN INSPECTION LOOKING FOR COLLISION DAMAGE.

input: Thirty minutes after takeoff i received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from the crew 'status maximum fl100/mea with first officer left/right (directions) stat first officer tat are we really restricted to 10;000 ft.' i advised the crew to standby while i confer with maintenance. I had reviewed the quick reference handbook and the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring non normal procedures. All the information there stated first officer (fo) stat inoperative systems - first officer pitot; left stat; right stat; first officer tat - crew awareness. Nowhere in either of the manuals does it reference 10;000 feet/foot restriction. After i told the crew to standby so i could get with maintenance; he stated 'been talking to local maintenance for 20 plus minutes'. Neither i nor maintenance control knew anything about the situation until the crew asked about the 10;000 feet/foot restriction. The only reference to 10;000 feet/foot restriction was on his electronic centralized aircraft monitoring the crew asked where you want us to go and where is the part. Maintenance control advised the part was available in zzz. Either going back or landing zzz; the aircraft would be landing overweight. The flight also had a failure - no phc 2 [probe heat computer] data idcfds. Based on these facts; the safest course of action would be to land zzz; long runways. Did not want the flight to stay in the air any longer in the event they lost or the other side iced up. The aircraft would then have no reliable air data. Plan was made to land zzz approximately 8;500 pounds over maximum landing weight. Message was sent to crew to attempt to burn extra fuel on the way to zzz. Then only a walk around overweight landing inspection would be required. Flight landed zzz taxied to the gate. Captain called dispatch and advised it was smooth landing; it was not a hard landing. Maintenance did the walk around inspection; changed the parts that failed and the flight continued to destination. Dispatch did check the flight history of down links from the aircraft. There were 2 failures and 2 warnings; takeoff minus 12 minutes - failure fuel level sensing; takeoff plus 1 - warning anti ice first officer tat; takeoff +1 warning anti ice first officer right stat; takeoff +2 failure no phc 2 data/idcfds. Once again; based on all available information; landing overweight was the safest course of action; rather than allowing the aircraft to fly for at least 2 more hours to burn the fuel off.original cause was in part; a lack of communications from local maintenance and/or flight crew to dispatch. Not knowing about a problem until 28 minutes after departure is; in my opinion; unacceptable. Local maintenance should have advised maintenance control in dispatch of the problem also. Neither was done. The reason the decision to land over weight was deemed to be the safest course of action at the time. [i] did not want to keep the aircraft in the air any longer than needed. Suggest company policy is changed about overweight landings. We have procedures in place for overweight landings based on manufacturer data. You cannot just simply say we will not land overweight. If the crew had been allowed to continue flying the aircraft for another 2 hours; i believe would have been a violation by allowing the flight to continue in unsafe condition.
output: A321 Dispatcher is informed almost 30 minutes after the fact; by the crew; of a Probe Heat Computer failure that will require returning or diversion for repair. A diversion and overweight landing is then accomplished; where the aircraft is repaired before continuing to destination.

input: I have been working as a pilot flying a traffic rptr over the roads of louisville; ky; monday through friday for the past 7 months. The aircraft owner has an letter of agreement with air traffic control allowing us to use an assigned squawk code and call sign. I have had an excellent working relationship with the controllers in the louisville tower except for one who seems to be very difficult to work with. On oct/tue/04 this controller was working; and i recognized him by his usual denials to my requests; even though the traffic situation did not seem to warrant his denials. This controller has a tendency to always state 'remain 1 mile e' or '1 mile westbound of the departure and arrival, arrive corridors.' on oct/tue/04; i asked him to clarify intermediate fix he meant 1 mile from the ctrline or the corridor; and he said 'ctrline.' to ensure that i follow his instructions; i will on occasion ask him to verify that i ante meridiem federal aviation regulation enough east or westbound for his taste as i parallel the runway(s) at one point; i was flying north 1 mile westbound of the runway(s) 35l departure course. I requested to cross over the departure corridor to the east to cover a traffic issue. There appeared to be no departing traffic at the time; but he still very abruptly denied my request. I always respect a controller's instructions; second officer i; therefore; continued nbound until i was below the shelf of class celsius airspace. I then informed the controller that i was turning east to transition north of the river. He stated 'approved' (something i actually did not need approval for). When reaching 1 mile east of the departure corridor for runway(s) 35r; i xmitted that i was turning south and would stay east i received no acknowledgement to my transmission but the controller was talking to other traffic at that time. As i proceeded sbound; the controller then very abruptly asked me to state my direction of flight i replied that i had just xmitted that i was turning sbound but would stay east of the departure course. He told me to turn to heading 090 degrees and immediately exit class celsius airspace; which i promptly did. I requested a frequency change; communicated with bowman (lou) tower and flew along hwys east of the class celsius airspace; but remained under the class celsius shelf. I then turned back westbound along highway 71 and lou tower told me to contact sdf tower the same controller then told me to remain outside class celsius airspace; which i did. I asked intermediate fix there was a problem and all he did was repeat this demand. I complied with his instructions; but this now prevented me from doing my job. This specific controller has in the past had a habit of denying me crossing requests; except for allowing me to cross directly over the numbers even though the traffic load was no higher than at other occasions with other controllers other controllers would easily accommodate me; but maybe sometimes after a slight delay intermediate fix the traffic situation warranted it. I fully respect any controller's right and authority/authorized to coordination my movements with other traffic but the controller in question habitually denies my requests for no reason apparent to me. After i landed; i called the sdf tower and asked them to pull the tape; explained to them that i was just trying to do my job; and that i can't do my job intermediate fix i ante meridiem to remain clear of class celsius airspace. Apparently when i stated that i was turning south and would stay east my transmission was not on the tape according to the supervisor the supervisor informed me that he would not violate me and i'm still trying to figure out intermediate fix he actually could; since i had had a valid transponder code and had been maintaining 2-way communications with sdf for the time/event in question. Even though the controller did not reply to my transmission i did not repeat it; since the controller had me on radar and i was already taking precautions to stay out of everyone's way. Intermediate fix the controller had let me cross when i had requested to cross east i would not have had to parallel the highway again to try to get a look at the highway from the east side. Since the controller did not allow me to cross; i needed to go south and look at the traffic from the east i make a habit of transmitting my intentions comprehensively; courteously and briefly; and i asked the supervisor intermediate fix any of the controllers had complained about me since they all probably are used to my xmissions. He said that he had no complaints about me and that he was not aware of any prior problem i told the supervisor that intermediate fix there was anything i should do differently; to please let me know; and maybe he could try to figure out why there is inconsistency in how i ante meridiem treated by this one specific controller compared to all the others. Furthermore; in the future; i will ensure that every single transmission i make to a controller is replied to; regardless of which airspace i ante meridiem maneuvering in.
output: C172 TFC WATCH PLT EXPRESSED FRUSTRATION WITH SDF ATC HANDLING DURING AIRSPACE TRANSITION OPS.

input: I was receiving flight following services from air traffic control and i had recently descended from 10;500 feet/foot to 8;500 feet/foot for traffic. As i was in the vicinity of a large class celsius airport; my engine started to run rough. I turned on the fuel pump and switched tanks in an attempt to remedy the situation; but the engine was still running rough. At that point; i advised air traffic control of the situation and my intent to make a precautionary landing at the nearby class celsius airport. This request was approved; and i descended and landed on runway 26l without incident. On the ramp for the fixed-base operator i did a series of ground checks. I found no issues at that time; and the problem appeared to have cleared itself. Concluding that the aircraft was airworthy; i made an uneventful flight to my planned destination. In hindsight; i believe the issue may have been a fouled spark plug due to my failure to lean the mixture as i made my initial climb to 10;500 feet/foot the problem appeared to resolve itself during ground checks at the divert airport.
output: A pilot failed to lean his PA-28-151 engine during climb out and fouled spark plugs may have been the reason for a rough running engine; which resulted in a precautionary diversion.

input: After leaving the holding pattern and starting to proceed inbound to stl; a crossing restrict, restricted, restriction was issued by zkc to cross the stl vor and dme (co-located) 078 degree radial 45 vor and dme (co-located) at 15000 feet/foot we were at fl220 and approximately 85 vor and dme (co-located) when clearance was given. We made several deviations for thunderstorms while trying to proceed inbound on the stl 078 degree radial. As we made our last turn around the last thunderstorm we were called by center (at stl 078 degree radial 47 dme) and asked intermediate fix we would make the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction we then initiated descent and crossed the 45 vor and dme (co-located) at approximately 18000 feet/foot and leveled off at approximately 37 vor and dme (co-located) as the pilot not flying i was performing duties associated with leaving holding; (acars message to dispatch) and arrival, arrive (atis for stl and called stl ops); after the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction was received. After these items were completed; i focused my attention on the weather deviations supplemental information from acn 303652: failed to keep in mind descent clearance due to weather deviation distr.
output: ALTDEV ALT UNDERSHOT IN A NON ADHERENCE TO ATC CLRNC INSTRUCTION. ALT XING RESTR NOT MET.

input: Ztl gave us a clearance to descend to 11000 feet/foot 40 mile north of clt at 250 knot(s) capt was pilot flying he began to descend and called for descent checked at this time flight attendant came into cockpit (approx fl240 at this time; she had a question for us). Through 18000 feet/foot we set local altimeters. As pilot not flying i began the chklist a little later than usual due to the fact that i was answering flight attendant's question. Flight attendant left cockpit; we switched to approach and completed the chklist. Approximately 30 seconds after leveling at 250 knot(s) capt noticed he leveled at 10000 feet/foot instead of 11000 feet/foot (11000 feet/foot was in altitude window). He immediately climbed to 11000 feet/foot at which time approach told us to descend to 7000 feet/foot no word was mentioned about the deviation by air traffic control i believe we lost altitude awareness because we were preoccupied by answering flight attendant's question and completing the descent chklist at a lower than normal altitude supplemental information from acn 477202: combination of weather avoidance and extra conversation in cockpit distracted us second officer that we didn't hear altitude warning horn. Did pilot not flying make normal calls? Center switched us to approach control about the same time.
output: A DSNDING DC9-30 FLC OVERSHOOTS THEIR ASSIGNED ALT OF 11000 FT WHEN DISTRACTED WITH FLT ATTENDANT IN COCKPIT 35 MI NW OF CLT; NC.

input: While the aircraft was out of service for other scheduled maintenance i replaced the gaseous o2 bottle assembly that was due for its 36 month. After going through all the leak checks and purging procedures as outlined in the procedures for the system. I safety wired the manual shut off valve in the closed position on the regulator; it should have been safety wired in the open position. During the time the aircraft was back in service; the o2 system quantity showed full.five days later i was contacted by the pilot stating the o2 system was full but no flow to the service ports. I was unable to quickly determine what was wrong and i was thinking while the medical interior was going back in the aircraft one of the clear flex o2 tubing was pinched; which would require a removal of the overhead and side walls of the cabin interior. We had the spare ec135 at our base so i made the call to move the crew over to that aircraft. I spent the rest of my time that night preparing the spare aircraft. I reach the end of my duty day after the spare aircraft was ready. I passed on the o2 problem on to the second base mechanic. He went thru the system and determined that the manual shut off was in the closed position. (note in the [company's aircraft configuration] the manual shut off is not used as with other stc's aka pilots shut off.)two days later i came back to work and started to work the ongoing air conditioning minimum equipment list during the course of the day i started to put the aircraft back together; i read the pass down note of where my partner left off and realized my mistake. I safety wired the manual shut off valve to the on position; verified o2 flow and installed the cover to the bottle.i have been here for about 2 months. During this time frame both of the mechanics have average over 60 hours a week dealing with scheduled and unscheduled maintenance on this aircraft with very little off time. A week before my mistake on the o2 system; i was in the hospital for a day and a half for a heart issue and i am currently on a 30 day 24 hour heart monitor. Not using this as an excuse but it is a contributing factor.it was an honest mistake made by me. All leak checks and purging was checked prior to the safety wiring of the valve. I would suggest that instead of just reading what is on the indicator and calling it good that the medical crews do a quick flow test daily as part of their routine. It was 5 days from the mistake with the safety wire and from the time it was found; 2 of those days was with the aircraft back in service for medical duty.
output: During scheduled maintenance on a Helicopter ECD-EC135 a mechanic safety wired an O2 bottle manual shutoff valve in the closed position when it should have been in the open position.

input: While en route to hou from shv; our clearance was changed from das1 standard terminal arrival route to roket arrival, arrive the flight management system has database of vors and airports but intxns must be manually entered using latitude/longitude. The originally filed and cleared standard terminal arrival route was entered prior to departure the pilot not flying began entering the revised clearance while i flew the descent it was a very busy phase of flight and i was unable to verify the latitude/longitude of all the waypoints. I did back up the course to be flown with vors; but didn't have the standard terminal arrival route in front of me to verify distances between fixes. The pilot not flying had transposed the minute(s) of the latitude for the final fix (drxlr intxn) where we were told to depart heading 300 degrees he entered '54' instead of '45.' this caused us to initiate the turn approximately 10 nautical mile early. The rerte happened at a very busy phase of flight as did the turn at drxlr. Air traffic control queried us and we responded that we were initiating the turn to 300 degrees as instructed at drxlr. He responded that we were about 10 mile off course and issued us a turn back on course. The pilot not flying immediately rechked the latitude/longitude and found the error. We chastised ourselves for not always having the pilot flying back up the pnf's entries. However; as pilot flying i was quite busy following the descent profile and speed crossing restrs as well as accomplishing the chklists for descent transition level; and approach and trying to help with radio tuning. The pilot not flying also had his part in all these actions along with radio calls to distract him. In retrospect; i should have had the standard terminal arrival route in front of me to back up the distances in addition to the radials for vor and dme (co-located) backup.
output: A CPR FLC OF AN LTT ENTERED THE WRONG COORDINATES FOR A NAV POINT IN THE FMS AND DUE TO THIS STARTED A TURN TOO EARLY.

input: We received the final weights via the automatic communications addressing & reporting system printer. The trim was set as called for and verified. As a cross check; i entered the mac on the takeoff page in the flight management computer and it's trim setting was very close to the final weight message. During the takeoff roll; with v speeds properly set; i attempted to lift the nose off the runway at the rotate command; but it was very hard to do so. I had to pull very hard and had to add nose up trim. The nose finally came up. During manual flight i noticed the aircraft difficult to level off and after adding trim inputs; it was if i was over trimming. It seemed out of balance.
output: A B757 Captain reported unusually high stick forces required at rotation due; he believes; from faulty weight and balance calculations by load planners.

input: I was conducting ojti on the r-side of sector 34. This is the developmental's first r-side. Sector 34 primarily provides final sequence of arrivals to sfo from the east coast. As the morning arrival push began we were abruptly interrupted by a coast target that had been pvd'ed to our scope. At the same time; the flm came to us while we were training/working the sector and told us; 'that coast target is an unmanned balloon and the coast target was an approximated position and altitude gathered from [internet] maps.' when i asked the flm for more information and why; the response was; 'there's nothing we can do; the balloon belongs to [a company] and they can do whatever they want.' the coast target indicated the balloon was right in the arrival path of aircraft descending over mod for sfo. Approximately 30 plus aircraft were scheduled within the next hour. While we continued to work the sector; we also researched the phraseology to alert aircraft of the balloon. Once we were relieved from the position; i approached the outer marker on duty to ask more questions and gather more information. I was met with defensive posture by the outer marker that indicated i should take my complaints and safety concerns elsewhere. The is an extremely dangerous situation. The explanation i finally got was that [the company] was in compliance with far's. The balloon does not have a transponder therefore i don't think traffic alert and collision avoidance system would alert the flight crew of a collision course; and we don't get a radar target on the balloon so we have no way of separating from the balloon. Furthermore; its position; in the middle of our busy arrival path leads to a high potential for a catastrophic event with loss of life. Recommendation; amend far's; bring [the company] here to see what type of hazard they are creating. Stop the balloons; period. At a bare minimum; add a transponder to the balloon. Management needs to relay this type event information more timely with less distraction.
output: ZOA Controller voiced concern regarding a balloon operation in the vicinity of the MOD air carrier arrival flow into SFO; the reporter suggesting the balloon should be equipped with improved identification gear.

input: Both aircraft called for taxi from spot 5; a new procedure at cle; i issued taxi instructions which would have kept them in trail. When i observed them one was on a taxiway j and one was on the ramp going to spot 5 side by side. I had to assert which was which and issue additional instructions. I asked the pilot about the new procedure and he wasn't sure. An unsatisfactory condition rpt has been filed about this procedure it has not been published; the spots (1-6) are not marked on the ramp and the procedure has created other safety issues. Users and airport management agreed to this and air traffic control is still being briefed. This is a hazard and could pose several safety issues. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated that the new taxi procedures for the ramp area were put into effect prior to the 'hold areas' (spots) being painted on the ramp surface. He had to direct aircraft around the ramp area in order to prevent a conflict or collision. Normally flight crews are cleared to a spot and receive their taxi instructions while holding at the spot. He felt that it was a major safety problem subsequently; the 'holding areas' (spots) have been painted and the procedures are clear to the flight crews.
output: ATC GND CTLR CONCERNED WITH NEW TAXI PROCS AND HOLDING AREAS AT CLE.

input: On jan/xa/00 in clt (dark); aircraft was heading south on taxiway celsius and entered the cargo ramp at taxiway c8. The aircraft made an almost immediate left/right (directions) turn nbound and followed the marked ctrline of the taxiway to the parking area. The ground handlers were not providing any guidance to the capt who had total control of the aircraft the aircraft struck a food catering truck parked approximately 56 feet/foot left/right (directions) of the taxiway ctrline with the left/right (directions) wingtip. The area where the truck parked was not lighted in anyway and because of the glare of the loaders flood lights it was very hard to see in the dark areas of the ramp. I never saw that the truck was parked too close to the taxiway the ramp was cluttered on both sides of the aircraft with loading equipment vehicles and cargo containers. The federal aviation administration inspector considered this an incident and not an accident. I recommend the following things: 1) the area where the truck was parked should be better lighted. 2) no vehicles should be allowed to park in this area. 3) txwys should be properly marked. 4) clutter of equipment on both sides of the aircraft moved to a safer distance from the aircraft 5) lighting should be positioned second officer as not to blind the flight crew note: the b727 wing span is 108 feet/foot supplemental information from acn 460270: after the aircraft was chocked; i opened the cargo door and noticed the damage to the left/right (directions) wingtip. The ground personnel remarked that they did not see us hit the truck. Supplemental information from acn 460268: i was at my flight engineer desk; doing my flight engineer duties; second officer i didn't really see anything; but did feel a bump -- felt like a chock had been run over.
output: A B727 FREIGHTER HITS A PARKED TRUCK WHILE SELF PARKING AT THE CARGO RAMP IN CLT; NC.

input: At dca when landing runway(s) 18 or runway(s) 36; clearance most often received is 'continue to runway(s) 21' (if land s) or 'continue to runway(s) 33' intermediate fix north as i assumed control of the aircraft i lifted fo's hands off throttles and said 'i have it.' he queried; 'you have the acft?' and i repeated my stated remark. During this tower issued what i heard to be 'continue to runway(s) 31' -- in fact; they said 'continue through runway(s) 33.' first officer asked intermediate fix i got that; second officer i said 'roger' to the tower first officer apparently did not hear or understand the clearance after i called tower on phone they told me there was no problem but wondered what had happened. He said this clearance is usually given with clearance to land; or at least before landing which it was not. Resolution: 1) for controller use different terminology such as 'rwy 33 not available' or 'do not turn off on runway(s) 33.' 2) issue clearance at better time. For pilots clear in that first officer should have advocated uncertainty regarding the clearance and capt should have confirmed verbally with full clearance tower reassured me; there were no problems supplemental information from acn 352091: we landed on runway(s) 36 at dca and tower had wanted us to taxi 'through' the intersection of runway(s) 33 and clear at taxiway south the capt had heard 'rwy 33' in the instructions and exited the runway(s) there instead of at taxiway s.
output: NON ADHERENCE TO ATC CLRNC INSTRUCTION FOR LNDG ARR TFC; AN ACR LGT TURNED OFF ON RWY INSTEAD OF TXWY. UNAUTH RWY ENTRY OP.

input: We were cleared for takeoff runway(s) 25r; lax2 departure commuter express on runway(s) 25l was cleared for takeoff right after us. Air traffic control told them to maintain visual separation with air carrier departing runway(s) 25r. At approximately 1000 feet/foot above ground level we got a resolution advisory from the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii giving us vertical guidance; monitor vertical climb the resolution advisory on the navigate, navigation display showed right over our aircraft plus 300 feet/foot climbing we adjusted our vertical climb no one in front of us. Looked back in our 7-8 o'clock position and i saw the commuter express aircraft this was at a very critical phase of flight i feel the air traffic control and the commuter express pilot as at fault; not to establish a safe departure interval behind the aircraft in front; both flying runway(s) heading. On a visual approach it is the pilot's responsibility to establish the safe landing interval behind the aircraft he was instructed to follow. I could not find anything about visual departures when aircraft depart that way in sfo on runway(s) 1's; air traffic control will give heading to fly to keep a safe interval between aircraft lax air traffic control did nothing. Very unsafe. Let's find a fix. Thank you. Capt of a320.
output: A320 DEPART RWY 25R LAX. COMMUTER EXPRESS DEPART RWY 25L TO MAINTAIN VISUAL ON TFC OFF RWY 25R. A320 GOT TCASII RA ALERT AND SAW TFC 7-8 O'CLOCK COMMUTER EXPRESS. REDUCED CLB RATE FOR FURTHER SEPARATION. NO COMMENT FROM CTLR.

input: We started both engines and turned off the auxiliary power unity upon taxi; i noticed an acrid/dirty socks/musty smell when i added power. As i backed off the power on taxi; the smell seemed to dissipate. On power up taking the runway (xxl); the smell returned. I made the decision to continue the takeoff and said to the first officer that if this doesn't dissipate and go away we should return and he agreed. Once airborne; it got even worse and became a significant fume event. We donned o2 masks and goggles; i [advised atc] due to fumes in the cockpit and we returned to land on [runway] xxl. The first officer flew and landed. I talked to air traffic control and ran the fumes/odor/smoke checklist. We landed uneventfully 2;000 lbs overweight. Holding short of the runway; i called back to the purser and asked him if he smelled anything. He said he didn't but would check in the back. I told him what we had experienced and that we would be returning if it continued. According to the flight attendants after landing; the smell was significant in the back of the plane and they said their eyes were burning as well. Upon arriving back at the gate; we were met by arff personnel and [company] maintenance. Firefighters boarded the plane and noticed the fumes as well; which were still present. The mechanic said they had done a 'compressor wash' the previous night and that it was his opinion that oil may have been freed from the compressors and entered the cabin. I was handed a smoke/fumes/odor form to fill out; which i did and returned it to station operations. Although some of the flight attendants complained to me about headaches and eyes burning; they declined to be checked out and told inflight operations they were fine and good to continue. I called the [duty manager] and we completed the human factors checklist. My chief pilot called to check on us and we said that while we may change our fit-for-duty status; for now; we were ok to continue. After talking about this more with the first officer; we decided we were no longer fit for duty and advised the [duty manager].
output: B737 flight crew reported a significant fume event shortly after takeoff resulting in an air return.

input: The first officer (first officer) and i arrived into the gate; and were running late due to up-line air traffic control delays. The first officer proceeded to our gate; and i stopped on my way to get some food. When i arrived at the aircraft; i was surprised that all 175 passengers had already been boarded. I was told that we had a company pilot jump seating and he had been on board when they were boarding. When i began to unpack my things; i realized that i had left my ipad at the last aircraft. I ran up the jet bridge and informed the agent that i had to run back and get my ipad. When i returned a few minutes later; the agent shut the door and followed me down the jet bridge. Within a minute of sitting down to start my preflight duties; the agent shut the aircraft door. I had not even started my preflight duties; nor had i signed the release. The first officer said we needed to reopen the door because he had not done his walk around yet. We opened the door prior to his pulling the jet bridge back and i spoke with him; informing that it was going to be 10-15 minutes before we were ready. It was obvious to me that he was in a hurry to get us out. We finally completed our preflight duties; signed the paperwork and pushed back.later; during the flight; i was told by both the jump seater and the fa's (flight attendants) that the agent had begun boarding with no pilot monitoring the aircraft and no power on the aircraft other than the ground service bus. One of the fa's informed the agent they could not board without us and went so far as to show him the bulletin in her manual. He told the fa's that there is a new procedure and they could now board without the pilots. So when the jump seater boarded and popped his head into the cockpit to check in with us; the crew; (we had not arrived yet) he witnessed another agent or csa trying to start the auxiliary power unity and get power on the aircraft. At that point; the jump seater took over; powered up and babysat the aircraft until my first officer arrived.i spoke with the inbound captain; and he was told by his agent (different from ours) that the through passengers had been deplaned and was not getting back on. Therefore; this captain elected to terminate the aircraft rather than run the new procedure of leaving the aircraft powered.i have several concerns about what transpired. First; the agent has a very new employee number and was being supervised by either another agent or a supervisor. It was obvious that he was under a tremendous pressure to close the door and get us going. I was definitely feeling like i was being rushed. Of course; i set the tone and the pace and the first officer and i were making sure we were not hurrying through our preflight and checklists. Closing the door and pulling the jet bridge back before i had even settled in; much less checking with me; the captain; to see if i am ok with closing the door; is completely unacceptable. It seems our agents are under so much pressure to close the door that is compromising safety. I was told by the supervisor that they only had to verify the count with the 'a' before closing the door. It should be standard operating procedures to check with the captain before closing the main cabin door. My second concern is that we obviously have operations(s) personnel misinterpreting this new procedure of 'aircraft on gate services without pilots' or their procedure is wrong. They are not allowed to board without the aircraft powered and being monitored by an operating flight deck crew member. Third; i am concerned that the agents are under so much pressure that they are not listening and heeding the information given to them by the fa's. If the fa's say they can't board; then don't do it. My fa's had very serious concerns. The intercom system does not work when the aircraft is not powered. If they need to order an evacuation or if they have other passenger safety concerns; there was no way to make a public address or communicate with each other via the interphone. The other concern was that the lavatories did not work;so the passengers could not use them until power was restored to the aircraft.
output: The Pilot of a Boeing 737 reported that passengers were boarded prior to the flight crew arriving.

input: While enroute [to] cyqb; we had 3 close calls with wake turbulence due to aircraft separation of only 1;000 feet. Departed for cyqb. There were 2 route changes after new york air route traffic control center handed [us] to boston air route traffic control center boston center cleared [us] to climb to fl290; then changed it to fl270; then fl250. Then; boston advised [us] of crossing traffic right to left b747-400 at fl260. Boston advised a frequency change; we contacted boston for a heading change to avoid wake turbulence. The b747-400 crossed ahead of our flight path and barely gave us enough time during a frequency change (boston) and ask for a heading change to avoid the wake turbulence.the second separation occurred 30nm south of mpv vor and dme (co-located) at fl370. We had an airbus 321 at fl380 pass right to left; off the nose with only 1;000 feet separation. Again; we contacted boston for a heading change to avoid the wake turbulence. Boston air route traffic control center handed [us] to canada air route traffic control center five minutes after entering canadian airspace; at fl350; the controller advised an airbus crossing our flight path at fl360 right to left. Then; canadian air route traffic control center cleared [us for] a descent to fl290; which kept our flight path away from the wake turbulence of the passing airbus.suggestions: smaller private jets including the cessna citation xl/xls should be operating above heavy airplanes; not below. The wake turbulence generated from heavy aircraft (b747/b787 & airbus) descends more than 1;000 feet below their flight path; should be avoided; and could detrimental to smaller aircraft.
output: CE-560XLS Captain reported multiple routing and altitude changes from ATC to avoid wake encounters.

input: Sfo automatic terminal information service reported cig 1800 broken few 1200. Cleared for the instrument landing system 28l; on 10 mile final with bridge and airport in sight. Given the air traffic control instruction to maintain 220 or better to the 7 mile final; we were at 240. Pairing traffic to 28r visually acquired by both pilots and communicated this to air traffic control who then told us to maintain visual separation. Both pilots recognized excessive closure rate to e170 and pilot flying started to pair airspeed towards 220 by disengaging autothrottle and using manual thrust (idle). Around this point (@9miles) air traffic control instructed 'slow to 180 knots to san mateo bridge'. Approaching san mateo bridge; we entered instrument meteorological conditions (bkn layer) with e175 @ 500 above; offset to 28r facility (final approach course); and slightly in trail. Pilot monitoring advised air traffic control that we were instrument meteorological conditions and lost sight of pairing traffic. Air traffic control responded with 'maintain visual separation'; to which pilot monitoring advised we were unable due to instrument meteorological conditions air traffic control instructed 'go around; maintain runway heading' (emphasis mine). By this point; we were visual meteorological conditions with field in sight again (@1400ft) but e175 was in the layer above. Pilot flying disengaged autopilot and began a methodical go-around conscientious of the presence of the e175 above and slightly in trail and that winds at altitude were @220/25kts. With this in mind; pilot flying instructed a slight offset upwind of rh to pilot monitoring to enter into heading window and @275 was entered with pilot flying executing a reduced rate climb back into the instrument meteorological conditions air traffic control nearly simultaneously instructed a left turn towards a downwind and remainder of frequency modulation ga/mapp was executed.
output: B737 flight crew reported entering IMC conditions and losing visual separation with landing aircraft on parallel runway while on an ILS approach. Go-around and missed approach conducted.

input: At fl340; we got a master caution light; followed by a low oil pressure light within 7-10 seconds. We immediately requested lower. Air traffic control gave us fl330 and within 1 minute(s) or second officer the engine seized and we declared an emergency we then asked for radar vectors for zzz preferring a longitude and wide runway(s) we ran the appropriate chklists for the engine shutdown; secured the engine and proceeded to zzz and landed without further incident.
output: AN LJ35 AT FL340 DECLARED AN EMER AND DIVERTED DUE TO MASTER CAUTION FOLLOWED 1 MIN LATER BY THE ENG SEIZURE.

input: We received our aircraft in zzz approximately 4 hours late. The aircraft had minimum equipment list 24-16 inoperative elec light dated several days prior. The minimum equipment list had two provisos; 1st; a standby powered checked done at the time of deferral and 2nd a checked of the battery charger prior to flight using the procedure spelled out in the minimum equipment list we completed our preflt and also did the battery charger check. It went as published. En route during my cruise flow i was checkeding the elec panel and noticed that the inv on the air conditioning / alternating current side was un-powered. When we arrived at our destination i called maintenance control to talk to them about the write-up in the logbook concerning the minimum equipment list and the deferral. The deferral stated nothing about the standby powered checked being completed when the elec light was deferred. This was not a specific maintenance procedure but just a proviso in the minimum equipment list the first officer and i decided to do a standby powered checked just for our own comfort. We used the standby powered checked for -700 aircraft that was in the minimum equipment list the test failed. The air conditioning / alternating current standby bus was unpowered. I then called maintenance control back and we ran thru another checked and decided that the air conditioning / alternating current standby bus was not powered. I wrote the aircraft up and we were assigned a new aircraft the original minimum equipment list deferral said that at startup; the elec light illuminated. The signoff was a very simple 'ok to continue per minimum equipment list 24-16.' i was signed off by a mechanic it is my thinking that at the time of the deferral; the standby powered checked was not done but the battery charger checked was. Intermediate fix this were the case then this aircraft flew for several days without an operating air conditioning / alternating current standby bus. I would recommend that as a part of this minimum equipment list a procedure be put in place to require a standby powered checked prior to the first flight of each day.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the 'elec' annunciator light was deferred per the minimum equipment list and it was obvious the required special procedure checked of the standby powered test was not accomplished at the time of deferral. The rptr indicated the only minimum equipment list special procedure required by the flight crew was a checked of the battery charger and not a standby powered check. Rptr suggested this be changed to add a battery charger and not a standby powered checked prior to flight with this minimum equipment list deferral. Reportedly this airplane was operated for several days with the air conditioning / alternating current standby inverter inop.
output: A B737-700 WAS DISPATCHED WITH AN 'ELEC' ANNUNCIATOR LIGHT DEFERRED PER THE MEL. THE ACFT WAS UNKNOWINGLY OPERATED WITH AN AC STANDBY BUS THAT COULD NOT BE POWERED FROM THE BATTERY. RPTR RECOMMENDS MEL SPECIAL PROC REQUIRE FLT CREW TO CONDUCT STANDBY POWER CHK PRIOR TO DAILY FLT.

input: Flt attendants rpted 12 times passenber were smoking in lavatories. Heat sensors don't go off until 175 degrees or fire gets real big. The flight attendants extinguished (put out) 3 smoldering trash cans in lavatories. I don't know intermediate fix you have had other rpts of this. Our company has a no smoking (at all) policy.
output: 3 SMOLDERING TRASH CANS WERE DISCOVERED DURING OVERSEAS FLT. FLT ATTENDANTS RPTED THAT PAX WERE SMOKING IN THE LAVATORIES. FLT ATTENDANTS EXTINGUISHED.

input: I was pilot in command (pic) of an air carrier flight. I refused to fly the aircraft after conversing with dispatch; maintenance control; the maintenance shift supervisor; and the director of operations; who was serving as duty officer. I believed that the aircraft was unsafe to fly due to a compromised rudder control system which was being deferred using an minimum equipment list that neither applied to the problem nor was fully complied with.upon acceptance inspection of the aircraft i found a [safety] wire connecting the captain's rudder pedal adjustment handle to an open screw hole in the pitot static isolation panel. The wire was approximately six inches long. The panel was being pulled out of position by the wire's tension as the panel was only being held by one of its two attachment screws. An minimum equipment list sticker was placed near the wire. The sticker and release indicated that the aircraft was operating under minimum equipment list 27-20-2 titled rudder pedal adjustment. The original write-up stated that the rudder pedals would not stay adjusted. That is; the rudder pedals were slipping during use. On the dash-8; rudder inputs are carried through the adjustment mechanism and the entire mechanism moves to translate the input to the rudder control actuators. Therefore; the rudder pedal adjustment levers and rudder input mechanisms cannot be compromised in any way. If they are; pressure on the rudder pedal may result in movement of adjustment lever within the adjustment mechanism and no actual movement of the rudder controls. The rudder pedal adjustment system consists of a handle attached to a flexible shaft that translates the adjustment input to a screw jack and adjustment levers that change the position of the pedals. Minimum equipment list 27-20-2 allows the aircraft to operate if the rudder pedal adjustment input is inoperative. Step one of the maintenance procedure states: turn the rudder adjustment handle; ensure the pedal adjustment shaft does not move forward or back. Meaning that if movement of the rudder adjustment handle does not result in movement of the adjustment shaft the aircraft can be deemed airworthy provided all the conditions of the mel's maintenance procedure are met. This air carrier used an operative rudder [pedal] adjustment handle to prevent the pedals from sliding. This means that the aircraft was depending on a piece of [safety] wire and a partially detached panel to ensure the rudder pedals remained functional. It also meant that the mechanical defect or wear that prevented the pedals from remaining adjusted as designed was not addressed. The rudder control system was compromised. By disabling the rudder adjustment handle with wire; step one of the minimum equipment list cannot be complied with. Therefore the minimum equipment list cannot be applied. The minimum equipment list does not allow for the use of wire or the removal of screws from other components. When i informed maintenance control that i did not believe the aircraft was safe they offered to send a mechanic to the airplane to adjust the pedals to fit me. I asked how they were going to do that and they said the mechanic would rewire the handle in a position that fit me. Based upon what i saw; my knowledge of the dash-8; and maintenance's explanations i determined that the minimum equipment list did not apply to the problem at hand and; baring that; was not being complied with. I informed the flight's dispatcher that i felt the aircraft was unsafe and that i was refusing to fly it. The dispatcher transferred the call to the dispatch supervisor who then conferenced the director of operations; who was serving as duty officer; onto the call. I explained my concerns to the director of operations who asked me when the original write up took place. I informed him it was written up ten days ago. He then asked if i thought all of the captains that had flown the plane since then were wrong to have done so. I told him it was not my place to judge them. He then hung up. The dispatch supervisor informed me that the flight was going to be changed to an available aircraft that was on a neighboring gate. I was then called by the dispatch supervisor and informed that the director of operations had ordered that i be removed from the flight. The crew; with a new captain; was later returned to the aircraft i refused and the flight departed with revenue passengers on board. This safety concern was begun by this air carrier's improper use of an minimum equipment list and was compounded by their refusal to correct the mistake when it was brought to their attention and their decision to remove the reporting captain from flying rather than the aircraft. The aircraft remained in service for a total of 10 days in that condition before repairs were made.
output: A Captain reported he refused to fly a DHC-8-Q400 aircraft because he felt the aircraft was unsafe due to a comprised rudder control system which was being deferred using an MEL that neither applied to the problem nor was fully complied with. Captain was removed from the flight; which departed with another Captain.

input: Following an instrument flight rules flight from pvc; mostly in instrument meteorological conditions with light rain and turbulence with reports of thunderstorms in area; was vectored extensively to avoid terminal control area penetration (common in boston area). Finally; when 3 mile from area with airport in sight; cancelled instrument flight rules and contacted tower made normal entry to left downwind but at a faster speed than normal. 2 aircraft were on downwind in closed traffic and i entered ahead of them; judging the distance to be ok. Controller advised other traffic to follow aircraft which had 'just entered downwind dangerously'. I probably was too close to other traffic which was not easy to see in the hazy light conditions. Had i seen them i would have been reluctant to execute a 360 degree turn without advice from air traffic control regarding other aircraft factors: too fast following extensive vectoring; poor visibility; no advice from air traffic control poor judgement of closing speeds.
output: REPORTER ACFT ENTERED ARPT TRAFFIC PATTERN AHEAD OF TRAFFIC ALREADY IN DOWNWIND PATTERN.

input: Engine's 6th cylinder rod broke in half. Engine indicated drop in manifold pressure approximately 4 inches. An aircraft nearby said smoke was trailing behind. Diverted to closest major airport but engine failed prior to reaching it. Turned to second choice airport for landing propeller still wind milling. I shut down the engine and when the magnetos were turned to the 'off' position the engine ceased; propeller stopped; and oil covered the windscreen. Landing was assured; and we glided in with no problem nor any further damage to the airframe. Intermediate fix oil pressure drops off; you can plan on an engine to fail shortly afterwards. Second officer intermediate fix you can land with some power better than none at all.
output: A PA32 DIVERTED AND LANDED IN EMER CONDITION DUE TO ENG FAILURE CAUSED BY #6 CYLINDER CONNECTING ROD FAILURE. INFLT ENG SHUTDOWN.

input: Pilot declared an emergency upon clearance to land due to an engine out situation. The aircraft landed uneventfully and came to a stop off the runway and taxiway and on the ramp on the west side of the airport. It was determined that a fuel calibration issue with the garmin g-1000 and the manual fuel gauge created a false reading indicating one hour of fuel remaining reading at the time of fuel starvation. Manual readings indicated same. After consulting with maintenance; a ferry permit was secured to ferry the aircraft with full fuel for repairs to the fuel calibration system on the aircraft per the manufacturer's specifications.
output: A Kodiak 100 piloted by an instrument rated Private Pilot accompanied by a more experienced Commercial Pilot suffered engine failure due to fuel starvation on the last of several legs for which they had planned fuel required based on fuel gauge readings and computed fuel burnouts for all planned legs. They managed to glide power off to a safe landing it their destination airport.

input: After pushback; we received a wave off from the ground crew. We completed our after start flows and the after start chklist. We extended our flaps to the 5 position we called ramp control and we were released to ground control we called ground control and we were cleared to taxi. We cleared the outside left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) and i spooled up the engs to breakaway thrust. Just as the airplane started to move; a contract ground operations(s) truck approached us from the 1 o'clock position and blocked our path. 2 people jumped out. 1 person ran to the communicationss panel on the left/right (directions) side of the airplane. The other person ran in front of the nose and gave me the stop signal. It appears that they had failed to close the door on the communicationss panel and they came back to close it. My problem is that they should have made radio contact with us when approaching the aircraft after wave off. We cleared both sides of the aircraft before taxi; and we were fortunate that the first officer did not go back heads down after clearing outside. I did not see the truck approaching until after the first officer told me to stop and the person appeared in front of the nose of the airplane. Follow basic safety procedures and make radio contact with an airplane before approaching after wave off.
output: ACR FLT CREW REPORTS GROUND VEHICLE BLOCKING THEIR TURN OUT OF PARKING TO GET THEIR ATTENTION AND ALLOW THE CLOSING OF A COMMUNICATIONS PANEL WHICH HAD BEEN LEFT OPEN.

input: At approximately xa15l we were operating on approach control vectors for a visual approach to bdl airport we were under an overcast in visual flight rules conditions; crossing between the ridge lines approximately 15 nautical mile nw of bdl. The airport was in sight; and we were just about lined up with runway(s) 15. We had been cleared to descend to 3000 feet/foot (apch ctl's mva). At approximately 3500-3700 feet/foot mean sea level we got a ground proximitypa warning terrain; followed shortly by a pull up. An immediate climb was started in accordance with regulations the ground proximitypa warning continued through about 4200-4500 feet/foot mean sea level about that time approach control called questioning our climb he stated that there were no traffic conflicts; and reclred us for approach to runway(s) 24 because of the altitude i called him after landing and he indicated that he had no problems with our actions as there were no traffic conflicts. He also told me that his minimum vector altitude in that area is 3000 feet/foot second officer we were well above the terrain. I rechked our altimeter settings and both were correct. I have flown this particular approach many times in the past with no prior problems i talked to a mechanic after landing and he indicated that several aircraft have rpted a similar experience recently. He could offer no suggestions as to cause; but did hypothesize that a ski area near the point of occurrence has a snow maker that may cause the radio altimeter to trigger.
output: FLC OF MLG ACR ACFT TOOK EVASIVE ACTION IN RESPONSE TO THE ACFT GND PROX WARNING ALERT DURING A VISUAL APCH.

input: I assisted agent in closing aircraft door. [i] pushed down on door handle and after 2nd attempt; it locked into place. Door was then properly armed. Upon take off roll; i could see light coming from back of door and extreme air noise. I could see door was not completely closed. Upon rotation i attempted to call cockpit but when they answered they could not hear what i was saying due to the extreme wind noise. We continued to climb and i then had the number 3 flight attendant go to the back of the aircraft to phone the captain and let him know what was happening. Due to weight of fuel we had to circle for nearly an hour before being able to land. Landed and went to gate. Maintenance came and opened door and after several attempts we able replicate the door not closing completely on the side of the frame of the door towards the rear of the aircraft. Flight attendant should not assist agent close door.
output: B737 Flight Attendant discovers during takeoff the the forward entry door has not been properly latched due visible light and extreme wind noise. Flight returns to departure airport.

input: This is not a safety problem only rpting an error in instrument approach procedures see attached. Brownwood runway(s) 30 as marked is really runway(s) 31 (that's what's painted on rwy). Don't know who else to rpt this to.
output: GA PLT RPTS AN INCORRECT MARKING ON AN INST APCH CHART ARPT DIAGRAM.

input: [we] aborted first takeoff due to a slow airspeed indication after a long takeoff roll. I thought the student (5 hours total time) was dragging the brakes. We taxied for a second takeoff. I took the controls to perform a short field procedure. I held the brakes; applied full throttle and noted the proper static rpm and engine indications. After a normal length ground roll; i pitched for climb out attitude; shortly after noticing airspeed indication of 40 knot(s) i lowered the pitch attitude to maintain a safe airspeed indication and noted only 200 feet/foot per minute and decreasing climb rate. I notified air traffic control and circled from the takeoff runway to land on closest runway at an altitude of approximately 300 feet/foot above ground level. The engine seemed to be operating properly throughout; but i decided to maintain a safe airspeed indication to prevent a stall at low altitude. I circled to non-active runway due to low altitude; with closest safe touchdown point.
output: The instructor and student pilot of a Cessna 152 aborted takeoff due to a slow airspeed indication. Following a taxi-back; the instructor assumed the controls for another takeoff. After a normal length takeoff roll; he pitched to a normal climb attitude then noticed the airspeed indicator at 40 KTS. He lowered the nose and returned to ensure a safe airspeed and returned to the field; landing on the closest runway.

input: Our c12 is equipped with the iec 9002 flight management system (gps sensor) and uses a commercial chart database (updated every 28 days). To properly utilize the flight management system you must input the origin and destination i was coming from abq to nzy (abq; nautical mile -- naval air station north island). I was subsequently cleared for the baret 4 arrival, arrive (baret.baret4) off the imperial (ipl) transition. The department of defense flight information publication (terminal) civil sids; standard terminal arrival route and profile descent procedures booklet; page x lists the baret 4 under nzy (as well as san). The flight management system lists the baret 4 under san only. Therefore; i must change my destination on the flight management system to fly the baret 4 and then reprogram the flight management system once finished flying the baret 4 and then put nzy back in the flight management system as my destination too much work down low in the terminal area. Can we correct the database? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr called back. He stated that he felt this was a problem for the crews going into north island. A lengthy discussion was held; with the rptr finally conceding that the flight to north island would have to be a visual approach in any circumstance and the flight management system was not needed or utilized for that. He was simply curious as to why this final destination could not be in the database for the flight management system rptr did not sound like he wanted to make a further issue of this subject.
output: MIL BEECH UC12 FLC HAS A PROB GOING INTO NZY; NORTH ISLAND NAS. THEY CANNOT PROGRAM THEIR FMS TO PERFORM THE STAR TO SAN; BARET.BARET4 STAR.SAN. THENCE ONTO NZY WITH NZY AS FINAL WAYPOINT IN THEIR LEGS OR RTE PAGES. THEY MUST REPROGRAM THE FMS ONCE COMPLETED WITH THE STAR; HAVING USED SAN AS THE FINAL DEST POINT.

input: On takeoff after accelerating to 50 mph a group of mule deer (6) ran across runway(s) in front of aircraft from ramp hangar area (w) across runway(s) to east side of runway(s) i was able to lift off short field technique. In feb of this yr (1992) the same situation happened when 20-25 deer ran across in front of my takeoff position which was stationary at that time. Thinking enough time had passed (all the deer were across rwy) i initiated takeoff at 30 mph another (4) deer ran across runway(s) within 500 feet/foot in front of me. I reduced throttle and braked heavily coming to a stop 100-150 feet/foot from path of deer. No rpt was filed. There is no wildlife barrier around this facility 2 similar occurrences within 3 months and 3 visits to the same airport indicate a very possible hazard. Intermediate fix it would have been after dark; i may not have seen the approaching deer. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states as he taxies on the parallel taxiway he tries to look between hangars for the deer. They tend to blend second officer well; it is hard to see them however; second officer one never knows what to expect. He knows of airport in flagstaff that recently put up a 14 feet/foot fence around airport to eliminate this same problem. Analyst encouraged rptr to follow up with state agency and federal aviation administration hotline as well.
output: ENCOUNTER WITH DEER ON RWY ON TKOF ROLL. MAKES UNPLANNED SHORT FIELD TKOF TO AVOID CONTACT.

input: In block altitude fl370/390; encountered severe turbulence; descended to fl350 to light turbulence. All crew and passenber seated....no injuries...atc and dispatch notified. Shortly after the turbulence encounter; the #1 hydraulic system failed. Accomplished the appropriate check list. Continued to [destination].....and landed [safely]. We were able to clear the runway (no nose gear or body steering). Shut down the engines and got towed into the gate. Debriefed with the base chief pilot.
output: Upon descending to exit moderate to severe turbulence; the flight crew of a B747 was met by a hydraulic system one failure. They continued to descend to an efficient altitude and landed uneventfully.

input: Upon descent from 6000 feet/foot to san carlos; we switched tanks from a very low tank; approximately 10 gallons; to a tank that had approximately 30 gallons. At this time; the engine hesitated. We then turned on the boost pump and this eliminated all engine malfunctions. We had already deviated from our instrument flight rules clearance to head to the nearest airport second officer i declared an emergency i thought that since we were over the city and there was an airport we should land. Intermediate fix we were in cruise; we would not have landed; but because of our location; we landed. We ran the engine several times inbound to moffett. We decided since we were now on final; we should land. Upon landing we drained fuel from all sumps; did a longitude runup; and decided to proceed to san carlos. The engine hesitation was a result of switching tanks to slowly. While passing through the off position i don't think the tank was dry due to the gauge indicating 8-10 gallons; and the fact that we could still drain fuel from it.
output: C210 LOST PWR MOMENTARILY WHEN SWITCH FUEL TANKS DURING DSCNT FOR LNDG RESULTING IN DECLARATION OF AN EMER AND DIVERT FOR AN IMMEDIATE LNDG.

input: A traffic alert and collision avoidance system system check was performed before flight and indicated ok. During climb; a traffic alert and collision avoidance system fail annunciation was noted by both crew members. I; the second in command and pilot monitoring; stated that a report to air traffic control was required for traffic alert and collision avoidance system failure; which may or may not result in being unable to operate in rvsm airspace. The pilot in command declined to make a report; stating 'it does this sometimes; probably a weight-on-wheels switch'. I again insisted that it was a requirement; but he reiterated his position that he didn't want the hassle of reporting it and getting it on the record. He then asked what i would do if i were making an oceanic crossing and traffic alert and collision avoidance system failed. I stated that i would report it to air traffic control as required; which if before coast-out may result in denial of entry into oceanic airspace. He questioned my judgement on this; saying 'sometimes you gotta do what you gotta do for the flight; and just keep quiet.' i then stated that we needed to file a report via the company; which he dismissed. I'm filing this report independently for my own protection.
output: Air taxi First Officer reported the Captain did not report to ATC a malfunctioning TCAS system.

input: Working sector 26 had just combined back with sector 6. Aircraft y was level at fl240 over tadpo and about to land at mth which is close to tadpo. Aircraft x was coming from havana over tadpo at fl200. My d-side told me i had control from havana to turn and climb aircraft x. I climbed aircraft x to fl230 which the pilot read back. I needed to start aircraft y down and keep aircraft x climbing. Around tadpo i told aircraft x to fly heading 310. Apparently he read back climbing to fl310 which i missed. A little later i observed aircraft x hadn't turned and i told him again to turn. In the read back aircraft x acknowledged the turn but also told me he was responding to an resolution advisory i thought the resolution advisory was because he was under aircraft y now and maybe he had climbed to fast and the resolution advisory was forcing him down. I was able to turn him away from aircraft y and started aircraft y down to get my separation back.the sector was really busy and probably should not have been recombined but we had no staffing.
