In particular; kk45k; kk45i; kk54i; among possibly others. The nomenclature used here leads to easily juxtaposed clearances; readbacks; and/or data entry errors into navigation systems. While enroute we were given a clearance to one of these points; the first officer and myself both believed we were cleared to kk54i; when it appears the controller intended kk45i. We're not sure if the controller made the error; or we made the error on our readback. We flew for a period of time towards kk54i until the next controller queried us about it. Having intersections named this way so close together is a problem.
output: An air carrier pilot commented that identical letters and sequential numbers; such as KK45I and KK45K; leads to track errors because they are easily misunderstood.

input: Fo was flying. Weather was visual flight rules with low level wind shear advisories in effect as there had been previous thunderstorm activity in the area. On final approach to runway(s) 16 in den; the approach was very normal (flaps 30 degrees reference speed 136 knots indicated airspeed target speed 141 kias); when a b737 in front of us rpted a 20 knot(s) loss at 100 feet/foot over the runway(s) i told xx to make our target speed 150 knots indicated airspeed then upped it to 155 knots indicated airspeed -- about 2 mile out. Aircraft was on profile and stabilized. As we approached the threshold; the airspd increased to approximately 170 knot(s) then; at the 50 feet/foot callout; the aircraft seemed to just drop; consequently; landing much harder than anticipated. At the time of touchdown; the windshear alert system activated in the cockpit. After touchdown; i immediately grabbed the controls to keep the aircraft on the ground and on the runway(s) 3 flight attendants and 2 customers were injured and escorted to the hospital for a chk-up. Because some panels came down in the cabin; maintenance did a 2 hour inspection and found the aircraft to be airworthy. Ferried aircraft to chicago. Supplemental information from acn 440710: i hand flew the approach it was smooth and stabilized. As we approached the threshold; i disconnected the autothrottles; and at the moment i did second officer the airplane was on speed and on profile. At the ground proximity warning system 50 feet/foot call; just as i was beginning the flare and bringing the power back and as i was transitioning my visual attention down the runway(s) i perceived that the headwind component was increasing. I stabilized my pitch to avoid floating in the flare. Then it seemed like the headwind abruptly dissipated and the airplane dropped to the rwy.
output: A B747-400 FO MAKES A HARD LNDG AT DEN; CO. PAX AND FLT ATTENDANT INJURIES.

input: On clbout on flight abc from zzz to zzz1; we had a low oil pressure light come on for #1 engine we referred to communications procedure and also contacted the company; and relayed to them the problem all engine indications were normal. We were instructed to continue to our destination once there; we were in touch with maintenance by phone and company decided to minimum equipment list it. We returned to zzz with no problems i believe our mechs were giving wrong information and we should have returned back to zzz. Company is saying i should have returned to zzz and not listened to maintenance control why is maintenance giving bad advice when the pilot is looking for good advice? The federal aviation administration will probably be involved; and want to know why i continued on to zzz1.
output: A B727-200 CAPT EXPRESSES CONCERN OVER ADVICE GIVEN BY A MAINT CTLR TO CONTINUE WITH #1 ENG OIL LOW PRESSURE WARNING LIGHT ILLUMINATED. ALL OTHER ENG INDICATIONS NORMAL.

input: While taxiing for takeoff from sba runway(s) 7; we back-taxied on runway(s) 7 for about 500 feet/foot and were given instructions from the tower to taxi into position and hold. I was going to fly this flight as we turned the airplane into position for takeoff the capt told me that i had the airplane. Since we were already taxiing on the active runway(s) i felt sure that we had been cleared for takeoff i set takeoff power and the aircraft accelerated to at or near rotation speed at approximately rotation speed the controller told us to abort. At the time the controller told me to abort; it was obvious to me that i had adequate speed and distance (from the aircraft crossing our flight path) to takeoff and be well above the c150 by the time we reached the rwy(s) intersection the c150 was landing on runway(s) 15 (l or r) as we were taking off on runway(s) 7. Other than a maximum effort climb to miss the cessna; no other evasive action was needed and we crossed behind and above the cessna's flight path about 200 feet/foot or second officer the tower didn't notice or advise us to abort until very late in our takeoff run. Supplemental information from acn 379585: i called the tower supervisor on landing and they asked for everything.
output: NMAC BTWN A GULFSTREAM; G3; TAKING OFF AND FLYING OVER THE INTXN RWY ON WHICH A C150 WAS ALMOST READY TO TOUCH DOWN FOR LNDG. INCIDENT WAS CAUSED BY RPTR'S NOT HOLDING IN POS ON THE RWY AND NOT ABORTING WHEN TWR INSTRUCTED THEM TO DO SO.

input: Prior to departing chino; ca on a very smoggy low visibility day on a visual flight rules flight plan for scottsdale az; i requested and received from chino ground control a departure squawk and frequency (0245 and 135.4). After becoming airborne; i tried repeatedly to raise ontario departure at least seven (7) times. No answer; although i could hear the female controller talking to other pilots finally; just out of riverside airport i switched to 119.65 and immediately raised a controller he could not receive my squawk; and questioned where i had received the code. He switched me to 0254; and could still not receive my squawk. After climbing w/nw of a low mountain (nw of sunnymead;) i was finally picked up on radar; and given headings and altitudes i requested my flight plan be opened; which i had previously filed by telephone. The controller seemed disgruntled since i had departed 1:45 minutes ahead of schedule (xxx z). I was then vectored eastward and told to call ontario approach by telephone when i returned to scottsdale. (collect) i called and a woman refused to take the call per area manager all of this was somewhat concerning to me and a certificated pilot who was a passenber on the flight to my knowledge; there was no violation nor close call situations. Callback conversation with rptr revealed following information there is a corridor between the two arsas which pilot was trying to use to remain clear until communications established. Eastbound heading would keep clear of arsa; but ral air traffic area is problem intermediate fix remaining below arsa floor. Frequency assigned by ground brought no response during several attempts. Pilot used published frequency on chart to make contact. Controller very surprised; asked where and how pilot had gotten code to squawk. 'most unusual proc' was the response. Rptr upset that call was not accepted after being told to call collect. No follow up by faa.
output: UNAUTH PENETRATION ARSA; ATA.

input: Fo; pilot flying rpted loss of rudder/nosewheel authority/authorized at 60 knot(s) indicated air speed during takeoff roll. Aircraft experienced no sudden movements to indicate wind affecting airplane. Aircraft drifted 10 feet/foot off ctrline. Would not return to ctrline. I called the abort. Taxied back to gate. No abnormalities were found. First officer had over 500 hours in airplane. Wind was 270 degrees at 20 knot(s) gusting 32 knot(s) within demonstrated 27 knot(s) crosswind component taking off runway(s) 33 at zzz. There were very dark clouds to the north over the mountains with tops of approximately 10000 feet/foot and bases down to 1000 feet/foot over the mountains. The clouds started about 10 mile north the airport was vfr.
output: A CANADAIR CL65 REJECTED TKOF AT 60 KTS DUE TO LOSS OF RUDDER NOSEWHEEL STEERING. NO MECHANICAL CAUSE FOUND. CAUSE UNKNOWN.

input: The aircraft had flown before our crew's scheduled flight the inbound crew had written up the #2 epr gauge as being unreliable. Write-ups from previous days also indicated a short history of #2 epr problems maintenance replaced #2 epr gauge and the aircraft discrepancy was signed off; clearing the aircraft for flight engine start and taxi were normal. When the throttles were advanced for takeoff #2 epr again appeared unreliable; as it was very low. #2 was then set takeoff power by setting 92% n1; which matched nicely with engs #1 and #3. All other engine #2 indications (except epr) were at normal takeoff settings and matched up with engs #1 and #3. #2 throttle position was ahead of engs #1 and #3. The takeoff and gear and flap retractions were normal. As we attempted to set climb power using n1; this now also appeared to be unreliable. Engine #2 n1 was lower and n2 was higher than engs #1 and #3. Climb power was set by using fuel flow. At 10000' the f/e rpted #2 engine constant speed driven 'in' temperature in the caution range. The f/e then performed the abnormal for this situation. Faced with not really knowing what was happening to #2 engine the capt elected to return to cincinnati. I completely supported his decision. The engine was not shut down and a normal approach and landing were made on runway(s) 27l. Rpts from maintenance indicate the cause of the problem was a crossover bleed duct that had ruptured.
output: FLT CREW OF LGT EXPERIENCED ABNORMAL ENGINE INDICATIONS FROM #2 ENGINE. SMALL DUCT FAILURE.

input: On the published departure from the eagle vail airport (ege); co; i failed to follow the prescribed routing taking off on runway(s) 25. The procedure is to turn immediately to a heading of 215 degrees and climb to 13500 feet/foot passing 9000 feet/foot intercept the 322 degree radial of the red table vor and dme (co-located) and hence...! I intercepted the 322 degree radial but was flying inbound instead of outbound; when the controller told me i was in the wrong area. I had spent several minute(s) prior to takeoff studying the procedure but obviously failed to understand it thoroughly. There is no question that i erred. I have to believe; however; that i ante meridiem not the only pilot who has committed; or will commit this same error because of its complexity. A simple; but much safer way to present this departure is to have it on a graphic; horizontal depiction with a broad black arrow overlaying the route this is common for many other departures and in much less hazardous terrain. Also; in the written departure instructions; insert the words; 'intercept and track outbound on the 322 degree radial....' i know these 2 changes would have certainly kept me from making this mistake! Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr has a lot of experience flying and controling still; he flew the wrong direction for the departure rptr had taken off to the east several times; but this was his first westbound departure he was not expecting a westbound departure when given the westbound departure he spent 3 minute(s) reading and reviewing the departure still; he flew it incorrectly. Rptr admits his error; but feels he would have flown it correctly had it been presented as many other departures are presented. That is; with a geographic layout with altitudes written along the departure path. He feels the depiction from a verbal description leaves out clarity and can obfuscate what is intended.
output: A B200 KING AIR TAKES OFF FROM EGE; CO; AND FLIES THE DEP IN REVERSE. DEP INSTRUCTIONS ARE CONFUSING TO RPTR.

input: Early this summer i was with a primary student on approach to land behind an airliner. Suddenly the airliner; for no apparent; reason decided to go around. Of course following close behind i had instructed my student to stay high and land past the point that the airliner was going to touch down. When the airliner decided to go around it created a tremendous wake event. I alerted the tower that i would need to take immediate evasive action and turned ninety degrees to avoid the wake. In over twenty years of flying i have never had this happen and it made me think that this is not something we teach students. I think this should be an issue that is included in textbooks. I certainly will alert my students to this possibility in the future.
output: C152 Instructor Pilot reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to AUS when the air carrier aircraft preceding him executed a go-around.

input: Briefed a flaps 30 approach and landing runway 35r. Due to gusty winds planned for a ref of 145 and a target speed of 160 knot(s) air traffic control vectored us off of the arrival and had us parallel the course with a heading and descent while pointing out multiple traffic eastbound to intercept final for 35l. Twice approach control gave us direct points on published instrument landing system for us to join for the visual approach to runway 35r requiring changes to the flight management computer normal configuration was commanded along with the landing checklist. At approximately 6;500 feet/foot while hand flying the airplane i called for flaps 30 and target speed. All was normal until about 400 feet/foot when we received a ground proximity warning system alert for 'too low terrain.' i double checked the gear was down; speed was target plus about 5 which was roughly 165 knot(s) i then noticed that the flaps were still set at 15 degrees. Due to our higher than normal target speed we were well above the yellow band on the airspeed indicator; pitch was not abnormally high. I added about another 5 knot(s) and landed the aircraft.
output: A distracted B737 crew landed with Flaps 15 in gusty winds as the GPWS TOO LOW TERRAIN warning alerted at 400 FT after a task saturated the First Officer failed to hear the Captain's Flaps 30 request.

input: On takeoff 1 or more tires failed on the left/right (directions) side and the takeoff was aborted on runway(s) 22l at boston logan international airport abort was initiated at approximately 120 knot(s) (v1 was 148 kts). We remained on the runway(s) ctrline and were able to clear the runway(s) on a high speed taxiway. There was no fire and we did not have to evacuate/evacuation the aircraft there were no injuries and we deplaned the passenber via the forward stairs. Passenber were then bussed to the terminal.
output: FLC SENSED BLOWN TIRES; ABORTED TKOF.

input: I was working flight data during a busy and complex session where we were using 'multimode' radar rather than our usual fusion mode. I heard a pilot on frequency that he was maneuvering to avoid a visual flight rules aircraft. He then asked the radar controller if a visual flight rules target had been seen. The answer was no. I feel that due to the complexity and workload at the time it would have been difficult to see the traffic. After the incident happened i observed the visual flight rules tag behind the regional jet. While observing over the next few minutes i saw an intermittent altitude readout of 8500 feet. I tagged up the target manually and asked if the adjacent approach control would continue to track the aircraft to see if we could get their perspective on the event.i think the complexity and added workload contributed to the controllers failure to give a traffic advisory. When the main radar site is out of service we go into multimode which requires us to coordinate departures and arrivals into and slows our automation as well as changes our radar quality and video display. We also had outages that involved frequently used radio frequencies creating a situation that required telephone calls to center for coordination. All of this more labor intensive work takes away from our ability to watch the traffic on the screen and provide as good a service.several hours later i was informed by our supervisor that the problem with the radar was not serious enough for our tech ops to work on it and that we should not have been in multimode for most of the day. I think there is a problem here because no one informed us about what the malfunction was; nor when it was fixed/determined to be not worthy of fixing. The status of the equipment was definitely not relayed as it should have been; causing higher workload and a higher potential for reduced attention and service; possibly reduced safety overall.i would recommend a review of the communication lines from the terminal radar approach control facility and tech ops and how information is relayed about equipment outages; especially when no one from tech ops is actually working. I wonder if sometimes terminal radar approach control facility calls techops; leave a message; and never follow up so nothing gets taken care of. I don't think the radar outage caused the near midair collision but it may have contributed to the ability of the controller to give traffic advisories.
output: PWM TRACON Controller reported he observed a NMAC reported by an aircraft with an unidentified VFR target during a partial radar outage.

input: Our facility management is still requiring 5 hours and 30 minutes on position each day. They are accomplishing this by opening sectors with no traffic and staffing unused positions. The managers are only focusing on maximizing time on position; and not sector needs. I was assigned to work the d side and traffic was starting to build. The supervisor continued to put more controllers on d sides at other sectors with no traffic. The supervisor was not paying attention to our workload and we quickly became overwhelmed with multiple approaches and high altitude traffic. A visual flight rules that we were providing flight following to went below our frequency and radar coverage; and we did not notice it because we were busy with the instrument flight rules traffic. The visual flight rules disappeared from radar and we noticed it about 5 minutes later. We tried to relay to the aircraft; but did not have the time to do a full search since we were still busy. I tried to contact the supervisor; but supervisor was not even in the area. All of the controllers plugged in to the dead sectors were talking loudly and the distraction became overwhelming. The traffic slowed down long enough for me to give a briefing. The supervisor was still not around; but the radar controller continued to look for the aircraft. I took a 30 minute break and came back and a new supervisor was in the area and assigned me to the same sector d side with a new radar controller working. They still had not found the aircraft; but i assumed they were looking for him. The sector was still showing numerous tracks for the next several hours and we had not split it yet. Another controller came back from break and i thought they were finally going to split the sector; and i saw they supervisor send that controller to sit on a d side of a sector with 3 aircraft. I called the supervisor over and requested the sector be split by that controller. He agreed and we split the sector. I then asked if they had found the previous visual flight rules aircraft and the supervisor looked at me puzzled. The operations manager was called and came down and said that since there was no flight plan outbound they did not know where to start looking for the plane. I would think landing airport would be a good place to start. So the radar controller and i started to look for the plane on our own. I called the airport manager where the plane had come from and asked if the plane went back. The controller confirmed that the aircraft landed 10 minutes ago; so we informed the supervisor that we found the aircraft. Over an hour had passed since we initially lost radar contact with the aircraft and not a single management official had started a search. Fatigue and complacency are becoming rampant at this facility due to this time on position requirement. Managers are so distracted with keeping everyone on position for over an hour and a half; that they are not focusing on safety and running the areas.
output: ZJX Controller described possible lost aircraft event that went unnoticed by the supervisory staff; allegedly due in part to their focus on time on position requirements; rather than operational responsibilities.

input: Chked in with phl approach control and was told to expect visual to runway(s) 27r. We were on vectors for that approach when air traffic control said to intercept the liberty visual for runway(s) 27l. It turns out that we were already on the mxe 108 degree radial and we did not have time to adequately brief and review the 'liberty' procedure we were asked by air traffic control intermediate fix we had the traffic lined up on runway(s) 27r and we replied 'negative.' it was at this point that i began to review the liberty procedure and approach plate. It states that you must be at or above 3000 feet/foot at 33 vor and dme (co-located) and at or below 2100 feet/foot at 27 vor and dme (co-located) we were at 31 vor and dme (co-located) at this point; second officer i started down to make 2100 feet/foot or below by 27 vor and dme (co-located) going through 2700 feet/foot the first officer asked air traffic control intermediate fix we were cleared for the approach and he responded 'negative; maintain 3000 feet/foot do you have the runway(s) 27r traffic in sight?' we quickly returned to 3000 feet/foot and called the traffic in sight. We were then cleared for the approach we crossed the 27 vor and dme (co-located) at 2800 feet/foot instead of the 2100 feet/foot or below. We continued the approach to landing uneventfully; maintaining visual contact with the traffic on runway(s) 27r final approach a lot of confusion could have been prevented with more heads up notice of the 'liberty visual' clearance we were cleared to intercept without the benefit of reviewing the approach plate.
output: B737 LNDG PHL GIVEN LAST MIN VISUAL APCH CLRNC CHANGE; BEGINS DSCNT PRIOR TO CLRNC.

input: I was notified that an aileron cable was found misrouted; i witnessed the assembly and system test of the component and did not notice a misrouted cable. This was accomplished on jobcard #xx-xx-xx. Safety and security inspection was accomplished and all checkouts listed in the document; with no issue's noted.
output: Two repair station inspectors report about a mis-routed aileron cable at an aileron bus drum in the left wheel well of a customer airline's B737-800 aircraft.

input: Fe radio was not functioning. I (the capt) went off the radio to contact company to inform them we were in range. This was a ferry flight from ord to mdw. Much confusion. First officer was flying the plane. When i came back on to air traffic control we were on a 2 mile final in the landing confign. We landed and taxied clear of the runway(s) however; apparently the first officer had not received a clearance to land. Our radio was still on the approach freq.
output: B727-200 CREW LANDED AT MDW WITHOUT CLRNC.

input: Nav deviation due to vlf/omega position error. Climbing out of scottsdale; az; at approximately 15000 feet/foot we were cleared direct to zun vor and dme (co-located) we were below the altitude where we could receive zun vor and dme (co-located) second officer we were navigate, navigationing solely by the global gns-500 vlf/omega. Either zab or phx departure informed us that we were about 20 degrees off on heading for zun. At the time the global was showing a 120 knot(s) crosswind and we informed dep/ctr that could be part of the confusion. The next sector informed us that we were 20 mile westbound of our intended course and gave us a heading for zun. When we were able to receive zun vor and dme (co-located) we saw that we were in fact off course. We initialized the global over zun and had no more problems on the flight on the return flight we were talking to zdv and received clearance direct from the denver area to inw vor and dme (co-located) again we were out of range of the inw vor and dme (co-located) and were navigate, navigationing by the global unit. Center informed us that we were 15 degrees off of a heading direct to inw and we corrected. When we got within range of a vor and dme (co-located) where we could checked our position we discovered we were off course by 28 nautical mile normal procedure for us is to initialize the unit at the departure airport this was done in both cases. Because the airport reference point can be as much as 2 mile from the end of the runway(s) we usually reinitialize the unit at the first vor and dme (co-located) that we cross over. In both cases we were cleared direct to another vor and dme (co-located) before reaching a vor and dme (co-located) to reinitialize the unit. Usually this means that we could be up to 2 mile off; but we are able to correct this once we are in range of the vor and dme (co-located) the unit is being sent to maintenance because we have had problems of this sort once before. One unusual factor was on the first leg we had no passenber and we made a 45 degree bank; 120 degree turn after departure when given a new heading perhaps the global could not follow such a rapid heading change? Note: the problem was apparently due to the annapolis very low frequency being taken off the air and its frequency reassigned to the hawaii very low frequency (see enclosed notice). Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states following suggestion from the manufacturer; the company deselected both annapolis and hawaii stations. There were 5 stations in the system and the deselect leaves 3 to work with. This should allow a navigate, navigation error that is acceptable; not an error of 20 mi.
output: LTT CHARTER FLT HAS 20 MI NAV ERROR DUE TO OMEGA VLF STATION BEING SHUT DOWN WITH NO NOTICE AND FREQ REASSIGNED TO HAWAII.

input: Tkof and initial climb normal. While climbing through fl300; automatic fail light illuminated and pressurization system automatically switched to standby operations(s) cabin altitude was climbing through 9000-10000 feet/foot manual operations(s) attempted per rapid depressurization chklist and outflow valve checked full closed. Cabin altitude still not stabilized. Emergency descent accomplished per chklist to 11000 feet/foot mean sea level cabin altitude continued to climb and passenber oxygen masks dropped. Flight attendants and passenber donned masks. Cabin altitude did not stabilize until aircraft level at 11000 feet/foot mean sea level dispatch contacted and returned to kansas city uneventful. Postflt inspection discovered aft cargo door seal had blown out.
output: A B737-300 CREW; CLBING THROUGH FL300; EXPERIENCED A RAPID DECOMPRESSION; AND INITIATED AN EMER DSCNT AND A RETURN TO MCI.

input: While flying into burbank at night pilot flying (pilot flying) / pilot in command (pilot-in-command) elected to do visual to [runway] 15. Clearance was granted around janny [and] pilot flying took a course that meant we would intercept the final approach course from the left of centerline. Post meridiem (pilot monitoring) noted that we were left of centerline and that there was terrain in the area. We crossed over the ridge line at the standard 5;500 ft. But thereafter while still left of centerline the pilot flying started a descent. Post meridiem had terrain display up on mfd and was watching; there was never a yellow or red terrain ahead of the aircraft at anytime. Yet post meridiem noticed that the radio altimeter was showing a reading while still left of centerline. The radio altimeter reading went below 1;000 ft. And got to around 800 ft. The post meridiem called out the altitudes as soon as they were decreasing below 1;000 ft. And the pilot flying took evasive action by disconnecting the auto pilot and stopping the descent. Almost immediately after the radio altimeter reading went away and we continued a normal descent to landing on [runway] 15. Taking a visual to [runway] 15 at night is unnecessarily risky. With margins very tight on the left side of the approach course; situational awareness is reduced at night. The benefits certainly do not outweigh the risks. We never received a ground proximity warning system yet we came within below 1;000 ft. Of terrain on around an 8 mile final. It is easy to become complacent with your surroundings when you can not see them; so don't bother putting yourself in this situation... The company needs to put into writing that visuals to [runway] 15 should not be allowed at night. As post meridiem i should have called an immediate go-around the second i saw the radio altimeter go below 1;000 ft.
output: Air Carrier flight crew reported flying uncomfortably close to terrain on a night visual approach to Runway 15 at BUR; and suggested that the procedure be restricted to daytime operations.

input: during light to moderate turbulence in instrument meteorological conditions conditions we detected a strong electrical smell of some system getting very hot. I requested the #1 flight attendant to turn off all the items on her lighting and electrical panel. We ran the quick reference handbook cabin fire/smoke chklist and shortly the smell and haze in the cabin disappeared. We called dispatch and maintenance and discussed the problem and continued uneventfully.
output: A B757-200 FLT CREW EXPERIENCED ELECTRICAL ODOR AND FUMES IN THE CABIN. AFTER THE FLT ATTENDANT TURNED OFF PWR THE ODOR AND FUMES DISSIPATED AND THE FLT CONTINUED TO DEST.

input: Upon arrival, arrive i called dispatch to see what the fuel load that was planned for flight to ord. I was told it was 75000 pounds and i asked for it to be upped to 90000 pounds i was challenged by the dispatcher as to why and said i will not fly with less because the forward fuel pumps in tanks #1 and #4 become uncovered when flying with light loads due to the acceleration and deck angle needed to maintain v2+10 on initial clbout. 1 hour prior to departure i picked up the paperwork and the fuel load was still 75000 pounds i called back to dispatch and was told to talk to system operations(s) i did and was informed that company had determined that 75000 pounds was the fuel load for that flight (zzz-ord) and 3 other scheduled flts. I told system operations(s) that the forward fuel pumps still became uncovered at that fuel load; light payloads. I was told that the dispatcher had come up with that number. I then told them i had been in discussion with him about this and said that when i could see documentation that says the fuel pumps can be run for longer than momentarily uncovered i would do it; second officer system operations(s) said they would authority/authorized the fuel load to 90000 pounds the only documentation that has been given to me to date pertained to the b747-400 with baffled fuel tanks; the b747-100/200 does not and a boeing operations(s) manual bulletin from 1980 that basically tells you to have enough fuel for the flight plus reserves; avoid rapid acceleration; reduce pitch angles to keep the forward pumps covered. No time length is mentioned. I have seen pumps be uncovered through 10000 feet/foot depending on the clearance given and not recovered until the aircraft has accelerated through 250 knot(s) i have flown 27 of these flts in the last 60 days and on every flight that i requested additional fuel i have been challenged about my request and repeatedly told that it is company policy that 75000 pounds is all the fuel that these flts get. I have flown these flts with varying fuel loads from 75000 pounds on up and the minimum load that does not uncover the forward fuel pumps during all aspects of the flight is 90000 pounds minimum equipment list 28-1 for an aft fuel pump in tanks #1 and #4 is inoperative requires a minimum fuel load in that tanks to prevent the forward pump from being uncovered is 24254 pounds balance that across the aircraft by 4 and it is 97016 pounds second officer a compromise i feel is 90000 pounds the other reason the company gives me the cost of carrying the extra 15000 pounds of fuel. On the last 27 flts i have only blocked in 5 times below the flight planned block in fuel and that was due to vectoring by air traffic control or extended taxiing. On all of these flts i was above the planned burn at top of descent per the flight plan second officer that argument is invalid on these short flts. The main question is do i as capt have final authority/authorized on what i deem is a minimum safe fuel load for the flight or do i not. Regardless of the present perception that i; dispatch; and system operations(s) have joint responsibility for the flight i and my crew alone have the sole mortality on that flight that in my opinion; outweighs everything else.
output: B747-200 CAPT IS CHALLENGED ON HIS REQUEST TO ADD FUEL. CAPT FEELS THAT THE FUEL IS NECESSARY TO AVOID UNCOVERING FUEL PUMPS DURING CLIMB.

input: After a uneventful landing the cockpit crew smelled a strong odor of ammonia. As i slowed to taxi speed and began to turn off runway one of the jumpseaters came up to report that there was smoke in the jumpseat area. I told my international relief officer to go back and investigate. I took control of radios and told tower we have smoke in aircraft. He said he was rolling the trucks. As i taxied the smoke became much thicker and started to overtake the cockpit. I stopped straight ahead and ordered an evacuation of the aircraft out the left side and to meet at the nose of the aircraft. My international relief officer blew the slide. My first officer started to look for the evacuation checklist but i instructed him to leave the aircraft and i ran some of the checklist from memory. I set parking brake; shut down all three engines and blew the bottles to the engines. We all evacuated the aircraft and when we met at the nose of the aircraft airport rescue and fire fighting was just arriving. We had no known hazmat on aircraft. I asked everyone if they were ok from the evacuation or the fumes. Everyone said they were and we all declined medical assistance. We waited for airport rescue and fire fighting to clear the aircraft so we could then clear customs.
output: An MD11 Captain reported that after landing the forward cabin and cockpit filled with smoke. The aircraft was evacuated.

input: Aircraft departing ont on the prado departure are assigned the riverside sector frequency of 135.4. After riverside talks to the departure; the next frequency will be 134.0 for the hemet sector. A b737 departed and by passed 135.4 and called 134.0. When asked where he got the frequency he replied it was on the chart. The chart has incorrect frequencies in that 134.0 and 119.65 should not be used for ont departures. The danger is that hemet has control for these aircraft and may think that the riverside controller no longer needed an altitude restriction and climb the aircraft when in fact the riverside controller never spoke to the departure. If the riverside controller had traffic for the departure and issued an altitude restriction; then the departing aircraft calls hemet on departure; and hemet issues a climb it could cause a dangerous situation. Change the frequencies on the chart!
output: SCT Controller voiced concern regarding the frequencies published on the PRADO SID from ONT; noting operational needs and concerns.

input: Manifest indicated dangerous goods on board; lead agent verified none loaded. Before closing all doors; i received notice through on-board manifest printer that there was dangerous goods on board. After verifying with ramp agent; he notified me that there was none loaded nor any paperwork that he received. After arriving at mex; i had checkeded with lead agent about any dangerous goods aboard while off-loading cargo; and he initially said no. After completely off-loading cargo; he advised me that he had found dangerous goods in the rear of either bin #3 or #4; buried behind the rest of the cargo.
output: B737 CAPT ASKED ABOUT A DANGEROUS GOODS SHIPMENT ON THE ACFT. THE ONBOARD PRINTER INDICATED DANGEROUS GOODS WERE ABOARD. THE DEP LEAD AGENT SAID THERE WAS NOTHING ABOARD. DANGEROUS GOODS WERE FOUND AT THE DEST.

input: We topped off the fuel in sju to go to ewr and the flight plan called for 3 hours and 36 minute(s) to reach our destination as we approached sie vor and dme (co-located) we were given holding instructions. After 20-25 minute(s) of holding as we were reaching our efc time; air traffic control told us to extend our holding 'indefinitely.' the capt told him that we needed a firm efc and that fuel planning was a consideration. He also told him that our filed alternate was bdl; but phl was closer and we even had it in sight. He responded that he would work on getting an approach time and that phl was better option for him because we would have to fly up and around ewr in order to proceed to bdl. As i was listening to phl automatic terminal information service and getting ready to tell the company of our intention to go to phl; another aircraft of our company told us that phl still had trouble with snow on the ground and that they had backup delays for landing then they cleared us to ewr. The next controller told us to hold again and we told him that we could not hold any more and we were proceeding to bdl. He cleared us to bdl. Then again to ewr and told us that the next approach sector wanted us to go over sax for spacing. We told him we did not have the fuel for that and that we wanted priority. He asked how much fuel we had and we told him 35 to dry tanks. He said we would be on the ground before that. The capt told him we wanted to go to ewr now. His reply was that unless we declared an emergency we would have to go over sax. The capt said 'in that case we declare an emer.' at that point we were given a vector directly to ewr and landed without further problems we had 5000 pounds of fuel at touchdown.
output: FLC DECLARE EMER BECAUSE OF LOW FUEL DURING IMC.

input: We were assigned 210 knots on downwind while on the arrival.... After turning us north on a vector toward final; the controller switched us to the final approach controller. The final approach controller cleared us for a visual approach.... In my experience; if a controller wants us at a certain speed to the final approach fix he will usually assign it with the approach clearance. We did not get a speed assignment with the visual approach clearance. The captain asked me if we could now slow down since we were cleared for a visual approach; and i said 'i think so.' he began to slow and configure since we were going to join the final approach course right at the final approach fix after a minute or so; the controller asked us to say our speed which i reported as 190 knots. He said that for future reference; we should maintain the speed previously assigned until told otherwise and then told us to maintain 180 knots to the final approach fix and switched us to the tower.
output: B737-700 flight crew commenced slowing the aircraft for final configuration after being cleared by ATC for a Visual Approach. ATC advised that the previously assigned speed was to have been maintained until the Final Approach Fix.

input: We were taxiing into the [fbo] ramp in lax. The marshaller was instructing us to park on the north side of the ramp usually reserved for larger commercial aircraft. We were just south of the zipper line for autos in a non-movement area when the airplane stopped. The marshaller continued to tell us to move forward; but we were unable. At this time we heard on ground control frequency that the asphalt had failed under our right main. We shut down the aircraft and came out to find the tire had sunk approximately 6 inches through the asphalt. There was no damage to the aircraft.i think the only way to avoid this scenario would have been if we parked in a different location.
output: G-IV FO reported the asphalt ramp pavement at a LAX FBO failed under his right main gear; making further taxi impossible.

input: Prior to the final approach fix we lowered the landing gear. We had no green lights or electronic centralized aircraft monitoring indicating that the gear was down and locked; however it 'sounded' as though the gear was down. We executed a go around at approximately 1;500 feet/foot above ground level earlier in the approach we flew through moderate rain-producing clouds which generated excessive static electrical discharges. We were clear of clouds and rain approximately 5 miles outside of final approach fix in visual meteorological conditions we flew north of the airport to work the problem. We first consulted the aircraft frequency modulation and found no procedure addressing the problem of no gear down indication. We then; through automatic communications addressing & reporting system asked dispatch to call us to discuss our situation with them along with maintenance control. However; after numerous attempts we were unable to make contact with them. After debating all options we decided to declare an emergency; and return lowering landing gear normally and make a normal approach and landing. When we lowered the gear outside the final approach fix all indications were normal. Landing was uneventful. Maintenance believes that we probably had a lightning strike and that we had momentarily lost our 1 lgciu.
output: A320 pilot reports no green gear indications or ECAM indications after gear extension during approach. After trouble shooting a second approach is accomplished and the gear indicates normally. Flight flew through clouds which generated excessive static electrical discharges during the first approach.

input: As aircraft climbed through 1000' above ground level clean up started and power was reduced on the thrust management computer (tmc). During clean up and power reduction; abnormal nose down trim was felt. In the process of sorting things out (clb; clean up; heading change; abnormal trim); the aircraft descended 300-400'. The autothrottles were coming back. The warning 'don't sink' on the ground proximity warning system went off. The f/o responded by pushing the power levers back to climb power i pulled the nose up and resumed the climb profile. I still don't know intermediate fix the trim ran away; autothrottles malfunctioned (nose down trim); or intermediate fix i just plain screwed up. 27 yrs in aviation; i've never had any problem i have been going through some family crisis and emotions have certainly been frayed. Watch out for complacency in the glass cockpit!
output: ACR LGT EXPERIENCES UNNOTICED AND UNEXPLAINED ALT LOSS DURING FLAP RETRACTION AND SPEED INCREASE PORTION OF INITIAL CLIMB.

input: The flight was in a twin engine be-76 leaving addison for local instrument flight rules training at night. Aircraft performance through takeoff and climb was normal. As the takeoff progressed through about 200 feet/foot above ground level i happened to glance out my left/right (directions) window at the left/right (directions) engine i was completely surprised to see the bottom of the engine cowling wreathed in a blue flame. I notified tower that we had a possible engine fire and that we were returning to land. Tower asked intermediate fix we needed the equipment i declined as at this point; power had been reduced and most of the flame had dissipated. An uneventful landing followed. Post-flt investigation showed no signs of fire. Upon consulting several other pilots and an a&p; it was determined that this was in fact normal behavior for the aircraft under certain atmospheric and engine conditions; the engs can produce quite a bit of flame. However; nowhere in the pilot operating handbook or in my training; or in my study; was i ever told to expect flame from a 180 hp engine in my case; the result was 2 minute(s) of terror and a little embarrassment. However; had the weather been worse; or had i elected to secure the engine the outcome might not have been second officer happy. I consider myself to be a competent pilot i had flown the aircraft many times at night; but had never seen this phenomena; which turns out to be quite common. This whole incident could have been avoided intermediate fix someone; be it beechcraft; a certified flight instructor or an federal aviation administration air conditioning / alternating current on flying twins had bothered to tell me to expect this common; rather unnerving phenomena.
output: PLT INST TRNEE RETURNED TO LAND AFTER TKOF DUE TO WHAT APPEARED TO BE AN ENG FIRE DURING THE START OF A NIGHT INST TRAINING FLT.

input: Initiated takeoff roll; reaching 70+ knot(s) noted vibration on left main gear. Retarded throttles; assumed tire failure. On deceleration left main gear collapsed. Aircraft listed heavily to left and departed runway and came to stop. Notified tower and secured aircraft.
output: BE-55 pilot reported his left main gear collapsed on the takeoff roll.

input: While doing clearing turns with a student; the pitts came across our path from below and left/right (directions) to above and left/right (directions) following this maneuver; the pitts did an abrupt 180 degree turn; and crossed from upper left/right (directions) to lower left/right (directions) then departed the area.
output: NMAC BTWN A C152 PRACTICING BASIC FLYING MANEUVERS; AND A CHRISTEN PITTS; S2; MAKING STEEP CLBING AND DSNDING PASSES THROUGH THE CESSNA'S FLT PATH.

input: On approach to cvg; air traffic control issued a base turn to the instrument landing system runway(s) 18r (cvg) to a heading of 090 degrees during our base turn; we had approximately 50 knot(s) of tailwind; and our ground speed was over 300 knot(s) the weather was approximately 600 feet/foot 2 miles and the capt elected to fly this approach with raw data (no flight management system flight director; autothrottle; or autoplt). I was pilot not flying and chose to update the mode control panel for myself and xchk his approach as we turned to final; the wind shifted to a 45 knot(s) headwind. On final; air traffic control issued a speed of 200 knot(s) because we only had a 500 feet per minute descent on final. Air traffic control said maintain 3000 feet/foot speed 180 knot(s) to logoz intersection cleared instrument landing system runway(s) 18r. The capt was at flaps 20 degrees 180 knot(s) and approximately 1.5 mile from logoz. The capt commanded the gear down. Prior to logoz (1 mi); air traffic control asked us our speed and i responded 'we are just slowing to final spd.' air traffic control said 'you slowed too soon.' after landing he told us to call the tower supervisor on the telephone. The capt called and talked to the supervisor and told him why he slowed (because of the instrument flight rules weather and this is the normal time to slow at the faf). I think that the tower controller did not believe we were at 180 knot(s) due to the 45 knot(s) headwind; and his traffic was creeping up behind us. Again; the weather was instrument flight rules and we were doing standard company procs.
output: CVG CHALLENGES B757 FLC SPD CHANGE ON FINAL WITHOUT PRIOR COORD AS FLC ENCOUNTERS WX.

input: When departing celsius concourse on what appears to be taxiway cn; traveling east on the north side of the concourse to control then ground cleared us to cross lima; taxi to runway(s) 17r on mach number as we taxied; he realized we had a longitude air traffic control hold and cleared us to runway(s) 17l on taxiway ed left/right (directions) on taxiway p to hold on p9. As we taxied on ed; an airplane landed on runway(s) 17r over the top of us. When ground was questioned; he stated; we were told to hold short of ed. Even looking back it appears we were on ed since leaving the gate on the north side of concourse celsius reference pg 10-9. How do you hold short of a taxiway you are on. I do not believe we were told to hold short of ed. There would have been an immediate question of that clearance since i believed we were on ed. This needs to be clarified on the charts and in the terminology used by the ground ctl.
output: CLRNC DISPUTED - ACR MD-80 IS OVERFLOWN WHILE ON THE TXWY XING THE APCH END OF THE PARALLEL RWY. GND CTLR CLAIMS THAT THE FLC WAS TOLD TO HOLD SHORT OF THE TXWY.

input: Crew illness due to suspected food poisoning. After blocking into xyz at xa12z; one of the augmented crew members informed me that the augmented flight engineer (on rest) had become very ill. I immediately talked to flight engineer to find that he had severe abdominal pain; was frequently vomiting and that the illness came on suddenly after our arrival, arrive in xyz. Further; he had a headache; extreme nausea; chills and was very weak. He further stated he did not feel he could continue to operate in his condition in which i fully agreed. His condition did not appear perilous or require an emergency response; however; i immediately called the duty manager and established a conference call between flight engineer an inflt medical service physician and the duty manager while i arranged to get medical help locally for flight engineer through the station representative. On the initial leg of the trip; flight engineer had consumed a meal from the zzz1 uploaded catering. He was the only crew member to consume a meal with sausage on the breakfast entree. Aside from this; similar items had been consumed by all the other operating crew (eggs; fruit; etc). The entire crew also shared common items from the subsequent uploaded catering with no mal-effects. Symptoms from severe food poisoning usually take hours (approx 10-12) to manifest themselves. After talking with the inflt medical service physician and duty manager we established that flight engineer would be taken to a hotel to get medical attention and rest. The local station representative arranged a hotel room and physician's house visit for him. I asked the crew tracker to assist him in contacting his spouse after he reached the hotel second officer he could advise that he would be in good care.
output: B747 RELIEF SO GOT SEVERE FOOD POISONING FROM A COMPANY PROVIDED CREW MEAL.

input: During cruise portion of flight from mem to sfo; the flight attendant rpted that smoke was in the cabin behind first class. After investigation; i decided to divert to den while accomplishing the chklist for smoke in the cabin. When a pack #1 was shut down (2-3 minute(s) later) the smoke stopped. We continued to den for repairs.
output: A320 SMOKE IN CABIN DIVERTS TO DEN.

input: I briefed a practice area navigation 36l visual approach at mco. When cleared for the visual approaching amebe at 3000 feet; flaps 5; 180 knots; i selected lateral navigation with auto pilot on. I then selected 500 feet in the altitude window and vertical navigation the aircraft captured lateral navigation and started to climb. After trying to figure out why it was climbing i disconnected the ap at 3250 feet to hand fly the approach. While getting the gear down and flaps extended tower asked if we could take a visual to 36r at approx. 1800 feet. I accepted and moved over. While the first officer was looking up the instrument landing system for 36r we missed the call/extension to 25 flaps. At the 1000 feet check we saw the flaps at 20 and executed a non eventful go around; approach and landing.when doing a visual and accepting a visual to a parallel runway both pilots should stay heads up until the landing check list is complete; then if time permits look up and tune the ils.
output: A B757-200 flight crew reported executing a go-around after an unstabilized practice RNAV approach.

input: Tcas resolution advisory 'clb now; clb.' deviated to 8600' from 8000' assigned. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution cleared rpted to air traffic control target indicated red; 1300' below. Air traffic control indicated target was instrument flight rules smt assigned 7000'.
output: ACR LGT ALT DEVIATION EXCURSION FROM CLRNC ALT IN RESPONSE TO TCASII RA.

input: While in cruise at fl310 over the north atlantic we experienced an autoplt malfunction that resulted in a left/right (directions) bank of 1 or 2 degrees that was not detected by the crew. The capt noticed the sun was not where it should be. He selected heading select which had no effect. We selected the other autoplt and returned to our desired track. The flight mode annunciators displayed inertial navigation system track. We informed gander center of our equipment malfunction. The rest of the flight was without incidence.
output: A DC10 FREIGHTER DEVIATED FROM INTENDED AND ASSIGNED COURSE DUE TO UNWANTED BACK INPUT CAUSED BY A FAILED AUTOPLT.

input: After an uneventful flight from zzzz; we checked the rjaa automatic terminal information service and obtained the latest weather. Although we had planned for gusty winds and discussed this with the dispatcher; we were not expecting what we saw. A frontal passage was occurring and the winds were significantly higher than what we expected -- gusting to 38 knot(s) it was my leg and we briefed for a flaps 25 landing. The reference speed for our weight was 140. We added the full correction for winds and gusts of 20 knot(s) as we entered rjaa approach airspace; the controller started issuing windshear reports of -15 and then -20 knot(s) on 3 mile final. Our fuel load was predicated on no alternate; with just a little extra for the time that the gusty wind operation would entail. Thinking ahead; we obtained the burn to the downtown tokyo airport from dispatch. We also got the weather there -- it was worse than rjaa -- gusting to 42 knot(s) we were faced with making the best of the situation at rjaa. As we positioned on downwind for runway(s) 16r; approach issued a micro burst advisory with a loss of 33 knot(s) this was getting interesting. I notified approach that we could not continue with the approach to landing with conditions like that. Almost simultaneously; approach came back and notified us that they were changing the runways to a north operation. They gave us a 180 degree heading and told us we would be number one. They had several aircraft yet to depart off of the runway(s) 16's and we were vectored accordingly. I discussed the fuel situation and the operating conditions with the first officer we decided that the safest course of action was to continue with rjaa. We would have fuel for one missed approach; vector back and one more attempt before things got to the extreme. All of the reports of windshear had been north of the airport second officer federal aviation regulation and we would be the first operation to land north. We briefed the approach and were mindful of the pws and ground proximity warning system windshear procedures; as well as microburst guidelines. We were instrument meteorological conditions until approaching the final approach fix at which time we broke out visual meteorological conditions radar was painting numerous patches of magenta returns north of the airport. Tower gave us a gust to 22 knot(s) at the runway and blowing dust kept us from seeing the approach lights until about 3 miles out. The ride had been fairly smooth for the conditions and we'd experienced minus/plus 10 airspeed fluctuations on final. We never got any windshear indications from our onboard systems. Once i had a good visual on the runway; i told the first officer that i didn't want to miss this approach and have to go into the area of really bad weather. Approximately one mile from the approach end of runway(s) 34l i began to intentionally allow the aircraft to situate under the normal glideslope. Given the conditions; i chose to fly the aircraft in a flatter and faster profile than normal. I verbalized this to the first officer and asked her to maintain watch on the airspeed and i would remain focused outside. The airspeed continued minus/plus 10 through the approach with moderate turbulence. Since runway(s) 34l has a displaced threshold; i intended to be somewhat lower over it and touch down just after it. At about 100 feet/foot above ground level the first officer called airspeed 170. This was higher than our planned target; and i attributed it to the gusty wind. We touched down about 500 feet/foot past the displaced threshold in a normal crosswind landing; normal reversing; and autobrakes at level 3. We turned off at the usual high speed turnoff uneventfully and taxied to the gate.
output: B777 FLT CREW ELECTS TO ABANDON THE APPROACH TO RWY 16R AT RJAA AFTER RECEIVING A MICROBURST REPORT FROM TOWER. A SAFE LANDING ENSUES ON RWY 34L.

input: Final approach stewart newburg; ny; vor and dme (co-located) runway(s) 27. Small aircraft (private) appeared on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii screen 100 feet/foot below us at a distance of approximately 1 mile we initiated a climb immediately after initiation traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii issued resolution advisory to 'clb.' traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii then issued 'monitor vertical spd.' we showed 500 feet/foot separation as aircraft passed below us. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii issued 'clr of conflict.' we resumed approach called approach control after landing this was the traffic he had called to us at approximately 11 mile on final. He asked tower to not pass us over yet till clear of traffic (we were told this on telephone). We were in climb when approach called the traffic again. We did not respond to his call due to avoidance of other aircraft we were told this is not an isolated occurrence in this area. More frequent ta's during the approach would have light emitting diode to an earlier avoidance of his altitude we were within 5 mile of the field.
output: FO OF ACR LGT ACFT TOOK EVASIVE ACTION IN RESPONSE TO A TCASII RA AND THE SIGHTING OF ANOTHER ACFT DURING AN INST APCH.

input: We all have been complying with mask use at zzz to 'stop the spread' and for public image. I see the policy becoming more and more restrictive; and gets interpreted differently by people. Yes; we must wear a face covering while in the public. Yes; if we are unable to maintain social distance; we should also be wearing a covering outside of public area. What this does not address is the long term health effects of wearing a face covering every day of the week for hours at a time. Extended mask use can cause and is not limited to:1.shortness of breath and light headedness2. Headaches3. Dermatitis4. A weakened immune system ( your body is unable to rid toxic cell normally because they wind up staying in your face covering which causes bacteria to stay in your mouth. Having bacteria stay in your mouth leads to health issues such as dental issues (root canals; infections; etc.) healthy oral hygiene is a necessity for heart health and overall health.5.chronic respiratory issues
output: Customer Service Representative reported health related concerns with wearing face masks at work for extended periods of time.

input: Acft had routine maintenance on right mlg which involved removing and replacement of right mlg upper and lower torque links. Maintenance was performed per maintenance manual 32-11- 04 of foreign mlg type aircraft problem was discovered inflt after pilot attempted to retract gear and above 500 feet/foot above ground level on a ferry flight for aircraft positioning pilot made decision to return to field. Pilot got air/gnd advisory and lift dumper inoperative or do not deploy. Upon maintenance investigation on ground could not find any problem with sensors on landing gear through onboard bite test of proximitypa box. Upon jacking aircraft and putting it in the air; maintenance could not retract mlg without using the gear override. Performed bite test of mlg sensors. Found right mlg air/gnd sensor shows federal aviation regulation position (in air sensor should show near.) prob/solution: adjusted. Right mlg air/gnd sensor target. Suggested final solution to avoid future problems maintenance manual should be changed to reflect aircraft must be jacked and then accomplish channel test of air/gnd proximitypa sensors per maintenance manual 31-41-00-710-815. The maintenance manual allows you to perceive that jacking the aircraft is necessary only intermediate fix you removed and replace the sensor. However; since the target is on the upper torque link; intermediate fix you remove and replaced the link the factory drilled holes may vary from the original equipment therefore; jacking the aircraft is necessary even intermediate fix you haven't removed and replaced the sensor due to possible target misalignment. Supplemental information from acn 244096: this was my first dealing with the foreign mlg maintenance manuals. I found they have a different way of doing things. I went back to the maintenance manual to see intermediate fix i had missed something; and how. On the first page of the mlg torque links removal/installation it lists the tools needed; materials needed; parts needed and at the bottom of the page 'referenced procs.' in this list of procedures was a reference to a different air traffic area 31; operations(s) test of the proximitypa switching system i guess i completely overlooked this. The target for the proximitypa switch is attached to the upper torque link. Possibly; i was tired from working all night and was on about my 10th or 11th hour i was tired and we had already broken about 2 etr's and i was hurrying to try to get the aircraft out the doors second officer i could fly. After talking with the mechanic that worked on the problem after the return to field; he said that the test of the proximitypa switching system wouldn't and didn't make a difference. He said the only way to avoid that kind of problem is the aircraft has to be completely jacked. The maintenance is pretty void in this area. It states the only reason to jack the aircraft is to change a proximitypa switch. We did not change a switch in the original problem all that was done was the replacement of the torque link. I feel the maintenance manual needs to state more clrly to jack the aircraft after changing the torque links and swing the landing gear.
output: ACR MLG HAD TO RETURN LAND FROM FERRY FLT ACCOUNT UNABLE TO RAISE GEAR. FAULT FOUND IN AIRLINE MAINT PROC WHICH WAS GOVERNED BY THE PROC AS SPELLED OUT IN THE ACFT MAINT MANUAL.

input: I departed from rochester; mn; at approximately xa30 local time. Before taking off i had completed a thorough preflt and runup (including fuel quantity and quality). The main tanks were topped off -- 100 gallons of fuel. The oil level was at 10 quarts north each engine on the runup the magnetos dropped 50 revolutions per minute each. The propellers were exercised and all engine gauges were in the green. There was no indication of any engine problems on the runup or on takeoff upon reaching fl190 all engine gauges were still indicating in the green. After being at cruising altitude (fl190) for 5 minute(s) the left/right (directions) engine failed. I was approximately 20 mile north of dubuque; ia. I started a steady descent and informed air traffic control as air traffic control vectored me to dubuque i attempted to restart the engine the engine did not restart. I tried one more time to restart the engine then i went ahead and shut it down. I had a safe landing at dubuque. After looking at the engine my guess is that it had blown a rod. Under the circumstances i did everything i could. There was no indication of engine problems prior to its failure. I calmly handled the situation and the flight came safely to rest at dubuque. The aircraft was light (i was the only one on board) second officer i had no problem maneuvering and maintain altitude with 1 engine i was in and out of clouds during the descent but encountered no icing. Dubuque was visual flight rules the aircraft was a cessna 340.
output: PLT OF AN SMT TWIN ENG ACFT MADE AN EMER LNDG AFTER 1 ENG FAILED DURING CRUISE.

input: At pwk the approach end of runway(s) 30r is not visible from the tower due to a hangar. Tower personnel are unable to monitor the progress of aircraft taxiing onto an active runway(s) controllers are already restrict, restricted, restriction from taxiing an aircraft into position and hold at the full length and require the aircraft to taxi up to a point where they are visible. Therefore aircraft are still on the active runway(s) in the non visibility area. The only way to alleviate this problem is to either remove hangar 3 or create access to the runway(s) a few hundred feet/foot north of the non visible area. Continuation of the operations(s) as it is; is unsafe.
output: RPTED SIT IN WHICH THE APCH END OF A RWY IS NOT VISIBLE FROM THE CTL TWR DUE TO A HANGAR. RPTR SAID ACFT ON THE APCH END OF THE RWY ARE NOT VISIBLE UNTIL THEY ARE A FEW HUNDRED FT DOWN THE RWY. RPTR FEELS CONTINUED OPS AS IT IS; IS UNSAFE.

input: In order to understand the situation; air carrier y's gates face south and my air carrier's gates' face west. For the aircraft to get out to the runways; taxiway charlie can be accessed by several taxiways; one of those taxiways being taxiway bravo. Shortly after air carrier y's airbus pushed back off of their gate and subsequently taxied out to taxiway charlie via taxiway bravo; i; ground support personnel; being the pushback tractor driver on air carrier x's 757 gate; was given permission for pushback by [our] air carrier x's pilot of the 757-200 outbound flight and proceeded to push the above aircraft back into the ramp area behind air carrier y's gates. I had already stopped once for air carrier y's airbus that had bypassed the bravo taxiway that leads into the ramp area for both air carriers; while using caution since aircraft are always arriving and departing. I had no sooner resumed the pushback from our gate pushing my air carrier x's b757-200 towards the ramp area behind air carrier y's gates; when i had to do a rapid; but safe stop of the outbound b757 flight due to a 2nd airbus a321 aircraft from air carrier y that rapidly came flying into the ramp/gate area off of taxiway bravo; narrowly clearing/missing the back of our air carrier x's b757-200. My lead also stated that he too saw the events above happen as well.
output: A ramp ground support tractor driver describes his efforts to safely push a company outbound B757-200 off of their west facing terminal gates past another air carrier's south facing gates to access Taxiway Bravo. Although cleared for continued pushback; an inbound A321 aircraft suddenly appeared; taxiing into the ramp area narrowly clearing; missing the back of their B757 aircraft.

input: I was landing on a clear morning with light winds from the south (my left). My approach speed on final was about 72 knot(s) with two notches of flaps. I had a bounced landing and tried to recover and save it in lieu of a go-around. The yoke was a bit 'sticky' and i began to porpoise and left the runway to the right. The aircraft taxied down a gentle side slope and slowed to 5 to 8 knot(s) before coming to the bottom of the slope and sticking the nose wheel in a soft muddy ditch. The prop struck the mud and tall grass and the engine stopped. The nose gear was pushed backwards into the firewall causing two wrinkles in the lower portion of the firewall and some slight floor damage (1' push toward the rear of the aircraft) and about a 1/2 inch upward 'saddle' of the outer skin. No structural damage was done to the aircraft and none was done to the nose gear. The prop sustained a nick about 1/4 deep about 5/8 inches from one tip.we removed the plane from the ditch by manually lifting the nose gear and inserting plywood under it and we did the same with the main gear then slowly towed it forward up the slope and back onto the rwy.no damage was done to runway(s) lights or other airport property.
output: C172 pilot reported minor damage resulted from a runway excursion following loss of directional control during landing roll.

input: We had just executed the published missed approach at zzz after determining that given the weather conditions it was not a safe option to land off the vor and dme (co-located) approach to runway(s) which we had conducted; due to limited visibilities and very strong crosswind conditions coming off and offset approach to the runway(s) of intended landing we were using continuous ignition during the approach phase due to the rain and strong wind situation the missed approach was conducted normally and upon contacting zzz1 approach with our missed approach call; our intentions were requested. We determined that a diversion to zzz1 was in order. As the first officer communicated our intentions and began to set up the flight management system i as flying pilot decided it was time to discontinue use of continuous ignition. On the gulfstream 5 the continuous ignition is directly above and in very close proximity to the engine run switches. Although i advised the first officer what i was doing; i did not have him verify my actions and i inadvertently selected engine run switches to the off position instead of the continuous ignition switches. Needless to say i realized very quickly what i had done as the engs spooled back. In the time it took my first officer to declare an emergency i had restored the run switches to their run position and the engs restarted very quickly with minimal loss of airspeed or altitude. It took us several minute(s) to regain all systems lost during the initial loss of generator power; but all systems were restored successfully. In communicating with air traffic control we advised them we had restored normal operations(s) however they attempted to provide us with expedited vectors for the approach after unsuccessfully getting the aircraft in a position for the approach to runway(s) we asked for vectors for the instrument landing system and that gave us the time we needed to completely restore the aircraft to normal operations(s) landing was uneventful. Certainly better crew coordination in deselecting the continuous ignition would have averted this incident. Since the location of the run switches are in such close proximity to the ignition switches; there needs to be a redesign to develop a guard for the run switches second officer as to bring into question which switches one is trying to deselect. Intermediate fix my hand would have hit a guarded switch; my mind would have been challenged to ask; 'is this really the switch i want to turn off at this time?' obviously the issue of attempting to do something during a critical phase of flight that could have been done at a later time; is worthy of consideration. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that he was totally at fault and that he realized instantly what he had done. He turned the fuel control switches on immediately and the engs started immediately. When asked about the shape of the two switches; he indicated that they were completely different and that he was in a hurried state and threw the switches very quickly. The switches can easily be seen and are not in a position that is difficult to observe. He indicated that he did not look down to confirm what he was touching. Supplemental information from acn 596851: i reached back to get the commercial chart book out of the holder and the capt announced he would turn off the continuous ignition. He reached for ignition; but put his hand on the fuel control and selected both engs to 'off!' the switches are co-located on the base of throttle quadrant. I ante meridiem guessing it took 15-40 secs for the engs to spool back up after the capt immediately returned the fuel controls to 'run.' all electronic flight instrument system went black; instrument meteorological conditions gusty 40 knot(s) winds at 2500 feet/foot the capt's electronic flight instrument system reverted to battery power and we use communications 1 for that reason; second officer no comm was lost. Callback conversation with rptr acn 596851 revealed the following information the rptr (fo) indicated he felt that the switches are too close to each other and that the inadvertent securing of the engs could occur again. Although the switches for the 'continuous ignition' are push to activate type switches and the 'fuel and ignition' switches are pull up andmove from the detent type switches; the rptr feels that the switches should be relocated. He felt that there was a lot of schedule pressure that particular day and that the crew was task saturated.
output: GULFSTREAM-V CAPT; DURING A MISSED APCH; INADVERTENTLY SECURES BOTH ENGS. THE CAPT MANAGED TO RESTART BOTH ENGS AND CONTINUE TO THE DESTINATION.

input: Was on a visual flight rules training flight for stall training and spin awareness; climbing out of lot. Normally; i stay low until well clear of class b airspace; but today i instructed student to level off at 3500 feet/foot mean sea level 100 feet/foot shy of ord class b airspace; second officer we could get out of everyone's way. I tried to leave a little room below the class b airspace; even though by the time we could realistically have reached that altitude we should have been well clear of the class b airspace. Well; traffic rpted coming from the north entering a crosswind for runway(s) 27; which we had just departed; and were currently about the area of a crosswind leg. I had the student level off briefly to look for traffic after spotting traffic i instructed him it was alright to climb he continued to climb as i was looking outside scanning for other traffic as i brought my head back into the cockpit; i looked at the altimeter to see we were at 3600-3700 feet/foot mean sea level i yelled at the student to level off and informed him of the situation and that we may be in violation. I took his sectional chart and estimated that we had to be clear of the class b airspace by approximately 3-5 mile but that it was close. I then instructed him to turn further south and away from the class b airspace; and then to continue the climb a little further away. I think the lack of situational awareness on my part was a contributing factor. I should have been paying closer attention inside the aircraft as we approached our altitude and closer attention to where we were in regards to the class b airspace. I also should not have allowed myself to be second officer distraction by the traffic to lose supervision of my student's actions. The student should have also been more aware of his altitude and our location. Especially after being reminded of what altitude we were climbing to. To correct for this situation and to avoid another close call as we were not in violation; hopefully; better situational awareness is needed; along with better supervision of my students. I cannot relax my supervision while being distraction outside. I also can probably leave a little more room for error when departing the area; or use my normal method of staying low until well clr.
output: C152 INSTRUCTOR AND STUDENT POSSIBLY ENTERED ORD CLASS B AIRSPACE WITHOUT CLRNC.

input: Plane equipped with wheel-skis had landed earlier on a frozen lake with fairly deep snow which had piled up on skis around wheels and brakes. Returning to gfl decided to land on glen lake to checked intermediate fix brakes had frozen. They had and wheels were locked. Kept sliding wheels on rough ice and snow to try to break them loose. Hit slushy spot- plane nosed up striking propeller should have stopped and freed wheels manually.
output: PLT OF A PA-18; SUPER CUB NOSE UP STRIKING PROP WHEN ATTEMPTING TO BRAKE LOOSE STUCK WHEELS AND BRAKES DUE TO ICE.

input: Having received clearance to fl280; the capt programmed the flight management system to descend to fl280 by a point 35 mile westbound of mei. The aircraft started the descent early; second officer the capt changed from an flight management system descent to a vertical speed descent at this time 'alt arm' light was illuminated for altitude capture at fl280. At approximately 250 feet/foot below fl280; the altitude warning horn sounded at which time the descent was stopped and the aircraft was returned to fl280. No conflict was noted. Standard callouts were accomplished. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr flies the md-88 for a major united states air carrier he likes the aircraft and calls it 'an old aircraft with new software.' he thinks this episode was primarily a 'software prob.' he agrees that he should have been watching the aircraft more closely. The aircraft has made him more aware and watchful. There was no word from air route traffic control center it is highly probable that the controller did not notice. The rptr's acr's policy is to avoid changing the altitude mode within the last 1000 feet/foot of capture second officer as to avoid losing the altitude capture feature. The crew did not change the altitude mode.
output: ALTDEV ON DSCNT.

input: Severe turbulence encounter approximately 100 nm east at fl280. Encountered a 10-15 second period of severe turbulence. Conditions were instrument meteorological conditions with light precipitation and light chop. Pax were seated at the time; fas (flight attendants) were not because we were well west of the convective activity (although aft fas were self seated). There was no indication of convective activity in front of the aircraft on the radar. All convective activity was behind the aircraft by approximately 30 nautical mile altitude loss was approximately 400 ft. Air traffic control queried us about our altitude and we responded with a severe turbulence report and that we were returning to fl280. After exiting the turbulence area; we immediately checked with the fas for injuries and cabin condition. There were no reported injuries; and since there were no carts out; the cabin condition was good. [reports] were recorded for severe turbulence and automatic communications addressing & reporting system inoperative via [commercial radio] voice with maintenance control.
output: An A320 encountered severe turbulence at FL280 flying through the Midwest and lost 400 ft; however no one suffered injuries. As a result of the turbulence the right front windshield outer pane cracked. The flight continued to its destination.

input: On nov/thu/03 myself and another technician installed a flap control unit using maintenance manual. A couple weeks later the technician that removed the unit questioned me about input crank bolt being difficult to access. On dec/sun/03; i discussed this with the other technician that assisted on installation and we could not remember tightening the bolt in question. On dec/sun/03; we contacted our maintenance control to request a technical service item against aircraft to rechk security of bolt in question. Maintenance manual abc sub task 123; step #8. It was determined on the night of dec/sun/03 that bolt was tight. I fault myself for not signing turn-over rpt up to the step i completed instead of signing off complete installation.
output: A B737-400 WAS DISPATCHED AFTER A FLAP CTL UNIT WAS REPLACED. TECHNICIANS WHO REPLACED UNIT QUESTION WHETHER THE INPUT CRANK NUT WAS TORQUED.

input: On initial contact; pilot was issued the following clearance 'acr x; austin departure radar contact. Turn left/right (directions) heading 070 degrees intercept and resume the austin 1 departure climb and maintain 12000 ft.' the aircraft flew this heading for several mile then turned towards the cwk vor and dme (co-located) instead of flying the air traffic control assigned heading when queried; the pilot stated that he was flying the departure proc.
output: AUS CTLR RPTS DISPARITY BTWN ISSUED DEP CLRNC AND UNEXPECTED ACFT RTE FLOWN USING FMS.

input: During cruise we experienced a fault with the #2 inertial reference system/unit performed the procedures outlined in the quick reference handbook checklist and the problem was corrected.
