The aircraft was pressurizing at an excessive rate; so he ran the quick reference handbook procedure and tried to manually control the pressurization system but the left side was unresponsive; the right side worked on the manual mode and was able to control the pressurization at that time. During level flight we had an engine indicating and crew alerting system msg. 'cabin alt auto' so we ran the quick reference handbook and complied with quick reference handbook instructions and were able to control the cabin pressurization manually. During cruise left outflow valve would display full open; and full close indications in manual and in auto. This was confirmed by mechanic who was onboard. The mechanic tried to troubleshoot by opening central monitoring computer (cmc) on the center control display unit cmc confirmed multiple failures of the pressurization system involving both channels of pressurization system and the failure of the left outflow valve. Status messages cabin alt auto b; and cabin alt auto a were displayed on status page. During cruise; cabin altitude would periodically initiate excessive rates of climb for no apparent reason. Cabin was stabilized and in manual mode; and would have to be stabilized manually. We had to be completely dedicated to monitoring the system to maintain a constant cabin altitude and differential pressure. This task was very consuming in addition to normal flight duties and other distractions; acars/ satcom failure; high frequency communications; redispatch flight plan; and weather avoidance. The relief pilot had flown this aircraft a week prior with the left outflow was on minimum equipment list he briefed the crew about it. We looked at the history of this airplane and found multiple write ups about it. The pressurization system had been written up numerous times; and was never properly repaired. This situation led to a complete loss of pressurization automatic control. Manually controlling pressurization on a seven hour leg was a big distractor and a safety issue. Maintenance needs to be properly diagnose and fixed to ensure safe operations.
output: A B747 First Officer experiences pressurization anomalies from right after liftoff and throughout the seven hour flight. The pressurization system will only operate in manual mode and then with occasional erratic climbs and descents of the cabin altitude. The problem had been written up numerous times and never properly repaired.

input: I was doing a diversion exercise with my student on the north side of sna arsa above the 91 freeway. He chose to take as ground reference point a small lake at the ne edge of the arsa in order to give me heading and time to the diversion point which was orange county airport after he gave me heading 210 degree and time estimated at 6 minute(s) he began his process. We were at 3000 feet/foot mean sea level i knew he was going through the arsa. I waited a little bit hoping he will realize it and change his heading i then told him and we exited the arsa. But when we landed we had to call orange county tower i then realized we were just in the path of orange county instrument landing system and then we made a big mess. I take the total responsibility in this mistake and i realize being a certified flight instructor i should have never let my student enter in the arsa with the hope he would realize the error. Student only admit their errors and mistakes when they are actually doing them. Nevertheless; nobody should ever violate an airspace consciously and i will never let my student do it again -- experiences are sometimes the result of mistakes.
output: UNAUTH PENETRATION OF AIRSPACE.

input: Flt x from hou to dfw was holding short of runway(s) 12r at hou. The tower controller cleared us into position on runway(s) 12r to remain westbound of runway(s) 17. As the aircraft lined up on runway(s) 12r well westbound of runway(s) 17; a different tower controller cleared us for an immediate takeoff traffic was cleared to land on runway(s) 17. The first officer advanced the throttles and the takeoff warning sounded stabilizer. The first officer restarted the throttles. I rechked the settings and seeing nothing abnormal; the throttles were advanced again and again the warning sounded. The aircraft was still well west of runway(s) 17. I informed tower to cancel our takeoff clearance tower ordered us to hold our position and added we should not accept takeoff clearance unless we were ready to go; and that he did not have a place for us to go. Knowing there was arriving traffic and not knowing their exact position i declared an emergency to alert everyone of the situation after redirecting some aircraft tower cleared us to the westbound ramp. We were able to reset our system and solve the problem we canceled the emergency and departed hou. Upon arrival, arrive at dfw we made the appropriate entries and maintenance found the stabilizer trim adjustment out of limits.
output: TKOF WARNING SOUNDED ON PWR APPLICATION. TWR STATED ACFT SHOULD NOT TAKE RWY UNTIL READY. WHEN TOLD OF PROB; CREW DECLARED EMER WHEN TWR INDICATED PROB WITH CREW PROC.

input: Fl320 slop (strategic lateral offset procedure) r1. We were behind a wide body aircraft. Started to encounter wake turbulence. We moved to slop r2. A little while later the wind shifted just enough all of the sudden we encountered moderate wake turbulence. Pilot flying put in slop r3 to avoid any possible severe wake turbulence. We were distracted momentarily with the turbulence issue and seating everybody. We did not get to notifying air traffic control of the r3 deviation in a timely manner. A few minutes later were informed via cpdlc about the deviation via ads-b. We immediately returned to slop r2 which did keep us out of the wake from the preceding aircraft at this time.
output: B777-200 Captain reported encountering wake turbulence from a preceding wide body aircraft in cruise flight over the North Atlantic.

input: After disconnecting the towbar and going to hand signals with both engs running; operations(s) determined we needed to move baggage for center of gravity. The initial bag handlers came up and waited to approach the airplane till we got a hold of operations(s) and found out what needed to be done and shut the #2 engine down. After we received the signal that all was complete and could restart the engine another baggage vehicle came up and ran in to add another bag. The marshaller saw him and gave me the signal that all was not clear and hold my engine start. The first officer also saw the individual and told me it was safe to start the engine while this turned out to be a non event; the potential for a serious incident was definitely there. Intermediate fix after being cleared to start the engine and intermediate fix we had initiated the start; both of us could have been monitoring the start and not seen the individual run in or the marshallers signal not to start. When anyone is approaching the airplane after the ground crew is cleared off; they need to be sure that they have been seen by the flight crew. A good way to have handled this situation would be to have the ground crew come back on interphone till all activity was complete; and then be cleared off again. We had an federal aviation administration inspector on board and he indicated that he would be mentioning the situation in his rpt. He did not see a problem with the way we handled the situation but he indicated that there was potential for a prob.
output: A B737 FLT CREW NOTICE A RAMP WORKER APCHING THE ACFT WITH A BAG AFTER THEY HAD STARED THE ENG.

input: Non-compliant passenger.during our flight i was informed of non-compliant passenger; passenger x seat xx6; who apparently was continually reminded of face covering policy. Flight attendant woke passenger to remind them to mask up. I was informed of this during a bathroom break an hour before landing. The passenger followed the flight attendant to first class cabin to complain about being woken up.captain made public address 'reminding all passengers of policy.'i told the passenger we need to get a commitment for mask and he agreed and then made a complaint about being hurt by flight attendant.flight continued without further incident and customer service supervisor met aircraft.
output: Air carrier Captain reported a passenger was not complaint with face mask policy during flight.

input: Acr xx flight xx planned lax to mia on a routing over elp; then ne toward lit to vuz; then se along the west coast of florida due to thunderstorms over se texas and srn la/ms. On flight monitor xc; i noticed the flight near msy and checkeded flight plan versus actual routing. The flight had accepted clearance from near mas direct to cyy; which would take him over the gulf. This was nowhere near his planned route of flight and he never advised me of the rerte. I also checkeded the aircraft status and determined it was not equipped for overwater flts. I sent an automatic communications addressing & reporting system to the flight advising them of the lack of life rafts or life vests. The flight then deviated back toward shore after being approximately 75-100 mile off the coast. The crew did not advise of the rerte; they accepted an overwater route for aircraft not second officer equipped; and intermediate fix i had not been familiar with the limitations of the automatic communications addressing & reporting system system i would have never been able to get them a message. Also; intermediate fix this had been the previous day when flight monitor was inoperative i would not have been able to advise them of the situation as it was; the only reason i looked at this flight a little closer was due to the fact i had routed all my flts away from the iam-msy area due to the severe thunderstorms in that area.
output: A DISPATCHER'S RPT ON THE FAILURE OF A B757 PIC TO COORD A CHANGE IN ROUTING AND THE ACCEPTANCE OF AN OVERWATER ROUTING THAT THE ACFT WAS NOT LEGAL TO FLY; NEAR CYY; FL.

input: The event began during the takeoff roll. The captain was the pilot flying and advanced the thrust levers normally. As the aircraft began accelerating; his charts binder became unstable [in its] bracket and began to fall rearward due to accelerating forces. While trying to handle the control yoke; thrust levers and generally control the aircraft during the takeoff; he attempted to catch the binder and place it back on the bracket. During this time we accelerated through 80 knots and shortly thereafter through rotation speed. The captain did rotate after the 'v1; rotate' call; but his binder was still not settled. We were assigned [a] departure...and made the initial turn to a heading of 039 and then 060 passing 500 feet. Still trying to get the binder back on the bracket; the captain engaged the autopilot with lateral navigation now past the 500 foot; 060 heading turn; the next instruction is to turn left heading 290 reaching 4 dme.... With the lateral navigation engaged; the aircraft began correcting to the right. At the same time air traffic control gave us a left turn to heading 220 as the captain was still trying to right his book and operate the autopilot. Throughout the ordeal the captain had become increasingly agitated. I had a hard time understanding the heading assigned by air traffic control due to the captain's struggle and initially read back 020; but promptly corrected to heading 220 by confirming with air traffic control at that point; air traffic control requested we keep the turn tight to the left. Having received that instruction the captain grabbed his binder and forcefully threw it behind him; then grabbed the yoke and rapidly rolled the aircraft to the left; pulling back on the yoke and for a second to a second and a half; the stick shaker activated. The captain quickly recovered and shallowed out his initial corrections. The remainder of the flight was uneventful....i have had similar incidents happen to me on takeoff; whether it's the checklist or my binder falling; i let it go because flying the aircraft is my first priority as the pilot flying. The post meridiem should have the same information out and available if i need to ask anything or correct me if need be. There are two of us for a reason and that is to back each other up. If the captain had just let his binder go or maybe even transferred controls for a moment if so distracted; i doubt any of this would have happened. The captain failed to prioritize his workload during this event. Here again we see how something small can be the beginning of a chain that leads to an undesired aircraft state.
output: An EMB-145 First Officer reported that the Captain; distracted by a publication binder that came loose from its bracket on takeoff; became agitated and over controlled the aircraft on the departure resulting a momentary stick shaker.

input: We leveled off at cruise at 12000 feet/foot en route to the ukn vor and dme (co-located) we did our normal weather briefings and noticed no unusual weather rpted until msp which was our final destination our radar was painting an area of green just ne of the ukn vor and dme (co-located) about 5 mile from the vor and dme (co-located) we noticed an increase in airspd and the aircraft climbed we pulled the power back to flight idle and pitched down; yet we were climbing 2000 feet per minute we ended up 700 feet/foot above our assigned altitude and then we encountered about 15 seconds of hail. The flight was surprisingly smooth and no significant weather was encountered again until we got to msp where we were painting thunderstorms we immediately returned to our assigned altitude and continued. The problem was weather related and radar failed to give any signs of its presence. We gave the rpt to zmp second officer they could pass along the word to anyone else in the area. Supplemental information from acn 319321: as we flew along the sw side of the cell we encountered severe hail for approximately 15 seconds followed by an intense updraft of approximately 2000 feet per minute 1 minute(s) later; we were in visual meteorological conditions conditions and noticed the aircraft had sustained damage to its leading edge. All of the acft's engine indications appeared normal second officer we continued to our dest.
output: COMMUTER ACFT ENCOUNTERS SEVERE UPDRAFT AND HAIL AT CRUISE.

input: Arrived at aircraft xxx and found #1 engine running unattended. Cockpit door was locked. Start/stop selector was at stop; but engine was running. Red engine indicating and crew alerting system warning was present; main door open. Previous crew left aircraft without shutting down eng.
output: AN EMJ FO; PERFORMING HIS PREFLT AT BOS BEFORE THE CAPT ARRIVED; QUICKLY DISCOVERED THAT THE #1 ENG WAS LEFT RUNNING BY THE PREVIOUS CREW.

input: On approach we were kept high and fast then cleared to intercept localizer to the runway. Initially told to maintain 250 knot(s) and then 210 knot(s) once on the localizer we were still high and fast. In trying to ensure a stabilized approach we may have slowed sooner than approached would have liked. We were sent around and given a phone number to call. Once at the gate my captain called. He was told we were sent around due to spacing of the aircraft behind us. Air traffic control did not get specific about us possibly slowing too soon.
output: A B757-200 was told to execute a go-around when spacing with the following aircraft became questionable.

input: I was en route visual flight rules from mdg to mwc. Cruise altitude 5500'. High pressure was centered over il and it was very cold on the gnd---5 degrees fahrenheit visibility was virtually unrestricted. Approximately 8 mile south of dec i contacted the tower to advise that i would be overflying the airport at 5500'. The tower controller gave me the airport information which included a notation of the visibility of 2 mile at dec. (the field was instrument flight rules due to a local power plant [or factory producing large amounts of steam. The restriction of visibility was extremely localized.) the tower controller told me to contact champaign approach since it was cold in the cockpit and i was wearing bulky mittens; and would have to take them off to change frequencies i simply continued on my merry way. As i got directly over the field; i realized that i had just entered an instrument flight rules control zone w/o a clearance at first call-up of dec tower i didn't possibly imagine that any part of the state of il would be instrument flight rules and i forgot to engage the instrument flight rules rules section of my brain. I was thinking that i only needed clearance to enter the ata--i didn't take into consideration the control zone.
output: AN SMA PLT ENTERS A CTL ZONE WITHOUT CLRNC WHILE ON A VMC FLT AT 5500'.

input: I was the trning capt; giving instruction from the right seat; shooting an instrument landing system runway(s) 30 lgb. The pilot flying started descending prior to the outer marker we crossed the outer marker 400' (approx) low. At the same time; the tower called traffic 2 o'clock; 1 mile westbound i replied negative contact. About 15 secs later the tower issued us a low altitude alert and requested an immediate climb we complied; and as the smt passed approximately 150' below us; the capt rpted it looked awfully close. The pilot flying began a dsnt too soon because of a misinterp of a new electronic flight instrument system presentation.
output: LTT ON PRACTICE ILS APCH TO LGB DESCENDS BELOW ASSIGNED ALT AND HAS NMAC WITH AN SMA THAT WAS CUTTING THROUGH THE APCH COURSE.

input: Flying olympia 1 arrival, arrive at seatac airport we departed fourt heading 340 degree cleared to 3000 feet/foot we leveled at 3000 feet/foot with no approach clearance at approximately 10 vor and dme (co-located) approach asked us intermediate fix we were making our turn? We started a turn and confirmed clearance for the bay visual 16l. Behind us an ltt air carrier y was cleared for the bay visual 16l and confirmed he had us in sight. Air carrier y now turns inside our flight path. Air carrier y is now inside our turn; below us; faster on a collision course and we do not have air carrier y in sight. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii then transmits a resolution advisory to climb which we complied with. After climbing to 3300 feet/foot we align ourselves with the glideslope talk to approach and comply with a second traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory approach now realizes the problem and issues clearance for both aircraft to switch runway(s) i ante meridiem not sure ltt ever saw us; he passed 2-3000 feet/foot ahead and 500 feet/foot below us. Supplemental information from acn 203362. This approach was lackadaisical at best. Laziness and inattentiveness on the part of approach why cross 2 planes on a loc?
output: POTENTIAL CONFLICT IN TCA.

input: Our original flight plan was filed as kzzz..orl..lbv..krsw. Our clearance was radar vectors lamma direct bitho direct. As we taxied out air traffic control wanted to clarify our route; lamma bitho direct; which we confirmed. As we approached the end and called ready we received a new clearance; runway heading expect radar vectors rsw. In the air and switched to zma we were given a 140 heading. After flying the wrong direction i queried air traffic control on how long on this heading; he responded; 'i don't know why they sent you this way?' after that we received a 180 heading; then the controller cleared us direct mommo. We were switched to ft. Myers and as we were crossing mommo the aircraft had just started to turn towards rsw vor and dme (co-located) when the controller asked if we were on the shifty arrival. We answered that we were not cleared an arrival. The controller responded ok; turn to a 240 heading. A few moments later the controller came on and said no fault of yours we are just trying to get this straight; what was your clearance; which we explained as direct mommo. He said contact fort myers; the flight continued to the airport with no more comments. After being on the ground; ft myers called me and asked me to contact miami center. I called and he asked me about the flight and clearance. I explained as above the numerous changes. He stated that he listened to the tapes and said everything you said is correct; you were not cleared via the arrival even thought the controller had put it on the strip. His only concern for me was why i did not query the point after mommo. He then went on to say; 'let me think about this and whether or not to file a pilot deviation.' i explained that i would need to file a report and would like to know. I told him that i thought it was unfair considering that his controller put the arrival on the strip and never cleared this way. Suggestions; i have encountered numerous complaints to the shifty1 and think that is needing a overhaul.
output: Fractional Jet departure described confused routing clearance to RSW; later to discover ATC was considering a pilot deviation; reporter claiming ATC erred in the routing and that the subject routing was problematic.

input: During departure from zzz everything was normal at the gate other than running slightly behind schedule. The gate agent was very busy with boarding passengers and other duties. After a normal taxi; takeoff; and climbout; we received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from dispatch while passing through flight level 260. The messages stated the following: 'you have slides in your forward cargo bin. The weight was accounted for correctly; however; the gate agent forget to give you the hazmat paperwork.' i am paraphrasing; that was the basic message. We felt safe to continue to destination without further issues. Mistakes happen. My only suggestion would be if possible; when hazmat is on the aircraft; include that in the remarks section of the [weight and balance]; that would be another possible way to catch missing paperwork.
output: B737-700 Captain reported receiving notification during climbout that HAZMAT flight documents were not included on flight crew release.

input: During the ground roll of the takeoff run from a pvtly owned sod runway(s) high grass retarded acceleration of flying speed and it was necessary to abort the takeoff while slowing down (about 30 mph) the left/right (directions) wing struck some small saplings on the side of the runway(s) causing the airplane to ground loop. Both wings suffered leading edge and tip damage but no spar damage. There were no personal injuries or other property damage. A factor contributing to this occurrence was past experience operating from the field under a variety of conditions and believing a successful takeoff could be made despite the high grass.
output: A CFI LUSCOMBE 8E PLT ATTEMPTS A TKOF IN HIGH GRASS AT A PVT ARPT. DURING THE ABORTED TKOF THE ACFT IS DAMAGED BY A TREE STRIKE NEAR OH96; OH.

input: On departure from burbank after turning 210 degrees per van nuys 7 departure procedure socal departure told us to turn to 360 degrees and intercept the 218 degree radial to palmdale. The capt turned to 360 degrees and set in the 038 degree course. Shortly after this; he got a vor and dme (co-located) capture and turned the aircraft per command bars to intercept course (approx 030 degree hdg). To back him up; i plugged inbound course to pmd into gfms and noticed that we were not yet approaching the course. That's when i remembered this exact thing happened to me last month; second officer i immediately told the capt that i thought the vor and dme (co-located) capture notification was incorrect. He began turning back to 360 degrees at the same time; departure must have noticed that we had turned to approximately 030 degrees and requested that we turn back to 360 degrees which the capt was already doing. I responded to socal; told him we were going back to 360 degrees to intercept the course and also told him this false vor and dme (co-located) capture had happened to me before. Socal responded that he'd seen it happen before also. Socal never mentioned the incident again. In my opinion; intermediate fix socal wants us to fly off the departure procedure second officer soon; they need to give us a 360 heading only. Then once we are high enough over the mountains to get good reception from pmd; we should be cleared to intercept the course inbound. There is second officer much happening as one takes off on runway(s) 15; turning; climbing cleaning up; responding to radio calls; that we'd have to ignore the false capture; which we'd not know was false (until we had a chance to tune and id). Hard choice to make given the information one has at the time. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr advised that subsequent departures from bur via the van nuys 7 prior to lange intersection confirm a pmd radial deflection when approaching 4;000 ft.
output: DEPING BUR VAN NUYS 7 SID; MD80 FLT CREW TURN EARLY FROM A SOCAL HDG CHANGE TO INTERCEPT THE PMD 218 DEGS R DUE TO A FALSE SIGNAL WHILE CLBING THROUGH 4;000 FT. FO AND SOCAL DEP RECOGNIZE ERRONEOUS TURN AND CALL FOR CORRECTION.

input: Departed zzz on an instrument flight rules flight plan to zzz1. About 1 hour into the flight the weather at zzz1 had improved to visual flight rules at this time i cancelled instrument flight rules and went direct zzz1. I asked to stay on frequency for visual flight rules advisories. Halfway between zzz and zzz1 vors around zzz2 vor and dme (co-located) i was told advisories were cancelled and to squawk visual flight rules and try zzz approach i contacted them and they to told me that i was outside their airspace and to try again in 10 miles. I decided to fly between zzz and zzz1 vors. This would have kept me just outside of the power plant at zzz2. When i finally saw the stacks we looked closer than 10 miles (about 8 miles). I immediately turned right to put more distance between us. A couple of miles later i was getting advisories from zzz approach i had received an instrument flight rules weather briefing before the flight the night before i mapped out all the power plant locations on my visual flight rules sectional. After looking at the airway; it outside of the 10 nautical mile ring. Contributing factors are non precise locations of plants (example xa mile ne of x city). Would that be nautical or statute miles. Is that from the city; the airport or vor and dme (co-located) latitude and longitude information would provide for better avoidance. Changing the symbol of the plants on visual flight rules sectionals would also help. The plants are denoted with the obstruction symbol with the words plant and cooling stacks. These words are around the symbol and are never in the same locations around the plant or symbol. Using the obstructing symbol (tower) in a group of 4 or 5 other towers in the area makes it hard to tell where exactly the plant is located. Lastly i could have been a little more vigilant. While staying on victor airway light emitting diode me to believe that i would be clear of all restrict, restricted, restriction areas i let my guard down a little bit. Lastly the stacks i looked to be 8 miles from may have been the ones 5 miles to the sw of zzz3 or the plant by zzz2. I ante meridiem not 100 percent sure.
output: A POSSIBLE INADVERTENT ENTRY INTO A TEMPORARY FLT RESTR AREA.

input: During passenber deplaning at dfw the flight attendant in charge 'faic' request that i stay aboard to talk with her after the passenber had left the aircraft she explained that there had been 137 passenber not 136 as our release showed (final weight and balance also showed 136). We were full in first class with 12 and supposed to be full in coach with 136. She explained that as we were descending into the dfw area she went into the coach section and noticed a female passenber seated in the seat designated 'flt attendant load factor only'. The 'faic's' investigation revealed that during the boarding phase in sat the female passenber mentioned above; left her assigned seat to go the restroom. When she returned to take her original seat she found it occupied and simply got in the 'load factor seat'. Fcia stated that her own passenber count in flight en route to dfw indicated 137 in coach. The 'load factor seat' is with the passenber seats; and is not a flight attendant jump seat; and is identical to a normal passenber seat except for the 'load factor' designation.
output: AFTER LNDG CAB RPTED TO PIC THAT THEY HAD 1 MORE PAX ON BOARD THAN SHOWN ON THE MANIFEST.

input: Fo was flying the aircraft on descent into dfw with a clearance to cross porks intersection at 11000 feet/foot and speed 250 knots indicated airspeed i was attempting to get automatic terminal information service which was in the process of being changed to find out about severe weather approaching the field. I was also using the radar to checked the storm's position passing fl180 we both missed changing our altimeters. On leveling at 11000 feet/foot i caught the mistake -- 29.92 set instead of 29.55; putting us approximately 350 feet/foot low. We immediately climbed back and were in the process of correcting when zfw changed us over to dfw approach on contact with approach they gave us a turn to intercept the localizer for runway(s) 31r and a descent to 5000 feet/foot which we complied with. No mention was made of the momentary altitude deviation no traffic conflict existed to our knowledge.
output: WX DISTR AND TASKS WERE CITED AS CONTRIBUTING TO FLC'S ALTIMETER ERROR; AND CONSEQUENT ALT OVERSHOOT.

input: Recently it has become necessary to reboot or in other ways work on the individual desk computers. The system to switch the keyboard between 2 computers seems to cause the problem most often. Today it was necessary to reacquire the system nearly 8 times in a 6-hr timeframe. Eventually the one computer locked up without recourse. It was necessary to reboot the other computer; but then the track ball system for the first computer wouldn't work after reboot. I called the computer technician to replace the keyboard and track ball. That resolved the situation but i was without a computer for nearly 30 minute(s) i used other dispatchers' computers to flight follow; but i was without access to downlink messages from aircraft for that entire time.
output: AN ACR DISPATCHER REPORTS RECURRENT COMPUTER PROBLEMS PREVENTING THE ACR FROM TRACKING AIRBORNE FLT.

input: Unsafe gear indication caused us to execute a low approach for gear verification then a landing with emergency equipment standing by.
output: COMMUTER SMT MADE A LOW PASS FOR LNDG GEAR VERIFICATION.

input: All seat belt and no smoking signs are out/mel. The flight attendant told myself of section 2. Federal aviation regulation 91.517: at least 1 sign/placard must be visible to each passenber discussed with dispatcher/dispatcher supervisor and was told by them and maintenance that minimum equipment list overrode flight attendant manual and federal aviation regulations back cabin was totally dark.

input: Clred for and shooting runway(s) 13 circle-to-land runway(s) 31 (gls) instrument flight rules ils/loc 13 approach in instrument meteorological conditions with haze. Runway(s) lights runway(s) 31 on bright. Runway(s) lights runway(s) 35 very low and no controls in effect. While shooting the approach the alternator cuts out and circuit breaker (60 amp) for alternator pops. Passenber gets scared; i turn off landing lights; pitot; strobes; storm scope as circling on approach in turbulence push circuit breaker in over 6 times and it keeps popping out. Apparently the tower told me to land on runway(s) 35. I apparently did not hear that or got confused dealing with the circuit breaker and scared passenber i landed on runway(s) 31. I was told i was told to land on runway(s) 35 by tower later; found short in wiring by mechanic and parts to prevent were available from cessna and fixed.
output: PLT OF C206 ON CIRCLE TO LAND APCH TO GLS EXPERIENCES ALTERNATOR FAILURE AND DISTRESSED PAX. FAILS TO HEAR LCL CTLR CLRNC TO LAND RWY 35 VICE RWY 31 AS ORIGINALLY CLRED.

input: Aircraft x was originally going to land at zzz; however; 2 new notams entered the system just before starting an instrument approach regarding standing water and ice on runway 20 and the taxiways. Due to the wind and previous icing encountered; he decided to not land at zzz. I put him into the published holding at jadgu at 120. We discussed his options for many other close by airports; but due to forecast and known icing and moderate to severe turbulence throughout the area we were having a hard time coming up with a good airport. Aircraft x was also not fuel critical; but did not have a lot of reserve fuel. During this; i was working departures and arrivals into/out of den with moderate turbulence. I advised aircraft x that publication was 60 miles northeast; and had visual flight rules weather with no known icing. I advised him that he would have to climb to 160; but only for a few minutes and they could descend to 140. Aircraft x decided to go to publication airport. I climbed aircraft x to 160 and he asked if it was about a 050 heading. I concurred; but he needed to climb first due to terrain before i could turn him there. He accepted the climb and then asked again about the heading. I told him to remain in the published hold and climb to 160 and i would have the turn on course above 130. He advised me that he was already turning to a 050 heading but was climbing to 130. At this point the minimum safe altitude warning alert was going off; but he was through130 in the 130 mia. I reiterated the climb to 160 and told him the terrain climbed rapidly and to expedite as much as he could. At this point; aircraft x was climbing through 140 heading into the 160 mia. I advised aircraft x the minimum instrument flight rules altitude is 160 and to report reaching. I should have issued a heading south as soon as he advised me he was already turning to publication i know the highest mountains in that area are not above 140; but the terrain climbs so rapidly in that area i should have known he would not have topped the 160 mia even though he did climb above the 130 mia. He also reported turbulence and icing at this time.the pilot should not have exited the published holding without a clearance to do so. I should have issued a south heading as soon as he told me he was turning out of hold. It was poor service on my end. I know all of the moderate reports and constant transmitter changes did not help the situation.
output: ZDV Center Controller reported an aircraft experienced a CFTT event while diverting due to weather.

input: During the final cockpit preparation we received takeoff data from the flight management computer and automatic communications addressing & reporting system for runway 28. However we were unable to get info for runways 32 and 34; the longer runways in use. I called dispatch and learned that this minimum equipment list had been applied to our aircraft due to local maintenance discovery. The first officer did not notice this on his walk around. Dispatch advised that we were not legal for takeoff on any runway due to the severe weight penalty. The company canceled this flight after exhausting all possible relief from this mel.my concerns and questions:1) why did the flight crew not receive an alert regarding this change to the original signed release?2) why did we receive takeoff data for runway 28?3) why does the [release] not print in sequential page order?
output: B787 Captain reported that an MEL weight penalty resulted in a maintenance action and flight cancellation.

input: We were almost ready to depart when it came to my attention by the gate agents and flight attendants that we had a prisoner onboard with escort. The problem was that there was no paperwork to indicate the presence of the armed escort or the prisoner. Seems the problem was that air carrier y was going to be the original carrier; but they cancelled. The prisoner and his escort were brought over to us and put on our plane. It was pointed out that when the agents first noticed the prisoner in the terminal; he was handcuffed to a leather belt device; but when he was put on our plane; he was not shackled. He did have an escort; but there was no paperwork for the capt or the flight attendants. Good news that the agents got on the phone and got more information and did take the prisoner and escorting officer off the plane. The problem apparently was due to the change from air carrier y to our carrier. This could be a possible security breach with some major implications. Please check into the procedures second officer that this type of glitch does not occur again. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the flight attendant was alerted that something was out of the ordinary when a passenber was observed to be shackled. She had previously noted the passenber handcuffed in the gate area. She notified both the gate agent and the capt. Rptr said the escort and prisoner were in the process of being removed when he went to the cabin. The capt submitted a rpt to the company. Air carrier notified the capt the incident is under investigation; but no conclusion has been reached at this time.
output: MD80 CREW HAD A PRISONER AND AN ARMED ESCORT BOARDED ON THEIR FLT. THE COMPANY DID NOT PROVIDE ANY NOTIFICATION TO THE CREW OR FLT ATTENDANTS OF THE PRISONER OR ARMED ESCORT.

input: I took off out of zzz on runway(s) 12l. Started left/right (directions) turn out to the westbound when flight attendant called up and informed us she had smoke in the cabin from around runway(s) 27 back. It was cloudy back there and smelled 'metallic' she said. I had the first officer declare an emergency and we went around and landed on runway(s) 12r as an overwt landing (134700 lbs). Landing was uneventful and smooth. Emergency vehicles followed us to our gate and came onboard to investigate and found nothing. No abnormalities were ever seen by us in the cockpit. 2 write-ups were made in logbook. One for the smoke in the cabin and the other for the overwt lndg.
output: MD80 CREW EXECUTED AN EMER RETURN TO THE DEP ARPT FOLLOWING AN UNUSUAL SMELL AND SMOKE IN THE CABIN.

input: The flight was progressing normally through taxi and initial departure off slc runway(s) 17. The first officer was at the controls in the left/right (directions) seat. We were assigned a 280 degree heading and a climb to 10000 feet/foot it was a cool morning and we were light; thus had a good climb going. Through 7000 feet/foot or 8000 feet/foot we got a traffic advisory i looked at the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii display and saw the traffic indicated at our 10 o'clock position level at 11000 feet/foot i looked out my window pausing to look at my pfd noting a climb rate of around 3000 feet per minute thus giving me an explanation for the traffic advisory i then saw the brasilia where the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii had indicated. We were now going through 9000 feet/foot and i told the first officer to 'get the nose down.' i continued to keep the traffic in sight. Getting at or near 10000 feet/foot i pushed forward on the yoke to arrest our rate of climb then looked back out the window to keep the traffic in sight. The traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii then issued an resolution advisory 'monitor vertical clb!' looking back inside; i noticed we were still in a slow climb second officer i told the first officer to 'get the plane back down to 'ten';' and ran the manual trim wheel forward to facilitate the descent at this point the aircraft finally started to descend the maximum altitude the aircraft reached was approximately 10250 feet/foot but at no time did we reach or go above 10300 feet/foot after confirming the aircraft was in a descent i looked out the window to see the brasilia appear to pitch up slightly and bank to the left/right (directions) as it passed overhead. We again reached 10000 feet/foot and the flight continued normally. In 5 yrs of flying with company x; this is only the second person i've had to 'push forward on the yoke;' to induce leveloff; and the only time an first officer 'froze up' and wouldn't fly the aircraft i will need to be more assertive in the future intermediate fix i see this situation recurring. Having that aircraft second officer close and wanting to make sure something more serious wasn't about to happen kept me looking out the window and trying to monitor all that was going on. I will be more aggressive in prevention of this sort of situation in the future. Supplemental information from acn 540256: unfortunately; in striving to stay below 250 knot(s) while executing a smooth leveloff; i did not apply aggressive enough forward pressure on the yoke or reduce the power enough to arrest our rate of climb before we had exceeded our assigned altitude this problem was caused by my failure to correctly take into account the high rate of climb we had and apply aggressive enough control forces and power adjustments to avoid exceeding our assigned altitude further training in procedures to follow in the citation excel when you have short climbs or dscnts combined with speed limits would be helpful. In particular; the citation excel has significantly better climb capability than the jets i have flown previously and i have been slower than i expected in developing the procedural habits for dealing well with this situation in addition; i was somewhat distraction by looking for the traffic i need to learn to rely more on the other pilot for this when i ante meridiem flying the plane; ie; better cockpit resource management would also help.
output: C560 CITATION FO OVERSHOT INTERMEDIATE CLB ALT DURING CLBOUT RESULTING IN THE CAPT TAKING CTL TO HELP LEVEL OFF AND RETURN TO ASSIGNED ALT; AND AN EMB120 TAKING EVASIVE ACTION IN RESPONSE TO A TCASII RA. DEP CTLR HAD ISSUED TA TO THE CITATION.

input: Cabin crew got lightheaded and dizzy; followed by pax same; spread from aft to whole cabin. No odor; fume detected. Multiple cabin crew and pax had symptoms. Decision to make a cautionary divert.established at fl320; got call from aft cabin flight attendant that two of them were feeling lightheaded and dizzy; we agreed to cool down cabin and told them to keep us informed; less than five minutes later we got another call that some passengers also were feeling lightheaded and dizzy; we called [maintenance] and dispatch on conference call and all agreed that aircraft was nominal and we'd continue to monitor while thinking of a possible divert; less than fifteen minutes since initial call we also got a call from the purser that the entire cabin crew were also getting lightheaded and feeling dizzy.the decision to divert [was] made and we called the international relief officer (international relief officer) back to the cockpit from his break; air traffic control gave us expedited handling to zzzz where an overweight landing was made following the  'cabin air quality procedure' and 'overweight landing' procedure as well as normal approach and landing. F/o (first officer) was directed to don oxygen mask as the flying pilot as part of normal zzzz procedure.landed rolled to end of runway(s) using reverse and min braking to minimize heating of brakes. After exterior inspection by fire and rescue we taxied unassisted to [the stand] where we were met by emt who took care of affected crew members and passengers; aircraft handed over to maintenance and flight crew went to the hotel.
output: B767 flight crew reported that the quality of air in the cabin caused the cabin crew and some passengers to become light headed and ill. The ozone converter was reportedly a contributing factor in the event.

input: At about 1300 feet/foot on departure out of anc we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii climb alert to climb at 1500 feet per minute we maintained takeoff thrust and accomplished the climb at about 1700 feet/foot we received clear of conflict. At 11 vor and dme (co-located) we started our left/right (directions) turn to 330 degrees as per the standard instrument departure it was necessary to level at 2000 feet/foot to regain airspd lost in the climb with flaps extended; bank angle was limited to 15 degrees as we initiated the turn; we received a call from anc departure that they had a low altitude alert and asked us to increase our climb and turn left/right (directions) to 290 degrees we proceeded without further incident. We never saw the conflicting acft.
output: WDB CARGO LINER HAS TCASII RA DURING INITIAL CLB.

input: Cleared to descend to cross sweet at 7;000. Aircraft in front of us reported a glider to air traffic control upon reaching sweet; glider was spotted just north of our position.
output: B737 flight crew report a NMAC with a glider over SWEET intersection at 7;000 feet.

input: Cruise phase to zzz was plagued with speed adjustments; unplanned altitudes and off-course vectors. Projected fuel on board slowly went from 7.0 early in cruise to 5.0 at top of descent at about 12000 feet/foot on descent air traffic control gave us a hold. (fuel on board was now 4.8.) we told air traffic control we could not hold because we were at minimum fuel. He asked intermediate fix we were declaring an emergency we said we were declaring minimum fuel and any delay would cause us to have an emergency he said we could not continue unless we declared an emergency second officer we declared a low fuel emergency we were cleared on to zzz with little delay. We blocked in with 4100 pounds of fuel. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated his flight plan was from zzz1 to zzz. When the crew rpted minimum fuel; the center controller advised that the terminal radar approach control facility would not accept them unless an emergency was declared. They declared emergency and were taken direct to zzz. He said they had taken on 2000 pounds of extra fuel at their departure airport but that was used up quickly with a number of unplanned altitude changes; speed adjustments; and several off-course vectors for spacing by the center before handoff to terminal radar approach control facility no one contacted them after landing supplemental information from acn 636525: during the arrival, arrive into zzz; we were given a hold just prior to xxx intersection as a result of an unplanned altitude and off-course vectors for spacing; we instructed air traffic control we were unable to hold because we were at minimum fuel (4.3 pounds arr). Air traffic control asked intermediate fix we were declaring an emergency we responded; 'no; but we cannot accept a delay; and therefore; unable to hold.' air traffic control said; 'advise when ready to copy holding instructions.' at that point we had no choice but to declare an emergency we arrived at the gate with 4.1 pounds we terminated the flight without further incident.
output: AFTER SOME UNEXPECTED SPD ADJUSTMENTS; UNPLANNED ALTS; AND OFF COURSE VECTORS; A B737 CREW REFUSED HOLDING AND DECLARED LOW FUEL. CTLR IGNORED LOW FUEL UNLESS CREW DECLARED AN EMER.

input: While doing some research on emas for runway(s) 12l; i discovered that msp uses a 'declared' distance on runway(s) 12l in order to have appropriate overrun to eliminate the requirement for an emas. The declared distance is 7620 feet/foot the federal aviation administration airport/facility directory commercial chart 10-9; apg; and other publications show the distance for runway(s) 12l as 8200 feet/foot that would mean that pilots and dispatchers are using take-off performance data 600 feet/foot more than what they actually have. This eliminates any safety margin. This runway(s) has had overruns in the past. I ante meridiem wondering intermediate fix the federal aviation administration would find a pilot at fault for using federal aviation administration published information.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that at least one air carrier has used the tora data instead of the asda. The rptr feels this misapplication puts the flight crews at risk of an overrun event without emas available should a reject be required using the 8200 feet/foot full runway(s) available. The rptr's intention with this rpt is to make airport users aware of possible data misuse.
output: A RPTR CAUTIONS THAT MSP RWY 21L TAKEOFF RUN AVAILABLE LENGTH MAY BE ERRONEOUSLY USED IN LIEU OF THE AVAILABLE RWY LENGTH DATA BECAUSE NO EMAS IS INSTALLED.

input: While replacing fuel nozzles for scheduled change the possibility exists i did not install two nuts on a fuel nozzle on # 1 engine. The aircraft flew for approximately 38-hours and developed a slight seepage of fuel from the nozzle. Maintenance action was to install two each nuts. Company's inspection program is being changed to make this a required buy-back item.
output: An Inspection Authority (IA) rated Mechanic reports he may not have installed two locking nuts on a Cessna 208 fuel nozzle. Time constraints; distractions and workload saturation were noted as factors.

input: As we were climbing after takeoff a strong smell of something burning filled the cabin. Myself and a flight attendant in the middle of coach cabin simultaneously called the capt to alert them of the smell. The cockpit tried several things to alleviate the smell; yet nothing seemed to work. Since the cockpit could not identify the problem we declared an emergency and returned to jfk. I was very pleased with the quick reaction of the cabin crew and the positive feedback from the cockpit. Communications was key and it worked. When we returned to jfk; the aircraft was quickly taken out of service i'm very confident in my co-workers after this event. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that the crew did not have to prepare the passenber for an evacuate/evacuation as the capt told them it was to be a normal landing there were no unusually upset passenber -- most took it in stride. The plane was taken out of service for maint.
output: CABIN ATTENDANT RPT; A300; JFK-AUA; SMOKE IN CABIN. EMER DECLARED. RETURN TO JFK. PLANE TAKEN OTS.

input: I was working the bosox sector radar position at zbw. There was no radar associate assigned. Air carrier x; an md80; was landing at psm. Air carrier y; an a320; departing boston. I intended to stop air carrier y at 16000 feet/foot but went to work separating 2 aircraft landing on longitude island. The second aircraft in this string had increased speed and was rapidly catching up to the aircraft ahead. Also at this time a bdl departure was in conflict. After fixing this situation; i noticed air carrier y climbing through 16700 feet/foot and expedited his climb i had inadvertently issued fl230; which is the altitude most aircraft from boston are climbed to. The closest the 2 aircraft got were 4.2 mile and 2400 ft.
output: ZBW CTLR EXPERIENCED OPERROR AT FL180 WHEN INADVERTENTLY ISSUING AN INCORRECT ALT TO A CLBING ACFT.

input: I was paged back 15 minutes into eating my lunch due to an aircraft in distress. Aircraft x was stuck on top of overcast; not instrument flight rules qualified; and running low on gas. By the time i got in dre controller had already gotten the basic info and we started trying to find any airports that were visual flight rules neither us nor surrounding facilities had one without an overcast layer. Ind was reporting the best weather; sct010 bkn015 ovc020. I was put on position to work only aircraft x and given a controller who was instrument flight rules rated as an assist. We vectored the aircraft for the instrument landing system 32 since it was the closest and we wanted a second chance before fuel ran out. We gave him the approach info and learned the co-pilot had some basic instrument training. The terminal radar approach control facility worked together to keep other aircraft away from him. We got him established on the localizer slowed and gear down and we brought him to the minimum vector altitude continuously soliciting base reports from aicraft operating at ind. At the marker i issued descent to the decision height rounded up to 1;300 feet. We helped give small corrections as he drifted back and forth on the localizer he got the ground and runway in sight out of 1;900 feet and landed without incident.[recommend] just keep staffing the federal aviation administration with dedicated people who come together when it matters.
output: IND TRACON Controller and Front Line Manager (FLM) report of a pilot that was not IFR rated had to descend in IFR conditions due to weather. ATC got the aircraft down to decision height where the pilot could see the runway and landed without incident.

input: Due to a re-route; i was scheduled to deadhead zzz-zzz1. After boarding had completed; ground operations requested four people move up from the back of the aircraft to sit in rows 2-8 for weight and balance (x-zone count). Since the passengers had just finished sanitizing their seat areas they were reluctant to move; so no one did. A second public address was made; specifically telling the passengers at the very back of the aircraft (all deadheading crew members) they were going to have to move up. I was required to abandon my social distancing and sit in row 2. After re-sanitizing my new seat; i sat with a passenger directly in front of me; one directly behind me; and one directly across from me. I had to sit there for about 20 minutes; before takeoff; and waited until the ride smoothed out and moved back to the back of the aircraft to space myself away from other passengers and crew. This event compromised my ability to protect myself as much as possible.crews need to be specifically exempted from moving to accommodate a zone count and this procedure needs to be implemented immediately; and pushed to all operational groups.
output: Deadheading pilot reported that passengers in the back of the aircraft were told to move to seats at the front of the aircraft to accommodate a zone count; which required abandoning social distancing and sanitizing new seats.

input: At xa00 ante meridiem the tower experienced a minor power fluctuation( or 'bump'). The tower emergency generator automatically activated; although commercial power was almost immediately available. The asr-9 was knocked out of service actually; the asr-9 antenna continued turning without interruption; but the radar displays in the tower and terminal radar approach control facility received absolutely no data from it -- no primary radar; no secondary radar; no automated radar terminal systems the outage lasted for 23 minute(s) zau assumed control of our airspace; while cid became a visual flight rules tower the supervisor while on the phone with the radar technician; was able to reset the power supply and the asr-9 was returned to service problem asr-9 is not on an uninterruptible power supply. We had another 'bump' in power on aug/xx/94 around xb00 post meridiem and again lost the asr-9; albeit only for a couple of minute(s) thunderstorms and lightning also cause the asr-9 power supply box to lock up. Airport facilities says putting the asr-9 on uninterruptible power source will solve this problem another problem is that our tower emergency generator is of 1940-50's vintage and isn't capable of handling the load required by all the new equipment (asr-9; mode-s; etc). We need a new generator to prevent interruptions in service and possibly very unsafe sits. New generator has been on order for yrs. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated supervisors and ctlrs-in-charge are not trained in restoring the radar after a power surge. Rptr stated the present emergency generator is adequate intermediate fix it only had to handle air traffic control equipment airport facilities technician told the rptr a ups system would prevent the power surges and would solve the problem of radar failure.
output: PWR SURGE CAUSES ATC RADAR FAILURE.

input: I was a first officer on an lgt x departing tampa valley airport (hayden; co) for san jose; ca. Yampa valley airport is unctled with a common traffic advisory frequency (ctaf) of 123.0. Before takeoff an instrument flight rules clearance was received from zdc. They requested a call airborne. After reading back the clearance we switched back to common traffic advisory frequency (123.0) to broadcast our departure and monitor other airport traffic after takeoff we made a left/right (directions) turn direct to the che vor and dme (co-located) and maintained 14000 feet/foot (our air traffic control clrnc). At about the che vor and dme (co-located) and 14000 feet/foot we called zdv. They seemed angry at us for not calling them sooner. That is the point of this rpt. We felt we should stay on common traffic advisory frequency until safely clear of the airport instead of calling them immediately after leaving the ground a complicating factor was another aircraft holding at 15000 feet/foot at the che vor and dme (co-located) that couldn't begin the approach until center talked to us. To prevent this problem in the future the pilots and controllers should have a better understanding with each other exactly when contact will be made after takeoff supplemental information from acn 197987: air traffic control had cleared our aircraft to climb to and maintain 14000; left/right (directions) turn direct to the che vor and dme (co-located) and to 'call airborne.'
output: ACR LGT DELAYED MAKING FREQ CHANGE TO ZDV FREQ THUS DELAYING THE DSCNT APCH OF ANOTHER ACR HOLDING FOR CLRNC TO DSND AND LAND AT A NON TWR ARPT.

input: Departed lax via loop 2 departure procedure dag transition. After dag routing was direct pgs direct publication just after passing dag; zla cleared us 'direct las vegas; nv; direct.' the sic acknowledged the clearance to zla; found las vegas on the high en route chart and entered the identify 'lvs' into the global positioning system the kln 90b identified 'lvs' as 'las vegas' and the new course was a slight turn to the left/right (directions) all looked reasonable as we began tracking to 'las vegas.' a few minute(s) later; zla asked our heading then told us 'las vegas; nv; is las; turn left/right (directions) heading 030 des; when able proceed direct.' we complied then asked center intermediate fix we had caused any trouble. He replied 'not at all.' we proceeded uneventfully. Commercial charts and high altitude en route charts show lvs and las named 'las vegas' without identing which state. Also; the king kln 90b global positioning system shows both vor's named 'las vegas' without identing the state. Everything looked reasonable to us en route to lvs as the course was only a slight heading change and it is not uncommon to navigate, navigation direct to fixes several hundred mile away. Also; since we had just passed dag and our next fix was pgs; we expected to find this new routing beyond pgs rather than closer than pgs. Familiarity with this area would have helped us greatly. I'm sure we are not the first to make this mistake. Adding the state name to these 2 vor's on the charts and in the global positioning system database could prevent this confusion in the future to other pilots callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr confirmed that they were flight planned via dag direct pgs direct publication and further to the east rptr also confirmed that the controller did in fact clear them direct las; nv; then direct publication and fpr. Rptr stated that they just made a mistake because their global positioning system readout indicated lvs; which seemed reasonable to them. He also stressed the point that both pilots were not familiar with that part of the country; since it had been months when they were last out there.
output: C525 CREW BEGAN TO FLY TOWARD LVS (LAS VEGAS; NM) RATHER THAN LAS (LAS VEGAS; NV).

input: Was flying direct at 7;700 msl with flight following. I was handed off to center and was assigned a barometric pressure of 30.18; which was in line with my previously assigned pressure. I could see a front off in the distance but didn't consider any pressure change. Center was busy; so my attention was reduced from the radio as most of the radio chatter was for others. Someone came over the radio and stated that they were showing traffic at 7;500 at their same altitude. I can't remember if there was any talk of course or altitude change as my focus went out of the cockpit. A few moments later a high wing cessna flew over us at 100 ft with a nearly head on course. A few moments later a radio report goes out to me that traffic is 0.25 miles same altitude. I report back that he is too late. The other aircraft states that he saw us on the adsb and was climbing prior to our close call to avoid. He also requests a number to file a complaint with flight service station specialist i'm asked to check my altitude and i tell him i'm at 7;700 and my pressure is 30.18. I'm told that the controller had me at 7;500 and that i should have been given a pressure of 30.11 which put me at a physically higher altitude.since i was flying into a front i should have known that the pressure would be changing and that i should be adjusting more frequently. Since the last time i got a pressure setting was when i entered approach airspace and the center's pressure was the same i reported my altitude lower than i physically was. I have foreflight and a stratus so i could have been more proactive with adjusting my pressure as well as seeing my global positioning system altitude for comparison. I also realize now that flight following is not a flight plan or a visual flight rules version of an instrument flight rules plan and that it gets low priority to all other traffic.
output: C172 pilot reported an incorrectly set altimeter led to a near mid air collision.

input: I tore the crew listing off the blank automatic terminal information service sheets to put on the captain's side by the hgs dim control knob. The hgs was mel'ed and had a stricter under the dim control knob. I didn't want to cover up the sticker; so i elected to try and put the crew listing on the ledge above the lower du. When i tried to balance it there; it slipped behind the lower du. I should have stopped what i was doing right then; told the captain; and called maintenance. Instead; i elected to do my walkaround and inform everyone after; in case i found something else on the walkaround. I completed my walkaround uneventfully and got sidetracked with conversation with the gate attendant; flight attendants; and captain as i completed my preflight duties and completely forgot about the crew listing slipping behind the lower du. After completing the flights for the day and getting to the hotel; i remembered i didn't report the incident. I called my chief pilot and the on call chief pilot to report it. I talked to the maintenance rep and told him the story too. The maintenance rep told me the aircraft was due to land in zzz and they would check it out; but felt it was not a going to be a problem.
output: First Officer reported that distraction caused him to forget to inform the Captain and Maintenance about an issue.

input: Atl dtw; mlg; federal aviation administration inspector on jump seat. During descent #2 oil temperature gauge started spiking. A closer examination showed gauge was for an mlg a aircraft yellow arc and red radial line in the wrong place. Federal aviation administration inspector insisted grounding aircraft in dtw until repairs made. Federal aviation administration inspector's headset jack was broke; was having to use coplt speaker for phone patch to mia tech services autoplt was broken on ci; i was handflying; talking to approach navigating. Federal aviation administration inspector had list of items for coplt to relay to miami-tech. I did not have time to consult proper charts. I had to take a shortcut second officer looked up next navigational aid inbound leg; dialed it in; flew it. Approach yelled at us. Told us we were off the arwy; turn left; get back on. The controller's voice sounded like we may have caused a prob/conflict. Federal aviation administration man was on f/o's speaker; unaware of any off arwy problem later review of arwy revealed a significant dog leg on arwy. The federal aviation administration man; his broken autoplt; too much confusion; too much going on during approach all contributed.
output: DISTRACTED BY ACI AND FAILED TO FOLLOW VICTOR AIRWAY WHEN DOGLEG DEPICTED ON CHART.

input: Freezing rain and ice at fl190 between slc and den. Lost 1500 feet/foot asked for block altitude and was given 16000 feet/foot through fl190. Was able to maintain control and slowly climb back to fl190.
output: SMA E OF SLC UNABLE TO MAINTAIN ALT BECAUSE OF ICE BUILDUP ON AIRFRAME.

input: Ltt x at fl330 was given clearance to fl290 to clear air carrier y fl310 approximately 60-70 mile apart. Ltt x did not descend at the rate described in the federal aviation regulations ltt x was then issued an expeditious descent clearance pilot still did not comply. Clearance to turn was issued and was ignored and pilot continued to argue. Supplemental information from acn 233069: during a flight between mia and phl; zjx told us to descend to fl370. I replied that i would like to stay at fl410 as longitude as possible as we were 350 mile out of phl; and that; intermediate fix i came out of fl410; i would like to stay at fl370 80 mile from phl. Zjx said he would relay the message but that i would have to descend to fl370 now. When in washington's airspace; i was told to descend to fl330. I requested discretion. Washington denied the request. Shortly thereafter; washington further descended us to fl290. Once again; i reiterated the enormous fuel burn at low altitudes to no avail. Through fl330 to fl290 i was told to make a left/right (directions) turn to 360. A few seconds later; another controller said turn even further to 340 expedite through fl290 and descend to fl240. I rpted out of fl290. Washington after a minute(s) gave me a phone number of quality assurance control to call when on the ground due to the lack of separation. Realizing that intermediate fix there were any delays going into phl i wouldn't have the required fuel; second officer i opted to deviate to acy. In retrospect; i do not feel that the controllers were keeping up sufficiently with the aircraft involved. The controller realized the traffic conflict too late and hence overloaded; making a bad situation worse. It is my understanding that one of the controllers was a trainee; and that is why she was relieved. In talking with the quality assurance control person; they said that i was not descending or turning at a rate that was acceptable to them. However; nowhere in the federal aviation regulations does it specify rates; nor for that matter of fact did the controllers it's my opinion that intermediate fix turbojet aircraft are going to be brought out of the higher flight levels 350 mile from destination pilots should be forewarned prior to departure to avoid these sits in the future. At no time did we not comply with the controllers flight planning for fuel is predicated on flying in the high flight levels. An ltt jet burns the same amount of fuel at idle on the ground as it does at fl410.
output: LTT X NON ADHERENCE TO ATC CLRNC INSTRUCTIONS SLOW DSCNT FAILED TO COMPLY WITH RADAR VECTOR HAD LTSS FROM ACR Y. PLTDEV.

input: Apch control asked us to keep speed up (190 kts) to approaching outer marker for runway(s) 24l cle. At 3000 feet/foot mean sea level assigned; cleared for approach tower cleared us to land; runway(s) in sight. At flaps 5 degrees speed 190 knot(s) first officer flying called 'gear down;' flaps 15 degrees speed etc. On glide path for instrument landing system i noticed flaps did not go past 5 degrees with leading edge devices at mid position green lights. No split flap indication; circuit breakers in. Referred to quick reference handbook got speed for vref 40+30 knot(s) i told first officer to continue and land. Speed was already at or near vref 40+30 knot(s) and stabilized. First officer made a very good landing after runway(s) turn off and taxi in; flaps operated normally up and down. Put incident in aircraft logbook and called maintenance suspect possible bad flap indicator gauge; or some other component.
output: B737 FLT CREW PERFORMS A PARTIAL FLAP LNDG WHEN FLAP INDICATORS SHOW THE FLAPS STOPPING AT 5 DEGS ON FINAL APCH TO RWY 24L AT CLE; OH.

input: I was flying the approach; when calling for gear down; the nose gear light did not illuminate green. We also had a gears door indication on the engine indicating and crew alerting system i performed the go around and captain handled the quick reference handbook and air traffic control communication; [another] captain was traveling as a non rev and offered assistance. We figured another set of eyes and ears would be helpful; especially since we had been flying all night.i transferred control to captain and we proceeded for another approach. If i remember correctly; we had a gear doors indication on engine indicating and crew alerting system only. We thought possibly a bulb could be burnt out. Tower asked if we'd like to do a low pass and they would attempt to look at our gear. Initially we said no because that is not a written procedure. [non rev] captain and the tower thought it would be worth a try. We checked our fuel and we were all comfortable with the fuel on board (fob) that a pass would be okay and might yield more information. It was still dark. At this point we lowered the gear for the second approach. This time we got a gear disagree and gear unsafe engine indicating and crew alerting system we did a low pass and it was confirmed that our nose gear was not down. I attempted to flash the nose gear lights and both tower and airport rescue and fire fighting (arff) confirmed it was not down.a second attempt at running the gear disagree checklist by myself and the captain was successful in getting a 3 green indication i could also feel and see with the landing light the gear had extended.the rest of the approach and landing were normal.
output: B757 flight crew reported they got an indication that the Nose Landing Gear (NLG); did not deploy as verified by ATC. They cycled the gear and the NLG came down normally.

input: After preflt an federal aviation administration ramp inspector found a small pin missing from a main door hinge cover that i missed on the preflt on my walk around. I was concentrating on the main gear wheels the brake debooster and the lower gear doors and as i walked around the landing gear i failed to look up at the gear door attach point. Intermediate fix i had i could have seen the pin missing. This error i believe was caused by complacency; lack of a positive attitude due to job security and events unfolding at my airline and a short over night (10 o'clock) layover. I had only 4 hours of sleep.
output: A SO RPTR TELLS OF AN ACI FINDING AN ACFT MAINT DISCREPANCY ON AN LGT AFTER THE RPTR HAD PERFORMED HIS PREFLT PROC. PLT TECHNIQUE PREFLT PROC CRITICIZED FOR MISSING ACFT EQUIP PROBLEM.

input: In sum: after a proper weather briefing and launch of several pibals; a hot air balloon pilot launched from a site familiar to him in the late afternoon. He drifted towards a residential area and sought winds that would steer him away; but to no avail. As darkness was approaching the rptr selected a cul-de-sac for landing his ground crew tied off his dropline to a stop sign that was uprooted; then later 'replanted.' the basket touched a roof on the way down. The balloon was removed to the street; then packed up with no damage to the balloon or any structure except the stop sign. The rptr believes that this incident was caused by an unusual overcast condition that did not allow the usual weather pattern to develop.
output: A HOT AIR BALLOON PLT HAD TO LAND IN A RESIDENTIAL AREA. HIS DROPLINE UPROOTED A STOP SIGN IN THE PROCESS.

input: On takeoff roll from grass strip on a no-wind; dry; early morning; [the] little c150 begun to pull to the right. I tried to correct by applying left rudder and brake but aircraft kept pulling to right; turned 180 degrees and stopped at right side off runway in brush. The left gear was completely detached with the rudder cable broken.
output: A C150 pilot reported losing control on takeoff roll; ground looping and leaving the runway which resulted in damage to left gear.

input: We were dispatched to our destination in spain with visual meteorological conditions forecast for arrival. The company provided notams that all approaches were out of service. During the cruise portion the weather went below visual meteorological conditions and we asked what they wanted us to do. They told us an airport surveillance radar approach would be available. Upon descent the dispatcher informed us that no airport surveillance radar was available. We held then diverted to a nearby military field and eventually timed out. The captain looked up the military notams [while there] and found that the airport surveillance radar was notam'd out from [the middle of the previous month to the end of this month]. The company dispatcher failed to give us that information in our paper work.
output: An MD11 crew dispatched to a forecast VMC European airport for which all approaches were OTS had to to divert to a nearby military field when low ceilings emerged and the promised radar directed approach proved to be fictitious.

input: My student and i made a full stop landing at isp after completing several takeoff and landings on runway 24. The controller was operating on one frequency for ground and flight. The controller was extremely busy and did an excellent job in controlling traffic. We made an uneventful full stop landing on runway 24 and turned off at bravo. The controller was extremely busy and handling both the tower and ground positions. The controller rapidly gave us a taxi clearance to 'taxi via taxiway bravo (b) charlie (c) sierra (s) cross runway 10 (non-active runway) via taxi way (a) to our fbo'. I believe i properly read back the clearance and my student then proceed to taxi. Instead of crossing runway 10 (non-active runway); we turned right and proceeded to taxi to the alpha (a) taxiway via runway 10. I noticed my error as i approached the hold line for runway 24. I held my position; did not taxi pass the runway 24 hold line and advised the very busy controller that i was holding short runway 24 at the intersection of 24 and 10. The controller immediately became concerned; rightfully so. He ordered me to hold my position; which i did. At no time did i cross the hold line for the active runway 24. No runway incursion occurred and i was fully aware of my position on the airport. I believe this situation occurred because of a few reasons. The very fast ground clearance; the controller being busy and my mistake by not confirming immediately to the controller that i had turned on the non-active runway instead on crossing over it. I believe that this situation could have been prevented had the tower been manned with two controllers on tower and ground. I thought the controller; although very professional and competent; was on occasion overwhelmed with the with the very busy airport traffic pattern and ground operations. I am very familiar with federal aviation administration procedures. My reasons for reporting this incident is two fold. I believe that one controller operating two positions at a very busy time of day is not safe. My intentions for reporting this situation is for safety and i believe had i not been experienced; i might have caused a serious runway incursion at the intersection of runways 10-24 because the controller was too busy to notice that i had turned on an non-active runway.
output: An Instructor Pilot reported a near runway incursion at ISP claiming the combined ATC position operation and workload was a contributing to the confused tax instructions.

input: Acft was parked in spot 1 at jfk. The aircraft was facing se. The surface winds were rpted at oh:31 estimate, estimation at 290 degree at 32 knot(s) peak winds were obtained from tower the aircraft was shutdown. The nosewheel was chocked as per standard procedures and both propeller restraints were in place. The emergency parking brake was set 'on'. During boarding of flight i was in the capts seat and f/o was entering the flight deck returning from her walk-around. I was double checkeding to make sure the 'seatbelt' and 'no smoking' signs were on when she yelled 'the plane is moving.' i immediately depressed the brake pedals; but the aircraft continued to fishtail from left/right (directions) to left/right (directions) the plane came to an abrupt stop. The left/right (directions) elevator and stabilizer struck the passenber van; which was parked next to the left/right (directions) rear of the aircraft the elevator pierced the top of the bus; there were four paxs on board the aircraft standing in the aisle from row 8 back. F/a notified me that everyone was alright. The paxs were offloaded and f/a escorted them to the terminal and made sure that correct incident rpts were submitted. There was no rpted injuries and all the paxs were rebooked on a later flight to dca. The aircraft next to us on spot 2 had also moved due to the winds as explained to me by jfk ramp personnel. The aircraft was secured and i called pou dispatch and maintenance supplemental information from acn 167539. I had 4 paxs about to situation down when the f/o said the plane was moving the rest of the paxs outside were running away from the plane. I evacuated the paxs like an emergency and lead them away from the plane. I made sure everyone was ok; there was no injuries. I informed to the agents outside that we needed statements from each passenber and called to see of anything else was to be done. The accident only lasted 5 secs or more.
output: PARKED COMMUTER ACFT BLOWN INTO PASSENGER BUS.

input: [two] aircraft arrived krdm from the northwest on the visual approach and made approximately 180 degree turns to final close into the airport. When they made the turns the data block went into coast mode even though i was still showing a good radar target during the turn. Appears to be some type of tracking issue where eram cannot track even though a valid transponder return is being received. I don't recall if the first aircraft had a 3 nautical mile separation symbol (ball and i believe it was a beacon slash only). However; the second aircraft had a 3 mile golf ball symbol during the turn along with a good target return; yet still went into coast mode for about 3-4 hits. After landing; it tracked back up. Adjust eram to provide tracking through out a turn when good/valid radar data is still being received.
output: ZSE Controller reported momentary loss of tracking for two aircraft arriving RDM. Both aircraft were in a turn on a visual approach; but the ATC system appeared to be receiving good transponder returns.

input: I was pilot not flying copying automatic terminal information service and listening to air traffic control i looked up to see the lear cross below us/head on. I noticed the pilot flying was 300 feet/foot low and called altitude as the pilot flying arrested the descent i estimate that had we not arrested the descent that a collision was probable. No traffic alert was issued.
output: A CPR FLC FLYING AN MU300 NEAR DET AT 18000 FT RPTS AN NMAC WITH A LEAR JET BELOW THEIR ACFT.
