input: Aircraft x was on approach to the airport. He later called the airport in sight for a visual approach; which i gave him. At some time before or after that; tower called and asked for a clearance from the ground for aircraft y; visual flight rules to an intersection; then to [destination] airport. I tried to give him a clearance from over the intersection; but he wanted a clearance from the ground. I told the tower controller that i was unable to issue a clearance from the ground; as i had inbound instrument flight rules aircraft. He said no; visual flight rules to the intersection; and i again stated that i could not issue the clearance; whether or not it was an instrument departure procedure (idp) or visual flight rules conditions to the intersection; as both clearances start at the airport; and require instrument flight rules separation. I told him they can wait on the ground until the aircraft on approach arrives; or get his clearance from over the intersection.the clearance he got was from over the intersection. I waited until i got the call of the arrival of the first of my two aircrafts; aircraft x; then i cleared aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) for the approach. As aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) was maybe 15 miles northwest of the airport; aircraft y popped up on radar; and after taking radar; i called traffic between the two aircraft.some people think this is not a problem in our facility; and this situation was covered in an interpretation binder; but that binder was removed from the floor years ago; and out staff and management fail to issue any direction on this matter. To me this is not a visual flight rules climb on course; where you can climb through another instrument flight rules aircraft; and being on a visual flight rules flight plan is different from being on an instrument flight rules flight plan; whether or not you are in visual flight rules (or vmc) conditions or instrument flight rules conditions. One is about protecting instrument flight rules aircraft from other instrument flight rules aircraft; and the other is visual flight rules vs instrument flight rules flying conditions; i.e. The weather!whether the aircraft choses or is issued the instrument departure procedure; or gets to the intersection; where his routing starts; matters not; if he has a clearance from the ground; he is instrument flight rules from the ground!
output: A Center and Tower Controller disagreed whether an aircraft with an IFR clearance including an initial VFR leg could be released with simultaneous IFR arrivals. The Tower departed the aircraft with an aircraft on approach.

input: High crew workload resulting from an overloaded air traffic control situation in the sat area; compounded by additional stress on the flight crew resulting from a near miss and a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory event. The primary focus of this report is for probably landing without air traffic control clearance at sat. The crew responded to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory approximately 5-10 minute(s) prior to landing second officer it is being included as a contributing factor. Zhu was working our flight as we descended on the marcs arrival, arrive into sat. Center issued our flight numerous heading altitude and speed changes and amendments. Because of all the changes being issued by air traffic control the crew got behind on our crew briefing; in-range chklist; and passenber briefing duties. Atc's and our workload was very high. Center descended us to 6000 feet/foot when we were level they handed us off to sat approach without providing us with a traffic advisory for the visual flight rules traffic which was about to cause our traffic alert and collision avoidance system event. When we switched to approach frequency we could not make contact initially due to frequency congestion. Before we could establish communications with approach we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory followed quickly by an resolution advisory to climb at 3000 feet per minute the crew complied with the resolution advisory and climbed 300 feet/foot before the resolution advisory stopped. At the top of our climb the conflict traffic passed 400 feet/foot directly below our aircraft on our traffic alert and collision avoidance system (6 mile display). The first officer caught a glimpse of the traffic as it passed under us as it was approaching from our 2 o'clock position at top of climb we established contact with approach and advised we were climbing for a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory the approach controller also had a very high workload and seemed to be overloaded. We were now rushed to complete our remaining duties; with adrenaline still pumping from the resolution advisory event we were quickly vectored on to a 12 mile final and cleared for a visual approach to runway(s) 30l. Approach control forgot to hand us off to local tower control we failed to notice and landed. We contacted ground control and taxied to the gate. At the end of the landing roll i realized that i was still listening to approach control and hadn't contacted the local control tower we contacted ground control they gave us no indication that we had landed without clearance and instructed us to taxi to our gate. I should have omitted the passenber briefing portion of my duties when it became apparent that our workload was getting high. I doubt intermediate fix that alone could have prevented this event. The federal aviation administration needs to take some type of action to prevent their controllers from becoming as overloaded as the zhu and sat approach controllers were that day.
output: EMB145 CREW REPORTS TCAS RA ON ARRIVAL TO SAT AND THEN FORGETTING TO CONTACT TOWER FOR CLEARANCE TO LAND.

input: During landing roll on runway(s) 22 at lga; upon raising thrust reverser sublevers; thrust levers dropped into idle cutoff position aircraft was coasted to high speed turnoff and past hold line second officer active runway(s) was not blocked. Equipment was dispatched by tower not at crew request. Pins to block thrust levers not deployed fast enough; but then blocked thrust levers in idle cutoff position problem resolved with circuit breaker resets and aircraft taxied to fixed-base operator no maintenance corrective action believed to be required. Thrust reversers will be activated in slightly more deliberate manner in the future.
output: LTT ENGINES INADVERTENTLY SHUT OFF DURING ENGINE REVERSE THRUST APPLICATION.

input: On final the capt called for gear down and when i selected gear down only the mains showed down and locked. I cycled the gear and still only the mains showed a down and locked indication. We flew by the tower and they confirmed the nose gear appeared to be down and locked. As soon as we landed and the nose wheel made contact the green light for the nose wheel came on and worked perfectly. I assumed the capt would fill out an irregularity rpt on the occurrence; but i never followed him up on the issue.
output: COMMUTER FLC RECEIVES INDICATION THAT ONLY MAIN GEAR IS DOWN AND LOCKED.

input: [i received] a gate call [on a dc-10] with an air system fail alert on pre-flight air system test. After getting the minimum equipment list to do the logbook entry; the circuit breaker would not reset. I collared [the circuit breaker] to prevent anyone else from trying to reset it. After looking into the system schematic manual chapter 21-26-0; i realized that the breaker just controlled the number 3 fan. I was trying to prevent any further aircraft problems. It also had no history for that discrepancy. I figured the system was inoperative and [that i was] collaring a breaker that would not reset; [so] i just collared it. I collared the breaker just to prevent anyone else from trying to reset. There was no question about safety of flight. I did the research to make sure the breaker did not affect any other components. I should have contacted maintenance control. I will contact maintenance control and make sure i go by the minimum equipment list to the letter and will not deviate. [i will] collect all information and with maintenance control; make a decision. Use my resources. I have seen where they put out maintenance alert about this type of problem in the last couple of day. Minimum equipment list 21-26-05; is a good [reference] to be used if you have a bad cooling fan that fails an operational check; [but] not if the circuit breaker pops.
output: The Maintenance Technician attempted to comply with the MEL for an avionics cooling fan fault; but discovered that the circuit breaker would not reset. He utilized the MEL and collared the circuit breaker thinking that is was only affecting that fan. By doing so; he did not comply with the approved MEL procedure.

input: While at fl320 in completely smooth air we encountered a jolt of moderate turbulence lasting approximately 2 seconds. This was followed by another jolt of turbulence lasting 2-3 seconds that was moderate to more than moderate; but not fitting of the definition of severe in intensity (fom); and about 3-5 seconds after the first encounter. In our vicinity an airplane had just passed in front and above us and was abeam our aircraft when the turbulence was encountered. I immediately suspected a wake encounter. This occurred about 100 miles south-southeast of bil. We asked air traffic control what kind of aircraft it was and he said his designation was a heavy airbus a300. A flight attendant in the rear of the aircraft reported bumping her head. No other injuries to passengers and crew.
output: A319 flight crew reported an 'aggressive' roll resulted after encountering wake turbulence at FL320 from a crossing A300. A Flight Attendant hit her head during the encounter.

input: Giant killer called to advise me that whiskey 107 was going active. I pointed out 3 aircraft to them; one southbound and two northbound. One of the two northbound was aircraft x which was 20 miles east of azezu about to cross b24 northwestbound direct camrn. They approved aircraft x direct camrn descending to 9;000. After i hung up; a few minutes later i witnessed some targets entering w-107 and heading in the same direction at aircraft x. I called giant killer to ask them what the targets were doing and they said they were going eastbound. I asked them if they were still ok with my point outs and they said yes. A few more seconds go by and i noticed that the military targets are not going eastbound but are headed directly for the aircraft x. I then called w-107 and asked them what they were doing again and they said now they were stopping the targets at 20;000 ft. So i told the radar controller and she stopped the aircraft x at 21000. By that point the aircraft x advised they had an resolution advisory alert and were climbing to fl220. After military targets were eastbound and away from aircraft x the radar controller reissued the descent clearance.giant killer needs to be in better contact with the pilots. One of the w-107 controllers advised that they were having trouble communicating with their traffic.
output: ZNY Controller reports of an airspace that is going to become hot. He coordinates with the airspace authority to have one last aircraft go through this airspace; which is approved. Minutes later the Controller sees targets entering the area going towards his pointed out aircraft. Coordination ensues; and his aircraft is still approved into the airspace. His aircraft is stopped above the other targets and the pilot reports a RA due to the fast moving targets.

input: I was flying an orientation flight from fcm to syn; visual flight rules i made all my traffic calls for runway(s) 27 as i approached from the nw including 10 nautical mile 5 nautical mile overflying the airport circling to enter downwind; downwind; base and final; and concluding every transmission with the statement 'any traffic in the area please advise.' my aircraft was lit up with its landing running; strobes; and navigate, navigation lights on. While on short final for runway(s) 27; i received a call on 122.8 common traffic advisory frequency stating 'acft landing at stanton; do you see the ultralight who departed on runway(s) 36 and is turning right towards you!' i didn't see the traffic at first; but in seconds; i saw a dark colored ultralight appear over the runway(s) from a darkly colored plowed field just to the north of runway(s) 27. He was aimed right at me. The ultralight was pitched up quite high; no running lights. I'm not sure he even saw me -- climbing quickly in my direction. I quickly made the decision to descend due to my confign and true air speed (full flaps; and 60-65 knot(s) descending at 500 fpm). I pulled the throttle out and pushed the nose down to quickly descend to the runway(s) below. We missed by less than 50 feet/foot the ultralight climbing over the top of us. On my landing due to the dramatic nose down pitch; my true air speed increased. My flare slowed me down to the point of touchdown; after a slight ride in ground effect. I believe my touchdown was approximately 400-500 feet/foot down the runway(s) (rwy total length 1950 ft). When i touched down; i could not slow the airplane down on the dry grass runway(s) and i applied full brakes; which eventually locked up. The aircraft finally slowed down; but at the end of the runway(s) ran off by a few feet/foot (less than 5 ft) while trying to turn around. The airplane was stuck in the dirt and i had to have some help pushing it out. After getting the airplane unstuck; i checkeded over the aircraft for any damage. The aircraft had a small nick on the propeller (most probably from a rock); but nothing i believed would make the aircraft unairworthy. I flew the aircraft back to fcm. I then called my flight release officer to notify him of what had transpired.
output: C172 PLT CAME WITHIN 50 FT OF HITTING AN ULTRALIGHT AT SYN.

input: I wish to express my concern about the competency of a 69 year old pilot mr x. March/1989 xa ante meridiem i received a call at my home from a controller at kona tower inquiring who was the pilot in command of sma that departed that morning. Mr x (pic) and mr y (coplt). Controller and i listened to the tower tapes to find out more about the incident with flight inbound for landing to kona and civil air patrol sma departing from kona en route to hnl that morning. Initially controller told me that the 2 aircraft were close; but not enough to file a near miss report. Sma was off tower frequency shortly after leaving the pattern and within approximately 2-3 miles from the airport the tower made many attempts to contact; but was not able to warn sma of the inbound air carrier in the opposite direction. The pilot did see the sma and put on lights to make a higher visibility for the sma that seemed not to respond to the conflicting flight paths. The pilot in command of air carrier after taxiing to the ramp called the tower and questioned why was that sma not responding to the traffic and in that airspace. May/89 (approx) mr x (pic); mr y (coplt) inbound for hnl cleared by air traffic control for a left base to runway(s) 4l. Sma crossed over the approach end of 4l and landed 4r. The controller informed sma that they had landed on the wrong runway(s) and mr x argued with the controller that he had not landed on the wrong runway(s) coplt mr y confirmed to mr x that the tower had in fact cleared him for 4l. Mr x (pic) and cfii mr zulu time (utc/gmt) (coplt) inbound for landing molokai airport cleared to land runway(s) 5. Mr x initiated an approach to runway(s) 35 and was unaware until mr zulu time (utc/gmt) informed him he was not cleared to land on runway(s) 35. Mr zulu time (utc/gmt) was warned by chief pilot to keep an eye on the pilot mr x; that he was not a safe pilot and has some problems with his flying ability. Mr zulu time (utc/gmt) also told me that the mr's flight expertise is equal to a student pilot on his 2nd solo flight and does not have some of the basic safe flight techniques generally learned in the early stages of flight training and that he is a dangerous individual in an airplane as pilot in command he further stated his landing flare is consistently initiated much too high and could get him into trouble some day when encountering a crosswind landing that he is not set up properly. Please take appropriate action to prevent what could be a deadly accident in the future. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: reporter states he almost lost his position and membership in the squadron as a result of his letter. The incompetent officer involved is a vicious man. However; 3 or 4 others also wrote letters and the man is now on a training status in the squadron. Reporter does not know what action federal aviation administration will take. Felt some action necessary when second officer many instances of poor ability were brought to his attention from second officer many different aspects.
output: LETTER TO LCL FSDO REGARDING PLT INCOMPETENCY AND CITING OF SEVERAL INCIDENTS TO CORROBORATE.

input: After pushback from the gate; while starting engs; prior to movement under own power we noticed a van moving backwards from another gate. After a short time; we noticed a person on the ramp chasing after the van. It then became apparent that the van was unoccupied (couldn't see driver's side or the van); and was going to strike our aircraft we immediately shut down engs (prior to impact). Van impacted aircraft just forward of left/right (directions) engine at approximately 5-10 mph. Tug driver came back out and plugged in; and i inquired intermediate fix we had any apparent leaks (of fuel); with none being observed. Called dispatch to see intermediate fix we needed to leave aircraft and van untouched until investigation complete; or intermediate fix maintenance could remove van. Dispatch said let maintenance take charge of situation. Maintenance and other supervisors then arrived to take charge of situation. Van was removed from under aircraft and aircraft towed back to the gate; where passenber were deplaned. Debriefed with supervisors and chief pilot callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter could supply no information beyond that given in the report except that the aircraft was taken out of service.
output: A319 FLT CREW REPORTS BEING STRUCK BY DRIVER-LESS VAN SHORTLY AFTER PUSH BACK AND PRIOR TO TAXI.

input: We mistakenly ran the wrong minimum equipment list procedure resulting in the deployment of oxygen masks in the cabin. No emergency was declared. We complied with quick reference handbook procedure for for cabin altitude message. Remainder of flight normal. A contributing factor was time constraints which caused us to be rushed and also an insufficient attention to detail; we did not read the minimum equipment list closely enough.to prevent a repeat i suggest flight crews read minimum equipment list instructions and minimum equipment list numbers very closely and make sure both crew members understand what is required or not required for each minimum equipment list item. If there are complicated mels make sure to set aside time to read them very carefully without any distractions or time pressure.
output: A CRJ flight crew utilized the wrong procedure for the pressurization system MEL number; which resulted in the cabin not pressurizing and the ultimate release of the passenger oxygen masks.

input: Inbound aircraft had various write-ups that maintenance cleared. Those included an automatic communications addressing & reporting system reporting issue; lavs overflowing; and autobrakes failing to arm. One write-up that wasn't cleared was the landing gear lever lock solenoid was not working properly thus crew has to use the override procedures. It was deferred [a few days prior]. Aircraft was dispatched and departed. Shortly after reaching cruise altitude we passed a waypoint but the howgozit did not update with actual fuel and time. Dispatch then sent a message asking about our delayed takeoff. I then pulled up automatic communications addressing & reporting system prog id/sensor page which displayed air/gnd in ground flight manual procedures and systems involved were nonexistent. Very disappointing. Crew felt a normal landing could be made at destination. Several hours later; near coast in; flight attendant notified flight deck that the mid lavs were overflowing. Did not know at the time that the drain mast heaters still were in ground mode which is inadequate at altitude. Normal landing at zzz. Zzz maintenance was shown a printed page of the automatic communications addressing & reporting system sensor page showing air/gnd in ground outbound crew was briefed on aircraft issues. Hindsight says air/gnd switch should have been tested [at other airports]. As important; the flight manual needs to have systems that are related to this switch.
output: The flight crew of a B767 reported that various systems were inoperative due to a defective air/ground sensor.

input: Zny had cleared us to cross 20 east of etg at fl220 then gave us a frequency change to contact zob. After initial contact and just prior to leveling off at fl220 cleveland asked us intermediate fix we could be level at fl220 in 2 minute(s) reporting traffic to us at 12 o'clock and 12 mile at fl230. We told him we'd be level in 10 seconds; as we were second officer close to leveling off. We believe we met the crossing restriction; and there was no conflict with the tfc.
output: ATC QUESTIONED REPORTER FLT AS TO WHETHER OR NOT THEY WERE GOING TO COMPLY WITH CROSSING RESTRICTION.

input: Prior to 1 apr 1988; all flts were smoking flts; and turning on the no smoking sign prior to landing acted as a signal to the cabin attendants (ca's) that landing was imminent and that it was time to be seated and secured for landing after 1 apr 1988; only those flts over 2 hours are smoking flts and on those under 2 hours the no smoking sign is to be left on for the duration of the flight to indicate smoking is not permitted. This change in the far's caused no procedure changes on flts over 2 hours as the no smoking sign would be used as it always had; a signal to be seated for landing however; on flts over 2 hours the no smoking sign is to be left on during the flight this means another way must be found to notify the ca's to prepare for landing our airline put out a bulletin stating that the new procedure is to make a passenber announcement prior to 10000' to alert the ca's that it was time to be seated and secured for landing on fri; sept 1988; on a flight from stl to mci; landing at (xxy hrs) 1:24 flying time; we landed at mci w/o making the appropriate passenber announcement. The flight was uneventful; routine; smooth and all procedure and chklists were followed; except for the passenber announcement. This flight was the last flight on the 3rd day of a 4 day trip; and the 1st leg of the trip under 2 hours one of the ca's was still standing when we landed. On the before takeoff chklist; the 1st item is 'cabin alert' with the response being 'alerted.' however; on the 'lndg final' chklist; alerting the cabin is not mentioned. Since the no smoking flts are new and since they entail a change of crew procedure and a change of old; well rehearsed habit patterns; certainly a better way must be found to assure the cabin team is safely seated than a bulletin telling the flight crews that they should now make a passenber announcement to seat the flight attendants on flts less than 2 hrs! Certainly; a chklist change would serve to do this better than memory!
output: NO LNDG ANNOUNCEMENT. FLT ATTENDANT NOT SEATED.

input: During my preflight exterior inspection i noticed that there was hydraulic fluid on the pavement just below the right main gear strut. I also observed a leak coming from the strut aft on the inboard side. I entered my discovery as a discrepancy into the logbook. After notifying my dispatcher i was transferred to maintenance (mx) control who informed me that a mechanic would come out. After a few minutes a mechanic showed up and said that he did not see any leak on the right main gear strut. I showed him the pictures that i took during my walk-around and pointed out the leak. He disappeared and a few minutes later a second mechanic came up to tell me that it was not a hydraulic leak but just grease from when they serviced the gear. Again i disagreed; showed him the pictures and told him that i touched the fluid with latex-gloves which revealed a clear reddish fluid not consistent with grease. Also; i showed him the origin of the fluid on the strut which was not near a grease point. He left the cockpit and at which time i received the logbook back. My write-up was signed off as 'no leak found'. Obviously i had an issue with that. I recalled the mechanic (a third one; not the same as the first 2) and asked why it was signed off as no leak found when i had actually shown them where the leak was. He replied that they had wiped off the strut; observed it for 20 minutes and did not find any 'new' leaks. I told him that this is what i would have expected to see in the corrective action box rather than the 'no leaks found' comment which makes me look like i was imagining things. He said that this is how they signed it off and if i had a problem with that i should contact mx control. I said that i will take the airplane as is; but that i still would prefer the logbook to show what action really was performed the next time around (backing my view on that issue are the comments made by mx in flight following [system] stating the steps they did to clear this discrepancy. It's in [flight following system] but not the logbook. Why?). As we were ready to push when the lead flight attendant (fa) called me up regarding a sick passenger on board. We decided to have the gate agent contact medlink in order to get guidance on how to deal with the sick passenger. While this was going and since i had some spare time i decided to re-inspect the right main gear strut. Even though the airplane had not moved yet i again observed a leak on the strut. I called dispatch; the duty pilot and mx control (all on a phone-patch at the same time) and informed them that i would have to put that back into the logbook as a discrepancy. Soon after the call the same mechanic who handed me the logbook (the third one) came back up into the cockpit; told me that after a hard landing when the gear moves some of the o-rings can become unseated and that this would be normal. I said that is fine with me as long as it is acknowledged that it is leaking and that a certain mx procedure is followed assuring the pilots that a certain leak (drops per minute; quantity or such thing) is acceptable. I told him that i would not accept a sign off stating that no leak was found. In a rather condescending voice he belittled me by saying that he will sign it off and make an addition to the sign off explaining how the gear works. I do know how the gear works....it might be him who needs remedial training on how a leak looks like. I did not say that in order to remain professional though. The decision was made to deplane and switch airplanes. I still do not know why suddenly mx changed their mind about the airworthiness and found the airplane not dispatchable; but i informed the gate agent of the decision and we deplaned. What i find very odd is that the mx comments in [flight follow system] say that even the second time around they did not find any leak; despite the photographic evidence to the contrary; but still swapped airplanes to do an inspection and possible repack of the strut.corrective actions: mx needs to pay closer attention to what the pilots are saying. It is incomprehensible to me how 3 mechanics can't find a leak that was that obvious and then proceed to tell me that the source is something that it wasn't (how can they mistake hydraulic fluid with grease?). Also; if a corrective action is performed it should be reflected in the logbook. Fixing (or trying to fix) something and then then signing it off as if it had never existed in the first place is just wrong. Also; why was the plane taken out of service after i refused the sign-off as 'no leaks found'? All i wanted was a comment like 'leak within tolerance' or similar. Unless of course a leak of any kind is not acceptable; but then they should not have just wiped it off and re-dispatch the plane in the first place.
output: MD-83 Captain reported that the aircraft was pulled out of service after three attempts to inform Maintenance of a hydraulic leak from the right main landing gear. The Captain was not satisfied with the initial logbook write-up by Maintenance.

input: Due to construction at jfk airport the controllers in the jfk area at the new york terminal radar approach control facility were ordered by management to work a nonstandard procedure the runway(s) confign was; land runway(s) 4r and to depart runway(s) 31l. The controllers have had no formal training on this airspace and the procedures associated with this runway(s) confign. I made a specific request for a written description of my airspace and was told that it would not be provided. Historically due to the complexity of this confign; this operations(s) was used only on a shift with 1 controller owning all of the airspace and only under light traffic conditions. The situation that makes this set-up unsafe; is that all of the arrs' and deps' flight paths will cross at some point. During my shift; numerous aircraft did not fly the departure standard instrument departure correctly. Some of the aircraft turned wide off of runway(s) 31l; others turned early and to the left/right (directions) directly towards the arriving aircraft landing on runway(s) 4r. The scariest and most dangerous deviation occurred when a heavy airbus turned left/right (directions) off of runway(s) 31l towards the runway(s) 4r arrs. The aircraft had to be given an immediate turn and climb back to the left/right (directions) it is my understanding that none of the pltdevs were investigated. I do not understand why i was not given a proper briefing along with my co-workers on what airspace and procedures were being utilized on this runway(s) confign.
output: N90 CTLR EXPRESSED CONCERN REGARDING LACK OF BRIEFINGS AND THE USE OF NONSTANDARD PROCS FOR JFK TFC DURING ARPT CONSTRUCTION.

input: While taking off; the engine lost power and i was forced to land. Since i was still over the runway(s) with about 3000 feet/foot still in front of me; i continued straight ahead and landed without incident.
output: AN EXPERIMENTAL ACFT PLT; DEPARTING BCT; EXPERIENCED AN ENG FAILURE AT 200 FT. HE WAS ABLE TO LAND STRAIGHT AHEAD ON REMAINDER OF RWY.

input: At xa55 jul/xa/00 we departed the gate for lansing; mile the takeoff was normal and at 3500 feet/foot mean sea level the aircraft was yawing to the left/right (directions) and vibrating followed by a loud bang and flash of white light. The #2 engine failed. We completed all the memory items for engine fire/severe damage inflt and completed all appropriate quick reference handbook procedures an emergency was declared with cvg departure control right after the engine failed. We decided to return for landing at cvg. Air traffic control vectored us for the instrument landing system runway(s) 18l; and the landing was uneventful and normal. We were told that another aircraft was ready for us to fly the lansing flight company advised us there was no crew available. The capt; the first officer and the flight attendant refused to continue. Rpt time xa20. Duty day 12 hours 53 minute(s) emergency occurred on the 7th leg. Intermediate fix we accepted that assignment our duty would exceed 14 hours we went home after this incident and resumed the trip on the following day at xp25.
output: ENG FAILURE ROUTINELY HANDLED BY CREW OF CL65. AFTER RETURN TO DEP ARPT CREW REFUSED FURTHER ASSIGNMENT DUE TO ALREADY LONG DUTY DAY.

input: On departure at 3;000 feet/foot began to smell hot fumes/smoke. Flight attendants called forward and said they smelled smoke/fumes. Donned oxygen masks and decided to return to the airport of departure. Contacted dispatch and notified of decision to return. Notified air traffic control and requested emergency equipment to meet the aircraft upon landing. Landed without incident fire crew inspected the outside of the aircraft then we taxied to the gate. We suspect the left pack may have been providing excessive heat.left pack cooling fan was on minimum equipment list procedure called to not turn on the pack on the ground. This was briefed prior to pushback. After engine start the left pack was inadvertently turned on and not caught by the crew. The minimum equipment list sticker was located on the center console and not on/near the switch for the left pack.
output: An MD82 returned to the departure airport after smoke/fire/fumes odor was detected in the cockpit and cabin. The inadvertent actuation of a deferred pack prior to takeoff may have contributed.

input: We were being vectored for the instrument landing system to runway 4r in newark. We were southwest of the airport; level at 3000'. Air traffic control gave us a traffic advisory for a visual flight rules aircraft 500' below our altitude. No more than 5 seconds after that advisory; we were given a traffic advisory from the traffic alert and collision avoidance system followed immediately by an resolution advisory to 'climb'. I disengaged the autopilot and began to follow the resolution advisory guidance while the first officer let air traffic control know we were in a traffic alert and collision avoidance system climb situation. Air traffic control acknowledged and told us to climb no higher than 3500'; as there was other traffic above us. As we leveled at 3500'  we received another resolution advisory to 'monitor vertical speed'. This command was for us to just stay level at 3500. I then saw the visual flight rules traffic (appeared to be a cessna model) pass directly below us at what looked to be less than 1000' lower than our current altitude. After clearing the traffic; air traffic control issued us a clearance back down to 3000 and we continued towards the approach.the main threat in this situation is congested airspace; with the addition of light general aviation traffic on days where the weather is nice. I am unaware if an error on the part of the visual flight rules pilot contributed to our traffic alert and collision avoidance system to generate an ra.i will continue to maintain a vigilant scan for traffic; especially in good visual flight rules flying days.
output: First Officer reported maneuvering for a TCAS RA; while being vectored for an ILS to EWR; that resulted in a second RA with another aircraft.

input: During preflight; we reviewed our flight plan which showed a filed route to zzz of fwa3 fwa dct vhp dct bwg ....zzz. We received our pre departure clearance which showed us -cleared as filed- dtw fwa3 fwa vhp bwg .... The pre departure clearance further stated feet/foot wayne three/ ctc departure 125.52 maintenance 10000 feet/foot after takeoff; when we first contacted departure control; departure told us to turn left and intercept the 202 radial to cavvs. The fwa departure is on the 217 radial second officer this immediately got our attention. I queried departure about our route; and was told it was remote id (identification) departure watertown; v467 remote id (identification) iiu bwg... He spit the route out second officer quickly that i had to ask him to repeat it. I told departure we had a pre departure clearance in hand which stated the fwa3 fwa.....zzz. Departure then told us to expect radar vectors to cavvs then the route he had given us. I don't know how a mistake like this is made; but i kept all the paperwork from this flight; and there is no mistake about what was on our flight plan and pre departure clearance during taxi out is usually when you would hear from air traffic control about a re-route; but nothing was said to us.
output: ACR FLT CREW RECEIVED A PDC WHICH INDICATED THAT THE FLT WAS CLEARED AS FILED. AFTER TKOF; ATC INDICATED THAT THEY HAD EXPECTED THE FLT TO BE NAVIGATING A DIFFERENT SID AND ROUTE.

input: Landed on runway(s) 22 new bern; nc. Taxied clear and contacted ground control on taxiway a. Was directed to taxi and hold short of runway(s) 13. We acknowledged hold short instructions. I became distraction discussing the approach with the first officer i was reminded by the ground controller to hold short of runway(s) 13. We came to a stop just past the hold short line; but still short of the runway(s) the other aircraft (c150) was just beginning takeoff we were fortunate that the ground controller was paying close attention to the situation no one was endangered; but i learned an important lesson.
output: A DH8A CREW; TAXIING TO THE GATE AT EWN; TAXIED PAST A HOLD SHORT LINE.

input: During descent into klga on the nanci arrival, arrive we were given the standard clearance to cross somto intersection at 11000 feet/foot we were level at fl260 having made a vertical navigation path descent to cross the kerno intersection at fl260. Upon receipt of the clearance we set 11000 feet/foot in the mode control panel altitude window and verified that we had indeed programmed somto at 11000 feet/foot we also noted that our touchdown point from our intermediate altitude of fl260 was 25 nautical mile our pitch at that point was vertical navigation air traffic control then requested that we start our descent immediately to cross somto at 11000 feet/foot after selecting the descent page we observed our capture prompt to be missing; (indicating at active capture descent in progress). We then selected a vertical speed descent of 1000 feet per minute and after descending approximately 500- 600 reselected vertical navigation and observed an immediate return to the capture mode. We then entered into a brief discussion concerning the relative merits of a speed descent versus a path descent and did not notice the fmc's apparent failure to compute a path based on somto at 11000 feet/foot and its failure to capture a path that would have crossed somto at 11000 feet/foot that discussion was interrupted by atc's query of 'are you going to be able to make somto at 11000 ft?' we both quickly referred to: a) vertical deviation on the descent page and b) distance from somto on our route legs page. It was then that we noticed the failure of the flight management computer to compute and capture the proper path. When i saw how close we were to somto (4 nm) i expected to see a +10000 feet/foot or second officer on my vertical deviation but in fact it was showing a - 400 feet/foot from a downtrack waypoint constraint; wezul at 3000 feet/foot we advised air traffic control that we would not be able to meet the restriction and he asked us to expedite through 20000 feet/foot which we did. No further comment was made to zdc concerning the somto clearance and we subsequently made a normal frequency change to new york approach control analysis: during the capture descent that we had been second officer careful to verify; our path somehow changed (or was deleted). It was obviously not deleted by either pilot but it inexplicably disappeared from our descent page. (this is where i wish i had a video tape of the descent to more closely scrutinize the actual chain of events.) we do know this; when air traffic control questioned our ability to make the somto restriction and we quickly analyzed our relationship to the displayed path; the vertical navigation 'light' was not on. By definition; that means the mode cannot be disengaged. More accurately in this case; i suspect it also meant that the mode was not engaged. The first officer was quick to select a different pitch mode; level change; deployed full speed brakes; and an indicated air speed command of 340 knots indicated airspeed to expedite our descent we had the opportunity to fly the nanci arrival, arrive 2 more times during this 3-day trip pairing and each time we tried to duplicate the chain of events with no success. (we made the somto restriction each time with normal indications.) conclusion: even though we properly programmed the descent path; we failed to monitor that descent and its subsequent capture of the proper path in order to meet the somto restriction. Thankfully; there was no traffic conflict. Recommendation: due to complaints from other pilots on this particular route concerning their inability to program certain altitude constraints; perhaps there is a peculiarity about this particular arrival, arrive that may cause problems within the flight management computer regarding path computations. I recommend that industry experts examine this particular crossing restriction to insure that some sort of anomaly does not exist that might cause another crew to make the same mistake.
output: ALTDEV ALT XING RESTRICTION NOT MET.

input: For the third time in the last two or so months we were assigned runway 17l as the landing runway by approach. For the third time i 'refused' the runway assignment. While the tables tell us a 425;000 lbs [heavy air carrier] can land on that runway i see no reason to do so while a tiny jet at what; maybe 60;000 lbs is occupying the longer runway. The question simply is not can we do it but why do we do it? Is there a better way?according to air traffic control the runways get assigned by 'the computer.' maybe 'the computer' needs to be educated or overruled. If you cannot accommodate international arrivals on the west side give heavy aircraft longer runways than you give regional jets. It's simply the smart thing to do. Longer runways decrease wear on equipment; lessen failure rates and allow crews that have been flying for 10-16 hours a greater safety margin.
output: Heavy aircraft First Officer reported that ATC computer assigns shorter runways for bigger aircraft.

input: Our flight was operating at fl370. Approximately air vor and dme (co-located) the controller cleared us to; 'cross 50 mile from eey 270; cleared direct to eey; hurry to fl310; pilot discretion after that.' we were still quite a distance from that point; and a good distance from our start of descent point. The f/o; at my request; asked intermediate fix we could just have pilot's discretion. The reply to the best of my knowledge was; 'hurry down to fl350 for now.' we complied. At fl350 we encountered light turbulence but also noted an aircraft proceeding left to right directly under us. At what altitude we didn't know; but i guessed fl310 or fl330. At this time we still thought we were cleared pilot's discretion to fl270; and i commented to the first officer 'i wonder intermediate fix the controller knew about him (the other acft)?' we had been level at fl350 for no more than 2 minute(s) still encountering light turbulence and after the other aircraft had passed; i started descent simultaneously advising the controller 'lgt x is picking up light chop and is out of 350.' no traffic advisory was given of the other aircraft shortly thereafter we were cleared to descended. About 5 minute(s) later we were advised we had an altitude excursion and intermediate fix we desired further information to call the watch supervisor cle air route traffic control center which we did. The next day i also called the quality control officer who explained the situation to me. His only comment about the controller was; 'he could have used better phraseology;' but did say the tapes replayed said he told us to; 'hurry to fl350 now; lower later;' or words to that effect. We did not remember that. Both of us were sure hurry to 350 and pilot's discretion to 270 was our clearance i was equally surprised when the aircraft passed under us and that it was at fl330. Had we started out of fl270 and hurried to fl310 as was our first instruction; i believe we would have been very close to that aircraft i believe the real problem is that the controller had to have us at fl350 or lower to hand us off to the next sector whose boundary was approaching very rapidly; as we were still a longitude way from our top of descent point.
output: FLT CREW MISUNDERSTOOD DESCENT CLRNC AND DESCENDED INTO CONFLICT WITH OPPOSITE DIRECTION TRAFFIC.

input: Departed shenendoah valley regional (shd) xa00; visual flight rules en route batavia; ny (qvc) elevation 1201 feet/foot cloud base 5000 feet/foot visibility 10+ mile began below cloud base to north arrived cumberland regional. Automatic weather observing/reporting system rpting 3300 feet/foot scattered 4000 feet/foot overcast tops of terrain not obscured; 10 mile visibility. Proceed north of bedford. Automatic weather observing/reporting system not rpting turbulence encountered just before attempt to call altoona flight service station specialist inadvertent instrument flight rules tried to climb from 3400 feet/foot to higher; but encountered icing. Tried lower. Began left/right (directions) turn. Turbulence made altitude hold impossible. Approximately 90 degree turn to left/right (directions) struck top of tree on ridge line. Approximately altitude 3100 feet/foot continued turn to south until visual flight rules again. Landed bedford without incident. Aircraft leading edges damaged. Left/right (directions) rear elevator and stabilizer damaged. No change to flight characteristics. Cause: too close to cloud base because of attention on cockpit (radios) and loss of visual ref.
output: GA PLT STRUCK TREE DURING INCLEMENT WX.

input: Flc on clbout got hydraulic pressure light. On further inspection found loss of fluid on left/right (directions) hydraulic system went to pom and accomplished abnormal procedure but still lost all hydraulic fluid in the left/right (directions) system i declared an emergency and returned to dfw for landing procedures were discussed and reviewed. Weather in dfw was overcast and instrument landing system to runway(s) 17l was executed. We used 20 degree flaps and speed of 152 knot(s) a normal landing was made; the runway(s) was wet and a crosswind from the left/right (directions) the nose wheel steering was inoperative as was the left/right (directions) engine reverser. Automatic spoilers were also inoperative on touchdown i applied steady braking and went in reverse on left/right (directions) engine the aircraft veered to the left/right (directions) i came out of reverse and had full left/right (directions) rudder and hit left/right (directions) brake to get aircraft straight. I then started back to ctrline of runway(s) and went back into reverse. Aircraft came to a stop. 4 tires on left/right (directions) side were blown. No one injured; and no other damage to acft.
output: LGT DURING CLB HAS HYD PRESSURE LIGHT. LOST ALL L HYD SYS FLUID. MADE EMER LNDG WITH BRIEF LOSS OF ACFT CTL.

input: I was distraction changing the waypoints on the global positioning system when unbeknownst to me; the autoplt disconnected. The airplane slowly rolled into a very steep turn and the nose dropped; which accounted for the loss of altitude when i had the plane under control i climbed back up to 11000 feet/foot and continued on course.
output: A BE36 PLT CRUISING IN IFR CONDITIONS WAS DISTR WHILE PROGRAMMING THE GPS AND; WHEN THE AUTOPLT DISCONNECTED; MOMENTARILY LOST CTL IN A VERY STEEP TURN.

input: Upon initial contact with approach we were told to expect the visual or area navigation runway xxr. At approximately mid field right downwind we were instructed by approach control to contact tower. Upon contact with tower we were cleared to land on runway xxr. We continued our descent and approach. A little while later; tower instructed us to return to approach. Approach control advised us of a possible pilot deviation as we were not cleared for an approach. We were given a base turn and asked if the airport was in sight. We were then cleared for a visual approach and again instructed to contact the tower. In hindsight; the instruction to contact the tower came at an unusual time; mid field left downwind. But when cleared to land by the tower; i thought nothing more of it. It was the instruction to return to approach and the subsequent notification of a potential pilot deviation that causes me to question the initial instruction.pay closer attention when instructions are given in a non-normal order/environment.
output: Air carrier flight crew reported they were informed by ATC of a possible altitude deviation.

input: During cruise flight we had gotten the stick shaker (both control columns) 4 different times; twice at fl310; .85; 320 knot(s) fl360; .86; prior to descent. Each event lasted 5 to 45 seconds. All other indications were normal. The aircraft was being operated well within the normal cruise envelope. Air smooth. After the 4th event and just prior to top of descent we contacted maintenance advising him of the problem as a follow up to the [write-ups] we had submitted earlier in the evening. Maintenance had us pull and reset 2 c/bs (circuit breakers) affecting the multiple inputs to the warning systems. After i discussed this with the rest of the crew we were still concerned about the erroneous stall warning indications and agreed that we should pull the stick shaker c/bs prior to the approach and landing. Maintenance concurred with our decision. The 2 c/bs were pulled for the stick shakers. The approach and landing were normal.
output: A B747-400 Captain reported multiple false stick shaker events in cruise flight.  After consulting with Maintenance; the appropriate circuit breaker's were pulled to prevent nuisance alerts on approach and landing.

input: Flt was normal until my coplt and i made our initial descent for landing into beaumont. After making a descent at flight idle i was in the process of adding power to both engs when i noticed a yaw. I glanced down at the engine instruments to find the right engine still at approximately 58% ni. About 5-7 secs after the left engine spooled the right engine then came up to speed i; of course; know that this situation is abnormal. I told my coplt that 'when we get to beaumont; let's have maintenance take a look to see what's wrong.' we did not experience any more problems after the initial problem until slowing for the approach gear down; flaps takeoff approximately 6-7 mile out. I added power to both engs to stabilize the speed at 130 knot(s) when i noticed again the right engine not spooling up. Since the right engine was maintaining minimum 58% i elected to feather the right propeller instead of shutting down the engine completely; since we were inside of the marker i elected to declare an emergency and make the landing then advise air traffic control on the ground of the situation which i did. After arriving at the gate; i advised maintenance on the company radio of the situation. They in turn told me they would meet me at the gate which they did. After deplaning the passenber the mechanic and i then taxied the airplane to maintenance and attempted to recreate the problem with the right engine again which we did successfully except the difference being the engine would only spool to approximately 35-40% ni on the start and that's all. We then shut the engine down and i then asked the mechanic 'do you want me to write this up on the form 1?' he said; 'no; i'll make the appropriate entry in the log form.'
output: ACR LTT ENGINE FAILURE IN FLT. FAILURE NOT ENTERED IN ACFT LOG BOOK.

input: We were delayed due to being swapped to an aircraft that maintenance was repairing. Maintenance was clearing a discrepancy on the left engine intake anti-ice. After maintenance cleared the discrepancy and released the aircraft; we got underway. Everything went without incident until we were in our climbout at about 14;500 feet/foot and about 20 miles south of zzz1. At that point; a cwp warning sounded an air conditioning master caution. Looking at the overhead panel we had a right bleed closed light illuminated. As the captain was the pilot flying; he called for identify and cancel; which i did; and then an emergency non-normal checklist for environmental/air conditioning. Before i could pull out the pom/checklist; we received another caution for a right duct over temperature. We completed the appropriate checklists and were instructed to 'wait a while' for the duct over temperature light and bleed valve light to extinguish. We 'waited for a while;' approximately 2-3 minutes; and the lights were still illuminated. The captain shifted control of the aircraft and #1 radio to me while he tried to get further guidance from maintenance about how long 'a while' was before we should follow the next part of the checklist; which was to 'land at nearest suitable airport.' it took the captain approximately 5 minutes to contact maintenance. In the meantime; the duct over temperature light would cycle randomly off and on which would also activate master caution warnings. After conferring with maintenance; it was decided that turning back to zzz was the best course of action. Dispatch ran our numbers and agreed that returning was the safest option. The captain resumed control of the aircraft; we obtained a new clearance from air traffic control and returned to zzz without further event. I would like the emergency non-normal checklist to be more specific as to how long to wait for the lights to extinguish. As it is presently worded; 'wait a while;' it is impossible to accurately gauge how long to wait.
output: SF340 flight crew encounters engine bleed and pneumatic system CWP warning messages and decide to return to departure airport for maintenance.

input: Acr x inbound to air traffic control on the longitude side transition to downwind was instructed to descend to 10000 feet/foot mistakenly instead of 12000 feet/foot which i meant to issue. The aircraft entered the air traffic control departure controller's airspace without coordination i noticed the aircraft descending below 11000 feet/foot and instructed the aircraft to climb and maintain 11000 feet/foot there are several factors that i feel contributed to this error. We were very busy. I was controling 9 or 10 arriving aircraft i was concentrating on the short side arrs since they were coming into my airspace at minimum in trail with speeds up. I had to vector them off the arrival, arrive for spacing; since our finals were already full. Descent to 10000 feet/foot is normal practice for this short side traffic thinking of the necessity to get these aircraft down to 10000 feet/foot i must have misspoke that altitude when descending a longitude side aircraft supplemental information from acn 306048: i was working the d handoff the center was feeding us at minimum interval and we were getting no relief from flow control (tmu). The sector was overloaded. I coordinated directly with the center to give us a gap. They did but an aircraft that went missed approach filled that gap. Tmc was coordinating with me telling me they had stopped arrs at logan; when the controller issued a short side altitude to a longitude side airplane. I missed the clearance and readback. The aircraft descended into dep's airspace.
output: ACR X UNAUTH UNCOORD PENETRATION OF DEP CTL AIRSPACE. OPDEV.

input: I ante meridiem an instrument rated/mel private pilot. I departed sjc in a seneca v/g on an instrument flight rules flight to gardenerville; nv. Ceiling was 2000 feet/foot i had just flown; as a passenber in another aircraft from gardenerville to sjc second officer i was more familiar with the en route weather than normal. I also had received two weather briefings prior to the flight when i landed in san jose there was a thin overcast layer and light rain over the airport with a broken layer to the east of san jose. In preparing for departure from sjc to mev it took me longer than normal to prepare for the flight and obtain the instrument flight rules clearance departure from sjc was normal. On climb out at approximately 3000 feet/foot certain instrument panel lighting malfunctioned; i attempted to diagnose the problem but was unable to do second officer at this point i attempted to turn on my flashlight but dropped in on the floor. In the process of attempting to find the flashlight and further diagnose the instrument lighting i misplaced my glasses. Simultaneously i was attempting to engage the autoplt; which usually is a simple task; however; i was unable to do this either; and thus continued to hand fly the airplane. Due to the several problems i was experiencing in the cockpit i may have missed some of the air traffic control radio calls as i was focusing on flying the airplane. At one point air traffic control was asking me a question about the 'legality' of something which i did not understand. I informed air traffic control that i did not understand the question. Because of these distractions the airplane deviated from its assigned altitude and heading air traffic control instructed me to 'dsnd to 5000' which i initiated. Once in the descent the airplane inadvertently began to climb again due to the extremely difficult lighting and the cockpit problems at hand. At some point during all of this air traffic control suggested that i return to sjc and i requested vectors to do second officer as i solved the problems at hand i flew the assigned altitudes and headings back to sjc and landed without incident. In retrospect the weather deteriorated federal aviation regulation worse than forecast and it had been a longitude day.
output: PLT OF PA34 LOSES COCKPIT LIGHTING; FLASHLIGHT; GLASSES AND CTL OF THE AIRPLANE DURING NIGHT IFR DEP FROM SJC. ALERT DEP CTLR ASSISTS A SAFE RETURN TO SJC.

input: Ground personnel utilized wireless headsets for cockpit communications during pushback. The problem wasn't immediately obvious: when we were contacted 'ready for pushback;' our baggage doors were still open and we told the ground crew. We were immediately advised 'i'm looking at them and they are closed; let me re-cycle.' during this time; we were instructed to 'release brakes;' to which we did. We observed the bulk cargo door close and then re-open. Ground inquired 'how's that?' and our response was 'we are still showing rear main cargo door open and the bulk door still open.' ground followed with 'sir; i'm showing you haven't released your brakes' so we cycled several times; our parking brakes and even re-pressurized the system to assure proper pressure. When he said our brakes were still on; i asked him how he knew; and i was told 'the aircraft wouldn't budge;' which was odd because we hadn't felt a single movement or strain on our nose gear as is usually felt. Our cargo doors finally showed closed and a different voice appeared on the interphone system saying 'is this gate x?' and 'are you ready to push?' to which i responded again 'yes; ready for push; but do you show our brakes still set?' a routine; procedural pushback followed and just prior to normal ground interphone disconnect; i noticed a walker in front of the plane wearing headsets with an antenna for wireless operation; and that is when it started to dawn on all of the crew what possibly had been going on! I made several non-routine comments and discovered the walker in front on my nose was able to communicate with me in addition to the man below on the tug and i think there was possibly some others on [the] same frequency. It then became obvious that there wasn't a problem with our door indications or the brake indicator light; that we probably were talking with another push crew dedicated to another gate. I had never heard of these wireless headsets before. I think they are new. I don't know if they are intended for all pushes now or are only intended during times when lightning in the area is present.if these style headsets are to be routinely utilized (in either normal operations or during lightning conditions only); and if it is determined that in this case; we were; in fact; unknowingly communicating with another gate operation; extreme measures need to be implemented to prevent it from happening again. Color coding or numerically dedicating to a specific gate or restricting use to one-at-a-time or something is imperative to assure multiple headsets operating on a same channel or frequency is required. If these style headsets are intended to only be used during storm activity and therefore different to normal operations; then possibly an additional non-normal requirement of the ground personnel upon establishing contact with the cockpit be made that would go something like: 'ground crew standing by for push; be advised wireless communications are being utilized; all users on this frequency/channel are to be working aircraft xxx; on gate x-xx; please respond with confirmation [if] that is the case.' if there is someone who is hearing this communication in error on another gate/aircraft; procedurally respond 'hold operations; this is gate x-xx receiving in error;' or something of the sort.
output: Air carrier Captain reported on pushback from CLT that ground crew was utilizing wireless headsets and the Captain was communicating with a push crew from another gate.

input: I was acting as a line checked airman; giving a capt chkout on the b737-200 to capt. We were scheduled for an ord-day-ord turnaround with an federal aviation administration inspector giving capt his initial capt's en route checked the inspector got on the aircraft at the gate and proceeded to give the aircraft (and crew) a thorough cabin and cockpit inspection. He notified me that the forward lavatory door did not have an ashtray installed on it and that either one must be installed or the forward lavatory had to be 'inop'ed.' i responded that this was a no-smoking aircraft and he said that did not matter. I notified maintenance who; a short time later; showed up with a copy of the maintenance minimum equipment list which showed no ashtrays were required on the lavatory doors. The federal aviation administration inspector said that it was required and needed to be fixed/installed. When the maintenance person said the minimum equipment list didn't require it again; the inspector turned into the cockpit and said he could not fly on the aircraft and give the checked with an open discrepancy on the plane. At this point; when he left the aircraft a new maintenance release came over our automatic communications addressing & reporting system printer. It did not show an open write-up (or any write-up) about the lavatory or ashtray; and there was nothing in the maintenance logbook about it. I asked maintenance on the aircraft intercom intermediate fix the aircraft was ready to go and they said yes; that the ashtray was not required. When we returned from dayton; another federal aviation administration inspector met the aircraft and wouldn't let it leave until another door was installed with an ashtray on it. Before the inspector got off the plane; he told me he was going back to his office to checked on the situation; and would possibly meet us after our return from dayton and give the checked on our next leg to phl. That did not happen. It seems the airline minimum equipment list did not agree with the minimum equipment list that the federal aviation administration had; and that the federal aviation administration said theirs is correct. Thus; the question: did i depart with an open discrepancy and an aircraft with an incomplete equipment list? I don't think second officer as the only written materials i had available to me were our airline minimum equipment list maintenance release and logbook; all of which showed 'no opens' and 'not required.'
output: FAA INSPECTOR CANCELED A CAPT'S INITIAL ENRTE CHK FLT IN A B737-200 DUE TO THE LACK OF THE FORWARD LABORATORY DOOR DID NOT HAVE AN ASHTRAY OR THAT THE LABORATORY WAS NOT PLACARDED AS 'INOP.'

input: Cvg; runway(s) 18l. Pushback taxi; before takeoff normal. Initial takeoff roll; aircraft rolled over bump and aft cabin door light flickered on and off twice and then remained on. I initiated an abort. The speed was less than 60 knots indicated airspeed the control tower was notified and aircraft brought under control and exited the runway(s) after clearing the runway(s) we asked the f/a's to push the aft cabin door handle down. The aft cabin door light then extinguished. The f/a stated the door handle was up slightly. Based upon this information and after referring to the minimum equipment list and pilot's operating manual i elected to continue the flight to destination at destination i told a mechanic about the abort. The mechanic took upon himself to checked the door. He said the door was working normally. Based upon this incident i would like to see the federal aviation administration clarify the far's concerning aircraft log book entries after aborts.
output: FLT CREW OF MLG ABORTED TKOF BECAUSE OF A DOOR WARNING LIGHT. DID NOT MAKE LOG BOOK ENTRY.

input: Clbing through 32500' leveling at 33000' the cabin rapidly went from 5500' to 10000' with altitude horn sounding. We started aircraft in a rapid dsnt from 33000 to 10000'; doing chklist on way down. Passenber or deployed at cabin altitude 13000'. No action would hold cabin. At 10000' the pressurization did descend to 5500' and worked fine to landing at den. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: f/o rptr was contacted and added that o2 masks were donned by the flight crew; although the capt showed some signs of being slow to don his in an act of disbelief of the situation. When queried; the f/o stated that he felt that the 1 yr second officer could have caught the cabin or rpted it sooner than he did as he had been watching it in its climb from 8000' up to the 10000' level where the horn sounded. The aft was on its second leg after being accepted from a contract maintenance base operated by another large air carrier aircraft was later ferried to overhaul for aircraft checked this was f/o's second loss of cabin pressure that month.
output: EMERGENCY DECLARED WITH AN EMERGENCY DESCENT EXECUTED AFTER LOSS OF CABIN PRESSURE CTL.

input: The flight plan of aircraft x was passed to approach (non radar adjacent facility that controls surface-10;000 ft). The estimated time over nld vor and dme (co-located) that was passed was xa:47z at 8000 feet. At some point a flight plan was copied from approach regarding a lrd lander. Because approach requires non-radar separation they would need to de-conflict any conflicts through their airspace. Aircraft y populated on my radar scope when he was descending from 11;500 feet to 5;000 feet. At the time; i did not have this flight plan in my strip bay. Upon noticing the conflict i immediately called approach to make sure they were stopping the traffic at 9;000 feet above my coordinated overflight at 8;000 feet. By the time i got a hold of the approach controller and issued him a control action of maintaining 9;000 feet the aircraft y was out of 8;700 feet in the climb back up to 9;000 with 8 miles lateral. Furthermore; i must mention that not having a direct and quick line to approach is a safety hazard. We must manually dial a 7 digit number and wait for a response; to then be passed over to the approach controller. We must have a direct and quick line that allows us to speak to an adjacent facility. Approach was applying non radar separation to aircraft transitioning through there airspace.
output: ZHU Center Controller was not made aware of an aircraft estimating their airspace from an adjacent non radar facility that was descending into a conflict with their traffic.

input: I was cleared to taxi from the fixed-base operator to runway(s) 10l at pdx via the outer taxiway (alpha). I was almost to the departure end of the runway(s) when i felt the right wing dip sharply. I thought i had a flat tire or damaged gear strut and was contemplating my course of action when the plane suddenly returned to a level condition. My passenber pointed out a wdb jet on the adjacent ramp which we had just passed behind. It had been pushed back to the edge of the ramp; perpendicular to the taxiway i would estimate the distance from the tail of the jet to the taxiway as 200-300'. The jet was apparently using breakaway thrust just as i passed behind it.
output: PLT OF SMA TAXIING ON TXWY ADJACENT TO TKOF RWY ENCOUNTERED JET BLAST CREATED BY WDB STARTING TKOF ON RWY.

input: Low flight over homes. Brushed roof of home. Good landing in the street. Was not in class b airspace and i had contacted the tower and advised we were flying over 5 miles from the airport. Other balloons were in the area.
output: A balloon pilot reported landing in the street after brushing a house.

input: Weather was instrument flight rules in denver. Automatic terminal information service was reporting 1/4 mile; and tower calling 6;000 runway visual range captain was flying and briefed clear air turbulence 3 autoland. We reviewed the procedures together using the briefing guide and notams as well. Air traffic control told us to slow to 210 knot(s) which we did. Our altitude was 7;000 feet/foot and we were on a dogleg to intercept final. Tower gave us a heading to intercept; maintain 7;000 feet/foot until on final; cleared for the instrument landing system at this point; i told the captain that we should slow down since we were approaching final. He did and put 180 knot(s) in the speed window. At this point; the localizer was alive and he armed the approach. We went through final and the captain decided to click off the autopilot and stated that he was going to hand-fly the aircraft to clear air turbulence 1 minimums. He caught me off guard and i was trying to figure out in a timely manner if this was legal. The captain got behind the aircraft. By fom criteria; we were not 100% stable at 1;000 feet/foot as the speed brakes were still out and we were not fully configured; airspeed was high and checklist not complete. I had asked him if he still wanted to continue and he said yes. I should have been more aggressive and just told him to go around; but did not. He caught up to the aircraft just as we reaching clear air turbulence 1 minimums; and saw the approach lights. We landed and taxied to the gate. We discussed what happened; and he also stated that we should have gone around.
output: An Airbus Captain elected to hand fly a low minimum approach but he got behind the aircraft. Attempts by the First Officer to suggest a go around when the approach exceeded stabilized approach criteria were ineffective.

input: On the morning of mar/tue/04; around xa00; i was cleared into the ne practice area by phoenix (deer valley) tower controller along with a law enforcement helicopter aircraft y. After establishing where aircraft y was going to operate within the practice area; we moved east for separation. As part of the clearance air traffic control informed me that aircraft y was operating in the practice area. After flying and setting up an approach for a landing in a clear area in the desert; an aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) appeared at about 25 feet/foot from the intended landing spot. I took the controls from student; said some choice words about the other aircraft and began a go around while initiating the power recovery; the wind blew me closer toward the other r44 helicopter path. The other helicopter had a problem with control but managed to move out of the way of my downwash. I then called dvt tower and asked controller how many helicopters were in the practice area. Controller advised 1 helicopter and then called for aircraft y to rpt in. I then advised dvt tower there were 3 helicopters in the ne practice area. Both helicopters were undamaged; but needed to take evasive action to avoid a collision. I think dvt tower should have been diligent in knowing the number of helis.
output: NMAC BTWN AN R22 AND R44 HELI IN A TRAINING AREA 3 MI NE OF DVT; AZ.

input: I was conducting an first officer initial operating experience and was flying the first leg of our sequence; as is customary with our cyy3 arrival, arrive proceeding normally; when approach control handed us off to mia tower with a frequency on contact; what we thought was mia tower cleared us to land (rwy was not mentioned -- and i do not remember whether the tower name was spoken). When we were on short final; about 2 1/2 mile the tower controller said; 'acr x; where are you.' the first officer replied as to our location; '2 mile out for runway(s) 9l;' tower said; 'acr x; you are on the wrong frequency this is fort lauderdale tower contact miami twr;' which we of course did and got a proper clearance to land on runway(s) 9l. This was a series of human errors. Approach control mistakenly gave us feet/foot lauderdale tower frequency feet/foot lauderdale mistakenly did not issue cleared runway(s) we did not notice those omissions. It is extremely fortunate that feet/foot lauderdale caught the error when they did. Lesson for me is to be vigilant about hearing the name of the proper facility and then making sure that the cleared runway(s) is also specified in the landing (or tkof) clrnc.
output: APCHING MIA RWY 9L AN ACR IS ON THE TWR FREQ FOR FLL.

input: On a climbout; there was an unusual level of noise in the aircraft. After checking hatches etc; the aircraft turned back and made a precautionary landing at zzzz.on landing; it was found that an exhaust manifold pipe had dropped off and the resulting hot gases had burnt part of the engine cowling. The missing pipe was recovered intact from the local golf course.apparently this was a known problem with this exhaust configuration. An investigation is in progress.
output: SR22 pilot reported that the exhaust manifold pipe fell off during climb.

input: At 10 miles northeast of gyi; my student (pilot flying) called the tower to establish two-way communication and request landing. The tower instructed us to follow traffic 10 miles north of gyi on a long final to runway 17l and report 4 miles north. At the time; there were several other pilots on the frequency. The tower controller seemed workload saturated but was not to the point of instructing arrivals to remain outside the airspace. With this amount of traffic; my situational awareness was perhaps moderate; and my student's minimal. While we were maneuvering north of the airport; i heard another pilot request a practice approach for runway 17l. The practice approach was approved by the tower with the instruction to remain east of the runway 17l. At around 5 miles north of the airport; the tower asked our position; which i reported as close to 4 miles inbound. Within 30 seconds later; i saw the practice approach aircraft flying head-on opposite of straight-in to the runway; approximately 100 feet below us in the path of our descent. I made an immediate steep turn to the right and informed the tower of the deviation. Based on only brief visual contact with the conflicting aircraft; i estimated our horizontal separation was less than 500 feet. Without a turn; we would have overflown the traffic with negligible separation.chain of events- high density traffic. - lack of radar service. - inadequate situational awareness. - lack of coordination. Human performance considerations- tower controller may have issued unclear instructions that would not result in separation of inbound and outbound traffic. - tower controller may have lost awareness of the practice approach aircraft's location. - the practice approach pilot may have been unaware of traffic already on final approach in the opposite direction. - my awareness of that aircraft's location was inadequate. - i could have improved my situational awareness by asking for more information about the practice approach traffic. - my student was operating in a situation beyond his level of experience in avoiding collisions.
output: An instructor pilot with student on a visual approach to GYI Runway 17L reported taking evasive action during a near miss from an aircraft on a practice to the same runway but flying opposite direction.

input: On approach to zzz; noticed rh fuel indication had dropped to 300lbs lower than the lh fuel indicator. No action taken in the air as i was on the instrument landing system approach and total fuel was not low.upon landing and parking; i noticed a substantial fuel leak and local airport operations and fire department were notified due to the size of the spill. The spill was contained and the aircraft grounded until a replacement part could be installed. Initially became aware of the fuel problem in flight on approach into zzz. The cause of the fuel problem was identified on the ground after shut down. After conferring with zzz1 maintenance; it was determined that a quick drain plug had come loose and fell out of its place during flight.
output: SA-227 Captain reported a fuel imbalance during flight led to discovery of a fuel leak after landing.

input: Event occurred during takeoff from cap-haitien airport haiti. After 2 haitian owned/operated turboprop aircraft landed on runway(s) 5 at cap-haitien airport the tower controller called me on the phone at pm15 to advise me that he was closing the tower and he asked me what my intentions were. I told him we still had adequate visibility and visual reference (sunset is at pm00) to attempt a takeoff he acknowledged and gave me the local weather (10 mile visibility; winds ne at 20 knot(s) altimeter 30.12 inches). The first officer was the pilot flying for this leg of the flight to fll. We ramped out at pm26 and back taxied on runway(s) 5 for takeoff as we accelerated down the runway(s) at pm30; we noticed a certificate of waiver walking in the grass off to the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) which is a normal occurrence since that airport is not fenced. When we rotated off the ground the certificate of waiver attempted to cross the runway(s) about 200 feet/foot in front of the aircraft we cleared it vertically by 50 feet/foot the rest of the flight was uneventful.
output: AN SA227 FLT NARROWLY MISSES A COW ON THE RWY DURING ROTATION AND LIFTOFF DURING A DUSK OP AT CAP-HAITIEN ARPT; MTCH; FO.

input: The name change of runway(s) 36r to runway(s) 36c was confusing when i reviewed the government approach plate and found 3 parallel runway(s) i wanted to find a center runway(s) when i queried the tower as to which runway(s) i was lined up with; the controller said runway(s) 36c. This was very confusing since i had actually lined up with the taxiway when i saw the blue lights of the taxiway i immediately took evasive action to correct the approach to runway(s) 36c and made a safe landing there. My estimate of 500 feet/foot missed contact with aircraft on the ground is based on my altimeter reading when i made the slight turn to get onto runway(s) 36c. I never intended to land on the txwy.
output: SMA ON APCH TO CTR RWY ALIGNS WITH TXWY INITIALLY; THEN BECOMES ORIENTED.

input: During clbout from london heathrow; cleared direct stu and fl280; i requested fl310 (passing about fl267). We were then cleared fl310 and i read that back (including our call sign). Later passing fl286 we were given an immediate vector of 190 degrees and told our altitude clearance was only fl280. During the turn (and dscnt) i sighted traffic above and to the right. London called the distance about 3 mile after that we were cleared direct shannon vor and tacan (co-located) (snn) and fl310. I don't know how the problem arose; second officer i can only guess that it was a mistake to give us fl310 or there was some communicationss failure/mistake. The area is near the london/shannon control boundary and opp direction traffic was involved.
