Upon reflection; i realized that the previous sector had leveled aircraft x for a couple of minutes for other traffic; and it appears to me that the pilot 'zoom climbed' at more than 6000 fpm when given the clearance to fl400 by zdc. I don't think that zdc expected the learjet to climb nearly that rapidly and probably (my professional opinion) did not consider aircraft y as traffic. Because the learjet 'zoomed' into the climb so quickly; conflict alert processing could not give a timely alert to me or to zdc until it was far too late. This was a very serious situation that the air traffic control system; both with regard to controller expectation of pilot actions and with regard to automation features such as conflict alert; were not expecting. If this 'zoom climb' had begun just a couple of miles earlier; it could have resulted in a possible midair collision that perhaps even traffic alert and collision avoidance system would have struggled to prevent. [does traffic alert and collision avoidance system expect aircraft near fl380 to be climbing at rates in excess of 6000 fpm?] please note: none of the choices presented under the 'causal & contributing' factors seem to exactly fit this situation. While i don't know that the pilot technically did anything wrong; clearly the rate of climb was completely out of conformance with what any controller would reasonably suspect in that situation; and so i checked the 'non-conformance with a clearance: altitude' box because it most closely describes what happened.in my opinion; this event was not a normal loss of separation; but was in fact a potentially deadly occurrence precipitated by a completely unexpected pilot action that the controllers and the automation were not prepared for. While controller training and an automation review (e.g. Conflict alert; tcas) might be warranted; this event should be brought to the attention of the pilot community through federal aviation administration safety briefings and the like; as an example of how such action can threaten safety.
output: ZID Controller reports of a loss of separation between two aircraft; one level and the other in what he calls a 'Zoom climb' of six thousand five hundred feet per minute.

input: While using uret at sector 73 -- i fell behind significantly while working moderate traffic once i got busy -- uret became a hindrance -- i could not find the flight plan information necessary to know where each aircraft was going (its route of flt); type aircraft and requested altitude as i look over at the uret screen -- the print is second officer small  that it takes a moment to find the flight plan -- then you have to try to stay focused on this flight plan's line of information and follow across to find the rest of the information as the screen is always changing and moving these flight plans -- this is very distracting -- as i got busier and tried to work with the uret screen -- i eventually fell second officer federal aviation regulation behind that i had to rely on my flight plan readout feature on my crd on the radar scope -- this was faster and allowed me to stay focused on the radar scope instead of being distracted by uret. Also; there are no times available on the uret screen to get an estimate of when this aircraft might enter my airspace. The flight data strips that we have been using are much better; they put all the information needed in an easy to read spot with legible print. Also when using uret; it is hard (if not impossible) to make information visible to the r-person when necessary for coordination (ie; control given to another sector; pointout information routing changes; etc). Uret is a distraction and intermediate fix we use it exclusively -- i cannot work nearly as many aircraft as i could with flight data strips.
output: ZNY CTLR EXPRESSED CONCERN REGARDING URET FUNCTIONALITY.

input: Zdc gave us a clearance to cross jaybo intersection at 15;000' which is 35 vor and dme (co-located) on 085 radial nottingham vor and dme (co-located) when given the clearance to 15;000 we were at fl290 with about 45 mile to go to the intersection i told the f/o we were doing 9 mi/min second officer he could plan the descent which would have taken 45 mile at 3000 feet per minute descent he began the descent initially at 1500 to 2000 feet per minute second officer i told him to increase the rate of descent to 3500 feet per minute he did slowly. We were on an arrival, arrive which was rather hectic with several vors and several course changes (at least 5). We only had one vor and dme (co-located) operating; my vor and dme (co-located) was deferred for later maintenance i told him several times to keep the rate at 3500 feet per minute he asked me to tell center that we would not make the restriction and he began to shallow the descent at that point i increased the descent to 4000 feet per minute we were still 70 knot(s) below vmo. We should have made the crossing restriction with several mile to spare but instead missed it by 4 mile and 300'. Nothing was said by air traffic control i feel that with operating in the ne corridor and congestion as it is; air traffic control could have cleared us to 15;000 sooner; and the f/o should've maintained a constant 3000 feet per minute descent to make the crossing having both dme's operational would have made the xchking much easier and this particular arrival, arrive should be simplified (dupont 3).
output: ACR MLG ON DUPONT 3 STAR TO PHL FAILS TO MEET 15;000' CROSSING RESTRICTION AT JAYBO INTERSECTION; CITES LATE CLRNC FOR DESCENT AS CONTRIBUTORY.

input: Flt was assigned aircraft x initially. By the time i reached the airport it was aircraft y checkeding the inbound log; there were 4 open items (2 cosmetic and 2 safety of flt). I called dispatch to ask about the status of the open items before releasing the aircraft and was told that he did not know. I called maintenance control who said it was a local issue. I called line maintenance and was told that intermediate fix i wanted the engine 2 high pressure valve fault addressed i needed to refuse the aircraft i did. The flight was into known icing conditions on an arrival, arrive that is a steep descent over the mountains. This is the exact reason for the high pressure valve to open and provide the needed hot air for anti-icing. Within minute(s) of refusing the aircraft i was paged by flight operations(s) station maintenance was calling to tell me the gate lead mechanic had already fixed and signed off the log item. Upon questioning; i was told that they had fixed the problem and run the engine with no issues. I released the aircraft and went to the gate. I checkeded the maintenance release and saw that they had cleared all log items. Due to the late departure i did my flows and briefings and we got underway. During the flight i asked the first officer what he had seen line maintenance do and he said they had retrieved some information from the box (fmgc) and left. I asked him about the engine run and he said he had no knowledge of any engine run-up. On descent into zzz; in icing conditions; we got the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring for the engine #2 high pressure valve and completed the procedure on the ground i went into operations(s) called dispatch; and spoke to maintenance control regarding the entire incident. It is clear i was lied to in order to expedite a departure to an outstation with no maintenance 'after' i had refused to defer it due to safety of flight as an airline capt; i have become used to the pencil whipping of maintenance items for expeditious movement of aircraft i have seen first hand the 'shopping' of broken aircraft to whichever capt will fly it. I have also experienced the normal 'we will not fix anything until you refuse the acft' routine many; many times. However this is the first time i have been openly and brazenly lied to in order to take an aircraft i have refused due to a safety of flight issue. This nonsense has to be stopped and it is clear that only the federal aviation administration can do it! Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter stated this issue of having to refuse aircraft because of safety of flight issues; just to get maintenance to fix an item; places undue pressure on flight crews. Being lied to when; in this case; going into a known icing conditions with the #2 engine high pressure bleed valve not functioning correctly and maintenance in essence; pencil whipping the write-up to get the plane out; is another indication of his company's unsafe maintenance practices.
output: AN AIRBUS A319 CAPTAIN REPORTS ON HIS COMPANY'S MAINT DEPARTMENT'S ATTITUDE OF LYING TO HIM; PENCIL WHIPPING AND TELLING PILOTS THEY HAVE TO REFUSE ACFT BEFORE ANYTHING WILL BE FIXED.

input: I have flown into myf several times on an instrument approach; instrument landing system 28r. Every time; i am given headings and vectors to final. I have asked for the full approach sometimes; but usually given vectors. The issue is that the altitudes and heading make it very difficult to fly a controlled and standard approach. This last approach i was given a heading to the final approach course at a higher altitude; then turned right and left and then back to final and then a steep descent to be able to get back on the right altitudes for the approach. This has happened about 5 times and usually the same sequence. I am kept high; then a step descent; various headings and then cleared for the approach at the last few minutes. It makes it very difficult to manage speed and altitude. Also; when in instrument conditions it provides an opportunity to become spatially disoriented with the turns and the assigned descent profile. I believe it would be much safer to be given the full approach and follow the listed altitudes. I can tell there is a lot of traffic and a lot of training going on in the area; 2 parallel runways at myf also present a challenge for controllers; but we should find a way to make the instrument approach be according to the plate. I believe this will make it safer for us all. I respect the approach controllers and they are dealing with all the traffic the best they can. It just makes the approach more difficult to fly correctly. If the approach is not workable; perhaps it should be revised.
output: Private Pilot reports on non-standard Air Traffic Control procedure at MYF.

input: Approximately 5 minutes after departing; we were given direct to the initial approach fix for the vor/dme-a at airport zzz. Once we were approximately half way to the initial approach fix both the instructor and [student pilot] noticed the oil pressure fluctuating between the caution range and back into the green range. [the instructor] contacted approach and advised we would return to [departure airport]. Once a 180 degree turn was made; the oil pressure continued to fluctuate and became worse. At that time the air traffic control advised that the airport zzz1 was the nearest airport. Instructor diverted the aircraft to zzz1 at that time and was cleared for the visual approach. Once contacting the zzz1 tower the engine also began to run rough and the instructor requested emergency vehicles as a precaution. The aircraft landed safely and was able to taxi to the ramp and shutdown without further incident.
output: A flight instructor in a SR20 reported a fluctuating oil pressure indication that resulted in a turn back towards the departure airport. The indications became more severe and the engine also was reported to be rough running; so the flight was diverted to the closest airport where a successful landing was made.

input: "this is in reference to the violation i incurred during the airshow at	 zzz airport the violation was for deviating from federal aviation regulation part 91.211(a)(2)(3). The federal aviation administration aci who was the enforcing official was mr x. The aircraft being flown was a cessna 207 and leased for skydiving. During this day the conditions were visual meteorological conditions 'clr and a million;' with winds out of the westbound at 8-10 knot(s) on the ground and 30-40 knot(s) out of the north at altitude the flight was scheduled to begin at xa00 and the 'jump' was to occur after. Prior to leaving the ground the aci spent over 20 minute(s) inspecting our aircraft and 10 more minute(s) discussing the discrepancies; and finally cleared the aircraft for flight i launched with 4 skydivers for 16500 feet/foot mean sea level the prearranged jump altitude during the clbout the pro jumper and i decided 14000 feet/foot mean sea level was high enough. During the process of clbout and after reaching 14000 feet/foot i had noticed considerable updraft and downdraft activity. Once i had reached 14000 feet/foot mean sea level i reduced power to 20 inches of manifold pressure (mp) and 2400 rpm's. This was approximately 10 minute(s) prior to the scheduled launch time. 5 minute(s) prior to launch; we were told to delay and plan the jump for 12 minute(s) later for incoming aircraft during this delay i was still experiencing the same updrafts. At the time of the delay call i was asked by the air boss to rpt my altitude as the jumpers exited the aircraft after the 7 minute(s) delay; and the jumpers creating an aft center of gravity; resulting in constant pitch changes; i launched the jumpers and once again the air boss requested; 'the federal aviation administration would like to know your altitude say alt.' i was squawking 1200 and in class east airspace. When asked; i was honest and forthright; i responded with 15200 feet/foot mean sea level i descended to the south and did a low pass along runway(s) 8-26; from the east to the westbound after landing on runway(s) 30 and returning to the parking area i was greeted by the aci. He first asked me; 'what altitude were you at when you released the jumpers?' once again; i told him the truth; 15200 feet/foot mean sea level he responded by asking me; 'does your aircraft have oxygen?' i told him it did not. He then asked; 'what altitude do you need oxygen?' i responded with; '14000 feet/foot mean sea level and above.' he then asked for my ticket; and told me 'i try to have selective hearing; but i ante meridiem required to do this by law.' in addition i would like to bring one more point to bear regarding his inquiry as to the presence of oxygen on the aircraft during his 20 minute(s) inspection he scrutinized all parts of the aircraft including; but not limited to; the interior; the cockpit; and the fore and aft baggage compartments. Prior to the jump; he was aware of 2 things; the aircraft did not have oxygen and the scheduled jump altitude of 16500 feet/foot mean sea level he still allowed the jump to commence and requested an altitude confirmation. I ante meridiem a safe pilot and i have never had a violation before. This incident was inadvertent; and i was not intentionally trying to break a federal aviation regulation in the conditions present; the updrafts compounded by the constant movements of the jumpers; i was unable to maintain the jump altitude of 14000 feet/foot mean sea level i ante meridiem first and foremost concerned with flying the plane and keeping my passenber safe. The c207 has a history of flat spins caused by aft center of gravity. During jump runs; i ante meridiem concerned with maintaining the acft's airspd; and staying away from those potentially dangerous stall/spin scenarios. By the time the delay had taken place and the jumpers were out the door i realized i was too high; and began to descend immediately. I broke the rule. However; i feel these issues mitigate the circumstances highly. I ante meridiem requesting a full investigation of the inadvertent violation; and mr x's actions."
output: A C207 SKYDIVING PLT IS CITED AND HIS 'TICKET' LIFTED AFTER A LCL FAA ACI CITES A VIOLATION REFED TO HIS FLT ABOVE 14000 FT WITHOUT OXYGEN PRIOR TO THE JUMPERS LEAVING HIS ACFT OVER ZZZ; US.

input: We were taxiing (at night) from the d-8 to runway 24l at e-8. I reviewed the taxi plan on the jepps chart with my first officer since i had not been back to lax since the runway 24l construction project began. I taxied slowly but still found it to be extremely difficult to get to 24l at e-8 from this direction due to poor taxiway line markings and confusing taxi lights at night. This is a serious night hazard that deserves immediate attention so we don't damage an aircraft; have an inadvertent taxiway excursion or (worse) a runway incursion. Also; i believe it would help if the jepps 10-7 page had an enlarged diagram showing this specific taxi area in better detail.
output: A Captain taxiing at night to LAX Runway 24L via Taxiway D-8; E-8 became confused because the signage and lighting were reportedly not clear.

input: Acr flight abc den-yvr we encountered some weather at approximately fl300. We had leveled at fl290 when we asked for higher. Fl310 was approved. During the climb from fl290 to fl310 we asked for a deviation for weather it was a cell with a red center there was some confusion about which side we could deviate on. We wanted to turn 20 degrees left/right (directions) but then air traffic control said there was inbound traffic to denver to our left/right (directions) and told us to turn left/right (directions) i turned back approximately 20 degrees left/right (directions) of course; hand-flying. We encountered moderate turbulence and i gained approximately 500 feet/foot air traffic control then asked about our altitude but we were already correcting.
output: B737 CREW HAD ALT OVERSHOOT IN ZDV CLASS A.

input: The aircraft was being flown by the capt and was being vectored for an instrument landing system approach to runway(s) 27 memphis; the aircraft was headed nw and was south of ctrline descending to assigned altitude of 4000 feet/foot the aircraft was then cleared to 2000 feet/foot on a 290 degree heading and cleared for the instrument landing system approach the aircraft was about 15 nautical mile from memphis descending through 3000 feet/foot to 2000 feet/foot on it's final heading the acfts airspd was about 230 knot(s) the capt leveled off at 2000 feet/foot slowed down; configured; and operated the flight to a normal landing after some thought a few days after the flight i reviewed the memphis terminal control area area chart. The terminal control area chart reveals that the aircraft was operated below the terminal control area floor above 200 knot(s) conclusion: must review terminal control area area chart for all airports flown into. Must be able to assert this information to the capt flying the aircraft (apch control will assign altitudes to aircraft that will take the aircraft below the terminal control area floor. Therefore; concluding that the pilots must always be aware of their altitude and position relative to airport terrain; and type airspace.
output: ACR CLRED TO DSND BELOW TCA FLOOR ON ILS APCH WHILE STILL AT 230 KTS.

input: While in the climb out at approximately 28400; the autopilot disengaged while simultaneously the captain's pfd and mfd lost all indications. I transferred control of the aircraft to the first officer we stopped the climb and descended out of rvsm. The amber; inertial reference system/unit fault light along with the master caution; inertial reference system/unit lights had illuminated. I ran the corresponding quick reference handbook checklist for the inertial reference system/unit fault. We operated with the inertial reference system/unit selector switch in both on right. I established a radio patch with dispatch and a subsequent conference call with maintenance. We discussed what had happened and the possibility of diverting. I ruled that with the loss of redundant attitude; airspeed; and altitude indications; the continuation did not seem like the best plan of action. We [advised atc] and diverted. The landing was uneventful and normal.
output: B737 Captain reported losing his primary flight display and IRS. He transferred control of the aircraft to the First Officer and diverted resulting in an uneventful landing.

input: Aircraft checked on my frequency slightly off route ; no issue. I descended the aircraft to fl270 ; updated his route in uret and handed the aircraft off to zjx sector 66 . Everything appeared to be working fine ; i was not busy at  all or distracted ; it was business as usual. I noticed the aircraft stopped flashing to j66 and switched it to j66' s frequency as usual . Later ; i switched the following air conditioning / alternating current to j66 and went to go drop the aircraft x data block off my scope ; but somehow still had track control of the aircraft. The target was no longer in ztl airspace and was now in zjx airspace which alarmed me. I called j66 to make sure they were aware of the aircraft and that everything was ok and when i asked if they had radar(track control) on aircraft x ; j66 said yeah ; no problem . I hung up the line ; reflashed aircraft x to j66 . The datablock flashed just a few times and stopped flashing . I reflashed the aircraft a 3rd time ; and j66 took track control of the aircraft . I'm not sure why it took so many times to flash the aircraft before it was accepted ; but this is not normal . I spoke to a fellow controller about this situation and he said he has seen this issue at other sectors in the past ; but never at ztl sector 32 . It may have been an automation issue with this one aircraft ; i'm not sure . The problem was solved via coordination ; and no unsafe situation regarding separation was noted. Since i believe this was a rare occurrence and might have been the result of an unknown automation issue ; i don't see any way this could have been prevented ; but i will alert my supervision and fellow controllers to keep an eye out for this kind of anomaly in the future .
output: Enroute Controller described an automated hand off problem when the data did not transfer to the receiving controller as expected.

input: During the after start chklist the ramp individual indicated that the tail stand was removed by a hand signal. Immediately after takeoff tjsj operations(s) called on the radio and stated that the tail stand was still attached to the aircraft we contacted tower for a left/right (directions) downwind and returned to tjsj. We maintained a level landing attitude; taxied to parking; tail stand was removed; mechs inspected the tail section and we departed a few minute(s) later. Over the past few yrs; the tjsj ramp has been operating by hand signal alone to indicate that the tail stand has been removed. Although this procedure is not stated in the station operations(s) manual or airline transport rating aom; it has become common practice. Obviously; this practice should be avoided and all personnel be reminded that the tail stand must be shown to the capt in accordance with our manuals.
output: ATR72 CREW DEPARTS WITH TAIL STAND ATTACHED TO AIRCRAFT AFTER GROUND CREW FAILS TO REMOVE IT.

input: Got clearance around weather from tokyo radio; 50 nautical mile to north needed 75-80 mile to get around weather xmitted location on 121.5; 128.95. Turned lights on and descended 500 feet/foot stayed in visual conditions; then returned back on course.
output: B747 WX AVOIDANCE ALTDEV ARR NARITA USING CAPT EMER AUTH.

input: On takeoff from denver stapleton on runway(s) 35l at rotate point that was abeam of 35r runup area. This rotate point was due to a light takeoff weight for a flight to cos. At rotation an abrupt yaw motion and movement to the left was encountered along with a moderate left roll. The action was ctlable but dramatic. The coplt was on controls. After discussion with crew we all remember an xxx wdb on z-4 facing 35r and believe that this thrust was the cause of our roll and yaw motion. This movement was also observed by myself while jumpseating to my home on an mlg some weeks prior but we did not notice intermediate fix an aircraft was on z-4 or not. The movement of the aircraft was the same. Recommend that hold takeoff on 35l with heavy aircraft on z-4 for takeoff on 35r.
output: ACR MLG JET BLAST ENCOUNTER DURING TKOF ROLL ON RWY 35L AT DEN. ACR WDB HOLDING ON TXWY 90 DEGREES TO TKOF RWY.

input: This is a fatigue report. I had landed [early morning] after flying the all night from hawaii. As usual; we must be phone available during our rest period. I attempted to sleep once i arrived at residence that morning. My phone rang three times including a call from the crew desk who assigned me a trip for a departure the next morning. I accepted the assignment but was extremely fatigued having been up for over 24 hours at that point. I slept for 5 hours that night and when the alarm went off early for me to now get ready and drive to the airport; i was almost incoherent. I called crew scheduling and advised i was unfit to fly. I would have had less than 7 hours of sleep over two segments in the previous 48 hours. This airline continues to assign these unsafe situations including early short calls after all nighters and it must stop. We cannot do this sort of thing in the name of health and safety. It is egregious to expect a pilot to fly three different shifts in a three day period and perform to expected safety standards for the amount of responsibility we assume with this job.
output: B757 First Officer reports a fatigue call after being unable to get proper rest for a flight departing 24 hours after arriving on a Red Eye flight.

input: I was advised prior to sjc tower by bay approach that i was following a warrior and to slow my speed down to 140 knot(s) after switching from bay approach to sjc tower i heard them sternly advise a warrior about crossing over the departure end of runway(s) 30 at 1500 feet/foot when he was supposed to cross midfield at 2000 feet/foot they were telling him to turn left/right (directions) downwind for runway(s) 29 and to call the tower after landing a minute(s) or 2 later tower instructed me to follow the warrior and to cross midfield at or above 2000 feet/foot i was still searching for the warrior when i was advised of other traffic as i was just crossing midfield at 2000 feet/foot i then advised the tower negative on traffic and lowered my wing to look under and beside me as i crossed over runway(s) 29. Tower then comes on the radio and tells me to turn left/right (directions) to avoid the departure end of runway(s) 30 and to call the tower when on the ground i then clarified with tower that i was cleared to land runway(s) 29. A person insisted that i crossed over the departure end of runway(s) 30 at 1500 feet/foot and that 'i had an aircraft departing and climbing through 1000 feet/foot creating a hazard.' when i attempted to explain that i was over midfield at 2000 feet/foot not 1500 feet/foot over the end of runway(s) 30; he cut me off and asked 'what's your prob
output: A PIPER PA34 PLT FEELS HE WAS MISIDENTED AS AN ACFT THAT FAILED TO FOLLOW INSTRUCTIONS AT SJC AND MAY HAVE ACTION TAKEN AGAINST HIM.

input: At cruise altitude fl350; we experienced a gradual loss of 'a' system hyds. Approximately el paso vor and dme (co-located) the third in command announced a loss of 'a' system hydraulic compared to block out quantity from iah. We blocked out with approximately 4 gals on the gauge and at the point of discovery was down to 1 1/2 gals. With the loss not getting any worse; or still at a gradual decrease; we reviewed procedures for total loss; which included manual gear extension. At approximately 3/4 gal of 'a' system hydraulic and on the arrival, arrive into phx; we declared an emergency and received priority into phx. After slowing to minimum gear and flap speeds we lowered landing gear normally. Flaps also lowered to 15 degrees (normal landing flaps for loss or leak chklist). Landing was uneventful; with a normal taxi to ramp. We did not experience a total loss of 'a' system supplemental information from acn 345806: on post flight inspection hydraulic fluid was found on the starboard wing. Solid knowledge of aircraft system prevented the situation from degrading any further.
output: B727 FREIGHTER SUFFERS A SLOW LOSS OF FLUID IN 'A' HYD SYS ENRTE TO PHX. EMER DECLARED IN LNDG PROC PHX. COMPLETED SAFELY WITH MINIMUM FLUID LEFT.

input: We experienced compressor stalls climbing out after takeoff on the left engine. Accomplished appropriate checklists. Declared an emergency and returned to [departure airport]. On approach the same engine that compressor stalled failed. We accomplished a go-around in order to re-assess. We then returned for a single-engine instrument landing system approach followed by an overweight landing. We then taxied to the gate under aircraft power.
output: B767-200 flight crew reported experiencing compressor stalls and subsequent engine failure shortly after takeoff. They declared an emergency and returned to departure airport.

input: On climb out after 5 min. For approximately 15 min. Flight attendant (flight attendants) 3 and 4 reported smelling sweet glue like odor that went away in about 15 min. About 35 min. Into flight flight attendant 3 reported a headache and flight attendant 4 reported headache and nausea. Flight attendant 2 reported the smell was faint but did smell it but felt ok. Flight attendant 1 and flight deck did not smell odor. The odor was noted from row 10 to aft of aircraft. The flight attendant 4 reported feeling worse at 35 min. Into flight so we elected to return to zzz. 1 passenger in 13a reported slight irritation in nose and slight headache. On return to zzz as a [prioritized] aircraft on descent through 10;000 ft. Flight deck and cabin noticed a distinct odor like elmer's glue. Uneventful landing with flight deck on o2 and cabin use of 4 portable o2 bottles. Flight attendant 4 went to hospital remaining crew felt fine and continued on new aircraft to zzz1 as rescheduled.the probable cause was possible oil leak but no indications in flight deck.dependent on maintenance findings.
output: A321 Captain reported a cabin fumes event during initial climb resulting in a return to the departure airport.

input: I was at 6000' and cleared for elz vor and dme (co-located) transition to localizer approach at olean; ny. Transition altitude is 4000'. I thought as i was cleared for the approach i called center that i was leaving 6000 for 4000'. I may have descended more than 300'. Center asked me to maintain 6000'. I got a call for federal aviation administration on 4/91 that center had rpted altitude deviation. During this i found out i had let my medical certificate lapse. I got a new one the same day. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rpts states he has received letter from federal aviation administration and has responded. They have discussed remedial training. It appears controller cleared for approach but also instructed to maintain 6000'. He plans to listen to tapes to be sure. Says he misread the date on his medical and thought he had a yr to go.
output: SMA PLT DESCENDS BELOW ASSIGNED ALT ON TRANSITION TO APCH.

input: After a full flap; no autobrake approach to fll runway(s) 27r in visual meteorological conditions daylight conditions; upon touchdown the aircraft pitched down rapidly and aggressively decelerated. No unusual vibration or noise was apparent. The first officer continued to steer to the ctrline. The deceleration was akin to a rejected takeoff stop. During the rollout the first officer noted 'prk brk' on the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring in amber. I cycled the brake handle and took control of the aircraft as it stopped. Thinking that the brakes were locked; i had the first officer cycle the anti-skid and nosewheel steering switch. The aircraft was clrly disabled; unable to move and we advised the tower immediately that we were unable to clear the runway(s) we asked the tower what they saw and they responded that they had seen smoke earlier at touchdown but now there was no smoke or fire. We asked that they roll the equipment as a precaution. They responded immediately and confirmed no fire or smoke. They advised that all main wheel tires were blown. We made numerous pa's to the passenber to remain seated. The engs were shut down and communicationss with operations(s) established by cell phone; arrangements for passenber deplaning by stairs and buses with fll operations(s) ground power and air were furnished. Flight attendants were reminded to disarm the slides prior to opening the cabin doors. Relevent chklists completed and logbook entries were made. We supplied gear pins and collars to maintenance contractor. Command of the aircraft was turned over to the contract mech.
output: A320 FLT CREW LANDS WITH PARKING BRAKE SET AND BLOWS ALL THE MAIN GEAR TIRES AT FLL.

input: This incident involved a c172 and a 2 step; collapsible ladder. A young man; on his first flight was with me. I'm explaining the preflt; to him; and he was asking many questions. I checkeded the fuel in the left/right (directions) wing; using the ladder to get to the fuel civil air patrol took the ladder around to the left/right (directions) wing and had him checked the fuel in that tank; instructing him to make sure the fuel civil air patrol was secure. I continued the preflt; not personally assuring that the ladder had been removed. He must have moved it forward of the left/right (directions) wing and to the left/right (directions) i did not see it. We strapped in; completed the chklist; started the engine received taxi clearance pulled out and to the left/right (directions) when contact was mae. My initial thought was that the left/right (directions) main gear had contacted something. I stopped; shut down the engine got out and discovered the ladder pieces; on the ramp. I removed them; inspected the left/right (directions) main gear and the propeller and determined the aircraft safe to fly. The federal aviation administration met us on our return; 1 hour later. Moral: make absolutely certain area is clear of everything; before starting the engine and taxiing.
output: INSTRUCTOR; WITH FIRST TIME STUDENT; TAXIES INTO LADDER USED TO CHK FUEL.

input: It was the final leg of the duty day and our flight had been delayed due to a late inbound aircraft. I felt slightly more fatigued than normal prior to the start of the flight. Before the inbound aircraft had arrived at the gate i had complained to the crew of some minor cold symptoms; but i thought i was still fit to fly. We decided to proceed with the flight as normal and we accepted the flight release. After push back there was a lengthy delay in taxi time and it took a great deal of time to reach the runway departure point. Upon reaching the departure point i resolved that i was still feeling good and we proceeded to depart. Everything was normal up until about an hour or so into the flight at cruising altitude. We were cruising at 38;000 feet and getting close to about an hour and 20 minutes left on the flight time. I began to feel cold and grabbed my jacket to cover up and keep warm. As time progressed into the flight i started to break out into a cold sweat along with a warm body temperature. It was at this time i feared that my cold symptoms were worsening and my body temperature was beginning to elevate. To make matters worse i started to feel an elevated heart rate and shallow breathing. At this point i decided to inform the captain that i might be feeling symptoms of hypoxia. The captain immediately checked pressurization of the aircraft and we both crosschecked that the pressurization was normal in the cabin and there was no need to don the oxygen mask. However; as a precautionary measure we decided that i should wear the o2 mask and try breathing normally to see if the symptoms would improve. I tried to take normal breaths from the o2 mask; but my symptoms only worsened gradually. We also asked for a descent to a lower altitude to get to a lower cabin pressure to see if my breathing would improve. This also did not help me. The captain inquired at this point that i might be getting sick. I agreed with the captain and said to him that if the symptoms worsened i might like to deviate from the planned course for a landing at the nearest airport. We decided to continue on course for what seemed like another 20 minutes until i decided that my symptoms were not getting any better and i was becoming increasingly ill. At this point i became concerned about my ability to safely perform my duties as pilot monitoring and as a side of caution for my fellow crew and passengers i asked that the captain would [advise atc] and divert to the nearest suitable airport. We utilized cockpit resource management and the captain made a precautionary declaration to air traffic control that we needed to divert. We were cleared and began our course change. The captain contacted the company via acars and informed them of my condition. He also got in touch with stat md for the required medical information on my physical state and other information. I did my best to perform my job functions and provide the captain with the landing weather automatic terminal information service and runway numbers; but my symptoms were getting bad with what seemed like an increasing body temperature and possible fever. I informed the captain of my state of being and from there we requested emergency medical equipment on the ground. There was light snow in zzz but the weather conditions were good for a normal clear air turbulence i instrument landing system and we were able to get down quickly. We arrived at the planned gate with the emergency equipment standing by. The captain opened his cockpit window and we were greeted by medical staff. They inquired my condition and concluded that i might be dehydrated and that they would perform further tests to see about my condition. At this point the flight was safely terminated and i was escorted into the terminal for a blood and temperature check. It was concluded by medical staff that i was running a high fever of 103 degrees with some dehydration along with it. After further medical care it was determined that i had a cold virus that caused me to have the fever. The fever is what gave me the symptoms of shallow breathing and rapid heart rate. In the interest of safety we did not take these symptoms lightly; and i believe we made the best decision to terminate the flight early. Cold and fatigue symptoms should not be taken lightly. If these symptoms occur in the future i will call off the trip or ask for a fatigue call. Better communication with the crew and company on my condition prior to departure is also important.
output: A regional jet pilot reported experiencing multiple physical symptoms resulting in an inability to continue the flight. A diversion to a suitable airport to seek medical help was accomplished.

input: General weather conditions were marginal visual flight rules all metars in the area were reporting marginal visual flight rules conditions. Pvj is my home base and upon return to base i encountered ceilings below 800 feet/foot automatic weather observing/reporting system at pvj has reported ceilings as missing for in excess of 2 months i have reported this on several occasions with no corrective actions.
output: A pilot reported PVJ AWOS was not reporting ceilings for more than two months but is now NOTAM'ed as unreliable.

input: I was working the night of dec/thu/02. The next morning (dec/fri/02) between xa-bx00; while auditing the minimum equipment list update list for the -300 type aircraft i found that minimum equipment list 25-11 had exceeded the mel's 2 day 'drop dead' time limit. Aircraft was not in a maintenance base and the minimum equipment list was still open. I realized that a major error had been made. This aircraft had been grounded in zzz all day dec/thu/02 from xe00 until xa25 on dec/fri/02 due to bad weather in zzz. I thought this aircraft would remain in zzz and the minimum equipment list worked because a maintenance routing/work request was issued to planning and dispatch on dec/wed/02 to work and clear this time limited minimum equipment list zzz maintenance was never assigned to work this aircraft without maintenance ctl's knowledge or approval; planning reassigned the minimum equipment list to maintenance the next day and dispatch routed then flew to zzz1. I informed my team lead of the situation and we both decided; in light of the error already made; to submit an minimum equipment list extension. My team lead then notified the director of maintenance as required; for the approval of an minimum equipment list extension. The minimum equipment list extension was approved and submitted. I fully understand there is no extension of an 'a' category minimum equipment list due to required weather related maintenance affecting a multitude of aircraft in the ne; this extension error was not realized at the time by me; my team lead; or the direct of maintenance there are designed chkpoints that should have caught this mistake. These chkpoints seemed to have erred in this particularly unusual sit.
output: A B737-200 WAS DISPATCHED IN NON COMPLIANCE WITH AN OBSERVER'S SEAT DEFERRED 2 DAYS OVER THE MEL LIMITS.

input: Traffic at sector 34 was very busy and it required complete attention to keep up. There was a considerable amount of sector to sector coordination to accomplish. There were multiple atcscc (air traffic control system command center) initiatives out which gave us a higher than usual and unsafe traffic volume. This higher than usual and unsafe traffic volume combined with the agency's de facto policy of not leaving sectors combined when there is not an inherent need to have them split caused this error. De-combining sectors unnecessarily does not provide the experience required to maintain proficiency in all types and volumes of traffic. The radar controller was overwhelmed and had anxiety about meeting a crossing restriction per the ztl letter of agreement this led to him taking unnecessary risks which ultimately led to a loss event.1. Stop de-combining sectors and allow controllers to maintain and train on all types and volumes of traffic.2. Dissolve traffic management units and the atcscc because they are wildly ineffective at maintaining safe volumes or managing traffic flow in an efficient and orderly manner. Flow initiatives should not cause errors; they should help prevent them.3. In the event traffic management is continued to allow to exist; do not put out routes that will increase volume without an afp (airspace flow program) in place.4. Instead of traffic management controllers talking about non air traffic control related business; laughing; taking care of personal business and carrying on (i have heard all of these happening on recorded lines and witnessed them in the flow management area); they should be proactively managing the rate at which airplanes enter each sector and the order in which they do so to reduce congestion and organize traffic flow.5. If the next center has miles in trail restrictions; the last sector in the center should not be required to achieve this in trail restriction from three different streams and blend them into one. All affected miles in trail aircraft should enter the center at the same fix.
output: ZJX Controller reports vaguely of a loss of separation; but his major complaint is about the lack of work and planning that he thinks the TMU (Traffic Management Unit) does.

input: The chart-arpt diagram for tulsa commercial chart is outdated. Evidently; taxiway celsius south of runway(s) 26; isn't pictured on this chart. input: While climbing out at approximately 7;500 feet the left/right (directions) air conditioning / alternating current bus caution light illuminated followed by the left/right (directions) tru; left/right (directions) elev horn heat; left/right (directions) stall warn. First priority was to exit icing conditions. After that the emergency abnormal checklist was attended to. Trying to isolate the emergency; we tried the left/right (directions) tru circuit breaker to reset; nothing. Realizing then it was an actual bus fault the proper checklist was administered. After completion of that; the first officer and i formulated a plan. 1. Contact company talked to our dispatcher. [we] told him of the emergency; and our intentions. 2. Talk to maintenance control. 3. Air traffic control. There was no hurry to contact air traffic control as we were out of icing and the decision to continue was made. Told air traffic control we were declaring an emergency; [number of] souls on board continuing; no equipment needed. Flew without further incident.
output: DHC8-100 Captain reports loss of right AC Bus climbing through 7;500 feet. After exiting icing conditions and complying with checklist procedures; the crew elects to continue the short flight to destination.

input: Climbing out of 8000 ft had a bird strike to the right engine. N1 on the right engine had a momentary drop of 10%. Then came back to normal. Very strong dead bird smell in cabin. We [returned] and landed (overweight landing). Taxied off the runway and fire trucks pulled up and said there was no damage. We asked to taxi back to a gate. Aircraft would not move; brakes were locked. Vans were sent out and passengers deplaned via air stairs.
output: B737 flight crew reported a bird strike on climbout that resulted in momentary power reduction.  After an overweight landing; the crew encountered locked brakes.

input: We reported fuel truck numbers xx53; x41; x38; and x04 to [supervisor] at [company] with the concern of leaking fuel and oil on the ramp. [three months later] we reported truck numbers x37; x43; x18; x14 and x04 with the same issues. [two days later] we reported truck numbers xx26; xx98; xx53; xx69 and x18 also with the same issues. [three weeks later] these trucks are being reported as well: xx69; x18; x43; and x41. This is an ongoing slip and fall hazard as well as an environmental protection agency issue.
output: Air carrier ramp personnel reported numerous fuel trucks leaking fuel and oil on the ramp creating an environmental hazard as well as a safety issue.

input: On aug/sun/03 in oma ne; we were given taxi to runway(s) 14r by ground control my first officer read back 'taxi to runway(s) 14r.' while taxiing out i thought we were given runway(s) 14l; after seeing taxi signs for runway(s) 14l. As we were approaching runway(s) 14r on taxiway foxtrot my first officer was looking down programming the flight management system system when ground control said; 'acft x stop! Stop!' i stopped the aircraft abruptly on taxiway foxtrot about 10 to 15 feet/foot short of the hold short line for runway(s) 14r. I looked around to see why the urgency for the stop. As i looked to the left/right (directions) i saw an aircraft already on the go around their gear was up and were already beginning their climb. As the aircraft passed by we determined the aircraft was a b737. After the aircraft was clear we were given instructions to cross runway(s) 14r. I quarried the ground controller to confirm that we were given runway(s) 14l. She said 'negative runway(s) 14r.' i then apologized for my misunderstanding. The ground controller then gave us taxi instructions back around to runway(s) 14r for departure prior to takeoff the tower gave me a phone to contact the tower supervisor when we got back to memphis. After landing in memphis i gave the tower supervisor a call; he then informed me the tower had to file a pilot deviation rpt to the federal aviation administration in short i admit my mistake for taxiing to the wrong runway(s) but at no time did ground control give us taxi instructions the first time to runway(s) 14r. Nor did i cross the hold short line for runway(s) 14r; and my first officer recalls not crossing it as well; when i stopped the aircraft i feel the go around of the b737 was conducted prematurely due to the communication between the tower and ground controllers although in the interest of safety it was probably justifiable.
output: CARJ TAXIING FOR DEP AT OMA IS CONFUSED WITH RWY ASSIGNMENT; STOPS ABRUPTLY AND CAUSED GAR.

input: Pittsburgh international has been on your signage list before. input: We were inbound to pwm. It was night; weather was clear and i briefed a visual approach to runway(s) 29. Pwm has a charted visual; the 'harbor visual 29;' second officer i asked the capt whether we should expect that procedure or a normal visual flight rules pattern. The capt had extensive past experience operating into and out of pwm (albeit some yrs earlier); yet he was certain that air traffic control would want us to execute the published procedure for noise abatement. All our charts (both company and federal aviation administration info) indicated the airport area is extremely noise sensitive; second officer the capt's reasoning seemed perfectly valid. (i; too; had prior experience at pwm; but not in jets; second officer i was not as familiar with noise abatement procedures as the capt.) approach control vectored us for the downwind; then cleared us for the visual and told us to contact tower twr cleared us to land. As we turned base; i began to maneuver to follow the waterways surrounding downtown portland; which makes a considerably wider pattern than a normal visual flight rules rectangular pattern. At this point; tower came up on frequency and politely said 'no big deal; but the harbor visual is not authority/authorized at night. Just continue; you're still cleared to land.' we landed uneventfully and there was no conflict with other traffic 2 things could have prevented this occurrence. First; intermediate fix there was any doubt; and there was; we should have asked the controller exactly what we were expected to do. Since a visual approach is somewhat discretionary; it was easy for us to think it was ok to follow the published procedure track; even though that specific approach was not mentioned by name. Nonetheless; we still should have asked. Second; nowhere in our company information nor the approach plate itself; is it written that the procedure is not authority/authorized at night. Having that information would certainly have cleared up some of the confusion. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr indicated that the capt was very familiar with the airport and briefed on the use of the harbor visual to runway(s) 29. They flew the approach only to be informed on the dog leg to final that what they were doing was not proper. The harbor visual was not to be used at nighttime. There were no indications on any commercial or federal aviation administration charts to indicate a time restrict, restricted, restriction the flight made contact with the controller after landing to inquire about the validity of the harbor visual. They were informed that when it is used at nighttime; too many flcs line up on the wrong runway(s) with all the lights at nighttime; there is a disorientation that seems to cause this. The controller did clear them for a visual; but did not specify a harbor visual. The flight crew feels they should have made an inquiry regarding the lack of a specific assigned visual.
output: A B727 MAKES AND IS CLRED FOR A VISUAL APCH TO PWM. THE FLC PERFORMS THE HARBOR VISUAL TO RWY 29 APCH. AFTER COMPLETING THE APCH THEY ARE INFORMED THAT THEY ARE NOT TO PERFORM THIS VISUAL AT NIGHTTIME.

input: We were cleared for takeoff on an instrument flight rules flight plan. When we began the takeoff roll i noticed that the battery was showing a discharge. We elected to abort the takeoff and check it out. It looks like we inadvertently had turned off generator 1 at some point. We reset it and ran the checklist. The battery was then charging properly and we elected to takeoff which was done without further issues.
output: PC12 Captain reported noting during the takeoff roll that the battery was discharging and elected to reject. Generator 1 was found to be turned off.

input: Took off from salt lake municipal #2 to the south and requested to transit salt lake class b to the north to logan. Was told to squawk discrete code and turn east to pick up highway; then head north along highway. Handed off to second controller ctlr advised to maintain at or below 8500. After passing abeam salt lake international we turned toward nw to pass westbound of hill air force base controller asked for heading then said he had told us to stay east of hill air force base we turned to pass east of hill air force base then exited the class b airspace. Two things contributed to this event. The first was that i was checking out a pilot in his newly acquired mooney and the radio intercom had a tremendous amount of static. I simply did not hear the instruction to stay east of hill air force base the second item was that after the controller advised us to resume normal navigation we turned nw to follow the shoreline westbound of hill air force base since the personnel at the municipal airport indicated that this was a good way to remain clear of the airspace at hill air force base in retrospect; it was not a good idea to take the student into such busy airspace when the radio intercom combination was not working correctly and was full of static. A contributing factor was that we had briefed our flight route on the ground before takeoff and were expecting to fly westbound of hill afb.
output: MOONEY ACFT TRANSITING CLASS 'B' AIRSPACE WAS INSTRUCTED BY ATC TO REMAIN E OF HILL AFB. RPTR ISTR DIDN'T HEAR THOSE INSTRUCTIONS; OSTENSIBLY DUE TO RADIO STATIC; AND ERRONEOUSLY ENTERED CLASS 'D' AIRSPACE.

input: After coast out at gander vor and dme (co-located) on a north atlantic track; inertial navigation system #1; #2; and #3 began to drift about 15 nautical mile off course. A course correction by gander radar back to course was made. All 3 units continued to show an error of about 15 nautical mile decided to return to ewr due to questionable navigate, navigation performance on inertial navigation system air carrier x ewr to rom. No federal aviation regulation violation occurred. Track airspace was not violated. Center also advised x to return to domestic airspace. Flight landed at ewr without further incident. Ins's #2 and #3 were found to be drifting excessively. Ins's were rebooted by maintenance and checkeded ok. What caused the sudden drift is unknown.
output: INS ERRORS INCREASE TO THE POINT FLC RETURNS ACFT TO DEP STATION RATHER THAN FLY OVER THE ATLANTIC WITH THOSE ERRORS.

input: While descending in reduced power spiral from 11000 feet/foot mean sea level to approximately 5000 feet/foot mean sea level unknown circumstances developed which prevented both engs on my cessna 337 skymaster from developing power restart attempted for both engs; without success. Had ample fuel on board; no prior indication of problems made pwr-off approach toward capital city airport but when i saw i could not reach the airport i decided to leave the gear up and make a water landing lndg was successful; no injury to myself or damage to plane (other than effect of being in water). I had been on my way to canada to have the annual inspection performed. Aircraft is registered in canada. Possible cause of dual engine failure could have been vapor lock or flooding of engs.
output: OFF ARPT EMER LNDG IN SMT TWIN.

input: At rotation; fuel lamp on mode annunciator panel lit and first officer rotated aircraft acft banked left/right (directions) and first officer corrected with control input similar to power loss and engine failure. Checkeded engine gauges and all appeared normal. Climbed out and did after takeoff chklist. I asked for control of aircraft to see intermediate fix we had a control problem i thought we might have a stuck or broken trim tab; control disconnect or similar. First officer checkeded cockpit and discovered a fuel imbal of 1700 pounds left/right (directions) wing heavy aircraft response improved with airspd. Returned for landing at cle. Maintenance opened refueling panel and found left/right (directions) defueling valve open. This allowed transfer of fuel from left/right (directions) wing to left/right (directions) wing tank. Aircraft was fueled; passenber boarded; receiving checked weight and balance and before start checked were all completed within 5 minute(s) of departure from gate. Fuel was checkeded 3 times in this 5 minute(s) period and all looked normal with a 2000/2000 pounds split between tanks. Transfer occurred during the 15 minute(s) taxi from gate to being #1 for takeoff on the before takeoff checked there is no checked fuel item. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr is flying the brasilia.

input: At end of landing rollout just prior to taxiing; aircraft struck a ridge on the grass runway(s) and nosed over striking propeller and damaging cowl and part of the rudder post. Problem caused by bump on the runway(s) and insufficient airflow over the elevator to keep the tailwheel down. Better preflt knowledge of runway(s) condition may have prevented the occurrence.

input: While en route from tol to cvg; crew received a 'r engine fire' warning. output: LTT SHUT DOWN ENG DUE TO FIRE WARNING AND DIVERTED TO LAND.

input: Background information: fai airport traffic control tower is a combined tower/tracon. Approximately 1 week ago; staffing related issues caused the facility to begin operating as a visual flight rules tower; with only 1 controller staffing the mid-shift. This drastic change was swift and nobody involved seemed to have been prepared. Additionally; it can be demonstrated that the staffing existed and continues to exist (through the judicious use of overtime and shift changes) for fai to operate the terminal radar approach control facility on a 24 hour a day basis. An letter of agreement between fai and zan was hastily drafted and revised multiple times during the subsequent week. As a result; the procedures are completely new and controllers at both facilities are largely figuring it out along the way. Due to zan's inability to vector aircraft to final at fai; instrument flight rules aircraft must execute the full procedure when utilizing instrument approaches. The potential for delays as a result of the utilization of a full procedure instrument approach and zan's increased separation requirements above a terminal radar approach control facility are undeniable. Unfortunately; the potential for the compromise of the system's safety also exists -- as demonstrated to me by the following description of observed events. Observed situation: working visual flight rules tower on mid-shift. Weather was 7;500 feet/foot broken; 7 statute mile visibility; light snow. Instrument landing system runway 1l approach in use. A scheduled air carrier was inbound to fai from the east-southeast. To my knowledge; the aircraft had been given instructions by zan to proceed to a fix and join the instrument landing system runway 1l approach. A private beechcraft king air was inbound; but further out; to the south of the field. To my knowledge; at this point; this aircraft would also be flying the instrument landing system runway 1l approach. When the air carrier was approximately 6 nautical mile south-southeast of fai; i noticed on the dbrite that the data tag went into 'coast.' i initially thought this was due to the aircraft beginning a turn to intercept the localizer outbound; however; on closer examination the aircraft seemed too far east of course to be initiating such a maneuver. The king air then checked on my frequency on a visual approach for runway 1l. I glanced back at the dbrite and the air carrier data now indicated the aircraft was visual flight rules however; i had not received any official notification from zan. A moment later the air carrier checked on frequency on a base leg for landing runway 1l; but without mention of a visual approach. On rollout; i queried the air carrier if they had canceled instrument flight rules with zan and they indicated that yes; they had canceled instrument flight rules at this point the king air's pilot thanked the air carrier. This transmission confirmed my suspicion that the air carrier had canceled instrument flight rules in order to minimize the delay to the king air; which would have been forced into a hold by zan had the air carrier continued with a full procedure instrument landing system runway 1l approach. To summarize; in my opinion; our new procedures of operating as a vfr-only tower during mid-shifts is potentially resulting in aircraft taking reduced levels of air traffic services in order to reduce delays to either themselves or other aircraft. In the years i have been at this facility; i had not seen an air carrier cancel instrument flight rules either inbound or outbound from fai until this series of events. I do not believe it is safe to train pilots that it is better to reduce your level of air traffic services simply to avoid a delay.
output: FAI controller voiced concern regarding new facility policy classifying Tower as VFR only during late night operations; reporter alleges policy could result in unsafe practices.

input: Pf was capt. Hand flying on hgs. Momentarily distracted away from hgs on navigate, navigation display. Pilot not flying was line checked pilot in first officer seat. Pilot not flying was reviewing standard instrument departure procedure momentary altitude deviation of 500 feet/foot above assigned altitude of 13000 feet/foot corrective action taken when altitude alert chime of 13250 ft.
output: B737-800 CAPT ON AN IOE CHK FLT BECAME DISTRACTED WHILE HAND-FLYING ACFT AND CLBED ABOVE ASSIGNED ALT. ACFT ALT ALERT CHIME BROUGHT THE ERROR TO THE ATTN OF BOTH CREW MEMBERS.

input: At fl290; approximately 10 nautical mile sw of ekn; clearance was received to cross 30 nautical mile sw of mgw at fl240. Pilot not flying acknowledged clearance and pilot flying entered restriction in flight management computer (flt was operating in vertical navigation and lateral navigation modes of autoplt.) after entry in flight management computer pilot flying noticed a 'bypass' annunciation in flight management computer routing in association with the entry of '30 sw of mgw' fix. This was due to improper entry of this fix between mgw and 'roton' intersection as opposed to where it really was; between ekn and 'tygar' intersection pilot flying was attempting to resolve this problem when it became apparent that initiation of descent was necessary to meet restriction. Pilot flying attempted to use vertical speed to initiate descent but aircraft remained at fl290. It was then noticed that altitude 'set' window was still at fl290; disallowing autoplt to descend altitude was reset to fl240; descent was initiated concurrent with inquiry from center as to ability to meet restriction. We responded 'unable' and flight was given a 50 degree left/right (directions) turn; presumably to avoid a potential conflict. At fl250; flight was cleared direct mgw to resume routing. This situation occurred because of pf's failure to follow his own standard operating procedure in such a circumstance which is to 1) reset altitude 2) make a quick determination intermediate fix aircraft is near the required descent point and initiate a descent using vertical speed or level change intermediate fix necessary; 3) make appropriate entries in flight management computer and use vertical navigation for descent intermediate fix appropriate. Pilot flying did these out of sequence and became distracted by an flight management computer irregularity; thus overshooting descent point.
output: AN MLG ACR MISSED A XING ALT.

input: Prior to departure; maintenance control transmitted a maintenance report stating that the batteries were out-of-date and no revenue flight could be flown until the batteries were replaced. Further discussions with maintenance control revealed that the batteries have been out of time for several days. The captain and first officer had just flown a flight in this aircraft. It appears that although the maintenance release stated that the plane was in an airworthy condition; the release was in error. No further information available at this time. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following information: reporter stated their maintenance control monitors when their aircraft main batteries require replacement. During a recent aircraft overnight at another line station; maintenance was supposed to have replaced both main batteries. Instead; maintenance just checked for proper volts and amps on each battery and signed off the paperwork. Reporter stated he was in the cockpit with the same first officer; preparing for another departure; when maintenance control sent a message saying the aircraft could not be released for revenue service.
output: A Captain reports he and his First Officer had just flown an A320 with aircraft batteries that had been out of date for several days. Their Maintenance Release was in error.

input: Selected flaps 2 degrees indication slats only with electronic centralized aircraft monitoring warning; performed electronic centralized aircraft monitoring actions and quick reference handbook procedures after executing missed approach proceeded to holding pattern and advised air traffic control to declare emergency when apparent a no-flap landing would result. Advised passenber air traffic control and company and made uneventful lndg.
output: AN A320 FLT CREW DECLARED AN EMER AND PERFORMED A ZERO FLAP LNDG WHEN THEIR FLAPS FAILED TO EXTEND.

input: At xa18 local and xa48 local while working east and westbound control combined at the t-35 position all full data blocks went into coast at one time for a period of 5 seconds both times.
output: DATA BLOCKS WENT INTO COAST STATUS TWICE WHILE CTLR WAS WORKING POS COMBINED.

input: At approximately xa30z in 9/88; another pilot whom i'll call d.l.; called zla and asked about restrict, restricted, restriction areas r4806w and r4808s; and told them that his aircraft and another aircraft were heading westbound through beatty vor and dme (co-located) zla told d.l. That the restrict, restricted, restriction areas were not active at this time and that we could fly directly from st george; ut; where we were starting from to the beatty vor and dme (co-located) both of us left at approximately xa50z from st george and flew westbound at about xx30z i called zla and asked for following. They told me to contact nellis air force base which i did. Nellis personnel told me that i had flown through a restrict, restricted, restriction area. I gave them the above information they said that only part of the restrict, restricted, restriction area was inactive. I told them that zla had say that it was not active and that we could fly through it. Nellis said that one of the restrict, restricted, restriction areas was always active 24 hours a day. At that point i was confused. I will investigate and become thoroughly familiar with restrict, restricted, restriction areas and the procedures for flying through them. I quote from my commercial chart; 'most restrict, restricted, restriction areas are designated joint use; and ifr/vfr operations(s) in the area may be authority/authorized by the controling air traffic control facility when it is not being utilized by the using agency.' the charts show lax air route traffic control center as the air traffic control facility intermediate fix i did violate restrict, restricted, restriction airspace; it was unintentional and was caused by misinformed from the controling agency. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr had received an inquiry from nellis air force base and returned a complete explanation of the incident. No further information from nellis to date. Feels he would have been more comfortable had he received his own briefing versus second hand. Was on a fly in to st george and most of the other pilots deviated around the restrict, restricted, restriction area. Does not feel he is in error because the center advised the restrict, restricted, restriction area was not hot. Not aware intermediate fix the other pilot is being investigated.
output: POSSIBLE PENETRATION OF RESTRICTED AREA THAT WAS HOT.

input: Forgot to switch communications radio from approach frequency to atl tower frequency after passing outer marker inbound to runway(s) 9r. Crew was distracted by traffic alert and collision avoidance system info.
output: TCAS DISTR. LANDED ATL WITHOUT CONTACTING TWR FOR CLRNC.

input: Working the worst session i have ever worked here in zjx; weather was blocking the departure corridor from mco and tpa complexes. All arrivals and departures were opposite direction traffic descending and climbing respectively. All aircraft were crossing on the boundary with sectors 30;17;88;16; and zma 08. Immediately prior to first loss of separation 17 told 16 no more departures until darbs19 procedures go into effect. Darbd19 is not possible with active w470; acmi; and nova airspace hot up to fl240 and fl250. The r-side at 16 started turning every departure to 250 headings to miss sector 17. Then sector 30 said no more hand offs or point outs from us because they cannot see data blocks in that area. The r16 turned departures southbound to miss sector 30. During the southbound heading; an e135 was given a climb to fl270; both r16 and i did not notice the excel at fl270 immediately behind the e135. I may have been coordinating on another line; or maybe i missed it during the mayhem. The excel was supposed to be below fl250 per sops. I tried to coordinate the e135 descending back lower with d88 but they had already descended the excel. Then after that problem separated r16 climbed the e135 and a lr31 to the same altitude. At that point a tracker 16 was trying to get in place to help and conflict alert went off again. Both departures (the e135 and the lr31) made a full 360 degree turn before proceeding on course. Immediately following these situations the tracker 16 called 88 and 14 and shut departures off. There were too many unsafe situations during this period to remember all of them. The sector was out of control. Recommendation; northbound and southbound route/s in this area that are not on a bunch of boundaries. More help from tmu and military areas. W470 should not have been hot; we needed darbs19 procedures along with more organized routes and ground stops to mco and tpa complexes.
output: ZJX Controller described possible multiple loss of separation events when inbound and outbound traffic was routed in opposite direction/s due to significant weather impacts; noting both Traffic Management and the Military; i.e. 'release of airspace;' could have assisted in this scenario.

input: Designed runway(s) heading for departure on runway(s) 34. At approximately 900' above ground level forward cabin door ajar warning annunciator illuminated. We were still under tower control at this point i cleared the airspace to my left to prepare for a left downwind pattern to land on 34. Tower was busy talking to someone else; second officer i began my turn to enter downwind. Tower finished talking with the other aircraft and then asked me why i was not on runway(s) heading i explained the annunciator light problem and he cleared us to land on 34. We landed without incident. There were no other aircraft in the area at the time. There are many reasons for my immediate turn back towards the airport i do not have complete confidence in the door latching mechanism on this aircraft our company recently experienced an inflt door opening and subsequent airstair door sep on this type aircraft the airstair door in question in located directly in front of the left propeller the aircraft that experienced the opening and sep of this door miraculously made it to a runway(s) in one piece. Our company's most experienced ltt pilots (myself included) and our most trusted mechs all believe that the next time a door comes off this type ltt it could prove catastrophic. Looking back; i believe i did the proper thing when i immediately turned back toward the airport at that instant; i did not know intermediate fix it was an indication problem or intermediate fix the door was going to open. The problem turned out to be an indication problem which i contribute to poor preventative maintenance lack of the proper number of mechs to work on these aircraft during the few; short night time hours that are available.
output: COMMUTER LTT DEVIATED FROM CLRNC HEADING FOR IMMEDIATE RETURN LAND DUE DOOR WARNING ACTIVATED AFTER TKOF.

input: During my first solo flight the following happened: after being in the traffic pattern with my instructor we first did 2 touch-and-goes and we did a simulated engine failure on downwind. We then did a go around and then landed for a full stop. I then took off for my first solo flight i did my first pattern and did my first landing came in for my second landing which also was ok. Both lndgs were not really smooth but safe. When i came for my third landing i was not correctly aligned and not established on final; second officer i initiated a go around the next landing was supposed to be a full stop. I was stable on final; but started my flare too high (according to my instructor). I misjudged my ht at that moment; i bounced hard on the runway(s) i did not react correctly on the bounce; which was followed by a nosewheel landing i felt heavy nosewheel shimmy; and i stopped the plane on the runway(s) it turned out that the nosewheel was flat. Nosewheel was damaged; as well as the nose strut and engine mouth. The cause of the damage/prob was my fault; to flare too high above the ground and that i did not react correctly on the bounce by not initiating immediately a gar.
output: SPI FLARES TOO HIGH ON LNDG. ACFT DAMAGED.

input: Clred direct cedar creek vor and dme (co-located) (114.8). Had bonham vor and dme (co-located) (114.6) tuned in error. Our vor and dme (co-located) tuner readouts are liquid crystal display unit displays which are fine when new; but with age; wear and tear; etc; become hard to read. After discovering our error (thanks to atc) it was still hard to tell the .6 from a .8 on the liquid crystal display. This problem is made worse by partial failure of the back-lighting (a common occurrence); damage to the display unit due to poor design and placement (placing a non sealed liquid crystal display unit on a horizontal pedestal where it is subject to use as a 'table' and frequent liquid spills). In this case; 2 arrival, arrive vors are placed almost in-line on the standard terminal arrival route and only about 20 mile apart -- also the displayed frequencies appear similar; especially with degraded displays.
output: DEV FROM RTE AND CLRNC WHEN PIC OF B737 TUNES IN WRONG VOR AND PROCEEDS DIRECT. FAILED TO IDENT FREQ AND BLAMES LIQUID CRYSTAL DISPLAY UNITS FOR POOR DESIGN AND IMPAIRED READOUTS.

input: Tower cleared us for takeoff while a b737 was approaching the crossing runway on a one mile final or less. The first officer pushed the power up partially and immediately returned to idle when we noticed the 737 approaching from aircraft right. Our jet rolled 50-100 feet/foot and controls were transferred back to the captain. We immediately notified tower we were not taking off. The 737 performed a go-around. We cleared the runway and taxied back for takeoff. Later we called the tower. Tower told us on the phone they don't know how the event happened. They were somewhat busy; but it was visual flight rules and the controller could clearly see both aircraft visually from the tower. The controller was either complacent or inattentive or both. The crew rejected the takeoff clearance avoiding the disaster and calmly taxied back for takeoff. Tower controllers need to pay more attention and quit being in such a rush that it compromises safety.
output: B717 flight crew rejected takeoff at a low speed when they note a B737 landing on an intersecting runway.

input: In 2/89 during a flight (vfr) to osceola; ia; in my own sma; i experienced an engine failure and landed in a field 1/2 mile south of unionville; ia. I departed k27 with full tanks of fuel and 50 minutes later; aircraft appeared to fail due to fuel starvation. After all attempts of starting failed; i landed in the most suitable field covered with snow. Unfortunately; a small draw in the middle covered with snow sheared off the nose gear. My son and his friend both 14 years old were paxs. There were no injuries. I notified the fort dodge flight service station specialist within the hour. I suspect some sort of fuel problem.
output: ENGINE FAILURE ON SMA IN CRUISE. ACFT SUFFERED MINOR DAMAGE ON FORCED LNDG. NO INJURIES.

input: The following narrative is based upon events described to me by my student who undertook the 300 mile solo cross country flight that forms the basis of this rpt. The student obtained both an initial detailed and follow-up weather briefing from; and filed a 3 leg flight plan with; bridgeport flight service station specialist the flight was to be from westerly to concord to danbury back to westerly. The student opened his flight plan; shortly after departure through the norwich vor and dme (co-located) when he attempted to close his first leg flight plan through the bangor flight service station specialist upon arriving at concord; he was advised that he had submitted a 'round robin' flight plan; although he indicates that what he had requested was a flight plan with three separate legs. While at concord. The aircraft was refueled. The student departed concord at ab30z. He contacted westover and windsor locks on his way to danbury. The weather which to this point had been as forecast; deteriorated due to reduced visibility (haze) and lowered ceiling. When the student attempted to contact danbury tower he was unable to obtain a response even though he was able to hear the tower talking to many other aircraft attempts to navigate, navigation by the carmel vor and dme (co-located) (and other area vors) were unsuccessful. The student was flying at 3000 to 3500 feet/foot (low clouds prevented him from climbing higher) to increase his chances of obtaining a usable vor and dme (co-located) signal. The student at this point became uncertain of his position when he sighted orange county airport he landed and replotted his course to danbury. Upon arriving in the danbury area; the student advised the tower he wanted to land and to refuel. The tower advised him that there would be a longitude wait for fuel because there was an air show in progress (apparently no notice to airmen / of air missions was issued for this air show). The student interpreted this to mean that he would have a longitude wait for a clearance to land. Because he was concerned about fuel and about completing the flight before sunset; the student decided not to wait and departed the area for bridgeport's sikorsky airport while in the pattern at sikorsky; the tower requested a 360 degree turn for spacing. While in the turn; the engine quit. The student advised the tower and was cleared for an immediate landing the engine restarted and failed twice while on final. The student declined an invitation to declare an emergency and landed without further incident. After refueling and a complete runup; he took off and returned to westerly without further incident. At about bc00z; danbury tower called westerly to ask intermediate fix the student had landed. Upon being told 'no' and that he was 'due;' the controller said that they had spoken to him about an hour before when the student had contacted the tower for landing instructions. The controller indicated that there had been a local air show with numerous aircraft in the pattern.
