I disconnected the autoplt; went to toga; and immediately started a climb and a shallow bank to the left/right (directions) since i could see the aircraft was slightly left/right (directions) of our course and i figured it would create a little bit more separation as he passed off our left/right (directions) side. At the same time that we started the evasive maneuver; we got an resolution advisory to climb and followed the commands as directed. We did not get a traffic advisory prior to getting the resolution advisory as we initiated the climb i saw the aircraft coming toward us and held my breath hoping he would miss us. When the traffic alert and collision avoidance system indicated clear of conflict; we returned to normal thrust and autoplt and continued the descent with a turn from air traffic control to intercept the localizer the controller asked intermediate fix we needed to take evasive action to which i replied; yes; considering we had just responded to an resolution advisory we continued the approach to a normal landing and taxied to the gate.
output: A320 ON ARLIN ARRIVAL TO PHX HAS NMAC WITH VFR ACFT. TRAINING IN PROGRESS FOR APCH CTLR MAY HAVE BEEN A FACTOR.

input: After completing a visual flight rules flight from huntingburg; indiana (hng) to wilkes barre; pennsylvania (avp); the ground controller asked me to call the indianapolis center. Center informed me that their computer track showed that i had flown through the corner of restrict, restricted, restriction area r-3403b. I should have entered the area 7 1/2 mile south of the nw corner and exit the area 4 mile westbound of the ne corner. The computer track also showed that i made a turn directly to wilkes-barre after exiting the restrict, restricted, restriction area. During this portion of the flight i was monitoring louisville approach on 124.5; indianapolis approach on 127.15 and indianapolis center on 128.55. I was fully aware that the restrict, restricted, restriction area was active. A flew in a direct line from 3 mile east of huntingburg to north vernon using long range navigation and xchk with north vernon nondirectional radio beacon after sighting north vernon airport visually; i crossed 1 mile east of the airport on the same heading as direct huntingburg and held that heading for 5 minute(s) then i reset the long range navigation to direct wilkes-barre and flew the new heading i also xchked the corner of the restrict, restricted, restriction area using area navigation nabb vor and dme (co-located) 14 deg/31.6 knot(s) an apparent conflict exists between the track i flew and the computer radar track. Intermediate fix i would have been receiving inflt following or advisories from center; then this would have been avoided. All of this makes me question the accuracy of my navigational equipment and the center's computer tracks.
output: ALLEGED ENTRY INTO RESTRICTED AREA DETERMINED BY COMPUTER TRACK.

input: Preferred arrival, arrive route printed on all alb arrs should only print on nonstandard routings. This nearly caused an operational error on mar/xx/93. On mar/xx/93 the radar controller at the danbury sector b20 made a save; turning 2 airplanes apart which had veered together at the same altitude these aircraft a bos arrival, arrive and an alb arrival, arrive had been delivered at fl240 as per letter of agreement on parallel rtes. Unfortunately; the alb arrival, arrive had a slight difference in his route than what was automatically coordinated by the preferred arrival, arrive route automation. This difference was not noticed by the 2 veteran controllers working at r56. Why didn't the controllers working r56 pick this up? Because every alb arrival, arrive has the preferred arrival, arrive route printed on the route in red; whether or not the aircraft is on the preferred route or not. Zny-510 was asked to consult with us on this matter; and looked up a pdn from oct/92 which illustrated this same problem this pdn listed the complaint about the redundant preferred arrival, arrive rtes as not necessary and distracting. Obviously; this situation has proved to be more than a distraction -- this condition is a safety hazard and has the potential to cause operrors. Zny-510 looked up this pdn in his file of active automation projects; and indicates that the technical center had acknowledged this as a problem which had been rpted by several facilities. However; this problem has not been dealt with and is on hold for some reason. The technical center project to correct the processing of these preferred arrival, arrive rtes needs to be moved out of hold status and expedited before a problem is caused that isn't saved. These preferred arrival, arrive rtes have the potential to do a great service to the operations(s) by assuring that descending aircraft are on preferential routings as soon as possible in their current form; however; they are a distraction with the potential to cause operrors; and intermediate fix corrections are not forthcoming; then consideration should be given to disabling all the preferred arrival, arrive rtes used in zny.
output: CTLR CLAIMS THAT THE PREFERRED ARR RTE (PAR) IS PRINTED ON ALL FLT STRIPS WHETHER THERE IS A CHANGE IN FILED ROUTING OR NOT.

input: Final approach runway(s) 23 at bct; wind was 190 degrees at 10 knot(s) was on stabilized approach with the correct crosswind corrections input. Once the mains came down; i lowered the nose gear and began to apply brake pressure to slow down and exit the runway(s) while keeping the crosswind correction in. Suddenly the left/right (directions) wing of the aircraft lifted up; causing the aircraft to veer off to the left/right (directions) when this happened; the aircraft went completely off the runway(s) for a short time then i was able to bring the aircraft back onto the runway(s) i firmly believe that it was windshear that caused the aircraft to be blown off the runway(s) in the opposite direction of the xwind.
output: C172 PVT PLT LOST CTL OF THE ACFT DURING LNDG RESULTING IN THE ACFT GOING OFF THE SIDE OF THE RWY. RPTR REGAINED CTL AND BROUGHT ACFT BACK TO THE RWY.

input: Flt to lga airport cleared to descend via the korry arrival, arrive was unable to cross brand intersection at 11000 feet/foot crossed brand at 11600 feet/foot by the time i noticed it; i could not inform air traffic control in time. Looking at the arrival, arrive i noticed you have 6 mile to descend 2000 feet/foot at the time; we had a 110 knot(s) tailwind. Plus; during the descent air traffic control told us to cross the next fix; korry at 10000 feet/foot at 250 knot(s) in a transport category aircraft it is extremely difficult to meet those altitude restrs with no tailwind and speed restrict, restricted, restriction safely. The flight management computer was unable to calculate the vertical navigation path in time for it to be of any use. This is a bad arrival, arrive procedure in reference to the 2 crossing altitudes at brand and korry. You do not have the distance to safely and smoothly meet those restrs. I have flown that arrival, arrive many times since this event and have yet to meet or see the other pilots meet those restrs. I now tell air traffic control in advance that i might be high over those fixes every time i ante meridiem above those alts.
output: B737 FLC CONCERNED WITH COMPLIANCE WITH RESTRS OF KORRY STAR INTO LGA.

input: Flying en route from plattsburg air force base to albany co airport we received the current alb automatic terminal information service albany's weather was visual flight rules with light winds; landing runway(s) 28 and taking off on runway(s) 01. On initial contact with alb approach we requested runway(s) 01; we were approximately 50 mile north after a while alb approach indicated we would be unable to land on runway(s) 01. After handoff to the next alb approach controller we again requested runway(s) 01; the controller immediately snapped; 'unable runway(s) 01.' when asked intermediate fix the pattern was saturated the controller snapped intermediate fix we wanted to talk about it to call him on the ground we were cleared for a visual approach to runway(s) 28 and switched to tower on initial contact with tower we requested runway(s) 01. Our position was approximately 15 mile from the airport on a right base. Tower advised us to continue and standby on the request. We configured and lined up for runway(s) 28. Two mile out the tower cleared us to cross the airport and enter a left downwind for runway(s) 01. Landing and taxi in were uneventful. The only other aircraft around was an sma and not a factor. Ground control asked us to call the tower on the tower telephone. When the aircraft commander called; a supervisor answered and wanted to discuss the incident. He was informed that runway(s) 01 had been requested for the following safety concerns: 1) we both were unfamiliar with alb; 2) runway(s) 01 has precision vertical guidance while runway(s) 28 does not (vasi 3.35 degs); and 3) runway(s) 01 is 7200' longitude while runway(s) 28 has only 5999'. The supervisor then wanted to contact someone at our home base to 'take care of this prob!' he doesn't want people asking for the takeoff runway(s) for lndg! He was given the aircraft commander's name and our command post's telephone number. I find this method of control to be 'heavy handed' and counter-productive. Our safety concerns are valid. It would be hard to explain why we accepted the short (barely legal for us) runway(s) that does not have precision g/s at an unfamiliar airport when a more acceptable runway(s) is available; to an accident investigation board (wind was not a factor). Domineering; intimidating control such as this may well be a contributing factor in a future alb incident/mishap. We complied with all far's and instructions; and have found this to be an isolated event and not a nationwide trend. Supplemental information from acn 87921: no procedures were violated in this incident; but i'm rpting it because approachs altitude was extremely uncooperative and their motives were unclear.
output: MIL AIR EVAC ACFT ASKED FOR RWY OTHER THAN ASSIGNED AND WAS REFUSED TWICE BY APCH CTLRS; THEN WHEN REQUEST MADE TO TWR; REQUESTED RWY WAS GIVEN. REPORTER STATED POOR ATTITUDE BY APCH CTLRS.

input: Tonight captain; first officer and myself were operating a flight to libreville; gabon. Captain was the flying pilot and i was the non-flying pilot. Over disak waypoint we received a frequency change and direct to valku. I checked in with the controller and got a response to our position. Approximately 15 minutes had gone by and we received a call on 121.5 from control. We were then given a new frequency were they said that they had tried to reach us several times without a reply. None of us had heard a call being broadcasted to us. Control then gave us a new frequency so we switched over and checked in. Approximately 5 minutes later control told us that we are being intercepted by the military to verify our aircraft because they lost contact with us for approximately 15 minutes. The military knew before the point of intercept that we were in radio contact again but still wanted to check and verify our aircraft. They intercepted us at fl310 on un855. Military aircraft came up on our right wing for approximately 2 minutes and then left.
output: Air carrier flight crew reported being contacted on 121.5 and told to switch to a new frequency by ATC. On the new frequency they were informed that they have been out of contact for 15 minutes and were being intercepted by the military to verify their identity.

input: Engine stopped in midair and i landed on [a highway] with no incident and called [the] airport for a mechanic and fuel. It was delivered and the tech checked out the motor and found no problem; did find that fuel gauges are incorrect. Added fuel; restarted motor; ran up and tested; found no problems. I took off on highway and went to the airport that was 9 miles away with no problems.
output: C182 pilot reported landing on a highway after the engine quit because of fuel starvation.

input: Flap failure en route to destination landed 0 degrees flaps with trucks standing by.
output: A CARJ CREW EXPERIENCED A FLAP FAILURE ENRTE; 80 NM S OF CVG.

input: While being vectored for the localizer runway(s) 23 approach at bhm; flight was cleared to 2500 feet/foot mean sea level 8-9 nautical mile from airport when we leveled off at 2500 feet/foot mean sea level a ground proximity warning system warning was received (both light and verbal) for 'terrain.' i immediately executed a climb to 4000 feet/foot mean sea level (the aircraft was instrument meteorological conditions and at night). Approach control was notified of the ground proximity warning system warning and the climb to 4000 feet/foot mean sea level immediately. The ground proximity warning system was tested after landing at bhm. No problems were found.
output: SCHEDULED CARGO FLT MAKES MISSED APCH IN A NIGHT OP; IMC; AFTER RECEIVING A GPWS WARNING.

input: Aircraft had engine wash [the] night before flight. During taxi and takeoff noticed foul stench from aircraft conditioned air. Went from bad during takeoff roll to worse on initial climb. Slowly dissipated but not without crew consideration of in flight return. Finally tolerable at about 6-10 thousand feet and didn't notice again until descent below 10 thousand feet. Odor was foul but not threatening.
output: B737 flight crew reported a 'foul stench' during taxi and takeoff which dissipated and returned on descent. Captain suggested the likely cause was a 'compressor wash' on the overnight layover.

input: This is a correction. Departed from zzz on the departure and was vectored for altitude climb for vxx [airway]. The departure was normal and the aircraft was stable in the climb. While passing 7;000ft mean sea level i notice a rise in the cht in cylinder 1;4;& 6. Temperatures where stable prior of takeoff and in the beginning climb at 356f. At 7;000 ft. Mean sea level temperature jumped to 386f than 2mins later to 400f with several quick spikes in the egt sensors for cylinder 6 and followed later by 1 & 4. Prior to reaching 11;000 ft. Mean sea level the temps with the cht began to climb faster to 420f. Reaching 11;000 ft. Mean sea level i began to; trying to make small adjustments to throttle and mixture to cool the 3 cylinders down. The adjustments were not making a difference and the engine began to sputter and quit. I panic for a millisecond realizing the problem was worsening and noted the mountains; west of the zzz1; i was about to travel over. With a quick decision i informed approach as i felt still in control of aircraft and still had somewhat of power available. I began a quick left turn to an airport on my left about; maybe; 30 miles and tried a steep descent to see if i could cool the engine down and get power back. Zzz2 was chosen with the help of approach and prior to the threshold of the runway power came back and engine was cooled down to 345f. Quickly did a landing checklist and through flaps in and landed safely on a 13;000 ft. Runway. Was met with arff and military police. Informed the operator/owner of the problem and concluded that the magnetos left/right (directions) side went bad possibly in the climb after taking a video after the landing to show him what i was seeing. Mechanics came out on date to find more problems on the engine that may of been a caused to the performance decrease with the help of the left/right (directions) side magnetos. Aircraft is currently grounded and is in the process of being repaired.
output: Pilot reported problems with the engine overheating and having to make an expedited landing.

input: Doing initial operating experience training on day 1 of 2. Repos ferry flight to iad. Arriving on the prtzl 1 arrival, arrive over psb which brings you in on the east side of iad. Automatic terminal information service rpting landing on runway(s) 1l and runway(s) 1r with calm winds and visual flight rules checkeded in with potomac approach and was told to expect visual to runway(s) 1r. We set up instrument landing system runway(s) 1r and briefed the approach to runway(s) 1r. Switched to next potomac approach and he cleared us to ticon for visual to runway(s) 1r. We did all our chklists and were on a left/right (directions) downwind approximately abeam the field when switched to final controller he descended us and turned us on a base leg. Final approach control called traffic and asked intermediate fix we had traffic and/or field in sight. We called the field and said we were looking for the traffic he cleared us for the visual and told us to contact tower we switched to tower and reported that we were on the visual to runway(s) 1r. Tower cleared us to land runway(s) 1l. We were at 2000 feet/foot descending and approximately 5 mile out. I informed tower that we were set up for runway(s) 1r and intermediate fix we couldn't get landing clearance for runway(s) 1r we would need to go around. This decision was made by the capt because i ante meridiem still going through my initial operating experience training and wouldn't feel comfortable making a side-step to runway(s) 1l on a short final. Tower said stand by; then came back and told us to fly runway(s) heading and maintain 2000 feet/foot which we did. Tower switched us back to approach the first controller we spoke to told us it would be vectors to runway(s) 1r. I asked that he confirm that; and he did. I repeated vectors to runway(s) 1r; and he agreed again. Vectored back to another left/right (directions) downwind; expecting runway(s) 1r. Switched to final approach controller and he told us it was vectors to runway(s) 1l. I told him we were expecting runway(s) 1r and he repeated runway(s) 1l. We configured for runway(s) 1l; re-briefed; and made a rushed but normal visual approach and landing to runway(s) 1l. The final controller was upset with us and said he had told us on our first approach that he was changing our runway(s) to runway(s) 1l. We never heard that transmission and definitely did not acknowledge a runway(s) change.
output: CRJ200 CREW WITH IOE FIRST OFFICER ON VISUAL TO IAD 1R IS SWITCHED TO 1L BY THE TOWER. THE INSTRUCTOR CAPTAIN REQUESTS TO REMAIN WITH 1R OR GO AROUND. THE TOWER CONTROLLER THEN ISSUES GO AROUND INSTRUCTIONS.

input: Normal landing in las. Ground temperature was 95f. Brake temps at the gate were at 425 on one side and not increasing. We had a 2 hour layover in las. Since the brake temperatures were not over 500c; brake fans were not procedurally needed since we had a 2 hour layover. The ground temp increased to 105f while we were away from the aircraft. Consequentially one of the brake temperatures increased and melted the thermal plug which deflated the tire. We did not notice the tire being flat until the people and cargo were loaded on the plane. I praise the ground crew for recognizing the situation; which prevented a more serious matter. Maintenance personnel at las told me to always turn on the brake fans when the ground temp is above 100f. That is not in our procedure. There is a conflict of opinion in the flight department and the maintenance procedures in the use of brake fans. When departing the ground temp was 102. The aircraft was on the ground for less than an hour. Brake temps on takeoff were around 200c. Upon landing in las normal reverse was used with little braking to make the turnoff. I feel that ground temperatures over 100f contributed to the higher than normal brake temps on hour 2 hour layover in las. I feel that a common procedure in the use of brake fans must be agreed upon with the flight and maintenance departments.
output: A320 Captain experiences a tire fuse plug failure at the gate after landing at LAS with OAT of 95; increasing to 105 before departure. The hottest brake was 425 C upon gate arrival; with a two hour lay over; and the brake fans were not turned on.

input: After flight sna to iah; arrived at gate x at iah. Federal aviation administration aci and his 'assistant' greeted the aircraft and informed capt that we were operating a 'non-airworthy' aircraft since this aircraft did not comply with ad 88-07.07. Aci said he was going to make an 'example of (our) airlines' and we were the 'sacrificial lamb.' this was due to the method the f/a's used to secure the new girt bar retaining straps. Prior to departure from san to arrival, arrive at iah; all slides were fully functional and properly armed. The discrepancy occurred after disarming slides at arrival, arrive callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr states; 'when we were accosted bythe overly officious aci; the capt called the chief pilot who came immediately to the aircraft and suggested to the aci that the flight crew be removed from the problem since maintenance had certified the aircraft to the flight crew and they had no part in the alleged violation. The aci grudgingly backed off and neither the capt nor i have heard anything about the incident.' the alleged violation concerns the velcro strap which is part of the latching mechanism for the emergency slides. The strap was apparently to be modified in 3/90 and had not been accomplished by maint.
output: ACR MET THE ACFT AND ADVISED FLT CREW THEY WERE IN VIOLATION OF AN A.D. ORDER THAT HAD NOT BEEN ACCOMPLISHED.

input: On jun/xx/94; i was plting a be-18 from phl to lorain county. After takeoff at am15z; while retracting the landing gear; there was not a positive landing gear-up indication. After troubleshooting with the appropriate chklist; i consulted my company's maintenance department via radio communications the maintenance manager instructed me to use the override switch to retract the gear; and also assured me that it would extend normally later. He then advised me to continue the trip as scheduled; and to call after landing at lorain county. I then used the override as instructed and was able to retract the landing gear; and successfully extended the gear prior to landing at lorain county. Because the landing gear worked satisfactorily; maintenance recommended that i fly back empty from lorain county to willow run with the gear down; second officer that they could troubleshoot later intermediate fix necessary. I did second officer and landed at willow run without further incident. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated that the uplock solenoid had failed causing the need to override the gear handle selector switch to retract the landing gear. The landing gear can be retracted and extended normally when using the override lever located next to the gear handle behind the instrument panel. The aircraft was a beech 18 and rptedly has several variations of the landing gear system he was directed to retract the gear on the empty outbound trip intermediate fix there was a need. It was suggested to leave the landing gear down intermediate fix possible second officer the system could be checkeded more accurately.
output: PLT OF AN ATX BE-18 USED THE LNDG GEAR OVERRIDE SWITCH TO RETRACT THE LNDG GEAR AFTER TKOF DUE TO THE LNDG GEAR NOT LOCKING IN THE UP POS.

input: The incorrect fastener hole was inspected due to the error the amt made while accomplishing the first step of the process (engineering order x); which is to remove and discard the specified fasteners. This step does not require a buy-back to ensure the correct fasteners are removed and discarded. The accomplishment of the subsequent steps relies on the first step being accomplished correctly. Additionally; the subsequent 'ndt;' 'i;' and 'rii' steps do not refer the inspector to figure which shows the structural rework.
output: DURING B727-200 ENG PYLONS #1 AND #3 UPPER SKIN AND STRUCTURE INSPECTION AND FASTENER REPLACEMENT PER AN ENGINEERING CHANGE ORDER HAD SOME INCORRECT FASTENERS INSTALLED AT WRONG LOCATIONS. ACFT WERE RELEASED FOR SVC.

input: Upon descent and transition from air route traffic control center to approach; we requested the area navigation (rnp) 30 approach. The approach controller cleared us from our present position (approximately 40 miles southeast of the field) to rokny. We referenced the approach chart and saw ronky as the initial approach fix from which we planned to commence our approach. We didn't catch the fact that when controller pronounced rokny that it differed from what we saw on the approach plate - ronky. Because the flight management computer was presently sequenced to the mso vor and dme (co-located) (our cleared/planned route); rokny was not an available option listed when the pilot monitoring (pm) pressed the dir button; so post meridiem hand typed ronky into the dir to field. The temperature inertial navigation system orange dashed line showed a turn to 180 degrees magnetic which obviously didn't make sense. We queried the controller as to the spelling of the waypoint; at which time controller phonetically spelled r-o-k-n-y. The post meridiem had trouble initially inserting this correctly as he was mentally convinced that it was what he was reading on the approach plate (ronky). I mentioned that the controller spelled it rokny; at which time we inserted the correct waypoint and verified it on the nd. We cleaned up and verified the flight plan in the flight management computer and executed the approach from the rokny initial approach fix and landed without incident. Upon landing; i called the duty phone and got a hold of the chief pilot. I relayed what had happened and conveyed my concerns for the next crew who might be flying into mso using that approach/iaf. Coincidentally; an employee of jeppesen heard about this event and contacted me so they are likely aware of the error. The approach plate is mso 12-21 dated 18 may 18. I verified this against the nga (national geospatial agency) product; which shows the waypoint correctly spelled rokny.suggestions: create process to validate all waypoints/coordinates in our jeppesen products.
output: Air carrier First Officer reported that while on the MSO RNAV Runway 30 approach; it was discovered the waypoint ROKNY is misspelled as RONKY on the Jeppesen chart.

input: Rwy 26r is fast becoming unsvcable -- really rough on rollout. Flight attendants riding in aircraft jump seats have complaints of sore backs -- not the landing but the rollout is the culprit (i have just heard this: not on this flt). Runway(s) 26r at den should be chked! We have at least 8 months to go at stapleton.
output: CABIN ATTENDANTS GETTING SORE BACKS FROM THE ROUGH RIDE DURING LNDG ON A ROUGH RWY.

input: While on approach to atl runway(s) 27l; 320 degree heading 5000 feet/foot first officer flying; approach control switched us to a new frequency after checkeding in; i mistakenly put in the tower frequency over the last assigned approach control frequency realizing we needed a lower altitude i discovered my mistake and switched back to the last assigned frequency they gave us a turn and a lower altitude (360 degrees 3000 ft) and a new frequency which i managed to get wrong. After not being able to reach anyone and with the airport getting closer; i contacted atl tower frequency and asked them for the right frequency they told us to stay with them; asked intermediate fix we saw the runway(s) and cleared us to land. On the ground i was asked to call terminal radar approach control facility in my conversation with them; they were concerned as to where we had gone (atl tower apparently did not tell them that they had us) and advised me that they were also concerned because we were on a heading toward north side traffic and they could not get a hold of us. I advised them what i had done and that it was my mistake. They asked that i be more careful in the future but understood how the mistake could be made.
output: ON VECTORS TO ATL ILS RWY 27L; B757 FLT CREW INCORRECTLY SET WRONG FREQ; EVENTUALLY REMAINING ON TWR FREQ FOR VECTORS AND LNDG CLRNC. CAPT DISCUSSES INCIDENT WITH A80 SUPVR.

input: We started and taxied out without any abnormality from the engine instruments upon our pushing the power and setting the takeoff epr; i looked outside to maintain runway(s) alignment as the pilot flying at approximately 60 knots indicated airspeed the capt called airspd alive and i checkeded my airspd indicator and the engine gauges briefly. At that moment the flight engineer pointed out that n1; n2; egt; and fuel flows didn't agree with what the epr was on the #3 engine the capt called for the abort and the abort was initiated between 60-70 knots indicated airspeed the airplane came to a stop easily within the remaining runway(s) we taxied back in to the ramp and maintenance mel'ed the epr gauge. We taxied back out and took off using n1 to set power per the minimum equipment list the engine performed normally and all remaining gauges indicated the engine was at takeoff power. I was later told that maintenance worked #3 eng's epr system but never ran it up. It was later determined that epr line that is connected to the bullet on the jt8d engine was blocked. I ante meridiem slightly concerned that with all the engine problems the company has had recently; it seems to me; as a pilot intermediate fix you worked on the engine you would run it up after completing the work to make sure it is working normally. This could have turned out a lot worse had we continued the takeoff and not recognized that #3 wasn't putting out full power. There very well could have been a similar accident to that years ago. That flight had ice blocking sensors on the engs which caused the epr gauge system to read full power when all other indications the engine wasn't making full power. It also helps that capt listened to the engineer and also recognized that something was wrong. Cockpit resource management definitely worked in this case. I feel that the federal aviation administration should look into putting out an advisory circular or airworthiness directive for aircraft using epr. Epr should not be used as the primary method of setting power. I feel setting power by the n1 revolutions per minute is much safer.
output: AN ACR FO REPORTS REJECTED TKOF DUE TO LOW EPR ON CENTER ENGINE AND QUESTIONS THE EPR MEL APPLIED BY MAINTENANCE WITHOUT AN ENGINE RUN-UP.

input: Aircraft x showed overdue in our edst (enroute decision support tool); we talked to zse10 (where the aircraft would have been before entering zlc30) they hadn't heard of him. Their supervisor did a spurt (or whatever that search function is called that supervisors trust beyond reason because they're not taught to think for themselves just to look at numbers on a screen that are usually wrong and make knee-jerk and bad decisions based on those numbers) and it showed that we had rs'd (remove strip) the flight plan in our airspace. We had not rs'd the flight plan. I'm pretty sure what happened is that the aircraft was an in/out/in flight with zse and erams (enroute automation modernization) flawed flight plan tracking requires the rs of the exiting flight plan so that it doesn't conflict with the entering flight plan. Because of this dangerous requirement of the eram system zse10 never received the overdue status and should in fact have obtained the alert before us. Luckily we found the plane (had returned almost immediately to [its original departure airport]) and there was no need for an alnot (alert notice); however; had it been a real emergency and a plane had gone down; the time added to the alnot and search and rescue due to an automatic rs function could have been the difference between life and death.not only was zse blissfully unaware of the aircraft that never entered their airspace and they probably should have been worried about; but when we asked about it; they were even more blissfully unconcerned because the computer told the supervisor not to worry and that we were the ones that rs's the flight plan.i wouldn't have paid for eram; but i guess we can't go back and fix one of the most fiscally irresponsible things the federal aviation administration has ever accomplished; so going forward i would train supervisors to think about what their job actually is; remind them that probably no action ever accomplished by a supervisor without the concurrence of an actual air traffic controller has ever been a good decision in regards to the naval air station (national airspace system); and change eram's 'rs' policy. If it requires so much concurrence from the controller (a logic check) it is dangerous and irresponsible to allow that command to be entered by a computer that obviously has no idea how the naval air station actually works.
output: ZLC Controller reported of an overdue aircraft notice. Aircraft was found to have returned to the departure airport soon after takeoff.  Reporter blamed ERAM and supervisors for not knowing where the aircraft was.

input: We found on our flight plan that morning notes from dispatch indicating fuel added to accommodate running the auxiliary power unity the entire flight. The reason was; a new auxiliary power unity was installed and an inflight start of that auxiliary power unity was required. They needed at least 2 hours cool down period prior to in flight start attempt. Since we did not have 2 hours to cool down the auxiliary power unity prior to entering extended range twin operations maintenance requested that we keep the auxiliary power unity running until 2 hours prior to our top of descent. At that point we were to shut down the auxiliary power unity for 2 hours then attempt the restart at altitude. I shut down the auxiliary power unity as instructed; 2 hours prior to estimated top of descent i then attempted the restart at altitude fl390 after 2 hours cool down. The restart attempt was not successful. Egt raised normally and began reducing as usual but was followed by an auxiliary power unity fault. Subsequent attempt during descent below fl350 was not successful as well. I then entered my full report of the scenario in the maintenance log book. During the preflight phase of our flight we received multiple automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages from dispatch confirming the procedure to follow which we confirmed. Additionally; during the auxiliary power unity shutdown period; we received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from dispatch asking if we had made our maintenance log entry. I responded by telling dispatch that we were in the middle of the procedure and would report the results in the maintenance log. Dispatch responded with a thank you.do not attempt a procedure like this while operating under extended range twin operations rules again. Domestic flight would have been a better choice for this kind of required check.
output: B757-200 flight crew on an ETOPS overwater flight reported they were tasked with testing the APU with an inflight start; and the APU would not restart. Reporter recommended they do these kind of tests on domestic flights.

input: I recently flew a b777-200 aircraft from zzzz to zzz1. One of the flight attendant's on this flight was doing safety checks in the lower lobe crew rest area and he tried to open the (cabin floor) escape hatch above him. He was unable to even get it to move (even) a little bit. He called for a mechanic and they discovered that the carpet over the hatch had been glued down and even they could not open it. They did manage to cut the carpet to make the hatch usable. This flight attendant brought this to my attention; so i told him that i would send a report concerning this matter. I don't know if this practice of gluing the carpet down over the hatch is common on all lower lobe aircraft; but perhaps it is something that should be checked out. That hatch could be the only means of escape from the lower crew rest area and the thought of it not opening when needed; is scary. Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.
output: A Flight Attendant reports that while doing cabin safety checks in the Lower Level Attendant rest area; he was unable to open the escape hatch on a B777. The carpet covering the cabin aisle floor hatch was larger than the size of the hatch and glued to the surrounding floorboards beyond the hatch.

input: Lear 24 en route from zzz to zzz1 climbing through 40500 feet/foot for fl410. Heard a 'pop' and left/right (directions) engine instruments indicated flame-out (ie no egt; windmilling revolutions per minute and reduced oil pressure). No other adverse indications of engine seizure or fire. Requested immediate descent to fl240 (for engine restart envelope). Some delay from the center due to traffic i elected not to declare an emergency yet; as things seemed 'otherwise normal;' but did not want to delay descent as maintaining altitude would eventually not be possible. Cleared to fl290 with a delay at that altitude for approximately 3 minute(s) controller asked why we wanted descent i told him it was necessary for restarting engine received descent to fl240. Passing fl295 restarted engine all indications normal. Climbed back to fl390 (after clearance received). Maintenance investigating cause of flame out. (fod; stator area mismatch; fuel ctl?) callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the airplane has not been worked on but is awaiting a borescope of the stator vanes in the compressor. Intermediate fix found ok then the engine fuel control will be replaced. The rptr stated that the same engine flamed out 40 days ago.
output: A LEAR 24 IN CLB AT FL405 HAD THE R ENG FLAME OUT. DSNDED TO FL290 FOR RELIGHT. ENG RELIGHTED AND RETURNED TO FL390 WITHOUT FURTHER PROBS.

input: We were assigned an initial cruising altitude of 33;000 feet/foot once we reached our initial altitude we were in a haze layer and there was pretty consistent light chop and thought that if we went up to fl370 we might get a better ride have a better view of any weather ahead of us. We climbed to fl370 and were still in the haze but had no returns on our radar screen. It was mostly smooth with some rare ripples of light chop and since we had been dealing with the weather/turbulence earlier in the day the captain decided to leave the seatbelt sign on. We were in communications with the flight attendant about the possibility of turbulence the whole flight. Air traffic control assigned us m.77 for spacing into dca. As we were over the luise intersection we were issued a descent clearance to fl310. I spun in the altitude; verified it with the captain; and set a descent rate of 1;000 feet per minute on the vs selector. As soon as we started our decent the aircraft pitched up and began about a 2;500 feet per minute climb. I instantly pulled the power to idle and overrode the autopilot to put us into a stable descent attitude and once the aircraft was established in a stable descent i reengaged the autopilot. During all this the captain advised air traffic control that we were unable to hold altitude and that we would advise when we were established back on our descent. The whole event only lasted 10 or so seconds and after that the flight continued smoothly and without incident. The turbulence wasn't the normal jarring bumps as it was more of a gentle sensation as if you were riding atop a wave. Dispatch called us a minute or so after the event to tell us that we should be crossing the worst of the weather in the next few minutes. While the captain was talking to dispatch i advised air traffic control that we would be unable to maintain m.77 due to the weather and slowed the aircraft. No passengers or crew were injured and there weren't any conflicts with traffic. The aircraft operated normally throughout the whole flight and event. We knew we were crossing weather and were very active in monitoring the situation. We made multiple calls to air traffic control asking about how the rides were at our altitudes. All sop's were complied with.
output: An ERJ flight crew encountered what appeared to be wave action when starting a descent and; instead; gained 500 FT prior to establishing a controlled descent.

input: We were on an instrument flight rules flight plan from eyw to sfb in mixed conditions when told to descend from 9000 feet/foot about 1 minute(s) or second officer later; zma called and said to expedite descent for traffic and got upset saying they tried calling several times without a reply from us. When they handed us off to orlando; they did the same thing and said they tried several times to reach us. There were 2 pilots on board and neither of us heard these multiple calls. We fly the same route all the time and have never missed a call from air traffic control it was obvious that the controller was working more than 1 frequency we missed the traffic by 900 feet/foot vertically and at least 700 feet/foot horizontally the traffic was visual flight rules at 7500 feet/foot we were about 6650 feet/foot intermediate fix the traffic was more than 1000 feet/foot vertically we wouldn't be making this rpt. The traffic didn't concern us because our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii didn't show a conflict; our concern was the blame for missed calls. I think the controller using more than 1 frequency played a large role in this. His attempts to call us couldn't have been on our frequency because we heard all xmissions on it. I can see missing 1 call at the most; but repeated? After the first complaint by air traffic control of not responding; we were extremely alert for our call sign. When air traffic control again said we didn't respond after repeated calls for frequency change; we knew for sure it was their mistake. On the other side though; air traffic control was very busy and i'm sure had his hands full. Another controller to help him would have definitely helped the sit.
output: IFR C414 PLT IS QUESTIONED BY ZMA CTLR REGARDING LACK OF RESPONSE TO ATC XMISSIONS.

input: Faa complained to air show director that i made slow roll passes; although i had presented documents indicating federal aviation administration qualifications to do the maneuver from ground level. Federal aviation administration observer complained to air show director that i crossed the show line (middle of runway(s) 1 and therefore was too close to crowd). 1) wind was a factor. B) i was concerned that another plane below me might pull up to my altitude when i rolled. Correction: 1) start maneuver further away from show line. 2) make certain other plane(s) will not interfere with the maneuver by increasing distance laterally between aircraft second officer maneuver can be started and completed on show line. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr states that he has current aerobatic waiver no altitude restriction he attended the show briefing and signed the show waiver. Therefore; he should be able to perform all briefed maneuvers at any altitude the real problem seems to be that he possibly crossed the show line and flew too close to the crowd area. This was primarily caused by spacing problems with another aircraft flying at the same time but not in formation.
output: FAA AIR SHOW MONITOR COMPLAINS ABOUT MANEUVER AND LOCATION OF REPORTER FLT.

input: This was a cross country flight from lafayette; in; to oshkosh; wi; with planned stops at kankakee; il; de kalb; il; and watertown; wi. While on the leg de kalb to watertown; i experienced some unexpected headwinds and; because of the 5 gallon fuel capacity; a gas stop was unavoidable. The lake lawn airport at delavan; wi; seemed the closest alternate; second officer i landed and was then informed that the airport was closed until xx00. Departure time from lafayette; in; was xa00. Before departure i had called flight service and telling the briefer my intended stops; he replied saying that there were no notams. As a precaution against repeating this mistake; i feel i should ask the briefer for notams on any airports that could be used as alternates; asking about them by name.
output: AN ULTRALIGHT PLT LANDED AT A CLOSED ARPT.

input: Coming in to land 8 mile east of btl; air traffic control advised us to keep the speed up and enter a final for runway(s) 31. We started our descent from 2500 feet/foot mean sea level at 145-155 knot(s) air traffic control then advised my student and i to turn our aircraft left/right (directions) towards the numbers because we were on more of a left/right (directions) base for runway(s) 31 instead of final. At this time; i decided we were going to do a no flap landing in order to approach the field a little faster. Coming in to land; we were 110-120 knot(s) on a half mile final when final approach for the cirrus sr20 is 85 knot(s) (no flaps). Over the numbers we were still 20 knot(s) fast second officer i put 50% flaps in to help slow the aircraft our aircraft then slowed to our normal approach speed but we had already used half of the 5000 feet/foot runway(s) we then entered ground effect and continued to float down the runway(s) i then applied full back pressure once we landed and did not immediately apply brakes. The flight school's policy is to only apply brakes below 50 knot(s) finally; we were coming up to the end of runway(s) 31 second officer i started to apply heavy braking and started to turn towards the taxiway at the end of the runway(s) we had to exit into the grass because we were going too fast to continue the turn onto the taxiway once we entered the grass and missed the taxiway light; we turned back onto the taxiway and started smelling the overheated brakes. My student and i should have never come in that fast for final approach we did not execute a go around when we should have. Additionally; a no flap landing in a cirrus should not have been attempted without proper glidepath and approach speed this is a valuable lesson learned and i ante meridiem very thankful no damage or injuries occurred during this mishap.
output: AFTER ATC REQUEST TO KEEP THEIR SPEED UP; SR20 STUDENT AND INSTRUCTOR LAND FAST AND LONG BEFORE DEPARTING RWY.

input: Both aircraft were on vectors and descending when separation was lost. Supplemental information from acn 596657: both aircraft were given vectors and an expeditious descent given to one of the acft.
output: ZID RADAR CTLR AND ASSOCIATE CTLR RPT OPERROR BTWN A DSNDING E135 AND MD80 WHICH CONFLICT WHEN LATERAL SEPARATION IS LOST.

input: I was making a standard rate turn to 040 heading to capture the [runway] 1c instrument landing system every part of the flight was stable until the autopilot picked up the localizer. As the plane made the turn to 010; i had a green needle and the localizer was centering. At that time the plane hit severe turbulence; the autopilot kicked off; and the plane turned and pitched up. Within a few seconds; i had the plane stabilized. I turned back on course; and as i did; i got a traffic advisory to climb. I think the plane behind me had closed in (within five miles); which set the traffic advisory air traffic control gave me a 270 heading and i broke off the approach; circled around; and made the second approach without any incident. I am not sure what caused the problem. It may have been wake turbulence: there was a warning about a b757 in front of me. The wind was 280 at 14-28 on the ground; it was 290 at 34-38 at 5;000 mean sea level i do feel the controller had us too close: he wanted me to hurry my turn to final. After looking at the flight path on flight aware; i did not get far off course. This happened in a matter of seconds; and as i turned back on the localizer; the traffic advisory came. At that time i felt the controller made the correct decision to pull me off the approach. It was an instrument meteorological conditions day and we were stacked up. When i got the plane stable; it was heading to the east; and i had gained 100 feet/foot or so. I did react to the traffic advisory and climbed to 5;600 feet/foot i feel that if there had been more separation; i could have continued the approach without any problem.
output: A C525A in single-pilot operations encountered what was likely wake turbulence on approach to IAD behind a B757.

input: Upon landing rollout; an estimated 15 mph crosswind caught the aircraft and spun the tail to the left/right (directions) causing the plane to slightly skid sideways; putting a side load on the landing gear; bending it. It is my opinion that this was only a roll out incident; since the only apparent damage was to the landing gear and the fiberglass wingtip -- there were no injuries and no insurance claim. This incident might not have occurred intermediate fix i had more experience in this plane and had been more aware of the crosswind i do not believe that this was a reportable incident.
output: A PLT OF A THORP-MILLER T18 EXPERIMENTAL HOMEBUILT ACFT BENT ACFT LNDG GEAR IN A XWIND.

input: Had a split flap on initial retraction with attendant flap asymmetry lockout at 1 1/2 degrees of trailing edge flaps and leading edge devices extended. No asymmetrical control inputs were necessary. Per aircraft restrictions; we proceeded to destination with limitations of 230 knots indicated airspeed and fl200. Made an uneventful landing at destination exercised extensive cockpit resource management in determining proper course of action.
output: UNABLE TO RETRACT WING FLAPS AFTER TKOF BECAUSE OF A SPLIT FLAP CONDITION.

input: We departed ord off of runway(s) 32l at taxiway t10 with a clearance of 'rwy heading to 5000 ft.' we were very light second officer our climb rate was 3000-3500 feet per minute passing through about 3000 feet/foot we were switched from tower to departure prior to checkeding in with departure we got a distraction which took my attention from monitoring the aircraft (i was the pf). The autoplt did not capture 5000 feet/foot and continued to climb i realized it did not capture at about 5100 feet/foot and our altitude peaked at just under 5500 feet/foot prior to a rapid return to 5000 feet/foot there was no other traffic to cause a conflict; and the event was unmentioned by air traffic control it's a good reminder of how important it is for one pilot to constantly monitor what the aircraft is doing -- especially when things are happening second officer quickly.
output: CL65 CREW HAD AN ALT EXCURSION ON CLBOUT FROM ORD.

input: Before this situation occurred it was noted that there were too many airplanes in the airspace with the amount of deviations occurring and no tmc (traffic manager coordinator) staffed to help with the traffic volume. The whole situation started with aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) from the west that was on an unusual vector to avoid weather. Aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) was the first aircraft i had that would eventually encounter the weather to the north. The final was full and aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) needed to be turned to a downwind heading. The pilot refused the instruction; fly heading 340; because of weather and was consequently taken across the final behind another airplane using divergence for resequencing. This had a cascading effect on the sequence as multiple aircraft were subject to this pilot's inaction. I had to repeat the instructions three times. Fly heading 130; fly heading 160; he finally started turning and i had him roll out on a 070 heading to pass behind. I just needed the aircraft to turn.resequencing that aircraft caused other aircraft to extend on the east downwind. All of the aircraft were contained in final's airspace. There were multiple aircraft left at higher altitudes such as 5000 ft because of how far out i was turning to final and i didn't want to impact other sectors with aircraft at lower altitudes and potentially going outside the class b airspace. I was busy communicating with my airplanes in the airspace due to the prior situation and i was continuing to formulate my plan to work around the weather deviations and reel the final back in. I then noticed another aircraft; aircraft y; from another sector out of place and in my airspace. Aircraft y was southwest bound level at 5000 ft; heading right for aircraft x and i immediately issued a traffic alert. The aircraft x pilot said they had the aircraft on traffic alert and collision avoidance system but not in sight. I wasn't sure what the other controller was going to do so i instructed the pilot to turn left immediately heading 230 to avoid a potential collision. This was a clear airspace violation and a potentially dangerous situation due to the split focus between low sectors in bad weather and the inaction of the other controller once the ca (collision avoidance) alarms went off and they realized the grave state of affairs. Aircraft x and the other aircraft were sequenced appropriately following this event and all landed safely without further incident. We had at one time at least 16 seattle arrivals deviating for weather with a 46 arrival rate which is not the instrument landing system rate into this airport. All the sectors were combined up. This has been a continuing trend at this facility and these kinds of events have been noted in the past. I'm just glad i had a backup plan. Due to the weather deviations and the lack of traffic oversight the arrival rate should have been set appropriately. The lack of awareness in the room as to what the weather was doing; how it was moving and interacting with final and other sectors is unacceptable; especially after the controller in charge (controller in charge) was made aware by another controller before i sat down and i gave them a heads up too. Having positions combined up during significant weather events is a bad idea and inherently dangerous given the current event stated above. The thought process of every controller in the building should be at minimum these two things: scanning for potential conflicts (they may not be in your airspace 'yet') and say something if it looks wrong or out of place. The second thing is too stay out of the final controller's way and out of final's airspace; period.
output: TRACON Controller working combined sectors with weather deviations observed an aircraft entering their airspace without a handoff conflicting their arrivals.

input: On departure at 10000' i understood departure control to say 'maintain present heading to intercept the 296 degree left/right (directions) of dxo and climb to 13000'.' i read back the clearance to 13000' and received no response from departure control we began climbing and at approximately 10800' departure control called us and said that we were only cleared to 10000' and that 11000' traffic had passed off to our right and behind us. He then cleared us to 13000' and told us to contact zob. The f/o was preoccupied with an inoperative primary stabilizer trim and did not hear the initial clearance intermediate fix we did misunderstand the clearance to 13000'; departure control also failed to pick it up when i read back the clearance to 13000'. This incident emphasized the need for better communications and i know i will work harder on that in the future.
output: ACR MLG ALT DEVIATION OVERSHOT IN CLIMB POSSIBLY IN RESPONSE TO A TRAFFIC CALL.

input: During takeoff roll; the #2 engine fire indicator illuminated. The takeoff was aborted; memory items were completed as well as associated chklist. Evacuate/evacuation was commenced with no injuries.
output: AN ACR BE1900D EVACED ITS PAX ON THE RWY AFTER A FIRE WARNING ON TKOF ROLL.

input: Passenger x was removed for testing positive for covid virus. Plane was not deplaned and sprayed. Passenger was on board 20 minutes with face covering not covering nose.
output: Flight Attendant reported that a passenger who had tested positive for COVID-19 was removed from the aircraft; however; other passengers were not deplaned and the aircraft was not sanitized.

input: Established on the instrument landing system approach to runway xxr prior to glideslope capture. Called for gear down. As the gear started to extend the aircraft pitched up and added power on its own. I disconnected the autopilot and autothrottles to regain control of the aircraft. The flight management system appeared to be in the go-around mode and the airspeed bug was stuck around 180 kts and unable to select it back to the vref speed of 136 kts. The flight director and head up display were commanding a pitch up of greater than 10 degrees and a deflection of more than 10 degrees left. Runway was in sight and continued the approach with raw data and manual throttles to an uneventful landing. A maintenance write up on the prior leg described a similar event. As a side note the flight management system databases were both out of date and deferred per the minimum equipment list also the go-around button was deferred [at our departure airport]. Instrument landing system xxr approach was hard tuned per the minimum equipment list this event occurred after a 7 hours and 20 minutes flight with a 2 pilot crew [early in the morning] with high terrain in all quadrants.
output: MD-11 Captain reported an anomaly with the FMS while conducting an approach to an international airport resulting in both speed and altitude deviations. The pilot quickly reverted to hand flying the aircraft; continued the approach; and landed uneventfully.

input: Exceeded 210 knot(s) restriction on the arrival due flight control issue discovered 6 miles prior to intersection. Declared emergency and advised air traffic control of intentions. Received priority handling and landed without further incident after completion of appropriate quick reference handbook procedure.
output: A MD-82 crew failed to slow for a 210 KTS intersection constraint because they were dealing with a flight control malfunction.

input: I was the first officer on flight dfw to hou. After an uneventful landing on runway(s) 12r at hou; we rolled to the end and were told to contact ground on taxiway mach number ground instructed us to proceed north on taxiway mach number and hold short of runway(s) 12l at taxiway o. I acknowledged those instructions. While on taxiway mach number an mlg landed on runway(s) 12r and took the high speed taxiway westbound we were told to give way to mlg; and then mlg was told to proceed north on taxiway mach number and cross runway(s) 12l and runway(s) 4/22 at taxiway celsius mlg acknowledged and proceeded. As we turned left/right (directions) on taxiway o; i told the capt that we had not been cleared across runway(s) 12l. He replied that we were cleared across behind aircraft i replied that i had not acknowledged that clearance by this time we had crossed onto runway(s) 12l; tower immediately called us to say that we crossed onto an active runway(s) our capt replied to ground that lgt was cleared across runway(s) 12l and 4/22. Tower replied that clearance was for mlg and that an sma had to abort his takeoff we were then cleared to our gate. Contributing factors: 1) we were told to hold short of runway(s) 12l while on taxiway mach number but mlg was cleared across runway(s) 12l in front of us; even though they had landed after us. 2) the ground controller told us to give way to mlg and then proceeded with mlg clearance without getting an acknowledgement from us to give way. 3) we were switched to ground frequency after landing even though we would have to cross an active runway(s) this did not allow us to monitor tower frequency and conflicts that might arise; i.e.; the sma given takeoff clearance on runway(s) 12 after mlg and before us. Human performance considerations: 1) not stopping to confirm a clearance 2) keeping aircraft on tower frequency until across all active runway(s) (as is common practice at most major arpts). 3) making sure all clrncs given are given time to be acknowledged and are! At no time was the sma ever in danger of striking our airplane.
output: LGT MISINTERPRETS CLRNC; TAXIES ACROSS ACTIVE RWY.

input: After a normal approach and landing to ril runway(s) 26; the aircraft slid off the end of the runway(s) on final; the braking action was rpted as 'mu 35-45' (poor to fair). Actual braking action was nil. No apparent damage to aircraft since the airport was unctled and had not been shut down; we elected to move the plane off the dirt to clear the ctrline in case another aircraft attempted to land. This incident serves to re-emphasize the need to exercise extreme caution on landing in mountainous/cold weather airports and the need to be skeptical of any information supplemental information from acn 570339: normal touchdown and brake application. Rpt of mu 35-45; actual mu 15-20.
output: A GLF4 CREW RPTED THAT THE RWY BRAKING ACTION RPTED FOR RIL; CO; WAS INACCURATE; CAUSING THEM TO DEPART RWY 26.

input: Taxiway a2 is not depicted on mke jepp chart 10-9 18 may 18. This is confusing since the [information page] for kmke states: 'after landing runway 25l -- be aware; taxiway bravo intersects taxiway alpha abeam a2'. After landing on 25l; air traffic control routinely issues the instructions; 'use taxiway alpha to bravo to the ramp.' they expect you to join taxiway bravo where it intersects with taxiway alpha abeam a2. When briefing this for arrival it was difficult to determine what the [company information page] was referring to; since a2 isn't on the jeppfd-pro chart.
output: B737 First Officer reported that Taxiway A2 was not depicted on the Jeppesen MKE 10-9 Chart.

input: I was working the busy late morning arrival bank and it became busy enough to have an assistant local controller assigned to the position. I was working two converging landing only runways and each runway had added complexity due to the following conditions. Runway 19r had a disabled aircraft blocking the first high speed exit and runway 12 had multiple taxiway closures forcing all arrivals to roll out to the far end of this 10;500 feet/foot runway to exit. Additional spacing had been requested from approach control to provide the necessary interval for arrivals to clear the runway at the far end. I believe 5 mile and 170 knot(s) was requested; but it was not being provided. This required intense monitoring on my part and occasional 's' turns on final on my part to achieve the needed spacing. The incident in question concerned aircraft y as the leading aircraft and an aircraft x as the trailing aircraft. I was closely watching as the lead aircraft was starting the turnoff at taxiway y; 9;600 feet/foot down runway 12; as the trailing aircraft x approached the landing threshold. At this point; the assistant local controller was already coordinating with the other local controller; lc1; for traffic and missed approach instructions. I was about to key the mike and issue the 'go-around' instructions to the aircraft x when the aircraft pitched up initiating a missed approach. I then immediately issued appropriate missed approach instructions. As the reason for initiating the missed approach; the pilot cited the aircraft y at the far end of the runway. The pilot of the aircraft x was vectored for another approach and landing without any further comments. Our approach control routinely disregards the requests made of them to provide what the tower needs to facilitate safe and efficient service to the users. Approach should strictly apply and adhere to the needs of the tower when requested.
output: IAD Local Controllers described a pilot initiated a go-around when landing traffic failed to clear the runway; the reporter allege PCT failed to provide required arrival separation given the circumstances.

input: Upon takeoff out of zzz at 100 knot(s) the master caution light illuminated with the forward cabin door light illumination. We continued the takeoff and the light extinguished. Upon leveloff the capt checkeded with the #1 flight attendant and checkeded door handle down. Door handle could not be selected all the way down. We communicated with maintenance control and they sent a message advising to not fly under these conditions because the door could come open. We diverted to zzz1 and had maintenance look at the situation and after further review with mechs and maintenance control we proceeded to destination zzz2. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter stated the fwd door closed and latched properly when operated at the diverted airport. His company has emphasized a policy for the pilots to inform the cabin flight attendants prior to takeoff to recheck the cabin door handles for proper latching. Reporter also stated his carrier has had several rejected takeoffs) due to cabin door warning lights coming on during takeoff resulting in blown tires; overheated brakes and aircraft damage. This is a major safety concern and financial issue for his carrier.
output: UPON TKOF; A B737-800 ACFT MASTER CAUTION LIGHT ILLUMINATED WITH A FWD CABIN DOOR LIGHT ON. TKOF CONTINUED; LIGHT EXTINGUISHED. DOOR HANDLE FOUND NOT FULLY CLOSED. ACFT DIVERTED ENROUTE.

input: Rejected takeoff at approximately 100-110 knot(s) after getting an engine indicating and crew alerting system (r) rev indication.
output: A B757-200 FLIGHT CREW NOTED A (R) REV INDICATION ON EICAS DURING TAKEOFF AND ELECTED TO REJECT.

input: On day 1; i was working with person x to give him a pass-down from the day shift workload. We were in a 6 feet by 6 feet office for about 15 minutes. Later that evening; after my shift was done; person x went to the hospital and was positive for covid-19. I was never contacted by anyone from management or the cdc about being exposed to covid-19 positive person. I also worked on day 2. I then started time off on day 3. While on time off a coworker told me about how person x was in the hospital and positive for covid-19; which occurred on day 1. I used time off for 14 days before i returned to work. Luckily i never showed symptoms or infected any other person. I took it upon myself to stay away from work for 14 days to protect my coworkers.
output: Mechanic reported being unknowingly exposed to a COVID-19 positive employee and not being notified of the exposure by company management.

input: (minor tail pipe fire on start.) during taxi out for takeoff (on taxiway rb near runway(s) 8l) we attempted to start #3 engine. While below maximum start tgt (turbine gas temperature); we were advised by another aircraft and air traffic control of flames coming out the rear of #3 engine. We stopped the aircraft to secure the problem. (emer equipment was called by ground ctl.) we aborted the start; shutting off fuel and motored the engine until the flames were out and tgt below 100 degree celsius according to procedures we asked the fire department to confirm the fire was out; and taxied back to the ramp for inspection of damage; by air carrier maintenance everything checked good; and another start was made. All cockpit indications; as well as visually by maintenance checked out normal. We released the fire truck and continued our taxi for takeoff passenber evacuate/evacuation was not necessary; and after evaluating the problem it appeared to be a minor tail pipe fire; as the engine operated normally for remainder of flight all abnormal procedures were followed regarding engine start and communicating with passenber etc.
output: FLAMES OBSERVED BY ATC AND OTHER ACFT FLT CREW COMING FROM #3 ENGINE DURING START. NO APPARENT COCKPIT INDICATIONS.

input: After landing on runway(s) 1 requested to switch to ground frequency after performing all required post landing chklists we taxied to the ramp. There was no traffic moving near us or in the vicinity second officer we were not alert to the absence of air traffic control communicationss upon arriving at gate we realized we were still on tower frequency we were not sure intermediate fix the radio switch got bumped because ground frequency was tuned in standby but not up and selected yet. No corrective action was necessary and no known conflicts occurred. I believe fatigue was a factor. I had worked my second job which i must have to provide for my family at this wage. It is a non flying job second officer isn't considered in rest requirements. I only got 4 hours of sleep the night before doing 6 legs in 6 hours of flying and 9 hours of duty. Until wages and working conditions improve these fatigue induced occurrences will continue. I don't believe any conflicts occurred and only increased vigilance on my part would have made us aware we were not over on ground frequency my capt had also just finished a longitude commute to work second officer may have been tired as well.
output: TAXI ACROSS RWYS WITHOUT CLRNC.

input: Day two; leg two with very familiar captain. Good crew rest; briefs; and all pre-departure items normal. Passing 13;000 feet/foot at approximately 290 knot(s) with autothrottles/autopilot; lateral navigation and vertical navigation aircraft experienced three bangs/pops with noticeable associated yaws. Captain (pf) disengaged autothrottles/autopilot and established level flight. First officer (pm) noted more noise from number 2 which sounded like metal in a blender. Number 2 had pegged out egt with complete red dial; but other engine indications were similar to number 1. Captain and first officer agreed to apply memory items for engine limit. Autothrottles were already disengaged so captain guarded number 1 and first officer reduced/closed number 2. Engine still had thrust with no aircraft vibrations; but crew agreed indications from the bangs and metal noise were not normal; and decided to shut the engine down. Captain guarded number 1 and first officer cut off number 2. First officer declared emergency and requested vectors for immediate landing while captain continued flying. Air traffic control did a nice job giving a base turn and pilot discretion descent to runway and giving time to get souls on board and fuel. First officer ran clean up checklists while coordinating with air traffic control while captain let flight attendants know we had the engine secured and were returning so they should secure the cabin. Crew had completed engine limit/surge/stall memory items and since engine was shut down ran the engine failure/shutdown checklist. After completing that; we ran the one engine inoperative landing checklist. Crew noted the landing would not be overweight and calculated landing speeds to use flap 15 speeds and programmed flight management computer air traffic control changed runway's so first officer setup flight management computer and navaids appropriately while captain got plane down on profile. Air traffic control switched to unified tower frequency with fire chief monitoring; which was helpful to coordinate their inspection of the aircraft after an uneventful southeast landing with autobrake 2. While captain coordinated with fire chief; first officer briefed passengers and flight attendants about engine problem and safe landing; why the fire trucks were inspecting; and finally that all was well so we were returning to the gate. First officer called operations to coordinate gate and csr for transfers while captain coordinated with air traffic control for taxi since cleared by fire chief. Passengers seemed fine; flight attendant supervisor; captain and assistant chief pilot checked with flight attendants to make sure they were okay (which they determined they were) and returned to their base. Maintenance notified crew number 2 engine turbine blades were toast. In hindsight knowing the extent of the damage; we might have followed the engine fire/severe damage/separation checklist; but other than the three pops/bangs we did not have excessive aircraft vibrations and other engine indicators were about the same other than high egt; which went in limits once the throttle was closed. This would have resulted in pulling the fire handle; and maximizing se general aviation thrust as opposed to our path; which we determined we did not need it given our light weight in the one engine inoperative checklist.
output: B737-700 flight crew experiences an engine failure during climb out indicated by banging and high EGT. The engine is shut down and the flight returns to the departure airport.

input: Cruising at 37;000 feet/foot experienced severe to extreme clear air turbulence. We had 1;000 feet/foot altitude loss; speed increased 30 knot(s) and aircraft banked 30-60 [degrees] to the left. Aircraft then gained 1;500 feet/foot airspeed decreased to 60-80 knot(s) with a violent roll to the right. Regained control of the aircraft and reestablished airspeed and altitude. Air traffic control was notified. Once the aircraft was stable i went to the back to checkout the airplane and to re-stow all of the items that were thrown about the cabin.
output: Hawker 800XP pilot reported encountering extreme clear air turbulence at FL370 that resulted in temporary loss of control of the aircraft.

input: Due to last summer's weather; the airport authority for sitka; alaska; have not repainted the runway markings. At night in bad weather the only visual cues are the visual approach slope indicator (which half of the display is presently out) and the runway lights. The rest of the runway environment was darker than the inside of a certificate of waiver with its eyes closed and tail down. The landing lights reflected off of the rain on the runway just barely enough to give the first officer (who had never been to sitka before that night) the visual cue to flare in time. I doubt that with the current lack of markings classify this runway as marked for instrument flight rules or night operations let alone both. Nor does this runway qualify for reduced takeoff minimums since there is no centerline or runway distance markings. Repaint runway as soon as possible. Issue notams to inform crews of missing runway markings. Consider raising minimums for instrument flight rules approaches. Raise minimums for instrument flight rules departures. Fix visual approach slope indicator lights that are out.
output: ACFT ON NIGHT APCH TO SIT FLARES JUST IN TIME TO AVOID A HARD LNDG DUE TO ISSUES WITH VISUAL CUES. RPTR CLAIMS RWY MARKINGS REQUIRE RE-PAINTING.

input: In sum: an air carrier mlg experienced a #1 hydraulic system failure. Dispatch was contacted. A decision was made to continue to an alternate destination clt. A proper briefing was made to the flight attendants and passenber a jumpseat rider was put to use reading chklists and operating an electrical flap switch. The landing gear was extended manually and; with the remaining hydraulic power the landing gear doors were retracted. An emergency had been declared; second officer the equipment was at the end of the runway(s) the aircraft was towed to the gate. 2 high pressure seals had failed causing the loss of fluid.
output: ACFT EQUIP PROB MALFUNCTION REQUIRES DIVERSION TO ALTERNATE ARPT. EMER DECLARED LNDG.

input: Pax was served 3 double gin and tonics. We cut him off. Flight attendant #2 served him #7 when he complained. We told passenber to remain in seat for duration of flight he became belligerent and started verbal abuse of nearby passenber pax around complained. #4 flight attendant talked with passenber he became more abusive (argumentative). I talked with passenber we made agreement he would settle down and remain in seat. He did. Upon landing and deplaning; passenber pushed his way from seat #xxx to #yyy. Yelled about getting out of aircraft said he was a soldier from afghanistan. Aircraft was met by lax police who handcuffed passenber they were still talking with him when flight attendants left jetbridge.
output: B757 PAX BECAME INTOXICATED WHICH RESULTED IN HIM BECOMING BELLIGERENT; MADE VERBAL ABUSIVE TO PAX AROUND HIS SEAT. WHEN GETTING OFF THE ACFT HE PUSHED FROM THE BACK OF THE PLANE TO THE FRONT AND YELLED HE WAS GETTING OUT OF THE ACFT AND WAS AN AFGHANISTAN SOLDIER.

input: We missed resetting our altimeter from 29.92 to 30.36 passing fl180. This error caused us to be about 440 feet/foot high at locke. (technically though; i believe the 11000 feet/foot restrict, restricted, restriction was removed because we were given a descent just before locke. Restrict, restricted, restriction removed or not though; we had a 440 feet/foot error in our altimeters.)
output: WRONG ALTIMETER SETTING USED IN DSCNT PROC DURING STAR ARR IN A NIGHT OP. QNE NOT RESET TO A LCL QNH. ALTDEV ALT UNDERSHOT IN DSCNT.

input: On sep/sat/00; i was given aircraft xyz to work on. Previous shift maintenance had replaced the epr xmitter for a throttle split problem and had accomplished an overnight checked the epr xmitter was installed but needed an 'o' ring on the sense line. My partner installed the 'o' ring and verified that the new part was installed. I took the aircraft to the run-up area and ran the engine at the power setting as per the maintenance manual. Everything checkeded out and i delivered the aircraft to the gate. There was no sign off for the installation of the part; second officer i had to sign for the removal and replacement of the epr xmitter which i was not happy about. There was no mention of initiating a follow-up in the logbook. All of the open items on the log page were signed off second officer i signed off the airworthiness. Unknown to me; there was a follow-up requirement for minimum equipment list 27-14 that had to be done on the overnight that was not done. I did not checked the minimum equipment list sticker on the logbook cover; but i assumed that the minimum equipment list was continued on previous shift. The crew took the plane and flew a couple of legs until the discrepancy was noticed in xxx. Xxx complied with the follow-up and notified zzz maintenance who in turn notified me. I did not investigate the minimum equipment list on the aircraft before signing the aircraft airworthiness; but assumed that the previous shift had addressed whatever maintenance was required whether it was working on the system or deferring it.
output: AN MD88 WAS DISPATCHED IN NON COMPLIANCE WITH A DEFERRED ELEVATOR PWR ON INDICATING SYS OUT OF TIME LIMITS; DUE TO CARELESS PAPERWORK MGMNT.

input: During his exterior preflt inspection; the first officer discovered that the bolt in the left/right (directions) aileron control rod was installed backwards. He stated to me that he was generally aware of this item because of a recent article he had read in an airline safety-oriented publication (he could not remember which one). We rpted the item to line maintenance (acars and voice); and our mechanic confirmed that the bolt was in fact installed backwards; and that this was a 'safety of flight item.' he stated that; as installed; the bolt could more easily become detached; causing probable loss of aircraft control the item was corrected and the flight departed 22 minute(s) late.
output: A B737-300 HAD A BOLT IN THE R AILERON CTL ROD INSTALLED INCORRECTLY. BOLT REMOVED AND INSTALLED CORRECTLY.

input: A flight was delayed due to a maintenance issue. I was advised by the crew via automatic communications addressing & reporting system that maintenance was taking the aircraft out of service. At that time i posted a dcn (document change notice) on the flight to allow the operations coordinator enough time to find a suitable aircraft. While on celsius zzz sent an estimated time of departure (estimated time departure) request through the watch system for a xa50z departure time. The system automatically overrode my dcn and posted this time without my concurrence therefore exercising operational control over my flight and overriding my dcn posting. This issue has been brought to the attention of the director many times and to date a fix has not been implemented. The far's and company policy are clear of the dispatchers responsibilities for operational control and this is a clear violation.
