output: FLC OF B727 ON LNDG HAS ANTI-SKID BRAKING CYCLING ON ROLLOUT. THE RWY HAS EXCESSIVE RUBBER BUILDUP ALONG ENTIRE LENGTH OF RWY CAUSING DETERIORATION OF BRAKING.

input: During start of left/right (directions) engine capt's finger slipped off left/right (directions) engine start switch. Engine start was aborted. During taxi-out engine clear procedure accomplished per communications wind 180 degree 12 knot(s) taxiing north to depart runway(s) 18. Second start attempt. Msn tower informed us that we had flames in rear of engine second start attempt terminated. Tower then informed us that flames were visible in engine inlet. Engine fire chklist preformed (gnd) 1 fire bottle used. At no time was there a cockpit indication of fire warning. Fire equipment called for. They examined left/right (directions) engine and stated no fire visible. We taxied back to departure gate and notified company. No emergency declared and aircraft was not evacuated next time more consideration should be given to a tailwind when clearing an engine after start aborted. Also controllers should be more aware of what they see related to some common start problems the event was text book as federal aviation regulation as procedures and training. I don't see anything the flight crew could have done more effectively.
output: ENG FIRE ON START.

input: A gii departed teterboro airport on the dalton 19 departure procedure. The aircraft did not follow the procedures and entered class b airspace coming within close proximity of an aircraft on final approach into newark airport. Recommendation; the dalton procedure should be terminated and re-evaluated to see if it can be re-designed to meet air traffic control separation criteria. Aircraft routinely come within close proximity of each other.
output: N90 Controller described a potential conflict event between a TEB departure and a EWR departure; the reporter suggesting the Dalton procedure be eliminated and/or modified.

input: South of vxv; air traffic control cleared us direct to bugme. The problem is both the first officer and i thought we heard bkw (beckley). Both these fixes arguably sound the same. We even read back; 'company flight number; direct beckley.' we then line selected bkw on the flight management computer and executed it. Approximately one to two minutes later; center asked us where we were going; and said; 'your course was way right of direct to bugme. Turn to 360 and proceed direct bugme; flight planned route.' we re-input bugme and proceeded direct; then flight planned route. I'm not sure what we could have done differently. Both of us thought we heard 'beckley.' we even read it back as beckley. Air traffic control is in my understanding required to correct us. But; we thought we were doing as instructed.
output: A flight crew heard an ATC clearance to Beckley (BKW) but BUGME; 130 NM away on J91; was intended.

input: Missed nondirectional radio beacon approach at ump. Approach then gave heading altitude and runway(s) assignment for instrument landing system at ind. I missed 1 communications because passenber was asking questions. Approach gave intercept heading altitude and approach clearance for instrument landing system 23r. I tuned in 23l which i had overshot; then intercepted and tracked into a landing on 23l. I called approach on phone after landing and the supervisor was very nice. He didn't think his controller did anything wrong and i agree 100 percent. I was behind the aircraft and was not keeping up with situation. I should have flown the aircraft first and talked to passenber after we were on ground should have been better prepared for my altitude arpt.
output: A CPR SMT LANDED ON 23L. IT HAD BEEN CLRED TO 23R.

input: Acft struck fuel truck while parking at gate with wingtip. Aircraft during taxi in at gate; struck parked fuel truck. Wing walkers were in proper position and seemed to be paying attention as one was by the fuel truck and was giving a thumbs up as we passed him. The guideman continued to give a taxi forward the entire time. Aircraft parked and shut down.
output: TAXIING S80 HITS FUEL TRUCK WITH WINGTIP DURING ACFT PARKING PROC AT GATE IN ORF; VA.

input: The anti-ice duct warning message illuminated during descent. This changed to an amber anti-ice duct message by the time i was able to run the quick reference handbook we picking up ice at the time; and expected to remain in poh-defined icing conditions for the balance of the flight. We had already briefed the clear air turbulence ii instrument landing system into dayton.once the wing anti ice was selected off per the quick reference handbook my priority became step 2; 'leave icing conditions.' it was not possible to do this via exiting the cold cloud; either up or down. We were at 280 kts. And descending. I could not remember the sat to tat equation off the top of my head (a check of google says tat = sat + (tas/100)^2); but i did recall the main point; that it was in proportion to the square of the speed. Therefore; a small change in true air speed would result in a large swing in tat; allowing us to directly control the tat as limited by the sat and the speed envelope of the airplane. (per the equation; 300 kts. = a nine-degree increase; 400 = 16; 450 = 20.25; etc. There is little change at speeds below mach number 0.2).i immediately called for the first officer (first officer) to increase speed to 320 kts. In order to increase the tat. (i had no time to explain why until later. He complied immediately; though. Nice work). We were out of icing conditions forthwith. And so we remained; but had to exceed 250 kts. Below 10000 ft. In order to do so. This required [us to advise atc]. As we got lower we were able to maintain adequate tat at normal speeds; and so cancelled the [event] before landing.i wanted to have a viable plan in case i was unable to stay out of ice on the approach. We got weather for the alternate from air traffic control it was no good for our purpose. I asked dispatch for the best/closest ice-free airport in my fuel range; and concurred with his recommendation of zzz. We informed air traffic control of that contingency. I was prepared to continue with my desired speed and altitude per emergency authority if necessary. Air traffic control was very helpful; and i'm sure we could have worked it out quickly.we did not run test items with the flight attendants. I was pretty sure the issue would be gone before landing; it did not involve the cabin; and i was way more interested in their normal procedures for the clear air turbulence ii at that point. I did make the regular clear air turbulence ii announcement on schedule.atc reported negative ice from aircraft in front of us on the approach. We flew cowls/no wings with a tat of seven to nine-ish on final. It was above 10 below about 500 ft. I flew the clear air turbulence ii; of course. We broke out just below clear air turbulence i mins and landed normally.[maintenance] showed that both loops detected a leak along the right side of the fuselage.
output: Captain reported while in icing conditions; the ice system malfunctioned and the Captain's need to use emergency authority.

input: We were on the rokit 7 arrival, arrive going into iah. Air traffic control gave us vectors off the arrival, arrive for spacing. Air traffic control then told us to go direct reptl and hold as published. Reptl was not part of our transition on the arrival, arrive it took some time to locate reptl on the arrival, arrive we needed to locate the fix on the chart to get the proper spelling for the flight management system and to determine the proper entry for the hold. By the time we put the fix in the flight management system and hit direct; we were basically right on top of reptl. We had insufficient time to set up the hold and determine the entry. The flight management system would not accept the hold because we were too close to the fix; second officer we needed to use the flight management system to fly direct to the fix and use the green needles (vor radial without fms) for the hold. Reptl was off a vor and dme (co-located) (that was not on the arrival, arrive second officer we needed to locate it to find the freq) at a vor and dme (co-located) distance. By the time we had set up for the hold and determined the proper entry; we were past reptl. Second officer we told air traffic control that we were going to make a left/right (directions) turn back to reptl to enter the hold (on the protected side). We turned back to reptl and entered the hold. We entered the hold at approximately 300 knot(s) we also forgot to inform air traffic control that we entered the hold until our second turn in the holding pattern. We entered the hold fast because we were busy getting set up for the hold. I believe the contributing factors in this situation were: the lack of time to get set up for the hold; and the crew being unfamiliar with the arr.
output: HOLDING PATTERN ENTRY OVERSHOT AT TOO HIGH AN AIRSPD BY THE FLT CREW OF AN EMB145 WHEN AN AMENDED CLRNC FOR THE HOLD CAUGHT THEM BY SURPRISE ON THE ROKIT 7 ARR INTO IAH; TX.

input: We operated aircraft x from zzz to [destination.] after our initial cockpit set up my first officer went down to do the walk around. After he came up he told me that 'they are de-icing our wings and tail.' no communication had been established between us and the deicing team. We had no opportunity to configure for deicing. De-icing had commenced without our knowledge. I contacted de-icing control and requested to talk to a rep. A few minutes later i was talking to the team leader of the crew de-icing our jet. He said that they are now trained to go ahead and start the deicing procedure (at the gate) as long as ground power is plugged in and gate air is connected.
output: A320 Captain reported communication breakdown between flight crew and deicing crew.

input: On final approach to runway(s) 30r msp (3500 feet/foot msl) we had flaps 15 degrees and gear down. We got a climb command (red) with no yellow traffic advisory before the command. We did not visually see the traffic but it was on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii screen 300 feet/foot directly below us. We climbed up to 3800 feet/foot mean sea level the traffic disappeared on the screen second officer began a descent again. Then we got a yellow traffic advisory (same -300 feet/foot directly below) second officer we executed a go around we came back around and landed without any further alerts. In both cases we notified air traffic control of first our climb then eventually the go around they said that they observed no traffic conflict. After blocking in we wrote up a maintenance ticket on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and also notified maintenance by phone.
output: FLC OF AN MLG HAD A TCASII ALERT ON AN 8 MI FINAL APCH CAUSING THEM TO MAKE A GAR. APCH CTL RPTED NO KNOWN TFC. THE TCASII EQUIP WAS WRITTEN UP FOR A MAINT INSPECTION.

input: Just after leveloff at fl310; the xfer lock-out light and standby light on the pressurization control panel came on. The cabin began to climb the red cabin altitude annunciator came on; and the horn sounded. We donned our oxygen masks; began an emergency descent and declared an emergency i called the flight attendants to brief them about the items saying we would be landing in dfw within 10 minute(s) and that an evacuate/evacuation was unlikely; we were not worried about the integrity of the aircraft i made a public address to the passenber to use their oxygen and to follow flight attendant instructions. A flight attendant then called to say the masks were not deployed second officer the first officer manually deployed them. During descent i asked air traffic control to please notify air carrier about our divert and emergency on downwind; once chklists were complete; i was able to notify dispatch on the radio. The first officer continued to fly and land. He did a great job and followed all procedures the flight attendants took care of all cabin duties; calmed the passenber and were prepared to land. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information this acft's pressurization system per discussion with maintenance after landing was found to have a history of similar problems this crew had similar indications during climb through 6000 feet/foot but they were able to clear them through normal procedures these indications are quite normal and; intermediate fix cleared by procedure do not require a maintenance log item. At the time of the second lockout light and standby light the cabin climb rate was 1500-2000 feet per minute but not considered explosive. The passenber oxygen masks were deployed manually below the cabin altitude that would have activated them automatically.
output: AN MD80 FLT CREW; AFTER LEVELING OFF AT FL310 IN ZFW'S AIRSPACE; EXPERIENCED DEPRESSURIZATION; CAUSING THE CAPT TO PERFORM AN EMER DSCNT AND LNDG AT THE DEST ARPT; DFW.

input: We landed in cyfb at xa07l for a tech stop en route from eggw to bur. While fueling; we uplinked our flight plan via datalink. Our clearance was delivered by a canadian comrdo at approximately xa45z while holding short of runway(s) 35. At xa47z; we were released and departed with an immediate takeoff in front of a hawker on a 4 mile final to our runway(s) we proceeded to our first fix yte and were instructed to rpt reaching fl340 to montreal center it appeared that our datalink flight plan in the flight management system did not correspond to our clearance correcting the problem manually revealed discrepancies within our current flight management system database. Realizing a problem with our clearance we needed route verification after yte. While climbing our communications with center gradually deteriorated and upon our leveloff; we advised the controller that his radio was weak and requested another frequency barely audible; he provided us with a very high frequency frequency of 127.6. After multiple attempts to reach the controller we returned to our previous frequency but could not re-establish contact. We tried to reach arctic radio on all the published high frequency frequencies but received no response. Air-to-air provided no assistance to us as well. All the while; we maintained a listening watch on 121.5. We were also unable to locate any phone numbers to dial any canadian air traffic control facilities through our satcom. After about an hour we finally reached arctic radio and provided him with a full position rpt. Communications was difficult at best; and when we asked for a route verification; we received no audible response. After some time; we reached winnipeg on a published very high frequency frequency and were instructed to 'ident.' the controller advised us that we were not on the published airway and was east of our cleared route we asked him intermediate fix we should correct our course; but he advised us to proceed direct to yyl. He informed us that he was required to complete the paperwork regarding a gne. After review of our cockpit procedures i feel the error could have been avoided had each fix had been properly xchked by each pilot individually. This particular leg of our flight should have been handled much like our overwater flts; where both crew member xchk each other on the flight management system after talking to colins; the airway was apparently dropped from the database because of some inconsistency with the commercial chart provider. Unfortunately; we did not notice the airway missing until it was too late. Some valuable lessons were learned and i have adjusted my procedures accordingly to prevent this from happening in the future. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr revealed the airway in question was j540. The reason given for its being dropped from the database was duplication of waypoints along the route his company is presently investigating the matter. The primary complaint expressed by the rptr is the lack of information forwarded to the crew's forewarning them of such omissions when they occur.
output: A CL60 CREW; ENRTE FROM CYFB TO BUR; WERE INFORMED; BY ATC THEY WERE NOT ON THE PUBLISHED AIRWAY; TRACKING E OF THEIR CLRED RTE.

input: At approximately 3200 feet/foot while en route from nh40 to fdk; i asked a passenber who had helped with navigate, navigation for many yrs; to notify me when we got to within 20 mile of allentown class celsius airspace; as i wanted to contact them for advisories. After a few minute(s) i asked to see the latest position plot on the sectional. The latest plot showed us within 1 mile of the class celsius boundary. I immediately turned 50 degrees to the east to avoid entering class celsius airspace. I do not know intermediate fix i penetrated the airspace. In the past; i have flown in aircraft with side-by-side seating. It was easier for me to glance at the sectional. In the husky; we had to pass the missed approach point back and forth. Lesson learned is to never depend on a non pilot for help with critical navigate, navigation decisions no matter how many yrs of experience they may have.
output: PLT OF A HUSKY A1 TANDEM SEATING ACFT BELIEVES THAT HE MAY HAVE PENETRATED CLASS C AIRSPACE DUE TO RELYING ON HIS PAX DOING THE NAV.

input: Flight pushed at ewr and after push automatic terminal information service and metar changed to indicate -pl which would leave an allowance time of :10. Captain called and said no pellets just rain. While talking with captain automatic terminal information service and metar amended to delete pellets and show just -ra. Captain questioned whether as an onsite observer he could say no pellets just rain. Called chief and he stated that if company x was not reporting pellets then we were legal to go. Captain concurred and flight took off. Captain automatic communications addressing & reporting system later to say the following:fyi we will do a reportabout the rapl weather at ewr..seems like a lot of.conflicting guidancebetween the fom+ the hot automatic communications addressing & reporting system lwe info..it would be good to see what is the.master weather source..atis..eyeballs..or lwe..our weather service reported nothing but rain during the entire event.
output: B737 flight crew and Dispatcher reported confusion concerning the legalities of a departure with -pl on the ATIS and only RA on the Hold Over Time app.

input: Fl320 in icing conditions with wing and engine anti-ice on; the pressurization flow light illuminated. The cabin altitude started to climb and we determined the left pack had failed. Followed quick reference handbook procedures but the cabin altitude continued to climb. Descended to fl250 but since the cabin altitude was still climbing we continued the descent to 10;000 mean sea level during the descent; the right pack was found to have failed as well. Declared an 'emergency' and diverted to a nearby airport for an overweight; uneventful; landing.
output: An MD80 operating at altitude in icing conditions and unable to maintain cabin pressurization declared an emergency; descended and diverted to a nearby airport; landing over maximum structural landing weight.

input: Acft was parked on a remote hard stand. During preflt duties while passenber were boarding; a maintenance man came into the cockpit and asked to speak to us. He said he was the maintenance personnel and that the number four tire had a bolt head broken off. It was rpted that it was discovered last night and that the maintenance controller was notified and ok'd the flight to zzz for repairs. We were told that the problem had no safety implications and the bolt only held a ring in place and had nothing to do with holding the wheel on. I went down to look at the wheel and asked to speak to the maintenance supervisor i was introduced to the same individual that i met in the cockpit. He assured me again that there were no safety implications and the maintenance controller was aware of the problem i asked for a placard and was told the maintenance controller did not want to placard the aircraft but wanted me to fly the aircraft to zzz for repairs. I did. On the ground we were told we flew with a no-go item. Supplemental information from acn 628352: during preflt in zzzz; a maintenance technician came on the aircraft and told us there was a bolt on the #4 tire that had a bolt head sheared off. He said he had been working with the maintenance controller since the night before; and that they were aware of the problem he went on to say that there were no tires in zzzz and we were to fly to zzz where the tire would be replaced. The capt looked at the tire and asked intermediate fix we needed a placard. The technician said that the maintenance controller said there was no need and everyone was aware of the problem he went on to say that the bolt was no big deal and was not needed to hold the tire on the aircraft upon landing at zzz; we were informed by chief pilot that the bolt in question was a no-go item. Callback conversation with rptr acn 628345 revealed the following information the capt stated the local ground crew had been counseled. The capt also said the next time he would have written it in the maintenance log to either be deferred or signed off.
output: A B757-200 CREW FLEW WITH A BOLT HEAD BROKEN OFF FROM NO 4 WHEEL.

input: Just before liftoff i felt a rumble and i wondered about the tires. At that [same] time i saw an intersecting runway go by so i attributed the rumble to an uneven intersection. Approaching our destination i received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message that tire debris was found on our departure runway. I [advised atc]; followed quick reference handbook procedure; briefed flight attendants; and briefed passengers. On landing there was a strong rumble as we decelerated and i then knew for sure we had a blown tire. After stopping fire rescue confirmed the blown tire and we were towed to the gate.i would like to make special note that when i looked in the electronic quick reference handbook there is no mention of landing on a flat tire procedure. That same page in the paper quick reference handbook does list the procedure. This needs to be corrected quickly. This initially caused me to believe there was no procedure. Only as a last resort when i searched the electronic quick reference handbook for the key word 'tire' did i find the procedure.
output: A B737-800 Captain reported suspecting a tire failure during takeoff and was notified in flight about tire debris on the departure airport runway. During approach; an electronic QRH index search listed no 'LANDING ON A FLAT TIRE' procedure but the procedure was contained in the document; simply mis-indexed.

input: While executing the area navigation approach in to zzzz. We were told by air traffic control to execute a missed approach due to drone activity over or near the airport. We executed the missed approach; entered holding and were vectored back for a second area navigation approach; this time uneventful. On the first approach we also came within 1/2 a mile of a paraglider at our altitude in the vicinity of the zzzzz intersection.
output: 777 First Officer reported an ATC initiated missed approach due to drone activity.

input: On approach to zzz my instructor and myself were given a left down-wind approach and runway xx was active. We were coming in from the west; and there was another plane approximately 6-8 miles directly behind us same altitude. We crossed runway centerline; and joined the left downwind for the runway. The aircraft behind us continued in and was also given a left down wind pattern entry. In my plane we did a touch and go which we were approved for and i believe asked to continue upwind before turning. What we hadn't realized is that air traffic control had asked us to continue directly into the side of the other aircraft. We didn't have them in sight; and i received a notification of a converging situation from foreflight. The nose on the climb was obscuring the view of the other aircraft. Upon receiving the notification; the upwind path was deviated from; due to zzz's poor tower controllers. This has been an ongoing issue with poor traffic management. This is the second time i've had a near miss in the last year or so training out of this field.
output: C172 pilot reported NMAC and cited reoccurring issues with ATC Tower.

input: Initial contact with lax approach control told us to expect instrument landing system runway(s) 25r with mudde 4 arrival, arrive capt (pnf) inserted the mudde 4 arrival, arrive while the first officer got his charts. Approximately 4 nautical mile east of mudde (14000 ft); we switched to the second approach controller who told us to fly present heading (230 degs) to intercept localizer runway(s) 24l; expect instrument landing system runway(s) 24l; runway(s) 24l glideslope out of service at that time; i (pnf) inserted instrument landing system runway(s) 24l and briefed the first officer on the approach calling out initial altitudes minimum descent altitude (with airspd out - 580 ft); missed approach procedure minimum safe altitude localizer identify inbound. I manually inserted localizer ident/inbound course and selected localizer only approach on the nav/rad page. We were cleared for approach and first officer descended to 2200 feet/foot approximately 6 nautical mile prior to romen. After he leveled off; approach control told us to contact tower at romen; cleared for approach at that time i looked at the navigate, navigation display which showed ff24l and not romen; second officer i looked at the approach plate to confirm where romen was and noticed i hadn't set time to missed approach i started to set it and told the first officer to set minimums (580 ft) and by the time i figured the missed approach time we were descending out of 1500 feet/foot and i figured it was too late. After looking out for the runway(s) i decided we were too low and told the first officer to stop his descent at about the same time air traffic control asked us what our altitude was. We had not yet crossed romen and were still talking to approach he told us the altitude restrict, restricted, restriction was 2200 feet/foot at romen -- we were approximately 900 feet/foot he asked us intermediate fix we could make it from there and i asked for missed approach instructions. He asked intermediate fix we were instrument meteorological conditions and i told him we were visual meteorological conditions we flew according to his missed approach instructions and continued around for landing at lax. The human factors involved in this incident are as follows: 1) the last minute(s) runway(s) change rushed both of us and consequently the approach was not thoroughly briefed nor understood. The fact that the approach was changed from an instrument landing system to a localizer only (gs was ots) compounded the issue. There is more to brief in terms of technique when flying a non precision approach 2) effective communications broke down. Both of us got absorbed in our own little worlds of 'preparation' and stopped communicating. Every 'incident' i have been involved in; however minor; has been a result of at least 1 person not saying what was on his mind. I should have asked the first officer what his intended technique/action would be after romen (ie; to either use vertical speed or level change to mda). 3) there was no xchk. I didn't realize until the controller gave us the frequency change at romen that 'romen' was defined on the flight management system and navigate, navigation displays as ff149 with a hand altitude of 2200 feet/foot also; when i told the first officer to set minimum descent altitude i should have said 'preselect' and he should have corrected me and reminded me that we were to cross romen at 2200 feet/foot 4) finally; the distraction in the cockpit caused by a lack of a good brief. At the time i should have been xchking the fo's position and altitude i was concerned with time to missed approach finding romen; the turnoff point on the runway(s) and the fact that i considered the first officer slow in catching up and minding the store. The 2 contributing factors that i think are necessary to bring up are the fact that we were both tired; not from excessive duty times; but from the simple fact of changing from daytime duty period to nighttime duty period. Also; lax's really bad habit of last minute(s) runway(s) changes.
output: AFTER LAST MIN CLOSE IN APCH CHANGE; HVT CREW CROSS FAF 1300 FT LOW PRIOR TO MISSED APCH AT LAX.

input: A c172 called for departure and was cleared for takeoff on runway 28r. The flm alerted me to the crossing emergency vehicle and i canceled the takeoff clearance. Recommendation: i was super busy and a split of the positions would have complicated things in briefing and would have been unsafe. I should have used the runway placard to remind me of the crossing traffic. The pilot complied with my instructions and any problems were averted. My flm was the one who caught the mistake and was aware of the situation.
output: Tower Local Controller described a potential conflict event when after clearing an aircraft for takeoff he was advised by the Supervisor of a crossing vehicle down field; prompting a cancel take off clearance.

input: When we checkeded on with ord approach they offered us to deviate for weather as we desired; and rpted moderate to severe turbulence was rpted 5 mile ahead. We deviated left/right (directions) of course (nw) around a cell on radar when we got the r-hand engine fire warning. The 25 minute(s) flight from spi had almost continuous light turbulence with occasional moderate turbulence we were in light turbulence at the time. I initiated the engine fire memory items and the first officer and i completed them to the point of going to the chklist; the fire warning remained after discharging 1 fire bottle. The chklist commands the second bottle. The chklist is kept in our personal manuals; not in an aircraft book as is probably normal. During the time it took the first officer to get out his chklist (30 seconds); the warning went out. Also during this 'dead time' i informed air traffic control declaring the emergency in case we needed to quickly come in to land. We ran the chklist and talked to company dispatch; then air traffic control informed us of severe turbulence and windshear rpts at ord. Rfd was the nearest airport but with the en route weather as it was; turbulence and heavy rain; i was hesitant to go there -- especially knowing that there is no airline service at rfd; and i would have to baby-sit passenber for who knows how longitude dispatch read us the sequence rpts for several airports and i decided msn was my most comfortable option. I've been there many times; and it was good visual flight rules this may not have been the best 'by the book' federal aviation regulation correct alternate; but i was most comfortable landing single engine there; rather than flying into weather that doesn't paint well on radar and may be deteriorating. I briefed the first officer en route that i was suspicious that the fire warning was erroneous and we could restart the r-hand engine intermediate fix there was trouble with the left/right (directions) we talked to maintenance control and consulted the flight attendant. She didn't see or hear anything out of the ordinary; and gave a short briefing to the passenber (fo). Total time on a single engine was 20-25 minute(s) landing at msn uneventful.
output: A D328 CREW; APCHING ORD; EXPERIENCED AN ENG FIRE WARNING. ENG WAS SHUT DOWN.

input: Logbook that was left/right (directions) on our aircraft was for aircraft #5ab. Our logbook was on aircraft #5ab. We were on aircraft #5co. Apparently logbooks were reversed; during the night.
output: WRONG LOGBOOK FOR ACFT FOUND DURING FLC TECHNIQUE PREFLT PROC AND CHKLIST USE.

input: Inflt illness. Passenber had sporadic; uncontrolled vomiting; indicating possible heart attack symptoms. Attendants provided help/assistance; paged doctor. Doctor provided help with o2 and aed therapy. Landed in zzzz for medical attention. Flight origin zzzz1 to zzz; air interrupt due to above. Observation/comment company passenber flight attendant call system poor!!! Passenber was initially unable to flag flight attendant attention due to design of armrest control location. This passenber panel is not easily visible; due to blocked access. Passenber continually push the wrong buttons; which rings call chime in flight attendant galley areas. Design in panel is such that 1 black square button is for the reading light; adjacent black button is for flight attendant call. Passenber continually hunting on panel; located at leg level; for reading light. Each panel is opposite to the seat next to it!! Therefore; intermediate fix you ask passenber next to you; how he turned on his reading light; he would tell you it was the 'forward' button; which is the wrong button on your own seat! Bad; poorly devised and poorly located panel. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the airplane was a b767-300er and was wbound over water when the passenber displayed signs of serious distress. The rptr said the passenber was unable to contact any cabin attendant due to confusion with the armrest control panel. The rptr stated the first problem was locating the panel then activating the call button which is the same color as the reading light switch.
output: A B767-300ER CABIN ATTENDANT RPTS THAT IN A RECENT MEDICAL EMER THE SICK PAX WAS UNABLE TO FLAG CABIN ATTENDANT ATTENTION DUE TO DESIGN OF ARMREST CTL LOCATION.

input: Upon landing; touched left main gear then right main gear; felt a 'wobble' in rear right main gear; touched nose wheel down and then felt the collapse of the right main and nose wheel which pulled me off the runway.
output: PA28R pilot reported the right and nose gears collapsed on landing resulting in a runway excursion.

input: Upon landing in zzz that morning we got an engine 2 rev fail message on the engine indicating and crew alerting system as soon as i parked the aircraft at the gate; i wrote up the aircraft and then called maintenance (mx). The contract mx worker showed up some time later and wrote up the reverser as being deferred. We then amended the release; boarded up and headed to zzz1. Upon landing in zzz1; the same engine indicating and crew alerting system message appeared again after we noticed #2 reverser was not gated and the thrust lever did go into reverse. Engine 2 rev fail appeared again on the engine indicating and crew alerting system and when we arrived at the gate; i wrote up the reverser as not being properly deferred by the contract mx in zzz. Two mechanics then showed up in zzz1; they went through the roughly 15 step process to defer the #2 reverser. The contract mx in zzz did not go through the process whatsoever to properly secure the reverser and as a result; another delay was taken by us to get the situation resolved. We need to have reliable mx in place at zzz. Since i no longer can trust the mx [in zzz]; there will be a serious hesitation in knowing that the proper steps are taken when something breaks in the future.
output: ERJ-175 Captain reported a failed thrust reverser was not properly deferred at a contract maintenance station.

input: After departure we flew through a line of rain showers westbound of the airport heavy weather indicated by radar and lightning flash was to the north and south of us. New york approach told us to turn to 090 degrees replied unable due to weather told again to turn 090 degrees said again unable. Told that we had to be either ebound or sbound. Said unable due to weather and that we may have to declare emergency approach said turn left/right (directions) to 090 degrees and descend to 5000 feet/foot we started slow turn to the east and descended as cleared air traffic control asked intermediate fix we were declaring an emergency replied no. Air traffic control said something like i will declare one for you. We turned to 090 degrees and were able to avoid cells with much maneuvering. Were able to comply with all further air traffic control instructions. Nothing more said about emergencies air traffic control could have been more helpful in our attempts in staying away from hazardous weather had the weather been just a bit more of an issue; i would have declared an emer.
output: FLC OF F100 INITIALLY REFUSED TURN INSTRUCTIONS DUE TO WX.

input: Before departing from freeway airport an unctled airfield; numerous attempts were made to contact apch/dep on 124.55; 125.65; and flight service station specialist on 122.2 to activate my instrument flight rules flight plan. I got no response on the radio. I departed runway(s) 18 at freeway airport and immediately contacted potomac departure on 124.55 and requested they open my flight plan and advise me of my assigned transponder squawk code. They advised me that the airport was located within an air defense identification zone and i was supposed to have the proper squawk code before departing. I then advised potomac departure that i was told to squawk 1200 upon landing at freeway airport 10 minute(s) prior to my departure upon calling the new york flight service station specialist the night before to file an instrument flight rules flight plan for this flight the flight briefer was totally unfamiliar with the air defense identification zone procedures in the area i was flying into. She had to put me on hold numerous times to confer with a supervisor to ascertain the information that i needed to properly perform my flight into and out of the air defense identification zone airspace. I was not properly advised of the air defense identification zone procedures that were currently in effect for my route of flight also; upon initially departing from republic airport for the first leg of my flight i was also advised by new york departure that the instrument flight rules flight plans that i filed the night before were mistakenly entered into the system as visual flight rules flight plans.
output: FOLLOWING THE FSS BRIEFING; A C210 PLT; UNABLE TO CONTACT PCT TO OBTAIN A DISCRETE CODE AND ACTIVATE HIS DC ADIZ FLT PLAN WHILE ON THE GND AT W00; TAKES OFF WITHOUT ACTIVATING FLT PLAN.

input: We got our load closeout on taxi out and ran the chklist and were legal for standard power we then got a message saying that the close-out was canceled and were asked to get another one which we did. We were once again good for standard power and we took off. Shortly after takeoff we got a revision 02 to the closeout and the revision 03. Numbers were still good. output: B757 RECEIVES MULTIPLE FINAL WT MANIFEST REVISIONS AFTER ALREADY TAKING OFF; ONE OF WHICH CAUTIONED THEM NOT TO TAKE OFF.

input: Qa audit wrote shop up for material on hand with vendor expiration dates past. Historically [computer program] used to determine [company] shelf life. Per [company document] life not established or not controlled. My supervisor has ordered the shop to disregard [company] shelf life and go by vendor expiration dates. The material in question is mostly shrink tubing. Sign off sheets have been established to check vendor expiration dates and sign off that this has been accomplished. input: My employer has established a new sick leave policy that; for all practical purposes; forces pilots to fly while sick. In the past few months; company pilots have taken actual pay cuts of 45% or more. The plts' pension has been changed to a defined contribution plan. output: AN AIRLINE CAPT RPT ON NEW COMPANY SPONSORED PLAN OF LOSS OF PAY SUFFERED WHEN CALLING IN SICK; AND THUS LOSING PAY FOR A 5 HR PERIOD FROM THE PAY CAP OF 85 HRS AT ZZZ; US.

input: Inbound to runway(s) 24 and on extended ctrline 4 mile out. Heard local control making blind calls for a king air. Then local asked me for an updated position gave position rpt and advised local that there was a traffic information system warning for traffic at my 6 o'clock position 500 feet/foot above and descending less than 1 mile behind me. The king air overflew me at less than 400 feet/foot vertical separation. Controller has no radar in the twr! And the king air was not talking to the tower even though he was in the class d. When local control saw the king air; he gave me a left/right (directions) 360 degree turn. The king air contacted the tower and subsequently did a go around i talked to the local controller later in the day and found that this was another case of new york terminal radar approach control facility making a late handoff to the tower the king air pilot later told the local controller that he had me in sight! This airport is plagued by late handoffs from new york terminal radar approach control facility add to that; there is no radar in the bdr tower the fix is that somebody has to hold new york terminal radar approach control facility accountable to their letter of agreement on handoffs and; a radar screen is longitude overdue! Need i say more?
output: RV6 WAS INVOLVED IN A NMAC WHILE ON FINAL APCH. THE CONFLICTING ACFT WAS NOT IN RADIO CONTACT WITH TWR.

input: Apch to runway(s) 36l dfw. The aircraft prior to our approach rpted no problems at approximately 2500 feet/foot afl we encountered severe windshear with all appropriate aircraft warnings. We executed missed approach and requested climb to 3000 feet/foot with left/right (directions) turn to 090 degrees to avoid weather and continued turbulence severe. Tower then approach then departure frequencies all busy with missed approachs arrs; etc. Still in moderate to severe turbulence on clbout; we requested higher altitude and deviations for weather and given heading and 5000 feet/foot we maintained assigned instructions as we could; deviated approximately 400 feet/foot above or below due to turbulence and windshear. Finally found clear air; flew assigned headings and altitudes held for 10 minute(s) then diverted to austin without further incident. Returned to dfw after refueling and dfw weather cleared during windshear recovery and missed approach i exercised capt's authority/authorized to maintain safe control of acft.
output: AN ACR FK10 FLC ENCOUNTERED SEVERE TURB ON APCH RESULTING IN A GAR AND DIVERSION TO AN ALTERNATE. THE RPT RELATES THE DIFFICULTY THEY HAD WITH CTLING THE ACFT DURING THESE MANEUVERS IN SEVERE TURB.

input: On descent/arrival we got a #2 source off light. I called for the quick reference handbook first officer ran the checklist. After completing the checklist the source off light went out but the #2 bus off light came on. I called for the quick reference handbook after running the checklist the #2 bus off light stayed on. A short time later the autopilot disconnected. I tried to reengage it. It was inop. When i tried the electric trim i found it to be inop. So now i was hand flying and using the manual trim wheel to trim the aircraft. One by one we had additional failures on the arrival and approach. These additional failures were battery discharge light; both engine eec (electronic engine control) lights; first officer flight management computer inop; first officer inboard display unit inop; first officer outboard display unit inop; two out of four wing electric fuel pumps inop; left electric hydraulic pump inop; pseu (proximity switch electronic unit)  light on; speed brake do not arm light on; and lastly the trailing edge flap gauge. Upon selecting flaps for the approach we noticed that the flap gauge was not working. We believed the gauge to be inop because the right side of the forward instrument panel (where it resides) was basically dead and it felt like the flaps extended normally. The leading edge devices were verified to be extended via the overhead panel. Upon selecting flaps 10 on approach; the aircraft went into an unusual and unfamiliar shudder. Believing this to be a stall buffet i lowered the nose and increased power. I told the first officer that we must assume that we have no trailing edge flaps (meaning the flap gauge could indeed be correct). I asked him to bug me to 200 knots and select max auto brakes. We left the flap handle at 10; increased to 200 knots and landed. The landing was completely normal despite our non-normal configuration. We did not use excessive runway and made a normal turn off at high speed turn off.
output: B737 flight crew experienced a Gen 2 Source Off light during descent. After switching to the APU generator; the Transfer Bus Off light illuminated. After completing the Transfer Bus Off QRH; they started to experience numerous other electrical failures; among them the flap gauge. When flaps 10 was selected and the aircraft slowed; a rumble is felt and a flaps up landing procedure was followed.

input: On departure; we received an overheat condition on the left bleed air. I pulled the power back and called for the checklist. When running the checklist; the light went out. If the light went out; the checklist ended. Had it not; we were to land as soon as practical. We discussed diverting or continuing. We were well over landing weight; and i determined it was best to continue to burn fuel rather than risk an overweight landing. I have landed overweight in the past for emergencies; but we were not an emergency aircraft; and i did not want to create an emergency by doing so. I considered the situation over since we had taken care of the overheat. I continued to discuss our alternatives with the first officer. We had a bleed air switched off after the checklist was run; and we decided not to fly up to fl450 as planned.a single bleed air can support the cabin; and some bombardier aircraft only have one pack. If i had to do it again; i would have chosen to level at a lower altitude and diverted once our fuel was burned off. We descended lower later in the flight. Bleed leaks are a common issue in learjets. The indication went away and we had tested the fire detect system in flight again to make sure it was working properly. If there was a secondary problem; we were not covered by redundancy.
output: Learjet 60 Captain reported an overheat condition on the left bleed air. Light went out after running checklist. Flight continued to destination at lower altitude.

input: L brake seized up and locked during taxi and pulled craft to left/right (directions) -- left/right (directions) wing struck runway(s) sign and damaged left/right (directions) wing.
output: PA28 PLT HAS BRAKE MALFUNCTION WHILE TAXIING AT CCR; DEPARTS THE TXWY AND STRIKES A RWY SIGN DAMAGING THE R WING.

input: Number 3 engine oil was full on departure. By the time we reached 50w; we had less than 2 quarts remaining. Contacted [operations] as to where we should go in the event of an engine shutdown and determined we had fuel and acceptable weather to proceed to [alternate]. After further consideration and discussion with the fact that the engine was maintaining steady oil pressure and stable oil temperature much longer than we had anticipated; we elected to proceed to our original destination. On approach; the oil pressure started to fluctuate so i elected to secure the engine with the concurrence of my crew so there would be sufficient oil remaining to maintain a positive windmilling oil pressure and prevent further damage. We landed without incident.
output: A B747 Captain reported losing oil quantity on #3 engine enroute. Sufficient oil remained to operate the engine until approach was begun; at which the time the engine was shut down.

input: This was a maintenance test flight for annual completion; and for an engine change. Initial two hour break-in; at 4;000 mean sea level  six ground runs had taken place for leak checks. Some repairs where performed after each run. I was asked by the owner and maintenance supervisor to take the aircraft on its initial break-in flight per the engine manufactures recommendations (lycoming). The flight was to last two hours. For the test flight i had the aircraft fueled with 36 gallons of fuel. I should have completed the two hour flight with approximately 16 usable gallons of fuel. Flying a 1.5 to three nautical mile vor and dme (co-located) arc around the airport; one hour and fifty minutes into the flight; i switched to the right tank. The engine sputtered maybe thirty seconds after; i immediately switched back to the left tank. I moved the throttle and mixture controls. I verified that the electric fuel pump was on. Checked fuel gauges; they read just shy of ten gallons each; right where they should be. I don't trust them anyway. While doing this i turned for the airport and placed the aircraft in best glide speed. Declared an emergency with approach control; told them i was contacting the tower. Contacted the tower declared my emergency and intentions. The engine fired briefly during the downwind run to the airport. Altitude was now at 2;200 feet/foot  having reached the traffic pattern; i turned base at 2;000 feet/foot perpendicular to the numbers on an angling base turn to final aiming for the 1;000 feet/foot markers. The high winds 100 at 25 gusting to 35; began to push the aircraft to the west and away from the runway. As i was getting pushed west; i realized that my only recourse to make the runway or the airport was to increase airspeed. Dropping the nose i soon realized the runway was no longer an option as it was no longer in reach. I asked the tower to verify that my gear was down; they confirmed it was altitude now 1;800 feet/foot  seconds later i touched down approximately 400 feet/foot short of the runway in the approach grassy area; after landing i had approximately a 100 foot ground roll to a stop and the prop stopped. Normal shut down procedures commenced. After sitting still for several minutes i exited the aircraft. I verified no damage to the aircraft and no injuries. A check of both fuel tanks revealed they were empty. Company support personnel soon arrived at the scene. The top cowling was removed. Investigation revealed that the main fuel line to the engine driven fuel pump was not tightened. Fuel was leaking over board. The front landing gear was covered with fuel stains. The engine case near the fuel pump was stained with fuel. Further investigation revealed that the underside of the airframe was dripping and stained with fuel. The fuel line was tightened; fuel pump was activated. No leaks detected; engine started. Shut down engine. Cowling installed. We pulled the aircraft onto the runway. Engine restarted and the aircraft was driven under its own power back to the fixed-base operator  federal aviation administration investigation follows: a paperwork check revealed no issues. Statements where provided freely to the tower and the federal aviation administration investigation team. Fuel was drained from the tanks. Right tank had one quart of fuel. The left tank revealed about 2.5 gallons of fuel. After thoughts: i could have taken more fuel. This could have prevented or delayed the issue as this problem may not have revealed itself until the next flight perhaps on a cross country. Ten more minutes of flight is all that was required. More fuel was not taken in the event something did happen such as fire as this was a test flight. Three point six hours of fuel was taken for the two hour flight; more than well within regulations. Approximately 16 gallons of fuel was pumped overboard. Fuel gauges where not accurate; they should have read empty. Too many hands were the major reason for this event. No less than three mechanics worked on this engine not to mention the annual. Who did what;i hope is in the paperwork. Failure to tighten the line was inexcusable.
output: PA28 pilot reports engine failure during a test flight at 4;000 FT while orbiting the departure airport; field elevation 900 FT.  High winds foil the gliding approach and the aircraft lands short of the runway with no apparent damage.

input: Capt flying standard instrument departure i turned to 140 degree heading as directed by standard instrument departure at 400 feet/foot above ground level and continued to climb shortly thereafter; i was given 090 degree heading and immediately complied. Before reaching 090 degrees we were told to stop turn at 130 degrees then; shortly thereafter; we were given a 280 degree heading and told to call the federal aviation administration when i got to dfw. In talking to the federal aviation administration they said the noise sensitive area was overflown by me. I told him that i did everything exactly as depicted by the standard instrument departure and he said okay. We were heavy 144000 pounds which may have delayed the turn due to slower climb and longer takeoff roll.
output: DURING DEP FROM BOS; AN MD-S80 CREW RPTED THAT THEY FLEW THE SID AND FOLLOWED THE CTLR'S INSTRUCTIONS. THEY WERE TOLD BY THE FAA AT THEIR DEST THAT THEY HAD OVERFLOWN A NOISE SENSITIVE AREA.

input: It was dark and visibility was good. There was little or no ground traffic some military c130's were doing touch and goes on what i 'assumed' was runway(s) 14/32 (the active according to atis). Our taxi instructions were to exit the ramp on taxiway celsius and hold short of what i thought he said was 'the salt rwy.' as i was taxiing slowly northeasterly on taxiway celsius i'm looking for the 'salt rwy.' i had no idea what ground was talking about and the only runway(s) shown on my airport diagram were runway(s) 14/32; 05/23 and 01/19. Even after at least two requests for clarification i was still uncertain. As i approached runway(s) 14/32 i stopped well short in an effort to maintain extra caution and vigilance; as a result my tail was hanging over into the unmarked taxiway that i had just crossed and appeared to be clear of taxi traffic ground and tower were combined on one frequency as i came to a stop i heard tower tell someone to 'go around.' as i looked to my left/right (directions) i could see a c130 go missed from what appeared to be either a huge overshoot or an attempted landing on the taxiway i had just crossed and even yet encroached. Needless to say i was confused and feeling somehow responsible for someone else's go around. It became clear that what they were saying all along was 'assault rwy' and that this terminology somehow referred to the unmarked 'txwy' shown on my airport diagram. I ante meridiem submitting this to you because i don't know who else has the 'juice' to fix this potentially disastrous operations(s) as a result of my complaints; i thought the new plates would clrly identify this 'rwy;' it clearly is not. I also thought they would add some new signage on the field. As of january 2000 they had not. I find this completely inexcusable; to allow anyone (mil not excluded) to use an unmarked taxiway as a runway(s) and then to use non-standard verbiage while doing it. Additionally; i ante meridiem continually opposed to any use of 'combined' frequencies i firmly believe that a majority of our problems are either initiated or promulgated as a result of this practice. The controllers are just not able to handle multiple frequencies as efficiently as one when there is more than one aircraft in the area of their jurisdiction. I believe this situation is just another very good example of that fact.
output: A TAXIING DASSAULT FA20 IS GIVEN CONFUSING TAXI INSTRUCTIONS TO; '...HOLD SHORT OF 'SALT' RWY.' RPTR; PIC; HOLDS SHORT OF THE ACTIVE RWY; (RWYS 14/32) AND NOTES A C130 PERFORM A GO AROUND. THE FA20 WAS; OBVIOUSLY; IN THE LNDG AREA OF THE 'ASSAULT STRIP' AT YNG; OH.

input: Flight planned to operate an aircraft with auxiliary power unity (auxiliary power unit) inoperative. Zzz weather was moderate to severe icing; wind; snow. Night flight. Zzz1 (an airport in mountainous terrain) was forecasting wind; snow; freezing precipitation; icing. I decided that this environment was not the time to be flying around without an auxiliary power unity i called dispatch; conferenced with [maintenance]; and refused the aircraft. I then contacted zzz [operations] and advised of the refusal; and suggested we start looking for an alternate aircraft. One was coordinated- we flight planned; loaded the pax (passengers); and departed. Arrived zzz1 about 1 hour late. First officer (first officer) was included in my decision making process. I followed proper established procedure/ protocol for the refusal. I utilized company procedures to achieve a successful - and safe - resolution to the issue.
output: Flight Crew reported refusing an aircraft with an inoperative Auxiliary Power Unit due to anticipated severe weather.

input: A passenber boarded the aircraft with a bottle of beer and approached a first class passenber and said 'why are you withholding information from me?' the first class passenber looked at the man and did not respond. The man repeated the question and began laughing loudly. As the man approached me; i told him i needed to take his drink or he needed to get off the aircraft he said 'that man is withholding information from me;' at which point i smelled alcohol on his breath. I repeated my request; and he gave me the bottle and proceeded to his seat. I notified the #1 flight attendant and the capt that this man was obviously intoxicated. We then notified the gate agent that we needed someone removed and she immediately guessed who he was (which tells me he should have never been allowed to board in the first place). I asked the first class passenber intermediate fix he knew the man and he did not. I proceeded to the back of the aircraft to find where the man was seated and to monitor him. I located him and observed him and his companion 'play' fighting; which was causing them to bump the seats in front of them (which contained an infant in a car seat) and disturbing the passenber behind them as well. When i passed their row to ask them to calm down; they were using profanity; second officer i asked them to please watch their language as well. They complied; but continued their rowdy behavior; once i returned to the back of the aircraft when the agent came to close the door; she asked me to point him out; which i did; and she removed him from the flight i told her i thought the man's friend was just as bad; but nothing was done with him. The flight proceeded and numerous passenber complained that other passenber were drunk; rowdy and were using foul language.
output: CABIN ATTENDANT RPT; B757; ORD-LAS. INTOXICATED PAX BOARDED; CARRYING BEER BOTTLE AND WAS VERBALLY ABUSIVE. CAPT HAD PAX REMOVED.

input: Acr x was in a holding pattern at cetus intersection (djb 310 degs/36) and cleared to continue dsnt to 14000'. Due to deteriorating weather at cetus; air carrier x was reclred to sandusky vor and dme (co-located) and instructed to hold westbound on v6. Approaching sandusky vor and dme (co-located) we received xmissions re: lightning strikes at detroit metropolitan airport and the company ramp control tower being evacked due to a tornado. Our fuel was approaching the point where we were making the divert to grand rapids; our landing alternate. This was the point in time when we entered holding at sandusky. With numerous aircraft entering holding patterns; diverting to alternates; the uncertain status of the company ramp operation; the fuel situation on air carrier x and the considerable congestion on zob frequency as well as the workload on our #2 radio; the cockpit in air carrier x was very busy! We believed we had a clearance to 10000'; as that altitude was indicated on my scratchpad and set in the altitude alerter. Consequently i rpted entering the hold at sandusky and rpted 14000 for 10000' and then began a dsnt after a female controller's voice responded; 'acr x; roger.' an air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) flight also in the pattern at 12000' queried zob about our dsnt. At that time; air carrier x queried air traffic control intermediate fix we were cleared to 10000' and air traffic control responded 'negative;' at which time we immediately initiated a climb from 13600 back to 14000'. Shortly thereafter; air carrier x departed to our landing alternate at grand rapids; and en route zob advised us to contact them re: the incident. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr was contacted about his callback to air traffic control supervisor about altitude deviation. Rptr stated there were several company aircraft on the frequency some with similar a/n. The air route traffic control center supervisor informed the rptr an altitude deviation violation was going to be processed because the tape playback did not show any altitude change issued to air carrier x. Analyst suspects air carrier heard clearance for another company aircraft rptr stated he was not informed he conflicted with another aircraft analyst suspects less than standard separation with an aircraft holding at 13000'. Error detection program computer detected error. Air traffic control supervisor second call to rptr indicated that the rptr rpted with callsign leaving 14000 for 10000'; and the controller acknowledged with air carrier x call sign. Air traffic control supervisor stated that an operational error was being filed against the controller and a pilot deviation because air carrier x was never issued a dsnt clearance supplemental information from acn 156079: flight specifics: air carrier x from norfolk to detroit; detroit weather was severe thunderstorms and low visibility. Contributing factors: 1) hazardous weather severe thunderstorms throughout the area; heavy turbulence rain and lightning. 2) heavy radio chatter; numerous aircraft in holding; call signs were being cutoff; lots of requests for different airspace. 3) our fuel state was rapidly approaching divert level. 4) human factors: stress; fatigue; frustration brought on by weather delays. The capt was trying to talk to our company and both radios were jammed up. We heard a clearance to 10000' that we thought was for us. The capt called air carrier x descending from 14000 to 10000'; and we got an 'acr x; roger;' and i began a slow dsnt. An air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) in the pattern below us at 12000' asked center intermediate fix she had cleared us through their altitude she said negative. I immediately asked intermediate fix we were cleared to 10000'. She said negative. Second officer i started an abrupt climb from 13600' back to 14000'. Total time away form 14000' was approximately 30-40 secs. Corrective action: none required. A minor mistake was made--ours and the ctlrs--and we took positive and professional corrective action immediately to fix the problem factors affecting human performance: to the above human factors add fear. With lightning whirling around the aircraft and thunder second officer loud it could block out radio xmissions; yes i was little scared. I wish i was as perfect and as fearless as the air traffic control computer.
output: ACR X HAD LESS THAN STANDARD SEPARATION WITH ACFT Y. SYSTEM ERROR. ACR X UNAUTH ALT CHANGE. PLT DEVIATION.

input: I was on a routine training mission en route from fvx to hef with 2 non-plts on board. I had established contact with potomac terminal radar approach control facility for ra's (flt following) and was identified as radar contact in the vicinity of gve at 5500 feet/foot mean sea level direct to csn vor and dme (co-located) conditions were visual meteorological conditions with a layer of haze at about 4500 feet/foot mean sea level clear above with unrestr visibilities. Shortly after radar contact was established; the terminal radar approach control facility issued an advisory that traffic was at our 12 o'clock position descending we began to scan the area in front of the aircraft along with the front left/right (directions) seat passenber and the rear left/right (directions) seat passenber i scanned the area and could not identify the target's location. Just as i was beginning to refocus my scan to the 10-11 o'clock position the front seat passenber said; 'there it is!' i looked to my 1 o'clock high position and a single engine low wing aircraft probably a piper aircraft passed just above and to my left/right (directions) of the aircraft the aircraft had come from my upper left/right (directions) quadrant maybe 10-11 o'clock position and passed abeam my 4-5 o'clock position the aircraft was; second officer close that i could easily see the registration numbers in white over a red stripe. I estimated that i saw the aircraft for a fraction of a second before it disappeared over my left/right (directions) wing. I immediately rpted that i saw the aircraft and may have said it almost hit me. No further acknowledgement from the terminal radar approach control facility was noted. I routinely fly on either an instrument flight rules flight plan or receive ra's while flying. Under the circumstances; the training flight was for aerial observers involved in aerial surveillance operations(s) which required numerous changes in directions and altitudes hence; flying on an instrument flight rules flight plan was not a viable option. During this particular phase of flight the training for the observers had been completed longitude before this phase of the flight commenced. Following the training; i requested flight following and was receiving advisories. Prior to descent i commented that the once clear windscreen was covered with a lot of dead bugs. I told the front seat passenber that the dead bugs were causing problems with identing traffic because my eyes were focusing on the bugs rather than distant targets. Prior to the flight each passenber had been briefed on how to scan for traffic in the aircraft and that they were to rpt my 'perceived' conflicts to the pilot in command up until that point; they had both identified numerous targets. Following the traffic advisory from air traffic control we began scanning the sky. After i could not identify the target; i did not notify air traffic control that i did not have the traffic in sight. Instead i continued to scan and gave directions to the passenber to continue to look for a descending target at our 12 o'clock position anticipating that the aircraft was very close; based upon the elapsed time of the advisory; 1-2 minute(s) i placed both hands on the controls and took the aircraft off autoplt with the anticipation of maneuvering the aircraft to avoid the target. We continued to look and did not hear any communicationss from air traffic control for either our aircraft or other aircraft in their sector. In retrospect; i should have immediately rpted that i did not have the traffic in sight in the hopes that air traffic control would reissue the target's new position issue a traffic alert or recommend a change in heading or altitude once the passenber yelled she had the aircraft in sight; i spotted the plane; however; i could not react. By the time i identified the plane; the plane was out of sight and i could not dive or turn the aircraft away from the target. I was surprised at how suddenly the aircraft appeared and was even more surprised that i did not have a quick enough reaction time to maneuver our aircraft to avoid a possible impact even though i was prepared to do second officer the combination of our high wing aircraft and the descending acft's low-wing contributed to the near midair collision. I perceived that i was at a safe enough altitude near the gve vor and dme (co-located) because i wrongly believed that most aircraft would start their dscnts further out to land at the few airports in the area. The lack of airports in the area gave me the impression that gve was more on an en route navigational aid where aircraft would generally be flying at an en route phase rather than an approach phase. Although i recognized that extra vigilance wasrequired near vor's; i felt that i was at a safe altitude and felt reassured that since i was in radar contact i would have helped in identing targets. Our aircraft is equipped with a global positioning system a satellite weather downlink and a mode south transponder in this instance; the traffic information system (tis) was not available since i was too federal aviation regulation from the washington dc class b airspace infrastructure. I was not relying on the system since it was flagged with the term 'tfc unavailable.' had the 'tis' system been expanded to outlying areas bordering the washington class b airspace; the 'tis' system would have alerted me to the target and that it was not actually at my 12 o'clock position but was instead at my 10-11 o'clock position i could have maneuvered the aircraft to better identify the target.
output: A HIGH WING SEL ACFT AND A LOW WING DSNDING SEL ACFT PASS WITHIN 100 FT OF EACH OTHER AT 5500 FT EVEN THOUGH ATC TA WAS GIVEN.

input: On bridge flight management system visual runway(s) 28r sfo; closely spaced approach with aircraft y. We were lead aircraft with aircraft y maintaining visual with us. Spacing was very close and trailing aircraft appeared to be in a 'sucked' (mil term) position relative to us. I saw the aircraft at our 7 o'clock position lost sight (although he was following us) and received a 'tfc; tfc' alert. Before the first officer could secure the traffic mode; we received a 'clb; clb' resolution advisory since the descend resolution advisory was inhibited due to our altitude and believing the intruder to be above us; i ignored the resolution advisory shortly thereafter; i reacquired visual on the other aircraft as he corrected back to runway(s) 28l ctrline; passing us in the process. At no time did we cross the extended ctrline of runway(s) 28r; and in fact purposely set up to the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) we had a slightly overshooting crosswind which should have caused the intruder to undershoot. I have extensive military experience in formation flying (3 yrs jet instructor pilot in multi-plane formation) and would estimate our separation to have been 2-3 wingspans prior to my losing visual with the intruder; prior to our resolution advisory i ante meridiem extremely upset with the intruding aircraft crew for failing to maintain separation while at the same time putting my aircraft into a 'box' where the proscribed procedure (a go around from landing confign) was a questionable one due to the proximitypa to the ground and the inhibition of descending resolution advisory when i believed the other aircraft to be above.
output: A319 CREW AND ANOTHER ACR ACFT HAVE A CLOSELY SPACED SIDE BY SIDE APCH ON THE 28'S AT SFO.

input: Flt was scheduled to depart iad at xa30z for zzz. The capt likes to be very involved in the flight planning stage. The capt is aware that the iad station prefuels the aircraft hours before the capt arrives for flight planning. The plane is often prefueled to the wrong amount since this capt regularly works with his dispatcher to fine-tune the flight plan originally proposed by the dispatcher. Being concerned that the plane will likely be prefueled to an amount in excess of the amount the capt is planning for the trip; he makes a call to the zone controller to advise not to fuel until the capt has finalized the fuel load. This heads-up call was made from the motel on the night before the flight the morning of the flight the capt called zone control to remind them that he had called the night before with instructions not to fuel the plane until the fuel load was finalized. This call was made 3 hours before scheduled departure the capt offered that it was safe to prefuel up to but no more than 40000 pounds of fuel. The crew arrived at the flight office and started flight planning. The release was signed for an approved fuel load of 44000 pounds (this was a reduction of 19000 pounds from the dispatcher's first suggestion due to carrying ferry fuel). The capt was concerned about en route turbulence and wanted the plane to be light enough to climb above the turbulence area. There was predicted moderate turbulence between fl240 and fl370 in the second 1/2 of the flight the flight plan; with the ferry fuel; was restricting the flight to fl350. The route was through the turbulence area. By reducing the planned fuel load to 44000 pounds the flight would be capable of fl390 initially; and then fl410 approaching the moderate turbulence box. The dispatcher and capt agreed to make the final fuel load 44000 pounds instead of 63000 pounds the capt called control to inform them that it was now ok to fuel. He was informed by control that they had already fueled the plane to 63000 pounds the capt told control that with 70 minute(s) to go; there was time to remove the excess fuel. Control refused to do it. When reminded that they were told twice; with plenty of notice not to fuel; control told the capt that it did not matter; he was not going to defuel. The plane had been fueled almost 2 1/2 hours before scheduled pushback. At the plane; the capt was approached by a flight manager and the station chief pilot after hearing the story; the capt was told that it was important to get the flight out on time; and that the fuel could not be removed. The capt said that while not unsafe; the excess fuel was making the flight less safe than he had planned with the dispatcher; and that the fuel had to be removed to clear a turbulence box. When the chief pilot could not convince the capt to take the existing fuel load; the capt suggested that he could be replaced by another capt willing to take the fuel load. Second officer as to keep the flight close to schedule; the chief pilot removed the capt from the flight instead of removing the excess fuel. Problem aircraft was prefueled to a fuel load that was not approved by the capt. Solution: program computer with a fuel block flight command. This command could be used up to 48 hours before pushback; only by capts interested in planning their fuel loads jointly with their dispatchers. The fuel sheet would be blocked from printing. No one would be able to override this command. The command would deactivate after 1 of 2 events: 1) the capt signs the release; or 2) at 45 minute(s) to go; the fuel sheet would automatically release with the dispatcher's suggested fuel load; intermediate fix the capt had not yet signed the release. In this case; capt's authority/authorized and his concern about turbulence was ignored. The capt gave sufficient notice not to prefuel. The station ignored the capt's instructions. Further; the company wanted the flight out on time second officer much that they preferred to remove the capt and find one who was willing to take their fuel load. The chief pilot when asked by the capt; admitted that he had not reviewed any weather charts prior to confronting the capt about fuel.
output: PIC'S DELAYED FUELING REQUEST IS IGNORED BY THE OPS DEPT WITH THE PIC REPLACED AFTER HE REFUSES TO ACCEPT THE ACFT WITH MORE FUEL LOADED THAN HE DESIRED. CAPT OF ACR B757-200 HAS FUELING REQUEST IGNORED BY THE OPS DEPT AT IAD; AND IS REPLACED AFTER HE REFUSES ACFT THAT IS LOADED WITH MORE FUEL THAN HE DESIRED.

input: We were pushing back from a gate for departure cannot see the tug from the cockpit; but we were in direct communications with the driver through the intercom. Aircraft engs were started during the pushback. Aircraft came to a brief stop then started forward. This is normal as the tug driver ctrs the aircraft on the taxi ctrline. We were never told to 'set brakes' which is standard procedure at the completion of a pushback. Through the intercom could hear heavy breathing and cursing. At that point the aircraft slowly veered to the left/right (directions) then heard over the intercom; 'no brakes.' i assumed that the driver meant the tug had lost its brakes and was rolling free. Did not want to damage the aircraft nose gear by hitting the brakes too hard; assuming that the tug was still attached to the aircraft second officer the aircraft brakes were eased on and the aircraft came to a stop. It was then that the crew was informed that the towbar had actually broken and we had rolled over the top of the tug. Immediately called over the very high frequency radio for an ambulance. However; before it arrived; we were informed that the driver of the tug was not hurt. At this point with help on the way; we shut down the engs. As people came to the aircraft the intercom was disconnected. We had to call over the very high frequency radio to find out what was happening. We did not know the status of the driver; the tug; or the aircraft we were eventually towed back into the gate. I feel this could have been prevented intermediate fix standard phraseology by the pushback crew had been used. Company has recently hired people with little or no aircraft experience to push back aircraft intermediate fix at the first sign of trouble the crew had been informed of the problem or been told to set the brakes as is standard; the whole thing would have ended with just a broken towbar. Although it should not be needed because of the intercom system a wing walker that is visible to the crew could also have prevented this situation.
output: FLT CREW REPORTS TOW BAR BREAKAGE DURING PUSH BACK AND ENGINE START; ALLOWING ACFT TO ROLL OVER THE TUG. COMMUNICATION FROM TUG DRIVER IS NOT TIMELY OR HELPFUL.

input: Flt requested to climb to fl370. Zfw asked intermediate fix able to climb to fl370 in 4 minute(s) capt responded yes. Cleared to climb to fl370 by zfw. Out of fl355; asked intermediate fix above fl370 in 90 seconds and i said yes. Out of fl360 we knew we could not make the time limit we told zfw. Zfw instructed us to turn 60 degrees left/right (directions) for traffic the turn reduced our climb rate to 200 feet per minute no traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alert and we observed traffic inside of 10 mile on radar as we finally leveled at fl370. Chop (light) also reduced climb out of fl355.
output: UNABLE TO CLB TO ALT IN THE TIME RESTR GIVEN AN A320 IS VECTORED CLR OF CONFLICTING TFC.
