The flight proceeded normally to destination. The captain and first officer discussed the flight plan cruise altitude of fl220. High task loading occurred during the climb due to the short duration of the flight. The air traffic control query created doubt to the flight crew as to whether we had received and responded to the air traffic control climb clearance properly; particularly with regard to the reduced ability to see the altitude selection window on the flight control unit and the airbus altitude window potential for digit 'skipping'.they 'why' of the event is because air traffic control queried the crew about the assigned cruise altitude; therefore it appears that air traffic control did know or remember what altitude they cleared the flight too. Improve the illumination of the flight control unit unit altitude window.
output: A320 captain reported that an air traffic control communication issue combined with glare and visibility issues on the flight deck resulted in an altitude deviation.

input: Weather was bad at tpa and with 100 foot ceilings reported. We were number 3 being vectored for the instrument landing system runway 18l. The first aircraft had gone missed approach and it seemed as though the controller was unsure of that aircraft's intentions. Number 2 was another carrier ahead of us that air traffic control broke off the approach and gave them vectors back around (possibly due to the aircraft ahead). We were told to fly 180 to the final approach fix and had just been vectored across final and given a reintercept heading from the east side of the localizer course. We were then told that the approach lights for runway 18l were inoperative. The current automatic terminal information service did not reflect that nor did the notams that we had for the field. The captain elected to hand fly the aircraft with the head up display for the clear air turbulence ii approach into runway 18l. The approach was flown to near minimums with runway lighting acquisition and an uneventful landing. I think that the approach controllers should have been more proactive as to the lack of available instrument lighting for the approach to that runway. We were not informed until after the approach had already begun as to any failure of airport equipment. Clear air turbulence ii approaches are flown so infrequently that maybe further training as to required equipment would be helpful.
output: B737 flight crew is informed during a clear air turbulence ii instrument landing system approach that the approach light system is out of service. Approach is continued and runway lights are acquired prior to minimums.

input: Had incorrect barometer (30.27 vs 29.55) setting which resulted in leveling off approximately 700 [ft] below assigned altitude of 13;000 feet/foot while descending into chicago airspace. Received a message from dispatch prior to descend stating 'attn crews: automatic terminal information service is reporting old info. Please check with dispatch for updated weather the weather request page is still accurate.' we read the message but did not realize this was 1- specifically for us and 2 was referring to chicago automatic terminal information service we sent for and received chicago automatic terminal information service just prior to descent which gave the barometer setting as 30.27. We did not notice the time on the arrival information was invalid. Shortly after this we received descent instructions including changes to crossing altitudes and speeds which created additional activities while descending. While inputting the arrival restrictions we passed transition level; set 30.27; completed the checklist and then leveled off at what we thought was 13;000 feet/foot approach air traffic control contacted us; asked to confirm our altitude and informed us the correct altimeter was 29.55. We reset our altimeters and climbed back to 13;000 feet/foot we requested another automatic terminal information service which was completely different from the first one and also incorrect. We listened to the audio automatic terminal information service which gave the correct info and said at the end that the automatic terminal information service was 'unreliable.'the message from dispatch could have been clearer in describing the problem we were about to encounter which i have never in my entire aviation career encountered before (display of completely incorrect automatic terminal information service information). For instance: 'attn flight x: chicago digital automatic terminal information service is invalid or inaccurate. Here is the current correct weather at kord: do not rely on the automatic terminal information service from kord!' plain language would have alerted us to the gravity of the situation. Chicago should also not send known incorrect weather information via digital automatic terminal information service they should shut the system down until it works correctly as expectation bias of always receiving the most up to date automatic terminal information service crept into this situation compounding it.
output: A crew was on the ord trtll 2 area navigation leveled at 13;000 feet/foot and was queried about their altitude then notified the digital automatic terminal information service was wrong and their aircraft was 700 feet/foot low. Digital automatic terminal information service nationwide was apparently in error.

input: Level at fl370 left/right (directions) aft entry door light on. Pressurization was normal. Per quick reference handbook procedure; cabin crew was instructed to verify door handle was closed. It was slightly raised; and per procedure; cabin crew moved handle to closed position. Warning light initially extinguished; but re- illuminated. Cabin crew reported handle rose up again. Per quick reference handbook procedure; as handle was not in closed position; we elected to divert. Dispatch was notified and they concurred with divert decision.
output: B737-800 captain reports a left aft entry door light on at fl370. The cabin crew finds the door handle slightly raised and moves it to the closed position extinguishes the light. The door warning light returns and the handle is found slightly raised again and elects to divert for maintenance.

input: During climb out we got a master warning and tail compartment temperature high light. The first officer was the pilot flying and i confirmed that he would continue flying while i ran the procedure. We accomplished the red box items and then i ran the appropriate procedure. The warning light did not go out after two minutes; as specified in the checklist; so we declared an emergency and got vectors back to our departure airport. During the descent; after power was reduced; the high temperature light went out. We then had some pressurization problems including a pressurization flow light. We added sufficient power to keep the aircraft pressurization descending schedule. We advised center and approach that we wanted crash fire rescue equipment to meet the aircraft to confirm there was no fire or high temperature in the tail before taxiing to a gate. I talked to the flight attendants and advised them of the situation and gave them ten minutes to accomplish their primary emergency checklist without brace commands. I made a public address to the passengers explaining that we'd had a warning light; which was now extinguished; but that we still needed to turn back and for them to pay attention to the flight attendant briefing. I also mentioned that we would be met on the ground by airport safety vehicles as a routine precaution. We accomplished the emergency landing checklist; briefed the visual approach and finished the descent and mechanical landing checklists. We accomplished a short visual approach to runway 28 and turned off at the tango taxiway where arrf inspected us and saw no evidence of continued high temperatures in the tail area. They then followed us to the gate. Maintenance found a broken clamp from the pack system coalescer bag which was porting bleed air into the tail compartment.
output: An md80 returned to the departure airport following receipt of a tail compartment high temp warning.

input: While cruising at fl380 we noticed the a side engine driven hydraulic pump low pressure light illuminate intermittently. We pulled out the quick reference handbook to review procedures when the light illuminated steady. We completed quick reference handbook procedures and noticed the a side fluid level at 18%. Pressure was normal at 3030 [psi]. We then began to review the quick reference handbook procedure for a system loss. At this point we noticed level continuing to drop. We notified dispatch via automatic communications addressing & reporting system and after a few minutes dispatch recommended diversion to [a nearby alternate]. We concurred and notified air traffic control of our intention. We then notified the flight attendants of our plan and instructed them to begin securing the cabin. We then notified the passengers. Since we did not completely lose the system; we were able to lower the gear normally. We informed air traffic control [of our runway preference]. They informed us that [coordination would need to be made] to be able to use that runway. [atc was advised] and we landed without incident; taxied off the runway and were inspected by crash fire rescue equipment we were then released by crash fire rescue equipment to taxi to the gate where the logbook was filled out and maintenance notified. Passengers completely understood as we switched aircraft and eventually departed uneventfully. First officer and crew performed flawlessly.
output: B737-700 captain reported diverting to an alternate airport after fluid loss in the 'a' hydraulic system.

input: We were conducting the area navigation 27 approach in day visual meteorological conditions conditions to san with a tailwind during most of the arrival and initial approach phase. The captain was the pilot flying. When cleared for the approach he followed the typical routine of arming approach mode which quickly captured lateral and vertical guidance and began descending on the glideslope. At the time we were at flaps one with about 10-15 kts buffer under the flaps 1 redline of 235. Because of the tailwind and the somewhat steeper than normal approach angle; the aircraft started to accelerate after capturing the glideslope and quickly oversped the flaps by approximately 5-10 kts. The captain began to intervene immediately with use of the speedbrakes but the acceleration trend carried us into the red line. After removing the aircraft from approach mode and taking us off the glideslope; the aircraft slowed below the red line and we continued configuring and landed normally. We wrote up the overspeed at the gate in san.i believe that the core reason for this was a misunderstanding on the part of the pilot flying (pilot flying) about what the aircraft would do once approach was armed. The pilot flying said repeatedly that he thought the aircraft wouldn't overspeed with the automation set up with a selected speed and approach captured. Because of the tailwind and the aircraft's priority to follow the glideslope without regard to selected speed; an overspeed was possible. He may have been thinking of flight envelope protections in normal mode which would have protected an extreme overspeed but will allow the aircraft into the redline before they intervene.as the post meridiem (pilot monitoring); i should have spoken up when approach mode was about to capture the glideslope to caution that an overspeed was possible. We had briefed during the approach briefing that a threat in san was the likelihood of being fast and high but i will add in the future that flap overspeeds; especially on the initial stage of the approach are possible. Additional emphasis in training about automation priorities where the aircraft will follow vertical guidance without regard to airspeeds may also be beneficial.
output: A321 first officer reported flap overspeed during a coupled approach with a tailwind.

input: Aircraft x checked in climbing to 14;000 feet on a 017-heading. The heading was unreadable to me. Radar controller cleared to climb; he was pointed out to sector 47 already. The pilot checked back and made a correction to the initial heading he gave us; he said instead he was on a 180 heading. The radar controller acknowledged and cleared the aircraft direct buzrd; on course. Aircraft read back and verified what sounded to us as buzrd. Shortly i noticed the aircraft was making a sharp right turn into sector 47's airspace. I notified the sector 18 radar controller immediately and initiated a call them with sector 47 radar controller. I initiated a point out as i didn't know what the aircraft was doing; heard the sector 18 radar controller issue a left turn which i passed along to 47; and the sector 47 radar controller stopped his traffic at 16;000 feet. After that call; we quizzed the pilot as to what had happened. He advised us that he was cleared via the blzzr3 standard instrument departure while we showed him cleared via the ssoxs4 departure. Once we verified his routing; we got him back on course. It turns out the flight plan the aircraft showed as issued and what the pilot had in front of him were two different things. The pilot says he was cleared on the blzzr3; and he was reading back direct blzzr. To us; the aircraft would have no reason to read back blzzr; it's not on the ssoxs4 departure and it sounded to me like an odd pronunciation of buzrd. Also note that it seemed that the co-pilot and pilot were sharing radio responsibilities and i remember hearing two distinct voices reading back at different times.the controller in charge (cic) happened to be there to observe the whole event and he took over the situation of discovering what happened with the routing.change buzrd fix to something not similar to other departure fixes; in this case blzzr. This should never be an issue if the aircraft's routing is correct; but they sound very similar and this is now a confirmed issue.
output: Zbw controller reported of a similar sounding fix that the pilot had entered and was flying towards. Aircraft was questioned and the confusion of the fix name was determined to be part of the problem. Air traffic control had one clearance the crew had a different one.

input: Acr x appeared 3 vor and dme (co-located) north of gqe as a real return. Air carrier x was actually 60 mile nw of gqe. It appears that this must have been some form of second time around.
output: Mem terminal radar approach control facility controller described single false radar target incident.

input: While being vectored for an approach (ils 5 lbt); the controller informed me there was no traffic following me; and i said i would probably miss and follow the published missed approach procedure. However; actual weather (asos was reporting 500' broken) turned out to be a thin scattered layer - no problem landing. Lbt is a non-towered airport with no remote communications outlet; and i had weak or no cell phone reception to call to cancel instrument flight rules so i taxied back and departed into good visual meteorological conditions called fay approach control to simply resume the missed approach procedure. I was informed there was a conflict; and in a subsequent conversation with the air traffic control facility was reminded to ask for a through clearance if spending any time on the ground. With hindsight; once i was airborne again; it was my mistake to use the term 'missed approach'; i should have just called to cancel the instrument flight rules and request clearance for the next leg. Still; i tied up the airspace for less time than if i had remained on the ground and searched for a land line telephone to cancel instrument flight rules on.
output: Ifr aircraft on instrument landing system 5 approach to lbt elects to land and taxi back for departure without cancelling instrument flight rules or notifying air traffic control of intentions.

input: Clbing out of pit; mid day; thunderstorms many aircraft deviating; we got an resolution advisory traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning to descend at approximately 1200-1500 feet per minute (we were climbing at about 3000 fpm.) we followed the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii instructions. Upon calling pit departure to rpt the resolution advisory the controller would not acknowledge it. I; as capt; finally refused the frequency change until he acknowledged my resolution advisory he finally said there was an air carrier flight above me and that 'there wasn't a prob.' upon speaking to his supervisor later; i confirmed this controller was swamped; working 2 sectors with weather deviations going on. Supervisor said he was overseeing this controller but he initially used the phrase 'i came over to him....' there was not enough help for this controller and he was definitely overloaded! During this type of wx/tfc situation all hands should be on deck.
output: B757 crew had a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory in pit class b airspace.

input: Launched balloon heading approximately wsw at 8 knot(s) special event was in effect and i followed the special event balloon for approximately 45 minute(s) across the first section of the lake. The special event balloon landed; i threw at the target and flew on seeking first available landing site. No sites available and overwater once again; with 40% fuel remaining; i flagged down a 70 feet/foot cabin cruiser to tow me 1/2 mile to shore. I landed on the deck; secured the basket and we proceeded for the marina. Once near the shoreline; i released the balloon from the deck and flew to the shoreline. I landed at a lakeside house without injury or damage to my aircraft no emergency services were required or contacted. I believe that i used poor judgement concerning direction of wind and speed for this flight i could have possibly landed safely prior to seeking the target throw; but failed to do second officer accordingly. This was my second flight in this area; but a new direction to me. I did feel that competition and restrs to landing within 1500 feet/foot of a target area contributed to my situation i do feel that i made all the correct decisions once i discovered that i was potentially in trouble near official sunset that evening. I feel i stayed in control of the situation and kept calm through the ordeal. I regret that it probably could have been avoided.
output: Hot air balloon pilot landed on boat deck after being over lake and running low on fuel. Boat went to shore and pilot flew balloon off landing nearby on shore.

input: We were turning base to final for the visual to runway(s) 1 at dca and extending flaps for landing while extending flaps 10 degrees we got a leading edge flap in-transit light on the forward instrument panel while we were on final approach we then broke off the approach and got radar vectors while we were doing the irregular procedure we accomplished the 'leading edge flap transit light (forward panel) on' irregular chklist. We then tried to contact dispatch via voice and were not successful. We could hear them; however; they couldn't hear us. We were at 3000 feet/foot mean sea level and i suspect that this was part of the problem in being at a low altitude i then consulted the irregular landing distribution chart that told us we needed 3500 feet/foot for landing which was ok for our runway(s) we were finally able to get an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message off to dispatch and told them our problem and that we felt it was ok to land at dca. They agreed and; in turn; declared an emergency on our behalf. Additionally; we declared an emergency ourselves. I told the flight attendants to prepare a cabin advisory. We then told air traffic control we were ready to land and landed uneventfully. On rollout; i had the first officer tell the flight attendants to remain seated. This action was probably not necessary; seeing that i had the cabin prepare for an advisory. We then pulled off into the runway(s) 19 run-up pad and requested the emergency equipment to inspect the brakes; which turned out to be fine. We then proceeded to the gate and were met by maintenance i then called dispatch and conferred with them.
output: A b737 capt rpted that a leading edge flap problem caused him to execute the missed approach at dca and then to declare an emergency and return for lndg.

input: After landing on a recent flight to lax i noticed an area of concern while taxiing. After clearing runway(s) 25l on high speed ap and proceeding on taxiway air conditioning / alternating current via the taxiway ctrline green lights we held short of the runway(s) 25r hold line at taxiway p by approximately 50-75 feet/foot it is my belief that had we proceeded any further and brought the b777 to a stop with the nose just short of the hold line the left/right (directions) wingtip would be in a position to penetrate the extended hold short line; impinging upon the runway(s) 25r protected area. The angle the air conditioning / alternating current taxi line approachs the hold line on taxiway p is very shallow and unsafe in my opinion. Not only do i believe the wingtip extends into the protected area of the runway(s) but from that position the pilots have no view of the approach end of runway(s) 25r when they do get clearance to cross the runway(s) due to the necessity to taxi straight forward prior to making any turn in order to assure left/right (directions) main wheel clearance from the taxiway edge lights. It's not until they crossed the hold line a good amount and are basically on the runway(s) that they finally get a safe view. The taxi line/green lights for the turn from taxiway air conditioning / alternating current to the taxiway p hold short line needs to be an arc with a much rounder radius allowing the aircraft to be in a near perpendicular position to runway(s) 25l; never giving a wingtip a chance to protrude beyond the hold short line as well as having the tail remain clear of the runway(s) 25l protected area. By observing the rubber scuff marks on the taxiway federal aviation regulation removed from the painted ctrline/green lights it's obvious many pilots are ignoring the taxiway ctrline and establishing their own turn radius to put themselves in a safe position at the hold short point. This shouldn't have to be the case; it's a brand new taxiway and should be properly striped and lit.
output: A b777 pilot believes the acft's right wing extends onto lax runway(s) 25r while holding short on taxiway p because the taxiway centerline arcs toward the rwy.

input: The workload on all shift dispatch desks has reached unacceptably high levels. In addition; we are experiencing an unprecedented amount of computer problems i have not worked a single shift in months without experiencing some form of computer problem some severe enough to impact safety and some more minor in nature. We are not getting any improvement or even acknowledgement of the problems from management or those in it (the computer people). We spend a significant amount of time on the phone just trying to get someone to address the computer problems we are experiencing; our point of contact (it) is frequently unwilling to call programmers at home or disturb them while we are experiencing significant safety ramifications from the loss of automatic communications addressing & reporting system flight planning; or current weather data. Today when i arrived on shift at xf30 ante meridiem the previous shift dispatchers had been trying to get flight plans all night. They had called it repeatedly all night longitude beginning at xa00 post meridiem yet it was not until xh30 ante meridiem that a programmer was called by it at home to address the problem today; while i was buried by workload resulting from a severe front impacting se alaska; surface winds gusting to 50 knot(s) with multiple diversions; an inoperative fuel truck and red turbulence plots requiring altitude changes. We lost all automatic communications addressing & reporting system data. Flts departed everywhere; including the stations most impacted by weather and i had no information on fuel loads; etc. It was not until over an hour into the outage that it called a programmer to correct the situation and this was only after being notified by the chief dispatcher that he was going to escalate rpt of the problem to his director. This type of outage or problem can be handled when workload is at acceptable levels; but at current levels the situation rapidly escalates. We had a safety audit performed which showed dispatchers working too many flts without the ability to get relief. Over time we have added flts and aircraft as well as significant additional responsibilities to the dispatcher. We are deluged with memos and pop-up warnings which alert us to ever changing requirements; we are not given any tools to reduce workload but instead are frequently expected to perform increasingly time consuming tasks. In the past; the chief dispatcher could relieve the dispatcher of some workload; this is no longer a viable option since their duties have kept pace with ours. Chief dispatchers are routinely consumed by flow programs; air traffic control conference calls; ferry flts and charters; etc. Dispatch has become the point of contact for all calls; even those totally unrelated to safety for the fodo; yet workload continues to increase. Whether it is slippery runway(s) criteria; braking action; extended range twin operations global positioning system turbulence plots; increased minimum equipment list penalties being flown for days; leg specific tankering which requires pulling multiple flight plans; weather and load criteria impacting tankering; necessitating increased communications with operations(s) weight and balance with more lapses in operations(s) falling to dispatch; there are many more examples not cited here. The bottom line is; dispatch has become saturated with work and it is now to a point where safety is being compromised knowingly or unknowingly on a daily basis. We desperately need to reduce workload; either by increased staffing or by acquiring much more sophisticated and reliable tools. The issues with reliability of dispatch products is critical. A contributing cause of this problem is the reliance on in-house products which are both inferior by design and have extremely poor support. We need to establish a much higher priority for the reliability of all computer programs; in my opinion this can only be done in a move away from in-house products. Ultimately we should have a system in place to continuously monitor workload; just as total numbers of pilots and flight attendants are tied to aircraft numbers; second officer should the total numbers of dispatchers.
output: Dispatcher rpts increasing workloads caused by understaffing and poorly maintained and dated computer sys.

input: At 300' on takeoff electronic centralized aircraft monitoring aural; master and overhead warnings of smoke in minimum equipment bay. Made immediate landing evacuated aircraft on rwy.
output: Acr wdb experienced smoke related emergency immediately after takeoff return land and passenger evacuation on rwy.

input: During our departure from teterboro; nj; we were assigned the ruudy 2 area navigation while proceeding on the ruddy 2; the new york departure controller asked if we were able to go to elvae intersection. The new york controller spoke very quickly and i was not exactly sure what he had said to us. I thought the new york controller said the elbee intersection. I stated back to him that our clearance was to white intersection and he gave us a heading to intercept the 350 radial off of colt's neck vor and dme (co-located) the frequency for the colt's neck vor and dme (co-located) is not on the ruudy 2 standard instrument departure because it is a area navigation standard instrument departure however; it is on the teterboro six standard instrument departure i tuned in the frequency for the captain flying the aircraft and he used the radio magnetic indicator bearing pointer making a turn to intercept the 350 radial. He actually intercepted the 010 degree radial of colt's neck. The new york controller caught the captain's error and told us to fly 230 degree heading to intercept the 350 degree radial. After climbing to our assigned altitude; i reviewed the ruudy 2 standard instrument departure chart. It was now apparent to me what the new york controller had asked earlier when he inquired if we were able to go to the elvae intersection; which is depicted on the ruudy 2 standard instrument departure our confusion was in the way the new york controller spoke so quickly and was not clear in his direction to us and his pronunciation. Our error was not realizing that the new york controller had said elvae and the captain flying intercepted the wrong radial to colt's neck. In the future; i will double check all sid's to become more familiar with the routing and the captain flying will go to short range navigate, navigation and will use the bearing pointer only as a back up.
output: A corporate jet pilot reported departing on the teb ruudy 2 area navigation and being asked to fly to elvae intersection which the reporter confused with the elbee intersection because of rapid speech and unfamiliarity. The controller wanted aircraft on the col 350 left/right (directions) which is described on the teb6 sid.

input: During pre-flight of aircraft; it was determined that due to excessive amounts of airframe ice; aircraft needed to be de-iced. After being de-iced and received de-ice report; and told that aircraft was clean; we continued with taxi whereupon we noticed ice still adhering to the windshield wipers. I decided to return to the gate to have the first officer further inspect aircraft for other signs of ice and found aircraft still had large amounts of ice adhering to the tail; winglets; flaps and radome. I informed the ground crew that the aircraft needed to be de-iced again whereupon aircraft was de-iced for a second time. I instructed first officer to perform another check and he reported ice still adhering to airframe. After this i spoke directly to the gentleman de-icing the aircraft who informed me that it was his first time de-icing an aircraft and asked what else he should do. I explained company's 'clean aircraft' policy and informed him that he needed to get out of truck to reach some parts of the airframe and how all ice needed to be removed in order to depart safely. After 3 attempts at de-icing the airframe it was determined that the aircraft was finally safe for flight operations. De-ice ground crew should receive better training on use of and procedures for de-icing aircraft. Supervision should be provided by the station to ensure these events do not transpire again.
output: Crj200 flight crew discovered ice on aircraft after having been de-iced. Flight returned to gate for additional de-icing.

input: I would like to highlight a potential safety issue related to air-to-ground communications in a specific geographical area. In the airspace above mrb (martinsburg; west virgina); within the class d airspace; according to the tower controller i queried; effective communications can not be established with the controlling air traffic control approach/departure facility (potomac terminal radar approach control facility pct) until reaching approximately 2;200 mean sea level  yet; upon departing mrb; the tower will typically instruct the departing aircraft to contact pct upon leaving 1;500 mean sea level approximately. During my flight (in a c172) with a student; i was executing a published missed approach on the vor and dme (co-located) a approach (mrb) climbing to 3;000 mean sea level  i was instructed to contact potomac by the tower; and did so; but there was a minute or so (prior to reaching 2;200 ft) when effective communications were not available/established. The result is that i got the sense that the potomac controller had perhaps given me clearance information (pertaining to my next requested clearance; the instrument landing system for runway 26) that i did not receive. He presumably heard me well enough to respond with clearance information; yet i could not effectively hear him. Received communications were weak and broken until reaching 2;200 feet/foot  as such; confusion between me and the controller resulted. Upon reaching 3;000 feet/foot i held altitude momentarily and did not climb to the 3;400 initial approach altitude associated with the instrument landing system approach. We (the controller and me) worked it out; and i don't believe any safety issues resulted in this particular flight; but i nonetheless thought that the communication situation perhaps should be assessed in the mrb area. Perhaps a note should be inserted in the approach notes that effective communications can not be established until 2;200 feet/foot when departing mrb; and as such; aircraft should  wait until reaching that altitude before attempting to contact pct. It seems like it would decrease the chances of confusion between pilots and controllers in that specific airspace during departure or a missed approach.
output: General aviation pilot voiced concern regarding the limited communications available with air traffic control during instrument flight rules operations at mrb airport; suggesting that the potential communications limitation be published on approach charts.

input: Departed with enough fuel to put us on at jfk with about 2000 pounds over reserve plus alternate due to load/altitude constraints. Dispatcher and i watched weather with a consideration of stopping for fuel. Zny issued a hold at jenno. I advised dispatch and said i was considering diverting to our revised alternate. Dispatch said most of the aircraft ahead of us had diverted and flights were now getting into jfk. Weather reports indicated the winds had let up some and in less than one turn in holding we were cleared on along the arrival. Alternate fuel was 5727 pounds and reserve fuel was 4591 pounds i set my bingo fuel at 11000 pounds we turned onto the localizer at 2500 feet/foot with 12000 pounds of fuel gear down flaps twenty 170 knot(s) in moderate turbulence. Almost immediately after rolling out we encountered severe turbulence that included a forty knot speed increase causing a flap over speed. A go around was begun and air traffic control advised of the severe turbulence. We obtained a clearance for our alternate and upon checking fuel at the top of climb; i was concerned to see only 7600 pounds i told air traffic control that i was only a few hundred pounds from declaring a fuel emergency and ask for as direct a route as they could give me. Air traffic control declared an emergency for us and cleared us direct. We landed without further incident with 4700 pounds i entered both the severe turbulence and flap over speed in the maintenance log. I believe the decision to continue from jenno based on the current reports we had received was reasonable. While we did land at our alternate with just over reserve fuel that would not be the case had i not started to go around with 12000 lbs.? I believe that the fuel figures for go around are suspect and should be reviewed. I am going to add 2000 pounds for the 757 until we have looked at them. Also; in the future; i will declare the emergency myself as soon as i begin thinking it necessary.
output: A b757-200 crew reported executing a go around during an approach to jfk because of severe turbulence. An unexpected fuel burn during holding required the crew to advise air traffic control about the possible low fuel. Air traffic control declared an emergency for them and cleared them direct to the alternate airport.

input: After having penetrated a thunderstorm for approximately 5 minute(s) i encountered moderate-severe turbulence instrument meteorological conditions hard enough to hit my head on the ceiling of the aircraft i immediately asked center for vectors to the nearest airport still encountering turbulence once i was back in the clear i noticed i had lost 1000 feet/foot altitude from my assigned altitude of 13000. Although flight watch had rpted severe thunderstorms in the vicinity; no lightning was visible; nor did the stormscope show any activity ahead. Furthermore; the line of thunderstorms was only 20 mile wide as rpted. Altitude loss was probably due to a combination of power reduction to obtain va as fast as possible; downdrafts; and to the fact that i had my hands full keeping the plane controled in the turbulence and in instrument meteorological conditions corrective action: once i discovered the altitude loss; i immediately started to climb at about the same time; air traffic control cleared me to 11000. To prevent this occurrence; intermediate fix weather says there is a severe circuit breaker in your path; believe them!
output: An sma deviated from its altitude during thunderstorm activity.

input: Parked at the gate and ready for departure; 30 minutes late due to late inbound aircraft. Doors were closed; all checklists complete; cabin ready (doors armed); and talking to push back crew; who said they were ready for departure. Called for push and got clearance to release brakes from push crew. Received push clearance; and were then informed by push crew they had 5 more bags. Contacted ramp; they canceled push clearance; and i informed the push crew they could load the bags. About this time the jetbridge began coming back to the aircraft. I informed the purser; and reset the parking brake. There was no warning the jetbridge was coming back; and as the flight attendants were already well into their demo; (not aware the jetbridge was coming back); this had potential for disaster with a slide deployment. Due to the cycling of the brakes; the automatic communications addressing & reporting system showed return to blocks; and had to be reinitialized; the flight attendants had to repeat the demo in its entirety as another passenger was boarded; and we re-accomplished the pushback checklist and confirmed once again the ground was ready; all bags were done; and we could again call for push clearance. This was a great effort on the part of the agent to get this passenger on the flight; but based on the timing of events to this point it had the potential for disaster. In the past; management has been reluctant to make such an effort for late passengers in a situation like this. Perhaps that was for a good reason; and this is a good example why. In the future; there needs to be better communication in situations like this; especially with the captain; and it should not be left to chance that the crew sees the jetbridge returning. For whatever it's worth; the push crew either didn't notice the jetbridge returning; or they did and said nothing.
output: Late bags and an additional passenger boarded after original brake release for pushback results in a breakdown in standard operating procedure  poor communications were cited as contributing.

input: I was on a ride as a company instructor with a line pilot to zzz who had not experienced large westerly wind conditions. We had two passengers from zzz1 to zzz. The pilot was landing 30 at zzz with a westerly wind. We caught a sinker (downdraft) on final; about 50 feet up off the runway. In my opinion; a stabilized approach could have been maintained by adding slight and brief increase in throttle to arrest the effect of the downdraft. The pilot elected to go full throttle and initiate a go-around. We did not catch any downdrafts during the go-around. I was watching the winds on the approach; and winds at the surface appeared to be about 15 knots out of the west (quartering headwind for 30); and the wind socks were remaining steady. I noticed a few errors during the pilot's approach such as getting too low during the base leg and being overly aggressive on throttle adjustments to counter up and down drafts. I have operated hundreds of times in that same wind condition safely; i believed a safe approach could be made; and therefore wanted to attempt the approach. I made a stabilized approach to 30; but upon touching down; got a large wind gust that got the airplane slightly airborne again. I cushioned the landing with a little throttle and set the airplane back down again with plenty of runway remaining. I saw the far wind sock snap like a whip; and another wind gust hit and we became airborne a second time momentarily; but then quickly subsided; and the airplane settled to the ground a third time. At this point the airplane ground speed was low; but was still wanting to fly due to the increased headwind gusts i was experiencing; even at idle power. I saw the wind sock snap again as another gust came down the runway. I had a little over 1000 feet of runway remaining (out of 2;000 feet; and runway stopping distance became in doubt. I initiated a go-around. While the go-around turned out fine; if any downdrafts had occurred; the obstacles at the far end of the runway would have been too close for comfort. I recently helped develop a new company standard operating procedure that is in the process of being codified; about not trying an approach again if a go-around was initiated due to weather conditions. I believed that the first approach could have been made; but lack of pilot experience in that particular weather condition compounded with lower time in make/model of aircraft was a contributing factor.i erred in the decision to attempt the approach again. The weather was dynamic; and conditions at the surface were worse than they had appeared on the first approach. I stand by the standard operating procedure that was made; and even if there is a more experienced pilot on board; the approach should not be made again; unless on an actual training flight. If a pilot has not experienced a particular weather condition; it is best to make a training flight for that flight; not just ride along like in an initial operating experience scenario. Other contributing factors: it's been more than a month since i had flown from the right seat. Proficiency may have been a factor. Mitigations: the company [weather briefing] was showing wsw winds from 15-19 during the time that the flight risk was assessed. [the local] forecast was showing winds up to 30kts out of the west for the day. However; we had not seen winds that strong at that point. Another weather tool was showing winds less than 20 at the surface; but in the low 20s at 300 feet. The zzz flight winds were risk assessed at 20-24 kts out of the west; giving a 'release approval required' in the flight operations management system from the do (director of operations) or cp (chief pilot). Release approval was granted. As a mitigation; i decided to fly with the pilot. Upon return to the home airport; after a review of the [off site weather station data]; winds were recorded as gusting into the low 30s from the west. I believe that this data would have been a better indicator of current conditions at zzz than the forecastmodels that we were using. In the future; i will be diligent about checking the [off site weather data] to help prevent this same scenario from occurring. Anything above 30 showing out of the west will most likely make zzz unsatisfactory for operations. This can be added specifically to the wind training for new hires.other mitigation: i debriefed with the left seat pilot; who gained a better understanding of westerly wind operations at zzz.
output: Instructor pilot of an air taxi operation reported attempting to land in windy conditions.

input: Atx x departed hou-aus climb 4000; atx y at 5000 wbound to sgr 4 south hou. Traffic issued to atx x reported in sight. The atx x vectored behind and just inside or ne of atx y. Turned the atx x to 300 degree and climbed to 6000' to apply course divergence with atx y. The aircraft were on other side from each other than originally thought which caused error. Error occurred due to incorrect application of course divergence.
output: Incorrect application of course divergence caused less than standard separation.

input: Departed with minimum equipment list 36-6 issued for auxiliary power unity bleed valve. After we arrived in zzzz; we attempted to start the auxiliary power unity for its generator. When the auxiliary power unity master knob was moved to 'run' position; the 'apu fail' message was displayed on engine indicating and crew alerting system i contacted dispatch who then started a conference call to maintenance control i described the situation to the maintenance controller who then issued minimum equipment list 49-1 to defer the entire auxiliary power unity maintenance control dispatch; and i failed to notice that minimum equipment list 36-6 cannot be in effect with minimum equipment list 49-1. Dispatch informed us en route about the discrepancy. The xref between the mel's was only marked for minimum equipment list 36-6; and no one thought to look at the earlier issued minimum equipment list to help avoid a similar event in the future; it would be helpful to have more complete xrefing of mel's. In addition; a more careful review of all issued mel's would have caught the error. Supplemental information from acn 810286: dispatcher working this aircraft on next flight leg caught minimum equipment list discrepancy and brought it to my attention i contacted maintenance controller who originally issued minimum equipment list with me. He; in turn; reviewed minimum equipment list book with his supervisor i reviewed minimum equipment list book with my supervisor and advised crew (via acars) of discrepancy. My supervisor sent an email to flight department requesting minimum equipment list book correction/clarification. Maintenance control supervisor also requested correction/clarification from flight department supplemental information from acn 810293: crew anticipated a slight delay in obtaining ground power they attempted to start the auxiliary power unity second officer they could use the auxiliary power unity generator for ground power when the auxiliary power unity master was selected 'on' the 'apu fail' caution message was displayed on the engine indicating and crew alerting system the capt and i elected to minimum equipment list the auxiliary power unity under 49-1. There was already an minimum equipment list open on the auxiliary power unity bleed system issued under minimum equipment list 36-6. Minimum equipment list 49-1 can be issued provided mel's 36-1; 36-3; nor 36-4 have not been issued in conjunction with this minimum equipment list the minimum equipment list was issued and crew placarded.
output: Emb145 is dispatched with incompatible mel's that ground the aircraft upon arrival at destination. Lack of cross referencing in minimum equipment list book is cited as cause.

input: At cincinnati; the crews typically land to the south ramp control almost always has us enter at spot x or y. Ground will typically say 'call ramp when clear good day' or 'enter spot zulu time (utc/gmt) have a good day.' when contacting ramp control the ramp controller will change the spot to enter. Almost always it isn't a problem today it was. Ramp told us to enter at spot y (after ground said spot x). We went to spot y. Unfortunately 2 air carrier aircraft were taxiing south on the taxiway this created a conflict. After personally talking to an irate supervisor on the telephone; i learned that ramp has no authority/authorized to change entry spots given by air traffic control ramp has the usual procedure here of changing entry spots from air traffic control that apparently is not correct. In good weather this is minor. Intermediate fix it were low visibility; the potential for aircraft damage is there. There needs to be better coordination between air traffic control facilities and local ramp controllers -- maybe designated entry spots that will always be followed. Intermediate fix the flight crew had been a little more aware; we could have also been more emphatic about entering at spot x.
output: Lack of coordination between tower ground control and company ramp control leads to traffic conflict.

input: Descending on left downwind for runway(s) 27l at ord from 7000 feet to 5000 feet with the autopilot engaged; at about 5500 feet during the descent we encountered a severe rolling moment to the right along with moderate turbulence. The first officer was flying and disconnected the autopilot and after a moment we seemed to have flown out of it. But a second moderate turbulence event along with another severe rolling moment was encountered. We reported to air traffic control that we were having difficulty in controlling the aircraft altitude because of the severe rolling moment. The first officer leveled the aircraft and began a slow climb back to approximately 5500 feet and after another moment we seemed to be out of it once again. We asked the controller who we were following because we just felt like we encountered wake turbulence and the controller said we were following a regional jet on final. Following the encounter and after a brief exchange with the ord ground controller; we believe that we may have encountered wake turbulence from a heavy jet on approach to runway(s) 28c. However we are not clear on the proximity of that aircraft to us.
output: B737-800 captain reported encountering wake turbulence on approach to ord; possibly from a preceding heavy jet.

input: All interphones in the cabin are incorrect showing the wrong placard. Attached shows photo only the interphone and shows a previous airplane write up which shows the correct placard needed.
output: Flight attendant reported placards for cabin interphone handsets are all incorrect.

input: While making an aerial application to a corn field; my helicopter's right skid became entangled in what may best be described as a well wire no longer in use. The wire didn't break away; instead dragged right side of aircraft into corn field; causing right spray boom to make contact with corn; [resulting in] damage. I tried to escape the drag placed on the aircraft by the corn and i was able to gain altitude but my egress routes were limited to downwind and uphill; or crosswind and over tall trees or headwind and over 50 feet power lines. I chose to attempt upwind and over power lines but still entangled in well wire and unable to gain enough altitude to clear the power lines. I did make contact with and subsequently broke the chin glass on aircraft and caused the power line to break. After hitting power line i was able to recover and safely land aircraft with no further damage to myself or aircraft. After landing and during post incident inspection a large amount of well wire was found wrapped around right skid.my perceptions are saving more critical areas prone [to] more obstacles till the end of the application would have given me a lighter and more responsive aircraft; if during ingress and egress an obstacle is suddenly realized. Extra care during recon of older abandoned home sites and possible hazards they may present; also more information from land owner prior to application in regards to potential hazards.
output: Helicopter pilot reported his aircraft became entangled in wire from an abandoned well during an aerial application flight. During the escape maneuver the helicopter contacted power lines.

input: Upon touchdown; we heard a loud pop followed by a veering to the right and a large vibration. We stopped the aircraft on the runway without braking and advised air traffic control we were unable to clear the runway. [we] ran the 'landing with a flat tire'; the 'after landing;' and 'shutdown' checklists and advised the passengers [of the situation]. Upon the arrival of airport vehicles we ran the evacuation checklist and the passengers deplaned. The tire was changed by company maintenance on the runway and we taxied the aircraft to the gate without further incident.
output: When a tire blew out on landing; the flight crew of a ce402 stopped on the runway; deplaned the passengers to utilize ground transportation; and taxied the aircraft to the gate after the tire had been replaced.

input: It was brought to my attention; at birmingham airport traffic control tower that we may be misapplying procedures related to non-radar rnav/gps approach clrncs to aircraft i believe the problem is systemic and the entire federal aviation administration from coast to coast; are also misapplying these procedures due to the lack of proper training and understanding of the non-radar rules from washington d.c. All the way down to the facility level. Intermediate fix this is true operational errors are taking place hundreds of times a day nationwide. A detailed explanation is difficult unless you have an understanding of the non-radar rules and their application concerning rnav/gps apches. Specifically pilots cannot be allowed to navigate direct waypoints (random area navigation rte) in a non-radar environment without radar course monitoring as per the 7110.65. In my experience even people who show up at the facility for evaluations and audits do not possess this required knowledge.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the reporter indicated that the airline transport pilot certificate 7110.65 procedure in question was paragraph 4-4-2; g & h.
output: Bhm controller voiced concern regarding alleged misapplication of non-radar rnav/gps approach procs.

input: Departed the local fixed-base operator at night announced intentions to taxi from parking area to runway(s) 11 and activated airport lights on common traffic advisory frequency frequency i completed run-up and announced on common traffic advisory frequency that i was moving into position for takeoff on the runway(s) once into position a private vehicle drove onto the runway(s) from another taxiway and drove past me (on my immediate l) and departed the runway(s) on the taxiway that i had been on. This happened while i was on the runway(s) despite the fact that the vehicle had its hazard lights on i never expected it to drive onto the runway(s) no radio call was made on the common traffic advisory frequency with runway(s) incursions on the increase; this is another example of unsafe operations(s) the vehicle should not have been operating on txwys or runway(s) without a radio. Ground personnel need to be included in the current awareness program. Airport access should be more secure (i believe this was a private vehicle -- not part of airport ops).
output: When the pilot of a c210 taxied into position at mean sea level an unctled airport a vehicle entered the runway(s) and drove past his acft.

input: I was approaching to land at creve coeur airport had been using zkc for flight following. Center passed me off to stl approach and i asked approach for vectors to my destination and advised them of my altitude after some vectors from approach he advised me that i was in the terminal control area and that i should descend immediately. I then did second officer w/o any other problem i suppose that my problem was lack of knowledge; i assumed that a controller would not bring me into the terminal control area w/o permission. I realize now that this is a problem of education. I believe that there are many private pilots who are not aware of the procedures necessary to enter a terminal control area possibly some trning of controllers might be in order; too. This is not the first terminal control area that i have flown in and this has never occurred before. Intermediate fix possible; i would like to have some printed matter on this subject. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr has done some research and now thinks he was in error; but at the time he thought the vectors were implied clearance into the area. Rptr has been advised that intermediate fix his destination is not the primary airport in the terminal control area he would not get a terminal control area clearance his destination lies under the stl terminal control area rptr is not sure; but believes he was using a discrete code when working with the center.
output: Ga sma unauthorized penetration of stl terminal control area while being vectored to nearby arpt.

input: We were cleared into position runway(s) 27 to hold behind a landing air carrier a flight after taxiing into position tower told us to exit runway(s) to the right. As we started forward the tower again told us to exit to the right immediately due to landing aircraft on short final behind us. I elected to make an immediate right turn off the runway(s) to comply and protect passenber we found ourselves with nose and fuselage off of runway(s) but main gear still on runway(s) due to apparent lack of weight bearing surface we did not go further forward. In summary; to protect people and aircraft and to comply with twr's request to exit runway(s) immediately 'to the right.' we moved all but the empennage of our aircraft from beneath a landing air carrier b jet. The air carrier b jet was told to go around on very short final.
output: While attempting to comply with air traffic control request to immediately clear runway(s) reporter aircraft apparently entered non-stressed surface. Unable callback.

input: An aircraft part going [from] zzz that was not hazmat. On paper work it said hazmat. It is not hazmat if it come from vendor. This part was checked by looking and smelling and computer that it came from vendor. This makes it a not hazmat; but paperwork from window says hazmat. Policy is to check if from vendor it is not hazmat to get the parts out on time. He did that. We have different policy on shipping potential hazmat. It depend on were the part is going. If it is a potential hazmat; we use to ship it like a domestic flight. We check to see; smell; [and check] computer work to see if it is hazmat by policy. Now today; they say if it is potential hazmat going overseas; ship it as it was hazmat. We would like some help in this. We really do not have a great idea at this time but we need to report this matter.
output: Commercial airline lead technician reported documentation discrepancies during shipping and receiving of aircraft parts due to confusing company handling procedures.

input: We were cleared for takeoff on runway(s) 30l by tower at hou. Read back clearance and took off. After breaking ground we saw a bonanza at about 80 feet/foot taking off runway(s) 35 at hou; climbed and turned left/right (directions) to avoid conflict. Asked tower intermediate fix he was cleared for takeoff they said no; he was not. Tower was discussing it with him when we went to dep.
output: Mlg crew had near midair collision with a bonanza. Bonanza pilot departed on another rwy.

input: On the lynxx8 arrival to bur passed janny intersection we are level at 8;000 feet mean sea level military aircraft is crossing path underneath at 7;000 feet right to left then parallel our path on our left wing about 3 nautical mile ahead. When we first received the traffic alert from traffic alert and collision avoidance system we thought it was that aircraft; but quickly realized it is a different aircraft about 10 o'clock 300 feet below us and pointing right at us. At the same time that air traffic control gave us a turn east and told us about a traffic (not sure if it was the one causing the ra) we received an resolution advisory 'climb; climb'; followed a few seconds later by 'adjust vertical speed'. Pilot not flying (pnf) responded to air traffic control that we are responding to an resolution advisory to which he replied roger; when able maintain 8;000 feet.we got visual of the traffic climbing through 8;700 feet; leveled at 9;000 feet before returning to the originally assigned 8;000 feet. Reaching 8;000 feet jcf approach instructed us to contact socal. Socal's first reply to checking was a new altimeter (was 30.28 now 29.89) with an 'i show you 200 feet low.' we told him we just recovered from an resolution advisory response and are level now at 8;000. No further incidents.it sounded like the military aircraft had a nonstandard request for their flight route/altitude and even checked with jcf if they are okay with that. This seemed to 'distract' the controller and possibly caused the late response to the traffic causing our ra.
output: An air taxi captain communicating with joshua reported a near miss with military aircraft while flying the bur lynxx eight arrival near the janny waypoint.

input: Sitting on runway(s) 9 at bos awaiting takeoff clearance we understood 'acr y cfa cleared for takeoff runway(s) 9.' believing the clearance was for us i ordered the f/o to verify that was air carrier x cfa cleared for takeoff runway(s) 9. He made two calls with no response either time. I then made one call; with no response. With the next call (f/o's third); we heard the tower give go around instructions to an aircraft and tower told us we were cleared for takeoff and that we were screwing things up. During takeoff roll i explained what had happened but tower didn't seem to understand. The tower controller seemed upset when he sent us over to departure control frequency second officer before switching; i again informed (the tower ctlr) what the problem was and his reply was 'acr x cfa maintain radio silence!' and i said 'acr x cfa switching to dep.'
output: Acr mlg requested takeoff clearance verification but before clearance could be confirmed airport traffic control tower local controller gave an air carrier on final a go around clearance and admonished the flight crew for failing to start tkof.

input: While at fl350 in instrument meteorological conditions conditions; with no weather cells displayed on the radar and capt's radar screen displaying a spoke pattern just prior to the event; aircraft encountered moderate turbulence for approximately 3 minute(s) followed by severe turbulence accompanied with hail for approximately 1 minute(s) the first officer was flying the aircraft (on autoplt). I announced/placed the mode control panel/spd monitoring system to turbulence mode. Fo's l-1 window outer pane then cracked from a hail strike. I immediately took control of the aircraft and disengaged the full flight regime autothrottle system entry airspd was approximately mach .84; sat m47; tat m12 and gross weight 204.0. I disengaged the autoplt in order to maintain wings level while the first officer and flight engineer monitored the speed engs were remaining within limits (we had turned on the engine ignition upon initial encounter of turb). Entry into this unknown weather was sudden and degraded rapidly. Throughout the entire event; no abrupt control movements were made; as my main concern was structural loading of the aircraft once clear of the wx/severe turbulence we performed a structural damage assessment of the aircraft and performed the procedures for a cracked windshield outer pane. We slowed/configured the aircraft early in the chance of a structural/gear/ctlability issue in order to provide the additional time window to work a potential problem the aircraft and its system were operating normally; and we landed without further event. The event was also rpted to air traffic control after block-in; the aircraft was noted to have radome damage and paint chips missing from the wing's upper leading edge. I believe the event would have been avoided with a normally functioning color radar as you can't avoid what you can't see. Minute(s) prior to the severe weather encounter; my radar planned position indicator intermittently displayed spokes. I asked the first officer (as the pf) intermediate fix he displayed the same pattern on his ppi; to which he responded; no. We were starting to pick up light to moderate chop in instrument meteorological conditions conditions; and i did not want to select the alternate receiver xmitter as this type of system can take up to 1 minute(s) to paint weather after switching receiver xmitters inflt. Being in moderate chop while in instrument meteorological conditions i deemed it better to have at least 1 ppi painting weather than none; while the alternate receiver xmitter pwred up. Fo's ppi was not displaying 'spokes' or any defined weather cells prior to the severe turb/wx encounter. The radar installed on this particular aircraft is the older generation with monochromatic ppi's without the capacity of displaying weather cell intensity information weather encounter on this event was due to a malfunctioning radar system however; even when this older system operates normally; it lacks the performance required for safe flight operations(s) imho. I believe that all united states certificated turbojet (high alt) operators should be required to use radar that displays weather cell intensity as a minimum standard (color would enhance safety even more). Example for this reasoning: departing out of an airport in the intertropical convergence zone like cali; columbia; with high terrain throughout; strict adherence must be given to the departure course in order to avoid controlled flight into terrain since the intertropical convergence zone will always have the convective weather yr round; deviating around weather is quite routine. Cali; with its small nbound departure corridor (defined by a high terrain on both sides); leaves little room for weather avoidance. When departing here at night or in instrument flight rules conditions; having a radar system that displays a storm's intensity is essential for minimum safe flight operations(s) and radar with color ppi's is even more of a safety enhancement. Given the fact that weather radar is primarily for complete weather avoidance; it is sometimes necessary to determine intermediate fix a cell tops out at 5000 feet/foot with light precipitation or goes to fl550 with extreme precip/turb as in the above example on a departure with high/close terrain in all quadrants. This is why i believe that acrs should not utilize these older (less capable) weather radar system plus; these system are usually over 30+ yrs old and more prone to malfunction just due to the component's age. Again; this weather encounter was due to a radar malfunction; but i felt this would be a good opportunity to address the issue of lacking radar spec/performance with regards to flight safety. Just as traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii was implemented and now required in order to provide collision avoidance; industry improvements should be mandated for airborne weather radar minimum performance specifications for the type of flight operations(s) being conducted by the acrs.
output: B747 flight crew encounters severe turbulence while at cruise alt.

input: After repeated attempts to reach flight service station specialist from the motel room; with no success i departed waynoka municipal (ok79) waynoka; ok; en route to salina municipal (sln) salina; ks; in light rain. I remained visual flight rules on top; but was having to climb at 5000 feet/foot mean sea level i contacted mcalister radio for a weather update for my route of flight mcalister was very helpful and gave me a full rpt with no significant weather other than high clouds with low level cumulus near hutchinson; ks; with salina showing visual flight rules mcalister offered me flight following or to air file an instrument flight rules flight plan. I was at 5500 feet/foot mean sea level on top and elected to file instrument flight rules for a possible let down through clouds closer to sln and relayed the required information i was asked to contact zkc on 118.35. They cleared me to hut vor and dme (co-located) then direct sln. I rpted crossing hut and was cleared down to 5000 feet/foot mean sea level shortly after this i lost my ability to transmit or zkc lost its ability to receive. I maintained 5000 feet/foot mean sea level and continued trying to raise center i could hear them trying to re-establish contact with me. I was in light clouds during this time. Approximately 30 nautical mile north of hutchinson i broke out of all clouds except for some high light clouds and a few broken clouds below and in visual flight rules conditions; as mcalister had said. Still unable to contact zkc; i left 5000 feet/foot for 3500 feet/foot mean sea level and contacted salina tower on 119.3. I explained to them my communications problem and asked intermediate fix they would contact zkc for me and see how they wanted me to proceed. Salina tower called me back and asked me to contact zkc on 134.9; which i did. I explained to the controller that i was in visual flight rules conditions. He asked intermediate fix i wanted to cancel instrument flight rules i told him i did. I continued on to salina and was cleared to land. I have no idea why my transmitting capabilities were compromised. I realize the boundaries were close; the anthony sector (118.35) and the hutchinson sector (118.8); but we are always instructed to change frequencies prior to losing one. My transmission into salina and subsequently to center showed no problem both of my radios are well maintained and have never caused me a prob.
output: A general aviation private pilot on an instrument flight rules clearance loses contact with zkc and has to obtain a new frequency from tower controller at sln; ks.

input: At btr; runway(s) 13/31 is under repair; and has been for several months. During this period; other surfaces have also been closed to accommodate work crews. Initially; taxiway a; where it crosses 13 was closed to repair this portion. During this time; all aircraft weighing more than 50000 pounds had to back-taxi on the runway(s) either going in or out. This resulted in an extreme amount of opposite direction situations; in which separation could not always be insured. This project was only supposed to last 21 days; taxiway 'a' was closed on or about x may. On or about x aug; taxiway was reopened. A 21 day project that took about 75 days! The work crews did not work on holidays or weekends; and that's when the weather was best! Now the airport has decided to close runway(s) 4r/22l; which will leave us one runway(s) most controllers here have never worked one runway(s) operations(s) second officer i believe safety will by severely compromised. A suggestion was made to wait until the nw portion of runway(s) 13 was completed before closing runway(s) 4r. This would push back closing runway(s) 4r/22l about 3 weeks! Plus; it would allow the controllers to land smaller aircraft on runway(s) 13 to hold short of runway(s) 4l/22r; thus increasing the safety of flying into btr. This suggestion fell on deaf ears at the airport mgrs office. He would not budge. Obviously; safety is not a concern of the airport here in btr!
output: Ctlr complains about runway(s) construction delays and schedule plan for other runway(s) closures.

input: I was a relief pilot and had just assumed my shift after being on break. Dispatch sent us a message via automatic communications addressing & reporting system recommending a reroute to the westbound of cleared cus via 10 degrees south 160 degrees westbound to avoid cumulo nimbus activity associated with tropical cyclone 'osea.' the capt (just before leaving the cockpit for his break) said; that 'she (the dispatcher) was overly helpful and that most of the weather was behind us and we should have smooth sailing.' he could not have been more wrong. Going by what the capt said; i had the other (non-flying) first officer tell dispatch that our current flight plan looked ok. Within 15 minute(s) of that; an intense; 100 nautical mile wide return started to grow on our radar 200 mile ahead. I tried to convince the other first officer that we should ask for 10 degrees south 160 degrees westbound reroute as recommended. He thought it was too federal aviation regulation off course and suggested that it looked better to the east i agreed to that and we asked to deviate 40 nautical mile left/right (directions) of cus. As soon as we started left/right (directions) (s) the line we were trying to go around appeared to grow on our cathode ray tube i had him ask for 70 nautical mile and soon for 99 nautical mile (the most the software will allow; this was a 'fans' rte). During this deviation it got increasingly turbulent to almost continuous moderate. The other first officer was involved in fans communicationss as i was flying the aircraft and we forgot to give a position rpt at 11 degrees south and 155 degrees westbound we also didn't do a plot while deviating. As we cleared the end of the cumulo nimbus line and asked for direct to 14 degrees south 153 degrees westbound or to continue our left/right (directions) offset for a while longer; tahiti responded 'unable.' we inquired as to which was unable; the direct or the offset; the next center auckland asked for our position we were abeam 13 degrees 27 minute(s) south 157 degrees westbound (our fir checked point). Second officer we gave an estimate to that point; and auckland cleared us to go direct to the succeeding point; south 27 degrees westbound 170 degrees during this deviation the workload seemed high to me; because the other first officer (non-flying) was having some difficulty with the flight management computer and responding to air traffic control on the flight management computer we made the mistake of not 'executing' the 99l offset (just using the dotted line) and that affected his ability to use the 'pos rpt' screen to respond to air traffic control quickly. I thought about awakening the capt when i realized we had missed a position rpt and a plot; but it looked like since we were giving the present position to akl; this situation was solved. In hindsight; i should have advocated more strongly to follow dispatch's recommendation for a reroute request. I also should have been made aware of how the other first officer was keeping up on the position rpt and plotting chart.
output: B747-400 aircraft on oceanic route encountered area of severe weather and had to divert around weather flight crew had some difficulty programming the flight management computer properly for offset plus high workload. Flight crew forgot to plot position and give position rpt. Both pilots in cockpit were fo's and the capt was on break sleeping. Flight was fans flt.

input: I was acting as check airman for a route check. The event occurred on final approach. At 4;000 feet/foot we were asked if we wanted the visual behind another aircraft. We declined when we were unable to acquire the aircraft. I could see the airport behind us but was behind us at a steep angle and [we] were just below the clouds. We were subsequently cleared for the global positioning system 6r [and told to] 'maintain 3;000 until crossing the iaf.' the intercept vector was at a steep angle causing the autopilot to overshoot final and was setting up for a very large correction. The pilot flying intervened and began to fly the airplane manually. By this time the airport was well insight. Inside of the initial approach fix to final approach fix the minimum is 2;700 then [a] descent to minimum descent altitude i called the runway insight to approach control and was switched to tower. A few miles prior to final approach fix the pilot flying began a descent for landing and said 'visual.' ultimately we passed the final approach fix about 400 feet/foot below final approach fix altitude. I had made note that we had not gotten officially cleared for the visual approach and debriefed the event to standard. The federal aviation administration inspector did not agree that this could be dealt with as a debrief item and altitude deviation may need to be further investigated.
output: A federal aviation administration inspector objected to a ce-680 check airman allowing the pilot flying to descend below the global positioning system approach final approach fix altitude in visual meteorological conditions conditions because air traffic control had not yet cleared the flight for a visual approach.

input: During cruise flight fl310; 1 flight attendant brought to cockpit a live 12 gauge shotgun shell a passenber gave to her. Passenber was sitting in row xa and found it on the floor. Flight attendant looked around for more and found none. No passenber claimed the shell. Dispatch was notified and they sent automatic communications addressing & reporting system message back saying slc will be notified and meeting the airplane. Upon arrival, arrive in slc no one special met the airplane and they claimed no one notified them at all. Passenber deplaned normally. I was disappointed someone dropped the ball and thought at the very least they would have some security personnel there to hand search everyone deplaning carry-on luggage. The station manager had cabin service give the jet an extra good search as well as my flight engineer and no other live ammunition was found. Return trip to dfw was normal. You would think they would find such items at the security screening chk-points but there's no way telling when or where it passed through and at what airport and it could have been on our jet's floor for days before found.
output: Pax of an air carrier b727 found a live shot gun shell on floor. Flight crew notified company to have security meet aircraft upon arrival, arrive passenber were not screened by security upon deplaning; but company inspected the cabin.

input: Opening broadway sector; frequency stayed in the on position on both main; standby and buec eventually a new frequency was added to the position but not before coordinating with another sector to assume my airspace.
output: Zny controller expressed concern regarding a frequency outage at his sector requiring another sector to assume affected airspace.

input: The flight planning system is 'unsafe'! It is too slow to safely and effectively perform the necessary functions for the aircraft dispatcher. Today i had to change alternates due to an inaccurate forecast. Some flights were airborne and some were still on the ground. Crews received the changes in an untimely manner because the computer could not calculate the changes fast enough for the crews to get the information. This slowness has gotten slower as we get busier. The automatic communications addressing & reporting system portion of the system was sending 'mas fail' alerts after the information was sent to the aircraft. The message was in error as the crews were receiving the information and acknowledging the messages. Because of the error the dispatcher now has to go back and verify whether or not the crews received the information thus slowing down the amendment process for other crews. As has been previously reported; the computer is slow to change between tabs and you can easily send automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages to the wrong tail. Minimum equipment list retrieval has gotten even slower than previously reported. With these problems it is very difficult for the aircraft dispatcher to keep up with the workload and still maintain a safe; legal; effective; efficient and timely operation.
output: Dispatcher reported the problems with their computerized flight planning system.

input: Normal operations until 5 hours into flight.we operated in 'econ' which showed greater fuel and still an on time arrival; and very near flight planned m.84.
