We operated and climb near as the flight plan indicated; and we held steady at 200 to 400 pounds ahead on fuel; and 200 to 500 pounds under burn; again until 5 hours into flight.at crew change we first went to 600 pounds behind from 200 pounds ahead and to 600 pounds over burn from 300 pounds under burn. We received air traffic control clearance to cruise m.83 for the crossing as this was close to 'econ' and indicated about 1;200 pounds better fuel at landing. Tailwind had drop about 20 knot(s) from flight plan.fuel flows where averaging under the flight plan. The burn and fuel was noted to relief crew. Upon return from rest increased over burn was noted to me at 140w as 2;100 pounds and behind 2;000 pounds gross. Inflight highest over noted as 2;600 pounds if memory serves. We noted a 6;000 pounds over burn after landing; but i failed to check number carefully as we subtracted planned flight burn from the total burn (not the flight burn); the over burn was 1;386 pounds when subtracting the flight planned fuel burn from the actual flight burn; there was 2;900 pounds taxi out burn; and 2;000 pounds taxi in burn. We took off 5;000 pounds under flight plan weight; so i do find it strange that we burned extra fuel; we were able to save another 1;000 pounds as air traffic control cleared us direct to fix on the approach deleting the arrival and we did a constant descent saving that 1;000 pounds which if added to the 1;386 pounds = 2;300 pounds very close to the highest over burn calculated in cruise near the end of the flight. There are good notes on the master flight plan to be utilized in the investigation. I have noticed that the burn and fuel does well and then starts slowly over burn about half way into flight; winds aloft and ground speed difference and temperature. Difference don't seem to explain this change half way into flight. We did request a reweigh of the cargo. Normal operation approach; landing; taxi in; shutdown and post flight.the crew and i wonder about cargo over weight; as there has been some cases of this in past; and perhaps fuel bias problems. Our error in calculating the over burn once on the ground was not helpful as well to the most accurate information; but i've corrected that calculation in the report and other will look at this as well. Continue to look into the cargo weight and fuel bias; thanks for your time and effort. I attached some pics of the master flight plan; not best quality; but may help in short term.
output: Boeing 777 captain reported a discrepancy in the flight management computer fuel remaining estimate. Initially it showed they would be landing with extra fuel; then 5 hours into the flight it showed they would be landing with less fuel than planned. It may have been due to an un-forecasted wind shift.

input: After repeated spacing vectors; airspd assignments and altitude changes; we were given a vector to intercept runway(s) 25l localizer our company procedures specify an lateral navigation intercept at that distance from field. As pilot not flying i proceeded to build an intercept off a fix on the approach as we were close to the localizer already; we flew through it before i could get the intercept leg in the box. I was heads down with the control display unit work and both of us missed the intercept on raw data.
output: B757 crew overshoots turn to final on arrival, arrive to las.

input: While on an instrument flight rules flight plan and executing the instrument landing system 17 approach to circle to land runway 27; we encountered an airplane conducting acrobatic maneuvers (loops; rolls) directly over the airport at our flight altitude; above and below. A notice to airmen / of air missions was issued that the 'acrobatic box' was active and we were aware of it. Reviewing the notice to airmen / of air missions we learned that the federal aviation administration had issued a waiver for pilots to conduct acrobatic flight within one mile from the center of the airport between 700 and 4300 feet above ground level this was not a public airshow. There is a direct conflict between instrument flight rules and visual flight rules aircraft. No separation exists.this is an unsafe waiver - should be withdrawn.sec. 91.303 -- aerobatic flight.no person may operate an aircraft in aerobatic flight--(a) over any congested area of a city; town; or settlement;(b) over an open air assembly of persons;(c) within the lateral boundaries of the surface areas of class b; class celsius class d; or class east airspace designated for an airport;(d) within 4 nautical miles of the center line of any federal airway;(e) below an altitude of 1;500 feet above the surface; or(f) when flight visibility is less than 3 statute miles.for the purposes of this section; aerobatic flight means an intentional maneuver involving an abrupt change in an aircraft's attitude; an abnormal attitude; or abnormal acceleration; not necessary for normal flight.
output: C182 pilot on an instrument flight rules flight plan executing a circling approach noticed an aerobatic aircraft flying acrobatic maneuvers directly over the airport above and below their flight altitude. Reporter stated there was a waiver in place for the acrobatic box over the airport; but feels it was unsafe and should have been modified or withdrawn.

input: I departed summit airport (n92) en route to red lion (n73) at approximately xy11 local time. Initial climb to 2000 feet/foot and turned to a heading of 090 degrees i was having trouble identing the ood vor and dme (co-located) when i looked up and saw the smt pass immediately in front of me. I hit his wake turbulence immediately afterwards. I contacted the pilot via radio. He said they had me in sight and were waiting for me to 'break off' (my heading 090 degrees smt heading 010 degs). Factors: balky radio equipment in plane occupied an excessive amount of my attention (unable to identify vor). Thus i was not looking outside the aircraft when i should have been. Pilot in smt had right-of-way by 'rules of the road;' but chose to stand on them when he had me in sight; and suspected i didn't see him.
output: Sma hit wake turbulence of smt while in cruise. Unicom conversation between the aircraft showed that the smt saw the sma but chose to insist on his right of way. Sma did not see smt until it was too late to react.

input: Approximately 1-2 seconds after touching down on [runway] xxr at [zzz] in a normal wheel landing; the airplane began to shake consistent with a flat left main tire. The tube inside the tire was losing air rapidly and the airplane began to sag to the left. Because the leak did not result in an immediate; completely flat tire; i was able to retain directional control of the plane during rollout. Only when the plane reached a very slow speed was the tire finally so flat that directional control was no longer possible. The plane stopped roughly 10 feet off centerline; about 300 feet short of taxiway b at [zzz]. It was not possible to taxi; applying engine power simply pivoted the airplane around the flat left main tire. I advised the tower controller of my situation and was told to shut down the aircraft in position and work the airport operations team to remove the plane. Because no suitable towing equipment was available for tailwheel aircraft; we changed the tube on the runway and taxied the airplane to parking uneventfully. No damage occurred to the plane or the airport. No injuries occurred. Upon inspection of the failed tube; a small tear was found at the base of the valve stem; where it joins the rubber of the tube itself. It is likely that when the wheel touched pavement; the tube shifted and the rubber at the base of the valve stem 'pinched' against the hole in the rim through which the valve stem protrudes; resulting in the tear. The tire itself had been replaced approximately 6 months ago and had about 40 hours of flight time. The tube in the tire had been in service for approximately 1 year; or about xxx hours of flight time.
output: Light sport pilot reported flat tire on landing rollout.

input: I have just recently noticed the abbreviation u/s being used a lot in the notams. I looked it up and it means 'unserviceable.' it seems to now be used instead of out of service (out of service); but i'm not sure it's the same thing. What is 'unserviceable' exactly and is it the same as ots? For example; if a notice to airmen / of air missions shows the approach lights are u/s for a period of time; are they out of service?
output: Pilot reported confusion between the difference in out of service and unserviceable in notams.

input: An a320 was at fl320 requesting fl360 because they were getting a choppy ride. I told him that i had his request; there was and aircraft at fl340 flying right over the top of him. Once he cleared the fl340 traffic i climbed him to fl360. Before i climbed the a320 i did a quick traffic scan thinking in the back of my head he was at fl340. Thinking that he was at fl340 rather than fl320 i did not see any traffic for him and climbed him. There was an air carrier southbound at fl330 missed the traffic because i thought the a320 was at fl340. I turned both aircraft 30 right; one second later; both were responding to a resolution advisory double check the altitude of the aircraft requesting higher and note the data block.
output: Zab controller described a loss of separation event when neglecting to properly scan the data block altitude information before assigning another altitude.

input: Another pilot and i were conducting a training flight near csm. In a weather briefing received before departure there was a notice to airmen / of air missions for ice/slush on runway(s) in spots. The state had been hit with several winter storms and many airports were rpting these conditions. Even our departure airport had ice in patches. However; the runway(s) had been plowed at our departure airport and the ice was not much of a problem i had made an assumption that csm would be in a similar condition. It is a twred airport (part-time) with a 13000 feet/foot runway(s) i expected there to be patches of ice/slush similar to our departure airport we were on a practice instrument landing system when i noticed the spots of ice on the runway(s) by short final; i could see the runway(s) in strips under the slush. The tower was not open at the time and we were in class g airspace. It was clear aircraft had been using the runway(s) before our arrival, arrive we continued the instrument approach procedure with a planned full stop. The moment we touched down; it was obvious that the runway(s) had not been plowed and that the ice spots were actually as high as an inch in some places. This resulted in a very irregular landing surface. The ice was not slush; but very solid and did not yield under our weight almost immediately; the aircraft jumped over an ice ridge and this caused an excessive yaw to the left/right (directions) i applied left/right (directions) rudder and brake; but the ice prevented any real control the aircraft then bounced to the left/right (directions) almost perpendicular with the runway(s) again; i applied left/right (directions) rudder and brake. The aircraft began to straighten out; but not before it slid off the left/right (directions) edge of the runway(s) it came to rest in the muddy clrway along the edge. There was no damage to the aircraft and there were no injuries. The aircraft was towed to a hangar for inspection. I believe the main contributing factor was the lack of detail in the notice to airmen / of air missions intermediate fix it had specified that the runway(s) was not plowed or included the depth of the ice; i never would have considered it safe. I honestly believe intermediate fix an airport is going to be in such a condition that its runway(s) is unsafe; the airport should be notamed closed until it thaws or is plowed.
output: Flc of a lear jet 25 lost directional control due to runway(s) ice during landing roll; resulting in skidding off the side of the runway(s) into mud. There was no damage to the acft.

input: While enroute at 5;500 mean sea level the aircraft engine dropped about 200 revolutions per minute momentarily and then returned to normal. A few seconds later; the rpm started dropping and lost approximately 600 revolutions per minute and the engine started running rough. I went through emergency procedures; including fuel; mixture; throttle; carb heat and mags; but the engine rpm stayed around 1;800 revolutions per minute i advised approach that we were having engine problems and that we would need to land at zzz. I [advised atc]; because i felt this would mitigate the risk to others; should the situation deteriorate further. In the descent; the engine returned to normal operation. I figured that the power loss could possibly have been carb ice. Nevertheless; i felt the safest course of action would be to get the aircraft on the ground to investigate what had happened.on the ground at zzz; i was able to locate a mechanic who was able to provide assistance. He looked over the function of all of the engine controls; but found nothing wrong. Generous sampling of fuel provided no indications of contamination. At the mechanic's suggestion; i took the airplane out and did a full power run up and checked the function of carb heat; mags; etc. The aircraft performed perfectly. I assumed that the problem was carb ice. I flew a pattern close to the airport as a precaution in case anything was wrong and then flew the aircraft to altitude to see if any problem could be detected. The aircraft performed flawlessly.
output: C150 pilot reported diverting due to engine power fluctuations possibly caused by carburetor icing.

input: I was the pilot flying on a visual approach to zzz on an air ambulance flight we were a lifeguard flight and are usually given priority due to this and cleared to land on the larger and closer runway(s) (rwy 35r). When approach control handed us over to zzz tower my capt (pnf) was working the radio and they cleared us on runway(s) 35l. The capt also read this back to the tower (as he heard in the tower tapes). I was busy flying and looking for visual flight rules traffic that was shooting practice approachs on runway(s) 35r (ils). I thought i heard us cleared for a visual and to land on runway(s) 35r; second officer i continued my approach to runway(s) 35r. The capt did not say anything to the contrary. On a short left/right (directions) base for runway(s) 35r; i saw traffic on final for runway(s) 35r (a c172). I pointed it out to the capt and he and i both thought this was the traffic practicing instrument landing system approachs and that this traffic would be going missed approach since we were much faster and the tower didn't say anything except for a traffic advisory we continued and landed on runway(s) 35r. Upon contacting ground we were told to contact the tower the capt called the tower and also went up to the tower to talk to everyone involved.
output: Fo of an ambiguity smt jet landed on the wrong parallel runway(s) due to habit instead of listening to the actual clearance given by the controller this mistake caused a c172 on final to gar.

input: After departure from wiley post airport in oklahoma city on an instrument flight rules flight plan to kansas city downtown; significant turbulence light emitting diode to altitude deviations of from 200-500' from assigned. Especially from per to emp on v354; turbulence from a developing thunderstorm cell was significant. Because the arwy centerline lay directly in the cell; i advised center of my course deviation to the westbound my deviation; although 15-20 mile westbound of the cell; was insufficient to keep me out of major up and down drafts. I lost at least 500-1000' before regaining aircraft control and exiting the area of turbulence center shifted me to wichita approach after my call for assistance in circumventing/avoiding further weather after the aircraft righted itself after a 45-50 degree updraft bank and altitude loss; clear weather reappeared. I advised wichita i believed i could proceed direct emp. I was transferred back to center. I advised center of my reappearance on frequency and my climbing to resume altitude assignment. Center cleared me direct emp and the flight continued otherwise uneventfully to mkc. Comment: evidently; some radar cannot pick up significant thunderstorm activity. Had weather conditions not been visual meteorological conditions or mvmc with 5-15 mile visibility; it's my belief i would have continued unaware into the middle of a storm i later learned dropped 8' of rain in se ks. In other words; i'm glad i wasn't in imc.
output: Sma twin experienced brief loss of control and altitude excursion in thunderstorm activity.

input: We were cleared for takeoff [at a foreign airport] and as we rolled out onto the runway; electronic centralized aircraft monitoring activated the fuel page with all indications 'xx'. We requested and were granted an exit from the runway to taxiway to troubleshoot our problem. Just as the airplane was stopped on [taxiway] and brakes set; a very noticeable acrid electrical smell started to permeate the cockpit. Scanned to overhead panel and noted all secondary fuel indicators were blank and no cbs were popped. Two loud bangs were heard coming from the east & east compartment and the smell of electrical fumes increased.elected to call for the fire brigade to respond to our location as we shut down the engines and removed all electrical power from the airplane. Disarmed both doors and opened both windows and l1 door to ventilate cabin. Fire brigade responded and provided a stair truck for us to leave the aircraft.the fire captain confirmed acrid fumes in the east & east compartment and completed their duties then turned the aircraft over to our mechanics. Aircraft was towed back to the ramp for further inspection.components in east & east compartment shorted out.
output: A300 captain reported shutting the aircraft down on the taxiway after electrical fumes were noticed as well as two loud bangs from the e&e compartment.

input: On sep/wed/04; while relamping a reading light at seat position x; a zzz1 amt found an oxygen generator safety pinned with the red 'remove before flt' streamer attached. The generator was reactivated and the remaining first class and coach generators were inspected to insure they were activated. No other generators were found pinned. A logbook entry was made; a maintenance operational rpt was completed and quality assurance was notified. The signoff on the job instruction card was completed under an airworthiness directive on aug/mon/04. I ante meridiem an amt in zzz base maintenance my signature and employee identify are in the signoff block. Although i ante meridiem ultimately responsible for the signoff; there are several contributing factors for the incident. First; there are numerous jic's and operations(s) for the passenber oxygen mask/generator replacement/inspection. Confusion results from ea's (engineering auth) and airworthiness directives conflicting with each other. Furthermore; several amt's were assisting with pulling the safety pins/streamers. The risk of human error was multiplied. I ante meridiem not passing blame upon anyone else; since my signature is in the block. Finally; i verified that all safety streamers/pins were pulled but may have inadvertently left one installed. To prevent this occurrence in the future; i would suggest having separate signoffs for each row of seats. When we install floorboards; there is a separate signoff for each floorboard. Also; having a 'second set of eyes' such as an inspection signoff after the mechanic signoff would help rectify the ambiguity.
output: A b757-200 while accomplishing an airworthiness directive and an engineering authority/authorized to all passenber service units one oxygen canister was found pinned.

input: At the given time and place; i was out and was doing some currency work among them emergency (eng out proc) approachs and lndgs from different altitudes and into different fields. Trying to surprise myself; i cut (the pwr) when it seemed most unfavorable in all the situations. In this particular approach i cut the engine at 1500' above ground level i-93 runs parallel to the river down the valley; but it seemed too easy second officer i went for the river because of the congestions on the interstate. I knew of 2 pwrlines crossing the river; but both of them were federal aviation regulation away from me. I took myself down lower than i normally do to see intermediate fix i would have made it in a real situation. I was just about to go around when i saw a set of wires right in front of me. Due to my speed (vglide) i realized that i would not be able to climb over them since i already was on collision course with the lowest set; and my power was not regained second officer i tried to dive under them. Maybe not the best decision; but i didn't have all the time in the world to make a decision. Knowing that people had been using this part of the river for seaplane lndgs was maybe the reason why i considered it to be safe; but now i know better. The lowest wire cut off a part of my horizontal stabilizer i was able to fly the airplane back to the airport and none of the wires were damaged. Knowing that a 2-3' higher altitude would have killed me; it is needless to say that i ante meridiem not taking any kind of chance again. At least i ante meridiem able to warn other pilots against flying low in terrain you don't know 100%. One thing that surprised me was that none of the wires were marked with any kind of markings; knowing that people have been using that part of the river for seaplane lndgs. I think that some markers would have prevented the incident. When this is said; it is no doubt that i put myself into this situation w/o having all information about that area; and that is my responsibility; and the only thing i can say is that it taught me that safety is no accident; it has to be planned.
output: Sma practicing forced lndgs struck power lines.

input: #3 engine vibration warning followed periods of sensed vibration. Engine shutdown completed; and drift down to fl280 begun. Subsequently descended to fl260. Requested quiet/discrete frequency a couple were given; but several further frequency changes made. Landing was made at dfw w/o incident; runway(s) 17l. A single quiet frequency could have prevented a lot of interruptions during chklist and engine review; as well as in event of further emergencies after considering weather and flight conditions; emergency was not declared.
output: Engine shutdown on lgt account vibration.

input: Our frequency has been well documented that we have a hard time communicating with aircraft at lower altitudes in the sector. This affects approximately 3 or 4 airports in this sector. Normally this sector is combined with another sector and we have fewer problems since we can change aircraft over to the other sector frequency. This event is from [a recent time of high] activity in the area. An airport in the sector was split because of the volume of traffic; we had to split off the sector by itself. This left me with few options in talking to aircraft during a tremendous amount of inbound traffic that were either on instrument flight rules flight plans or on visual flight rules flight following to this airport. It is my understanding that a new antenna is supposed to be installed that would fix this issue but still has not been done. This issue on the frequency caused a very unsafe operation in this airspace. I think at one point i had 6 or 7 inbounds that all of the aircraft could not hear my transmissions. Just get the frequency fixed as soon as possible; we have been waiting on this and it could have helped us a lot if the frequency was in working order prior to the amount of traffic coming into the terminal area.
output: A center controller reported losing radio contact with numerous aircraft during a busy period in an area with known poor radio coverage that has not been fixed.

input: Enrte to destination cruising at fl270. Capt noticed hydraulic quantity in the #3 system was lower than normal. This situation does not give any other indication in cockpit but the synoptic page showed the quantity as white instead of green. After speaking with maintenance as longitude as quantity was steady (which it was) and pump pressures were good (which they were); no action was necessary and maintenance would greet the aircraft at the destination as the descent was commenced into the destination the fluid quantity decreased further. We were cleared for the approach to runway(s) 5 and glideslope intercept; the landing gear was selected down. The system fluid then decreased to zero and the nosewheel came down and locked; but the gear did not. A landing gear warning and hydraulic caution were soon heard. The first officer initiated and flew a go around and then the capt ran through the appropriate checklists. The gear had to be extended manually. It indicated that all 3 gear were down and locked. The only real concern at this point was that there would be no nosewheel steering upon landing and only 1/2 the brake system would be working. An adjusted landing distance was calculated and the runway(s) was more than longitude enough. The capt then took over flying and an uneventful landing was made and the aircraft stopped on the runway(s) a tug was then called to tow us to the gate. Hydraulic fluid was seen leaking from the fuselage bottom on the postflt. The mechanic later found at least 3 leaks in the system it would have been nice for there to be some sort of warning that the hydraulic fluid was low enough; required a diversion or gear extension to assure the gear extended normally. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated when on the ground the gate technician rpted 3 separate hydraulic leaks in lines and fittings but did not disclose their location. The rptr also said this airplane should be equipped with a hydraulic reservoir low level warning sys.
output: A canadair cl65 on final approach at 3000 feet/foot executed a go around due to loss of #3 main hydraulic system landing gear extended manually. Caused by leaking lines and fittings.

input: I leveled aircraft off at 6000 feet/foot and set cruise power noted lower than normal airspd. Checkeded gear and flaps and found them to be retracted. Airspd dropped further (slowly). I added power and checkeded for ice; suspecting pitot ice. Noted outside air temperature was -2 degrees celsius and only a trace of ice on the wings. On this particular aircraft the anti-ice switches are on the left/right (directions) sidewall near the capt's knees; and are hard to see in dim lighting. I looked and thought i saw pitot heat on. During this time; evidently the altimeter and vsi froze somehow. Air traffic control cued me in to this as they said first i was at approximately 7800 feet/foot mean sea level then a few moments later; at 10700 feet/foot mean sea level altimeter read approximately 5950 feet/foot vsi indicated zero feet per minute and airspd indicator read zero. I was able to level the aircraft off briefly and then turned on all switches on the left/right (directions) sidewall in the row with the deice equipment a few moments later; all indications came back to normal. Altitude wound up to 10300 feet/foot mean sea level airspd read 160 knot(s) and vsi approximately zero. I think i might have failed to turn on pitot heat in the dim light as the switches are hard to read. The emergency was declared when air traffic control indicated i was at 10700 feet/foot after everything came back to life; the flight was uneventful.
output: Pa31 pilot declares emergency when he experienced erroneous pitot static indications because pitot heat switches were off.

input: While flying from mem to fmh at fl410; the acft's constant speed drive motor; which runs the main air conditioning / alternating current generator; overheated. The emergency procedure dictates turning off the constant speed drive (essentially securing the main air conditioning / alternating current generator); switching the air conditioning / alternating current load to the auxiliary power unity and then landing as soon as possible at this point; we were 30 nautical mile westbound of aml and requested a divert into dulles international airport weather conditions along the ne were low instrument meteorological conditions due to snow and fog. Teb was closed due to snow on the runway(s) and other new york area airports were experiencing delays due to weather dulles was the primary divert for those areas. Washington approach was very accommodating; vectored us into the flow of traffic for an instrument landing system to runway(s) 19r. The pilot in the left/right (directions) seat flew the approach and landing and decelerated the aircraft on the deck. I was in the left/right (directions) seat and once we reached a safe speed took controls brought the aircraft to a full stop on the runway(s) just past a taxiway we requested a 180 degree turn to exit the runway(s) quickly. Needless to say; we were not quick since we did not use the high speed taxiway and the aircraft behind us on the approach had to execute a go around after we parked the aircraft we received the infamous call from tower who very calmly (thankfully) expressed his concerns. Contributing factors: 1) experiencing an electrical problem in the goo and landing at an unfamiliar and busy airport with a 'land asap' emergency presented a challenging situation for us. 2) we were tired; having flown 4.8 hours for the day; on the last day of a 3- day trip. 3) as military pilots we have very little experience operating at busy airports especially where time means money. It is a different environment for us to operate in. 4) it appeared all players were having a tough time due to the weather and heavy traffic flow. This included approach control tower and ourselves. Basically; the entire crew was focused on safely landing the aircraft since we were tired; we were concentrating on putting the aircraft on the deck and not past that point. Neither pilot verbalized the use of high speed txwys and we did what we always do at home at the end of a longitude sortie -- full stop on the runway(s) complete a 180 degree turn and exit at the mid-field taxiway lesson learned: use the high speed txwys intermediate fix they are available.
output: Mil flight crew of hu25 falcon jet has constant speed drive failure which leads to overheat of the main air conditioning / alternating current generator. Divert to iad as the best airport in instrument meteorological conditions after landing full stop on runway(s) leads to go around for aircraft following.

input: On oct/sat/99; on a flight from zzz to lax; we were in the aircraft preflt phase. 10 minute(s) before departure i had already done my cockpit preparation and all system were normal. I was the first officer on the flight my cockpit preparation was completed 30 minute(s) prior. The ground handler came up to the flight deck. He was talking about the air carrier broken b727 next to us. It was on a mechanical and would not be leaving for awhile. In his hand he had a temperature probe. I asked him what the probe was from and he replied from the broken airplane in a joking tone. I then said the airplane over there must not be in good shape at all. He agreed. He also joked about some airplanes break a lot. I then got up and went to the bathroom. When i came back into the cockpit the ground handler was leaving. While taxiing out; all system were normal. We departed zzz. On clbout. The tat (total air temp) was +50 degrees celsius this temperature is normal on the ground before takeoff but inflt normal is +10 degrees celsius to +20 degrees celsius on clbout. I pointed this out to the capt i also noticed a light to the left/right (directions) this is the windshear inoperative light and it was on. This light was pointed out to the capt also. Both were put into the logbook and maintenance was notified on arrival, arrive in lax. As the capt was speaking to the maintenance person; i got up to do my required duties. While the 3 of us were waiting for transportation to our operations(s) the capt noticed that the temperature probe was missing; i then thought back to what we were joking about in zzz. When we were talking about a temperature probe falling off it was not a joke; he was serious. He meant our airplane. This is no joking manner. This is people's lives. With the confusion of the broken air carrier b727 i thought he meant that air carrier b727. While all of us were joking we all misunderstood. This is a very serious safety issue. The ramper should have never been joking about aircraft parts and maint.
output: A b727-200 was dispatched in non compliance with the total air temperature probe missing. Damage incurred by ground vehicle undiscovered in preflt chk.

input: On right downwind for [runway] xr in zzz; and after being cleared for the visual approach; we received a gen 2 off caution message. Once on base; the tower controller asked where we were parking. I told him; and he asked if we wanted [runway] xl. The captain and i both agreed we would stick with xr. After the captain had the aircraft fully configured; he stated he was comfortable with the approach; and asked me to run the quick reference handbook checklist for gen 2 off message. I opened the quick reference handbook and found the checklist for gen 2 off message. The first item on the checklist says to move the gen 2 switch to off/rest then automatic i looked up at gen 2; looked back at the checklist; then accidentally moved the gen 1 switch to the off/reset position. This caused the air driven generator to automatically deploy. The captain turned on the auxiliary power unity and continued the approach and landing normally. I advised the tower controller that we may lose radios for a few seconds once on the ground. On the rollout the captain asked me to press the transfer override button to transfer power to the auxiliary power unity generator. We were already running behind and were scheduled to get in about 15 minutes later than scheduled. When we got the gen 2 off message; my mind began to wander. I started thinking that the plane would be delayed severely or grounded. Then i thought about how the next crew was going to be delayed; and how it might affect their day. Once it came time to run the checklist my mind wasn't completely on the task at hand as it should have been. I will definitely confirm and re-confirm what i'm doing while running any checklist. This was a mistake that i made; and should have paid more attention to what i was doing.
output: Crj700 flight crew experiences a number two generator off message during a visual approach and elects to continue. The first officer is asked to review the quick reference handbook and inadvertently turns off the number one generator while attempting to comply with the reset procedure causing the air driven generator to deploy. The auxiliary power unity is started and the flight continues to a normal landing.

input: At approximately 5 nautical mile on final for runway(s) 9l; all aircraft on tower frequency were advised that braking action on the runway(s) was good; but conditions were icy after turnoff. After a normal landing and speed deceleration the capt had planned to turn off approximately 2000' short of the end of the landing runway(s) when were told by the tower controller to 'take it all the way to the end.' as we reached the end of the runway(s) with approximately 10-15 knot(s) of forward ground speed the capt applied the brakes and we began to slide on a solid sheet of very thin ice. The capt applied full thrust reverser on all 3 engs in an effort to stop the aircraft after sliding through 2 runway(s) end lights. He was able to stop the aircraft approximately 500' into the overrun with the nose approximately 30 degrees to the right of runway(s) heading ord airport authorities arrived on the scene and asked us to attempt to turn the aircraft second officer we could taxi. We attempted 4 times to apply very little thrust and turn the nose; each time sliding straight forward. We elected not to make any more attempts because having the area around the aircraft de-iced was of no assistance and we were concerned about any further maneuvering causing us to exit the prepared surface. Numerous veh's were sliding as they applied sand to the overrun. A company tug was finally able to achieve enough traction to pull us out of the overrun and onto the de-iced runway(s) after having our landing gear inspected; we started the engs and taxied to parking.
output: Slid onto overrun area due to ice on rwy.

input: A band of showers had moved through my airport's area from west to east. I had been monitoring the weather via adds.aviationweather.gov. The band had moved out of the area and conditions had become visual flight rules a nearby airport was reporting visual flight rules conditions; but two other area airports were still marginal. I had decided to depart with the intent that if conditions were not good; i would return to my departure airport. Upon departure; the weather in the area was holding up as expected. Although there was residue clouds from the band of showers; i had positive visual contact with ground references and otherwise fair horizontal visibility. I continued on a 180 degree heading from at 1700 feet/foot mean sea level at approximately 3 miles south of my departure airport; i found myself in a cloud. I remained in level flight while i composed myself for a gradual 180 degree turn to return to my departure airport. Before i could execute the turn; i was out of the cloud. At this point i again had positive visual contact with the ground; but the horizontal visibility was vastly improved. The conditions continued to improve; and i was able to begin a climb as i was now under the 3000 feet/foot mean sea level shelf of the class b. Visibilities and conditions continued to improve; and i was able to maintain 5500 feet/foot mean sea level cruise altitude for the remainder of the trip. Upon reflecting on what could have gone wrong at any time in this flight; i reminded myself that the area in question has enough risk without contending with marginal conditions; and should have never been attempted. This situation does not reflect the decision-making process that i use when flying. I plan to review and use techniques for decision-making that i saw at an federal aviation administration safety seminar.
output: An m20 pilot reported departing his airport in marginal weather only to encounter instrument meteorological conditions conditions for a short time after takeoff. He continued to his destination in clear weather.

input: Approx 15-20 mile ne of karla intersection on byp 5 arrival, arrive to dfw; visual flight rules weather descending to 11000 feet/foot with speed brake out and approximately 2500 feet per minute descent passing 14200 feet/foot we were asked by zfw (124.87) at the last second to level at 14000 feet/foot we were unable to comply and stopped descent at 13500 feet/foot and then climbed back to 14000 feet/foot we told air traffic control and they very much apologized for the last second request and said we had visual flight rules traffic north of us at 14500 feet/foot as the reason for the request. We saw no traffic visually nor on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii most probably past us by this point. This controller was extremely busy; talkative; and seemed very stressed; definitely handling too much traffic also; there were other aircraft with similar call signs including a company aircraft and a few other similar call signs on frequency this ftw controller sounded as intermediate fix he could not talk fast enough; resulting in aircraft missing/repeating calls. I write this rpt not mainly because we were unable to comply with an impossible request by air traffic control short of pulling g's; but because these last minute(s) clrncs/requests are occurring more often; creating a less safe air traffic control environment. Maybe the air traffic control environment can't handle the increase of aircraft ie; 10 rjets or smaller versus 1 b737/757. Maybe air traffic control controllers are overworked and undermanned and losing too many senior people. Whatever the problems these issues need to be addressed. Or will it take a serious midair/loss of life before someone takes this seriously? Pass this rpt on to air traffic control and the faa!
output: B757 capt expressed concern regarding zfw controller's performance with regard to workload and staffing.

input: Flt crew squawked horizontal stabilized pitch trim paint marks on tail. At neutral pitch trim; leading edge of horizontal stabilizer did not line up exactly with neutral paint mark on vertical fin. Ran pitch trim to mechanical stops full nose up and nose down; those paint marks lined up. Put high lift truck at tail and viewed neutral up on the stabilizer; leading edge at upper edge of mark. A planning item was generated to repaint the mark. These marks have nothing to do with the rig of the airplane. Maintenance manual installation procedure for paint mark says; 'pos stabilizer to neutral position (0 units trim) and paint; intermediate fix required; index marks on vertical fin to align with mark on stabilizer leading edge.'
output: A b727-200 flight crew rpted stabilizer positioned at 0 degrees neutral trim did not align with neutral paint mark on stabilizer leading edge with vertical fin mark.

input: Lubbock automatic terminal information service was calling for a scattered layer around 2000 feet/foot when approximately 15 mile out tower said clouds were moving in from the north and an approach would be necessary. I flew the instrument landing system runway(s) 26 circle to land on runway(s) 8. I was cleared by the tower to enter a left/right (directions) downwind and cleared to land on runway(s) 8. I was able to make visual contact with the runway(s) at the minimums on the chart. I was expecting to break out much higher based on what the tower was saying. After becoming visual with the runway(s) i could see that it was getting worse to the north and ceiling was dropping fast. Instead of entering a left/right (directions) downwind; i flew a low approach over the runway(s) followed by a teardrop and landing for fear of losing the airport by entering the downwind. While on final; i advised the tower that the weather was getting lower in places. Immediately after i had made that advisory; tower came on and said new automatic terminal information service was available still calling for 1500- 2000 feet/foot scattered. Again while taxiing in; i again advised them that it was around 300 feet/foot overcast in certain areas around the field. While flying the low approach i descended about 150 feet/foot below the circling minimums unintentionally because i was watching the clouds and airport outside. Factors that i felt that contributed to the problem was inadequate information from the tower not once do i recall being informed about the lowering cloud deck.
output: Plt of a be18 twin beech failed to follow twr's circle- to-land instructions when passing over the runway(s) instead of making a left/right (directions) downwind for circling due to low clouds in the circling area.

input: At cruise center cleared us direct to 'drake' is what she said. Since drake was not on our flight plan i input the fix drake. The next controller asked where we were going and i replied drake. He said we were cleared to the drk vor and dme (co-located) not the fix. We entered in drk and continued. I guess we should had clarified with the first controller but she said 'drake' not drk. Both sides should have clarified the clearance since there is a fix and vor and dme (co-located) of the same name and somewhat in line with each other flying east bound. Clarify the clearance.
output: Air carrier flight crew reported they flew off course when cleared direct drake which is the name and same pronounciation of a vor and dme (co-located) in arizona and an airspace fix in colorado.

input: A b747 was en route zzzz and i called piarco center to coordinate the flight over 18n060w. The controller at piarco center said a couple of times that i was coming in weak and could not hear me too well; i could hear them loud and clear. She asked me to repeat the time; altitude; and air speed. I cannot recall if she read back the data or if she just said approved; but at the time we disconnected the call i was under the impression that piarco center had the correct data for this flight. I was relieved by another controller and developmental coming in to train and when i came back from break they had informed me that piarco center had called saying that the b747 had come over to them at fl380 and that they had shown the flight coordinated at fl360. The data on our end showed coordinated at fl380. Piarco center said that the difference in altitude was not a factor for them; but they were still having problems hearing us. Recommendation; i would recommend installing a better voice line between zny and piarco center since we are always having problems hearing them or visa versa. As you can see this weak phone line could have had catastrophic results; had piarco center had another aircraft close to the b747 at f380.
output: Zny controller described confused altitude coordination with piarco center; recommending the land line between the two facilities be improved.

input: Repositioned t28b; from rfd to isp with a fuel stop at cak on aug/xa/97; visual flight rules conditions at 11500 feet/foot cruising altitude approximately 3 1/2 hours en route flight distance approximately 745 nautical mile with no problems some weeks later; the new owner of the aircraft called me and said a local federal aviation administration inspector was asking him how the aircraft arrived at isp; as the operating limitations attached to the pink special airworthiness certificate experimental/exhibition; called for a 600 mile radius limit for proficiency flts. I submit this rpt that this was not a proficiency flight and simply a reposition to the new aircraft home base. No federal aviation regulation exists for the definition of delivery to a new home base; the paperwork is too vague and subject to different interps.
output: Plt of a north american t28 exceeded the acft's special airworthiness certificate operating limitations when delivering the aircraft to a new owner located beyond the distance specified in the operating limitations.

input: During climbout; approaching the flight levels the autopilot pitched down rather quickly to maintain the climb speed schedule with vertical navigation engaged. To make the flight more comfortable the captain elected to use v/s to continue the climb to fl390. Approaching the low fl300s i began looking in my publications and took my eyes off the instruments. Shortly thereafter the captain gasped and i looked away from the efb and noticed our airspeed had deteriorated significantly since i last looked moments earlier. The aircraft was at a speed just shy of the amber header. Meanwhile the captain lowered the nose to gain speed. Altitude loss was minimal and this occurred around fl370. Air traffic control never queried us and we continued our climb to fl390 once the aircraft returned to a normal energy state. The captain noted the mode control panel window had a flashing a. No other buffet alerts or stall indications were activated.
output: B737 flight crew reported that during climb the autopilot pitched over to regain airspeed.

input: After initial takeoff from zzz; departure notified the crew that zzz tower found a tire and suspected aircraft x had blown a tire either during taxi or takeoff. The crew had already raised the gear and flaps normally with no indication and decided to continue to zzz1. En route; the crew ran all appropriate checklists and decided to conduct a low approach for visual confirmation of landing gear status. The crew conducted a low pass at 500 ft. Above ground level and zzz1 tower indicated that both tires on the right main landing gear appeared to be missing. The crew climbed to a safe altitude and made the decision to [advise atc] and divert to zzz2 due to runway considerations. Zzz2 offered a longer; wider runway. The crew briefed and flew the approach to runway xx and elected to land on the left side of the runway to keep the drag in the center and reduce the chances of departing the runway. The crew landed on the left then maintained centerline due to the drag. The crew stopped the aircraft on the runway and egressed normally.the brakes on aircraft x had been changed [five days prior]. The brakes appeared to be stiff throughout the trip with a noticeable pull to the right.
output: Flight crew reported both right hand main tire and wheel assemblies fell off the aircraft at take off.

input: Was given block of airspace for training. Concentrated training. Strayed out of block. Disagreed with controller on limits of block. No known conflict with any acft.
output: An instructor pilot and student flew beyond the blocked airspace near msn.

input: Climbing out of lga on the lga5 departure; coney climb; we were told by air traffic control to maintain '300 knots indicated airspeed on the nose'. The aircraft was configured in a manner to accelerate toward 300 knots. The aircraft had reached 280 knots when we realized the aircraft was still under 10;000 mean sea level the aircraft was at approximately 8000 mean sea level when we noticed the deviation. The aircraft was immediately slowed to 250 knots until we reached 10;000 at which point the aircraft was again accelerated toward 300 knots. Air traffic control made no comment of the deviation and we continued the flight without further interruption. I was unfamiliar with and fixated on the departure procedure. I failed to control operation of the aircraft below 10;000 msl.
output: Captain reports having a speed deviation below 10000 feet departing lga; citing cause as fixation and unfamiliarity with the departure procedure.

input: Student and i called luk ground after receiving the automatic terminal information service and were instructed to taxi to runway(s) 3r. Many additional aircraft were also arriving/departing runway(s) 3r and the controller's workload was very high. As our flight proceeded down taxiway celsius toward runway(s) 3r; we volunteered to hold for a challenger to pull out of fixed-base operator and taxi ahead of us to runway(s) 3r. Following the challenger and trying to maintain situational awareness with the aircraft around us; we continued along taxiway celsius while searching for the standard yellow hold short lines. As we slowly rolled onward toward the threshold of runway(s) 3r; it became apparent that we must have missed them. Second officer we stopped immediately; still well clear of any operations(s) on runway(s) 3r; and looked behind us. Sure enough; the remnants of the very heavily worn and faded hold short lines could just barely be seen along the edges of the taxiway and were almost invisible on the remaining width of the taxiway our aircraft had rolled approximately 15 feet/foot past the line but was still at least 30 feet/foot from the left/right (directions) (or closest) edge of the runway(s) the runway(s) itself was 150 feet/foot wide. We were shortly thereafter cleared for takeoff without further incident. Even though the hold short lines were very worn/faded; we should still have been able to identify the holding point using the red/white txwy/rwy intersection markers. While we were both concentrating to see the hold short lines; i honestly do not remember seeing the red/white intersection markers. In the future; i will be more alert to multiple means of identing a particular spot; route etc; and not allow attention to become overly focused/limited on 1 item; no matter how busy the workload. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he has had no follow-up on this incident. He was quite shocked to look back and see these 'pieces' of yellow lines from the edge of the taxiway that faded into nothing on the center taxiway area. His reference to red/white markings is referring to the runway(s) signs one would see beside the taxiway indicating the runway(s) ahead. He has learned; as has his student; to monitor more than 1 indicator.
output: Instructor with student taxi past very worn hold line.

input: When the crew arrived at [the aircraft]; maintenance control had deferred the ground idle portion of the eec's (electronic engine control). Myself as the captain looked over the ddg (dispatch deviation guide); talked with the two mechanics on board and found that everything was written off properly. The mechanic and i discussed the ramifications a little bit on the referral. The plane blocked out on time with a normal engine start and normal taxi to [the] runway. However upon takeoff clearance and bringing the thrust levers up to approximately 70% we noticed the right engine was accelerating quicker than the left engine. It wasn't exceeding any limitations but still as the captain and because we had the deferral concerning the situation ; i felt it would be better/ conservative to just bring the thrust levers back and taxi off the runway and discuss what was actually going on with the mechanics in a safe environment on the taxiway and that is what i did. I asked the first officer to cancel takeoff clearance and that we would like to clear the runway and discuss a possible maintenance issue. So we cleared the runway; i spoke to the mechanics about the situation and it is quite common on most of the 767 200s for the right engine to accelerate quicker than the left engine. I don't know why this is but i've noticed it on many different airplanes. So we cleared the runway.i spoke to the mechanics about the situation. I remembered talking to maintenance control the day before and he informed me there are no time limits for the engines to accelerate together. At this moment on the taxiway i confirm that with the two mechanics that only the two engines had to match and then accelerate uniformly after takeoff thrust button was pushed and takeoff power is set. After clearing the runway there were no checklists to be run since there are no engine indicating and crew alerting system messages or abnormal events. I just wanted to understand that everything was fairly normal. The break chart was not needed to be consulted since we never really release the brakes for takeoff. Takeoff power was never set. By definition in the fom a rejected takeoff was never really performed since take off power was never set however i am going to treat this like a rejected takeoff just in case. The two mechanics and the first officer and myself discussed that we would perform the takeoff again.... Let the engines both stabilize at approximately 70% and then push the takeoff thrust button and if the engines accelerated absolutely perfectly symmetrically to takeoff thrust then we would continue the takeoff. This is exactly what happened on the second takeoff and this is normally what happens on most of the 767 200s. The engines do not accelerate to 70% symmetrically all the time but they do accelerate from 70%to takeoff thrust symmetrically. Maintenance control and the mechanics confirmed there is no time limit to where these engines have to accelerate to the 70% setting. The takeoff was normal.
output: Captain reported a rejected takeoff after number 2 engine acceleration lagged significantly.

input: I departed ral instrument flight rules to visual flight rules on top in 4 mile visibility 3000- 3500 feet/foot overcast with tops at 5000 feet/foot at approximately xa45. I departed on runway(s) 27 direct to pdz vor and dme (co-located) with a clearance to maintain 4000 feet/foot above ground level i was handed off to socal approach from ral tower at about 1500-2000 feet/foot i was directed by socal approach or vectored off my direct heading to pdz vor and dme (co-located) approximately 2 mile prior to the fix by socal approach and told to turn to a heading of 140 degrees which i did and climb and maintain 4000 feet/foot as i was coming up through 3000 feet/foot i was amended to maintain 3000 feet/foot i had autoplt set for 4000 feet/foot by the time i reached the knob to reset to 3000 feet/foot and set pitch for descent i was climbing through 3600 feet/foot the aircraft did not respond quick enough second officer i turned off autoplt when approach announced traffic alert 12 o'clock position approximately 3 seconds later i was at 3000 feet/foot with manual control and i heard aircraft at 12 o'clock position announced. He was instrument meteorological conditions when i was visual flight rules at 3000 feet/foot i was told to call 619 area when i landed which i did at calexico. Note: i believe the controller should have let me continue to pdz vor and dme (co-located) as was initial clearance and not vector me into a 12 o'clock position on-coming aircraft the traffic alert was given within 30 seconds after vectoring me in his direction.
output: Plt of a piper pa30 twin commanche overshot departure altitude resulting in a conflict with other aircraft the pilot blames this incident on air traffic control giving a late clearance to stop climb at the altitude passing through and autoplt slow in responding to a descent back down to the newly assigned altitude rptr disengaged the autoplt and returned quickly to assigned alt.

input: I left during visual flight rules conditions to spread cover on a crop 5 miles south of the airport. When i reached the field the weather quickly closed in on me to less than 1 mile visibility and less than 500 ft ceiling trapping me against the ground. I was able to stay at 100 ft above ground level and follow my last global positioning system track back to [the departure airport]. I passed over the city at about 100 ft above ground level in order to maintain ground contact and reach the airport. Forecast weather did not call for instrument meteorological conditions conditions until later in the day.
output: Thrush s2r pilot reported overflying a city at low altitude after becoming caught beneath an overcast layer.

input: While waiting in line for departure; it became apparent it was the beginning of the early morning push for departures interspersed with a steady stream of arrivals. Runway 25r was in use for arrivals/departures along with operations being conducted from the runway 19l/r complex. I cannot adequately provide the color to the story except to say that there had been a go-around from the runway 19l/r complex and a hot air balloon that made multiple unanswered calls to the las tower. Earlier; [the] balloon had checked in with las tower to report operations six miles west of the airport at 4000 feet. The controller eventually did answer [the] balloon; advising [him] to remain clear of class b airspace. Balloon responded by saying they would be operating six miles west of the airport at 5000 feet. The controller did not acknowledge the transmission. A b737 had been cleared for takeoff on runway 25r. Holding short of 25r; las tower asked if we had that [b737] in sight. We replied that we had the [b737] in sight as the b737 was just beginning its takeoff roll. We were subsequently cleared to line up and wait on runway 25r. Taking the runway; we were cleared for takeoff by the tower. Aligning the airplane on the runway; i noticed two things. One; the b737 wasn't airborne yet; and secondly there was a flight of two hot air balloons operating west of the airport. I delayed our takeoff roll; since the b737 wasn't airborne. I asked the first officer to confirm we were cleared for takeoff. The first officer was initially unable to do so as the controller had cleared the airplane behind us to line up and wait. The controller confirmed we had been cleared for takeoff. We began our takeoff roll as the b737 became airborne. During our takeoff roll; the tower advised arriving 25r traffic to prepare for a go-around. Flying the cowby6 area navigation departure; at 600 feet above ground level we encountered the b737's wake turbulence. The wake turbulence continued until the initial turn passing rbell to roppr intersection with the worst rolling moment of the wake turbulence occurring during that turn. The wake turbulence made flying the lateral portion of the cowby6 area navigation departure difficult particularly turning toward roppr intersection since the turn had been begun late due to having to manage the wake turbulence. Keep in mind; the flight of two hot-air balloons operating west of the airport.
output: B737 captain reported a track deviation resulted departing las after encountering wake turbulence in trail of another b737.

input: I was working sector 30 and was advised by the adjacent controller that air carrier x was heading towards my sector and that he was having radio problems and could only transmit and receive on 134.57 (and 121.5). Air carrier x departed zzz enroute to zzz1. The 134.57 frequency is not a frequency we can transmit or receive on. That meant we could only communicate indirectly with air carrier x; using other aircraft to relay to him on 134.57 or 121.5. Apparently the command center was aware of this problem; and the supervisor was coordinating with adjacent facilities. As we weren't busy at the time we objected in principle to the situation but had no real pressing need to talk to the aircraft as it transited zmp airspace. However; not being in direct communications with an aircraft for extended periods of time; heading to a busy destination such as zzz1; creates an unsafe situation; as well as additional workload for the controllers. The aircraft should have been ordered to divert to another airport to fix the equipment malfunction before being allowed to proceed to a busy east coast airport such as zzz1.
output: Zmp controller voiced concern regarding the decision to permit an air carrier; limited to only one frequency; to transit multiple airspace environments and land at a busy east coast airport.

input: After a 10 hour flight; and upon approach to runway xy; approaching 1;400 feet above ground level i asked for flaps 25. When first officer moved flap; handle to 25; the 'leading edge slat disagree' light illuminated. I told the first officer we would go-around; & he relayed the info to the tower. Tower then gave us runway heading & climb to 3000 feet. Flaps indicated 25; & we left them there on climb out. During the initial climb out; airspeed got to 220 kts; which is an over speed for flaps 25. It was a momentary speed & we quickly reduced the speed to 170 (flap 25 speed is 180). I was flying the aircraft & talking with air traffic control the first officer & relief pilot went through the proper quick reference handbook checklist. I told tower we wanted to land on the [longer parallel runway] & that was approved. First officer then went thru the landing checklist again; in its entirety; & i told tower we were ready for the approach. We were in & out of icing throughout the entire event. I [asked air traffic control for priority] due to the uncertainty of the positioning of the flaps & slats; & the poor weather conditions at airport zzz. Braking conditions were not available for the runway; but tower said it had been cleared. The relief first officer checked the runway length required for landing; using wet runway with braking action poor. [parallel runway] far exceeded our length requirements. The landing was smooth & uneventful. The arff trucks followed us to the first available high speed taxiway. We stopped the aircraft once clear of the runway; & had arff check the aircraft for any damage or anything unusual. The report was negative; & we were cleared to taxi to our gate. Upon taxi in; we contacted aircraft maintenance & they said to leave the flap handle in the 25 position. No pax reported injuries; & the deplaning was normal.
output: A b767-300er flight crew experienced receipt of a l/e slat disagree message upon selecting a landing flap setting of 25 degrees and the pilot flying called for a go-around during which the landing gear was retracted; autoflight modes and autothrottles were deselected or misemployed...due in part to the blaring landing gear warning horn which was a substantial distraction until silenced. A subsequent flap over speed occurred when the thrust levers were not retarded in a timely manner. They advised air traffic control completed the associated quick reference handbook and checklists; requested a longer runway and landed safely.

input: Crew had planned a practice auto-land. After localizer intercept; second autoplt armed; capt called 'gs alive.' no glideslope indication on first officer side (pf). First officer said 'no glideslope indication.' at intercept; capt said to start down. Still no glideslope indication on first officer side. First officer said 'you have the aircraft as i have no gs.' capt said 'i have the aircraft stand by for gar.' capt flew down to glideslope manually while first officer configured aircraft for landing (gear; flaps 15 degrees 25 degrees 35 degrees target; and reset speed brake which had been pulled slightly aft of armed pos). Aircraft stabilized by 1000 feet/foot normal landing glideslope written up. Intermittent glideslope at 1300 feet/foot and 1100 feet/foot slide glideslope at 1000 feet/foot to ground on first officer side. Possible airspd exceedance on flaps 25 degree setting. Should this have been on automatic go around even in clear air turbulence i conditions? Inoperative glideslope created high workload and rapid control xfer and confign.
output: Role reversal occurs in the cockpit when the fo's glideslope indicator on the b737-700 fails when glideslope is alive for instrument landing system runway(s) 4r at ewr; nj.

input: About 20 minute(s) before landing a call light went off. #4 flight attendant answered it and it was a lady complaining of not feeling well. Paxs beside her thought she may have had a seizure. She was pale and couldn't see well. #4 gave her water and asked intermediate fix she was on any medication. Capt was notified to have paramedics meet the flight we landed and got to the gate only to have jet bridge in wrong position second officer we waited for a tow to get to jet bridge; paxs were advised to remain seated. Paramedics got to her row and immediately the gate agent announced that rows fwd of her could deplane. All those people got up and then paramedics needed to get back off the plane to get supplies and were trapped by deplaning paxs. Another announced was made to tell people to get out of the way. She was removed from the plane and treated in the terminal area.
output: Md80 flight crew landed with an ill passenber and had emergency medical personnel to meet aircraft after boarding and checking paxs; the medics were blocked in deplaning for getting needed medical equipment due to deplaning paxs blocking their way off the acft.

input: Because of the controller's accent it was difficult to understand his instructions to begin with. We were approaching anu from the wnw and were cleared to the nondirectional radio beacon second officer we proceeded as cleared we questioned the controller on 3 separate occasions what his intentions were after we reached the nondirectional radio beacon and also for the weather conditions since they were marginal for us to even begin any approach we finally received some weather found it to be adequate for our intentions and continued. As we were in very close proximitypa to the nondirectional radio beacon we once again asked for the controller's intentions and received once again a 'roger'; meaning absolutely nothing to us. Once we reached the nondirectional radio beacon we asked the controller intermediate fix he wanted us to proceed outbnd on the 070 degree bearing; because we were unsure of the approach in use at the time. We received a 'roger' and in the hurried state we proceeded on the nondirectional radio beacon 25 since this corresponded to the 070 bearing without realizing there were 2 ndb's on the field. We flew the procedure for nondirectional radio beacon 25 off zdx nondirectional radio beacon but never descended from our 2500' assigned altitude because we were never cleared for the approach we informed the controller 2 separate times of our position with no disapproval. As we turned inbound to zdx the controller after we once again gave our position off zdx; informed us the approach in use was the ndb-a circle runway(s) 7. We then proceeded back to the appropriate nondirectional radio beacon and flew the approach and landed without any further problem. I feel this all could have been avoided intermediate fix the controller had made his intentions known from the beginning. We also feel the manner in which he spoke could have been more clear and concise and a little slower. We all were unfamiliar with the airport with myself being the only one having been there once before.
output: Flt crew of lgt commenced approach on wrong nondirectional radio beacon approach communications difficulties.

input: Shortly after liftoff; we had multiple cockpit failures. The first officer airspeed indicator was rapidly accelerating; the altimeter was increasing at a highly accelerated rate; and the vvi was pegged at 6;000 feet per minute climb. There were multiple cockpit warnings both aural and visual. Both the warning and caution lights were illuminated. There were multiple engine indicating and crew alerting system messages. At a minimum i saw overspeed warning; aileron lockout; and rudder ratio. When i looked across the cockpit; i saw the captain's instruments were indicating a normal climb out. We were quite close to the ground; so i silenced the bell and told the captain her instruments were indicating correctly. (by the way; unusual attitude training was helpful in this case to not react in an inappropriate manner). As we climbed out; the instrument indications returned to normal and eventually all the cautions went away. As we climbed above 10;000 feet/foot we began to troubleshoot and determined it was a problem with the air data computer. After referring to the flight manual and conferring with dispatch and maintenance; we decided to return to the departure airport to get the airplane fixed and press on to our original destination. Shortly after we made this decision and began our turn back; we got the same cockpit indications. This time; we selected the captain's air data computer to repeat on the first officer's side. Periodically; i would return to the first officer air data computer and it would be indicating normally and at other times; it would be in a state of failure; so we decided to leave the first officer instruments on the captain's air data computer. Once the decision was made to return to the departure airport; we began to dump fuel to get closer to max gross landing weight. As we flew back; we began to review the fom and flight manual to ensure we hadn't missed anything. After reading overweight landing verses fuel dumping i advocated that it didn't make sense to land overweight. It seemed an easy decision to delay landing by an hour to ensure no damage to the aircraft as opposed to having to wait at the end of the runway for an hour for the brakes to cool off possibly damaging tires or brakes. We had no dire emergency that would cause us to land immediately. The captain ultimately decided that was what we were going to do: wait until our landing weight was reached to ensure the safety of the passengers and to prevent damage to the airplane. While we were in holding burning fuel; we received a cell call. The dispatcher wanted to know why we didn't want to land overweight. I was pretty surprised that the dispatcher was asking all these questions (including page numbers and our rational) while we were in the middle of an emergency. Shortly after that; the duty manager cell called us. I was stunned to find out that he was trying to convince us to modify our decision in the middle of an ongoing emergency. He was not trying to point out something we missed that would cause injury. He was trying to point out a misinterpretation of a chart. I couldn't believe that the duty manager would try to convince a cockpit crew in flight that the decision they made was too conservative. It would have been more appropriate to wait until after landing to point out the chart misinterpretation. Unfortunately; being human; for the rest of the flight; i was second guessing our decision. Instead of thinking of the safety of the airplane; i was trying to make sure i wouldn't be reprimanded for making a poor decision. I found myself worrying about my job on final instead of being fully engaged in the cockpit. The emergency itself was relatively inane and not difficult to manage. The second guessing (while in the cockpit of an emergency aircraft) was disturbing and distracting. I have 2 recommendations. First; a duty manager should never call an emergency aircraft in the air unless his concern is for the safety of the flight. Certainly not to recommend a less conservative path than the one the crew has already chosen. Second; i would recommend renaming the b767 brake cooling time table chart to b767 maximum effort/rto brake cooling time chart.
output: A b767-300 crew reported a first officer air data computer malfunction shortly after takeoff. The decision was made to dump fuel then return to the departure airport for a normal landing. The company dispatcher and duty pilot questioned the decision to not land overweight making the crew uneasy.

input: During landing rollout in pit; the crc master warning sounded and electronic centralized aircraft monitoring showed a landing gear unsafe indication momentarily; and then subsequently disappeared. Next; a nosewheel steering fault appeared and nosewheel steering was lost. The aircraft was stopped on the runway(s) ctrline and air traffic control was notified. Air traffic control asked intermediate fix we required any assistance and we replied negative. I set the parking brake; recycled the brake and nosewheel steering switch; and recovered nosewheel steering. We then exited the runway(s) and taxied to the gate. Air traffic control dispatched the emergency equipment as a precaution.
output: A319 suffers loss of nosewheel steering on landing roll. Set brakes and cycled brakes and nosewheel steering switch and proceeded to gate.

input: This was the first leg in this aircraft. There was heavy rain enroute through the eastern half of the flight. The flight was uneventful until engine shut down at block in. At engine shut down; i leaned over to open the cockpit door. When i did; i smelled a strong electrical burning smell. I turned to the first officer to ask him about the smell and i looked at the instruments to see if there were any other indications of something burning. He suggested that it was possibly the engine exhaust we could be smelling as there was wind and the cabin door was open. The smell lasted a short time; approximately 10 seconds. Having no other secondary indications of an issue; the smell had since dissipated; this seemed reasonable. We had a 37 minute turn so we boarded the jet for our return flight. While taxing out; the first officer elected to use the radar for departure; as the weather was moving in. I turned on my radar as well. I did not receive any radar returns for the first several sweeps. I then got returns for several sweeps; to again have them disappear. The first officer radar was intermittent as well. We cycled the radar on and off several times to have the same results. We took the gain from automatic to maximum and settings in between. We tested all ranges; mirroring both ranges on each side and then separate ranges. The results were the same. We did not receive any failure messages. We elected to taxi back to the gate as i wanted a mechanic to examine the radar as opposed to a circuit breaker reset. This was due to the nature of the failures accompanied with no failure warnings and the weather along the flight. I informed the flight attendants we had to return to the gate and the first officer let operations know. When we got back to gate and shut down the engines. Immediately the a flight attendant reported that he smelled a strong electrical burning smell. I asked him the location and to describe exactly what he had smelled. He described the same smell i had experienced in the same area; again a short duration. The area was right by the cockpit door. (please note that i had not discussed the smell i experienced on the previous leg with the flight attendant. The first officer took care of write ups while i went to the jet bridge and called dispatch. I asked the dispatcher to patch me through to maintenance and stay on the line. I explained to maintenance the issues we had. While i was talking to him; the a flight attendant came told me that the passenger entertainment system had cycled on and off when we had taxied out. (we had started both engines at the gate). I reported that to maintenance as well. In addition; while i told maintenance that i did not feel this was an issue; but i was giving him everything we saw; i had quick sporadic flashes of messages at the top of my pfd at power transfer. Maintenance said that we would not be taking the jet anywhere with a burning smell twice in a row. We told him we felt the same way. I briefed the contract mechanic. It is my opinion that he was not very interested in speaking with me as he wanted to talk only to maintenance. He did not ask me any questions or spoke any further with me; only to ask what maintenance was asking him to ask me (over his cell phone). He went to the cockpit to test the radar. He ran the tests pattern on the radar and tests through the jets computer. I was up in the cockpit with him and told him we had not received any failure messages but had lost the return of the weather several times. (thinking the radar may ground test ok; but not work when turned on). We had told him we would configure the jet as we had before (engines running; and out where we could turn on the radar and show him what we had). We were not asked to do so. The contract mechanic had also opened the avionics bay to check for a smell and had not detected any odor. I told him that this was well after the smell had dissipated; so it was not unexpected that he would not smell anything at this time.i did not see the contract mechanic again. The first officer; i and the flight attendant crew stayed on the jet. The first officer asked if i knew the flight attendants had a legality issue. I did not. He said that the gate agents had received a call regarding it; they go illegal in an hour and fifteen minutes and they passed this information on to us. I verified this with the flight attendants. We were told the jet was released and that they were going to board the aircraft for departure. We had not heard anything from maintenance regarding the jet. We had not received a maintenance release. We had no information on anything regarding the status of the jet or what was found. The first officer worked with the gate agents to hold off on the boarding; explaining the situation to them; as i got on the phone again with maintenance. I asked maintenance what was causing the electrical smell. He said he did not know yet; that it might be the passenger entertainment control unit and that might be deferred.
