I told him that was a big assumption and how did we know that was the cause. He stated that was why they were still looking into the issue. I asked him why he released the jet. He said he had not released the jet and he would not until he could track down the smell. (he was very good to work with and it is unfortunate we both had conflicting information as to the status of the jet). I told him that we were told the jet had been released and the new maintenance release was down in operations. The gate agents had passed on the information to us. He had no information on this and stated he had not released the jet. The first officer had just received the new maintenance release and all 3 write ups had been signed off. I called dispatch back to update him. I let him know we were not taking the jet until we could get some information on what was causing the smell or some reasonable explanation. He concurred. He said that they would most likely send in an engineering crew to ferry the jet to a maintenance base. At this point the flight attendants went illegal. The flight was canceled about a half an hour later. We stayed on the jet. [analyst summary: the captain reported a dispute developed when maintenance claimed the crew had not cooperated with maintenance to solve burning smell issue. Maintenance attempted to force the crew to fly the aircraft by stating no more maintenance would be accomplished and an engineer crew would not be sent to ferry the aircraft. The crew refused a ferry flight the following day because maintenance had not completed any troubleshooting or prepared a brief for the crew. The crew was approved to taxi out and configure the aircraft for takeoff as they had done the previous day when the burning electrical smell appeared. The burning smell returned on taxi back and shutdown.]
output: An a319 radar malfunctioned during taxi for takeoff so the crew returned to the gate where a burning electrical smell was detected on engine shutdown and where a passenger entertainment system anomaly was also noted. Interaction issues with maintenance developed.

input: Detected slight left/right (directions) engine roughness and partial power loss. Noting a high fuel pressure; low egt; and no differential magneto drop; i diagnosed the problem as a clogged fuel injector. Elected to continue to home base at reduced left/right (directions) engine power no emergency declared; or asked for most direct routing. Air traffic control cooperated. Emergency equipment out at destination though not requested by me. Had past experience with this type of engine anomaly.
output: Pa30 pilot had rough engine with power loss.

input: We were on an instrument flight in a c172. During the course of the flight; we climbed to 12000 feet/foot (per atc) in order to stay on top of the haze layer and reduce turbulence. We were over the a regional airport at 12;000 feet/foot and we were in communication with approach. At that point; the controller directed us to 'descend and maintain 9000 ft.' flight conditions were instrument meteorological conditions -4 degrees celsius and no airframe icing was being encountered. We reduced throttle in order to descend; within a few seconds of reducing throttle; the engine stopped running. After quickly completing the 'engine failure checklist;' with no success; we declared an emergency with approach and received expedited handling. The controller directed us to squawk 7700; which we did. We continued on our present heading with the intent of making an emergency landing at a nearby common traffic advisory frequency airport; which was very close and below us. Upon further discussion  with the controller; however; we elected to instead head for a nearby class d airport because of the fact that the controller had weather information there; and not at the first airport; and also because better emergency equipment was available. At our altitude of 12;000 feet/foot a glide to the airport (-15nm) was within reach at that point; per the poh. The weather was reported to us by the controller as overcast 3500 feet/foot with light rain and 7 miles visibility. As we descended through 9000 feet/foot (still in imc) we were able to restart the engine; although it was still running roughly at that point. We continued to descend towards the airport and broke out of the clouds into good visual meteorological conditions at approximately 4800 feet/foot at that point the engine was running smoothly and at full power. We cancelled our emergency status with approach; and he once again cleared us to our original destination; the controller returned us to our original transponder code. Upon further analysis; it is clear that this engine failure incident was caused by severe carburetor ice -- just below the freezing level; in cloud; with visible ice crystals in the cloud. Although the ice crystals were not of the type that created airframe ice (no airframe ice was reported in our area); it was ideal for causing carburetor ice; which built up more rapidly than we were able to clear using carburetor heat. As we descended into warmer air; the carburetor ice cleared and the engine ran normally. No other anomalies were found with the airframe or the engine.
output: A c172 pilot at 12;000 feet/foot descending in instrument meteorological conditions with no visible ice; experienced an engine failure because of carburetor ice. An emergency that was declared with air traffic control was later cancelled after the engine was restarted at 4;880 feet/foot in vmc.

input: I was working the north arrival, arrive sector at phl. During this session the winds had increased to the point that our secondary runway(s) (35) was not being utilized for arrs due to the tailwind component. The supervisors on duty decided to run an operations(s) called 'saprs1.' this procedure is rarely used and caused a vast amount of confusion to all arrival, arrive sectors. I do not believe all required coordination was completed; associated airspace to run this procedure was not obtained from adjacent facilities; and personnel working these arrival, arrive sectors were not told who the first aircraft to run this procedure was. Since this is a seldom used procedure trying to implement it during a heavy arrival, arrive bank without ensuring all personnel understand their responsibilities is a severe safety risk. At the minimum phl should have stayed 'status quo;' until all personnel were briefed and were comfortable with the operations(s) additionally i feel this procedure should become a mandatory briefing item quarterly to keep personnel familiar with this proc.
output: Phl approach controller expressed concern regarding a change to the rarely used saprs1 procedure during busy traffic period.

input: Flight is scheduled for a flight time 7:58. Actual flight time 8:57 with a duty time of 11:38! This flight consistently goes over 8 hours and because the original scheduled flight time is under 8 hours the crew is not entitled to a rest break if the crew rest seats are sold. Fatigue is dangerous and although this month's schedule has the flight over 8 hours there is no consistency with this flight as scheduled flight time varies from month to month; but only by a 5 minute window! This practice is unsafe and this flight (and others like it) should always have a scheduled crew rest.
output: A flight attendant explains that a flight scheduled under eight hours consistently exceeds eight hours but no crew rest seats are provided.

input: While in cruise at fl410; the #2 transfer bus off light began to flicker and then the 'b' autopilot kicked off and the #2 drive light illuminated. We coordinated with air traffic control for a lower altitude while running the drive light quick reference handbook procedures. While running the quick reference handbook we noticed an acrid smell in the cockpit followed by notification from the flight attendants of the same smell throughout the cabin. We then accomplished the quick reference handbook items for fumes in the cockpit and began to coordinate with air traffic control for an even lower altitude and request for diversion to a nearby airport. We also declared an emergency at this point and notified dispatch and the flight attendants as well as getting the divert airport weather and getting performance calculations and getting out the appropriate approach plates and keeping the passengers informed as well as running the descent and before landing checklists. We coordinated for emergency response vehicles to meet us after clearing the runway to confirm there was no fire and that it would be safe to taxi to the gate. They cleared us to the gate and then the captain contacted dispatch/maintenance control/and chief pilot on call after debriefing the emergency response crew. A logbook entry was made.
output: A b737-700 #2 generator control unit (gcu) and generator malfunctioned in flight illuminating the #2 transfer bus off and generator drive lights as well as creating electrical fumes in the aircraft so an emergency was declared and the flight diverted safely to a nearby airport.

input: Local show time was approximately xa:00. This was 55 minutes prior to scheduled takeoff time. (xa:55z). Airfield conditions were night operations with no visibility issues. Upon arriving at the aircraft at gate; maintenance informed us of a write up requiring deferment (auto speed brake system). There was also a problem with the captain's seat belt. The maintenance issues lead to a block out time of xb:45z (:50 late). During taxi out; #2 deu failure caused a return to the terminal. After maintenance was performed; the aircraft blocked out for the second time at xd:36 (2:46 late). Ground control cleared us to taxi to runway xxl and [along the route hold at] taxiway x. Taxiway x and taxiway y are both at the approach end of runway xxl with open tarmac between them. Taxiway y is nearest the beginning of the runway. Also; there is a flange on the west end of taxiway y to facilitate a high-speed turn off from runway xyr. The width of the widest part of this flange is approximately equal to the runway width.approaching hold point taxiway x; tower instructed us to hold short of holding point taxiway y. There was a wide-body aircraft holding at taxiway x; which was subsequently cleared for takeoff. As that aircraft was rolling for takeoff; we were instructed to taxi into position and hold. We entered the runway area via holding point taxiway y. A yellow runway exit line curved to the right toward the runway centerline from hold point taxiway y. Hold point taxiway x was to the left; which allowed the full length of the runway. We expected full length. There was open tarmac between these two runway entrances; so we turned about 45 degrees left to maneuver the aircraft to a position closer to the beginning of the runway. When the aircraft was turned right to align with the runway; the yellow line leading to the runway centerline was not evident and the right runway-edge line was mistaken for the runway centerline. The captain set the brakes and transferred aircraft control to the first officer. During the turn to the right to align the aircraft; the first officer was scanning for possible malfunctions associated with the multiple maintenance issues leading up to this point. After transfer of aircraft control; i noticed there was a notable lack of runway markings in this hold position. In my mind; this was attributed to being on an open ramp area prior to the beginning of the runway. I expected normal runway markings to be just ahead. A lack of familiarity with this runway and the large open tarmac between the hold-short area and the runway contributed to this misperception. After receiving takeoff clearance and during the initial part of the takeoff roll; the first officer's attention was inside focused on setting takeoff power. During this time; the aircraft was aligned with the right-side runway edge lights. As the flange narrowed from right to left to meet the edge of the runway; it became apparent that the centerline was to the left. With rudder pedal steering; the aircraft was maneuvered to the left to join the centerline. The maneuvering occurred after setting takeoff power and runway centerline was achieved just prior to 100 knots. All maneuvering was in the low-speed regime and it was not apparent that we impacted any runway lights during the takeoff roll. We elected to continue the takeoff. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. After blocking in at zzzz1; we discovered that one of the nose wheels sustained notable damage to its sidewall.
output: While taxiing the aircraft onto the runway for takeoff; b-737 crew was unable to see the yellow line leading to the runway centerline and mistook the right runway-edge line for the runway centerline. Crew recognized the error; corrected to centerline by 100 knots and continued the takeoff. On post-flight inspection the crew discovered damage to the nose wheels sidewalls.

input: This airport's rotating beacon is located 1.4 nm ne of the airport; well outside the airport boundary. Though very non-standard; it is not mentioned in the flight information publication (flip) or depicted on the ipp plates. Even the green bay sectional could show the correct position; instead of the standard symbology which implies the beacon would be found on the airport.only the jeppesen instrument charts depict it accurately.this secret non-standard placement could result in disorientation and worse; at least give pilots a chance by publishing it.
output: Pilot reported the rotating beacon located 1.4 nautical mile ne of imt airport is at a non-standard location and could potentially result in pilot disorientation. Pilot also stated the beacon location is not mentioned in the flight information publication; nor depicted in the ipp plates.

input: Having previously flown as the pilot flying into bhm just once or twice; and then in mvfr/ifr conditions; i was the pilot flying. As such; i had never personally seen the 2;049 feet/foot tower depicted on the instrument landing system 06 approach chart. Unfortunately; today i completely overlooked this potential obstacle when i briefed the visual approach for runway 06 backed up by the instrument landing system we had been cleared down to 3;000 feet/foot approximately 10 miles southeast of the field when bhm approach cleared us for the visual and told us to contact tower. I then dialed the final approach fix ('mcden') crossing altitude of 2;200 feet/foot into the mode control panel altitude window; began a descent to that altitude; and proceeded direct to mcden. The plan was to level off at 2;200 feet/foot some three miles prior to mcden and then continue slowing and configuring. At approximately 2;300 feet/foot the captain noticed and called out the tower; which was nearly directly in front of us; at an estimated distance of 1.5 miles; and looking nearly at our same altitude. I immediately clicked off the autothrottles and autopilot and commenced a gentle climb (we reached nearly 3;000 ft). Just after i commenced the climb; the egpws sounded 'obstacle.' the captain then contacted bhm tower; advised that we were high; and requested that we be allowed to cross then return to the localizer from the opposite side; in order to conclude a successful approach. The tower approved and cleared us to land. Crossing the obstacle tower; i continued configuring and slowing and; after we crossed the localizer; a 30-degree banked turn and a 1;000 ft/minute descent allowed us to be configured; stable; and on the localizer and glideslope at approximately 1;000 feet/foot above ground level the remainder of the approach and landing were uneventful. Closer attention to detail on the approach plate; and to other notes and warnings provided in our [chart] package; would likely have caused me to notice; brief; and better avoid this obstacle. However; i also find it curious that air traffic control never mentioned what i suspect is a commonly encountered threat; at least for aircraft arriving from the southeast conducting visual approaches to runway 06.
output: An air carrier aircraft egpws alerted caution terrain on the downwind for a bhm runway 6 visual and so the crew climbed slightly to avoid the tall tower but were high on final requiring delaying turns.

input: I was flying with a high minimums capt from mkg to dtw. The capt performed all takeoffs and lndgs. I would fly every other en route leg from the completion of the after takeoff chklist to the completion of the descent chklist. The automatic terminal information service was indicating landing runway(s) 21l and hold short of runway(s) 27l. The capt told the controller on initial contact that we could not hold short. After some discussion between the capt and myself; we determined that we could hold short of runway(s) 27l. Control of the aircraft was transferred and we were handed off to the next sector. I was working the radios. I checkeded in. By this time we were established on the instrument landing system for runway(s) 21l. The controller queried us about the hold short and i told him that after further investigation; we could hold short of runway(s) 27l. We were told to contact tower marker inbound which we did. At 900 feet/foot above ground level the capt noticed both hydraulic lights illuminated on the annunciator panel. I checkeded the hydraulic pressure gauge and found it indicating low and dropping. The capt called for the quick reference handbook (quick reference handbook) hydraulics/nosewheel steering. I went through this chklist. We then noticed smoke in the cockpit. The capt had me checked the cabin; it did not seem to have any smoke in it at the time. We then performed the smoke removal chklist from the quick reference handbook this did not remove the smoke and by this time the cabin was starting to fill with smoke. Tower cleared us to land and hold short of runway(s) 27l. The capt said we would not be able to hold short of runway(s) 27l and i told tower we had smoke in the cockpit. We talked about landing with 1/2 flaps; the gear was down and flaps set to half; the capt called for flaps full. I selected full flaps and watched as the hydraulic pressure went to zero and the flaps stopped at 3/4. The capt was concerned about the gear; since hydraulic pressure helps hold the gear down. We did have 3 green indication. I ran through the emergency gear extension from the quick reference handbook we landed without incident; and turned off on taxiway fahrenheit crash; fire and rescue was there and the capt called for an emergency evacuation due the smoke in the aircraft we evacuated the passenber without incident; and i stayed with them all the way to terminal. The tower supervisor called our dispatch and asked to talk to the capt. He wanted to know what the confusion was about concerning the land and hold short. The capt explained about the hydraulics failure and the fact that he did not want to be limited in the available runway(s) during all the chklists and trying to analyze the situation we never declared an emer.
output: Acft equipment problem hydraulic pressure lost on final apch.

input: After takeoff; when 'gear up' was selected; the left main landing gear (mlg) indicated an unsafe 'up' position. The appropriate check was executed; which also concluded that the left main gear door was in an unsafe position. We advised air traffic control declared an emergency; and contacted flight control for an aircraft return to zzzz. The landing was uneventful. After landing; the mechanics found a broken bracket on the [main] gear door; had been the cause of the problem. Electronic flight instrument system fms/fmc.
output: An md-11 captain reports that after takeoff; when 'gear up' was selected; the left main landing gear (mlg) indicated an unsafe 'up' position. Emergency declared; aircraft returned to field.

input: Pnf pulled flight guidance circuit breaker to simulate loss of electronic flight instrument system this breaker also controls autoplt; altitude alerter; and pressurization controller clearance was to fl210. I overshot altitude by at least 1000 feet/foot before catching mistake. Pilot not flying also failed to monitor instruments pilot not flying asked for lower altitude and we were cleared to the altitude at which we already were. There were no traffic conflicts and controller did not say anything. Contributing factors were: lack of planning or pre-brief on pnf's part. Pilot flying did not slow down and was distracted while trying to maintain speed during descent in the future this crew will pre-brief simulated emergency in this ce525; pilot in left/right (directions) seat should fly rest of leg; as this position has full instrumentation. Pilot in left/right (directions) seat would then monitor instruments and do coms.
output: A c525 crew; during a self induced emergency overshot their assigned alt.

input: Ifr weather runway(s) 7 and 15l/r in use. Sma x was on instrument landing system apch/missed approach runway(s) 7. Missed approach instructions were nonstandard and coordinated by radar controller runway(s) heading until 700'; then turn right heading 200 degrees climb and maintain 2000'. Sma y called for departure instrument flight rules to visual flight rules on top runway(s) 15l. Release was obtained form radar. Sma y was given traffic (sma x) 2 mile final runway(s) 7 and cleared for takeoff runway(s) 15l runway(s) heading climb to visual flight rules on top 2000'. Sma x executed missed approach 1/2 mile final; was instructed to fly runway(s) heading until departure end then turn to 200 degrees sma y was now 2 mile south at 1300' talking to departure sma x began turn to 200 degrees approximately 1/2 mile beyond departure end. Sma x target went no beacon on radar. Radar controller gave sma x right turn to 100 degrees while aircraft was still on local frequency sma y heard the heading issued the sma x and turned left to 100 degrees targets passed within 1 1/2 mile of each other; altitude of the sma x was unknown. Local was unable to provide visibility because of the weather the radar controllers rpted the loss of sep. The aircraft never saw each other. Local controller was decertified for the operational error not providing initial sep of successive departures local controller was aware of the situation but judgement was poor in assuming sep would exist when sma x turned. Positive sep was not ensured.
output: Acft took heading intended for another aircraft after departure resulting in less than standard separation.

input: I was in contact with phoenix approach for flight following. I was about 25 miles southwest of sky harbor and had reached my cruising altitude of 10;500 feet/foot and had leaned the mixture for this new altitude. About 30 seconds later; the engine began losing power. At first; i believed this to be due to over-leaning the engine; so i richened the mixture. This did not clear the issue; so i added full mixture and full power and still had intermittent power from the engine. I contacted phoenix approach to announce the engine issue and turned back to mobile airport; which was just a couple of miles behind me. While troubleshooting the engine; i circled the airport as we descended to around 5;000 feet/foot at that point; full power returned to the engine. I continued to circle over mobile airport until i was able to climb back up to 10;500 feet/foot after the engine power remained stable at full power for about 20 minutes; i requested a return to my departure airport and was cleared to go directly there and chose to remain at 10;500 feet/foot for as long as possible; because while i believed the engine issue to be resolved; i wanted to have sufficient altitude to reach any airport just in case. I was cleared to descend through bravo airspace and then handed off to my departure airport's tower; and was able to land without incident. The engine made full power and appeared to have no problems after the point where power was restored. The fuel tanks had been topped off the night prior to the flight; and no water was seen when sampling the fuel on the day of the flight just prior to departure. It was a hot dry day; so water and carb ice were not suspected. I have since contacted my mechanic; and he is currently checking the engine and fuel system to see if any issue is seen.
output: C172 pilot experiences a rough running engine upon leveling off at 10;500 feet/foot and leaning the engine for cruise. The reporter elects to spiral down over a nearby airport but when the engine returns to normal he decides to climb back up to 10;500 and return to the departure airport. This is accomplished successfully with no further engine troubles.

input: Clbing out of zzz we got a left/right (directions) hydraulic psi low annunciator light. Hydraulic psi on the left/right (directions) side was zero. We ran through the chklist and decided to go back to zzz. We did not declare an emergency but did have crash fire rescue equipment waiting in case the auxiliary pump failed. There was some confusion on the runway(s) assignment. We wanted xx and they had us on xy. We asked them intermediate fix we could sidestep; and they let us. Landing was uneventful. Upon taxiing in to the gate; we were informed a first class passenber was having heart problems we advised the company and pulled in to the gate. The paramedics arrived shortly after.
output: An md80 experienced loss of hydraulic pressure on climbout. The flight crew elected to return to their departure airport with equipment standing by.

input: Atc frequency error. On frequency change from zjx to mco approach my first officer read back and entered wrong frequency by the time we figured this out we were too close to mco to make sure descent to runway(s) 18r. We received vectors to descend and came back for an uneventful landing on runway(s) 18l. Both the first officer and i were very fatigued at this time due to an early sign in and a longitude duty day.
output: B737-700 crew entered an incorrect communications frequency when changing from zjx to mco approach ctl.

input: Passing over zzz at fl240; we heard a thump immediately followed by a significant pressure change in our ears. I immediately looked up to the tiny cabin pressure gauges to see intermediate fix we were losing cabin pressure; in anticipation of a rapid depressurization. I could tell that my jumpseat rider was thinking the same thing as we both simultaneously leaned over the center console and looked up at the gauges. It was apparent that we were not losing pressure; and queried each other as to what we thought the noise and pressure jolt might be. At that time we got a body duct leak engine indicating and crew alerting system message. The first officer was flying and i opened the quick reference handbook to the body duct leak chklist. During this time; the cabin call chime was ringing; but we were not able to hear anything over the interphone. Within seconds; there was rapid and loud pounding on the cockpit door. My jumpseater asked permission to open the door; which i granted. The flight attendant said there was a lot of smoke and debris in the aft cabin; and it looked like there was a fire. The flight crew immediately performed the initial action items for smoke; and put our full-face oxygen masks on and established communications i looked at my horizontal situation indicator and saw that we were just a little sw (maybe 20-30 mi) from zzz. I informed the crew that we were going to divert to zzz; called air traffic control declared an emergency for smoke in the cabin; requested an immediate descent and a turn direct. We were immediately cleared for a left/right (directions) turn direct to zzz with a descent to 11000 feet/foot the 'body duct leak' chklist was quickly completed as i thought this might help the situation in the back of the plane; and the coplt aggressively turned the plane towards zzz and descended with full speed brakes. Given the information i had received second officer federal aviation regulation i believed the safest course of action was to treat this emergency as an inflt fire. There has been an emphasis on the smoke and fire scenario over the yrs in the company's initial and recurrent training programs. Establishing and maintaining communications with the back of the aircraft is critical. With the coplt flying; i attempted to talk with the crew in the back of the plane. The static was overwhelming and made the use of the interphone nearly impossible. I turned to my jumpseater and asked him to work the interphone; pa's; and get me whatever information he could; concerning our situation. Between this time and landing i noted mention of smoke and also a lessening of smoke. It appeared things were not getting worse. I turned my attention to getting the aircraft on the ground we received vectors to an instrument landing system all normal chklists were accomplished. (note: the approach plates for zzz were in our new airway manual; and this worked well.) the flight crew performed their duties wearing full-face oxygen masks. The weather was better than 2000 feet/foot and 5 mile with winds nearly down the runway(s) at about 12-15 mph. I chose to have my coplt fly the approach and landing second officer that i could continue to monitor the situation in the back; as well as continue briefing what i planned to do after landing there was second officer little time; and i wanted to be sure everyone knew what to expect; and what was expected of them. My biggest concern at this time was whether we would need to emergency evacuate/evacuation on the ground or that panicked passenber would open doors. The jumpseater assured me that the passenber had been instructed to stay in their seats until they received instruction from the crew. The rest of the plan was for him to leave his seat as soon as the aircraft was stopped; quickly ascertain the situation and essentially be my eyes and ears again. I had no interphone for communications with the cabin. Fo's landing was excellent. After stopping on the runway(s) the jumpseater provided me with the information i needed to decide an emergency evacuate/evacuation would be unwarranted. The passenber were again told to remain seated; and that as a precaution the airport fire crew would look over our aircraft prior to taxiing clear of the runway(s) the fire crew examined the aircraft and informed us there was no sign of smoke; fire; or damage. We then cleared the runway(s) and requested a gate. This took some minute(s) as there was some uncertainty asto whether a b767 would fit at any of the gates. I informed the crew that we would deplane normally through the jetway.
output: B767-300 developed a 'body duct leak' during cruise. Smoke was reported by the flight attendant second officer the flight crew declared an emergency and landed at the nearest arpt.

input: During taxi to ramp after landing ground control 121.4 was advised by me that we were in a rental aircraft unfamiliar with the airport and requested progressive taxi directions to ramp. Ground control guided us to taxiway mach number beside the ramp at which time maintenance personnel used hand signals from the ramp indicating we should taxi around to the sw corner entrance. This entrance can be seen coming from runway(s) 9r/txwy left/right (directions) on the attached airport diagram. We advised ground control of our requirement to continue taxi from taxiway mach number out taxiway h; up taxiway left/right (directions) wbound in order to enter ramp. Ground control asked intermediate fix we could make the turn from taxiway h onto taxiway left/right (directions) which i advised yes we could. As we made the turn the left/right (directions) main gear came about 5 feet/foot off the taxiway into the mud. Aircraft movement stopped and we shut down all engs to prevent foreign object debris damage. The national oceanic and atmospheric administration 'arpt facility directory' does advise the txwys are 50 feet/foot wide or less but nothing is stated that these txwys are unusable by large aircraft (over 12500 lbs). Also; being unfamiliar with the airport as we advised; ground control should have advised us of a better taxi route -- such as utilize runway(s) 9r and not taxiway left/right (directions) we were the 4th large aircraft in recent months and the second large aircraft in 2 weeks to turn short on kfll txwys. Kfll airport (rwy 9l and ramp area) has been upgraded to handle jet aircraft but all txwys have not been upgraded which creates confusion and problems small non-upgraded txwys should be notamed as non- usable for large aircraft and ground ctl/atis should advise flcs.
output: Excursion from txwy.

input: We were forced to take evasive action three times during a visual approach to runway 17 at trm; due [to tcas] ras. Approach seemed particularly anxious to have us cancel instrument flight rules during descent. Ultimately; we did cancel about 8;000 mean sea level air traffic control did advise us of visual flight rules bonanza traffic at 10;500 feet/foot which we attempted to avoid by leveling off at 11;000 but which triggered our first resolution advisory which resulted in our first evasive action. This was followed by two more evasive actions at approximately 6;500 and 4;000 respectively. It should be noted that the weather was perfect with unlimited visibility. Upon arrival we had a discussion with fixed-base operator manager about our experience. She informed us that this is the busiest day of the year for them. While fueling we noticed traffic departing and arriving on 17 and 35 without incident. In my opinion; the exceptional weather was a factor. We would not have experienced any of this in instrument meteorological conditions conditions. As far as the airport goes; the unicom is listening only; no airport advisories. We did successfully communicate our intentions with two aircraft during arrival; and at least two during departure. My recommendation is to have a controller from the psp tower man the unicom at trm for holiday weekends during season.
output: A cl60 experienced multiple traffic alert and collision avoidance system ras with visual flight rules traffic while inbound to trm on a brilliant visual meteorological conditions day.

input: Bottom line: did not see general speed restriction on jeppesen standard terminal arrival route details: descending on jknoxx.hhood4 standard terminal arrival route into pdx using vertical navigation profile in flight management computer first speed restriction in flight management computer was 270 kt. At bayyr. There is no speed restriction listed directly next to mytoe and jknox; the first two points on the standard terminal arrival route in the vicinity of mytoe; the center controller asked our speed. Pilot not flying; ca (captain); answers with 300 kts. Center controller asks us to fly the 'published' speeds. The ca and i rechecked the star and saw the 270 kt. Restriction at bayyr as the first speed restriction. The ca responds that we're slowing to 270 by bayyr. Center controller instructs us to go ahead and slow to 250. Once on deck; the ca and i reviewed the standard terminal arrival route and found a note written in the top right corner that says for turbojets to descend via mach number until intercepting 280 kt.; maintain 280 kts. Until slowed by the standard terminal arrival route we did not see this note real time in the aircraft and were about 20 kts. Fast for a portion of the standard terminal arrival route between jknox and mytoe. I was responsible for complying with and should have seen the note and will certainly double check for them in the future. However; i believe the following are contributing factors of why the note was missed by both aircrew. On the vast majority of stars; speed restrictions are almost always listed directly next to the points they apply to. Thus; we are not conditioned to necessarily search for speed restrictions elsewhere. The speed restriction at flavr on the ziggy7 standard terminal arrival route into ont is a good example of a speed restriction written prominently directly next to its respective way point. The general speed restriction on the hood4 standard terminal arrival route is written in magenta against a black background. While it was daytime; the jeppesen flight director pro application was being run in night mode to conserve battery for the 6+ hours of scheduled block time that day. Post flight; when i switched jeppesen flight director pro to day mode; the note was more prominent/easy to see with a white background. The speed restrictions that are listed directly next to the points also show up in the flight management computer when the standard terminal arrival route is loaded. Every speed restriction that was listed on the standard terminal arrival route directly next to the way point showed up in the flight management computer creating an incorrect expectation bias that if a speed was not listed by the flight management computer and not listed directly next to the way point on the standard terminal arrival route depiction; then there was no speed restriction for that point. Suggestions: ensure general speed restrictions are depicted more prominently on stars in both day and night modes of the jeppesen flight director pro application. List general speed restrictions next to the 'routing' section of the standard terminal arrival route so they'll be easier/more likely to be seen. For points such as mytoe and jknox on their hhood4 standard terminal arrival route that have a 'general' speed restriction; place an asterisk next to the point; as well as next to the general speed restriction. This asterisk would cue aircrew to important information located elsewhere on the standard terminal arrival route depiction to locate and read. Insert an 'arrival' page into the airport briefing guide for pdx and insert a section describing this general speed restriction on the hhood4 star.
output: B767 first officer reported an airspeed deviation during arrival on a standard terminal arrival route that contained vague charting.

input: We had aircraft x holding short of [runway] 8l flashing for release. There was a carrier on final for [runway] 26l who had previously arrived from the south and vectored outside of 10 mile final for approach. There was also aircraft y 15 miles south at 5;000 feet on a north easterly heading on approach. Socal released aircraft x with a 4000 ft. Restriction reference aircraft y. We had to wait for the aircraft on final to touch down [on runway] 26l. When the aircraft was short final we lined up aircraft x on runway 8l. Aircraft y was still at 5;000 feet heading north-eastbound. We cleared aircraft x for takeoff and then we noticed that aircraft y turn a seven mile base for [runway] 26l. Immediately we got on the line with socal and notified them that aircraft y was going north through the final and that they were going to be switched back to them reference the departure and an additional carrier arrival. Opposite direction arrivals/departure procedures entail that the departure has to be in their turn before the arrival reaches 10 mile final. Socal released our aircraft x departure with the restriction reference aircraft y and then turn him inside the 10 mile final to try and get aircraft y in before another carrier. I'm not sure if they forgot they released aircraft x or assumed we weren't departing aircraft x before aircraft y. We also were working under the assumption that since they gave us an altitude reference aircraft y and released the aircraft that they would not turn aircraft y in for final reference the 10 mile opposite direction rule. I recommend that there be clarification to the opposite direction order. The order says 10 mile radius but operationally we always use established final for the departure/arrival. If they do not intend for it to be 10 mile final and want a 10 mile radius there needs to be clarification from management on this. The majority of both socal and ont cpcs (certified professional controller) understand work on the premise the aircraft has to be in their turn before the aircraft reaches 10 mile final. Also if it is radius versus final their needs to be an altitude limit as well because we wouldn't be able to clear aircraft within the 10 mile radius even if they are at 15;000 ft. I also recommend that the inter-facility coordination be improved. If socal questioned the order of the arrival/departure sequence or whether they could get aircraft y in before the aircraft x departure; they should have initiated coordination with us. Socal did not ensure separation between the departure they released [and] with the arrival they cut in; inside the 10 mile restriction. If socal wanted to put aircraft y before the departure they released reference aircraft y; they should have called and canceled the release on aircraft y.
output: Ont tower controllers describe a situation where an opposite direction arrival is turned in towards the airport while a approved departure is released; losing separation with the arrival.

input: Due to severe turbulence and difficulty in controling the aircraft at fl350; a descent was made prior to receiving air traffic control clearance although i had requested a descent clearance some 5 minute(s) prior to this incident; communicationss between commercial radio; air traffic control and the aircraft are cumbersome and time consuming. I felt the safety of the aircraft and those on board was somewhat in jeopardy; and thus initiated this descent the aircraft was turned off the arwy and a call made to all stations on 121.5. Additionally a call was made to sfo advising them of our intentions. During the process of descending a clearance to fl310 was received from air traffic control more expeditious clrncs and better communicationss would be a great help in preventing this type of occurrence.
output: Acr wdb encounters severe turbulence enroute hawaii and is forced to leave altitude and track prior to receiving air traffic control clrnc.

input: Our contingency manager advised us [a station] had reported a mercury hazmat spill and that [the station] has determined a mercury hazmat package was loaded on one of my flights but was unable to confirm if the spill was from that package. The hazmat help desk advised that our hazmat did not have any incompatibility issues with the other packages in the same container. I reviewed the situation with the director of operations. What is known at this time is three drops of mercury were found on a package belt and that there is a mercury hazmat package on my flight. Our procedure requires the package to be 'six side' inspected before loading in a sealed uld container; and that there were no incompatibility issues with other packages in the container. The director of operations; who also has experience as the director of safety; reviewed the information and decided there was no confirmation that the package [on our flight] was leaking; there was no safety risk to the crew or aircraft at this time and; therefore; confirmed a decision to continue the flight.
output: When three drops of mercury were discovered in the cargo preparation area the dispatcher for a cargo carrier did his best to determine if it might have come from a hazmat package aboard one of his flight. After reviewing all available information the flight was allowed to continue.

input: We made a visual approach to runway 27 in good visual flight rules conditions backed up by a 5 mile extension from runway 27 in the database and a 3 degree path. The 600 feet runway extension at ptpn has been completed for months and the touchdown zone markings are properly painted on the runway approximately 1;000 feet from the threshold of runway 27. The runway 27 precision approach path indicator is still located at the original position which is now approximately 1;600 feet from the new threshold. The aircraft database appears to coincide with the runway 27 precision approach path indicator with a 3 degree path intersecting the runway approximately 1;600 feet from the threshold. [chart website] has an info page for ptpn stating that the longest runway is 6;600 feet. The jan. 2013 [chart] still shows runway length to be 6;001 feet. The mar. 2012 [chart] still has construction notes stating that the extension is not usable including the turnaround.
output: An air carrier pilot reported that the ptpn runway is now 6;600 feet long but all current airport charts indicate it is 6;001 feet.

input: After receiving a climb clearance from 16000 feet/foot to fl260; while maintaining visual separation on a preceding aircraft and climbing through fl200; we noted a convergence of our aircraft and the preceding aircraft in addition; as we approached an upper level cloud deck; we notified center that we may not be able to maintain visual contact. Zjx directed us to turn to heading 350 degrees intermediate fix contact was lost. We elected to turn to heading 350 degrees immediately in order to ensure separation. During this process; we received a traffic advisory followed by an resolution advisory to reduce climb during this resolution advisory visual contact was never lost; climb was reduced; and then resumed following a 'clr of conflict.' center indicated a minimum separation of 1.5 nautical mile when queried. Although zjx did not indicate a problem we felt that we had gotten uncomfortably close during this separation maneuver.
output: Use of visual separation in the class a airspace results in a loss of separation.

input: We called the fixed-base operator upon taxiing in. Line service said park anywhere up front. I found a yellow parking line and offloaded the passengers. Line service said we were parked in the 'airline area'. There were no sida (secure identification display area) red markings anywhere. Line service said we could either start up and move or he could tug us. I requested the tug. He brought the tug and asked me to release the brakes. I went on board; shut the door and released the parking brake. I went in the back to tend to the cabin. The plane was slowly moving backwards at what i perceived to be a normal towing speed. I happened to look up and see the tug not attached to the plane. I pulled the emergency brake and stopped the aircraft. The nose wheel scissors were spun 180 degrees exceeding the 90 degree restriction. I asked the line service guy what happened. He said the plane started to roll when he was hooking up the tug. The plane didn't hit anything and did not depart the paved surface. It rolled about 75 feet.i should have double checked the line guys work and made sure the plane was chalked before i released the brakes and not just trust his release the brakes request. Also the ramp should be marked as a sida area with red lines as normal. The fixed-base operator should be clear when they're not out to park us and not say just park anywhere up front.
output: Ce680 pilot reported they parked in an area designated for commercial aircraft because it was not properly marked and had to be towed to the correct area. The tug driver told the pilot to release brakes and the aircraft rolled backwards prior to being attached to the tug.

input: Acft with call sign ending in xxx called lhd tower (lake hood tower a visual flight rules tower located in anc twr) from the north inbound with information (current atis). Aircraft was told to rpt a point. Aircraft rpted said point and was cleared to land. I became distraction and did not observe aircraft touchdown. I then scanned the area; many parts of which are not in sight from the tower and attempted one call to the aircraft i then informed the controller in charge that i did not see the aircraft land and clear this is a common occurrence at lhd due to many obstructions from the tower it happens daily. I believe all aircraft should always give a 'clr' transmission and that air traffic control should not have to rely on other rpts to ensure an acft's clrnc.
output: Anc-lhd controller expressed concern regarding limited tower visibility with lhd operations(s) and lack of procedures for tower notification of landing clear of rwy.

input: Pnf read back 25 left and switched mcdu to fly 25 left/right (directions) instrument landing system transition after river. Approach advised that we should be on 24l around taroc at approx. 8500 feet. And issued vector to join 24 left procedure which we complied with immediately. I believe this was a readback / hearing mix-up. Could also have been an air traffic control error. I didn't specifically recollect hearing the change to 25left that the first officer read back. I try to make a habit of asking the pilot not flying to query clearances if i don't hear them clearly. Very little traffic this particular evening and i just didn't catch it. No loss of separation and when advised to change to the 24 left path we complied immediately. In short... If you don't clearly here a clearance and your flying partner advises what he or she heard... That is always a good time to ask for a verification.
output: Sct approach control cleared flight crew for approach to lax runway 25l. Then advised that clearance was actually to runway 24l and reissued the approach clearance.

input: An unreported; unlit crane approximately 600-700 feet/foot above ground level existed at 3.2 vor and dme (co-located) on the final approach course to the vor and dme (co-located) y runway 06 at mygf. The mygf notams for mygf did not contain temporary obstructions nor did they include amendments to the vor and dme (co-located) y runway 06 instrument approach procedure on initial contact with mygf approach; the approach controller did not alert our crew of the temporary obstruction. Prior to the valry final approach fix the approach controller cleared our crew for the vor and dme (co-located) y runway 06 approach. Marginal visual flight rules conditions prevailed with cloud bases reported at 2;800 feet/foot after passing valry; the pilot flying initiated a descent to 700 feet/foot mean sea level while established inbound on the 069 final approach course. At approximately 3.7 vor and dme (co-located) the pilot not flying alerted the pilot flying of a crane existing on the final approach course to runway 06. The pilot flying stopped the aircraft's descent and maneuvered right of the final approach course in order to avoid the unreported crane. Given that marginal visual flight rules conditions prevailed; the crew proceeded to execute a visual approach to runway 06 and landed without further incident. The crane was resting on-top of a ship that was docked at the harbor southwest of the airfield on the final approach to runway 06. If instrument meteorological conditions conditions prevailed; the unreported crane would have posed a serious threat to the safety of our flight given that it existed exactly at the 3.2 dme/ 620 feet/foot step down fix. A notice to airmen / of air missions should be issued for this obstruction and its location should be passed along to aircrews conducting approaches to runway 06. In addition; the vor and dme (co-located) y runway 06 approach should not be utilized during this crane's presence.
output: A flight crew on the mygf vor and dme (co-located) y 06 approach took evasive action from a crane extended to around 600 feet/foot 3.2 miles from the approach end and were told after landing that the terminal radar approach control facility controller should have notified them and further that only visual approaches were conducted during the crane's presence.

input: After takeoff from bwi and shortly after being handed off from bwi departure to washington center we were climbing to an assigned altitude of 13000'. The aircraft was on automatic flight control i was the 'flying plt' and my f/o was the 'non flying plt.' center gave us a heading of 230 degree because there was considerable background noise (from center) i asked my f/o intermediate fix center had said 'two three o'. My f/o who apparently did not hear any of the transmission reacted by setting 23000 in the altitude select window of the mode control panel. This caused the aircraft to continue climb to about 13400' before i could disconnect the autoplt and return to 13000'.
output: Alt overshot on climb.

input: Served as international relief officer (intl relief officer) on flight bwi-aua. Offered and completed the walk-around inspection; but did not preflt flight plan or release with capt. Once we entered ar8; capt realized we needed high frequency radios. We relayed our position through air carrier y and air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) there were no automatic direction finder or vor and dme (co-located) facs defining the arwy; and we were only equipped with irs's; not ins's. Lastly; the aircraft was not extended range (er); and we were definitely more than 162 nautical mile from shore. Not well planned or executed by either dispatch or crew. This was my first experience as an international relief officer and i certainly learned to watch what's going on. I was trying to be helpful and stay out of the way (ie; just do preflts; etc). Will be more involved next time.
output: Acr mlg made an extended over water charter flight without required radio or safety equipment.

input: Approx 40 nautical mile ne of csn; zdc told us to turn left/right (directions) to 260 degrees to intercept j48. I advised center that a 260 degree heading would take us off the airway. They said we were south of course. I looked at our missed approach point which showed us on course. We did have 'dir' on our missed approach point second officer we did turn to 260 degree updated our position off the csn vor and dme (co-located) and then went to navigate, navigation again. Center then called to say we were south of course again. This time we corrected and flew the remainder of the flight using vor/airway radials and used the 'map' mode as a backup. No further incident occurred. I was not overly concerned; since all of the navigate, navigation problems could have been just on our aircraft however; on wed/aug/94 i flew the same flight again; and although i did not experience a navigate, navigation problem i heard zdc talk with another aircraft that was 'off course.' this occurred near csn vor and dme (co-located) very strange. Zdc told this other aircraft 'we have had a lot of trouble in this area.' my question is; is anybody doing anything about this navigate, navigation prob? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rpting capt was flying lga-tys over csn when this anomaly occurred. He thought nothing of it until he heard a controller say that it happens all of the time. The rptr was flying the md-88 with an ahars instrumentation system this is not an inertial navigation system or inertial reference system/unit aircraft the rptr has not talked to other pilots flying through this area to see intermediate fix inertial navigation system or inertial reference system/unit aircraft have the same sort of navigate, navigation problems according to the ctlrs.
output: Zdc alleged that the rptr was off course in the vicinity of csn.

input: While climbing to our cruise altitude the captain and i began to hear a noise coming from the cabin that sounded to us like a pressurization leak in the airplane. Shortly thereafter the captain received a call from the cabin crew; i believe notifying him about the same noise we were hearing. We then asked air traffic control for a lower altitude in hopes of the noise stopping. Shortly after that the captain received another call from the cabin crew; when he hung up the phone he told me we were returning to our departure airport zzz due to claims of smoke or fumes in the cabin. I then donned my oxygen mask and notified air traffic control with our intentions to return to zzz. We were then given a lower altitude and vectors. We conducted the smoke/fumes checklist. We also decided zzz1 airport would be closer and notified air traffic control we would be landing there. We landed in zzz1 without incident where we had the arff (airport rescue firefighters) search our aircraft for any hot spots while still on the runway. After no hot spots were found we taxied to the gate where we deplaned normally. The pressurization leak that caused a loud noise and i never heard what the cabin crew smelled in the cabin. I really can't come up with any suggestions that would have prevented this event without knowing what caused the leak and what caused the smell.
output: A321 first officer reported a cabin fumes event during climb and cruise level off resulting in a diversion. The fumes were reportedly caused by a pressurization leak.

input: I can't speculate as to why the event occurred. There was packed ice on the ramp and txwys; i have no idea intermediate fix this contributed to the situation. We were on taxiway south turning southbound onto taxiway s1. We were cleared for takeoff. As i was turning onto taxiway s1 to access runway(s) 27l there was a radio broadcast from a fellow pilot in another airplane behind us: 'acr x hold your position. Do not attempt to take off. Your right landing gear is cantered about 50 degrees from its normal position.' we held our position. Shut down engines. Called maintenance i used my cell phone to contact my dispatcher. Sent out buses to pick up our passenber and crew and return them to the terminal. The right main landing gear truck was indeed cantered 50 degrees to the left/right (directions) of its normal position. I don't have any recommendations.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated during pushback from the gate the movement of the aircraft by the tug did not feel normal but attributed the movement to the ice and snow present on the surface. After the pushback the brakes were set and the rptr noted that the tug was at the nine o'clock position to the aircraft vice fwd of the fuselage. This was prior to the tow bar being disconnected. Rptr stated that this was unusual; but once again attributed it to the environmental factors present and the difficulty with the pushback. The taxi out to the runway(s) appeared normal. When clearance for takeoff was received; the aircraft had to be taxied slightly left/right (directions) of the taxiway and then turned left/right (directions) to arrival, arrive at the runway(s) during the sequence of events the rptr stated that the aircraft came to a stop and he was unable to move the aircraft further. Simultaneously; a flight crew in another aircraft alerted the flight crew to the left/right (directions) main gear being out of alignment. At this time the aircraft was secured; the company notified and the passenber deplaned. The rptr stated that discussion with company maintenance personnel after the incident indicated that the problem with the main gear has occurred before. This was during periods of rough icy conditions on the txwys. The rptr stated that the comments regarding previous incidents could not be confirmed.
output: B757 flight crew has left/right (directions) main gear malfunction during taxi for tkof.

input: We were being vectored on a left downwind for a visual approach to runway 27 at iah. Aircraft were being turned on to about a 25 mile final. Aircraft were also given a descent to 2000 feet and told that they would be outside the class b airspace. I am concerned because this area has a lot of visual flight rules traffic; many of whom do not talk to approach control and there is no way to guarantee that they have an operable transponder that is turned on and accurate. Even when the 'heavies' reach the class b ring they are at the very bottom of protected airspace. Most visual flight rules pilots in this area feel they are safe from airliners if they remain outside (below) class b airspace. Descending airliners into a busy general aviation flying area; one that includes a practice area for student pilots; is a very hazardous practice.
output: A320 captain reported approach control assigned an altitude below the class b airspace into an area known as a visual flight rules student pilot practice area.

input: We diverted to hou because of thunderstorms over iah. After refueling we were dispatched to iah upon taxi out to runway(s) 04 thunderstorms were in the vicinity of hou; other traffic was requesting thru ground control specific headings on departure to avoid the weather we had our radar tuned up as we were taxiing. I thought i had a good handle on the route and i was monitoring the radio traffic and radar to missed approach point our departure strategy. Between glancing at the radar; trying to figure the best departure and thinking runway(s) 04 was further ahead i found us on the departure end of runway(s) 04 and radioed us to clear the runway(s) and tower sent an aircraft on final around. I believe the causes are clear my sole attention should have been on taxiing the aircraft to the runway(s) i'm sure its and old story: your sure you know where you're going second officer you let your attention slip to other planning factors. Only its obvious now that i wasn't that familiar. I have been to hou before but it was during the day; not on a dark rainy night. Although this was clrly my fault one mitigation factor should be examined. The hold short line at runway(s) 04 is identified with a painted standard line and sign. Since it intersected a taxiway to runway(s) 35 i believe it should have the elevated flashing guard lights. Supplemental information from acn 538888: as the first officer i could have been more careful; looking outside as the capt taxied to aircraft i have been to hou many times and found one thing that concerned me. Runway(s) 04/22 red sign was marked 04/35 and they had no flashers. I find the yellow sequential flashers the best insurance in preventing a runway(s) incursion. Another factor was fatigue. Diverting from iah we had to go around weather and turbulence that really exercised all my airmanship abilities.
output: Potential ground conflict with an aircraft on final to runway(s) 04 after a runway(s) incursion by a cl-65 at hou; tx.

input: We were on a repositioning flight to zzz on an instrument flight rules flight plan in visual flight rules conditions. Upon being handed off to approach; air traffic control instructed us to descend to 2000 feet and fly a westerly heading to join a right downwind for runway 9 at zzz. We reported the airport in sight for the visual. Air traffic control said that we would fly for several more miles to allow for a departure. Air traffic control then instructed us to fly a heading of 360; cleared us for the visual approach; and to contact zzz tower. We complied with all instructions. As we turned a 5-mile base to final; we attempted to contact the tower three times as we continued our descent. At 900 feet; the tower finally responded and told us to immediately turn to a heading of 120 and climb and maintain 2;000 feet. As we began the turn and initiated a climb; tower announced several times in the same radio call that we needed to expedite our climb as there was traffic at 1;000 feet at our 12 o'clock; less than a mile. We aggressively climbed from 1;000 feet to 2;000 feet and was instructed to contact approach for further vectors. Air traffic control vectored us to a 9-mile right base and once again cleared us for the visual approach. We landed without further incident. After clearing the runway and asking ground control for a phone number to speak with the manager. The controller asked if it was about what just happened. We replied yes. She stated that it was approach that gave the suggested heading of 120 that put us in direct conflict with the general aviation traffic that was at traffic pattern altitude on the right downwind for runway 9. She said that it was approach's fault and offered the terminal radar approach control facility phone number if i wanted it. I declined and informed her that i would file a national aeronautics and space administration report and that the midair was entirely too close.
output: Captain reported taking evasive action and climbing aggressively to avoid a near mid air collision.

input: I had [priority requested] by my number 2 aircraft in my sequence who was following a slow moving citation jet. I vectored out the citation and made the [priority] aircraft number one and gave them direct to the airport. After achieving what i initially thought was enough space between the 2 instrument flight rules aircraft i turned in the citation jet and soon realized i didn't have enough room behind the [priority aircraft]. I vectored the citation back out and leveled him at 14000 feet by the time i had my spacing he was in conflict with the jump zone i called traffic to both the sky dive aircraft and the citation i then turned the citation an additional 30 degrees right to clear the confliction of the sky dive aircraft however he was still in the sky dive area. Soon after the citation began to descend i told him to maintain altitude but he advised me he was responding to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory he descended and exited the sky dive area without further incident. During the incident i had a [priority aircraft] i was coordinating with the controller in charge and approach as well as some frequency congestion working a high and low combined at the time. As well as working a much larger scale than normal made the conflict harder to see.i shouldn't have assumed the sky dive aircraft would have ceased his sky dive activities when calling traffic to him; i believe i failed to tell him the traffic would enter the jump area as well as allowing the instrument flight rules aircraft to descend to an altitude that would put him underneath the sky divers jumping from 14500 ft. I should have gone further away from the jump zone not just separating from the aircraft.
output: Atc center controller reported vectoring an instrument flight rules aircraft for sequencing behind a priority aircraft through a parachute jump zone and below the altitude of the jumpers.

input: I have an aerial advertising company and was contracted to fly a total of 4 hour and 15 minute flight over a concert. The federal aviation administration requirements are that aerial advertising aircraft are to be at a minimum of 1000 above ground level while towing banners over populated areas. There were continuous mild to moderate up and downdrafts over the venue area. I was flying a 5 ft letter banner approximately 120 ft long. Most of the time i was at 1100 to 1200 above ground level to cushion any downdrafts that normally show up. Probably 4 or 5 times in the 3 hours i was over the venue; i got into a moderate downdraft of 1000 feet per minute descent from a little more powerful downdraft and my initial power applications were not enough to stop the descent before dropping to 900 above ground level  i have a garmin 496 global positioning system that has a very accurate vertical speed indicator that i use to detect downward vertical movement. Maybe two of those times i was also being directed by approach control to look for approaching aircraft that were in my general area and my attention was diverted for a little more outside time than my normal scan and i got a late start on the power application. Corrective actions would be to be a little more aggressive on power applications. That being said we also have to consider the noise issues of the people we are flying circles around. The more power the more potential for complaints. I will also try and be 50 to 100 ft higher to have a little more cushion on that 1000 ft minimum when we have the potential for stronger downdrafts.
output: Banner tow pilot reported operating below the federal aviation regulation mandated floor of 1000 feet above ground level while circling an outdoor event due to turbulence and downdrafts.

input: We were filed into ord on the trtll4 standard terminal arrival route kansas city center cleared us direct cashn intersection at max forward speed. We complied and cruised at .80 mach. After the handover to chicago center we were given vectors off the direct we were previously cleared and a slow down to minimum forward speed. I told air traffic control that the speed for our altitude would be .76 mach number the controller okayed it. After two headings ranging from southeast to northwest and a descent to fl290 we were cleared direct to vinca intersection. We could see ahead of us another aircraft descending at around 10 miles on traffic alert and collision avoidance system the vectors and slowdown was given to us in order for us to be positioned behind that aircraft on the trtll4 standard terminal arrival route the flight was an md11 aircraft as we later found out. At 10 miles behind him and fl290; we encountered moderate chop/turbulence. From experience i knew that this was wake turbulence. I immediately turned the seat belt sign on. As i prepared to make a public address announcement; the aircraft experienced a right abrupt rolling moment; to about 45 degrees. The first officer was the flying pilot and autopilot 2 righted the aircraft back to level flight. I immediately asked air traffic control what kind of aircraft were we following and he told me that it was an md11. I told the controller that we experienced wake turbulence and that we need a vector off; in order to get upwind of the aircraft. The winds were from the northwest at only 25 knot(s) we were initially doubted by the air traffic control controller. After i reported the event he told me 'but you have 10 miles; this is the first time i heard of something like that!' on top of that; the [md11] pilot mocked us saying over the frequency 'hey; why don't you offset!' as if we were in oceanic airspace! Not only were we put behind a heavy; in very light winds aloft; while the heavy descended on top of us; we were also ridiculed for experiencing wake turbulence because of the poor air traffic control traffic management and at the same time another pilot tried to tell us how to fly our aircraft. Completely unacceptable behavior by both air traffic control and [the md11] pilot. The controller; after giving us the vector that allowed us 15 mile separation; asked us what was the intensity of the wake turbulence and we told him exactly what we experienced.
output: A319 captain reported encountering wake turbulence 10 miles in trail of an md11.

input: On departure from tri; cleared to hmv shine 5 arrival, arrive clt. After passing hmv; set and tracked outbound on the 094 degree radial vice 156 degree radial (radial off vxv on shine 5 arr). Center called at 15 vor and dme (co-located) and gave heading of 170 degrees to intercept 314 degree radial clt. Capt was off frequency copying automatic terminal information service for clt and getting gate assignment. Cause: misread standard terminal arrival route in moderate turb.
output: Mlg flight crew on standard terminal arrival route uses wrong radial. Rptr misread the radial due to turb.

input: The aircraft had been operated with generator 4  mel'd prior to the departure. Per the minimum equipment list procedures; the auxiliary power unity had been running during the entire flight to provide a 4th generator. In cruise at fl360; without warning or any erroneous indications; the auxiliary power unity automatically shutdown; with the associated master caution and engine indicating and crew alerting system message auxiliary power unity fail. We also saw a lightning flash nearby; and feared that the failure was associated with a possible lightning strike. The captain ran the appropriate quick reference handbook which directed us to not attempt any restart of the auxiliary power unity since it failed in flight. He then contacted dispatch and maintenance through automatic communications addressing & reporting system to discuss our options to either continue or consider a diversion. After several confusing messages; he contacted dispatch/maintenance via voice. It was eventually decided that given our present position; a diversion was the best course of action for a precautionary landing. The subsequent arrival and landing were uneventful.the cause for our concern was that due to the generator minimum equipment list and with the auxiliary power unity failure; we were now down to 3 operating generators. Any further generator failures would present a further degraded electrical system and the loss of electrical components. The aircraft was technically un-airworthy; operating outside of the guidelines per the generator minimum equipment list after several automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages with dispatch and maintenance; the captain decided to contact the company to have a verbal discussion. Further compounding the issue was confusion on the part of maintenance in helping us deal with this malfunction. The quick reference handbook clearly states that if the auxiliary power unity fails in flight; to not attempt any restarts. At least 2 automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages and then several times the captain was verbally instructed by maintenance to restart the auxiliary power unity and that 2 attempts were permitted. Unfortunately; maintenance was reading the 2nd half of the quick reference handbook procedure which address auxiliary power unity failure during a start attempt; and presumably while on the ground. They had skipped over the first indention of the procedure which pertains to in flight failures. We had discussed the situation; and agreed that we were going to comply with the quick reference handbook and not attempt any restarts. It is imperative that everyone involved understands where to find appropriate procedures; and how to read and apply them. Several minutes were wasted trying to convince maintenance that he was reading the wrong part of the quick reference handbook procedure; and that what he was instructing us to do could have had detrimental effects. Eventually; the captain simply told him that we were not starting the auxiliary power unity and that we were going to divert.
output: Emb-145 first officer reports being dispatched with the number four generator inoperative and the auxiliary power unity generator taking its place. In cruise at fl360 the auxiliary power unity fails and the crew elects to divert to a suitable airport.

input: In 10/90; i launched my hot air balloon from a field well clear of the albuquerque international balloon fiesta. I was aware that there was a restrict, restricted, restriction airspace around the fiesta's launch field that extended out 2 mile my launch site was well away from this airspace. During my flight the winds had changed direction and i was unable to avoid the restrict, restricted, restriction airspace. In addition it was not possible to make my approach to landing in accordance with the unrealistic interpretation that the federal aviation administration has re: balloons and minimum altitudes my approach however; was safe and appropriate as seen fit by the ballooning community. Note: the federal aviation administration should really review the practicality of their interp.
output: Balloon unauthorized penetration of airspace.

input: Was making an approach to landing on runway 36 at igq. At about 200 feet/foot above ground level and just 10-15 seconds from touchdown was overflown by a high speed f16 just 100 feet/foot above my aircraft. Aircraft was rocked by the wake and jet blast and my attention was taken away from the landing. The f16 pilot did not follow any of the published intercept procedures and frankly created an unsafe situation by 'buzzing' the aircraft on short final. The actions of the f16 pilot were entirely unnecessary and could have been avoided by the f16 simply circling the field for just 60 second to confirm we were landing to allow ground authorities to address the situation. We had announced our position and intentions on the common traffic advisory frequency at 20; 15; 10; and 5 miles. [i] was unaware of a pop-up tfr in the area. There was no mention of the tfr on the automatic terminal information service we received more than 20 miles out. The [website] did not have a graphical tfr depicted for this pop up tfr when we checked the night before. The ads-b real time broadcast from the federal aviation administration did note the tfr's but none that extended as far south as we were. Bottom line is the tfr was poorly communicated and i missed it. The f16 pilot was reckless in his actions that did not comply with any published intercept procedures. The f16 pilot's actions endangered my life and all of the passengers aboard my aircraft.
output: Be58 pilot reports being 'buzzed' by an f16 as he is about to land. He is informed after landing that he has entered a vip tfr although it is not visible on foreflight with stratus or via ads-b (weather; notams; tfr's).

input: Vhf communicationss had been poor for about 30 minute(s) mostly because of thunderstorms in arkansas and missouri; but we had been able to talk to air route traffic control center well enough to get a vector to ddy; and air traffic control requested that we climb to fl330 at about the sgf vor and dme (co-located) for 5 minute(s) or second officer prior to the incident; our frequency was basically unreadable due to a probable stuck microphone it was not our xmitter causing this. As soon as the stuck microphone problem was corrected; we received a call from zkc to turn left/right (directions) 30 degrees for traffic which we did. Within seconds; we received a selective calling from air carrier zulu time (utc/gmt) who told us to contact zkc on a new frequency that there was a traffic conflict; and zkc could not communicate with us or the other aircraft due to a stuck microphone it appears that an air carrier y flight at the same altitude was converging head on during the communicationss blackout. That crew acted upon a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning and changed course to avoid a collision. I ante meridiem not sure how close we came; but after discussing it with zkc; i do not believe we came close enough to file an federal aviation administration near miss rpt. As federal aviation regulation as i know; no one in the air or the ground made an error. The system temporarily failed us; and i ante meridiem thankful that air carrier y had an operating traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii because it saved us all a lot of trouble; to put it mildly. Perhaps until traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii is universally required; we should all monitor guard channel (121.5 or 243.0) as a backup; as the military currently does. I hope it works better in the civil community than it did while i was in the military however.
output: Tcasii of other aircraft helps save the day by directing aircraft to take evasive action on converging courses.

input: All events through pushback were accomplished without note. During pushback; a puddle on the ramp aft of the normal oil spot was noticed behind the #2 engine. Puddle was not present on the walkaround. A stream of drops along the ramp was also noticed while the #2 engine was run. After five minutes the fuel leak had not stopped and we towed back to a gate. Maintenance was called; ran several tests; and two engine runs. The leak dissipated as the tests were completed. No fuel appeared to be leaking while engines were running; except for one within limits from the heat exchanger. Forms were completed to indicate it. Aircraft pushed and started again. No leaks were noted.shortly after takeoff/cleanup; captain announced a split in the thrust levers.
