The air carrier x pilot rpted the traffic in sight after the climb traffic was medium. No system error or deviation happened. The controller exchanged traffic and had air carrier x clear of svn.
output: Acr x traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory had conflict with visual flight rules military aircraft see and avoid concept. Evasive action taken.

input: I was assigned to replace a triple seat in a b737-400 aircraft. My lead mechanic and i researched the part number (p/n) using company illustrated parts catalog (ipc) and component maintenance manual (cmm) to confirm the correct part to install. We found the part; i installed the seat; and signed it off as completed.this morning i was informed that the company had submitted a self-disclosure because the wrong seat for that position had been installed. This was due to the company not updating the ipc and cmm. My lead and i did everything by the book; but the book was inaccurate. Make sure all company documents are kept up to date. Also; simplify the charts for the seats installed on the aircraft.
output: A line mechanic was informed he had replaced a triple seat assembly on a b737-400 aircraft with an incorrect seat; even though he and a lead mechanic had followed the manuals. Their company illustrated parts catalog (ipc) and component maintenance manuals (cmm) had not been updated and were inaccurate.

input: The top cowling became unsecured on the co-pilot's side. The cowling was secured on the pilot's side and stayed on the aircraft. I slowed the aircraft and continued the approach and landing. I shut down the engine upon landing as a precaution since the top cowling was loose and was towed to the fbo.
output: A pa28r pilot reported the top cowling became unsecured on approach. Landing was continued normally.

input: The drop tubes at dab are out of service. I; as a radar controller have to look at the scratch pad of every departure to determine the acft's destination intentions; etc. Here at dab; all we do is practice apches; second officer for almost every departure i have to write a progress strip with all the approach requests while working all my traffic this is an extremely dangerous situation and the maintenance people will not fix this. This will definitely end up with airspace deviations; separation errors; and possibly mid-airs; and the federal aviation administration is not doing anything about it.
output: Dab controller describes lack of maintenance efforts to repair departure drop tube; resulting in extra controller workload and potential safety concerns.

input: I started our dept's c185 and taxied from the hangar area to runway(s) 12 at brd. The east side of runway(s) 5/23 was covered with a thin layer of ground fog. This was causing the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) which is located on the ne side of the airport to give the weather as: wind calm; visibility 1/4 mile vertical visibility 100 feet/foot conditions over runway(s) 12/30 were clear high thin cirrus; and unrestr visibility. Since i planned to depart visual flight rules and the wind was calm; i chose runway(s) 12. While taxiing out; i noticed the commuter on their ramp. The engs were shut down. Upon arriving at runway(s) 12; i did my runup. The fog was burning off rapidly. I listened to the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) on communications #2. It was still saying the field was instrument flight rules i then contacted princeton flight service station specialist and gave them a visual flight rules pilot report and asked about departure with the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) still giving instrument flight rules conditions. I was advised that since the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) was still rpting instrument flight rules i would have to get a special visual flight rules from zmp to depart. Upon contacting zmp and requesting a special visual flight rules departure i was informed that there was an arrival, arrive and some other operations(s) and it would be a while before they could give me an special visual flight rules i informed them of the visual flight rules conditions and that only a few wisps of fog remained in the vicinity of the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) these conditions were confirmed by a flight that was on an instrument landing system final to runway(s) 23 at brainerd. Still the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) was rpting instrument flight rules and center would get back to me. This took approximately 10 minute(s) what little fog was left was gone second officer i listened to the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) again. The rpt was wind calm; 6 mile visibility; sky 100 scattered. To make sure i heard right; i listened to the sequence again. This time it gave the visibility as 8 mile upon hearing this; i contacted zmp again to cancel my request for an special visual flight rules and advised them i could now depart visual flight rules i had heard the flight that had landed earlier call clear of all runway(s) and taxiing to the ramp on common traffic advisory frequency 122.7. My radio transmission was 'brainerd traffic cessna departing runway(s) 12 brainerd and will be wbound.' i then taxied onto the runway(s) and began my takeoff roll. Since this is my home base of operations(s) i'm familiar with the blind spot caused by trees that block the view of the takeoff ends of runway(s) 12 and 23 and tend to look in that direction as i take off. Shortly after breaking ground and clearing the trees; i saw a commuter aircraft about 1/2 way down runway(s) 23. Having enough speed and altitude i was able to make a climbing left/right (directions) turn before reaching and crossing over runway(s) 23. Since i hadn't heard any traffic on the radio; i xmitted asking where the commuter aircraft had come from. I was thinking they had just arrived. To my shock they had aborted their takeoff and replied they had xmitted their departure 3 times. I honestly did not hear one of them. Even after announcing my intentions before departure i heard no response. Thinking back to how this could have occurred; these are the events and actions that seemed most prominent. After taxiing to runway(s) 12; i was parked for my runup facing the approach to the runway(s) in this position i would not have seen commuter taxiing from their ramp to runway(s) 23. One of the biggest contributing factors i feel was having the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) rpt; prohibiting visual flight rules operations(s) when in fact excellent visual flight rules conditions existed and were verified by another aircraft in the immediate vicinity. Even though common traffic advisory frequency was being monitored; between talking to flight service station specialist zmp; listening to automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) and transmitting my own departure call; i could have missed commuter's departure call. Finally i could have given more than 1 departure announcement; since i knew the takeoff end of an intersecting runway(s) is blocked from view and during calm wind conditions when multiple runway(s) may be in use at an unctled airport such as brainerd. Supplemental information from acn 415632: the first problem was the other aircraft departing the intersecting runway(s) was visual flight rules when the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) at the field was calling visibility between 1/4 - 1 nautical mile the field was clearing up quickly. I saw him sitting at the end of the runway(s) 12 when we taxied to runway(s) 23. I thought he was waiting for the field to go visual flight rules the second problem he was not monitoring common traffic advisory frequency when we made 3 calls stating our intentions of departing runway(s) 23. While we were on the roll; the other aircraft announced his intentions of departing runway(s) 12. Another thing that should be corrected is the tree line at brd that blocks the view of both aircraft at runway(s) 12 and runway(s) 23. Callback conversation with rptr acn 415833 revealed the following information rptr states that the commuter made a rpt to his company; but no other follow up has occurred. The automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) is located near a hillside and the fog hangs in there a bit longer than in open areas. This is not the first time this problem has occurred. Since it is a non tower airport pilots chose the runway(s) to use in calm wind conditions. Many pilots like the 'big super slab' on runway(s) 23. The trees in the area are about 40 feet/foot tall and block the departure ends of runway(s) 23 and 12. Callback conversation with rptr acn 415632 revealed the following information rptr states that he filed/spoke to his chief pilot who contacted the other acft's chief pilot pilots then wrote letters to each other stating their view of the incident. Commuter pilot had waited 1 1/2 hours for weather to reach 1/4 mile second officer he could depart. Since he listened to the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) 4 minute(s) prior to the departure he finds it difficult to believe that the weather had changed from 1/4 to 8 mile in such a brief time. Also; there would be no possibility of an special visual flight rules clearance until weather was 1 mile and pilot could remain clear of clouds. He does admit the weather was much better at the end of runway(s) 12. He believes the trees are a great problem as he could have seen the movement of the other aircraft intermediate fix they were cleared he thought the other aircraft was not moving until he sighted the cessna near the runway(s) intxn.
output: Plt of c185 on takeoff at non tower airport sights a commuter on takeoff roll on intersecting runway(s) cessna pilot lifts off and makes an abrupt turn to avoid the commuter aircraft commuter aborts his tkof.

input: We were given a crossing restrict, restricted, restriction at manes at 11000 feet/foot mean sea level (plt discretion). We were at 16000 feet/foot mean sea level at the time. Center controller didn't ask intermediate fix we had remembered our crossing restrict, restricted, restriction being on duty 2 days in a row more than 12 hours and 3rd day of a 3 day trip for more than 13 hours crew fatigue (tired) played a major role. We made the turn at manes intersection and realized we were still at 16000 feet/foot mean sea level we forgot the crossing and were starting down. I asked did we cause any conflicts. There was no answer from center except to contact cvg approach on 123.87; second officer we did and started down at 2000 feet per minute to add to this; it may not be the controller's responsibility to make sure flc's make their altitude restrs; but when something like this happens giving the crew some feed back intermediate fix there was a conflict or not would be a plus. Not to just leave the crew out of the loop.
output: Flc forgot altitude restr.

input: We are supposed to run our [specific equipment] to reduce covid exposure; yet i was flight planned with [specific equipment] inoperative. When i queried the dispatcher why it was dispatched that way; his response was 'i don't know.'  i refused the aircraft.after refusing the airplane the dispatcher stated [i] was to speak to flight operations. The dispatcher also had me talk to maintenance to confirm i 'understood the nature of the mel.' this sounds a lot like pilot pushing to me.
output: Air carrier captain refused the aircraft due to a specific equipment meled inoperative; which is reportedly used to reduce covid exposure.

input: We landed on 9r in philly and tower told us to cross 9l at echo and contact ramp. Tower did not tell us to contact ground nor did they specify which ramp frequency to use. I chose to contact ramp on 130.57 because that is the frequency for the area of the ramp where we were parking. I called ramp and told them we were on echo and our parking gate. Ramp control told us to taxi to the gate. When we exited echo and taxied across spot 11 we noticed a company aircraft under maintenance tow on the north side of the east gates. I was watching him to see where he was going and then looked to the right and saw a dash 8 very close to us approaching spot x from the north. I told the captain and he stopped. The dash 8 did not have his taxi light on and was painted black. After we stopped he continued to taxi to his gate between us and the maintenance aircraft. We called ramp control and asked about it; but they did not see the dash 8 and were not talking to him. When we reached the gate we contacted ramp control on 129.75 and asked them about the incident. They told us they had seen it; but they were also not talking to the dash 8. Even though tower did not specify which ramp controller to contact and ramp did clear us to taxi to the gate; if i had contacted ramp on 129.75 he may have been able to give us a heads up on the dash 8 earlier. The dash 8 should have been in contact with ramp and should have had his taxi light on. Ramp should not have cleared us if they did not have our entire route in sight. Tower should have specified which ramp frequency to use. If tower or ground were talking to the dash 8; they should have told them about us or at least coordinated with ramp.
output: A b737 crew was given taxi clearance by phl ramp control to their gate after landing. Enroute the reporters encountered an aircraft under tow and taxiing dhc8 neither of which were reported as traffic. The dhc8 became a threat and reporters had to stop for them. Ramp control did not see either conflicting aircraft.

input: We received our clearance pre departure clearance and it included flying the wlkkr3 area navigation departure from runway 16r at vny (climb via standard instrument departure except maintain 4;000 feet). The captain and i reviewed the departure chart and it shows on the plan view that we are to cross the vny d1.5 'at or below 1;750 feet;' and then to 'climb to 1;303 feet.'this is; at best; confusing. The narrative is slightly better; except that the narrative doesn't include the detail about 'at or below 1;750 feet.' note also that the 'at or below 1;750 feet' restriction was not in the flight management system and neither the plan nor the narrative makes it clear when you are to climb above 1;303 feet.we contacted clearance delivery by radio to ask what it was that we were expected to do. We were told that the 'at or below 1;750 feet' was a limitation; but the 1;303 feet was there to prevent airplanes from running into terrain. So we were to comply with the 'at or below 1;750' at 1.5 vor and dme (co-located) and then climb to 4;000 feet'.change the chart to clarify that the 'climb to 1;303 feet' only pertains to the minimum altitude before making the turn to pprry (which isn't much of a turn at all); rather than appearing to be a limitation on how high you can fly. Also; the presence of the shaded circle adds to the confusion; because its purpose isn't apparent. If the shaded circle were not there; it might have been more apparent that the 1.5 vor and dme (co-located) from vny vor and dme (co-located) was essentially at the departure end of runway 16r.
output: Cl-350 pilot reports confusion regarding the initial climb segment on the area navigation standard instrument departure chart and climb restriction was not in aircraft database.

input: I was in zzz to replace an outboard flap; inboard trailing edge panel. I noted wrong part number was delivered. Worked with engineering to rectify part number issues. Got verbal saying it was interchangeable; difference was in the inboard end rib of panel. Differences visually noticeable; took picture of area with notes; submitted to engineering. Got reply back saying it was a bonded channel. Installed trailing edge; got engineering change for use interchangeability and signed off paperwork along with quality control inspection. Returned to yyy that day. Aircraft returned to service when i got back to work; i pulled up a drawing to do a gut checked on some information received on channels and found fasteners in drawing not installed on trailing edge rib channels. I notified line maintenance supervisor maintenance control and engineering. Appropriate actions were taken by all. Engineering contacted bombardier and has since got a re-dispatch for aircraft for return to service as is. Just did a self-chk and didn't get a good feeling of the answer i got from engineering about pilot holes in rib channels and did a little more research and found fasteners to be missing in channels. Notified maintenance supervisor maintenance control which swapped out aircraft with spare; and engineering contacted for more information lack of documentation on interchangeability as to what is required when changing parts and conflicting drawings. When dealing with interchangeability issues; ensure all documentation on differences accompany the engineering change for proper install of new part. Not just a statement saying they are interchangeable.
output: A mechanic on a field trip replacing an outboard flap; inboard trailing edge panel on a dehavilland dhc-8-400 aircraft notes the visual differences from the removed panel. Engineering still approved the use of panel.

input: During a very busy arrival and departure session. It appeared that ztl center started to vector aircraft off of the arrival and towards my departure corridor. Tmc (traffic management coordinator) and the supervisor told me after the fact that they released my airspace to center without my knowledge. Tmc told me they told center to call me with a point out but i never talked to center. Approximately 5 or 6 aircraft entered my airspace without approval or point out from me and at the time i had multiple departures climbing underneath this operation; then the supervisor approved them to hold an aircraft again in my airspace without my approval. I asked the supervisor after this situation why this occurred and why we didn't have center go into holding. The supervisor told me that i should have known what was going on and that it was ok for someone else to approve operations in my airspace. I stated this was unacceptable and a very unsafe practice. After the first aircraft was coordinated; the tmc should have went in to holding in the appropriate location. The supervisor should have seen what was happening and also discussed holding the aircraft. The supervision was very poor in this entire situation.
output: Clt terminal radar approach control facility controller reported that his supervisor assigned some of his airspace to ztl center without his knowledge.

input: Prior to touchdown; a snowmobile crossed the runway(s) at about midfield. I made a gar.
output: C170 pilot about to land at 66s; an unctled airport went around when the pilot saw a snowmobile crossing the rwy.

input: Flt crew was on the runway(s) 12r instrument landing system at approximately 5 mile final when switching to tower frequency we heard a slight noise and yaw from the left/right (directions) engine immediately followed by a master warning light and chimes. We noticed a left/right (directions) engine oil light on with also an indication of 0 torque on the left/right (directions) engine no fire was noted. It seemed that the left/right (directions) egt was slightly lower than the left/right (directions) we had approximately 20-25% torque on both engs before this incident. Being on final and with gear down and flaps at 20 degrees we completed memory items and contacted tower i informed tower that we had a left/right (directions) engine failure and declared an emergency tower replied affirmative and cleared us to land. Approach and landing were uneventful and we contacted ground and taxied to the gate.
output: Saab-340b flight crew has engine failure during apch.

input: Thirty minutes after a vip tfr ended at a class-c airport; i was cleared to land while on an instrument landing system approach in instrument meteorological conditions a few miles from the airport; i emerged into marginal visual flight rules conditions. During my flight; i received no traffic advisories to advise of a helicopter operating near and above runways. Before my flight; in a telephone briefing from flight service station specialist i was read a list of notams at my destination; and these did not include any that warned of helicopter operations. As i touched down on the runway; i heard the tower advise a cessna; which was number two for landing behind me; to go around. At the same time; my skywatch traffic surveillance avionics (similar to tcas) called out 'traffic! Traffic!' i discovered the problem by looking over my left shoulder; where i was surprised to see a military helicopter flying parallel to me at approximately 100 above ground level and 300 feet/foot from the runway centerline. The helicopter was faster than me as i was landing at less than 80 knot(s) and it overtook me as i slowed down on the runway. The helicopter continued circling the runway vicinity at low altitude for at least another fifteen minutes. Occasionally i heard tower or ground make calls to '[x] helicopter;' but i never heard any warnings given to traffic of the conflict that the helicopter posed. I believe the helicopter's operations endangered my safety by presenting a significant hazard to traffic.contributing factors include: a lack of a notice to airmen / of air missions a lack of an air traffic control advisory to alert inbound pilots to the presence of the helicopter; and marginal visual flight rules conditions that made it impossible to visually discover the helicopter until late in the approach. I do not believe that i was given adequate separation. If air traffic control is unable to keep adequate separation of general aviation traffic from a helicopter performing a mission after a vip tfr; then the federal aviation administration should at least issue a notice to airmen / of air missions to advise pilots of the hazard. This notice to airmen / of air missions should indicate the nature of the hazard and it should define how long the hazard will persist; so that pilots can plan their flights to avoid the hazard.
output: A pilot emerged from instrument meteorological conditions on the cid instrument landing system to see a military helicopter 300 feet/foot from him on short final with no communication from air traffic control about the near miss traffic.

input: Right after rotation on takeoff a small flock of ducks or mallards got into the aircraft flight path. A bird strike occurred and some birds remains were ingested into the left/right (directions) (#3) engine causing a power loss on that pwrplant. Fuel dumping was coordinated with air traffic control after bringing the aircraft to its landing weight and instrument landing system approach to runway(s) 21r in dtw was executed. Normal approach and landing no injuries resulted from such an incident.
output: Bird (duck) strike right after takeoff caused power loss to 1 engine return to airport after making fuel dump to get down to landing wt.

input: I recently began my private-multi training in the piper seminole pa-44-180. Myself and my instructor (right seat); were involved in an accident due to a failed right main landing gear. After completing our lesson; we returned to the airport for two successful touch and go's. During the third approach; we had established on the downwind for runway 04 with gear down. Current wind conditions were 350 at 12 knot(s) gusting 17 knot(s) [and] a crosswind less than both my demonstrated ability as well as the aircraft limitations. Once established on final; i completed the final check to ensure landing gear was down; three green lights illuminated; and could verify with gear down in the mirror. Tower updated winds to 360 at 12 knot(s) gusting 21 knot(s) [and] a crosswind that was manageable and within mine and aircraft limits. Final approach speed was approximately 80 knot(s) to compensate for crosswinds and gust factor. Proper crabbing methods were used and with winds from the left side; i touched down with the left main wheel; then the right; followed by the nose wheel. Before i was able to lower flaps or add power for the touch and go; a loud noise was heard and the right main gear gave way. The aircraft was aggressively pulled to the right; despite full aileron and rudder to remain on centerline. In order to avoid the grass and risk digging the propeller into the ground; we tried to exit on the taxiway. My instructor managed to safely exit the active runway; stop the aircraft; secure the engines; and allow us to safely exit. Since the gear were verified in the down position numerous times before touchdown; and because we had completed two prior landings in the same crosswind manner; we believe the cause of the accident was due to a faulty right main landing gear. In the future; i truly do not know how this could have been prevented. A thorough pre-flight walk around was conducted and nothing faulty was noted with the landing gear. The gear was verified down in-flight; and functioned normally on prior landings.
output: Pa-44 student pilot with instructor; experiences a right landing gear failure while landing with a left crosswind.

input: Another dispatcher asked for my assistance on how to work up and send an update request to the crew for ci500 for a flight to nrt. [we] sent an email to our lone fpsa/senior manager but no answer. As we don't expect him to be available to us 24/7; this can be a safety issue not having sme's to assist the 4 sabre desks operating 24 hours a day. We were able to get an answer from a sme from [a different facility]. It is alarming that the company considers this situation safe. Let us not wait for time critical safety issues to happen and we cannot get an expert to assist us.
output: Air carrier dispatcher questions how to work up and send an update report to the crew for a ci500 [cost index] and where to get help after hours.

input: Ifr flight from dan to gsp and had just reached cruise altitude of 6000 feet/foot mean sea level 20 nautical mile north of gso. Engine abruptly and without warning lost all power i notified control of my problem and they gave me vectors to the nearest airport shiloh. While gliding toward the airport i switched tanks and turned on boost pump with no result. At about 1000 feet/foot above ground level i determined that i could not reach the airport and turned toward a field that i had picked up. I landed in the field gear up; and slid down the field approximately 200 yards and went through a fence at the end of the field. No injuries and aircraft damaged consistent with gear up landing federal aviation administration visited site and confirmed approximately 30 gallons fuel remained in each tank. As of this writing; cause of engine failure not known.
output: Single pilot had an engine failure and made an emergency landing in a field.

input: L-hand engine had a compressor stall. Smoke and fire was sighted coming from it by crew and passenber in main cabin. Loud noise and moderate shaking of aircraft plane flown to lax; no evacuate/evacuation normal lndg.
output: A b757 flight attendant rpt on an engine failure; inflt engine shutdown; within 2 minute(s) after takeoff from sna; ca; and a diversion to lax; ca.

input: Aircraft x initiated contact. As per standard operating procedure; i looked for the corresponding flight strip in order to assign the flight a beacon code. When i did not find the flight strip; i requested the flight plan from host and discovered that the flight plan was not stored in host. I requested a beacon code from host and assigned it to aircraft x. After positively radar identifying the aircraft; i proceeded to type in aircraft x's flight plan. From this point on; i worked the flight as a routine arrival. There was no loss of separation involving aircraft x during this event. I subsequently found out that the cause of this event was a typographical error during input of aircraft x's boundary estimate into the atop system. The atop controller had inadvertently typed in an estimate that was ten hours later than what was intended to type (jx00 vs. Ax00). There are currently numerous logic checks within the atop system concerning aircraft data such as weight category; cruising speed; ceiling altitude; etc. These logic checks; while not always correct; do have value as they draw attention to potential typographical and/or other errors. It is puzzling why there is not a logic check pertaining to boundary estimates. A logic check of boundary estimates would have drawn attention to the typographical error since facilities do not pass boundary estimates that are that far into the future.
output: An oceanic controller enters a arrival time estimate with a ten hour typo from actual. When the aircraft contacts the receiving radar controller; the problem is identified. Controllers noted that the atops system checks many parameters but not this one.

input: I took off in the late morning local time; heading northwest to practice turns; climbs/descents; shallow bank turns to get comfortable with airplane. On return to the airport; setup for landing on the runway. After touchdown the landing gear collapsed and props struck runway. There were several eye witnesses; including the airport manager that indicated that the landing gear doors were open and the gear was down. I am not sure what caused the landing gear to collapse. Perhaps the switch that locks the gear malfunctioned.
output: A pilot reported his m20e landing gear collapsed after what appeared to be a normal approach and landing with the gear extended.

input: Working air carrier x in for instrument landing system 5 approach to follow a c560 on a visual approach cleared x for the instrument landing system 5 approach the citation then slowed to 100 knots indicated airspeed ground speed second officer i slowed x; noticing that i would not be able to maintain separation unless i issued the c560 traffic to x and he would be able to see it and follow on a visual approach or turn x out for resequence. I tried for the visual when x did not rpt the c560. I inadvertently gave x a left/right (directions) turn to 360 degrees and 2600 feet/foot x gave the appropriate readback and hearing it; did not realize that the left/right (directions) turn was issued; x started the turn at which time i realized he was in the left/right (directions) turn and issued a climb to 3000 feet/foot mean sea level for obstruction clearing and a heading of 180 degrees for traffic -- a falcon on the instrument landing system approach x made the turn; however; was slow in climbing to 3000 feet/foot falcon traffic was issued and the altitude of 3000 reissued. Traffic passed and x was resequenced for the instrument landing system 5 apch.
output: Ctlr turned air carrier x wrong way had less than standard separation from falcon jet. System error.

input: I had requested climb from fl280 to fl330 at stevn. Later at bakon; i made a position rpt and sfo radio read back my position rpt and stated cleared to fl330. I had not requested fl330 since my first request at stevn. The high frequency radio reception was marginal; second officer we requested that sfo radio confirm 'clred to fl330.' he stated cleared to fl330. We read back the clearance 'clred to fl330.' about 10 minute(s) later; the capt rpted to sfo radio; 'level at fl330.' a few minute(s) later; sfo radio called and asked us to confirm level fl360. We stated; 'negative; we are level fl330.' a few minute(s) later sfo radio called back and asked when did we receive a clearance to fl330. We stated at bakon at approximately pm40z. A few minute(s) later; we were told that oakland had never received a clearance and that we were to call them when on the ground probable cause: poor high frequency radio reception may have caused a communications problem supplemental information from acn 362540: due to static on both high frequency frequency we had had problems with air-gnd communicationss during first part of flight we acknowledged leaving fl280 for fl330. I rpted level at fl330; due to the coplt being busy. Shortly thereafter; sfo radio called back to say he had us at fl360. We stated we were at fl330. Sfo radio then called back and said oakland now cleared us at fl330; but no original clearance had been given to fl330 and to call oakland oceanic supervisor when able. Poor radio reception for both aircraft and ground each asking a question that was answered with a reference to fl330 was an underlying cause. Supplemental information from acn 362541: my impression is that we were cleared by mistake by sfo radio. It seems odd to me that both the capt and first officer mistook the radio call. However; we are using very old technology that is poor at best -- high frequency radio. I can receive live tv coverage on any of a hundred channels from any point on the globe; yet we are flying passenber across the pacific in unctled airspace using wwii technology handed down from the controling agency -- where are our priorities! In the future; i will try to listen (best as i can) to all radio xmissions. I usually listen to all calls; but was not as attentive on this call because it was initially a position rpt.
output: Acr wdb had asked for fl330 on previous position rpt at fl280. At next position rpt sfo radio gave what was interpreted as clearance to fl330. Flight crew confirmed with a repeat clearance from sfo and then climbed to fl330. Rpting in level; sfo radio paused and after checkeding with zoa; stated that the clearance to fl330 was never issued by center ctlr.

input: We arrived at the aircraft for an xa40 departure and found a discrepancy on the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring hydraulic page indicating a line was pressurized from the blue electric pump box to abeam the ram air turbine/ram air temperature (ram air turbine). The line was amber from that point up; indicating low pressure. Previous experience told me we had a faulty pressure switch or cannon plug in the blue hydraulic line. We observed a previous day write-up of the same which was signed off with an minimum equipment list this minimum equipment list had been removed before our flight i notified maintenance and got 2 technicians working the problem then we notified maintenance controller of issue. I was told that we would be mel'ed under the previous number. I told them the minimum equipment list was not appropriate as it didn't address the specific fault. The response was fine maintenance controller out. Nothing more. I re-established contact several minute(s) later and got a new controller apparently there was a shift change in progress. I re-explained the problem same response; same minimum equipment list i again refused relief under this minimum equipment list as i considered it inappropriate. Maintenance controller said he'd get back to me. Indirectly; i guess he did; as 10 minute(s) later; 2 technicians returned with the singed off logbook and minimum equipment list sticker on front. I again refused and they simply replied they were doing as told by maintenance controller now 20 minute(s) after scheduled push with a full aircraft i again called maintenance controller to refuse the minimum equipment list now a 3rd controller insisted that since the minimum equipment list addressed the indicating system and the switch provided pressure indications; the minimum equipment list was correct. I replied the minimum equipment list addressed the indicator; not the source of the information and therefore was inappropriate. He stressed; again; it was the correct minimum equipment list and i should fly the aircraft i asked him intermediate fix he would be as adamant intermediate fix an federal aviation administration was standing over my shoulder and he assured me he was absolutely positive; 100% certain; it was a good minimum equipment list against my better judgement; i relented; for 2 reasons. One; i hate delaying my passenber from their homes; families; or meetings. Two; i did not consider this one issue related to the critical safety of the flight after expressing my reservations at least 6 times to at least 2 technicians as well as 3 maintenance controllers i yielded to their interpretation and accepted the minimum equipment list once airborne; i had time to further examine the minimum equipment list book and realized that even to accept maintenance controller logic connecting the indicating system to the pressurize switch in question; which i don't; this minimum equipment list addresses the 3 hydraulic pumps indications specifically; not the pressure system in general. It was the wrong minimum equipment list now for even another reason. Maintenance controller had twisted this minimum equipment list to fit this fault because there is; in my opinion; no relief in the minimum equipment list for this fault; as well as the fact that there were no switches available. I sent a text message while en route requesting the switch be replaced. They responded there was not enough time on quick turn. I then threatened to revisit the validity of this minimum equipment list when we arrived. Lo and behold; we were met with a team of technicians to fix the problem also; we were met by the assistant chief pilot as maintenance controller had rpted to him that i had been uncooperative and obstinate. He listened to my account of events; reviewed the minimum equipment list book; and determined i was right to challenge. The reason for this as soon as possible are 2-fold: 1) address this maintenance issue in the minimum equipment list it is a fairly common occurrence. Until it is addressed in minimum equipment list do an in-house evaluation of this fault and establish what; intermediate fix any; relief is available. Then; advise all technicians and maintenance controller what procedures should be followed until it gets addressed through the minimum equipment list (also; how about keeping a few switches at each out-station that services our busses...) and 2) address the mindset of a few of our controllers who feel their job is to push airplanes; rather than address the maintenance needs to satisfy the safety; as well as the legal requirements; of maintaining the schedule. It is extremely frustrating to have maintenance controller disregard my input; as a capt; that directly affects my license and livelihood; as well as my safety.
output: An a320 crew arrived at the aircraft to find a repeated hydraulic system abnormality. The flight crew felt that the maintenance minimum equipment list assigned was inaccurate. After several discussions the crew flew the aircraft but later felt it was not a legal maintenance minimum equipment list assignment.

input: Pa44 was executing an nondirectional radio beacon runway(s) 11r circle to runway(s) 4 approach be90 was issued the exact same approach clearance 8.5 mile in trail when the pa44 passed the approach gate. The vrb tower was talking with both aircraft when i observed on radar the pa44 fly to the airport and then reverse course to a point 4 mile sw of the field. As soon as the be90 left my frequency his radar target deviated off the nondirectional radio beacon runway(s) 11r and tracked towards a 4 mile straight-in to runway(s) 4. The be90 was supposed to fly the nondirectional radio beacon then circle to runway(s) 4. The outcome of this has been charged as an operational error to the radar controller who provided non radar rules and separation. Every other controller that works this sector was trained to do the exact same rules and procedures it is unknown at this time intermediate fix the vrb tower controller turned either one of these aircraft are aircraft allowed to circle or start their circling maneuver 7 mile from the rwy? I feel this was a pilot deviation intermediate fix the second aircraft had flown the approach separation would never have been jeopardized.
output: Zma controller observes 2 non radar aircraft divert from vrb approach and conflict. Controller alleges procedure 'ok' because that was the way he was taught.

input: On about a 120 degree downwind vector for an instrument landing system approach; the controller issued a descent to 3;000 feet. The pilot monitoring read back the clearance and we dialed it in the mode control panel window; verified; and continued the descent. Being very familiar with surrounding terrain; i thought this seemed a bit low; but chose not to query the controller. Passing through 3;100 feet; he gave us a 'low altitude alert; check altitude immediately; maintain 3;500 feet.' i disconnected the autopilot and climbed quickly to 3;500 feet. We completed the rest of the approach with no other issues. It was a poor air traffic control clearance; and i knew it. I should have asked him to confirm the descent to 3;000 feet.
output: Air carrier flight crew reported air traffic control descended them below the minimum vectoring altitude.

input: Rental aircraft sma xx based at san antonio int'l airport san antonio; transmitter is not mode celsius equipped. I contacted houston center watch supervisor 'rooster'; pr federal aviation regulation 91.24(d)(3) requesting a mode celsius authorized deviation for an instrument flight rules flight from houston-hull (sgr) airport to houston-baytown (hpy) in aircraft xx via telephone. Verbal consent was given for this flight approximately 40 minute(s) after this telephone conversation; the flight departed from houston-hull on an instrument flight rules flight plan. After initial contact to approach on 123.8 the approach controller noted he was not receiving an altitude readout. I responded that i had obtained a mode celsius deviation. The controller requested who i contacted for this deviation. I responded 'with houston center'. The controller said i should have made the request thru the houston-hobby arsa. The flight proceeded normally after this exchange of information it appears that the appropriate ctlr(s) are not being informed of authorized mode celsius deviations in a timely manner. Clarification of side-by-side (or adjoining) terminal control area and arsa airspace should be provided to pilots and controllers concerning mode celsius responsibilities (ie; why aren't arsa approach controllers notified of a mode celsius deviation in their airspace intermediate fix authorized).
output: Sma transgressing hou arsa with mode celsius deviation queried by terminal radar approach control facility who gave authorization.

input: Violation of federal aviation regulation 121.471 flight time limitations scheduled to fly zzz1 to zzz3 reassigned to fly zzz1-zzz3 via zzz2 with a departure as flight xxx. We arrived at zzz1 airport around xa30 and found the aircraft park at the terminal. After a lengthy delay for fuel we left the gate at xd42. During pushback a tug operator broke the towbar and the aircraft could not be returned to the gate. After nearly 4 hours we were finally able to continue the pushback/tow to deicing and takeoff for zzz2. We finally arrived in zzz2 at xa47 local time and with a total flight time 5.05 hours more than 2 hours prior to our arrival, arrive in zzz2 we were reassigned again to fly to zzz4 instead of zzz3. Zzz2 to zzz3 equals 2.17 hour flight plan. Zzz2-zzz4 equals 4.20. When we arrived in zzz2 i contacted our crew tracker and the chief pilot to inform them of the 8 hour limitation and our illegality. I was informed that due to the 'divert' further informed them that our flight to zzz2 was not a 'diversion' and that we had been reassigned to zzz2. Furthermore; that we could not leave the gate at zzz2 for zzz4 (and a 4.20 flight plan) and knowingly fly over the 8 hour limitation. Both the tracker and the chief pilot continued to declare that we were legal and given relief from said federal aviation regulation i disagreed. The capt also contacted them and was told the same thing. Crew tracking was well aware that we would be in violation of the federal aviation regulation well before we arrived in zzz2. They had the time and the opportunity to either reassign another crew; deadhead a crew into zzz2; cancel the flight or even to have capt and i fly a legal and scheduled sequence to zzz3 and then have another crew fly zzz3 to zzz4. They chose to falsely declare our flight as a 'diversion' to circumvent the far's. They further violated federal aviation regulation 121.471 reference part 1; 8.3 paragraph (b)(3) and part 1; 8.3 subpart left/right (directions) paragraph (c). Over 9 hours aloft they failed to give us proper crew rest in zzz4 of 11 hours 18 hours as required under sub part left/right (directions) there was never a diversion. There were however many reassignments.
output: B757 crew is rescheduled to fly over the 8 hour flight time limitation.

input: Notams at mgw are not always timely and accurate/valid. Also; there may be a misuse of purpose of notams. The issuance of a notice to airmen / of air missions that closes runway(s) 5/23 and 24/7 may be being used; unfortunately; for a purpose other than safety; namely; to build a case to close runway(s) 5/23 permanently. Runway(s) 5/23 is the prevailing wind runway(s) in feb and march; the crosswind component for my aircraft and 2 commuter aircraft (there may have been others) were exceeded and the only choice was to land on runway(s) 23; intermediate fix a landing was to be made at mgw. Each aircraft chose runway(s) 23. However; the airport manager has determined that he will close the runway(s) permanently and has stated second officer publicly. The city council and the mayor with support from the aviation community have stated that the runway(s) will not be closed. It is speculated that the use of the notice to airmen / of air missions in the fashion in which it is being used is a way to build the case for closure. Current construction will last for several months. With respect to the construction equipment located near the end of runway(s) 23; this can be moved and located elsewhere during non working hours an additional issue is whether the markings being used on runway(s) 5/23 to designate that the runway(s) is closed are appropriate. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr restated in considerable detail his opposition to the manner in which the airport is run. Most specifically and in greatest measure the alleged intent of the airport manager to eventually close the runway(s) in question. He stated the notice to airmen / of air missions issue; while of some concern; was mostly a means to get awareness of his greater concern in the public view...ie; national aeronautics and space administration involvement.
output: Rptr alleges agenda driven airport manager at mgw is misusing runway(s) closures and notams to support the city's desire to eliminate a runway(s) alleges airport notams are untimely and inappropriate.

input: During boarding passenber call button at row 10def. Passenber advised me that entire row of seats was loose. The passenber then demonstrated by rocking the row with their body weight while sitting down. I observed the entire row rocking off the floor; both front and back floor mounts. I immediately rpted this to the capt. Maintenance immediately came to the aircraft we were at departure time and the decision was made by dispatch to minimum equipment list the seats and depart on time. The passenber were reseated to row 11def. This is directly behind the minimum equipment list row of 10 def. How could this be allowable? The company placed passenber in a row aft of the minimum equipment list row and there were passenber sitting in the row forward of the minimum equipment list row 9def! As a flight attendant; i ante meridiem shocked that an exit row of seats; not bolted to the floor; could be safe. It would seem that in the event of an accident/evac the stress limits would not be met and the row would shift and block egress. The actions of passenber egressing would also shift the row of seats to become a safety hazard. The aircraft was dispatched with the above described condition. It was also dispatched from zzz with the same mel.
output: An a320 cabin attendant rpts maintenance mel'ing the aircraft with the entire emergency exit row of seats not bolted to the floor.

input: The crew had just finished 6 hours 8 minute(s) of charter flight into an unfamiliar airport sjc. We had yet a 4 hour 30 minute(s) ferry from sjc to xyz late that evening. It was my leg. After takeoff we were executing the loupe 9 departure procedure during the climb he cleared us to the sjc vor and dme (co-located) and to join the departure procedure as published. Because the controller cleared us to 17000 feet/foot we ignored the crossing restrict, restricted, restriction at sjc vor and dme (co-located) at 12000 feet/foot therefore; we continued our climb higher than 12000 feet/foot prior to reaching sjc vor and dme (co-located) later; the controller 'queried' us on the restrict, restricted, restriction there was no incident or conflict with any other aircraft i believe the mistake resulted in a combination of being slightly fatigued; and confusion in the communications between the controller and the crew. Corrective action may have taken place on both sides due to the fact we were unfamiliar with the airport and our call sign was unfamiliar to the controller intermediate fix the controller would have stated 'cross sjc vor and dme (co-located) at 12000 feet/foot then maintain 17000 ft;' there would have been no confusion. Second; it was part our responsibility to query air traffic control rather than assume during a confusing clrnc.
output: B727 flight crew ignores crossing restrict, restricted, restriction on departure from sjc.

input: Enroute from teb to zzzz we were given direct to an intersection and accidentally flew to a different intersection. Our route was teb elvae col dixie prepi owenz linnd azezu l453 paepr..... Along airway l453 there are 2 fixes with similar sounding names; lexad and lexim. Before prepi we were given direct to lexad but we heard and saw lexim along our route. We both confirmed lexim and read back to air traffic control direct to lexim. Neither air traffic control nor us caught the error. About 10 minutes later we were asked what we were flying to and i responded lexim. He asked when we were given that clearance and i mentioned it was given to us earlier. He asked if lexim was even along our route and i confirmed that it was. He mentioned that there should not have been 2 fixes along our route with such close spelling and that it was their fault for the error. It was then that he said we should have been going direct to lexad. He said to continue to lexim and he would try to work out direct to lexim. Before freq handoff i apologized and asked if we had a problem. He said nothing to apologize for and thanks for bringing the situation to his attention.
output: A fractional captain reporting being cleared direct to lexad intersection. The pilot read back lexim another fix on their route. Air traffic control did not notice the read back and the pilot proceeded to the wrong fix.

input: In the vicinity of terrell; transmitter airport (trl); numerous operators/aircraft/other airfields use same common traffic advisory frequency frequency 122.8; which results in highly cluttered frequency which is barely usable. Numerous 'stepped-on' calls occur. Evaluating local area radio frequencies and amount of radio traffic on 122.8 in this location; changing some if necessary; would enhance aviation safety!
output: Pilot landing trl experiences excessive use of the common traffic advisory frequency 122.8 resulting in stepped on and missed communications. Reporter suggests that the frequency be evaluated and perhaps the number of airports in the area using 122.8 could be reduced.

input: I was relieving the radar controller. Controller covered all required items including aircraft status. A b737 was on frequency with standard restriction to cross zzz at fl190. Briefing over; i sat down and observed the b737 crossing zzz level at fl230. At that moment; the b737 announced on frequency that they would not make the restriction at zzz; but that they would miss it by 3 or 4 miles. The controller i relieved had not yet left the area; and confirmed that the b737 had checked on with the crossing restriction. The pilot of the b737 then made several transmissions asking if that had been a problem; are we all set here; are you going to file paperwork because if you are then we will; and so on. They missed the restriction by several more than just 3 or 4 miles.i read the recent briefing sheet that stated that crossing restrictions were the shared responsibility of pilots and controllers; and i disagree. A crossing restriction is issued by the controller to ensure that; at some future time or place; the altitude of a specific aircraft will be known; so that other tasks; such as concentrating on other separation scenarios developing in the sector; can be accomplished. Many pilots now 'hang it up' so they can perform 'flight idle descents' to an assigned crossing restriction; so it is not unusual for an aircraft to appear high; to a controller; for a particular restriction. Short of questioning each aircraft that has been issued a restriction if they are planning on complying with a restriction (and this does not assure compliance either); i do not see how a controller could manage a moderately busy sector; and thus; my opinion remains unchanged that an acknowledged crossing restriction; for which the controller has assured a good readback; is the sole responsibility of the flight crew. I have no recommendation on how to prevent a re-occurrence of this event. Until there are consequences for the offending flight crews; restrictions will continue to be ignored; and the results may prove to be ugly and newsworthy.
output: Artcc controller reported an air carrier missed a crossing restriction; then discussed who was responsible.

input: We were making our turn over zzz vor and dme (co-located) and joining zzz1 when center inquired about our routing to zzz6. We informed that we were cleared as filed via cpdlc. What was on our paperwork was zzz zzz1 zzz2 zzzzz zzz3 zzzzz1 zzzzz2. He was showing us after zzz going to zzz5 and the north wind route. He filed us direct zzz4 zzzzz1 zzzzz2. At the gate in zzz the route that loaded was the southern route not the north one over zzz5; which matched what was on our paperwork release 2. When we got our cpdlc and it said as filed; we executed and flew. After the conversation with center we acars'd our dispatcher. Who took over from the one who planned our flight. He said that revision 1 had north route over zzz5 and revision 2 of the release had the southern route. Not sure where the confusion in routes happened; but we executed and flew what was on the latest revision we had; when we were issued our clearance.
output: B737-700 first officer reported discrepancy between cpdlc clearance; and air traffic control clearance.

input: It was day visual meteorological conditions and we were on initial approach into mht. We called the field in sight; but were told to expect approach clearance to runway(s) 17 in a few mile we were on a vector that was basically an extended right base for runway(s) 17; and we were told to descend to 2500 feet/foot the first officer was hand flying. Shortly thereafter; we were cleared for the visual to runway(s) 17. My first officer and i saw a mountain ridge with an antenna farm on top of it which was directly ahead of us on the vector we had been left on before being cleared for the visual. Even though we had clear visual contact with the mountain; we decided it would be prudent to stay at the air traffic control assigned 2500 feet/foot until clear of the ridge. As we passed over the ridge; we received the aural warning 'terrain; terrain; pull up; pull up!' i quickly checkeded to ensure that the first officer had indeed leveled at 2500 feet/foot (he did); and that we were not descending (we weren't). Before any evasive action was taken; the warning ceased. After landing i called boston terminal radar approach control facility on the phone. I wasn't second officer much alarmed at what had happened to us; but intermediate fix we'd have been instrument meteorological conditions or at night; it would have been a different story. Terminal radar approach control facility informed me that in instrument meteorological conditions they leave planes at 3000 feet/foot over the ridge until within 3 mile of the localizer but because we had the field in sight; they dropped us to 2500 feet/foot they said we weren't the first airplane to complain about this specific incident. In retrospect; we had about 750 feet/foot clearance over the antennas and the ridge. I had my terrain display on; but was unable to see it because it isn't a very bright display; and the sun setting behind us was shining right onto my mfd. I don't feel that safety was compromised on this particular flight however; i feel that boston terminal radar approach control facility should raise their minimum vector altitude to 2800 feet/foot over this ridge; because even in clear conditions with the hazard in sight; we shouldn't be getting egpws warnings at air traffic control assigned headings and alts.
output: Acft inbound to mht experienced ground proximity warning system alert while on controller vector at mva.

input: After cleared for the bdega one star and established in the descent (clearance was 'descend via...') norcal approach informed us to expect runway 28l at ksfo and runway 28r is on request. We were level at the final altitude of 11;000 feet mean sea level and 1 nautical mile past corkk intersection we failed to confirm that runway 28l was programmed in the flight management system as a result the flight management system directed the aircraft toward the routing for runway 28r; which was previously loaded in the flight management system by the crew. Norcal approach queried us to confirm we are on the runway 28l transition and issued a right turn to heading 140. We updated the flight management system with runway 28l; the remainder of the flight transpired with nothing significant to report. The flight terminated as scheduled at ksfo.heading into sfo is really a pilot nightmare. It is a general consensus that no matter what you load in the flight management system you will get a different clearance. For example during this arrival and approach we had the instrument landing system to 28r programmed and the quiet bridge visual approach programmed in and yet we got a third approach issued to us (as is the norm). This causes distraction in the cockpit during the descent and arrival phase of flight that is already busy with other required checklists. As a prudent pilot; i have an approach set up and an arrival and approach briefed at the top of descent so that both pilots can focus on other required duties. When the arrival and approach info changes from what is expected it causes undue stress and distraction in the cockpit which further leads to pilot error. Frequently on arrival to sfo; the automatic terminal information service lists three approaches in use. It would be helpful if expected arrival and approach information could be pushed out to pilots sooner; by the top of descent from cruise altitude so that the cockpit could be already configured for descent and both pilots can be focused on flying the aircraft along the required flight path instead of having one pilot reprogramming and the other pilot now briefing a new approach during the arrival phase. With most commercial traffic having access to digital media it would be helpful to have a pre departure clearance clearance sent one hour out from landing issuing the arrival clearance; or at a minimum have the center pass the expected arrival approach to aircraft prior to transitioning into the arrival phase. With sfo being a melting pot of aviation and with english as a second language for most international carriers; giving more time to understand the expected arrival and approach would benefit many.
output: Descending on the bdega one standard terminal arrival route into ksfo; corporate jet flight crew received clearance to runway 28l which had not been programmed in the flight management system after aircraft turned toward routing for runway 28r; air traffic control issued vectors and crew reprogrammed the flight management system ongoing problems associated with changes to expected routing on ksfo stars were noted by the reporter.

input: Smt was instructed to enter left base runway(s) 19l. Sma in right closed pattern runway(s) 19r. Smt rpted 2 mile base; was told to turn right and follow another aircraft downwind past the approach end runway(s) 19l. Smt did not comply and appeared to be proceeding directly to the approach end of runway(s) 19r at a high rate of speed (much faster than i felt was appropriate for traffic pattern). Smt was given traffic (sma on short final runway(s) 19r). I also instructed him to then continue straight ahead past the tank farm nw of the airport then make a 270 degree turn and enter base for runway(s) 19r. I had given him this last instruction of continuing straight ahead because he was heading directly to runway(s) 19r. There was no base to final and sma was within a 1/4 mile final runway(s) 19r.
output: Smt did not comply with air traffic control instructions and came in close proximitypa to another aircraft on short final.

input: There seems to be some miscommunication between operations and cargo. There have been some guidance changes in reference to the carrying of dry ice in the front cargo compartment of the a320 [series]. On [date] cargo put out the following bulletin that states dry ice can no longer to loaded in the front pit of a a320 [series aircraft]. It would have been nice for the largest division at [company] to pass this info on the front line. Does this new requirement require all checked luggage that is within limits to be loaded in the rear? Advisory: dry ice shipments can no longer travel in the forward pit of the airbus a320 [series]. This change will lead to a reduction in the amount of dry ice that can be carried on the a320 [series]. [company manuals] are being updated with the new limitations to ensure dry ice shipments are not improperly manifested to the airbus. Why: during recent discussions with airbus; it was discovered that [company] lacked a ventilation modification that would allow for the safe carriage of dry ice in the forward pit of the a320 [series]. [company] is required to follow all manuals and technical guidance from airbus to ensure a safe and compliant operation of the airbus fleet.
output: Ground agent reported communication breakdown between operations and cargo [load planner] regarding the carrying of dry ice in the forward cargo pit on the air carriers a320 series aircraft.

input: I was assigned to inspect the forward (fwd) cargo compartment of a b767-300 aircraft in accordance with the specified job card. After the aircraft had been released for flight; i was notified that i had signed-off the required inspection items (rii); but had overlooked a few unairworthy fire discharge nozzles. The fire discharge nozzles had apparently been taped over.
output: A line mechanic was informed he failed to notice during his a-check that fire extinguishing discharge nozzles were previously taped over in the forward cargo compartment of a b767-300 aircraft. The extended range twin operations aircraft had been released months earlier from a heavy maintenance check at a contract maintenance repair station.

input: Somehow the flight management system kicked out several fixes that were previously in the flight plan route as both the captain and i checked the route and all fixes on the ground before the flight. All fixes were there before we departed. As we were climbing we were assigned a new air traffic control frequency and the controller said he was showing us 2 miles off of our filed course; that's all he said then he passed us over to another controller and he said that he was showing us 3 miles off course; we then asked for direct to stl as that was the fix we were going to on j134; that was approved with no issues. We got out the paper chart to verify proper course and fixes along with the filed flight plan and legs on flight release. It seems that the flight management system somehow kicked out several fixes on j134. Both the captain and i checked all of the fixes in the flight management system with the flight release and pre departure clearance on the ground before the flight and all fixes were in the fms.
output: The crew verified all flight management system fixes in the flight plan route prior to departure. During the climb out air traffic control advised the crew of a track deviation. The crew requested and received a new clearance for direct routing.

input: The crew reported for duty for a part 91 flight to pick up the airplane owner. Prior to departure the crew conducted a full preflight. No anomalies; malfunctions or defects were noted. As a result of the preflight inspection the crew determined the airplane was in airworthy condition and departed to pick up the owner and return to home base. No defects were noted upon return. The day before the crew had experienced a partial malfunction of the pilot and co-pilot pfd displays that was temporary in nature. During initial climb on the last leg of the day the flight director failed; the altitude preselect stopped displaying an altitude and the background momentarily went white. Almost immediately the system reset itself and the background returned to normal. Initially the flight director did not reappear in spite of attempts by the co-pilot (pilot monitoring) to reset it. The altitude preselect showed an altitude as soon as the altitude knob was twisted clockwise and was reset to the original assigned altitude. The second attempt from the pilot monitoring to bring the flight director back into view was successful. Once everything returned all systems and displays continued working normally for the remainder of the flight. All displays and modes were crosschecked against standby instruments and navigation receivers. No anomalies were noted. As a result of the display malfunction the crew had missed an altitude assignment that subsequently became a matter of great concern to the crew. The crew discussed what could have caused the partial and temporary display malfunction and determined the likely cause to be a jolt that we felt through the nose wheel as the airplane accelerated at v1. The nose wheel hit some kind of bump on the runway and this was felt through the airframe. In other words; we determined that the likely cause was an event external to the airplane; not a fault of the electronics themselves. Upon arrival the captain contacted the chief pilot. The incident was reported and discussed. The chief pilot requested a report in writing from each pilot. Post flight checks by the crew revealed no anomalies/malfunctions or defects. The next day; upon return the crew discussed the previous day's display anomalies with one of the maintenance technicians. Maintenance expressed no particular concern during the conversation and remarked that they had received similar observations of soft failures that reset in flight and that upon inspection could not be replicated. The crew stopped by the chief pilot's office and discussed the reports to be filed. They were filed later that evening. The crew received no response about these reports until three days later. The airplane was released by the company for an international trip; part 91; for the airplane owner to be started in two days. The crew reported for duty; and conducted a full preflight. No defects were noted and the crew with the owner departed. A total of 4 legs were flown that day; during two of which the crew encountered instrument flight rules conditions with moderate rain and turbulence. An instrument approach had to be flown into tucson; az for a fuel stop; followed by an instrument departure in rain and turbulence. Throughout all 4 legs that day there were no malfunctions experienced. The trip ended without incident. The crew was contacted by the company a day later about the lack of a discrepancy write-up concerning the partial and temporary display failure. The crew had not filed a discrepancy report because there were no hard failures of any of the displays or avionics; the temporary display interruption was thought to have been caused by a temporary external event; and because the crew was preoccupied with the altitude deviation. As pilots we have no training in aircraft systems matching the level of a&p; yet we are expected to be able make a determination as to the airworthiness of the airplane before every flight. We are considered to be competent to do sofrom a private pilot on up. However; our decision making is now being questioned; even after a federal aviation administration licensed a&p inspected the equipment; could not duplicate the faults on the ground; and returned the airplane to service. The lessons learned are to: 1. Not take anything for granted. 2. Not to get distracted from the cause (why did the malfunction happen) by the effect (missing the altitude assignment).3. Back up your thinking with the expertise of other professionals.
output: Ce525 first officer experienced momentary pfd failure during takeoff which is quickly corrected; but not before an altitude deviations occured. The crew is chided by the company for not entering a maintenance discrepancy in the logbook.

input: We were the second aircraft on final when tower told the plane in front of us; aircraft y; to turn left to rejoin the downwind with no explanation as to why; even though we had been making right traffic. He continued to give directions to other aircraft telling them to turn left but never said my tail number of aircraft x; so i was confused as to what was going on. Aircraft y continued to ask how they were supposed to rejoin the downwind since they were asked to turn the opposite direction; all while there was a jet on final. Finally; tower exclaims for me; aircraft x; to turn left to get out of their way. Aircraft y however was much closer as they had crossed the final to rejoin the opposite downwind; so aircraft y and the jet had a near midair collision. I believe this event happened because of a mix up in tail numbers and giving the smaller planes confusing directions.
output: C172 pilot reported an near midair collision with two other aircraft in a traffic pattern.

input: While performing the flight deck preparation oxygen mask test procedure; i noticed the oxygen pressure dropped excessively; by about 400 psi. I called maintenance to have them check the oxygen bottle shutoff valve and they found it partially closed. This is a recurring problem and our procedures are not designed to detect it. I always check for pressure drop although it's not required and have caught this issue several times because of this. In my opinion; our current airbus normal standard operating procedure - flight deck preparation - oxygen mask test procedure could be improved to reduce the risk of operating with partially closed crew oxygen bottle valves by requiring the crew to check for excessive pressure drop.unlike the boeing standard operating procedure airbus pilots are not currently required to check for excessive pressure drop during flow testing. Although there are obviously design differences between the two fleets; both have rotary shutoff valves that could be left partially closed. The airbus has a regulator low pressure electronic centralized aircraft monitoring message that the crew is required to check after testing; but it only serves to warn the crew of a fully closed shutoff valve and is ineffective against a partially closed valve. Obviously; a partially closed valve may not provide enough flow for all the flight deck occupants.in my experience those valves are occasionally left partially closed after crew oxygen bottle replacements. When that happens; the aircraft may keep operating in that undesirable state for extensive periods of time. Typically; partial valve closures are only noticed when a crew dons the o2 masks for a restroom break and notices a lack of flow; even though they may have performed the published masks test procedure correctly.so far; on our airbus fleet; i have personally experienced the issue three times and i am aware of at least one incident resulting in a diversion. After my last as soon as possible report on the subject a couple years ago i was told that changing our flight operations procedure was not necessary because maintenance procedures were changed to prevent the issue from happening again. However; it still is happening. The last time i witnessed maintenance perform an oxygen mask test after a bottle replacement; they didn't check for excessive pressure drop. So; it might be a good idea to look at their procedures as well.given the recent change by the federal aviation administration regarding the use of oxygen mask during breaks; i'm concerned it is more likely that an issue with the o2 valve may remain unnoticed until the masks are needed in an emergency. That obviously could have very negative consequences.
output: A321 captain reported finding an oxygen pressure drop while checking the crew o2 masks during preflight that was caused by a partially open shutoff valve on the crew oxygen cylinder.

input: Radio frequency 134.47 at zfw (decod hi sector) has been causing numerous problems for up to 7 days. The frequency 'burps' frequently; and on occasion cuts out. These problems have been rpted to airway facilities; but to date have not been corrected. These problems cause an unsafe situation on a busy sequencing sector where there is no room for error intermediate fix radio failure occurs. Pilots have trouble hearing air traffic control and miss many calls. This problem could be related and a causal factor in an operational error that occurred on this sector may/xx/93.
output: Freq 134 pt 47 megahertz is intermittent and impacting controller work.

input: On the loupe 9 departure from sjc; began turn at 1.8 vor and dme (co-located) remained within 4 vor and dme (co-located) at all times (30 degree bank turn). As we entered our climbing turn to a 120 degree heading the dep/apch controller called traffic at 9 o'clock position we were around 3700 feet/foot mean sea level as we were in our turn now heading about 090 degrees the controller called another aircraft to our attention at around 2 o'clock. We were looking; but did not see traffic at approximately 4600 feet/foot mean sea level as we were about to level off at 5000 feet/foot mean sea level we got a traffic advisory on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii this was just as we were completing our turn to 120 degrees at 4800 feet/foot mean sea level we got an resolution advisory telling us to descend we had not yet leveled at 5000 feet/foot mean sea level i stopped the climb and began a descent the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii showed traffic now at +200 feet/foot above and in front of us. At this point the controller told us this aircraft had us in visual contact and to continue our climb to 12000 feet/foot then he came back and said to expedite our climb to 12000 feet/foot at that moment the capt grabbed the yoke and began an immediate climbing turn to the left/right (directions) it looked as though our traffic the twin cessna; just saw us also. Aircraft #2 quickly veered to the left/right (directions) and descended immediately. We did not continue climb because resolution advisory was telling us to descend we began climb after traffic was in sight. Airspace for departure should be class b. Departure is too busy to be looking for visual flight rules traffic at our alt.
output: Md80 crew had near midair collision in sjc class celsius while on the loupe 9 sid.

input: I was flying wdb climbing out of heathrow; bound for nyc. Capt (pnf) was calling shanwick oceanic clearance for our clearance across the north atlantic. I was flying and talking to the local high sector controller while the capt was getting his clearance the oceanic controller asked him to estimate our oceanic entry point (ackil); (54n 10w). Because the aircraft clock was a drum/digital type; the hours set of numbers had rotated; at about 55 minute(s) past instead of 59 past (or 00). The capt mistakenly gave oceanic; a wrong estimate of time. Oceanic accepted this time estimate. The capt changed frequency back to the local high sector radar controller shortly thereafter; the radar controller quizzed us about our estimation of ackil. Rechking this; the capt corrected his mistake; to the radar controller who said he would pass it on to oceanic. For some reason he did not do this; second officer when we showed up; on the oceanic controllers frequency he was surprised; and had to issue us a climb clearance from fl350 to fl390 because of conflicting traffic (we were visual flight rules conditions on top). Contributing to this incident was the fact that we had transversed second officer many time zones in 24 hours it was a time change from daylight to standard in us; we were using universal time coordinated (zulu/gmt) not local etc. I also think the mechanical time clock in the cockpit is an additional factor; since the hour drum of numbers rotated to the next hour; before the last hour was finished.
output: Equip problem plus a communicationss mixup cause wdb to approach a rpting point a hour early.

input: Lost power left/right (directions) engine aircraft yawed; remained full throttle on both engs. Left/right (directions) engine only put approximately 50 percent power cleared for climb on course; made u-turn (1500 feet/foot above ground level estimated) and requested land opposite direction of pattern traffic (none in pattern i could see or hear). Psp tower cleared me for a landing any runway(s) after i informed tower of engine power loss. Landed without event. Did not tell approach i was switching back to tower as i was busy setting up for a possible single engine flight and landing did not need to feather left/right (directions) engine as it maintained partial pwr.
output: The pilot of an smt has a partial power loss in the left/right (directions) engine after takeoff and was able to reverse course and land successfully in the opposite direction of traffic with tower approval.

input: I was returning to my home airport (rkd) late in the evening. There was a broken layer below me and a solid overcast above by maybe 1500-2000 feet/foot as i flew past bangor heading south the undercast became closed in and the overcast began to come down. By the time i realized all the ground lights had disappeared and the overcast had closed in; i was deep in a series of broken and solid clouds. Even though i knew where i was and had my instruments tuned in; i quickly decided to call bangor approach control to help with vectors to their airport i knew they could get me o the ground with a surveillance approach jut about as soon as i did a 180 degree turn; the undercast returned to broken; but i still used the controller to help with vectors and altitude suggestions.
output: Bgr controller provides radar surveillance approach to a c172 caught between cloud layers.
