(i may have passed out; i'm not sure.) my hand must have hit the radio switch because when i got myself oriented again i was down to about 2000 above ground level in a left/right (directions) spiral dive just westbound of oma; in their arsa. After resetting the radios; i contacted oma approach who gave me radar vectors to mle. Landed uneventfully although i was still shaken and somewhat dizzy.
output: Unauthorized uncoordinated penetration of airspace. Proximitypa of arsa.

input: I was in the nw practice area at about 6000 feet/foot when the engine started to slowly lose power finally; nearly all power was lost and i tried to restart and go through the emergency chklist but nothing worked. I saw an open road and called 'mayday' several times on vgt frequency but received no response. The plane reached critically slow speeds on final and stalled. The airplane veered to the left/right (directions) and impacted nose-hvy. I set up for a 60 knot(s) approach straight-in for a highway and kept a straight final until the plane stalled and veered to the left/right (directions) it impacted at approximately 30-40 knot(s) road upward grade approximately 5 degrees stalled at 15-20 feet/foot above ground nose gear and propeller damaged. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr discussed incident with the federal aviation administration and was relieved of responsibility for incident. Federal aviation administration took action against the flight school because student pilot had not received instruction on carburetor icing detection or elimination in the aircraft rptr stated that training was from a reputable flight school; yet; in 35 hours rptr had 3 different instructors -- 'they kept leaving for other jobs.'
output: A c-152 flown by a student pilot developed carburetor icing. Aircraft stalled during force landing on the highway.

input: On descent into mvy we were setting up for what looked like a right downwind for runway 24. We were given a descent to 2;000 by air traffic control and told to make rapid descent because of traffic. As we approached 2;000 air traffic control issued a heading of 030 to get around the traffic. We had not been able to make visual contact with the other aircraft.while we were still in the turn we got a 'descend' resolution advisory we complied with the resolution advisory and advised air traffic control what we were doing. As we received the clear of conflict message from traffic alert and collision avoidance system the flying pilot began to roll wings level. At this point; the non-flying pilot in command made visual contact with the aircraft. It appeared to be a single engine. [however; as] the flying pilot rolled wings level a second aircraft was in our front wind screen. The flying pilot took evasive action by descending and turning left.the second aircraft was a twin engine piston aircraft; perhaps a cessna 402 that looked to be headed for mvy. As the flying pilot was taking action the traffic alert and collision avoidance system gave resolution advisory call outs with which we complied. We were approximately 500 feet/foot from the second aircraft at the same altitude. After this we told air traffic control about the second aircraft and [then] went on to land on runway 24.
output: A g-iv flight crew suffered two consecutive conflicts with aircraft in the vicinity of their airport of intended landing. They followed a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory to avoid the first then came nose to nose with the second from which they took undirected evasive measures.

input: We departed lvs around x ante meridiem on a charter for the blm on an aerial survey. First contact with nellis control was in the north boundaries of a481. I instructed nellis control that i had the blm onboard and needed to inspect some land just north of the lv terminal control area and south of the desert national wildlife range. After receiving a squawk code; i was instructed to stay clear of the lv terminal control area as we went behind the ridge i heard nellis control call several times; but they could not hear my xmissions. They continued to transmit to me in the blind to contact control on 126.95. After contacting control on 126.95 i informed them that i was going to squawk 1200 and would be continuing up highway 93 and would be too low to maintain radio contact. All transmission were acknowledged. As we proceeded northbound we entered the desert moa-salley sector still squawking 1200 and monitoring nellis control on sector frequency 124.45. As we proceeded up kane springs i heard no calls from nellis control for sma but could hear nellis control contacting several aircraft inbound to nellis. When we were approximately 5 mile sw of elgin on the ridge line east of the delamar; we encountered a single fgt at our 2 o'clock position passing through a gap in the ridge. It was starting a left-hand turn toward us; but turned slightly back to the right passing approximately 200' off our left wig tip. Bout 1 mile later; still proceeding northbound along the ridge; we encountered 4 more low level fgts at our 2-3 o'clock position breaking over the ridge. 2 of the fgts broke hard to the left between the ridge and ourselves; the other 2 continued straight ahead and after passing us made a turn southbound at that time we turned nw up the gorge past elgin and blm personnel radioed his dispatch re: the encounter. I felt that the first fgt that saw us should have notified the other fgts of our position after landing we learned that nellis tried to warn up about th fgts. Not being able to contact us; could they have contacted their own acft? Corrective action: the fgt flts are now scheduled 90 days in advance and will be given to nellis to be put on their daily flight schedule. Nellis control will be contacted by aircraft before entering the military operating area nellis control will be contacted by phone by dispatch at least 1 hour before the flt.
output: Air taxi pilot flying in military operating area and in communications with air traffic control has near midair collision with 5 fgts.

input: While on a night visual meteorological conditions final for visual approach to runway 30l sjc the extremely bright stadium board display lights were on at full illumination and were an extreme visual distraction to us and other pilots on final approach. Sjc tower acknowledged our report and added that all pilots had commented on the distraction. The worst problem will be night games at the stadium when the weather is instrument meteorological conditions and instrument approaches are in effect at sjc or nuq. The condition may create a problem of flicker vertigo for pilots.
output: B737 captain reports being distracted by the new stadium display during a night visual approach to runway 30l at sjc.

input: The following rpt had been filed with the federal aviation administration general aviation district office jacksonville; flight level to mr ab; inspector: after an instrument flight rules letdown to bunnell-flagler county; flight level an unctled airport i was on final approach to runway(s) 06 when i observed a man on a bicycle riding on a closed runway(s) 17/35 (which is also a txwy) that crosses runway(s) 06 about 1500' from the end of runway(s) 06. I was about the point of flaring for landing when i first observed movement on the closed taxiway and could see that a collision would occur about the time i would t/d. I added power and slowed the aircraft and held it in the air second officer as not to hit the man on the bicycle and landed beyond him. I rpted the incident to mr weather airport manager he had given permission to my yz to ride the bicycle on the closed runway(s) but not the active runway(s) mr yz admits to having a pilot's license; but refuses to give me his qualifications or pilot number. I feel that both the airport manager and the bike rider have learned a lesson; but this incident would not have occurred intermediate fix the airport manager was doing his job and managing the airport for aviation uses only.
output: Sma pilot on landing approach had to avoid bicycle rider.

input: Established at cruise altitude of fl330 approximately abeam zzz on an overwater segment; the lead flight attendant rpted an acrid burning odor in the forward galley. I then had the odor confirmed by another flight attendant and the first officer we ran the quick reference handbook for smoke or fumes. Determined zzz was the nearest suitable airport for diversion and diverted direct to zzz. Declared emergency en route to zzz. Maintained 250+ knot(s) until 15 nautical mile from airfield. After clearing the runway(s) in zzz; the aircraft was inspected by the crash crew. Crash cleared the aircraft second officer we proceeded to the gate and offloaded passenber i then turned the aircraft over to maintenance and crash crew.
output: Md88 flight crew reports acrid burning smell in the forward galley and after complying with quick reference handbook procedures; diverts to nearest suitable arpt.

input: While flying on nat track u; #3 engine compressor stalled at fl330. It was possibly caused from turbulence encountered. We were in light turbulence and got a couple good jolts and then it stalled. The first officer began descent out of fl330 and turned 90 degrees north away from the track. Capt (pnf) and second officer completed the engine failure chklist while first officer (pf) broadcast mayday on gander oceanic. Second officer and i saw nothing obvious wrong with the engine and attempted a restart. First officer (pf) turned parallel to the track 25 mile offset and leveled at fl280. Second officer broadcast on very high frequency position after engine restarted; we called gander and were reclred on track u at fl290. We called dispatch on high frequency phone patch through stockholm radio and got confirmation to continue to frankfurt. High frequency phone patch was poor. Maintenance was also notified. Supplemental information from acn 404549: engine #3 compressor stalled and was shut down. Pilot flying (fo) broadcast mayday on gander oceanic high frequency frequency only real problem was horrible communicationss with gander oceanic on high frequency radio; as dawn was approaching communicationss were 2 by 2 on high frequency and messages had to be repeated several times. I passed several broadcasts on very high frequency to let other aircraft on nat tracks know our situation position and where turbulence was encountered.
output: A dc10 leaves north atlantic track u and altitude when #3 engine suffers a compressor stall and is shut down.

input: Lead flight attendant did not relock cockpit door after entry. Following her exit; passenber mistakenly opened cockpit door. Relocked door and briefed flight attendant about locking door. This problem is caused by manufacturer's design of a320 cockpit door lock. Unlike other transport aircraft this door does not always remain locked; and must be relocked after entry via key.
output: A320 aircraft in cruise; flight attendant came to cockpit and when departing forgot to relock the cockpit door. Later; a passenber opened the cockpit door; no doubt looking for the restroom. Flight crew locked door.

input: Aural altitude alert did not function. Autopilot; flight director; mode control panel and autothrottles all worked well. I forgot that aural altitude alert is required for rvsm airspace. This was the first revenue flight for this aircraft. I assumed that this was the normal configuration for this aircraft. We had reviewed differences prior to departure in the quick reference handbook so that should have given me heads up that it was not correct.in the future when something is not ordinary; check the ddg (dispatch deviations guide). This would have prompted note to maintenance and write up of aircraft in this circumstance.
output: B747 captain reported that an aircraft was operated in rvsm airspace without a required component.

input: After landing at mco on runway(s) 35 and clearing at taxiway h3; during taxi the 'apu fire' warning activated. The chklist memory items were executed and fire bottles discharged. Neither air traffic control air carrier ramp tower nor other aircraft rpted signs of fire. Maintenance confirmed no fire or smoke upon inspection. The passenber were deplaned normally at the gate.
output: A canadair cl65 on taxi in to gate experienced an auxiliary power unity fire warning requiring fire bottle discharge caused by a false warning.

input: I read back clearance to cross snrkl at 12000 feet/foot at that time; i switched frequencies to company operations(s) to order a wheelchair for a passenber upon returning back to approach frequency i noticed 10000 feet/foot set on the mode control panel capt told me we were cleared to lax from snrkl via the mitts one arrival, arrive as we descended past snrkl from 12000 feet/foot i rpted leaving 12000 feet/foot for 10000 feet/foot at 11000 feet/foot we got a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning 'clb; climb now' sounded. We looked at the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii display and saw traffic at our altitude on our nose. We never had a visual on it. We immediately stopped the descent until we were clear of conflict. That evening we were given 2 arrs and 4 runway(s) changes inside of 90 mile from lax -- unacceptable. We called approach control via land line upon landing they said we did nothing wrong. They were 'overloaded' and 'should have put airplanes in holding patterns' longitude before this situation ever developed.
output: B757 crew had poor air traffic control handling on the mitts 1 into lax.

input: In the approach phase we were given information regarding 1 mile visibility and 1;000 ovc for weather snow. Braking action was 5/5/5.approach was stable and on good speed. Anti-ice for engines and wingstab was on.touchdown in the touchdown zone and we had good braking action. We slowed down to taxi speed and were slowed about halfway down the runway.tower stated that we had traffic on final and asked us to either expedite or hurry to the end of the runway which was the taxi way that was briefed and anticipated based on automatic terminal information service report.began applying brakes about 1;000 feet prior to reaching the taxiway located at the end of the runway and were not receiving deceleration. Released and smoothly applied pressure again and then began to feel the slide. At this point i tried to continue controlling the airplane with smooth brake applications and shallow maneuvers to avoid runway and taxiway lights.
output: Emb-505 flight crew reported a runway excursion that resulted in contact with a snow bank after they encountered icy conditions on rollout.

input: Acft #1; an sma x; was cleared for a straight-in landing while 7 mile from runway(s) 29; to call 4 mile final. At 4 mile an sma y approached from the left/right (directions) rear belly-up to aircraft x and passed within 100 feet/foot cutting in front of aircraft x. At this time; the sma y contacted the tower and was cleared to land. When i asked the tower why the sma y had not contacted the tower before entering the air traffic area the answer given was 'he was still with ctr.' the y said he never saw us in sma x. This is the second time this has occurred to me at this airport in the same place and with the same excuse offered by the tower 'he was still with ctr.' the time before; aircraft 2 was an air carrier ltt with 19 people aboard. In each case; the airport was visual meteorological conditions and no reason can be found for the center (zla) to not release the aircraft to the local controller prior to reaching the air traffic area recommendations: 1. Center release aircraft to local controller when the airport is rpted 'in sight' and prior to 5 mile from the airport 2. No more than 1 aircraft allowed on the straight- in final at a time within the ata.
output: Nmac at non approach control tower fac.

input: This report is submitted as evidence of a very poorly managed and extremely bad policy implemented by flight management and maintenance management at [this] airline. Effective june 2012; flight management rescinded the requirement for pilots to check tire pressure gages on the external preflight.february 2013 morning; i began normal preflight duties at the gate on an md-80 aircraft. As i began the external preflight; i observed what appeared to be two; new; nose wheel tires installed on the nose gear. While acutely aware of flight management's directive of; not checking the tire pressure gauges; i decided that since gages were installed on the new tires; the safe and prudent action would be to verify the pressure on the gages. As i approached the tires; i noted that both tires 'looked' exactly the same in size and shape; with no noticeable differences or abnormalities. Upon close inspection i saw the left tire gage indicated a normal 160-psi while the right tire gauge indicated about 60-psi.i was quite surprised and alarmed at the different readings especially in light of the june 2012 directive. I decided to call maintenance personnel out to verify the tire pressures on the new nose tires. When the maintenance technician arrived; i went down to observe his verification of the tire pressures. Upon testing the right nose tire; he stood up and said; 'we have some issues here!' he then proceeded to order two new; nose tires to be installed.in my 13-years of flying the md-80s at [this airline]; this is the 5th occurrence for me of finding a 'flat' tire during external preflight. This is my first report for this type of event; as we have never been encouraged to report this type of problem to flight management; and now they are planning to remove all tire pressure gages from all fleets. This can only be described as a desire by management to strip a safety check away from the pilots operating the aircraft. I believe that five possible aircraft incidents were prevented during my md-80 career by [my] inspecting tire pressure gages on preflight! Surely the federal aviation administration will not approve/allow [my airline] to continue removing tire pressure gages from all aircraft! My personal experience in this matter scares me; in that i cannot believe flight management could demonstrate such a callous disregard for a vitally important safety item for pilots and passengers. I implore you to decide for yourself if [this airline's] policies and procedures are providing required safety margins for the traveling public. Please require tire pressure gauges on all of our aircraft.
output: A first officer expresses his concerns about his air carrier's policy of removing tire pressure gages from all of their aircraft wheel and tire assemblies. He also believes tire pressure gages helped prevent five incidences from occurring; due to low tire pressures that could not be noticed by just looking at the tires.

input: A little after xa00 local time (xh00z) i departed hollister (307) en route for san jose (sjc). After listening to automatic terminal information service at sjc; i made my initial call to norcal approach approximately 8 nautical mile wnw of 307 on 120.1. I was given a transponder code of xxxx and told to identify within a minute(s) the controller came back with 'radar contact' with a position relative to sjc and told me to 'proceed direct to pruneyard 2500 feet/foot for sequencing.' this is the usual clearance when approaching sjc from this location. The pruneyard is a visual flight rules waypoint a few mile sse of sjc. Flying inbound to the pruneyard; i continued to monitor air traffic control but heard no other transmission directed to me. There were several other aircraft on frequency second officer this didn't surprise me. I proceeded towards the pruneyard via the foothills westbound of the runway(s) 30l final approach corridor. I initially climbed to 4500 feet/foot mean sea level but almost immediately started a visual flight rules descent at some point between receiving my last call and arriving over the greater san jose city area; i believe there was a change in controllers sometime before the incident; i heard a call for a cessna (acft #2). I don't remember his n-number or destination but his desired heading was 120 degrees due to the cloud cover; he asked to stay at 3500 feet/foot the controller acknowledged and gave him a heading of 140 degrees after this; i heard a call to his aircraft that included 'tfc 12 o'clock position less than 1 mile type unknown; altitude 3500 ft.' he acknowledged i think that he would turn left/right (directions) almost immediately; i saw a cessna at my 1 o'clock position roughly 200 feet/foot above me. I watched as the cessna flew over me after which it started a turn to the left/right (directions) when at my 7-8 o'clock position at that point; i figured that the 'type unknown' traffic was probably me. In a short amount of time; say 1 or 2 minute(s) i arrived over the pruneyard. I was expecting that at or before my arrival, arrive over the pruneyard i would get a handoff to sjc tower (124.0). When i arrived at the pruneyard; i called norcal approach informing them that i was at the pruneyard. They replied back with something like 'who is at the pruneyard?' i repeated my call sign and was asked to standby. I informed them that i would circle to the south they came back with a new transponder code yyyy and then handed me off to sjc tower where i landed. I accept that under visual flight rules flight rules i ante meridiem responsible to see and avoid. I did notice the other traffic but by that time; it was probably no more than .75 mile away. Given that the cessna was above me and i was already descending i didn't take any additional measures. I believe that the approach controller lost track of me; possibly during a controller handoff the controller did not call out any ta's and seemed surprised when i called up over the pruneyard. Also; the assignment of a new transponder code leads me to believe that he needed to 'get me back into the sys.'
output: Be36 pilot and a cessna had an near midair collision in sjc class east under nct ctl.

input: The coplt was flying and i was pilot not flying we were in cruise at fl200 33 mile sw of nabb; when i heard zid; 'dsnd and cross sargo at 11000 ft' second officer i read back descend and cross sargo at 11000 feet/foot and we started down. Passing fl180; zid asked what our altitude was; and i read back descending through fl180 to cross sargo at 11000 feet/foot center came back and said our last clearance was fl200. I got back on the radio and said; 'i heard and read back cross sargo at 11000 ft.' center said; 'that was for other acft' and he got their readback. I asked intermediate fix he wanted us to climb back up to fl200 and he said; 'no; descend to 17000 ft.' and then he switched us to a new controller i asked intermediate fix he wanted us to call when we got on the ground and he said; 'no; no prob.' we completed the flight i believe there was a miscom on the controller's part. We started down after there was no correction of my readback.
output: C560 altitude deviation near lou.

input: Departed runway(s) 24 at teb on the teb 5 departure at airport boundary; called 'flaps up; autoplt on.' aircraft started to pitch up to 15 degrees at this point. Power was reduced and aircraft continued to climb at a rapid rate. At 1400 feet/foot both pilots attempted manual level off; autoplt disconnected because of high climb rate; aircraft reached 1700 feet/foot before a descent to 1500 feet/foot was established on a heading of 280 degrees controller advised crew of altitude deviation and reason for the 1500 feet/foot level off altitude when asked intermediate fix there was going to be a problem; he responded 'no problem' and cleared us to 6000 feet/foot still on the 280 degree heading. Flight continued to destination with no further problems with the autoplt noticed by the crew.
output: Flt crew deviated from published altitude utilizing autoplt on dep.

input: I am a reserve captain; and was finishing day 5 of a 6 day stretch. I was released to rest at 2150 after completing a flight at 2135. I had not received a prior notification of short call reserve for the following day via phone call or email; and had not confirmed via our automated phone system (i was not legally or contractually required to do so). As per the fars and union instruction; i believed myself to be in rest for 10 hours; after which i expected to be contacted for further assignment on my last day of reserve. This is commensurate with a letter from our vice president of flight operations; stating that 'all pilot reserve activities and schedules are considered 'short-call' and are conducted pursuant to the provisions of 14 crash fire rescue equipment 117.21'. To be eligible for a short call reserve assignment; i am required by federal aviation regulation 117 to receive 10 hours of rest from my previous assignment.i awoke the next morning around 8 ante meridiem to a missed call from scheduling that occurred at 1201 ante meridiem with a voicemail 'confirming me' for a short call reserve period starting at 10 ante meridiem i took this as my notification; but upon further inspection; noticed that i had received a missed assignment. I contacted scheduling and was told that since i did not answer my phone at midnight; during my federal aviation regulation mandated rest period; i was removed from my assignment for the day and would be given the disciplinary mark on my record. I placed this call at 930 ante meridiem and reminded the scheduler that i was still available and had not yet missed any assignment. They stated that the missed assignment would remain on my record and only the chief pilot could remove it.i contacted the chief pilot immediately after. I explained the situation and was told that the union and company were actively discussing the disagreement; that i was not the only one who was in this situation; and that the missed assignment would remain until it was sorted out via the normal grievance process or other negotiations. He said several other pilots had recently been terminated for similar issues; and were being told by the company to 'grieve it into the street'. The implication was that; even if the company was in the wrong; pilots would face the difficult choice of breaking an federal aviation regulation or being terminated and trust that the grievance process would restore their jobs.this incident is an example of a pattern of recent behavior by the company towards its reserve pilots regarding federal aviation regulation 117. After failing to reach a negotiated settlement to bring our contract in line with the federal aviation regulation update that occurred over a year and a half ago; the company decided to unilaterally change its interpretation of our existing contract and enact new rules regarding how we were to be confirmed for future assignments. This has led to mass confusion on the part of schedulers; pilots; and managers. Different schedulers interpret the rules in different ways; leading some to believe pilots are all long call reserve until converted to short call; while others believe all pilots to be on perpetual short call reserve. Any disagreement with a scheduler's interpretation by a pilot will generally lead to a threat of punitive action in the form of a missed assignment. This occurrence was an example of a scheduler not understanding that i was in rest and unable to legally answer my phone; and then managers being unable or unwilling to remove this disciplinary mark on my record due to company/union politics. This is a dangerous environment for pilots and passengers. Pilots are unsure as to how fars are being interpreted by the company via the individual scheduler calling them; and management is attempting to intimidate pilots into complying with illegal assignments or scheduling practices by threatening and enforcing disciplinary actions when pilots attempt to follow fars (some of which may have been accepted by the company a week or two before). This uncertain and hostile environment leads to pilots either flying tired or illegally; or facing termination from employment for following fars. It is an unsafe environment and unbecoming a part 121 air carrier.
output: An air carrier reserve captain reports receiving a missed call from scheduling after going into a federal aviation regulation 117.21 mandated ten hour rest period. The company disagrees with the pilot union on how this federal aviation regulation should be interpreted.

input: Was given late descent clearance into eidw on osgar 1l arrival requiring a high rate of descent was given altimeter setting of 1023mb. First officer (fo) reconfirmed and was given 1032mb. Continued shortened arrival for instrument landing system runway 28. Encountered visual meteorological conditions at 2;000 feet. Runway contact at 1;500 feet. Noticed several unusual lights on runway that resembled vehicle tail lights. First officer asked tower if any vehicles on runway and response was no. Continued approach; at 1;000 feet captain inquired if any vehicles were on runway. Tower said that there had been pilot reports of unusual lighting around taxiways e3 and r4 but no vehicles on runway. Continued to normal landing. On roll out first officer noticed 'distracting' lights coming from runway abeam taxiways e3 and e4. We exited runway at taxiway e6 with normal taxi to gate.
output: A b757 flight crew reported noticing unusual and distracting lights during their approach to runway 28 at eidw.

input: Unable to lower landing gear either normally (hyd) or manually. The weather was not a problem and sufficient fuel (time) was on board to try different solutions. Landing was made with gear up; no fire after landing all paxs and crew deplaned in an orderly manner. Cause of malfunction is not known at this time; however; suspect hydraulic pressure in the gear up position at all times.
output: Acr lgt gear up landing at ord. Flight crew unable to extend by normal or alternate proc.

input: Atc had issued a climb to fl220. Out of 21500 got traffic advisory at about 21800 got descend resolution advisory  first officer; who was flying; followed descend resolution advisory  i advised air traffic control of resolution advisory and was told traffic was level at fl230. Got clear of conflict command at 21500. Returned to fl220. We were instrument meteorological conditions the whole time and never saw traffic. Only 1000 feet vertical separation and aircraft was climbing at a high rate.
output: B757-200 flight crew responded appropriately to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system ra.

input: We operated an a320 flight to ont. Upon our arrival, arrive at gate it became immediately apparent that the jetway was not operating properly. The jetway was able to move in all directions except forward. Several gate agents and a gate supervisor tried numerous times to move the jetway forward; but were unsuccessful. They then requested a jetway technician for assistance. During this time; i made the necessary public address announcements and made numerous attempts to contact ont operations(s) to see intermediate fix it was possible to relocate the aircraft to next gate. It was my intention to move the aircraft in order to facilitate a more expedient off-loading of the passenber unfortunately; i was never able to contact the operations(s) agent; as he was occupied on the ramp; off-loading bags. Approximately 10 minute(s) after our arrival, arrive the jetway technician arrived and began the necessary repairs to the broken jetway. During this time; with the jetway positioned approximately 10 feet/foot away from the aircraft i observed an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring message that we were being refueled. I immediately began several attempts to contact ont operations(s) to stop the refueling process because all of the aircraft doors were still closed and the jetway was still positioned away from the aircraft once again; my attempts to contact ont operations(s) were unsuccessful because the operations(s) agent was still on the ramp. Having no other recourse; i opened my flight deck window and yelled to the gate agents that were still in the jetway; to tell the aircraft fueler to stop refueling the airplane. Additionally; i asked the gate agents to tell the operations(s) agent to return to the operations(s) office; second officer that we may contact him via the radio. After establishing radio contact with the operations(s) agent and requesting that the refueling process be stopped; i was informed that the refueling process had already been completed. I explained to him that the refueling process should never have started because the aircraft doors had not been opened. Furthermore; i attempted to explain why operations(s) personnel should remain in operations(s) in a situation such as this; second officer that necessary communications can occur. His reply was that he was working with a skeleton crew and that he was required to assist in the various ramp functions in order to turn the aircraft this; in my opinion; is unacceptable. I believe that the gravity of this event completely escaped him. His sole interest; as well as all personnel in ont; seemed to be to turn the aircraft as quickly as possible. In summary; i believe that this event could have been avoided; or at least minimized; intermediate fix ont operations(s) had been appropriately staffed and had maintained personnel in the operations(s) office during our irregular operations(s) during such an occurrence as this; communications is paramount. Additionally; i believe that some education; or re-education; is required for our station personnel and contract vendors regarding refueling procedures with respect to door position and egress.
output: An a320 pilot in command tells of illegal ground refueling procedure while his aircraft is at the gate but unable to exit the passenber because of an inoperable jetway and no station personnel to talk to at ont.

input: We landed in bis on runway(s) 13 as the tower was closing for the night. We exited the runway(s) with a right turn onto taxiway d; followed by a right turn onto taxiway celsius we were both unfamiliar with the airport and had the airport diagram in front of us. The diagram appeared to show that i could make a left turn onto c4; then a right turn at either of two places onto the ramp. My intent was to take the first right turn off c4 onto the terminal ramp. However; after making the left turn onto c4 we realized that the txwys from c4 to the ramp were only vehicle service roads. C4 was not wide enough to make a u-turn; second officer we called operations and requested a tug to push us back onto taxiway celsius once this was accomplished; we taxied to the gate. First; my acr's airport directory was less than helpful in our preflight planning. The airport directory says that the terminal is located on the east side of the airport when in fact it is on the west side. Second; both 'txwys' depicted on the airport diagram connecting c4 to the terminal ramp are not aircraft txwys. The first officer had only been to bis once before; and i had never been. Given our unfamiliarity and the nighttime blowing snow cover; we did not realize our mistake until we had already turned down the wrong taxiway update the airport directory with accurate information! Also; adding a note to the airport diagram page to indicate which pavement is service road and not for commercial acft.
output: At bis a medium large transport jet pilot taxied onto narrow taxiway abeam c4 because the commercial airport chart indicated a taxiway with dimensions similar to c.

input: Apching rogers; ak; from the north we saw the airport visually at approximately 15 mile we called the airport in sight and were cleared for a visual approach we remained in contact with razorback on approach frequency and with our discrete code. The controller informed us of traffic also approaching rogers ahead and to the left/right (directions) of us at a lower altitude his instructions were to increase our speed on final to position ourselves ahead of the other traffic closer in; the other traffic (who was also on the same razorback approach freq) said he had us in sight above him. We also had him displayed on our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii equipment before we passed him; my coplt said he saw him. I altered my descent profile to maintain 500-600 feet/foot separation vertically above him until our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii display showed him behind us. I then initiated a normal descent to the runway(s) the controller continued to transmit advisories to both of us. When on the short final (approx 2 mi); the controller advised us to change transponder codes and contact advisory frequency i believe i was both complying with the controller's advisories for sequencing and separation and using traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and visual sightings to maintain a safe distance from the other traffic the pilot of the other aircraft complained to me on the ground that i had come too close to him after we passed him. I tried to point out the facts to him. I thought i had used all the information at my disposal to apply safe sequencing actions. Primarily; i believe this situation occurred because of a lack of situational awareness on the part of the other pilot secondarily; perhaps it would have been helpful intermediate fix the approach controller had also given a speed advisory to the other aircraft supplemental information from acn 537839: we maintained a safe distance from the c172 until we passed him. On the ground the other pilot of the c172 came up to us and stated he didn't like the stunt we pulled. We told him what we were advised to do. He then stated the controller is going to take a hit on this one then. I was shocked that he was upset about this. I felt the c172 had understood we would be passing him overhead. With approach control working both of us; we felt this would cause no alarm.
output: A c172 pilot gets upset with the air traffic control procedure used during the approach of a c750 jet that descended through his altitude during visual approachs to rog; ar.

input: The rotating beacon at the sulphur springs municipal airport has been inoperative for several weeks the light shines; but the beacon does not rotate. Last summer; it was also similarly inoperative for several weeks as were the runway(s) lights inoperative for several weeks it seems the city of sulphur springs may not be placing as high a priority as they should in seeing that the beacon stays operational. Be advised this is not an old; worn-out beacon nor is it one of the small; almost useless types. The city should give top priority to seeing that the beacon is kept in good working order at all times. Intermediate fix it 'goes down;' get it fixed immediately! We are very fortunate to have a large airport beacon. Even with the sophisticated; electronic navaids that are available to most pilots today; a night visual aid can be of significant importance. As a pilot i can speak from experience. I ante meridiem enclosing a copy of an article which i believe greatly exemplifies what i'm talking about. Finally; the beacon should be relocated back to its original site on the airport which is several feet higher in elevation than its present location. Every feet/foot of elevation helps in the distance that the beacon is visible. The current beacon was installed at the present location a few yrs ago when a new runway(s) was constructed and new lights installed. The old beacon was moved to the mt pleasant municipal airport no one has ever been found that will accept responsibility for not having the new beacon installed on the site of the old one. I have enclosed a copy of an airport layout which shows the present position of the beacon as well as the original location. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he has not talked to anyone at the airport this time because all he got was a run around last summer when he tried to get some action. The airport manager is an employee of the city. He rpts to the city and has no power beyond that. Last summer the beacon was out for about 3 weeks this time is almost a month already with no action. The old site of the beacon is about 10 feet/foot higher than its present position analyst referred him to the federal aviation administration hotline for further action on his part.
output: Rptr concern regarding malfunction of airport beacon at non tower arpt.

input: I was instructed by the controller in charge (there was no flm on duty) to relieve the radar north (rn) controller; as he wanted leave and it was to be approved. As i plugged in to monitor the position; i could see that there was moderate traffic with a little complexity. Both radar sectors that were open were running arrivals to intersecting runways; as well as some arrivals to other satellite airports. The controller working rn seemed overwhelmed and confused. I observed the rn controller gave a be36 a heading to avoid a tbm8; who was on vectors to runway 28. At this point; i assumed that the rn controller had given adequate vectors to both the be36 and the tbm8 to ensure some sort of separation (lateral; passing/diverging courses; etc.); so i initiated a relief briefing. The briefing was convoluted; but i felt it was best to go ahead and get the controller off position; as there was nothing more that he could do that would be productive. Upon relieving the rn controller; i proceeded to clean up the sector. As the relieved controller was doing his 2 minute overlap; he said 'watch those two guys;' pointing to the be36 and the tbm8. At this point; the tbm8 was level at 5;000 feet/foot and the be36 was climbing through 5;800 feet/foot +/- 100 feet/foot i am not sure if there was 3 miles lateral separation or not at this point; but there was certainly not 1;000 feet/foot vertical between the aircraft at that time. Within seconds of him pointing out the possible conflict; vertical separation was achieved anyway. There was nothing i could have done to alter the situation; as other matters in the sector were far more pressing and no action i could have taken would have expedited/maintained separation. As such; i took no action and chose to let the situation resolve itself without causing unneeded alarm to the pilots.i have several opinions/ideas; reference this scenario: 1. The controller that i relieved is unsafe. I don't say this lightly; as this sort of poor sector management and panic is commonplace when he works traffic. As he is only 4 or 5 months from mandatory retirement; i doubt that any recurrent training or skill enhancement would be productive. However; his experience could be useful in administrative duties. I am sure he would probably be relieved to be off the boards; and our staffing is such that it would not be difficult for management to make this happen. 2. Increase the number of flms in the building from 3 to 4. Often; cics seem unwilling to give their co-workers/friends orders concerning how they work traffic. I believe this could have been a contributing factor in this scenario; as the controller in charge knew that the rn controller was having difficulty working; but was reluctant to tell him what to do. Having more flms would reduce the number of times when cics have to run the shift and monitor the operation. 3. Don't pressure the relieving controller to take a position that is not 'cleaned up.' it would be helpful if our local management would encourage this. Often; we are pressured to relieve weaker/overwhelmed controllers because they cannot keep up with what is going on. Rather; it should be that people help the weaker controllers to get their sector under control first; and then once things are resolved; the relief briefing can take place. This would be a much safer method; as well as one which would probably help to build up the skills of controllers who need skill development.
output: Tracon controller described a probable loss of separation event when trying to relieve a controller who was overwhelmed; the reporter suggesting increased flm coverage and delaying position take overs during these conditions.

input: "taxiing into the gate; the visual docking system was reading stop"" but the marshallers were continuing to wave us in. Stopped and called operations(s) who said they were looking into it. Marshallers continued to wave us in. Had to call operations(s) again; who said they weren't sure if it was working. We advised them to turn the system off so we were not receiving conflicting information; and after several minutes of all the marshallers trying to wave us in; one of them finally went over and reset/turned off the system. We discussed the situation; and being good daylight visibility; taxied in using the marshallers only. This is not the first time i've had conflicting information between ground crew and the system; usually with the display advising ""stop"". I am not seattle based so don't see the system every day but i have used it fairly often; and i think we are just setting ourselves up for potential issues if we get in the habit of not trusting or ignoring the system sometimes and relying on it other times. The system should either be working and used or completely off when we're relying on marshallers."""
output: During taxi into the gate; airline pilot reported receiving conflicting directions from the marshaller and the automated docking system.

input: Due to heavy volume going into zzz and air traffic control turning the airport take-off/landing configuration; all aircraft landing there were told to expect holding. Everyone was getting a hold at the zzz vor and dme (co-located) i was entering that hold as per the standard terminal arrival route in the flight management system i was having difficulties getting the flight management system to take the information. Suddenly; the flight management system gave an unusual message in the scratchpad and then blanked out completely. We were then assigned to hold at zzzzz intersection on the standard terminal arrival route the flight management system had returned to its normal condition and i proceeded to enter the hold. As we were entering the hold we were constantly given descents. I announced to air traffic control that we were entering the hold. She responded worth another descent. Then another controller came on the frequency and told us to tighten up the turns in the hold and that our pattern was too large. We checked the flight management system for any errors and found none. We did notice that the autopilot was performing half-bank turns. There was no notification on the flight mode annunciator on the pfd that this mode was active. We responded to air traffic control that we would fix the problem. Again; we went through the default settings to see if there was some reason why this was happening. Then we were given a heading by air traffic control and vectored to rejoin the arrival. The flight continued without incident. Upon landing as i checked the flight information; i noticed that it looked as if the flight management system had timed out; saying the flight was only 46 minutes long; which was incorrect. But; we surmised that 46 minutes ago was about the time the flight management system had initially timed out.the only explanation i have for why the autopilot was flying the holding pattern the way it was is due to the strange occurrence when the flight management system gave me the error message and blacked out. We checked and double checked the flight management system programming. We scoured the approach plate making sure we didn't program the hold incorrectly. We rechecked the flight management system settings for any anomalies that could have been set in the defaults. And we could simply find no reason whatsoever to explain the strange actions of the autopilot and fms.
output: Cl-350 flight crew reported that the autopilot was flying a holding pattern in an irregular pattern when it got an error message and blacked out.

input: I was vectoring several aircraft to airport in particular; the dc10 was coming in from over the mountains to the east of anc. I had no reason to doubt the reliability of my radar presentation; second officer i descended the dc10 to 7000 feet/foot as he appeared to be within that minimum vector altitude area. I further vectored him to follow the dh8 that appeared to be on a dogleg final to runway(s) 06r; using close to minimum separation. The dc10 never saw the dh8. When my colleague and i remarked that the headings of the aircraft looked wrong; we discovered that the azimuth of the radar -- not the missed approach point presentation -- was off by about 30 degs! Maintenance was doing something to the radar and we knew nothing of it. For several minute(s) i had no primary targets; no background video; and no way to ascertain where my aircraft actually were. At that point; i had 5 aircraft on the scope in my sector. I do not know intermediate fix the dc10 was descended below the minimum vector altitude or intermediate fix i had placed him in unsafe proximitypa to the dh8. When we got after maintenance they corrected it; but they were trying to downplay the impact; saying that it should only have been one sweep! It was totally irresponsible for them to be tinkering with the radar without anything being said to air traffic control and worse that they tried to cover it up. It is also important to note that dc10 was in the clouds for nearly all of his dscnt.
output: Apch controller vectoring a dc10 inbound over the mountains and descending him to the minimum vector altitude to follow a dch8; discovered that the azimuth on his radar was 30 degrees off. Maintenance was doing some uncoord fine tuning of the radar and rptr concerned he may have put the dc10 too close to terrain and the dhc8.

input: On this flight; while level at fl270; we experienced a dual pack shutdown and as a result; declared an emergency in order to start a expedited descent to a lower altitude. At the time the packs shut down we had just finished deviating around rain showers; had just broken out into the clear and were in the process of securing the anti-ice system. Prior to the packs shutting down we had been in icing conditions with the complete anti-ice system turned on. The system had been turned on prior to entering the area of precipitation and had been on for at least 20-25 minutes by the time we exited icing conditions and this event occurred. We never had any indications of a problem with the system. After breaking out into the clear i ran the tail de-ice and at some point during the process i noticed the pressurization flow light had illuminated. Still with no indications of any issues with the anti-ice system i initially assumed the flow light had illuminated due to the system switching between the tail and wing; a temporary anomaly. It became obvious after a short period of time that the cabin was continuing to climb and both packs had inexplicably shut down. I immediately asked air traffic control for a descent and then decided to declare an emergency to make sure we got down before the cabin reached 10;000 feet. At approximately 16;000 feet i noticed the left pack had started working again and had the first officer level the aircraft there. A short time later the right pack came back online. I told air traffic control that we were no longer an emergency aircraft and started a gradual climb back up to our cruising altitude of fl300. The cabin never climbed above approximately 7000-7500 feet. I called dispatch on the phone to let them know of our situation and we agreed that since the pressurization system had stabilized and we had enough fuel we would continue to zzz. We landed at zzz with just under 6000 pounds. The aircraft was taken out of service with the cause yet to be determined as i complete this report.
output: A captain reports about a dual air conditioning pack shutdown in flight at fl270; resulting in an emergency descent. The md-82 aircraft had just exited icing conditions with the complete anti-ice system turned on. At approximately 16;000 feet/foot the left and right packs came back online. Aircraft was removed from service after arrival.

input: I took a hand off from pvd on a visual flight rules aircraft landing 5b6. About 30 seconds after i took the hand off the radar system dropped the target which was at 5500 feet/foot  i realized that the aircraft was missing from my radar scope and began to try and locate the call sign. The aircraft was not in my coast/suspend list. I called over to pvd to see if the aircraft had cancelled because there was another aircraft just entering my airspace on a 1200 at 5;500 feet/foot  pvd said no and was not familiar with the aircraft in question. I did not have a beacon code or call sign. The aircraft finally checked in. I had him identify to see if it is the aircraft squawking visual flight rules  there was no identify observed and i immediately called the aircraft 'radar contact lost'. The pilot showed a little concern saying 'what do you want me to do then'. I advised him to maintain visual flight rules to his destination and explained the situation. The aircraft dropped off at fmh 264/028. I finally got him back after about 10 miles of flight. This is an on going issue with this radar. We are now getting into the busier traffic and i fear this may result in an aircraft incident. Recommendation; truly fix this radar so that it works properly. A huge amount of work has been done to the asr-8; including a new beacon system. This has not solved the problem; because everyday a situation like this happens. We mitigate it some by placing the automated radar terminal systems in a radar flash to the maintenance scope; but that is not an efficient way of handling aircraft.
output: K90 controller described losing a visual flight rules target; noting similar situations are commonplace and the facility asr-8 system needs requires attention.

input: While climbing through fl210 to fl220 we noticed the number 2 engine itt (inter turbine temperature) rising. We stopped our climb and asked air traffic control for fl200. While descending to fl200 the right engine vib (vibration) icon appeared. Our flight attendant (flight attendant) called up and asked what was going on; i told him; 'we are working on a problem and will be landing soon. I do not have a time at the moment.' we reduced the thrust to near or at idle. I told air traffic control that we were having engine problems. Air traffic control gave us a lower altitude. Then we received a fwd and aft lav smoke warning messages. We smelled smoke. We decided to switch controls from first officer (first officer) flying to ca (captain) flying. The first officer ran the left/right (directions) engine oil abnormal procedure checklist. It was the only engine indicating and crew alerting system message that was most prevalent at the time; other than the fwd and aft lav smoke messages. We decided to secure the engine first then assess the lav situations. After the engine was secured; the lav smoke messages went away. I told the passengers that we will be landing soon and that we had multiple problems with the aircraft. The first officer did notify the fa's that we would be emergency landing in 10 minutes. We ran the single engine procedures checklist and then the descent checklist and the landing checklist appropriately. The landing was uneventful and we taxied to the gate after crash fire rescue equipment (crash/fire/rescue) checked us out; and deplaned the passengers. I debriefed the crew and then called dispatch; maintenance and our chief pilot.
output: Crj900 flight crew experiences high itt and vibration from the number 2 engine during climb through fl210. The engine is brought to idle and descent is initiated. The foreword and aft lav smoke detectors activate and the engine is shut down. Flight returns to the departure airport for a single engine landing.

input: This is concerning the events of aircraft on the date of jan/tue/07; with the very high frequency #3 antenna found being loose with skin damage; cracking in this location. I became aware of this problem on jan/wed/07. The date of this inspection occurred on jun/wed/04 to checked inspect the very high frequency navigate, navigation mounting location for structural support; to verify whether or not it was in place. This event happened 2.5 yrs ago; and i will try my best to bring back to memory everything that i recall in this event. On jun/wed/04; i was given the inspection job card. I went to the aircraft did the open up; inspected the internal area of the antenna. And at that point made a determination of what i saw. Looking at the inspection job card today in my opinion is straight forward in that it asks to look for 2 possible structure types; to determine which one is installed intermediate fix anything at all. Once again very straight forward in my opinion. On the actual signoff of inspection job card i checkeded off structure was not installed. On the following page item 3a; i checkeded off no for doublers installed. On the very last page (comment page) again i express my views what i'm looking at and write no doublers on outside or inside. As i stated earlier this inspection job card is straight forward and understanding. I have had a number of days to think about this; to recall what has happened and have come to the conclusion that one of 2 things has happened. #1: i didn't understand what the inspection job card was requesting or #2: i entered the information on page 5 in error. I realize that i made a mistake but don't understand why item 3a was checkeded as a no and figure 3 was clrly stating that no doublers was installed and on the comments page again i state no doublers installed inside or outside. Why this did not raise a red flag or concern with whoever reviewed this paperwork in 2004. In ending this; i find it very difficult to accept today that i didn't understand the inspection job card back in jun/xa/04. That this inspection job card signoff was an error on my part.
output: A b737 was discovered to have #3 very high frequency antenna loose with skin damaged and cracked. Special inspection for skin doublers was not accomplished correctly.

input: Our flight of apr/xx/95 was initially cleared by air traffic control on a route overland. The clearance was changed to an overwater utilizing one of the atlantic rtes. Clearance said 'we're going to clear you like yesterday' and gave us the overwater clearance there has been change; and pending change; in the offshore limit for various aircraft recently. I had not flown for a month and after discussing it with my coplt; i decided that our md-88 could exceed 50 mile from shore per changes in policy that had been pending; and which i thought had occurred. I later found the md-88 is still limited to 50 mile offshore. We were sometimes on vectors; sometimes direct; but operating around the atlantic rtes and very likely exceeded 50 mile from shore. Factors contributing to this were: 1) air traffic control clearing us overwater saying the flight had gone that way the day before. 2) pending changes in offshore limit that stayed unresolved for some time. 3) a ton of constant changes and revisions that come in from a great number of various sources. It all begins to get vague with second officer much coming from second officer many sources. Suggestions: act on proposed changes promptly and disseminate results. Ask air traffic control not to clear md-88's down the atlantic rtes. Supplemental information from acn 302167: when we called clearance they asked intermediate fix we were the same crew as the previous day because we would be flying the same routing. They then came back and cleared us on a routing that took us out over the water. The key was when clearance said that it was the same route that the previous crew had flown.
output: Amended clearance route change accepted by flight crew unauthorized overwater operations(s) determined after the flt.

input: On the morning of nov/xa/97; the capt and i departed iad with thunderstorms in the area. After deviating for weather and climbing to our cruising altitude the capt noticed a small fire/glow in his ccs (coms) box. The smell of smoke was filtering through the cockpit; second officer we decided to declare an emergency and land as soon as possible the capt and i evaluated the situation in the cockpit after we both donned our oxygen masks. Air traffic control advised us that we were closer to iad than to phl; with frederick being the closest airport the capt and i agreed that iad was the best choice considering the level of emergency assistance available at iad. As we were en route to iad; we contacted our company to receive assistance. We tried to pull a circuit breaker to eliminate the fire; but it did not work. To eliminate smoke in the cabin; we raised the cabin altitude to our cruising altitude air traffic control vectored us for the instrument landing system runway(s) 19r approach and we landed safely. Emergency vehicles arrived at our aircraft as we were evacing the acft.
output: A ba32 jetstream in cruise declared an emergency and diverted due to a fire in the capt's communications panel.

input: Cleveland center issued descent clearance to 12000 feet/foot level at 12000 we were given frequency change to detroit approach checkeded in with detroit approach called level 12000 feet/foot detroit approach issued descent clearance to 11000 feet/foot with vector heading 040 degree both pilots copied 11000 feet/foot and 11000 was set in autoplt altitude selector. Descent was made to 11000 feet/foot after several minute(s) detroit approach called us; 'confirm altitude clearance 12000 ft'. I responded; 'negative; cleared to 11000'. Detroit approach issued an immediate vector turn for us and an immediate vector for a commuter airliner. Traffic in the area was normal. The radio frequency was not cluttered. Transmissions were not being blocked.
output: Close proximitypa cpr ltt commuter ltt on vectors into dtw.

input: On a training flight instrument flight rules received an instrument flight rules clearance on ground control clearance read: 'clred to port angles airport as filed; climb to 8000' paine 1 departure contact zse 128.5; squawk (?); cleared to taxi to runway(s) 34l a4 intersection contact tower when ready and advised you have ifr.' after student preformed run-up and preflt at a4 intersection student advised the tower he was instrument flight rules read for takeoff at 34r a4 intersection tower advised cleared for takeoff tower was very busy; and after takeoff runway(s) heading student contacted departure upon contacting departure dep asked intermediate fix we were instrument flight rules we said that we were; and had an instrument flight rules clearance departure said that we did not. Tower had not called departure and advised them we were coming. I feel the problem was that tower confused our sma with one that took off before us; vfr.
output: Twr controller failed to hand off instrument flight rules training flight to departure ctlr.

input: On visual approach to runway 17c we were assigned 170kt to 5 miles. We were fully configured when i pushed the speed selector to establish managed mode so the aircraft would slow to approach speed. I noticed when passing through 1;200 ft. That the aircraft was still maintaining 170 kt. I re-selected managed speed; but in the descent with a tailwind the aircraft was still approximately 40 knots fast and we were approaching 500 ft. I knew we would be too fast at 500 ft. So i told the first officer (first officer) we had to go around; said 'go around toga' while advancing the thrust levers to toga (takeoff/go-around). I had experienced a previous go-around about 2 months before where the first officer had set toga and srs (speed reference system) never engaged; so i left the thrust levers in toga for a 3-count; then said 'climb' and selected climb thrust. Air traffic control gave us a 140 heading; and as i started turning i noticed the flight mode annunciator (flight mode annunciator) still displayed 'land'. I was distracted and went through our heading. Air traffic control clarified the assigned heading and we turned back. The first officer restated the altitude assigned was 2;000 ft. I saw we were at about 2;250 ft. And returned to our assigned altitude. I don't believe i heard the original air traffic control assigned altitude because i was trying to make sure the automation was correct before restoring the autopilot; so my expectation was we were going to 3;000 ft. All in all it was a very messy go-around. Primarily; the airplane did not do what i expected it to; resulting in my becoming task saturated and distracted. The initial reason for the go-around was selecting managed mode didn't resulting in the aircraft slowing to approach speed. I could have trapped that error by confirming the blank window and verifying in the flight mode annunciator this alone would have likely resulted in a stabilized approach and a normal landing. A contributing factor was the tailwind. We may have been able to be stabilized at 500 ft. - hard to say for sure. The rest was caused by task saturation when the expected automation did not engage. I still do not understand why because i deliberately advance the thrust levers to toga and left them there for a 3-count. Foqa (flight operational quality assurance) told me the data shows we only went to mct/flx (manual thrust mode). I know where i moved the thrust levers to because i was calm but deliberate in my actions. I made the mistake of not verifying srs in the flight mode annunciator but even if i had looked and it still said 'land'; which it did; i do not know what the procedure is or if one exists except to fly the airplane; which i did. Once corrected by air traffic control on the heading; we returned to our assigned heading and altitude. I do not recall if air traffic control corrected our altitude - we were only off by 250 ft.; still unacceptable; but i believe my first officer advised the altitude deviation. If you were to tell me air traffic control queried our altitude i would believe you - i was attempting to avoid over speeds because the auto throttle did not engage as commanded. The soft go around is supposed to be a calm; slow procedure. When the automation did not do what i expected; we as a crew had a difficult time putting the pieces back together. The decision to go-around was the right one because we were unstable. I believe i did the procedures correctly until i ran out of procedures. I think training on re-establishing automation would be extremely helpful. We fly considerable more visual approaches than instrument procedures; yet the majority of our training focuses on procedures that we have robust standard operating procedure (standard operating procedure) for with back-up support documents. The only guidance provided for a manual go-around without srs engaging the go-around mode assumes a system failure. I have seen this twice now in 2 months; in both cases the thrust levers were advanced to toga; yet go-around phase was not engaged. Training on how to 'put humpty dumpty back together' would significantly reduce the distractions caused by confusion about re-establishing automation. I don't know for sure because i was focused on flying; but when i called 'set speed 210' and 'open climb' i do not believe anything happened with the automation. 'land' was still displayed until we were well into the go around procedure and we were able to re-establish automation by cycling the flight director (flight display) switches; pushing the auto throttle button; and i commanded 'autopilot 1'.
output: A321 captain reported the automation for a go around did not engage; resulting in an altitude and heading deviation.

input: I wanted to maintain instrument flight rules proficiency and hence filed an instrument flight rules flight plan from sac to ont on a cavu day. Prior to approaching the palmdale vor and dme (co-located) i was given the following clearance 'clred to the ontario airport via the cajon 5 arr' by line of sight angeles center on 127.1. Later edw approach was controling the flight just prior to arriving at the palmdale airport on 126.1. Since cajon 5 arrival, arrive indicates the procedure to follow the 104 degree left/right (directions) and shows 10700' minimum enroute altitude (i was at 11000'); i wanted to verify intermediate fix my clearance still was as given to me by line of sight angeles center. I asked edw approach on 125.1 to verify intermediate fix i was cleared to ont via cajon 5 arrival, arrive while still at 11000' and prior to arriving at palmdale vor and dme (co-located) there was a pause; then he said; 'affirmative.' at palmdale i rpted leaving 11000'. Shortly thereafter the flight was handed over to la center on 128.2. By the time communications was established; i was at 10700' (the published minimum enroute altitude for the segment). The controller asked to verify altitude when i replied 10700'; she was unhappy and asked me to climb back to 11000'. Shortly thereafter the flight was handed over to ont approach on 127.25. They cleared the descent and vectored the flight to ont. I discussed the above matter with a member of flight standards district office sacramento office on 6.thu/88. His opinion was that perhaps she did not know the mea's for 'cajon 5 arr;' for intermediate fix it is a published procedure you are expected to follow it. Rptr reiterated that he had contacted an federal aviation administration employee at a flight standards district office and he said that aircraft should descend to the minimum enroute altitude when flying a standard terminal arrival route as the rptr had done in this case. Counseled rptr to be aware of the difference between stars and profile dscnts.
output: Plt thought he was cleared to descend to the mea.

input: Flying inbound on the coyot 1 arrival, arrive at 8000 feet/foot and 250 knot(s) inside brusr intersection about 25 vor and dme (co-located) from phx vor and dme (co-located) approach gave us a 080 degree heading for small aircraft traffic at 1 o'clock position and 7800 feet/foot and climbing in the turn we got a 'dsnd; descend now' resolution advisory commanding a 1500-2000 feet per minute rate. We complied and i called approach to inform them what we were doing. We could see the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii target indicating inside 1 mile and 100 feet/foot separation but never had visual contact with the aircraft at 7300 feet/foot the resolution advisory ended and we received a 'clr of conflict.' i called approach to tell them we were starting a climb back to 8000 feet/foot and returning to course. Immediately after we received a call from approach to turn to a 180 degree heading and climb to 8000 feet/foot approach said there was visual flight rules traffic at 11 o'clock position and 7000 feet/foot and 3 mile while we were complying with this clearance a second resolution advisory sounded 'clb; clb.' the capt spotted this traffic visually and we got the 'clr of conflict.' from looking at the class b airspace chart; it looks like the first conflict was from traffic exiting the terminal control area we depend on approach control to have the radar picture of all the traffic and during a conflict to turn us away from further danger. During the phone conversation while in the blocks at phx with phx terminal radar approach control facility operations(s) supervisor the capt questioned intermediate fix a left/right (directions) turn wouldn't have been a better choice during the first conflict. Supervisor reply was that it was up to the flight crew to make the final decision and overrule an air traffic control clearance intermediate fix needed. We had no time to discuss other options or question approach with the closure rate we were experiencing.
output: Md80 on descent for phx experienced 2 traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii ra's.

input: During our approach into jfk we were being vectored behind an a380 approx. 7 miles ahead of us...we encountered a sudden and abrupt wake turbulence event which rocked our aircraft pretty good...we told air traffic control what happened and asked for extended vectors...approach control sounded irritated about our report of wake turbulence and told us to let him know when we were ready to turn to intercept the approach course to vor and dme (co-located) global positioning system 13r into jfk....after receiving a heading to join the inbound course and cleared for the approach we proceeded to join....we were told by approach control we were showing about a half mile off course when our instruments showed we were on course.....we were told to maintain 3;000 feet and contact tower.....looking at the flight management system i noticed asalt fix was behind us and started to descend to 1;500 feet to cross cri.....after handed off to jfk tower the controller said that approach controller wanted to know why we started our descent early...we noticed we had deviated by about 300 feet below the assigned 3;000 feet....... We stopped the descent and crossed asalt at approx. 2;700 feet and continued the approach on profile......the wake turbulence and the query of air traffic control about our course offset had the crew frustrated and the attitude of the approach controller was somewhat irritated in nature causing us to deviate briefly in altitude during the approach........the approach was completed normally as expected.i believe that after experiencing this type of wake turbulence that air traffic control should review the guidelines regarding separation of aircraft behind heavy airframes generating wake turbulence....especially with regards to an a380........and also air traffic control should be more understanding of situations that flight crews are reporting instead of displaying a defensive attitude.
output: A crj-900 flight crew reported encountering 'sudden and abrupt' wake turbulence in trail of a super a380 on approach to jfk that led to track and altitude deviations. The flight crew stated they sensed some irritation on the part of air traffic control when they asked for more spacing.

input: The outside air temperature at the destination was 33 degrees celsius below zero (negative 33 degrees c). As a crew; we discussed the ramifications that this lower than standard temperature would have on our indicated altitudes at cache intersection on the instrument landing system and our decision altitude that evening flying the instrument landing system 1l approach to fai. Given the temperature at the airport (negative 33 degrees c) we would expect to cross cache (5 vor and dme (co-located) off the 1l instrument landing system at pafa) on the glideslope at an indicated altitude of 2374 feet/foot mean sea level not the charted value of 2047 feet/foot mean sea level the nonstandard; and much colder temperature at the airport would cause the altimeter to read some 327 feet/foot higher when we were on the glideslope at cache intersection than it would read intermediate fix the temperature was international standard atmosphere (isa) at the airport conversely; intermediate fix we flew to an indicated altitude of 2047 feet/foot we would be actually the same 327 feet/foot but lower and closer to the ground than we would be intermediate fix the temperature was international standard atmosphere at the airport as we were being vectored; the approach controller assigned us a final altitude to intercept the localizer of 2200 feet/foot mean sea level it was clear to me that should we descend to 2200 feet/foot mean sea level we would not intercept the glideslope until we were inside cache intersection (5 dme) which serves as the final approach fix for the purpose of verifying our glideslope crossing altitude checked i complied with the clearance descending to 2200 feet/foot mean sea level and we did intercept the glideslope inside of cache intersection we were in and out of instrument meteorological conditions and i had the terrain in the vicinity of the airport in sight. Later on the same night we flew into fai a second time and i asked to intercept the glideslope at 2500 feet/foot mean sea level not the 2200 feet/foot mean sea level we had been issued earlier. The later and second approach worked out much better. I believe in canada vectoring altitudes are compensated for nonstandard temperature and i also believe that vectoring altitudes are compensated for nonstandard temperature by united states military controllers regardless; air traffic control vectoring altitudes should be modified for nonstandard temperatures in the united states. Most of the time it isn't a major issue; however; when the temperature is colder than 30 degrees below zero it takes on greater importance. When it is much colder than standard temperatures flying the same published altitudes or assigned altitudes will result in the aircraft being closer to the gnd.
output: Acr pilot described very low temperature operations(s) at fai and the altitude adjustments necessary; suggesting federal aviation administration adopt procedures to adjust alts.

input: Weather at our destination was 500 feet/foot overcast with heavy rain; winds at 230/20; altimeter 29.36. At approximately 4000 feet/foot in instrument meteorological conditions all anti-ice on approximately 20 miles from the airport and 3 miles from instrument landing system intercept; i the pilot flying; noticed the left throttle would not retard to less than 1.35 epr. I directed the first officer to declare an emergency and consult the quick reference handbook for a procedure. The auxiliary power unity was started. The first officer efficiently completed all tasks. We decided to leave the engine running until landing rollout. Descending through approximately 2000 feet/foot the tower reported a microburst alert with 40 knot(s) gain. Our airspeed increased from 150 knot(s) to 175 knot(s) i initiated an escape maneuver go-around. Tower gave us instructions to climb runway heading to 4000 feet/foot i elected to divert to our nearby alternate where the weather was better. Terminal radar approach control facility gave us vectors for instrument landing system i landed on and upon touchdown had the first officer shutdown the engine with the fuel lever. Because the throttle was stuck forward; the spoilers deployed and then retracted. The first officer then redeployed the spoilers. We taxied clear of the runway and had airfield rescue and fire fighters check us over. We then taxied to the gate.
output: On final approach a md80's left thrust lever was stuck at a mid range epr and would not retard. An emergency was declared but a go-around was executed because of a microburst on short final. The crew proceeded to their alternate and after touchdown secured the engine before taxiing to the gate.

input: While established at cruise; fl340; with smooth ride and air traffic control reporting the same; we encountered a momentary jolt; three quick bumps with no greater intensity than moderate chop. We suspected wake turbulence from a passing aircraft above. It was a surprise to both crew members as the passing aircraft was shown on traffic alert and collision avoidance system as 5;000 feet/foot above our cruising altitude.
