Again this is the 2nd time in two day there has been a dangerous situation due to him.the only recommendation i have is to remove him from the boards until some type of training is complete.
output: Controller in charge reported that another controller operated in an unsafe way by letting an aircraft land when it should have been sent around.

input: I was assigned by detroit approach to climb from 3000 feet/foot to 7000 feet/foot due to severe winds/turb of moderate nature. Was experienced throughout climb clb through the clouds and possibility of icing; combined with turbulence created distraction that light emitting diode me to perceive that i had leveled off at assigned 7000 feet/foot when; in fact; i leveled off at 8000 feet/foot error was one of human performance and my being distraction by checkeding for ice; activating de-ice equipment and still hand flying aircraft in turbulence of moderate to occasional severe nature. I cannot identify any specifics that contributed to this error of human performance. I was well rested and had only flown approximately for 15-20 minute(s) before this dev.
output: C401 pilot levels off 1000 feet/foot high on a departure in bad weather conditions near dtw; mi.

input: This flight was a positioning flight to move the airplane to the maintenance facility where it was to receive its normal annual inspection. There were no known issues with the plane; and the work was expected to be done with little trouble found. After a normal startup; taxi; run-up; and takeoff the engine began misfiring and lost much of its normal power this began when just over the departure fence; and at an altitude of less than 200 feet/foot power was sufficient to maintain level flight in the takeoff confign (10 degrees of flaps); and was continued through departure section of crosswind and downwind section of pattern until approximately abeam the approach end of the runway(s) at which time the engine stopped producing power altogether. The landing glide was short; and required a 90 degree turn at a very low altitude to make the runway(s) the airplane stalled as just as the wings were brought level; but the left/right (directions) wing caught the top of a small bush; causing some damage; and a low speed nose-over. There were no injuries; fire; or property damage. The aircraft was righted; and towed back to its normal tie-down space. The pilot has considerable experience with this aircraft and though the airplane is old; its maintenance record is excellent; and it is considered a reliable plane. During the past week our area has gotten an unusual amount of rain; and i suspect that because of the design of the fuel fill ports; water had collected in the shallow dishes surrounding the caps and contaminated the fuel. Because of the low temperature on the day of this event; the water was probably in the form of ice until the engine had run longitude enough to melt it. The botched landing was due to a combination of things; and could have been avoided intermediate fix the pilot had acted as though the engine would quit immediately instead of counting on a continued production of partial power a straight-ahead landing in a number of pastures surrounding the airstrip was possible; though bringing the plane back safely to its home base seemed a powerful enough incentive to preclude an off-field lndg.
output: C150 loses power shortly after takeoff power fails completely while attempting to complete traffic pattern.

input: After completing deicing; we called ground for taxi clearance. First officer and i both understood 'follow air carrier x on taxiway for runway 17r. We followed another air carrier x until he pulled over to an off gate parking area. We then were able to see beyond the air carrier x and air carrier y inbound on taxiway. Obviously this was not going to work; so i stopped airplane and mid ramp and set parking brake. About this time; ground called and asked 'if we were still with them' so we answered affirmatively. We were told to contact ramp and give a frequency. After being dressed down by ramp control; we were cleared through on taxiway and to contact ground at the normal exit spot. No aircraft clearance or opportunity for aircraft damage ever occurred. Study of possible taxi routes from deice station; told us that most probably another taxiway to runway 17r would be expected. We received the clearance expected; and went on our way. At no time did first officer or myself hear an instruction to contact ramp; or given a frequency. This was my first time on the denver airport. First time deicing on a 737; so my attention was give to those two details. In hindsight; it would make sense to contact ramp; but having been on ground in a departure; i was ready to continue on ground frequency then on to tower.
output: Air carrier is counseled by ramp control regarding taxi procedures with respect to ramp vs. Air traffic control operations; reporter noting unfamiliarity with airport and procedures as causal factors.

input: Aircraft x was level at 110 in a 120 minimum instrument flight rules altitude (mia) en-route to fmn. I didn't realize that aircraft x was below the mia until it was in my airspace for a couple minutes. Zab started the hand off about 10 miles south of my airspace and i believe the aircraft was in a 112 mia when they started the hand off. The mia changes from 112 to 120 at the zdv/zab boundary. Minimum safe altitude warning (msaw) was not flashing and i didn't realize the aircraft was about to enter a 120 mia.aircraft x didn't check on freq until about 1 mile into my airspace. A minute or two later; i realized he was below the mia. I asked if he has good visual with the terrain and if he could maintain his own terrain and obstruction clearance for the next four minutes. The pilot responded affirmative to both. Based on the weather conditions; the aircraft performance; and the proximity to lower mia; i didn't feel it was necessary to climb the aircraft. About 1 minute later; minimum safe altitude warning started flashing. A few minutes later; aircraft x entered a 100 mia.no specific recommendations. I'm curious as to why minimum safe altitude warning didn't alert until the aircraft was halfway through the 120 mia. It was a strong reminder to me not to rely solely on automation. The zab controller and i need to stay diligent in paying close attention to routes of low altitude aircraft in reference to mia's. Zab shouldn't have handed me the aircraft at 110; but i should have recognized it earlier and called them to climb the aircraft.
output: Zdv controller reported receiving an aircraft below the minimum instrument flight rules altitude.

input: Flight was dispatched with minimal reserves for landing in visual flight rules conditions at phl. With 3500 pounds required for visual flight rules reserve the flight departed with 4200 pounds forecast on landing at phl. Throughout the 4 hour flight forecast reserves continued to be 3900 pounds to 4000 pounds at phl; with good weather and no delays forecast. During the last hour of flight and during descent; with forecast winds decreasing; reserves began to drop to 3500 pounds dispatch was kept advised and diversion plans discussed intermediate fix needed; but with good weather still holding at phl; the flight continued to destination. However; with increased fuel burn during approach the flight landed with 3300 pounds with no further incident.
output: Dispatched with only 700 pounds more than federal aviation administration minimum planned at landing modest delays result in a319 landing with less than that required for dispatch.

input: Very simply; the first officer received a departure clearance for the reno 3 departure and loaded the mustang 6 departure in the flight management system during the taxi checked i asked him to brief the departure i believe he stated that we had the reno 3; but he read the departure from the mustang departure i've asked myself how this could happen and how i missed it. The things that i feel contributed to us flying the wrong departure were: 1) we were on day 7 of a busy 8 day tour. We were also on the 5th leg of a very busy day with short turns. Our day had started early and combined with our cumulative fatigue; we were very tired. 2) the electronic charts we use are a continuing source of frustration to me. We now have a mounting bracket on the coplt's side; which puts the unit directly in the sun. The pilot in the left/right (directions) seat has trouble reading it and the pilot in the left/right (directions) can't see it at all. Had i had a chart that i could see; i may have caught this mistake.
output: Be40 flies mustang vice reno standard instrument departure as cleared from rno. Cite difficulties associated with electronic flight bag.

input: On my approved flight student pilot of 150 nm with 3 full stops. Everything was great and was planning on landing runway xx that had been temporarily closed due to crane being up in the air. I was told i had to land on runway xy which posed a 70 degree crosswind at 9 kts. Which is outside my minimums by 1 kt. However; i decided to make approach. Upon touch down; i did not like the position of the plane so i full powered back up and did a touch and go. I then noted i should get fuel and was not sure if the wind would calm back down at zzz. I decided the closest place to land with gas that also had a runway that aligned with the wind was zzz1.although i was not approved for zzz1; i have been there 6+ times sitting in the passenger seat with my good friend's plane. I was familiar with the airport and decided to land there and get fuel; re-collect; and then head back to zzz when the weather calmed down. After re-fuel; i checked weather conditions and they were better. I headed out of zzz1 and back to zzz; when calling into tower; they advised that the automatic terminal information service i received was actually low of what they were reading and their reading on the winds was higher (and outside my minimums) however; the winds were perfectly aligned with the 'closed' runway. I inquired about why the runway was closed and they said it was only for another hour; and it was because a crane 300 feet tall was 3 miles away.i knew that i would be nowhere close to that crane and decided as pilot in command (pilot in command) that the safest option was to land on runway xx regardless that the tower said they could not authorize the landing and that i would be landing at my own risk. Ultimately i made it back with a perfect landing and safe. The increase and change in wind direction was unforecast and after my long flight had changed enough to be outside my minimums.
output: C172 student pilot reported that they elected to land on a closed runway due to unforecast winds that exceeded personal minimums.

input: The student entered the traffic pattern at felts field and apparently did not receive or understand the radio call from the tower telling the student to give way to an aircraft in distress (rough eng). The student then entered the traffic pattern and did not follow another aircraft in the pattern; and proceeded to start his crosswind leg while another aircraft was on his crosswind leg farther up the upwind leg. The student eventually exited the traffic pattern to return to the base of operations(s) felts field tower called the office and informed the instructor of the incident. The problem stemmed from the fact that the student did not understand the instructions given to him by felts field tower to evade and give way to the aircraft in distress. The student cut in front of the aircraft in distress and subsequently put both of them in danger. Intermediate fix a more structured communications vocabulary were established; then it is possible this event would have been unworthy of rpting. The student has been made aware of his actions and is presently undergoing intense communicationss training and is purchasing a scanner to facilitate the learning process.
output: Student pilot of an sma sel training aircraft inadvertently cut in front of an aircraft in distress when entering the traffic pattern after being told to give away to the distressed acft.

input: After selecting gear down; we heard a loud pop. Hydraulic quantity went from full to empty in about 2 seconds. Main accumulator pressure also dropped to zero. Emergency and inboard/outboard brake accumulators remained charged. We went around leaving the gear down and did the abnormal chklists. A no flap landing was made. After clearing the runway(s) port authority/authorized rpted hydraulic fluid leaking from nose wheel well area. We shut down there on taxiway and bussed the passenber in to the terminal.
output: Flc of an ltt went around to evaluate failure of the main hydraulic system on final and then made a no flap lndg.

input: Possibly deviated from assigned altitude reasons for deviation longitude duty day; possible mountain wave caused by strong winds aloft after frontal passage. Distraction by other cockpit duties.
output: Excursion from assigned altitude by crew of an air carrier ltt due to turbulence caused by mountain wave condition.

input: Please see mmsd's 13-1; takeoff and departure section; runway(s) 34 at night. It says 'not applicable.' what does that mean? The situation follows: nw winds at about 12 knot(s) few clouds at 3000 feet/foot visibility 10 statute mile no known limitation on the use of runway(s) 34. Our xoral 1 clearance follows the engine failure procedure for 17 miles. The capt; dispatcher and i agreed that taking off from runway(s) 34 would be the most safe and prudent course of action. Any clarification would be appreciated.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr advised that he had had no response from his company regarding the meaning or intent of the phrase in question. Rptr stated that the flight crew was unable to determine the meaning of the language despite a thorough review of the supporting documentation from the supplier.
output: Md80 flight crew is unable to determine the meaning of the comment 'not applicable' on the mmsd airport page regarding night takeoffs on runway(s) 34.

input: Assigned to jfk finals sector vectoring aircraft for instrument landing system runway 22l and instrument landing system runway 22r. Surface winds were on automatic terminal information service 320@13. On the sector wind readout wind was showing 340@13. This is a quartering tailwind and unacceptable for any runway especially a short runway. A relief briefing was started. I state wind 340 at 13 and say this is not good or acceptable. I was advised that frg airport (under the jfk operation) is using runway 32 (aligned with the wind) and due to numerous visual flight rules aircraft and the frg operation the jfk arrivals were higher than optimal. I assumed the position. Aircraft x is issued a descent from 5000 feet to 4000 feet. Descent is only to 4000 feet because aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) is slow descending to 2000 feet. Aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) is only leaving 3500 feet in its descent. Aircraft x is issued a left turn to a heading of 280 degrees and also issued a descent to 3000 feet. Aircraft x is finally observed descending out of 3900 feet. Conflict alert activates. Traffic is issued to aircraft x for traffic into lga at 4000 feet; aircraft y. Aircraft x advises aircraft y traffic in sight. I tell aircraft x to maintain visual separation. Aircraft x says 'visual aircraft x.'this was going to be an error regardless of who was on the position. That it happened roughly 1 minute after i assumed the position was just my bad luck. The aircraft were not descending optimally because of wind and that there were numerous visual flight rules aircraft under the shelf of the class b airspace and under the jfk operation that we had to keep them a bit high to avoid the visual flight rules traffic. This is the operation the jfk tower wants to be on regardless of the wind. It's the best operation for the tower over aircraft safety. The tower doesn't want to use runways 4l and 4r because it's harder for them to taxi aircraft. In the towers eyes let the approach control fix their ground control problems in the air. The tower says 'the users' prefer this operation or 'the customers and command center' want this operation. Why are the 'users' or 'customers' telling the tower what runway they want? When an aircraft rolls off the end of the runway (it may happen with these bad tailwind landings) are the 'users' or 'customers' going to accept responsibility or is it the controller that will hang for it. The controller will be left to hang!also an issue is the airspace design. Lga arrivals are above the jfk instrument landing system runway 22l and 22r approaches at 4000 feet. They should be above the approaches at 5000 feet. This allows jfk to keep the arrivals at 2000 feet and 4000 feet. This keeps the aircraft at the class b altitude not under it (the class b is at 3000 feet northeast of jfk). Lga arrivals are above the jfk instrument landing system 22l and 22r approaches at 4000 feet. They should be above the approaches at 5000 feet. This allows jfk to keep the arrivals at 2000 feet and 4000 feet. This keeps the aircraft at the class b altitude not under it (the class b is at 3000 feet north east of jfk). Also the class b airspace northeast of jfk needs to be lowered from 3000 feet to 1500 feet. Jfk lands runway 22l and 22r very often. It is amazing that helicopter and light fixed wing traffic can legally be at 2500 feet and fly above or below aircraft into jfk legally and not even be talking to air traffic control the volume of traffic into jfk makes it necessary to use 2000 feet and 3000 feet to maintain separation with the arrivals but we also have to dodge visual flight rules traffic that we are not talking to. Again it's only a matter of time before there is an accident. Also if the jfk operation could stay at 3000 feet and 4000 feet on the 22l and 22r operation it is much better noise abatement for the communities that are under the jfk 22l/r operation. The biggest problem is jfk tower making us use runways with tailwind operations. It amazes me the pilots don't complain but only when we tell them the wind; then they start to complain. But that still doesn't help.
output: N90 controller vectored an aircraft for spacing on the final approach course into the path of an aircraft in the adjacent sector.

input: The b737 was cleared to 6000 feet/foot to avoid conflict with the pa32 at 6500 feet/foot the pa32 mode celsius was showing 6300 feet/foot but the altitude was confirmed. The b737 got an resolution advisory from traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and climbed through the altitude of the pa32.
output: With issued traffic by bhm; b737 executes a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii climb that conflicts with visual flight rules pa32.

input: Arriving on the visual [approach]; configured gear down and flaps 20 degrees-all normal. I called for flaps 30 and the first officer advised me that the left flap indicator showed 30 and the right flap indicator showed 20. I considered continuing the approach and landing; since although i felt the asymmetry; i didn't think it would prevent a safe landing. Being new to the 757/767 fleet and my first officer having been on it for 3 years; i quickly considered a go-around to solve the problem; based on: having excellent weather conditions; and having 2 hours of fuel on board. I called for a go-around; asked the first officer to advise the tower. We executed a go-around and i instinctively called for flaps 20. My first officer asked if i was sure and i realized better to deal with the known than the unknown. I said no leave 30; then asked for gear up and of course immediately realized the error; as the gear warning went off. So we immediately lowered the gear so we could hear each other and be able to think.we executed the go-around first to 3000 ft and then to 5000 ft per air traffic control i tried twice to engage the ap at 3000 ft and again at 5000 ft. It kept engaging for about 10 seconds then it would disengage. I flew the airplane manually. I had a handful as it felt very wing heavy on one side (i can't remember which). I called for the flap asymmetry checklist. We ran the checklist and there was no solution to our problem. We [advised atc] and asked for vectors back to [the runway]. We requested that crash fire rescue equipment be available for our landing; briefed the fas; and asked air traffic control to advise dispatch; as we had little time to do anything else. We landed without incident. Crash fire rescue equipment followed us and i had the first officer ask if they noticed anything unusual. Crash fire rescue equipment replied no. I then advised the first officer to tell air traffic control we would taxi to the gate; but have crash fire rescue equipment follow. I asked the first officer to leave the flaps down and we taxied to the gate without any incident. Once at the gate; i made a public address to the passengers. Crash fire rescue equipment came to the aircraft and i asked him what he saw. He said that the flaps did not look the same. He said that one side was extended more than the other.
output: B757 flight crew reported they executed a go-around after noticing a split trailing edge flap condition.

input: The trip was from ot2 to ome via little diomede visual flight rules for sightseeing purposes. The air defense identification zone had been moved east since we had done this same trip previously. We penetrated the air defense identification zone outbnd while talking to flight service station specialist while not realizing it. We made the trip at slow speed second officer as to conserve fuel and not be a high-spd return on radar. Although we informed flight service station specialist of our intentions; no one reminded us of the air defense identification zone or mentioned any problem with our planned trip. Alerting flight service station specialist personnel about this problem and a note on aeronautical charts stating penetration requirements would be helpful.
output: Ga sma unauthorized penetration of foreign airspace and failure to follow air defense identification zone proc.

input: We were on the localizer (back course) runway(s) 11 approach to fresno; ca. I was pilot not flying we had been cleared for the approach to maintain 1800 feet/foot mean sea level until established. We intercepted the localizer and descended to 1500 feet/foot mean sea level as i completed the landing chklist; i looked up to see that the capt had begun descent to the minimum descent altitude at about 6 vor and dme (co-located) before passing 'stack;' the final approach fix i said 'we're low for out here' as we passed about 1100 feet/foot mean sea level he was looking outside as well as inside; and since we were in visual meteorological conditions conditions with good ground contact; i decided he had the runway(s) or airport in sight. I went back to instrument scan and called out '200 feet/foot 100 feet/foot minimums.' i had lost situational awareness; but it really came back at just above minimums how federal aviation regulation we were from the runway(s) i said 'go around!' the capt started a go around just as the tower advised us of a 'low altitude alert.' we flew the published missed approach until instructed to higher altitude (3000 ft) and a turn. During the approach we were flying in and out of rain and light to moderate turbulence during the missed approach we entered moderate rain and instrument meteorological conditions the second approach was uneventful. My lapse in situational awareness was just enough to keep me from backing up the pilot flying at a critical time!
output: Established on course; back course instrument landing system approach pilot flying capt; lost situational awareness and descended to minimum descent altitude much too early. Rptr first officer called for a go around at the same time air traffic control called low altitude alert.

input: Significant freezing rain event the day of this flight led to 1/4 to 1/2 inch clear ice covering the entire aircraft. There was no attempt to de-ice the aircraft prior to the crew arriving for preflight. The engine inlets needed to be de-iced prior to block out so that we could start the engines after block out. This de-icing of the inlets took a considerable amount of time due to the significant accumulation of ice in the bottom of the fan section of both engines. By the time we were able to block out (2h 39min late) and taxi to the remote de-ice pad a; a short distance from our ramp; the de-ice trucks had run out of fluid and trucks needed to also be refueled. Another significant delay ensued. Almost an hour after block out; de-icing began. The entire airplane was de-iced with type i fluid since there was no precipitation falling. Aircraft was fully de-iced and inspected by the de-ice team. We then proceeded to our departure runway and prepared for takeoff. The reason for this safety report became clear as soon as we began the initial climb segment immediately after takeoff. We began shedding ice from the entire fuselage and this shedding continued through 12;000 ft.; approximately 7-10 minutes after takeoff. All four crew members could hear the ice departing the aircraft and felt the airframe vibrations as large chunks of ice tumbled down the length of the fuselage. All four crew members each have 20-30 years of aviation experience; and no one had ever experienced anything like it. In my 30 plus years of heavy transport category aircraft operation i have never experienced this kind of ice shedding event. I believe that the de-ice procedure was completely ineffective for this amount of clear ice that covered the entire aircraft. With that amount ice being shed from the aircraft for that long; we had a significant amount of ice still adhering to the airframe when we took off. The engine vibration was well within limits even during the climb out and so the crew chose to continue the flight. I was concerned about airframe damage from that amount of ice departing the aircraft; and because of that concern; i recorded an aml entry asking that the aircraft be inspected for damage after arrival in zzzz. [cause was] inadequate de-icing for the amount of clear ice that was adhering to the airframe. Also the de-ice crew was possibly unable to see the ice after de-icing; since it was clear ice and fully covering the aircraft; and the airplane was still wet from the de-icing fluid used. [suggest] re-evaluate the process of de-icing when so much clear ice is adhering to the airframe.
output: Air carrier captain reported inadequate deicing procedures resulted in departure with significant airframe icing.

input: After landing a passenger approached the flight attendant asking if he could tell the crew about a possible maintenance issue. The passenger came to the flight deck and said he saw a tool used by maintenance stuck in the area underneath the right flight spoiler; and described the tool. After the description i believed he saw something. I walked around lifted the flight spoiler and spotted a tool used by maintenance; it was a mirror attached to a bright orange handle. I tried to get it out but it was stuck in the position. I returned to the flight deck and notified dispatch of the situation.
output: A crj-900 passenger saw a mechanics tool under a spoiler in flight and notified the crew at the gate.

input: While descending into las on the creso 2 arrival, arrive we picked up a contact on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii at 12 o'clock and 10500 feet/foot at approximately 4 to 5 nautical mile approach control called traffic at 12 o'clock and 4 nautical mile we were in a descent but started to reduce the rate of descent at this time. Shortly thereafter; a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory sounded to climb we stopped the descent visually acquired the traffic an sma; after the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alert and started to climb to comply with the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii we were in a climb when approach control called traffic at 10 o'clock. We visually acquired the 10 o'clock traffic an other air carrier mlg on the radio call from approach i started the aircraft back down and watched the sma y pass down our left/right (directions) side; 1000 feet/foot below and 1/2 nautical mile laterally. No other calls were received from approach control to indicate there was a problem with our actions.
output: Altdev altitude undershot altitude excursion during flight crew response to traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii ra.

input: Prior to the tower opening at xa00 local i had the student taxi to the end of the runway(s) 23 for departure on a local instrument flight rules training flight we called cleveland apch/clrnc for our instrument clearance but got no answer. We tried reaching them several times on 121.85. We made an announcement on the tower frequency 118.5 stating intentions. By the time we realized (xa01 or xa02) we were not receiving any communicationss from approach or tower we returned to the ramp. I called the controller in the control tower to explain the events. He gave me warnings about moving onto active movement areas without 2-way communicationss he explained that i was congesting the frequency with my xmissions and it appeared he was aggravated with the situation i apologized many times and informed him i was aware of the restrs when the tower was open. I explained we did not intentionally try to cause problems and apologized some more. He seemed to settle down by the end of the conversation. There seemed to be no operational conflict.
output: A flight instructor and a student taxied to the runway(s) shortly before the tower opened and attempted to call approach control for an instrument clearance unable to contact anyone on the radio; they taxied back and called the tower on the phone.

input: The issue is concerning a mural painted on a retaining wall at lex; ky. Over the last 2 weeks we have had at least 6 documented comments and/or complaints about this mural. They range from things such as 'nice distraction;' to 'an accident waiting to happen.' lex services air carrier and taxi as well as general aviation the pilots rpt the mural as confusing and an impairment to depth perception. This mural is at the end of runway(s) 22; which is the most used runway(s) with an instrument landing system callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr indicates the subject mural is at the end of a frequently used runway(s) on a retaining wall and has prompted a number of concerns expressed by pilots especially those unfamiliar with the airport the mural is reportedly very 'lifelike' presenting an illusion and distraction the rptr said that one pilot stated that the mural affected his/her depth perception. The rptr indicated that a number of taped comments by flight crews have been forwarded to the airport operator; but to no avail. The rptr stated that in his/her opinion the mural is an 'accident waiting to happen.'
output: Lex controller expressed concern regarding a painted mural of a bridge at the approach end of runway(s) 22 that has promoted a number of complaints by plts.

input: On oct/xa/98; slc approach control changed the specified arrival, arrive altitudes for landing south on the bearr 3 and brigham city 1 arrs. The published stars state to expect to cross bearr at 15000 feet/foot and expect to cross cartr at 16000 feet/foot on oct/xa/98; changes were forced upon zlc requiring swapping the gate altitudes now bearr at 16000 feet/foot and cartr at 15000 feet/foot the stars have been updated many times in the last 13+ months; yet they still state 'expect to cross' at the old altitudes this is an ongoing safety issue as well as breach of procedure i have filed a ucr at my facility and have had zero action taken. Calls to the federal aviation administration administrator hotline yield no results. My first level supervisor has told me he will not go to the facility manager any more because of the almost violent reaction it draws! I spend each session on this sector restating/correcting altitude restrs and verifying altitude restrs to pilots who are looking at a chart expecting to hear one thing and hearing something else. No one (non ctlrs) in the federal aviation administration is willing to acknowledge this is a problem now 13+ months later there is no action in the works to rectify the problem it is only a matter of time until an ever diligent controller misses a bad readback and an aircraft descends to 15000 feet/foot instead of 16000 feet/foot please put forth an effort motivate the federal aviation administration to correct these pubs or procedures callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated that he has to correct on the average of 10% of traffic on the standard terminal arrival route routing with regard to the altitude expected and desired for the crossing fixes involved for the past 14 (now) months since the stars charts have not yet been changed to reflect the new altitude he stated that all controllers spend extra time with each pilot in order to emphasize the new expected altitude which is not yet depicted on the pilot's chars.
output: Artcc radar controller complains that 2 standard terminal arrival route arrival, arrive charts to the slc airport need to be amended to reflect the actual expected crossing altitude for 1 main fix which has been in use for the past 14 months. This has caused the controllers to take extra time to restate the normally used altitude since pilots do not always pick up the change and have prepared their acft's flight management computer for the old depicted alt.

input: My trainee and i had returned from debrief and break after training on the west departure sectors combined (tyson/fluky) and were assigned to train on east departure (krant). While we were gone the east sectors were split; this is not unusual but also not frequent. Another trainee was sitting at the spare scope to the right of krant so i didn't do my normal routine of setting up that scope to watch training on my preferred setting.a departure off of adw sparked a conversation between myself and the trainee on the new pre-coordinated climb between krant and another sector southbound. The conversation grew to involve all controllers working and the supervisor. At some point during the conversation the trainee climbed aircraft x. He was not quick looking the fluky sector whose airspace krant has pre-coordinated climb through as long as no traffic. I scanned the tyson scope which is to the left of krant for traffic (white tags) but with fluky open they would be green. Fluky is too far from krant to see. I didn't notice that the trainee wasn't quick looking fluky. The trainee told me later he had never worked next to tyson with fluky split off. I never observed the conflict with aircraft y.independent of the conflict i noticed he was not quick looking fluky. We went through his preferred setting and quick looked the sectors that i look at and saved the new preset. Soon after fluky asked if we were quick looking him and we said 'we are now.' the operations manager came over and informed us she needed the strip on aircraft x for a possible loss of separation. I should have asked if the trainee had ever worked with fluky split off from tyson. Sometimes there are multiple targets around a satellite airport (gai) where the fluky traffic turns and makes it hard to tell what aircraft are there. A technique used before you climb is to look at tyson for white data tags in the area but if fluky is spit they won't be on tyson.stars (standard terminal automation replacement system) came to pct around six months ago. There have been constant changes/briefings since its implementation. The operations manager asked me if the 'quick look region' was on during the event. I said we were not quick looking fluky; but corrected it and saved the changes. I have become aware in discussion since this event that stars can make airspace that will quick look all planes in a certain area if the function is turned on. I strongly recommend at pct each area identify these quick look regions and make it an 'opt out' function. Presently they are 'opt in' (the controller has to turn it on). These areas should start on and if the controller wants to turn them off they can do so. That would have broken the chain of events in this situation. The reality of the situation is we have been briefed so much we have forgot how to turn on many of the tools. These quick look regions for pct's high volume pre-coordinated airspace areas need to be turned on and force those who don't want to use good techniques to turn them off.
output: Pct controller conducting training did not realize their trainee did not have the radar display setup properly to observe a possible conflicting route from an adjacent sector. The trainee climbed a departure into the path of another departure on the conflicting route.

input: I went into the control room to relieve the rx2 controller at xa00z. I received a position relief briefing and there was nothing out of the ordinary that was given to me. There were a couple of frequency notes given to me with zzz1 [center]; but other than that there was nothing different from normal.all during this time apparently zzz2 [center] was atc-0 and we in area x were never told about this going on. When i came in that evening there was no notice; and no one was told that a zero event was going to be taking place. The controller on rx2 that i relieved was never briefed about zzz2 [center] being atc-0. When i took control of the position i had aircraft x on frequency and he was turning towards zzz [vor]..zzz [airport]. This is the routing that per the letter of agreement we give to zzz2 [center]. The aircraft was level at fl340. After a few minutes i gave the aircraft a crossing restriction to cross zzz [vor] at 100; what we give these aircraft again per the letter of agreement  his route of flight was going to clip airspace x if the aircraft stayed up high before meeting the restriction. I placed a pvd [plan view display] on airspace y that auto-directed to airspace zulu time (utc/gmt) as normal for that time of night. When the aircraft started to descend the point out had still not been accepted; so i called to the sector and got no answer. I tried a few times to no avail. I then tried to call zzz2 [center] airspace x and got no answer from anyone.the controller on the low side rx1 said the shout lines with zzz [approach] were down; maybe the zzz2 [center] lines were down as well. By this time i had hollered for the flm to come down and explain if they knew what was going on; and it was then i was told that zzz2 [center] was atc-0. At this time the aircraft had already entered zzz2 [center] airspace without approval; and my main focus was to handle the aircraft towards zzz [airport] approach. We pulled up the approach plate at zzz [airport] and i told aircraft x to maintain 110 to not enter approach's airspace and gave the aircraft i think xyz.ab to switch over. Not two minutes later; zzz2 [center] comes back up and helps me with necessitating the hand-off. Not at any time was anyone working traffic aware of this issue with zzz2 [center]. After this aircraft handling was done; i called area b controllers and asked if they knew about the zzz2 [center] zero event and they said no that they had not heard anything. Area b also is adjacent to zzz2 [center] airspace.later the flm came back down to let us know the zzz [approach] lines were back up and running. This makes this zero event even more frustrating to us in area a since the routing and altitude that we give zzz2 [center] aircraft going to zzz1 approach requires us to call zzz approach for a point out. So during this zero event; we had no clue that we were actually in it; and then if we did know we would have had to do extra work just to get the procedure to work with zzz approach.another part of this is that the controller on rx1 never knew about this event as well because he had a zzz [airport] departure at fl230 during this time as well; and according to the atc-0 procedures we are to radar identify the aircraft when they come over to us. I cannot be sure that this was done. This aircraft... I don't recall the numbers or where he was headed. Communication is a big deal in what we do. It is highly irresponsible to not be told about something as important as an atc-0 event in the facility. All i needed was to know was who and when and we could have handled this situation the correct way. We have routing for this exact situation; we have the procedures posted in the area; but if no one tells me what is happening then this type of event will continue to happen.
output: Center controller reported an air traffic control zero event at another center facility resulted in communication issues and an airspace violation.

input: Minot air force base approach control does not open until 7:00am central standard time on monday mornings. While we do have a frequency at mot we do not have complete radar coverage until between 25 and 30 miles southeast of the mot vor and dme (co-located) due to an oil boom in north dakota; mot sees a fair amount of traffic early in the morning. A crj-200 requested clearance and was issued one departing mot to msp via federal aviation regulation as filed. I had 2 inbound aircraft to mot that were greater than 60 miles away at the time the clearance was issued. I had descended a cessna 441 down to 11;000 feet mean sea level and when the crj-200 departed mot i climbed him to 10;000 feet. Intending to separate them in radar. Initially i was using altitude separation. I informed the descending c441 that i had departing traffic not within radar; i then radar identified the crj. The crj and the c441 advised they had each other insight. The c441 then said he lost the crj because the aircraft turned off their landing light. Then c441 said he had the crj back in sight as the aircraft had turned their landing light back on. I had the c441 restate they had the crj in sight and then advised the c441 to maintain visual separation from the crj and to descend to 5;000. The c441 read back that he would maintain visual from the crj and 050. I let the crj know the c441 had him in sight and was maintaining visual separation in a descent. I am nearly positive the c441 read back his call sign correctly when reading back the visual separation clearance. But in the back in forth of establishing him having the crj in sight i may have missed it. About the time the c441 passed off the side of the crj; the pilot of the crj advised me they had received an resolution advisory that the c441 had passed a little close to them and they responded with a slight turn off course but were now correcting back to course. I asked the pilot if he needed anything else; he said no. I advised my supervisor of the resolution advisory the pilot did not sound alarmed or upset. Once standard separation was restored i climbed the crj to his flight plan requested altitude. When i applied visual separation i did not issue that 'targets appear likely to merge.' it looked as if the range i was operating on the targets would just pass off each others right sides. After the crj advising me of the resolution advisory i find it would have been prudent to advise the pilots 'targets appear likely to merge' as a precaution. Recommendation; it would be preferred to have minot air force base radar piped into our radar system to make the flow of traffic in and out of mot more efficient when minot air force base radar approach control is closed. I will start applying 'targets appear likely to merge' when i think aircraft will be less than 2 miles apart due to mosaic radar limitations.
output: Zmp controller described a conflict event with aircraft operating to/from mot during the tracon's closure; the reporter noting that having access to mot radar would prevent these types of occurrences.

input: Our landing was very smooth. The aircraft came to a stop after a short taxi and the capt made a public address that was not clear to me except at the end when he said that we would be at the gate in 10 minute(s) flight attendant #4 looked out of a window on the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft and said that emergency equipment was approaching i called the capt to ask what was happening and he said that the airplane was ok; we just needed a tug to pull us out of a snow bank. A few minute(s) later he made another public address that it would be 30 minute(s) before we would be at the gate. When we arrived at the gate; the prepare for arrival, arrive public address was made and a routine deplaning was accomplished.
output: Md80s aircraft slid of taxiway into snow bank. Tug pulled aircraft out and to the gate.

input: Approx 25 nautical mile from las and slightly westbound of the 190 degree radial; we were advised of a visual flight rules parachute-drop aircraft maneuvering at our 12 o'clock position that would pass overhead. The first officer and i acquired the aircraft both visually and on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii at about 5 nautical mile it appeared to be a cessna heading north at 11000 feet/foot to 12000 feet/foot mean sea level we rpted sighting the visual flight rules aircraft and approach cleared us to 8000 feet/foot the controller then asked the visual flight rules pilot to rpt sighting the company b737 (our acft) to his left/right (directions) and emphasized that he was not cleared to release his jumpers; as our aircraft would pass directly beneath his position which was now less than 3 nautical mile off our nose. The visual flight rules pilot replied that he had just kicked the last jumper out the door. I reacted immediately as approach gave us a left/right (directions) turn to 340 degrees and warned us of possible parachute jumpers in our immediately vicinity. I had already pulled the power back and begun descending to 8000 feet/foot when the lower half of my vsi displayed a red arc as the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii issued an aural traffic alert. I stopped descending but maintained a 30 degree left/right (directions) bank making it impossible to see the other aircraft the first officer advised air traffic control that we had the visual flight rules aircraft in sight but had no contact with the jumpers. Within seconds of the traffic advisory we received a 'clb' resolution advisory as the red arc on my vsi extended well into the upper half of the display. The visual flight rules aircraft had apparently begun a spiraling left/right (directions) dive to follow his jumpers; resulting in a high rate of closure as he passed through our altitude at that moment i had no clue as to what rate of turn or descent the other pilot was using. Between the radio xmissions and traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alerts i had not heard anything from my first officer that assured me we would clear the other aircraft second officer i complied with the 'clb advisory. I applied maximum thrust and rotated to go around attitude. The first officer advised air traffic control that we were climbing to avoid the other aircraft 2 of our flight attendants were in the process of securing the cabin and were knocked to the floor during the maneuver; but later stated that they had not suffered any injury. The first officer estimated that the other aircraft passed within 1000 feet/foot horizontally in a nearly inverted attitude with its belly towards us. I have no idea intermediate fix the other pilot was aware of our position or totally focused on trailing his jumpers. We remained busy for the remainder of the flight as air traffic control slowed and vectored us repeatedly in order to fit us back into the sequence for landing on runway(s) 1l. This incident arose as a result of conflicting usage of airspace in the las terminal area; which is limited due to terrain obstacles and the runway(s) confign in use at the time. However; it would not have posed a threat to operational safety had the other pilot complied with the controller's instructions in accordance with the letter of agreement by which he was bound. I can only speculate as to what other factors may have contributed to this pilot's poor decision making. With las arrival, arrive and departure procedures currently in a phase of transition due to problems implementing lateral navigation operations(s) it might be a good time to address the issue of whether or not this drop zone can safely co-exist with such a busy airport however; in fairness to the skydiving operators; prior to this event and throughout my 18+ yrs of operating in and out of las with company; i have never experienced any conflicts with these aircraft supplemental information from acn 564762: operating under air traffic control ta's and federal aviation administration letter of agreement aircraft was unable to drop jumpers under radar service at oc7. Pilot canceled radar service but maintained communications with las terminal radar approach control facility dropped jumpers and proceeded to agreed clb/dscnt box. Was advised by air traffic control of traffic and when i raised wing to look; saw b737 closing on position tightened up turn and increased descent rate. Traffic was then no factor. Improved communications between pilot and controller and earlier notification may have alleviated the problem callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the jump aircraft had been delayed for 30 minute(s) by air traffic control before being allowed to release jumpers second officer radar service was canceled. The release was made under the visual flight rules rules of the letter of agreement after jumpers were released the aircraft proceeded to the approved climb descent area for descent it was here the conflict occurred. The jumpers were approximately 3 mile away.
output: Conflict between an air carrier b737 and a c206 when skydivers are released without coordination near las vegas; nv.

input: This was a routine training flight with my student which was to include an approach into cgi; go missed; and continue to vih for the second half of our flight plan. Zme asked us to get current information from cgi and relay this information back to them. However; what we were not informed from notams or memphis; communications between the cgi tower and zme were out of service since the night before. I informed zme we would like to execute the instrument landing system 10 into cgi; go missed; and continue on our filed flight plan. He told me cgi tower would have to approve that approach which i realized. Zme gave me my clearance to vih even though it was already on file. From there; i was radar vectored for the instrument landing system 10 and then cleared for the approach i was then told to contact the tower and tower cleared me to land. After landing tower told me to taxi clear of active. At this point; i'm starting to realize something was not right. After shutdown; i went to call flight service station specialist but all lines to the outside were out -- even the tower this meant i would not be able to takeoff and continue my flight because it was instrument flight rules and other planes were possibly trying to get in. However; i was able to talk with a commuter plane over the unicom frequency he needed to get in cgi and did not know intermediate fix i had landed or not. He relayed the message back to air traffic control that i had landed safely. He gave tower a clearance void time for me from air traffic control tower wanted me to inform zme; after my departure the commuter airplane had landed safely. We all had to work together as a team to make the situation work. I believe intermediate fix i had known about the communications outage; i would have informed tower i was just going to do a stop and go and continue on my flight i will definitely use this as a learning experience. The rest of the flight went great.
output: Due to a lack of communications for handoff air route traffic control center did not know intermediate fix an sma training aircraft had made a landing at an airport on the filed flight plan.

input: During the taxi out to runway 28r at n5; i noticed how horrible the taxiways have become at ord. Our taxi took us down b to n2 to north to n5 for takeoff on 28r. It was dark and i only had my limited taxi light working. I had so many potholes come up all of a sudden requiring me to brake quickly or try and taxi around them that i was swinging my flight attendants around during their takeoff demo. I even tried to slow to a crawl as i made my way over the constant potholes and poor patch work holes but even then i was banging and bouncing all over the place. These taxiways were easily the worst taxiways i've seen at any airport anywhere in a while. Ord needs to repave or at least repatch up those taxiways to keep us from hitting pot hole after pothole on taxi out. Based on the undulating and bubbled cement on all the taxiways; i think just repaving them would be the best option.
output: B737 captain reported the condition of the taxiways at ord have become poor with multiple potholes and other pavement irregularities.

input: I misread the approach thinking i had to be at or above 11000 feet/foot mean sea level at brand. The approach reads 'cross brand at 11000 ft.' previous points had been to cross at or above.
output: Acr capt misreads standard terminal arrival route and undershoots crossing restr.

input: Departed myf under tower control on runway 28l. Prior to departure; i asked the tower to request flight following for me. Two minutes into climb out the tower passed me over to socal approach. Socal approach immediately indicated i was in class b violation. Why did the tower let me fly into the class b airspace without clearance?
output: Cessna pilot reported that air traffic control did not help him with class bravo clearance when he requested flight following on the ground.

input: The departure and cruise segments of the flight were uneventful. While initiating an initial descent i heard a pop and noticed arcing on the electrical terminals on the window directly in front of me. I brought it to the captain's attention. Almost immediately a torch-like fire occurred at the terminals making a loud hissing sound. Shortly after that; the torch like fire ignited the plastic in the vicinity of the electrical terminals causing a flame. We donned our oxygen masks and started fighting the fire. We transferred controls of the plane while i discharged the fire extinguisher at the fire. The flames ceased; but the arcing occurred again which reignited the fire. I discharged the fire extinguisher a second time and the fire flared up again. At that point we transferred controls back and i increased airspeed to vmo while the captain ran check lists and coordinated an evacuation plan with the flight attendant. I informed air traffic control of our intentions and they pushed us to the tower frequency shortly thereafter. Once we were on short final approach we configured the aircraft and landed without incident. Once on the ground we transferred controls as normal turned onto a taxiway and stopped short of a parallel taxiway and executed the emergency evacuation procedure as planned. Everyone exited the aircraft without injury and met up at the rally point. Since this event involved the window heat; perhaps a maintenance inspection at specific intervals may prevent a recurrence of this event
output: Dash-8 201 flight crew reported a persistent fire caused by arcing at the first officer window terminals.

input: Upon rotation; fo's airspd indicator and altimeter inoperative returned to cle; overwt landing (normal descent rate and lndg). Contacted cle operations(s) they called dispatch. Emergency declared through company. Ran all appropriate chklists.
output: Return and land for a b737 flight crew when the fo's air data computer fails at rotation. Company declared emergency overwt lndg.

input: While climbing to fl410 i noticed cabin climbing in altitude stopped climb with permission from zjx. Cabin altitude was still climbing crew donned oxygen mask and initiated a descent to 10000 feet/foot as a precaution with zjx's blessing and proceeded back to tampa; flight level with no special assistance with no problem all chklist were followed to the letter.
output: Lj25 flight crew suffers pressurization failure. Return to departure arpt.

input: During takeoff controller thought he assigned runway(s) heading crew thought he assigned 310 degrees for hdg.
output: Flc of a beech 1900 airliner be02 were advised on departure that they were assigned runway(s) heading for departure and not the heading to which they had turned.

input: Helicopter enroute to  regional medical center flew into un-forecast light icing conditions at 3500 mean sea level  pilot in command immediately identified light build up of ice on the aircraft windshield and initiated a descent down to 1500 mean sea level with no further incident. Pilot in command contacted flight service station specialist weather briefer once on the ground to obtain updated weather information and pass on information about the icing incident.
output: Helicopter pilot encountered un-forecast icing conditions at 3500 feet/foot descended to 1500 feet/foot which was ice free.

input: Aircraft intercepted a false glideslope twice during an instrument landing system approach to runway 08 at tjsj.
output: B757 flight crew reports capturing a false glide slope during instrument landing system to runway 8 at tjsj in visual meteorological conditions and prior to localizer intercept.

input: I was flying with my student for his private pilot practical examination when the situation occurred. We arrived at the airport early; second officer i decided to go over possible pitfalls that his designated examiner may introduce during the flying portion of the practical examination one of these pitfalls would be an accidental approach into a nearby closed airport 1 mile westbound of zzz is the old zzz airport which is closed. The 2 airports are close together and both have the same runway(s) headings of 18 and 36. I showed my student the closed airport and then turned north to show him another airport he would likely be asked to divert to during the navigate, navigation part of the practical examination i told my nervous student to relax while i flew us there. I took the flight controls and he slid his seat back to relax. I looked out the left/right (directions) window for possible traffic at the new zzz. I was about to announce my nbound departure from the area when suddenly i smelled smoke. My reaction to the smell of smoke in the cockpit was to land immediately. The quickest way to land would be to enter a left/right (directions) base for runway(s) 18 at zzz. I immediately announced my intentions. I then asked my student intermediate fix he smelled the smoke. I got no response from my student. A second later; i heard someone on the frequency say; 'be advised zzz left/right (directions) tfc.' i had been monitoring the zzz frequency and was keeping track of the arpt's traffic in my head. I thought all of the traffic was on the gnd! When i heard 'be advised left/right (directions) tfc;' i thought that i must have heard part of a transmission and maybe someone was in the pattern making left/right (directions) traffic i announced that i was turning left/right (directions) base. No response! I vigilantly began looking for the potential traffic i continued to scan for the traffic unable to see anything; i asked my student intermediate fix he saw any traffic again; i got no response from my student. Once i had the runway(s) made; i looked inside the cockpit to glance at the engine gauges. Should i pull the mixture? Does the smoke smell like an electrical fire or gas? Maybe i should turn off the master switch! I glanced at my student to see why he wasn't reacting to the situation after all; it was his airplane that was potentially on fire. That was when i realized where the smoke was coming from. There; to my left/right (directions) sat my student -- headset around his neck -- smoking a cigarette! This took me by surprise for a couple of reasons: 1) i didn't know my student smoked; 2) i've never seen anyone smoke in an airplane before. I felt amazingly dumb at that particular moment. I looked at the approach end of the runway(s) and noticed 3 confused cessna pilots holding short of runway(s) 18; where i thought they should be; probably wondering why i was making left/right (directions) traffic i believe that this situation occurred because of lack of communications between my student and me. I believe that this situation could have been avoided intermediate fix i had assessed the situation a little longer instead of jumping on my first reaction. I also believe that in the event of an emergency cockpit resource management should be higher on my list of priorities.
output: Instructor pilot makes a precautionary landing after detecting smoke in the cockpit. Source of the smoke was the student pilot smoking a cigarette.

input: Had a master warning tail compartment temperature high light on clbout through 10000' mean sea level accomplished appropriate emergency procedures solved situation; and returned to dfw and made an uneventful overweight landing at 131000 pounds problem was suspected to be a bleed air leak in tail compartment; and post-flt maintenance confirmed that and replaced some ducting clamps and seals. Everything went by the book and no difficulties were encountered. We did declare an emergency and made the landing back at our departure station (dfw).
output: Aft equipment bay overheat due to pneumatic leak on air carrier mlg.

input: All operations were normal; including our clearance to line up and wait on the runway. The captain noted that a vehicle appeared to be in the distance; however it appeared to me that is was very far away and probably on a taxiway past the end of the runway.immediately after taxing onto the runway we were cleared for takeoff; fly heading 220. I made the normal callouts; and after the 80 knot(s) call i looked up and the captain called out abort takeoff. I saw the vehicle approaching; and 1 or 2 seconds later the tower told us to cancel takeoff clearance. The captain recognized that there was in fact a vehicle on the runway and it was driving towards us. As we slowed to a roll the vehicle exited the runway on a high-speed exit roughly 1;000 feet in front of us. The tower controller advised us to exit the runway and contact ground control; and apologized for making the mistake of clearing us for takeoff while a vehicle was inspecting the runway. No further contact with air traffic control was required regarding the event.being more cautious and vocal with air traffic control concerning vehicles potentially on the runway. It would be helpful if inspection vehicles were on tower frequency; or if air traffic control would announce or advise when vehicles will enter onto and off of an active runway.
output: Air carrier flight crew executed a rejected takeoff after seeing a vehicle on the departure runway.

input: I was notified by scheduling that i was junior man to fly a 4 day trip out of base. The scheduler said 2 junior fo's called in sick. She said it was an international destination trip with a deadhead. As i had over 2 hours before i had to leave home; i cleaned up the work i was doing in the garage; came in; packed and showered. Then i went to the computer to checked the flight up to this time; i had assumed the international destination trip was for the following day. As it turned out; it was for that night; and the 2 junior pilots had not called in sick but fatigued. Since it was getting late; i just went to the airport for the trip. I was in coach for deadhead and could not get a nap. I arrived for the international destination flight 30 minute(s) after departure time and didn't have time to prepare for the flight second officer i suggested that the relief pilot and i change places. During my 2 1/2 hour crew break; i tried to nap but was unable due to turbulence when it came time for descent and landing i was having such a hard time staying alert; i once again traded places with the relief pilot and had him situation in the first officer position at landing i had been up for over 24 hours looking back; i should never have accepted this assignment as it was inevitable i would be fatigued by the time we arrived. Using out-of-base pilots to cover back-side-of-the-clock flts is inherently dangerous. I certainly would not want my family on an international flight with a pilot who was on duty for 24 hrs.
output: B777 relief pilot was sent out of base to fly on the back side of the clock because two other pilots had called in fatigued.

input: Tug with bag carts had to dodge between 2 aircraft problem arose because ramp is unctled. Speed of all 3 was too high (a) (b) (c). I will prevent repeat occurrence by reducing taxi speed and not assuming actions of other aircraft and vehicles.
output: 2 air carrier mlgs almost collide with tug hauling baggage carts while approaching their gates in stl. Tug driver steered clear between the 2 aircraft rptr pilot in command states that the ramp is unctled.

input: Upon return of circling maneuvers (period photos) engine began to run rough and vibrate. Engine temperature oil temperature oil pressure displayed no indication of temperature increase or drop. All remained stable; within green indications. Manifold pressure dropped only 1/2 inch to 1 inch and fuel flow was proportional for the power set. An attempt to smoothen engine operations(s) was not successful; problem worsened. Result was a loud bang sound from engine which resulted in propeller coming to a complete stop. A forced landing was made in residential street; gear down; all electrical and fuel secured. Normal landing in street and no injuries to passenber people or ground or to pilot cause of engine failure was connecting and bolt failure (sheared) and exited engine case and cowling.
output: Sma pilot on photo mission has engine failure; off airport lndg.

input: In the tops and instrument meteorological conditions noticed a traffic advisory that appeared to be moving toward us. Target was 500 feet/foot above. As target closed it became an resolution advisory at about the same time air traffic control issued a clearance to turn toward the target. We declined the turn and turned about 10 degrees away from the target and we received the 'monitor vertical spd.' target passed without further incident. We told air traffic control we had an resolution advisory and the target passed as close as 400 feet/foot directly above us as determined by the traffic alert and collision avoidance system in 5 mile range. Air traffic control said the target was visual flight rules we never saw the target; as we were instrument meteorological conditions air traffic control gave us a heading to return to. Nothing further. It would have lessened the stress intermediate fix air traffic control would have pointed out the traffic second officer we knew she was considering it.
output: Sf340 in instrument meteorological conditions receives an resolution advisory and a subsequent turn from air traffic control towards the traffic that was 500 feet/foot above them.

input: As we went into position and hold on runway(s) 15; tower changed departure instructions; new clearance climb and maintain 3000 feet/foot and 230 degree heading cleared for takeoff shortly after; told to keep visual separation with a departing dash8 aircraft track of the dash8 was on the dca 185 degree radial. Takeoff was normal. After area to our left/right (directions) was cleared we made a early turn to help air traffic control with separation off departing aircraft from runway(s) 1. While executing the turn we were instructed to contact departure aircraft in a left/right (directions) bank and climb of 2500 feet per minute both crew members continued to maintain visual with the departing dash8. Departure was contacted with no delay; using proper phraseology; flight number; current altitude alt climbing to; heading turning to. As i released the push to talk switch we heard the last part of an air traffic control transmission we waited to hear the acknowledgement from air traffic control next transmission was 'flt number; you on freq?' we acknowledge; 'affirmative.' air traffic control response; 'maintain 2000 feet/foot you have a dash8 off your left/right (directions) 1000 feet/foot above.' we immediately stopped the climb current altitude 2000 feet/foot shot through the 2000 feet/foot by 200 feet/foot corrected and maintained 2000 feet/foot this was followed by 7 clrncs to turn and climb i feel this created a safety hazard. Overloaded crew watching engine parameters; traffic callouts; and physically flying. The t10 phase is one of highest workloads and most dangerous times. Air traffic control at dca pushes the safety envelope; by rushing crews with multiple instructions; last minute(s) changes and relying on aircrews to make it happen. They are not taking into consideration a transmission on departure might be missed intermediate fix they get too aggressive and step on aircrew's transmission air traffic control also needs to keep in mind crews might be dealing with an emergency dash8 aircraft should not have been turned toward the departing aircraft all was depending on leveling off at 2000 feet/foot too close and too aggressive by atc.
output: Do328 crew had airport traffic control tower local controller and departure controller interfacility coordination failure departing dca.

input: I was training a d-side developmental at sector 18/19 and [controller a] was the left/right (directions) side. We got put in the hold for lga and the left/right (directions) side began issuing holding instructions to the first aircraft. We called phl approach to coordinate use of the holey holding pattern and they gave it to us under the condition we would work the visual flight rules traffic that they had previously pointed out to us that was doing air work in the pattern. The visual flight rules aircraft was at 12;500 just north of the davys intersection. The second lga arrival (aircraft y) had not been issued holding and was at 13;000 the r-side descended the aircraft to 11;000 and started to issue holding when conflict alert went off with the visual flight rules about 5 miles in front of the lga arrival. The left/right (directions) side turned aircraft y 30 degrees left; but it was too late and they got a resolution advisory with the visual flight rules the aircraft got very close together and the pilot of aircraft y later reported they nearly collided. 15 minutes later the same situation occurred with aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) in nearly the same manner. When she descended aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) out of 14;000 for 11;000 i physically pointed at the airplane and said 'its going to happen again stop aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) at 13'. She did not and they had another resolution advisory and about 1.5 miles of separation. [controller a] has been off the floor for several months for a medical issue and she was only re-certified 1 day before this incident with the bare minimum recertification training completed. This was a terrible oversight this controller is incompetent in her duties and should not have been re-certified in this amount of time. I would recommend that [controller a] be de-certified and removed from the area completely. She is an unnecessary danger to the nas.
output: Zdc controller reported recertified radar controller repeatedly failed to separate traffic resulting in multiple ra's.

input: The purpose of flight was for aerial photography. Location was a shopping mall in mountain view. Operating between the altitudes of 800-1000 feet/foot mean sea level i was given an altitude restriction from moffett ('at or below 1000 ft'). I noticed my altimeter 850 feet/foot mean sea level i kept visual separation while maintaining a safe flying altitude terrain in the area was approximately 50-150 feet/foot when returning from the flight i received a message to call the san jose flight standards district office i returned the call and spoke to inspector and gave him a verbal rpt. Note: after approximately 10 minute(s) i left the area to go to other locations for the photographer. I departed the area at 1000 feet/foot mean sea level some factors that needed attention was various aircraft that were departing moffett field. Visual separation was not a problem apparently 2 rpts were filed with the san jose flight standards district office of a low flying aircraft of which i was flying. The altitudes at which i was flying was appropriate for the photographer's needs and within safe parameters.
output: Sma flies below federal aviation regulation minimum safe alt.

input: This approach now brings aircraft too high to land on glidepath from minimum descent altitude i know it has a steeper glidepath; that is not the problem. The problem is that the glidepath puts aircraft too high at minimum descent altitude to make a normal landing. The precision approach path indicator is all white. I was able to land only because i broke out 500-600 feet/foot above minimum descent altitude the week before; the ceiling was close to minimum descent altitude and aircraft had to go-around. Please have federal aviation administration flight check technicians call me; as the prior reports do not seem to be understood by company and union representatives.
output: An md-82 captain reported that when flying the area navigation runway 27 approach to san the charted glidepath (3.5 degrees) inside the final approach fix failed to place the aircraft vertically at a point from which a stabilized approach and touchdown could be accomplished. Per a later conversation with the first officer of that flight the reporter learned the problem appears to have been resolved via discussions and subsequent actions between government; airline and pilot union representatives.

input: Unable to establish communications with aircraft for period of time exceeding 20 min enroute; followed by a second instance still ongoing. Flight was in area over south china sea out of very high frequency datalink range; unable to transmit acars message via high frequency data link. No fault of dispatcher or crew; problem caused by placing insufficiently equipped aircraft (i.e; satcom; reliable high frequency data link) on overwater routes. Company in violation of federal aviation regulation 121.99 for not providing means to maintain rapid and reliable communications.[suggest a removal of] 767 fleet from [this regions'] routes until such time as they can be equipped appropriately for the mission. Otherwise; only flight plan them to stay within guaranteed very high frequency datalink range and spend the extra money on time/fuel for the resulting longer routings.
output: Dispatcher was unable to maintain high frequency data link contact with crew during a trans-oceanic flight and recommends that the company discontinue the use of this type of aircraft on these routes until better data link radios are installed.

input: We were cleared on a heading of 310 degrees to intercept the 085 degree radial of abq vor and dme (co-located) and the miera 2 arrival, arrive to abq. Later received clearance direct to corona vor and dme (co-located) miera 2 arrival, arrive cross miera at 15000 feet/foot started descent and crossed miera at 15000 feet/foot but failed to make turn to go direct to corona. Center informed us of our mistake. No conflict with other traffic this was the last leg of the day after about 8 1/2 hours flying for the day.
output: Acr crew receives and acknowledged clearance but does not fly it at the end of a longitude day.

input: Prior to takeoff we had a left global positioning system fail. We stopped; ran the quick reference handbook contacted dispatch and maintenance and minimum equipment list 34-53-01a(c) was issued. We completed the logbook; ran our checklists and departed for zzz. During cruise i began to setup for the instrument landing system approach that would be required due to low ceilings. When i switched the frequency to active; i immediately got the localizer / g/s caution flags on the primary flight display. We ran the quick reference handbook which told us we could not do an instrument landing system we also could not fly an area navigation because of the global positioning system inop minimum equipment list we called dispatch and decided we would divert to zzz1. We continued without further incident. Here is my issue. Had part of the procedure for the global positioning system inop had us check other navigation systems (ils) we would have found the instrument landing system to have also failed. From what i understand they are part of the same (box). Could that be added to maintenance procedures for minimum equipment list 34-53-01. Thank you.
output: Pilot reported a diversion caused by additional navigate, navigation systems inoperative and not addressed in an minimum equipment list applied to a global positioning system system.

input: B737; zzz [airport]; gate xxx: fuel reported leaking from the refuel manifold following ground refueling. Maintenance discovered rag/cloth fragments protruding from the manifold poppet valve. This prevented closure of the valve and resultant leak. I suspected the debris came from the ground refuel pit or truck during the refueling process and that there could be additional contaminates in the aircraft fuel tanks. Consequently; i refused the aircraft. The following day i reviewed the aircraft electronic logbook and discovered that the aircraft was returned to service without inspection of the fuel tanks. This is an unsatisfactory decision. Aircraft fuel tanks should be examined for debris and refuel pit/truck should be inspected to determine source of possibly contaminated fuel.
output: B737-800 pilot reported refusing an aircraft after it was found to be leaking fuel from the refuel manifold. Maintenance discovered rag cloth fragments protruding from the poppet valve which reportedly prevented proper closure of the valve.

input: At approximately xa45 central standard time flight received taxi clearance from houston hobby ground control to 'taxi to 12r; hold short of 12l on e.' the aircraft taxied on the ramp area to the point where taxiway east joins the ramp area. This area is the site of extensive construction with minimal taxiway lighting in operations(s) the aircraft missed the lead-in line to taxiway east and proceeded in a northerly direction parallel to the westbound side of concourse celsius and then made a left/right (directions) turn onto an access taxiway which dead ended into a ramp and a corp hangar. The aircraft was promptly stopped wbound on this taxiway and a transmission was made to ground indicating that the aircraft had made an inadvertent turn and may be in need of assistance. Ground responded by asking it we could make a 180 degree turn. It was determined that the apron area next to the hangar provided sufficient clearance and a right 180 degree turn was accomplished. Normal taxi with clearance from ground was made to runway(s) 12r and normal takeoff occurred. After landing the flight crew was informed of possible damage to hangar doors at houston hobby. This problem arose because taxiway lead-in lines were missed and not followed.
