Contributing factors were the lack of visibility at night; extremely poor taxiway lines and markings due to extensive construction where ramp joins taxiway east and failure by the crew to question ground when there was any question as to acft's location on the field. Corrective actions include better taxiway lines and markings in the large area where east leads off from the ramp. In this specific case; the aircraft could have been towed back to the ramp area or a second engine could have been started to assist with the 180 degree turn maneuver.
output: Non adherence to air traffic control instruction in taxi clrnc.

input: I was working an inbound push on buj seavr 1 (ne corner into dfw). Traffic was very complex and aircraft abcd; an l329; descending to 6000 feet/foot over sasie intersection entered regional approach with no handoff i made a frequency change thinking the handoff was complete. My d-side then alerted me that no handoff had been made. I initiated a handoff to regional approach approach control issued an immediate turn (a 360 degree turn) when they talked to the aircraft for traffic i was busy with new dsr equipment (looking for input keys 'heads down') and was distraction i should have had a handoff person on the sector for the workload involved. Also the database on aircraft abcd was incorrect which inhibited the automatic handoff feature. The federal aviation administration should have allowed more training time with the new dsr equipment to allow more familiarity during busy periods.
output: Rptr let aircraft x penetrate apch's airspace without a handoff or prior coordination being accomplished. This resulted in an opdev.

input: Standard separation between simultaneous departures off the parallel runway(s) at atl is; according to the handbook 7110.65; that the flight paths must diverge by a track of at least 15 degrees immediately after takeoff however; the area navigation departures published off runway(s) 27r state that the turn to rojrs must start at or above 1200 feet/foot this allows the aircraft to climb on runway(s) heading for an unspecified distance as longitude as the turn is above 1200 feet/foot in this instance; a b717 remained on runway(s) heading for 3 miles. The south wind caused the aircraft to track toward or converging with a departure off of runway(s) 26l. The local controller prompted the departure controller to take action. When the pilot was asked intermediate fix he was turning towards rojrs; he said; 'we will turn now.' controllers and pilots both followed procedures correctly and the area navigation departure procedure as published caused a conflict -- which was unreported by atl management due to an organizational commitment to make the area navigation departure procedure successful.
output: Atl local controller expressed concern regarding area navigation departure procedures that reportedly result in conflict intermediate fix aircraft are delayed in executing turns.

input: With 15 minutes left in flight; we took our jumpseats and noticed once we sat a strong pungent smell that smelled cheesy and musty coming through the cabin. I notified the other fas (flight attendants) and they also smelled it. Smell continued until the boarding door was opened. My throat was burning and a headache came about.
output: A321 flight attendant reported pungent odor on descent that continued until deplaning at destination. Flight attendant also reported minor health issues.

input: Capt and first officer detected electrical smoke in cockpit. Accomplished smoke chklist. Declared emergency diverted to closest field (jax). Uneventful apch/lndg. After landing maintenance personnel discovered electrical component had fried and caused the odor. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information first officer rptr stated that the aircraft was a b767-200. The crew; as part of their chklist procedure did ask the cabin attendants intermediate fix there was any anomaly in the cabin. Cabin attendant rpted some reading lights and passenber entertainment system inoperative this helped to pinpoint the problem as the crew then asked for direct to jax. The multiplexer mixing unit for the passenber entertainment system (channel selectors and video) and lights had fried. This unit is in the e&e compartment next to the equipment cooling fan. There is no other warning or alerting system for this type malfunction other than the flc's 'nose sensor.' the plts' union was also notified of the event.
output: A b767-200 flight crew diverts to jax after perceiving electrical odor and smoke in cockpit.

input: At gate; the external power tripped off 2 times during flight attendant briefing; and then i started the auxiliary power unity due to the aircraft being unpwred for a while we had serious #2 engine problems on start that required a return to gate; reset of fadec by maintenance and 1 hour 30 minute(s) delay. This also snowballed with delays the rest of the day on that aircraft the first officer had seen a ground guy wiggle the external power cord and at first we thought it was his wiggling the cord that caused the problem but when we arrived back in zzz after a maintenance carry-over turn we returned to gate and were connected with external power and it again tripped off on its own and we had to start the auxiliary power unity the incoming capt said the power had been bad at this gate for over a week intermediate fix that's the case; please don't use it and have the crews use the auxiliary power unity loss of power on an airbus results in many problems usually not found until after push and start.
output: An a320 capt rpts gpu at a gate in zzz trips power off airplane causing disruptions of system and programs incurring delays.

input: Arts 3.06 problems the conflict alert and low altitude alert portion of the automated radar terminal systems at stl tower are not functioning correctly. On numerous occasions the 'conflict alert' or 'low alt' flashes on the bright radar indicator tower equipment with no associated aural alarm. At other times the aural alarm goes off for no apparent reason. When the bright radar indicator tower equipment scope is expanded out the aircraft causing the aural alarm has been found to be 15-20 mile from stl; this aircraft is being worked by the terminal radar approach control facility this condition started with the installation of a3.06. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated problems with the new automated radar terminal systems program 3.06 have been corrected.
output: Atc equipment problem radar. New automated radar terminal systems program 3 pt 06 gives no aural alarm with low altitude alerts or conflict alerts.

input: After starting the auxiliary power unity i noticed a dirty sock smell coming from the vents. Having smelled this before i disregarded it at first. We decided to start both engines during push to shut down the auxiliary power unity bleed. After a few minutes of taxiing; the smell continued and i noticed a dull headache; nausea; and burning; itchy eyes. I mentioned this to the captain and she commented that she had a headache. We contacted dispatch and maintenance control and we all agreed to return to the gate. The flight was canceled and medical services were notified. They came to the hotel to evaluate those involved.
output: A319 first officer reports a 'dirty sock' smell when the auxiliary power unity is started and the packs turned on. After engine start the smell persists and headache; nausea; and burning; itchy eyes are experienced by both the captain and first officer. Aircraft returns to the gate and flight is canceled.

input: On teaming gates; the lack of push qualified agents has caused some issues with close departure times between two gates. In order to achieve on [time] departures; some have been advised to have a non-push qualified agent sit on the tractor and ask for brake release until a qualified push agent is able to take over.
output: Reporter wrote that in order to achieve on time departure some have been advised to have a non-push qualified agent sit on the tractor and ask for brake release until a qualified push agent is able to take over.

input: When lined up on runway(s) 13 at lga; we switched both compasses from magnetic mode to directional gyroscope mode and aligned compasses with the magnetic heading of the runway(s) (134 degs) (due to steel pilings under rwy). After takeoff we followed the normal noise abatement procedures and accomplished the published whitestone climb procedures we were given a clearance to climb to 15000 feet/foot and subsequently a left/right (directions) turn to 290 degrees at this time; and climbing out of 5000 feet/foot we returned the compasses to the magnetic mode; and rolled out on a 290 degree heading during the climb we noticed we were converging with other climbing traffic and asked departure about it. We were asked our heading and told to level at 10000 feet/foot it was then we discovered our magnetic compasses differed from the standby compass by about 40 degrees departure gave us gyroscope failure turns until we were able to return our magnetic compasses to normal. Supplemental information from acn 224027: intermediate fix we had been instrument meteorological conditions without clear air turbulence ii; only controller vigilance could prevent conflict/collision had conditions (acft proximitypa and flight profile) light emitting diode us closer.
output: Hdg track deviation due to aircraft equipment problem operating procs.

input: Working arrivals; visual flight rules weather with very good visual approaches. The session was very busy with westerly winds complicating the situation. The bases were fast and compression on the final was substantial. Aircraft x requested an instrument landing system autoland approach for currency. I cleared aircraft x at the marker for an instrument landing system approach and assigned him 160 knots to 5 mile final. I brought aircraft y behind him and slowed the aircraft down early to maintain wake turbulence separation. I cleared aircraft y for the visual approach with 5.5 miles separation and assigned the flight 160 knots to 5 mile final and i instructed him to contact the tower. As i monitored the final i realized that aircraft y was compressing too much on the heavy aircraft x; i immediately called the tower and i instructed them to break aircraft y out to a 270 heading and to climb and maintain 4000 feet. Aircraft y was still within the wake turbulence parameters at 5.01 nautical mile behind the heavy. The local controller replied 'i think we have visual...hold on'; 5 second break then 'yes we have visual'. I let it go and it compressed further to 4.8 nautical mile as i thought about the situation and knowing that the tower controllers cannot waive wake turbulence separation unless the aircraft waives it with visual separation i was left wondering if that is what the tower meant. As this was a specific occurrence due to bad winds and compression i see no recommendation i can give. This was a very busy session with difficult winds; maybe there should have been a consideration to using a different runway.
output: Tracon controller reported of two aircraft on final that were going to lose wake turbulence separation. Terminal radar approach control facility controller advised tower controller to break the trailing aircraft out and relayed go around instructions. Tower controller advised terminal radar approach control facility controller they would apply tower visual separation between the aircraft.

input: About 30 mile north of miami at xa11z; the #1 engine strut overheat light illuminated. Followed procedures and light did not go out. Declared an emergency and shut down the #1 engine at xa16. Touched down at mia at xa26z. All other indications were normal. Informed passenber that fire equipment would checked us out. Aircraft looked good; taxied to gate.
output: B727 engine strut overheat. Engine shut down.

input: Was the relief pilot on flight abc; zzz to zzz1. While at the gate; the ground crew tried to motion to the capt that they had no headset for engine start and that they wanted to use hand signals. The capt refused and told them to find an operative headset. After some search; ground crew returns and says he has one that he thinks will work. As we push back; he clears us to start. The autostart function on the left/right (directions) engine fails almost immediately as we attempt to start both engs simultaneously. We notify the ground personnel of this and tell him to not disconnect because we have a problem he says fine. About this time we have finished our pushback and are still connected to the tug. We refer to the manual engine start chklist and the left/right (directions) engine starts normally. At this time; we notify the ground personnel that we have 2 normal starts and that he is cleared to disconnect. He replied he'd see us out front. The next thing we realize is that the airplane is rolling forward and that the ground crew had in fact disconnected the tug without ever telling us to set the parking brake. Although nothing occurred; there was a tremendous opportunity for an accident to happen; to either the ground personnel or the aircraft should have contacted either the ground personnel or the tug; as the aircraft rolled forward.
output: A b777 after engine start and with no ground to cockpit communications the ground crew disconnected the tug and towbar. The airplane rolled forward endangering the ground crew.

input: I was working the radar at the time of this incident. There was a broken line of storms in the western half of the sector that all aircraft were deviating around. The traffic at the time was not difficult in complexity and there was not a lot of volume in the sector. I took radar contact of both aircraft in this incident. Aircraft x and aircraft y. Both aircraft were coming from the adjacent sector and were level at 34000 feet on the same standard instrument departure aircraft y checked in on frequency and asked about descending in altitude or a route offset due to wake turbulence that the aircraft encountered prior to checking in on frequency. I offered the aircraft an altitude change up or down and i did make a traffic call about the heavy airbus 300 which was approximately 7 miles in front. I offered the aircraft a climb to get above the wake turbulence instead of descending with it. The aircraft requested a climb to 36000 feet and i issued the altitude. That was the last communication i had with the aircraft and i was relieved from position. I was told later in the shift that the aircraft diverted due to injuries sustained from the wake turbulence encounter. After discussing the incident with the operations manager; i was advised to file a report. Since i talked to the aircraft after the incident happened; i was unable to prevent it. After watching the falcon radar replay from the beginning of the flight; it would of been helpful if an advisory was given to the pilot so that they knew a heavy aircraft was climbing in front of them.
output: A center controller reported an aircraft reported a wake vortex encounter and diverted due to injuries.

input: The runway lights at the bqn airport are set excessively bright at night. This condition results in excessive ambient illumination inside the aircraft that can produce glare that may cause uncomfortable squinting; eye tearing; and even temporary blindness during the landing phase. The airport is not equipped with a pilot control lighting system to adjust the runway illumination when the tower is closed.
output: Air carrier captain reported excessive brightness of the runway lights at bqn airport.

input: We departed on the standard terminal arrival route off of runway 25r. Passing through approximately 9;000 ft; the autopilot disengaged; first officer's (fo) flight director disappeared; and fo's flight mode annunciator (fma) arm; roll; and pitch mode windows went blank. The captain's side was still working and we switched flight director (fd) selector operative system. We ran the quick reference handbook procedure for a blank flight mode annunciator and after a few minutes the autopilot disengaged again and both flight directors and flight mode annunciator blanked. We leveled off with air traffic control approval below rvsm airspace; and coordinated to return to the airport. While descending; the flight directors started working again. We landed uneventfully. This aircraft has multiple pieces of equipment in the cockpit that are different from the other aircraft in the fleet. Crews must maintain a vigilant crosscheck of these systems to ensure they are operating as expected. Differences in flight management techniques due to the lack of vertical navigation and different type of flight management system controls should be thoroughly briefed prior to departure.
output: Md-80 first officer reported during climb the autopilot disconnected; the first officer's flight director disappeared; and the flight mode annunciator's arm; roll; and pitch mode windows went blank.

input: During descent given clearance from 14000 feet/foot to 10000 feet/foot read back clearance and leveled off at 10000 feet/foot after landing told to call center on telephone. I was advised that i leveled off at 10000 feet/foot and should have leveled off at 11000 feet/foot because 11000 feet/foot was my clearance altitude i never acknowledged or read back an 11000 feet/foot clearance i do recall that the controller was extremely busy; issuing many clrncs to numerous aircraft he was also denying radar advisory service to many aircraft because he was second officer busy and overloaded with instrument flight rules traffic i do not recall receiving or acknowledging an 11000 feet/foot clearance there were no traffic conflicts or traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii advisories. Intermediate fix i was at the incorrect altitude why did the controller allow me to continue flight at that altitude i never received any altitude corrections or advisory about altdevs until i returned the telephone call; once on the gnd.
output: Atc alleges that an a300 was cleared to descend to 11000 feet/foot clearance disputed as flight crew insists they were cleared to 10000 feet/foot aircraft got to 10000 ft.

input: Pushed back from the zzz gate x; during push back; we received the okay from ground crew personnel that we can start engine 1. During engine start of the number one engine; it was noted that we had a hung start as the n2 gauge only got up to about 31 percent. Once the captain and i noticed the indications; we went into shutdown procedures of the number 1 engine. We did note the engine 1 itt temperature rapidly increase; before it decreased. After shutting down the engine to prepare to restart; ground crew personnel attempted to notify us that there was a fire. However; due to faulty headsets of ground personnel; this information was hard to make sense of. At this point to confirm a potential fire; we contacted the flight attendants to check the rear of the aircraft and look out the windows to confirm the fire potential. The flight attendants did not see any flames or smoke. The decision was made to open the main cabin door; to allow the pilot in command to visually verify there was a fire threat. After the pilot in command visually inspected the area; he was able to confirm that there was a fire and we promptly called for an aircraft evacuation of the passengers and crew. Fire units were notified promptly by ground crew and notification to zzz ground control of evacuation of passengers on the ramp. The captain and myself (first officer) continued to do the engine fire (on the ground) emergency procedure checklist and the passenger evacuation procedure checklist.
output: Crj 900 flight crew reported that ground crew observed a fire on an engine during start and evacuated the aircraft.

input: Departed runway(s) 29 cae. Clearance was climb to 2500 feet/foot at 400 feet/foot above ground level we switched to cae departure they said; 'clb to 10000 feet/foot cleared direct choo choo vor.' we were climbing at 3000 feet per minute at 2600 feet/foot mean sea level cae said; 'maintain 2500 ft.' we missed the mooney visually by leveling at 2800 feet/foot we need traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii on all freighters and we need it yesterday; not tomorrow!
output: An air carrier b757 freighter aircraft was cleared to climb through an occupied altitude and an near midair collision was the result.

input: Ogg cargo rpted omitting a container resulting in a 4500 pound weight and balance closeout error. Also maintenance indicated tailskid would not extend due to a tail strike. Capt keeps paperwork from all his international flts. Ptow for this flight was 337600 pounds closeout tow was 331936 pounds capt determined weight difference to be fall off in cargo. Departed ogg runway(s) 2 wind 050 degs/10 knot(s) first officer leg. Capt observed normal rotation and liftoff. No indication of tailskid contact. On approach to lax after extension resulted in after extension of gear resulted in illumination tailskid light. Chklist crew awareness resulted in normal landing by first officer write-up made for tailskid light illuminated upon gear extension. Looking back a few months of typical takeoff stabilizer trim for b767-300 out of ogg is 1.7 to 2.7. Closeout stabilizer trim for this flight was 3.6. Additional information tailskid light illumination. Action taken: maintenance removed and replaced tailskid control module vlv per maintenance manual 32-71-01-4 leak checked and operations(s) checked good. Only valve replaced. This does not indicate tail strike. A 31 day history of hydraulic and gear system showed no record of tailskid indicator trip. No record of crushed tailskid cylinder. No record of tail strike inspection. No tail strike. Miscom between maintenance and chief pilot that there was tail strike.
output: A rpted tail strike on a b767 is determined to be erroneous after repair history of the aircraft is reviewed relative to a tailskid malfunction log item that was made after that flight the flight that had been issued erroneous weight and balance information when 1 cargo container was not loaded.

input: On apr/fri/06; both the primary and back-up atop/ocean 21 channels experienced complete simultaneous critical failures. This left air traffic control controllers without any aircraft position tracking functionality for at least 10 minute(s) this tracking functionality updates and ensures the position of aircraft operating within the system during this outage; any aircraft that may have actually experienced a problem resulting in an 'overdue acft' rpt would not have been rpted. The failure caused many aircraft operating in the system to indicate to controllers that they were now overdue. This dual failure also resulted in a loss of the conflict probe functionality; which is used to detect and ensure required separation standards that maintain the safety of the system beyond the basic safety aspect; requests from users for altitude and route changes could not be processed due to the controller's inability to ensure the position of many aircraft the above is a recurring situation as on apr/sat/06; both the primary and back-up atop/ocean 21 channels experienced complete simultaneous critical failures for 1 minute(s) and on apr/sun/06; both the primary and back-up atop/ocean 21 channels experienced complete simultaneous critical failures for 18 mins.
output: Zoa controller states ocean atops system is unreliable.

input: Taxiing in to the gate at dsm; i was following the instructions of the ground signalman. There were 2 yellow lines and turning the corner i was at first unsure what line i was supposed to use. I lined up on the yellow line that i was getting marshaled to and the signalman was giving me the straight ahead signal. When we were approaching the place i expected to stop; i was given a hard left/right (directions) turn. I followed these instructions and the left/right (directions) wingtip contacted the jetway. I was not at any time until after contact was made to stop. The wing walker was trying to tell the signalman to stop me but for some reason he didn't hear or see him. A contributing factor was having 2 lines and not giving me good signals as to what line he wanted me on. Also; ramp congestion and other smaller aircraft parked nearby added to the problem the best corrective action i could recommend is to have just 1 line; better attention to the wing walkers by the signalman and intermediate fix ever in doubt; stop the aircraft and establish interphone contact with the cockpit.
output: Marshal signal ground crew failed to signal flight crew of an md80 to stop prior to the left/right (directions) wingtip striking the jetway during parking.

input: I noticed a mild burning (plastic) smell and eventually smoke pouring out of every crease and opening from ceiling. I notified cockpit and we made an emergency landing the capt and myself experienced symptoms from chemical exposure. A few first class passenber complained of throat and eye burning and were coughing too. Cockpit shut down power to first class galley. We diverted. I went to the doctor and was treated with medication for chemical exposure and situational anxiety.
output: Md80 declares emergency and lands when smoke and fumes are noted in cabin by cabin attendant and pax.

input: On approach to mem we were cleared the visual approach to runway(s) 36l. We had the instrument landing system tuned and identified and were flying the localizer and glideslope approach control was very busy at the time. At about 2300 feet/foot to 2500 feet/foot we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory and instructed to clb! Clb! Clb! By the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory we cleared the area and proceeded to climb putting the vsi in the appropriate ãƒâ¾greenãƒâ¾ climbing range. The capt instructed air traffic control of our go around and why. Air traffic control gave us a clearance to level at 3000 feet/foot at 3000 feet/foot we still had our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory active second officer we continued our climb as traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory required. The climb resolution advisory ceased at approximately 3500 and said ãƒâ¾monitor vertical spdãƒâ¾ and we told air traffic control we could level at 4000 feet/foot a different voice answered from air traffic control and cleared us to ãƒâ¾level at 4000 feet/foot runway(s) heading 190 kts.ãƒâ¾ we complied and the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii declared ãƒâ¾clr of conflict.ãƒâ¾ we followed air traffic control clrncs to another approach to 36l and landed without further incident.
output: Lgt on approach has traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory climbs and tells air traffic control go around given altitude to level; still has resolution advisory continues climb until clear indicated; notifies atc.

input: Following marshaler's instructions; we stopped inches away from hitting the jetway with our left/right (directions) engine the marshalers did not regard wing walker's instructions to stop. I believe that due to lack of training and proper supervision of new hires this was a tragedy nearly avoided. An obvious newly hired ramp marshaler nearly directed us into a jetway disregarding other ramp agents' attempts to stop us short of the left/right (directions) engine hitting the jetway. The gate is a turn in gate and needs a qualified; experienced ramp agent to handle a turn in gate. Ramp wing walker was summoned to capt to explain why we had to be towed back to deplane passenber i contacted chief pilot better training and supervision of new hired ground personnel.
output: A320 captain reports inexperienced marshaler failed to heed direction from wing walker to signal for a stop. Collision with misplaced jetway narrowly averted.

input: We (capt and i) were given clearance to cross 'hoggs' intersection at 19000 feet/foot we were on arrival, arrive from south to new york. I (coplt) misread chart; next intersection is about 8 mile further. Read that one instead of hoggs. Capt asked 'if i was going to make the crossing at hoggs.' i increased our descent by using speed brakes and we crossed ok. The capt started 'fussing about planning ahead' etc. We were given our next clearance to cross cameron at 11000 feet/foot since the capt was involved with his 'lecture' to me; i missed the part of the clearance that we were to cross cameron at 250 knot(s) also. Consequently; we crossed cameron at 11000 feet/foot and 300 knot(s) instead of 250 knot(s) as requested. Now the capt is really excited. He says 'you're going to have me having to answer to the general manager of flying. Why weren't you 250 knot(s) at cameron!' i slowed immediately to 250 knot(s) we continued and landed at jfk airport with no response from center or approach about the excessive speed at cameron. I think the problem was caused by a breakdown of crew resource management by the capt. Had he been as vigilant in monitoring our letdown arrival, arrive progress into new york as he was intent on 'lecturing' the coplt on an oversight in reading the chart; the excessive speed at cameron would not have occurred. I talked to a representative of professional standards. Perhaps they will send a representative to discuss this with the capt. The capt had about 300 hours in the aircraft at the start of our trip several days before.
output: Lgt aircraft makes speed deviation on arrival, arrive proc.

input: Scheduled flight time was over 12 hours and the fuel load was 229;000 pounds start up; taxi and takeoff was normal. The takeoff required the use of flaps 15 due the gross weight which was 611;000 pounds air traffic control directed a heading of 320 and a climb to 3;000 feet/foot after takeoff. I called for heading select after gear retraction and began a turn at 400 feet/foot above ground level as soon as the turn was initiated i saw a flock of 6-10 birds immediately in front of the aircraft. One bird hit the center of the forward windscreen and i heard two thumps in very rapid succession. We were at approximately 180-190 knot(s) at impact. Although my windscreen was covered with bird tissue; the windscreen was not damaged and visibility was not impaired. I looked at the engine panel to access any engine damage and observed a red over temp box around the right egt. There were no other indications of engine damage or stress. We operated the engine normally for the remainder of the flight. I called for flaps 5 to begin the flap retraction process. Realizing that the bird encounter would necessitate a return; i instructed first officer to get us a level off at 3;000 feet/foot mean sea level versus the new cleared altitude which was 10;000 feet/foot at the same time we saw that an area of weather within 10 miles on our nose would require immediate attention. There were other aircraft making radio calls on the frequency and we were unable at first to make it known to air traffic control that we had taken several birds strikes with potential engine damage; needed to remain at a lower altitude than our last clearance and needed to make an immediate right turn to avoid severe weather. We elected to declare an emergency at that point. After that; our handling and communications became much smoother. I instructed the relief first officer to contact dispatch and maintenance control. I instructed the second relief first officer to inform the lead flight attendant of our status and our intention to return. After that he was to make appropriate announcements to the passengers. We obtained clearance to 7;000 feet/foot for fuel jettisoning. Rather than holding air traffic control put us on a series of vectors in the area. First officer began fuel jettison in accordance with the emergency checklist. At first our intention was to dump to maximum landing weight; 460;000 pounds which would take about 27 minutes. We had about 225;000 pounds at the beginning of jettison. We discussed our options for landing. We were concerned that the same area of weather the necessitated our immediate deviation on initial climb could possibly delay or even prevent our return. Maintenance control gave us the okay to land overweight and dispatch sent us the appropriate landing data. First officer coordinated an immediate return and reviewed the overweight landing checklist. We stopped jettison at 5;000 feet/foot in the descent with about 148;000 pounds remaining. A 30 flap landing with autobrakes 3 was planned. First relief first officer reviewed the diversion checklist on her company issued ipad. The landing [and] rollout were normal. We exited the runway; stopped the aircraft and shut down the right engine for inspection by the emergency crew. Rather than restart the engine for taxi or taxi overweight on one engine; we elected to have the aircraft towed to the gate. Weight at touchdown was 533;000 pounds with 147;000 pounds of fuel on board.
output: B777 flight crew describes the crew actions after several bird strikes at 500 feet/foot above ground level on departure. An egt over temperature is noted initially and the crew elects to return to the departure airport. Fuel is dumped but approaching weather leads the crew to terminate that process and land overweight.

input: No narrative supplied.
output: Ctlr rpts loss of separation westbound of iiu.

input: Acr x flies into sgf several times a day from zzz. They check on every day saying that our automatic terminal information service appears to be out of service. When asked what frequency they used; they always give the wrong one. I spoke to one of their pilots about it and found out that the charts that their airline uses do not have the current automatic terminal information service frequency in them for sgf. Our automatic terminal information service frequency changed about 6-8 months ago to 135.125.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr confirmed problem still exists; even with the latest chart revisions.
output: Sgf controller voiced concern regarding a commercial chart provider that has not updated automatic terminal information service frequency change.

input: Inbound to o'hare; automatic terminal information service rpted landing in progress 22r and 27r/l. Traffic level was very heavy and we were following 2 company aircraft with very similar call signs. We were vectored by approach control for runway(s) 22r. Intercepted localizer and were cleared for approach when switched to tower frequency at outer marker it was apparent someone had a stuck microphone on tower frequency 126.9. 2 attempts to contact tower for landing clearance were unsuccessful. Aircraft ahead of us landed. First officer started to select another tower frequency on communications #1 when i tuned communications #2 to 126.9; when a strong transmission overrode interference on frequency clearing us to land. We landed on runway(s) 22r but were unable to exit runway(s) on the high speed taxiway because 2 aircraft holding short of runway(s) 27r (for landing tfc) were occupying it. With no other place to go; we continued to rollout on runway(s) 22r to runway(s) 27r hold short line. Tower frequency was again garbled and tower was unable to exercise control of traffic holding short of 27r. With traffic to land behind us and no tower communications we switched to ground frequency while still on the runway(s) ground control (apparently tower local ctlr) advised us to immediately cross runway(s) 27r and turn off runway(s) 22r onto 'old scenic' taxiway we observed traffic rolling out runway(s) 27 and deeming the separation adequate; we immediately crossed runway(s) 27r and exited runway(s) 22r. When clear of both runway(s) we advised ground control we were clear at which point the real ground controller got us confused with the similar call signs holding short of runway(s) 27r in the high speed several xmissions were required to clarify our position and obtain taxi clearance the margin of safety is lowered by conducting simultaneous operations(s) to intersecting runway(s) on runway(s) 22r at ord; there is no place to clear the runway(s) without crossing the other active runway(s) (27r) intermediate fix the high speed turnoff is blocked or missed. Any failures - - mechanical; communicationss coordination etc; lower the margin to 0. In my judgement; simultaneous landing operations(s) on runway(s) 22r and 27r at ord; are imminently unsafe and should be discontinued!
output: A stuck microphone causes gridlock at the intersection of runway(s) 22r and 27r during simultaneous lndgs on these rwys.

input: The parachute jump area was active vfr/145 at xs90. This area is controlled by aus app and they notify sat app and zhu rnd sector 92 when active. The jump plane was climbing in the area southbound and spilled out of the depicted protected airspace. Meanwhile aircraft x was on the setzr standard instrument departure from sat climbing to fl230. As the targets began to merge i turned aircraft y to mercr intersection on the standard instrument departure to pull south and issued an initial heading of 15 degrees right to help expedite the vector. This turn kept him an addition 2 miles south of the depicted jump area (the standard instrument departure takes departures along the southern boundary of jump area). After reevaluating the situation i stopped aircraft y at 14000 below the jump plane at 14500. Aircraft x was climbing unusually slow. Majority of the time jets will top this area. As soon as i un-keyed the jump plane began a decent. Aircraft x responded to resolution advisory and reported seeing traffic 400 ft above.this has been an ongoing issue for slow climbers or turbo props on this standard instrument departure with the parachute jump areas active. As stated above the jump are sits just off the standard instrument departure were the east departures off sat intercept on a northeast heading then turn east on standard instrument departure this jump area is located within sat app who owns 13000 and below and aus app who owns 12000 and blow and our 92 sector. I do not have control for turns from sat until out of 13000 and have active military operating area at 8000-12000 south of the standard instrument departure for many reasons this is an unsafe place for jump are:1) in a major departure corridor for sat app.2) jump planes spill out of depicted area.3) sat app does not ensure departures top jump planes.4) aus app does not keep them in areas.1) don't allow parachute jump operations in or near a major departures or arrival corridors.2) move standard instrument departure south.3) cap jump area altitude to 12000/13000 and sat app should be required to ensure separation via alt or vector before shipping to 92 sector.4) aus app needs to monitor their jump planes to prevent spilling out.
output: Zhu controller reported a near midair collision between an air carrier and a jump plane due to the proximity of the jump area to the standard instrument departure routing.

input: Obtained weather at sgf for instrument flight rules flight to ads. As i got closer to pallas on the fingr 3 arrival, arrive weather worsened; and due to worse than expected headwinds; arrived over dallas about 1 hour later than expected. input: This was the second leg of a charter from zzz to zzz1 carrying a full load of military personnel. I was the captain. We had 2 maintenance personnel and 2 ramp personnel in addition to our 14 flight attendants. We received our final weights and the center of gravity was about 21 percent resulting in a trim setting of approximately 3.5 units. At trim settings this far forward; the 747 will display a second portion of the stabilizer greenband; which is lighter in color. Our trim was set just at the border of the darker section of the band. This often causes a 'stab greenband' engine indicating and crew alerting system caution message; but did not today. All normal checklists were accomplished during taxi out and the trim confirmed at 3.5. We were cleared for takeoff. The tower had cleared a beechcraft musketeer to take off in front of us and gave him a turnout to the south. He was drifting left of centerline with the wind and was not starting his turn as we began our takeoff roll. I was concentrating on keeping him in sight as we began the takeoff roll in case there was a flight path conflict after takeoff as we climbed out. This put more of my normal scan outside the airplane. I was the pilot flying. Takeoff power was set and the normal 80 knot(s) call was uneventful. Our v1 was 134 and vfr military training routes was 145 with v2 at 154. Our takeoff weight was approximately 596.0 thousand pounds i heard the aural warning sound and glanced inside at the upper engine indicating and crew alerting system screen. I thought i saw a red configuration gear message on the screen. The aural warning was steady and the engine indicating and crew alerting system message steady. I glanced at the airspeed indicator and the speed was roughly 10 knot(s) below v1. The v1 call had not been made by the first officer. I aborted the takeoff bringing the throttles to idle and selecting reverse thrust. The autobrakes engaged and the airplane began a rapid deceleration. I evaluated the remaining runway; determined we didn't need maximum braking to stop and called for the autobrakes to be turned off while simultaneously reaching for the selector myself. The first officer got there first and turned off the autobrakes. This occurred between 70 and 90 knot(s) the first officer told the tower we were aborting and would clear the runway. They asked if we needed assistance and i requested that they roll the fire trucks and we suspected our brakes would be hot. We cleared the runway and stopped on the parallel taxiway. I did not set the parking brake. I held the brakes as gently as possible and after 3 minutes of cooling we shut down the #2 and #3 engine to reduce our thrust. I said i thought i saw configuration gear but the first officer said he thought he saw configuration stabilizer either message will generate the aural warning; a red warning light and its respective red engine indicating and crew alerting system message. I looked down at the stabilizer position indicator and the lighter portion of the greenband had disappeared and only the normal darker portion remained. Our trim setting was right on the edge of the green band. I selected the brake temperatures synoptic on the lower engine indicating and crew alerting system screen. The temperatures were beginning to rise from zero. Captain asked our weight and the flight management computer showed 594.5. I guessed our speed at the abort to be about 120-125 knot(s) based on our v1 and i told him to use the 600.0 weight on the chart. We determined we would have to wait 50 minutes to 1 hour for the brakes to cool. Based on the temperatures and our weight and the numbers; i determined it safe enough to taxi a short distance further down the taxiway and off to a holding area to clear the taxiway for the tower. The fire trucks followed us; we started the auxiliary power unity shut down the remaining engines and requested the fire marshal place chocks under the nose gear tires. The fire marshal scanned each wheel and his readings corresponded with our brake temperatures on the screen. The hottest brake was 280 degrees. We observed the brake temperatures and one brake rose to 6 (the scale goes to 9); 3 went to 5; and the rest never went above 4. Peak temperatures did occur as advertised about 15 minutes after the rejected takeoff. We requested stairs from the fixed-base operator and when they arrived; our maintenance personnel went down to check the wheels and tires. The right forward tire on the right body gear was now flat-spotted and frayed and would need changing. I went down and inspected all the tires and concurred with the mechanic's assessment. The brakes were warm but not hot. We requested a belt loader from the fixed-base operator and pulled the spare tire we carried and the jack from the flyaway kit in the aft pit. The 2 mechanics and the 2 ramp men changed the tire. By the time the tire was changed; the brakes had all cooled to zero. We surmised that as we approached v1 and the nose began to rise and the strut extended; the lighter portion of the stabilizer greenband disappeared and our trim was set just outside the darker band. This would account for the 'config stab' warning. For the next takeoff; the weights and trim came in roughly the same. I directed the first officer to increase the trim just a bit to get it inside the edge of the darker greenband. He set it at about 3.7 units. During the subsequent takeoff; i also kept a little extra forward pressure on the control column until i started the rotation at vfr military training routes i wanted to ensure the nose strut would not extend prematurely. I am very familiar with the issues we have experienced on the b747 at very light weights and low trim settings. The pressure sensor in the nose gear can cause a 'stab greenband' engine indicating and crew alerting system message. Aft center of gravities or an over-serviced nose gear strut usually causes this. Our irregular procedure is adequate to deal with these instances when they occur. I had not seen a case where the lighter portion of the greenband would disappear and leave the current trim setting outside the darker greenband. I plan to follow up with engineering and boeing to see if there have been any other reports of this. The glare on the upper engine indicating and crew alerting system screen made it difficult to read the warning message clearly. If i had seen 'config stab' instead of what i thought i saw (config gear); i may have reacted differently; especially so close to v1 and knowing the stabilizer trim was at the edge of the normal greenband. The small airplane on climbout ahead of us was a distraction. The steady aural warning and the red engine indicating and crew alerting system message elevated the severity of the situation and training kicked in; as it should.
output: A b747 engine indicating and crew alerting system alerted 'config stab' at about 115 knot(s) on takeoff roll because of the aircraft's light weight and forward trim setting. The captain deiced to reject the takeoff and found the stabilizer trim at its limit. A tire change was required before the next takeoff.

input: Assigned job to remove and replace #2 engine fuel shutoff cable on aircraft xxx due to worn area. Removed cable and was rerouting new cable from the turnbuckle in the forward cargo pit to the #2 engine the first pulley in that run is in the air condition bay. The cable was routed correctly and the pulley was installed without tightening the nut. I had a family emergency arise and i left at xa30. What action; intermediate fix any; have i taken to correct this? The next morning i phoned my partner i was working with to see how everything went and mentioned the pulley in question. She decided to contact the supervisor on duty to stop aircraft and have the pulley looked at. Supplemental information from acn 749254: i was working on the wing section for #2 engine fuel shutoff cable run (ref log page). I removed 3 pulleys outside of the fuselage and they were documented on a maintenance form. Another technician was working in the forward cargo bay area and behind the aft wall (acft bay). He installed the new cable. It was pulled through from the turn barrel (in the cargo bay ceiling) to the #2 engine pylon quadrant. I was working on installing the cable guard on the #2 pylon quadrant when the other technician was called away on a family emergency i gave a turnover to the next shift mechanic on the area i worked on. The next day when talking to the mechanic on next shift about the job; i mentioned the difficult pulley behind the cargo aft wall and he was unaware of it. I was not sure the nut was torqued. What action; intermediate fix any; have i taken to correct this? I notified my supervisor he contacted maintenance control the aircraft was looked at. Supplemental information from acn 749434: at beginning of shift; i took turnover for an engine fuel shutoff cable replacement. The cable had been routed and hooked up at both ends. Reference log page xxx. I completed the job per maintenance manual and all documented items on form xxx. The next day; i was asked by the mechanic who turned over the job to me; intermediate fix i had looked at any of the cable pulleys in the aft section of the cargo pit (christmas tree area). My reply was no. Apparently; there was some question about whether or not all the pulleys in this area were secure. There was no documentation that any pulleys in this area were in any way suspect. Supervision was notified; as well as maintenance control the aircraft in question was stopped; and the area inspected. Supplemental information from acn 749253: i was the inspector involved with load planning #2 engine fuel shutoff cable installation; it was brought to my attention today that one of the cable pulleys (that was not documented on the maintenance form) may not have had its nut tightened. The aircraft was stopped on the ground at zzz1 where technician found the nut hand tight and secured the same. Note: amm states -- the removal and replacement of cable does not mention any loosening and/or removal of cable pulleys.
output: A b737-500 aircraft #2 engine fuel shut-off cable was replaced. Nut securing cable pulley not tightened in fwd cargo air conditioning bay (christmas tree area).

input: Bna is in desperate need of a ramp controller. On this flight; we had four airplanes pushback simultaneously; unnecessarily crowding the alleyway. input: Yesterday a motor vehicle accident occurred between a catering van and a ramp agent driving a tug pulling a cart. I was driving as the team leader was coming towards my direction. As he was coming forward he didn't realize the van was coming out already. Once he realized he then tried to avoid the collision but in that instance the cart on the bag of the tug swerved back in. When the cart came back in that's when it collided with the van. Immediately as i see this take place i notified [a supervisor] over the radio and told him that an accident had just taken place. When he came over to my gate he asked (3) questions! Did i see what happened? What had taken place? Who was at fault? I then gave him the run down as to what had taken place. I went back to uploading and pushing out my flight. After [pushback] a supervisor was still at the gate and i asked him if he had wanted my statement in which he then told me that it was stated that there were no witnesses to this incident. He then took me to the office to write out my statement.
output: Ramp agent reported an accident between a catering van and a tug pulling a cart.

input: Somewhere outside civet we were cleared and i read back the civet 5 arrival, arrive runway(s) 25r. Somewhere after civet we were told to switch to frequency 128.5. I knew this was wrong. When we checkeded in the controller asked intermediate fix we were going to runway(s) 24r. I said no; we were cleared for runway(s) 25r. The controller said change to runway(s) 24r; frequency 108.5 and cleared for that runway(s) we did; no further incident. This happens way too often; and way too late in the arrival, arrive phase. We had an flight management computer that was slow to respond to our inputs; and on more than one occasion gave the message 'single flight management computer op' and 're-syncing other fmc.' this compounds to the problem as there are way too many intxns and step-down fixes to comply with in a logical manner when the flight management computer is slow and approach gives you last second changes to comply with.
output: B767-200 flight crew has clearance change in close during civet arrival, arrive to lax.

input: A b737 reported the airport in sight approximately 10 northeast of the airport. This caused an adjustment to the sequence from this aircraft being number 3 to it now being number 1 ahead of 2 other aircraft; one inbound from the west and the other inbound from the southeast. To ensure proper spacing on final; the b737 was instructed to 'maintain at or above 030 until base; turn base within 7 vor and dme (co-located) cleared visual approach runway 2'. As the b737 was reading back this clearance; another aircraft; a helicopter checked in on another frequency blocking the read back of the b737. To ensure the read back from the b737 was complete and accurate; i repeated the clearance and had the b737 repeat the read back. The helicopter was a visual flight rules helicopter; checking in over mcgregor point; inbound to ogg. I proceeded to issue the helicopter a squawk for radar identification. By the time the helicopter was radar identified; the b737 had started his base turn and was now head-on with the helicopter at the same altitude. When i attempted to re-restrict the b737; the aircraft did not respond. After another attempt; there was still no response. I then issued the helicopter the traffic and this aircraft reported the b737 in sight. I then called ogg tower and the tower said that the b737 was on their frequency. I advised the tower that the helicopter had the b737 in sight. This aircraft had gone over on its own. The main problem that led to this event; and many similar events that occur on a daily basis; is the fact that the procedures were established based on ogg approach operating as 2 different sectors. R9 is designed to work all arrivals and r10 is designed to work all departures. When working these positions combined; all instrument flight rules (both arrivals and departures) aircraft are on one frequency. This works well when all you have to work is instrument flight rules traffic. But this is hardly ever the case when working maui approach which is designated as class charlie airspace; requiring visual flight rules aircraft to check-in and establish communication prior to entering the airspace. You would think this would be enough to ensure visual flight rules aircraft stay away from the instrument flight rules aircraft operating in the charlie airspace; but not in the case of ogg approach; where the airspace just east of mcgregor point is not charlie airspace but is right along the final approach course. The issue is that an aircraft can be outside of the designated charlie airspace and still; because of the close proximity to final; be a factor for an instrument flight rules aircraft on a visual approach or even the instrument landing system runway 2. Because you never know when these aircraft are going to check in; they constantly block transmissions. The best recommendation is to have maui approach operate as 2 sectors from 9 am to 5 pm everyday when visual flight rules traffic is most likely to interfere with all of the arriving instrument flight rules traffic and frequency congestion and 'stepping on' and 'blocking' would be greatly reduced.
output: Hcf controller described a conflict event between an instrument flight rules and visual flight rules aircraft listing combined position procedures as a contributing factor.

input: April 2013 at station zzz1; mechanics changing # 8 main wheel assembly reported tang washer was missing when they removed the wheel. Back in december 2012; mechanic y and myself (mechanic x) changed the # 8 main wheel assembly. Installing and removal procedures [were] done in accordance with maintenance manual (mm) 32-41-01-2. It was late at night finishing; and the middle marker procedure was followed and no discrepancies were found. On short notice of the findings by zzz1; i was notified [approximately] five days later and i investigated to see if we may have missed the tang washer as found in the middle marker 32-41-01-2; page 19; item 8. I called our air carrier company representative who works with the vendor concerning [landing] gear assemblies. He gave me our company's receiving report which showed no abnormalities from the contract tire/wheel vendor as to the tang washer being left with the removed main wheel assembly. He informed me that i would need to check the shop report that the contract vendor keeps; that documents everything they found during the shop visit.i then contacted the contract vendor representative to get a copy of the shop report. The report on the tire wheel assembly was at an off-location and had to be retrieved. The following afternoon the vendor representative informed me that there was nothing mentioned about finding a tang washer during disassembly of the tire/wheel assembly [we had removed in december]. As a precaution; i had him check the shop report for the tire/wheel assembly just removed in zzz1; to make sure that somehow the tang washer was not left with the tire [that zzz1 mechanics had removed]. The wheel assembly we had installed in december also had a clean report. I do not remember the exact details of the main wheel change on the dc-10 in december 2012; but i do follow the middle marker on all work accomplished on any aircraft i work. It is not only required and company policy; but all aircraft have differences in the way they are built that it is necessary to consult the middle marker to keep the aircraft safe. I am answering this due to the incident brought up by management; i do not know exactly what happened to the missing part in question; however i will attempt to answer what may have happened somewhere. The tang washer probably stuck to the wheel bearing grease being removed and would end up on the wheel going into disassembly. [recommend] when removing the old wheel assembly; the wheel bearings should be wiped off and an inspection done to the wheel prior to installation of shipping caps. This would help to identify any other problems with the aircraft that may contribute to wheel change. Such as; flat spots on tire beyond normal wear; discoloration of heat shield; loose or broken beam rotator keys.
output: A line mechanic describes his efforts to locate a tang washer found missing from a # 8 main tire/wheel assembly he had previously changed on a dc-10 aircraft.

input: Jeppesen plate instrument landing system 5 orf. Note 3 towards top of page states: glideslope unusable for coupled approaches below 744 ft. input: During the preflt; i checkeded the cabin logbook to find no write-ups; but for some reason did not checked the aircraft maintenance log. I left that to the capt (my first mistake). He apparently looked at it quickly; but did not notice that there was an open write-up. The write-up was the outboard landing light on the left/right (directions) wing was inoperative it was left the night before for contract maintenance in phl. But for some reason it was never taken care of. We departed phl and proceeded en route to cleveland and didn't known about it until we arrived when maintenance came out to the aircraft to fix it and sign the book. Because no word ever made it to maintenance personnel the night before; there was not any indication on our flight release and flight plan regarding any minimum equipment list however; there is no excuse why we did not pick up on the write-up when there it was in black and white. I believe that complacency had a lot to do with the situation as well. Thank god it wasn't a serious write-up.
output: B737 departed phl with an open log item.

input: While climbing through fl360 to our assigned altitude of fl370 we encountered severe wake turbulence from a preceding md-11 aircraft; which was at an altitude of fl390 and on a diverging heading. Our aircraft suddenly made a violent left banking roll and pitched up. The bank exceeded approximately 30 degrees of roll. We also had momentary loss of aircraft control. I was the pilot flying and immediately disconnected the autopilot and had to aggressively apply pitch and roll input in order to get the aircraft back under control. We immediately contacted air traffic control to report the incident and to dispatch via automatic communications addressing & reporting system we also contacted the flight attendants to check their status of any injuries as well as the passengers. The flight attendants reported no injuries to themselves or the passengers. One flight attendant did report she had fallen on top of the passengers but was ok. Approximately 30 minutes later the same flight attendant notified us that she was not feeling well and wanted to get replaced once we arrived. We asked her if she needed any medical attention and she refused. We continued with no other issues. Once we landed i called dispatch; maintenance control; and the chief pilot on call. A logbook entry was made due to the severe wake turbulence.
output: B737 flight crew reported a momentary loss of control climbing through fl360 after encountering severe wake turbulence from an md-11 at fl390.

input: I had one of the aircraft owners in the cockpit and he was actually flying the airplane. We were on base to final turn on a visual approach. We had been descending at a fairly high rate about 1;500-2;000 feet per minute we were leveling off at about 1;500 feet above ground level when air traffic control notified us of a low altitude alert. I suspect it was caused by the high descent rate. There was no danger as we were already correcting.
output: A corporate pilot and the aircraft's owner were provided a low altitude alert from air traffic control the pilot suspects that it was due to a high descent rate.

input: Acr aircraft x; inbound flight xxxx; outbound flight yyy; jan/sun/05. Due to confusion on my part; the above mentioned acft/flt did not receive a required checked (daylight version). The normal scheduled equipment type is a b737-800. As per air carrier operations(s) bulletin xx-xx; which was issued jan/wed/05; the b737-800 no longer requires this checked unless it remained on ground for 5 hours or more. The next day (today; jan/mon/05); bulletin #yy-yy was issued which does away with the requirement for that checked when i realized that a mistake had been made; i notified my supvr.

input: In the course of completing the normal preflt of our b737-300; as well as the required paperwork; our release and all other paperwork indicated that this aircraft was equipped with cfm26-b2 engs. During the cockpit setup; information displayed in the control display unit indicated that the software was for b1-pwred engs. Given the preponderance of data which told us to expect b2 engs; this one entry on the computer display could easily be missed by crews operating this aircraft as i assume it was by the crew who brought this aircraft to mex. Our maintenance department indicates that some portion of our fleet has been equipped with a switch; which they can change from one engine rating to the other without having to complete extensive; time consuming procedures should a derating or engine replacement be necessary. Their supposition in this case is that this switch might have been inadvertently bumped and switched to the incorrect position this situation highlights the problems faced by today's airline crews utilizing advanced technology equipment which provides access to almost unlimited information but can; on occasion; provide incorrect data which affects safety of flight the perceived infallibility of this equipment (computers) leads to a complacency which could be fatal.
output: Capt of a b737-300 found the control display unit (cdu) set to the wrong engine problem caused by a switch used by maintenance when a slightly different model engine is installed.

input: While flying the localizer approach to runway(s) 10 ord; the page for the instrument landing system or localizer runway(s) 10 shows a final approach course of 093 degrees both capt and first officer had 093 degrees in the obs; 'man/exp' selected for the horizontal situation indicator the course deviation indicator was ctred and the track was showing 3 degrees off from the course line for the entire approach the winds were calm. During rollout; the track and course were still not overlayed. The track was indicating straight up (090 degs) while tracking runway(s) ctrline during rollout while the course was still 3 degrees off. Intermediate fix the course deviation indicator remains ctred up; the track line will be overlayed with the course line. The track information appeared to be accurate as confirmed with visual indications while lined up with the runway(s) in zero wind conditions. I have doubts as to the accuracy of the final approach course that is published.
output: B737 captain reports that the localizer course for runway(s) 10 at ord appears to be off by 3 degrees. 090 degrees appears to be the correct localizer course and runway(s) heading.

input: Acft engine abruptly quit following takeoff a glide was established and aircraft turned slightly left/right (directions) to land in another small lake. Just prior to landing power was restored by activation of the aircraft electric boost pump. The aircraft was close to the second lake surface and touched down momentarily; but with power restored; and due to the small size of the second lake; the aircraft was lifted off again. While the aircraft was being operated from its fullest tank; it is believed that the engine suffered from temporary fuel starvation due to unporting of the fuel tank line during step taxi prior to tkof.
output: Plt of an sma ambiguity single engine land aircraft made an unscheduled touch down on another lake than used for takeoff when the engine quit due to fuel starvation.

input: Upon landing gear extension on approach we received an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring caution for nosewheel steering. We executed a go around to evaluate the situation and completed the quick reference handbook follow-up for the nosewheel steering malfunction. I elected to have emergency equipment standing by for landing second officer we declared an emergency with approach i informed the flight attendants of the situation and to prepare for a precautionary landing as i was not anticipating the need for an evacuate/evacuation i also notified the passenber of the situation and assured them everything would be fine and after landing we would likely be stopping to be towed to the gate due the steering malfunction. Since the nosewheel steering fault was not accompanied by the shock absorber fault; the first officer and i felt confident the nosewheel was ctred and just the steering was faulted. Dispatch was acars'd of the situation and the station was notified via radio. As our fuel was at 5000 pounds we felt that with all procedures complied with; a complete discussion with dispatch and maintenance was not necessary or possible. The landing was made smoothly and i was able to taxi clear of the runway(s) using differential braking. I elected to have the aircraft towed in to the gate due to the close proximitypa of other aircraft in the gate area. I greeted the passenber on deplaning and all appeared in good spirits and many thanked us for a safe journey.
output: An a320 capt experienced an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring message for nosewheel steering after gear extension on approach. Flight crew declared emergency and continued to a safe landing.

input: Clrnc given to 'dsnd and maintain 1-0-thousand.' readback given: '1-0-thousand.' upon descending through 10600'; air traffic control stated 'your assigned altitude was 1-1-thousand;' and then clearance given to 10000'.
output: Flt crew understood 1-0-thousand. Controller corrected to 1-1-thousand.

input: Shortly after top of climb pilot not flying observed using 'rsv fuel' message on the flight management computer pilot not flying corrected performance page reserve fuel amount to comply with company policy. Center tank fuel pumps turned off at 1000 pounds quantity to comply with ad. 20 minute(s) later; pilot not flying observed imbalance of 400 pounds on left/right (directions) engine (#1) and commenced crossfeeding to balance fuel load. Fuel configuration returned to normal after wing tanks balanced. 15 minute(s) later pilot flying noticed imbalance on left/right (directions) engine (#2) of 800 pounds pilot not flying commenced crossfeeding to rebalance wing tanks. Pilot not flying also observed total fuel quantity decreasing at an abnormal rate and called for quick reference handbook chklist inflt engine fuel leak. Leak was confirmed by crew; but crew was unable to identify source. Diversion to zzz was initiated after contacting mx and dispatch of problem flight continued to zzz without incident. Upon landing and turn off for taxi; noticeable odor of fuel detected and engs immediately  shutdown. Fire crews notified crew of no fire or danger thereof; and aircraft towed to gate for passenber deplaning. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information maintenance determined that there was a leak from the hydro mechanical unit of the fuel control the hmu had recently been replaced. This was done because the carrier had noted that their engs had not been producing thrust per specifications. They determined that it was not caused by a software problem in the fuel control system second officer they were changing out of hmu's for investigation of the problem the reinstallation of the unit is apparently difficult and requires a special tool due to the location of some of the fasteners securing the unit. There have been other rpted incidents at the airline. One of these included an engine flame out. The flight crew was questioned about their apparent non compliance with the quick reference handbook procedures which included an engine shutdown. During simulations of the problem at their training facility it was determined that they; with the condition described; handled the situation appropriately.
output: Having difficulty with a fuel imbalance condition in a b737-800 the crew determines there may be a fuel leak at an unknown location. Diversion is accomplished and engs shutdown for a tow to the gate when fuel fumes are detected after lndg.

input: First officer (fo) entered flight deck for preflight. First officer immediately noticed musty odor on flight deck. Odor was not noticeable throughout rest of aircraft. First officer went to do walk around to check exterior for possible causes; and suspected odor may be gone upon return. The maintenance log was not on board. The first officer also noticed work being done in the forward avionics bay from terminal window prior to boarding the aircraft. This occurred after an equipment change on the sequence. Upon returning from the walk around; the odor was still present and very strong; but only on the flight deck. First officer asked flight attendants if they noticed any odors in the cabin; they agreed there were none. One flight attendant accompanied first officer back to flight deck to check for the odor. The flight attendant agreed that there was a strong old sock smell only on the flight deck. The first officer tried to gather more information about the aircraft by calling operations (ops) and maintenance to inquire as to the reason for the equipment change and the reason the maintenance log was not on board the aircraft. Ops did not have any information on the equipment change; and maintenance said they were working off some write-ups on the log but did not explain what they were. The captain was not yet on board; the first officer made a decision to report the odor to maintenance; hold off boarding and inform the flight attendants as to the issue. When the first officer reported the odor to maintenance via the maintenance frequency; the respondent asked the first officer if the auxiliary power unity bleed was on. The first officer responded that it was on. The respondent request the first officer turn off the auxiliary power unity bleed. The first officer immediately turned off the auxiliary power unity bleed. As soon as the auxiliary power unity bleed was turned off; the odor began to dissipate until it was barely noticeable within about 3 minutes. After the bleed was turned off; the first officer went to the top of the gate to inform the agent to hold off boarding. The captain was there printing paperwork. After being joined by the captain and maintenance representatives; the first officer promptly completed an odor report and sent it; as well as filled out a discrepancy in the maintenance log. The station chief pilot called the first officer and informed him the form was never received. The first officer resubmitted the odor form and it seemed to have went that time. The first officer also; at the request of the chief pilot; emailed screen shots of the report to the chief pilot and submitted report. The first officer did not follow the quick reference handbook for fumes due to being at the gate and having access to maintenance. If i had it to do again; i would have also pulled out the qrh.
output: A321 first officer reported musty odor in the flight deck during preflight; which was diagnosed; albeit without reference to the qrh.

input: A flight of two b52s were enroute to yuma range complexes r2306 and r2308 at fl350. We do not have a letter of agreement with yuma range control that would depict agreed upon altitudes for aircraft to enter the range control. Zab r65 called yuma range control to coordinate entry for the b52s flight. Yuma range had to call cibola range to coordinate. After coordination took place between with cibola and yuma; yuma called r65 and told us to have the b52s flight enter the range at or below fl300. R65 coordinated with r91 (r91 owns fl260 to fl330 and r65 owns fl340 and above) and after pointing out the aircraft to r91 they gave the b52s an altitude of fl280. B290; terminated the aircraft and put the b52s on cibola range control frequency. Cibola then descended the aircraft to fl250 without coordination. The b52 flight came within close proximity to a b737 descending to phx on the geela4 arrival. Recommendation: we need to have some sort of agreement with cibola range/yuma range that pertains to procedures entering and exiting the range. There should also be something put into place where there is no ambiguity on what range control has control for communication. Zab sectors also shouldn't have to go through a third party to achieve any kind of coordination that would result in an undue delay to these aircraft. There also seems to be a real issue with cibola range on what they control.
output: Zab controller voiced concern regarding the lack of formalized procedures with two military range operations; suggesting an letter of agreement be developed to clarify responsibilities.

input: Acft leveled at 10000 feet/foot with autoplt engaged. While slowing to 250 knot(s) was given a heading change and also a runway(s) change from runway(s) 1 to runway(s) 19. As aircraft was in turn; aircraft descended to 9500 feet/foot without an altitude warning from the altitude warning system disengaged autoplt and climbed back to 10000 feet/foot supplemental information from acn 370799: after finding the new approach plate all 3 crew members noticed simultaneously that our altitude was 9600 feet/foot the autoplt altitude capture had failed to arm. Contributing factors: momentary distraction of a runway(s) change given less than 1000 feet/foot from leveloff altitude crew fatigue due to inbound leg from europe. Xa00 rpt time for this flight this was day 3 of a 9 day pattern to europe which included 6 ocean xings.
output: Arr dc10 descends below assigned altitude when altitude automatic capture feature of the autoplt fails to level the aircraft at 10000 feet/foot flight crew was distraction with an amended clearance and a runway(s) change; retrieval of other approach plates.

input: I was working satellite at mci combined north and south (multiple freqs). Traffic was extremely heavy and the position should have been split in the interest of safety. A b190 took a descent clearance meant for c210 on another frequency i did not hear both aircraft respond to the clearance i had approximately 13-15 aircraft on frequency at the time with constant coordination from 4 different towers 1 approach control and 2 different zkc sectors. During this time; i was barely able to complete all work functions and had to tell multiple visual flight rules aircraft to call back later; yet management wouldn't open another position for relief. Another factor was staffing. We were extremely short staffed during this time.
output: Mci controller described event when readback was missed; allegedly because of staffing; combined positions and frequencies and traffic volume.

input: Outbound crew rpted to maintenance that aircraft would not take ground power (we were unaware of this issue.) while we were doing preflt checkeds i noticed the avionics door open below. I asked the first officer intermediate fix he knew what maintenance was doing. He was also unaware. I went downstairs to talk to mechanic he informed me of the ground power issue. I asked him intermediate fix we needed to write it up as we did not see a write-up. He said yes; and we did second officer after he did his checkeds he came to the flight deck to let us know he could not find any issues. He said that the ground power worked; our system showed no faults; and they could not find a reason why ground power could not be used. We informed him that we had no ground power light on overhead panel when plugged in; and questioned logic of why everything showed normal but we could not use ground power and questioned intermediate fix this could be an indication of some other problem in the electrical system we were not seeing. He said that he had checkeded all circuit breakers down below and ran all the tests on the system and ground power but would ask his supervisor our question. He came back and stated that the supervisor stated it was 'weird' but they were going to defer the ground power on aircraft as we were talking to the mechanic he got a call from maintenance (over his radio; as we could hear as he was sitting talking to us). Maintenance asked what he was doing. He stated; talking to the crew about the issue. At that point maintenance responded to him to release the jet; even though we were clearly not done discussing the issue. We told the mechanic we were not yet done and that he needs to work with us regarding this; as he was (the mechanic at the jet was very good to work with). Maintenance did defer the ground power and we took the jet. After pushback and after engine start (on a jet that just flew in) the #1 generator dropped off line. We reset; and the generator operations(s) normal. In cruise my radio; which had been operating properly; was unable to transmit although i could hear air traffic control loud and clear i was also unable to talk to the flight attendants through my radio. I tried both #1 and #2 on my side and could not transmit i checkeded to see intermediate fix headset was correctly plugged in -- it was. I checkeded all toggle switches on my side including the handheld microphone and still could not transmit -- all of them inoperative the first officer radio at that point worked; second officer he made radio calls. I sent an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message to dispatch to let them know and we informed air traffic control the first officer a few minute(s) later; could also not transmit he also tried #1 and #2 radio.
