I did not advise the passengers to leave all their belongings; but i did ask them to move in an orderly fashion and to stay close to the airplane. I did not contact ground services to help contain the deplaned passengers; though i did notice some ground personnel approaching the airplane soon after deplaning began.in retrospect; i wish i had made a more thorough deplaning announcement; but on the other hand; i am glad that i didn't waste much time in getting the people off the airplane. I also wish i had called for firefighters. After deplaning the passengers; someone asked me if i had called them. I answered no and he said he would do it for me.all company personnel were very helpful and professional.i have operated the auxiliary power unity with bleed air open and recirc fan off in the past for short spans of time to help communication in the flight deck (e.g. Getting a clearance; calling clp/dispatch) and have never gotten hot ducts or smoke in the cabin. Maybe this is a place to be more cautious in the future.i'm glad that i have spent time in the past thinking of how to handle emergencies at the gate. We don't have specific procedures for handling such events and we don't train them.there was a moment when i thought i could try to evacuate the smoke and continue with the operation in that airplane. That did not last long and i decided to get the people out right away. Maybe the lesson is; don't mess with smoke.this event was good practice in prioritizing tasks. My attention was consumed by four different mel's and talking with several different people about their part in dealing with the various pieces of malfunctioning equipment on the airplane. There were also communications problems as noted above. When the flight attendant said there was smoke on the plane; i had to drop all that and switch into a completely different mode. Without our training and time spent imagining various emergencies; it would have been harder to make this transition.
output: Bombardier q400 captain reported orderly evacuation due to smoke in the passenger cabin.

input: Gar was started on runway(s) 36l mem due to severe turbulence on short final at 300 feet/foot above ground level from a line of weather 10 mile north of the field. At approximately 1000 feet/foot above ground level a gain of 35 knot(s) and a red windshear warning was encountered; windshear escape maneuver applied and successfully exited the shear. Air traffic control assigned 030 degree heading and 3000 feet/foot this was into the storm and we were experiencing severe turbulence at the time. While struggling to control the aircraft we continued the turn to 180 degrees and elected to descend to 2000 feet/foot to exit the weather as soon as possible and return to stable flight notified air traffic control of the deviation we were obscured to air traffic control due to a transponder malfunction and the weather upon exiting the weather we had an uneventful landing to runway(s) 36r mem.
output: A b727 flight crew deviate from their clearance after experiencing severe turbulence and bad weather and after going around due to windshear.

input: While operating in the traffic pattern we were given a landing clearance while on downwind abeam the numbers on runway 2. We were told that we were number 3 for landing behind two cessna 172s on final. At this point we turned base and checked the final to identification our traffic ahead. We then cleared the extended final to our right and saw no conflicting traffic either way. We turned final and heard tower communicating with a c172 but we didn't hear the conversation because of instructional activity. After we turned final and began our final approach; tower asked us if we were on a one mile final behind another cessna. We saw a cessna ahead in the flare over the runway so we confirmed. The tower controller told us to go-around and to sidestep left of the runway. I added full power and sidestepped the runway to the left. As we climbed we suddenly saw a c172 climbing out of the right side window very rapidly. We were approximately 10-15 feet/foot laterally from the other aircraft. I continued the turn to clear the aircraft and then flew another normal traffic pattern to land. The student was on an initial solo. I spoke with the instructor and he advised me that the student had 60 hours of flight time and this was his first solo. He clearly had english comprehension issues. The ground controller advised us that he was having trouble understanding the instructions. It appeared as if the other cessna was on an extended straight in approach and that he was cleared as the number 4 aircraft behind us on base. He must have thought that he was supposed to follow the aircraft already on final and he did not look at the based to see if there was conflicting traffic. Spoke with the student and instructor on the ground to talk about collision avoidance and traffic pattern operations.
output: A c172 encountered a very near miss with another c172 on final approach at the airport.

input: This was a training flight for an instrument flight. We were reviewing vor and dme (co-located) holds from the ffu vor and dme (co-located) to the east. Altitude was 7;500 feet/foot mean sea level also we were on salt lake approach receiving traffic advisories. We initially got a call out for the other traffic; air traffic control advised us of the traffic south of our position we were a heading of roughly 270. The other traffic was also on radar with salt lake approach talking. The next call from air traffic control he recommended a turn to the south to avoid the traffic. I continued to look for the traffic and turned south bound. The next call from air traffic control was to turn to the south west to avoid the traffic. Once we reached a heading of roughly 220 a traffic alert from my twas system inside the aircraft came up for the first time for this aircraft; the target was directly on my position and indicating 0 feet of difference. At that same moment i spotted the aircraft to my left side same altitude less than 100 feet horizontally opposite direction. By the time i had seen the traffic their wing was slightly ahead mine; because of that there was no time to react and turn to the right. The other aircraft had seen me at the last moment and started a hard turn to there right to avoid. The other traffic advised air traffic control that they saw me and that we were very close. In my opinion if the other aircraft did not see me at the last moment there would have been a collision.
output: Two aircraft near ffu had a near miss at 7;500 feet/foot after salt lake approach control pointed out their mutual traffic and issued suggest headings but still neither aircraft saw the other until the last second.

input: Den ground instructed us to taxi to runway(s) 17l from e4 via mike; hold short of ed. Once on mike northbound ground instructed us to turn right at ed and hold short of the approach end of runway 17r. The first officer (first officer) was in the process of completing his delayed engine start flow as i started the turn on ed. At this point i noticed traffic on short final to runway 17r and thinking to myself that it didn't seem right to turn on ed. I stopped the aircraft as soon as it was straight and pointed east on ed. I asked the first officer if he saw a sign or hold short line on his side. I saw no signage in front of us and now felt extremely uncomfortable with our proximity to the runway 17r approach path. At this point the ground controller told us we were supposed to stop 50 ft. Further back. I looked behind us and noticed the left wing tip was over the east edge of taxiway mike. I could not see a hold line below the wing. We were switched to tower. The tower controller gave us a number to call for a possible pilot deviation. Shortly after writing down the number we were cleared for takeoff. As we rolled down the runway i realized we failed to complete the final items.i spoke to the tower supervisor later that day and explained the events as they occurred. He admitted that this hot spot is an ongoing issue; the hold area is not well marked and the controller's intent was to have us pointed east to help move aircraft through the runway 17r approach path faster. Unfortunately the tower had to send around the landing traffic i was distracted with during the turn because they were not sure if we would stop. I have flown in and out of den since the day it opened and have never been issued a clearance like this. I have always been instructed to hold short of ed when aircraft are landing runway 17r. I believe this type of clearance should be avoided; specially in an area that is a hot spot. The aircraft behind us which received the same clearance had to confirm the clearance and the intent to hold short immediately after turning.
output: Air carrier pilot crew reported ground control instructions and the charted version of this hotspot at den airport are confusing.

input: [we were on a] visual meteorological conditions ruudy 2 departure. Lateral navigation and vertical navigation engaged and approaching 1;500 feet/foot mean sea level for initial level off restriction. Some bit of turbulence (maybe?) caused the yaw damper and autopilot to disconnect. We overshot the restriction prior to the 'cross at 1;500 feet/foot msl' requirement. During the correction we overshot the descent back to 1;500 feet/foot mean sea level and finally corrected to 1;500 feet/foot mean sea level prior to the crossing restriction. The airspeed was around 270 knot(s) indicated air speed as the autothrottles didn't respond during the altitude corrections. Speed control became a factor and was corrected immediately to conform with requirements for altitude and airspace. No actual violations occurred during this event.
output: G450 flightcrew reports exceeding altitude and speed requirements during the ruudy3 with the autopilot engaged in lateral navigation and vertical navigation and autothrottles set for 200 kts.

input: I was conducting a part 91 day; visual flight rules flight from van nuys to san luis obispo. I pre-filed an instrument flight rules plan for an xa25 departure the weather was clear second officer i elected to depart visual flight rules without opening the instrument flight rules flight plan. After departing van nuys airport using runway(s) 16r; i turned downwind at 2000 feet/foot mean sea level and began a slow visual flight rules climb taking care to stay below 3000 feet/foot mean sea level until my global positioning system showed me clear of the burbank class celsius airspace that extends from 3000 feet/foot to 4800 feet/foot mean sea level over van nuys airport when i was about 3500 feet/foot mean sea level i contacted socal departure to obtain flight following to san luis obispo. After identing me on radar; the controller asked me intermediate fix i saw the md80. He then went on to explain that during my climb from van nuys; he expected me to remain at 2500 feet/foot mean sea level until north of the burbank localizer he explained that he turned an md80 that was on the instrument landing system to runway(s) 8 at burbank because i climbed above 2500 fi mean sea level before i was clear of the burbank localizer although i do not believe that i breached the overlying class celsius airspace; i believe that i did climb above 2500 feet/foot mean sea level before i was sufficiently north or the burbank localizer i believe that this situation occurred because i failed to make note and read back the instructions of the van nuys tower controller to stay at or below 2500 feet/foot mean sea level until north of van nuys airport this was aggravated by the fact that i did not attempt to contact the socal departure controller until several minute(s) into the flight had i been in communications with socal; i would have been reminded to remain at 2500 feet/foot until clear of the burbank localizer for the future; the air traffic control controller suggested that i request a transponder code from the van nuys tower prior to departure second officer that i can be identified on radar as soon as i ante meridiem airborne. Then; i should request a frequency change to socal before departing van nuys class d airspace second officer that i will be under positive air traffic control control before climbing out. I will take this suggestion to heart and plan to always be in contact with socal departure when departing the van nuys area.
output: Atc vectors an air carrier off the instrument landing system localizer to bur to avoid a departing aircraft from the vny airport; rptr climbed above the 2500 feet/foot clearance when north of vny; as instructed by vny tower prior to tkof.

input: While on a vector to intercept the final approach course; the first officer answered a call from the a flight attendant indicating that he detected a dirty socks smell in the passenger cabin and that he was feeling dizzy and lightheaded as a result and was very concerned for his health. We declared a medical emergency; requested paramedics meet our flight; and expedited the approach; landing and taxi in. While on approach; the first officer donned his oxygen mask; then i donned my mask. I observed that the first officer was holding his mask to his face (upon debriefing; i learned that while the first officer's oxygen mask provided 100% oxygen; the retraction function of the head straps failed to release from the donning/straps pressurized mode). Upon arrival at the gate; both air conditioning packs were shut off. The a flight attendant called the cockpit asking if we wanted the cabin doors open; i responded yes as the jetway had been connected to the aircraft; the report was that the passengers were aware of the fumes yet calm; the engines were shut down; (the open cabin doors would facilitate purging the fumes from the cabin). The paramedics arrived and examined the a flight attendant (and the entire crew later) after the passengers had deplaned. The crew conferred with maintenance and the station supervisor in a nearby conference room. Then the crew was transported to a hospital emergency room for examination and treatment if necessary. After release from the emergency room several hours later; the crew overnighted at a hotel and dead headed home the following day. We do not know the cause; twelve minutes transpired from the time of the initial call from the a flight attendant until parked at the gate. We suspect; through post flight debriefing; that the air contamination was delivered through the air conditioning system; possibly from engine bleed air. An international group of aircraft manufacturers; airline pilot; flight attendant; and maintenance engineer representatives; and medical research specialists should be assembled to study cabin air contamination issues; develop general procedures for flight crews to address such issues and ultimately employ design changes and maintenance procedures to eliminate cabin air contamination. During this research time; the traveling public should be informed and advised of the known hazards. Perhaps the traveling public should be informed of the possibility that smoke hoods can be purchased and carried on board airliners as a precaution. Regarding the failure of the first officer's oxygen mask headbands; i would suggest a test of that function be included in maintenance routine check procedures.
output: Emb190 captain is informed by the a flight attendant that he detected a dirty socks smell in the passenger cabin and that he was feeling dizzy and lightheaded. A medical emergency is declared to expedite landing; and the crew was transported to a hospital emergency room for examination. The first officer's oxygen mask head strap malfunctioned.

input: A heavy jet was on visual approach to runway 8r straight in on about 10 mile final. This aircraft was being worked by final center sector. Aircraft x was on the downwind for runway 8l. I was conducting training on final north as he turned aircraft x south bound for the visual approach; [trainee] told aircraft x that there was traffic on the south runway. When aircraft x said field in sight [trainee] cleared him for the visual approach without giving him the 30 degree turn to final and the pilot flew past the final and got in the wake remnant of aircraft y.next time i will ensure that my trainee understands the importance of the 30 degree turn to final to prevent this situation from happing again.
output: I90 terminal radar approach control facility controller's trainee did not use proper procedures to ensure wake turbulence separation between successive arrivals.

input: During flap retraction from 5 degree to 2 degree amber leading edge flap light remained on. Visibility inspection confirmed #5 leading edge device on left/right (directions) wing extended. Decision was made to go to mco because of fuel and altitude considerations. With air traffic control concurrence; fuel was dumped second officer as to arrive mco at maximum landing weight approach and landing at mco were normal. Visibility inspection on post flight found fuel access door open and locked. Company maintenance at mco released aircraft after functional checked of leading edge devices. Fuel door appeared closed after fueling; maybe install warning light on fuel door access panel.
output: After takeoff air carrier lgt finds it cannot retract a portion of the leading edge device because it is blocked by an open fuel access door.

input: During preparation for arrival at lax the automatic terminal information service was reporting winds that resulted in a 9.4 tailwind component for landing. Subsequently a special weather automatic terminal information service observation was reported and the winds including gust factor brought the wind over the 777 tailwind landing limitation of 10kts. When we checked in with la center; we advised them we would be needing a landing to the east due to the winds. They acknowledged our needs and after a little while came back and told us that lax was landing west and would not change the configuration; what was our alternate. After that they turned us up to the northwest until we could come up with a plan. As we were proceeding to the northwest; air traffic control came back to us with winds that were below limits; told us lax was considering changing to an east flow; so they turned us around and we continued towards lax. We flew the standard terminal arrival route and planned for a normal landing on runway 24r; with a tailwind that was approaching but did not exceed our limits. While descending on the downwind leg; the approach controller advised us that he heard we had a problem landing with a tailwind; so they were planning to switch us to 25l as it is a longer runway. I informed him that the problem we had is an aircraft limitation; not a runway length issue. He told me that that he understood; but the winds had been blowing out of the east all day and most of the day above 10kts. He said he would switch us to the 25l; clear us for the approach and when the tower gives us a landing clearance; if the wind exceeded our tailwind limits; they would plan for our go around. Subsequently we were cleared to land and the winds were in excess of our tailwind limits and so a go around was executed. During the go around we were advised that we would be taken out to catalina to hold for a bit; before being brought back for another approach. When i queried the controller about which approach; i was told for runway 25l. I told him that the problem is the wind; not the runway length and he understood and told me that the lax had considered turning the airport around 'however; they had too many airplanes on the ground waiting to depart to the west'. I didn't say anything about that comment; however i was dumbfounded! Not only about the priority of aircraft on the ground vs. Aircraft in the air; but also the fact that so many flights were landing and departing while exceeding the 10 kt. Tailwind limitation that i know many; many; aircraft have! We continued with vectors toward catalina and prepared for landing at ontario; as we were running low on fuel and decision was going to be required shortly. Ontario had winds out of the east as well; however they were landing to the east; so there was no problem landing there. Approach gave us that the latest automatic terminal information service and the winds were acceptable on the automatic terminal information service we asked if he could find out what the tower was presently 'calling' the winds and he responded that his supervisor told him that all he could give us are automatic terminal information service winds and that there were no gusts at the present time. Again; we were a bit taken back by the fact that we couldn't get as much information as we needed to make a decision. However; with the information we were given; we had just enough fuel for one more shot at landing lax to the west; so we headed toward sli; were vectored into sequence and made our approach and landing at lax; with no further reports of wind that exceeded our limitation. After we landed; as we taxied in toward the gate we observed a 737 executing a go around as well. It seems to me as lax was having a weather event day (not just a diurnal wind reversal); that the airport should have been turned around for an east configuration long before our arrival and that there should have been a greater emphasis on the needs of the aircraft in the air; over the aircraft on the ground. It appears that air traffic control (tower controller) declined to provide aircraft in the air with priority over those on the ground. That too many flights were accepting landing and take-off clearances with winds exceeding what i believe to be the 10 kt tailwind limitation that most aircraft are required to observe. That human nature to continue to accept the unacceptable or the inertia to continue to do what we have been doing; as to change things would require too much effort; or otherwise be disruptive.better education of air traffic control controllers as to the fact that most aircraft have a 10kt. Tailwind limitation and once winds exceed 5kts and are forecast to either exceed the 10kt. Limit; or are going to continue approaching the limit; the airport should be turned to operate into the wind. Pilots need to be better aware of tailwind situations and should be more proactive in refusing to land or takeoff when tailwinds exceed aircraft limitations.
output: B777 captain reported lax and sct controllers would not change the runway landing direction even though the winds had been from the east all day and were exceeding the 10 knot tailwind limit for most aircraft.

input: During final brief; i was interrupted by staff while briefer gave the local sequence and i missed 700 feet/foot overcast we have had strong visual meteorological conditions the past week and got complacent with what appeared to be another 'clr' morning with 10 mile visibility. At 700 feet/foot i entered clouds until 1500 feet/foot after takeoff normally i'm able to reach oak tower for the standard instrument flight rules clearance day or night -- ifr/vfr. This was a serious mistake; especially given the airspace. Although it was early; it could have had serious consequences. I've been jumping back and forth as a mechanic ground instructor; and flight inspector and need to settle down in my pilot duties and get back to basics.
output: C421 pilot takes off visual flight rules from hwd; ca; when weather conditions require an instrument flight rules flight plan and clrnc.

input: Coplt flying. Takeoff on runway(s) 13 whitestone climb turned left/right (directions) to 175 degree heading i noticed the coplt did not show a vor and dme (co-located) after i turned the air conditioning packs on. I dialed in the correct frequency 113.1 and vor and dme (co-located) read 4.0 vor and dme (co-located) he started left/right (directions) turn to 040 degrees when departure said to tighten the turn and roll out on 360 degree heading my vor and dme (co-located) was set to bwz 114.2. The flight management system was set up prior to taxi; he must have changed frequency between initial taxi and takeoff attention was on takeoff with no pack on at maximum gross weight for rwy.
output: An air carrier mlg crew failed to follow the whitestone standard instrument departure properly.

input: I got the briefing for operational supervisor/controller in charge (os/cic) and went on break; after i had taken radar from the previous controller; i got a phone call from the pilot of aircraft x. I took down the information he gave me about an event that took place earlier. He informed me that earlier that evening he was doing an instrument landing system approach into rvs visual flight rules and was switched to advisory frequency. He said the approach controller then vectored aircraft y to the same runway instrument flight rules  from what i gathered from the information; i thought that the helicopter was not being provided instrument flight rules separation services. He said that he was inbound on the approach and decided to break off the approach and was nearly missed by aircraft y who was closing in behind him. He said that when aircraft y checked on advisory frequency; there was not enough time for him to respond with a position report. Brief all controllers on the appropriate procedures for having an instrument flight rules aircraft being vectored for the visual approach behind a visual flight rules aircraft conducting the instrument approach into an uncontrolled airport.
output: A tul tracon controller reported of a helicopter that was on an approach being followed by a jet. The helicopter elected to break off the approach because of the close proximity. The controller wanted the facility to brief all controllers on the appropriate procedures for having instrument flight rules aircraft vectored for the visual approach behind visual flight rules aircraft.

input: Level at 16;000 ft just north of zzzzz intersection we observed traffic on traffic alert and collision avoidance system below and to the left of our position; climbing at a high rate. Air traffic control never informed us of any traffic in our vicinity. Within seconds; we received a resolution advisory to descend. The captain immediately started to comply with the traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution and started a descent until clear of conflict. I; as the pilot monitoring; tried to immediately notify air traffic control of the conflict; but i was unable to for about five to ten seconds due to radio congestion. As soon as possible; i notified center that we were descending to comply with traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution. It seemed that air traffic control was not even aware of the traffic in our vicinity otherwise he may have given us at least an indication that there was another aircraft climbing towards us. Center then asked us what kind of resolution it was and at what altitude we had descended to; to which i replied a descent resolution and 15;000 ft. We were then handed to approach and continued the visual approach without further incident.
output: The flight crew of a 737 reported the need to comply with an resolution advisory to avoid an airborne conflict that air traffic control was seemingly unaware of.

input: We received a 'wheels up' time with our clearance in las. As we followed another air carrier twin jet to runway(s) 1r; i could see we were approaching our wheels up time. Clear skies with unlimited visibility and a brisk north wind prevailed at the airport after an air carrier landing the tower operator cleared the twin jet in front of us into position and in what seemed to be the same breath; cleared him for takeoff and me into position as i taxied into position behind the departing jet; i could see another jet on a 3 or 4 mile final approach to this runway(s) 1r). In a panicky voice; the tower operator cleared me for takeoff before the traffic down the runway(s) lifted off; advising me that he would be turning east and i westbound i at least waited until the traffic in front of me lifted off before beginning my takeoff an uneventful takeoff ensued. I appreciate what i hope seemed to be an attempt to meet our wheels up time by the controller however to do it over again; i would have refused clearance onto the runway(s) until there was a sufficient interval between the departure or after the arrival, arrive had landed. I have noticed a tendency to squeeze departures (more than arrs) together at las and phx. The pressure of expediting the takeoff combined with decreased performance of jet aircraft at high density altitudes makes for a very uncomfortable situation at times. For everyone's sake; departures and arrs should be staggered. We're not in that much of a hurry!
output: Operational error. Tower local controller cleared acr-mlg for takeoff before preceding acr-mlg had crossed end of runway(s) and did not advise mlg of traffic on final within 6 miles per 7110 pt 65.

input: I was working controller in charge on the mid shift. An a319 was handed off from zse to p80 via other-than-coordinated routing and altitude. I became aware of the unusual event when the hood controller said the a319 was level at 13;000 feet/foot in a 13;400 feet/foot minimum vector altitude hood verified the aircraft's assigned altitude and the pilot confirmed they were assigned 13;000 feet/foot and cleared direct bonvl; which is a fix on the bonvl6 standard terminal arrival route the a319; by the zse/p80 letter of agreement should have been cleared via the bonvl6 arrival landing west which involves crossing bonvl at 10;000 feet/foot at 250 knots indicated airspeed the routing assigned by the center controller appeared to not be on the arrival routing but rather a radar vector. Once the hood controller verified the a319's altitude he asked the pilot to maintain separation from terrain and obstructions; and the pilot concurred. Once the aircraft was over the next lowest minimum vector altitude 6;200 feet/foot the hood controller vectored and descended the a319 for a visual approach at pdx. I called zse several minutes later to inquire about the a319's clearance. The controller responded with direct bonvl and assigned 13;200 feet/foot i told them the a319 had descended to 13;000 feet/foot and that our minimum vector altitude was 13;400 feet/foot i am not sure of what the center actually gave the a319 for altitude or routing; all i know is he was going direct bonvl off the arrival and descended below our minimum vector altitude without pointing fingers this appears to be a case of 'mid rules' where the center has a common practice of clearing arrival aircraft; especially those landing pdx; via other than letter of agreement routing without coordination. Most of the time this is not a problem; but in this case even if the a319 had been issued 13;200 feet/foot they would still be below p80's minimum vector altitude and on other than expected routing. This put the hood controller in a stressful and uncertain situation and the aircraft in unsafe proximity to terrain. My recommendation is for zse to follow the letter of agreement regardless of what time of day it is; and if aircraft are routed otherwise to coordinate it; because we almost never unable their requests. Appreq's are fine with me all the time but aircraft below mva's is not.
output: P80 controller described a below minimum vector altitude event during late night operations involving an arrival routed via an non-standard clearance. The reporter suggested all routing be pre-approved if other than letter of agreement standards.

input: Just prior to gate departure the security coordinator for my flight from cdg-dfw brought up the security form for my signature. I asked as to the number of selectees; intermediate fix any; on my flight and was told he did not have to tell me. I again asked since he did not have to tell me the number of selectees aboard my flight would he tell me and had been told not to tell the capt the number of selectees on board the flight i cannot read his name from the form; but his employee number is xyz. As the inflt security coordinator; i feel this is important information which the security coordinator should know as to the security situation on his specific flight intermediate fix someone attacks my door or passenber (crew in flt); i would like to know intermediate fix there are any individuals present who could be accomplices. Why are the capts not being told of the number of selectees on their flts?
output: A b767 capt rpted his dissatisfaction at not having complete information regarding his flight before dep.

input: Rejected takeoff due to slow loss of #1 engine power likely caused by faulty fuel control unit from preliminary maintenance 'look.' just prior to v1/vr loss of power on #1 engine became evident/signaled by engine failure caution light. Capt called abort and took control of aircraft engine reversers and wheel braking normal application brought aircraft to a controled stop on the runway(s) supplemental information from acn 487687: we stopped on the runway(s) and taxied clear at the end of the runway(s) called for fire coverage to inspect the brakes and had the aircraft towed to the gate. Supplemental information from acn 487690: had emergency equipment follow.
output: A b727 crew aborts their takeoff when the #1 engine rolls back associated with an engine fail caution light at atl; ga

input: During landing roll; air traffic control clrd us to the ramp via runway(s) 19 and charlie taxiway due to operational consideration we exit the runway(s) at taxiway just past runway(s) 19 and turn sw on parallel taxiway and south on runway(s) 19. We did not see any taxi signs. Preceeding down runway(s) 19 and halfway down air traffic control informed us it was closed. Air traffic control then advised us to cross runway(s) 33 and proceed to the ramp. First of all; it was a bad time to advise us when and where to taxi. The taxiway sign was obscured by snow. Runway(s) 19 was closed due to snow; but was clear as the txwys. I feel better communications between air traffic control and pilot are needed. More federal air marshal trips would help when the weather is bad.
output: Acr mlg followed wrong route to ramp and taxied on close rwy.

input: While returning to 0w3 to land in a glider i noticed that parachutists were maneuvering directly over and west of runway 01/19 which the majority of traffic was using. It is my understanding that the agreement with the parachute operation on the field is that parachutists will maneuver east of 01/19 and land on a target which is east of that runway. The wind favored 01. I was at an altitude of approximately 1200' above ground level but in heavy; (600'/minute); sink. I orbited approximately 1/2 mile west of the airport in the hope that the parachutists would be able to clear the runway environment; and that i would be able to land. After 2 turns in that area my altitude was approximately 800' above ground level and i had to turn for the runway. I attempted to stay as high as possible and displace left of the centerline of runway 01 by about 100' in order to stay as clear of the parachutists as possible. At that time i transmitted on 122.8 that i was on a left downwind leg for 01 attempting to steer clear of the canopies that i could see; but that they were maneuvering west of the runway; and i didn't have enough altitude to modify my pattern and land downwind. I understand that parachutists don't have radios; but i hoped someone on the ground might be able to wave them back to the east side of the runway; or otherwise communicate with them. Someone; presumably a jump pilot; retorted on frequency that i didn't need to avoid any canopies and everything would be ok. As i crossed aldino rd south of the runway at approximately 200' above ground level a tandem parachutist slightly below me; and over runway 01; turned west and directly into my flight path. The parachute pilot was wearing a black; or very dark; jumpsuit and a black helmet. He flew along and over the hangars west of the runway then turned back to the east and toward the drop zone. I continued left of centerline toward a point where i hoped i would be able to 'sidestep' right with my remaining altitude and land on the last part of 01. The parachutist; (who must have seen me on his first turn due to the close proximity of my glider with his parachute); then turned sharply back to the west and into my flight path again. I turned left to avoid him and my right wing tip passed within 40 feet of his shrouds at about 100 feet above ground level  after passing the parachutist i deployed full air brakes and slipped aggressively to get the glider on the ground on the very northern part of runway 01.
output: A glider pilot landing at 0w3 reported taking evasive action at 100 feet to avoid a parachutist by 40 feet on final to runway 1.

input: On clbout out of msy while deviating around thunderstorms we were initially cleared to fl230. The clearance was changed to fl180; then fl190. The controller asked us to fly a 050 degrees for takeoff and weather which we did for a short time. Because of weather on that heading; we needed and asked for a 030 degree heading established on that heading; we heard another flight on the frequency the controller called that traffic out to us at 10-11 o'clock position at fl190. We repeated we were level at fl190. The controller came back with immediate instructions to fly heading 070 degrees and descend to fl180. We complied with those instructions. We never saw the traffic either visually or on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii we did not take evasive action only followed the controller's instructions.
output: A dc9-50 flight crew was given an immediate descent and heading to avoid conflicting traffic near msy. Separation was never lost.

input: After taking off; the left main gear did not retract. We leveled off at 2000 feet per clearance; advised departure of our problem and the first officer (pm) began to run the checklist. We did not declare an emergency; we were vectored on a right downwind for landing. [it] seemed very quick; we were told to turn on a right base; but we were just finishing up our checklist so requested to extend some. We were informed we were approaching [another airport's] airspace and need to turn base. (we did not seem that close at the time; but i was a bit distracted.) we turned base and began to complete the normal cruise; descent; approach and before landing checklists. I felt rushed because of the vectoring; and would have liked a minute or two to sit back and review what we had done to confirm we had not missed anything. In hindsight; we did complete all of our required checklists correctly. I let myself be rushed by air traffic control they did not seem to be aware that abnormal checklist take time to complete and we still have the normal duties involved with flying the airplane and communicating with air traffic control and flight attendants. I also could have asked for a 360 degree turn or two to give me time to review what we had done. If air traffic control would have been aware of the time we needed; only an additional two or three minutes; the whole procedure would have been more comfortable for the flight crew. I should have told them or they could have asked.
output: An atr-72 captain reported feeling rushed by air traffic control during vectoring for a return to land because of a landing gear that would not retract.

input: While practicing emergency procedures in the traffic pattern; a landing gear failure was experienced on the third landing on the first approach the circuit breaker for the landing gear was pulled. The gear was let down with the emergency handle. The circuit breaker was pushed in but 'popped' out after 2 or 3 seconds. The second approach was performed to confirm the circuit breaker would not pop again before we continued training. On the third approach the gear deployed normally and was confirmed with the indicator light; a visual outside the aircraft and a lack of warning horn; the landing gear collapsed on touchdown and no injuries occurred. The airplane suffered very little damage and no property damage was observed. Supplemental information from acn 446807: the circuit breaker for the landing gear was pulled; and the gear was let down with the emergency handle. The circuit breaker was pushed in but 'popped' out after 2 or 3 seconds. Second approach was performed to confirm the circuit breaker would not pop again before we continued.
output: A cessna cardinal 177rg had the landing gear collapse on landing at 50r.

input: As required; prior to pushback; i checkeded the aircraft surfaces for contamination. I determined that de-icing was required. Very light drizzle; or mist; was falling with a rpted temperature of 31 degrees fahrenheit. The first officer and i agreed that both type i and type ii de-ice fluids would be used. The aircraft was de-iced using these fluids; with an application time of xa43. The first officer and i determined that due to the very light intensity; the 'holdover time' would be 20 minute(s) therefore; the 'holdover time' would expire at xb03. During taxi for takeoff the precipitation stopped for a time; and began again. The length of this cessation was not measured by the flight crew and we did not change our 'holdover time.' some air traffic delays were incurred prior to takeoff as required the first officer performed a 'pretkof chk' within 5 minute(s) of our takeoff at xb03; we received clearance for 'pos and hold' on runway(s) 13. (at takeoff the aircraft was free of contamination.) our takeoff roll began after xb03; approximately xb04; and therefore our original 'holdover time' had expired. The flight to destination orf was routine.
output: Acr mlg performs takeoff after deicing 'holdover time' expires.

input: When the move team pulled the aircraft to the gate; the first thing i noticed was a nonstandard fuel panel configuration. Both right fuel pumps were on and displaying a fault and the cross feed valve was open. There were multiple electronic centralized aircraft monitor (ecam) cautions related to the right fuel pumps faults and low pressures as right wing fuel tank was completely empty. The plane also had a 10000-pound fuel imbalance...all fuel was in the inner tank of the left wing. First problem is; how did this happen? Second problem; was a checklist even followed by the move team? To have such an abnormal fuel configuration should be a red flag to anyone with the slightest knowledge of airplane systems. I talked with maintenance control and had a mechanic come out to see the condition the plane was brought to the gate in and to help the fueler with the imbalance. That mechanic indicated the plane should not have been moved with all the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring cautions and the extreme imbalance...both things i cannot confirm to be true; but i would not have taxied the plane in this configuration.
output: A319 captain reported that the electronic centralized aircraft monitor; electronic centralized aircraft monitoring indicated a massive fuel imbalance: captain questioned the tow procedures under such a state.

input: I was notified july 2012; that bearings were incorrectly installed on (4) b747-400 main tire/wheel assemblies; inboard side. Four; b747-400 main tires were built in july 2012. Two have been located and brought to the shop and two remain out in the system. The one tire assembly that i worked on has not been verified with wrong bearing; but all four were built on the same day.
output: Two tire shop mechanics were informed that four b747-400 main tire/wheel assemblies that were built-up in their shop; were found with incorrect wheel bearings installed on the inboard side.

input: On a classic high speed descent executing the sls one arrival, arrive descending to 2000 feet/foot by sigas; aircraft began to lose cabin pressure at rates of 2000-3000 feet/foot this was preceded by loud air noise in the cockpit. No engine indicating and crew alerting system message or aural warnings; switched to mode 2 with no effect. Then went to manual with no effect. I was hand flying and becoming preoccupied with the problem fly the airplane stupid. I settled approximately 100 feet/foot below 2000 feet/foot also missed the transition altitude of 4000 feet/foot reset at 29.77. Now almost 300 feet/foot low. Corrected immediately...still confused at prob...decided that no threat existed other than discomfort and ears popping. Pressed on and landed without any further attempt at a correction. On ground flight attendants said a lot of air noise and curtains waving. No complaints from passenber wrote up in log. Mechs could not duplicate. Aircraft went to dfw and was tracked; no problem i figure the air/gnd logic change cured the problem for now. Could not understand the problem with no engine indicating and crew alerting system i do not believe it was airframe. Either fault with outflow or ee cooling. Moral to story: capt designates who will work the problem and who will fly the aircraft seems i've heard that somewhere before; about 500 times.
output: B757 aircraft in high speed descent started losing cabin pressure. Flight crew attempted to control it to no avail. The distraction resulted in descent below assigned altitude aircraft checkeded by mechs and no known cause found.

input: We departed dfw and retracted the gear and heard a loud bang in the nose gear area and lost system #1 hydraulic pressure and fluid. We declared an emergency and ran the appropriate chklists. We did not land overwt. We stopped on the runway(s) and waited for maintenance to arrive. While on the maintenance frequency i told a female our problems and a male got on frequency and told us to taxi off the runway(s) he insisted that we could even though we could not. I then got the capt on frequency to tell the man we could not taxi. He then realized that we were an f100. The bottom line was the 2 people in maintenance did not communicate and then would not accept my request.
output: F100 crew had nose gear retract mechanism failure which resulted in main hydraulic system failure while departing dfw.

input: Climbing out of den on the spazz departure off runway 17r; climb via except maintain 10;000 ft. Hand flying. Approaching 10;000 ft; controller gave us direct spazz. Turned the aircraft and then controller called traffic one o'clock; ten miles; i thought i heard him say 'out of 11'. I thought it odd that he'd turn us towards a descending aircraft and proceeded to slow the climb. As we looked for traffic i made a remark to the first officer that i 'didn't like this'. As we were looking for traffic i may have climbed slightly above 10;000 ft. Controller then said '(call sign) verify you're climbing to 11;000 ft.' thinking i'd screwed up; i immediately raised the nose and started the aircraft towards 11 when the controller corrected himself and said '10;000 ft'. At that time we were about 10;350 ft. First officer and i looked at each other and there was an immediate discussion about what we were cleared to since the next waypoint we would've had was raydr; which is at or below 10;000 ft but once turned off the standard instrument departure that shouldn't have applied. The aircraft was headed back down to 10;000 ft when we acquired and called the traffic. Controller then gave us a turn to 120 degrees. Started the turn and controller then gave the 'possible pilot deviation call this number'. When we got to [our destination] we called. Air traffic control said the controller's instruction was 'direct spazz; maintain 10;000 ft.' neither of us recalled hearing the 'maintain 10;000 ft' and post meridiem responded with 'direct spazz' with no altitude mentioned. They also claimed we'd not leveled off at 10;000 ft and got as high as 10;500 ft; and that we were at 10;300 ft when the controller queried us. They did acknowledge that the controller did say 11;000 ft at first and then corrected himself. They said that since we had the aircraft in sight; there wasn't a conflict but they would have to pass it up for review and would get back with us. I believe this was more of a controller error because when he asked us to verify we were climbing to 11;000 ft set the stage for the confusion that followed.
output: Pilot reports of a confusing transmission and instruction to climb to a different altitude then assigned and then descend back to the previously assigned altitude.

input: On a vectored climb we were deviating around thunderstorm cells with high precipitation we went between 2 cells using our weather radar. We encountered a severe updraft that climbed us 2000 feet/foot in 40 seconds. We notified air traffic control encountered another cell within 10 minute(s) as we tried to navigate, navigation through this area. Second incident; an updraft took us 1000 feet/foot up in less than 5 seconds. Both events decoupled the autoplt. We cleared the area and no other incidents of severe weather were encountered. Postflt revealed some minor nose cone damage from small hail.
output: Citation ce560xl flight crew encounters severe turbulence during which caused a deviation from assigned alt.

input: #4 first officer window cracked inflt. Pulled out the quick reference handbook window damage chklist and identified it to be the outer pane. 'no restrs' except for window heat off and dialed up land altitude to 10000 feet/foot and proceeded without further event. Later we discovered that the middle pane had cracked and not the outer as we suspected. It is very difficult to identify which window pane is cracked from viewing the windows from inside the cockpit. Suspect a previous bird strike on this window may have caused weakening and subsequent cracking.
output: B737-700 first officer window cracked during flt.

input: In cruise at fl380; 37nm northeast of tunto (on a590) we passed below an opposite direction b-747 at fl390. Shortly after passing; we encountered wake turbulence of a moderate degree. The airplane shuddered and then rapidly rolled approximately 20 degrees right. The autopilot commanded a left roll to counteract; but then kicked off. The captain assumed control and steered us away from the wake. There was no altitude deviation or loss of separation. Dispatch; maintenance control and air traffic control all notified of event after we returned on course. Aml entry was made as a precaution; even though no limitation exceedence of any kind was observed. [the cause was the ] 1;000 foot rvsm separation and the direct tailwind that washed the wake directly over us.
output: Md-11 flight crew reported encountering wake turbulence that resulted in a 'rapid roll' from opposite direction b747 1;000 ft above their altitude of fl380.

input: While training in radar; flights of military fighters were inbound to runway x. I was letting the trainee run with his plan. I asked him how many miles we need between non-standard flights. He said 3; i said 4; and the controller in charge concurred. During the session the two flights were both getting close to 4 miles of separation with the preceding aircraft. Both times i had the trainee break the flights out to re-sequence. During debrief we looked up 7110.65; 5-5-8.c. The phrasing is such i'm not sure what the separation should be. I've asked different controllers and management and gotten different answers. More research is being done. Recommendation: the paragraph needs to be rewritten.
output: An approach controller providing on-the-job training experienced an operational deviation allegedly due to the less than clear separation standard listed in the 7110.65 regarding flights and the procedures required.

input: Aex; runway 32; pilots and tower controller. Received a take off clearance with a heading 180 degree instruction that was very unusual for direction of flight. We were heading east; and always received some heading north-by-northeast. Flight crew queried heading instruction and was told by air traffic control heading 180 degrees was for traffic in the area. First officer read back: 'aircraft x; cleared for take off; runway 32; fly heading 180 degrees; climb and maintain 10;000 ft.' tower did not correct the read back. I think tower responded affirmative; giving us the mindset; that a right turn to heading 180 was correct. Departure provided vectors for and a clearance to proceed enroute. Departure then asked us to call them once we landed. We were told the take off clearance was to make a left hand turn; not a right hand turn on course. Cause; the left turn was a turn away from our intended departure direction. This was very unusual for aex. Suggestions; 1. Flight crew to be provided with direction of other traffic; to put us in the situational awareness loop; i.e. 'traffic northeast; on departure; turn left heading 180. 2. Controller catching and/or requiring; or expecting left/right read back due to unusual direction of turn. 3. Controller in tower seeing us on his scope turning the wrong direction; and correcting if able. 4. Pilot not flying reading back left turn 180 or right turn 180. 5. When controller heard read back of heading 180 from pilot not flying to query and ascertain intentions were to turn in the correct direction.
output: Air carrier departure from aex was issued an unexpected turn for traffic; the direction of the turn not clarified resulting a possible airspace incursion.

input: After returning from my rest break in the cabin; i was informed by the capt that the weather radar was not functioning properly and that they were talking to dispatch about routing to sbgl. I inquired and was told by the other first officer that dispatch was confident that we could avoid thunderstorm activity in the vicinity of 10's latitude intermediate fix we rerted on a different airway to the east i advocated continuing to sbgl as the path of least risk; considering the fact that the sun would be rising in about 2 hours heading sbound and that we were already almost 1/2 way there; and turning around and returning to iad (our only other option) would put us in night flight the rest of the flight and take us through areas of thunderstorms we had already passed through. The capt decided to return to iad. We returned to iad without further incident.
output: B767-300 crew returned to their departure airport after the weather radar malfunctioned. They were in the intertropical convergence zone in tncf airspace.

input: Our aircraft was on a regular training flight the student being on one of the last flts before his private pilot checked ride. We were performing a diversion from cuyamaca lake to on the rocks private airport a common diversion frequently chosen by local examiners for the checked ride. Not more than 1 minute(s) after overflying on the rocks; i noticed a high wing retractable gear aircraft emerge from below us; headed towards our 1-2 o'clock position horizontal separation between the 2 aircraft must have been non-existent; vertical separation couldn't be more than 50 feet/foot since at that point the 2 aircraft were on diverging course; no evasive action was taken from our side; we remained south of see loc-d contacted see tower appropriately; and conducted a safe landing at see runway(s) 27l. On tower frequency we heard an aircraft reporting an near midair collision and after verifying the visual features of that aircraft match with our observation we confirmed our aircraft was the other plane involved in the incident. Weather conditions at the time of the incident were visual meteorological conditions no clouds; visibility p6sm. We were communicating on frequency 122.75 megahertz the common traffic advisory frequency for the san diego practice areas. No evasive actions had been taken from my side; since by the time i had visual contact with the other aircraft it was 'already too late.' corrective actions: 1) in the future i will exercise extra caution when crossing any instrument flight rules approach path; and in the immediate vicinity of these approachs 2) i will try to fly well clear (above or below -- airspace and terrain permitting) of the approach altitudes 3) when flying in these areas i will consider monitoring the appropriate air traffic control frequencies (in case dual radio units are installed); while on air-to-air.
output: Instructor and student pilots aboard c152 have near midair collision during practice diversion.

input: Due to covid customer service agents should not be touching the airplane phones to make announcements. Both arrival and departure announcements are not necessary. Passenger and airline have the technology to get current gate and baggage claim information. All the agent is; is in the way when making any announcements in the aircraft doorway.
output: Ground employee reported that during covid-19 customer service agents should not use the airplane phones to make announcements.

input: Arriving to lax on the sadde 4 arrival, arrive we were cleared from smo vor and dme (co-located) for the stadium visual and a visual to 24r lax. Upon turning base over the stadium; i lost sight of the north complex runway(s) due to the sun and haze and overshot runway(s) 24r centerline. By the time i started turning back towards the runway(s) we were approximately midway between the north and south complex. At no time was any evasive action taken by myself or any other acft.
output: Arpt visual signature lost in visibility reduced sun position and air carrier wdb creates a heading track position deviation on the lax stadium visual approach proc.

input: Long 2 1/2 hour ramp delay due weather had to return to terminal from ramp area because of a diabetic passenber while being towed into gate area; we developed an unstoppable fuel spillage through fuel vent. Called airport rescue/fire fighting and decided to deplane passenber via rear airstairs onto ramp as no gate was available. The 94 passenber deplaned and were safely escorted across ramp to gate xx. All went smoothly. Crew did a great job. Notes: fuel spill alert came from mechanic on tug. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the cause of the fuel spillage was the 2.5 hour ground hold in the hot sun and expansion of the fuel as the tanks heated up. The rptr said no one was injured in the aircraft evacuate/evacuation as it was accomplished through the aft airstairs.
output: A dc9-30 on returning to the gate after a 2 pt 5 hour ground hold declared an emergency and evacuated the aircraft due to a wing vent tank fuel spillage.

input: Vmc day on approach control frequency and level at 9000' mean sea level being vectored to a downwind for 36l at clt. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system on and in use. Both pilots qualified in traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory issued with verbal; 'tfc; tfc;' followed shortly by an resolution advisory and a verbal; 'clb; clb;' vvf command of 2500 feet per minute climb coplt (pf) disconnected the autoplt. I told him to climb as i searched visually for the traffic (y). Traffic was spotted in a climbing turn toward us and below us (1000' lower; 1/4 mile and at our 11 o'clock pos). I simultaneously called clt approach and told them we had climbed to 9600' in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory clear of conflict; we descended back to 9000'. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system announced; 'clr of tfc.' approach called out the traffic to us only after we had climbed and had called them. Back on the ground i talked to the approach supervisor concerning the incident. He said he was required to submit his own rpt on the traffic alert and collision avoidance system induced deviation. He indicated the conflicting traffic (y) was at 7400' and climbing to an assigned altitude of 8000' when we departed 9000'. From the trning we received; likewise we must follow the resolution advisory assuming no conflicting information not to. Even intermediate fix the conflicting traffic is spotted visually; are we sure that's the traffic traffic alert and collision avoidance system is alerting us to? It seems to me that a false resolution advisory can be generated by a quickly clbing/dsnding aircraft even intermediate fix the aircraft intends to level off 1000' below/above my aircraft is this going to be a common occurrence? Are we still getting the bugs out of the system at a time when it is being operationally put out into the field?
output: Apparently false traffic alert and collision avoidance system alert leads to altitude excursion for air carrier mlg flight crew.

input: When parked at gate in zzz; cockpit crew were doing normal preflt activities while boarding aircraft flight attendant was looking outside to see intermediate fix everyone was on board and noticed a massive fuel leak out of the left/right (directions) wing! No one had said anything about this to us prior to the flight attendant even though there were several ground personnel around the aircraft this included the baggage loaders currently loading bags and the gate agent who was boarding the aircraft as soon as the flight attendant informed me of this situation we started deplaning the aircraft as a precaution. I then pulled out the gom and followed procedures exactly as spelled out (fuel spills). The problem that i had with the situation was that the gate agent; after the flight attendant and i had told the passenber to deplane; told them to go back on board and grab their bags and let them just mill around the aircraft i then went and told the passenber to go inside the terminal and informed the gate agent that they were not allowed back on the aircraft the fuel truck was left running next to the aircraft as well as several baggage carts and the baggage loader instead of being driven away from the spill per our procedures despite me telling them to do so.
output: An emb145 developed a fuel leak or spill at the gate. The aircraft was evacuated; but an emergency was not declared.

input: While taxiing into the gate at ord; i smelled smoke. I turned to look into the cabin; and it was filling with smoke in the middle of coach. I notified #1 flight attendant. She was unaware but notified capt. Passenber were starting to panic and were getting up. Capt didn't make a public address until we were pulling into the gate. He didn't call the flight attendants. We were not sure intermediate fix we were going to evacuate/evacuation first officer told us to 'prepare for arr.' at this point it was really getting smoky. Passenber deplaned normally. We never were told what happened.
output: As the b757 approachs the gate at ord; cabin attendant observes and smells smoke in cabin. Flight crew notified.

input: Visibility was low and ceiling was rpted at ftw at 1400 feet/foot overcast visibility 3 mile in mist. Fws was observed to be broken 2000 feet/foot visibility 5 mile in haze. I called the tower on the phone to query the airspace class at fws and was told it was class g when tower was in or out of operations(s) with this information i decided it was legal to do a series of visual flight rules touch-and-goes in the pattern. After a series of 3 or 4 lndgs; i noticed there was no clouds and 3-5 mile visibility. I contacted the tower and requested to track the localizer outbound and do a 'practice' 90 deg/270 degree procedure turn and track the instrument landing system inbound. This was approved by the tower i was told to remain visual flight rules and rpt the marker inbound. Tower called to rpt a bonanza 10 mile south cleared for the instrument landing system i was 1 mile south of the outer marker inbound; instrument landing system runway(s) 35l approach i was established and called the marker and was cleared for 'the option.' the bonanza's pilot told the tower he nearly hit me (1/2 mi). Tower said on the phone that approach control broke off the bonanza's approach i should have been monitoring approach control looking back at the situation and it could have been avoided.
output: On a visual practice instrument landing system approach to a class g airport with tower authority/authorized an aircraft has a conflict with another aircraft on the same approach that had a terminal radar approach control facility clearance for the same apch.

input: We were flying the clear air turbulence ii instrument landing system 04r approach to bos. The weather had been called 100 overcast 1/16 runway visual range 04r-8v14. It was reported runway visual range 60 shortly before we landed. We were on the localizer inbound with clearance to 3000. From about 2-3 mile south of nabbo to past miltt; i tried to obtain approach clearance i could not because the frequency was saturated. We were past miltt before i could talk to the controller the controller said he thought he had given us clearance for the approach he then brought us around with a quick pattern and we landed without further incident. The controller apologized for our missed approach i later talked to another airline crew that was in a wdb behind us on approach they said they did not hear us get a clearance they added it was hard for them to get a clearance because of the frequency saturation. I would like to state that the controller was calm and collected during the process and handled it well. I feel his performance was above the standards considering the conditions. I do not know how many aircraft were on the final approach frequency but we went 7-8 mile trying to make radio contact but were unable to do second officer because second officer many different voices were on the frequency when we are flying to clear air turbulence i or ii minimums; from a safety and operational viewpoint; it seems we should be able to make radio contact in no more than 30-40 seconds. I might add that our fuel state was such that we were within a few minutes of heading to our alternate.
output: Acr unable to obtain approach clearance account frequency congestion.

input: I was working west radar. En route sector 4 advised me aircraft x was carrying a critical passenger. I advised both h radar and v radar as well as input a scratch pad entry 'crit' into the data block of aircraft x. I looked at my asde-x repeater display and observed no instrument flight rules traffic moving on the airfield. I advised v radar of this and heard her call someone in hnl tower and apreq aircraft x critical; requesting direct to the airfield. This was approximately 10 minutes prior to aircraft x's arrival time at the airfield. When aircraft x was approximately 10 nm from hnl airport i noticed on my asde-x repeater that aircraft y was moving onto runway 8r. I remarked to both h and v radar controllers that i thought it odd that an aircraft would be put in to position with aircraft x in the departure corridor. I then called local control 2 (the controller of runway 8r) and asked 'you do know about aircraft x direct to the field?' he replied in the affirmative. I then noted from my asde-x repeater that aircraft y appeared to be on takeoff roll. I immediately advised the left/right (directions) radar departure controller that a heavy aircraft y was departing opposite direction to aircraft x and that he would likely have to take immediate action. Aircraft y did depart with aircraft x approximately 7nm from hnl airport and appeared to be exactly opposite direction; climbing and accelerating. I noted that aircraft x turned southwest while aircraft y turned eastbound.it is my opinion that standard radar separation was not maintained between these aircraft and that it is likely that aircraft x was below the minimum vectoring altitude when it turned southwest. I do not know what control instructions were issued to either aircraft.i do not know if the v radar controller coordinated directly with the local control 2 position for approval to enter their airspace with aircraft x. I do know that it is a common practice for most terminal controllers to only coordinate with the local assist position for anything that may affect anything at the airport traffic control tower rather than communicate directly with local control 2 regarding their airspace (local assist is mostly focused on aiding local control 1) and that it is also common practice for en route controllers to only coordinate with the westbound position for anything that may affect anything at the terminal radar approach control facility rather than communicate directly with the controller of the airspace in question (w radar is mostly focused on aiding h radar). It seems that some focus should be made on ensuring controllers are communicating directly with the controller responsible for the airspace in question (or their direct assist position) rather than using the two assist positions as catch-all coordinators. This allows better decision-making based on situational awareness of the airspace they are monitoring.
output: Zhn center controller reported a conflict between opposite direction aircraft.

input: On this particular day; i was returning to pell city airport from charleston; sc; having filed a visual flight rules flight plan; flying my cessna skylane. As i neared anniston; i checkeded weather with atlanta and found that it was much worse than i had expected from my preflt weather briefing. However; i had over half my fuel remaining; according to the gauges; and felt that i could make a weather checked at pell city and still have plenty of fuel to divert intermediate fix necessary. As i neared pell city; i contacted birmingham approach control and again was warned that the weather was below visual flight rules minimums; but i proceeded on to checked for myself. At this point; i noticed that my fuel had decreased significantly to less than a quarter of a tank on each of my 2 gauges. Arriving at pell city; it was apparent that the weather was indeed below minimums for visual flight rules and it was apparent that the fuel had decreased rapidly. I contacted birmingham approach which asked my intentions; and i informed them that i needed to land. Somewhere amidst all the stress and radio xmissions; i finally was put in touch with mr y. I declared an emergency he immediately asked me what he needed to know to get a grasp on the situation and confirmed that i had practiced airport surveillance radar approachs in my training. At this point; he began giving me vectors; while keeping me informed about the ceiling and visibility; and filled me in on the approach and runway(s) in use. Following his calm lead; i was vectored in for the approach and descended to the altitudes he gave me. The visibility was second officer poor that i saw the runway(s) lights only when i was almost on top of them. I now spell relief 'lndg on that runway(s) via mr y.' it gives me a hollow feeling when i think about how much worse it could have gotten had i not been given such good help by your people.
output: Rptr flew visual flight rules into imc.

input: [in pre-dawn darkness] mmmx ground control cleared us to push and release 'short of bravo; facing bravo.'  i passed those instructions to the ground crew; and they read it back to us correctly. We stopped; were cleared to start; and i cleared the ground crew to disconnect. The nose of our aircraft was over the ground vehicle roadway painted on the ramp; but not on or over bravo. During the start sequence the first officer; said; '[my name]!' and pointed to the left. A b747 was in a high-speed taxi; and the right wing tip and large winglet appeared to be heading right toward our cockpit. The ground crew was still there (but with the headset disconnected) prior to the salute; and our #2 engine was not yet up to idle. Our only option to avoid decapitation would have been to unbuckle and hit the deck. A radio call would be useless due to the speed of the b747 and because of how quickly this event took place. Just then we noticed the green nav light 'moving on the windscreen' and not on a collision course. We watched the large winglet pass ten to fifteen feet in front of our cockpit. It is unknown whether or not the [b747] crew saw us; or; due to the darkness; whether or not the [b747] captain was on the bravo centerline. (that entire area is regarded by many pilots as a 'black hole.') i made a radio call to mmmx. For your reference; please see jeppesen mmmx charts 10-7z; 10-9; and 10-9b. I would suggest that the mmmx ground crews be instructed to release our aircraft at least 20 feet prior to the painted ground vehicle roadway northwest of taxiway bravo.
output: B737-800 flight crew reported they were parked near taxiway b after pushback and were almost hit by a b747 taxiing past them. Darkness was a factor; and the crew suggested push procedure should not position them that close to the taxiway.

input: Dsnding on the green one arrival, arrive we were cleared to cross the garrd intersection at 11000 feet/foot approaching 11000 feet/foot we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory followed immediately by an resolution advisory to monitor vertical speed and descend we descended to about 10800 feet/foot when we saw the traffic at 12 o'clock position about 200 feet/foot above us as we passed under him. We advised air traffic control of our actions. Center said the traffic was visual flight rules and they were not talking to him. Aircraft was a single engine low wing. I feel we would not have seen the traffic intermediate fix we had not gotten the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii warning.
output: Acr avoids visual flight rules small aircraft by 200 feet/foot as the result of a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii ra.

input: Flt xxx departed elp-hou. Before departure i had amended his release to change his alternate from crp to sat; and iah also had similar amendments; and a convective significant meteorological information was in effect for a trw line on a shv-ggg-cll axis moving from 2840. I briefed the pilot in command on all this. The normal air traffic control route was elp-j2-fst-j138-sat-lissez-hou. Later; the trw's developed further sw along the axis; and extended to crp; stilling moving 2840. I accessed the national weather service radar at gls; and it appeared that the line was 40-50 nautical mile from iah/hou. I contacted xxx via company radio abeam sjt and advised him of all this; plus my recommendation that he slow from u74 to lrc to delay his arrival, arrive including holding in the ela area second officer as to allow the weather to clear hou; and an approach from behind the line. The capt concurred. I expected to hear from xxx in the ela area about 30 minute(s) later; but didn't; and was unable to reestablish contact via radio. I was advised that xxx had contacted a nearby company station; and relayed the message that he was proceeding to crp to go around to the east side of the line. The line was about 10 nautical mile out of iah/hou at this time; and my repeated attempts to contact were to no avail. Flight xxx shot an approach to hou runway(s) 4; but missed approach due to the weather and came around and landed on 30l. The weather hit shortly thereafter. As i later discussed with the capt; while i wasn't trying to usurp his pilot in command authority; i was concurrently trying to keep the operation safe; and trying to minimize economic impact to the company. Had xxx held over ela area (as other company flts were); he would have only consumed another $300 in fuel. I chose to spend that money to prevent exposing the crew and passenber to a trw event; and to also prevent the flight from getting trapped on the east side of the line (which built to almost lrp after xxx turned it at crp). Had xxx not made it into hou; i would have diverted him to bpt (a non company station) and held him there until the line cleared there; 2 hours later. The total cost for such a diversion (fuel; acft/crew time; hotels for misconnected pax) would have come to about $7000. After almost 15 yrs of dispatching; it continues to amaze me how little some crews and management really understand about operational control and how it affects the airline. Since most dedicated airline departments disappeared after 1978's deregulation; more responsibility falls upon us; but we often get only minimal company support (computers; decent very high frequency communications system staff; etc); and indifference from many crews who don't/can't see us for the resource that we are.
output: Acr mlg flight crew failed to respond to dispatcher's recommendation and proceeded to destination.

input: Taxiway romeo in phx has a new bridge over it. The automatic terminal information service notams [and] 10-9 airport page make no mention of it. Seeing the bridge at last minute and being committed; and seeing a b-737 going under with plenty of clearance; [i] made the judgment call that we would clear; and proceeded under. Second thought; after thinking about it awhile and talking to people; should have tied up the airport for indefinite time to throughly research the issue before proceeding. Was not able to turn around before proceeding. Would like to see some information on 10-9; 10-8; notams or automatic terminal information service addressing the issue.
output: A b757 captain reported being surprised and confused by a newly constructed bridge over taxiway left/right (directions) that is not reported in notams or shown on airport diagrams.

input: Deferred item xxx [maintenance procedure (m/p)] was called out [to be accomplished] on aircraft x; a b757-200 aircraft located at terminal gate xx. I complied with the maintenance requirement in minimum equipment list chapter 27-21-00; but on aircraft y; a different b757-200 aircraft located on an adjoining terminal gate. I signed-off complied with deferred item maintenance procedure and sent the maintenance release to aircraft x. After questioning by the flight crew of aircraft x; whether they had the correct maintenance release; i realized my error and then performed m/p required on aircraft x. A new maintenance release was sent to aircraft x; before brakes were released at the gate. Situations sometimes occur when an individual is assigned multiple gates with similar aircraft types at same times.
output: Two line mechanics performed a power control unit operational check to satisfy a continuing minimum equipment list 27-21-00 deferral for a b757-200 aircraft. Mechanics realized they had completed the power control unit check on the wrong b757 after the captain questioned whether he had the correct maintenance release.

input: Not late-not in a hurry. Right at pushback we got the runway and departure change. During engine start first officer grabbed the performance computer and began programming changes. Then we got a pre-taxi air traffic control call about construction issue near our gate. While stopped; i decided to go through the runway taxi and departure changes and went into departure takeoff mode. Out of sequence now; i inadvertently overlooked the before taxi checklist before taxiing. During taxi we both knew we were out of sequence; so i said i wanted to re-review the departure and performance data. That's when the first officer noticed the flaps at 0 and instinctively grabbed the handle and set to five. So flaps were reset on the move. We then re-ran the before taxi checklist and reconfirmed all configure/takeoff and departure items. I should not have allowed first officer to begin performance computer changes during pushback. I should have waited until after the before taxi checklist was completed prior to addressing the clearance changes.
