I am unsure if tower recognized that the pa28 had drifted left and extended so far out; but i am assuming that they did not as no call was made informing me of their position or the potential for conflict.overall; my own misjudgments of my timing and distance; mistake in missing calls for other aircraft to have an idea of what is going on big picture (as i would have been able to recognize that i would essentially be following an aircraft in the right traffic pattern); and the pa28's over extension and drift on the departure leg contributed to this event.
output: Single private pilot reported a conflict in the traffic pattern.

input: Ivanpah solar on arrival to las. Mirrors supposed to focus on towers however northern most facility was out of control and beaming laser like streams on our aircraft as we proceeded on kepec arrival. The intensity was that of a green laser i have experienced in the past. The result was blinding spots that continued for the subsequent hour after arrival. This not only affected the flight crew but the passengers on the right side of the aircraft. We missed the approach checklist at the appropriate time to protect ourselves from the light and warn the passengers.
output: The captain of a b737ng reported encountering glare from the ivanpah solar farm while on approach to las airport.

input: We were aware of the turbulence forecast area near the mountains by den; and that we may be transiting the lower corner of it en route zzz1. We were flying econ cruise of mach .78 at fl390 (because of weight although dispatched at fl410). As we approached air traffic control queries and rpts indicated only light chop/turb with air traffic control stating it existed up to fl380 and lasting only a few minute(s) for e/w travel. Second officer it appeared only 'light' and below us. As we approached slightly nw of santa flight engineer nautical mile the light chop began as the seatbelt sign was put back on. It started to worsen second officer i sat the flight attendants down. The chop did indeed worsen even more shortly thereafter. Within a minute(s) or second officer the light chop suddenly and instantaneously turned into moderate turbulence with some mountain wave action. As i started to pull power to slow to mach .76; the airspd literally jumped to mach .82 with clacker in about 2 seconds. I was stunned at how quickly this happened with only 'light chop' conditions reported at altitudes below us only. I had to further pull power all the way to idle with the speed continuing upward to mach .84 where it stayed for about 10 seconds (while at idle)! The speed then slowly dissipated over the next 15 seconds or second officer as i gradually added power to intercept mach .76. Within the next minute(s) or two; the rough ride went back to light chop; then smooth until; amazingly; about 20 minute(s) later; approaching abeam ama; some slight mountain wave was again encountered for a couple of mins! After the encounter; we looked in the fom to see intermediate fix reaching vmo +20 knot(s) or mmo +.02 mach (design limit speeds of 340 knot(s) mach .84) required a logbook write-up and maintenance inspection (i thought that they did with recent emphasis on the fact from flight ops). I was also unsure of the potential maintenance inspection timeline requirements (ie; immediate; or within a certain number of days; or... Etc). This maintenance inspection requirement knowledge turns out to be a critical customer service issue inbound to a station after even only touching design limit speeds (also for flap overspds). We found an fom appendix page that talks about 'unscheduled maintenance chks...exceeding design speed (vmo +20 knot(s) or mmo +.02 mach).' since we did not 'exceed' the design speed but only 'reached' it; those words convinced us that no maintenance action or inspection delay would be expected reaching destination we knew a mechanic would be there to confirm our assumption also. It was not until after talking to maintenance control on landing and their grounding of the aircraft for inspection (approx 1-2 hrs) that i discovered this in the fom on the previous pages. The fom appendix talks about 'items that require guidance from maintenance ctl' but only an 'info' write-up: operational exceedances that do not require maintenance inspection: 1) vmo exceedance of less than 20 knot(s) 2) mmo exceedance of less than .02 mach. This is; apparently; correctly worded regarding real world operations(s) however; it contradicts the fom page guidance that one must 'exceed' design limit speed to actually trigger the inspection requirement (ie; 361 knot(s) mach .85 ). Because of our confusion in thinking no inspection was required; passenber were already boarding as we got the news from maintenance control that the aircraft required an inspection which could take a couple of hours since we were a couple of hours from destination when the overspd occurred; we could have informed dispatch via automatic communications addressing & reporting system of the event and inspection requirements well ahead of time for other arrangements and aircraft swap planning to be done to inconvenience our passenber the least. Therefore; i believe that the following changes need to be made to the fom: 1) the page should read; 'reaching and/or exceeding design limits speeds of 360 knot(s) mach .84 (vmo +20/mmo +.02). 2) the fom limitations should include; somewhere; the definition of 'design limit spd' and then state that reaching and/or exceeding those speeds 'require' grounding of the aircraft at destination for a maintenance inspection (possibly a couple of hrs); second officer contact dispatch and/or station operations(s) as soon as possible of the overspd second officer that passenber and aircraft swap planning can commence. (the same is true for flap speed exceedances). Also; why not blatantly state that maximum operating speeds vmo/mmo (clacker) are 340 knots indicated airspeed mach .82; there also?
output: A b737-700 at fl390 experienced moderate mountain wave action with mach/airspeed deviation exceeding vmo/mmo limits and requiring inspections.

input: We were making a night cross country the cross country was to include 5 lndgs to a full stop at a control towered airport the flight started without a hitch. All of the alternators were showing a good charge during run-up and takeoff prior to the practice instrument landing system approach we checkeded the instruments again. One alternator was showing a really low charge; however; that is normal for the airplane. Shutting down the other alternator makes it show a full charge. The instrument landing system and the later pattern went well. We practiced a landing without the panel lights on the third approach to landing we practiced a landing with just the navigate, navigation and beacon lights on the 4th landing feeling good about ourselves; the 5th and final landing was to be a normal landing on downwind; we were cleared for the option early. After gear down abeam the touchdown zone; i requested a verification on the stop-and-go clearance after 2 unanswered calls; i realized that the radio was not displaying the 'tx' icon. Hoping it was just my push-to-talk switch; my student made 2 unanswered calls. We quickly tuned the standby radio and still no response. During a quick checked of the systems; we found both ammeters at zero. We recycled the alternators and still no response. A checked of the landing lights on the wing verified that we were on battery power and fading fast. The landing gear had used up all the available watts of power we went dark on short final and we landed without the use of our electrically operated flaps. The student made an unbelievably soft landing and we exited on the second taxiway we stopped short of the first intersection and called airport operations(s) on a cell phone and asked for assistance. We were met by the emergency response and airport personnel for an escort to a maintenance facility. The problem that got us is that we didn't catch the electrical failure soon enough. The baron ammeters usually read low. This is because all but one flight are flown during the day and the electrical load is very low. Also; one alternator seems to read zero and the other carries the small load most of the time. The idle alternator switches every flight second officer either the left/right (directions) or the left/right (directions) will read almost zero in most cases. Even though it was night; a low ammeter reading or zero reading really didn't draw much attention to itself. I will certainly verify that it is because of the load that it reads second officer low. It was very fortunate that we were cleared to land already and had the gear down. We wouldn't have had the chance for light signals; because during a phone call with tower after the event; we were told that we were invisible without our lights. The 2 practice approachs were a great life saver because the student was well prepared for the real thing. The cause of the dual alternator failure was that the belts had come off both alternators. The mechs are looking to make sure that they don't fall off again. I ante meridiem not sure what the cause would have been and what actions they take to prevent it. One other thing that we should do is have atc's phone numbers in the aircraft with us. We had a current airport/facility directory but the number listed was the airport operations(s) and not the control tower with the millions of cell phones today; the ability to call the tower to rpt an emergency would be a blessing. Then they would be aware of our issue and be able to assist us over the phone.
output: Be55 instructor reports total electrical failure while practicing night landings with student. Student lands uneventfully with no lights.

input: Had #1 autoplt go inoperative on inbound flight when maintenance release came for subsequent leg it did not contain any placard information it should be on there. Had to pull the minimum equipment list card in order to retrieve the information (turn clear air turbulence iii placard over; other autoplt must be operable; no clear air turbulence ii; iii approachs etc).
output: B737-300 flight crew has incorrect minimum equipment list for autoplt inop.

input: I was taking a short trip to the coast from pao with a brand new garmin navigation database update into a brand new class b change for the sfo area. The new garmin update included the new class b inromation. The global positioning system showed me that the base of the class b changed from 4000 to 8000 not to far from osi vor and dme (co-located) this was a change; since it had been a shift from 4000 to 6000. I was briefly over 6000 before descending. When i returned; i double checked the new chart and found that the global positioning system data was wrong--the base was 6000 not 8000. I later checked with the also brand new database in the garmin receiver in my other airplane. It also showed incorrect information as to the base of the class b in that same area. It also showed 8000 instead of 6000.bottom line is that i relied on the newly downloaded database; which was supposed to accurately conform to the new changes in the class b. Although the new database in both airplanes seemed to conform to the many changes; it was inaccurate as to this area. This occurred only 2 days after the class b changes; so i am planning on informing garmin of their error. Both airplanes; with 2 separate garmin products; both with 2 new garmin database downloads were consistent but wrong.
output: Ga pilot reported the garmin navigation database was incorrect referencing the new sfo class b airspace.

input: Flt from dfw to shv. All weight and balance parameters given to the crew within limits. Rotation; takeoff cruise and descent normal. Landing at shv on runway(s) 5 with first officer flying. Smooth touchdown on the mains at vref of 120 knot(s) however; nose stays up throughout deceleration despite fo's efforts to push yoke forward. I take control of aircraft and move power levers out of beta and apply slight forward thrust which in conjunction with forward yoke pressure brings nosewheel down onto runway(s) uneventful taxi to gate. Rampers rpt unusually heavy bags and several heavy pineapple boxes. Conclusion: cargo weights given to us at dfw were obviously not what was loaded into the cargo compartments. Aircraft must have actually been aft of its center of gravity limits. In 5 yrs of flying this aircraft have never encountered such a characteristic on landing after 1 1/2 hours after passenber deplane; maintenance personnel come up to cockpit and ask about the condition of the tail and whether we scraped it anywhere. That's when we get out of the airplane and to my amazement and shock notice scrape marks on the aft tail strakes and lower portion of the tailcone albeit very subtle but nonetheless there. First officer rpts not having noticed anything unusual during post and preflt walkarounds at shv and i did not notice anything unusual while handling the tailstand. Landing at dfw was very smooth and normal second officer anything there is out of the question. As federal aviation regulation as the landing in shv; we had not even given the remotest thought about the possibility of any part of the aircraft having made contact with the runway(s) because we never had any physical feedback; vibration or heard any noises. Nor did the tower flight attendant or any passenber rpt anything of that nature. Therefore we were not in a mindset to look for any scrape marks on the aircraft but realistically; i'm sure that's where it happened and we did not feel it. Maintenance person later stated that there is no way the crew could have seen it on a walkaround such as is accomplished on a turn. However; there may have been an opportunity to discover more had the rampers perhaps communicated better with myself by having been more specific about the problem they were having and how much they knew and bringing matters that come to their attention first and foremost and in a timely manner to the attention of the pilot in command rather than keeping the crew out of the loop until departure time and contacting maintenance without informing the pilot in command this is where i think we need to apply cockpit resource management beyond the cockpit and involve all departments however; the main safety issue with this occurrence is the need to revise the current procedures at dfw for weighing and loading cargo and communicating the numbers to the crew. Obviously there was a gross discrepancy between weights given to us and actual weights on the aircraft perhaps rather than using the standard 23 1/2 pound bag; all bags should be actually weighed to prevent further occurrences such as this. Company rpts made; meetings held and performances evaluated. Effective immediately; some new procedures have been implemented concerning aircraft loading and more recommendations will follow. Hope this is a useful rpt.
output: Flc of an sf340b had difficulty lowering the nosewheel to the runway(s) after landing due to the aircraft aft center of gravity limits had been exceeded by excessive baggage weight the tailcone had also been struck during one of the lndgs as evidence of small scrape marks on the fuselage tail cone.

input: It was brought to my attention during my last uio flight that another capt had raised an issue as to how the operations(s) agents -- especially the former dispatchers -- are handling the flts out of uio. I have been to uio many; many times over the previous yrs. I ante meridiem willing to say that the uio operations(s) is by federal aviation regulation one of the best and safest in our system i was distressed to see that one of the key agent/former dispatchers was temporarily not being utilized in operations(s) on the day of my last flight instead; a temporary from gye was being used to see how different the operations(s) is. The assistance from a former dispatcher; and someone who knows the field and airport and how the conditions change; is invaluable in uio and all of our hit cities. I have seen these agents point out valuable information to both old and new crews while operating out of uio. This has always been in a most professional way. I hope that we continue to utilize these agents with their extremely important knowledge -- it is one of our important safety nets. I hope that they are not told to not offer their advice. This would be contradictory to our mission statement and federal aviation regulations to utilize all available resources when planning our flts.
output: A b757-200 pilot in command rpt on the non use of operations(s) agents; former dispatchers; in the dispensation of information to flcs at sequ; fo.

input: Apching lax; from the north on the fim 6 profile; we were advised by approach control to initiate base turn as soon as practical after passing smo; and that an ltt would follow us to 25l. During base; left/right (directions) turn; we were advised the ltt would turn inside us for visual to 25r. When we rolled wings level on final for 25l; we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory followed by a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory calling for a climb as we were about to initiate the climb to avoid the unknown traffic we observed the ltt at 1 o'clock; 100 feet/foot below and about 250 feet/foot to our left/right (directions) visual contact was then maintained until both aircraft touched down on 25l and 25r respectively. A contributing factor to the proximitypa of the 2 aircraft was the north crosswind which caused the ltt to overshoot final for 25r. Also; both aircraft being in a turn at the same time made visual contact difficult. I believe a hazardous situation was unnecessarily created; as this was not a busy arrival, arrive period. We only heard 2 other aircraft arriving at this time. It was not necessary to turn traffic second officer close together. One comment on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii frequently we are lulled into treating ra's in runway(s) proximitypa as 'nuisance' alerts. Had we not seen the traffic when we did; the outcome of this event could have been quite different.
output: Commuter aircraft cleared to turn inside mlg for parallel runway(s) traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory close prox.

input: We received an aircraft at the start of our trip with three mel's. The mel's were: 34-20 no 2 radio altimeter; 34-12 no 2 flight director; and 32-27 pseu system. The original logbook discrepancy was for a spurious 'minimums/minimums' automated callout. The me'ls resulted in higher weather minimums for the aircraft. (the a/c was downgraded to clear air turbulence i only; no lower than 4000 feet or 3/4 mile visibility.)  we flew the aircraft and at touchdown; the 'minimums/minimums' callout occurred. After arriving at the gate; the first officer and i discussed the existing mel's and felt that we were okay to continue. We thought the intent of the mel's were to prevent us from being distracted by the spurious callout in a low weather; low altitude situation by setting higher approach minimums. We continued on to our next destination. On the next flight; the first officer and i further discussed the mel's. We realized that we didn't know if the deferrals were actually intended to prevent any further callouts form occurring. If that was the intent of maintenance control with the mel's; further maintenance and or deferrals were needed. Upon arrival at our next destination; the callout occurred again. I contacted maintenance control and talked with the contract mechanic. With the version of software on this new aircraft; the answer was unclear. The contract mechanic thought the callout was normal. The maintenance controller decided the ground proximity warning system system needed to be deactivated to silence the automated callouts. At this point it was still unclear whether we violated any fars. After doing more research with maintenance control; they told me that this automated callout would be standard on all aircraft {tail number} onward. Determine if these automated callouts should or should not occur. Either de-activate them or publish guidance for flight crews to use if the callout will be standard on our new aircraft.
output: B737-700 flight crew reports accepting an aircraft with mel's to deal with a spurious 'minimums minimums' automated callout. On the first landing the callouts occur. Maintenance control is unsure if the minimum equipment list actions were meant to silence the callouts or even if they are anomalous or just part of a software upgrade in newer aircraft.

input: The memphis vor and dme (co-located) (mem) is out of service and will be down for 2 more months. Our routes continue to be filed and we continue to be cleared via arrivals that are based on the mem vor and dme (co-located) is this legal? Should pilots accept this clrnc? Why can't a temporary vor and dme (co-located) be used? Also is it legal to use the vor and dme (co-located) for crossing restrictions when the azimuth portion is in operation? Intermediate fix the vor and dme (co-located) is out isn't the vor and dme (co-located) also considered decommissioned? How could most people get the ident?
output: Acr mlg complaint about being given clearance involving vor and dme (co-located) that is notamed out of service.

input: On takeoff from bzn experienced engine failure and fire on #3. Started a fuel dump; leveled aircraft at 800' above ground level to retract flaps. Advised bzn flight service station specialist we had an engine failure and fire and would be returning to land bzn runway(s) 12. Also asked to have the equipment standing by. Started to run chklists. On emergency chklist followed instructions and fired 2 bottles into #3 engine fire light did not go out and fire bell kept ringing intermittently. Terminated dump and started to turn final just outside outer marker at bzn. Completed all chklists and asked flight service station specialist intermediate fix he could see either smoke or fire coming out of #3 engine was advised by either flight service station specialist or taxiing aircraft #3 engine was still on fire. Told flight service station specialist to have equipment meet the aircraft after landing and that i planned to evacuate the aircraft on runway(s) advised f/a's nd paxs on p/a to plan evacuation after we stopped aircraft on the runway(s) since by that time we were on short final. Landed aircraft and after it was stopped i called for evacuation on the left/right (directions) side only. The fire department immediately reached the aircraft and extinguished the fire on the #3 engine paxs and crew evacuated the aircraft with no injuries; evacuation chklist completed. Supplemental information from acn 154267. I believe the first indication of engine failure was the 'eng failure lights' on the capt's and f/o's glare shields. I terminated the dump and noticed out of the corner of my eye that the #3 start valve open light was on steady. I informed the pilots on final approach an aircraft waiting for takeoff xmitted that we had alot of smoke coming from #3 but he saw no flames. Supplemental information from acn 153837. Paxs evacuated out left/right (directions) forward and aft slides and a couple of people went out over wing exit. No panic or confusion with pax's.
output: Acr lgt had an engine failure at 200' on climb out from bzn mt. Flight crew stated fuel dumping and completed the engine shut down and fire checklists. Fire warning continued until landing where fire equipment extinguished the fire. Passengers evacuated.

input: Climbing out; at about fl260; i pilot flying (pf) noted the engine indicating and crew alerting system became de-cluttered. I pointed it out to the captain; and we found engine 1 lp vib to be at 4.0; which is in the yellow caution range.we leveled at fl280 and the captain ran the quick reference handbook while i remained in control of the airplane and took over the radios. As instructed by the quick reference handbook we were able to get the engine 1 low pressure (lp) vibration stabilized at about 78% n1. At this power setting; we were still able to maintain altitude and airspeed; so we discussed the possibility of continuing to [destination]; checking drift down; fuel plans; and other precautionary items.during this time; the captain also contacted dispatch; maintenance; and ops; and included them in the loop. He had them rerun the flight plan at fl280 and our current speed. They concurred that we could continue to [destination].no further issues were noted.upon arrival; we were met by maintenance. They determined that we needed to do an engine run-up check with them. The captain and i coordinated with operations(s) and air traffic control performed the run-up with mx; which was satisfactory. Maintenance signed off the writeup; '...could not duplicate...' and we loaded up passengers to continue our next leg.
output: Emb-175 first officer reported they received an engine indicating and crew alerting system message engine 1 lp vib. Flight continued to destination after running the qrh.

input: Departing via the area navigation standard instrument departure from runway 8r at atl; at approximately 500 feet/foot the tower controller gave us a clearance to precede directly to the second fix. Captain selected that fix in the flight management system then asked that i verify that it was depicted correctly. I verified that it was indeed depicted correctly on the display and in the box; and he proceeded to execute it. We then both verified that the dashed white line turned to a magenta line to that fix. We had by then reached 1;000 feet/foot and upon request; the captain dialed in half rate; climb power. While he was doing that i noticed that the flight director was commanding a high bank angle of turn for what should have been a fairly small amount of heading change; and so while leveling the wings i informed the captain that something was wrong with the flight management system as we both looked at it we immediately saw that what should have been the active waypoint had been dropped and the flight management system was trying to steer directly to the next fix which was approximately 90 degrees off our wing. Captain immediately informed the tower controller that we were area navigation unable and that our flight management system had malfunctioned. The tower controller gave us a heading (which was very close to the heading we had already established) and informed us that there had been no conflict of any kind. To our knowledge; no procedural mistakes were made by the crew. I have heard from other pilots that this is a reoccurring problem on this departure. I would suggest determining if there is a history of problems with this departure and if so terminating this area navigation departure procedure if a history is discovered.
output: After departing on the atl runway 8r area navigation an air carrier's flight management system dropped the active waypoint and sequenced the aircraft to the next point. The crew requested a vector and believe that this anomaly has occurred previously.

input: After finishing a behind the clock flight (xa:30 -- xh:30am) the previous day; this entire crew left hnl for ppt at xx:00 post meridiem on 1/93. The flight to ppt was without incidence however; everyone on this crew mentioned how tired we felt. Once on the ground in ppt; the capt went into the local office to pick up the flight plan and weather data for our return flight to hnl. Upon his return he said he wanted 74000 pounds of fuel and we have 15 minute(s) to turn the plane which usually requires an hour and a half. Meanwhile i was loading the inertial navigation system and omega information being second officer tired nobody even thought to checked this load with the flight planned load. After takeoff on the climb out the flight engineer realized we didn't have enough fuel for our flight which prompted an immediate course reversal with air traffic control to return. While in our turn; hnl commercial radio called with a phone patch from our dispatch; saying to return. We arrived back in ppt without incidence and refueled to the correct load and flew to hnl. I think a combination of fatigue and rushing made the 3 of us overlook checkeding our flight planned fuel with our actual fuel load. After speaking to our chief pilot about this; we came to a solution of putting a block 'flt planned fuel' on the flight engineer's fuel loading sheet right next to fuel load.
output: Hvt departs with insufficient fuel for their trip. Return land.

input: While preflighting my o2 mask i noticed the pressure gauge reading slightly over 2000 psi. The mask checked normal after the 5 second check. I was curious about the gauge reading over 2000 psi. I thought that if we have so much pressure it wouldn't hurt to do a prolonged check to try to get the pressure to read normal. After about a minute the o2 stopped flowing from the mask while the overhead pressure still indicated slightly over 2000 psi. Obviously an empty o2 tank and bad gauge. Maintenance confirmed the o2 bottle was empty and replaced it. Maintenance said the previous installation of the o2 bottle damaged the sensors for the o2 pressure gauge. I'm sure you see the seriousness of this and like me wonder how many other airplanes are showing abnormally high o2 pressure with actually very very little o2.
output: A 737-800 pilot performed an extended crew oxygen system test due to a high pressure indication; only to discover that the oxygen bottle was near empty.

input: Acft was level at 21000'. Inertial navigation system lateral navigation vertical navigation and left/right (directions) autoplt engaged. We were given a turn to 030 degrees and to slow to 250 knot(s) i set 250 knot(s) in crz page and mode control panel indicated air speed window; and both showed fl210. The autothrottles were at idle and airspd about 285 knot(s) at this time autothrottles went to climb power and autoplt pitched up 12 degrees both were disengaged and aircraft was leveled at 21400' and returned to 21000' assigned. Atl center made no mention of this event. All system worked normal; autothrottle and autoplt; remainder of flight and no known reason for this aircraft irregular autothrottle autoplt action. I did submit a crew irregular operation rpt to my chief pilot atl office.
output: Lgt with automated cockpit has equipment malfunction resulting in altitude deviation.

input: Approx 1 hour after departure the flight attendant notified me that the access door from the lavatory to the cargo compartment was ajar. I instructed the first officer to investigate the situation. When he returned i was informed that the cargo access door had; what appeared to be; a manufacturer defect. The latch did not align with the lock. We assumed that the access door opened from fuselage flexing during flight i instructed the flight attendant to inform me of any passenber that used the lavatory while we evaluated the situation. After approximately 2 minute(s) she informed me that 2 passenber in the back; had used the lavatory more than once and that one of them was at that time in the lavatory. I then instructed her to 'seal' and not to allow any further use of the lavatory. Meanwhile; the first officer and i continued to evaluate the situation and found that all that we had was an open access door; with no evidence of tampering; and a couple of passenber who appeared normal other than using the lavatory more than once.
output: Access door to cargo compartment from lavatory to cargo compartment found ajar.

input: Cruise flight at fl350. We had a recurring pack 1 fault and pack 1 was shut off per procedure shortly thereafter; we had a pack 2 fault. An emergency descent was initiated and an emergency was declared with zob. After leveling at 10000 feet/foot pack 2 was able to be reinstated as per procedure we canceled the emergency with zob and climbed to fl200 to finish the flight to ord after taking fuel burn at the lower altitude into consideration and checkeding with dispatch. The cabin pressure never exceeded 9000 feet/foot i made a public address concerning the descent but i believe the entire event went pretty much unnoticed by the pax.
output: Fk100 executes emergency descent after losing pressurization system in zob airspace.

input: During taxi out for takeoff; we received the following message: captain you have to return to the gate or at least the alley because zzz ramp did not secure the hazmat in accordance with federal aviation administration required guidelines. We returned to gate; and parked the aircraft. While i coordinated; the ramp crew properly secured the hazmat; and once we confirmed that we were legal and our rls was still valid to continue; we departed without further incident.
output: A319 captain reported a ground gate return due to improperly secure hazmat cargo in cargo compartment.

input: Acr x received traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory followed by a resolution advisory climbed from 35000 to 36000. I notified controller who said no problem. He had no traffic in our area at our alt.
output: Acft equipment problem traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory resolution advisory false ghost target. Air carrier x evasive action taken clb.

input: While awaiting takeoff with aircraft landing and departing; confusion arose over rpts of icing on departure all of us on frequency heard 'there are no official rpts of severe icing.' moderate icing was mentioned. We were cleared for takeoff with no mention of icing at all from the tower controller on departure we pilot report of light icing; as did other aircraft later i heard that pilots were rpting severe icing on approach to cleveland; then were landing with no ice on their aircraft severe icing is defined by our operations(s) manual as 'unable to control the accumulation with anti-ice/deice equipment and inflt diversion is required.' obviously; as the aircraft did not divert; there was no severe icing. I feel that invalid meteorological rpts are hazardous as they could; in this case; require aircraft following to divert prior to entering severe deicing conditions; and perhaps cause low fuel problems at alternates. I would recommend air traffic control inquire simply 'is the ice accumulation ctlable and are you requiring a divert?' then they could rpt; accurately; intermediate fix severe or moderate. Of course; pilots need to be more precise in this rpting also.
output: An air carrier capt regrets that other air carrier pilots cannot rpt icing properly in their required pireps.

input: I was handed paperwork from my supervisor while on position. The paperwork provided a brief description of what to expect from a flight that was to fly through my airspace (aircraft x). The paperwork said aircraft x would orbit in nttr for 2+00 hrs. When the aircraft checked on; he asked to proceed to kl45m and hold for two hours. I said proceed as requested because i thought that was a part of the pre-coordinated route that had been established. Once i realized he was turning towards the restricted airspace i called and asked nellis if aircraft x could in fact come in and hold as he requested. They said unable and he had to stay out of the airspace. From that point; i got busy at the sector and was trying to get answers from management as to what i needed to do with this aircraft since he was not allowed into the restricted airspace like we had planned. I put aircraft x on a heading to stall and try to find answers. When i tried to issue him holding instructions he informed me that he is unable to accept 'faa holding instructions' and was just requesting a 'delay.' i have no idea what issuing a 'delay' does and how i can possibly ensure separation or ensure i know what the aircraft is doing if i simply tell him to delay as requested. I was then handed paperwork on an area of airspace and instructed to ask the aircraft x pilot if he was familiar with 'the ops area northeast of las.' the aircraft was not familiar. The whole thing was a cluster and i was busy with other airplanes and normal complexity of an already busy sector. I felt like my entire area had no idea how to handle the situation; including the mos (military operations specialist) who had been called down to help me or try to provide answers. Aircraft x ended up just flying in circles in my sector with no real 'holding' instructions established because he couldn't accept them. There was no incident but it was a safety issue because the level of distraction that this one operation caused me put my sector in an unsafe situation.these drone operations need to be more clearly defined and the pilots need to be made aware of the requirements. They can't just expect to get to hold and not be able to accept holding instructions. I'm not sure what went wrong; because i'm not the mos and not familiar enough with the drone operations to recommend a good solution. I just want to make atsap aware of the distraction this caused myself while working a busy sector; and the distraction it caused my entire area.
output: Zla controllers reported a unmanned aerial vehicle that could not accept holding instructions and was not allowed in restricted airspace. One controller was confused and had busy airspace. The mos did not have any special instructions to help and the unmanned aerial vehicle made circles until a resolution was found.

input: During the normal 30day/100hour hydraulic fluid change; while system was draining; i removed and serviced [the oxygen system] bottle and reinstalled. I then finished the servicing of the hydraulic system. I then signed off the pre-completed logbook page for the hydraulic system service. The pilot did the inspection of the hydraulic system and signed the log page. We then proceeded to move the helicopter out of the hangar. I had forgotten to mention the servicing of the [oxygen bottle] to the pilot and i did not remember to write up a discrepancy for the servicing of the [oxygen]. The next time the helicopter flew the crew had a warning on the ventilator of low pressure. The ventilator and attaching lines were checked; all good. The pilot checked the [oxygen] bottle and found the one feed line not connected.
output: The maintenance technician did not record an oxygen discrepancy on an as350. He also did not complete the bottle installation after servicing; which led to a low pressure condition.

input: The problem arose when i took someone sightseeing. It was clear visual flight rules and no wind. This person wanted to fly near the statue of liberty. I then flew down the hudson river; underneath the class b of new york. I flew between 1000 feet/foot and 500 feet/foot above ground level after passing the george washington bridge. After i returned to my home airport i was told by fellow flight instructors that they had heard there were temporary flight restrs for the excursion. I had called; earlier in the day; the millville flight service station for a weather briefing. However; i did not anticipate flying down the excursion. As a result; the briefer did not inform me of the restrs. This was of no fault of the briefer. I failed to request these restrs because i was unaware of them. The only thing i can think of to prevent something like this from happening again; is to have control towers aware of restrs such as these. In turn; they might be able to forewarn pilots of the restrs and advise them to call the nearest flight service station specialist i blame only myself for neglecting to obtain the appropriate information i do not hold the flight service station specialist or the controllers responsible for my actions.
output: Erroneous penetration of temporary flight restrict, restricted, restriction area along hudson river corridor near teb.

input: While en route to den we were advised via automatic communications addressing & reporting system of den being a 2 runway(s) operations(s) due to 'staffing issues' in den. We were told that we might be slowed and/or held going into den. Luckily; i had uploaded some extra fuel. We continued and were slowed to 240 knot(s) approximately 150 nautical mile out. We continued in and were progressively descended on the dandd arrival, arrive around dandd we were vectored westbound and descended to 13000 feet/foot mean sea level we were told to expect runway(s) 35r. We set up and briefed an approach to runway(s) 35r. It was night and we were instrument meteorological conditions 2 controllers later; as we were being vectored to final; when we were approximately 7 mile from the final approach fix we were given our approach clearance the controller gave a standard type clearance that included a heading minimum altitude until established and then 'clred for instrument landing system runway(s) 35l.' as we usually are during that phase of flight our cockpit was busy with aircraft confign and chklists -- the frequency was busy also with numerous arriving aircraft triple simultaneous instrument landing system approachs were being conducted. I read back the clearance and hesitated at the '35l' part. I asked my coplt intermediate fix we were on the left/right (directions) or the left/right (directions) she replied on the left/right (directions) i asked the controller what runway(s) we were cleared for; he responded that we were cleared for the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l. At that time i said we were not set up for the left/right (directions) and he climbed us and vectored us in a box pattern to set us up for the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l. We scrambled to get set up and brief the new approach we were vectored and flew the instrument landing system runway(s) 35l with an uneventful landing intermediate fix i had just said 'clred for the apch;' and continued for runway(s) 35r; or intermediate fix my readback had been stepped on; would there have been a 'conflict?' what intermediate fix i had accepted an aircraft with an inoperative tcas? Or some other aircraft had inoperative traffic alert and collision avoidance system how would having 2 or 3 aircraft responding to ra's have impacted that op? At night and instrument meteorological conditions i know myself and my first officer were both fatigued and i have to wonder intermediate fix terminal radar approach control facility was fatigued also. What was the staffing issue?
output: B737-300 arriving den is given vectors to intercept instrument landing system 35l when they were told to expect and were set up for the instrument landing system 35r. Aircraft was then vectored for another approach to 35l.

input: Boarded aircraft and found maintenance personnel on the flight deck performing duties to include deferring open items and performing extended range twin operations release checks. Of particular interest to me was the minimum equipment list deferral of the traffic alert and collision avoidance system system and a maintenance log entry from the previous flight of the air traffic control transponders; both 1 and 2; being reported by air traffic control as intermittent. Maintenance personnel told me they had replaced the traffic alert and collision avoidance system computer but did not have the equipment to test it so the minimum equipment list deferral remained. An aircraft test of the transponder system was performed and the system test passed; the transponder system was signed off as operational. The maintenance extended range twin operations release was received from maintenance control; the preflight duties were performed by the flight crew and the flight departed on time. On taxi out for takeoff; tower advised negative transponder readout for our aircraft; we switched to the other transponder but it was also reported as inoperative. Realizing that our flight into rvsm airspace required at least one working transponder and for safety of flight considerations i made the decision to return to the gate and have the transponder system checked. I made an entry in the maintenance logbook. Maintenance personnel changed the air traffic control transponder control box and the #1 transponder and performed an aircraft system test which passed; then signed off the system as operational in the logbook. I asked that they also do a test with air traffic control of the transponder readout; but we found out from air traffic control that the transponder readout is inhibited at the gates and the test would have to be done away from the gates on taxi out. We departed the gate a second time 151 minutes late. On taxi out; tower reported the transponder readout as normal. The transponder system operation was normal during taxi; takeoff and climbout to fl360. Approximately 100 nautical mile out air traffic control reported radar contact lost no transponder code or altitude readout; only primary radar target. With our transponders intermittent or somehow restricted in range; i asked air traffic control to coordinate our entry into rvsm airspace with transponders inoperative; negative rvsm; per fom. I then contacted dispatch via automatic communications addressing & reporting system and advised of our situation. Air traffic control responded by clearing us as filed; fl330. We descended to fl330; reported level and advised dispatch of clearance. Flight proceeded ops normal enroute. Approaching the west coast; contact with oak center was established and a transponder code received and entered in the air traffic control transponder. Primary radar contact was made but transponder readout delayed; we were given a descent clearance; started our descent then radar contact established approximately 100 nautical mile from our destination at about fl250. Transponder worked normal with oak center until we switched to norcal approach. Norcal reported our transponder readout as intermittent. Due to the hour the tower was closed; conditions were clear; and norcal cleared us for a visual approach; but we set up for an instrument landing system the aircraft was configured for landing; flaps 20 and gear down. Outside the final approach fix with the gear down three green we received a trailing edge annunciator light; te flap disagree engine indicating and crew alerting system message; and a te flap lockout status message. The flap position indicator showed the flaps as symmetrical; down at between 5 and 10 degrees. I followed quick reference handbook but considering we were flying into an uncontrolled airport; with no traffic alert and collision avoidance system and; at best; an intermittent transponder i did not want to go around and made the decision to land with the flaps we had available. Our weight was less than 260;000 pounds vref; flaps 30 speed was 130 knot(s) and i chose to land at vref30 + 30 (about 160 kts). Approach and landing proceeded normally with no further incident. On arrival i made maintenance logbook entries for the inoperative flaps and intermittent transponders. After much needed crew rest; the following morning we proceeded to the airport for our next flight. The maintenance logbook showed the flap system reset and tested and thelower air traffic control transponder antenna removed and replaced and the 2 air traffic control antenna switching units removed and replaced; the system aircraft tested (but not tested with atc) and the system signed off as operational. On taxi out; tower confirmed our transponder code readout and takeoff was normal. On climbout about 8;000 feet/foot norcal departure reported radar contact lost but then reestablished climbing through 10;500 feet/foot oak center reported radar contact until about 100 nautical mile out at which point radar contact was lost until approaching destination. Like the day before; we coordinated with air traffic control to continue into rvsm airspace with intermittent/inoperative transponder; negative rvsm and notified dispatch. Clearance to proceed as filed; fl360 was received and once again i had dispatch confirm clearance oak. Flight proceeded without incident; approximately 100 nautical mile out; air traffic control reported radar contact and normal transponder code and altitude readout on descent; approach and landing.
output: B767 captain reports flying two pacific crossings with weak transponders after attempts by maintenance to make repairs. The first flight ends with a te flap disagree engine indicating and crew alerting system message; and a te flap lockout status message. Captain elects to land with existing flaps at vref30 + 30 kts.

input: In brief; i landed about 50 feet/foot short of the boeing field runway(s) 31r threshold line. This was at the end of a 1.6 hour first flight and chkout in an sma type 2; and after a longitude day at work. I had made 3 good lndgs and this was to be the final one. I wanted to try a short field landing and to set down on the runway(s) numbers. On final approach my attention was drawn to a taxiing wdb freighter under the approach path and to maintaining a flight path on the visual approach slope indicator although i feel i remained on the visual approach slope indicator my instructor said he felt that; while i was on the visual approach slope indicator i was a little low on it and showed a trace of pink on the bottom light at one point. With my concern about keeping the flight path high; i subconsciously pulled back on the yoke; and my airspd dropped from the desired 65 knots indicated airspeed to 60 knots indicated airspeed once over the paved portion of 31r; i reduced power to set down on the numbers; but the sink rate was greater than i expected. At about 50 feet/foot above ground level i still thought the landing flare and subsequent float would carry me onto the numbers. In fact; the plane exhibited no float at all; and we landed about 50 feet/foot short of the threshold line. The touchdown was not a hard one and was on paved runway(s) there was no damage or harm of any sort. However; as my instructor vigorously pointed out; landing 50 feet/foot short at some airports can mean not making the runway(s) at all. I made 2 main mistakes which caused this event: 1) i picked an intended touchdown point too close to the threshold; the problem being the numbers are an obvious; but perhaps not safe; target for a spot landing perhaps i also shouldn't have attempted a spot landing on a runway(s) at which flying the visual approach slope indicator is second officer critical. 2) i let the speed drop to 60 knot(s) and expected the aircraft to perform about the same way it did at 65 knot(s) i did this in an unfamiliar aircraft which; as it turns out; flares normally and floats slightly at 65 knot(s) but sinks like a stone at 60 knot(s) the sma type 1; with which i ante meridiem much more familiar; and which feels the same in many other respects; floats slightly even at 60 knot(s) i probably shouldn't have tried a spot landing in a plane i had only landed 3 times before. Fatigue and a headache brought on by 'headset squeeze' were contributing factors in my poor performance.
output: Plt trainee in training on type lands short of displaced threshold of active rwy.

input: While in cruise we had the left engine oil light illuminate indicating low oil pressure. The oil pressure gauge confirmed the low oil pressure. Following our checklists we shut down the left engine. We requested to change our destination to zzz. On about a 10 mile final we realized the airspace was extremely busy and we [advised atc] in the hope of avoiding the need for a diversion or go-around. We landed at zzz without incident. After landing we discovered that the left oil filler/dipstick cap had developed a gap in the o-ring allowing the engine oil to escape. When the o-ring was replaced and the oil replenished; the engine ran fine.
output: Falcon 10 flight crew shut down left engine due to low oil pressure. They discovered the o-ring on the oil filler cap had a gap that allowed oil to escape.

input: I was on a filed instrument flight rules flight plan for the purpose of simulating instrument flight and doing practice approaches. We flew the area navigation 28 into zzz and proceeded to zzz2 for the loc/dme back course 18. We were instructed to climb to 4;000 feet/foot there was no cloud cover at that time. As we got about 20 nautical mile from zzz2 we had an overcast ceiling of about 2;700 feet/foot we were flying a robinson r-22 helicopter which is not certified to fly in instrument meteorological conditions conditions. We requested a frequency change to contact flight service station specialist who gave us the weather at zzz2 and zzz3. When we got back on with control and requested to proceed direct to zzz3 for the vor and dme (co-located) 21; we received the clearance to proceed direct and maintain 4;000 feet/foot when we were about 30 nautical mile out we received the clearance to descend to 2;700 feet/foot and we responded that we were unable to descend into the clouds. The controller said that we were on an instrument flight rules flight plan and couldn't understand why we were declining to descend. We responded that our aircraft was not certified to go into the clouds and that we could not descend at that time. The controller said to advise when we were able to descend. About five minutes later; the cloud layer broke and we started our descent. We went down to about 3;600 feet/foot and the controller said that we were not cleared to descend and that we needed a clearance to descend and we were now cleared to descend to 2;700 feet/foot once we got back to our home base; the federal aviation administration contacted us to find out why we had filed an instrument flight rules flight plan and would not comply with the order to descend into the clouds. I now understand that i cannot fly in a visual flight rules on top condition even though on an instrument flight rules flight plan if i can't stay in visual flight rules flight.
output: R-22 instructor and student pilot on an instrument flight rules flight plan declined an air traffic control request to descend into instrument meteorological conditions because their helicopter was not instrument flight rules certified.

input: First let me say; we caught the error and did not fall into the trap. But given another day i could easily see myself making this mistake under the circumstances.we were repositioning a plane to zzz. I set up and briefed the area navigation approach to xy. The weather started to deteriorate making that approach not usable. So i set up and briefed the instrument landing system yz. We were then told that there had been an accident and that the instrument landing system was unusable. We then began to get conflicting information as to whether we could shoot the area navigation to yz. Which i set up and briefed. We were then told that we could not do that approach but that another airplane had gone into runway zz and that was available although the ceilings made it marginal. At this point i did not brief that approach. At the same time we were talking to dispatch which wanted us to divert to zzz1 which we did. We set up the instrument landing system and were heading into the downwind when dispatch called and said we could go back and land at zzz and that they had received information that supported that. That information was not accurate. At this point dispatch started to become a threat because they were continually calling and the information they were giving us was not accurate. I am not placing blame on them it's just what it was.we diverted back to zzz. Then the controller also was confused as to whether the runway was a go to land on or the approaches were temporarily unusable due to the accident. He again offered runway 2 and said that a previous aircraft had made it in.we asked for holding at zzzzz to buy us time to think through the options. He put us at 5;000 feet i briefed the area navigation to yz because now the controller said the area navigation was doable. It turns out it was not. We talked to dispatch and told them that contrary to popular belief there was still ambiguity as to whether or not yz/xy were usable due to the crash. [captain] had contacted the tower and was trying to get some information. During the next minute or so the controller heard what he thought was us asking for the approach...we had not. He cleared us for the approach. I did not bite because we were at 5;000 feet and that in order for us to have a reasonable descent i'd need something like 3;000 feet. So i didn't bite i told him i wanted to stay in the hold. During this the controller then came back and told me the 'the national transportation safety board was on the scene now and said we could not fly any approaches to yz/xy' great. But that zz was still usable.i then started setting up the approach for zz. Obviously we were getting tired by now. I think i had briefed something like 5 approaches at this point. I started briefing the approach and expanded the approach plate on the ipad. You know that little note that says 'runway zz not authorized at night' was now off the screen. [the captain] also looked at the back of the 10-9 plate and we were making notations of all of the runway notes etc. However that note for runway zz was out of my field of view. There was more discussion with dispatch and that we were going to try runway zz. Almost simultaneously we got a message from dispatch and i scrolled the chart down and noticed that notation. However i have to be honest we came very close to shooting that approach. I told air traffic control that we could not shoot the approach because of that note. They said they did not have that note on their charts and that another plane had just made it in and were kind of wondering what we were looking at. Regardless we said we could not do it.we contacted dispatch and told them we were then heading to zzz1. Which we did and landed safely.i think i set up and briefed maybe 5 to 7 approaches; a couple over again because we had just so much going on. We did three diverts and a hold and were being lead down paths with incorrect information from air traffic control dispatch and tower controllers; cleared from altitudes on approaches which would of made for radical descents . We managed the workflow well and avoided all of these traps that were l aid for us. We almost though bit on the runway zz approach. Why because air traffic control kept offering it; another plane had just made it so our expectation and bias was that it was usable. Yes we should always scroll up and down on the ipad to ensure all information is seen; that's our job. But given the saturation and the nature of the ipad and the fact that it was yet another approached briefed after 5 or 6 or i had lost track how many were briefed it is an easy enough miss. I wish that the really important notes were grouped into one place or that at night the release had some remarks. I bet you that if you did this as a line oriented flight training (loft) scenario 50% of pilots would bite. We didn't not because i think we're better but because we just happen to catch it as did dispatch but late in the game. We came oh so close to making the mistake that i felt i should as soon as possible it.
output: Flight crew reported that the primary runway at their destination airport was closed due to an aircraft incident. Several times they were given conflicting information regarding the availability of another runway; ultimately resulting in a diversion to an alternate airport.

input: On visual approach to runway(s) 23l at tys; we were 4-5 mile left/right (directions) dogleg base to runway(s) 23l at 2600 feet/foot mean sea level when we received a ground proximity warning system warning. We had 15+ mile visibility; runway(s) and airport in sight. We started a climb and at 3000 feet/foot mean sea level ground proximity warning system warning stopped. The following morning; looking at arrival, arrive from the east there are several short sleeper hills along that approach area that probably set off the gpws.
output: F100 receive ground proximity warning system alert when turning left/right (directions) base at tys and execute clb.

input: We were in cruise at fl360; about 50 minute(s) into a 1:43 minute(s) flight halfway there between zzz1 and zzz2. We received a hydraulic 3 hi temperature message on the engine indicating and crew alerting system and followed the pom chklists from there. We were operating with pump 3a deferred; second officer with having to turn off pump 3b; we had lost a hydraulic system and some necessary hydraulic services like landing gear extension; nosewheel steering and inboard ground spoilers. The associated chklists light emitting diode us to declaring an emergency diverting to zzz and a 12000 feet/foot runway(s) with favorable winds. We tried to automatic communications addressing & reporting system dispatch; and we briefed the flight attendants for an emergency and an unlikely possibility of evacuate/evacuation we performed an emergency gear extension; and landed without incident with arff standing by. The station was unable to tow us to the gate as we requested. Second officer after the passenber had been bused to the terminal; under maintenance guidance; and after the #3 hydraulic system had cooled; we started up the engs and taxied the aircraft to the ramp. When we received the aircraft for flight we noted that hydraulic pump 3a was deferred. When we read the minimum equipment list it was a little unclr as to how to operate the aircraft in that condition as the usual operations(s) is with 3a on; and 3b automatic to back up 3a or come on during various flight regimes for redundancy. Maintenance said that 3b just stays on in this instance in place of 3a. In reviewing the original write-up that light emitting diode to hydraulic pump 3a being deferred (hyd system 3 had experienced a hi temperature earlier that day already); it appeared that in the previous event the problem may not have been adequately addressed. The write-up said that after pump 3a caused an over-temp the crew had switched to pump 3b; and though the system had cooled some with the pumps both off; pump 3b was causing the system temperature to rise also. We really have no way to know intermediate fix this was anything other than an incident that happened to occur. Although it appeared that both pump 3a and pump 3b were causing the temperature in the #3 hydraulic system to rise at the time of the original write-up. It could easily have been that the minimum equipment list was correctly assigned and the associated condition deteriorated even faster than anticipated. Or it may have been a misdiagnosed problem that could have been handled more effectively in another way.
output: A crj900's #3 hydraulic system hi temperature engine indicating and crew alerting system message alerted in flight with the 3a hydraulic pump deferred. An emergency was declared and the flight diverted to a nearby arpt.

input: We operate a cpr bombardier global express. We were planning an xa00 departure out of iad. As we prepared the aircraft it did not occur to us that there would be any problem exiting the ramp. And during the external walkaround; the only reason that i could think of why i did not notice this potential problem to exit from cargo was probably because it was blocked by 2 relatively large aircraft and from a distance this would make the distance between them difficult to judge. There was a dc8 loading cargo on the left/right (directions) and a boeing bizjet on the left/right (directions) completely shut down and closed up. It was not till the line crew came up to the cockpit just prior to engine start and pointed out that they were trying to move the boeing; but were not able. They indicated that they thought that we might be able to squeeze out. Of which we agreed to pull out and take a look; but told them that we needed a lot of assistance as federal aviation regulation as men on each wing; and knew that this could amount to nothing more than a look see. Which would also secondly make a point to the people at xxx that they indeed have boxed us in; and this is not good. We pulled out and made the left/right (directions) turn; toward the 2 aircraft but as we progressed it was convincingly apparent that there would be no way. We positioned in the best possible way second officer as not to get anyone stuck; but as we progressed the line crew continued to motion us forward; and thinking that there was some reason to take us further forward; we continued; but it became very obvious that they were intending to take us into a very unsafe position motioning us to go under the wing of the other aircraft this; of course; was not an option and we stopped well short of that prospect. But close enough to concern the dc8 crew; though they did not jump out and ask us to stop. We shut down the left/right (directions) engine and the capt got out to explore intermediate fix there was any quick resolve; such as the moving of the dc8; but they were not going to budge till they were through loading their cargo. And the boeing crew was nowhere to be found; second officer we were left to shutting down and waiting the 30 minute(s) till the dc8 got pushed back. It was not till later when talking to the crew of the dc8 that i was informed that they were loading ammunition. As the lineman was leading us; the thought certainly crossed my mind; was it ok to take 1 wing under the other; intermediate fix he was able to lead me safely in that situation? This is not a good thought. In reflection of that thought; there were some human factors involved which not till now did i realize have influence but as yet have not caused me to do anything unsafe. But in this case it light emitting diode me into a situation that could unknowingly influence judgement or at the least continue to bring stress into the cockpit. The capt on this flight asked our lead passenber intermediate fix it would be ok to stay another night in washington rather than move the aircraft empty the night before; and the boss agreed. We had given ourselves at least 1 hour 15 minute(s) extra; but i think getting to our destination and in position for the pickup was an extra added pressure because of the fact that the pilot in command had created the timetable. Secondly this pilot in command has been with this department for 15+ yrs and during that tenure he has had an earlier incident with the boss on board. And i notice that when flying with him although he seems cool as a cucumber; i ante meridiem on alert that he will occasionally try to push that limit; to be put in the right light with the boss. In this situation; i think i did feel a bit of pressure coming from him in regards to taxiing up and taking a look. But that was leading me into a situation that could take us into trying something that we would rather not try. I need to be aware of my own limits in any situation when flying with him or anyone else. This awareness may very well assist in many other situations that will allow me to look at the circumstances and not any pressure coming from other seat to the side of me or any seat in the cabin. And this situation has also given me new resolve to take the mindset i have had for years. The lineman is merely advisory and they would go home and think nothing intermediate fix two wings met on a ramp; wile at a minimum i would carry that for the rest of my career. I ante meridiem rethinking how very serious the operations(s) on the ramp are; and just how much insidious danger awaits there. The bottom line is that two wings are never to cross on the ground or in the air. I think the contributory elements to this situation are: 1) everyone is trying to meet deadlines that really are not that important. 2) the fixed-base operator felt that they would show they were trying; by doing the impossible; because they were responsible for making sure that we would get out and that they did not set us up to be impeded. For their lack of anticipation an apology is probably better suited. 3) the perception in and around larger aircraft that distances are more difficult to judge. 4) we were on an angle to the two aircraft before we began to taxi out; and from there it did seem there was an adequate distance between the aircraft 5) not having a tremendous amount of time in this aircraft it is difficult to conceptualize the wingspan in comparison to situations like this. Helpful to remember: 1) the linemen are advisory only; though extremely helpful they have no tests or medicals to pass. And their motivations may not be your own. 2) scout it out and plan ahead. 3) and have a good sense of where your wingtips are and when in the slightest doubt wait it out. 4) make sure wherever you are on the airport that there is plenty of room for ground operations(s) 5) and finally the fact that you never know what the aircraft you are taxiing by might be carrying. I learned a lot.
output: A global express 700 first officer rpts refusing to taxi out of an iad cargo ramp with insufficient wing clearance from a dc8 and a boeing bizjet.

input: Enrte petaluma airport (o69) to palo alto airport (pao) 6500 mean sea level called zoa to enter arsa and eventually terminal control area (127.8). Position at that time approximately north shore of san pablo bay outside arsa. Radar identified (mode c) and accepted in arsa as per requested route. Called center again to request terminal control area clearance was advised 'will hand you off to bay in a minute; cleared direct pao; vfr'. Due to frequency congestion; it was a little longer than a minute before handoff. Contacted bay and was advised that i was in the terminal control area without a clearance turn left 060 and descend to 4500'. A couple of minutes later may advised clear of terminal control area cleared direct oak airport east of lake chabot descend to 2000. Bay advised 'no conflict'; no problem; (maybe for him!) oak; (on initial clearance to pao) did not advise 'remain clear of tca' neither was i formally cleared thru the terminal control area with specific wording as usual. Suggest filing this one under communicationss i feel like mom said 'take a cookie' and split; dad came in and found me with my hand in the cookie jar.
output: Sma enters oak terminal control area without proper clrnc.

input: While en route from tde-lax at fl350 the following occurred: the fuel synoptic was selected on the secondary engine indicating and crew alerting system screen to monitor the center tank scavenge pump operations(s) during this time the secondary engine parameters 'popped up' on the secondary eics. This was caused by the #1 oil quantity decreasing at a higher than normal rate and the quantity turned to magenta at 9 quarts remaining. Over the next 15-20 minute(s) we observed the quantity drop to 4 quarts at which time the decision was made to divert to narita international we advised tokyo center via tokyo radio of the nature of our problem and our desire to go to nrt. We also began requesting fl290 which the highest altitude we could maintain on 3 engs. As the oil quantity fell we reduced engine thrust to idle to allow engine cool down prior to shut off. Request for course reversal and lower altitude were repeated. When oil quantity indicated zero the #1 engine was shut down and air traffic control was advised of this along with more requests for descent in addition; fuel dumping was initiated as the airspd decayed toward the yellow minute(s) arc; with still no descent clearance we declared an emergency turned off track to the north and began a descent to fl290. Air traffic control then gave us clearance to fl290 and back to nrt. Maintenance found a broken oil pressure line on #1 engine intermediate fix air traffic control had provided prompter assistance in the form of lower altitudes a disruption of traffic could have been avoided. Even after the emergency was declared with nrt weather at 200 feet/foot and 1600 meters; air traffic control sandwiched an aircraft into final ahead of us for runway(s) 34 with only 2 mile separation setting up a potential 3 engine missed approach in bad weather as for the oil indication; the advanced cockpit wdb with 4 engs has had an indication problem on oil quantity for engs 3 and 4 since the beginning of delivery. After start and departure the oil quantity on 3 and 4 fall from 20/24 quarts to 9 and sometimes 5 quarts; causing the display to indicate magenta quantities and negating the alerting function of 'pop up' and color change when oil quantities fall. Intermediate fix we had broken a line on 3 or 4 we would most likely have missed the problem until the engine was severely damaged. Aircraft manufacturer or engine manufacturer need to rectify this problem asap.
output: Acft equipment problem.

input: After a normal landing at sna; i cleared the runway(s) as soon as practical because an airline aircraft was on a 2-3 mile final behind me. Immediately after departing the runway(s) the coplt attempted to contact ground control 3 times without success. The distance between the active runway(s) and taxiway is very short. It is also the last taxiway on a short runway(s) -- by large aircraft standards. By this time i turned on the taxiway and stopped immediately when i saw a small plane approximately 1200-1500 feet/foot away taxiing toward me. Then the small plane stopped. The coplt checkeded the ground frequency and had inadvertently inserted the wrong frequency (121.8 versus 120.8). After selecting the correct frequency ground control was contacted and i remained stopped until the small aircraft was cleared to taxi and taxied around me. There was no danger to either aircraft at any time in as much as both aircraft stopped (with over 1000 feet/foot of clrnc) until ground control had control of the situation the ground controller was correct that i did not have clearance onto the taxiway however; intermediate fix i had stopped before entering the taxiway the airliner would have been unable to clear the runway(s) sna has only a single runway(s) for large aircraft and is one of the most highly congested airports in the world. My attempt to clear the runway(s) and onto the taxiway was an honest attempt to keep traffic moving. With the ground control frequency at times; being congested; often there is a delay in contacting the ground controller on this occasion it was compounded by inadvertently selecting the wrong ground control frequency because of the heavy traffic and limited txwys often aircraft are facing each other on the same taxiway the situation basically results in making the decision: 1) clearing the runway(s) stopping immediately (until ground control is contacted) with no space for an aircraft behind to exit resulting in possible delays and even missed approachs 2) intermediate fix unable to immediately contact ground control (for whatever reason) taxi onto the taxiway and stop until contact with ground control is established.
output: A private mlg flight crew clears runway(s) 19r at sna and turns off onto taxiway d then; without talking to ground control continues onto taxiway a; where they block another aircraft temporarily. The rptr admits to being on the wrong frequency but also complains about the difficulty of clearing the runway(s) without proceeding onto taxiway a due to the length of his aircraft versus the shortness of taxiway d.

input: I thought that the buckeye military operating area was hot 30000 feet/foot and below when it was actually hot 50000 feet/foot and below.
