output: Lgt guided to ramp by marshallers who let aircraft with no shut down. Crew tried to contact to determine loading area and then cleared to taxi by ground hit fuel truck.

input: Clbing to assigned fl200; i entered clouds and almost immediately begin picking up moderate mixed icing. I was on vectors (hdg 200) to intercept the standard instrument departure upon ice penetration; i informed controller and advised i was turning to heading 090 degrees to descend to visual flight rules breaking out at about 15500 feet/foot i canceled instrument flight rules and proceeded to destination visual flight rules air traffic control did not advise of any conflicts; and was extremely helpful.
output: Sma pilot runs into icing on clbout. Turns aircraft as he advises air route traffic control center radar controller of his intent to descend out of the icing.

input: Ground gave us clearance to taxi and hold short runway 13 from the gate via b3 and b taxiway. Upon turning from b3 intersection onto taxiway b; i noticed there was no sign confirming i was actually turning onto b taxiway. There was a small yellow sign with an arrow to 13 '13 ->;' but no actual taxiway b sign. I had to stop and refer to my commercial chart along with coordinating with my first officer to confirm we were on the correct taxiway. All taxiways should be clearly marked with a taxiway sign on either side of an intersection. This becomes even more critical if one of taxiways; as b3 does at crp; leads to a runway. If we had turned wrong; we could have ended up with a runway incursion at this intersection. Very hazardous.
output: An air carrier captain reported poor markings at crp airport; at the intersection of taxiway b and b3.

input: The first officer entered the cockpit after completing the exterior inspection. She rpted that ramp employees were loading boxes of lithium batteries into the aft pit of the aircraft she asked intermediate fix they had a dangerous goods manifest for the batteries. They replied no; and added that the batteries did not require a dangerous goods manifest. The only label on the boxes were written in chinese except for the words 'lithium batteries;' or 'lithium battery packs;' which were in english. She then asked the ramp employee how many boxes were being loaded. He said about 1000 pounds the only reference i could find in the fom for the loading of lithium batteries was for personal use on 13.10.16. There also is a reference to a maximum limit of 55 pounds of dangerous goods in an inaccessible compartment. I called dispatch and we agreed that at a very minimum we would need a dangerous goods manifest. I also wanted to determine the maximum amount we could legally carry. The dispatcher said he would call acr's dangerous goods to verify what we could legally carry. A ramp employee came to the cockpit and could not answer my questions to my satisfaction; only to say that he 'thought' we could take the batteries and he was 'not sure' whether or not we needed a dangerous goods manifest. He then said they would remove the batteries from the aft cargo pit and place them on a later flight second officer we would not take a delay. En route i spoke with dispatch. I told him that ramp wanted to send the batteries on another flight he spoke to a dispatch shift manager who called airport operations(s) and said they could not load the batteries on another flight until everything was sorted out. That was the last of my involvement in the situation.
output: B737-500 flight crew refuses shipment of lithium batteries boarded without a dangerous goods manifest.

input: Atis was rpting winds 120 degrees at 13 knot(s) i corrected for the crosswind and my airspd was 75 knots indicated airspeed it was a normal landing the main wheels touched down first then the nosewheel. As i began to slow down the plane veered to the left/right (directions) i immediately tried to correct but realized i was going to strike one of the runway(s) edge lights; i applied full power took off again but the left/right (directions) wheel cover struck the runway(s) edge light. The tower after inquiring intermediate fix everyone onboard was all right; cleared me to land on runway(s) 14. I rpted to the tower that i thought the left/right (directions) tire had burst second officer they had a fire truck stand by at runway(s) 14. The plane landed with no further incident. I believe the plane was about 1000 feet/foot down runway(s) 19l when it veered and hit the edge light. After securing the aircraft i inspected it for damage and found that the left/right (directions) wheel cover and the rear left/right (directions) side of the nosewheel cover had damage. There was also 2 scratches on the left/right (directions) door.
output: A cessna 182 pilot struck the runway(s) edge lights during a go around at ict. Emergency equipment called out for lndg.

input: Lax taxiway markings inadequate/non-existent as to names/numbers. Clrncs should just specify via 'ramp;' 'inner;' 'outer' to simplify. Turnoffs and crossing txwys need clear lighted identifiers. Hold line instruction/signs not readily apparent and no indication of such is on taxi chart. Even gate markings (terminal 5; at least) are poor and unlit.
output: Another flight crew complaint about taxiway markings at lax.

input: Conducted 2 pre takeoff runups; no problems at altitude en route lost left/right (directions) alternator. I did not realize warning light for left/right (directions) alternator had failed en route experienced near total electrical failure. Greater knowledge of system and troubleshooting would have prevented 'pucker factor.' landed just fine.
output: Lost both alternators enrte.

input: 119.05 is automatic terminal information service frequency for sgf. 119.05 also used by dfw arrival, arrive traffic for dfw approach intermediate fix you are descending into sgf and above 8000 feet/foot mean sea level obtaining the automatic terminal information service is next to impossible because traffic inbound to dfw blocks it out. Intermediate fix you wait until below 8000 feet/foot mean sea level on descent you're too close to safely leave the frequency i talked with tower supervisor about it and he told me that there was nothing that he can do. All that needs to be done is to change the automatic terminal information service frequency can you cut through all the bureaucratic horse-pucky and get this done?
output: Plt rptr complains about dfw automatic terminal information service interfering with sgf automatic terminal information service while approaching sgf.

input: During a part 91 reposition flight on leveloff we received a flaps fail caution message. At the same time we were cleared to 17000 feet/foot before reaching the fix; we were given direct to another fix down to 11000 feet/foot at the same time the pilot not flying was running quick reference handbook items for a flaps fail caution message; and in the process of contacting company on communications 2 regarding a flaps fail caution message. Air traffic control was also advised of the flaps fail; informed that our maximum speed was limited to 250 and that we might need delay vectors or a hold in order to sort out the caution message with company. (during this whole time we also received several hdofs.) we then requested and received a delay vector; while on the vector we continued the descent down to 11000 feet/foot at 12000 feet/foot we received an resolution advisory on the traffic alert and collision avoidance system and initiated a climb to 13000 feet/foot during the climb air traffic control also gave us a climb to 13000 feet/foot air traffic control also stated that we were not cleared below 13000 feet/foot we believe that we were still cleared down to 11000 feet/foot during this time (between 13000 feet/foot and 11000 ft) company advised us there was no way to fix the problem in the air. Second officer we declared an emergency advised air traffic control that our flaps were stuck in a position that was indicating up; and our landing speed would be considerably higher. We requested the longest runway(s) and to have emergency equipment standing by. The landing was uneventful; no injuries; or damage to the aircraft we had the emergency vehicles verify that our tires and brakes were not on fire and taxied to the gate. At the gate maintenance was brought out to the aircraft i believe the cause of the resolution advisory was either us missing a radio call to stop descent at 13000 feet/foot or the controller issuing the vectors not knowing that we were cleared down to 11000 feet/foot by the previous controller in either instance; the only correction that i know of would be better communication between aircraft and atc.
output: While working an inflt equipment malfunction; flight crew may have missed an altitude clearance and overshot assigned altitude resulting in traffic alert and collision avoidance system ra.

input: Clbing through approximately fl246 on our way to fl250; the first officer noticed the cabin altitude was about 9800 feet/foot and remarked it seemed excessive. I asked center to descend to fl240. The controller responded 'roger.' at that point; the cabin altitude went above 10000 feet/foot and we received the cabin pressure warning. We; the first officer leveled off as we began the aom procedures i asked the controller for the descent again right before the warning. He said 'i have your request; say your altitude now.' during this exchange; the first officer had started his descent as i was putting on my oxygen mask. Once we were on oxygen; i advised center we were declaring an emergency due to cabin pressurization and would like to continue descent eventually at 10000 feet/foot after following all chklists per operating manual; the pressurization was stabilized by using the manual mode. After conferring with company dispatch and maintenance control the decision was made to continue to dfw. There was no doubt of structural integrity. Since we no longer required priority handling; air traffic control asked intermediate fix we wanted to cancel the emergency we said yes and continued to dfw without event. I'm not sure what caused the excessive cabin altitude but my lack of situational awareness in scanning the cabin pressurization panel during the clbout prevented us from remedying the problem ie; cabin altitude above 10000 feet/foot before it got to that point which dictated a descent or emergency descent since the controller didn't issue a descent right off; we had to declare the emergency and descend since the cabin altitude had reached approximately 13000 feet/foot since we rarely go above fl190 on our short trips; the pressurization is not usually an issue. Most of my trips recently have been short flts; around 10000 feet/foot this has probably light emitting diode to the lack of scan. Needless to say; this occurrence has renewed my scan of all system during clbout. There were no injuries or aircraft damage. I believe the only emergency was to descend in order to assure the cabin altitude descended there was no decompression in any manner. The manual mode did pressurize the aircraft the pressurization is always an issue; to re-explain; it's just that the pressurization checked on the chklist is only on the initial climb chklist and on the descent chklist. One should scan the system at regular intervals of course; but having another pressurization checked on the cruise chklist might help; even though in this case; we were still a few hundred feet/foot from cruise altitude possible causes for the excessive cabin altitude which was a gradual increase; could possibly have been the automatic controller at fault or the secondary outflow valve being cracked open by the manual know being misaligned or accidentally brushed against by something. At this time i don't know.
output: Sf340 flight crew declared an emergency and descended due to noticing the cabin altitude climbing to an unacceptable alt.

input: During climb from dca at night; using nw departure dca departure control cleared us to 17000'. At approximately 9000' departure control cleared us direct ldn which gave us a heading of 260 degrees at 11000' they rpted traffic at 11 o'clock; 17500'. We observed only 1 aircraft in that area and responded; 'tfc in sight.' the aircraft was at the 10:30 high position opp direction; approximately 20 mile and would pass clear to the left. Departure then switched us to dulles approach control at approximately 12000' and had us rpt that we had the traffic on initial contact; approximately 13000'; with dulles approach we rpted 'tfc in sight.' dulles approach then cleared us to 'clb to 270 pilot's discretion.' we hesitated a moment before reading back the clearance as we had not heard the term 'plt's discretion' used before in relation to a climb with visibility traffic we then read back the clearance but omitted the pilot's discretion in hopes that the controller would clarify the instruction. Instead he acknowledged the readback and immediately started talking to another aircraft at this same time the autoplt/fms leveled the aircraft off at 17000'. We then reprogrammed the altitude select and engaged the vertical navigation to start the climb we were well clear and maintaining visibility sep from the traffic and did not see any other aircraft ahead. The autoplt/fms was slow to leave 17000' as it performed a transition to climb during this transition we spotted a second aircraft at 11:30 slightly high; 1 mile opp direction that had just turned on its landing lights. We disconnected the autoplt and remained level at 17000'. The second aircraft passed overhead. Approximately 45 secs later we asked approach control the position of our traffic to confirm which aircraft was the rpted traffic approach replied; '5 o'clock 10 mile 17500'.' he then asked intermediate fix we saw the traffic and we replied; 'yes.' at this point we still had visibility contact with the first aircraft at our 7:30 position and what looked like our same altitude we then reconfirmed our clearance to fl270 and started a climb shortly thereafter approach control switched us to center and we continued the flight to dfw. At no time during this sequence of events did either dca departure or dulles approach mention any other traffic nor indicate that we may see more than 1 aircraft in the 10-12 o'clock position also; when the second aircraft went overhead the first aircraft was at our 9 o'clock position and appeared to be 3-4 mile level at our altitude although we were maintaining a watch for other aircraft we were unable to see the oncoming second aircraft head to head from below until he turned on his landing light. The lack of advisories from dca departure or dulles approach as to other traffic in that area light emitting diode us to believe that we had the only conflicting traffic visually and were tracking a safe course. It is a poor practice to allow 2 aircraft to converge head on in that manner; even with visibility contact when there is a possibility of confusing traffic and identing the wrong aircraft there should be mandatory horizontal radar sep to ensure that a margin of safety is maintained.
output: Close proximitypa acr-mlg unk-vfr aircraft opposite direction traffic at night.

input: Aircraft x was a visual flight rules full stop with taxi back. After taxiing back to runway 31l (temporary runway); aircraft x crossed the hold short line without a clearance. There was no impact; or other traffic. The hold short line for the temporary is the same as it was for the regular runway 31l prior to construction. It is located in an unexpected place.the hold short lines should be placed in a normal distance from the temporary runway.
output: Psp tower controller reports of a runway incursion due to the markings of the hold short lines and construction at the airport.

input: [in cruise flight] fl310 we noticed the cabin altitude climbing above normal level. After reference of checklists etc we were still unable to control the cabin altitude from climbing. We descended to fl250 and subsequently descended to fl230. This stabilized the cabin altitude just below 8000 feet. The cabin continued to descend with our lower cruise altitude. We contacted dispatch; [maintenance] and after careful consideration of factors and available resources (checklists; weather; notams; fuel; aircraft state; maintenance; performance; passengers; crew) we elected (with dispatch and [maintenance] concurrence) to divert to [a suitable airport]. We continued a gradual early descent in order to lower the cabin altitude in a comfortable manner. No sops or fars violated. No discomfort issues with passengers or crew. Air traffic control was notified of our condition. We made a normal uneventful approach and landing.
output: B757 flight crew reported diverting to an alternate after loss of automatic pressurization control.

input: The ground person on the headset just prior to push; did not state 'gnd to cockpit; pre-dep checked is complete.' instead; i believe he said 'ready to push.' he has a difficult time communicating over the headset; in the english language. I stated; 'after the rj; you are cleared to push for a westbound taxi; the brakes are set.' shortly after; i felt the tug trying to push the aircraft with the brakes set. I asked the ground person intermediate fix he had tried to push the aircraft with the brakes set. I believe he had a difficult time understanding my question; he eventually said yes. I asked him to get someone else on the headset. The other ground person that came on the interphone; told me that he was training the previous person. I told him that due to the language communications safety was being affected; i would rather have him on the headset during pushback. He stayed on the headset with me for the remainder of our time; at the gate. We incurred a 30 minute(s) delay while maintenance inspected the nose gear and provided a new maintenance release.
output: A b767 capt rpts nonstandard communicationss with tug driver during pushback; resulting in an attempt to push with the brakes set.

input: Lmp (lower minimum performance) was downgraded to 'not clear air turbulence ii' due to r-hand autoplt and thrust management on minimum equipment list on day 10 of the minimum equipment list the autoplt was fixed yet the thrust management remained on minimum equipment list to circumvent the 10 day restrict, restricted, restriction of the minimum equipment list i was instructed by management to clear the placard and reissue it using new authority/authorized to restart the clock. This is in violation of gpm 16-14b page 2.
output: A b757-200 was dispatched in non compliance with the aircraft thrust management system out of the 10 day limit but with a new deferred item issued extending the 10 day limit.

input: Assigned standard instrument departure ali 1 a from vidp. This was loaded in flight management system and efb as published. It was flown in navigate, navigation on autopilot. After takeoff we were advised by departure control that the standard instrument departure was revised 15 days ago and we were flying the old standard instrument departure we were then given radar vectors. The controller reported 'no problem.' standard instrument departure change was the same number as the old one. It was not revised on our flight management system or efb (or the paper charts also). In the us intermediate fix a standard instrument departure or standard terminal arrival route is changed it is renumbered. The standard instrument departure change was not listed on our chart change bulletins. Standard instrument departure change was listed on page 10 of 18 pages of notams for vidp which we missed. When second officer many notams are given to us to review; most of which do not apply (different dates or times etc); it is extremely difficult not to miss something at some time. The notice to airmen / of air missions system is outdated and not specific to our flight (date; time; items which do not apply to our operation).callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr has not been back to vidp and has not checked to see intermediate fix the procedure has been updated in the aircraft that he flies.
output: Acr capt reports departing vidp using outdated procedure for the ali 1a standard instrument departure the flight management computer efb; and paper charts have not been updated.

input: With bwi approach control [potomac]; we were vectored onto a visual approach to 33l. They put us in between 2 b737s which where only separated by 5 nautical mile by referencing the traffic alert and collision avoidance system map. We were told to slow to final approach speed. We configured to flaps 22 and gear down. Passing through 150 knots indicated airspeed and approximately 1400 ft above ground level with the autopilot on; the aircraft began to roll to the right and suspected wake turbulence. As we continued to roll to the right passing 25-30 degrees of bank; i decided to take control of the aircraft and autopilot automatically disabled when rolling the yoke to the left. I continued to roll the yoke to the left to the stop. I had no more aileron input to the left and we continued to roll through 60-70 degrees. At this time the pilot monitoring decided to push the power to full forward helping in any way to regain control the aircraft. Audial 'bank angle' was heard and we continued to roll. At this time i decided the best course of action was to stop trying to roll the aircraft level to the left and let the aircraft to continue to roll and try to maintain a 1g roll with the direction of the wake. We had no control of the aircraft as we passed 80 degrees bank. At about 90 degrees bank; with the engine spooled up; we regained control of the aircraft and recovered from the unusual attitude. We apparently were no longer in the wake of the aircraft in front of us. Recovering from the excessive bank; we executed a go-around. We told bwi tower that we encountered wake turbulence and called the go around. We were vectored around for another visual and landed. Bwi terminal radar approach control facility [potomac] seems to put aircraft very close on visuals. I know separation can be reduced to 2.5 nautical mile on visual approaches within 10 miles of runway; but 3 miles might be safer with an rj behind a b737-800. In doing some research; a 737-800 can have the same wake at max landing weight as a 757. Would suggest to at least move to 3 [miles].
output: Emb-145 flight crew reported a loss of control and aircraft upset following a wake turbulence encounter on approach to bwi in trail of a b737 which caused a 90 degree bank.

input: Fatigue without relief pilot during my last trip to ogg (flt x) and my return to zzz (fly y) some fatigue issues arose. The trip was not scheduled to have a relief pilot because of contractual flight time limits (any flight under 8 hrs). Limits that were just changed. My previous 2 trips to this location this month had a relief pilot on board. The ogg arrival, arrive was basically uneventful and we got to the hotel around xa00 post meridiem i went for a run. I then returned to the hotel; went to expected approach time and was asleep by xe45 post meridiem i was wakened by the sun shining in my room around xc30 ante meridiem the rest of the morning was spent visiting the island. I got back to my room around xl00 post meridiem and took a nap. I then took a shower and made a pot of coffee; getting ready for our xn25 post meridiem pick-up for the xp10 post meridiem departure to zzz. About 4 or 5 mile from the airport the van driver told the capt that operations(s) had just called and that there was a maintenance delay. We would now depart at xu00 post meridiem we then returned to the hotel and reset for another pick-up at xt00 post meridiem having already had a few cups of coffee; i knew that another nap would not be possible. I received another call later -- again rescheduling our pick-up time. I began to realize how longitude this trip was going to be for both myself and the capt without a relief pilot on board. After finally arriving at the airport things were uneventful. We departed for zzz at __00 post meridiem after a scheduled departure time of xp10 post meridiem having no relief pilot on board; plus flying on 'the back side of the clock;' both i and the capt were very tired. I'm not proud to say that at some point over the ocean; i must have fallen asleep for a short period of time. This occurrence has greatly disturbed me. The capt agreed with me that we both needed a nap in order to be rested for the safe operations(s) of the aircraft he told me to take a nap in my seat intermediate fix i needed one; and that he would stay awake. In the essence of safety he felt that he also needed a rest period as well; but could wait until over lax or close to that area. At no time were we both sleeping simultaneously. We arrived at zzz at xa32 ante meridiem i know that contractually no relief pilot is required on flts under 8 hours but with 'flying on the back side of the clock' compounded; in this instance; with a lengthy maintenance delay just does not pass the common sense test. We are for the most part goal-oriented people. We want to get the job done for the passenber and the crew members alike. We need to take a hard look at returning the relief pilot to flts that truly need them. Zzz departures to ogg and hnl -- both with scheduled flying times of slightly under 8 hours -- are 2 such flts. Supplemental information from acn 514967: our flight y ogg to zz was scheduled to depart ogg at xp10 post meridiem with an xn25 post meridiem pick-up at the hotel. Roughly 10 minute(s) before arrival, arrive at the airport the van driver received a phone call from our air carrier operations(s) that our flight had been delayed due to mechanical problems and that our new departure would be at xu30 post meridiem with an xt00 post meridiem pick-up. We returned to the hotel. At approximately xr30 post meridiem i received a call from our air carrier operations(s) that the part had arrived earlier than expected and could i round up my crew and return to the airport at approximately xs30 post meridiem we again departed for the airport after completing all preflt duties; the flight departed at xu00 post meridiem (scheduled departure xp10 post meridiem arrival, arrive zzz xi01 am). We were in constant chop (light to moderate) for the first 3 hours we arrived in dfw almost 4.5 hours after scheduled arrival, arrive flying all night and dealing with at least 3 hours light to moderate chop and with no scheduled break is not a good operations(s) without question; fatigue was a factor on this flight this is a legal 2-man operations(s) but not a wise one in my estimation. The relief pilot needs to be reinstated on this flight and flts like this.
output: B767 crew was given a new departure time by the air carrier after they were almost at the arpt.

input: We were on the visual approach to 18l in mco. We were cleared to descend to 2;500 feet/foot we were slowing to configure for landing while descending. Air traffic control told us again to descend to 2;500 feet/foot and pointed out traffic ahead. I explained that we had to slow while descending to air traffic control i had a visual on the cessna traffic to our right; and also a twin that appeared to be climbing directly ahead i told the captain to turn right and climb shortly after that; traffic alert and collision avoidance system commanded a climb.the main cause of this was poor communication between flight crew and air traffic control i do not believe any other company operates its fleet like our airline; requiring us to slow to within 10 knot(s) of clean maneuver or minimum flap speed before selecting our next flap position. I say this because when we are away from airports that handle lots of our flights air traffic control seems perplexed by our need to slow so much to configure. Also this causes a greatly reduced descent rate that air traffic control does not anticipate.
output: When cleared for a visual approach to runway 18l at mco; a b737ng experienced traffic conflicts and a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory with respect to traffic ahead of them. The reporter cited a company policy requiring crews to slow within 10k of minimum knots indicated airspeed for the existing flap setting before extending greater deflection. He believes this policy results in the company's aircraft following significantly different vertical descent tracks from those of most carriers which do not utilize the same vertical planning regimen.

input: Aircraft had 2 mel's on it. Pack 1 was inoperative and the ram air dampers. On initial climb out; we received a bleed 2 overpressure. The quick reference handbook procedure was run and [it] did not reset the message. We continued the quick reference handbook procedure which led us to use crossbleed which didn't work. The procedure led up to [a landing] at the nearest suitable airport. Because pack 1 was inoperative we had no pressurization as well since we lost pack 2 with the bleed overpress and crossbleeding didn't work. The aircraft had a history of bleed 2 overpressure.
output: Emb-175 flight crew reported returning to departure airport after the sole remaining air conditioning/pressurization pack failed in flight.

input: Flt clt-ord. F/o flying. Aircraft departed clt en route to ord. F/o had been flying this trip all month and was familiar with the route our clearance was hornet one departure stann left/right (directions) (clt 347 degs) htm as filed. Takeoff and clbout was normal; f/o proceeded outbnd on the clt 347 degree left/right (directions) as cleared at 50 vor and dme (co-located) he turned direct htm. Shortly thereafter center called and asked our heading i told him 305 degrees he then asked why we had turned. I turned to the f/o and he said at 50 vor and dme (co-located) on the departure we turned to the next fix. On closer examination of the fine print; the f/o had misunderstood the departure and second officer did i. I have since highlighted that trap on my departure plate for future reference. I had flown several times in the past with this particular f/o and i feel he is highly competent. I think i placed too much confidence in his familiarity with the route and should've been checkeding closer; especially since i had not flown this route in the past.
output: Flt crew of mlg departing clt made turn at 50 vor and dme (co-located) per diagram. Controller wanted heading until advised.

input: After preflt inspection; all system working; taxi normal. At rotation it was apparent i had no aileron control and little rudder control we notified departure that we wanted to return to the airport given vectors i could not hold heading and departure gave us discretion on our altitude i asked to maintain heading to burn off fuel and give me time to work on the problem after about 30 minute(s) i was able to turn the plane back towards sat; and i realized we could not fix our problem from the cockpit. Air traffic control gave me the choice of landing at sat or sks; we took sks because of wind direction and length of the runway(s) after a safe landing we think what may have caused our problem was a locking pin used during a 6 month inspection was left in place under the fuselage of the plane; and may have come out upon landing after an inspection of the plane; with all the controls working normally; we flew the airplane back to sat without any problems callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he truly believes the problem was a locking pin that was not removed prior to departure the mechs stated that they had trouble keeping the pin in place while working on the aircraft and removed the flag. Without the flag the pin would be very hard to see during the walkaround. Since the aileron movement was ok during taxi everything seemed normal. The pin was never found and the mechs claim that all pins are accounted for. There is no damage to the aircraft or scarring on the cables as there would be intermediate fix a part would have moved in or out of place during the flight the aircraft has been flown about 6 times since the incident and the problem cannot be duplicated. The lr25xr is designed second officer that aileron movement will allow the pin to fall out and rptr believes this happened on landing the design works well.
output: Lr25xr has rudder and aileron control restrict, restricted, restriction after takeoff return land after burning off fuel.

input: The 6th evening of a 7 day trip began with a re-rte dlh- ind-mem in lieu of the scheduled dlh-mem; resulting in the mem hub turn being shortened from 3 1/2 hours to 1 1/2 hours after the hub turn; on the way to grr; the event occurred during cruise at approximately xa10 on the scheduled mem-grr leg (after the hub turn) with the first officer as pilot flying throughout the week a routine had been established of initiating the descent approximately 70-75 vor and dme (co-located) out after receiving air traffic control clearance to descend at pilot's discretion at least 30 mile prior. Hypnotized by the routine (no excuse); the pilot flying initiated an uncoordinated descent from fl330 at 65 vor and dme (co-located) from grr. Both the pilot flying (fo) and pilot not flying (capt) were initially distracted by what appeared to be a repeat of a previously noted autoplt pitch knob write-up. The pilot not flying realized we had begun descent without air traffic control clearance as he made the required descent radio call at 32600 feet/foot i was the second officer on this week longitude trip. As per our procedures i stay on the communications radios as back-up except when i need to get automatic terminal information service make the tkof/lndg data card and call in-range to our station. I was off the radio at the time of the occurrence; performing my duties to call the station prior to our descent as i returned with the crew; i noted that they were simultaneously clicking off the autoplt; leveling off; talking to air traffic control and then continuing with the descent with a clearance after it was under control they explained to me they had begun to descend and when the capt called in the altitude leaving; for the new altitude he realized we had no new altitude to go to. The air traffic control controller responded with a clearance to descend to 11000 feet/foot although the pilot flying (fo) says he accepts full responsibility for descent without a clearance i will try to accomplish all my duties a little sooner; intermediate fix possible. (sometimes our radios don't pick up communications with the station that federal aviation regulation out.) i also will not always assume that the crew is fully alert; as our flying hours are at physiologically difficult times. Supplemental information from acn 402665: called zau as being 'out of fl330.' as is my habit i glanced up at the altitude alerter after making the call and saw fl330 set. I realized at this point we had not been cleared to descend second officer we immediately kicked off the autoplt and climbed back to fl330. We had descended approximately 400 feet/foot at the point of correcting. Although a 5-6 hour stint in the cockpit doesn't seem bad to the uninitiated; working on the 'backside' of the clock is deleterious to normal xchking and flows. As companies flying at night push harder to 'optimize' the efficiency of the flight schedules; they do not factor in any compensation for the biological clocks of the crews. 10 hour layovers; with debrief; shuttle times; hotel checked in; bodily functions; eating and stress/forced sleep cycles; are a ticket to more mistakes in the cockpit. 10 hour layover equates to maybe 5-6 hours of sleep. Supplemental information from acn 402847: although fatigue may have been a contributing factor; there is no excuse for initiating a descent without clearance in the future; i will establish a routine of xchking the altitude selector in addition to coordinating with the pilot not flying prior to initiating any dscnt.
output: A b727-200 freighter crew experiences an altitude excursion when the first officer starts a descent from habit and an expected clearance the flight crew notes this after 400 feet/foot of dscnt.

input: During takeoff from runway 28r from intersection east at sfo; we experienced significant engine thrust turbulence from a landed b747. Air traffic control cleared us into position on runway 28r from east intersection after the b747 passed by from landing on the same runway. The [b747] aircraft exited 28r on k and held between 28r and 28l. Air traffic control cleared us for takeoff after [the b747] cleared runway 28r on k in quick [succession]. During the takeoff roll and as we approached the b747; it appeared the aircraft was very close to runway 28r. Our aircraft actually reached v1 and became airborne just prior to intersection k where the b747 was waiting to cross runway 28l. As the flying pilot in the left seat; i glanced over and saw that the rear third of the large aircraft appeared to be still protruding across the 28r runway. As we passed by at approximately 50 feet; we experienced significant turbulence and airflow disruption from the idling b747 on taxiway k between 28r and 28l. I don't think air traffic control (sfo tower) should clear any aircraft for takeoff when a large b747 type aircraft is holding between the parallel runways 28l and 28r. I don't believe there is enough room for that size aircraft to hold short of runway 28l and be fully clear of 28r especially on k taxiway. I also feel the jet blast is significant enough to disrupt the airflow enough or case enough shear to have a significant impact on safety. Certainly if the b747 was cleared to cross 28l on k taxiway and powered up its engines as we passed by at low altitude and low airspeed the outcome could be catastrophic. I would also like to see the ground surveillance radar on this event to see just how much of that b747 was intruding into the south side of runway 28r at k intersection. From east intersection; the aircraft appeared clear and we also relied on tower to confirm that landing aircraft is clear of the runway which i don't think they could or did.
output: Corporate jet captain reported experiencing significant engine thrust turbulence from a b747 that had exited their takeoff runway and was holding short of a parallel runway.

input: Called for flaps 25; the 'trailing edge disagree' light came on and the flaps did not move from flaps 20. Executed a go around. At level off; called for flaps 5. Flaps stayed at 20. Ran quick reference handbook checklist. Planned flaps 20 landing. Did not call dispatch or maintenance. Fuel was a concern at 5.9 with flaps stuck at 20. Landed uneventfully. Unable to move flaps [with] hydraulics or electrically.
output: A b757-200 engine indicating and crew alerting system alerted trailing edge flap disagree at about 1;000 feet/foot on final; so a go around was executed. Delay vectors were requested while the quick reference handbook was complied with. With fuel considerations; a normal 20 degree flap landing was completed.

input: During clbout; had a left/right (directions) engine oil strainer clogging annunciator light. Performed abnormal procedure and reduced power returned to harlingen and replaced oil filter.
output: An air carrier mlg had to return land.

input: Completing gear retraction a loud 'growling' noise started on left side of aircraft. Engine vibration n2 5.0 was only indication of an abnormal situation. A few minutes after takeoff there were three jolts with no indications from the engines; a call from flight attendants alerted us to smoke coming from engine number one with each of the jolts. Once air traffic control was notified; dispatch/maintenance consulted and checklists completed. We dumped fuel to maximum landing weight and returned to [departure airport]. Notified on ground of bird strike; crew debriefed and critiqued.
output: A b747-400 relief pilot reported experiencing high vibration and loud noise from #1 engine after takeoff. They returned to departure airport where they were advised they had struck a bird.

input: On takeoff from cle runway 6r; just after rotation; witnessed a bird pass from right to left close to the aircraft. All engine and aircraft systems continued to operate normally. During climb; aircraft developed a slight vibration. All engine and aircraft systems continued to operate normally. Uneventful landing. Upon postflight; found #1 engine had damage.
output: A300 flight crew on departure from cle experienced a bird strike.

input: We were on the ruudy departure from teb off runway 24. As we leveled at 1;500 feet/foot before wentz tower said we had navajo traffic (do not recall if he gave direction) and i thought tower said he has you in sight. When i looked the resolution advisory went off to 'climb' and i saw the navajo turn sharply right and dive to avoid us. Pilot flying had disconnected the autopilot and started to react to the resolution advisory and the navajo was behind us. I do not think the navajo saw us when he reported to teb tower he had us in sight. When he saw us his hard right turn and dive avoided what looked to me like a midair. I do not know if the pilot flying would have been able to avoid it even though he was reacting to the resolution advisory because the autopilot comes off we were about 10 degrees off course but not very far off course when we corrected our course. I do not even know if our off course would have been detected by radar. Departure did not say we were off course. I told departure about it; he sounded very surprised asked if we knew the area and asked if teb tower issued the traffic. I said yes and it was very close. I do not recall what he said or i said because i was busy making sure we made the next altitude. In this airspace see and avoid is very questionable. It seems like there should be more positive control. It is easy to think you have traffic in sight and you may be mistaken as there is so much traffic.
output: A fractional airline crew reported a near miss with a navajo on the teb ruudy 4 standard instrument departure at 1;500 feet/foot approaching wentz intersection.

input: While we were in visual conditions descending into las airport approach control gave us a descent out of 8000 for 6000 feet/foot with the autoplt on; 6000 feet/foot was set in the altitude selector of the autoplt; confirmed by both pilots by cockpit xref and a descent begun. We were on a left/right (directions) downwind to runway(s) 25l. Approaching 6000 feet/foot approach control gave us traffic to follow at our 9 o'clock position which we confirmed we had in sight and were then told to follow. We were in the base turn to follow the traffic when approach control told us to checked altitude as we were below 6000 feet/foot we looked up at the altitude selector and it was at 5000 feet/foot and we were descending out of 5700 feet/foot we immediately climbed back to 6000 feet/foot at which time approach control cleared us for the visual approach to runway(s) 25l. Neither one of us; the coplt nor myself; had set 5000 feet/foot in the altitude selector. The major factor was getting distraction by following the 9 o'clock traffic and not watching the leveloff at 6000 feet/foot with the autoplt on. The visual conditions also could have been a factor. To correct the situation close attention to the leveloff should be adhered to -- even with the autoplt on.
output: An md82 on approach into las; nv; descends through assigned alt.

input: I was conducting an intro flight in aircraft x. We had begun our take off roll and got to rotation speed; the aircraft left the ground and was slow to climb. I was pitched at about 10 to 12 degrees.the aircraft then had a reduction in power about 75 ft. Off the ground before the engine surged back into full power. Once realizing that we were not going to have sufficient power to maintain the climb i immediately pulled the power back to idle and landed on the remaining runway. Air speed was approximately 95 kts. We landed with about 300 ft. Remaining which resulted in a runway excursion of approximately 5 ft. There was no damage to the aircraft or airfield lighting. I taxied the aircraft back to the ramp and was able to shut down; no further incidents.
output: Pilot reported aborting takeoff at 75 feet above ground level after engine power loss and landing on remaining runway.

input: B737-800 aircraft [rudder] balance arm weight did not have any paint on it. The repair deferral was listed in the summary sheet of the aircraft logbook. The repair authorization was listed as 'nef' (non-essential fixture) [function]. The raw material of this rudder flight control [balance weight] was delaminating. Pilot ordered to fly.
output: A line captain raises concerns about the use and effects of specific type i de-icing fluid on numerous b737-800 aircraft and the deterioration of their rudder balance weights. Also noted was their company practice of deferring eroded and corroded balance weights under a non-essential function (nef) deferral; instead of a regular minimum equipment list deferral for a flight control surface.

input: [event occurred] during a charter flight; in a gulfstream g200 with one passenger; two pilots and one flight attendant. The conditions were clear visual meteorological conditions and we were vectored for a visual approach. On short final a hawk flew in front of us and i decreased the descent to avoid hitting the hawk. Within approximately 15 seconds the right hydraulic system failed with numerous messages indicating the failure. We initiated a missed approach and the tower gave us a vector and altitude. We notified the tower of our problem and after we had been handed off to departure air traffic control declared an emergency. After evaluating the situation we decided to leave the gear down; slats down; and flaps at 20. Then we decided it was best to go to [another airport] where there is a gulfstream service center and [a long] runway. The flight attendant briefed the passenger on the circumstance and our intentions - then briefed for the emergency landing. We received excellent help from air traffic control along the route and decided to hold for a while to burn off extra fuel. During this time we notified [the company] of our situation and spoke with maintenance and gulfstream tech ops. Air traffic control had made [the divert airport] aware of our problem and intentions - fire/rescue trucks and gulfstream personnel with vans and a tow truck were waiting for us. We had plenty of time to go through the checklists several times and to discuss our options. When we felt that we had done all we could do and discussed this with [the company] and tech ops; and that the fuel level was sufficient for the landing; then we left the hold and started a visual approach. We reviewed the appropriate landing checklist - no brakes or anti-skid (only emergency brakes); no thrust reverser; and no nose wheel steering. We did put the flaps back to 40. Then we made the landing and all went well. The airplane was stopped on the runway and the fire trucks came; then we shut down the airplane and opened the door. Since there was no fire we decided to stay in the airplane. We walked around the airplane to see the damage and were told about the hawk hitting the right main gear and damaging the hydraulic lines. We discussed the situation with gulfstream personnel in the warmth of the airplane while waiting for a tow truck to arrive to take the airplane to gulfstream. The passenger was taken to [the fbo] in a van escorted by one of the pilots. A limo was arranged to take her back to [her planned destination]. She was frightened and shook up but thanked us all for getting there safely. The airplane gear was pinned (including the main gear) and the airplane was towed back to a hangar with a mechanic in the pilot seat. The rest of us rode to [the fbo] in a warm van. I filled out paperwork for the fire/rescue personnel basically stating what type airplane and who was on board.
output: The crew of the chartered g200 attempted to avoid a bird on short final; but was unsuccessful. The birdstrike caused damage to the hydraulic system; so the crew performed a missed approached. They elected to divert to another airport with a longer runway and better facilities. The landing was successful.

input: Approaching white sands testing area; air traffic control warned us that 'radar jamming' was being tested/used. While at cruise; we were 'jammed' numerous times. Warnings that would be expected with this process occurred numerous times. The nav accuracy was downgraded and upgraded to normal the first few times that we were jammed. Then; electronic centralized aircraft monitoring notified of global positioning system 1 failure and then went away. A few minutes later electronic centralized aircraft monitoring notified of global positioning system 2 failure and then went away. We incorrectly concluded that the global positioning system systems had reset themselves; but the navigate, navigation accuracy downgrade notice never went away (on the nd). After checking global positioning system condition on the flight management computer it became clear that we had no global positioning system positions left. We advised air traffic control that we needed a non-rnav arrival. They provided vectors to a visual approach.stop jamming commercial air traffic.
output: A319 pilot reported that while approaching white sands testing area in new mexico; air traffic control warned of 'radar jamming' which affected global positioning system following several global positioning system 1 and global positioning system 2 electronic centralized aircraft monitoring alerts; all global positioning system position reporting was lost for the remainder of the flight.

input: As we were taxing out in smf to runway(s) 35l; the taxiway narrows and becomes a general aviation taxiway with a weight limitation. I was the first officer and i was running the before take off checklist when the captain stopped the aircraft and informed me that he had missed the turn to the runway. He said that he had been distracted by his pfd that had gone blank for a moment. We informed air traffic control and they said that they were going to send out a tug. The aircraft didn't go past the intersection more than 5 feet; but it was to tight to make the turn; so we waited for the tug and were pushed back a few feet. After completing the push back we continued with the normal operation of the flight.
output: Air carrier pilot crew reported inadequate warnings available for weight limitation change for a taxiway at smf airport.

input: Receiving a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory reacting to its command; and then seeing the b737 300 feet/foot above and slightly behind you is an experience one would hope never happens. An event like this occurring while under terminal area radar control in clear skies; should never happen. My flight was flying on a longitude extended straight-in instrument landing system approach to runway(s) 25l. Air traffic control advised us to look for a b747 in our 1-2 o'clock position maneuvering for one of the 'n complex' runway(s) 24l/r. After the controller's second inquiry intermediate fix we saw the b747; i acknowledged the aircraft in sight. About a half minute(s) later; we received and complied with a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii descend resolution advisory upon our notifying the controller about our resolution advisory he responded the conflicting target was a b737; behind us. He stated the pilots have us visually in sight and were flying a visual approach to runway(s) 25r (500-700 feet/foot lateral offset). The controller claimed he previously advised us of this b737 aircraft but we never heard or acknowledged the advisory. The situation startled me. My concentration became focused on the other plane's proximitypa the other plane flew above us; below us; behind and ahead of us until landing i had difficulty maintaining attention to my acft's performance during the critical stages of short approach and landing i have experienced many side-by-side; wingtip-to-wingtip approachs to closely spaced parallel runway(s) under the concept of 'visual apch.' none of these were very comfortable to fly. Several times; i never saw the other plane due to it being slightly behind my viewing capability. Most of the pilot's effort is on avoiding a collision; when we should be concentrating on flying a safe; stabilized approach to landing the separation of parallel runway(s) at lax; sfo; and sna airports is less than 700 feet/foot inflt maneuvering can bring aircraft separation much closer. When will the minor slip in judgement occur; or the unexpected turbulence arise; or the mechanical mishap happen to cause the unthinkable collision and loss of life? Flying dangerously close to another aircraft is not condoned as normal operating procedures do we not have separation standards that trigger a near miss rpt when not met? Intermediate fix an air traffic controller tells one pilot to follow another plane visually; does this mean the separation standards do not apply? What assurance does the leading pilot have that the following guy will not collide into him by mistake? After all; i have at times seen the 'wrong' plane i was looking for.
output: Flc of a b757 descend in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory air traffic control advised of a b737 as causing the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory who was just behind them and on a visual approach to the other parallel runway(s) than that which they were assigned. The rpting capt complained that aircraft should not be allowed to become too close unless in formation flt.

input: R-hand main gear #4 tire has broken tie bolt.
output: A dc9 found with #4 main wheel 1 tie bolt broken.

input: About 20 minute(s) from zzz at fl300; our left/right (directions) generator tripped off. Following company chklist; we attempted to start auxiliary power unity with no luck. Several more attempts were made at different altitudes with only 1 generator; we decided to declare an emergency and requested direct zzz. At 10000 feet/foot we were finally able to start auxiliary power unity and told approach we'd like to cancel emergency status. We landed without incidence.
output: Md80 flight crew at fl300 has left generator trip offline; they declared an emergency until successfully starting the auxiliary power unity at 10;000 ft.

input: While cruising enroute along our planned flight path at fl430 we had experienced several hours of calm high cirrus instrument meteorological conditions conditions. We were approximately 50 nautical mile from the closest radar echoes of a significant and widespread storm system when we experienced a partial loss of flight control systems including autopilot/ auto-throttles and yaw damper. The system reset properly and we decided to abort our mission and look for the clearest path to our destination. Shortly thereafter the partial system failure happened again along with a loss of both p (pilot) and cp (co-pilot) airspeed systems (the standby knots indicated airspeed true air speed and glideslope appeared to be working normally at this point; however). Again we reset the system leading to a partial recovery of some flight control systems.deciding to stay at altitude until visual meteorological conditions to avoid descending into inclement weather we were nearly over our destination when commencing our initial descent. At that point we once again lost our primary air data indications (cp's was reading near mach 1 and p's was reading an impending stall condition before eventually just showing 'red x's for kcas/ alt and vv). Furthermore the right engine started significant surging which led to severe yaw oscillations on the aircraft. We were also getting erroneous glideslope indications (showing 200kt tailwind) but our true air speed standby knots indicated airspeed and aoa indicator seemed correct. We had air traffic control provide us with updated glideslope readouts to ensure we were within parameters.at approximately 23;000' the air data systems returned to normal and the thicker air reduced the yaw oscillations until a safe landing could be completed normally.our belief; in agreement with the aircraft manufacturer who completed a thorough checkout of the pitot/static systems along with electrical continuity; is that we experienced a relatively rare high ice water situation. Extremely fine particles of very dry ice particles (that do not show on radar nor trigger icing indications) led to a partial blockage of our pitot/static systems. This led to a miscompare in all 3 air data computers eventually shutting down our primary air data display information; causing our flight control malfunctions; and leading to the right engine's compressor valve cycling as designed to shed ice from the engine to prevent a compressor stall/ potential flame-out. The aircraft checklists are designed for the loss of one air data computer where redundant systems can fix a mis-compare but not for the loss of all 3.lessons learned are avoidance of prolonged exposure to high cirrus clouds whenever possible is imperative along with backup plans to control the aircraft with whatever air data systems you can validate as still operational; and failing that; resorting to aoa readouts to ensure you are within speed parameters could be the only reliable information you have. At the end of the day; descending as soon as possible to warmer thicker air is the most likely action which will hopefully restore the air data systems and enable a normal landing.
output: G-v captain reported pitot static system anomalies due to high altitude icing.

input: On previous flight; high frequency antenna was found broken. Maintenance removed the antenna and mel'd [(deferred)] the high frequency system inoperative. The next day after much consideration; i felt that to minimum equipment list the high frequency system inoperative; because the antenna was missing; was not the proper minimum equipment list an minimum equipment list for the antenna missing or removed would be appropriate and it would also address the fact that the high frequency radio was affected; except there is no such minimum equipment list or cdl item. Several authorities both inside and outside the company agreed that the minimum equipment list was acceptable as written; so i continued to fly the aircraft; however i still feel that the minimum equipment list was not appropriate. The minimum equipment list addresses only one resulting problem caused by the actual problem; rather than addressing the problem itself. It would be similar to mel'ing the window heat inoperative because the windshield was missing. I would like to see an minimum equipment list or cdl addressing a missing or removed antenna (hf or any other) rather than using the minimum equipment list for an inoperative radio to cover a missing antenna. Maintenance entered an minimum equipment list that i don't consider appropriate. Had discussions with maintenance personnel; the flight duty officer (fdo); the union steward on duty and a cessna service customer service representative.
output: A first officer reports that an high frequency antenna; found previously broken on their cj3 (cessna 525b) aircraft; had been improperly deferred as high frequency system radio inoperative instead of antenna being missing. Adding to pilot's concern was the lack of any minimum equipment list or cdl language available for a missing antenna.

input: I planned a cross-country flight to p14. I checked the notams for all airports at about xa00 universal time coordinated (zulu/gmt) at xd10 universal time coordinated (zulu/gmt) i took off with my one passenger. We picked up some fuses and a landing light switch enroute to try to fix my aircraft's landing light since a significant portion of our flight was going to be at night. We installed the switch and replaced the blown fuse. When we tested the landing light after the repair; we blew the new fuse. We decided to continue since the weather was reported to be quite clear the whole way; our destinations were well lit; and i had done 3 take-offs and landings in the past week at night with no landing light quite comfortably.we departed at xe04 universal time coordinated (zulu/gmt) for p14. The weather remained clear and calm the entire flight. When we got to the vicinity of p14; we noticed the airport beacon was functioning normally and we clicked on the runway lights using the common traffic advisory frequency after checking automatic weather observing/reporting system i elected to land on runway 21 so i entered a left; rectangular pattern for runway 21. At about 5 feet above the numbers on very short final; i saw the numbers '21' but they looked odd - they had what appeared to be white rectangles scattered about. Initially; i thought perhaps they were reflectors on the numbers. I put in a touch of power and pulled the nose up slightly to land past the numbers since it looked strange. My passenger commented that they looked like milk jugs. I commenced an uneventful full-stop landing and pulled up to the fuel pumps. We noted that one of the taxiways had barriers. We decided there were enough odd things that happened during that flight that we should call it a day and continue our flight in the morning (landing light out; panel clock stopped midflight; runway numbers looked odd; barriers on taxiway). We pulled the plane to parking and tied it down. A pick-up pulled up. The driver mentioned the runway was closed and it was notam'd. I checked again and saw two notams closing both runways were posted at xe03 universal time coordinated (zulu/gmt) on that day; one minute before i started the engine for that flight. The driver also said that the ground vehicles that would be performing work (the reason the runways were closed) would have radios and that it should be no problem to coordinate with them to depart in the morning.the next morning; i called the phone number in the notams to request permission to depart. The individual who answered was with the city of holbrook and just said the airport was closed. I mentioned the notice to airmen / of air missions said i could call this number for permission to depart. He said he was unaware of this and gave me another city number to call. Since he didn't seem to understand the notice to airmen / of air missions system and since the number he gave me was not affiliated with the airport; i made the decision that contacting the construction vehicles at the airport (i was standing on the ramp by my plane) and coordinating with them would be safe and aligned with the intent of the notice to airmen / of air missions i did not call the number he provided. Before starting the engine on my aircraft; i spoke to them by handheld radio on common traffic advisory frequency they said to call them up when i was ready for take-off and they'd move. I started the plane; did my run-up; called them and they said they were clear of the runway which i was able to visually confirm before take-off roll. When i pulled onto the runway; i saw what was on the numbers. They were what looked like white; 20 pound sand bags standing upright on end. There were about two dozen arranged in an x. That would have significantly damaged my aircraft's landing gear had i landed 20 feet sooner. I used a taxiway that got me onto the runway in front of the sandbags and took-off uneventfully (there was still almost 6000 usable feet of runway). Having a minimum time between posting a notice to airmen / of air missions about an airport closure and actually closing an airport of at least 24-hrs would have prevented this. Disabling the airport beacon and/or runway lights for an unusable airport would have also been a clear signal not to land - having all the lights working at the closed airport was deceptive. The landing light may have shown me the sandbags in time to do a go-around but maybe not.
output: General aviation pilot reported landing at night with an inoperative landing light to learn that the airport is closed. The notice to airmen / of air missions closing the airport had been issued just before engine start for the flight; although an intermediate stop had occurred to attempt to repair the landing light.

input: Filed air defense identification zone and visual flight rules flight plan. While over brooke; quantico approach cleared us into the air defense identification zone they also warned that r6608a; b; celsius was in our path and offered that a climb or vectors would keep us out. We chose both. After getting over the restrict, restricted, restriction area; quantico put us back on course. Shortly after; quantico switched us over to potomac approach who told us we were not cleared into class b airspace. I made a 180 degree turn to sort out the airspace problem we did not anticipate (being cleared into the air defense identification zone and not class b). The owner of the plane indicated that as longitude as we remained between 2500-3500 feet/foot we would clear both airspaces. I kept us at 3200 feet/foot and resumed on course. Shortly afterward; we advised that we were in class b and to get out. I descended the plane rapidly to comply. On the sectional; the class b and restrict, restricted, restriction airspace boundaries coincide; second officer our course should have permitted a descent without entering the restrict, restricted, restriction airspace. After landing we again read the chart; and the floor of the class b was 3000 feet/foot contributing factors were the unexpected air defense identification zone clearance without a class b clearance the close proximitypa of the 2 airspaces; cockpit resource management in that neither of us flew with each other before; outlined responsibilities for the flight etc. I also inaccurately expected the owner to be familiar with the airspace because this was the area he most commonly flew in.
output: Ryan navion pilot was cleared into dcadiz by the nyg military approach controller after xfer to pct controller he informed the pilot that he did not have clearance into dca class b airspace.

input: After startup sequence exhibiting; as has been the case since last annual inspection; moderate engine skips at low revolutions per minute between 1000 and 1200 revolutions per minute performed uneventful visual flight rules flight from zzzz to zzzz1 and parked.approximately 30 minutes later; taxied for runway xx and run-up was similarly nominal. After being cleared for takeoff; initial climb exhibited a few engine misses and while continuing to gain altitude; called air traffic control with a request to land due to engine issue; possibly related to spark plug fouling.received clearance to land on any runway; and chose to perform a 80/260 reversal of course right-hand (due to terrain) and established on final 06. With reduced power; engine was shaking as if a cylinder was not operating; a fadec caution illuminated; and landing was calm and uneventful.requested to perform a run-up; on the western taxiway; which was unsuccessful; then requested taxi back to apron and the assistance of a mechanic.
output: Liberty xl-2 instructor pilot reported aircraft engine problems after takeoff resulting in a return to departure airport.

input: I was sent from base to zzz for a b737-700 aircraft with a #1 engine fuel leak. We arrived at night. We discovered that the #1 engine main fuel pump was leaking. We inquired about getting an inspector sent to zzz for the fuel pump replacement; but were told by maintenance control that no inspector was required. A fuel pump was sent to zzz. The [following] morning; we proceeded to replace the part. I did not see the computer link for the maintenance task [job card] in aircraft maintenance manual (amm) 73-11-01/401. I also was not aware that a [specific job card] was required. The aircraft was flown on a ferry flight back to base. Upon my arrival at base i was told that job card was supposed to have been accomplished with the pump replacement. I researched the maintenance procedures manual (mpm) chapter xx; table 10.1 and saw that the b737-700 main fuel pump replacement was not on the rii list. The aircraft was kept at base and the job card was issued that night during a routine overnight check (ron). The mpm rii list and the aircraft maintenance manual (amm) reference contradict each other. If table 10.1 of the mpm doesn't list this job as an rii then why does the maintenance manual have a maintenance task [job card] with an rii requirement? [this was a] failure to use job card.
output: After replacing a fuel pump on the #1 engine of a b737-700; a line mechanic was told he should have completed a specific job card that included an rii inspection. Maintenance control said no inspection was required. Mechanic questions why the maintenance procedures manual (mpm) and the aircraft maintenance manual (amm) contradict each other.

input: Working on an aircraft as quality control inspector for elevator tab checked we found a problem with the r-hand elevator tab hinge bushings and fixed the problem however; the next night when looking over the same paperwork on another aircraft it was noted that on step 3c. We complied with engineering authority/authorized x but did not comply with engineering authority/authorized y. We did comply with a tab free play and apply witness putty to the bolt heads as well as the system was inspected. However the ea (engineering auth) was not issued and needs to be complied with. The reason the problem or event happened was the paperwork was/is very hard to read and understand.
output: A b737-300 in a heavy checked had the left/right (directions) elevator tab bushings replaced per an engineering authority/authorized a second engineering authority/authorized was not issued with the checked paperwork and a required inspection signoff was not accomplished.

input: During our instrument landing system approach to zggg; we had a global positioning system loss of signal/gps signal interference for about 30 seconds.we were given a vector heading to intercept the instrument landing system to runway 01 about 20 miles from the runway. Just as we were intercepting the localizer; 'ads-b out l' engine indicating and crew alerting system (engine indicating and crew alerting system) alert appeared and the navigate, navigation display changed from global positioning system to inertial. I was about to switch the transponder to the left/right (directions) side when approach control advised us that they had lost our transponder signal. After switching to the left/right (directions) transponder; approach confirmed that they were receiving our signal. The engine indicating and crew alerting system alert blanked and the navigate, navigation display showed global positioning system about 30 seconds after the initial signal loss.after landing; we asked ground control to advise approach control of the global positioning system interference on the final approach. We had experienced our first global positioning system jamming/interference event on our previous flight. Due to our short layover in zzz and much needed rest; i chose to wait until our longer guangzhou layover to submit an [asrs] report per the fom x.xx mandatory report table. The table shows only an [safety report] and security reports are mandatory; the aml entry box has no 'x'. In the research for the report; i reread the entire bulletin xxx-xx-xx global positioning system 'loss of signal / global positioning system signal interference.' it was at this time that i discovered that i had misread the bulletin and neglected to make an aml (aircraft maintenance logbook) entry regarding the global positioning system interference. I have submitted a security report for both flights.as stated above; this [asrs] report is essentially applicable to this flight and our previous flight. The same causes apply to both.the cause of the loss of global positioning system was most likely due to jamming and/or interference.neglecting to properly document and communicate the global positioning system issue was primarily due to my misreading of the global positioning system bulletin. In a rush to reference the technical part of the bulletin to assist in troubleshooting; i skimmed the administrative paragraphs and missed the 'a detailed aml write up is required for any global positioning system discrepancies even if the global positioning system function returns to normal.' i made the mistake of assuming that; because the event was not caused by our equipment; an aml entry would not be required. The lack of an aml entry requirement in the fom (flight operations manual) x.xx table contributed to my error. The bulletin is controlling as it was issued subsequent to the current fom. Additionally; this was our first global positioning system event experience.our improper assumptions were additional causes. We assumed that a notification to air traffic control or [operations center] was not necessary because we never had a loss of navigation capability and we had no aircraft system malfunctions.in the future; i will notify air traffic control [operations center]; document with an aml entry; file a [safety report] and a security report for a global positioning system jamming/interference event.going forward; after a 'non - normal' event is complete; stabilized or we are blocked in; a detailed review of the quick reference handbook bulletin or other source document would be helpful. A slower review during a low workload time would help to avoid this type of mistake. A more detailed review would have led me to make an aml entry; notify air traffic control and [operations center].additionally; an update to the fom table x.xx for the global positioning system events would help to prevent this type of error.
output: Air carrier captain reported possible global positioning system jamming event during an instrument landing system approach to guangzhou baiyun international airport.

input: While in holding east of boston; air traffic control advised that field was closed indefinitely. Contacted dispatch for diversion to jfk. Dispatch issued us bdl and swf. Air traffic control said wall of red from pvd to alb second officer we elected to divert to jfk. Dispatch advised us that they could not legally give us jfk because of fuel numbers based on our departure from cdg. We calculated that we indeed had enough fuel to meet all federal aviation regulation legalities and proceeded to jfk under capt's emergency authority/authorized even though we never declared an emer.
output: B767 flight crew overrides company dispatch airport diversion due to weather deviation to pic's airport of choice.

input: Flt abc from ewn to rdu. We were expecting visual approach runway(s) 5r. After the approach brief and chklist; we were asked intermediate fix we could see a b737 2 o'clock position 7 mile we saw a jet in that direction; but we were not aware of another jet in the same direction; further out. We called traffic in sight and were cleared for visual runway(s) 5l behind him. As we turned; i noticed that the aircraft we were to follow didn't seem to be aligned with runway(s) 5l. I called the approach controller to inquire about that. Air traffic control was busy -- got no response. Noticed a target on my traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii which appeared to be on left/right (directions) side. Air traffic control came back to ask intermediate fix we had the traffic to our left/right (directions) at that point; i saw him we were flying parallel to each other. He was at least 1000 feet/foot above me 7-8 o'clock position we stayed visual the entire time and requested a go around we got heading of 140 degrees and 2000 feet/foot factors: traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii vor and dme (co-located) notamed out of service sun still low on the horizon affecting visibility. Most of all; not being notified about the aircraft nearest our position by the air traffic control ctlr.
output: A jetstream 3200 pilot in command initially follows the wrong aircraft for a visual approach towards runway(s) 5r at rdu; nc.

input: We refused aircraft for improper logbook documentation.the aircraft arrived in zzz with a write up that the aft; right service door light illuminated in cruise flight. I spoke to the inbound captain face to face who told me that the light illuminated twice in flight and per quick reference handbook procedure he directed the cabin crew to push the door handle down which extinguished the light.maintenance applied minimum equipment list 52-xxx which is for the door warning light system. This minimum equipment list applies if the door warning light system is malfunctioning. It is my judgment that the warning system was functioning properly. This function was tested again in zzz. When the door handle was lifted the light illuminated; and with the door handle fully closed the light extinguished. In other words; the malfunction was likely within the door itself and not the warning system.i discussed this with two b737 check airmen via telephone who agreed the minimum equipment list was inappropriate. I also spoke with a representative of the zzz chief pilot office and the duty pilot and told them i would gladly take another aircraft or accept the current aircraft if the door/sensor could be adjusted or if a different minimum equipment list or sign off could be applied to the logbook.the flight eventually cancelled.the cause of this event was the application of an minimum equipment list which did not address the actual maintenance issue.perhaps this minimum equipment list could be written in a matter to include other malfunctions of the door system.
output: B737-800 captain reported refusing an aircraft due to improper minimum equipment list application.

input: Apched the localizer runway(s) 27r see at approximately lardy intersection electrical system had started to fail approximately 5 minute(s) earlier. Lost all navigate, navigation communications strobes; lights; beacon. Flaps (electric) were inoperative passenber (non plt) was getting very anxious and appeared nervous. No traffic in sight second officer elected to turn inbound on final. Landed without incident (flaps up) and received green tower light to taxi. Called tower by telephone and all appeared ok.
output: Sma has total electrical failure on approach continues; gets green light.

input: Apch control cleared us for visual approach during busy time at airport and in cockpit. We never received call to change to tower and landed using last clearance without 'a cleared to land' from tower nothing was said to us when contacting ground control we never switched to tower we were still talking to approach on short final.

input: While on approach after descending to visual conditions (from moderate to severe icing conditions 5000-7000 ft); stall stick shakers activated at 145 knot(s) with flaps/slats 40 degrees after 'firewall pwr' was applied; we attempted to establish a shallow climb but shakers activated again. Aircraft did not feel like it was in a stall condition. It flew level ok with an increased speed a stall indicator failure came on after 5 seconds.
