output: B767 cargo flight on prado 5 standard instrument departure ont failed to comply with the 4000 feet/foot 6 vor and dme (co-located) pdz restrict, restricted, restriction restr is not in the b767 database and the capt failed to brief the procedure prior to dep.

input: I was approaching sun for landing t-210-1 mile final cleared for landing and i was slightly low on ideal glide path second officer added 2 inch manifold pressure and seemed to get no response. Then added more power and still no response. I then considered best glide to make it to airport which would have been a very close call to us. Slowing down going with full flaps and r-stol capability to land in smooth farm field short of the airport which seemed much safer. I decided to go for the farm field. While on final descent i continued emergency chklist and found low boost pump on and turned this off. At this point power started to return but i was second officer slow and low that i felt it was safest to continue with the landing lndg was soft with normal rollout through knee high barley. Engine was back to running smooth second officer i idled the engine 2 minute(s) to cool down turbocharger and then shutdown engine i announced to tower at onset that i had loss of power and may have to land on field. I then announced to tower i was safely landed without damage or injury and controller said we would send support equipment to help. Fire departure personnel came and inspected the scene and with their supervisor arrangements were made to transfer the airplane up to the airport service area where it was secured in fixed-base operator hangar for further inspection.
output: Emer lndg.

input: Eagle (f-15) had exited warning area 105 on instrument flight rules flight plan. Aircraft was not able to be handed off to us due to automation issue. We attempted numerous times to get control of aircraft data block; but the computer was not letting us take control of the information. Eagle (f-15) was pointed out to sector 47 descending to 110 direct baf airport. Approximately 5 minutes after we started working on getting control of the data block for automation purposes; the radar controller was able to drop the data block track on eagle (f-15). When he dropped the data block from our scope; it automatically removed the data block from sector 47. The radar controller immediately started another track and was in the process of making a manual hand off to bdl approach control when sector 47 put traffic on his scope; g150. Aircraft were approximately 12 to 15 miles apart on converging courses. Sector 47 had already sent g150 over to bdl approach control; so we had no way of turning the aircraft away from eagle (f-15). Bdl approach control called us and issued descent clearance to eagle (f-15) to 8;000 feet. Closest proximity with both aircraft at 110 is approximately 9 miles. The automation issue of not being able to get control of the data block to ensure proper automated hand off is the bigger issue between the two aircraft. If we did not have to make all of the attempts at getting control of the data block; when the original data block finally did get removed; it would not have dropped off sector 47 radar display. The data block dropping off sector 47 scope makes the issue worse; and then ultimately the radar controller at sector 47 forgetting about the eagle (f-15) flight at 110 did not help. Ultimately; in my opinion; all of this would have been avoided with proper automation and hand offs for eagle (f-15).
output: Zbw controller described a probable airspace separation event when the automated hand off efforts failed.

input: Clbing through approximately 1500 feet/foot mean sea level duct leak warning came on. Followed chklist items which light emitting diode to #1 engine being shut down. Informed flight attendant and passenber prior to shutdown. Declared emergency to air traffic control and returned to mco. Followed maintenance which discovered a bleed line that came loose. We launched as ferry flight (in same acft). At same geographical position and altitude same warning came on for same engine followed same procedure as above except we had no passenber on board. Declared emergency and returned to mco. Maintenance found a broken fitting on water separator for deicing boot bleed. Replaced fitting and resumed trip. Cockpit resource management worked as advertised. Delayed shutting engine down a little to complete notifications to flight attendants; passenber and company but no harm done this time.
output: Acft equipment problem broken bleed line caused warning of duct leak and subsequent engine shutdown. Flight crew declared emergency and returned for landing after maintenance found the loose bleed line and reconnected it; the aircraft was dispatched again as a ferry flight again; the duct warning came on and the flight crew returned. A broken fitting on the water separator was discovered.

input: My family and i were returning home from a short vacation. We had filed an instrument flight rules flight plan. We planned to refuel and then complete our trip to our home base. The instrument flight rules flight to our first fuel stop was without incident. Monitoring the automatic weather observing/reporting system prior to landing revealed the winds to be out of the west varying from 240-290 degrees at approximately 5-7 knots. Given that the winds were blowing essentially across the runway in a variable fashion such that the preferred runway would also be variable; a call was made on the common traffic advisory frequency requesting the airport advisory. It went unanswered. The last report from the automatic weather observing/reporting system as i was approaching the airport indicated the wind at 270 degrees; and so a visual approach and landing was made to runway 34 without incident. The airplane was refueled by me and topped off. A weather briefing was obtained using the foreflight commercial app. It revealed good visual meteorological conditions conditions through to our destination. Thus a decision was made to complete the last leg of our trip visual flight rules a weather briefing continued to reveal the wind to be variable across the runway from the west. A standard preflight inspection was done by me and did not reveal any abnormalities.the engine was started and initially it did run very rough; and this i attributed to the fuel vaporizing in the lines due to sitting in the sun and the hot engine from the recent flight - not an uncommon occurrence in my particular aircraft. Indeed; when the standby electric fuel pump was turned on the engine smoothed out and seemed to run as normal. As we taxied from the ramp i again listened to the automatic weather observing/reporting system it revealed the winds to be at 290 degrees at 7 knots; and thus i made the decision to depart from runway 34. The taxi itself appeared to be normal. A standard run-up of the engine did not reveal any abnormalities or anything that sounded unusual. Takeoff flaps were set at 10 degrees as per the poh. Given that we were fully loaded and the density altitude was significantly higher than field elevation; i considered using 25 degrees of flaps as specified in the poh for short field takeoff. I elected not to do this for 2 reasons. First of all; our home field is very similar to this airport with regards to its runway - a 4000 feet/foot runway at approximately 600 feet mean sea level i've made many departures under similar conditions without incident using the standard takeoff technique. Given that the aircraft is turbocharged mitigates the deleterious effect of density altitude. My second consideration was that since the winds were so prominent from the west; i was concerned that the added surface area of exposure with the additional flaps might make the directional control more challenging as the takeoff proceeded. Thus i made the decision to use the standard takeoff flap setting.the initial takeoff roll appeared normal; and a quick scan of the instruments revealed appropriate indications. Quickly however the takeoff progressed into something that didn't feel right. Despite using standard crosswind takeoff technique with aileron deflection into the wind it was challenging to hold the aircraft on the centerline. The aircraft also did not appear to be accelerating as quickly as i would've expected and felt very sluggish; almost as if we were dragging something. There was a strong tendency for the aircraft to yaw to the right. The aircraft came off the ground at approximately midfield and i held it in ground effect. The aircraft was very near stall speed and continued to feel very mushy with regards to control feel. I made a quick assessment that we had used up over half of the available runway and had significant obstructions at the end of the runway in the form of tall trees and power lines. I was 100% confident that we were not going to clear the obstructions. I made the decision to abort the takeoff and try stop in the remaining distance we had left. I immediately pulled the throttle to idle and the aircraft settled to the runway. I applied the brakes firmly but evenly and appliedappropriate aileron to counteract the crosswind. I immediately felt the same dragging force pulling me to the right as i had earlier. Despite my best efforts to keep the aircraft on the centerline i was unable to counteract the force that caused me to yaw to the right. We departed the runway to the right and as we went off the pavement i felt the right main gear buckle. The aircraft then slid parallel to the runway for a short distance before coming to a stop. I immediately verified that my family was ok; which they were; and asked them to exit the aircraft. I quickly shut off the master; alternator; electric fuel pump; and magnetos and exited as well. We then walked back down the runway to the fbo.as to my explanation of the cause; examination of the runway demonstrates a single tire skid mark generated by the right main tire which begins approximately at the point i recall touching down and continues until the point of departure from the runway. The single tire skid mark from the right main is joined near the point of departure from the runway by tire skid marks from the left main and nosewheel as well. The orientation of the three skid marks demonstrates that the aircraft was in a leftward yaw as it slid off of the runway; this in attempt by me to hold the aircraft on the runway with left rudder despite the significant drag to the right. The right main gear went off of the runway first and folded back; causing the aircraft to yaw to the right as it slid in the grass parallel to the runway before coming to a final stop. In my opinion a mechanical failure involving the right main tire and/or brake caused an anomaly during the takeoff; slowing my takeoff roll and thus increasing the length of runway needed to become airborne; as well as causing the significant yaw to the right. This persisted during my attempt to stop the aircraft after the aborted takeoff resulting in me being unable to maintain directional control on the runway.
output: Pa-32 pilot detected drag during takeoff and countered with rudder during the prolonged takeoff roll. Once airborne he realized obstacles would not be cleared and landed but ran off the runway end where the right gear collapsed. The right tire and/or brake were thought to be the cause of the takeoff drag.

input: On returning from a flight to mountain meadow airport (22b) i entered the traffic pattern at somerset airport (n52) and activated the gear down switch. I failed to get a positive gear down indication (no light) for the left/right (directions) main gear. I radioed somerset traffic (123.0) indicating my problem - - advised i was departing the pattern to checked out further. After approximately 5 attempts lowering the gear; i still did not get a positive gear light. I radioed somerset; requested a low pass for a visual checked as i flew over someone came out and appeared to indicate a 'thumbs up.' i added power realized i wasn't climbing properly; second officer i raised the gear and flaps. The plane was 'mushing;' i realized i would not be able to clear the trees; second officer i opted to land straight ahead; gear up. This occurred at approximately xx00 post meridiem eastern daylight time on jul/sat/95. Contributing factors: the runway(s) in use; (rwy 12) is not the runway(s) normally in use (rwy 30) the fixed-base operator building is close to the departure end of the runway(s) 12; consequently after confirming a visual checked (which really meant nothing -- since none could confirm a gear locked position -- hindsight) i had already passed the departure end of the runway(s) the small field and 50-60 feet/foot trees at the end did not allow me the time to gain airspd and climb corrective action: although i allowed myself to get too low and slow and fall behind the 'pwr curve;' the decision to put the plane down in the field (against all instincts to pull back and clb) was a very difficult one. You know you will do damage to the plane; possibly harm your passenber (or worse) and at least suffer embarrassment. However i know it was the correct decision since all 4 occupants walked away unhurt! Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated that the aircraft was a rockwell international commander 114. The federal aviation administration investigated the mishap and classified it as an incident since the damage was not considered substantial. No one could determine at the time the aircraft was 'ferried' away with the gear locked in the down position what caused the landing gear down indication prob.
output: Pvt pilot of an sma sel crashed off the departure end of the runway(s) due to being unable to climb over tall trees after low approach fly-by for gear inspection. There were neither injuries to occupants nor substantial damage to the acft.

input: This was a vip movement for [government aircraft]. The controllers working did not receive a briefing of any kind about the operation. Management was on several telcons prior; and relayed zero information to the front line controllers. That being said; there was not a clear line of authority. Who calls the ramp freeze? The airport operations? Secret service rep in the tower?since we had no briefing; that means there was a movement area violation by the [government] motorcade (between 20-50 vehicles). They came out on to taxiway a without the ground controllers permission or prior knowledge at the south end of fixed-base operator ramp; to the north end of fixed-base operator ramp. No prior coordination/notice had been given to the ground controller.second; there was a runway incursion. The two vehicles followed the aircraft for his taxi from the fixed-base operator ramp from the departure end of runway 13 left until the exit at runway 18 and on to taxiway alpha. Aircraft called for taxi. Those vehicles continued their movement area violations when aircraft departed by returning to the fixed-base operator ramp via taxiway alpha.third; since there was no briefing to the controllers; the 7110.65 says to give [certain government] aircraft 9000 above ground level on departure as initial altitude to the max extent possible. Our sids go to 8000 mean sea level about 7500 above ground level myself and the ground controller brought this up; and the flm (front line manager) in charge snapped at me in front of everyone in the tower cab; which included the atm (air traffic manager) and secret service rep; yelling that was not going to happen.fourth; there was also a discrepancy on how to read a new full route clearance to the pilot; and the atm stated that it could not be done in the tower cab; though the pilot was requesting it on frequency. The pilot eventually got the full route clearance.fifth; aircraft was delayed by between one to two minutes at the runway hold line by the local west controller and flm for an undetermined reason. Traffic was not a factor.brief the controllers on the operation. Our atm has a documented history of not providing briefings and also providing untimely briefings. We have had background checks; many have held secret or better security clearances. The operation details the day of are fouo (for official use only). We are allowed to know that information.
output: Dallas love controller reported not being briefed for a vip movement and what resulted afterward.

input: We were proceeding direct to imb and transitioning to bonvl 2 arrival, arrive to pdx; capt flying. He didn't turn right away to get on proper radial departing imb vor and dme (co-located) 50 degree difference between radial we were on and proper outbound radial finally noticed his error and started a 10 degree bank correction to get on course. At this time seattle center asked us to confirm our intentions of flying the bonvl 2 arrival, arrive i answered yes and that we were in the turn at this time; but at 10 degree bank angle we weren't setting any records getting over. And then to my surprise he only went 10 degree past the radial to intercept. At this time the radio magnetic indicator showed a difference of 40 degree between where we were and the radial we wanted to be on. I told the capt that he needed a bigger correction and he laughed it off saying he wanted to cut the corner. We were 50 vor and dme (co-located) past imb before getting on the radial. I recently downgraded from capt to first officer to stay in base. I have never seen such lax navigating as i've seen in the past 4 months; and with other capts too. I get the feeling they think close is ok. Not in my book it isn't.
output: Acr mlg track heading deviation on standard terminal arrival route into pdx.

input: While working local control west; the tower tmc made the call to depart and land runway 9 and also depart runway 15l. It has been brought to my attention that each and every departure off of runway 15l has been a potential conflict with the runway 9 arrival even though i was using anticipated separation and departing behind the arrival as well as providing traffic information reference the arrivals to runway 9. Recommendation; all departures [should go] to runway 15l so as not to create an urgency reference arriving and departing runway 9.
output: Iah controller described a probable procedural error during a runway 15l/runway 9 arrival/departure traffic flow.

input: While being vectored from the arrival to the ils6 approach we were issued confusing instructions between approach controllers. The previous controller issued us direct vings and maintain 2;000'. Then the next controller issued us 'heading 090 to intercept.' this is where the confusion started as we were already direct to a fix on the localizer (vings) and with the winds aloft (300@50) a heading of 090 pushed us off of the previous track to intercept. The frequency was busy so by the time we queried the controller about it; we were about to go through the localizer. Then there was a break in the frequency so we asked the controlled to clarify and the controller issued '030 to intercept the localizer; 2;000 until established; cleared for the instrument landing system 6 approach'. This new vector and clearance now made sense; but we had already flown through the localizer but and we continued the approach without incident. The causes were busy airspace; high workload on the controller; and breakdown in communication between controllers. This might have been avoided if we had informed the controller upon check-in that we were previously assigned direct vings rather than the controller assuming we were being vectored to the localizer.
output: Pilot reported receiving conflicting heading clearances during hand-off between air traffic control controllers on vectors for the ils.

input: Flight was delayed due to a late inbound aircraft. When we arrived at the airport i called dispatch for a brief and to discuss the proposed departure time. In the brief we discussed the minimum equipment list that was applied to the aircraft for the anti ice valves. The valve in question was wired to the open position and the minimum equipment list stated several things:mel #30-xx-xx-x: to (takeoff); engine override knob placed in the engine position for the entire flight/all phases. Engine ice on applied to the tlr (takeoff landing report); weight penalty applied; these stipulations were discussed in the brief.once i received my paperwork i reviewed the tlr and saw that the penalties had been applied in the [takeoff] section. However i missed that they were not applied to the landing section.on the arrival the first officer stated that the automatic communications addressing & reporting system wasn't giving speeds because of a note saying that engine a/i not required with temps above 10c. I then said then we would have to utilize the tlr to get our required numbers. This is where i noticed the lack of engine a/i on for the landing performance. I sent several automatic communications addressing & reporting system messages to dispatch stating that i needed these numbers. They replied that the computer system wouldn't allow them to select a/i on with temps above 10c. I said that something needed to be done because our landing numbers will differ from those without engine ai on. Also as a reminder the minimum equipment list states that the override switch must remain in the engine position for the entirety of the flight in all phases.i looked at the quick reference handbook to see if there was a performance chart that could be utilized to derive a landing distance and weight for the above condition. There wasn't one. I then reviewed the quick reference handbook procedures to see if there was a factor to apply to an unfactored distance. There wasn't one.in this time i coordinated with air traffic control for some delay vectors so that we could formulate a plan. Our fuel was about 800 pounds over divert. I mentioned to dispatch that we needed some numbers sooner than later and they replied that they were working to produce them. I informed air traffic control that we wanted to slow to 210 kts to save some fuel while we waited. They were happy to help with providing vectors just south of zzz. A short while later we heard back from dispatch that there were no weight limits for runway xxr for our configuration using flaps 45. We then noted that our fuel was showing 3;900 lbs over runway xxr (divert fuel was 3;881 lbs). We told air traffic control that we were ready for the approach. He vectored us to the approach and at this time we noticed that we were going to dip below divert (flight time remaining was about 6 minutes to the airport). Speed control in the descents played a part in the extra fuel used due to increased idle n2 settings with a/i on. Flaps were extended earlier than normal to aid in these speed and altitude changes. Upon landing we had 3;660 lbs of fuel which was well above our final divert of 3;188. After arriving at the gate i immediately called dispatch to discuss the situation. I asked how the numbers were derived and i was told that they told the computer that the temp was 10c to eliminate the messages. The temperature in zzz was 15c and our next trip was to zzz1 where the temp was 33c. I said that this wasn't a good solution because of the effects of temperature on performance. I then said that i was going to ask for a different aircraft since; at this time; there was no way to produce accurate landing numbers. A different aircraft was provided for the remainder of the flights.i also called my chief pilot to discuss the situation. I was asked if i planned to [report] the event and i confirmed that i was. The chief pilot then called me back to say that he discussed the situation with another manager who said that it seems like this might be a limitation with the software. I mentioned that the minimum equipment list shouldn't be used if there was such a limitation in the planning software.there seems that there were several chances for this event to be averted. However it was missed in the planning and implementation phases. I usually verify the headers and notes on the tlr but this time i overlooked the landing notes. It wasn't until i noticed that the automatic communications addressing & reporting system didn't want to provide info that i began digging deeper. Here is where i began the conversation with dispatch. We were very focused on our fuel to ensure that we had adequate supply. It was my intention to ensure the safe operation of the aircraft; as always. Thus the request for delay vectors from air traffic control while we waited for numbers from dispatch. I'm always trying to operate the aircraft by the book! However; in this case i missed my mark. I feel that we managed the situation the best that we could under the given circumstances. I must say that it was a frustrating situation; but one where i've learned.hopefully this event will shed some light on what seems like a software limitation that is critical in complying with the minimum equipment list i also hope that this [report]; while embarrassing and frustrating; will shed some light on an overlooked part of one minimum equipment list that can become more common as winter approaches.
output: Emb-145 captain reported during minimum equipment list operation; computer software was unable to compute landing performance for given conditions.

input: Fms developed an anomaly which light emitting diode aircraft to disconnect and proceed 20 degrees off heading discovered error and in process of correcting when air traffic control called and asked about error. Original arrival, arrive atl was erlin 2 salms transition; memphis changed arrival, arrive to erlin 2 mem transition cleared direct mem. Selected direct mem verified leg executed then selected erlin 2 mem transition flight management system looked right; missed approach point looked ok. Between re-clrnc point and mem route discontinuity developed mem/gpy/mem-devac-calco-rmg-erlin. Because of peculiar nature of error we discovered it only after aircraft did not turn at mem.
output: B767-300 flight crew fail to close route discontinuity on altered erlin standard terminal arrival route to atl. Minor track deviation occurs when flight management system goes to heading hold vice lateral navigation at point of discontinuity.

input: On landing runway(s) 6 at wilmington; nc; cleared to land. On left/right (directions) turn to final; tower rpted low altitude alert. Proceeded with normal approach and lndg.
output: A beech bonanza pilot was advised of a low altitude alert on the approach base leg to ilm.

input: Two events combined in this report. Weather had been between marginal visual flight rules and instrument flight rules throughout the day. Ladd army airfield (fbk/pafa) airport traffic control tower was closed all day. Aircraft x had departed eielson air force base (eil/paei) on a local instrument flight rules clearance for some practice approaches. After executing an approach to eil; aircraft x was requesting the ndb-a approach to fbk and was informed that no landing or weather information was available and issued the fairbanks (fai/pafa) wind and altimeter. While holding over chena nondirectional radio beacon (cun) had requested that i file an instrument flight rules clearance to anchorage (anc/panc) via the fdio. All this was accomplished without incident. Event #1: upon completion of some holding at cun; aircraft x requested and was cleared for the ndb-a approach to fbk. At an appropriate point the aircraft was given climb out instructions (fly heading 170; climb and maintain 3000') and changed to the advisory frequency. When aircraft x was approximately 5-6nm from the runway inbound; fbk airport traffic control tower called over the shoutline. I was on the phone at the moment; so the developmental in picked up the call and informed me that fbk airport traffic control tower was advising us that there was snow removal equipment on the runway. I immediately called fbk airport traffic control tower over the shoutline and informed them i was not talking to aircraft x at this point and that i would attempt to contact the aircraft on guard. I then broadcast in the blind on guard to aircraft x that there were personnel and equipment on the runway at fbk and received no response. Event #2: following the previous event; as i monitored aircraft x approach i noticed that upon reaching the runway threshold the aircraft began turning to the north of the runway. At first i thought perhaps the aircraft had visually acquired the snow removal equipment on the runway and in an attempt to not overfly the surface had deviated slightly to the right before executing their climb out procedure. This thought was quickly dispelled when the aircraft appeared to continue to remain north of the runway; so i initiated another blind transmission on guard and instructed the aircraft to fly heading 170; climb and maintain 3000; and contact me on 125.35. In my haste; i had given the west radar frequency; so i advised the developmental on west radar that aircraft x should be coming up on their frequency; but that he was radar contact and to put him on my frequency again. Aircraft x checked on with west radar and was radar identified and given instruction to switch to my frequency. When aircraft x checked on my frequency i redundantly re-identified him and asked what had transpired at the end of his approach. The pilot informed me he was circling for runway 7. I informed the pilot that circling is not authorized north of the runway on the ndb-a approach and after a moment the pilot indicated that he now noticed that restriction on the chart. At this point aircraft x was given his instrument flight rules clearance to anc and departed my airspace without further incident. Recommendation; reference event #1: at the time of this event there were no known notams issued regarding personnel and/or equipment on the runway at fbk. A printout of the notams for fbk at the time of the incident should be attached to this report. Appropriate dissemination of this information would have prevented this occurrence; as well as future occurrences. Reference event #2: the air traffic control system performed its function to monitor the approach and took immediate action to correct an observed abnormality. Had i been more inquisitive as to the nature of the approach request; i might have determined that aircraft x intended to circle to land. With that information i would have issued a more detailed approach clearance; which would have included a restriction to circle south of the runway. While this would have prevented the occurrence; the traffic situation at the time did not warrant that level of  detail as there was nothing to preclude the aircraft from executing the procedure as published. The publishedprocedure clearly includes a statement that restricts the circling maneuver to south of the runway. Therefore; i believe the problem was that the pilot's briefing of the approach was either incorrect or not detailed enough to include the circling restriction.procedure clearly includes a statement that restricts the circling maneuver to south of the runway. Therefore; i believe the problem was that the pilot's briefing of the approach was either incorrect or not detailed enough to include the circling restriction.
output: Fai controller described multiple errors when runway closure information was not disseminated properly; a flight crew did not correctly interpret charting information and a wrong frequency was issued; all leading to a potential closed runway landing event.

input: After getting a traffic advisory from zny; the capt (pf) mistook it for a climb clearance from 12000 feet/foot to 14000 feet/foot he dialed 14000 feet/foot into the altitude box and set the autoplt for a climb he confirmed the clearance with me. However; i told him there was no clearance and to maintain 12000 feet/foot by now we had climbed 50 feet/foot he reset the autoplt for 12000 feet/foot and it recaptured. However; approximately 1 minute(s) later the altitude alerter went off signaling we had deviated 250 feet/foot the capture of our autoplt must have disengaged. We descended immediately back to 12000 feet/foot there was no traffic conflict. Air traffic control never mentioned it. I don't know why the autoplt captured and then canceled its altitude hold. Probably more vigilance would have caught it sooner.
output: Flc of a dhc8 climbed above assigned cruise altitude due to the autoplt not capturing the return to assigned altitude and due to the capt's misunderstanding of an air traffic control ta.

input: I was flying eastbound at fl250. Outside air temperature was -10 degrees celsius. In the thin air; i fly on autopilot using global positioning system steering and altitude hold. At around 500 miles out from my destination airport the jack screw which adjusts trim froze up. This prevented my autopilot from being able to adjust trim and hold altitude. I was in visual meteorological conditions at the time. I then hand flew the altitude and let the autopilot steer the plane. An hour later; i entered into instrument meteorological conditions conditions. I was still flying the altitude by hand for the next 45 minutes. I worried about potential icing and requested a descent down to 17;000 mean sea level i figured that the descent of 8;000 feet/foot would change the temperature to +6 degrees celsius or 2 degrees per thousand feet/foot the adiabatic lapse rate. The temperature went to 0 degrees celsius and i began to accumulate ice. It was rime ice on the leading edge of the wing along with the windshield icing up. I had pitot heat and propeller boot heat on so no issues with the instruments. I informed center i was taking on ice and asked for 15;000 feet/foot mean sea level and i was still on an instrument flight rules flight plan. As i leveled out at 15;000; the ice started to melt away but due to the lack of autopilot controls and the accumulated ice i had some difficulty with the controls in maintaining level flight. The controller advised me that i was 400 feet/foot below my assigned altitude and i corrected. The controller gave me a standard terminal arrival route which took us to a lower minimum vector altitude so that i could descend further. Seeing that i was in visual meteorological conditions and i could maintain visual clearance on the mountains; i canceled instrument flight rules and went direct to the airport. I had checked weather before my flight and while there were no tops' reports; the ceilings were lower which normally makes for lower tops. This ceiling was very thick. The reported freezing level was around 18;000 yet i began accumulated ice from 19;000 down to 16;000 feet/foot i had the altitude hold jack screw freeze up before two years ago and had my shop remove the old grease and replace [it] with new grease and yet it froze up again. Next time when i see forecast ceilings over the [mountains]; i will choose a different route of flight; either flying further north or further south. I plan to talk with my shop on why my autopilot ices up and if the grease they are using on the trim is the correct product for flying in cold weather. I can't say enough about the controller and how well he took care of me in the icing conditions. I truly appreciate the assistance he gave me to get me out of the icing conditions and let me fly the plane.
output: A m20 elevator trim lubricant froze while in cruise flight at fl250 but a descent to 17;000 feet/foot resulted in rime ice accumulation so further descent to 15;000 feet/foot was made where the ice began to melt.

input: After performing the normal pre-flight inspection and after completing an extended warm-up and run-up to let the engine oil temp rise sufficiently; i departed. At about 200 feet above ground level with approximately 2/3's of the runway behind me; the engine lost significant power; i estimate at least a power loss of 75%. I immediately pulled carb heat; tried adjusting the mixture control and power control; but no action had any effect of restoring power. I did not have enough altitude to turn 180 degrees back to the runway. However; i had enough altitude and speed that if i just let the aircraft glide; it would impact pine trees beyond an open field just beyond the end of [the] runway. The field between the end of [the runway] and the trees has an upslope so i decided my only option was to fly the airplane into the field and use the long grass and small trees and the upslope of the field to hopefully bring the airplane to a stop prior to hitting the pine trees at the end of the open field. I secured the aircraft with the time allowed for a forced landing; opened the canopy; and tried to deploy flaps but impacted the ground prior to being able to deploy full flaps. I continued to 'fly' the aircraft up the incline doing my best to keep it under control while bleeding off speed. The aircraft came to rest about 200 yards in the field prior to entering the pine trees. The strategy of using the upslope and the grass and small trees to bleed off speed prior to impacting the pine trees worked. Once the aircraft came to a halt; i exited the aircraft. I sustained no injuries. The damage to the aircraft is not fully known at this time but the left wing and the landing gear are damaged.within the last few months; in two separate instances during climbout; i experienced engine roughness that was eliminated with the application of carb heat. In both of these instances; the air temp was near 40 degrees fahrenheit with visible moisture in the air. I attributed the engine roughness to carb ice due to the perfect conditions for carb ice and the fact that the application of carb heat resolved the engine roughness. Now; based on this last event; i'm wondering if the events are related; in that; there is a carb or some other malfunction that initially presented itself with the same manifestation as carb ice.
output: Aa5b pilot reported losing power shortly after takeoff and landing straight ahead in a field; resulting in some damage to the aircraft.

input: Was operating the scissor lift and bumped into the r-hand nose dock; which was not setting the 4 antiskid's brakes; caused the r-hand nose dock to move several inches and put a dent in the left/right (directions) front corner below the paint stripe on the fuselage next to the radome. The dent is approximately the size of a nickel.
output: An md80 was damaged when parked in a portable dock when a scissors lift struck the dock moving the dock against the aircraft nose skin.

input: This was a night flight from phoenix sky harbor to goodyear. I received clearance from clearance delivery to 'squawk xxxx; fly runway heading at 3000'; departure frequency is 123.7;' which was read back and confirmed. After liftoff on runway(s) 26r; the tower assigned me a heading of 220; which is in the direction of south mtn. Shortly thereafter the tower controller told me to 'contact dep.' i switched to comm 2; which was preset to 123.7; and called departure there was no response. I tried several times and still could not get a response. I tried several times and still could not get a response. I then entered 123.7 on comm 1 and tried ot reach departure on that radio. There was silence and no response. At that point i continued my climb through 3000' since i was aware that south mtn and its radio towers were 3000'. I tried both radios several times with no response. I then switched back to the tower frequency for a radio checked upon contact; i told the controller of my inability to contact departure she then told me to 'try another frequency 124.1.' i called on 124.1; made contact; and leveled off at 3700'. The departure controller immediately admonished me for climbing through an assigned altitude i explained what had happened; and he then cleared me to my destination i believe that tower should have informed me of a frequency change and the shutdown of 123.7 (especially since i was vectored towards a mtn).
output: Sma climbed above assigned altitude in arsa when unable to contact departure control on assigned freq.

input: After landing in phl on runway(s) 9r and clearing we were told to taxi via taxiway westbound and to hold short of runway(s) 9l which was read back (by the fo) and acknowledged by the capt. At this time i was finishing the after landing chklist and notifying the company that we were on the ground and receiving gate clearance then i looked at my airport diagram chart. When i looked up; we were approaching the runway(s) and the first officer and the tower almost simultaneously reminded the capt to hold short of runway(s) 9l which the capt had just started doing. The hold line is faded yellow which is extremely hard to see at night and there are no lighted signs that you are approaching the runway(s) (no runway(s) signs that are lighted). Braking was slightly harder than normal second officer when a departing wdb rotated 100 yards or second officer before us; some passenber had thought we had a near miss and expressed concern when they deplaned. Although we knew to hold short of runway(s) 9l; we may have crossed the hold short line a little since it was almost impossible to see. Being a little closer to the runway(s) than normal; and the positioning of the taxiway light emitting diode to the passenber concern. Ground taxiway and runway(s) lighting signs definitely need improvement in phl as well as elsewhere in the country.
output: An air carrier lgt taxied across the hold short line approaching a rwy.

input: Electrical fire smoke in cockpit from malfunctioning electrical equipment. Radio communication was temporarily lost due to power outage in plane. I turned off non-essential electrical; ventilated cockpit; and was able to re-establish radio contact with departure frequency. At that time i declared emergency due to smoke in cockpit. They cleared me to land. I was able to make [a] successful landing and the electrical issues were contained by turning off power.
output: Lnc iv pilot declared an emergency and landed after noting smoke in the cockpit from malfunctioning electrical equipment.

input: I ante meridiem a line checked airman for my company and was in the left/right (directions) seat while a new capt was getting his federal aviation administration observed line checked we had departed reno en route to lax; and were on an assigned heading of 160 degrees prior to intercepting j7. We leveled at 15000 feet/foot and had just gotten the handoff from reno departure to zoa frequency 128.80. Switched over; was waiting to get a word in; when we heard a citation checked in 'off douglas county airport out of 12500 feet/foot visual flight rules like to pick up our instrument flight rules clrnc.' we got the first hit on our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii at our 2 o'clock on the inner ring -- yellow; 1000 feet/foot below us; the 2nd hit we got was 12-1 o'clock; 500 feet/foot below us; and about 1 mile traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii immediately gave us an resolution advisory descend dsnd now; increase descent the pilot flying pushed the nose over; and caught the overspd warning clacker. The altitude alerter then went off because we were off our assigned altitude responding to the resolution advisory air traffic control was calling to see intermediate fix we had traffic 12 o'clock our altitude in sight; and the federal aviation administration inspector on the jumpseat jumps up; points at our 12 o'clock position 'i've got him!' the citation passed over us by 500-1000 feet/foot questions i have are why did reno departure not alert us to the traffic even intermediate fix it was only a primary target. Why did our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii not get the traffic until he was second officer close. Was his transponder working? Human factors: an federal aviation administration observed flight for a new capt is a stressful situation anyway. Add on to that; traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory air traffic control overspd clacker; and altitude alerter; plus the inspector jumping up and pointing out traffic and an airplane coming at you with a high closure rate in a 15 second window of time; and i think he did a fine job. There are times when a master mute switch would be wonderful.
output: Flc of an lgt descended below assigned altitude in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii ra.

input: Rear cargo door light on climbout. Returned to field. Check of the door verified door was latched and locked. Tapping on the lock cylinder from the outside caused the light to extinguish. Door was then unlocked and unlatched and visually checked on the inside. Nothing appeared to be out of the ordinary. The door was latched and locked and the light remained extinguished.
output: Citation flight crew reported a cargo door warning light resulting in a return to the departure airport.

input: During taxi out from gate; we were told that there would be a runway(s) change. Instead of choshi 1 runway(s) 16r; we were given the choshi 1 runway(s) 34l. Our taxi route was hn gateway h-d-a-rwy 34l. Our pace to the runway(s) was unhurried. In fact; we held for a couple of minute(s) just short of taxiway a before being cleared onward. During this time we completed chklists and all 3 of us were monitoring our progress to runway(s) 34l. There is an altitude restrict, restricted, restriction of 7000 feet/foot on the choshi 1 runway(s) 34l. As we taxied; the ground controller had us delete that restrict, restricted, restriction both the relief pilot and i heard the call and the first officer read it back with our call sign. After we taxied onto taxiway a; the air traffic control again called and told us to line up and wait. Again the relief pilot and i head the clearance and had the first officer read back with call sign. For some reason the first officer was having trouble understanding air traffic control i called for 'the final items' and proceeded to taxi from taxiway a to runway(s) 34l via taxiway a11. Being new to the aircraft i taxied slowly (5-6 kts) in the turn. I visually cleared the approach corridor and looked down the runway(s) before turning onto it. Meanwhile the first officer was completing the 'list.' both the relief pilot and i saw landing lights on short final for runway(s) 16r. I stopped immediately. Our nose was about 8 feet/foot into the runway(s) the landing aircraft was our sister flight the first officer told the tower we were still 'holding short;' whereupon the ground switched us to tower we checkeded in with tower and were told to hold short. As landing aircraft cleared at mid field; we were cleared into position the first officer called to verify our altitude clearance and we were given the 7000 feet/foot restr! We could have had a major runway(s) incursion and an altitude bust within 10 minute(s) upon reflection there were several red flags. The fact that ground cleared us into position for takeoff the other was the fo's difficulty with communications one other was air traffic control had their hands full with the runway(s) change. I can only attribute jet lag as the reason for our lack of response to these cues. We may not have been sleepy but we weren't rested!
output: B747 flight crew is confused with ground taxi clearance at nrt; crossing runway(s) hold line with traffic on final.

input: During navy tow mission #1 oil pressure started to slowly decrease with good oil temp/eng temperatures we terminated training mission and returned home base. Prior to landing we did a precautionary engine shutdown and executed an uneventful single engine apch/lndg.
output: Inflt engine shutdown.

input: Atl to bru. After an 8 hour flight and an uneventful landing at ebbr on runway(s) 25r; we cleared the runway(s) and we were issued taxi instructions to taxi to spot (jetway) via the inner taxiway (which paralleled runway(s) 25r). The controller was speaking in 2 different languages to various aircraft and we (the capt; myself and the relief fo) thought we heard to take taxiway mach number to the ramp. Upon approaching taxiway mach number there were 3 aircraft in front of us ready to take off on runway(s) 25r and on the inner taxiway past taxiway mach number to the left/right (directions) was an air carrier b767 under tow; second officer a left/right (directions) turn into the commuter apron leading to taxiway mach number made sense. Upon turning we noticed that taxiway mach number (200 feet/foot in front of us; narrow and asphalt) did not look adequate (which our commercial chart verified for b737-400 or less gross weight only). Ground asked us to stop and could we make a left/right (directions) 180 degree turn back to the inner. A dash 8 aircraft was 100 feet/foot to our left/right (directions) and a curb was 200 feet/foot to our left/right (directions) we asked for marshallers and wing walkers and started #2 engine again for the turn. We signaled 2 individuals near the dash 8 to checked our wingtip clearance and followed the marshaller's signals 200 feet/foot in front of our aircraft the relief first officer was stationed in the left/right (directions) window to observe wing walker's signals and wingtip clearance approximately 1/2 way through the turn; the capt stopped the aircraft as he was unsure intermediate fix the nosewheel would clear the curb 80 feet/foot in front of us. We asked for a tug when the marshaller signaled we had clearance and to continue the turn. Power was added with the dash 8 approximately 100 feet/foot behind us. I mentioned to the capt to limit his power as the acft/personnel might be behind us. The turn was made; a taxi was accomplished to the gate. We later heard that a wing walker may have injured his hand (could not confirm). The capt was asked to fill out a rpt of this occurrence for the airport manager tower personnel were present at this meeting. He stated that there was no damage to the dash 8 and the wing walker was fine and 'back on the job.' (capt related.)
output: B767 flight crew received confusing taxi instructions at a foreign arpt.

input: I was the technician that signed off aircraft change order #x. Several technicians were working on this step; but only 1 block was available to sign off. I was told that during an audit that 1 passenber service unit that was not modified was discovered. I cannot recall every passenber service unit that i worked on this acft.
output: A b737-300 had a passenber service unit modification accomplished. Later was found to have 1 passenber service unit not modified.

input: I became aware aircraft x was flying in our airspace to siver city; new mexico. I was curious why this aircraft had not responded to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory i asked the pilot to contact me once he was on the ground. He called and i asked him about the event. He informed me his traffic alert and collision avoidance system equipment only provided ta's. The equipment just advises him where the traffic and changes color as it becomes closer. I was not aware of any equipment in the system that did not provide an resolution advisory i thought that's how the system works and why controllers are not to issue any clearances to aircraft responding to a resolution advisory i have talked to numerous people; including people in aov; since this discussion and no one was aware of this type of traffic alert and collision avoidance system in the system. Air carrier y responded to a resolution advisory to descend due to the rate of climb of aircraft x. Aircraft x on another frequency responded to a control instruction to descend back down to fl400. One aircraft responding to a resolution advisory one aircraft responding to a control instruction sounds very similar to a midair in europe. We are briefing our workforce on this information. If it is the case that traffic alert and collision avoidance system equipment as described are in the system this information needs to be disseminated. There should be a way to recognize these types of equipped aircraft. If traffic alert and collision avoidance system is the failsafe system for this type event then all aircraft should receive ra's to prevent a midair.
output: A zab supervisor; investigating a traffic alert and collision avoidance system conflict event; discovered a misconception he and other controller's had regarding the limitations of various types of traffic alert and collision avoidance system equipment.

input: I took off from sna airport to go to hemet; ca; and pick up a friend. I had a heading of 80 degrees and reached 5500 feet/foot for this flight over saddleback (santiago peak); there was very strong turbulence the information i had from a fellow pilot was that there was a new runway(s) at hemet. Though i had been there many times; my last time was over 1 yr ago. I have been in southern california and line of sight angeles; flying since 1955. My heading was on course until i saw the runway(s) i landed! I had dropped 3000 feet/foot and landed at march air force base thinking it was the new longitude runway(s) the military police took me to base operations office for the rpts. After that; they let me go.
output: Wrong airport landing as an old veteran pilot meanders into the class celsius airspace without clearance and then mistakenly lands at march air force base without landing clearance suffering a runway(s) incursion at riv; ca.

input: Radar maintenance technician at lbg radar site (garden grove) interjecting 'test targets' with a beacon cone of 6667 and an altitude of 53;600. These targets are equidistant from the radar site and are distracting to controllers. The federal aviation administration takes a stance on reducing distractions in the workplace but the stars automation system continuously provides distracting information to controllers. Tech ops should take measures to prevent false data from displaying on the controller displays. Automation could be programmed to ignore certain beacon codes such as this particular 6667 code. Please conduct an independent operational analysis on the stars automation platform at sct.
output: Sct terminal radar approach control facility controller reported false targets on the stars display that were put there by maintenance. He recommended an independent operational evaluation on the stars system at sct.

input: While taxiing into the hangar area on taxiway b i came close to a helicopter approaching to land. He was approaching from my right and the landing spot was also to my right adjacent to the taxiway. I did not see him immediately as my view to my upper right is blocked by the sun-shield on my canopy. When i first saw him he was at my 2 o'clock at a low altitude as he was executing a go-around. I stopped immediately until he had passed in front of me. Then i proceeded and turned right two hangar rows passed the conflict point and as i exited that hangar row headed for my hangar row; i saw him making another approach in front of me. I immediately stopped to let him land. He saw me and hovered for a moment to make sure i was going to stay stopped. The normal procedure at this airport is: i am cleared to the ramp by the tower and told to monitor the ground frequency which i was doing. The helicopters are cleared to land by the tower at their own risk. If he is cleared to land after i switch from the tower frequency to ground; i will not hear that transmission. That was the case here; i assume; as i never heard him cleared to land. Since we are on different frequencies it makes for potentially dangerous situation. I have talked to the tower about this previously but got no response.
output: Small aircraft pilot reported a conflict with a helicopter while taxiing in the ramp area at ffz airport.

input: At start of shift; we were informed that notams had not been available since approximately xa:00z due to damage to the federal aviation administration servers. Several messages sent by [the] domestic manager to get notams by calling airport operations at our airports to obtain notice to airmen / of air missions information. However; this wouldn't work with many international airports due to language barrier (later resolved when international notice to airmen / of air missions access was restored;) and even with domestic airports; the information is only good until the phone call would be terminated because without new notams coming in; we would have no way of knowing if a new notice to airmen / of air missions was added later. Additionally; center; fir and fdc notams were not being updated either; so that information also not available as required by federal aviation regulation and fom.consequently; i elected not to release any of my flights until the notice to airmen / of air missions system came back up. I attempted to have the flights all prepped so they could be sent immediately when the notice to airmen / of air missions system started coming back; but i fell behind even doing that; and all 13 flights on my desk released late and took the associated delays. Contributing to the late releases were thunderstorms approaching zzz during the inbound and having to focus my attention on those rather than getting flight plans prepped. My purpose with this report is to both self-disclose the fact that i sent releases later than specified by the manual but also to raise concerns about management's solution to 'mitigate' the notice to airmen / of air missions issue. The manual is clear about our requirement to check all notams; and merely calling airport operations does not ensure that all notams are received. Some notams; like runway closures; taxiway closures; approach light outages; etc; may come from airport operations; but others may be issued by the federal aviation administration notice to airmen / of air missions office (fdc notams;) others are issued by the air traffic control centers. It's simply unrealistic and imposes too much of a workload on both international and domestic dispatchers to be expected to call dozens of airports (9 alone on one of my extended range twin operations flights;) along with multiple centers to try and get notice to airmen / of air missions information while also dealing with thunderstorms and all of our other flight following duties.it seemed very much that the overriding concern was getting releases out regardless of whether it was legal or prudent to do so. Apparently; the federal aviation administration puts the notice to airmen / of air missions servers on the top floor of one of their building. When thunderstorms moved through; the roof leaked and allowed water to soak all of the servers. Better server placement by the federal aviation administration would be a good start along with a robust backup system in a completely different location along with the necessary programming and bandwidth so that failing over to the backup system is a near-instant process rather than requiring hours.
output: A dispatcher reported notams were not available due to equipment outage so they could not release flights. The reporter stated the dispatchers were told by supervisors to contact airports operations to get notams but this was not sufficient and in violation of company procedures.

input: I was the post meridiem (pilot monitoring) for the flight and first approach. It started with a celsius hydraulic qty (center hydraulic quantity) engine indicating and crew alerting system in the terminal area of zzz. The quick reference handbook was completed. A area navigation global positioning system approach was conducted with the autopilot and autothrottles off. Weather was day/vmc. Immediately after gear and flaps were extended there was a complete failure of the celsius hydraulic system with the associated engine indicating and crew alerting system messages. I announced to the pilot flying (pilot flying) that we would have to abandon the approach and complete the quick reference handbook i coordinated a go around with tower. I explained our problem and our need to perform the quick reference handbook before another attempt to land. While talking to tower; i failed to monitor our airspeed after the first officer (fo) arrested the rate of descent. I had not given him any guidance as to maintaining a particular speed or altitude. The stick shaker got my attention. I called 'speed' just as the pilot flying added power and recovered quickly.tower handed us over to approach. I explained the need to perform the quick reference handbook the time needed to complete the quick reference handbook and that we would only have 2 of three hydraulic systems. A few minutes into working on the quick reference handbook procedure air traffic control advised us that they were [giving priority to] us. Air traffic control asked for souls on board and fuel state. The quick reference handbook was completed. I elected to become the pilot flying for the landing. The landing and rollout were successful. Emergency vehicles escorted us to parking.of course i wish i could do it over. I'm not happy with my initial performance with the problem. The system failure happened at the most inconvenient time. Nonetheless the decision to not land and fix the problem was easy enough. However; my initial execution was poor. After announcing the problem to the pilot flying i should have simply called go around. That would've put us back into the 'aviate' phase and eliminated the stick shaker activation. Then i would've told tower of the go around. Everything else would have sequenced properly for the remainder of the flight.
output: Flight crew reported having a stick shaker activation during a go around; which was attributed to a hydraulic system failure.

input: Cruise flight the left/right (directions) inertial reference system/unit fault light illuminated. Quick reference handbook completed; fault light still illuminated. Visual flight rules landing uneventful. Called maintenance control had filled in most of the blocks of the discrepancy section; ie; pdis; tail number; station; flight number; employee number; but not the actual discrepancy verbiage. Maintenance control wanted troubleshooting help. I turned the irs's off; pulled the 3 adiru circuit breakers; realigned the irs's; no fault lights; everything normal. Second officer i lined out all the entries; initialed all but didn't feel comfortable with the situation ie; not completing the write-up. Maintenance duty control looked at the history and noticed similar write-up the week before and decided a write-up was in order second officer i went to the next page and did a complete write-up. Maintenance from lax was supposedly sent with a new adiru. I suppose the federal aviation administration will nit pick either logbook page; especially the first one being lined out and the reasons why the first was lined out. Second is; how federal aviation regulation do we go to help maintenance and what can we do as pilots that is not considered mechanic only actions; considering how pwring down fixes many electronic probs?
output: Capt of b737-700 questions whether maintenance action and documentation he encountered at a non maintenance station was appropriate. Also concerned that he; a non qualified individual; was performing maintenance procedures via telephone direction.

input: I departed felts field in spokane on a visual flight rules flight to coe. Before departing; i failed to checked with weather service for weather conditions at coeur d'alene airport i began calling the coe tower on 119.1 about 5 mile westbound of the field but was unable to get a response. My altitude was 3100 mean sea level and visibility good. After repeated attempts to raise anyone on either 119.1 or 122.8 i entered a visual flight rules downwind approach announcing my intentions on 119.1 and 122.8. As i was turning left/right (directions) base for runway(s) 1 i noticed an ltt airliner on final for the same runway(s) i then proceeded with a go around well clear and to the left/right (directions) of the approach to runway(s) 1. I was then able to get someone on 122.8 who advised me that the airport was showing an 800 feet/foot ceiling and was under instrument flight rules conditions. I immediately departed the area and returned to felts field for landing i inadvertently entered controled instrument flight rules airspace while flying visual flight rules i had not checkeded with weather service in advance nor had i listed to the local automatic weather observing/reporting system on 135.075. The visibility was good and the ceiling appeared adequate second officer i did not expect instrument flight rules conditions at coe.
output: Unauthorized penetration of airspace. Proximitypa of control zone.

input: I was working 4 radar sectors combined with a large area of thunderstorm activity through the sectors resulting in excessive coordination and frequency congestion during a period of moderate (13 acft) traffic i issued a course deviation for aircraft y; be10 departing gnv; flight level en route to mco; flight level to avoid weather and an altitude of 9000 feet/foot per letter of agreement versus 7000 feet/foot requested on the flight plan. Aircraft x hs125 inbound to gnv; flight level from the south was also issued course deviation for weather then assigned a descent to 8000 feet/foot i assigned 8000 feet/foot thinking i had assigned 7000 feet/foot to the be10. The be10 climbed quickly and was level at 9000 feet/foot within 15 mile east of gnv. Aircraft x descended very slowly; leveled at 10000 feet/foot until about 12 mile from aircraft y then made a turn toward and descended into aircraft y resulting in a loss of separation (600 feet/foot versus 1000 ft). Aircraft x was at 8800 feet/foot descending 5 mile from aircraft y where aircraft y responded to an resolution advisory then climbed up to 9100 feet/foot changed the action then descended resulting in 600 feet/foot separation. I was involved in coordination at the time and was not aware the aircraft were conflicting as the new stars equip's conflict alert did not sound an alarm. Primary cause: i issued 8000 feet/foot to aircraft x thinking i had assigned 7000 feet/foot to aircraft y. Frequency congestion and coordination prevented me from doublechking altitude information which i would normally do. Contributing factors: aircraft x did not appear to descend at a standard rate and the response to an resolution advisory resulted in the aircraft climbing into aircraft y without my knowledge until after the aircraft had passed. The faa's conflict alert equipment did not alarm. Frequency congestion: the reduced strength of the frequencies being used in this large sector requires the use of multiple frequencies as aircraft progress through the sector. You must use multiple frequencies simultaneously or lose radio coverage with the aircraft human performance: the federal aviation administration began a policy about 1-2 yrs ago to increase productivity (reduce controller's time off pos) during a shift. Controllers are working considerably more time on position with less breaks resulting in tired controllers returning from short breaks to work heavy tfc.
output: Jax terminal radar approach control facility controller experienced operational error at 9000 feet/foot when climbing an aircraft to an occupied alt.

input: During normal visual flight rules approach to phx-26r we experienced a fair amount of thermal activity (outside temperature approximately 100 degrees f). Causing plus or minus altdevs from glideslope normal for this type of day. Aircraft (a-320) was being hand flown with autothrottles on. No flight directors or autoplts on. Below 200 feet/foot above ground level aircraft was on glideslope flare and retrad of power normal. Just prior to touchdown wind gust and/or thermal activity caused aircraft to climb from 10 feet/foot radio altitude to 30 feet/foot radio altitude airspd increased about 5 knot(s) over v approach intermediate fix landing had been 'forced' touchdown would have been beyond midfield second officer go around was initiated. Since throttles had been retarded to idle considerable time was required for engs to reach go around thrust. After passing 2500 feet/foot mean sea level we were switched back to approach from tower capt was operating radios and setting altitude assigned of 4000 feet/foot and confirming heading by the time 4000 feet/foot was assigned and confirmed by capt we were rapidly climbing through 3200-3500 feet/foot and experiencing the same ups and downs due to thermal activity. In attempting to smoothly level off in the bumpy air while still completing the aircraft clean up and turning the autothrottles back on; etc; i exceeded my altitude of 4000 feet/foot we were essentially level by 4150-4200 feet/foot and then once again 'ballooned' to approximately 4300 feet/foot due to thermal turbulence possible causal factors: failure on my part to be mentally prepared for go around and thus be more efficient in getting the system back on line to and in go around profile. Being #1 to airport in visual flight rules conditions with no traffic at hold short no reason to consider a go around capt was on only his second trip since training on aircraft (less than 100 hrs) and rather than trying to respond to questions about why autothrottles; etc; weren't on during go around etc. I should have asked him to wait until aircraft was on downwind. Corrective actions: always be mentally prepared for go around no matter how good the weather when flying with 'new to the equip' pilots or anyone without recent experience; review what will/will not work on go around this go around was very unusual in that throttles were already to idle and therefore autothrottles disconnected. Also fo's were off -- (flt director's) second officer there wasn't the usual vertical guidance to help with gar.
output: A-320 forced to go around due to thermal activity and resulting turbulence exceeds go around alt.

input: A line of thunderstorms oriented ne to sw lay se of the airport essentially stopping all departures as no one elected to depart through them. Bwi airport surveillance radar 9 showed the storms to be of level fire intensity with a few holes in between wdb requested departure and was put into position on runway(s) 15r to look at the x. The first fix on the route was to a point 180 degrees from bwi; and south of the line of thunderstorms the pilot looked at the weather and told the tower he saw a hole he could go through and there would be no problem going on course. I; as the departure controller released the flight wdb departed and immediately started deviating; eventually to a point 70 mile off course when he left my scope. Several other flts; holding north of the weather were affected; as they had to be moved out of wdb's way. When asked why he told the tower he would go on course and did not; the pilot basically said that it was just a ploy to be released; knowing that once airborne he could pick his way around the weather this created an unsafe situation as traffic was compacted already due to being stuck north of the weather and practically all holding altitudes were taken. In summary; what i encountered was a supposedly professional flight crew lying to get airborne; knowing they would not do what they had said they would. By doing second officer they endangered their aircraft as well as other flts already airborne.
output: A departing aircraft that had to deviate due to adverse weather caused problems for the air traffic control system.

input: We landed safely at dubuque. The weather at the time was rpted as 200 feet/foot overcast with 1 1/2 mile of visibility; light freezing rain; and braking action poor. We proceeded from the runway(s) to the company hangar with caution. We brought the aircraft to a complete stop at a distance we considered to be safe. We initiated the shutdown procedure and as capt brought the power levers out of reverse first officer pulled the propeller levers to feather at this point the aircraft slid forward hitting the hangar. The left/right (directions) propeller radome; and left/right (directions) spinner hit the doors of the hangar causing damage to each. Possible corrective action would be to assure a clear area in front of the aircraft prior to shutdown and establish a procedure for shutdown when the brakes are ineffective (ramp was ice- covered).
output: Smt cpr aircraft shuts down after parking and aircraft slides into hangar. Ice on ramp.

input: Procedure set up to get apa arrivals into apa airport with a descend via to keep them out of the way of denver arrivals. The procedure requires the arrival controller in the terminal radar approach control facility to use the automated point out function to point out the aircraft to west departure; south departure; arrival sectors as well as local 2 in the tower. This seems to be a common issue where everyone approves the point out for the procedure except local 2; and then we are scrambling last minute to stop the descent; call departure control; initiate a handoff to a different controller (that already took a point out) and coordinate new instructions to both the controller and the pilot who is on the area navigation arrival descending via. Yes; the procedure descends through tower's airspace; but the arrival was jointly created and is in the standard operating procedure (standard operating procedure) so all controllers are very familiar with the procedure. Lately it seems local control is saying 'unable' much more than in the past. Today local 2 waited until the aircraft was 9 miles northeast of den to say 'unable' and he did so using the automated 'un' function. By the time i observed the 'un' flashing; i have about 5 miles with the aircraft going 250 knots to figure out a new plan; do all the coordination; handoff the aircraft; etc. Meanwhile i have other aircraft calling and pilot reports to be issued and i was not anticipating having this additional workload put on me with no time to complete all of it. The worst part of this entire situation today was that not a single aircraft departed within 5 miles of aircraft x. I stopped the aircraft x at 11;000 feet; to keep out of the tower's airspace. Aircraft x continued on the lateral portion of the arrival and while the aircraft was over the tower's airspace; there were no aircraft departing; which indicates to me that the local controller did not have an actual reason to unable the point out. The 'descend via' clearance as published would've worked absolutely perfectly. Zero aircraft were departing denver; so no delays on the departing traffic; and then aircraft x would not have to have been delayed either. I asked the supervisor to call upstairs and ask why the local controller said 'unable' and was unable to accommodate the descend via through his airspace; and the supervisor would not tell me what the tower said. He instead stated that i needed to quiet down; and that it's their airspace and they have every right to say 'unable'. It is frustrating that the supervisor in the terminal radar approach control facility cannot communicate to me what the reason was and also doesn't seem to have my back; and instead takes the tower's side. There was no tm (traffic management) in the room at the time; otherwise perhaps that would've been the better route to go as far as figuring out why they couldn't accept the point out. If the tower isn't going to approve the puffr 4 arrivals descending via through their airspace; then the tm needs to be advised so they can coordinate with center so the aircraft are routed into apa airport a different way. This is getting ridiculous. If the tower controllers can't work with us; than the procedure needs to be changed and the aircraft routed a different way. As radar controllers we shouldn't have to scramble every time because the local controllers don't want to work something out; don't want to work hard; or feel it is easiest to 'unable'. Every time this happens it compounds the frustration in the terminal radar approach control facility and it seems tower just doesn't want to work as a team. If they actually have a reason to say 'unable'; then it is completely acceptable and understandable; but more often than not; they 'unable' the point out; and then we observe zero aircraft impacting what could have been an easy operation. Instead; the apa arrival gets vectored all over; and the departure controller who takes the aircraft last minute; at 11;000 feet; is scrambling because they have nowhere to go with the aircraft and if there was a sequence with another aircraft there is very little airspace to maneuver in.
output: Tracon controller reported the tower local controllers routinely disapprove point outs through tower airspace even without conflicting traffic.

input: After departure from yum airport we received a clearance to climb to 15;000 feet/foot we received a handoff to abq center at approximately 14;300 feet/foot after checking on with abq our attention was diverted for a few moments and the aircraft climbed through our pre-selected altitude to approximately 16;300 feet/foot we recognized the error and immediately corrected back to 15;000 feet/foot abq center recognized our mistake and verified our assigned altitude and that we were correcting. The dhc-8 has an altitude pre-select and an altitude sel button located on the fcp. You must always set a new altitude in the altitude pre-select window and also select the altitude sel button on the fcp. This 2 step requirement can make it easier to make a mistake. Also the fcp is very small with each button in close proximity. It is very easy to unintentionally de-select the altitude sel button when arming another mode such as navigate, navigation or heading (etc). All of this can be guarded against by making the id-802 a large part of your scan as it makes you aware of the modes you have armed. Both i and my first officer recall seeing the altitude sel mode selected several times during our climb. I believe the most likely thing that happened is that it was inadvertently de-selected when we intercepted the airway on the departure just after checking on with abq center and only moments before reaching 15;000 feet/foot i believe that the most common sense correction to this situation is a modification to the aircraft to allow for the pilot to select and altitude in the altitude pre-select window and that is the altitude the aircraft will next capture.
output: A dash 8 captain reported overshooting assigned altitude on climb; citing an overly complex altitude pre-select interface on the autopilot as contributing.

input: During a departure push from cle with scattered thunderstorms in the area; the supervisor decided to combine the yng sector and the dkk sector because of the lack of staffing for the evening shift. The combined sector was staffed with a trainee; an assistant; and myself the trainer. With 2 sectors and 2 frequencies the sector combination soon became difficult to manage. The trainee struggled with frequency changes while aircraft from the 2 frequencies checkeded in and covered one another. Numerous crossing situations needed to have altitudes amended while aircraft checkeded in and covered clrncs. Needless to say; this confusing situation would have been difficult for myself; let alone a trainee with only several hours on the sector. Zob management routinely refuses to call overtime to staff already depleted controller numbers necessary to operate an area. D-side position are left unmanned when they normally would have been manned to assist a busy sector.
