output: Zob controller described busy on-the-job training session when lack of staffing made operation of combined sector very difficult.

input: We flew a test flight on the aircraft earlier; which was satisfactory. Maintenance came to see intermediate fix test flight was satisfactory/unsatisfactory. He then took the logbook to copy the results of the test flight i thought he was sitting in the front passenber row to copy the information when in fact he had left the aircraft (with the logbook). I did not know he had left the aircraft he went to maintenance and was shortly called out to another aircraft before finishing with our logbook. The logbook was sitting on the table in maintenance passenber and release came shortly after maintenance man had left. We started the left/right (directions) engine and taxied out and took off. When i went to enter the times; logbook was not in the aircraft we returned to base; shut down the left/right (directions) engine got the logbook; and took off for syr. Round trip; and returned without incident. Recommendations: 1) first officer enter out-time in the logbook -- not on a piece of paper under his yoke clip; at time of taxi. 2) the word 'logbook' be added as item #1 on the before taxi chklist. It is not uncommon for maintenance to come to the aircraft take the logbook off the aircraft to bring it back shortly thereafter. It happens quite frequently. This incident was rpted to: coordinator on feb/xa/99 at xa50.
output: Sf340 takes off lga without logbook on board.

input: Sick passenger which required us to call stat-md through arinc. Using the very high frequency frequency chart on one of the last pages of our [release]; we attempted to call arinc; which we could talk to; but barely understood them. We tried a different frequency which was no better. We needed to talk to dispatch somehow but were unable to through arinc and our automatic communications addressing & reporting system showed automatic communications addressing & reporting system no comm. While we finally patched with stat-md and dispatch; we wasted around five minutes; which during those minutes we were doing nothing to get ahead of this sick passenger's situation. Automatic communications addressing & reporting system and arinc is not always reliable.
output: B737 captain reported a critical communication breakdown when trying to reach stat-md regarding a passenger illness.

input: We were shooting the back course mvy approach in weather rpted as 400' overcast and 1 1/2 mile in light rain and fog. While inside the final approach fix (16.0 vor and dme (co-located) mvy vor) we noticed deviations of 1/2 to 1 degree we corrected for what we thought were winds. Approximately 3 mile from the missed approach point (21.0 dme) tower advised us that we were 1/2 mile north of course. Our instruments showed that we were on course. At the missed approach point or just before reaching it we spotted the runway(s) to our right by 1/4 mile we turned right; lined up and landed safely. Later in the day we flew this approach twice and found the vor and dme (co-located) course to be drifting at some points on the approach by as much as 1 1/2 dots in relatively short time periods. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: commuter airline. Rptr very familiar with this particular approach stated sometimes ships in the channel cause the vor and dme (co-located) to swing. Allowable error on vor and dme (co-located) test (before flt) xchking the 2 vor and dme (co-located) instruments is 3 degrees believe 1 degree error at 21 mile would give approximately 1 mile off course. This is entirely possible on a back course at 21 mile from vor.
output: Reporter states mvy vor and dme (co-located) signal inaccurate.

input: I also submit this rpt on behalf of mr x (my fo/co-capt on this trip) and mr y (my flight engineer during this particular trip). On a recent trip with a part 121 supplemental carrier (my first as pilot in command for this carrier and under these regs); i believe my crew and i inadvertently under-rested after exceeding 24 hours of flight time in a 72 hour period (ref federal aviation regulation part 121.521). This is my first employment within the supplemental airline ranks and i have found the flt/duty/rest regulations to be a whole new and very large pill to swallow. By my calculations; as of nov/tue/05; we had accrued 27 hours 28 minute(s) of flight time during the previous 72 hours with legal rests; but we had triggered the necessity for 18 hours of rest following our arrival, arrive on nov/tue/05. Unfortunately; due to the pace of this trip; the irregular operations(s) of this trip; my own and apparently crew scheduling's lack of familiarity with supplemental regulations governing us; we departed on nov/wed/05 after only a little over 14 hours of rest. Our crew scheduling department intervened in no way; shape; or form. Point of view: the rules governing supplemental operators and their employees; like all flight and duty limits; require an attorney and accountant on staff to decipher and track. At all previous airlines in my experience; we have had crew schedulers/planners that were constantly looking forward and backward using their own knowledge of the regulations and backed up with the software to flag any problem areas to ensure that no violations existed or developed. The rules currently under discussion require a flight crew member to be constantly aware of multiple rolling clocks 24/48/72 hours not to mention the 24/7 rolling; 120/30 day rolling; the 300 in 90 day rolling; and of course the 1000 in any rolling 12 months. Intermediate fix you happen to conduct a domestic portion then; of course; the rules and limits change. Surely there must be a better way to ensure crew members are adequately rested without adding additional duress during the course of an already tiring trip caused by mysteriously convoluted regulations it's as intermediate fix one needs additional rest to recuperate from tracking the flight time and rest requirements. The complexity of the regulations and tracking requirements seem to defeat their own purpose.
output: Fatigued b747-200 flight crew for supplemental carrier believe they failed to obtain the required rest following an irregular international op.

input: On climbout; had some different trim requirements than normal; but not entirely abnormal for such a steep climb in such a light airplane. Received a spoiler fail and a spoiler open indication shortly after establishing in cruise flight and just joining up with the arrival into zzz. I was the pilot flying. Received an engine indicating and crew alerting system message of 'spoiler fail' and a 'spoiler open' indication. Followed the procedure; declared an emergency due to loss of a flight control; and determined that zzz was the best and most suitable option for our needs after carefully reviewing landing distance requirements and configuration requirements. Contacted dispatch and local operations to let them know of our situation. Landed without incident. Declared an emergency; followed the procedures; checked and rechecked performance numbers and configuration; asked for priority handling when air traffic control advised us that zzz was holding (didn't find it prudent to hold slow in light chop with a spoiler system that was not operating properly). Contacted dispatch and operations to confirm situation and discussed with dispatch to confirm our assessment of performance numbers for suitability of zzz as our point of landing. Due to configuration and increased landing speed requirements by the aom; i requested crash fire rescue to monitor the brakes once we were clear of the runway. Landed without incident. Crash fire rescue found brakes to be warm but fine for taxi (as were cockpit indications). Taxied in without incident. Folks removed for maintenance to figure it out and fix it right. After third attempt at departure; we gave up and called fatigued in order to force local maintenance to take the time and fix the airplane properly. We returned to a 'fixed airplane' only to have the same issue haunt us once airborne. This spoiler situation was a multiple repeat write-up. Caution on the part of any crew -- vigilance -- and asking the right questions was all we could do. Once the mechanics sign something off and is provided that long to 'fix what is broken' there is not much that any crew member can do. Our livelihood as well as that of our passengers is on their backs. If they do not have the tools or support from their management to do what they need; they need to make us (pilot in command) aware of the issue so we can elevate the issue to another level for resolution. There is no such thing as 'must go' in civil aviation. We forced the maintenance issues by using the excuse of 'fatigue' the evening before to give the mechanics time to address the issues with the airplane. We took the full hit of pay loss flight delay/deferral of the flight so the airplane would be taken to the hangar and properly fixed.
output: Emb135 captain reports 'spoiler fail; spoiler open' engine indicating and crew alerting system in cruise after three previous attempts to remedy problem by maintenance. Emergency is declared and flight continues to destination for uneventful landing.

input: Events best as i can recall. Departed cle; first officer flying. Cleared by departure to 17000 feet/foot contacted zob; cleared to fl230; then fl280. Center asked for climb rate of 1500 feet per minute was unable; could do 1000 feet/foot center asked us to hurry through fl220; then fl250. Cleared direct pxv out of fl240 for fl250. At some point we were handed off to next controller along with squawk change and clearance to fl310. Aircraft was in slow climb due to high gross weight and anti-ice. Pilot not flying went off frequency to make public address and returned to hear pilot flying talking to zid. Zid asked intermediate fix we were level fl280; to which he replied out of fl280 for fl310. No response. Several other aircraft checkeded in. Finally we asked to confirm altitude controller stated no one down here can remember clearing you to fl310. Call regarding possible deviation was pretty sure zob cleared us to fl310; but now wonder intermediate fix we got another's clearance similar company call signs on frequency that day. In addition; was last leg of a longitude day; as well as a busy frequency with ord traffic and weather in the area. Followed altitude setting procedures rigorously; but no good intermediate fix i set it taking someone else's clearance or center handoff isn't completed. Not a great way to end a trip.
output: Alt assignment confusion in zid class a airspace.

input: At fl350 and track 11-173w encountered moderate turbulence seat belt sign had been on for 10-15 minute(s) flight attendants were told to be seated. 5 minute(s) before encounter; a passenber got up to go to bathroom and was verbally told by a flight attendant to situation down. Passenber refused and went to washroom. On leaving the washroom she fell and injured herself. Injury unknown. Passenber claimed her leg was hurt and couldn't walk on it. 2 doctors were called on to checked on passenber they said there was nothing they could do; other than what the flight attendant had done. We called ahead for ambulance and medics. Also advised company of incident. Time of incident was xa23z. Supplemental information from acn 319975: she refused and went to the lavatory. Upon exiting the lavatory; fell and injured her leg. The injury could possibly be a broken left/right (directions) leg.
output: Pax injury during flight through moderate turb.

input: Acr x inbound to mia and cle. Automatic terminal information service at mia and cle issued following information 'apch in use instrument landing system runway(s) xx...notams g/s ots.' what they really meant was 'loc approach to runway(s) xx.' in today's busy air traffic control environment with 2-m cockpit crews; air traffic control can lead a flight crew down the primrose path expecting an instrument landing system instead of localizer upon questioning mia approach said a localizer approach does not exist for 09l at mia; but only for instrument landing system (with g/s ots). This is not safe. Last night i listened to the cle automatic terminal information service (info 'a' or 'p;' depending on which letter you listened to on their info) for 5 minute(s) before i deciphered that they were doing a localizer only approach try this with multi vectors; huge line; longitude runway(s) 23l out of service all summer and an automatic terminal information service giving a 5 minute(s) spiel to state they were shooting 23l localizer only; sidestep to 23r; 23r visual approach slope indicator ots!! Please tell federal aviation administration a localizer approach is localizer not ils! Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr was contacted about clearance interpretation analyst explained federal aviation administration policy as to the phraseology used for approach clearance and the information advertised on the automatic terminal information service the mia supervisor was correct in his explanation to the rptr. The approach is advertised as it is listed on the approach plate. Rptr then complained about the length of automatic terminal information service information analyst said this sometimes becomes a problem and the rptr should rptr it to the supervisor of the particular fac.
output: Atis approach information lengthy automatic terminal information service information.

input: We were tasked with a part 91 reposition flight and the flight was routine. After a second reposition flight on a different aircraft and while in a taxi to our overnight hotel we received a call from the crew taking the original reposition aircraft. They asked us if we had noticed any discrepancy with the overwing emergency exit door 'slide armed' indication. I advised them that i did not recall any malfunction and the slides themselves do not generate malfunctions to the fwc unless a cover is removed from the overwing exits. As we were a reposition flight only we did not arm the slides due to concern over inadvertent opening of an armed door during a non-normal operation. If the overwing slides were not armed it escaped our notice during the flight. We were only advised of a possible situation by the crew subsequently flying the aircraft we had repositioned. Failure of the maintenance facility to rearm the overwing emergency exit slides may have been a factor; however as i did not notice any slide malfunctions and we did not arm the slides prior to departure i cannot say that this may be the case. It may be helpful to add the overwing slides to the post maintenance inspection procedures and possibly add a slides armed item to the before start or after start checklist.
output: A320 flight crew is informed after the fact; that they may have flown an aircraft on a part 91 ferry flight with the over wing exit slides disarmed. The cabin doors were intentionally left disarmed but the crew did not notice that the over wing exit slides had been left disarmed by maintenance.

input: On a visual approach to runway(s) 35r dfw and inside of 10 nautical mile a flight attendant passed a note to the cockpit that said a passenber had gotten a clear fluid leaking from the overhead bin in her eye and was requesting medical assistance. Upon clearing the runway(s) first officer called the cabin to ascertain extent of problem the note we received had stated that it was not an emergency and the flight attendants verified this. The first officer notified ramp and requested emt's meet the flight we were on at xa48 and due to an occupied gate did not reach gate xx until xb10. Emt's boarded aircraft and rinsed female pax's eyes. She refused to give the emt's or the crew her name; but stated she felt her problem had not received serious enough attention emt's informed me that they found no indication of inflammation or irritation to pax's eyes; but that she was extremely upset.
output: Plt rpt; s80; msy-dfw; overhead bin leak in passenber eye; emt called on arr.

input: To start off i just want to say it involves an unsafe situation/event with the aircraft but also a safety issue with the constant actions and mentality of the controllers at the facility.starting with the event; aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) was one of four aircraft on final to runway 28r at fll. The aircraft order on final is as follows: aircraft x; aircraft y; aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) and aircraft a (aircraft a is the last aircraft for a good 20 miles). All aircraft are instructed to maintain 170 knots until a 5 mile final. When aircraft x drops off my scope there is 4.5 miles between him and aircraft y who is slowing because they are just inside a 5 mile final. We have a display (passur) at the left of the positions that show the ground radar at fll so we can see taxiing traffic and give gaps when necessary (i will note not all controllers do this). When i glanced at the display i noticed one aircraft taxiing and one waiting out there as aircraft x is short final; but that would be the gap to hit. When aircraft y drops off the scope there are 3.5 miles between him and aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) with a slightly faster speed so it is still compressing. When aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) is on about a mile to half mile final i notice he is at 300 feet and starting a climb. At this point aircraft a is 3.6 miles behind aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) and no one is behind aircraft a. I look at the passur screen to see if aircraft y was stuck on the runway or didn't clear; but what i saw was a departure rolling down the runway. Not only am i baffled as to why; but now i'm worried because aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) is straight out climbing and here pops up aircraft b a half mile in front of him climbing same heading and about 600 feet apart and closing. I know the tower can provide visual separation; but they did nothing [to] turn aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) or aircraft b until the departure end when the collision alert is going off because aircraft zulu time (utc/gmt) is speeding up and aircraft b climbs into them. This is completely unsafe and shouldn't have happened.the safety issue is with fll and the mentality they have there that lead to this incident and multiple others that have happened before this. It is a well-known fact that the controllers at fll have the idea of if i have a departure and no gap i'll just clear them for takeoff or line up and wait and send the next one around. This happens constantly and has become what i believe is the normal thinking for them and they just do it as seen above. They are constantly putting aircraft in gaps that can easily be seen as not big enough for a departure. All it takes is one stuck mike; radio failure or miss applied go-around procedure for a major accident to happen. When they are busy they have asked us to give them 5 miles between arrivals which we do; but how do [you] need 4-5 miles for a departure and yet put an aircraft in a 3.5 mile and closing gap. The mindset of these controllers is negligent and this is a major safety issue. They are going to get someone killed.we have two runways at fll and try to balance it as best as we can. We do have a best operating practice; that in times of busy traffic to send certain arrival gates to certain runways; but most of the time it is not a balanced arrival push so one runway gets hit more if you follow it. To not follow it (and balance the traffic to suit our needs) draws attention of certain supervisors who then yell and force you to do it. We also use 5 miles and 170 knots when we can to help them; but it is not always possible when we get so strung out. They are supposed to balance the departures between the two runways which is not always followed as well. We both need to balance the traffic better; in-air and on the ground. But this mentality of lock and load and go around has to stop. This has been going on for months now and it is getting worse; and for safety i cannot in good conscience let this continue without something being said.
output: Mia terminal radar approach control facility controller reported fll tower has a constantly practiced procedure of allowing aircraft to line up and wait while traffic is on a short enough final to require a go-around. They then have issued a takeoff clearance which creates a conflict on climbout.

input: Location: just north of runway(s) 35l; takeoff after takeoff at about 2000 feet/foot i noticed that the fo's window was cracked. It was a small area in the lower r-hand corner. My concern was that as the airplane pressurized the cracks would spread to the entire windshield. I elected to return to dfw. I advised departure control in my first radio transmission that we had a cracked window and would need to return to dfw. They began to vector us for landing as we climbed to 6000 feet/foot i did not declare an emergency because we did not require special handling. We just needed to fly a normal approach and land. I made a public address to advise the passenber and flight attendants. Then i called ramp to advise them of our impending return and asked them to advise maintenance as you are aware this was a very busy time. I should have called dispatch in a perfect world per the new procedures in reality; this new requirement did not even cross my mind. Intermediate fix i had thought of it; i do not think that i would have had time to contact dispatch in this situation they always seem to take their time answering the radio. My first priority is the safe operations(s) of the airplane. In my opinion downwind; base or final is not the place to be trying to talk to dispatch. That said; i will try to contact dispatch the next time something like this happens.
output: An s80 pilot in command notes a cracked first officer window and return land without advising dispatcher as per new procedure at dfw; tx.

input: Acr x (sh360) is en route pgv to clt; cruising at 6000 feet/foot 10 nautical mile north of gsb. Military y (a heavy kc10) departs runway(s) 26 at gsb. Departure gives him 360 degree heading and 5000 feet/foot departure calls him as traffic to air carrier x. Air carrier x rpts traffic in sight at 10:30 o'clock position air carrier x is not given 'maintain visual separation.' air carrier x is called as traffic to military y and military x rpts negative contact. Departure clears military y to 10000 feet/foot military y is on a line of constant bearing to air carrier x; and is now climbing towards 6000 feet/foot range is approximately 2 1/2 mile air carrier x begins hard left/right (directions) turn to avoid collision. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii calls for rapid descent air carrier x continues a left/right (directions) turn and begins a rapid descent and advises seymour departure of evasive maneuvering. Military y is now at approximately 5700 feet/foot and still has no visual with air carrier x. Range is less than 2 mile and decreasing. Seymour departure then instructs military y to maintain 5000 ft! Military y begins descent back to 5000 feet/foot range is still decreasing to less than 1 nautical mile and likelihood of vertical separation has been lost. Capt of air carrier x (previously pnf) has visual with military y. Midair collision is imminent. Range is much less than 1/2 nautical mile and closing. Capt takes the aircraft and initiates maximum rate climb simultaneously; the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii reverses to 'clb; crossing clb.' the 2 aircraft miss by minimal separation.
output: An air carrier first officer rpts their flight encountered less than standard separation from a kc10 that departed gsb.

input: During walk-around; observed excessive amount of oil or grease on belly of right side of aircraft. Area extended from aft of wheel well; to rear of aircraft; into outflow valve; to tail-skid. Made logbook entry and called maintenance. Maintenance advised that substance was sealant and aircraft would be scheduled for wash at a later time. Logbook stated that aircraft had already received wash four days prior. [we] contacted maintenance control who verified that aircraft had received a wash four days prior. Due to large amount of substance and color and also the fact that aircraft had recently been washed; refused to accept aircraft for safety of flight concerns until source of substance could be positively identified. [there was a] logbook entry 17 days prior for acm [air cycle machine] replacement; [another] logbook entry 13 days prior for odor in cabin. Advised maintenance control; dispatch and local maintenance.
output: B737 captain discovers an excessive amount of grease and oil on the belly of the aircraft during preflight; running all the way to the tail. When maintenance cannot positively identify the source of the lubricant the aircraft is refused.

input: I was pilot in command of an ec-130b4 conducting a [company] air tour flight from zzz to [a national park]. Four passengers were on board the aircraft plus myself. Prior to the flight; i conducted a pre-flight briefing and did not find any notams or airport recordings regarding area closures that would have alerted me to the situation i was about to encounter. Prior to my aircraft's departure; a us marshal prisoner transport plane was present on the ramp and not parked in its typical location; but much closer to the helicopter landing area and parking pads. The prisoner transport plane was in a parking place commonly used by other aircraft; so the presence of an aircraft at that location was not unusual. The us marshals' aircraft and officers had been present on the ramp for at least 15 to 20 minutes before [company] helicopters started departing the ramp. Two other [company] helicopters were also scheduled for departures and departed without incident about 5 to 10 minutes ahead of my aircraft; using the same departure. I lifted off the southern ramp parking pad and hover taxied to the helipad on the southeast corner of the ramp; the departure helipad used by [company]. Arriving at the helipad; i started a right 360 degree clearing pedal turn; looking above for inbound helicopter tour traffic. During the clearing turn i initiated contact with tower; requesting a...departure from the...ramp; which is standard procedure. In the midst of this call and with the helicopter passing through a northerly heading; i observed two men in plain clothes walking from the us marshal's aircraft toward my helicopter with what appeared to be ar-15 assault rifles pointed at the helicopter. The men waved me back with weapons pointed.... The men were approximately 100 feet from my helicopter and the us marshals' plane was approximately 200 feet north of my location.with guns pointed at my aircraft; i was concerned for the passengers' safety and backed the helicopter away from the armed men; repositioned; and landed near the [company] parking pads in an orientation where i could see further instructions from the men. During this repositioning i communicated my actions with the control tower and asked tower to have [local] police respond to my location in the interest of establishing communication and deescalating the situation. Police responded about ten to fifteen minutes after the request. While waiting for police to arrive; i remained at the controls with the helicopter running and stayed in communication with the tower. Once police arrived on scene; i shut down the helicopter and began offloading passengers.... I asked the officer to approach the us marshals and help establish constructive communication between me and the us marshals. The officer walked over to the us marshals and; when he returned; explained that the us marshals refused to speak with me. Shortly thereafter; the us marshals departed the area. The safety of my passengers; myself and any traffic in the vicinity was endangered; as during a clearing turn in a standard departure; i was forced to unexpectedly maneuver the helicopter in a low hover to gain distance from us marshals pointing assault rifles at the aircraft. There was no notice given that could have helped avoid this situation.
output: Helicopter pilot; doing a clearing turn on the ramp in the vicinity of a u.s. Marshal aircraft; was approached by two men pointing assault rifles at the helicopter. After a call for assistance to local police; the situation was resolved.

input: Aircraft experienced an engine rollback with extremely high egt (approximately 891 degrees c); leading to an automatic engine shutdown and engine fire indication. All memory items were accomplished and the engine fire checklist was accomplished as well (engine fire indication extinguished after the fuel control switch was placed to cutoff). An off-track divert was performed with a 15 nautical mile offset to the left. After the offset was established; a descent below fl280 was executed to fl205 initially. Contact with air traffic control was made through [arinc] and a clearance was received to maintain fl200 and cleared to divert. Upon arrival; the [flight] crew executed the instrument landing system landed safely overweight; and stopped on the runway for inspection from arff. Flight was towed to a remote parking site to deplane crew and passengers.
output: Boeing 777-200 flight crew reported that during cruise they had an engine rollback and fire indication and proceeded to divert uneventfully to an appropriate alternate.

input: I was flying the first leg of the day which was a ferry flight. Everything was standard and we were issued a descent clearance from fl350 to fl240 to try to get out of some light turbulence as we started down we were issued descend via the published star.i started to increase our rate of descent to try and stay ahead of the vertical navigation because the difference in our altimeter setting was 30.41 from 29.92. As i started to increase the altimeter to 30.41 our vertical navigation path dropped below us;  so i increased the rate of descent more and deployed the speed brake. I have never used the speed brakes in this airplane as they were a fairly new modification.i captured the vpath and the airplane was flying the descent and the indication in the aircraft flight control systems (afcs) was a magenta navigate, navigation and a magenta vpth. In order to maintain the speed that was requested on the arrival i had to leave the speed brake deployed and as the rate of descent finally started to arrest a few miles from the fix then i closed the speed brakes. This action seemed to cause the airplane to pitch down even more and as i looked at the altitude the airplane was still pitching down through 11;000 feet which was the mandatory altitude so i quickly disconnected the autopilot and started to correct for the deviation.we were still able to make the crossing at 11;000 feet. The captain and i discussed the matter after we arrived and decided that the speed brake retraction caused the automation to misjudge the rate of descent required for the vpth and that in the future changes with the deployment or retraction of the speed brakes should be made at least ten miles prior to the fix in order to assure the crossing altitude would not be a problem.
output: Embraer legacy 450/500 pilot reported the auto flight altitude capture feature failed to level aircraft.

input: Recently i flew 3 different 757-200 airplanes on a two day sequence. The first had the new quick reference 'book;' the second had the old quick reference 'hard card' and the 3rd had 'both' the new book and the old hard card in place in the same plane. We have yet to be completely trained with the new quick reference books and now we find them in a mixed bag in the planes. So; each departure brief is different; standard operating procedure out the window.on a different subject; in the first week of their use; about half of the new [normal] checklist cards i've seen are ripped. We went to a lighter material and they aren't holding up at all.
output: An air carrier b757-200 pilot advised that new and old quick reference checklist publications are on board the fleet in any one of three possible configurations: 1. Old. 2. New. 3. Both. He further reported that training on the new; more comprehensive; 'book' version is not complete. The result is significant cockpit confusion and the need to brief operations based on what resources are available on a given aircraft. Also of concern was the insubstantial nature of the cardstock used on their new 'normal' checklists; noting that about half he has used are already torn after only a week in service.

input: I was flying an sma at 11000 on an instrument flight rules flight in instrument meteorological conditions conditions when i encountered light rime ice on the leading edge of the wings. I explained the situation to the air traffic controller and asked intermediate fix could descend to 9000 feet/foot the controller cleared me to descend to 9500. At 9500 the temperature was 0 degrees celsius and while no more ice was accumulating on the wings; it was not defrosting either. While discussing with air traffic control the possibility of diverting south to san marcos (rzs) vor and dme (co-located) along v-25 (where the minimum enroute altitude is 8600) and then direct vtu; lax; and finally to lgb; i hit an updraft which caused the aircraft to climb while approaching 10500 feet/foot i asked air traffic control intermediate fix i could climb to 11000 feet/foot at 11000 it was visual flight rules between 2 layers of clouds. The controller asked me what my present altitude was. I told him 10500. He asked me who gave me permission to climb to 10500. I paused; then replied by explaining how an updraft caused me to climb and i continued to 10500 which was clear of clouds. The controller scolded me for climbing without permission and cleared me back to 11000 where it was visual flight rules i thanked him for his help and changed frequencies to the next controller it was clear to me; as a pilot it was more important to reach an altitude that was clear of clouds and moisture to stop the build-up of ice; than to continue to make a marginal situation worse. I could not control the air mass that caused the aircraft to climb initially. When i got out of the updraft; i was only a couple hundred feet/foot from 10500; and more importantly; a couple hundred feet/foot from visual flight rules conditions. I climbed to 10500 because the aerodynamics of an airplane are much better than an ice cube.
output: Altdev after inflt encounter with adverse en route weather factors.

input: [operations] advised pilot that [another helicopter] was '10 minutes or so' inbound to [the medical center] as well. After departure i received another call from [operations] asking if i had heard from [the other helicopter]; i responded; 'no.' landing was uneventful at the helipad. Three aircrew members boarded the aircraft. After performing the pre-takeoff checklist; a crew member requested and we received permission to lift and return to base. As i pulled power; i noticed a bright light flooded the cockpit. I immediately reduced collective pitch and looked over my right shoulder and saw a searchlight and then the undercarriage of a helicopter approaching the parking position from the northwest.i made a call to [operations] informing them that they had an aircraft landing. They requested that i hold my position. After [the other helicopter] went to flight idle; i made contact with them on area common [frequency.] both pilots and [operations] coordinated that [the other helicopter] would remain at the park position until i departed. We departed from the adjoining 'h' without incident.a long term solution would be to develop a universal tracking system where all flight operation centers can see the locations and id's of all emergency medical service aircraft. Pilots must be ever cautious and diligent when reporting their aircraft's current position and intentions when entering high traffic areas.
output: Ec135 pilot aborted liftoff from a medical center helipad when he observed the lights of another helicopter landing in close proximity.

input: Normal rated power applied for takeoff on runway(s) 11 at oak. Normal callouts were given at 80 knot(s) passing 110 knot(s) but prior to v1/vr the engine failure lights illuminated. The second officer announced 'eng failure; the capt (pf) initiated the abort and asked the first officer to notify the tower of our aborted takeoff a public address was made to the passenber as we exited the highspd taxiway normally. Once the aircraft was stopped on the taxiway the capt called for the chklists. We concurred that the #1 engine had failed. The hard card (quick reference chklist) was reviewed for the engine failure. Then the pilot's operating manual pwrplant abnormal section. 1 engine inoperative follow-up chklist was reviewed for the appropriate items. We requested firefighting equipment to follow us during our taxi to the gate. Supplemental information from acn 257941: thanks to our training program; it went just like the simulator!
output: Lgt takeoff aborted at high speed when an engine failed.

input: I was on an instrument flight rules flight plan from tulsa to topeka; ks; (forbes field). I was on v131 nbound; talking to kansas city center i had automatic terminal information service within 25 mile of the airport (i believe the wind was 210 at 8; landing runway(s) 22). The center told me to look for the airport at 11 o'clock and 5 mile and tell them when i see the airport i saw an airport and thought it was forbes. I was turned over to the tower at forbes and told them i had current automatic terminal information service they told me a different automatic terminal information service was current and to get the current information i again tuned in the automatic terminal information service and found the only change was the wind was 220 at 8. I called the tower an told them i had automatic terminal information service i was cleared to land on runway(s) 21. I was in fact was looking down runway(s) 22 at billard; thinking it was forbes 21. I proceed to land at billard. An sma y was ready to depart on runway(s) 18; the pilot of the sma y saw me and aborted his takeoff run. (the sma y pilot called me a little later when i was at forbes and told me he saw me and was surprised because the tower at billard didn't see me until i was on the rwy). Now i realized that i was at the wrong airport forbes tower said you must have landed at billard. Their tower frequency is 118.7. Billard tower asked the sma y pilot intermediate fix he wanted to file papers on the incident. The pilot said that he would not. Billard tower proceeded to chew me out and asked my intentions. I said to go to forbes. Billard gave me a clearance to depart on 18. When i arrived at forbes 5 minute(s) later; they asked me to call the tower they took my name and address and commented that it is easy to mix up the 2 airports because they are close together. Forbes questioned intermediate fix i was on the vor and dme (co-located) 21 apch? I said i was not and was cleared for the visual after i told center i had the airport in sight. Forbes said that he was not sure then what he was going to rpt. This is a dumb mistake and i ante meridiem disgusted with my performance. I have a form that i fill out before every flight i list all the frequencies for the arrival, arrive airport the elevation for that airport the visual flight rules pattern altitude on that form i write my clrncs; and every frequency change; heading change; and altitude change. I accept full responsibility for this error and i ante meridiem not trying to place blame on anyone else by giving excuses. The following comments are being submitted only because this form asked for human performance considerations. 1. Perhaps i let myself be distracted from the visual identify of the airport to get the current automatic terminal information service after i was close to the airport on a hot hazy day; with the sun in the sw limiting view of both airports at the same time. Perhaps the change of 10 degrees in the wind; rpted on automatic terminal information service should have been stated by the tower second officer that the pilot need not go back to tuning radios when the most important job was landing many times; wind changes are called out by the tower when you are on final; without being requested to do second officer by the pilot the airport was not busy. Automatic terminal information service was received within 25 mile of the airport and that radio was set to tower frequency ready to be changed. Perhaps i should have asked for a contact approach and intercepted the instrument landing system 31; circle to land 21. I was somewhat surprised that forbes tower did not know for certain that i was handed over to them on a visual landing and not on the vor and dme (co-located) 21 approach this rpt is submitted in total disgust and this incident is a draining experience i will never forget. Please excuse the typos in this rpt; i did it myself; i'm ashamed to let anyone else know about this.
output: Unauthorized landing at wrong airport creates a potential conflict with departure crossing tfc.

input: Plt rpted a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alert at 200 feet/foot and believed it was from a ship in the bay located off the approach end of the runway(s) no resolution advisory was given.
output: Acr x false traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory with ship on the water. Aircraft equipment problem tcasii.

input: Aircraft was in cruise on instrument flight rules plan in visual meteorological conditions another aircraft that was climbing appeared in front of aircraft and slightly to the left from below the nose of the aircraft in cruise. The approaching aircraft was taking evasive action via a hard climbing turn to its right. There was no notice of aircraft in the proximity given by air traffic control atc was notified of the near miss.
output: A be36 pilot on an instrument flight rules flight plan reported a near miss at 9;000 feet/foot with no advance air traffic control notification as the unidentified aircraft took evasive action.

input: Aircraft x called inbound from the southwest for a full stop landing. After initially telling him to make straight in for runway(s) 5; i changed his instructions and told the pilot to make right traffic for runway(s) 10 and to report a 3 mile right base for runway(s) 10. I noticed the aircraft on the radar display on the edge of the class delta flying nw bound through my final for runway(s) 5. I told the pilot to continue west so he didn't cut any other aircraft off on final for runway(s) 5. I observed the target moving westbound. I cleared the aircraft to land on runway(s) 10 and to hold short of runway(s) 5 for traffic. The pilot asked me to repeat my clearance; so i did; he read it back verbatim. I had aircraft y luaw [line up and wait] on runway(s) 5; i scanned all finals then cleared aircraft y for takeoff. I saw aircraft x rolling out on runway(s) 28; so i immediately cancelled aircraft y takeoff clearance. I asked the aircraft on runway(s) 28 who he was. The pilot gave me his callsign and stated that i cleared him to land on runway(s) 10. Both aircraft stopped in time and were about 1;500 feet apart. I told aircraft x that he landed on runway(s) 28 and not runway(s) 10. The pilot seemed confused by this and didn't understand that he actually landed on the wrong runway(s) i read the pilot of aircraft x the brasher warning and taxied him off the runway(s) and to contact ground control. Our staffing was very short due to management allowing the 3rd person that would've been there to change shifts. If that person had stayed on their original assigned shift; we would've had an extra set of eyes in the tower. Traffic was very busy the entire day due to it being a normal busy day and the pilots couldn't do pattern traffic after xa:30 post meridiem local time because of a tfr that would be effective for a sporting event. The traffic was very busy and complex until the tfr started that evening. All other controllers left; so it was just myself and one other controller in the tower until closing time. The flm [manager] was in his office downstairs doing the schedule.management should not have approved a shift change for the 3rd controller.
output: Laf tower controller reported an aircraft landing on the wrong runway and have a ground conflict with a departure aircraft.

input: In level cruise at 27000'; was given vector to intercept j52 ne of cae. That heading aimed us at buildup depicted on weather radar. Advised zjx we were deviating 15 more degrees right (to 060 degs). On that heading with traffic alert and collision avoidance system in ta/ra automatic had an intruder at 2 o'clock showing -800' relative altitude traffic alert and collision avoidance system announced; 'tfc; tfc;' as intruder popped up on screen. Moments later it commanded; 'clb; clb.' immediate climb was commenced at the specified 500 feet per minute the altitude alerter sounded. Then traffic alert and collision avoidance system announced traffic clear and we returned to altitude 27000'. Zjx did not seem to know what we were talking about when questioned. He did say an aircraft had been cleared to fl260.
output: Tcasii resolution advisory leads to altitude deviation for air carrier mlg in cruise at fl270.

input: During the approach to runway(s) 17r in aus with the instrument landing system tuned and identified we noticed that my glideslope indication was showing left/right (directions) on glide path while the fo's was 1 department of transportation low. We were visual at the time and at approximately 4 mile out on final. I thought that i was too low to be this federal aviation regulation out and checkeded the fo's side. We then re-tuned the instrument landing system and also tried switching the 'rad nav' switch. I attempted to try manual instrument landing system by turning off the flight management system nothing worked and the instrument landing system continued to show false on glide path information with no warning or comparator lights. This is a former air carrier y bird that has been modified. We might want to checked and see intermediate fix the wiring has a problem with this jet and others like it. This could be a potential problem and cause numerous missed approachs due to erroneous information with no warning flaps. A good xchk should catch it; but we should try and correct this quickly. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr said; 'my glideslope indicator was ctred; but looking outside the airplane it appeared too low on profile.' the first officer agreed and stated the left/right (directions) glideslope indicator was 1 department of transportation low while the capt's indicator displayed exactly on glideslope there was no warning flag or comparator alert. All other system operated normally. The rptr stated this airplane was a buyout airplane and has been modified to somewhat like the acquiring carrier's fleet. This difference is of great concern and is a potential problem maintenance cleared the rpt with removed and replaced. No other details. Callback conversation with rptr acn 638509 revealed the following information the rptr state that on final approach the capt remarked that he seemed low on profile and he was left/right (directions) 1 department of transportation low on the left/right (directions) glideslope indicator. All navaids were properly tuned and both system on correct frequency no warning of any kind alerted this difference. The logbook was cleared as re-racked units.
output: An md80 capt flying at 2000 feet/foot 4 mile final approach on glideslope noted aircraft too low. Fo's glideslope indicator 1 department of transportation low. No warning flags or comparator alert.

input: At 10;000 ft and 280 kts with autopilot and autothrottles engaged we saw engines 1&2 n1's cycle to idle as engine 3 n1 exceeded its limit; we saw as much as 124%. Upon seeing this i disconnected the auto throttles and moved throttle lever #3 to idle. The first officer reviewed the quick reference handbook for the indicated engine 3 exceedance. Not sure if this was real or just an indication issue we left throttle #3 at idle and operated the rest of the flight with throttles 1&2 only. Throughout the rest of the flight with the #3 throttle at idle we noticed the n1 indication for that engine continued to fluctuate even as high as 70%. We [advised] air traffic control and were given vectors to the instrument landing system we executed an autoland.
output: Md-10 captain reported that one of the engines had an erratic n1 indication.

input: I ante meridiem a flight instructor. I started the day with nearly a full tank of gas in both tanks; on my first flight i had a second flight immediately after the first flight i did a preflt; checkeding the fuel. The fuel gauges read over half on both tanks; and in an sma helicopter the main tank (19.2 gallons usable); and the auxiliary tank (10.5 gallons usable); and with a fuel burn said to be 8 gallons per hour i felt i had 14.85 gal of usable fuel. With that much fuel for a local training flight planned to be no longer than 1.5 (1 hour 30 mins) i should have had enough fuel plus 20 minute(s) reserve. As you might have already guessed; at the end of this training flight i was watching the fuel gauges because they were getting low. From past experience in the sma; when i would fill up; i would find they did not take as much fuel as the fuel gauges would make you think. With this in mind i believed i had plenty of fuel. But as we were in a transition through whiteman arpt's air traffic area the low fuel light came on. The sma manual says 'select the nearest safe landing area and make a normal lndg.' it goes on to say the engine may run out of fuel within 5 minute(s) i could easily be on the ground in 3 minute(s) at burbank airport and i felt it would take me just as longitude to turn around and land at whiteman airport the engine quit less then a minute(s) after the light came on. I always know where i would land intermediate fix there were a power failure because at 600 above ground level its too late after the engine quits. The last place i looked at was a park to my left/right (directions) the engine stopped and that is where i went. I lost a little airspd getting to the park. The landing was smooth; but not enough revolutions per minute gain to set it down without any damage to the aircraft the damage was hard to see to the untrained eye; but the tail cone did have a dent in it; this takes from the strength of the tail cone and that is why it is now called an accident.the total time of this flight was 1.5 to the best of my knowledge.
output: Heli on training flight has low fuel light activate. Engine according to manual should run 5 minute(s) it quit in 1. Emergency lndg.

input: Acft #1 was inbound to psc at fl310. Traffic in the sectors (47 and 48 combined) was moderate to busy. There was traffic for aircraft #1 in descent aircraft #3 at fl290; opposite direction; and aircraft #2 ebound out of pdx on j16. The aircraft were still quite federal aviation regulation apart and aircraft #1 was issued a pilot's discretion descent to fl240. I think i gave more attention to the opposite direction traffic and missed aircraft #2 as he converged with aircraft #1. There were numerous data blocks in a small area when the conflict alert activated. I immediately issued fl310 back to aircraft #1 and issued fl280 to aircraft #2. Aircraft #2 said he was out of fl290 and had an resolution advisory closest proximitypa was 1700 feet/foot and 3.2 nautical mile there was a developmental certified on the position working my d-side who also failed to recognize the traffic sector 47 and sector 48 are seldom decombined due to a poor design. I think the error was simply a failure to re-evaluate aircraft #2 as traffic on my ensuing scans. Supplemental information from acn 620131: after evaluating the situation my r-side issued a pilot's discretion descent however; due to the nature of a pilot's discretion descent clearance aircraft #2 was still traffic vertically i was performing my functions; coordinating as necessary; and discussing traffic sits with my r-side. We both missed the more immediate traffic supplemental information from acn 620127: the radar controller for whatever reason; didn't recognize aircraft #2 as traffic for aircraft #1. 15 controllers assigned to the shift. 9 controllers on position 1 developmental training. 4 cpc's on break. 1 cpc in training. 2 oj's on duty -- 1 on position in area; 1 in training.
output: Zse controller experienced operational error between fl290 and fl310 with crossing and descending tfc.

input: While on ferry flight from hnl to phx; we encountered a problem with the internal ferry fuel tank system we were between engin and etnic on r577 at 17000'. At engin; we were :18 minute(s) behind flight plan and 1700# of fuel over planned burn off. #3 ferry tank emptied around 995-1000 gals; after only :50 minute(s) of use. Capt recognized a problem due to his past ferry experience. The tank should not have run dry second officer early. We entered our etp airport ito; in the inertial navigation system and agreed it was closest. Aircraft had sufficient fuel in aircraft tanks to make ito and fuel still flowed from ferry tanks 1 and 2. Around n25 latitude w145 longitude calculated fuel and found sufficient amount to make hnl. We landed hnl with 4000# after 10:07 hours of flying. The ferry tank system has only crude sight gauges to determine quantity. Subsequently; we learned that maintenance discovered an improperly installed fuel line in #3 ferry tank. The line apparently crimped; not allowing fuel to xfer. I realize now that we could have made lax; but i ante meridiem glad we were conservative in our decision making.
output: Acr mountain daylight time on transoceanic ferry flight encounters bladder tank problems.

input: Taxiing out to takeoff in my open cockpit biplane (stearman) on an absolutely beautiful day; i gave the engine a complete run-up and looked very carefully for other traffic since there were glider operations(s) in progress. Seeing no one; i proceeded to takeoff on runway(s) 30. However; there are trees that obstruct your vision of the final to runway(s) 2 (grass rwy); and sure enough there was a piper cub on final to that runway(s) i saw him just as we broke ground it was obvious we were going to miss; which we did -- by about 500 feet/foot -- second officer i continued the takeoff it was a very sobering experience; however; in that i was very careful about looking for traffic and still ended up in this situation had i been a few seconds later on my takeoff we would have been a lot closer. I'll not only look next time at this airport i'll watch the x-rwy pattern for several minute(s) to make sure the 'blind spot' holds no surprises!
output: Plt of stearman departing at non tower airport encounters a piper cub departing from a x-rwy. Distance was enough that no evasive action was taken; but close.

input: Aircraft x was a departure level at 16000 feet on a westbound route. Aircraft y was on a southwest bound route. I initially climbed aircraft y  to 15000 feet and issued traffic to both aircraft. Aircraft y reported aircraft x in sight and since they were the only two aircraft in the vicinity and it appeared aircraft y would be crossing behind the path of aircraft x. I instructed aircraft y to maintain visual separation and climb to 23000 feet. I did not clearly understand aircraft y 's read back the first time so i restated and asked for clarification that he would maintain visual separation. He responded that he would. I then told aircraft x that the other traffic had him in sight and would be climbing visually behind him. At the point that i made the decision to apply visual separation rules. The speed and climb rate of aircraft y led me to think that he would be passing behind aircraft x and targets would not merge. Aircraft x then reported that he was responding to an resolution advisory (ra) and was climbing. I then verified again that aircraft y still had the aircraft in sight. Aircraft y responded that he did and i told him that aircraft x was responding to an resolution advisory and climbing now. Aircraft x then stated his concern for an aircraft getting that close to him and aircraft y stated that they weren't that close. I don't think i would leave separation decisions to a general aviation pilot when an airline carrying hundreds of passengers are involved. Although visual separation is a tool to expedite traffic flow in this situation it would have only been a minute delay before the aircraft could continue his climb.
output: Air traffic controller and air taxi captain reported another aircraft had to respond to an resolution advisory and told the controller the climbing aircraft was too close.

input: During cruise; left/right (directions) hydraulic system pressure and quantity dropped. Pressure eventually went to zero. Unable to restore pressure. Left/right (directions) hydraulic system shut down in accordance with chklist. Uneventful dscnt/lndg at bis; nd. Leak in brake line found after lndg.
output: A dc9-50 in cruise at fl310 diverted due to a loss of left/right (directions) hydraulic system pressure and quantity caused by a leaking brake hydraulic line.

input: Refused to operate aircraft with entire overhead panel lights inoperative. Lights would go full bright; dim; and off uncommanded at random intervals. Deemed unacceptable for night flying and totally unsafe for a late night flight to zzz with moderate/heavy rain; low clouds and over 20 kts of crosswinds. Refused at aircraft at gate. I believe the minimum equipment list that maintenance was going to use was not meant for the entire panel being dark.
output: B737-800 captain refused aircraft due to erratic overhead warning lights affecting the entire overhead panel.

input: Cessna assigned runway(s) 35 lined up for runway(s) 36. When recognized by the local controller the cessna attempted to line up on taxiway 'golf.' we have more and more occurrences like these. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated several rpts have been sent to aviation safety reporting system describing the problem at lnk with wrong runway(s) landings. The rptr stated the runway(s) were renumbered about a year ago from 36l and 36r to runway(s) 36 and 35. He said it has not helped and may have made the problem worse. He said they don't have a problem when traffic is landing south he said the tower location is not a problem even with the local controller position facing ne. He said the tower is equipped with bright radar indicator tower equipment radar; but is not much help determining runway(s) alignment. He estimates a wrong runway(s) landing at lnk occurs approximately two or three times a week. Mostly with general aviation aircraft but occasionally with commuter flts. The rptr said a number of suggestions have been rejected to renumber the runway(s) back to 36l and 36r. Also suggested was putting lettering or a large 'x' on the txwys to prevent inadvertent landings on non runway(s) surfaces. He said presently under consideration is a plan to put lead in lights on runway(s) 35.
output: Ctlr at lnk states there appears to be an increase of incidents by pilots using the north parallel runway(s) lining up and landing on txwys or misidentifying the runway(s) assigned.

input: I was cleared to taxi to runway 18 via the west parallel taxiway. Weather was day visual flight rules and there were no other aircraft operating at the airport at the time. While taxiing and accomplishing pre takeoff items; i failed to notice that there was a runway hold short line on the parallel taxiway. I was notified by ground control that i had taxied past the hold short line. The location of the hold short line on the parallel taxiway instead of adjacent to the runway is nonstandard and not depicted or noted on taxi diagrams. Recommend additional signage and notices in the fixed-base operator for the benefit of transient pilots; not to mention a call by ground.
output: Pilot taxied past hold short line without clearance. Reportedly; the hold short line is located unexpectedly distant on a parallel taxiway due to displaced threshold runway configuration. The hold short line is not depicted in airport diagrams.

input: Crew accomplished through flight on aircraft that previously flew same day with no items entered in maintenance logbook. A checked by maintenance was also completed at zzz by maintenance after airborne; first officer noticed engine indicating and crew alerting system computer switch in left/right (directions) computer instead of automatic position upon reposition to automatic position lower engine indicating and crew alerting system was inoperative unless engine indicating and crew alerting system computer switch placed to left/right (directions) computer selection. Sent 'fmr' message; checkeded minimum equipment list which referenced placing standby engine instruments switch to 'on' position and noted applicable contingencies in event of future display failure. Landed at destination without incident; maintenance reset computers; faults cleared recommend to aircrews and maintenance the importance of putting switches back into normal position and or writing up malfunctions second officer that future crews on through flts; etc; do not get stuck with a previously existing problem the through flight philosophy relies; to a large extent; upon checkeding certain items and relying upon most switches and system having previously been set and checkeded  intermediate fix no items entered in logbook; then the crews assume system works ok. It is difficult to detect insidious malfunctions like an engine indicating and crew alerting system computer failure when the other computer is selected and operations(s) normal.
output: A b757 flight crew failed to note that their engine indicating and crew alerting system computer switch was not in the automatic position during their use of the 'through flt' chklist out of mia; fl.

input: On approach into reno; we were cleared for the visual to runway 34l and advised that the localizer was not available. We loaded the area navigation to runway 34l for a backup and i asked the first officer to confirm the altitudes on the approach. They agreed with the 12-3 area navigation (gps) runway 34l altitudes. I followed the vertical navigation descent profile and received a ground proximity warning system 'pull up' warning in the vicinity of febak. The radar altimeter at that point showed about 900 feet/foot we executed a go-around and then got further clearance to land on runway 16r. I was watching the terrain and was aware visually that there was a hill below us as we continued for runway 34l. I am not sure why the ground proximity warning system alert went off; but followed the guidance to execute a missed approach when it did. We advised tower the reason for our go-around. When we landed; they asked that we call them on the telephone. I spoke with the tower controller who wanted to confirm the reason for the go-around was a ground proximity warning system warning and i concurred. Supplemental information from acn 830988: i cannot say why this happened. We were on the vertical navigation path. I would imagine that with the high terrain in the area we may have had a momentary descent rate increase that caused the ground proximity warning system system to activate.
output: A q400 got a ground proximity warning system terrain warning on the area navigation 34l approach to rno. The flight crew executed a go-around per policy and accepted a vector to a south landing.

input: Johnson county executive airport needs a serious revamp of airport markings and runway hold position signage. At night you cannot see their ground taxiway and runway markings. No reflective component is added to the taxiway marking paint. There is very low contrast between runway markings and pavement. Areas have non aeronautical information manual standard hold bars not authorized by federal aviation administration  each runway intersection should have a standard international civil aviation organization runway hold sign (red with white numbers). Perhaps they should also paint red runway hold markers at the hold bars. In any event the yellow lead lines and taxiway markings (especially on the southwest turnoffs of runway 18) need to be repainted with black contrast bars and/or reflective yellow paint --- it is very difficult to figure out taxiway at night. This is a safety of flight issue that should be addressed with johnson county airport operator.
output: C172 instructor reports ojc taxiway markings and signage are inadequate and in need of refurbishment with reflective paint.

input: On may/xa/99 at xa25; our aircraft was being parked in our spot in a very tight and cluttered space at the den airport the space is called the 'horseshoe.' once we came in to the 'shoe' we had to deviate away from the taxiing line to avoid a maintenance truck that was parked at the tail of another aircraft in spot x. When we cleared the truck and moved into spot y under normal marshaller's directions; i noticed our gpu on the left/right (directions) of the lead-in line in its normal position and a air conditioning unit on the left/right (directions) in our parking area. It did not appear to be a factor in parking our aircraft since the marshaller was still leading us in. The aircraft unit is new equipment for us and we did not know at that time it should have been parked out of the airplane's area. When the air conditioning moved out of my view on the left/right (directions) i looked to the marshaller for any abnormal signals. The marshaller gave a normal hand signal to stop. Simultaneously as the capt; the marshaller stopped the aircraft that is when the left/right (directions) propeller hit the corner of the air conditioning unit. At that point the capt shut down the left/right (directions) engine when the propeller went into feather; that is when it did most of the damage. When the plane was shut down and secure; we stepped out to the nose to see intermediate fix we were parked incorrectly. We were parked as standard on the line at the top of the 't.' was told that the aircraft parked in that spot just previous to us was parked 6 feet/foot short of the top of the 't.' intermediate fix we had painted markings for where equipment should be in the parking area or a wing walker when there is equip.
output: Dornier 328 propeller contacts ground cart while under the direction of a marshaller at den.

input: We were holding for a takeoff clearance (off the runway(s) 4r). We were holding for +/-15 minute(s) during this time i alerted the tower (hnl tower 118.1) of our holding position finally we got the clearance 'taxi into position and hold.' the student in the left/right (directions) seat alerted me of an approaching dc10 from +/-2 mile out. After passing the holding line i questioned the clearance the twr's response was 'make 180 degree turn stay clear of the rwy.' i took the plane controls over from the student and executed the clearance the dc10 landed. None of the pilots or flight engineer of the dc10 came over the radio. Holding again for +/- 5 minute(s) a new clearance was issued; 'taxi into position and hold runway(s) 4r.' this time on short final we noticed a caravan 1/4 mile out with a cleared to land on runway(s) 4r. Again i alerted the controller who promptly issued a new clearance 'hold your pos.' +/-7 minute(s) later we received our clearance to take off. At the time of both incidents; heavy traffic incoming as well as outgoing was observed.
output: Hnl tower twice issued clearance onto the active runway(s) with aircraft on short final to an instructional flt.

input: While on arrival descent to ord; air traffic control informed us that ord was changing runways and to slow to slowest practical speed. Last automatic terminal information service showed landing runways at ord as 14r and 22r. Winds were reported to be 200/26g39. New automatic terminal information service showed a change to runways 27l/r and 28; with the same wind. This had to put most landing aircraft beyond their crosswind limits. We asked air traffic control to confirm runways in use at ord. We turned our other radio to monitor tower and heard an aircraft go around attempting to land on 27l. At that point; the captain notified center we would not accept the runways in use due to crosswind. Controller sounded upset and immediately told us to hold at teddy. After that several more aircraft on arrival refused new runway configuration and were also placed in holding. About 15-20 minutes later air traffic control notified everyone new runway was 14r and to let him know if unable. My recommendation is for controllers to get general training on airframe capabilities and limitations. This runway configuration change was unsafe and not appropriate; when it put many aircraft out of crosswind limits. We need to get the controllers back into the cockpits on familiarization flights to have a better understanding of what pilots are experiencing in our air traffic system. This event also cost a lot of airlines fuel and unnecessary delays.
output: Air carrier inbound to ord commented on the runway in use; noting current wind components precluded use of runways; the reporter suggesting both additional controller training regarding aircraft limitations and the start up of the federal air marshal program to enhance controller awareness.

input: On departure from jfk to sju; encountered mod turbulence at 4000 feet/foot speed 220 knot(s) increased speed to 250 knot(s) in terminal control area at 5000 feet/foot turbulence became severe; speed increased to 280 knot(s) which is turbulence speed for lgt aircraft was not informed by departure of turbulence which it seems he knew about. I relayed moderate with occasional severe between 4000 feet/foot to 6000 feet/foot to both jfk departure on 125.7 and zny on 128.3. No mention of turbulence on automatic terminal information service ground tower or departure i advised dispatch and maintenance and logged severe turbulence in logbook. Aircraft appeared normal on climb out. Did not want to fly through turbulence again; continued on to destination no one hurt. All strapped in at time of turb.
output: Flc of lgt in climb out of jfk encountered severe turbulence between 4000 and 6000.

input: Clred by dorval ground (yul) to 'taxi to runway(s) 28 via taxiway a; call tower 119.9 at rwy.' read back 'taxi to runway(s) 28 via taxiway a; tower 119.9.' after some minor confusion regarding the location of taxiway a; we proceeded to runway(s) capt apparently thought we were cleared 'pos and hold' and taxied approximately 150 feet/foot past hold short line. I did not notice that we went past hold short line because: i was busy with pre-tkof checkeds (including extra 'first flight of day' chks). Hold short line is further back than normal; due to oblique angle between taxiway a and 10/20. Therefore we hadn't yet passed what would normally be a standard hold short distance. About the time i switched to tower i noticed that i couldn't see a hold short line in front of us. While querying the capt; tower cleared us for takeoff on runway(s) 28. No conflict occurred between us and any other aircraft on clbout air traffic control asked us to call dorval ground for a phone number for atc.
output: Cl65 capt overshot runway(s) hold line during taxi out. There was no conflict; but tower requested crew to call after landing at dest.

input: Parking the aircraft at the gate in tulsa; i followed the marshaller's instructions and stopped where i was told to stop. Afterwards; it was revealed to me that the jetway had been left in place from an rj departure before our arrival, arrive the marshaller had mistakenly parked me into the parking position for an rj and not a b737. The result was that my left/right (directions) engine had stopped about a foot from the jetway while still running. While securing my personal items; the night supervisor signaled to me to start my auxiliary power unity when it came on line; i simply xferred power secured the left/right (directions) engine and continued to secure the cockpit; thinking that was the way they wanted the aircraft for overnight cleaning; totally unaware of how close the jetway sat to my engine i saw the supervisor below my window; opened it and was told the tug was going to push us back 10 ft! Later; while helping with some wheelchair passenber one of the wheelchair attendants told me she'd never seen an engine that close before! I investigated and discovered what had taken place. I spoke with the night supervisor giving him my perspective while following the marshaller's guidance. Inspection of the engine revealed no damage.
output: B737-300 capt follows parking guidance from marshaller. Since jetway was in wrong location; aircraft stopped with just 1 feet/foot clearance from jetway.

input: I was on an instrument flight rules flight plan; in the clouds; nearing the tha airport. My plane was equipped with an instrument flight rules certified global positioning system system. I had planned the flight carefully (i thought) and had reviewed all necessary information and notams for the flight. I was being handled by memphis center. The controller asked which approach i wanted. Given that the ceiling was reported 2500 broken but variable; and just below the 3300 transition altitude; i told him that i wanted the vor and dme (co-located) 24 approach. He cleared me direct to the tullahoma vor and dme (co-located) (uxm) at 3300 and cleared me for the approach. I had been navigating using the global positioning system system in my plane and continued to use it to go direct to the uxm vor and dme (co-located) i tried tuning in the uxm vor and dme (co-located) on my vor and dme (co-located) receiver; but did not get a good signal. I told air traffic control that i was not receiving the vor and dme (co-located) he told me that he did not have any notams showing that the uxm vor and dme (co-located) was out of service. So i continued to use the global positioning system to navigate to the uxm vor--which is allowed--thinking that since the vor and dme (co-located) was a low powered one that i was just not yet getting a good signal. Another plane behind me asked for the vor and dme (co-located) 24 approach. Then he reported that he was not receiving the uxm vor and dme (co-located) either and asked for a different approach. I began to be concerned; but i knew that i could substitute my instrument flight rules certified global positioning system for an out-of-service vor and dme (co-located) legally; but i could not use it for navigation on the final approach fix. Soon i started getting needle movement on my vor and dme (co-located) receiver; but never a good signal. I don't know what this signal was--perhaps another vor? I continued to navigate to the uxm vor and dme (co-located) using my instrument flight rules certified global positioning system system and broke out of the clouds into visual flight rules conditions just before reaching the uxm vor and dme (co-located) i started to descend visual flight rules turning back toward the airport. While doing this; i reported to air traffic control that i had lost the signal on the uxm vor and dme (co-located) again; but that i was visual flight rules i cancelled instrument flight rules at that time--while visual flight rules and before having to navigate the final approach course for the uxm vor.as it turns out; the uxm vor and dme (co-located) had been notamed out of service (ots) and i had missed this notice to airmen / of air missions in the dozens that had to be reviewed. Air traffic control apparently also missed it; because the controller told me that he did not have any notams for the uxm vor and dme (co-located) the other plane behind me also missed the notice to airmen / of air missions because he also asked for the vor and dme (co-located) 24 approach using the uxm vor and dme (co-located) so two pilots and one controller did not know that the uxm vor and dme (co-located) has been notamed ots.certainly; i should have been more careful in my review of the notams. Having said that the notice to airmen / of air missions system is badly broken and the federal aviation administration is working on fixing it. As it stands now; pilots and controllers are supposed to review pages and pages of notams many of which are basically un-readable. Nonetheless; i should have seen the notice to airmen / of air missions and requested a different approach. I will be more careful in the future.i do not believe that any violation of the fars occurred. I was navigating the approach transition to the uxm vor and dme (co-located) using an instrument flight rules certified global positioning system system and broke out into visual flight rules conditions without using that system to navigate the final approach course. Having said that; missing the notice to airmen / of air missions was sloppy at best. But two pilots and the controller not knowing about the notice to airmen / of air missions testifies to problems with the notice to airmen / of air missions system as it is today.
output: An bonanza 36 pilot reported flying a vor and dme (co-located) approach using a notamed out of service vor and dme (co-located) reporter cited the poor formatting and presentation of notams as contributory.

input: Shortly after takeoff from seoul; runway(s) 32r; our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii system issued a 'ra' requiring us to stop our initial climb and subsequently avoided a collision with a military twin engine turboprop (king air 200 or similar). The airport automatic terminal information service rpted 35 scattered; 10 knot(s) visibility; 240/08 knot(s) 29.81 inches. I was the acting first officer and we had received a clearance from sel departure direct shrimp intersection and were climbing through approximately 13000 feet/foot to fl330 at en route climb speed we were in visual flight rules conditions and the initial 'tfc' warning showed the traffic 2600 feet/foot above us and distance decreasing. The capt was flying and disengaged the autoplt immediately and followed the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii advisory; pushing the nose over; stopping our climb i did visually spot the traffic at my 11 o'clock; moving to my 3 o'clock position and verbally informed the capt while maintaining visual contact. In addition i radioed sel departure and announced our actions and traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii 'ra.' sel departure would not reply or acknowledge the conflict. The conflicting traffic passed above us within 500- 700 feet/foot altitude at an altitude of approximately 14000-16000 feet/foot we did not deviate from our clearance at any time and once we were visually clear we continued our normal climb to cruise altitude the maneuver did not cause any disturbance to our service or passenber i feel that sel departure neglected to issue a traffic advisory and i do not know why they would not acknowledge the 'conflict.' i also feel that the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii system worked exceptionally well and averted a collision. Conflicting aircraft above; seemed to be in level flight and never realized conflict.
