output: Tcasii resolution advisory saves 747-400 from mid-air in foreign airspace.

input: There were several inactions that light emitting diode to my visual flight rules flight ending with a landing in ground fog at abilene regional airport at xa30 ante meridiem dec/xx/94. The first mistake was that our departure time was extended past the time for which my weather briefing at xc15 post meridiem dec/xx/94 (zfw) was valid. I only took into account the clearing trend; and not the ground fog which would develop as the nighttime temperatures lowered; and failed to call weather before we left arlington municipal at xx15 ante meridiem my second inaction occurred inflt. I didn't call for a weather update for abilene; nor did i listen to automatic terminal information service my first knowledge of abilene being instrument flight rules because of low ground fog came 30 mile out when i called approach control my third mistake was that i failed to request special visual flight rules clearance from approach instead; i simply asked to fly over the airport to see intermediate fix i could see the end of the runway(s) i was cleared for such actions; but apparently because the approach controller thought i might have a fuel situation i rpted i thought i had between 30 minute(s) and 1 hour of reserve. (once on the ground i calculated i had an hour and 10 minute(s) of reserve.) while; i never declared a fuel emergency my underestimation of fuel reserve caused the controller to declare the situation an incident. I did not know this until i called tower after we were down. Had i simply asked for special visual flight rules clearance the same outcome (a good lndg) would have occurred without the situation becoming an incident. I was able to see the end of the runway(s) asked for clearance to land; was given it and proceeded to land. I now know the importance of always calling weather regardless of how favorable the weather seems. I also know to listen to automatic terminal information service and get inflt weather rpts. Finally; i have already arranged recurrent training with my instructor in the area of special visual flight rules clrncs in arsa's. I have definitely learned an important lesson; 1 which will change my flying procedures for the better.
output: Pvt pilot of an sma sel landed below airport visual flight rules weather minimums.

input: Controller gave us descent to 7;000 from 13;000. I was in area of thunderstorms with moderate turbulence. Started descent mode in autopilot vs mode; hit severe updraft; autopilot disconnected; airplane gained altitude at a great rate. As i gained control of aircraft i had climbed 1;800 feet. Severe turbulence; moderate rain; night time conditions.
output: Beech jet captain reported large gain of altitude in descent from severe updraft in the vicinity of thunderstorms.

input: I was capt on an federal aviation regulation part 135 flight due to weather concerns; i had filed instrument flight rules with intentions of being vectored south then north the weather concerns were noted on our flight plan under 'remarks.' we receive the usual area routing instead. Approaching zzz1 from the east air traffic control advised that approach was no longer accepting traffic into the area. We chose to divert to zzz2. Once on our way there; air traffic control said traffic was now being accepted and asked intermediate fix we wanted to continue to destination i asked about any ride rpts and was told a dash 8 rpted moderate turbulence when he went through the area of weather along our route atc's tone of voice made it seem like it was no problem now and we decided to accept the offer to continue to our original destination once established again; we saw a solid line of weather just to our left/right (directions) we couldn't paint ground through it with our weather radar. Very soon after this; the turbulence increased to constant moderate to occasionally severe; with objects being lifted out of place and tossed about. Air traffic control then issued a heading that would take us directly into the heaviest weather we couldn't paint through. I refused citing the weather we were experiencing. Air traffic control became adamant to the point we had to declare an emergency due to weather we advised we were flying our own headings from that point to avoid the severe weather we were able to land safely at destination after landing we looked at weather radar for the area and found 'meso' activity in the area we were flying in. It seems the air traffic control routings are too rigid in the ne. I believe this situation would have been avoided intermediate fix we had been issued our filed routing. Also; air traffic control needs to be more helpful avoiding severe weather since our weather radar is quite limited in what it sees. We don't have the ground based nexrad that air traffic control should have access to.
output: Be20 described weather encounter in zzz airspace at various alts.

input: I was the first officer on flight on sep/thu/91. This was a scheduled passenber flight operating from tokyo (nrt) to jfk. This was a 4 engine wdb. I was receiving my initial operating experience (ioe) and was programmed to fly this leg. As we approached runway(s) 34 i was taxiing the aircraft the second officer rpted the door warning light for door 3r had come on. We had the same experience 4 days earlier departing jfk in the same aircraft the capt had sent the relief pilot down to checked the door. He moved the handle and the light had gone out. We proceeded with no further occurrence. The capt again dispatched the relief pilot to checked the door. Shortly thereafter; we were cleared into position at about the same time the second officer announced that the door light had gone out. Either the second officer or the capt (i was monitoring air traffic control and was not in the conversational loop) called down to 3r and told the relief pilot to take a seat in the cabin that we would be cleared for takeoff momentarily. We were then cleared to go and we began the roll. At approximately 100 knot(s) someone called out that the light had come on again. The capt took control of the aircraft and announced that he was aborting the takeoff by this time we had accelerated to approximately 120 knot(s) we were still well within the first half of the runway(s) the capt applied idle reverse and moderate braking. The aircraft began decelerating normally and was obvious we could easily stop on the remaining runway(s) with no additional braking or reverse. The capt applied a bit more reverse; activating the automatic brake system to maximum braking. This caused a very rapid uncomfortable deceleration for several seconds until the capt disarmed the system a turnoff the runway(s) was made and we began taxiing north at this time we received a call in the cockpit that the slide for 3r had deployed after we turned off the runway(s) the capt ordered the #3 engine shutdown and an assessment of our ability to continue taxiing. It was determined that we could second officer we continued to a remote spot. We warned the ground personnel of our hot brakes and the nose wheel was chocked. The brake temperature continued to climb and 9 of the fuse plugs melted and the tires deflated. My conclusions after reviewing the above events are that we need more information on the overwing doors and their relationship to operations(s) with heavy fuel loads. I have been a wdb second officer and first officer and did not know of any prohibition against operating the door with heavy fuel loads. I also think the application of maximum braking when not needed causes more problems than it solves.
output: Tkof aborted as door warning light illuminates on takeoff roll.

input: On departure from phl runway(s) 27l; we were cleared to 5000'. We were then cleared to climb higher and out of 2000'; proceed direct mxe. As we approached level at 12000'; f/o told zny we were passing 11500' for 12000'; when controller questioned our clearance controller said there was no conflict; but we were supposed to be at 10000'.
output: Acr lgt altitude deviation overshot during climb.

input: Cruise phase of flight. 45;000 feet experienced clear air turbulence. Aircraft began to pitch and roll uncontrollably. Airspeed fluctuations +/- 10-20 knots. Loss of altitude was approximately 800 feet. Regained positive control of aircraft after reaching 44;200 feet. No passengers were on board; no damage to aircraft was done. Air traffic control was immediately notified of occurrence and was issued a descent to 41;000 feet. Incident lasted approximately 15 seconds.
output: Lj31 flight crew reported encountering clear air turbulence and loss of aircraft control at fl450 with an altitude loss of 800 feet.

input: While en-route on a visual flight rules flight plan with flight following from approach i noticed a persistent fuel smell in the cockpit. I told them i had a fuel smell in the cockpit and wanted to know the closest airport with arff and then did divert to that airport. Air traffic control asked if i wanted to declare an emergency and i said yes because now i saw liquid dripping from behind the co-pilot's instrument panel. Air traffic control provided me vectors and the automatic terminal information service at the airport even though the flight was in visual meteorological conditions conditions. After reviewing the emergency procedures i decided to make a normal landing and to the ramp rather than evacuate on the runway. Upon landing arff equipment followed me to the ramp as a precaution. I shut down and deplaned the passengers without further incident.
output: A pa31 pilot diverted under emergency conditions to the nearest suitable airport due to gas fumes and liquid leaks behind the instrument panel.

input: While flying nw at approximately 700 feet/foot above ground level the da40 crossed our path; left/right (directions) to left/right (directions) approximately 30 feet/foot ahead; and 5 feet/foot below the main rotor of the helicopter i believe the wings of the aircraft may have even passed below the main rotor. The da40 was in a blind spot on the helicopter (behind the l-hand door frame) and could not be seen until it passed. I didn't have time to take any evasive action. The da40 passed too quickly. There were several factors which contributed to this near miss. 1) we were crossing the final approach path for runway(s) 4 at zzz however we were 4 mile away and below traffic pattern altitude (tpa). Although we were scanning for traffic we could not see the da40 as it was in a blind spot. 2) the da40 was not talking on the correct frequency for zzz. After confronting the other pilot i discovered he was making radio calls on the arpt's old common traffic advisory frequency frequency (currently it is up-to-date on charts and the airport facilities directory.) 3) the da40 was not above tpa prior to entry as the aeronautical information manual suggests. Further; the da40 did not fly a traffic pattern; he landed straight in. 4) upon confronting the da40 pilot he clrly demonstrated 2 of the hazardous attitudes listed in multiple federal aviation administration pubs: macho and invulnerability. I believe the only way to prevent this type of incident from happening again would be for the da40 pilot to receive remedial training on airport traffic pattern operations(s) and the importance of using an up-to-date chart and airport facilities directory for preflt planning.
output: Helicopter pilot reports near midair collision at 700 feet above ground level with da40 flying straight in visual to zzz.

input: [this was a] skydiving flight; fuel exhaustion on final approach to land. Pattern and approaches are always done very high; so some of the flaps were retracted; and a gliding landing was easily made. Fueling was done for these 3 skydiving flights after flying the airplane from the home airport to the airport where the skydiving took place. Fuel was checked in both tanks before leaving the home airport; and i mentally noted that one tank contained more fuel than the other; and that i had plenty of fuel to fly to the skydiving airport; and would get fuel there even if i did not fly skydivers. I think the reason this happened is that i forgot which of the tanks had the greater amount of fuel when checking fuel at the home airport. I therefore filled the tank that was already the most full; and did not have the reserve in the other tank as expected; because i did not specifically check it after filling the other tank. This also might have never been noticed if i had not used a steep bank from base to final. There is a large amount of unusable fuel in early model c182's; especially if steep banks are performed at lower fuel levels.
output: A c182 engine quit on final approach from fuel starvation after the pilot flew three skydiving flight and forgot that the selected tank did not have sufficient reserve fuel after using the other wing's full tank.

input: The city of cleveland is in the process of moving a very large pile of dirt that was in the path of the new runway(s) that is currently under construction. They are relocating this pile to a location that; i believe; may create a safety hazard. It is being moved to a point approximately 1/2 mile off the approach end of runway(s) 6r. The northern end of the pile is almost directly on the ctrline of the runway(s) i would estimate the pile to be 50 feet/foot high and growing. I believe this new location creates a safety hazard for aircraft departing runway(s) 24l that may experience an engine failure. At the very least this new obstacle should be taken into account by our runway(s) analysis. Also; runway(s) 6r is a clear air turbulence iii runway(s) and this new obstacle may impact the minimums for that rwy's low visibility approachs it is my belief that the best solution would be to remove this dirt to a new location much farther from the runway(s) ctrline. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information this dirt pile had been moved from a lateral position as referenced to the runway(s) to a more aligned position second officer as to accommodate the construction of a new parallel runway(s) to the se at cle. Rptr was just in cle and stated that the growth has stopped but the pile has been hydro-seeded for grass. Pilot stated that at 200 feet/foot above ground level there was about 150 feet/foot clearance pile being about 50 feet/foot high. The pile is lined up just to the edge of the runway(s) not extending to the ctrline. The seeding indicates that no movement of the dirt is planned in the near future. This situation has been brought up in the recent airline/faa review panel meeting; second officer it is being looked at officially.
output: A potential hazard to aircraft rpted by a b737-400 first officer a 50 feet/foot high pile of dirt exists 1/2 mile off the end of runway(s) 6r at cle; oh.

input: In sum: rptr received an instrument flight rules clearance after a normal briefing with a void time before the lgb tower opened for the day. Preparations were made for an on-time departure but there was a question as to whether or not the radios were working correctly. It was close to tower opening time and rptr made several nonstandard calls; which were not answered. He then planned to take off on time; make a call to departure control and intermediate fix not successful; return and land visual flight rules takeoff was successful; contact made and flight proceeded normally. Later a request was made to contact lgb tower to explain takeoff on a closed runway(s) no notice of the runway(s) closure was found in the duats briefing or with the flight service station specialist briefer. Problems of concern to the rptr are: 1) the lack of notice from any source about the runway(s) closure. 2) his lack of improper radio xmissions when the tower was closed and he should have been using common traffic advisory frequency calls. Tower said they would have answered a common traffic advisory frequency call indicating a takeoff on the closed runway(s) 3) the tendency for pilots to rush when trying to make clearance void times.
output: Plt takes off on closed runway(s) at lgb before tower is open.

input: Visual approach to runway 25l at las. Visual meteorological conditions conditions clam winds; 10+ statute mile visibility; clear skies. Was being rv by las approach on downwind to a visual approach to 25l. Was turning base to final when the ground proximity warning system alert came on. I was approximately 4;600 feet in a slight descent when the ground proximity warning system went off only once. I stopped the descent and started a climb to 4;700 feet. The terrain and tower was in sight and on the right side of a/c. I called out to the non flying pilot that i had the terrain and tower in sight and that it was definitely below and to the right of us. The ground proximity warning system alert stopped once i leveled off. The ground proximity warning system only sounded/alerted once. After i was sure that we were clear of any more alerts i continued my visual approach to 25l with a stable approach and landing. I believe with the aircraft in a turn/bank angle that the radio altimeter was picking up the side of the hill which is located due south of relin (faf). Aircraft was being hand flown. Speed 170 and flaps 20. Speed bug was set to 160 and aircraft was decelerating to 160 knot(s) and approach mode was armed. Aircraft was about 200-300 vsi down in a descent and 4;500 feet was set in the altitude window. Verify that just because air traffic control is giving you decent clearances/step downs while being radar vectored that the altitudes that they are descending you too is at or above the mva/ minimum safe altitude if unsure; then level off and question air traffic control i am very familiar with las and its surrounding terrain and i knew/saw all the terrain while being radar vectored but will request to fly the area navigation arrival to avoid unnecessary ground proximity warning system alerts. It is very common to get rv from skebr to runway 25l while arriving at las in the evening. They step you down while also giving heading instructions until you except the visual approach.
output: B767 captain experiences a terrain warning during a visual approach to runway 25l from the south in night visual meteorological conditions a slight climb was initiated as the radio tower that caused the alert was in sight below and to the right.

input: Atc facility: socal. Location: 20-30 mile east of kayoh on e- side arrival, arrive capt flying at 220 knot(s) air traffic control asked us to increase to 250 knot(s) i read back clearance capt kept 220 knot(s) air traffic control asked intermediate fix we were increasing. Thinking we would; i said increasing through 220 knot(s) capt maintained 220 knot(s) atc's 3rd call; capt said he'd have to slow at kayoh. Air traffic control said for now need 250 knot(s) capt stayed at 220 knot(s) air traffic control asked speed capt said say 240 knot(s) kept 220 knot(s) air traffic control said aircraft back at 210 knot(s) 10 knot(s) less ground speed obviously angry he advised us of our obligation to comply with clearance aircraft behind us turned to 180 degrees and 260 knot(s) for space. Next frequency 121.3 cleared instrument landing system runway(s) 19r. Instead of following lateral navigation command bars; armed localizer at localizer alive; went through localizer assigned heading 165 to reintercept localizer whole thing illegal. I do not like being unnecessarily exposed to possible federal aviation administration violation; nor do i appreciate being expected to bend the truth. Reason capt gave for maintaining 220 knot(s) was that air traffic control needed to learn not to fly our airplanes for us.
output: Fo rpt on failure of air carrier pilot in command to follow air traffic control request for speed increase on arrival, arrive traffic speed dev.

input: There has been a 'frequency problem' for 17+ years. The pilots are hearing a loud hum on 120.45. Center does not hear any hum. From 1700z through 1800z you can here numerous aircraft complain about what sounds like a stuck mic.
output: Zob controller voiced concern regarding a long standing frequency interference problem; the anomaly reportedly only occurs in the 1700z to 1800z time frame.

input: Was on break as relief pilot position was called to the cockpit at xa30z. Informed of pending serious condition of loss of oil quantity. Oil quantity was zero when i arrived in cockpit. I was tasked to call dispatch desk on comrdo. Capt and first officer were in process of declaring an emergency and exiting the atlantic track to divert to bicc. As i called dispatch; capt and first officer were very concerned about the zero oil quantity on #2 engine status messages were displayed; but no engine indicating and crew alerting system message was received. With oil pressure starting to decrease below 80 psi; capt and first officer elected to shut down #2 engine i concurred; of course. I coordinated our divert with dispatch. He alerted bicc and set us up with weather crash fire rescue equipment etc. My next task was to run the 1-eng drift-down chklist in the quick reference handbook we descended to fl210. Engine failure chklist also run. Still no chklist direction was displayed through the engine indicating and crew alerting system system next; we coordinated with iceland control via high frequency then shortly thereafter on very high frequency this was about 290 nautical mile sw bicc. Radar contact was received and we were cleared to bicc to eventually intercept the runway(s) 2 instrument landing system we began fuel dumping about 200 nautical mile from the field; dumped down to maximum landing weight we ceased dumping at about 10000 feet/foot and 25 mile from the field. Capt performed an excellent approach and landing at xb40z. First officer did a super job analyzing the problem and coordinating our departure from the track. Everything seemed to work as planned. One sys's note is that we never received an engine indicating and crew alerting system message which stepped us through the engine shutdown procedure and follow-on events. We manually recalled the appropriate electronic chklists. The bicc operations(s) personnel did a super job helping us on the ground no adverse items to rpt. Intermediate fix anything; we almost had too much help at first after we declared mayday. Too many folks were on the radio offering assistance. Supplemental information from acn 617555: decided to divert to bicc which was nearest alternate. Started shallow descent while turning off the track. Accomplished all appropriate chklists; including emergency landing chklist. Flew for approximately 1 hour on single eng.
output: Inflt engine shutdown when a b777 flight has to shut down #2 engine with zero oil pressure while on an extended overwater operations(s) 390 nautical mile sw of; and diverting to; bikf; fo.

input: Was told to descend to 4000 feet/foot was slow descent during time conversation with passenber unknowingly descended to 3500 ft.
output: Plt of sma on instrument flight rules flight plan is cleared to descend to 4000 feet/foot he descends to 3500 ft.

input: Received the automatic terminal information service at iad with the following notice to airmen / of air missions taxiway whiskey closed between whiskey one and whiskey ten. A review of the airport diagram 10-9; dated 10/xx/89; was made and whiskey ten could not be located. Since we were landing on runway(s) 1l; we asked the approach control the location of whiskey ten. input: On instrument landing system approach to runway(s) 8r at phx; localizer became unreliable with localizer light on instrument comparator. Since we had ground contact and airport in sight; continued approach checkeded identify on 108.3 and heard frequency modulation radio station. Mechanic said this is normal on rainy days. Mechanic said at least 5 aircraft had same problem in past 2 days. Interference from local frequency modulation station should be investigated.
output: Loc on instrument landing system runway(s) 8 at phx allegedly erratic.

input: We were cleared direct to the airport for runway(s) 8l. Approach called visual flight rules traffic below us which we cleared about 6 nautical mile east of the field. Although we had a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory i acquired the traffic visually and the first officer minimized the response to the resolution advisory by reducing the descent rate down to 6000 feet/foot our assigned altitude approach then cleared us to enter downwind north of the airport for runway(s) 8l. We then had a progression from a traffic advisory to resolution advisory for traffic above us. While searching for the traffic the altitude alert sounded; indicating that we were 400-500 feet/foot below assigned altitude my reaction was to advance the throttles and pick the nose up to return to 6000 feet/foot this was reinforced by approach calling and asking us to checked our altitude assigned 6000 feet/foot it wasn't until the resolution advisory increased in intensity that i pulled the throttles back and pushed the nose back over and directed the first officer to resume the proper response to the resolution advisory i immediately advised approach of our altitude deviation due to the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory approach advised us that the visual flight rules traffic had allowable vertical separation on us and was puzzled by the resolution advisory our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii gave us. We were then cleared for the visual approach runway(s) 8l; maintain 4000 feet/foot until on base; 3000 feet/foot until on final. We received 3 more ra's from different aircraft in the vicinity by the time we rolled out on final. Second officer with the 5 ra's and several (i lost track) ta's; there was more than enough confusion for 1 approach the first officer did a good solid job of flying and responding per the company's procedures i felt like i did more reacting than planning on my part. I ante meridiem concerned that my reflex action to initiate a climb back to 6000 feet/foot was contrary to ra's directive. The multiple ra's and ta's point up a significant problem the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii parameters for an resolution advisory are still too broad; especially in the traffic pattern. I spoke to the approach control supervisor who had been looking over the controller's shoulder during our approach he said all the visual flight rules targets had adequate separation for the controller's sequencing. He said a more prompt call announcing the deviation from assigned altitude would have prevented the controller's query about the altitude deviation i agreed. Cockpit communicationss between the first officer and myself had been good throughout the 3 days we had been flying together. The conversation got brief during the approach due to all the distrs. We had a chance to debrief the approach at length. The 1 real improvement we came up with to our coordination in the cockpit is the need to verbally state intentions to respond to an resolution advisory i agree that responding to an resolution advisory should be self-explanatory; but in this case; we had just cleared traffic below us when a new traffic advisory to resolution advisory sounded for traffic above us. I was still watching traffic passing behind us; while the first officer was reacting to traffic ahead. The first officer was ahead; i was behind and it took a moment to get back to the same point.
output: Mlg crew responds contrary to traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory instructions.

input: Departing teb on runway(s) 24 standard instrument departure first altitude was set to 1500 feet/foot per standard instrument departure sid calls for a climb to 2000 feet/foot at 4.5 vor and dme (co-located) after takeoff first call to departure controller was 'off teb; climbing to 2000 feet/foot on the teb 5.' controller asked for confirmation that we were climbing to 1500 feet/foot answer was affirmative. Controller asked intermediate fix we knew when to climb to 2000 feet/foot response was 'at 4.5 dme.' controller answered 'that's correct.' aircraft following ours checkeded in the same way; controller seemed annoyed and responded; 'you're the second one to checked in this way.'
output: A da50 (falcon 50) departing teb contacted terminal radar approach control facility with clearance to 2000 feet/foot and was questioned about his 1500 feet/foot restr.

input: On arrival; phx was experiencing wind-shear and microburst activity and a dust storm was approaching. On visual approach to runway 7r at phx wind-shear and microburst alerts were activating; pireps were reporting 20 knot loss of airspeed on final. Elected not to descend at the vdp; fly straight through initial and avoid wind-shear conditions. Weather conditions remained over phx airport and continued to degrade in the surrounding area. After 20 minutes of vectoring informed phx approach control that we will be reaching a fuel critical / emergency fuel state if not on the ground by then. Flight crew was coordinating with phx tower and approach control; company dispatcher; phx ramp control; to find the safest place to land. Exercising captains authority i decided to land zzz; [a nearby airport]. The landing was uneventful; ground support met us and we shut down; and the fuel system indicted total 10;800 pounds (200 pounds below our emergency fuel amount). The aircraft was serviced and after the severe weather was no longer a threat we took off and flew to phx. All agencies were coordinated with during this evolution and duty officer kept apprised of the situation and solicited for advice. Kudos to phx approach controllers; ground services at zzz and my first officer; who's new to the company and been on the line for 4months; all did a great job! Emergency was not declared; as soon a decision was made expeditious traffic handling got us over zzz in just moments. Weather forecasted other then what was actually encountered upon arrival. Give us more fuel! Closer monitoring of weather while enroute to destination.
output: Widebody captain reported encountering un-forecast windshear and microburst activity upon arrival at phx. After 20 minutes of vectoring the crew elected to divert; landing with 10;800 pounds of fuel.

input: While attempting to land at golden triangle airport i narrowly avoided landing gear up. Without the vigilance of the tower controller in warning me i ante meridiem certain i would have.
output: Iar sa barsov 823 pilot executes a go around due to landing gear in the up position at gtr.

input: During departure we received vectors over the north side of the ocean which was in the opposite direction of our filed route. These vectors and the resulting route change resulted in a significantly longer route than originally planned for. This new un-planned routing around weather resulted in the necessity to divert for fuel; due to no available alternate that would allow us to go to our planned destination then to our alternate and still land with 45 minutes of fuel. We confirmed with dispatch over automatic communications addressing & reporting system and due to the need to actually discuss the situation at xa:36z we used commercial radio for a phone patch to get a better idea of the weather situation. At xa:45z we declared a fuel emergency due to not being able to complete the flight as planned and the miscommunication with air traffic control we were very close to another airport and we had a window of opportunity with the weather that allowed a normal descent; and the other airport would also be in the clear shortly after we diverted allowed for a mostly visual flight rules flight to our planned destination once the severe storms passed over the field. At xa:50z we changed our destination to the other airport.the biggest threat with this flight was air traffic control taking us over a completely different route than our clearance! The filed route provided us with a 'hole in the weather' that would have allowed us to complete the flight without anything more than minor weather deviations typical of instrument flight rules flight in the summer. What happened after departure was a complete lack of communication from air traffic control as why they took us south and almost to the maximum 50 nautical mile from land. I felt that they sent us over the gulf route for traffic purposes that did not have anything to do with weather avoidance. There was no notification that they were going to [have us] deviate from our filed and cleared route while we were on the ground.now knowing that air traffic control completely deviating from the route we received is more a possibility i will be more inquisitive on the ground as to there intentions before the wheels are off the ground. I felt that during this flight air traffic control was always just trying to pass us on to the next controller and most likely should not have allowed us to take off if they couldn't handle our flight with the flights that were already in the air. This flight was planned very tight on fuel with the load we had. If we had received the longer route from air traffic control on the ground we could have very easily increased fuel to accommodate and avoid the diversion.
output: An emb-145 captain believed atc's failure to route them via their filed and cleared route resulted in the need to stop for fuel in order to remain legal to complete their planned flight.

input: I completed the air carrier provided phase 2 federal aviation administration approved training and determined i was not adequately trained to carry out my duties per the fars as the pilot in command of my aircraft fleet. I asked my flight management for additional training and they refused my request so i am left with no alternative but to remove myself from flight duties. I simply do not feel proficient enough to carry out my duties and responsibilities having read a draft copy of a revised flight manual that is riddled with numerous errors; a cbt program that directs you to changes that can be found in this manual and a program that lists profile maneuver and standard operating procedure changes but doesn't afford you an opportunity to practice or perform these changes. The sheer volume of changes is too much to absorb thru reading or cbt lesson that lists many changes as 'additions.' i am left with tremendous pressure to find a way to support my family; but i will not waiver in my belief in the extraordinary responsibility i have for the safety of my crew and my passengers. I will not return to the flight deck until i receive adequate training. How this training ever got by our point of interest is a mystery.
output: A b767 captain removed herself from flight status because the company's transition training was not structured to allow a pilot sufficient training in numerous new and modified operational procedures.

input: Atis gave visibility at 1 mile at iad; overheard runway visual range 3000 feet/foot on runway(s) 12. We were cleared for approach runway(s) 1r. Elected to perform autoland due to fog and light snow. After passing alert ht with everything indicating normal i looked outside and saw the approach lights. It took a few seconds but i realized we were headed for the approach lights. I disconnected the autoplt; flew it back to the glideslope and made a normal landing i then realized the 'too low; gs' aural had sounded and missed approach was warranted but my entire focus was on not landing in the approach lights and did not realize what the noise was about until after landing the mystery is why the approach was second officer low in second officer short of time when everything looked good.
output: Acr descent below glideslope while on coupled approach for autoland.

input: The rides had been bad and several aircraft had been asking for ride reports and i was spacing for the class b airport. An e170 was eastbound at fl350 and requesting fl330 because of the bad rides. The e170 was in sector x's airspace and i had just given sector x the first of two northbound arrivals at fl340. In the next couple of minutes i was distracted by a situation in the southern part of my sector. When i scanned back to the north; the e170 had entered my airspace and the first arrival northbound was in sector x. I gave the e170 a clearance for lower and conflict alert went of with an e145; the second arrival at fl340. I turned e170 20 degrees left to add more space between them. There was no loss of separation but it felt like a safety issue to me because they were closer than i usually let airplanes get and i had just been dealing with the other situation in the sector. I need to take a moment to refocus after some kind of distraction. When pilots are trying to get out of bad rides; it adds a sense of urgency to get them out of it as quickly as possible. If i would have taken just a moment to scan my entire sector again i would have made another evaluation at the traffic situation with the e145; and probably waited two minutes before descending e170.
output: Distracted by attempts to resolve 'bad ride' reports; an enroute controller experienced a near separation loss.

input: While departing from hmt runway 23; my student noticed an unmanned aircraft; that appeared to be a recreational use radio controlled aircraft operating in the area about 1.7 miles southwest of hmt. There appeared to be a miniaturized runway constructed of concrete on the ground with multiple radio controlled aircraft on the ground. The unmanned aircraft system appeared to be operating about 100 feet below us; and about 2000 feet laterally to our left. This would put the aircraft at about 500-600 feet above ground level the aircraft did not pose an immediate threat to us; however the aircraft and the field it appeared to be operating from are located in the flight path normally used by pilots performing a 45 degree entry to the left downwind of runway 23. There were no notices on the airport automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) or over any other frequencies.
output: Pa28 instructor pilot reported that a miniature airport for model aircraft is located 1.7 nautical mile sw of the hmt airport and one of the aircraft came in conflict with them nearby the radio controlled strip.

input: Boston weather was low and but still technically visual meteorological conditions as noted; and they were using instrument approaches to get into the airport. Given the wind they were landing runway 4r with the glideslope out of service thus utilizing the localizer 4r approach. The first officer was the pilot flying and elected to fly the localizer approach using the non-precision procedure commonly referred to as 'dive and drive.' everything was briefed and proceeding normally with a clearance to land when; after the final approach fix; kbos tower queried us by stating the altimeter setting and asking our altitude. We were previously cleared for the localizer approach and thus descending to minimum descent altitude after the final approach fix. Minimum descent altitude is 440 feet and we were descending through 620 feet at the time of the radio call. The pilot flying had seen the airport visually at this point and said so out loud. I looked out to see the field after having called back tower to give them our altitude as 'through 620 feet' and then i looked back at the instruments and the aircraft was still descending. I brought this to the attention of the pilot flying and a correction was made and at the same time the egpws announced 'too low terrain' as well as air traffic control asking our altitude again and telling us they had a low altitude alert on us. The aircraft position was corrected and a normal landing made.the weather in boston was a little squally and visibility was variable in flight so we didn't get the field in sight when we expected to see the runway but we still flew the approach according to procedures. The query by boston tower at 200 feet above minimum descent altitude and descending was a major distraction at a critical time; we had the altimeter setting and were on profile for the non-precision approach but asking a question like that causes a crew to recheck everything at a time when they should be focused on leveling at minimum descent altitude and watching for the vdp. I believe this question from tower caused to pilot flying to look outside where the field was sighted and then to remain outside visually. Because we had the runway in sight and the weather was visual meteorological conditions the slight deviation below a normal altitude was more of an anomaly than anything else but in the wrong weather it could have been a big deal.during periods of inclement weather; although technically visual meteorological conditions if air traffic control is utilizing non-precision approach procedures they should not be surprised to see aircraft flying these procedures as published. I believe actual weather on the approach was worse than reported and we needed to get to near the minimum descent altitude and fly to the vdp to see the runway; asking us a question that can cause second guessing at such a critical time of flight is an dangerous distraction at a time when it is least needed.
output: Bos tower called an air carrier crew near the localizer runway 4r minimum descent altitude causing a distraction. While trouble shooting the crew descended below the approach path and got an egpws warning.

input: The automated radar terminal systems 2e was losing all tracks on one sweep and retagging most of the targets on the next few sweeps. This situation occurred numerous times over a 30 minute(s) period. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr revealed that the problem has been resolved.
output: Rptr states the p31 automated radar terminal systems 2e was losing targets intermittently for a period of time.

input: Dep briefed for runway(s) 31c; mdw; with attention to standard instrument departure instruction to complete assigned turn within 4 nautical mile of mdw loc/dme. First officer who was flying on his first takeoff of 2-day trip sequence; acknowledged standard instrument departure restrs. (this is an experienced first officer though not personally known to capt; who was on his first trip following requalification after medical leave.) after gear retraction; first officer was late calling for flap retraction; and did not initiate left/right (directions) turn to 100 degrees as assigned. Capt reminded; 'begin your turn.' first officer initiated gradual bank. Capt reminded; 'flaps;' which were retracted. Capt reminded; 'increase turn.' controller asked us to increase rate of turn and said; 'you are outside the sid.' first officer appeared to be disoriented or confused: airspd increased above 250 knot(s) altitude increased to nearly 3200 feet/foot before capt could push yoke forward to reduce pitch. First officer did not call for climb power second officer capt disconnected autothrottle while pushing nose down and reducing thrust. Aircraft returned to standard instrument departure profile and control was returned to first officer for climb on vector. This episode has me wondering just how much leeway a capt may give a first officer before intervening in aircraft control this is a 'tight' standard instrument departure with an error imminent with the slightest failure to follow standard instrument departure procedures or aircraft handling techniques. I did not expect this from an experienced coplt. In reviewing this situation i'm not sure that i could have prevented these exceedences without having simply flown the departure myself.
output: A b737-200 first officer fails to follow the profile of the standard instrument departure from mdw and enters the class b airspace of ord during a slow rate of turn and an altitude overshoot event north of mdw; il.

input: While in cruise flight imc/oat=(-20) experienced an icing event (rate-severe; accumulation-moderate) in which the airplane developed a moderate vibration. I informed air traffic control and requested a descent and deviation to zzz. Descending thru fl120 (oat=(-5) the vibration stopped. I continued to zzz and with a normal approach and landing; and taxied to the fixed-base operator i conducted a thorough walk-around and visual inspection of the aircraft and tested all its systems as per the checklist and found nothing abnormal. Atc/tracon/tower all accommodated my request for priority handling and no in flight emergency was needed or declared. I refiled my instrument flight rules flight plan and departed to [my original destination]. The flight was normal.
output: Tbm-850 captain reported moderate vibration from severe icing event.

input: Immediately after takeoff i realized that the aircraft was not properly pressurizing. The f/o was flying and i asked him to slow the climb rate in preparation to level at 6000. Departure control approved level off at 6000'. Pressurization controller was functioning normally but aircraft would not pressurize in standby or manual. Several minutes had passed since takeoff and the #1 f/a began knocking on the cockpit door. Initially; i did not allow him access because he hadn't followed proper entry procedures but; when he did enter; i noticed a loud noise coming from the forward cabin which the #1 confirmed to be air leakage from forward entry door. It was interesting to note that as loud as the noise was; i did not notice it until the cockpit door was opened. Obviously; i was second officer involved with the situation at hand that this noise didn't get my attention we slowed the aircraft to 210 knot(s) to reduce the noise and discussed alternatives while contacting company. Company wanted the aircraft in ewr (dest) but left final decision to me which is of course standard. I left the cockpit to observe the forward entry door. The handle was down in the proper position and the door seemed to be closed normally (we had no door warning lights). We decided to continue the flight to destination at low altitude and reduced airspeed. My biggest concern being passenber discomfort due to the noise in the forward cabin area. Although this was not the most conservative decision; i believe it was a safe alternative to inconveniencing the passenber on board and also returned the aircraft to a major maintenance base where proper repairs could be made. The situation was explained to the passenber as we continued en route at arrival, arrive in ewr passenber deplaned with a few thank you's and for the most part seemed calm and satisfied with our decision to continue the flt.
output: Unable to pressurize aircraft due to main cabin door leak; mlg proceeds to destination at low alt.

input: Training flight at reid hillview airport (rhv) san jose; ca; jun/xa/02; times from xa45 local to xc00 local pacific standard time flight was a training flight with myself as flight instructor in left/right (directions) the entire flight was pattern work runway(s) 31r; left/right (directions) hand traffic aircraft traffic ranged from light to us being only aircraft in class d airspace -- rhv. Frequency congestion was minimal to none. Flight started normally; air traffic control professional and courteous; about 4 aircraft in airspace; shift change occurred with new controller on frequency immediately a piper j3 cub doing pattern work had to ask tower for clearance while he was on final. Tower was not providing him with clrncs until pilot asked or them during critical final approach phase; that aircraft terminated and the rest of the aircraft in the airspace had left the pattern. After landing we taxied back for takeoff runway(s) 31r and awaited takeoff clearance after about a minute(s) and a half and with nobody else on frequency we asked the tower intermediate fix he was 'all right.' he gruffly cleared us for takeoff to make left/right (directions) traffic runway(s) 31r. We flew around the pattern without receiving any landing clearance or other instructions. On short final i instructed the student to do a go around since we had not received a clearance to land. I then told the tower that we were doing a go around since we had not received landing clearance his only response was 'roger.' this happened 2 more times in a row with us going around and stating that we were going around because we had not received landing clearance his response being the same 'roger.' just before the third go around another aircraft called inbound to rhv and had received instructions. After the third go around and same response 'roger;' i asked him why i was not receiving any landing clrncs. Now no response at all. I then tried to contact the other aircraft about possible radio problems immediately the frequency was jammed with a stuck microphone for about 1 minute(s) and a half. Not aircraft noise; but office noises (or tower noises) were heard in the back ground the rhv controller then came on frequency stating that some aircraft had a stuck microphone then cleared us to land. We then terminated our flight the controller appears to have some mental or physical problem that restricts his ability to control safely. Intermediate fix another aircraft had an emergency during his stuck microphone an accident or injury could have resulted. This type of problem with this controller has been going on for over 1 1/2 yrs with numerous complaints to the chief and aviation safety reporting system rpts filed. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr said a particular controller at rhv has been harassing pilots for almost 2 yrs. He does a lot of flight instruction at rhv and usually lets the students work the radios from takeoff to landing but steps in when the controller starts yelling at the student. He said he has discussed the problem with the tower chief on several occasions without any change in the controller's behavior. Supplemental information from acn 550941: we had performed several patterns and lndgs without incident; a shift change in the tower occurred. We then did not receive landing clearance from the tower though we were the only traffic in the pattern. We then asked for a radio checked from another aircraft and immediately after the end of our transmission a stuck microphone was heard on frequency after about 1 minute(s) the controller returned and gave us a landing clearance we terminated then. I believe the controller stuck the microphone to prevent us from communicating. Callback conversation with rptr on acn 550941 revealed the following information the rptr states that it was perceived that the 3 gars were due to the voice recognition by the controller of the pilot's voice; that the pilot and controller had 'previous altercations; both on and off freq;' that the controller recognized the pilot's voice and 'willfully' caused the 'stuck mike' incident.
output: An rhv local controller is displaying unusual behavior while controling tfc.

input: I was scheduled to start my 4 leg post meridiem flying day in st louis. Everything was uneventful prior to arriving at the gate where we were informed the aircraft would be 25 minute(s) late. As the pilot not flying (for this leg -- stl to lit) and first officer i reviewed the weather and release. Upon descent into lit; i copied the automatic terminal information service which did not mention that the ne 800 feet/foot of runway(s) 4l/22r was closed. Approach control told us to expect a visual approach to runway(s) 4r. We requested and received a visual approach to runway(s) 4l. No mention was made by approach control of the shortened runway(s) status. Subsequently; we were given clearance to land runway(s) 4l by lit tower and again no mention was made of the shortened runway(s) status. The weather was clear with 10 mile visibility. The capt landed the aircraft flaps 30 degrees on speed at approximately 1000 feet/foot using regular procedures reverse thrust to 80 knot(s) before braking. My attention was divided between the runway(s) exit at taxiway j and the airspd indicator; as it is my job to call out 80 knot(s) to the capt to reduce reverse and begin normal braking. It became obvious a short time later that the capt was not going to exit at taxiway j; second officer i shifted my focus down the runway(s) to the departure end. At this time i noticed something on the runway(s) at the same time the capt began braking harder. There were 5 sandbags evenly spaced across the width of the runway(s) i would estimate we were doing about 30 knot(s) when tower advised us we were about to enter a closed portion of the runway(s) the capt steered between the sandbags and entered the closed portion at approximately 15 knot(s) ground speed did a 180 degree turn; and exited at the point which we had entered. Taxi to the gate was uneventful. The capt did an exterior inspection and noted nothing unusual. This entire chain of events occurred because a single notice to airmen / of air missions amongst all those in the weather package was not noticed. Something as important as the primary turbojet runway(s) being shortened (especially a relatively short runway(s) to begin with) should be in the automatic terminal information service and mentioned by both approach control and tower when assigning it for the approach and landing none of those actions occurred. Finally; using 5 sandbags to indicate a runway(s) closure is not visually adequate. The runway(s) looked perfectly useable until very late in the landing rollout. Supplemental information from acn 409613: the destination metar was missing and i spent a little time trying to find it in the package before i showed it to the operations(s) agent and requested current weather which he later provided. Unfortunately i missed the notice to airmen / of air missions on the second page of the weather package. The system was very intolerant of that simple error. There were three more opportunities that could have alerted me to the runway(s) shortening and they weren't there: the automatic terminal information service contained no mention of it; the approach controller when he cleared me for the visual did not say anything about it; and the tower controller made no mention when he cleared me to land.
output: A landing b737-300 inadvertently uses the closed portion of runway(s) 4l at lit. Approach controller and tower controller did not advise crew of the closed 800 feet/foot at the end. The runway(s) confign had been notamed but the flight crew missed that in their flight planning. Automatic terminal information service did not carry this information either.

input: The purpose of this form is to document operational shortcomings identified by crew members. Air carrier has initiated an internal evaluation process which encourages employees to inform management of operational problems or concerns. The crew was informed by the handling agent that brought the weight and balance to the aircraft that we had 2 tires on board in the flyaway kit. This was reflected in the ballast (other) block on our weight and balance as 280 kg's. We applied the rest of the information and departed on the way to zzz. Once airborne we reviewed the weight and balance books an at the time we realized that the agent had the wrong weight for the two tires. Aircraft table reflects the weight for two tires is 420 kg's for this aircraft not 280 kt's. It is not very clear intermediate fix by the statement the additional weight gets applied in the load planner or on the final crew form. We had flown the 2 previous legs without being informed that the tires were on board. We reviewed the other flight envelopes on the aircraft and realized that out of 16 other flts; only 1 was correct. We arrived in zzz and had the station superintendent meet the flight he was not informed of the tires in the flyaway kit; and explained that air carrier 1 does it different. He indicated that air carrier 1 applies the information to the weight and balance advisory on the flight release. All the air carrier 2 releases show are the basic operating weight including basic crew and not anything else. I asked that he make the changes. Air carrier 2 crew should be better informed as to what is on board the maintenance support items weight the information should be on the flight release; or by the information posted on the aircraft logbook. My concern is how many other air carrier 2 flts have not had the correct information since the implementation of the new weight and balance procs.
output: A b747-300 freighter was repeatedly dispatched with an incorrect weight for an onboard maintenance fly away tire kit.

input: While on the flosi3 area navigation arrival into newark after passing the crank intersection; air traffic control vectored us off the arrival heading 230 and assigned us to descend from 7000 mean sea level to 4000 mean sea level the vector placed us about 5 miles behind a visual flight rules aircraft at 3500 mean sea level the visual flight rules aircraft was also heading roughly 230. We were overtaking the visual flight rules aircraft with approximately 40 knots of overtake. There was a 600' broken cloud deck from 3500' to 4100' mean sea level which kept us instrument meteorological conditions air traffic control pointed out the visual flight rules traffic but we told them we were not visual (imc). At roughly 1 to 2 miles from the visual flight rules traffic and leveling at 4000' our traffic alert and collision avoidance system showed the traffic climbing. At inside of a mile (estimated based on tcas); i perceived an impending conflict based on the traffic alert and collision avoidance system trend and our over-take. I turned off the autopilot and initiated an aggressive climb. Moments after initiating the climb; the traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory aural alert sounded with an initial descend command followed immediately by a climb command. I followed the climb command with the vertical speed in the green until 'clear of conflict' was heard which happened at about 4500' mean sea level the captain informed air traffic control that we were climbing as a result of the resolution advisory air traffic control acknowledged and assigned us back down to 4000' mean sea level the rest of the approach and landing was uneventful.
output: First officer reported executing an aggressive resolution advisory traffic alert and collision avoidance system command in instrument meteorological conditions following atc's vectors off the assigned star.

input: After takeoff the cabin altitude warning sounded passing 10000 mean sea level during preflight we requested and received takeoff data for a flaps 5 bleeds on takeoff. During taxi out we received an error twice when attempting to get final takeoff data for flaps 5 bleeds on. This seemed a little unusual since our takeoff weight had decreased from the planned weight. We then requested and received takeoff data for a flaps 5 bleeds off takeoff.while holding number 1 for takeoff we told tower we needed a few minutes to complete our checklists. We then reconfigured the bleeds panel for a bleeds off takeoff and completed the before takeoff checklist. At this point neither of us remembered that we needed to start the auxiliary power unity which had been shut down after engine start.after takeoff i noticed the cabin was climbing quickly and placed the right bleed switch on and configure the bleed panel for normal operations. The cabin alt warning horn sounded briefly and the cabin descended immediately back below 10000 ft.
output: B737 flight crew reported a bleeds off takeoff from a high altitude airport with the auxiliary power unity shut down which resulted in the cabin altitude warning sounding at 10;000 feet.

input: Normal instrument landing system 24; upon t/d; when all tires were on the ground selected beta for deceleration. Once the power levers were over the gate i discovered i had no beta from the propellers i notified the capt. He initiated a go around but engs would not respond quickly enough. Capt aborted the takeoff capt applied full braking and beta did not function again. We encountered blowing snow the last 1/3 of the runway(s) and this prevented efficient braking. Slid off the runway(s) about 60'. Shut down and called the unicom to notify them of the situation. Contributing factors: no beta range for deceleration; blowing snow on the runway(s) high crosswind of 20+ knot(s) and no procedure exists for this kind of situation. 3 days after the incident company mechs were testing the power levers when one of the cables broke. They found where it had frayed and said it caused the binding i felt when selecting beta and when the capt selected go around pwr.
output: Ltt goes off end of runway(s) as reversers fail to operate and braking is ineffective on a snow-covered surface. Aircraft not evacuated.

input: During our approach into bozeman montana we were cleared direct to kicdo and to descend to 11;000 feet by big sky approach. Before reaching kicdo from the east at approximately 11;500 feet during our descent we received a terrain warning followed immediately by a terrain pull up warning. I executed the escape maneuver by disconnecting the auto pilot and putting the aircraft into go around mode. Our display showed no color terrain indication of any kind during this time. We climbed to 12;000 which is higher than the minimum safe altitude in that sector and the audio warning stopped. Once we confirmed the aircraft status; we notified big sky air traffic control of the warning indication and of our new altitude. We stayed at 12;000 feet until air traffic control cleared us down to 8100 feet and turned us on to final for the final approach to runway 12. At the time of the approach the weather condition was snowing. Prior to this event while cruising at 17;000; we had an automated 2;500 foot call out. We can only attribute this to the snowing condition with the radar altimeter.no other additional indication occurred after the terrain warning. We continued the approach and landed without any further incident. Upon contacting big sky approach by phone; i was informed that this abnormal indication have occurred to other aircraft in this area of operation in the past which is north of the airport. We show no terrain indication on either of our displays. Considering the lack of indication on our display and the fact that other aircraft have experience similar indications it seems to be an area of erroneous egws indication.
output: Air carrier captain reported an erroneous egpws indication north of bzn during descent to 11000 feet near the kicdo intersection. Evasive action is taken but no high terrain is actually present. Air traffic control indicated that other aircraft have experienced similar anomalies in that area.

input: I arrived at the airport from san francisco and although there was a cloud deck at approximately 600 feet/foot i had noted a number of holes; which i had deemed sufficient to fly through and get on top for visual flight rules conditions. In checking the conditions for the route the conditions were showing overcast at 600 feet/foot with 8 miles of visibility in the bay area and clear to the south and east with 12;000 few in the central valley. I had made the trip the day before under the same conditions with no issue. As i was looking to plan my route; i saw that there was a hole with clear sunlight over coyote hills; which meant asking for a special visual flight rules clearance with a cement plant departure and climbing on top as soon as i reached the hole. This was exactly what i had done the day before. In the worst case i had 8 miles of visibility so even with the low ceiling i could always make a u-turn and come back to the airport if there was a problem. I performed the normal preflight and asked for my clearance from the tower. Once i received this i taxied to the run up area and when i was ready i asked for a clearance. Just as i was taxiing onto the runway i was stopped by a large goose standing right on the 12 numbers which initiated a dialog with the tower. Eventually the goose left the runway and i taxied onto the runway for a cement plant take off. In the time i was in the run up and paying attention to the goose i had not noticed that the conditions were changing rapidly and that the fog was moving very swiftly. Once i took off and made a 20-degree turn off the end of the runway; as is the normal procedure and then proceeded to turn towards the cement plant. At this point i was at approximately 400 feet/foot and noticed there were a number of clouds below 600 feet/foot that i needed to avoid. I began to weave around the clouds when the tower called and inquired about my strange flight and if all was ok. I indicated that i was avoiding clouds and all was fine. At this time the tower called to hand me nct approach. At about the same time i lost sight of the cement plant and the hole i was flying towards. The situation was rapidly getting worse. At that time i decided to turn back to san carlos and radioed my intentions to the tower. I told the tower that i was turning back due to the clouds and proceeded to turn into a cloud. What i had not realized was the 8 miles of visibility had closed to 0 behind me within a matter of minutes. I was in a cloud with no visibility in any direction. I told the tower of my situation and tried to descend and see if i could get below the clouds. I was at 300 feet/foot and could not see the water below me and remembered the power lines so i began a steep climb. I then tried turning left and right to see if i could find any visual reference. At this point being a visual flight rules pilot in a cloud with complete white out conditions and no clue which way to go i began to panic. I tried to fly the plane and when i looked at the instruments i was descending at a rapid rate completely uncoordinated and given my height above the water did not have much time before i would crash. I stopped the descent at about 200 feet/foot and remembered my flight instructor telling me to stare at the instruments; as you will have no idea what you are doing otherwise. I can honestly say that until i stared at the gauges i did not realize i was turning at a 45-degree bank while slipping. I immediately began to stabilize the plane and was reporting to the tower my altitude to make sure there was no traffic that would be a factor. Once the plane was stable i began to fly coordinated with the instruments and realized that i had no clue of where i was and certainly could not find the airport. I decided to try and get the global positioning system set so i could use the moving map however after 5 tries it would not accept my input of direct to san carlos this may have been due to my hitting the wrong buttons in my state or a problem with the global positioning system i was lost over the bay in the clouds with traffic and obstacles all around. The tower was talking to me almost constantly and asking if i could see anything i reported that i was in total white out conditions. He asked if i was instrument flight rules certified and i reported i was not. He reported i was just about over coyote hills and that i should fly a westerly heading. I began to turn however i was still lost. I flew the heading and he told me there was an instructor in the tower to help. He had me verify my altimeter with his and the heading i was flying at that point he directed me to fly a heading and report when i can see anything. I flew that heading for what seemed an eternity however could not have been more than a couple of minutes. Eventually the ground below came into sight. I reported seeing the power lines and was able to make sure i was above them however i still could not see the airport. I kept flying and then the 101 highway appeared almost instantly. I reported the highway in sight and then the airport. At that point there was a large hole above the airport and there was very good visibility and not a problem to land. I made my go no go decision without paying attention to how fast the conditions were changing. As my hobbs meter indicted .6 from the time i started the conditions went from 600 with 8 miles visibility to complete white out within minutes. The visual reference points all disappeared including the ones behind me that would get me back to the airport in case i could not go forward. From a risk management standpoint the margin for error with a 600-foot ceiling was too narrow. In looking back the questions i should have asked myself were 1. What is the margin for error in this situation? 2. What are the consequences of failure if i am wrong? Given the answer to 1 is 600 feet/foot with power lines below and clouds all around the answer is very little. The answer to 2 is i will end up in a cloud and likely to crash into the bay. An easy answer in hindsight i should have stayed on the ground.
output: Pilot departing sql on a special visual flight rules clearance reports inadvertently entering instrument meteorological conditions and initially losing control. Control is regained using flight instruments and assistance from air traffic control is requested. With air traffic control assistance the reporter returns to visual meteorological conditions and a visual approach and landing is accomplished at sql.

input: Returning from a solo cross-country; i was established on the published visual flight rules arrival procedure for the flight schools; developed for williams gateway airport (iwa) at an altitude of 3;500 feet mean sea level in a small aircraft. (while i was in the gap i was not in iwa class d airspace however i was communicating with tower) i noticed a target moving my direction at approximately the same altitude on my ads-b. I was unable to visually see the aircraft due to its location in a blind spot created between my windscreen and the door jamb. With the aircraft at two miles and still at my altitude; i initiated a climb to avoid a collision. The climb was only 100-200 feet; so there weren't any issues with phx class b airspace. I finally obtained visual identification of the aircraft as it passed below me. Another plane from my flight school; with an instructor on board; noted that the aircraft missed my plane by approximately 100 feet and didn't seem to realize that he'd nearly caused a midair collision. Lessons learned for me as a student pilot include; improved scan for aircraft; including maneuvering the plane on occasion to check blind spots. Better radio vigilance.
output: Small aircraft student pilot reported an near midair collision in the vicinity of iwa airport.

input: The fo's forward windshield began arcing. Shortly thereafter it cracked in several places. We followed electronic centralized aircraft monitoring quick reference handbook and fom procedures descended to fl230 and ultimately landed in zzz2. All parties were informed. We saw it and heard it. Requested a deviation from air traffic control declared an emergency left the track. Conferred with dispatch. Apparently the windshield controller caused the arcing and subsequently the cracking of the windshield.
output: An a330 fo's forward window cracked at fl370. An emergency was declared with a diversion to a nearby arpt.

input: Location: ord 020 degree radial; 20 vor and dme (co-located) climbing out of ord on vectors; cleared and read back 'turn to 060 degrees climb to 15000 ft.' center asked what was assigned heading says 'no; 020 degrees assigned; now climb to 17000 ft.' i responded '060 degrees understood and read back.' no response. Turned to 020 degrees and climbed to new altitude 17000 feet/foot no traffic advisory or resolution advisory no further mention made by atc.
output: A b737 first officer attempts to clear the confusion regarding a previous clearance wherein the controller did not correct an erred readback for vectors out of ord; il.

input: I closed the left/right (directions) cowl flap and cut off the left/right (directions) mixture. I had my student perform the troubleshoot and engine secure chklist. With the engine secure i then had my student perform the air start chklist. The engine did not start on the first attempt second officer i vectored my student in the direction of zzz to minimize our time flying on 1 engine intermediate fix we couldn't start it. We were down to the single engine service ceiling before the engine started. When the left/right (directions) engine started it was producing no thrust. The left/right (directions) tachometer was indicating 1500 rpm's. We called approach and advised them of our situation and requested a straight-in visual approach for runway(s) 32. While flying towards zzz we tried to get the propeller to move forward or feather but it remained at 1500 rpm's and no manipulation of the throttle would yield any thrust either. Still in a descent at 1800 feet/foot mean sea level even while pitching for vxse (82 kts) i chose to make an off airport landing with the propeller not feathering; i put all the controls forward one last time hoping that the propeller would move forward and the left/right (directions) engine would produce thrust. As we neared our selected field; it was noticeably rough and rolling with alfalfa growing more than 1 feet/foot high second officer i chose to land with no gear. At approximately 300 feet/foot above touchdown; i extended flaps 25 degrees and closed the throttles about 50 feet/foot above touchdown. We made a belly landing touching down just under 70 knot(s) and sliding 600 feet/foot to a complete stop. We then secured the airplane and exited.
output: Unable to restore an engine shutdown for training; a pa44 instructor and student make an off airport single engine landing in a field.

input: I launched at about xa55 from our launch site on lower loop road. I briefed my passenber on what to expect on landing and what to do -- face the direction of travel; hang on tight; bend knees and to stay in the basket until told to exit. I lifted off in very normal condition for us as usual and started floating westbound as normal at 1-2 mph winds. My altitude was 100 feet/foot above ground level for that time. After about 30 minute(s) into the flight the winds shifted to the north at about 5 mph. Have gone this direction many times over the yrs of flying in second. My direction north was lining me up with a small field about 1/8 mile away for landing still at 4-5 mph. At about 1-2 minute(s) before landing the winds went from 4-5 mph to 20.9 according to my global positioning system and shifted direction slightly. Immediately i saw a small opening in the trees to land and did second officer landed in high winds. 1 passenber (a small girl 7 or 8 yrs old) upon landing bumped her little finger on a fuel tank. Everyone else was fine. No damage to the aircraft as a precaution; had the girl checkeded out at the local medical center where she was found to be alright; and 2-3 minute(s) before landing i did brief all of my passenber on what to do upon landing and that it was going to be fast and hard because of the high winds.
output: The pilot of a balloon and his passenber experienced a 'high wind' landing near sedona; az.

input: Dep off runway(s) 24 teb calls for runway(s) heading to 1500'; then turn to 280 degrees until 015 degrees bearing on nondirectional radio beacon then climb to 3000'. On earlier flight we departed same runway(s) as soon as airborne controller gave different heading than described in departure with climb to 3000'. On evening departure i was flying this leg as f/o. After takeoff we were given heading of 270 degrees by controller and assumed since we were not following departure off teb because assigned heading differs from that described in departure we were allowed to climb to 3000' as stated. Because it states heading of 280 degrees until 015 degree bearing; should we have stayed at 1500' on 270 degree heading until 015 degree bearing; then climbed to 3000'? Anyway; after assigned heading of 270 degrees we started climb to 3000' and were told to descend to 1500' by controller after which he then changed instructions to climb to 11000' before we could even get back to 1500'. What to do intermediate fix we were assigned different heading but not altitude was confusing. Also; when heading given; capt said; 'ok; up to 3000';' and i followed instructions assuming as he did that 1500' restriction was no longer valid. This should be clarified either in written departure procedure or by controller when headings differ from departure plate.
output: Alt deviation; excursion from assigned.

input: The aircraft was to transport 2 passenber and 140 pounds of cargo from an offshore structure to intracoastal city heliport. Upon landing at the offshore heliport; the helicopter was kept operating while the passenber and cargo were loaded. The aircraft flew to the on-shore helicopter without incident. After shutdown; i was informed that the cargo was a regulated hazardous material; flammable liquids n.o.s un 1993 package group iii; there were 2; 5 gal pails. The heliport dispatcher notified the federal aviation administration civil aviation security office in accordance with 49 crash fire rescue equipment 175.31.
output: Hazardous cargo problem - the pilot was informed that hazardous material had been put on board at the offshore oil rig along with the pax.

input: Ifr flight plan: lal vi57 gilbi direct fxe. Departure from lal was normal at approximately xx00 ante meridiem initial altitude assignment was 2000'. I was handed off to tpa approach on 120.65 and cleared to 5000'; 180 degrees assigned. After several minute(s) i was cleared to 9000'; still 180 degrees assigned. Tpa handed me off to zma on frequency 134.55. I ante meridiem very familiar with this route and have never been assigned this frequency the normal frequency is miami on 133.15. I checkeded on with zma and was told to continue on the 180 degree heading zma was extremely congested on 134.55 due to poor weather conditions in the tampa bay area with numerous aircraft asking and receiving weather deviations. After several more minute(s) i was cleared present position direct gilbi; to which i acknowledged and complied. During the next 30 minute(s) i continued toward gilbi at 9000' and received no further assignments or advisories from 134.55. At 10 mile nw of gilbi intersection i requested a lower altitude on 134.55. The controller responded somewhat confused by asking who i was. I stated we were instrument flight rules at 9000' assigned; to which he then asked my position i responded by explaining 8 nautical mile nw of the gilbi intersection after a short pause i was assigned zma on 133.55. I checkeded on frequency to be immediately queried as to why i did not communicate with them (133.55) earlier. I stated i was just handed off. The zma controller responded rather upset and wanted to know what our previous frequency was. I answered 134.55 and was told to descend immediately to 4000'; and that we must expedite our descent he also told us that we had been treated as a no-radio instrument flight rules for the past 20 minute(s) zma soon handed us off to zma approach on 119.7 and we continued on to fxe w/o further incident.
