input: Departed den after much confusion and miscom between the flight crew; dispatch; and den clearance delivery (atc) concerning a revised segment of the pre departure clearance may have inadvertently departed with an air traffic control clearance different than the routing in the amended dispatch release. After receiving the howgozit inflt; noticed a difference in the routing versus the air traffic control received routing. We received the pre departure clearance with a revised segment changing the departure to the den 4 direct oal and notified dispatch with the change. Also questioned intermediate fix method #1 still applicable. This also happened after a diversion the previous evening on our flight the change was sent to dispatch; the data checkeded and we received a release via automatic communications addressing & reporting system 'ok to depart and continue under method #1.' i was expecting the same answer based on our weight and routing being the same along with all the terrain considerations. Instead i received multiple messages that due to computer limitations are unable to flight plan that route either method #1 or #2. The flight was delayed trying to resolve the clearance issue and find a legal dispatch. We were told by clearance delivery that 99% of the time the filed plan of direct rif direct oal is revised to direct oal due to en route center restrs. Clearance delivery consulted with center to help us find alternative routing to send to dispatch. He mentioned that the center controller was aware of driftdown criteria. We were told that routing over laramie or alamosa were only acceptable alternatives and that information was relayed to dispatch. Dispatch advised us that air traffic control had also contacted them and they were refiling our flight plan. Rls 2 routing was rocki4 dbl j80 oal. We sat awaiting voice clearance and had to ask dispatch to refile again because den had not received a clearance when contacted by clearance delivery; they said 'finally received your company filed flight plan' -- and gave us clearance as 'den 4 oal 10000 ft.' i mistakenly assumed this was the refiled company flight plan due to terminology used. In trying to get flight out for passenber connections; i did not request copy of new flight plan because it was second officer similar to our original routing (and knew terrain and fuel were adequate); but which would have shown discrepancy. Realized that this was a larger and more complicated problem than we were aware of after debriefing with dispatch and dispatch manager via telephone after flight we discussed the need to be able to revise flight plans due to revised segments predep; but that limit prevents being able to flight plan on revised segments being issued by den. Was told that it is part of a complex situation concerning division of center sectors and that our databases are not programmed with the en route fixes used to prevent the conflicts. Was informed that this would be topic of discussion the next day with the air traffic control coordination to find a solution.
output: A b757-200 took off from den with mismatch between air traffic control clearance and company release.

input: We had a problem with the new area navigation departures out of clt today. Here was our flight plan: harray2.harray vxv direct. The clearance we received from air traffic control prior to departure harray2 harray vxv as filed. The way i understood it is that we were supposed to fly to vxv after harray. Intermediate fix the controller would have said: 'harray2 vxv transition' we would have programmed in the fix 'zavier.' 2 center controllers asked us about our route and seemed somewhat concerned; but they never came back with a definite answer. They just said they were going to look into it. Later; i asked clt clearance delivery (who did not know); and then his supervisor who i spoke on the phone with (who did not know) and never got a good answer. It seems like everybody is somewhat confused about how to fly these departures could somebody please enlighten us? Thank you.
output: An air carrier capt reported confusion flying new area navigation departure out of clt that apparently resulted in a track dev.

input: Acft x on overnight. Crew wrote up #2 capt's window beyond limits. I measured within limits. Also talked to capt and he assured me it was not in his field of vision. I signed off write-up in maintenance log. This occurred the day before also. I contacted planning to get the aircraft to a maintenance station with facilities to replace windows and change window. The window was changed wkend of aug/xa/06. Maintenance manual needs to be more specific; give limits intermediate fix exceeds must change not recommend change.
output: A b757 with a capt's #2 window delamination rpted twice is finally routed for window replacement. Technician believes manual needs to give more specific limits.

input: Shortly after takeoff we received clearance from mia #1 omega ambiguity light illuminated. #2 omega appeared normal. We started navigating to tadpo using #2 omega. #1 omega was updated using non precision method. Both omegas appeared to be functioning normally. Mia air traffic control gave us clearance and confirmation heading direct cayo largo nondirectional radio beacon it became apparent the #2 omega was now showing erroneous indications. Both 1 and 2 omega ambiguity lights came on. We notified first mia then havana of our problem then requested and received clearance to varder using raw data. Over varder performed unsuccessful precision updated to both omegas. After consulting with dispatch determined we could continue the flight using raw data only. All preflt -- runway(s) and after takeoff position checkeds were performed as per operations(s) procedure all checked normal.
output: Flc experienced dual omega failure.

input: I was at sussex; nj; over night on 7/sat/90 planning a departure from sussex 7/sun/90. The morning of 7/sun/90 i received a briefing from flight service station specialist reached by the 800 number from matamoras; public address which indicated a convective frontal system moving into the area after noon time that day. I was given a complete briefing but no notams for n63. I proceeded to the airport arriving approximately 30 local i went directly to the fixed-base operator office which is a relatively small area where the phone was located. There were a number of people in this area all talking in very loud voices immediately adjacent to telephone. The noise level was second officer high i was required to put one finger in my ear to hear the briefing i received from the millville flight service station specialist and second officer advised the briefer. On the basis of the briefing and while still with the briefer i filed an instrument flight rules flight plan n63 to lebanon; nh; and was instructed to pick up my clearance on the ground from ny terminal radar approach control facility again i was given no notams or n63. At approximately noon time i called ny terminal radar approach control facility and was given an instrument flight rules clearance to depart n63 with a void time of next hour plus 21. I then did preflt and monitored the published common traffic advisory frequency frequency of 122.7 taxied to about midway on runway(s) 21 announced i was ack taxiing runway(s) 21 for departure (with no response) did a runup on the end of runway(s) 21 still monitoring 122.7 then announced i was departing runway(s) 21. The departure was visual flight rules with good visibility. I noted no traffic nor did i hear any radio communicationss on 122.7. At approximately 2000' mean sea level i contacted my center departure frequency and proceeded in accord with my clearance . Approximately 3 days later i received a telephone call from a local pilot who advised me that the field was closed during my departure and that there was a helicopter in the air with a parachute jumper. He further advised me that the helicopters were utilizing 123.05 and were talking on that frequency he indicated there was a potential conflict but one did not occur. Factors. No field closing notice to airmen / of air missions given pilot in command in 2 complete briefings . Inappropriate noise level while receiving 2nd briefing and clearance no response or advisory on 122.7. Helicopter activity using a completely different frequency i received an instrument flight rules departure clearance for a time that the field was allegedly closed.
output: Reporter cites events that alleges that he departure from a closed airport and that although no conflict existed with a parachute drop from a clc helicopter; he should have had a notice to airmen / of air missions on the closure which reporter states was non existant.

input: We received taxi clearance prior to taxi from fixed-base operator to runway(s) 25r and as i proceeded taxi i started to cross runway(s) 25l and ground controller advised i had taxied onto active runway(s) and said to turn left/right (directions) and exit on next taxiway which i did immediately. We then received new taxi clearance to taxi on taxiway a to taxiway fahrenheit which i did. Both my first officer and i understood clearance to cross runway(s) 25l second officer there apparently was a misunderstanding. I would not intentionally cross an active runway(s) without clearance apparently there was confusion as to how the clearance was given and how it was received and understood.
output: Rwy incursion at lax is disputed.

input: Upon arrival, arrive we were given signals by the guide man to taxi into a dimly lit; undefined area. The area was not defined by a lead-in line or marked by an envelope and was between 2 aircraft (a regional jet on our left/right (directions) and a b737 to our r). It appeared that at one point there may have been lines on the tarmac; but they had been removed. The guide man was signaling us to enter the gate area approximately 15 feet/foot to the left/right (directions) of the established lead-in line. I brought the airplane to a stop adjacent to the beginning of the established lead-in line and signaled the guide man i would not proceed without wing walkers. The guide man attempted to urge me to continue. I declined. I again signaled that wing walkers would be required. The guide man stomped off to find some help and came back a few minute(s) later with someone to watch our left/right (directions) wing but nobody to watch the left/right (directions) wing. Furthermore; this wing walker was without a lighted wand; which i felt necessary for all involved to see him. Again; i declined to move and signaled the guide man that another wing walker would be required for the left/right (directions) wing and i lit up the ramp to indicate that lights would be required. Again; the guide man stomped off. Meanwhile; the first officer and i made repeated attempts to contact station operations(s) to no avail. I finally called dispatch on my cell phone to try to reach station operations(s) and the station manager intermediate fix necessary to rectify the situation. About the time the dispatcher got a hold of operations(s) (15 minute(s) from our arrival, arrive at the gate area) the guide man showed up with 2 wing walkers with lighted wands to guide us in. We then proceeded to park with caution and without further incident. While no damage was sustained to the aircraft or personnel; i ante meridiem deeply concerned by several factors: 1) there are no defined lead-in lines to what the agent later told me is a routine parking spot for overnight aircraft 2) the guide man attempted to park me in an undefined area without a clearly marked envelope and lead-in lines without the assistance of wing walkers. 3) we were unable to reach station operations(s) by normal means. This appears to be a total breakdown of company procedures by operations(s) and i believe needs to be looked at by corporate safety.
output: A319 capt stops aircraft after attempt by marshal to park him between two other aircraft in dimly lit; unmarked area; without wing walkers.

input: Shortly after i assumed the position i noticed that the previous controller's instruction for a b737 to expedite descent was not working as planned. I issued a turn to the descending b737 aircraft and called traffic with no reply from the b737. We have bad radios in the area; so i watch a second to see if he took the turn. I called a total of three times to the b737 before he took the turn. I had also called traffic to the c130 and the pilot reported traffic in sight. The projected path initially looked close but appeared separation would not be lost. I wanted the turn for extra comfort but as it played out it ended to be right at the minimums for separation as they passed. We have had frequency problems on 135.7 for an extended amount of time; but i'm not sure if i was blocked; pilot was not listening; or it was a blind spot. I believe if the b737 had taken the turn when i initialized it i would have had plenty of space. Proper frequencies would be great. We have been reporting those down for years. Maintenance seems to reset it; someone does a brief frequency check and it's called back up. The expedite descent clearance was not necessary in the first place. I should have just stopped descent vertically as soon as i sat down.
output: Zsu controller described a failed attempt to issue a descent clearance noting the frequency utilized has had problems for an extended amount of time.

input: Passenger brought to my attention that her 3-year old and 4-year old girls could not be secured in their seatbelts. On this a319 aircraft; it is equipped with the new acro seats and true enough we could not get seatbelt to tighten enough to secure the two girls. We ended up putting coats to secure them better-i know this is not the answer; but was the best we could do. I believe the way the seatback curves backwards makes the seatbelt obsolete for a small child. During pre-flight; it is recommend to change the seatbelts.
output: A flight attendant reports that young children cannot be properly secured in the new acro passenger seats installed on their airbus aircraft. The same seatbelts from the removed seats were reinstalled with the new seats; but will not tighten up enough to accommodate the increase curvature of the new seatbacks.

input: Level at 240 on kayoh arrival, arrive noticed radio was quiet; second officer asked for radio checked center replied 'loud and clr.' approaching kayoh; asked for lower altitude no reply. Became apparent we were lost on the frequency took several minute(s) to re-establish contact. Had to take vectors off arrival, arrive to descend no conflicts or other problems. Numerous notams for unauthorized radio xmissions in lax area. We wondered intermediate fix we had been a victim.
output: Lgt temporarily loses communications with air route traffic control center in the lax area.

input: Tcasii gave us a dive command. We had traffic at our 12 o'clock; descending to fl290. We were at fl280. After visually sighting our traffic i could not determine intermediate fix he had stopped at fl290 and traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii was giving a resolution to dive. I descended 500 feet/foot and that satisfied traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii no other aircraft were in the area. In the future; i will put more dependence on the altitude difference readout on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii scope and will disregard the ra.
output: An air carrier mlg crew descended in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii command.

input: Flt was from buenos aires to santiago. After navigate, navigationing the appropriate standard terminal arrival route i joined the localizer and rpted 'rwy in sight' to my crew (not the controller since this was our first time to santiago -- all of us). The approach controller who was obviously also the local controller said 'clred to land runway(s) 17r'. My approach plate showed only one runway(s) 17. Now i ante meridiem wondering intermediate fix i have the right airport all through final approach i questioned the controller as to the name of the airport confirm runway(s) 17r; etc. The only response was 'clred to land runway(s) 17r.' everything matched up second officer i landed. The problem often at night; for maintenance purposes; the chileans close the main runway(s) 17 and light a parallel taxiway for operations(s) the taxiway is concrete; 150 feet/foot wide and has runway(s) lighting. Perfectly safe. But; they won't tell you and it is not notamed. I think crews operating into santiago should be aware of this possibility second officer they don't go crazy like i did.
output: An air carrier hvt frtr landed on runway(s) 17r at scel. There is only one runway(s) but a taxiway can be used for lndg.

input: While cruising at fl350 aircraft encountered severe turbulence was unable to control aircraft altitude and heading advised center of situation. Turbulence lasted from near bancs intersection to past 46n; 502; estimated to most severe turbulence (when aircraft was close to uncontrollable) lasted approximately 5 mins.
output: Wdb trans-atlantic flight encounters sustained severe turbulence at 35000'; causing loss of control.

input: On j119 50 nautical mile north fagan intersection zjx 132.82 requested a 90 degree turn to the left/right (directions) off the airway. Unable to comply due to weather controller requested second time to turn 90 degrees left/right (directions) unable again; due to weather used capt's emergency authority/authorized maintained altitude + hdg.
output: Capt required to use emergency authority/authorized when zjx air route traffic control center radar controller twice requested crew to turn left/right (directions) off airway into wx.

input: Immediately after liftoff; we got heading disagreement warnings on both pilot electronic flight instrument system displays. This implies a loss of heading accuracy; which was not critical at that moment. Our departure procedure simply required a turn to track directly to a vor and dme (co-located) then outbound on a radial. The first officer did a good job of staying focused on flying the aircraft while i executed the normal chklists; talked to air traffic control and attempted to correct our compass problem we were well into the departure procedure when our flight management system system began warning us to 'chk pos.' on top of this; the compass system stubbornly resisted my attempt to fix it. Usually this is a simple toggle and switch throw. The controller then turned us to the first en route fix. When the first officer leveled the turn; i xchked the magnetic compass against the electronic flight instrument system and completed the heading correction; which cleared the heading warning. The first officer was heading directly to the fix; but air traffic control called to warn us that we were not quite headed properly. She (the ctlr) said 'your flight management system is wrong; turn 10 degrees r!' i could not tell how good or bad our flight management system information was; but we did continue to have our 'chk pos' warning even though i had repeatedly tried to reset the system relative to local navaids. I told the controller that we had been having a heading problem another controller came on frequency to simply direct us to the next on course vor and dme (co-located) we did this on 'raw data' easily. After numerous tries; i was finally able to help the flight management system find itself; and we naved successfully for the remainder of the flight using it. It is sad that our flight management system and heading becomes occasionally lost in new york (especially at lga) and florida. Obviously; we are capable of flying without flight management system but the system seems to be almost predictably unreliable at times. These failures usually correct themselves; but i was caught off-guard by the persistence of this multiple failure. I should have notified air traffic control immediately that our fms/heading information was suspect. I ante meridiem not looking forward to using this system in instrument meteorological conditions in highly mountainous terrain. Our company is aware of the weakness of this sys.
output: A departure carj flight crew gets some assistance from departure controller when their flight management system and directional gyros create a navigate, navigation problem for them after liftoff from jfk; ny.

input: After a normal landing at glw; propeller reverse was applied. After a hard yaw to the left/right (directions) the left/right (directions) engine reverse was released and i started hard braking until aircraft reached about 50-60 knot(s)  at this time i let aircraft coast to the end because they only have a turnoff at the end. When i reached the end; i started braking again; but braking action was nil. Runway(s) was wet and outside air temperature was 34 degrees the runway(s) was just freshly painted on a very smooth asphalt surface. I have noticed this to be the case at many airports lately. Aircraft continued straight ahead at about 10-15 knot(s) into the grass! Aircraft was shut down; pulled out by tug; and inspected by mechs. No damage to aircraft or property. Aircraft was returned to service after being inspected by mechs.
output: Plt in a be90 ran off the end of the runway(s) after slowing down and coasting to the end of the runway(s) at glw.

input: My intentions were to fly a c-172 from buffalo airport (9 mile south of amarillo; tx) to amarillo international and leave the airplane at amarillo international however; the airplane had just finished some maintenance work. Therefore; before i was going to fly the plane to amarillo international i was going to perform a taxi checked intermediate fix the plane would have proved airworthy; then i was going to proceed back to the hangar to call someone to pick me up at amarillo international and take me back to my car at buffalo airport as i was taxiing; i noticed some fresh dirt that had been spread over an area that leads to the runway(s) (the airport is all grass with no designated taxi rtes. It's an unctled field with a runway(s) on one side of it.) the area where the fresh dirt has been spread was between some t-hangars and a fence. After passing the t-hangars; pilots normally make a 90 degree turn to go to the other side of the hangars and proceed to the runway(s) however; parallel with the t-hangars were some holes that had been dug to build new t-hangars. (i was not aware of this at the time). Around the holes was fresh dirt; some of which had been smoothed out. In addition; some of the holes were identified with stakes in the ground however; the area where pilots normally taxi across had no warning signs except the fresh dirt. I decided to slowly taxi up to the area to see intermediate fix it looked safe. As i proceeded a little closer; i noticed some holes second officer i decided to turn around and figure out another route as soon as i started to turn; the nose wheel fell into a hole causing the propeller to hit the ground the hole was about 10 inches wide and approximately 2 feet/foot deep. The bottom of the cowling hit the ground before the nose wheel hit the bottom of the hole. The engine quit after the propeller made 2 strikes into the ground i immediately shut off all fuel and electrical switches. I had no injuries; but the propeller was slightly bent and the engine was going to have to be inspected. There was no other evident damage. The problem could have been corrected in many ways. First; the area of construction (approx 500 feet/foot by 20 ft) was second officer inadequately marked that it lead me to believe that it was safe. Second; it was only my third time at the airport second officer i was still relatively unfamiliar with its layout. After seeing the fresh dirt; i should have shut the airplane off and inspected the area by walking around; or by proceeding back to the hangar and asking airport personnel what their recommendation would be.
output: Rptr taxied into unmarked hole.

input: A dent was found in the aircraft skin in a rvsm area. While attempting to resolve the issue; using the srm; there was confusion due to the unclr maintenance instructions. The aircraft was inspected under direction of maintenance management maintenance control and engineering department engineering department specified how to inspect dent and to establish an engineering deferral. A few days later; while doing the on-line training for dc9 rvsm; i discovered that the procedures found there appeared to be different from those in the srm. Maintenance management and maintenance control were notified of my concerns. Later union air standards representative was notified. Aircraft was then re-inspected. Concerns: 1) discrepancy that exists between on-line training and aircraft manuals. 2) lack of clear instructions on procedures for dents in rvsm area in aircraft srm. Solutions: 1) creation of a specific chklist type paperwork for rvsm area dents. 2) srm corrected for clarity. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the repair for the dent became confusing with the differences between the on-line training and the srm and the maintenance manual. The dent was not repaired but was deferred per engineering authority/authorized which limits the airplane to less than fl290. This was to allow time to correct and standardize the repair procedures no consideration was given on the replacement of the static port heating plates which is not being considered in chapter 20 anti-ice. Callback conversation with rptr acn 651755 revealed the following information the manuals and the training program material are now seeing intensive action to bring the information together and standardize the repair proc.
output: A dc9-30 incurred a dent in the aircraft static port area (critical rvsm area) due to conflict with class 1 repair documents dent was deferred per engineering.

input: About 25 nautical mile due east of rbv; at about 12500 feet/foot mean sea level i caught about a 2 second glimpse of something go directly underneath the aircraft at first i thought it was another aircraft but i did not see any wings. I asked air traffic control intermediate fix they showed an aircraft that just passed beneath me. They said there was no traffic in the area. I asked the first officer he was flying the aircraft intermediate fix he saw anything but he said no; his head was down. It appeared to be a missile. The object was gray; had a round nose and cylindrical. It appeared to be traveling fairly fast. I did not see any contrail although there was a layer of clouds beneath the object and my line of sight. I thought about it for a minute(s) or second officer and concluded it looked more like a missile than anything else. I rpted this to air traffic control i cannot be absolutely certain it was a missile; but i don't think it was a bird or a balloon. It was definitely something; and it looked like a missile more than anything else.
output: A320 capt observed an unknown object that passed beneath aircraft at 12500 feet/foot while on n90 freq.

input: The event was a near miss between a heavy jet and a king air; with evasive action taken by the heavy jet. Visual contact from the king air to the heavy jet was never made. The event occurred somewhere within 1 mile to directly overhead; of the cross keys airport (17n) which is an active skydive drop zone. It's unknown to me where the near miss occurred; but given the localizer of the occurrence; the king air would have been in a short cruise at 13000 feet/foot followed by a turn back to the se and descent after releasing jumpers. The letter of agreement between the drop zone and the phl terminal radar approach control facility calls for all climbs and dscnts to be conducted south and east of the airport class b exits north and westbound of the field. Operations(s) of the king air was conducted in our allotted area and to standard operating procedure we were in direct contact with phl approach in fact; we were conversing about a dash 8 over the drop zone. Approach suggested that i hold my jumpers while it passed. This was done and reapproval was given to commence skydiving activities. Jumpers were dispatched and the king air made its normal dscnt-to-lndg in the approved operations(s) area. This was done exactly like approximately 1000 other operations(s) conducted by myself at this airport alone during this summer season. All rules; regulations and procedures were followed exactly as set forth in federal aviation regulation part 91; federal aviation regulation part 105; and by letter of agreement with the phl terminal radar approach control facility why there was no message received about additional conflicting traffic i do not know. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that; after the flight phl terminal radar approach control facility requested that he give them a call. He found out that the heavy jet had to take evasive action to avoid his aircraft the rptr felt that he had followed the letter of agreement between his company and phl terminal radar approach control facility and that he conducted this flight as he had the other 20-25 flts that day. This summer alone he has logged more than 500 loads. He recalled that he and his company have met with the phl terminal radar approach control facility team supervisors on a number of occasions. During the meetings the subject of the letter of agreement his company has with tampa and minneapolis; respectively; have been discussed. The rptr attributed the success of these loa's to the tracons' assignment of discrete codes to the jump planes second officer that the controllers knew what to expect of the pilots he rpted that the phl terminal radar approach control facility refuses to offer discrete codes. He also stated that phl refuses to coordinate with center but that the other class b tracons do coordinate with their respective ctrs. The rptr asserted that his workload is increased by phl's refusal to coordinate with center causing him to monitor 2 frequencies both of which issue ta's -- sometimes simultaneously.
output: King air jump pilot rpted that he had near midair collision with a heavy jet which he never saw. The rptr does not indicate how he knew that the heavy jet took evasive action to avoid him.

input: Flying the podde departure to the north the altitude restriction for kmart is incorrect. The commercial standard instrument departure chart shows altitude at or above 5500 feet/foot the flight management computer database for the point shows at or above 5000 feet/foot the date range of the database was verified as good. Departure control seemed unsure of the restriction; but upon prompting; verified the correct number was 5500 ft.
output: Capt of b757-200 rpts altitude discrepancy between flight management computer database and published chart at kmart waypoint on the podde area navigation standard instrument departure at dfw.

input: Both aircraft taking off at same time. Both aircraft announced takeoff but neither heard the other's transmission on 122.7. Both aircraft communicated with each other after takeoff and evasive action. We don't know why we didn't hear each other before takeoff wind was more in line with runway(s) 35. We couldn't see each other because of the trees.
output: 2 sma's made simultaneous takeoffs on intersecting runway(s) and had near midair collision trees adjacent to airport runway(s) blocked view of each other in takeoff position. Unable to read each others announcement of takeoff intentions at uncontrolled arpt.

input: During cruise at the noted location we encountered moderate plus mountain wave turbulence. We seated the passengers. We were initially in the clouds and we made a pilot report of loss of 15 knot(s) airspeed. A few minutes later we exited the clouds and were on top of all clouds with clear day visual meteorological conditions conditions. We noted some rotor cloud activity ahead at our 10 o'clock position. It was initially smooth with winds around 30 knot(s) we then encountered a series of strong mountain wave; winds aloft went up to 80 knot(s) and our airspeed gained 20 knot(s) (target + 20); then suddenly lost 50 knot(s) (target -30). We were within a couple of knot(s) of the yellow approach to stall speed and the altitude went up and down 300 feet/foot i believed we were very close to a potential stall and were ready to declare an emergency and [descend to a] lower altitude. After a couple of minutes it smoothed out. We [had come] within a few knot(s) of both overspeed and approach to stall speeds; however; no limits were reached. We reported this info to air traffic control dispatch; and maintenance. Maintenance misinterpreted our call and wrote up an overspeed condition (vmo+20 kts) which was not the case. We were only target speed (.82 mach + 20 kts).
output: A b777 flight crew reported significant airspeed and altitude variation as a result of weather and windshear.

input: While taxiing on tarmac just before turning in to gate at hou hobby; i ran into mud on small strip of grass that was not visible to me or first officer no lights; no visible marking sand not shown on plates. No damage. Towed aircraft out of grass. This airport has barriers all over that aren't lighted or marked. The latest charts do not show the tarmac as it really is. With tarmac and dark and wet; i could not see any visible markings anywhere. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information this incident happened at night. There were no lights marking the taxiways; only barricades. There were no paint lines to follow. Intermediate fix there had not been 2 days of rain; the aircraft would not have sunk into the mud and there would be no rpt. After the aircraft was unloaded; maintenance personnel taxied the aircraft out of the mud. Blue can-like markings were put into place after the aircraft went off of the pavement.
output: An lgt taxied off the edge of an unlit taxiway into soft grass with 1 main gear.

input: It was brought to my attention that some of the wide body belt loaders have had their steps used to climb up on the belt loader relocated from the left to the right side. In doing so this is creating an unsafe situation. After the belt is raised and in position on a wide body. It is extremely dangerous to climb on and off of the belt loader especially during weather events. I am deeply concerned that this will cause a serious injury or worse. I know that we have had fatalities with employees falling off of belt loaders and i do not want to ever see that happen here.
output: Air carrier ramp employee expressed concern about the safety of reconfigured belt loaders.

input: Tkof clearance received from gainesville flight service station specialist was to climb to 2000 feet/foot on runway(s) heading and contact zjx on 134.4 (unctled airport ops). At 1000 feet/foot on clbout 3 attempts were made to contact center with no answer. Aircraft leveled at 2000 feet/foot on runway(s) heading with 1 more attempt to zjx made. A short; broken transmission was heard; which light emitting diode us to believe we were too low to pick them up. Approximately 10-12 mile off the departure end of runway(s) 28 are 3 large towers the largest 1050 feet/foot high. Since we could not contact zjx and due to the close proximitypa of the towers and power plant; we started a left/right (directions) turn to north and began a slow climb while trying to contact center at 3500 feet/foot to 4000 feet/foot we were finally able to contact center on the second attempt after climbing and told them we were climbing out and turning north the controller questioned our last clearance and the reason for deviating from it. We told him we were unable to contact him and that we had become concerned with the ht of the towers we were given a clearance to climb and told to head direct to taylor vor and dme (co-located) radar contact was established at approximately 10000 ft.
output: Clred to climb on runway(s) heading to 2000 feet/foot then unable to contact atc.

input: The ground lighting in sfo is not adequate for clear air turbulence iii operations(s) and should be upgraded. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated sea has low visibility taxi rtes when the visibility is below 1200 feet/foot on runway visual range sfo and lax do not. Sfo operations(s) officer stated there is an advisory circular number 120.57 which covers this subject. Taxi rtes during low visibility operations(s) runway visual range less than 1200 feet/foot facilities have been granted an extension for implementation until jan/96.
output: Sfo airport not in compliance with advisory circular 120 pt 57. Low visibility taxi rtes during low visibility ops.

input: I was on an instrument training flight in visual meteorological conditions in a c172 with a student and was inbound from the procedure turn on the bzn vor and dme (co-located) 12 approach about 2 mile from the airport bzn tower advised he had an air carrier y b727 ready for departure on runway(s) 30 and advised by tower to terminate the approach i acknowledged this and requested a left/right (directions) climbing turn outbound to manni (iaf) for executing the instrument landing system runway(s) 12 approach this was approved by tower with the instruction to maintain visual separation with the air carrier y flight and was cautioned of wake turbulence of the b727. Since the air carrier y departed on runway(s) 30 and was outbound on what i presumed to be the 298 degree radial; i flew parallel to the 298 degree radial an estimated 1 mile to the nw. I had visual on the air carrier y flight at all times until he turned left/right (directions) and crossed behind and below me apparently turning on course. Air carrier y then called bzn tower and complained that i had not maintained visual separation. The air carrier y pilot needs to review federal aviation regulation 91.113 (b) and (f).
output: Nmac between a c172 in level feet/foot outbound parallel to the inbound instrument landing system approach and a b727 climbing out after takeoff and turning below and behind the c172.

input: Was climbing out of sjc off runway(s) 29; headed for rhv. At about 1000 feet/foot on upwind leg; asked controller intermediate fix i could make left/right (directions) turn for rhv. Did not receive a reply but proceeded with the turn; and headed out for rhv. On return; while taxiing back to parking; ground asked me to call tower after parking. Tower then informed me that they had asked me to make a left/right (directions) downwind departure and that my left/right (directions) turn had taken me across the flight path of a b737 taking off from runway(s) 30l. Due to relative inexperience; i misunderstood/did not properly hear this message. Will be more careful in future while communicating with air traffic control especially while entering/departing airspace of busy arpts.
output: Student pilot turns across takeoff path of b737 without clearance at class celsius arpt.

input: Departing 18l from dfw on the soldo 3 standard instrument departure we received a 'lateral mode off' (nav had been selected ; and was in navigate, navigation mode) engine indicating and crew alerting system message in the climb along with the loss of nav data on the mfd. Air traffic control was notified immediately and were given a heading. Very shortly after atc's instructions; all data and info came back online. Continued on; uneventful flight. Air traffic control advised us of no problem and no deviation. Possible satellite signal interruption.
output: Emb135 flight crew experiences a 'lateral mode off' engine indicating and crew alerting system message along with loss of navigation data on the mfd during an area navigation departure. Air traffic control is advised and issues a heading; but within seconds all navigate, navigation data reappears.

input: On clbout at fl260 nyc 134.6; cleared us direct mxe after vectoring us off the airway j75 while awaiting handoff on handoff to nyc 134.32; the new center wanted us to turn left/right (directions) to join j75. We were currently on a heading of 220 degrees direct mxe with an isolated thunderstorm to the left/right (directions) of the aircraft our position was mxe 040/10. We were unable to turn left/right (directions) to join the j75 because of the buildup and advised air traffic control atc insisted we turn left/right (directions) to heading 270 degrees because he had arrs to the left/right (directions) of us and zdc was not taking the next handoff we again told the controller that we were unable to comply. The controller then declared us an emergency and told us to squawk 7700 till the handoff with washington was accomplished. Emergency was declared at xx26z at mxe 040/10 heading 220 degrees and then terminated by zdc at xx31z. It appeared to us that the original nyc 134.6 who cleared us direct mxe did not properly pass the information along to the next controller during the hdof.
output: Flc of a super md80 did not accept air route traffic control center radar controller heading due to severe thunderstorm weather build-up; resulting in air traffic control declaring an emergency for them and assigning a transponder code of 7700 due to heavy traffic in the area. The crew believed that there was insufficient coordination between air traffic control departure and center ctlrs.

input: Upon acceptance of the dispatch release we noticed there was a [maintenance release] defect report stating that the cabin temperature was too warm; and that the crew was unable to control the temperature through normal procedures. The discrepancy report did not indicate whether the aircraft was on the ground; or airborne at the time of the malfunction. The corrective action indicated the fault was corrected and that all temperature perimeters were within the normal range; and that the aircraft was returned to service.with this particular [maintenance release] defect reported the day before; as well as the high surface temperatures; i elected to start both engines and assess cabin temperature from air supplied to the packs directly from the engine-bleeds prior to departure. Since the temperature of the conditioned air as supplied from the auxiliary power unity bleed; as well as the engine bleeds was satisfactory to the entire crew on the ground; we departed on time.at approximately 10;000 feet mean sea level we noticed the temperature of the air leaving the vents on the flight-deck becoming uncomfortably warm. Soon afterward the [lead flight attendant] called and stated same problem was occurring in the cabin.as we were unable to control the temperature normally; i directed the execution of the non-normal checklist for cabin temperature hot. If the cabin temperature cannot be controlled with the non-normal checklist; the procedure eventually requires descent to 10;000 feet mean sea level or below and opening the outflow-valve to allow better ventilation. It also requires an immediate landing at the nearest suitable airport.as we were complying with the non-normal checklist; i immediately [advised atc] in accordance with fom (flight operations manual) 2.10.1 as well as the fact that we would perform an overweight landing. I completed the test briefing with the [lead flight attendant] and the cabin was not prepared for evacuation. We informed the company of our plan to air-return and the passengers were briefed on the situation.we landed at [the departure airport] without incident and taxied to the gate without further assistance. Although temperature within the aircraft was uncomfortably warm; at no time did any crew member; and/or passenger ask for or require medical assistance.we debriefed maintenance personnel in great detail about the malfunction. I also conducted a de-brief in accordance with 'the debrief' checklist card and fom 3.70 with my first officer. Additionally; i called and debriefed the [chief pilot].i would like to take this opportunity to recognize my first officer and my [lead flight attendant] for their professionalism and proficiency during this event. In addition; terminal radar approach control facility as well as arff were outstanding.after a period of 20-minutes after my initial de-brief with the [chief pilot]; i called the [chief pilot] back and informed him that we were fit for duty and elected to continue the flight with another aircraft. We eventually completed the mission and safely delivered our passengers to [their destination].
output: B737ng captain reported that the temperature in the cabin and cockpit was uncontrollable and it became too hot.

input: During descent into our destination the airspeed indicators showed a difference of more than 25 knots. The autopilot failed. Engine control faults were cycling. The anti-ice had been on for a minimum of 15 minutes before entering into the precipitation. Due to conflicting airspeed indications and altitude indications; the first attempt at a landing was abandoned by me calling go around; as we were not established and stable. The second attempt was successful; but we lost communications with air traffic control due to the radio interference from the weather. I believe that this was a circumstantial event; and that maintenance was a large factor; but earlier recognition of the flights disparities would have eased the situation.
output: A c-680 on descent in heavy precipitation developed a 25 knot airspeed discrepancy along with autopilot and engine control malfunctions. A go-around was executed from an unstabilized approach with airspeed and altitude discrepancies.

input: While approaching top of climb fl350 for fl360; number 2 engine rolled back (no stall or noise). [this was] followed by number 3 engine rolling back (slight rumbling sound). I asked the flight engineer if [i] was doing anything to cause this? He replied 'no'. Departing from an airport not frequented by our air carrier; i was thinking about possible fuel contamination and becoming a glider. We immediately performed a rapid restart. The attempt was unsuccessful. I called air traffic control and asked for a descent to fl250. While descending through fl310; we attempted another start; again unsuccessful. As we were passing through fl290 we attempted another start. This start was successful. The engines stabilized; and we elected to continue to [our destination]. [we] contacted air traffic control for climb back to fl360. The rest of the trip was uneventful. The first officer was at the controls. No engine parameters were ever exceeded. No oil pressure lights were ever illuminated.the flight engineer came to me today and informed me that he thought long and hard; and that he remembered having a little different fuel feed going on at the time of the event; and that he had e-mailed the chief pilot about it. (outboard tanks to all engines) he was trying to even out the tanks. I not sure if this had anything to do with this occurrence; but i thought it is best not to omit anything.
output: A b747-200 crew reported that at fl360 the flight engineer was feeding engines 1/2 from the fuel tank 1 and engines 3/4 from the tank 4 when engines 2 and 3 shutdown. The engines were restarted descending through fl290.

input: I was cruising at 5000 feet/foot the air was smooth and the attitude of the airplane never moved from level. Occasionally the altimeter would jump about 100 feet/foot abruptly; then come back to 5000 feet/foot the airspd indicator and vsi would also jump. Zhu rpted that my encoder was showing 4700 feet/foot i replied that i was level 5000 feet/foot i knew i had a static system problem but this airplane wasn't equipped with an alternate static source. It was visual flight rules out and since this was a rental airplane; i didn't want to break the vsi. The altimeter started going crazy and went all the way down to 4400 feet/foot then back up to 4800 feet/foot where it stabilized. When i got on the ground at jan; i discovered the source of the static problem it had been a very longitude day. Before the flight i helped the aircraft owner (a&p and cfi) change the oil in the aircraft i helped put the cowl on and then went inside while he ran up the aircraft i had preflted the aircraft earlier and it was otherwise ready to go. My passenber and i jumped in the aircraft after the owner gave us the thumbs up. I didn't double- checked to verify that the oil civil air patrol was put back on; and it wasn't. Oil had streaked out of the cowling and down the side of the aircraft right over the static port. I cleaned up the mess; added oil and flew home. The encoder was 100-200 feet/foot low when i asked jan approach to give me the altitude showing on the way back to new. When the altimeter started jumping around; i did rpt it to zhu. Relearned an old lesson. Never the recreational uas safety test anyone; always checked the saying about people who assume rings true.
output: Plt of an sma sel aircraft experienced erratic indications of the aircraft transponder altimeter; altimeter; airspd and vertical speed indicators during level flight cruise.

input: We were on the ground at zzz for a prolonged time (approx 1.5 hours) due to a previous flap issue on arrival. After contract maintenance fixed the issue; we taxied to de/anti ice. That took about another 30 minutes before taking off. Prior to departure all takeoff protocol was followed with all checklists completed. The flight management system was set up per the zzz2 rwy xx departure company page of to-1/cmb-1 with flaps 2. We also used anti ice-all; with compact snow for the runway conditions. The terrain maps were configured to both our mfp's as well. Automatic terminal information service was reporting light snow/ 1 to 5 miles visibility with about a 7 kt headwind for runway 19 at the departure time. Temp was around -4 celsius it was also night. The first officer (fo) was the pilot flying. I believe we had around 24 passengers with 9200 pounds of fuel at takeoff. Once cleared to takeoff; we taxied into position on the runway 19 threshold and the first officer conducted a full static takeoff. We rotated towards the last one third of the runway and promptly retracted the gear. The first officer pitched into the flight director with over a thousand foot climb rate. Everything appeared normal. At about approx 30 seconds to a minute into the climb; the terrain aural went off. We then conducted the controlled flight into terrain profile and monitored our climb and speed. I paid particular attention to my resolution advisory which was showing -5 feet. I then looked at our course and we were perfectly centered on the course line and the terrain maps were showing nothing but green ahead. After the terrain warning seemed to be over; i pulled the thrust levers back to the toga detent. Once back in the toga detent; the terrain aural sounded again. Again; we conducted the controlled flight into terrain profile. I scanned my resolution advisory a second time and it still bounced around -5 feet. The terrain overlays on both mfd's still showed only green ahead and around us. Once the terrain aural silenced the second time; the first officer brought the thrust levers back into the toga detent. Tower then switched us over to center. After contacting center and with the terrain warning finally over; the first officer called for and i completed the climb sequence and after t/o checklist. Once everything was stabilized; both the first officer and i discussed at length what happened. We were both in agreement that we experienced an erroneous terrain warning. My resolution advisory continued to have the yellow bar and still showed -5 feet until about 10-15 minutes or 20;000 to 30;00 feet into the flight. The first officer indicated he thought his resolution advisory was faulty as well. Once we landed and were at the gate in zzz; i wrote up the terrain warning and the faulty resolution advisory and i called maintenance control. They had me run the resolution advisory test and returned the aircraft back into service. The controller told me that this can happen when the aircraft taxis on icy and snow covered runways/taxi-ways/ramps. After letting the controller know we had been on the ground in zzz for over two hours with those conditions; he was confident that's what caused our issues. He said when the ice and snow melts off the resolution advisory antennas; the resolution advisory returns back to normal. The subsequent flight to zzz2 was normal. I thought about this event and i'm not sure if i'm supposed to send in an as soon as possible but i finally thought it might be a good idea. Please contact me if you have any questions or need more data. I believe the ra's functioned abnormally due to their antenna's prolonged exposure to snowy and icy conditions on the runway; taxiway; and ramp at zzz airport. I suggest an advisory could be sent out to keep the crews from being startled when this occurs in the conditions explained above. However; remind the aircrews to still comply with the terrain warning; whether it's an erroneous warning or not.
output: Erj-175 captain reported erroneous egpws terrain warning during departure from a mountainous airport departure. Flight crew conducted a controlled flight into terrain profile and completed an uneventful flight to destination where maintenance attributed the warning to the resolution advisory antenna icing.

input: While flying an instrument landing system to runway(s) 4r at bos; air traffic control advised us that a tall masted sailing ship was in the channel. We replied that we had the ship in sight moving from (our) left/right (directions) to (our) left/right (directions) to the left/right (directions) of ctrline. As we flew over the channel the ship was just slightly to the left/right (directions) of the instrument landing system ctrline. The capt deviated slightly to the left/right (directions) and stayed slightly above the glide path. I observed the ship through the capt's left/right (directions) aft window as we went by. After landing we were notified that tower observed some damage to the top of the ship by wake turb.
output: Wake turbulence encounter.

input: When i studied the operating manual i read about the company's takeoff minimums and departure minimums. The takeoff minimums in some cases are less than standard. En route i listened to automatic terminal information service prior to my approach to maf. It said 1600' runway visual range and 0' ceiling. Somehow i mixed up my takeoff and my departure minimums and instead of 2400' runway visual range that is needed to even start the approach i began the approach at 1600' runway visual range approach controller said; 'clred for instrument landing system runway(s) 10. Runway visual range now is rpted 1500. That's right at minimum; isn't it?'; and that even made me more sure of my minimum. I replied; 'clred for runway(s) 10 instrument landing system and that's right at minimum;' and began my approach i saw the rabbit at 200' above ground level runway(s) threshold lights at 100' above ground level i landed; parked. No more was said until my fellow pilot told me i busted minimums. I got the manual out and studied it again and found out he was right. Lesson learned and action to avoid such a problem in future is to study your manual even more carefully and make sure you understand fully before entering instrument flight rules conditions with probably low minimums.
output: Atx smt made an instrument landing system approach to maf using takeoff runway visual range instead of landing runway visual range as airport minimums for lndg.

input: Dfw approach control (d10) started a handoff to me on aircraft x when i was working local control east and north combined. I saw aircraft x scratch pad that the aircraft wanted a downtown tour of the dallas skyline. I called the d10 controller to inform him that aircraft x cannot proceed with a downtown tour in the north flow (ry 31l/r) operations per our local standard operating procedures. The d10 controller said 'since when'. I told him it's been in effect for the last four or five years. His respond was 'oh; come on' and he hung up on me. The d10 controller took back the handoff and allowed aircraft x to proceed into my airspace for the downtown tour; without prior coordination or a point-out. I had another aircraft y who was on the letter of agreement (dinner tour) and is allowed to maneuver close to the downtown dallas skyline. When aircraft y started his southeast bound turn to parallel the finals to dallas love field at 1;500 feet (safe operation) he was in conflict with aircraft x; who i was not talking to. I called the d10 controller to get aircraft x out of my airspace; since aircraft y was only 4 miles northwest of aircraft x at 1;500 feet on converging courses. The d10 controller completely ignored my multiple calls to get his aircraft x out of my airspace. After 'screaming' over the landlines; i did observe aircraft x making a turn towards the southwest to leave my airspace and avert a conflict with aircraft y.in my career of working in multiple centers; approach controls and towers i have never seen another controller blatantly disregard another controllers request and arrogantly violated another controllers airspace. About 45 minutes earlier i had a d10 controller handoff another small aircraft for the downtown tour over dfw. I told him; i could not accept the handoff due to our local standard operational procedures not allowing downtown tours in the north flow. He seemed unaware of our local procedures but complied with my explanation. I recommend that when dallas love field management implement new procedures all surrounding facilities and customers know about our new procedures. I had a bonanza depart off the addison airport (6 miles north of dallas love field) requesting a downtown tour of the dallas skyline during this same session; working local control as stated above. Once again; i told the bonanza pilot i could not approve his request due to our local operating procedures. The bonanza pilot told me 'since when'. Once again; i had to apologize and inform him it's been in effect for four or five years. To correct this problem in the future; and avoid further conflicts between controllers and pilots; dallas love field management must inform adjacent facilities and pilots of our new procedures. No more thinking management can put these major procedural changes in a read and initial binder and expect controllers in both facilities to remember the new procedures. Many times new controllers at the new facility have no idea what was in the read and initial binder years ago. To ensure new major procedural changes are implemented correctly and avoid confusion to the users. Management must put these new procedures in a letter of agreement and not a read and initial binder. Controllers can't remember everything they have read in a read and initial binder years ago. But controllers do look at the letter of agreements to refresh their memories. For the pilots to remember our new operations we need to update the 'facilities directives' or 'green book'. I realize it would be difficult for management to classify every procedural change as major or non-major. But we owe it to our new controllers and customers the latest up to date information so everyone will be on the same page. Last but not least someone in management needs to talk to the d10 controller and explain to him his actions are not acceptable and completely unprofessional. This is one 'faa' and we must allwork together to make this the safest system possible. The federal aviation administration cannot afford or allow individual controllers to deliberately break the rules at their own discretion and not suffer the consequences for their actions. Just listen to the tapes and everyone will hear the blatant negligence of one arrogant d10 controller. It's obvious some controllers do not think rules apply to them.
output: Dal tower controller reports of an airspace violation by a d10 controller. The d10 controller then has his aircraft become a conflict for the dal controller's aircraft. The d10 controller wanted his aircraft to be able to do a downtown tour; but due to the runway configuration at dal it was not approved.

input: Fo landing runway(s) 23r at ind. Landing uneventful; though there had been mixed precipitation earlier; and the temperature was about freezing. Braking action was good on the runway(s) and we rolled slowly to the end of the runway(s) as we turned off the runway(s) at a crawl; we completely lost traction. The aircraft slid off the side of taxiway a12. Braking and steering were nil. We were prepared for poor braking during landing and knew the txwys would most likely be worse.
output: Md80 super 80 slides off taxiway as they turn off the runway(s) after landing they were taxiing at a crawl and completely lost traction.

input: No violations of any type occurred on this flight. Informational only; i've noticed on the pecan 1a and ocean 2a departures out of vhhh that each of these sids load with '5;000 feet/foot and below restrictions' (5;000b in fmc) for the first two waypoints (porpa; ramen on pecan 1a; porpa; td on ocean 2a) even though on the respective 'paper' sids neither of these restrictions exist. The only altitude restriction on the standard instrument departure is the 5;000 feet/foot initial climb clearance just below the plan view; but it does not state anywhere on these sids that those above mentioned intersections have to be crossed at or below 5;000 feet/foot the potential problem is that once hong kong departure clears one to an altitude above 5;000 feet/foot with the mode control panel is in vertical navigation (as it normally is); the aircraft will try to level off at 5;000 feet/foot until passing the second waypoint (ramen; td) even though it is not required. Further; on my last flight out of hong kong; the controller told us to climb to 'xx;000 unrestricted' (note: the controller did not say 'speed unrestricted;' he stated 'climb unrestricted' and it was to an altitude well above 5;000 ft) which would imply that there was some sort of altitude restriction that we otherwise would have had to comply with. None of us in the cockpit were aware that a restriction existed per the standard instrument departure nor were we given one in our initial clearance. So i'm submitting this report so that the '5;000b' restrictions can be removed from the sids in the flight management computer if they're not supposed to be there. A cockpit crew could get distracted with the autopilot on and not notice the plane isn't climbing when it should be if given a higher altitude by air traffic control leading to an altitude bust. If hand flying; the flight director will pitch for a level-off at 5;000 feet/foot when in fact the plane should be climbing to whatever altitude cleared to above 5;000 feet/foot if the '5;000b' is supposed to be in the flight management computer for the porpa; ramen; or td intersections and i'm missing something. I'd like to know where those 5;000 feet/foot or below restrictions can be found. If the location of these restrictions for these intersections is somewhere obscure (buried in a 10-1 page?); then a note should be placed on the 10-7 page for hong kong.
output: A pilot departing vhhh noted that the pecan 1a and ocean 2a have 5;000 feet/foot ramen and porpa climb constraints specified in the flight management system area navigation procedure; but while a 5;000 feet/foot is a general climb constraint; it does not appear to be associated with waypoints.

input: I was an a320 first officer on short call reserve and started a reserve assignment period (rap) at xa:00 [local] at my home. At xj:26 [local]; i was called by crew scheduling to fly. On the initial call; i expressed reservations about having sufficient time to arrive at the airport and fly the sequence before the end of my reserve duty period (rdp); as i lived two hours drive-time away; but not having the information in front of me; i didn't definitively know; so i accepted the assignment. After hanging up; i went to my computer and reviewed the sequence and saw that the computer was showing that my rdp would expire at xp:00 [local]. I called crew scheduling back at xj:34 [local]; where i was eventually transferred to a supervisor. I expressed my reservations about being assigned to this flight; as i did not think i had adequate time to get down to zzz and preflight the aircraft before i would time out. At that time; the computer data for the flight showed a departure time of xk:00 [local] (with a generated sign-in time of xj:00 [local]; which was 26 minutes before the first time i was called) and a land time xn:32 [at destination airport]. I realized that i wouldn't be leaving the house until xk:00 [local] at the earliest; and knowing that in perfect weather and traffic conditions; that it takes just under two hours to drive from my house to the parking garage at zzz airport. I did quick math and realized that if a xk:00 [local] departure time would result in a xn:32 [destination airport] land time; then a xm:00 [local] departure time would mean a xp:32 land time; leaving only 28 minutes of legality. I stated that that was for a xm:00 [local] departure time. Best case; i would be arriving at the parking garage at xm:00 [local]; not pushing back from the gate at that time. I made it very clear in this conversation that i would not be arriving at the airport until; best case; xm:00 [local]. I was informed by the supervisor that the computer showed a xm:42 [local] maximum off time (mot); and that the trip was therefore legal and that i had to take it. Because of this sense of urgency; i stopped my inquiries with the supervisor and hurried to get ready and leave; and with the delays from the second phone call and from driving at night on wet roads; i did not park at the parking garage at zzz until xm:24 [local]. While removing the bags from my truck; i was called by my captain to inform me that we had been cancelled. After he told me this; he told me that something had seemed wrong about this from the start; and that he had been looking at the federal aviation regulation 117 rules regarding flight duty periods (fdp) and rdps; and that he realized that i was never legal for this trip from the start.as stated above; i began my rap for the day at xa:00 [local]. I was initially called by crew scheduling at xj:26 [local] for what showed in the computer as a xk:00 [local] departure; with a xj:00 [local] sign-in (in other words; the sign-in time in the computer was 26 minutes before i was even called). I notified the scheduler that i was two hours away from the airport; but no times were changed in the system. When i called back at xj:34 [local] for my eight minute phone call with a supervisor; i also informed them that i lived two hours drive-time away; and that i would not be arriving at the airport until at or after xm:00 [local]. Even though i had repeatedly stated that i could not arrive at the airport any earlier than xm:00 [local] (and had i been sitting in my truck; with engine running; in uniform; bags loaded; when they first called at xj:26 [local]; i could not have arrived any earlier than xl:30 [local] with perfect road conditions). The only change to the departure time was that a delay of 15 minutes was entered at xj:42 [local] (the time that the phone call with the supervisor ended); making the new departure time xk:15 [local].these artificial departure times (of xk:00 [local]; later changed to xk:15 [local] after my phone call to the supervisor) showed me to be legal for a trip when in fact i was not legal. The xl:00 [local] and xk:15 [local] departure times created xj:00 and xj:15 [local] sign-in times. With a scheduled sign-in time between xj:00-xj:59 [local]; the maximum fdp is 11 hours and the maximum rdp is 15 hours; meaning that my rdp was legal until xp:00 [local]. However; since i wasn't even called the first time until xj:26 [local]; and that i had repeatedly stated that i lived two hours drive-time away; my scheduled sign-in time should have been no earlier than xl:30 [local]; or even more accurately; the estimated xm:00 [local] arrival time that i told them. If; after my phone call with the crew scheduling supervisor; the departure time for the flight had been changed to accurately reflect my estimated xm:00 [local] arrival at the parking garage as opposed to a completely inaccurate and useless 15 minute departure delay; then i would have immediately shown in the computer as being illegal for the trip; as with a sign-in time of xl:00-xo:59 [local]; the maximum fdp is 9 hours and the maximum rdp is 13 hours; meaning that my rdp would have expired at xn:00 [local]; well before the xp:00 [local] time that the computer was generating and that crew scheduling was using in assigning me the trip. Whether this incremental departure time change of xk:00 [local] to xk:15 [local] at the end of my phone call was done in ignorance or with knowledge aforethought; it set me up to fly an illegal flight. This illegal flight was only avoided by sheer luck; as had i not had reservations about having sufficient time and had i also been ready to immediately walk out the door after the first phone call; even with the imperfect road conditions; i would have likely arrived at the airport around xl:50 [local] with enough time to rush and possibly make the inaccurate xm:43 [local] mot (a mot based upon a rdp that expired at xp:00 [local] and not xm:00 [local]).this event occurred due to inaccurate times entered into the computer by crew scheduling; and an extreme sense of urgency from crew scheduling for me to leave the house and begin my drive; resulting in me just accepting the rdp times generated by the computer and not checking the fdp/rdp times myself.after being informed of the pilot's estimated arrival time (or at a minimum; the global positioning system derived drive-time); crew scheduling must immediately update departure and sign-in times accordingly in order to allow the computer to generate accurate legality times.
output: An air carrier first officer reported that artificial departure times showed a pilot to be legal for a trip when in fact the pilot was not legal.

input: While tracking the 138 degree radial to oak (116.8) on the jaws arrival, arrive to sjc at approximately 27-30 vor and dme (co-located) norcal approach cleared us to descend from 6000 feet/foot to 5000 feet/foot we received a terrain warning at approximately 5300 feet/foot i instructed the first officer flying to climb and rpted this to approach we were mostly visual flight rules and could see we were not in close proximitypa to the ground thinking that our equipment was possibly faulty; i inquired of approach intermediate fix they had any other aircraft rpt this problem approach indicated that several other aircraft had experienced the same warning. After landing i telephoned the approach control to discuss this. They have had complaints from other aircraft but said their minimum vectoring altitude was 4500 feet/foot in the area. We were approximately 10 nautical mile sw of sjc. The minimum safe altitude for sjc is 5500 feet/foot on the approach chart. I recommended to the supervisor that they investigate this apparent problem no separation deviation occurred.
output: A visual meteorological conditions descending md80 flight crew experiences and reacts to a ground proximity warning system alert at 5300 feet/foot about 10 nautical mile se of sjc; ca.

input: In sum: an atx pilot made an nondirectional radio beacon approach to runway(s) 34 at ciu; being under control of czyz. He lost contact with czyz at very low altitude as was to be expected by both parties. Due to navigate, navigation difficulties; the pilot was well off course when he broke out below and made a circling approach to runway(s) 16 and landed successfully. Czyz lectured him very harshly when he departed later. A phone call to a czyz supervisor straightened things out. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following: further investigation by the rptr centered on one of the alternators but then a bad antenna coupler was found on the automatic direction finder the general consensus of the pilots that fly into ciu regularly; is that the nondirectional radio beacon is rather weak. Only 3 mile away is an instrument landing system running parallel to this nondirectional radio beacon approach at cyam. Czyz controls both airports and; in this incident; was very concerned that there was an aircraft groping around that it had no control over or communications with. The czyz controller that talked with the rptr over the air was not as polite as the manual says that he should be.
output: An atx frt pilot had trouble completing an nondirectional radio beacon approach because of a faulty antenna coupler.

input: I was given taxi instructions to runway(s) 9l. I have flown in and out of oakland for over 10 yrs but never departed from the 9 runway(s) -- always 27r and 27l. It was very poorly marked and consequently i went past the intersection had to turn around; go over the end of an intersecting runway(s) (33) to get to number 9. In second officer doing i apparently went beyond 9l and was proceeding towards 9r when the controller advised me to continue on to 9r and cleared me for takeoff this is a very confusing area that should be more clrly marked. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he was on taxiway j and cleared to cross 33. Looking for a runway(s) he crossed 9l. As he looked at diagram after the fact; it seems impossible to cross 33 via j. He received a call from federal aviation administration inspector who said they have had problems with this taxiway area. Inspector suggested he go back and look over the area to see where he failed. Rptr did second officer with an instructor and requested 33 departure confirmed it is impossible to cross 33 from the stated taxiway. Signs are not clrly visible. When he called inspector back and told him the situation; inspector stated there was a group checkeding over the situation at that time. Inspector stated probably some remedial work would be required. Rptr asked; what are we going to do; go out and taxi all over the arpt? He has since been told no further action will be taken.
output: Sma taxies past desired taxiway; turns. Air traffic control clears to cross runway(s) 33; rptr crosses runway(s) 9l.

input: We pushed back with proper weights from load planning that showed we were legal. While climbing out we received a second set of weights that showed we were a thousand pounds heavier than we thought we were. These came in over the cockpit automatic communications addressing & reporting system printer 19 minutes after liftoff. Why we got corrected weights 19 minutes after liftoff is unknown to me; as this is not a safe way to operate.
output: An a319 flight crew was surprised to receive revised takeoff weight data well after having taken off.

input: After pushback and prior to taxi; we received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message that indicated we were out of balance and needed to block row 39. Prior to taxi these passengers were moved. During rotation; i noticed that the airplane was rather pitch sensitive. After the airplane was cleaned up; the airplane continued to be pitch sensitive. I noticed these same characteristics during the approach and landing. Additionally; the pitch trim system activated twice on approach. These two instances occurred below 1500 feet. I have never seen the pitch trim system activate during a low power phase of flight. I suspect that the airplane was still out of balance.
output: A b737 weight and balance blocked row 39 but during flight the aircraft was pitch sensitive and the pitch trim system activated trim during approach at low power. Balance may have been near the limit the entire flight.

input: Chked weather in zzz2 to find it marginal at best. Pulled release and found; once again; that the dispatcher realized that an alternate airport was needed due to conditions but the hold fuel column had not been amended to reflect current conditions per management direction not to change holding 'profiles' which had been recently reduced by more than half. 10 minute(s) of hold fuel remained unchanged because management is pressuring dispatch to fly with limited hold fuel to reduce 'costs.' 10 minute(s) of hold fuel into an airport with marginal conditions because the dispatcher does not want his/her name on the fuel list for the week printed and hung by management contacted dispatcher and after 'capt requested it' fuel was begrudgingly added to 20 minute(s) to accurately reflect the conditions. Low weather at an international destination with few alternatives close by and no gas to hold. Get management out of the dispatch process and stop pressuring dispatchers to cut fuel to below safe and normal levels. Create a profile for holding based on reality not bonus program of a few in mgmnt.
output: A emb135 pilot's int'l destination forecast marginal weather but dispatch chose 10 minute(s) of hold fuel to save money. Flight crew obtained an increase to 20 min.

input: With takeoff clearance tower rpted runway visual range 700 feet/foot after takeoff i knew something was out of place and rechked dispatch release. We had no takeoff alternate listed. Takeoff briefing before engine start had taken current weather conditions including a trend to lower visibility. Was preoccupied at departure end of runway(s) with tower ignoring our calls ready for takeoff tower was ignoring to help another air carrier who was in holding bay and not ready to receive a takeoff clearance before us. This type of unequal handling can be very distracting when it is second officer blatantly done.
output: Mdt was dispatched without a takeoff alternate in lowering visibility conditions. The capt had briefed for the weather at the time of departure yet did not notice that the alternate was not specified. Airport minimums for alternate airport takeoff alternate.

input: During the preflight exterior inspection damage to the number 2 engine cowling was discovered/failure of the material used to construct the inside of the cowling near the tips of the fan blades/a hole developed. The damaged engine cowling was placed on deferral using a tear down inspection ('tdi') as there isn't a cdl that applies. Aircraft was returned to service with the hole still in the cowling; no repair attempts were made before flights with revenue passengers on board. Subsequent flight crews operating aircraft may easily miss the damage to the number 2 cowling if the fan blades were parked in a manner that covered the hole. Tdis are not listed on dispatch release and there are no placards anywhere on the aircraft identifying the damage to alert the next crew. Please review and respond...was this the correct way to 'fix' this particular mechanical discrepancy? At the very least; please list all tdis on the dispatch release and highlight them on the cover of the aircraft logbook so that each crew is fully aware of the current condition of their aircraft. Furthermore; in hindsight i have concerns regarding the safe operation of company aircraft that are dispatched for revenue flights with holes developing in the engine cowling; cowling material eroding away without predictability - just millimeters away from spinning fan blades inside the engine cowling.
