output: A320 captain reported a hole was discovered on the inside cowling of the number 2 engine during the exterior inspection. Aircraft placed on a work order and returned to service with hole still in cowling. Captain is concerned about this procedure.

input: Clbing out of fl230; i observed an 'a' system low pressure light illumination along with the master caution. I requested to level off at fl250 and it was granted. Upon leveloff; the autoplt was disengaged; at which time i checkeded the quick reference handbook for the 'a' system low pressure illumination. The instructions were to turn the appropriate switch off; which was done. After a short time; the 'a' system pressure gauge needle began to fluctuate back and forth. At this time the quick reference handbook was reviewed for an 'a' system failure and the appropriate action was taken. The aircraft flew fine and there were no other problems associated with the aircraft maintenance control was notified and the situation reviewed. The weather was good and there was no known turbulence and none forecast for the route from zzz1 to zzz2. The chief pilot's office was also notified through dispatch; at my request; to make sure they agreed with my decision to continue on to zzz1. The aircraft was stable and felt solid on the controls aircraft x was hand flown back to zzz2 by myself and landed with emergency personnel standing by. The first was also instructed that we were going to treat this as an emergency and that we would be using the brace position for landing callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated when on the ground hydraulic fluid was all over the left/right (directions) side of the aircraft from the main wheel well aft. The rptr said maintenance later advised the loss of 'a' system was caused by a chaffed line in the left/right (directions) wing root aft spar; midway between the wheel well and the left/right (directions) engine the rptr stated this area cannot be inspected on a preflt checked unless the flaps were down and the spoilers extended and locked.
output: A b737-200 in climb at fl230 lost 'a' system hyds pressure and quantity. Caused by chaffed pressure line in left/right (directions) wing root aft spar.

input: Upon returning to cvg we shot the instrument landing system runway(s) 36l; ceiling was approximately 300 feet/foot overcast and visibility about 1 statute mile runway visual range was rpted for runway(s) 36l at 4000 feet/foot in snow and blowing snow. After contacting the tower inside the outer marker tower rpted braking action fair; rpted by several previous aircraft upon taxiing off the runway(s) my first officer (who did the lndg) rpted braking action fair. On our taxi to the fixed-base operator we were instructed to hold short of runway(s) 27 for departing traffic as we approached the hold short line for runway(s) 27; my first officer (who was taxiing) applied the brakes and we started skidding; he released the brakes and reapplied them -- still another skid and then we stopped 1/2 way through the hold short line. As we came to a stop; i looked up and saw the departing aircraft from runway(s) 27 lifting off. There was no conflict with the departing aircraft and just as i was going to rpt to ground that we skidded 1/2 way through the hold short line; he cleared us to cross runway(s) 27. I did rpt braking action poor on that taxiway but did not mention sliding 1/2 way through the hold line. We were probably about 10 feet/foot over the line. I took for granted that the braking action was fair on the taxiway since it was fair on the runway(s) bad assumption.
output: Flc of lr35 is unable to stop at hold line to hold short of runway(s) they had to cross during taxi due to poor braking action.

input: All chklist and procedures were routine. Engs start and cleared for pwrback from gate x at memphis; tn. All hand signals were promptly followed. At the come ahead signal i came out of reverse and waited for the taxi signal from the ground signalman. It did not come--a hold signal followed. From the action on the ramp i realized that something had occurred behind my aircraft unable to get any information from company radio. An agent yelled up that my aircraft had struck another (lgt) parked at gate y. At this time a f/a came to the cockpit and asked intermediate fix everything was ok. She stated that an unusual noise was heard from the rear of the aircraft f/a and passenber informed of problem engs were shut down and we were towed back to original gate. Logbook entries complete and chklist completed. A verbal rpt was made to flight dispatch. Aircraft change completed and flight continued to ord. Contributing factors: it is unusual to have an lgt on this gate. The lgt extends further out into taxi area than an mlg (normally at this gate). Also; my mlg model is longer than other mlg coming off of gate x. We are not allowed to use brakes to stop rearward motion. Aircraft could have been stopped via brakes intermediate fix signalman thought we were not stopping fast enough. Aircraft did continue back a few feet/foot coming to forward thrust. I did not realize that we had contacted anything and i believe our signalman did not realize this until pointed out. Damage: mlg left horizontal stabilizer trim tabs (dent/cut) and lgt upper rudder trim tab; right side (visual inspection only). Corrective action: 1) push back at all time using intercom. 2) not allowing pwrback by mlg and lgt when they are on opp gate since they; by their combined length; allow less maneuvering and stopping room. During company meeting with chief pilot i was informed that the company control tower (ramp) saw this incident about to happen. Also; the wingwalker saw the contact coming. He started running towards the cockpit to warn me/forward signalman (one i was watching). (i cannot see the wingwalker during pwrback.) wingwalker did not appear in my line of sight in time. I recommended to the chief pilot that an emergency stop hand signal for the wingwalker (to forward signalman) be used second officer capt could stop rearward movement by brakes. In my case only problem to result would be an upset (and possible injury to the f/a). They were standing; giving safety announcements. Braking when going rearward would probably result in nose strut extention. A standard signal to tighten or open the turn radius would also give signalman more control to direct capt. At present; signal is only to turn left or right; not amount of turn desired.
output: Struck aircraft parked at gate during powerback maneuver.

input: A t38 was northeast bound to bab restricted at 3500 feet/foot on a course to pass behind a b737 and just south of smf. The b737 was on the wraps5 arrival at 3000 feet/foot under control of the final controller. Traffic was issued to the t38 on the b737 and reported insight. The expo (east smf departure) controller advised me to keep the t38 out of the departure area. I advised the t38 and asked him to pass behind the b737 and fly northwest bound or keep the b737 to his right and fly northwest bound. The t38 replied he was already behind the traffic. While advising the final controller of the t38's intentions so they could advise the b737; i did not hear the t38 report that he was 'descending to de-conflict'. I pointed out the t38 to smf tower; asked him his altitude. The t38 reported descending through 1700 feet/foot he was 500 feet/foot above and behind the b737 and descended through the b737. I asked the t38 if he could maintain visual flight rules at 1500 feet/foot so he would not climb back through the b737. The t38 response was affirmative. I restricted the t38 to 1500 feet/foot transferred radar and radio communication to the final controller. I did not feel there were any procedural or equipment problems. I was advised upon returning to work; that the b737 had filed a near midair collision report. Recommendation; t38 was restricted above and advised he was passing behind the b737. Why he decided he needed to descend through the b737 is unclear.
output: Nct controller described a conflict event between a t38 and a b737 operating near smf when the t38; instructed to remain above and behind the b737; elected to descend through the occupied altitude.

input: Zjx put us on a vector to deviate east of a line of thunderstorms that stretched sw to ne through northern florida and georgia. Numerous aircraft were deviating east of the line; center gave us a radar vector of 215 degrees then told us to squawk 7700. As we were on a vector we followed his instructions. Other aircraft were also told to squawk 7700. We were clear of the weather on the east side of the line. We were concerned when the controller told us and other aircraft to squawk transponder code 7700; that he may have vectored us into a military restrict, restricted, restriction area.
output: A b727-200 pic's rpt on zjx controller having the flight squawk code 7700 when aircraft had been vectored into the military warning area during weather avoidance procedures east of sav; ga.

input: I was made aware that an engine was not properly secured after a flight with flight crew not in the immediate area. In trying to recall the events of that flight; i cannot recall specially if we shut the engine down or not and if an appropriate checklist was completed or not. I [did] know that this was the last leg of a four day and i was hoping to catch a flight home; and was feeling rushed to complete tasks so that i could duty out. It is likely that in my haste to pack things up and get out of the cockpit as quickly as possible; that we missed shutting down one of the engines and forgot to complete a checklist. I remember saying my goodbyes to the captain still sitting in his seat as i left the aircraft; whom i presumed would run the power down checklist. Also in my haste i forgot to do a post flight walk around. During the course of the trip; the captain had done a handful of post flights for me after taking a smoke break outside. This break from my usual flow; and added to my haste to catch a flight caused me to forget to do a post walk around that would have surely caught an unsecured engine.the main undesired state in this event was having an engine running without flight crew present. This was caused by being hurried and rushed to try and get the aircraft secured and shutdown as quickly as possible which resulted in errors of not properly completing checklists.specifically for commuting pilots; or pilots trying to get home fast; there is a sense of get there as quickly as possible. These moments should be recognized for their propensity to cause mistakes. Normal items that you do daily with regularity can be overlooked. In the future i will tell myself in these situations that nothing is more important that the safety of those on board and on the ground; and to just slow down and make sure everything is completed per the checklist and our om.
output: Crj-200 first officer reported they failed to complete power down checklist resulting in the engine operating with no flight crew onboard.

input: 10/sat/91 i was advised that on 10/tue/91 a flight i had built a release for had the incorrect aircraft sent to the pilot and filed with air traffic control release stated mlg type a; but actual aircraft was a different manufacturer mlg. Flight departed 1 hour 45 minute(s) after i was off shift. Dispatcher on duty was not notified of change by coordinator; therefore release was not amended and flight remained (and flew) as filed as a type a. The change of equipment occurred at xx ante meridiem local dispatcher on duty was notified of wrong equipment at the down line station.
output: Wrong aircraft type identified on dispatch release and filed flight plan.

input: Weather - clear beautiful flying day low wind; great visibility unlimited ceiling. Traffic - heavy traffic converging on un-towered airport from multiple directions and altitudes. Flight situation - initial approach was cautious due to traffic; got in the pattern and extended downwind to space landing traffic. At this point an aircraft (experimental rv-7 i believe) cut in front of me from above with smoke trailing and landed. I offset to the right of the airport flew to mid field turned right and executed a 360 gained 500 [ft.] above pattern and crossed the airport to re-enter the pattern on the other side (for normal left traffic for runway xx wind calm). I made common traffic advisory frequency announcements when i left final; when i did my 360 and when i crossed mid field stating my intentions to enter a downwind from a 45. As i crossed the runway no traffic was visible in the downwind. After crossing the airport i made a tight right 360 to lose 500 feet and enter the downwind at 2;400 [ft.]. Upon rollout i realized traffic had overtaken me from the left in the pattern during my maneuver. The traffic was directly in front of me and slightly higher. It was at a close but manageable distance. I immediately began slowing down to increase separation. The leading traffic reduced speed faster than i could reduce speed closing our gap to an unsafe distance. I then veered right and descended to avoid the traffic. The leading traffic also veered right and i lost visual tracking of the traffic; and could only see his shadow on the ground. The pilot asked where i was and i told him i had descended and veered right to gain separation. I then veered further right to provide additional separation. The leading traffic was later identified as a c150/152. There was an a36 bonanza behind me in the downwind at this point. I believed the safest thing to do was to stay to the right of the leading traffic and extend downwind to allow the leading traffic to land. I made additional common traffic advisory frequency announcements to communicate my intentions to the traffic. Contributing factors - loss of traffic awareness due to traffic data loss on gns530 in our aircraft. Human performance issues - heavy workload: heavy traffic from multiple directions and altitudes; uncontrolled airspace; evading previous potential incident. Human performance issues - hazardous attitude: the leading traffic was a student with a certified flight instructor they demonstrated anti-authority attitude and a lack of situational awareness as they cut us off in the pattern. They did not accept that their intention to pass on the left was unsafe.
output: C172 pilot reported a near midair collision with traffic failing to operate with proper pattern procedure which resulted in taking evasive action.

input: During an audit it was found my logbook review was past due and that my maintenance release had dropped off my maintenance record.
output: A technician rpts dispatching aircraft in non compliance due to an audit discovering logbook review and maintenance release authority/authorized expired.

input: I was conducting a discovery flight. Prior to start the engine i completed a through pre-flight inspection. After engine start i let it warm up for 10 minutes. Then i was on hold by the ground control another 5 minutes due to heavy traffic. The engine run up and take off was normal. We flew 10 miles west of the airport for the sight seeing discovery flight. There was no indication of any kind of engine trouble. During our flight back to the airport; 2.5 miles from the airport the aircraft engine started to surge up and down. I performed checklist items for emergency and verified all items need to be checked and secured. Then about 20 seconds later engine completely stopped running. I declared emergency and set up for a power off landing to the airport. I tried to restart the engine. It started for 10 seconds and started to surge again and shut off again. Then i briefed the passenger for emergency landing. I started to lose altitude and i realized that i did not have enough altitude to glide to the airport safely. So; after a quick search i found a remote grassy field suitable for a safe landing west of the airport. I used 65 mph recommended by the aircraft poh glide airspeed and landed safely. Then i called air traffic control to let them know our location and we are safe. There was no damage to the aircraft and no bodily injury to the passenger. In the future i will be attending safety seminars held by local federal aviation administration offices.
output: Lsa pilot reports engine failure while returning to the airport after conducting a discovery flight with a passenger. When it is discovered that the airport cannot be reached a grassy field is chosen and a successful off airport landing ensues. No damage results.

input: While cruising at fl350 had a cabin pressurization failure; deviating around weather had communications problem with air traffic control could not hear them until we came out of the weather they could hear us. Declared emergency started descent diverted to zzz.
output: A communication problem with air traffic control reported by a dc-9 crew during a loss of pressurization event while deviating around weather.

input: B737 at fl310; wbound on taxiway j6. Crj2 at fl350; wbound on taxiway j6; about 6.5 mile in trail. They were the same speed winds at the 2 altitudes were the same. Crj2 destination is sdf; which standard operating procedure says needs to enter the next sector at fl280. I issued a descent to crj2 and continued to watch the speeds they remained the same through fl330. Traffic was increasing; second officer i took care of some other things and came back. I noticed crj2 had accelerated to 470 knot(s) from 445 knot(s) ground speed i thought maybe it was a bad radar return; second officer i watched 2 more updates. Ground speed increased further to 485 knot(s) even though crj2 was slightly north of b737 track; i was forced to turn crj2 30 degrees left/right (directions) across b737's tail; due to conflicting fl330 aircraft ebound. I issued 30 degrees left/right (directions) to b737. Crj2 continued to increase ground speed to 495 knot(s) second officer i issued a 180 degree heading to crj2. I got no conflict alert until aedp went off. After getting the aircraft apart; i got them back on course.
output: Zid controller watches conflict developing between a descending carj and a level; en route b737.

input: Apching the dixon nondirectional radio beacon we received faulty bearing to the station. We were to join j174 after diw. Approximately 20 mile south i asked zdc for a heading to join the airway south of orf. This request was denied; as was our request for direct. To continue to fly j174 off the diw nondirectional radio beacon required a 40 degree turn to the westbound after this maneuver; we were directed back to a 040 degree heading and an air carrier aircraft was turned to the westbound factors to event: diw is a poor navigational aid global positioning system is not installed on these aircraft i did not ensure my request to air traffic control was clrly understood.
output: B737 crew has difficulty using an nondirectional radio beacon in the high altitude structure for navigate, navigation when signal is weak. Traffic conflict was the result.

input: Taxiing into park; at gate our ltt aircraft bumped wing tips (overlapped) with the next ltt aircraft on the left/right (directions) myself; as the first officer told the capt to 'slow down; we're pretty close.' then followed up with shouting 'stop!' the qualified ramper was still signaling to come forward. The capt put on the brakes and yet the aircraft still lunged 4 or 5 inches forward to meet with the adjacent acft's wing tip. Even after the 2 wing tips had met; the qualified ramper was still signaling us to come forward. Insignificant damage was sustained by both wing tips. Nonetheless; company policy called for a change of both wing tips. The parking arrangements on the company airline ramp are completely unsatisfactory. Measures are being taken to change the layout of aircraft position on the ramp. Also; further on-the-job- training is being dispersed to all the individual rampers. The ramper that was directing us into our 'parking space' has since been fired.
output: Commuter ltt hit wing tip to wing tip with company aircraft on the next ramp pos.

input: We initially attempted the instrument landing system prm (precision runway monitor) runway xxl approach into zzz. We subsequently went missed approach due to not having the landing environment in sight at the decision altitude. No abnormal navigation issues occurred during this approach. After executing the air traffic control climb out instructions; we were given vectors for the instrument landing system prm runway xy as the weather was improving. We reprogrammed and re-briefed the approach for instrument landing system runway xy. We were given a vector of approximately 300 degrees to intercept the runway xy localizer and subsequently cleared for the approach. As we started to intercept the localizer; the lateral deviation indicator started acting erratically and thus the autopilot started banking left and right to attempt to regain the localizer. The pilot flying noticed immediately and attempted to correct back on localizer centerline. Simultaneously; the pilot monitoring notified air traffic control that we were having a navigation issue. The prm monitor advised to correct back to centerline which we were doing. We were never deviated more than 1/2 dot either side of centerline. Air traffic control then told us to discontinue the approach. We were then given a vector and told to maintain 3;000 ft. Mean sea level furthermore; the pilot monitoring told air traffic control that we needed time to assess the problem with the navigation equipment. As were we on a downwind vector; the pilot monitoring noticed that the pilot flying didn't have the localizer identification of zzzz displayed on his pfd (primary flight display) while the pilot monitoring did; even though both very high frequency navs where tuned to the correct localizer frequency and course and we had no 'off' flags displayed. We both discussed the situation and elected that the pilot monitoring fly this approach as it appeared his very high frequency navigate, navigation was working correctly. We accomplished the instrument landing system prm runway xy approach and landed uneventfully. During the approach; the new pilot monitoring noticed his lateral deviation indicator acting erratically again. After landing; the captain called maintenance and dispatch to discuss the situation that had occurred. Since there was no navigation issue during the first approach (ils xxl); we did suspect that we had a bad very high frequency navigate, navigation 1. Thus; even though we were getting good localizer (localizer) and glideslope symbology while being vectored to final; neither of us noticed that the pilot flying did not have a good localizer identification until after being told to discontinue the approach. Another preventative measure that we discussed after landing was: since we had the instrument landing system programmed in the flight management computer we could have selected lateral navigation (lateral navigation) when the localizer was being erratic to give us good guidance to the runway centerline (while we were troubleshooting the issue) since prm approaches were being conducted. This would have more than likely prevented the approach monitor from giving a deviation call and reduce the task overload that was already occurring with an erratic localizer poor weather; etc. Until we either told air traffic control that we could not continue the approach; or resolved the issue.
output: B737 first officer reported a vhf/nav 1 anomaly resulting in a missed approach.

input: We were south of cew on a 250 degree heading to get around several large thunderstorms center had an emergency aircraft at our 12 o'clock position that was about to descend through our altitude air traffic control told us to turn 20 degrees left/right (directions) which we did. They then came back and told us to turn an additional 20 degrees left/right (directions) which we did. At this point we had the other aircraft visually and traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii showed him at our 9-10 o'clock position and about 11 mile and at our altitude and descending air traffic control then told us to turn left/right (directions) to a 090 degree heading we told him we could not accept that as it would put us in the storm. We got no response from air traffic control as he was very busy. We turned left/right (directions) to a heading of 320 degrees and told him what we were doing. Again we got no response. About the time we rolled out on the 320 degree heading he asked intermediate fix we were in our turn to 090 degrees we again told him we could not accept that due to the weather he then told us to turn left/right (directions) to 270 degrees and proceed direct to aex when able. We proceeded with no other problems i felt that intermediate fix i had accepted the 090 degrees heading i would have put my aircraft in danger. Also we had a visual on the other aircraft we were at least 10 mile apart and our courses were diverging.
output: Md80 crew experienced conflict with air traffic control instruction due to wx.

input: Flight from ord was parked at the concourse end and nearly perpendicular. After boarding was complete and all doors were closed; communication was established with the tug driver via interphone. All communications were standard between the driver and me. The first officer called ramp control for clearance to push and we were immediately given permission to push. There are no other communication procedures outlined in the ord briefing page for this gate. The tug began to move us and swing our tail to our left into the alley between concourses. It seemed to me that the push was following a normal pattern for that gate. When we had the aircraft swung around and continued to move in the alley the tug driver asked me if i saw the 777 on taxiway a moving from west to east on our right side. At that point the first officer and i looked up and saw a b777 moving down taxiway a at what i can only describe as an excessive speed. It was obvious that the 777's left wing tip was overlapping both our cockpit and the tug. The 777 made no attempt to stop or even slow down and their left wing tip passed over the top or our cockpit. At this point the nose of our aircraft was over the hold line for the alley to taxiway a. The pushback was completed behind the hold line and the engines were started and we departed. I did ask the ramp controller if he had seen the incident and he said he had. He also said he would try to find our who had been taxiing the 777. This happened so fast that we did not get the nose number off the 777 before it had moved down taxiway a out of our sight. My concern is that either there needs to be additional communication for aircraft pushing off the concourse end to coordinate with traffic on taxiway a; or the push crew had gotten us too far out in the process of the push. Looking at the location of the gate and where we were throughout the push; i don't believe the path we followed was too wide or the turn in the alley was made too late. It did not appear to me that the 777 did anything to account for our presence and at the speed they were moving there was nothing we could do to warn them. We were on ramp control and they were with ground control. The 777 crew should have stopped and waited for us to clear behind the hold line before continuing on to their gate. I don't believe they even knew where their wingtip was in relation to our position. If we had been in a 757 instead of an md80 there would have been major damage and probably severe injuries involved.
output: Md80 captain reports being pushed off the end of a concourse in ord coordinating only with ramp control. During the push the nose of the aircraft crossed the taxiway a hold line and conflicted with a b777 taxiing by.

input: After takeoff and during climb smoke started to come into the cockpit from behind the panel. Capt called for the 02 masks and quick reference handbook. While we were reading the 'smoke in cockpit' chklist; left/right (directions) engine instruments indicated the left/right (directions) engine was going to fail. We shut down the left/right (directions) engine secured cockpit and landed at sacramento executive airport without further clearance i feel that our training more than prepared us for this emergency situation.
output: Commuter aircraft has smoke in cockpit. Engine shutdown. Divert land.

input: Both the coplt and i misread the gland six arrival, arrive chart to expect clearance to cross 'gland' at 10000' and 250 knot(s) actually; it said cross 'gland' at 250 knot(s) expect clearance to cross at 10000'. When we were cleared to 'cross gland at 10000'' we discussed the clearance and decided that since the controller did not give a speed restriction; none was required. We were switched from center to approach at gland. The controller asked our airspd and we told him it was 290 knot(s) he said it should have been 250 knot(s) since that was a 'mandatory' not an 'expect' restriction. He said the slower speed was important for vectoring onto the approach it difficult to read small print on approach charts. Pilots anticipate mandatory restrictions only on profile descent charts. You see what you expect to see. Speed restriction not given by controller when 10000' altitude restriction given; since it was on the chart. I recommend an underline; shadow; or some other highlight for mandatory altitude or airspd restrictions on nonprofile charts. Controllers should restate mandatory airspd restrictions when altitude restriction is transmitted. Pilots should keep head out of ---.
output: Acr mlg flight crew fails to comply with speed restriction at 'gland' on gland six arrival, arrive to iah.

input: Taxiway that runs from 'c hangars' to 'piombo' has a significant and sharp depression in asphalt near the wash rack. The depression is about one inch deep and presents a danger when taxiing; either from direct aircraft damage; or by pilots attempting to squeeze around the area where they may hit another aircraft or equipment. This has existed for several months and has been reported to airport management twice. In july 2015; [airport representative] stated in a conversation that it would be several years before the pavement is repaired as the county is unwilling to fund the repair and they are waiting for the federal aviation administration  this is a simple fix that would require one bag of asphalt; yet could cause thousands of dollars of damage to aircraft.
output: General aviation pilot reports there is a depression about one inch deep that presents a danger when taxiing at sql. The depression is near the wash rack.

input: We were repositioning our lr25 from ewr to fnt; mile the lr25 had; previously that day; tipped on its tail due to a fueling error. The fuselage was full of fuel and the linemen were filling the wings. The capt was helping one of the fuelers when the coplt (not me) stepped off the airplane. That was enough momentum for the nose to come up slightly and; with the fuselage full and the tips and wings filling up aft first; for it to go on its tail. There was no structural damage; just a scrape on the tail; second officer the capt verified it was safe to fly. The first officer was hurt in the mishap when he tried to stop the nose from coming up. When he stopped off his hand got caught in the staircase and he dislocated his shoulder. This happened in the morning on oct/fri/94. Second officer they sent me to ewr from fnt to replace this first officer and bring the plane to fnt. The capt had been up a longitude time and was surely fatigued. The preflt to before taxi checked went normally; however; 1/2 way down taxiway left/right (directions) at ewr an air carrier jet told tower that a small jet in front of him was pouring fuel on the ramp out of his tail. We were really pouring in on the ramp. When we realized they were talking about us; the capt shut the #1 engine that was operating; down. We exited the airplane and the fire trucks came for safety. The fuel eventually stopped but the firemen plugged the fuel vent on the tail with clay. What the capt later realized is that initially we had thought it had something to do with the airplane falling on its tail earlier in the day but actually we left the fuel control switch in the transfer (empty) position which was taking fuel from the fuselage and trying to put it in the wings which were already full. The system worked just like it was supposed to. The excess fuel was venting out of the fuel vent in the tail. The capt and i both overlooked the part on the before start chklist which states the confign of the fuel control panel. First officer is new to jets.
output: Fuel spill.

input: In cruise; i noticed the fuel temperature gauge (l side of the gauge -- #1 side) was reading nothing (below the -45 hash mark). I called maintenance control and explained what i saw on the gauge that shows a #1 side and a #2 side in regards to fuel temperature there was some confusion initially as to whether it was the fuel tank temperature gauge on the left/right (directions) side of the instrument panel (of which there is only one for the left/right (directions) tank) or intermediate fix it was the fuel temperature gauge which has a reading for the #1 side and the #2 side on 1 single gauge located on the left/right (directions) side of the instrument panel under the landing gear handle. The problem was with the gauge with the readings for #1 and #2 -- the #1 side was indicating nothing. To clear up the confusion; i used the phraseology of; 'the gauge under the landing gear handle on the left/right (directions) side of the instrument panel.' maintenance seemed to be clear at this point. I next had to call my dispatcher to devise a plan as to either continue on to the destination or to go somewhere else -- we collectively decided to continue on to the destination before we terminated communications i made sure to ask maintenance and dispatch to get a hold of the local mechanic second officer he/she could meet us on arrival, arrive we landed and deplaned in zzzz without incident. I next called dispatch to see intermediate fix we could expect maintenance and was told that we can minimum equipment list the gauge over the phone with maintenance direction. I called maintenance and clarified the gauge once again and was told we could minimum equipment list the gauge; second officer we did. I then called dispatch to amend my release for flight back to zzz; due to the minimum equipment list being a dispatch advise item; and then departed and landed in zzz without incident. My crew and i had an equipment change in zzz and went on with the rest of our day. After our day was over; i found out that the gauge that was mel'ed was not an mel-able item. I immediately called maintenance control on the phone and asked about it (by this time it was a different maintenance ctlr); and was told that indeed we mel'ed an item that was not mel-able. At that instance; i realized that there was a gross miscom between me and the original maintenance controller and even though i thought that i repeatedly clarified the gauge; it didn't work. Another contributing factor was the minimum equipment list reference with 2 similar; but very different gauges. I contacted my duty officer and disclosed the whole experience with him and then i filled out the required irregularity form and faxed him a copy. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter stated the right wing tank does not have any tank temperature gauge. The left wing temperature gage is the only reference for wing fuel tank temperature although maintenance control gave him the ok for the deferral over the phone; and they departed; the minimum equipment list was not legal; as he found out later. Reporter also stated; although they carry their minimum equipment list manual onboard; the minimum equipment list shows only one fuel temperature gage installed and '0' required. The minimum equipment list did not discriminate; or differentiate; the left wing fuel tank temperature from the engine fuel temperature gauge which is a dual reading; but single gauge. After a review of their minimum equipment list manual; his chief pilot informed him the company would be revising the minimum equipment list procedures language to address this discrepancy.
output: A bombardier de havilland dhc-8-200 aircraft was dispatched under a maintenance minimum equipment list deferral with a fuel temperature gauge reading nothing. Minimum equipment list was not legal.

input: Filed to fly from maf direct ink; v94; molly; direct to lru. Proposed time off at xa40z; actual time off probably around xa55z. While en route i received clearance to go direct to ewm; a longitude leg; but i had filed as global positioning system equipped; making it possible. I received a frequency change to zab; and the controller informed me that my present course would bring me too close to the guadalupe mountains and that i should return to v94; which i did. I informed the controller how i was cleared and he called zfw; which denied that i was cleared that way. I traveled with my wife; who heard the clearance given me. Flight conditions were clear and unrestr visibility. I had the guadalupe mountains in sight longitude before this misunderstanding.
output: A c182 pilot ends up off course due to a clearance misunderstanding from zfw.

input: After receiving position and hold clearance tower controller told us it would be a couple of minute(s) before he could clear us for takeoff due to en route sep. Within 1-1 1/2 minute(s) we were cleared for takeoff on initial climb and at approximately 400' above ground level we saw a sma sing engine at about our altitude and headed directly toward us; out the right side window. We continued the departure and asked tower what the traffic was doing there; and did he know it was there? After a couple of attempts to get a response; he rpted that the aircraft (sma) had departed 36r and had us in sight. Since no evasive action was required; i waited to talk to a supervisor on the phone later that evening. His explanation was that when a swbnd general aviation aircraft departed at the same time as an air carrier the sma is given a 270 degree heading behind the jet after he rpts the jet in sight. This was 'standard proc.' standard or not; the aircraft was entirely too close to us. Evidently standard procedure was not used because it would not be possible for an sma and a jet to depart at the same time and the sma heading 270 degrees at 400' at the same time we are 400'. I believe he was cleared first and was given a 270 degree turn while we were in position i believe the tower controller on 36l was watching on en route spacing; got the spacing and cleared us for takeoff forgetting about the other aircraft or not knowing about him. Better coordination between local controller might have not let this happen.
output: Sma departs 36r; turns to 270 degrees and conflicts with air carrier off 36l.

input: Departing dca; our clearance was radar vectors to paleo intersection as filed. Dca departure procedure (prohibited area p56 avoidance procs) notes both nw and ne departures both paleo and our destination airport ewr; are to the ne of dca; therefore we planned and executed a left/right (directions) turn and successfully avoided p56. The tower controller directed us to 'expedite' our turn; and nothing more was said.
output: E145 crew concerned about controller's remark during climb in dca airspace.

input: Approaching jalyd initial approach fix from the east we were switched to tower as the aircraft was maneuvering to intercept the initial approach fix and the 12 vor and dme (co-located) arc. We were then directed to fly the 10 vor and dme (co-located) arc and report final approach fix inbound. The aircraft was already in a turn away from the initial approach fix which is 10 vor and dme (co-located) to intercept the 12 vor and dme (co-located) arc. The pilot flying (pf) switched to heading select to turn back to intercept the 10 vor and dme (co-located) arc by using the sia vor/ 10 vor and dme (co-located) on the fix page. The controller told us that we were trying to follow the 12 vor and dme (co-located) arc and we responded that we were correcting back to intercept. We continued on heading select following 10 vor and dme (co-located) arc and landed uneventfully. I later talked to the tower and told them our database and jeppesen all had the 12 vor and dme (co-located) arc. He had said the area past 10 vor and dme (co-located) was a special operating area (i forget the terminology.) i apologized and told him i would communicate these issues and procedures to the company. Our jeppesen and databases need to somehow be updated to reflect this base's procedures and possibly update the station guide and company pages. We really weren't given enough notice to make this happen when we were already at the initial approach fix intercepting the arc from an awkward angle the aircraft was trying to intercept.
output: Air carrier captain reported track heading deviation during approach to obbs airport due to the jeppesen database not reflecting specific airport procedures.

input: I was flying the landing to 24r; flaps 40 (in order to avoid published construction areas); approximately 10 miles in trail of heavy a380 aircraft. Approach was normal and stable with some rolling type turbulence (possibly wake turbulence) below 500 feet. At about 40 feet as i was transitioning to the flare; a large rate of descent became evident. I added some power to arrest the rate of descent and touched down with throttles above idle (i assume); although i attempted to reset them at idle at touchdown. The first touchdown was controlled and well within limits; but then the aircraft bounced and became airborne; the nose pitching up excessively. At this point the power was at idle and my first concern was to hold an attitude to prevent a tailstrike. Setting the normal touchdown attitude resulted in a very hard landing after the bounce. We contact the flight crew to ask about injuries or other issues in the cabin. All stated they were fine with no damage apparent.we also contacted maintenance via radio to advise of the hard landing and to have them meet the aircraft. The maintenance technician (mt) i spoke to said he would take a quick look at the tail before we made any logbook entry; i agreed. He reported no tail contact or other issues. I did not make a logbook entry.
output: B737 captain reported a hard landing resulted when he encountered wake turbulence at low altitude in trail of an a380 on approach to lax.

input: Flt from las to lax requested push from gate x from las vegas ramp control on frequency 124.4. Las vegas ramp control cleared flight for pushback. After pushback and engine start complete; then requested taxi clearance las vegas ramp control instructed flight to taxi via the ramp nbound to spot x for runway(s) 19l. The capt began the taxi north along the ramp area. The airport diagram (xxy and xxz pages from the commercial charts) show 2 teardrop hold pad areas along the ramp area in the direction of the taxi. The capt continued to taxi the aircraft north on the ramp when i noticed it appeared visually and from the commercial charts he was taxiing towards the 2 hold pad areas. The airport ramp commercial charts are a little deceiving because they show almost a straight taxi north along the ramp; but actually the ramp turns a little to the left/right (directions) toward the international terminal and you need to taxi between the international terminal and the north teardrop hold pad to reach spot x. I told the capt to stop because the aircraft was actually almost between the 2 hold pad areas at spot y instead and just to the westbound of this position was txwys d and south the capt stopped the aircraft i told him he would need to turn the aircraft and taxi to the left/right (directions) side of the north hold pad area which had an aircraft parked on part of it in order to get to spot x. The capt instructed me to tell ramp control our situation ramp control saw that flight was near spot y between the 2 hold pad areas next to taxiway d. Second officer ramp control then instructed us to continue on to taxiway d and contact las vegas ground control on 121.1. Then contacted ground control and told him we were just joining taxiway d for taxi. He instructed us to continue taxi to runway(s) 19l and stay on his frequency for release time for flow to lax. The flight was then released and departed to lax. Neither the ramp control or ground control (las vegas) at any time said they had a problem or seemed to make a big deal about the aircraft taxiing to the wrong spot/location. At no time did it appear that the aircraft actually taxied or protruded on to an active taxiway without permission. Initially when ramp control was contacted about being at the wrong location/spot he was told there was some confusion on the ramp layout. I believe part of the confusion was due to the airport diagrams; but also the taxi-lines; markings; and signs are difficult to see on the ramp area. Recently there has been a lot of construction around the concourses and ramp area which has been finished. Intermediate fix confused on a position either ask for progressive taxi or definitely stop the aircraft before continuing. Also during the event there were no other aircraft in the general vicinity that were taxiing on the ramp or to runway(s) 19l that were a factor.
output: Flc of a b737-300 were confused as to the proper taxi route to ramp holding spot due to the taxiway lines; markings and signs were hard to see because of construction in the ramp area.

input: I landed on runway(s) 1 at ilg (wilmington; de) after completing the instrument landing system runway(s) 1 approach on an instrument flight rules flight plan. Was a clear (vfr) night; but very dark; no moon. I was instructed by tower to turn off runway(s) 1 at taxiway k and switch to ground control frequency which i did. Ground instructed me to turn left/right (directions) off taxiway k onto taxiway b; taxi to runway(s) 27 and hold. I started to taxi down taxiway b; looking for signs for runway(s) 27-9 and almost immediately found myself crossing a runway(s) which turned out to be runway(s) 27-9. I notified ground control he said to do a 180 degree turn and hold at runway(s) 27; which i did. After turning 180 degrees i saw the runway(s) 27-9 sign; but it was not lit and very hard to see. The runway(s) 27-9 sign on the north side of runway(s) 27-9 was also unlit. I called ground control and told them the runway(s) 27-9 signs were unlit. They said they were unaware the lights were inoperative on reflection; i should have looked at my taxiway missed approach point before turning off of taxiway k. I would have seen that runway(s) 27-9 was very close and perhaps could have avoided the incursion. However; it was very dark. Without lighted signs; it would be easy to pass onto the rwy.
output: Rwy incursion at ilg; de; on a moonless night with inoperative runway(s) sign lighting.

input: Prior to flight the proper chklist was performed. The glider; a 103 grob; was taken in tow at hilltown; public address at 300-500 feet/foot the rear canopy blew open. I executed proper rope break procedure and landed back at the field. No injuries occurred. The rear canopy fractured and the plexiglas fractured. After landing i discovered that on 3 other separate flts the same thing happened. However; no damage was incurred. No further action was taken. I also discovered that this aircraft had an airworthiness directive on this canopy and i believe no action was taken because the airworthiness directive was for negative g.
output: Sailplane pilot has canopy open on initial climb he releases tow rope and makes an emergency landing at departure arpt.

input: Capt requested a change in air carts. Both carts were checkeded by automotive and found to be working properly. On the first start attempt on the left/right (directions) engine the air cart delivered 22 psi. The dc9 operating manual starting section page 13 has a caution; which states 'if starting pressure is below 25 psi; be alert for a hot or hung start.' on the same page in bold typeface it states the fuel lever goes to on 'at maximum motoring 20' n2 minimum; with approximately 5' n1; and egt at or below 100 celsius with 22 psi; we had a maximum motoring of 17 'n2 and 4' n1. This was clrly below the limits set forth in the operating manual and was unacceptable. I rpted this to the ground crew; who initially stated they had no other cart available. I said the cart's performance was not enough to start the engine while they looked for another cart an air carrier mechanic spoke to me through my window. I explained that the cart only gave me 17 'n2 and 4' n1. The mech's response was not in accordance with the standards outlined in the operating manual; he said 'capt -- just be brave and add fuel anyway.' i explained to him that such actions were not prudent; and that the possibility of torching a 2 million dollar engine did not appeal to me. He did not respond to that. Another cart was found and hooked up to the aircraft we ascertained from maintenance how longitude we had to let the left/right (directions) engine situation after the first start attempt to regain the full 90 second starter duty limit. While waiting for that time to expire; the new cart was hooked up; and we started the left/right (directions) engine with it. It gave 24 psi; and turned the left/right (directions) engine at slightly over 19 n2 and 7 n1. We started the left/right (directions) engine fine; it just took about 70 seconds to do second officer we augmented the air cart with running up the left/right (directions) engine and started the left/right (directions) engine the automotive checked may show the first start cart is fine; but in actual operations(s) the first cart did not provide the n1 and n2 revolutions called for in the operating manual for starting the left/right (directions) engine air carrier maintenance is charging me with an average of 1 delay per 3-day trip. In every instance; i have filed a rpt showing i ante meridiem in complete compliance with far's and air carrier standard operating procedures maintenance has yet to rebut me and show that i ante meridiem requiring more than the operating manual requires.
output: An md80 capt rpts being pressured to accept substandard air carts for starting engs that do not meet flight operating manual limits.

input: In an effort to avoid overheated brakes; the capt elected to roll to the end of the runway(s) and exit to the left/right (directions) since the company's cargo facility was on that side of the airfield. (the capt had just recently upgraded to the b747 and was not overly familiar with the jfk arpt.) as the aircraft neared the end of the runway(s) at a normal taxi speed the capt became distraction looking for a taxiway exit that; as it turned out; did not exist. To add to the distraction a perpendicular taxiway with blue taxiway lighting was visible just beyond the end of the runway(s) in the ensuing seconds of trying to determine how to exit the runway(s) the capt failed to notice the runway(s) end lights disappear under the nose of the aircraft (the first officer meanwhile; was talking to tower and referring to his airport diagram to resolve our situation and was; therefore; not immediately aware of our tenuous pos.) finally realizing that there was no apparent turnoff available; the aircraft was stopped but not before the nose gear had passed beyond the runway(s) end; damaging one runway(s) end light. A tug was summoned; and the aircraft was towed to the cargo facility having sustained no damage.
output: New capt taxied over runway(s) end light at jfk.

input: Aircraft departed taxiway due to loss of brake pressure and clipped a taxiway sign. Alternate braking system used to stop on taxiway. Aircraft inspected by mechanic and found airworthy. All appropriate checklists complied with. Contact was made with tower and airport manager.
output: A b17's brake system failed and caused it to depart the taxiway as the alternate brakes were applied. The aircraft was undamaged after striking a taxiway sign.

input: We were cleared by lax center direct blh as filed. We were filed for the blh geela6 area navigation arrival. I had programmed the flight management computer for the runway 7l transition; since runway 7r was closed by notice to airmen / of air missions kphx a0865/13 201308/0500 201308/1400 and our arrival time was during that entire period. This notice to airmen / of air missions was the first contributing issue to this incident; as i interpreted it as meaning that the runway was going to be closed continuously for 3 days; rather than the usual night time closings of various phx runways. If the runway was going to be closed each night but open in the morning; i expected the notice to airmen / of air missions would say (as it usually does) runway(s) 07r/25l clsd daily 0500-1400 wef 201308/0500 201308/1400. We had completed the arrival verification procedure before top of descent; and had been cleared direct to scole. After starting our descent to cross scole at fl250 we received the latest phx automatic terminal information service which showed arrivals on runway 7r. I attempted to load the 7r transition by selecting geela6/blh/ils 7r and had to do it several times before the route looked satisfactory and discontinuities were removed. During each unsuccessful attempt the autopilot was transitioning back and forth from vertical navigation path to vertical navigation speed with changing vtk error information and autothrottle activity. My difficulty was probably caused by our direct clearance to scole (bypassing blh) combined with my fatigue level; having been up all night. The net result was that my task loading went up very rapidly and my ability to figure out what i was doing wrong deteriorated. We did not have the chance to do a complete 2-pilot arrival verification procedure again after changing to the 7r transition because in very short order we got a frequency change to abq center; crossed scole properly at 280 knots and fl250; received and read back a clearance to descend via the geela 6 arrival 7r transition; set 4000 in the altitude window; and noted that we were high on the profile and the autopilot was correcting with a significant pitch down. My first officer (pilot monitoring) then asked; 'where did spink go? We need to cross at or above 240.' i didn't see spink on the horizontal situation indicator although i thought we had not yet crossed it. We were rapidly approaching fl240. I selected altitude hold and saw that spink had apparently dropped out of the active route. I didn't think i had time to reload the route so i selected direct to spink; saw that it was about two miles ahead of us; and executed it. The aircraft was in a steady pull up and had leveled at fl236 as we passed spink. The execution occurred too close to spink; because as soon as we passed it the flight management computer drew a right circle back to spink; the aircraft rolled into a turn to the right; and the active route ahead disappeared up to geela. I went into heading sel then direct to snrra and on the way was able to successfully reload and verify the entire route with no further issues. Apparently i had not properly loaded the blh transition; so the route i had executed was from scole direct to geela. Distraction and sudden workload increase occurred just as we needed to complete another arrival verification. My first officer clearly saved the day with good monitoring; i'm sure we would have crossed spink significantly lower if he hadn't caught the mistake. Air traffic control did not comment on our altitude or minor course divergence.fatigue; distraction; and a change to a different area navigation arrival transition caused me to fail to resolve flight management computer route change issues fast enough to prevent crossing an altitude restriction 400 feet/foot too low. I could have avoided the issue altogether by not attempting to change the runway transition until much later (for example; approaching cagor); when our ground speed was much lower; we had more time; and air traffic control had made a final decision on our runway assignment. In retrospect; as soon as my task loading spiked i should have said; 'i have the aircraft and the radio; would you verify the route right now?' i think that would have divided the workload and managed the distractions and task loading more effectively. It might be worthwhile to check notice to airmen / of air missions kphx a0865/13 to see if it is coded correctly; since that's what set me up to begin with. Regarding the fatigue issue; it is my opinion that most if not all of us flying schedules that require us to stay up all night are always in a degraded condition. Operating this way is the norm; and the effects of the fatigue do not become obvious until things go wrong. This isn't going to change with the new flight/duty time federal aviation regulation solving the problem will require the company to stop building pairings that clearly violate safe scheduling practices that have been well researched and publicized for years. The schedule i fly is legal under the new fars. It is; however; as my doctor puts it; 'just crazy.'
output: A fatigued captain described the complexity and confusion around a phx area navigation runway transition change after the initial descent began which resulted an altitude constraint overshoot after the constraining waypoint dropped from the flight management system during programming.

input: Working lax approach control from over smo. Approach vectored us for 24r -- all our radios and briefing for 24r. We were turned final and all lined up on 24r. At the very last transmission approach gave us 25r and tower on 133.9. Since we were much too close for a frequency mix-up; i changed to 120.95 which is correct for 25r. Tower cleared us for 25r then changed our runway(s) to 25l. We landed 25l. After switching to ground control we were requested to call tower on telephone. They (twr supervisor) wanted to know why we lined up for the 25's. Told him that was the last we heard from approach and were getting all our radios retuned for 25 vs 24. My first officer was flying and we both distinctly heard 25r. Apparently controller said 25r when he meant 24r.
output: Acr mlg wrong runway(s) approach lndg.

input: I was working the flight data position at fairbanks flight service station specialist and received a facsimile to issue a notice to airmen / of air missions for a taxiway closure at fai airport. I composed and transmitted the notice to airmen / of air missions after which i attempted to retrieve the notice to airmen / of air missions to verify its accuracy and to obtain the notice to airmen / of air missions number. The notice to airmen / of air missions was not in the system. I verified it was not on the suspense list. I then did an oasis evr using the weather/notam transmitted data feature for the last hour and entered 'twy' as a search string. The search did not return any transmissions with this string. Based on this information i assumed i had not transmitted the notice to airmen / of air missions and must have inadvertently pressed a wrong key. I then formatted the notice to airmen / of air missions again and transmitted it. I then retrieved and verified its accuracy and obtained the notice to airmen / of air missions number and recorded it on the faxed sheet. Fai flight service station specialist received a call from another flight service station concerning a notice to airmen / of air missions that was issued for ftw airport for taxiway 7. Evr data indicates that this was the first notice to airmen / of air missions i had attempted to issue for fai and had mistakenly issued it as an ftw notice to airmen / of air missions  i was then notified by the flm (front line manager) of the incident. I believe there is an inherent safety issue with oasis when it will allow you to issue a notice to airmen / of air missions for an airport that is not in your area of responsibility without first raising any red flags to the specialist. Also; there is no user friendly way for a specialist to go back and check what they have just transmitted that would give them a chance to correct any mistakes made. I attempted to do this and came up empty handed which led me to wrongly assume the error was a failure to push the right key for transmission. Another minor issue with oasis that could have helped alleviate this incident is that a transmission screen immediately disappears and cannot be recalled after the message is transmitted which does not give the specialist an opportunity to give it a final look before moving on to other tasks. Had any of these tools been available to me i would have been able to identify and immediately correct the error thus avoiding any incident. Recommendation; 1) have oasis (and it's replacement system) validate an airport for your area of responsibility according to those you have selected in the facility responsibility table and generate a warning box for any notams you attempt to issue for airports outside your area of responsibility. 2) have oasis (and it's replacement system) retain a transmitted message on the screen. The border should change color to indicate it was transmitted. 3) incorporate a recall feature that will allow you to bring up previously transmitted messages. Each press of the recall button will bring up the next oldest message. 4) the message response box should be more specific. Instead of just saying 'fp transmitted successfully' or 'notam transmitted successfully' it should say 'fp for notice to airmen / of air missions (id) transmitted successfully' or 'notam for fai transmitted successfully' and it should remain in the message response area until the next message is transmitted.
output: Fai flight service station specialist specialist described a wrong airport notice to airmen / of air missions issuance event suggesting oasis equipment be modified restricting any transmittal involving airports outside the area of responsibility.

input: I had made a public address to the passenber that the seat belt sign was on and to make sure that their seat belts were securely fastened. We advised air traffic control that we needed another 30 mile on this heading before turning back toward aus. Air traffic control concurred. Just as we started our turn back to aus; we hit a pocket of severe turbulence the autoplt was knocked off line and the aircraft climbed 300 feet/foot from our assigned altitude of fl220; and it turned 30 degrees left/right (directions) of course before i got it under control it lasted only 15 seconds. Air traffic control asked us why we had not turned at 30 mile and i answered that we had hit severe turbulence and were proceeding on course to aus now. He issued a pilot report to the aircraft behind us. I made a reassuring public address to the passenber and we proceeded to aus.
output: An air carrier md80 flight crew experienced severe turbulence and temporarily lost control of their aircraft which climbed and turned off course.

input: In bound to las we were informed that it was a no auxiliary power unity taxi in; we confirmed this with ops over the radio. Upon arrival at the gate; the power cord was not in place to be immediately connected to the airplane. So we had to leave the number 1 engine running; the marshaller on the left wing grabbed the chalks and walked in front of the running engine!!! Very unsafe!! After the jetway was moved up the power cord was finally hooked up. After finishing the checklists and exiting the cockpit; i went down to operations to discuss what happened; i was informed that the jetways in las will not function with the power cord not hanging in place; so pre-positioning is not possible. So the no auxiliary power unity taxi in is not actually possible; and with the engine running; we could end up with someone being seriously injured or killed. Besides the rampers not following proper procedure; we actually can not do an no-apu taxi in; safely in my opinion.
output: B737 captain was informed arriving las that ground power was available and leave the auxiliary power unity off. Ground power at las is not available until the jetway is mated with the aircraft; so the left engine is kept running. During this time the left wing walker grabs the chocks and walks directly in front of the running engine.

input: We entered aircraft x to find that both ram ipad mounts were missing. After waiting for paperwork we finally received the flight plan and in the mel/cdl (minimum equipment list/configuration deviation list) section mel/cdl 25-20-xx (nef) (non-essential furnishings) was listed. We set about to verify the validity of the applied minimum equipment list within the ddg (dispatch deviation guide). The minimum equipment list in the required column requires '0'; zero. We referenced section 4 of the nef program and found that the ram mounts were covered in the nef listing under flight deck item 30. 'efb (electronic flight bag) tablet ram mounts missing.' i will point out that the language states exactly 'mounts' as plural. Satisfied that we had complied with the regulatory requirements for maintenance dispatch of this flight we proceeded with an uneventful flight. Subsequently we found out that a conflict may exist between the company ddg/mel/cdl/nef program and the fom (flight operations manual). There is 'tribal knowledge' interpretation that implied within the paragraph personal efb (pefb) mount in the last sentence of: 'if necessary; utilize the single pefb dispatch or no pefb dispatch procedures above.' this sentence creates ambiguity. In our case both the ca (captain) and fo's (first officer) pefb's were fully functional. The fom draws one back to 'procedures above' and there is a reference to no pefb dispatch that leads one to 'coordination with dispatch is made to obtain hard copies of the pertinent: jeppesen charts for the route of flight and ddg pages for items on deferral'. The subsequent flights dispatched and the dispatchers after us evidently applied this logic and provided hard copies of all pertinent information. We were not afforded this fom application. Please keep in mind that we both had fully operational pefb's. We scoured the fom for more definitive guidance outside the above mentioned passages and can find nothing else related. To say the least this is perplexing and confusing and it would be very helpful if the [safety officials] would or could address this issue and drill down for an answer. If the [safety officials] can address this issue it would go a long way to clearing up much confusion with in the fom and the ddg/mel. Your help is appreciated.
output: Reporter states that there is inconsistencies in the application of minimum equipment list deferrals as well as conflicts between the information in the minimum equipment list and the flight operations manual in regards to the pilot efb (electronic flight bag) and the minimum equipment list associated with the efb mount on the aircraft when it is missing/inoperative.

input: Atc cleared us to cross boone intersection at 11000 feet. Since the captain's flight management system was deferred we were using the f/o's flight management system and the ca was the pilot flying. The f/o set 11000 ft in the altitude preselector and then put 11000' in the flight management system in what we thought was boone intersection. In reality the 11000' was set to looth intersection. I monitored the vertical navigation until it said 2000 ft/min to meet our crossing altitude and started my descent. About 7 miles from boone intersection i noticed that 2000 ft/min was not going to make the crossing restriction and descended at a rate of 4000 ft/min. This still wasn't enough and air traffic control asked us 1 mile prior to boone if we were going to make the crossing restriction and we said we were trying. We crossed boone at approximately 12500 feet and air traffic control center told us to contact ord approach. That was the end of that.
output: Air carrier flight crew failed to meet a crossing restriction at boone intersection when they confused it with looth.

input: I allowed a plt-wanna-be passenber to distract me. This caused me to not follow my before landing chklist; and i didn't put the gear down. After landing i realized the gear and stall horn were not working. It was not known to me beforehand; nor was it placarded. Being an active instructor; i'm used to distrs during all phases of flight why this was different; i don't know. No injuries and only minor damage.
output: A beech sierra certified flight instructor pilot lands his aircraft with the gear up when allegedly distraction by his passenber at md90; md.

input: Approximately 40 minutes before departure; captain called to advise me of a logbook write-up from the previous night. The logbook said that after landing and pulling off the runway; the number one engine shut down. Captain said that the maintenance response in the logbook was that there were 'no faults; no failures and the condition could not be reproduced.' the aircraft was certified as airworthy by the mechanic that signed it off. Captain said that he would not accept the aircraft because nothing had been done to fix the aircraft after an uncommanded shutdown. I told the captain that i supported his view and that i would research the issue. After calling the maintenance tech foreman; i was assured that the engine never shut down; and that it was just an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring fault. He said that it was basically like getting a check engine light on your car. I called captain on his cell phone to explain the maintenance theory. He replied that the logbook said engine shutdown; not electronic centralized aircraft monitoring message of a shutdown. He was not interested in flying that airplane without an explanation of how the aircraft was repaired. I agreed that we would not move the airplane without further information. When i asked the unit coordinator for another airplane; i was told that there would not be a replacement because maintenance said that aircraft was airworthy. I told him that the flight would not depart with that aircraft and i was advised to have the captain call his chief pilot. I was also told to cancel the flight and charge the cancellation to the crew for refusing a good airplane. I made several requests to contact the pilot that made the original write-up and he was finally located. After speaking with his chief pilot; the captain confirmed an uncommanded number one engine shutdown upon exiting the runway last night. The captain/dispatcher was pressured to accept an airplane that had an actual engine shutdown; and was not repaired.maintenance and the unit coordinator made assumptions that the reported engine shut down was a computer error instead of finding out for certain. This wasn't an issue of whether a coffeemaker was repaired; it was an engine failure. The mechanic should face severe reprimand for signing off the logbook without making sure that the problem was fixed. He signed his name that the airplane was airworthy; yet this aircraft has been out of service for 3 days and counting. Who know what would have happened if that plane took off on a short runway with passengers; and lost the engine at a critical moment.
output: A319 captain and dispatcher describe the events surrounding the capitan's refusal to accept an aircraft that had experienced an uncommanded engine shut down after landing the previous night. The maintenance response in the logbook was that there were 'no faults; no failures and the condition could not be reproduced.'

input: On descent into iah on coast 2 flight management system arrival, arrive we were given a descent clearance to 4000 feet/foot and a heading of 110 degrees for vectors to runway(s) 14l. I was off communications #1 (atc) calling iah operations(s) for gate information i returned to communications #1 and heard air traffic control asking us what our airspd was. I observed we were at 9200 feet/foot mean sea level and descending our airspd was 300 knot(s) i disengaged the autoplt and autothrottles and halted our descent reducing airspd to 250 knot(s) i informed air traffic control we were slowing to 250 knot(s) we were instructed to continue our descent to 4000 feet/foot and were given a new heading of 140 degrees we complied with the clearance and executed a normal approach and landing at iah. It was determined that the first officer had received the clearance to descend from 10000 feet/foot to 4000 feet/foot he was loading the flight management computer and did not realize the aircraft was in excess of 250 knot(s) the first officer stated that he thought he had entered 250 knot(s) into the mode control panel before engaging level change to begin dscnt.
output: An air carrier mlg exceeded 250 knot(s) below 10000 feet/foot federal aviation regulation violation.

input: Acft lost hydraulic pressure and fluid on 'b' system on arrival, arrive at aircraft we found #1 electric pump line burst. Checkeded hydraulic reservoir for fluid level. Level was between refill and empty. Removed and replaced flex line on #1 electric pump; with temperature line. Svced hydraulic system with fluid and operations(s) checkeded and leak checkeded line installed. All checkeded good. Operations(s) and maintenance control push for aircraft to be returned to service the case drain filter was not inspected.
output: A b737-200 was dispatched in non compliance after a 'b' hydraulic electric pump flexible line was replaced for fluid loss. Pump filter inspection not accomplished.

input: We (acft #1) were doing an approach with the pilot working on his instrument rating flying the instrument landing system runway(s) 23 approach at mmu. We were instructed to call when breaking off the approach to circle to land on runway(s) 30. We did second officer but received no acknowledgement from the tower as other aircraft on the frequency were keeping the controller very busy. We knew that there were two other aircraft inbound; but assumed that one was a longitude way off. On seeing one aircraft on final pass our wing; we turned base. At about the time of completion of the turn; the aircraft on final; a high wing; asked the tower intermediate fix there was a low wing aircraft below him. The tower said yes; and the next thing we knew; the low wing; a mooney; had turned left/right (directions) and was heading right for us. We went low and to the left/right (directions) and avoided the aircraft the first aircraft we saw landed; and we followed having gone past the ctrline of runway(s) 30; but having no trouble again lining up with the runway(s) this incident seems to have occurred because of too much traffic heading inbound at the same time. The controller said that our call was missed; second officer there was no awareness of our turning base when the mooney was waved off. Also; we failed to note the second aircraft on final; because we were not expecting a conflict on final. I do not believe that this tower has radar. It is a busy area; and the controllers need the additional eyes that radar provides in helping to exactly point out the position of the aircraft here; intermediate fix a conflict was developing; one of the aircraft should have been told to change course or do a 360 degree until proper sequencing could be accomplished. Note: it would have been better for the tower to have had the high wing aircraft go around and to have let the low wing; at lower altitude land. (no conflict with us.)
output: Nmac on base leg between a sma sel high wing on base leg and a mooney sma turning off final straight toward the rptr. The rptr descended and turned to avoid the mooney acft.

input: The midshift policy scares me. We are given 2 controllers; no supervisor and told to both remain in the operating quarters for the bulk of the shift. Per a recent memo in our read file our management has instructed us to take 'reasonable' breaks and stagger our breaks to meet the traffic conditions. The problem is that there isn't really a good time to take anything more than a small meal break. We are making control decisions while fatigued. If there are admitted periods of 'substantial traffic'; then why are there only 2 controllers scheduled? Perhaps 3 controllers or a supervisor would meet the traffic demand. Two controllers who are tired seems to be a recipe for bad things. We have been told that management has asked for additional staffing on the midshift; but our time on position doesn't support it. They are asking us to work more hours on position on a mid than a day or swing; and that seems very wrong to me. Considering the fatigue memorandum of understanding and national attention of about 5 years ago; someone needs to address why we only have 2 people scheduled for a mid when it is one of our busier overall shifts. We were encouraged to take fatigue breaks and sleep at work on the midshift before; yet this local policy seems to be in direct conflict with the fatigue guidance and common sense. Being scheduled for 2 midshifts at the end of our workweek seems to be normal here. To clarify this controllers are scheduled a swing; day; day; mid; mid week due to staffing.please take a look at this and ask if it aligns at all with the fatigue guidance that was jointly put out before. Further; take a look and see if it passes a common sense test. Additional staffing is needed on the midshift and at this facility in general.
output: Zau controller stated that having two people scheduled for the midnight shift is insufficient for staffing.

input: This rpt was to alarm all those in regulatory position of a potential concern with filing flight plans when you have a user profile on file with flight service station specialist on nov/xa/08 i had filed to fly instrument flight rules in a piper warrior. Due to a mechanical issue we opted to take my aircraft i explained to the briefer that i already had an instrument flight rules flight plan filed and briefing but needed to amend or create a new flight plan due to an aircraft change. The briefer pre-populated my information based on my stored cell phone number. Rather than a going block by block in the flight plan sequence the briefer asked me to fill in gaps. However; there were certain elements such as equipment type that had changed from standard. In addition; my alternate airport selection which was not entered. I was able to later amend this information and there were no further problems there was no major issue this day however; it appears that the user profile system with flight service station specialist might lead pilots to think they are all set but in reality take off with incorrect or missing information due to a joint effort to expedite the filing of a flight plan. Let's remember that this can result in a violation of a federal aviation regulation but more importantly result in an issue of safety.
output: A pilot filing an instrument flight rules flight plan revision because of an aircraft change discovered that incorrect information can inadvertently be included or excluded that may violate far's when a flight service station specialist briefer enters pre-populated data.
