input: I was issued descend via zzzzz1 arrival except maintain 8;000 ft. I was at 14;000 ft near zzzzz2 when given the clearance by approach. I experienced moderate turbulence at the time; which i then maintained altitude and got control of the aircraft; and then started my descent once safe of the turbulence. I reached zzz3 waypoint at 13;300 ft. And i was supposed to be 13;000 ft. Or below at that time. I went to contact approach to advise them; and they came on the radio and told me to descend to 8;000 ft at zzzzz4. I complied and had no other issues with the remainder of the flight.
output: Air carrier flight crew reported arrival crossing restriction not met due to pocket of moderate turbulence encountered during descent.

input: Enroute [while over the pacific ocean] i was notified by air traffic control and dispatch of a significant meteorological information that had a report of observed severe turbulence on our route and altitude. I attempted for one hour to get a new route north of the area or lower altitude below the reported/forecast area of turbulence. Approaching fix gitle after air traffic control was only willing to let me offset 50 nautical mile south into the forecast area to get a lower altitude and dispatch was unable to get air traffic control to change my route; i [exercised my captain's authority]. We turned 45 degrees north and offset 15 nautical mile then descended to fl270. Then we returned to our route. Fl270 was below the significant meteorological information area. I prepped the cabin for turbulence while we passed the area just in case. The flight was normal and air traffic control and dispatch were advised.
output: B737 captain reported deviating around an area of reported severe turbulence on a trans-pacific flight without air traffic control approval.

input: Due to coast clouds and fog i was being vectored by san diego approach control prior to landing at montgomery field. Approach released me and told me to turn towards the coast; find mount soledad and continue visual flight rules to montgomery. These instructions left me between miramar and lindbergh's traffic patterns and encroaching fog bank. I took the safest route possible in order to protect my paxs and myself and the other landing and departing acft.
output: Ga sma reported unauthorized penetration of airspace san tca.

input: Sma x was issued clearance to land on runway(s) 7l by local controller i was working ground i heard sma y on my taxiway alert the local controller that sma x was about to land on taxiway a. Go around instructions were issued in landing flare. Approximately 60 known aircraft have landed on this taxiway in the last 18 months. The airport manager has determined that additional marking is unnecessary. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated there have been 2 more unauthorized taxiway lndgs since he filed this rpt. On 1 occasion; an aircraft had to leave the taxiway to avoid collision. This situation has been rpted to facility management airports division western pacific region; and city airport manager with no action on any of their parts. The airport management did repaint the runway(s) numbers.
output: Sma x attempted to land on taxiway had conflict with sma y. Situation taxiway a at dvt has been mistaken for runway(s) 7l. Taxiway needs additional markings.

input: We were being vectored to intercept the xxr localizer. Suddenly; we lost most of the flight and engine instruments. We aborted the approach and asked for vectors so we could figure out what happened. We were given instructions to climb to 4000 feet. We climbed and while doing so saw that we had lost the left generator and the left air conditioning / alternating current bus. We went through the quick reference handbook procedure and were able to restore power to the aircraft. We were vectored around for another approach and landed without further incident. The incident was written up in the maintenance log and was explained to a mechanic.
output: A b757-200 flight crew experienced the loss of the left generator and associated bus while on approach. They executed a missed approach; ran the appropriate checklists restoring power to the lost buses and landed uneventfully.

input: We arrived at aircraft x with open write ups for the flight splrs and spoilerons. Mx arrived at the aircraft and preformed a [fix] which cleared the error and preformed a successful ops check. We departed to zzzz with indications through the flight normal including with use of spoilers. During approach; upon calling for gear down and selecting flaps to 30; we got the ib flight splrs and ib spoilerons msgs. We discontinued the approach; and requested vectors from air traffic control to work quick reference handbook msgs did not clear. We then switch to the longer runway; notified the company; and notified the fas (flight attendant) threat we were going to be making an emergency landing; the reason; and let them know we should not need to brace. I elected to call the fas opposed to using the 3 hi; log notification in order to reduce anxiety on their part. The fas worked great and effectively prepared the cabin. After completing setup for the other approach and an abbreviated brief (we had briefed instrument landing system xx approach on arrival expecting to get it; but were changed to xyl) we proceeded in for the landing; we landed without event; notified air traffic control and taxied into the gate. The error seemed to be associated with a failing sensor as explained by mx.
output: Crj900 flight crew reported ib spoiler and ib spoileron messages resulting in emergency landing.

input: During my first officer preflt flows before the flight to albany; the crew desk acars'ed a message for me to contact them. They informed me another first officer refused a jet due to a deferred traffic alert and collision avoidance system they asked me intermediate fix i was willing to fly the jet. I too was uncomfortable without traffic alert and collision avoidance system as it is vital equipment for air safety. I advised them i too was not comfortable taking the jet. I was then asked 2 more times if/why i will not take it and was told i needed to speak to the chief pilot at this point; still in the middle of my preflt during an lca checked ride; i became very stressed. I felt i was being pilot pushed 10 minute(s) before departure i did not speak to the chief pilot at that time due to my high frustration level. Instead; the phone call was ended. I stepped away from the jet and gate to calm my frustrations. I then called the chief pilot and advised him i did not appreciate the pilot pushing techniques utilized during these already stressful times. I completed the original trip and line checked as scheduled.
output: B737-300 first officer reports attempts by air carrier mgmt to have him fly an aircraft with an inoperative traffic alert and collision avoidance system system.

input: I experienced a near midair collision while flying a glider south of the zzz airport. Purpose of the flight was currency since the soaring season is mostly over apart from mountain wave flying. Typically; i take a tow into the mountains to connect with the excellent soaring conditions. The plan was to stay close to the airport and perform a short pattern flight. Before the flight; i thought about the extra vigilance required due to the flight in congested airspace. Flying in the mountains presents it's own set of challenges; but from a traffic perspective it's much less stressful than flying close to the zzz airport. Takeoff and climbout were normal; and we were established on an easterly heading in the 'glider box' climbing through 7;200 feet when i released from the tow plane. Normal release procedure is to clear right; release from tow; and perform a slight climbing right turn to deconflict from the tow plane while the towplane performs a descending left turn. This was accomplished; and i kept the turn going to a 270 heading. Once rolling wings level at 270; i was presented with the image of a blue and white piper cherokee rapidly filling my windscreen head on. Time from recognition to action was within a second and i dumped the nose to build airspeed/separation and rolled right to deconflict. The cherokee seemed to pick me up at the last minute; and i observed him making a slightly delayed climbing right turn. I estimated separation at between 100 and 200 feet. It was too close! If i remained on tow on an easterly heading; there is a very good chance the cherokee would have flown directly into me at my 6 o'clock. Very similar to a fatal midair accident that happened 10 years ago at zzz between a towplane; glider; and cirrus transitioning the area. I was on the zzz common traffic advisory frequency with the tow plane; and neither me or the tow pilot heard the cherokee making position calls. The cherokee continued it's flight eastbound and i made an announcement about the near miss and called his position to anyone else on frequency. Technically; nobody did anything wrong. The cherokee was not required to make position calls. However; in the busy airspace around zzz this is common sense. See and avoid worked; but just barely. I was squawking 1202 (glider transponder code per letter of agreement with tracon) with a mode south transponder. I confirmed the transponder was on during my before takeoff checklist and directly following the incident. I had a flarm collision avoidance system installed in the glider. This picks up mode celsius mode south and other flarm traffic. In the event of a conflict; there is an audible warning and the screen on the s100 variometer displays the clock position; distance; and altitude above/below of conflicting traffic. Very similar to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system it does not display resolution advisory/vertical speed required for deconfliction. The flarm alarm did not activate; and i didn't even look at the instrument. My eyes were outside the whole time and i was very lucky they were. This comes down to solid training and a good scan. The world war ii pilots had it right. 'keep your head on a swivel'. Don't trust your traffic avoidance system to show or alert you to everything out there. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system ads-b; tis; flarm; etc. All offer an absolutely incredible advantage in situational awareness and safety. However; it's not a 100% solution. Many gliders and older powered aircraft don't have transponders; and a traffic avoidance system won't pick up something they can't see. You still need to look outside the cockpit.the flarm/s100 system has certain configurations that can be set by the pilot on when to audibly and visually alert on a potential conflict. Due to flying in close proximity to the tow plane on tow; i believe it's a possible setting to inhibit warnings while on tow. Since this happened within seconds of release; it's possible that is the reason i didn't receive an alert. I'll need to do some reading of the manual and also investigatethe configuration of the s100/flarm system installed on aircraft x to further understand this logic. It's very possible this is my fault; and by configuring the system differently i could have avoided a slice of swiss cheese or two from lining up. It's not the people talking on the radio that will hit you; it's the people that aren't. A good scan is critical. Keep that head on a swivel and outside. When releasing from tow in the future; i'll start clearing not only my 3 to 4 o'clock but all the way to my 6 o'clock. It's unlikely i would have spotted the traffic doing that due to the headrest blocking my view directly backwards; but it's a good idea none the less. The local terrain and airspace setup cause a bottleneck between the mountains to the west and the class b to the east. You have a lot of airplanes flying visual flight rules in a fairly small corridor. That ups the chances for these types of incidents occurring. More education for pilots that not all traffic will be presented or presented accurately on their traffic displays. This is a perfect example. Many pilots think everything out there that can hit them will show up on foreflight; traffic alert and collision avoidance system etc. That's absolutely not the case. Better education about the 'glider box' at zzz. There is a note about it on the zzz airport website; and in the chart supplement. It's buried; and realistically not many pilots read those materials for airports they will overfly. There should be a note on the sectional about the specific dimensions/locations of the zzz glider box.even better; the federal aviation administration should make a database of this type of airspace and it's dimensions and allow it to be displayed as an overlay on tools like foreflight. Just like they do with tfrs. While the chart supplement is an awesome resource; my honest experience is nobody looks at it unless they are taking a checkride. Everyone uses foreflight these days. By presenting this type of airspace as a graphical overlay on these types of moving maps/apps; you have a much higher likelihood of awareness and compliance from the pilot population. This would increase safety tremendously! This wasn't a causal factor in this incident; but easily could be in a future one. All gliders should be required to have transponders. There are plenty of people flying gliders at 17;999 feet. In busy terminal arrival and departure corridors without a transponder. The battery technology exists for this to not be a problem anymore. I can fly all day with my transponder; radio; electronic variometer; and two moving map displays without running out of battery power.
output: A glider pilot reported a near midair collision with a fixed wing aircraft while in a published glider flying area that is close to a busy airport on one side and a mountain range on the other.

input: On the arrival route the two 'l+r hydraulic pressure' annunciation lights illuminated. For the duration of the flight they went on/off intermittently while during the last 5 minutes of the flight finally went to solid 'on'. The hydraulic pressure was zero. I notified approach control of the emergency condition. I shot the instrument landing system via vectors. I emergency extended the landing gear per the quick reference handbook without incident. I received 'three green indication' upon doing so. I landed without further incident.
output: Sa227 captain experiences loss of both hydraulic systems during descent for landing. An emergency condition is encountered and the gear is extended via the quick reference handbook resulting in three green indications. An instrument landing system approach and landing ensues.

input: Prior to boarding our auxiliary power unity failed for a second time. We called maintenance and they deferred the auxiliary power unity we boarded and handed out paper work when we found out the ground crew lost the pin to the door handle. The ground crew asked us to call maintenance to see if they had spare pins. I called dispatch who then handed me over to maintenance. Maintenance advised me that they would send the mechanics out to help look. While on the phone with maintenance i asked if it was okay with them for us to start an engine because the cabin temperature was dropping rapidly. They said they didn't see a problem with it. I asked the ground crew if it was okay to start engine #2 and they confirmed we were good to start and the aircraft was chocked and hooked up to the tug; but then they walked away. I went outside to make sure #2 was clear and the first officer (fo) started the engine. While outside i looked around to see if i could see the pin. The mechanics showed up and starting looking for the pin to the door. After a while of looking we could not find the pin and the mechanics disappeared without talking to the crew. I called dispatch to see what was going on and to see if there was any spare pins; or planes we could take. That's when dispatch advised me that we would probably be swapping planes. I told the first officer and he called operations to ask for the jet bridge back to deplane. A few minutes later the gate agent comes down and we deplane. After the last passenger gets off i go to the back of the aircraft to advise the flight attendants what was going on. At that point in time the flight attendants advised me of a possible duty issue for them. A few minutes later the first officer came back to tell us that operations had called and we are switching aircraft. A couple of minutes after that a mechanic ran on board and asked why the #2 was still running. Not knowing it was still running i ran up there and quickly shut the engine down. We then shut down the aircraft and took our bags off and proceeding into the terminal with no incidents. Better communication. Create a checklist for situations like this to warm the aircraft when an auxiliary power unity is mel'd in extreme cold conditions.
output: Dash 8 flight crew reported starting an engine for cabin heat on the ground; then leaving the engine unmonitored when they left the cockpit.

input: Over the last few days i have witnessed several aircraft attempt to turn onto a currently published; but closed (reopened in new location) taxiway. I received a phone call from a pilot who; among other things; said he had taken the closed taxiway ('g') to exit runway 18/36 to the ramp. Also somewhat linked; a new 'island' of taxiway lights has been installed on the non-movement portion of the ramp. This has resulted in several pilots attempting to pass between these lights to get to a parking area by the fixed-base operator please share this information. The purpose of a notice to airmen / of air missions is to amend currently published data about a facility. A currently published taxiway has been moved (a new one built). There is currently no way for a pilot to know that this situation exists. Until the old taxiway is demolished and airport diagrams updated; i believe a notice to airmen / of air missions could help pilots be aware of the new configuration of the airfield. For the taxiway lights on the ramp; i recommend in-pavement lighting to prevent aircraft damage and closer spacing between taxiway lights to better define the area.
output: Evv controller voiced concern regarding the absence of a notice to airmen / of air missions clarifying the status of taxiways and their usability.

input: I was the pilot flying capt was the pilot not flying on initial contact with ny approach control while flying the camrn 4 arrival, arrive were given expect instrument landing system runway(s) 4r. Instrument landing system runway(s) 4r at jfk was briefed; the flight instruments and bugs were set for landing runway(s) 4r. We were handed off to the next controller who instructed us to fly heading 340 degrees for rv to instrument landing system runway(s) 4r. Capt continued with the 'before landing chklist.' we were then instructed to fly heading 010 degrees of intercept runway(s) 4r localizer asked that we kept our speed up and would have speed reductions in a few miles. Intercepted course and was given a speed reduction i believe it was 180 knot(s) shortly thereafter. Approximately 30-60 seconds after speed reduction approach control asked intermediate fix we were intercepting runway(s) 4l. Capt responded 'no; we were instructed to intercept runway(s) 4r.' controller 'acr x just turn left/right (directions) and intercept runway(s) 4l frequency is 110.9 maintain...you are cleared instrument landing system runway(s) 4l.' made a left/right (directions) turn to intercept while capt set-up the aircraft for runway(s) 4l...intercepted the loc/gs inside 10 miles instructed to contact kennedy tower 123.9...received clearance to land and landed without further incident.
output: B767  flight crew is vectored by two successive controllers for instrument landing system runway(s) 4r at jfk. As they are intercepting the instrument landing system the controller informs the flight crew they were cleared to intercept runway(s) 4l instrument landing system and turn left/right (directions) to intercept.

input: We were on the final for runway xr performing the instrument landing system runway xr prm; in actual prm conditions; i.e.; low visibility; fog. While on the final; i noticed an aircraft quickly approaching our position in an apparent overshoot of the final on runway y. Just as i was asking my first officer if he had visual contact of that aircraft; the final approach controller asked us to break off our approach and climb and maintain 5;000 feet/foot i executed the standard go-around procedures and as we were climbing; he asked us to continue to track inbound on the localizer as we began to comply; the monitor came over the radio and asked us to get back; descend to 4;000 feet/foot we began to descend to 4;000 feet/foot again when the monitor asked us if we could try and get back down and perhaps shoot the approach from where we were. By this point we had full deflection of the glideslope so we declined and said we would prefer to go back around and get stabilized again as we were previously. He said that would be no problem. While this was transpiring; we had drifted off the localizer because we were in heading mode and we had a 26 knot(s) crosswind. The monitor asked us to rejoin the localizer we complied. We then were vectored back around and shot the instrument landing system 10 approach successfully. The infringing aircraft appeared to be a regional jet.
output: Flight crew of unspecified air carrier aircraft on an instrument landing system prm approach are instructed to go around by the monitor controller due to encroachment by the partner aircraft.

input: We are able to receive and occasionally transmit to aircraft operating with ind airport traffic control tower both towers local control frequencies are 120.9. We had ind air traffic over-riding aircraft operating within dpa airspace. On numerous occasions we had to wait until the ind traffic stopped transmitting before we issued control instructions to our aircraft otherwise we would just have to retransmit due to frequency congestion. Numerous aircraft commented that they heard a lot of other aircraft on the frequency a possible solution: change tower frequency to something else.
output: Dpa and ind towers have same local control frequency 120 pt 9 on occasion causes frequency interference.

input: During the second week of jan/01; i was diagnosed with an illness. On jan/xa/01; i began taking a prescription drug. I was unaware that federal aviation administration order 7350.4 requires notification of one's supervisor when taking prescription medication. When i heard about this requirement; i was unable to verify it; because our facility does not have a current copy of the above order. On feb/xc/01; the local representative of the national association of air traffic specialists; was able to obtain a copy of order 7350.4. After being shown the pertinent passage; i advised my immediate supervisor that i was taking a prescription drug. Intermediate fix the federal aviation administration expects its employees to follow a certain set of rules and regulations they must ensure that all employees have access to the rules and regulations we still do not have a copy of federal aviation administration order 7350.4 at my facility; the oakland fss.
output: Oak flight service station specialist specialist concerned with illness notification and lack of on-site federal aviation administration orders concerning illness notification procs.

input: Our company works in conjunction with the usda on the insect pest eradication program here in zzz; first officer we release sterile flies over the country in grid or block patterns. In the past; when the weather necessitated an instrument flight rules flight plan; we were cleared to our dispersal region at an altitude with further clearance back to location. A change in air traffic control procedure requested a block from between 2 radials and 2 vor and dme (co-located) settings from zzz vor and dme (co-located) while airborne. I gave the 2 radials between which i intended to fly and they cleared me to fly between those radials at 80-120 vor and dme (co-located) i accepted. Later when i realized that the vor and dme (co-located) distances would not allow full coverage of my region; i requested an amendment for a bigger block and was given an extension. Towards the end of my block i was unsure of amended clearance coverage needed to overfly some nearby islands; second officer stated my intentions of flying to them. It was acknowledged and i was told to maintain my altitude after leaving the original block; air traffic control informed me that i was not cleared to do second officer and i had violated my original clearance i requested further clearance which was given and completed the flight contributing factors include: 1) spanish/english language barriers. 2) my assumption of being fully cleared to fly outside of an assigned block. 3) change in air traffic control procedure leading to ambiguity. 4) heavy traffic flow on air traffic control frequency corrective actions: our base is planning a visit to air traffic control to discuss effective procedures and any concerns.
output: Be90 pilot and foreign controller had language barrier; readback hearback problems in a foreign location.

input: Conflicting visibility approach to runway(s) 03l dtw. Preceding us to land was wdb 6 mile ahead. Just prior to t/d in landing flare; left wing suddenly dropped. Touched down left main gear and commanded pilot flying to execute a missed approach normal missed approach and subsequent visibility approach and landing made on runway(s) 03l dtw. Upon landing and arrival, arrive at gate; conducted post-flt inspection to ensure aircraft integrity. Found left wing tip light; outermost wing tip spar and wing tip trailing edge lights damaged. Wrote up same in aircraft maintenance log book. Discussed damage with maintenance contributing factors: 1) left crosswind 2) very strong wind gust!; 3) suspect residual wing tip vortices from (just cleared rwy); 4) target flare spd/close proximitypa to ground 5) wind shear!
output: Wing tip strike during landing minor aircraft damage.

input: The instrument flight rules charts for sac have shown 118.8 as the approach control frequency for as longitude as i can remember. 118.8 has not been used at sac for at least 10 yrs! Approach is usually 125.25 and occasionally 125.6. This is confusing for transient pilots and should be changed. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that he believes the frequency was changed because bfl used the same frequency and there was sometimes a bleed over on the frequency which created confusion. The local pilots know the correct frequency by this time but a transient pilot would not be able to contact anyone on the 118.8 frequency which is listed.
output: Flt school instructor indicates a wrong approach control frequency on the sac charts. The frequency was changed about 10 yrs ago but is still published.

input: During pushback from gate x at the air carrier zzz flight center the tug driver began to turn the aircraft before it was clear of the passenber loading bridge. The aircraft contacted the loading bridge causing a 4-5 feet/foot cut in the skin below and behind the capt's window. The 2l door was used during boarding and the passenber loading bridge had been backed away from the aircraft as federal aviation regulation as it would go. When the passenber loading bridge first became visible to the cockpit crew it appeared close to the aircraft it took me a second or second officer to realize the aircraft was moving toward the front edge of the bridge instead of parallel to it. Before it could react; i heard the aircraft contact the bridge and immediately told the tug driver to stop. Contributing factors were that it was dark; raining; and early in the morning. There was considerable congestion on the ramp and a hard turn of the nose to capt's left/right (directions) was required to move the aircraft to the cleared location (txwy m). By the time the cockpit crew saw the passenber loading bridge it was too late. Intermediate fix air carrier operations(s) continues to push the aircraft from this gate to taxiway mach number with the tail to the nw; a spotter under the passenber loading bridge is a must.
output: A b757-200 on pushback from a congested ramp struck the parked jetway incurring a 4-5 feet/foot skin cut below the capt's window.

input: I performed the preflt inspection and found 5 or 6 mechanical discrepancies. I was met at the airplane by one of our chief pilots and some other individuals with whom i was not familiar with. One of the maintenance items was plastic erosion tape on the engine pylons. I had written up the tape on the left/right (directions) pylon; but not the left/right (directions) because the left/right (directions) did not appear to be damaged. The chief pilot asked me why i had not written up the left/right (directions) engine pylon speed tape. I told him that it did not appear to be damaged to me. He stated; 'well; i guess the preflt isn't complete then.' the other maintenance items were: composite erosion on left/right (directions) navigate, navigation light cover (wingtip); erosion tape damage on left/right (directions) horizontal stabilizer; cargo light mesh cover damaged; and cargo floor covering torn. All were legitimate mechanical discrepancies. Air carrier is attempting to intimidate its pilots into not rpting mechanical problems the chief pilot also asked me intermediate fix it was normal for the capt to do the preflt. I stated that sometimes i took the initiative to help out the first officer and that it was my right to do so.
output: Pic's rpt on company intimidation. Rptr feels that he is being watched because of a rash of logbook write-ups by company plts.

input: A husky landed and rolled off the side of the runway and up onto a taxiway. No damage to aircraft or airport. This was a non event until supervisor told us we needed to archive weather and fill out statements. We all did but this is over kill when nothing happens. We need better training regarding what is an occurrence and what's not.
output: Reports from a tower controller and a husky pilot describing a runway excursion during landing with strong crosswind.

input: Taxiway signs are difficult to impossible to read in west and northwest portion of rjtt airport with tall un-mowed grass obscuring them.
output: Air carrier captain reported taxiway signs obscured due to overgrown grass/weeds at rjtt airport.

input: I headed south climbing to 3500 feet/foot to cross san vicente reservoir; then westbound into myf for landing due to the turbulence caused by the santa ana wind conditions; i was distraction and climbed over 3500 feet/foot and was then taken to 4000 feet/foot by an updraft. The floor of the san class b airspace in this area is only 3800 feet/foot as soon as i saw i was at 4000 feet/foot i descended to 3000 feet/foot to ensure that i did not go above 3800 feet/foot again.
output: A private sma pilot was taken into the san class b airspace by an updraft. He had no clrnc.

input: This event was not a direct result of an error on my part but concerns a common practice by flight instrs. A fellow flight instr's student wanted to make a cross-country to an airport 70 mile away. The trip was to be there and back - direct. The route has many chkpoints and is flown by many students. My fellow flight instr was not available second officer i was asked to sign off the student. With the simplicity of the cross-country in mind; along with the thorough planning by the student; i signed the student off for the flight i remember feeling apprehensive about signing off a student i had never flown with. But i did second officer anyway because i didn't want to disappoint the student. The student had no problem on the flight to the destination but the return trip did not go second officer well. The student dialed in his home base vor and dme (co-located) and centered the needle with a 'from' indication. Since he was going to the station; what followed was the classic 'reverse sensing' scenario. The needle deflected to the left/right (directions) second officer the student turned left/right (directions) as the needle went further left/right (directions) and eventually went full scale; he continued to try to intercept the course. In the confusion; he lost track of his ground chkpoints and; becoming totally disoriented; ended up 20 mile off course. Realizing he was lost; he looked for a place to land. Unfortunately; the airport he selected was an air force landing strip in the middle of a restrict, restricted, restriction area which was 'hot' that day. Upon landing the student was met by a group of military personnel who informed him of where he was. They would not let him leave by himself and requested that a certified pilot fly him out. After paying a $100 landing fee; we flew him out with no further problems since i had never flown with this student; i was not aware of his trouble with vor and dme (co-located) navigate, navigation i should have followed my initial feelings and not signed off a student i didn't know. His flight planning was thorough; but just because a pilot can plan it right doesn't mean he can fly it right. My advice to other flight instrs would be to avoid endorsing students for cross-countries unless you've flown with them yourself. You never know who you are signing off. The favor your are doing for a fellow instr may be one to regret later on that day.
output: Student pilot on solo cross-country misinterprets vor and dme (co-located) indication; deviates in heading; penetrates restricted area; becomes completely disoriented and lands at restricted military arpt.

input: Conflict with a hawker jet occurred while transiting [near teb]. Cessna 172 was skirting the around the north side of teterboro class delta at 1200 feet/foot while attempting to establish communications with approach (127.6). Approximately 5 miles north of teterboro we did a random 'left wing up' clearing only to see a small jet pass off our rear quarter at approximately the same altitude (1200-1300 feet). I did not hear any traffic alerts given to the jet by approach control (we were squawking 1200 mode c). I assume the jet was on a long low final for runway 19 at teb and was talking to the tower directly. No evasive action on our part was required but a half second either way would have put both aircraft on the 5 o'clock news. We knew we were flying in a busy area and were on the watch for aircraft making their way in and out of teb. This one just sneaked up from our rear quarter. Pilot flying was in right seat. Non-pilot flying in left seat.
output: C172 pilot experiences a near midair collision at 1;200 feet; 5 nautical mile north of teb with a hawker jet on approach.

input: During climb at high altitude the left/right (directions) start valve light started to flicker. After 1 minute(s) the light came on intermittently. All the engine parameters were normal. We accomplished the memory items and the appropriate quick reference handbook procedure declared an emergency and returned to zzz. During the descent the light came on occasionally. We landed overwt; normal touchdown. During taxi; the left/right (directions) engine was shut down; but the light kept coming on and off. Maintenance rpted the valve was closed even intermediate fix the light was on.
output: An md80 flight crew experienced left/right (directions) engine start valve light on in climb. They ran the procedure; declared an emergency; and returned to their departure arpt.

input: Engine quit at approximately 200 above ground level on final approach. Hard landing on grass a few feet before threshold of runway. Aircraft rolled onto runway. Speculation that the problem occurred due to right fuel tank being used instead of switching to both tanks prior to entering the traffic pattern. Possible carburetor ice; carburetor heat does not function robustly; on run up; addition of carb heat only drops rpm by 30-40 rpm. Other possibility is that the fuel outlet on the right tank unported and air was drawn into the line.
output: The pilot of an amateur built experimental aircraft reported a loss of engine power on final approach that led to landing just short of the runway. Carburetor ice may have existed and the carb heat control may be inadequate.

input: Earlier in flight a high pitched squeal started and first officer noticed what appeared to be a 1 inch crack at the lower corner of the window. As a precaution we descended to fl210. Fl230 was recommended by maintenance and dispatch which had us landing zzz with less than federal aviation regulation 45 minute(s) we notified air traffic control of minimum fuel and were cleared direct zzz. Shortly after checkeding in with zzz center they advised us that we would have to declare an emergency or return to our original route we opted to declare the emergency at that time rather than fly the route anticipating that we would have less than 30 minute(s) when landing in zzz intermediate fix we did so.
output: After an a319 window cracked; the crew descended; declared an emergency to get routing direct to their destination because of fuel considerations at the lower alt.

input: Flt taxied in line for over 2 1/2 hours before reaching #1 for takeoff at jfk. Heavy thunderstorms and wind shear were causing the delay. Some aircraft were vectored to the south avoiding large buildups ten mile off the end of runway(s) 4. When we arrived at position #1; we were cleared for takeoff on the condition that we could maintain heading 080 degree for a minimum of 20 mile with no turns. Our weather radar indicated this would take us through a large well contoured cell at 10 mile we indicated this to the tower and requested a turn to the north or south they denied this and ordered us to taxi down the runway(s) and go the end of line; now over 40 aircraft longitude he then offered the same deal to the aircraft behind us. Two more declined the offer and were sent to the end of the line. One aircraft finally took off and flew through the cell. At this point we returned to the ramp. Before leaving i called the tower and told them i thought their procedure was unsafe. They told me i was disrupting their operation by making these comments on vhf.
output: Reporter complains that air traffic control will not permit deviations for weather at jfk.

input: At the aransas county airport i was in the touch and go pattern. I called turning crosswind on runway(s) 27. After turning downwind; the radio traffic was heavy with several aircraft checkeding in with position rpts. Several experimental aircraft were checkeding in with bad radios. There was; i would estimate; about 4- 5 aircraft coming in to land at the same time while i was in the touch and go pattern. One aircraft joined the downwind leg behind me and the experimental aircraft were some distance away and another aircraft kept calling longitude final into rockport. I never saw the aircraft on longitude final and as federal aviation regulation as i know; the aircraft did not join the pattern as per the aeronautical information manual at unctled airports i checkeded the traffic turning base from downwind and didn't see any; second officer i called the turn. Seems like the c172 on longitude final made another call; but with all of the radio traffic i didn't really pick up the call. I then called 'acft on longitude final say your pos' and didn't get a response. Second officer i turned from base to final; then the student in the front seat saw a shadow on the ground and then i saw the aircraft on short final. I estimate his altitude at about 100-150 feet/foot and my altitude at about 400-500 feet/foot i then flew through the extended ctrline and flew the aircraft up the left/right (directions) side of the runway(s) 27 to keep the landing traffic in sight. Runway(s) 27 is left/right (directions) hand traffic contributing factors: 1) radio traffic everyone rpting position and bad radios causing other aircraft to tune out the radios. 2) mix of high wing and low wing aircraft makes it hard to see each other. 3) longitude final. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states that the c172 pilot told him 'you need to call the fsdo' when rptr made the go around when he landed he made an attempt to talk to the other pilot but he was taxiing back to depart. Air traffic control at corpus christi contacted rptr and said the airport manager had called in response to a complaint. When rptr described the incident air traffic control indicated it would go no further. There are occasionally problems in the area with aircraft from an aeronautical club practicing at rkp and the airport manager wanted to checked out this incident. The d-45 is a certified version of the t34b mentor which is military and not certified.
output: D-45 (mentor) with instructor and student aboard has near midair collision with a c172 making a straight in approach at a non tower airport the mentor makes a gar.

input: Departing sfo runway(s) 1r; flaps 15 degrees normal takeoff upon flap retraction from 1 degree to up; the leading edge flap asymmetry engine indicating and crew alerting system came on. There was no adverse yaw or roll felt. Followed irregular procedure in flight manual. Takeoff weight was about 230000 pounds talked to air carrier maintenance and dispatch and coordination a return to sfo. We burned about 20000 pounds of gas to reduce landing weight i determined that an overwt landing was deemed as safe as continuing to fly with a secondary flight control problem emergency vehicles were standing by but no assist was required. Shut down engs and towed to gate because of hot brake considerations. A flight manager met us at gate for quick debriefing. Got us a new aircraft and we proceeded to bos.
output: B767 crew had engine indicating and crew alerting system warning of leading edge flap asymmetry after takeoff at sfo.

input: I am a pilot for a large unscheduled fractional operator. The [company's] fatigue inducing schedules are almost impossible to manage. I was forced to call in fatigued this time because two days in a row my scheduled duty start time forced me to wake up at 0300 one day and 0200 the next. These times reflect the time zone where i live. The workload is not the issue. The problem is that i am constantly being shifted back and forth on duty start times and it creates a constant state of fatigue while i am on the road. There are no controls or safeguards for this at the scheduling level and it is up to the pilot to call in fatigued. The company fatigue policy is supposed to be a no questions asked policy; yet i have been called into headquarters and asked why i have so many fatigue calls. This causes me to be uneasy about calling in fatigued and to push myself when i should not. Another issue i see a lot are very early duty start times--often between the 0300-0500 hour--with six to eight hours of sitting at the airport. After these very early wake ups and extensive sits i am often expected to fly another five or six hours. This causes fatigue. Management's practice of calling people into headquarters about fatigue calls has also created a social stigma among the pilot group where; if one deviates from the statistical average of fatigue calls; he/she is deemed an 'abuser' of the policy. Because our company is an unscheduled operation and pilots cannot bid trips ahead of time; schedulers often give certain pilots 'preferential treatment' with their schedules thereby skewing the fatigue numbers. This helps the company justify that only a few 'abuse' the fatigue policy by giving just a few the most 'fatiguing' schedules.
output: An hs-125 captain for a fractional operator alleged coercion of some pilots to fly fatiguing schedules and preferential treatment for others to avoid the same; resulting in flight crews being compelled to fly when not fit to do so.

input: After pushback and engine start and putting engine driven generators on line; 'electrical' amber annunciator light illuminated. After consulting quick reference handbook and minimum equipment list it was determined that battery charger was off-line since dc meters in battery position indicated -4 amps. Pulled back in to gate; called dispatch and maintenance duty desk. A reset procedure was verbally given over the phone which reset the battery charger. Maintenance also stated that due to numerous similar sits; after consulting with the company and federal aviation administration it was acceptable to proceed without a logbook entry and pilots were ok'ed to perform the reset proc.
output: A b737-700 was dispatched in non compliance with a maintenance procedure performed by the flight crew with no logbook write-up.

input: On taxi; immediately prior to takeoff i experienced tingling sensations in my hands. This tingling continued and at cruise altitude of fl390 my feet began tingling as well. Having previously experienced a slow decompression on a b737 and being aware that these sensations indicated i was going into a hypoxic state; i became quite alarmed. I asked my flying partner intermediate fix she was experiencing these symptoms and she replied negatively. She was also quite a bit heavier than i ante meridiem i called the cockpit immediately and requested an increase in air flow. I also asked the first officer intermediate fix they manipulated the air flow to increase fuel consumption. He replied that they did not. Within 1 minute(s) my hypoxic symptoms were gone. I called the cockpit to let them know this and the capt asked me to come up when they needed a break. I did this and the first officer left the cockpit. Capt then informed me that on 'long hauls' he did manipulate the outside air flow to increase fuel efficiency. At this point i realized that air quality (and my brain cells) was being compromised in the pursuit of fuel efficiency. I believe this situation is an alarming one and that all flight crews should be aware of the symptoms of hypoxia and the consequences of manipulating air flow to the detriment of air quality.
output: B737 flight attendant experiences possible hypoxic signs during cruise.

input: After receiving automatic terminal information service for slc; i contacted approach and told them where i was. They gave me a squawk and told me to contact tower i told them that i was unfamiliar with the area and was in severe turbulence he told me to contact tower i contacted tower told them that i was unfamiliar with airport he told me to follow the freeway; then asked me intermediate fix i saw the airport to the westbound i told him that i did. He told me to land on the left/right (directions) runway(s) he had given me the runway(s) number that i could not see. After telling him that i was turning for runway(s) i heard nothing until i landed; at which time he gave me a phone number and told me to call. Second officer i called and gave him my n-number and name. He told me that i had landed on a closed runway(s) and that he was going to fill out a rpt and asked me intermediate fix i could read a compass. I told him i was in turbulence and he certainly saw me line up with that runway(s) why did he not tell me at that time?
output: Pvt pilot of sma landed on a closed rwy.

input: Upon arriving at the aircraft we (myself and capt) were met by the incoming capt and first officer they briefed us on the current minimum equipment list (73-31-xx) on the aircraft they briefed us that during their flight into zzz they received the engine 1 fuel low pressure caution message 4 times. During this time all 4 of us discussed the minimum equipment list and the fact that there is no specific guidance in the minimum equipment list addressing whether the caution was normal during flight the inbound crew left at this time and capt and myself continued to investigate the minimum equipment list we determined that; with no specific guidance in the minimum equipment list addressing whether the above caution would normally be displayed inflt; in the event the caution did display we would follow the applicable quick reference handbook procedure at this time we reviewed that quick reference handbook (eng #1 fuel low pressure) and realized that intermediate fix followed we would be required to divert. With the understanding that the message would most likely be displayed during flight we saw no reason to take off only to divert. At this time we began to seek more information from outside sources. We agreed that intermediate fix we could get an official written procedure telling us that we in fact should ignore the engine 1 fuel low pressure caution; we would go. Capt called maintenance control and relayed this request to him. Maintenance said he would discuss it with the embraer representative and get back to us. When he did; he said they found a page in a maintenance manual that stated the caution message was associated with the minimum equipment list note that this manual is not available to pilots and in fact it took maintenance control over 2 hours to produce the reference the manual page was faxed to us and we reviewed with an zzz line mechanic we agreed that the page did prove the message was associated with the minimum equipment list but it did nothing for guiding us to run or not run the quick reference handbook intermediate fix received inflt. Shortly thereafter; we were made aware there would be a conference call with maintenance control pilot group safety representative; and us. During the call; maintenance correctly summarized our issue and proceeded to explain that it was indeed alright to ignore the caution inflt. He referenced the preamble of the quick reference handbook the intro to the minimum equipment list and some part of another manual that i have never heard of nor have access to. His explanation was sufficient; but unrealistic. He convinced me it would be alright to take the aircraft in the current state; but it was such an involved process of proof; i doubt i could reproduce it. First officer made the comment that the average line pilot would probably not be able to come to the same conclusion with our limited resources. Ironically; during the 3 hours of discussion about this issue; the part that was deferred became available and was replaced within 20 minute(s) took the flight with the new part installed. Supplemental information from acn 809716: updating the quick reference handbook and mel's in a timely manner when safety of flight issues are impacted. This is the company's responsibility and duty to ensure the resources are made available to flight crews for the safe movement of an aircraft we are limited by the tools the company provides to us to complete the required tasks. Intermediate fix such items are not available -- such as updated manuals -- the tasks cannot be safely completed by the pilot group.
output: Emb170 flight crew refuses aircraft with minimum equipment list that causes 'eng 1 fuel lo press' warning; due to lack of specific language allowing this message to be ignored.

input: During landing rollout my aircraft suddenly and abruptly swerved to the left and departed the runway. The approach speed was 95 mph and touchdown was made on the runway centerline several hundreds feet past the threshold. I was decelerating with all 3 wheels on the ground when the aircraft swerved to the left at approximately 40 mph. I don't know the reason for the sudden change in direction but i did find some heavy plastic material in the left wheel pan. The brakes have not been inspected yet. Nobody was injured and no property other than the aircraft was damaged during this incident.
output: A pitts s-2 became uncontrollable for unknown reasons and departed the runway after a normal landing.

input: During cruise flight we got an engine fire warning light on the left/right (directions) engine we proceeded with the appropriate chklist and upon retarding the power lever the warning light extinguished. We proceeded to our destination with reduced power on the left/right (directions) engine and found that there had been a fire. Because the warning disappeared upon power lever retardation; and without shutting down the engine or activating an engine fire extinguisher bottle; we thought the warning was erroneous. In hindsight; i believe that any engine fire warning should be treated as an actual fire; the engine should be shutdown; an emergency declared and a landing made as soon as possible.
output: Commuter aircraft has engine fire warning light activate. During chklist procedure light extinguished. Continued to des.

input: Base leg on visual to runway(s) 25l at lax. Given a heading of 150 degrees and cleared to 4000'. Told us to follow an smt low. When on base mlg y passed over us at approximately 500'. He stated that mlg y had visibility on us. I was looking at mlg y close on us and the sunlight was such that it appeared it was not moving or actually seemed to be flying formation with us. Approach did not point out mlg y till we were very close. Although we were at least 500' vertical from mlg y; he was not pointed out to us. He tended to distract us from our obligation of making a visibility to 25. Had approach informed us of mlg y earlier and gave us his altitude we would not have been distracted observing him.
output: Acr-lgt flight crew upset by the close proximitypa of acr-mlg while both aircraft were on visual approachs to parallel rwys.

input: After receiving clearance and taxi instructions (txwy k/b to taxiway b3 for runway(s) 27r dep) i inadvertently turned left/right (directions) onto the overrun for runway(s) 27c. After making the turn; i noticed the chevrons and immediately called ground control to clarify and ask for further instructions. I was told to make a 180 degree turn. I followed the instructions; got on the proper txwys. On the continued taxi; i was asked to call the tower when reaching destination i called from the airplane while still on the ground the person in charge returned my call later to tell me that what happened would be recorded only as to what happened. There was never a separation issue (as to other tfc) and i did not actually taxi onto an active runway(s) only the displaced threshold. We also discussed how poorly marked the displaced threshold is. There has been and is ongoing construction in this area of sfb. Many taxi areas are poorly painted or not painted at all. I believe this needs to be addressed with sfb airport auth.
output: Be40 rptr runway(s) incursion sfb. Rptr cites construction zones with poorly marked; poorly signed taxi routing and or instructions.

input: Currently; there is a need for safety over-runs at the cortland county airport; (n03) because of the type of aircraft flying into and out of the facility. Within the past two years; there have been two aircraft accidents at the cortland county airport (n03) both which could have prevented if safety over-runs were in place. It is my understanding funding is available for such safety enhancements and this report is the proper document to begin the process for the over-run request.
output: A pilot reports that there is a need for safety overruns at the cortland country airport.

input: Acft #1 was a student solo wishing to depart to the practice area. Developmental local controller cleared aircraft #1 for takeoff and issued traffic on a 3 mile final (acft #2). Pilot of aircraft #1 did not respond in a timely manner to the control instruction; second officer developmental local controller told pilot of aircraft #1 to hold short of runway(s) 17l. Both developmental and fpl local controllers heard the pilot read back 'hold short.' seconds later the fpl local controller saw aircraft #1 holding in position on runway(s) 17l. Developmental told aircraft #1 to exit the runway(s) and aircraft #2 to go around aircraft #1 turned around and exited the runway(s) but aircraft #2 continued his approach over the threshold; intending to land now that runway(s) was clear subsequent review of tape recordings showed that pilot of aircraft #1 read back 'hold short on runway(s) 17l.' contributing factors: 1) controllers were cued in on 'hold short' and missed the rest of the readback. 2) student pilot of aircraft #1 was not properly prepared for solo flight as he had no idea what 'hold short' meant. 3) aircrew of aircraft #2 was hell bent on landing (pressure to save money?) and made a bad situation worse by not complying with air traffic control instruction to gar.
output: Rptr and developmental local controller missed readback of aircraft #1 to hold short of the runway(s) pilot repeated hold short in position and went into position on the runway(s) aircraft #2 on final for the same runway(s) was issued go around but continued approach while aircraft #1 exited the runway(s) per instructions.

input: I was working a radar position at jacksonville air route traffic control center a large area of thunderstorms developed north over; and sw of omn vor and tacan (co-located) impacting the bitho6 arrival, arrive to mco. After an air carrier aircraft rpted severe turbulence the controller in charge and the radar controller at the affected position asked flow control to close the bitho arrival, arrive the flow control supervisor in charge would not close the route which forced aircraft that would normally fly the arrival, arrive to deviate westbound of course and head on with departing traffic from mco.
output: Request for flow control because of weather by controller refused by flow ctlr.

input: We were in cruise; level at fl230; when we were issued a descent to 17;000 feet/foot just after that call was received; several things happened. First; i noticed that the captain's eadi; ehsi; and the traffic alert and collision avoidance system screens all went blank. I received a red 'fd' and 'cross side data' flag on my eadi. Those events happened at almost the same time. Within a second; the screens came back on; and the flags went away. There was a master caution light illuminated now; and it was for an electric look-up light. On the overhead panel; the 'bus tie' connect and 'left generator' warning lights were illuminated. I called for the electrical; non-normal checklist. The captain worked through the checklist; and after the checklist was finished which lead us to declare an emergency; she then contacted dispatch and company while i flew the aircraft. We continued the arrival as filed. Later; closer to zzz passing 5;400 feet/foot air traffic control asked us 'were you assigned 6;000 ft?' to which we replied; 'no; we were assigned 4;000 ft.' the rest of the flight continued without incident.
output: Sf340 flight crew reports generator failure descending out of fl230. Checklist is complied with and an emergency is declared; followed by an uneventful landing at destination.

input: Avl has had a new runway construction for a few years now. The new runway is starting to get runway [markings] on the south end of the field. The new runway is east of the old runway and must be crossed to use the old active runway. On the south end of the field (runway 35) the runway hold short line for the new runway is painted (runway is not open yet). On the north end of the field (runway 17) the old [markings] are still there.as we taxied to runway 35 (old runway) we inadvertently crossed the new runway hold short line by a few feet for the new runway (remember the new runway 35 is east of the active old runway 35). The new hold short line is a long way from the old runway 35 (which is the active runway) and there is an uphill incline from the new hold short line to the old runway which makes seeing the old runway impossible in a low wing single engine aircraft. Due to the distance from the new hold short line to the old runway 35 a chance of this being a traffic conflict is very diminished.in addition to the notice to airmen / of air missions for the new hold short line i would recommend that the ground controller advise light aircraft who don't see the old runway 35 that the new line is quite a distance from the active runway (old runway). For example 'be advised the new hold short line for the active runway 35 is just after the a1 sign.'
output: Pilot reported a runway incursion at avl airport and cited runway marking issues as a contributing factor.

input: Apch to runway(s) 8l at atl was normal. Speed 145 knot(s) based on weight and gusty winds. Touchdown was normal and in the touchdown zone. Spoilers and reversers deploy immediately after touchdown and aircraft seemed to decelerate normally. Reversers stowed at approximately 75 knot(s) and braking initiated with little effect. Maximum braking applied but aircraft did not slow as we approached the last taxiway on left/right (directions) (b-15). I elected to attempt to turn aircraft 45 degrees rather than go off the end of runway(s) 8l. Aircraft departed runway(s) and stopped with nose gear and left/right (directions) main in grassy area which was very soggy and muddy due to constant rain that day. Notified tower of our position and that we were disabled. Checkeded on cabin; no injuries rpted. Eventually deplaned passenber through aft airstairs and bussed to terminal. Contributing factors were moderate rain and heavy rubber deposits on runway(s) 8l which made the last 3000-4000 feet/foot very slippery with braking action; nil. Some braking action rpts from the tower could heighten awareness of this potential problem experience on the 727 played some role; but the responsibility still rest with the capt and crew to anticipate potential hazards and try to avoid them.
output: Rwy excursion in a b727.

input: Flt slc-pdx was in climb on autoplt. Center pointed out traffic 10 o'clock at fl290. I made visual contact and verified altitude capture on vertical navigation traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advised descend first officer disengaged autoplt and aircraft ballooned to 28200 feet/foot first officer returned to fl280 immediately. No further action was required.
output: Flc of an mlg air carrier aircraft overshot assigned altitude during clb.

input: While flying towards dfw on scy 296 degree radial at 11000 feet/foot our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii displayed traffic at 11 o'clock 1800 feet/foot below and climbing a white diamond. Within seconds; the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii issued a yellow traffic then within 2-3 seconds issued an resolution advisory of 'clb clb.' we had the aircraft visually after the 'tfc tfc' advisory. Shortly after the resolution advisory i was about to lose sight of the intruding aircraft under the nose of our aircraft i then directed my coplt to climb and follow the resolution advisory we climbed to 11500. Just as we started climb i advised air traffic control we were climbing in accordance with traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii air traffic control verified that our traffic had leveled at 10000 feet/foot and we immediately returned to 11000 feet/foot and slowed to 210 kts.
output: Altdev.

input: With no warning my engine started running intermittently. I checkeded mixture; carburetor heat; switched tanks with no improvement. When the engine finally quit i made a landing on the highway with no damage to anyone or myself. Called my mechanic he suggested i drain all gas sumps which were clear of contamination. Restarted plane. Highway department stopped traffic for departure continued on with no more problems callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr has flown this plane for 17 yrs with no problems mechanic at destination checkeded and found nothing. Flew home uneventfully. Own mechanic checkeded found nothing. Concensus is that vapor lock occurred. Federal aviation administration rep came to scene and suggested rptr checked highway to see intermediate fix safe for takeoff highway department assisted; stopping tfc.
output: Engine failure; forced lndg.

input: As i was fixing drinks; i felt dizzy and lightheaded. A moment later the masks dropped throughout entire aircraft after realizing what was happening; i donned my oxygen mask; made public address and then went from mask to mask to make sure everyone was using masks and were ok. Went back and donned a walkaround oxygen and continued to make sure everyone was ok -- especially children and unaccompanied minors we landed in zzz and everything was ok.
output: Deployment of o2 masks alerts cabin attendant to loss of cabin pressure.

input: Our flight plan was j67 to lin; then j189 to ave. We had a wind from the north in excess of 60 knot(s) i had been looking at our bid sheet for jan and had placed it on the approach plate holder on the control column. On the mlg x; the yoke covers the horizontal situation indicator in most positions of the seat. You have full view of the horizontal situation indicator and the 'to/from' flag when the seat is in a forward lndg/tkof position in cruise i had moved the seat aft to a comfortable position and the yoke fully covered the horizontal situation indicator in order to see it; i would have to lean forward. Placing my big sheet on the yoke did not help matters either. Inbound to lin i had been referencing the f/o's horizontal situation indicator to monitor our course deviation; then xchking his horizontal situation indicator with mine. I last remember checkeding my horizontal situation indicator and making a slight course correction to the westbound i then heard the f/o say 'ok; it's 144 degrees outbnd and i'm going to avenal.' i said 'ok;' but what i failed to notice is that we had passed overhead lin. I did not see the to/from arrow shift. I checkeded the f/o's horizontal situation indicator and it showed us east of course (j189) and my horizontal situation indicator showed us east of course. However i was still set up on the 166 inbound to lin; and was flying outbnd. I should have been on the 144 degree out of lin. Of course the north wind did not help matters. Zoa asked intermediate fix we were intercepting the arwy. We said we were. They advised that they showed us approximately 7 mile westbound of course. It was then that i realized what had happened and corrected to intercept j189.
output: Acr mlg fails to fly new course passing lin vor.

input: Passing through fl180; the altimeter to be set was 29.71. Pilot at the controls (capt) set 30.71. After leveling off at 4000 feet/foot on the capt's altimeter; approach asked our altitude my initial response was our assigned '5000 ft.' that's what my altimeter showed along with what the altitude window showed. I quickly looked at the capt's altimeter and was shocked to see the 1000 feet/foot disparity. I immediately realized that the capt had set the wrong altimeter setting. However; i had also realized that i must have missed his mistake when completing the dscnt/apch chklist. After advising approach control we made an uneventful climb back up to 5000 feet/foot and was told that there was no traffic conflict. Lessons learned: because of the 1000 feet/foot split on the altimeter; i assumed the altitude was correct -- it looked correct! Both needles were at the 12 o'clock position in level flight in the future. I will ensure that i checked the numerical setting of the altimeter; along with the 1000 feet/foot prior aural altitude alert -- like i'm supposed to do! I learned a lot from this one!
output: B737 flight crew misset altimeter passing fl180 and overshot assigned altitude of 5000 feet/foot while on radar vector to pvd.

input: During a routine flight with a flight time of approximately 50 minutes at an altitude of 4500 mean sea level an outside air temperature around +10c. Tks system on high; inertial separator in bypass; heat on with the selector turned to the 9 o'clock position; the overhead vents opened; and side vents closed. I prepped aircraft for a normal winter's flight by doing a preflight test of the tks system. All tks panels were saturated with tks fluid and all systems operated normally. After engine start and during taxi to the takeoff runway i turned the tks system on high; and pulled the inertial separator to bypass. I maintained the system on high and inertial separator in bypass for entire flight. About 20 minutes into the flight i noticed a strange taste and a very faint odor of tks fumes. About 5 minutes later i noticed the beginnings of a slight headache. I put my oxygen mask on for the remainder of the flight. After the flight i walked around got some fresh air and a drink of water and the headache was gone.on the return leg i turned the tks on to the norm selection for about the first 15 minutes of the flight then turned the system onto high. Inertial separator in bypass; heat on at 9 o-clock position and overhead vents open. On the return leg i did not notice any fumes or get a headache.the difference between the 2 legs was on the initial departure i started the system on high on the ground during taxi; and on the second departure i started with norm and ran on norm for about 15 minutes. Another difference was the direction of flight. From initially i was flying into the sun and i'm sure the flight deck was much warmer.
output: After takeoff with the tks system set to high; a c208 pilot detects fumes and develops a headache. Oxygen is used for the reminder of the 50 minute flight. On the return leg the tks system is set to normal for the first 15 minutes then high and no odor is detected nor does a headache develop.

input: Prior to push; heard banging on the aircraft passenber and flight attendants also heard banging from below. First officer being blamed for ramp worked locked in baggage pit 3-4. We heard banging from below. First officer went down and let ramp worker out. Pit was empty and worker said he was resting in pit when it was closed. Please note this pit is not heated and at altitude worker would perish.
output: Ramp worked locked in md80 cargo pit.

input: Restricted areas r2914/15/17/18/19 overlying the vps complex are active fl240 to fl350. Traffic management unit (tmu) issued a restriction earlier in the shift for no traffic south of j2 which would clear this airspace. Shortly after the airspace went active the tmu restriction dropped off our board. I went to tmu to ask if this was going to be reissued. Traffic management coordinator (tmc) said they removed it and questioned why it was necessary to issue it in the first place. I stated that it now went active almost every day during the week up to fl400; just like the warning area's and flow needed to be issued around it. Weather was building northwest of these restricted areas and with no flow out zhu would allow aircraft to be routed into these hot areas with very little time to catch the route. This is an unsafe situation that is being allowed to happen.when the vps complex goes active issue flow around it.
output: A jacksonville center (zjx) controller questions why a restricted area that goes hot every day was removed from the information display system (ids) in the area. Traffic management unit (tmu) removed the information and questioned the controller as to why they needed it on the information page. The controller was concerned that the area was going to go hot without any flow control for it.

input: Left for ord. Ord weather rpting runway(s) 27l; runway visual range 1800 feet/foot v 2800 feet/foot shot 2 approachs to minimums both to a missed approach then diverted to dtw alternate airport notified dispatch of diversion through automatic communications addressing & reporting system en route dtw. Dispatcher acknowledged receipt of divert on automatic communications addressing & reporting system dtw weather was visual flight rules landing on the runway(s) 21. Several aircraft in pattern. We requested runway(s) 3r due to fuel considerations with missed approachs and vectors heavy both ord and dtw. Minimum fuel was declared (by ctlr) to accommodate. Landed safely. (note: dtw approach controller was irritable about our request. We were assigned runway(s) 4r for lndg.)
output: A b727 gets into a low fuel situation due to 2 missed approachs because of wx.

input: On approach into zzzz; we received a taws terrain alert; followed by an obstacle alert; and a pull-up command. We then executed the taws escape maneuver; and received clearance for another approach. We landed uneventfully the second time. We are not sure why we would receive the command; we were at proper altitude; verified by air traffic control and on course. The following morning; however; during my first-flight-of-the-day checks; the taws test failed; citing; 'internal global positioning system not navigating.' so it is possible that taws received a false position from the flight management system the night before. Callback conversation with reporter revealed the following information: reporter stated he does not know if maintenance was able to determine the cause of the inflight taws alert on the saab-340b; or the preflight test failure the following morning. Reporter stated he wondered if the pre-programmed database of all the obstacles was an issue or an flight management system position signal.
output: On approach; a saab-340b flight crew received a terrain awareness warning system (taws) terrain alert. During the following morning's first flight of the day checks; the taws test failed citing 'internal global positioning system not navigating.'

input: I was working the r1 position. Aircraft x was inbound from the south requested area navigation [runway] xx approach to get below the deck and requested to proceed via own navigation to zzzzz. I cleared aircraft x to maintain and cross zzzzz at or above 5;700 ft.; area navigation [runway] xx zzz approach. Aircraft y was inbound from the east; and instructed to hold east of zzz at 6;000 ft. For sequence behind aircraft x. Aircraft x was radar service terminated and switched to zzz tower. Zzz tower had not been advised of aircraft y in holding. At approximately 5.5 mile; zzz tower called and advised aircraft x was requesting a 360. I approved aircraft x request. When i observed aircraft x continuing to travel eastbound; i called zzz tower to verify aircraft x had canceled instrument flight rules zzz tower advised they had not canceled instrument flight rules when i observed aircraft x began to climb higher than 4;600 ft. Eventually up to 5;200 ft.; i issued aircraft y to continue in holding except to climb to 7;000 ft. Ca went into alarm; i issued a traffic alert to aircraft y and advised a right turn heading 360 and to climb and maintain 7;000 ft. I called zzz tower and asked them to switch aircraft x back to me. Aircraft x was still on tower's frequency and they rejoined the area navigation [runway] xx at 10.5 miles and continued inbound.on initial call from zzz tower; i should have verified that aircraft x had canceled instrument flight rules with tower. I could have instructed aircraft y to hold at 7;000 ft. From the initial call.
output: Controller reported previous instrument flight rules released to tower made unexpected climb towards holding traffic resulted in an airborne conflict.

input: Set off rops warning system on landing. Turned off at normal exit after moderate braking.
output: An airbus flight crew reported the activation of the runway overrun prevention system (rops) while landing at kord. They were in compliance with all landing parameters and safely exited the runway after using moderate braking.

input: With first officer flying; we established a downwind to boi runway(s) 10r. Abeam the airport i inquired with approach intermediate fix other aircraft were doing visuals or staying instrument landing system i could see airport from our current position and thought we could execute a visual from that point. Approach responded 'yes' and asked intermediate fix we had airport in sight.' i said 'yes.' he cleared us for 'visual to runway(s) 10r.' the first officer turned inbound and wasn't sure intermediate fix she had airport in sight. I gave initial headings to it as i did see the airport i then called the tower and they cleared us to land runway(s) 10l. Right after that; the first officer said she did not see airport and asked me to take aircraft which i did. I flew it to runway(s) 10r and; at about 300 feet/foot noticed another aircraft take the runway(s) i executed a go around we inquired why aircraft was on runway(s) 10r and tower replied we were cleared for landing runway(s) 10l. We finished the go around and came back to land on runway(s) 10r using the instrument landing system under visual conditions. I believe factors were confusing clrncs at same time of changing control of aircraft combined with some level of pilot fatigue as this was our 4th leg of a longitude day. The landing clearance came right as i was concerned that first officer could see runway(s) i accepted it and immediately became pilot flying first officer did not hear the landing clearance as she was trying to see airport supplemental information from acn 605313: i felt the confusion was caused partly by the clearance from an instrument landing system to a visual and no clear verbiage about a runway(s) change (ie; now clred).
output: B737-300 flight crew performs a go around after seeing another aircraft crossing their assigned runway(s) 10r at boi; id.

input: We were cleared 070 degrees to intercept runway(s) 9r localizer at ord. Capt briefed approach and subsequently selected the localizer for runway(s) 9l. I noticed instrument landing system vor and dme (co-located) was not coming in second officer stayed on ord vor and dme (co-located) for vor and dme (co-located) i did not checked capt's selected frequency or attempt to identify (as i normally do). Capt's localizer was captured and i saw a runway(s) at 12 o'clock. Ord approach called to say 110 degrees to intercept runway(s) 9r. I responded on localizer and approach responded localizer frequency 111.1. Capt set correct frequency intercepted and landed. Approach said later was no conflict. Capt said approach book was open to runway(s) 9l and runway(s) 9r; got localizer frequency from wrong page. Capt did not identify localizer as is required per operating manual and company policy. I should have identified (as backup to capt). I might have seen runway(s) as wrong runway(s) (visually) earlier; too. Lack of vor and dme (co-located) on original frequency should have been a clue also. Maybe having approachs to parallel runway(s) as consecutively numbered (and opposite each other in approach book) contributed.
output: Capt and pilot flying tunes in wrong instrument landing system frequency and is alerted to error by the twr.

input: My captain and i were ferrying an aircraft from zzz-zzz1. We were taking off runway xx and after takeoff our lavatory smoke detector alarm started beeping. After direction from the captain we [advised atc] and made the decision to return to zzz. We requested direct zzz to hold and set up for our return. As we were entering the hold the alarm had stopped; we decided to still return to zzz as it was the safest decision and we could not verify that there was no fire. As we were holding we set the aircraft up to return; calling company and following procedures for our return.
