After we finished setting ourselves up and getting ready we ran the checklists that we needed to; we requested vectors for to return to zzz and requested an instrument landing system we returned to zzz without any further issue and had fire trucks meet us on the runway to verify that there was no fire. After we verified there was no fire we taxied back to the ramp and shut down the aircraft. Lavatory fires or indications are handled by flight attendants; we did not have any on board so we treated this like a regular fire and returned to field in a safe and efficient manner.the captain's workload was extremely busy; my recommendation/lesson learned is to help the captain out sooner in any way possible including helping by offering to take flight controls and lessen the captains workload. Another recommendation is having a procedure for pilots in the event of [lavatory] fire for pilots when no flight attendants are on board.
output: Q400 first officer reported the lavatory smoke alarm activated after takeoff resulting in a return to the departure airport.

input: While on instrument flight rules flight plan from bvy to 39n; lost both communications radios after hartford departure control advised to shift frequency to contact ny approach control could not raise ny approach control and after reverting to previous hartford departure frequency could not raise air traffic control there either. After failing to raise ny approach on other frequencies as listed in airport facility directory and any station on 121.5; attempted to troubleshoot radio problem but concluded xmitters had failed. Switched transponder to 7600 and guarded voice frequency on navigate, navigation radio for sax vor and dme (co-located) which was next point on instrument flight rules clearance proceeded instrument flight rules in instrument meteorological conditions in accordance with last clearance until approximately 20 nautical mile east of hudson river at which time visual meteorological conditions was encountered. Descended visual flight rules to 2500 feet/foot above ground level and switched transponder to 1200 and landed at nearest airport greenwood lake (4n1). Called ny terminal radar approach control facility via land line to advise on ground and to verify instrument flight rules flight plan had been closed. Also advised fixed-base operator at 39n. However; later that night; local police checkeded 39n fixed-base operator regarding overdue airplane advisory from flight service station specialist apparently ny air traffic control had advised flight service station specialist of radio out situation before receiving my land line call and flight service station specialist was commencing ground checked prior to launching sar. Subsequent testing of aircraft could not recreate communications problem which may have resulted from loose audio panel or overheated radios.
output: An instrument flight rules c172 in instrument meteorological conditions experiences lost communications while attempting to contact approach control the pilot switched transponder to 7600 and continued on filed flight plan at 6000 feet/foot when visual meteorological conditions was encountered; the pilot squawked 1200 and landed at closest airport without further incident; then contacted approach control and canceled instrument flight rules flight plan. However; the cancellation was not relayed to flight service station specialist and an overdue aircraft search started.

input: I wanted to file a report over the notice to airmen / of air missions package that our carrier uses for operational procedures for our standard flights. This particular flight had questionable weather at bgr and an alternate was given for pwm. However; btv has the same direction runways. Because of the significant length of the notams and the similarity of the runways; i found it difficult to tell which airport some of the notams were referring to. It was possible to decipher the correct airport; but very difficult especially when we are trying to fly on-time and have all of our normal operational pressures. I took the time to accurately identify the notice to airmen / of air missions for the instrument landing system to runway 33 missed approach at bgr however; it was not easy. I could have easily read that as referring to btv instrument landing system 33. The notice to airmen / of air missions package is very difficult to read as the notice to airmen / of air missions context jumps around from one airport to another and does not easily show which airport the notams are referring to. The also jump around context referring to taxiways; approaches and departures and it's hard to follow the context even when i know it's for the specific airport.in addition to this particular flight; this problem is systematic for all of the [company] flights. The notice to airmen / of air missions packages for each and every flight have gotten significantly longer and i fear as a result; pilots legitimately aren't reading all of them as a human factors response to something that is very difficult to reconcile.a week ago or so; i did a trip that involved flights out of [3 airports]. While reviewing the notams; i discovered alternate missed approaches for almost all of the runways at all of these airports for various reasons. It is my belief that due to the nature of our current notice to airmen / of air missions package; a large percentage of our pilot group is simply not reading the notams; or at least not in an effective way so that they are comprehended properly. That would mean that we have a hole in our safety net and there are errors out there waiting to happen. Because of problems of interpretation and even comprehension of the massive amount of notams being given in an irregular order and in extreme detail; i recommend that the [company] notice to airmen / of air missions package be formatted in a more readable way so that approaches; departures; arrivals and taxiway notams are separated and labeled by airport and category. This would seem to me to be an obvious format that we would want so that we can comprehend what we are reading consistently as we read through the package. I believe this to be a significant problem and when bringing it up to a management representative; i was told to use the report program for this concern. While legal requirements are currently being met with this format; i do not believe human factors regarding the effectiveness of the notice to airmen / of air missions package are being considered in the decision making. Please help; so that we can much easier read and comprehend the notams relevant to our flights.
output: Air carrier captain reported his company's confusing notice to airmen / of air missions format which presents large amounts of route and airport data in a random fashion making reading and comprehension difficult. Notice to airmen / of air missions usability is questionable yet probably federal aviation administration acceptable.

input: I was pilot monitoring performing check airman duties with a first officer (fo) performing pilot flying duties during his line training leg. Flight was routine. We discussed landing issues/terrain during cruise; and checked fom for any applicable restrictions. Only fom restriction that i could find was 'no autoland'. Flap 25 landing at 179 tons (ils in vmc) with appropriate wind additive for headwind was planned. Landing was not smooth; but i did not consider it to be hard.on post-flight inspection; the right inboard trailing edge flap was found to be not fully retracted; and there was damage to one of the associated flap track fairings/canoes. Flaps had been selected to the up position after landing; and engine indicating and crew alerting system showed them fully retracted. Cockpit voice recorder was then pulled and systems control; management duty pilot and maintenance control were informed of aircraft damage.in the distant past; i believe there was a procedure for the pilot monitoring to set a different barometer minimums bug to then have him make a callout to help compensate for the lack of radio altitude callouts? This might have been helpful to the pilot flying. In reality; the new first officer undergoing training would have benefitted from some more recent flying experience or a simulator refresher prior to starting line training. In the future; i will delay flap retraction on any landing that is firmer than normal; as this may have prevented some aircraft damage.
output: B747-400 check airman described a hard landing by a new first officer; receiving initial line training; that resulted in damage to one of the flap track fairings for the right inboard trailing edge flap.

input: While approaching minuteman ma airport near nashua; the common traffic advisory frequency 122.8 was extremely congested. Even while over the uncontrolled airport at 1500' above ground level i could not get through to unicom except as broken garbles received from them. I could see no planes in the pattern but could see the tetrahedron pointing out the runway(s) i departed the area; descended to 1000' above ground level and made a 45 degree downwind entry; calling each action on the radio (probably only adding to the garble). I then turned base; and then final; calling on the radio. After turning final; a plane called out; 'didn't you see me on longitude final?' i did not; and he went around the pattern. He was sufficiently behind me that i had completed my landing roll and turned off the runway(s) to see him going around at the other end of the field; second officer i think he had more than 4 or 5000' of sep. However; i feel that part of the problem was the congestion of the radio frequency to the point of unusability.
output: Ga sma cut an aircraft out of the pattern at a non tower airport unicom.

input: The flight was on a positioning leg from teb-pbi. We were descending from cruise flight to 8000 feet/foot for vectors/visual approach to pbi from fl240. Capt was sitting in the left/right (directions) seat in the descent radioing ahead for services when the coplt descended below his assigned altitude of 8000 feet/foot there was no traffic at the time and approach had no comment on our mistake.
output: A gii cpr repos flight descends 500 feet/foot below its assigned altitude when the capt is off on a company radio call 20 mile north of fbi; fl.

input: At cruise with autoplt on; we experienced a rolling motion that had to be manually corrected with aileron control aircraft bank reached 40 degrees suspect a b747 15 mile ahead created wake turbulence that caused the rolling motion. No control malfunction indicated. No injuries. Maintenance notified; debriefed and a write-up entered in the logbook.
output: B737-300 involuntary rolled to 40 degrees during cruise at fl280 which had to be corrected manually with aileron after autoplt disconnected. There was no control malfunction indicated. Flight crew suspected wake turbulence from a b747 15 mile ahead.

input: I was making my final walk through during taxi. I made it to the back of the aircraft. I made my checks and then the b flight attendant said there was a passenger being unruly during the safety briefing. I had her point him out. He was making snide remarks about the masks when they were mentioned in the pa's. As i was conducting my walk through back to the front of the aircraft; i noticed this passenger had his mask down. I asked him to return his mask and started to confirm with him his compliance and need to not interject during announcements. During this conversation; we received the cleared for departure ding. The b flight attendant was not in a jump seat but was in the galley confirming i had the correct passenger and keeping an eye on me. I was trying to gain compliance from the passenger when the aircraft began to take off. I was in the middle of the cabin dealing with this passenger and had to end the conversation and climb my way into my jump seat. I did not confirm that we were cleared for departure with the pilots; nor did any other crew member.
output: Flight attendant reported standing in the aisle talking with a non-compliant passenger regarding face mask policy when the aircraft began the takeoff roll.

input: Signed in at sector 10; eram was in channel b. All of my altimeters were stacked in the upper left hand corner. The relieving specialist showed me a route display for a c130 that had the plane going to a gfs radial. I was redistributing my altimeters and asked all aircraft to standby; after i finished; i made a couple of transmissions before i noticed had turned east toward a hot restricted area and hot military operating area r2507/kane east. I asked the c130 where he was going. He said to work in kane east. I asked him if he was cancelling instrument flight rules and proceeding visual flight rules as the area was currently hot. He responded; no i'm on a flight plan. At this juncture the plane had already passed about 1 mile from r2507; and was heading toward kane east. The specialist at 09 jumped on the line with yuma; while i turned the c130 back to the west. The route display was entirely incorrect from the filed flight plan of this aircraft and it created a very dangerous situation. I'm informing you of this dangerous situation that eram creates with peoples settings! My attention is on setting my scope up; not with the planes. I have to drag about 12 altimeters from the upper left hand of the scope to their positions. Take eram offline. Do not bring eram back up until it can be demonstrated these and many more issues are fixed. I thought we worked in a safety first environment; not one that pushes flawed new systems through with words like; 'they're working on that; or; it'll get fixed on the next update; or there's a work around for that'.
output: Zla controller voiced concern regarding eram anomalies; suggesting eram be taken off line until some of the identified flaws are changed.

input: Received automatic terminal information service visibility ok. Received clearance to cps. Loaded plane. Started engs. Coplt's leg to fly -- taxied out via txwys y/k/f. Briefed coplt on takeoff procedures his duties; my duties. Departed #3 after 2 company aircraft -- cleared to takeoff on takeoff roll; visibility rpted as 5/8 mile visibility requirement 3/4 mile federal aviation regulation part 135. Contributing factors: attempting to avoid morning rush hour delay. Meet arrival, arrive schedule. Rapidly fluctuating visibility. Briefing coplt. 2 company planes departed ahead -- assumed that visibility was not a factor. Low ceiling. I feel that no safety was compromised; only visibility requirement may not have been met. Company policy is visibility to low '3/4 mile down to 0-0-' depart part 91 and pick up cargo at airport with visibility minimums. Several reposition flts made in last few weeks zone manager departed first assumed it was 'ok.' supplemental information from acn 336608: from departure end of runway(s) 31c to where i began my takeoff roll is about 1 nautical mile i could see from one side of the airport to the other end. I departed runway(s) 31c with what i could see as at least 1 mile visibility. On the following day; at mdw; i heard from company pilots that were behind me; that tower had rpted visibility as 5/8 mile i had heard no discussion of visibility less than what was rpted by automatic terminal information service (1 mi) on ground control or tower frequency before i departed. I do not believe safety was compromised in any way. I watched the preceding aircraft takeoff climb out and turn to the westbound until he was approximately at 2000 feet/foot mean sea level contributing factors: questionable accuracy in weather rpting at the midway airport recently found the airport on the instrument landing system to runway(s) 4f at 1200 feet/foot mean sea level weather rpted at the time 5000 feet/foot overcast and 7 mile visibility.
output: Air taxi cargo flight crew departs using automatic terminal information service stated visibility but visibility has dropped to five eighths of a mile takeoff below minimums.

input: Jax cleared our flight to fl260 which we heard and read back. At fl230 we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alert then resolution advisory to descend controller asked us intermediate fix we were at fl230. We were at fl235 and returned to fl230. There was confusion as to which altitude we were cleared to.
output: Tcasii. Clearance confusion.

input: We were being rerouted for thunderstorms affecting airports in the area. Initially; we were at fl320; in and out of turbulence. We descended to fl280 for a better ride. Shortly after level cruise; we felt a jolt; like wake turbulence. I saw no aircraft on traffic alert and collision avoidance system that could have been the cause. So we didn't think anything more about it. A little while thereafter; we heard a banging noise; and we looked at the engine gauges but could not determine which engine might have been the cause. I turned the right throttle off; thinking that might have been it. We retarded the throttle slightly to see if that would identify the cause. It ran smoothly; so we re-engaged the right autothrottle. As the engine was coming up; we got the bang again and noticed the fluctuation on the left engine. At that point; we turned off the left autothrottle and retarded the left engine. At that point; we decided we needed to run the checklist for that engine. We declared an emergency and asked for vectors to destination. We thought that was the best option because thunderstorms were at the field at our alternate and also between us and the alternate. We followed all checklists and accomplished a safe landing. We asked for fire trucks to meet us on landing; they checked out the aircraft; and we continued our taxi to the gate.
output: B777 flight crew experiences compressor stalls in the left engine during initial descent for landing. The engine is allowed to continue running and an uneventful landing at destination ensues.

input: A b717 aircraft came in for maintenance on jul/wed/04. A service checked was done on the aircraft and a number of faults were found on the r-hand engine electronic controller the faults were narrowed down to the b-channel of the engine electronic controller i went to change the eec (electronic engine ctlr) on the r-hand engine i pulled up the maintenance manual for changing the eec and replaced it. The aircraft went down to the flight line for the morning flight after the maintenance was complete. It was found that i missed a temporary revision in the maintenance manual for the eec change. This was found before the aircraft left for the flight second officer the steps in the temporary revision that were different than the maintenance manual were performed and the aircraft was returned to svc.
output: A b717 was released for service after the left/right (directions) engine electronic engine control was replaced per the maintenance manual. Prior to departure a temporary revision was discovered with revised chks.

input: Glendale issued a direct geu and descend to 5000 feet/foot handed to luke approach told to 'dsnd to 3000 feet/foot and cross goodyear at or above 2500 feet/foot because of targets at goodyear.' started my descent and approximately 15 mile from geu; luke approach issued 'clr for visual approach geu maintain 2500 feet/foot till goodyear contact geu tower 121.0 after crossing over goodyear' and started my descent and contacted geu; rpted 8 mile south landing geu. Geu issued 'clred to land runway(s) 1.' approximately 15 seconds later; geu called and asked what my assigned altitude was. I said 2500 feet/foot till goodyear; my altitude was 2289 feet/foot descending geu said i was not to descend till goodyear. I acknowledged that and told them goodyear was behind me! Geu told to climb back to 2500 feet/foot i stated that goodyear was behind me. He then said 'clred to land again runway(s) 1.' upon my landing roll and turning off at a7 and contacting geu ground 118.0; upon contacting geu was told to taxi to park monitor ground and to call goodyear tower after parking and shutting down; called goodyear tower spoke with tower controller she asked what my assigned altitude was. I stated 'maintain 2500 feet/foot till goodyear; cleared visual approach runway(s) 1 geu from luke apch.' she asked 'they didn't say 'maintain 2500 feet/foot until through the delta airspace goodyear?' i said 'no ma'am.' i said 'there is a large difference in maintain 2500 feet/foot till goodyear and maintain 2500 feet/foot till through the delta airspace of goodyear. She then said 'well; they were supposed to say 'till through delta airspace' which would have been in another 2 mile because i had a learjet on base; i had to turn because of your dscnt.' i apologized again but again re-stated my clearance from luke. She said ok and hung up. My question is this: why would luke hand me off 'clred for the visual' and not 'call' the traffic in front of me and again state 'maintain 2500 feet/foot till through delta airspace?'
output: Mu2 pilot has altitude deviation and enters class d airspace prior to landing at geu.

input: Weather at bdl was called at 1;700 feet/foot and 5 statute mile in light rain. We thoroughly briefed the vor and dme (co-located) knowing the weather could be a factor because of the high minimum descent altitude at bdl due to the terrain to the northwest of the field. We attempted 1 approach and never broke out of the weather and executed a missed approach. The automatic terminal information service was still calling good weather and the previous and subsequent flights were successful in their vors to runway 15. We got short vectors for 1 more vor and dme (co-located) to runway 15. During this approach; we got visual contact with the runway right at the calculated vdp. I disengaged the autopilot and began a descent to the runway. Just after starting down from the minimum descent altitude we received a terrain caution and executed a go-around. We diverted to pvd and landed there after an uneventful; but bumpy ride. The flight attendants approached the captain; and then me and voiced their distress over the 2 missed approaches and the rough ride during the divert to pvd. They decided they could not go on; contacted scheduling (i presume) and were replaced by another crew. The flight back to bdl was uneventful. Landed after an instrument landing system to runway 33. Winds from the east at about 8 knot(s) early on; when discussing the vor and dme (co-located) to runway 15; we contacted dispatch with our concern and they told us tower could offer us the instrument landing system to runway 33 if the weather became a problem. Tower did; in fact; offer us the instrument landing system to runway 33 after our first missed approach; but we were already on the downwind for runway 15. In retrospect and with winds permitting; having the field set up for the instrument landing system to runway 33 might have yielded better results.
output: B737ng makes two go-arounds due to weather and a ground proximity warning system terrain warning on the vor and dme (co-located) runway 15 approach to bdl. Divert in turbulent conditions to another airport from where the flight attendants refuse to continue.

input: Ztl on darc; midshift operations(s) light traffic pa32/g climbed to jwn descended to mtv handed off from zme/m41 (zme also on darc) to me at ztl/41. I enter code into bcn list and receive a 'duplicate flight ident' message. Target will not track; with a data block. However a 'free track' triangle appears. Airways facilities technicians summoned. Overriding the track (10k) results in the full data block appearing; however; there are now 2 tracked targets on top of each other for the same aircraft this causes the conflict alert feature to activate continuously. Subsequent efforts to change the bcn code; remove the flight plan; reenter the flight plan; suppress the conflict alert are all unsuccessful. The aircraft displays 2 tracked symbols throughout ztl airspace. There are no means to ascertain that there are no other aircraft involved; other than asking the pilot intermediate fix he 'sees anybody else out there at his alt.'
output: Ztl controller described darc anomaly that resulted in two data blocks on the same aircraft causing a continuos conflict alert.

input: While on a biennial flight review; the engine lost all power and we were forced to land on a county road. We were approximately 1500 ft. Above ground level when the engine lost power. We found a paved county road and landed safely.
output: Cessna 172 pilot reported engine failure which resulted in a safe forced landing.

input: We arrived at the aircraft for our flight to find the ramp closed due to heavy rain and lightning at the field. After a few minutes the lightning moved off the field and the ramp re-opened; but it was still raining. I went to the aircraft and found the main cabin door and cockpit door were left open during the heavy rain; resulting in water in the cockpit. When the captain arrived we discussed and decided to have ops bring us some absorbent pads to clean it up. With the cockpit floor now dry again we performed a normal preflight and departed uneventfully. Upon passing about 15;000 feet mean sea level we turned on the radar because of storms up ahead. The radar then failed in all positions (manual and auto; both sides). We discussed between ourselves and decided that continuing onto the oceanic tracks at night without radar; with storms in the area to be a bad idea. We had decided we would probably return to zzz; but would discuss with dispatch prior to commencing the return. The captain then attempted to make a call to dispatch on satcom 2; only to have it fail as well. At that point we theorized that the water we found in the flight deck upon arriving at the aircraft might have leaked down into the floor and to the [company] bay; causing shorts. The captain was eventually able to get through to dispatch on satcom 1; and all this information was relayed. After about a 15 minute call with dispatch and maintenance control; it was decided to return to zzz. We started the diversion and air traffic control was notified. When we started the descent; the aft fas (flight attendants) called to tell us that they smelled 'something burning' in the aft galley; but could not locate it. At that point the captain took the aircraft and requested priority handling. I took the quick reference handbook and ran the smoke or fumes in the cabin quick reference handbook checklist. We had enough time and were able to complete the entire quick reference handbook and all the required items before landing; pertinent to the diversion. About 10 minutes after the initial call the fas called us to tell us that the smell had dissipated and they were never able to locate the source. We landed on runway 8r and stopped on the runway to have airport rescue and firefighting in zzz confirm that they didn't see anything on the outside of the aircraft. After a successful inspection from airport rescue and firefighting we taxied to the gate and deplaned the passengers.
output: B737-800 flight crew reported water in the flight deck due to l1 door and flight deck door being left open during a severe rain squall.

input: I was visual flight rules en route to denver from ege. The en route weather was deteriorating second officer we climbed to stay well above mountains. I had ground contact the entire time but not much forward visibility. When i realized that i was at the altitude of the departure course from den to dbl; i hit the xfer button to listen to den approach then i heard the controller telling some aircraft that there was an aircraft flying visual flight rules in instrument meteorological conditions conditions. Second officer i figured that he was talking about me; second officer i started an immediate descent to a lower altitude after listening to automatic terminal information service i contacted approach with nothing else happening. After landing i was given zdv phone number. I called and was informed that there was an near midair collision and the other aircraft had to take evasive action to avoid me. The controller told me that he started pointing me at 8 mile and finally at 1 the other aircraft told him there was no way i was visual flight rules because he could not see me. I said well i did not see him but i had all my lights on. The controller said he got within 1/2 mi.
output: Plt of an atx smt cargo aircraft flew into instrument meteorological conditions while visual flight rules resulting in a confliction with another aircraft which had to take evasive action unknown to the rptr.

input: On 05/wed/03; i tried to contact clearance via telephone from the ground as there is not a radio frequency from anp. After repeated calls only to get a busy signal i decided to fly out visual flight rules and pick up my clearance in the air. During this time i squawked 1200 and flew straight out over the bay. I thought i was clear of all special airspace. I was later informed that i had strayed into the air defense identification zone i ante meridiem typically a conservative and careful pilot second officer this came as a surprise and will not happen again.
output: A mooney m20 pilot departs anp and inadvertently enters the washington dc adiz.

input: This was the first of three legs planned for the day after an 11 hour layover. I occupied the pilot observer position in the left jumpseat. The crew experienced and responded to a ground proximity warning system terrain warning during approach to oaix runway 03 via the instrument landing system procedure track from ginri (iaf). Departure and cruise were routine and uneventful. I occupied the crew rest bunk until shortly after entering afghan airspace as i anticipated flying the last leg of the day. The initial descent from airway m696; approximately point vuset; was via radar vectors to a location north of oaix and then a vector toward the southeast. Air traffic control directed 300 knots indicated airspeed during descent and we were in and out of clouds with occasional moderate turbulence and conditions conducive to icing. Turbulence subsided below fl180. During descent and shortly after being assigned the southeasterly vector; the pilots asked to fly the instrument landing system runway 03 procedure from ginri. This was approved with a clearance to proceed direct to ginri; descend and maintain at or above 12;500 feet/foot until ginri; cleared for the approach.soon after; the pilots asked for relief from the 300 knots indicated airspeed and that was approved by approach control. Around the 16 vor and dme (co-located) arc intercept point; air traffic control directed 'final speed.' the pilots had already begun slowing and extending flaps and they continued that effort; ultimately selecting flaps 20 and 155 knots indicated airspeed i believe the entire descent had been accomplished with vertical navigation selected on the mode control panel but i didn't verify that and did not note the specific vertical navigation modes indicated on the fmas of either pfd. After approach clearance was received; the pilot not flying noted aloud the clearance and asked to select a lower altitude on the mode control panel the pilot flying responded that he would wait until we were leveled off. I was familiar with the environment; and comfortable with the discussion based on our location; clearance and the mode of vertical automation that i assumed we were in; so i did not lean forward and visually back up the crew's actions during this portion of the approach.i failed to see or hear when; who or exactly how the altitude selector was set to 7;000 but that's where it was when; at a point between ginri and dapub (probably around the bgm 135-140 radial); the ground proximity warning system activated with a terrain; terrain; pull up warning. The pilot observer in the right jumpseat called 'go around.' the pilot flying initiated the ground proximity warning system response maneuver by disengaging the autopilot; raising the pitch and pushing the thrust levers forward. The airplane climbed immediately. The pilot flying didn't disconnect the autothrottles initially and the power came back when he removed his hand. The pilot not flying noted the speed decreasing in the climb and called 'speed' while he and the pilot flying pushed the thrust levers back up and disconnected the autothrottles. The airplane continued to climb and seemed to recover to an altitude above 12;500 feet/foot expeditiously. At the moment of the warning; the aircraft was in a steady descent. I believe the lowest altitude reached was in the 10;000 - 10;500 feet/foot range. If i had been deliberate enough in leaning forward to monitor the altitude that i could provide accurate details; i probably wouldn't need to write this report. I believe the pilot not flying announced to bagram approach that we were climbing due to a ground proximity warning system warning and the controller replied that the minimum vectoring altitude at our location was 11;500 feet/foot would we like a vector to join the localizer? With around 25 track miles to run; it seemed reasonable to continue for landing. The pilot not flying reset the control display unit as necessary. The pilots re-established full automation; complied with air traffic control vectors and descents; and the airplane was configured for and accomplished a normal approach; landing and block in.specific to the pilot observer in the left jumpseat: (background) since observing anything on the right pfd; the only one visible; is difficult from the left jumpseat due to distance; i've always emphasized backing up the operating pilots by listening to radios and copying clearances and weather so i can quickly interject on interphone to clear up any uncertainty with minimum delay during the critical phases of flight. This is clearly not adequate. 1. While all the complications of flying (speed and altitude control; navigation; configuration; radio calls; traffic; etc.) are being handled by the operating pilots; i should be backing them up very deliberately with basic instrument procedure compliance; i.e. Stepping through our progress to each waypoint and the associated minimum altitude; to include verifying actual aircraft altitude. 2. I should be more attentive to backing up the operating pilots on company standard callouts. That is; understandably; one of the first things to suffer when things get busy; so that's a great place for an observer to help. Strict compliance helps prevent an altitude deviation or mode control panel misconfiguration from occurring without immediate identification and correction. Specific to the pilot crew in general: 1. In this case; i felt that the crew maintained a professional environment and complied with sterile cockpit protocol; but we could probably benefit from being more deliberate about establishing sterile cockpit at 10;000 feet/foot above the ground; which would be 15;000 feet/foot mean sea level for bagram; or higher if you consider the terrain we are flying over. Many of us just focus on 10;000 feet/foot mean sea level regardless of where in the world we're flying. You still aren't going to get automatic terminal information service until you are in the descent due to the communications limitations with high terrain; but wrapping up as much as possible above 15;000 mean sea level would help keep all eyes forward during the approach procedure. 2. I honestly have no idea how the 12;500 feet/foot altitude constraint was deleted during this approach. The flying pilots have not been known; in my experience; to deviate from standard operating procedure for manipulating and coordinating mode control panel changes. I don't know if the altitude selector button was pushed after 7;000 feet/foot was set or whether the pitch mode was changed to flch speed at some point. I do know that they intended to be in vertical navigation and that being the case; it would be good to have the vertical navigation descent page in view on one of the cdus so that whenever we set approach minimums in the altitude selector; we can immediately verify that the appropriate altitude constraint is still active. Obviously; the selector button should not be pushed after setting a new altitude unless clearing an existing altitude constraint is desired. As a qualified pilot in an observer seat; i have no excuse for allowing this incident to occur. I really don't have a single; all-encompassing revelation to submit that will prevent a similar incident. We obviously did a poor job of avoiding and managing the distractions that could allow all four of us to miss a glaring altitude deviation during the same critical moment. The lesson for me is simply to stay engaged at a higher level when i'm on the flight deck.
output: Air carrier flight crew on approach selected the incorrect altitude for the existing autoflight mode and the aircraft descended too low in an area of mountainous terrain just south of the airport. The flying crew initiated an escape maneuver following receipt of a ground proximity warning system terrain warning. Of particular note was the reported reminder that the sterile cockpit environment is more appropriately described as 10;000 above ground level vice msl.

input: While on final approach the captain and i both observed a high cloud layer with a small area of thick virga underneath it develop directly over the field. Winds were reported gusty; and we were visual meteorological conditions with the runway and airport clearly in sight. A few miles from touchdown we received a warning of 'go around; windshear ahead.' at that point we executed the published missed approach. It was windy with turbulent air not exceeding moderate chop but we were still visual meteorological conditions with the field in sight. Air traffic control reported they were observing gusty winds with no adverse weather warnings.we accepted close-in vectors for a second approach and stayed within about six miles of the airport. We accepted a visual approach on the base turn and joined a five-mile final. On the second approach our radar picked up a small; about two-mile wide light green return over the approach end of the runway. Then air traffic control reported a microburst alert with a 40 knot wind change. We immediately performed a second go-around and took a south turn away from this small band of quickly developed weather. At that point our attention quickly turned to fuel. We were forecast to land originally with only 6.5 in gas; and due to a good weather forecast we had no alternate and little extra fuel. The captain reached out to dispatch via the ops frequency while i continued to fly the aircraft and looked up alternate options. We first looked at zzz1; which after brief calculations proved too far and had us landing with emergency fuel. I then suggested zzz2 as i knew it was close and had operated there at a prior airline. We checked the weather at zzz2; which was only around 50 miles away and it was visual meteorological conditions with light winds. However; we were shocked to find that zzz2 was not in our flight management computer database nor was it in our jepps plates. We began working with air traffic control to get information about zzz2 and we informed dispatch to get us performance data for the airport. At that point the small band of weather was observed to have moved off the field to the south. We queried with air traffic control who informed us the winds died down a bit and the microburst and windshear warnings were no longer observed. After getting the weather; runway length and localizer frequency for zzz2; we determined that would be the safest course of action if a diversion was required. We calculated the burn and determined we had the fuel to do one more approach attempt in zzz since the weather improved and then divert to zzz2 and land with 4.0 on the gas. We landed in zzz without further incident with 5.0 on the fuel. We should have more alternate airport options in our jepps and flight management computer in this case; we didn't have information on the nearest commercially served airport to our destination. I am surprised we don't have the plates for zzz2 and that it is not in our flight management computer database. It also makes me wonder how many close suitable airports to destinations we serve also aren't included. In an unlikely event such as unforecast weather; airport closure; runway closure; etc. The more diversion fields we have information for that are close to the destination the better. It would help immensely if we had approved alternate airports that were the nearest suitable airports to the markets we serve; especially when the nearest airport is a commercial one. This would allow us to better prepare; gather information; save time; get the performance; and set up for an approach. It would be safer. Also; it would be nice if [we] had a list of diversion options along with the distance from the destination airport. This would help in situations like this when fuel is low and quick decisions need to be made.
output: B737 first officer reported two missed approaches with lack of information about nearest possible alternate.

input: In exchanging aircraft with inbound crew; capt advised maintenance had been called to service the left/right (directions) engine oil. Not entered in logbook (not a required entry). Oil was svced from 12-21+ pints indicated. Further review of the logbook showed that from aug/wed/06 to sep/fri/06 the left/right (directions) engine had received 29 pints while the left/right (directions) had received 86 pints. Having no flight times to reference for oil consumption/flt hour and the engine being above minimum dispatch i elected to accept the airplane. My comment/event/question is this: with more than double consumption on the left/right (directions) engine over the left/right (directions) and no oil service request/confirmation entries required; and missing entries on the bottom of the logbook page for oil added; how is the flight crew to know whether consumption is excessive and is; in fact; receiving all svcing inputs and monitoring same?
output: B757-200 capt rpts how it is not possible to monitor oil consumption with no logbook entries. Left/right (directions) engine has more than double consumption over left/right (directions) eng.

input: Upon arrival, arrive in the dfw area we were vectored to a visual straight in on runway(s) 18r. Descending through 1000 feet/foot above ground level the capt announced that the before landing chklist was complete and we were clear to land. I then visually confirmed that all the tabs on the mechanical chklist were in the landing position as the last 2 tabs are unlabeled our practice is the first represents that we are cleared the approach and the second represents cleared to land. Our arrival, arrive was in the middle of a complex and the radios were saturated. This was my leg to fly and the capt was responsible for the radios. I landed the aircraft uneventfully and we taxied clear of the runway(s) on the second high speed we didn't receive any taxi instructions from the tower and the capt told me to contact them. I called for taxi instructions on the frequency the capt had selected and was informed that i needed to contact the tower that we were still with approach control i then contacted the tower and was told to hold short of 18l. We then discussed the possibility that we had landed without a clearance but were never told to contact air traffic control by telephone at the completion of the flt.
output: Acr landing without clrnc.

input: Before takeoff; we had a single channel autoslat failure during recall check. We cleared the runway and mel'd this item. After departure sometime below 10;000 feet we noticed the standby attitude indicator was displaying a red flag. Shortly thereafter the standby attitude indicator began to wobble and keeled over for good. All other indications were normal at this time; so we notified maintenance and dispatch and pressed on towards our filed destination. Shortly after reaching cruise; i noticed many of my instruments had red flags including my primary attitude indicator. We were down to one known good source of attitude information at this time and since we were instrument meteorological conditions we decided to immediately [advise atc] and get radar vectors to nearest visual meteorological conditions initially we decided to go to zzz; but on the descent i saw zzz1 just off the right side of the aircraft and completely in the clear; so we changed the plan and diverted into to [that airport]. The remainder of the flight was uneventful. We then swapped aircraft and took our passengers on to our filed destination.
output: A b737-300 crew reported many first officer instruments; including the attitude indicator; displayed red flags so the crew; now in night instrument meteorological conditions with one attitude source; diverted to a nearby visual meteorological conditions airport.

input: Location: 30 vor and dme (co-located) westbound of bos. Aircraft arrived with inoperative left/right (directions) inertial reference unit. Ground proximity warning system was placarded inoperative in accordance with minimum equipment list during ground checkeds traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii system checked failed. Capt and i misread minimum equipment list and assumed that traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii was ok; just failed checked due to left/right (directions) inertial reference unit off and ground proximity warning system inoperative maintenance advised that the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii is disabled by the ground proximity warning system being turned off; but the minimum equipment list doesn't address this fact or require a placard. Suggest the minimum equipment list be updated to reflect traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii loss with left/right (directions) inertial reference unit failure; and ground proximity warning system off; with placard warning added. We made an erroneous assumption and should have had the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii placarded before we departed.
output: B757 aircraft had inoperative left/right (directions) inertial reference unit which made ground proximity warning system inoperative flight crew thought the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii was still working; though the ground checked failed; but with ground proximity warning system inoperative the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii is inoperative minimum equipment list doesn't reflect that and rptr flight crew says the minimum equipment list should be updated.

input: Pomona 2 standard instrument departure ontario; on clbout; f/o (me); continued flying 255 degree hg instead of flying (intercepting) pomona 114 degree left/right (directions) controller had us stop climbing at 8500' and turned us to intercept 294 degree left/right (directions) of pomona. F/o (me) got locked onto 255 degree heading because second officer frequently we are given headings to fly to intercept. We were given our clearance to '255 degree heading pomona 2; gorman; as filed 12000'; expect fl390; 10 minute(s) later.' departure frequency 125.5; squawk; speed 250 knot(s) this was read back on being cleared for to; again; heading of 255 degrees nothing said about pomona 2 departure at a point where we would have turned we were given traffic to look for; but did not see. We continued to fly the 255 degree heading it was not said to fly the departure second officer i didn't! Supplemental information from acn 99963: i believe that the lack of communications between the pilots about the departure itself and the anticipated acft's performance for this takeoff contributed to the deviation.
output: Failed to comply with the sid.

input: My front line manager came back from the watch desk with a plan that i draw a line with the draw feature from the southeastern shelf of the [restricted area airspace] to the approach sector boundary. This new 'airspace' was given to my sector from 11000 feet to 23000 feet not by me but commanded by my supervisor. I didn't agree to it; since my knowledge of eram (artcc computer software) is that it is illegal to just draw lines on our scope to give airspace to another sector. This is because of lack of the 'autopop' feature because eram wouldn't know of the airspace change. I wished to take point outs like we do every day in the control room. I said i didn't want to draw the line but was forced to draw the line by my front line manager. I then said i wanted to be relieved because i think this procedure is illegal. I was relieved shortly afterwards. [adjacent sectors] whose airspace adjoins were not told about the 'airspace change.' flow control reroutes were not utilized when it should have been for these situations if management thought that point outs were too much workload; which in my opinion; they were not. Or maybe it was because [tracon] didn't want to point out or hand off the deviating aircraft.do not have the operation managers and front line manager's making plans behind the scenes that completely disregard safety and the mandates of the faah 7110.65. I felt like 'what is wrong with point outs?' from what i know; we are not allowed to draw lines on the scope for airspace changes. It goes against the safety culture we are trying to create. Why force two controllers from different sectors to work differently than the norm? First; to take care of point outs radar assists should have been in place if this was a problem. This was not done. Furthermore; if it was deemed radar assists wouldn't be enough to mitigate the perceived problem; then trackers can be brought in. When other sectors that surround the 'new drawn airspace' are not told about it this creates a safety issue. For example; another sector may point out an aircraft to my sector but if they are not aware all of my airspace is not mine; then they would violate the newly acquired airspace. Let's say an arrival was deviating east and another sector was working the aircraft northwest bound. Am i supposed to explain every detail of the new airspace configuration? I might say 'point out approved' thinking they knew about the airspace deal but in reality they might not know. They would descend the arrival; unknowingly putting the aircraft in conflict with departures that are transitioning northwest bound through my old airspace; not knowing that my sector had aircraft climbing through there. I would not be required to have data block on my scope if i gave that new airspace away. The aircraft would automatically appear on my scope because that's the way eram is designed. They would turn into nuisance data blocks; therefore creating workload. I'd rather have the point outs. The other controllers were still pointing out the aircraft to me because they felt the same way. They also filled out an atsap report.
output: A controller was told by his supervisor to temporarily change his airspace and create the boundary on his radar display with the draw feature. The reporter felt this was a violation of rules and unsafe as there was no coordination for an airspace change and the radar software was not adapted to accommodate the supervisor's airspace change plan.

input: On initial call to taxi-out from the ramp; tampa ground issued the following instructions: 'air carrier x; taxi via alpha; bravo 6; whiskey.' we waited to hear if he was going to say anything else but he didn't. We asked him to clarify and he re-stated those taxi instructions exactly as before. I responded with: 'ok for air carrier x you want us to taxi via alpha; bravo 6; and whiskey; then stop for further instructions?' the controller replied with a raised voice; 'no; i want you to taxi to runway 18r!' i replied that he hadn't cleared us to taxi to that runway and hadn't even mentioned the runway in his clearance. His reply was something to the effect of; 'well; the active runway is on the automatic terminal information service and you did say you had the atis.' tampa ground controller should be reminded of the importance of using standard phraseology when issuing taxi instructions. At no airport that i have flown to has the runway been omitted from the taxi instruction unless we have not been cleared to taxi to that runway. At no other airport have i been told that the runway to taxi to can be omitted because it is included in the atis.
output: Air carrier taxiing for departure at tpa questioned atc's lack of runway information contained in the taxi clearance. Air traffic control responded that the runway information was contained on the automatic terminal information service and not required in the taxi clearance.

input: I was assigned the extended range twin operations check on aircraft x; it was snowing and the aircraft had heavy snow accumulation on it; hindering the visual inspection. I asked for the aircraft to be de-iced; so i could complete the inspection. A discussion followed with management. The supervisor referred to the de-icing as a 'courtesy.' i have encountered this mentality in every extended range twin operations inspection during snowstorms. It will continue until the air carrier establishes a written policy on de-icing aircraft prior to extended range twin operations inspections. As far as i know; my aircraft was the only one de-iced to facilitate the walk around inspection. Air carrier needs engineering bulletins and a procedure manual reference to automatically de-ice airplanes for extended range twin operations inspections; or else an incomplete visual inspection may occur.callback conversation with reporter revealed the following information: reporter stated he was told; there was enough of the wings and fuselage visible for him to accomplish the extended range twin operations walk around inspection and sign off the check. Reporter stated his carrier does not seem to have any intention of developing written procedures; to address when de-icing should be used to properly complete an extended range twin operations inspection for maintenance personnel.
output: A mechanic assigned to perform an extended range twin operations check and walk around on a b777 with heavy snow accumulation; requests the aircraft be de-iced; to avoid an incomplete visual inspection. His carrier does not have a written policy on de-icing aircraft prior to extended range twin operations inspections.

input: Passenger was sold last seat in first class cabin at x6 this morning. He had a large service animal. X4 is still reserved for the x flight attendant (fa). While i was in the back doing service the gentleman in x6 put his items all over my seat and was asleep when i returned. During the flight we had continuous moderate turbulence for the last two and a half hours. I ended up sitting in the forward jump seat. The few minutes that we were able to get up to prepare the cabin for arrival; the cabin quickly became moderately turbulent again and i returned to take my seat; only to find that he had placed his backpack on x4; my seat. I again had to take the jump seat. When the passenger was finally able to stow his luggage; i took the seat at x4 for landing and the passenger started talking my ear off. I tried to quietly tell him i had to concentrate but to no avail. Could you please tell me why i had a passenger with a large emotional service animal next to what had been assigned to me as my seat; in the x position; when there were only xx passengers in the back? Is this considered to be a 'social distance' block? 1. Current assigned seat for the x flight attendant does not allow for safe distancing between passenger and flight attendant.2. Current assigned seat for the flight attendant was not available during the flight when moderate/severe turbulence hit. Took seat next to y flight attendant - this did not allow for safe distance between both the y and x flight attendants.3. Having passenger in x6 is distracting when trying to silently review safely evacuating the plane.i learned that i cannot safely socially distance when someone is sitting next to me. I also do not have an assigned seat when turbulence hits unexpectedly; unless i quickly push all of the passenger's belongings to the floor. It has also put me in an awkward position upon landing when i am supposed to be concentrating on my drills and safely evacuating the cabin when i have the distraction of a talkative passenger.
output: Flight attendant reported a passenger was seated in the company social distancing blocked seat.

input: A passenber told one of the flight attendants that he noticed a section of the wing which was wet. The flight attendant relayed this information to the capt and myself in the cockpit. No abnormal fuel usage was noted during the flight flt was continued uneventfully to bwi. Upon landing we asked maintenance personnel to inspect the wing area where a passenber had noted some dampness during flight since no abnormal fuel burn was noted; we did not enter a discrepancy into the aircraft logbook. This was our last flight in this particular aircraft second officer we do not know the results of the maintenance inspection.
output: The crew of an air carrier mlg failed to write up a possible fuel leak in the maintenance log.

input: We were flying lateral navigation to avsar intersection and getting numerous speed reductions for preceding traffic. At that time we also encountered towering cumulus and had to turn the eai (engine anti-ice) on. The controller gave that traffic a turn away from our path and gave us further decent to that aircrafts altitude of 12000 ft. The controller than issued us a left turn to 110 degrees for one min then back direct to avsar intersection. As i looked up to turn the aircraft to 110 degrees the stick shaker activated very briefly. As the capt. Was talking on the radio and looking outside for traffic i responded with immediate thrust and recovery. We both debrief this item and both agreed on how and why this happened. I can tell you i learned a valuable lesson on the importance of keeping my eye on the airspeed indicator; especially when the auto pilot is on; the aircraft is in a turn; and flying at clean maneuvering and the aircraft is flying below the flight path in the fmc.
output: B767 first officer experienced a momentary stick shaker while turning to an assigned heading at minimum maneuvering speed.

input: We had leveled off at fl260 and were tracking the junction 1 departure as cleared per the pre departure clearance shortly after leveloff; both vors showed on course. I had just tuned mine to the junction vor and dme (co-located) i was correcting about 20 degrees to the left/right (directions) to stay on course. Center questioned what we were doing and gave us direct to the centex vor and dme (co-located) direct to the san angelo vor and dme (co-located) perhaps we had some fluctuations of the vor and dme (co-located) signal to cause ctr's concern. It was center; zhu. The controller commented about a possible equipment problem on dec/xa/00 we flew the same route with a different aircraft we noted the junction 090 degree radial showed 1/2 department of transportation south when tracking out the humble 273 degree radial from 80 mile westbound of humble to 115 mile w.
output: Md80 flight crew drifted south of atc's intended course; following the published vor and dme (co-located) radial.

input: The airport was very busy. Crossing runways were being used. I was assigned runway 11; hold short of runway 16. On short final; i was asked to do a 360 for spacing. On resuming short final; the controllers were too busy to verify i was clear to land or recognize i was back on final. I was too close and low to safely go around due to the crossing runway; and i chose to land and hold short; as directed. It is not clear to me whether i had an authorized landing clearance; although the controllers did not complain. I believed landing was safer than going around at that instance.
output: A pilot landing at hpn was told to do a 360 on short final to runway 11. After the turn he was uncertain about landing clearance but landed as a precaution considering a go around over runway 16 to be unsafe.

input: Ils approach to runway(s) 16r at smf. Approximately 9 vor and dme (co-located) gear lowered. Indications: left/right (directions) -- down and locked; nose -- down and locked. Left/right (directions) -- no down and locked. Vectored around pattern. Recycled gear same results. Accomplished emergency procedures chklist. Declared emergency accomplished low approach to visually verify gear down. First officer verified visually. Notified crew and passenber for possible evacuate/evacuation touchdown and rollout normal except for gear door extend. No injuries. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated that no corrective maintenance action information was known.
output: An md80 on approach at 2700 feet/foot declared an emergency due to left/right (directions) main landing gear unsafe warning. Gear checkeded visually and aircraft landed uneventfully.

input: Maint was received at gate; 'chiller' (food refrigerator unit) was inoperative in aft galley. We called this in to ramp/maint immediately. Mechanic was sent up to aircraft i was told by flight attendant (around push time) it would be 'deferred.' as mechanic (another) got on headset; getting ready for pushback; i questioned intermediate fix a new maintenance document was forthcoming. He stated 'no' due to no write-ups. I stated we called into maintenance the 'chiller inop.' by now; the jetway was pulled back from the aircraft and ramp was stating we were blocking the gate space for an inbound aircraft the first officer and i discussed it; and decided we would call this in to maintenance to have it properly done: 'deferred.' i called back to the flight attendant; who was working with maintenance on this; and i questioned the status of where the mechanic left this? She then told me maintenance said 'to write it up later; enrte.' one causal factor: 1) flight attendants got to aircraft late (van was 45 minute(s) late). 2) misuse of terminology: i told flight attendant 'deferred' means to properly defer; not 'put it off to later.'
output: A defective food chiller is not properly deferred under the pressure of departure schedule and a misunderstanding of the term by cabin crew.

input: Socal assigned heading 320 degrees vector for instrument landing system runway(s) 6r vny. No new heading assigned or any other air traffic control transmission received for nearly 2 minute(s) changed to communications #2 and re- established contact. Socal assigned heading 180 degrees and advised radar contact lost. Radar contact established and instrument landing system completed to landing 2 days later; took aircraft to avionics shop. Technician tested radios; antennas; cables and connectors. No obvious cause; but suspect moisture or corrosion in connector was responsible for weak reception. Radios checkeded ok. We were very concerned because of the instrument meteorological conditions (clouds and heavy rain) and mountains obscured in clouds; which existed at the time of communications failure. Controller was unhappy with us when we re-established radio contact. We did our best; but equipment problems prevented receipt of air traffic control instructions.
output: Plt of king air cpr aircraft has brief lost communications situation radar contact lost as well; re-established and instrument landing system approach completed.

input: During signoff of defect; i used a q400 wire diagram reference instead of the correct crj reference incorrect reference q400 w--d 34-44-01. Correct reference crj w--d 34-44-04. All other references used in the signoff are correct. I used the correct reference when working at the aircraft when i returned to the line shack area; i left the manual on the table. During the time i was putting away my tools; the manual was returned back with the rest of the manuals. I also performed wing walker duties on an aircraft moving out of the hangar. When i returned; i grabbed the q400 wire diagram by mistake and used its reference in my signoff. I was scanning aircraft history for x and i noticed my signoff had the q400 reference told supervisor and filled out a safety rpt. Things were a little hectic at this time due to aircraft movement in and out of the hangar getting ready for morning flts. I was distraction because i was called upon to walk wing on an aircraft moving out of the hangar. Suggestions: 1) not become distraction during the times i ante meridiem performing my signoffs. 2) should have done the signoff before putting my tools away.
output: Mech rpts on using a q400 wire diagram reference instead of the correct crj-700 reference chapter during signoff of defect. Correct reference was used when working at the acft.

input: On the morning of aug/wed/00; i was acting as pilot in command and cfi/glider giving instruction to a private glider pilot in a katana extreme motor glider. This pilot had recently purchased a single place motor glider; and was seeking a self launch endorsement as per federal aviation regulation 61.31(j)(iii) to satisfy regulatory and insurance requirements. We had done about 2 hours of ground work the previous evening covering poh knowledge including limitations; normal and emergency operations(s) system and flight characteristics peculiar to this aircraft because of excessive xwinds; and the limited crosswind capability of this aircraft we delayed the flight training until the morning on aug/wed/00. The preflt briefing covered seatbelts; egress; emergencies pilot in command responsibilities; positive exchange of aircraft controls and what training we would accomplish. Using the private pilot glider pts as a syllabus; i briefed the student that among other things we would be practicing emergency procedures including simulated loss of power immediately after takeoff i briefed him that we would do 2 emergency engine out scenarios -- one below 200 feet/foot above ground level and the other above 300 feet/foot above ground level intermediate fix below 200 feet/foot above ground level i expected him to maintain control of the aircraft and land straight ahead on the remaining runway(s) above 300 feet/foot above ground level i expected him to; traffic and wind permitting; return and land on his departure runway(s) the extreme has the advantage of climbing well above its own glide path; second officer you can just about always return to your departure runway(s) intermediate fix you descend steeply enough and the winds cooperate. We taxied to runway(s) 13 (8600 ft) in calm winds; no rpted traffic in the pattern. After runup and pretkof chklists were complete; my student departed runway(s) 13 and initiated a climb at vy; climbing at about 1000 feet per minute and a fairly steep deck angle. At 200 feet/foot above ground level i retarded the throttle to idle and declared a simulated engine failure. He pitched the nose over; established proper approach speed and using dive brakes/spoilers; landed safely just beyond the mid point of the runway(s) after touchdown; i instructed him to stow the dive brakes; and again depart at full throttle. He again established a vy climb and we had reached 300 feet/foot above ground level as we crossed the departure end of the runway(s) i again reduced the throttle to idle and declared a simulated engine failure. He pitched the nose over; established proper approach speed made a left/right (directions) descending turn back to the departure runway(s) and using dive brakes/spoilers easily landed on the departure runway(s) in the process of turning left/right (directions) back toward the runway(s) we crossed over the general aviation ramp and hangar areas at approximately 150 feet/foot above ground level in a fairly steep nose down attitude. After landing he cleaned up the aircraft and then departed runway(s) 31. We continued our training in the practice areas away from the airport the following day; i did similar training with another glider student pilot with an engine out at 200 feet/foot above ground level and a landing straight ahead; followed by an immediate departure i don't recall any other aircraft in the pattern that morning either. Later in the week some colleagues brought to my attention a rumor that the airport manager had received complaints regarding the glider doing 'careless and reckless' maneuvers over the airport and was considering rpting a violation to the local flight standards district office i called the airport manager and determined that the above operations(s) were those in question. I discussed the matter with my chief pilot in the part 141 school of which i ante meridiem an employee. I discussed the operations(s) with the glider operations(s) inspector from my local flight standards district office the chief pilot and the flight standards district office inspector both believe that the training maneuvers were safe and appropriate for the aircraft being flown. I ante meridiem filing this rpt as a precaution against any charge that may arise from these events including 'careless and reckless' or aerobatic operations(s) over the arpt.
output: Motor glider was doing engine failure on takeoff training at pvu.

input: On departure from fca; mt; we were told by zlc to hold for instrument flight rules release. A cessna was doing an instrument landing system to runway(s) 2 in kalispell. The visual flight rules traffic was using runway(s) 20. We taxied out to runway(s) 20 and held for release. The cessna canceled instrument flight rules while inbound to kalispell. Center then released us for takeoff and cautioned us to the inbound visual flight rules traffic during that time there were several calls on common traffic advisory frequency and an aircraft was on a left/right (directions) base to runway(s) 20. We looked for traffic south of the airport and saw no one. We then announced our intentions to depart runway(s) 20 to the se. No one said anything. Then we taxied into position on runway(s) 20 and i saw a light in the distance which looked like a landing light. The first officer repeated our intentions and said; 'we are on the runway(s) do you see us?' the aircraft replied; 'i see ya' and continued to land on runway(s) 2 opposing us. The time factor left us no way to taxi clear which would have been to taxi down the runway(s) 3000 feet/foot to a turnoff closing the distance to the landing cessna. We stayed in position in disbelief the pilot would land in front of us; knowing we were on the runway(s) we had made our intentions abundantly clear to all traffic on common traffic advisory frequency we felt the visual flight rules inbound cessna was entering a left/right (directions) downwind with other traffic in the pattern. He gave no response to our intentions. I turned all our landing lights on to give this pilot a clear picture. He looked like he landed within the first 3000 feet/foot of runway(s) 2 and turned off on taxiway celsius while i did not feel he would come close to us; the fact is he landed on an occupied runway(s) we had approximately 5000 feet/foot of distance between us. I did not get his aircraft number and he never gave it; unfortunately. Hopefully; fca (glacier) tower will open soon.
output: A dc9 crew; in position at fca; witnessed another aircraft land opposite direction on the same rwy.

input: Acr x; a flight from south america to the united states; encountered weather at grann intersection and requested deviation around it. When i entered the deviation in atops to send it to the flight the computer responded 'fpap internal error' and would not let me probe the deviation to see intermediate fix it was good. I have no idea what 'fpap internal error' means. I tried replacing the flight plan with a new one but it gave me the same result. I could not probe a deviation for air carrier x. This happened at xa30 ante meridiem second officer there wasn't anyone around to get help from. I eventually assessed the traffic i had and determined that there shouldn't be anyone around that flight at his altitude and issued the deviation verbally through comrdo. I'm not supposed to do that because all clrncs need to be probed first to checked for traffic this is a safety issue. After talking to a few co-workers; this has happened to them also. This is one of many glitches atops has. A very flawed atops system has taken over the control duties and reduced us to being computer problem fixers.
output: Zny controller described atops failure during weather deviation requests; probe attempts unsuccessful; clearance issued without atops info.

input: Encountered wake turbulence from a heavy jet on approach. Autopilot disengaged; captain took manual control. Unstable approach; and unable to make 7000 ft at grabl due to wake turbulence encounter. Air traffic control sequencing was too close.
output: Emb140 first officer reports wake vortex encounter with preceding heavy jet during arrival to ord.

input: While landing on [runway] 30r; a light off the [northeast] side of the runway was very bright and distracting. I couldn't tell where it was coming from and mostly forgot about it. While taxiing out for takeoff; i noticed the light again and saw it was coming from a cargo operator's ramp. They had one of those temporary construction type generator light tower units. It had four light fixtures on top of the tower and was pointed and angled right at the displaced threshold of 30r. Multiple trucks were under it and it looked like they had a temporary sort operation going on in the ramp area. On the takeoff roll; the light was very distracting and bright. It affected my vision for several minutes after takeoff. This cargo operator could easily point the light in a direction away from the runway.
output: B737 first officer describes bright temporary lights set up on the cargo ramp at sjc that are aimed toward the approach end of runway 30r. These lights were on the right side of the runway and primarily affected the first officer's vision.

input: The ny metropolitan area had quite a bit of thunderstorm activity in the area. Jfk was using the cri vor and dme (co-located) approachs to runway(s) 13l. As we approached the cri vor and dme (co-located) ny terminal radar approach control facility advised us we were cleared for the approach and to cross the cri vor and dme (co-located) at 1000 feet/foot which we did. There was a rather nasty thunderstorm just westbound of the approach path. After we passed the vor and dme (co-located) we started a normal descent for the airport and picked up the lead-in lights for runway(s) 13l at jfk. About half way between the vor and dme (co-located) and the first lead-in light; the clouds from the bases of the thunderstorm appeared to be slightly below our 800 feet/foot normal altitude i might note here that the approach chart gives no suggested altitudes or altitude restrs once the approach lights have been sighted. We had a good visual on both the approach lights and runway(s) after leaving the vor and dme (co-located) and upon reaching 800 feet/foot i felt both the flight and altitude were safe. When it seemed we might lose sight of both runway(s) and lead-in lights intermediate fix we stayed at 800 feet/foot all the way around to final; which jfk likes for you to do for noise; the first officer started a slight descent to maintain the maximum possible altitude and keep both runway(s) and lead-in lights in sight. As we started our turn for the airport the tower controller voiced some concern that we were indicating an altitude of 450 feet/foot at that time. I told him of the lower clouds to the westbound and he said they were changing the approach to runway(s) 22 as we were speaking. I told him that we were fine and that we had both the lights and runway(s) in sight. I asked intermediate fix we were causing a problem and he responded with something like; 'no; i was just concerned because you were below the normal alt.' we continued the approach and landed on runway(s) 13l with no problem i was just concerned that he questioned what we were doing at the time.
output: Flc of an lgt warned of low altitude during a vor and dme (co-located) approach using lead-in lights for the last segment.

input: I was working d7 when aircraft x checked in on frequency at fl340. The r7 controller issued this aircraft a beacon code of [xxxx] then proceeded to start a track (as per hcf facility directive) for aircraft x over fapis. A minute or two later aircraft y checked in on frequency at fl360 and the r7 controller did the same thing for this aircraft; beacon code and started a track. The track for aircraft x showed a mode celsius altitude of fl360. This occurred for a couple of sweeps and i proceeded to bring this erroneous altitude readout to the attention to the r7 controller. The r7 controller then proceeded to reposition the track for aircraft x off of the target it was tracking (aircraft y). I have noticed this happening several times before. This is totally unacceptable to have data for one aircraft being started on a target of another aircraft. Before this track starting procedure was implemented; this had never happened before. The procedure requiring controllers to start tracks on no visible targets must be discontinued. Auto acquisition must be reemployed as a way of radar identification to ensure the data from the aircraft's transponder matches the data in the tab list. Starting a track does nothing to ensure instrument flight rules separation is maintained and only causes potential erroneous data being displayed as demonstrated above as well as unnecessarily increasing controller workload on the busiest sector in hcf.
output: Hcf controller reports of a new procedure where they tag up aircraft; not related to a primary radar return. Data tags swap at times causing confusion about the aircraft's position.

input: Requested instrument landing system runway(s) xxr and was informed out of service then requested vor and dme (co-located) xxr and was vectored onto approach noted not receiving vor and dme (co-located) on vor and dme (co-located) and informed tower twr said was not aware out of service couldn't continue approach for vor and dme (co-located) xxr with vor and dme (co-located) out of service unable to land on only remaining approach instrument landing system yy due to high winds exceeding tailwind component limitation. Ceiling was 1900 feet/foot broken and thought i need 2000 feet/foot ceiling for company limitations on circle to land procedures since instrument meteorological conditions and unable to complete any approach diverted to zzz1. Spoke with company dispatch on ground and discussed situation. Was determined i was incorrect on the ceiling requirement for circle to land and only needed 1000 feet/foot ceiling. We rarely perform circle to land in instrument meteorological conditions and i thought required 2000 feet/foot ceiling. Reviewed current weather at zzz and returned to zzz and completed the instrument landing system yy circle to xy. Reviewed release later for notams and noted amongst the 27 fdc notams there was a notice to airmen / of air missions for the vor and dme (co-located) out of service but was hard to spot as was listed in conjunction with the global positioning system approach for runway(s) xxr (we are not authority/authorized to complete global positioning system apchs).
