He did state the altitude to maintain correctly so i did not make a new transmission to get a different read back. I switched him to hou tower when he was at 019. Since he was the last aircraft for a few minutes; i remember taking a drink of my water and standing up to stretch my legs. The la (low altitude) alert sounded and i quickly called hou tower for them to issue the minimum safe altitude alert. The aircraft had descended to 010 on the localizer 1.5 miles from the final approach fix  the crossing altitude for the final approach fix is 020 and the minimum vector altitude in the area is 020 and the minimum vector altitude in the area is 2;000 feet. I did not notice his quick descent since the few seconds had elapsed from when i switched him to the tower.maintain a steady scan of all aircraft at all times until they are safely outside the area of my responsibility. Make sure every read back is 100% accurate; 100% of the time.
output: Houston terminal radar approach control facility controller reported a partially incorrect readback which lead to an aircraft descending below the minimum safe altitude in the area.

input: Twenty five to thirty minutes out we picked up our first automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) report: 300 scattered 5;000 overcast 1 1/2 miles visibility; mist. Shortly after that; dispatch called to report that the visibility had dropped to 1/2 mile but that it had improved. We also verified that our alternate; was still good. We monitored the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) as we were being vectored onto the instrument landing system approach. The weather was changing rapidly. It went to 300 broken 3/4 mile visibility then 300 overcast 3/4 mile visibility then 200 overcast 3/4 mile visibility. Then; as we were intercepting the localizer; the report was 200 feet/foot vertical visibility 3/4 mile visibility freezing mist. From the outer marker i could see the approach lights and most of the high intensity runway lights. During descent; as the angle of sight decreased; fewer runway lights were visible. With 3/4 mile visibility still being reported and a runway 2 miles long i was expecting to see about 1/3 of the runway at touchdown. From 200 feet/foot (dh) i could clearly see the green runway end identifier lights and at least 4-5 runway lights on each side. This seemed to agree with the 3/4 mile report. In any case it was more than 1/2 mile. I continued the approach and called 'landing'. By the time we got into the flare for landing it was clear to me that we did not have 1/2 mile visibility; but by that point i believed it was safer to continue the landing rather than initiate a missed approach. The landing was firm with some sideways movement; but not as bad as some landings performed by some new first officers. As we continued down the runway the visibility continued to drop. We taxied to the end of the runway and turned off. By that time the visibility was so low that we could not see the terminal. It was not safe to taxi unescorted. We stopped; asked for; and received an airport pick up truck to guide us to the terminal. Even as we were taxiing in; the automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) was still reporting 3/4 mile visibility.do not operate in low visibility environments without real time visibility updates. This automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) was reacting to and reporting the rapidly changing ceiling conditions but was not reporting the rapidly changing visibility conditions. This is not acceptable when conducting approaches to minimums; at night; at an uncontrolled airport. If i had to make an educated guess at what the runway visual range readings would have been if the airport had been equipped with runway visual range it would be 2;800-1;800-800.
output: B757 captain reports landing at an uncontrolled airport with an automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) reported visibility of 3/4 mile and an instrument landing system required visibility of 1/2 mile when actual visibility may have been less than 1/2 mile. A vehicle is required to lead the aircraft to the gate.

input: Wind calm/variable at 04 knots according to automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) i approached zzz from 10 miles to the north. Started making radio calls on unicom [ctaf] that i would use runway 14. No other calls heard. I entered downwind for 14 on a 45. Made call. Turned base. Made call. Final. Made call.saw no other aircraft. Landed 14. Upon landing; saw other aircraft coming towards me on the runway. Other aircraft just landed opposite direction 32. I called 'do you see me?' on [ctaf]. No response.other aircraft made 1st turnoff; so did i; without incident. After both aircraft stopped; other operator approached me and said he had heard no calls at all on his 'old radio.' said he had heard automated surface observation sys (or weather observation sys) but not anyone in pattern. Apologized to me as he assumes his radio was at fault.
output: C182 pilot reported an opposite direction ground conflict on landing at a non-towered airport.

input: I departed zzz and flew visual flight rules to zzz1 and attempted landing i hit something on the ground about 20 feet/foot after the beginning of the runway(s) and took off immediately. The gear did not retract; the main gear stayed down. I tried to recycle gear without success and proceeded to zzz2 where i landed. The front gear either collapsed or did not extend. Nobody was injured and the plane was removed from runway(s) customs clred.
output: A c182 hit an unknown object while landing the pilot executed go around and flew to a nearby airport upon landing the nose gear collapsed.

input: While accomplishing a routine work card; i noted the forward cargo door open and locked light was inoperative as per the work card intermediate fix this item is inoperative it is to be corrected or programmed for repair. Part to correct problem was not available; second officer i programmed item for repair. The next night i had the same problem with another one of our aircraft i then recalled that this item was to be addressed in a future minimum equipment list manual revision. Up to this point; it was standard procedure to program the item; there was no minimum equipment list requirement. I checkeded the recently revised minimum equipment list manual and noted the cargo door light had been incorporated. I mel'ed this aircraft work card should be revised to indicate item is now to be mel'ed intermediate fix inoperative -- not just programmed. I have notified company safety officials of this incident.
output: An a321 forward cargo door open and locked light was found inoperative rptr assigned item for a repair with no time limits. Later found revised minimum equipment list had added cargo light with time limit for repair.

input: The contract towers with radar routinely work visual flight rules aircraft on practice approaches in satellite airspace. We do not allow the federal aviation administration towers to do this; only the contract towers for some reason. They are not required to point out or coordinate these aircraft even though they are operating in our airspace. They issue these aircraft a discrete beacon code. We only see a partial data tag on our scope. It is impossible for me to separate my traffic from these aircraft because i have no idea what altitude they are climbing to; if they are going to turn left; right; climb; descend; etc. Since they are maneuvering on the instrument approach final for the airport; it puts them in the worst possible place for my ifr/vfr arrivals. I have complained numerous times to supervisors about this unsafe procedure and was told it is not my responsibility to separate from those aircraft because they are operating outside of class b. I even pointed out this potential situation to the supervisor on the wall a couple minutes before this happened. A be58 was an instrument flight rules inbound to gky that i had descended to 030 on a vector to gky. There was a visual flight rules aircraft on a gky tower tag that had been doing multiple practice approaches at gky and was southbound apparently for another approach. I issued traffic when they were 4 or 5 miles apart. I assumed the visual flight rules would stay at or below 025 but noticed him climbing higher. I tried to keep updating the be58 on the traffic and that the traffic appeared to be climbing. The targets merged with 200 feet/foot or less of vertical separation. The be58 never reported the traffic in sight until they were past. Recommendation; i am afraid there is going to be an accident because we have 2 controllers working airplanes in the same airspace with neither one knowing what the other is doing. I do not believe these contract towers even have the authority/certification to provide any type of radar services to begin with. The visual flight rules aircraft are asking the tower for service (why else would they be on a discrete code) and are issued a discrete beacon code so they probably believe that they are being separated from the other traffic. Since they are maneuvering on the instrument approach final for the airport; it puts them in the worst possible place for my ifr/vfr arrivals. It is impossible for me to separate my traffic from these aircraft because i have no idea what altitude they are climbing to; if they are going to turn left; right; climb; descend; etc. We do not allow any of the federal aviation administration towers to work visual flight rules practice approaches in our airspace. Why do we let the contract towers do it? Since these airports are below class b it is impossible to keep the arrivals in class b. They have to descend below it to land. With gky being in close proximity to dfw it is imperative to get the gky arrivals down as soon as possible which makes the situation even worse. Since the satellite controller is working the arrivals and departures already; it would only make sense that they also work the visual flight rules practice approaches like we do at all the other satellite airports. Another solution would be to have the tower restrict the practice approaches to maintain at or below 025. Then at least then we would have something to use for separating from them.
output: D10 controller expressed concern regarding the alleged practice of allowing local contract towers to provide radar vectors to practice approach aircraft; noting no procedures are in place to exchange traffic or provide separation from d10 traffic.

input: An md80 inbound to dfw on the jen9 arrival [was] cleared direct isabl intersection to clear other traffic in high altitude and to give a short cut. [the md80 was] cleared to cross isabl at 11;000 per letter of agreement. [there was also] a flight of 4/f16s proceeding direct to brownwood military operating area i called traffic to the md80 at 25 miles. I called traffic again at 10 miles. I was not talking to the f16s until they were just a few miles apart. The md80 said he was having a traffic alert and collision avoidance system alert. I then saw the f16s climb above the md80 and thought the traffic had cleared but i was unaware of the fourth f16 lagging about 12 miles behind and called this second traffic. The md80 said he was climbing due to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system alert. I only rogered the traffic alert and collision avoidance system alerts. I coordinated with dfw approach about the last traffic alert and collision avoidance system and told the controller in charge who reported to the amic. This type of incident as happened many times. Military aircraft will depart visual flight rules and fly straight to the brownwood military operating area head-on with dfw terminal arrivals. We need to come up with a procedure to get the military aircraft to the brownwood military operating area without being head-on with all of the dfw terminal arrivals. Maybe the traffic can depart out over the mqp vor and tacan (co-located) which is the departure gate. The last aircraft so far from the first aircraft caused another problem. I thought maybe i should have turned the md80 to the right but i was not talking to the f16s and did not know which way all 4 f16s were going. If we leave the dfw arrivals on the jen9 arrival then the incident just happens further west. The next time i will request early communications from dfw approach and give a hard turn to the right on the inbound traffic to hopefully miss all of the f16s that are not joined up.
output: Zfw controller reported military departures routinely climb visual flight rules opposite direction to dfw arrivals creating conflict.

input: After landing at dfw; ramp told us we had a 40 minute(s) wait for the gate. There were several aircraft lined up on taxiway left/right (directions) awaiting gates. Tower told us to turn left on taxiway left/right (directions) left on taxiway a. We turned left on taxiway left/right (directions) missed the turn on taxiway a; and got in line with the other aircraft tower told us we missed the turn and to contact ground gnd said no prob.
output: After landing super 80 missed assigned turn onto taxiway a.

input: Location: radar downwind sna runway(s) 19r. On radar downwind at 5000 feet/foot and 190 knot(s) i saw 2 traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii targets approximately 5 mile on my nose -- 1 co-alt; and the other 400-500 feet/foot below my altitude they were moving straight at my aircraft i announced to the socal controller a traffic conflict existed on my nose; co-alt. He gave me a left/right (directions) turn to 170 degrees as i started the turn; traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii announced 'tfc; tfc' on the co-alt target. As i started the turn; i xchked the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and knew that this was going to be close. I tightened up the turn by going to approximately 45 degrees of bank. The aircraft announced 'bank angle; bank angle' -- possibly blocking a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory as best as i can determine; i was within approximately 1 1/2 mile of the co-alt target during the turn. Oddly; the controller didn't believe the separation was much of a problem a telephonic debrief with the socal supervisor on duty was made after lndg.
output: A b737 flight crew exceeds their desired angle of bank at 5000 feet/foot in avoiding opposite direction same altitude traffic se of sna; ca.

input: During a taxi out for takeoff on runway(s) 33 at orh; a back taxi downwind was required. The winds were gusty and variable in direction from westbound to nw. All chklists were completed. During the takeoff roll; after takeoff power had been set between 60-80 knot(s) a high pitch intermittent horn sounded. I felt it was the stall vane but with the short runway(s) i chose the conservative approach also the lack of a stick shaker confused me. All engine parameters were normal. We told the tower that we had an aural warning. A taxi back to the gate and subsequent telephone conversations with dispatch and maintenance control personnel concluded that the horn was caused by the abnormal position of one of the angle attack vanes which resulted from the downwind taxi. Both angle of attack vanes were at normal position prior to our second taxi out and no further problems were encountered.
output: Acr mountain daylight time takeoff abort because of an unidented warning horn at start of tkof.

input: I flew; as pilot in command with clearance under an instrument flight rules flight plan. One non-pilot passenger was on board.while in contact with [the arrival airport] tower; i reported final approach approximately 4 miles from the runway. I was then cleared to land. The weather was clear and sunny with winds out of the north at 6 knots. I performed the gumpps checklist and continued my descent. On short final; i performed the gumpps checklist a second time and confirmed; among the other checklist items; that the gear deployment switch was in the proper position. I do not recall whether the single green light gear down indicator was illuminated. I glanced at the mirror mounted on the left wing to confirm that the nose gear was down. It appeared down.the landing was comfortably set up and standard until touchdown from flare. Things felt normal during touchdown; however; i realized something was wrong as the plane sank and the props hit the pavement. Smoke filled the cockpit. I maneuvered the plane to a complete stop then quickly opened the front door and unbuckled the belt so my passenger could exit the plane. I followed shortly thereafter as help arrived.[a local man] arrived in a pickup truck where the plane came to rest on the runway to provide assistance. He indicated that he had watched the landing and 'everything seemed normal with landing gear down; center of runway; normal sounds; etc.' the plane sustained obvious damage to the props and underside. It was later removed from the runway and transported to a nearby location.
output: The pilot of a beech baron reported a landing gear collapse during touchdown.

input: On clbout out to houston's hobby airport (dest dal) a developing storm was north of the route of flight with an overhang in front of the aircraft virga was apparently below the overhang. The capt and i discussed going under the overhang; through virga; as our destination was nnw. We decided the area looked too turbulent. About that time a sustained bolt of lightning flashed at our 12 o'clock (cloud to gnd) about 10 mile since it came from the storm developing to our north i turned 10 degrees left to avoid that area and asked the capt to get permission to deviate. At that time departure asked us to turn approximately 50 degrees right and he asked to delay turn about 10 mile the controller angrily shot back 'everyone else went that way; why can't you?' the capt calmly said; 'we must be out climbing the others.' the controller angrily shot back like a 2 yr old; 'just do what ever you want to do.' i turned 10 degrees left; flew 3-4 mile and when passing the area turned to the heading and flew through my assigned altitude by 800'. I had been climbing at about 3000 feet per minute and my attention was outside to avoid the weather it took 20-30 secs to stop my climb safely and descend to my altitude i failed to devote all my attention to flying the aircraft first in respect to the weather and assigned instructions. The controller was a significant distraction with his unbelievable attitude and then his who cares attitude.
output: Acr mlg track heading deviation avoiding thunderstorm activity; then altitude deviation when distraction weather avoidance.

input: I was descending to get under the class b airspace for mci to land at mkc. As i descended under the outer ring; i was getting automatic terminal information service to mkc. I reset my altimeter setting and realized that i 'may' have cut the outer ring close and had an incursion. What i learned: 1) get automatic terminal information service sooner; 2) obtain flight following; 3) give class b more space.
output: Rpt of a possible class b incursion at mci; mo.

input: On arrival, arrive into zzz we were taxiing in to gate and were about 3-5 feet/foot short. The guide man was in the process of bringing his arms up to stop us as part of a normal aircraft receipt and we got some abnormal hydraulic ecams. Since i was concentrating on stopping the aircraft which i did; and wasn't sure what happened; but when i looked down the electrical hydraulic pump was running. We still had both engs running. I asked the coplt to pull up the door pages. When he did; we saw both cargo doors open. I immediately called for shutdown of the #2 engine it appears the ground crew had opened both cargo doors as the airplane was taxiing. We had an federal aviation administration inspector riding the jumpseat who witnessed the whole process. I called station operations(s) and let them know all that had happened upon deplaning.
output: A320 captain reports baggage handlers opening cargo doors while aircraft still moving with engines running.

input: I unintentionally violated federal aviation regulation 135.265 (duty time and rest requirements) by flying a trip that made my 7 day total flight time projection exceed 34 hours company made a change to trip by adding 1 additional destination and; therefore; increasing total flight time for that trip by 37 minute(s) company did not distribute the updated flight schedule until after completion of the trip that exceeded my projected 34 hour limit. The information that i had available to me prior to departing on the trip in question light emitting diode me to believe that my projected 7 day total flight time would be less than 34 hours total flight time.
output: Part 135 commuter pilot in command exceeds his prescheduled 34 hours in 7 days.

input: Filed a flight plan from mei direct to pbf. Thought that i would be ahead of weather predicted ceilings were dropping and clouds were closing. Was using flight visual flight rules following. Near indianola advised intent to descend quickly. Center advised that greenville; ms minimums were a control zone and instrument flight rules only. Across the mississippi river a pilot was rpting ceilings above 2000' mean sea level i got into a pocket of foggy weather but visibility was 30 mile and sometimes greater. At their direction i landed at indianola and did not cross control zone. A good decision to land. Waited there until better circumstances.
output: Plt on visual flight rules flight plan with flight advisories from zme made precautionary landing at intermediate airport when he encountered less than forecast wx.

input: Location: lax company ramp. We were assigned gate on arrival, arrive it is a tow-in gate. The ground personnel hooked up the tow bar on arrival, arrive and proceeded to tow us in. They did a very poor job with a gross alignment. Without permission from company ramp; the crew proceeded to push the plane back into the ramp area. Company ramp notified us too late saying there may have been a conflict. Supplemental information from acn 455077: the first officer and i commented that the tow path seemed unusually wide. The other ground crew also signaled the driver that he was wide of the parking line. Very soon after stopping; the driver called to say that he needed to repos the airplane and not park the brakes. He then started to better align the plane. We soon realized that he was initiating a deep pushback and as the first officer reset his interphone panel to call company ramp control they were calling us to ask where we were going. They were concerned as another plane opposite our gate had called for push. We explained what had happened and they of course reminded us of the need to call before push.
output: The ground crew repositioned a b767 flc's aircraft without company ramp coordination at lax.

input: Takeoff from iah runway 15l; climbing via mmugs1 area navigation standard instrument departure captain checked in with houston departure control; advised climbing to 4;000 feet/foot the controller then cleared us to climb via mmugs1; except climb to 16;000 feet/foot the captain read back cleared to climb via mmugs1; except climb to 16;000 feet/foot after passing ttaps [and climbing through] 4;000 feet/foot simultaneously the aircraft kept climbing [so as] to cross botll at or below 5;000 feet/foot [but] i stopped the climb at 4;400 feet/foot due to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory for an aircraft on a 6;000 feet/foot downwind for runway 27 at iah. Simultaneously the controller asked the captain to verify that we were climbing to 5;000 feet/foot the captain advised him we were cleared to 16;000 feet/foot the controller said yes via the mmugs1. The captain replied in the affirmative; yes via the mmugs1. We were still at 4;400 feet/foot because of the traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory i had the autopilot engaged and lateral navigation and vertical navigation engaged. Autopilot was disengaged momentarily for the traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory to stop climb at 4;400 feet/foot so as not to get the traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory which would have been a more aggressive maneuver. The aircraft crossed ttaps at 4;000 feet/foot and was climbing for botll at 5;000 feet/foot or below on the mmugs1 area navigation sid.; based on the aircraft's fmc's navigational system.[our company's] b737-400's navigational system uses a single inertial reference system/unit as the primary navigational positioning platform with auto tuned dme-dme or vor-dme or vor-vor position updating; all of which gives the flight management computer the capability of being within 1/3 to 1/2 a mile of accuracy. [it is] not global positioning system accurate! The flight management computer cannot auto tune and update until after takeoff. Even then it sometimes can't update due to external or internal factors; or finding a viable vor and dme (co-located) and/or vor and dme (co-located) signal to auto tune. I have personally seen the flight management computer off by 10 nautical mile on 2 hour trips; because it was not updating properly. The federal aviation administration does not allow this type of navigational system to fly an area navigation approach to a runway using it for lateral and vertical guidance because it is not accurate enough; but thinks it is accurate enough to fly lateral and vertical guidance for a precise area navigation standard instrument departure that has vertical criteria to meet; with other area navigation sids off other close airports flying 1;000 ft. Above or below your precise altitude. Precise altitudes at three dimensional waypoints are only as good as the lateral precision your navigational system gives you![we should] not let navigational systems that use only one inertial reference system/unit with ground receiving updating (i.e.: no global positioning system updating or even 2 or more irus that talk to each other) fly precision three dimensional area navigation sids.
output: Confusion and disagreement reigned with respect to appropriate altitudes between air traffic control and the flight crew of a b737-400 assigned the mmugs area navigation standard instrument departure from iah departing runway 15l. A single inertial reference system/unit based flight management system was cited as a major contributing factor.

input: After takeoff oil quantities were checkeded and found to be normal (12-16 quarts). Approximately 1 hour later; the left/right (directions) engine was indicating 8 quarts of oil. In the next 20 minute(s) the oil quantity declined to 4 quarts. A radio patch to maintenance was established and our problem discussed. During the 10 minute(s) conversation; the oil further declined to 1 quart. Maintenance advised that there would be oil remaining in the left/right (directions) engine even after the gauge read 0 quarts. As we were still losing oil; the quick reference handbook was referenced and complied with. We elected to continue to our original destination as we were at the top of descent by then. We pulled the power to idle and declared an emergency we requested expedited handling to runway(s) 27l. We elected to leave the left/right (directions) engine running but only in idle as the oil pressure and oil temperature were within limits. When we turned final; we used only left/right (directions) engine thrust. At 5 mile on final; the first indication of low oil pressure was announced. We landed on runway(s) 27l without incident. When we cleared the runway(s) we secured the left/right (directions) engine and taxied to the gate on the left/right (directions) engine at the gate we shut the aircraft down.
output: Flt crew of md80 experience loss of oil quantity and subsequently oil pressure at top of descent to destination declared emergency and landed; securing engine after lndg.

input: After departure in climb approx. Fl320 we had a 'left engine fuel filter' engine indicating and crew alerting system indication. We referenced and accomplished the quick reference handbook for procedure and guidance. The quick reference handbook required 'land at nearest suitable airport'. After air traffic control and dispatch coordination; we elected [a nearby airport that] was a good option. In addition; the decision to divert was based on a combination of factors including; but not limited to; proximity in distance and time; emergency facilities; subsequent maintenance; and customer service options. Adding to this decision was this fuel filter issue had previously; earlier in our day; resulted in a significant maintenance delay. This aircraft inbound had the same engine indicating and crew alerting system indication prior to landing. Maintenance changed the fuel filter and fuel pressure sensor on the left engine. The filter showed contamination of a dark blue plastic/rubber matter. After completing their work; maintenance ran the engine and signed the aircraft back into service.
output: A b757-200 flight reported diverting to a nearby airport when they received a engine fuel filter engine indicating and crew alerting system message on climbout. Aircraft had shown the same symptom on the inbound flight.

input: Aircraft x was in a full 300 hour inspection for two weeks in zzz at base xxx. I was leading the project working the hours of xa:00 to xm:00 everyday. We were short on man-power and the ones that arrived to help were only able to help a couple days at a time and then another hand or hands would show up to help. The base mechanic out of zzz1 refused to come help. I started the inspection at the tail and was lubing the splines and got pulled to the front due to a crack found in the broom closet which turned out to be structural. We had to remove all the controls and the servo rack up top in order for the repair to get done. A vendor was called in to repair it which took a full two days and i was up there removing anything else he needed. We finished all the inspections and the aircraft went back to the base and after a flight the pilot noticed a nut sitting in the drain hole on the thrust reverser gearbox fairing. Base mechanic was called in and found the nut on the furthest aft hangar bearing bolt (there are one on each side); came off. The other bolt was still in and cotter pinned and the bolt was still in on the left side with no nut. I was having to do a bunch of jumping around due to different hands coming in on several different days and lost focus. I thoroughly believe i put the nut on but didn't cotter pin it.
output: Technician reported not installing a cotter pin in the nut for a bolt on the aft bearing hangar for the thrust reverser gearbox fairing.

input: We had just entered a left/right (directions) downwind to runway(s) 28 making all the appropriate radio position rpts on common traffic advisory frequency maintenance technician (mr x) called us on our company frequency and then someone said 'disregard.' mr x called us again just as we turned a left/right (directions) base and told us a c150 was doing touch-and-goes to runway(s) 11 and not in communications with anyone including common traffic advisory frequency as we rolled out on final; while looking directly into the sun just above the horizon; my first officer saw him and then immediately lost sight of him. I executed a go around and asked mr x to tell me when the c150 cleared the runway(s) we landed and parked the jet and mr x and his partner drove over and told us that there were 2 pilots an instructor and the owner/operator; on board and the owner became very indignant when mr x confronted him about what had just happened. The 3 of us went over to talk to the c150 pilots and the instructor did apologize to me. When i asked him intermediate fix he had access to a handheld radio; he said he did; but did not have it with him. I told him that was a poor decision for an instructor. And while the owner said very little; i could tell that he felt put out with our conversation. I have no doubt that he will continue to operate in this manner in the future; until he finally buys a radio -- intermediate fix he ever does buy one. Obviously; this could have had a very different and unfortunate ending. I strongly recommend that the company and federal aviation administration pursue this incident and contact the pilots before something very bad happens. I also recommend that the company acknowledge mr x's outstanding efforts in preventing a midair or ground collision. The federal aviation administration needs to contact the c150 pilots and reinforce the need to communicate on common traffic advisory frequency our company should tell all stations with unctled runway(s) to immediately advise airport maintenance personnel with radio access about this incident and the great job that mr x did.
output: Prompt action by a mechanic on the ground warns flight crew of b737-400 about traffic conflict with a c150 landing opposite direction not utilizing common traffic advisory frequency reporting. B737 makes a gar.

input: During preflt planning the capt and i complied with both company and federal aviation administration directives concerning the usage of area navigation departures from dfw. The departure and transition point (as assigned by clrnc) were correctly entered into the database and reviewed by both the capt and myself. Subsequent to departing dfw on this area navigation departure feet/foot worth center advised us that we were not on course to the anticipated intermediate waypoint. Upon review of the then resident flight management system waypoints; it was discovered that at least two; and possibly three; waypoints had dropped out of the database. The capt and i immediately reentered the missing; and previously correctly entered; waypoints into the flight management system and the aircraft returned to the air traffic control assigned course. Subsequent to arrival at lga; this flight management system malfunction was rpted to maintenance the mechanic informed the capt and i that other aircraft had been written up for similar occurrences.
output: E170 rpts flight management system loss of transition waypoints on area navigation standard instrument departure from dfw.

input: I finished a flight assignment as pilot in command in the morning at xa00. Immediately after landing and parking the aircraft at our hangar; i was notified i would be placed on crew rest for 10 hours to accommodate a flight assignment as first officer later in the day (part 135; 2 crew). It was actually a part 91 leg initially for this later assignment; to pick up a part 135 flight later. After this information i was told i was officially placed on crew rest; and my postflt duties were assigned to another on-duty pilot i relaxed for a few minute(s) prior to leaving the building; but not before understanding i would show at xk00 for a departure immediately following. The capt would be briefed on this show time. Later in the day; i showed at the airport after sleep and rest. As traffic was light; my drive took less time than expected; second officer i waited in the car for a few minute(s) to comply with rest rules. When i walked in the building; the capt told me to relax and we'd leave only when i was ready. Concurrently; we had to delay departure to xk45 to accommodate last minute(s) maintenance on the aircraft it seems perfectly honest to me; except that a disgruntled former employee claimed to the federal aviation administration that i had violated crew rest. I certainly did not set out to do this and believe i was in compliance. However; in the future; i believe i will demand at least 1 extra hour to account for any possible claim like this. It's unfortunate; but apparently necessary. I will also re-examine my own approach to busy schedules like this.
output: A federal aviation regulation part 135 pilot re-examines his approach to crew rest issues after having been accused of violating crew rest regs.

input: While on vectors for the localizer 16 approach for fyv we had to navigate, navigation through a line of developing thunderstorms the first officer was flying and the ride was not all that bad. After intercepting the localizer we could see the airport and runway(s) clrly from about 10 mile out. Rpted weather was 2000 feet/foot scattered; 4000 feet/foot overcast and 7 mile visibility. There were a few layers of clouds still and the approach was continued. We descended into the clouds and i noticed some low scud in patches below us. We broke out of the clouds into very good visual flight rules just prior to the missed approach point. We were high and began a steep approach to land. The ground proximity warning system gave us a sink rate warning followed by a pull up command. Since it was night we began a go around the tower told us to contact approach upon contacting approach we told them we were in visual flight rules and would like to try to receive a visual approach clearance the controller told us to maintain visual flight rules he then told us he had another aircraft on the approach and could not clear us. He then issued a heading for us to fly. We advised we could not fly that heading and maintain visual flight rules the controller then asked intermediate fix we would like an instrument flight rules clearance i had assumed we were still on an instrument flight rules clearance but the controller didn't seem to think second officer we told him we needed a clearance and wanted to come back and try the approach again. We received a clearance and vectors for another approach the line of weather we had come through was building rapidly and was between us and our alternate. We called the tower on the second radio and he advised the problem appeared to be a small area of low scud just off the approach end. The wind at this time actually favored a landing to the opposite end of the runway(s) from the localizer approach after being cleared for the localizer approach again we were told to contact tower we explained to tower that we were trying the approach again and intermediate fix we broke out like last time would like to receive a visual approach to runway(s) 34. Unknown to us it had begun to rain at the airport and the good visual flight rules conditions had deteriorated. We shot the approach and just prior to the missed approach point both the first officer and myself began to look outside the aircraft we glimpsed the runway(s) through a vertical hole as we passed over it. We looked back inside and saw we were past the missed approach point. We began a missed approach and at the same time the tower controller called and said we looked awfully low and for us to execute a missed approach we executed the missed approach and asked for vectors to our alternate. There appeared to be several problems this evening after reflection. I believe a true picture of the weather should have been passed to the approach controller this would have aided our decision to actually penetrate the first line of storms and begin this mess. The low scud layer was never mentioned on the first approach and the change in weather was not passed to us prior to beginning the second approach the next problem seemed to be terminology. On the first missed we told approach we were 'vfr and would like to get a visual approach clrnc.' i believe he thought we had canceled instrument flight rules and that caused confusion on our part. Next was the second approach the tower operator thinking we were low on the approach this could have been because of our slow start to begin the missed approach or the tower controller could have thought we were doing the circle to land. There was lots of confusion on approach frequency with approximately 5 aircraft being worked and deviating in all directions for weather our 'out of the ordinary' requests also served to confuse things worse. Our desire to land at the airport rather than fly through the bad weather between us and our alternate could have proven disastrous. This airport sits in a valley and a visual approach at night; in rapidly changing weather was a poor choice of things to try for. We should have just flown the approachs and executed the missed on both approachs instead of trying to have a better idea.
output: Commuter flight in an emb120 encounters weather between their position and the airport which has good visual meteorological conditions on missed approach they request a visual for a second try. Weather has deteriorated and they make a second missed approach divert to alternate.

input: After we took off; flight attendants still on the jump seats during climb i noticed a haze through the cabin and a smell. #1 flight attendant called the capt. He called the tower and he told us to prepare for landing the smoke went away before we landed. No one knew what really happened and i was not given any further reasoning for the smoke; other than it could have been from the deicing in den that could have been in the air conditioning.
output: Flt attendant rpt regarding haze and a smell in the cabin during climb capt notified and flight returned.

input: We were cleared the mount vernon visual runway(s) 1 circle-to-land runway(s) 33. Automatic terminal information service called winds at approximately 9 knot(s) out of the westbound as we were in the circling maneuver from base to final for runway(s) 33; another aircraft asked for a wind checked tower now said the winds were out of the westbound gusting to 33 knot(s) i immediately now knew i would overshoot final. I tried to correct for it and still blew through it. In attempting to re-stabilize onto final; i received a bank angle warning from the egpws; now trying to correct for that i then started getting bounced around pretty good by the gusty winds. I did not like this situation; especially this close to the ground second officer i immediately did a go around and circled back around requesting a straight-in approach this time to runway(s) 1 and informed the tower that in those conditions it just was not safe to attempt another circle to runway(s) 33. Had i known of the wind conditions prior to commencing the approach i would not have accepted the circling maneuver. It is my personal feeling after this experience that this approach is not a safe procedure intermediate fix winds are anything more than light and variable; especially when out of the westbound you are too close to the ground to really have a whole lot of time to correct for any abnormalities. Better communications of the conditions should have been made; without prompting; much sooner for us. Neither my for nor i had any idea that we would encounter those conditions.
output: Crj flight crew executes a go around from an unstabilized apch.

input: I was the co-pilot and flying pilot with no passengers. This was the third mission in this airplane and unlike the usual aircraft i fly this one has a glass cockpit with the mode control panel in front of the captain. We had worked together very well as a crew with excellent cockpit resource management we were descending to land at rno where the weather was about 1200 overcast with tops about 8000 ft and because of the temperature; icing was expected; level unknown. The autopilot was engaged. I had briefed the approach and we completed the appropriate checklists. We were getting step down descents and when we were cleared from 10000 to 9000 ft. I saw the captain select 9000 in the altitude preselect window but failed to notice the arm button was not pushed. I had just called for engine anti-ice to be turned on and we were discussing when to turn on the wing anti-ice. Then i noticed the airplane going through 8700 ft. I immediately disconnected the autopilot and started a climb back to 9000. Just as the airplane started climbing air traffic control announced 'stop your descent.'  we received further vectors and descents and accomplished the approach; landing in rno.contributing factors were i had little time on this glass panel airplane; night flight; instrument flight rules weather ahead with possible icing and busy time of flight. We lost situational awareness and my inaction was not confirming autopilot status and reliance on automation.
output: C550 pilots reported incorrectly setting their altitude during a descent to rno resulting in overshooting their assigned altitude.

input: Initial climbout; given instruction left turn northeast. Pilot flying (sic) observed difficulty in roll and pitch axis. Pilot monitoring (pic) made positive control exchange and verified the aircraft; hand-flown felt very heavy in the roll control and decided to return to airport of origin. At this point air traffic control noticed the deviation and queried the crew. Pilot in command decided to [advise air traffic control of the issue] due to difficulty in maintaining aircraft control and wanted freedom to deviate as necessary to mitigate the situation. Aircraft landed no flap without incident.
output: Pc-12 flight crew reported stiff roll control on takeoff and returned to the departure airport.

input: Atc gave us a descent to fl340 while in a left hand turn from a heading of 170 to 330. At roughly fl355; we received a traffic advisory on an aircraft left of our nose that we did not see and was not yet called out by air traffic control  we queried air traffic control about the traffic advisory traffic and as air traffic control gave us information; we received an resolution advisory of 'adjust vertical speed'. As pilot flying; i followed the resolution advisory commands in the cockpit and reduced our rate of descent and then visually acquired the traffic. Once we received the 'clear of conflict' audio; i lowered the flight deck angle in order to continue descent while maintaining visual of the traffic. I received an alert that i was 300 feet below our pre-selected altitude and quickly arrested the descent and climbed back to fl340. Our cockpit indication was that we descended to fl335 at the low point before recovering back to fl340. Air traffic control contacted us and gave us the phone number to call. After landing; we contacted air traffic control and they informed us that there was a 'loss of separation' of 800 feet and 3 nautical miles. Atc's threshold is 1000 feet and 5 nautical miles. We discussed the events that took place in the cockpit. I informed air traffic control of our failure to level off at the assigned altitude after reacting to the resolution advisory and that both pilots were scanning outside the cockpit to gain a visual on the traffic. We recognized our deficiency in maintaining an outside and inside scan throughout this evolution. In the near term; we will brief our team and review the pilot flying and pilot monitoring duties and responsibilities when searching for traffic; reacting to ra's and when we are within 1000 feet of planned level off.
output: While in a descent; cleared to fl330; the flight crew of a cl30 responded as directed to a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory followed shortly by an resolution advisory upon completion of the avoidance maneuver they continued their descent while monitoring the traffic visually. While doing so they inadvertently descended approximately 500 feet below their cleared altitude.

input: Normal takeoff from lax on runway(s) 25r for the loop departure cleared to 2000 feet/foot as we started to level off at 2000 feet/foot we got a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory to climb approach told us we had traffic at 2500 feet/foot and reiterated to level at 2000 feet/foot i saw a light aircraft at 1 o'clock position and diving below our altitude we followed the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii climb command and the light aircraft went below us when we were at 2120 feet/foot sct then cleared us to 13000 ft.
output: An air carrier flight crew flying a b777 rpts receiving a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory at 2000 feet/foot mean sea level departing lax.

input: We were in the final phase of the climb passing fl180 for fl190 when the aircraft's master warning system detected the aft baggage door was not secure. After complying with quick reference handbook procedures we contacted operations control and informed them of the situation. The aircraft was not losing pressure at this time. Initially we were given the option of returning to the departure airport or diverting. We chose to head for a nearby airport. With the exception of the indication of an open door everything else was normal until about 10 nautical mile north of the airport. As we were descending through about 5;000 feet/foot myself and the captain both heard a loud bang which was confirmed by the flight attendants who also reported a loud whistling noise. Around the same time we noticed a spike in cabin altitude as the door seal broke and the aircraft depressurized. Even though we were leveling at 4;000 feet/foot at this point and pressure was not an issue we were worried as to what the position of the door was; so the captain declared an emergency. We asked for a straight-in; however; by the time air traffic control coordinated that it was easier to continue the downwind for 1r. We were cleared for the visual. Emergency services met the plane as we exited the runway. We shut down the #1 engine and they confirmed the aft cargo door handle was unsecured and the door open.
output: A q400 master warning alerted the aft baggage door was not secured so the quick reference handbook was complied with. During the diversion to a nearby airport the aft baggage door opened and the aircraft depressurized at 4;000 ft.

input: Visual approach to runway(s) 17c at dfw. Scattered clouds; 10 mile visibility. Approximately 1000 feet/foot above ground level saw lightning flash westbound of airport tower rpted the start of rain at the airport during arrival, arrive about 25 mile out; radar showed no weather returns in the vicinity of the airport second officer radar was turned off. At 800 feet/foot above ground level tower rpted microburst alert for runway(s) 17r&c. Surface winds; visibility remained unremarkable. Approach was continued with no turbulence airspd gain/loss; or other indications of windshear activity. Aircraft landing ahead of us (3 mile ahead) did not rpt any indications of windshear; airspd gain/loss or turbulence approach was continued to a normal landing again with no indications of windshear or microburst. As we cleared the runway(s) the rain on the field became very heavy with increased lightning activity. Normal taxi to the gate. In hindsight; probably should have gone missed approach but lack of indications in the cockpit (turb; airspd fluctuation; windshear warning) made it hard to abandon the apch.
output: An md88 flight crew continues the visual approach to runway(s) 17c in spite of a last minute(s) microburst alert issued by tower when on 2 mile final at dfw; tx.

input: Aircraft x called from the northeast inbound and was instructed to enter left base runway 16l. Aircraft x read back the entry and runway correctly. Aircraft x entered the left downwind for runway 16l and was then cleared to land runway 16l. Aircraft x was a traffic conflict for a departure and was told to turn northbound into the downwind for that traffic. Aircraft x did not respond and was just told turn northbound. Aircraft x responded turning northbound and was again cleared to land runway 16l and read back the clearance correctly. Aircraft y was cleared for takeoff runway 16l. Meanwhile; an aircraft on ground was calling for taxiing which was on speaker over the local frequency. I responded to the ground aircraft. While talking on the ground frequency; aircraft y exited the runway on his own. When asked reason for the abort; aircraft y stated; it was for an aircraft landing on the opposite runway. At that time aircraft x was on short final for runway 34r and landed. I was working local; ground and controller in charge all combined. There were only 3 controllers after xa:00 pm on a busy visual flight rules day and no one was on break. We combined the positions. While the pilot turned the wrong direction on the downwind; i was working ground frequency and did not see the error in time.
output: A tower controller working local control; ground control and controller in charge combined positions cleared an aircraft for takeoff but did not notice an aircraft landing opposite direction to their assigned runway.

input: On the ewr4 standard instrument departure off of runway 4 we contacted departure after tower switched use. The initial controller gave use to climb to 5;000 ft. We responded with the altitude still on the standard instrument departure the same controller gave use a second climb instructions to 10;000 ft. And now we are turning west on the standard instrument departure we switched to the second controller and checked in still on the standard instrument departure he gave use a turn to 090 heading right turn. Then asked us why we are not on an assigned heading. We responded we never received a heading instructions. All four of us agreed we never heard a heading assignment on initial contact with departure. There was no aircraft conflict during the climb.
output: B777 pilot reported receiving confusing clearances from air traffic control while flying the ewr4 departure procedure.

input: Acft came in with a minimum equipment list for a standby magnetic compass. My partner and i were assigned to aircraft at xa15 i ordered the part number needed. I researched the maintenance manual to see what was involved to do the work. We observed that at the end of the maintenance manual it states in step 3 note: 'in the event the compass is removed and there are no modifications to the area and the same equipment is installed; there is no need nor requirement to swing the compass.' when we read this; i notified my lead technician. He also wanted to make sure intermediate fix we had to do a compass swing. Lead called line control line controller called maintenance control wide-body desk. Maintenance controller notified line controller that a compass swing was not required and a deferral was not needed. At this point; i went to the aircraft and replaced the broken compass as per maintenance manual. Aircraft departed at xc10. At xd00 my supervisor called me and said that maintenance control said that it needs a compass swing. I checkeded to see intermediate fix the aircraft was still here; but it was on its way to zzz1. My lead said that maintenance control scheduled a compass swing when it arrives to zzz1. Supplemental information from acn 729875: control center had called inquiring about standby compass removal and installation. Questioning intermediate fix a compass swing is required. With information line control had given; my input of their interpretation of the statement in the note of the removal and installation was of the same. Apparently the way worded it's ambiguous and obviously misleading. However now; after reviewing the amm standby magnetic compass maintenance practices; it's perfectly clear 'in the event the compass is removed and no modifications are made to the area and same compass reinstalled there is no need nor requirement to swing compass.' maintenance removed and replaced the magnetic standby compass; cleared minimum equipment list per amm and operationally checkeded system however failed to accomplish compass swing per amm. Immediate action. Discrepancy corrected during first maintenance overnight second magnetic standby compass was removed and replaced reference maintenance manual and compass swing accomplished reference maintenance manual new compass card installed. Follow up action. Recommending the note: 'in the event the compass is removed and there are no modifications to the area and same equipment installed; there is no need nor requirement to swing compass' of amm (removal and installation procs) be deleted or reworded as follows: 'if the installation location has no repairs and the same compass reinstalled; you do not have to do the tow around or calibration proc.' additional follow-up action. Suggest reviewing and rewrite all fleet amm magnetic standby compass r&r and swing procedures to ensure consistency throughout our maintenance procs.
output: A b767-200 aircraft standby magnetic compass was replaced. The required compass swing checked was not deferred nor accomplished prior to flt.

input: On nov/sun/05 my wife and i departed from dwh airport on a visual flight rules flight to madison; wi. We landed in sgf for refueling. At that time the weather forecast at the estimated time of arrival in madison and at least 3 other airports in the area was visual flight rules we departed springfield toward madison on a visual flight rules flight and requested and obtained radar flight following. About 100 mile from madison; the weather minimums changed to marginal visual flight rules and then to instrument flight rules several options discussed with the controller including returning to springfield or proceed to another airport at that time the nearest airport with visual flight rules weather was rockford; il; also 100 mile away. Fuel on board was 2.5 hours the flight was directed to rockford and radar contact and flight following was maintained. 30 mile from rockford; the weather also dropped below the visual flight rules minimums and became instrument flight rules the rockford tower started radar surveillance approach for landing descent and landing was done safely. I might consider returning to the departure or other airports with visual flight rules or marginal visual flight rules should a similar situation arise.
output: A non instrument flight rules rated pilot on a cross country accepted a surveillance approach to a nearby airport when his destination and nearby airports became imc.

input: After taking off out of teb the captain commanded me to put gear up. Then 400 feet/foot asks for flaps up; lateral navigation at the same time tower told us to switch to departure; while all that was taking place; our traffic alert and collision avoidance system had a guy in front of us about a mile or two away. While we both were looking for the traffic and cleaning up the aircraft i (first officer) did not hit the lateral navigation button and we did not level off at 1;500 feet/foot we noticed it at 1;700 and then descended to 1;500 feet/foot no problems were encountered.
output: A g-iv departed on the teb ruudy 4. During the climb; the newly trained first officer; distracted by a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory mistakenly hit flight level change instead of vertical navigation which caused the aircraft exceed 1;500 feet/foot before wentz.

input: It was my takeoff. On takeoff roll just after the 80 knot(s) call i heard increasing wind noise coming from the copilot sliding window. I notified captain and he noticed that the latching handle was not in the stowed position; even though the window appeared closed. He took aircraft control and performed a rejected takeoff at approximately 90-95 knot(s) we referenced the brake cooling charts and contacted maintenance; operations; and dispatch. During the before starting engines checklist the handle was physically checked by myself and crosschecked by the captain. The only thing i can come up with is that on taxi my headset cord became looped over the latching handle. I slid the cord back over the handle and may have inadvertently tapped the top of the handle and unlocked it. The handle must have slowly opened unnoticed during taxi and takeoff roll. In my opinion the button that is depressed on top of the handle seems very sensitive.
output: B757-200 flight crew reported that the first officer window was noisy and unlatched on takeoff; leading to a rejected takeoff.

input: On sep/fri/06; we took off at xa00z. During clbout on departure we made a turn to the westbound and the #2 autoplt disconnected during the turn. We leveled out and engaged the #2 autoplt again and continued on our way. We had been cruising for about 8.5 hours i was looking at my charts at the time because we were changing from one chart to another. We had entered some light turbulence and then had a feeling of the nose climbing this caused me to look at my instruments and i saw the vv1 tape increasing through 600-700 feet per minute of an uncommanded climb i looked over to see 37xxx feet/foot in the altitude window and quickly asked the first officer intermediate fix we were cleared to that altitude he said no and was already reaching for the altitude dial and turned it to 36000 feet/foot i looked back to checked my course; heading speed etc; and by that time the aircraft was leveling back to 36000 feet/foot i then selected altitude hold (we had not been in altitude hold before) and watched it carefully the rest of the flight without any other problems we entered a write up in the logbook of aircraft x and described the uncommanded climb event.
output: An md11f cruise at fl360 #2 autoplt began an uncommanded climb of 600-700 feet per minute altitude hold selected and airplane leveled at fl360.

input: We were cleared position and hold on runway(s) 16 left at sea. As we aligned with the runway the raas system announced 'on runway(s) 16 left' at the same time that tower issued instructions to an air carrier y flight exiting runway(s) 16 center down field. We had a much greater need to clearly hear the instructions to air carrier y -- whether cleared to cross or hold short of the runway our runway(s) -- than to hear a computer voice announce the runway(s) that we already knew we were on. Only when air carrier y actually crossed our runway(s) were we sure that they had actually been cleared to cross. Had tower actually told them to hold short and cleared us for takeoff prior to that; we would have been forced to ask for confirmation that air carrier y was going to hold short -- we were unable to hear their clearance due to interference from raas. Immediately remove the current raas. Re-install only intermediate fix it is upgraded with a crew-selectable inhibit function.
output: An air carrier pilot discusses the loud and unnecessary raas warning as the crew lines up on the departing runway(s) to hold for crossing tfc.

input: Climbing out from san we were told by air traffic control to cross pgy at 14;000 feet/foot we told air traffic control we were unable due to aircraft performance. We were then told to head 090 after pgy. After passing about 13;500 feet/foot we were told to rejoin the standard instrument departure the turn headed us back towards a daily; local parachute jumping plane supposedly at 13;500 feet/foot somewhere near pgy. This caused us to have traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory at about 13;700 feet/foot with a descent command. We complied telling air traffic control we were doing so. Air traffic control then told us we were descending towards the other aircraft. Not seeing the aircraft in question made this very distressing. Air traffic control then said we were clear as they had moved behind us. The other aircraft said they had us in sight but this was no comfort. They could be looking at the wrong aircraft. They could also have the wrong barometer setting and or could be climbing. We are trained that without knowing with certainty we have the other aircraft in sight we must comply with an resolution advisory even if air traffic control tells us we are causing a greater danger. The captain wrote up the traffic alert and collision avoidance system system but frankly i think something is broken in this recurring event that our mechanics could not fix. Move the parachute jumping away from pgy at 13;500 feet/foot this is an accident waiting to happen.
output: An air carrier flight crew flying a heavy aircraft on the san poggi two area navigation standard terminal arrival route could not make a 14;000' poggi crossing restriction and had a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory with a parachute drop aircraft at 13;500 prior to poggi.

input: Middle of night; unfamiliar airport i was called out on an air ambulance flight from lit to oma and back. Taxiing for departure from east general aviation ramp; ground control and tower was the same person. I was unfamiliar with the airport and was receiving progressive taxi instructions to runway(s) 14l. As i had completed the before takeoff checkeds on the ramp i was ready for departure at the end of 14l. As i rounded the corner i switched to the tower frequency before i could call him the tower asked me intermediate fix i was ready and said yes and was cleared for takeoff the approach end of 14l connects to runway(s) 17 which is much wider and more visible. Considering the above factors it is very easy to inadvertently line up on either runway(s) at that point. Again being unfamiliar and making a rolling takeoff without stopping at the approach end i began the takeoff on 17. After getting takeoff power set and checkeding the engine instruments for any abnormality i noticed my heading indicator was about halfway between 140 and 170 at which point the thought flashed through my mind that i could be on the wrong runway(s) this was at the point of rotation second officer i continued the takeoff in the interest of safety. After takeoff the tower handed me off to departure and informed me that i took off on 17. I think that there should be better markings distinguishing the 2 rwys.
output: Ga charter smt made a takeoff on the wrong runway(s) at oma.

input: A b737 was on a vector to the base leg to turn a 10 mile final; and a c208 a law enforcement aircraft was on an active mission approximately 1-2 miles south of the final approach course and maneuvering at 5;500 feet/foot mean sea level traffic was called to both airplanes more than once; however with other things going on; i failed to instruct either pilot to 'maintain visual separation'. The b737 was now on vectors to final and asked if they could square the turn to final and that he saw the visual flight rules c208. I wasn't able to approve it because there was a heavy airbus on final and immediately after i informed the pilot i was unable to approve his request i canceled his approach clearance; issued a heading of 170 and issued an altitude of 5;500 feet/foot because directly south of the aircraft was a 5;500 feet/foot minimum vector altitude this transmission was not acknowledged and 'someone on the air said blocked'. I then went back a second time and issued to the b737 'approach clearance canceled; fly heading 170 and maintain 5;500'; however this transmission also went unanswered. I went back and a third time issued the same previous instructions to the b737 and at that point he advised me he is in a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory descent and was around 5;100; but turning left to a 170 heading. I told the pilot to advise when he was complete with his resolution advisory and could accept the maneuver. By this time the b737 was southeast bound and there was no longer a conflict. First; i would make sure to ensure visual separation was being applied to one or both of the airplanes. Second; i felt compelled to work the c208 and not move him because he was on an active law enforcement mission at that moment. I thought there was enough room in the area; but the c208 suddenly moved towards the point where i was vectoring too. In the future; i imagine we shouldn't be able to approve any kind of mission whether it is a law enforcement or a photo mission in such close proximity to a busy final. There are lots of photo mission and law enforcement missions approved that always come very close to final. I think these should be approved less and with more awareness on impact of the standard operation and its safety.
output: L30 controller described a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory event involving a law enforcement aircraft and an air carrier arrival into las; the reporter expressing concern regarding the approval procedures for these types of operations.

input: Clbing out of san jose on the loup 9 departure i ante meridiem capt and pilot not flying departure gave clearance to cross sjc vor and dme (co-located) at 12000 feet/foot first officer started turn to vor and dme (co-located) i thought we were a little close but said nothing. Departure asked intermediate fix we would be able to cross at 12000 feet/foot we replied in the affirmative; knew that it would be close but thought we would make it. Instructed to switch to center we ended up crossing approximately 150 feet/foot low. Then proceeded on loup 9 to 8 vor and dme (co-located) fix to cross at or above 14000 feet/foot we crossed this approximately 200 feet/foot low. Center never made any comment on our altitude as the capt i should have been more involved and vocalized my feelings of turning a little short. It is easy to become complacent when not flying and then realizing that things are not right when it is too late. Not really a safety item but definitely not a professional altitude in the future i will make sure we have plenty of room; and vocalize my feelings sooner.
output: Flc of an mlg failed to make the altitude crossing restrict, restricted, restriction during 2 of the 3 fixes during climb out on a sid.

input: Tape covering total air temp/sat probe. Location: yvr. Total air temperature and sat were both reading 12 degrees higher than actual outside air temperature maintenance found tape around stem of rosemont probe which blocked numerous small holes resulting in erroneous temperature reading. Tape was very difficult to see due to its similar color as probe and proximitypa on airplane. Conspicuously colored tape used on aircraft might help make taped openings more noticeable and insure removal.
output: Erroneous total air temperature and sat readings; due to tape on rosemont probe.

input: Upon completing extended range twin operations 1 checked inspection on this aircraft an federal aviation administration inspector questioned item #8; pitot tube; static port; and angle of attack sensor inspection procedure he asked how i determined the tube had no insect obstruction. I explained that i checkeded it from the ground he explained that his interpretation is that you must put a stand up and visually checked up close. I explained we were trained that all inspections are done from the ground we also checkeded 'a' checked and 'b' checked paperwork inspection of this pitot tube and it states it is done from the ground item #6 on the extended range twin operations 1 checked states general walkaround accomplished from ground level. I feel the extended range twin operations 1 paperwork is contradictory with item #6 and item #8 and 'a' and 'b' checkeds reference work card x; 'b' checked and 'a' checked card 'a' states accomplished from ground i ante meridiem filing this rpt to have this issue clarified. Contradictory information causing entrapment of mechanic -- no specific proc.
output: During a b777 extended range twin operations checked an federal aviation administration safety inspector questions the method of checkeding pitot tube; static port and angle of attack sensors for insect obstruction.

input: Enrte mina vor and dme (co-located) to sac. Using a san francisco sectional; mar/xd/01; 66th edition. This missed approach point doesn't show any class d airspace around the airport and no ceiling at mhr. I called sac 20 mile out. They said to call back 10 mile out. I came close to another aircraft that was probably entering left/right (directions) downwind at mhr. I didn't catch mhr control tower when i didn't see dash line i assumed it was non operating control tower will you notify the department of transportation on the error on the map? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information an mhr tower specialist stated the tower has been in operations(s) for approximately 1 yr. In jul/01 the twr's class d classification went into effect.
output: A c210 pilot inadvertently entered class d airspace when it was not depicted on the sectional chart.

input: Gear up landing audible warning system did not sound. Gear lights too dim in sunlight.
output: C340 pilot landed gear up.

input: During flight from dmmn to fajs we experienced the typical conditions associated with operations(s) in the african non radar environment. Position rpts and air-to-air advisories were conducted at the appropriate rpting points. We attempted to contact libreville for approximately 30 minute(s) on all listed high frequency frequencies and ultra high frequency frequencies as well as xxxx for position and estimated time of arrival rpts. The first point of contact was 20-25 mile from lbv vor and tacan (co-located) at this time the controller was obviously upset. No traffic conflicts were experienced or stated. The high frequency communications frequencies are shared in this area by numerous other control areas in southern african which adds to this problem the entire crew has considerable experience in non radar environments as well as operations(s) in africa. While in this operating area of lbv we noted that we were not the only ones transmitting to lbv and not receiving a reply.
output: A b747 crew were experiencing communicationss problems resulting in delayed position rpting while flying over southern africa.

input: Sfo-ont coplt flying mlg. On cajon fix arrival; we were over pmd approximately fl230 with clearance to fl210. Next clearance was to descend to 14;000; which we expected for the majek restriction. Shortly thereafter center cleared us to 'dsnd to 13;000 at majek (pause) 250 knot(s) at 14;000.' what i had expected was majek at 14;000 and 250. Something didn't sound right second officer my response on readback was 'i understand; flight cleared to descend to 13;000; slow to 250 knot(s) upon reaching 14;000.' center response 'roger'. Airspeed in descent at that time was approximately 300 knot(s) at 14;000 the coplt raised the nose to slow; and reduced rate of descent to approximately 500 feet per minute about that same time an aircraft behind us was cleared 'cross majek at 14;000; 250 knot(s) then descend to 13;000.' we were at approximately 13;700'; 250 knot(s) when the coplt and i both decided that what center wanted was us at 14;000 until majek. He added power and pulled nose up; within seconds we were over majek and legal to go to 13;000. I read your national aeronautics and space administration reports all the time and i feel this is a classic case of 'punctuation and hearback'. Upon the original clearance to 13;000; intermediate fix the pause had come after 'dsnd to 13;000; pause; at majek; 250 knot(s) and 14;000'; that would have helped solve the problem. A normal sequence of 'majek; 14;000 and 250 kts' would have helped; or listening to the readback might have helped. The controller was busy; several aircraft on frequency but talking faster doesn't solve the problems. We could have had a serious incident or worse. And i'm sure intermediate fix the aircraft behind us hadn't been cleared over majek; we would have crossed at 13;000.
output: Alt deviation on standard terminal arrival route crossing restriction nearly voided. Clearance misinterpreted.

input: I rpted smell at 3l to pilots before takeoff they checkeded it. Thought it was new smell from factory. We took off. Inflt fuel was not adjusting correctly from tanks second officer we made an unscheduled landing in chicago. Pilots would not take aircraft over water.
output: Flc diverts due to fuel xfer difficulties.

input: I was working the lake sector; and at the time of the incident was taking care of some unusual procedures; including a medevac arrival inbound through our departure gates; very close in-trail departures out a different gate; and a instrument flight rules departure off of ogd that was going to conflict with my departures. The controller at the jordan sector called to coordinate aircraft x off of zzz; on a 090 heading; 130; my control; and the controller indicated he was 'not cleared.' i was little confused for a moment because the aircraft was in a 135 minimum vector altitude but i assumed (wrongly) that the 'not cleared' must mean he was visual flight rules since he was below the minimum vector altitude it is common for departures off that airport to depart visual flight rules and pick up an instrument flight rules in the air to avoid delays. The aircraft checked on heading directly into zlc sector 3 airspace and only a couple miles from the boundary; so i immediately turned the aircraft north to remain in s56 airspace; but i didn't have time to give him his clearance yet. At that time a supervisor came to watch me as my sector was fairly saturated. We discussed the medivac arrival; the close-in-trail departures; altitude conflicts with my ogd departure; and then focused on the aircraft x. He then left to talk to someone else; presumably the jordan controller. I climbed the aircraft out of the minimum vector altitude to fl230 in preparation for an instrument flight rules clearance. When the supervisor returned he told me that the aircraft was already instrument flight rules and was on vectors; but needed a clearance on course. At this time the aircraft was already above the minimum vector altitude i did not have a full strip with the destination as the route was truncated due to an ammendment; but the supervisor instructed me to clear him to the tch vor and dme (co-located) j15; boi; then as filed; and i did so. The supervisor then left. I am not sure why the jordan controller put the aircraft on the heading or altitude that he did (i do not work that sector and have not trained on it yet); but unclear communication and confusion about the ifr/vfr status of the aircraft (which i did not have time to go back and clarify with the jordan controller due to the unusual and busy situation in my own sector) caused a delay in my climbing the aircraft out of the minimum vector altitude altitude. In the future; when coordination is given to me that i'm not fully clear about; i will try to clarify that coordination rather than base my assumptions on common practices; even if the sector is busy.
output: S56 controller reported an aircraft was improperly coordinated off a satellite airport instrument flight rules below the mva.

input: Acr x inbound to dtw on polar arrival, arrive when air carrier x was 1 mile from traml another controller advised me that air carrier x had traffic at 2 o'clock at 12000 also. I issued traffic to air carrier x and descended him immediately to 10000. The target coasted for 2 sweeps. While in coast; i descended air carrier x to 6000. The beacon of the intruder re-acquired and now showed 11000; the same altitude that air carrier x was leaving! I advised air carrier x that the traffic now 2 mile away appeared to be descending they merged; the traffic disappeared. We brought up the beacon of the intruder; it turned out to be a ghost of air carrier x! We have asr-9.
output: Ctlr observes traffic on radar that is in conflict with an air carrier arrival, arrive at the same altitude the beacon target turned out to be a ghost target of the air carrier aircraft facility has asr-9 radar.

input: Dep from fll; clearance given and departure did not agree. Transition given did not agree with route given and loaded into flight management computer problem design of transition in the departure and pilot's overreliance on automated cockpit.
