input: I was called to look at some minor damage on the #1 thrust reverser actuator fairing; that was caused by a belt loader. The damage amounted to a small dent and scrape on the bottom of the fairing. We pulled the inspection (maint manual 05-51-062-02). The phase i inspection was complied with and no structural damage was found; other than the small scrape and dent on the fairing. This damage was documented and the aircraft returned for service i think the maintenance manual is vague in regards to when it is necessary to do more than the phase i inspection. It may help to delete the phase i inspection and just perform the phase ii inspection any time the engine has been contacted by ground equip.
output: A b737-200 incurred thrust reverser damage from ground equipment technician making inspection rpts phase i procedure inadequate.

input: Prior to pushback preflt indicated need for deciding due frost. Temperature was -1 degree celsius dew point -1 degree celsius visibility was initially rpted as 1/4 mile after deicing and during taxi to runway(s) 3; visibility dropped to 600-800 feet/foot runway visual range tower cleared us into position and hold on runway(s) 3 and said 'rvr 600 ft.' further inquiry revealed mid runway visual range to be 500 feet/foot now cleared into position and hold while waiting for runway visual range to improve. Holdover time of approximately 17 minute(s) was now exceeded. I (fo) went back to perform contamination checked no contamination. Shortly after i was again seated; we both noticed a slight vibration. All engine parameters appeared normal. Capt started to run up engs for clearing procedure and thought better of it at approximately 40% n1. Capt and i discussed it further and decided to return to gate suspecting fan blade icing. After returning to gate inspection showed 1/4 to 3/8 inch of ice on both fan and stator as well as considerable build up of ice on the back of fan blades. Contacted maintenance control and dispatch. Mechs heated the engs with conditioned air units and after another deicing of the airframe we departed with no further probs.
output: A b737-700's engs accumulated fan blade ice during taxi and extended hold for runway visual range improvement in dense fog and freezing temps.

input: Taxing for instrument flight rules release at destin. I tried to contact eglin clearance and clearance release on the published frequencies and finally managed contact with great difficulty! Contact with air traffic control while on the ground has always been; and still is; an admitted 'hit and miss' problem with eglin. This airport has a ctaf/unicom frequency and several different frequencies with which to communicate and try to maintain a safe operational environment. With no tower and the extremely close proximity to eglin air force base the operations at dts are growing increasingly more dangerous. That is an admitted fact by eglin air traffic control and base operations. Without a tower to coordinate the operations at the airport; it is just a matter of time until a serious accident happens there. Between the multiple frequencies that one must navigate through to get a clearance; taxi; get released; watch for abundant traffic and fly the airplane and be vectored; a tower with appropriate air traffic control personnel to coordinate departures and arrivals with all civilian traffic and abundant military is sorely needed. With so many frequencies to change and communicate on; it is very easy to get into a conflict or incursion on the runway with other traffic. With coordination of military traffic; civilian traffic and 'hit and miss' communications there; a tower with a clearance; ground and tower controllers would make destin a much safer place.
output: Ifr departure from dts voiced concern regarding the continued difficulty in establishing communications with eglin air traffic control for instrument flight rules operations; suggesting some type of improvement is critical to maintain safety.

input: Flight was operating to the west coast on a manually built route crossing the rocky mountains in colorado. The fight was originally planned and released with a method 1 (m1) terrain clearance solution. Maintenance deferred an engine anti-ice valve in the open position; so release two was planned and released with minimum equipment list 30-21 applied. This new flight plan was planned and released with a method 2 (m2) solution with den and lax as the listed m2 alternates. Once enroute; weather allowed for a more direct routing; so the dispatcher asked the crew to request direct from their present position (over nebraska a bit west of the spawn waypoint) to the bld vor and dme (co-located) (located in southern nevada). The crew acknowledged; requested; and was cleared direct to bld; and informed the dispatcher of that fact. Wishing to compute a new flight plan for this new direct route (in order to get new fuel burn and ensure terrain clearance); the dispatcher requested a flight management computer position report; which was entered in. The dispatcher then put the new route in and computed a flight plan. The error 'no point-circle crossing found for zzz' (or something to that effect) was displayed. To correct this error; the dispatcher went to the extended range operations tab and clicked 'default' (the flight had been planned with 'prep man' selected and alternate airports of zzz; den; and lax). This altered the extended range operations solution to alternate airports of lnk; inw; and lax; and produced a solution with no errors (other than perhaps the usual 'insufficient fuel' or similar error that is always generated when calculating an airborne flight). The dispatcher then released the flight with the new direct routing.immediately upon inputting release 3; the dispatcher realized that there was no terrain clearance solution generated. The flight was still east of the rockies at the time and crossing over areas of high terrain; so a terrain clearance solution would have been required. After changing the position report to input the more accurate; lower; zero fuel weight to attempt to force a m1 solution; and 'prep manning' the extended range operations page to input specific m2 airports; still no solution could be generated that provided terrain clearance. The chief dispatcher on duty was called and could not figure it out at first either. Eventually the chief dispatcher was able to generate a m2 solution when the extended range operations 'default' button was selected and den was removed from the list of available airports (cos was selected as the m2 airport). The dispatcher then put in release 4 with cos as the m2 alternate and provided the crew with the terrain solution and cos weather and notams. It should be noted that den was forecasting gusty variable winds; and thus would be considered unsuitable. However; 'ignore suitability' for den was attempted and still did not produce a valid terrain clearance solution.the safety concern here is that the dispatcher was able to plan and release a flight crossing an area that would require [our flight planning software] to generate a m1 or m2 terrain clearance solution with no error generated whatsoever to alert the dispatcher that this had occurred (additionally; a federal aviation regulation was unintentionally violated by issuing release 3 with no terrain clearance when it was required). It is conceivable that a m1 or m2 solution would not even be possible in certain circumstances and this would pose a safety risk.
output: A dispatcher described his difficulty manually revising an a320's inflight terrain clearance release over the rocky mountains. An engine anti-ice valve had been mel'ed open and special procedures were required because of the available alternate airports.

input: While pushing back; i discovered the contract pushback crew didn't seem to be following standard pushback procedures when they were ready for me to set brakes; the person on the interphone said 'set brakes and go to hand signals.' he apparently doesn't understand that it is the cockpit crew that tells the ground crew to go to hand signals; and not the other way around. Had i wanted him to stay on the headset for some unusual reason after setting the brakes; he would have already been disconnected and off the headset before i could have stopped him. When i looked outside to look for a wave off after performing my after start flows; i only saw 2 ground crew members walking away from the plane (they were about to enter the terminal building). Yet there were 3 crew members involved with the pushback but i was only seeing 2 people instead of 3 as i should have seen. I called operations(s) on the radio and asked that they send someone back out to give us a wave-off; and when the guy came back out; he seemed to have a bad attitude about coming back out and he let me know through his body language that he wasn't happy coming back out. It's important for the ground crew to realize that it's very important to follow proper procedures on pushback for their own safety. In this situation here; i was concerned that perhaps the third (missing) ground crew member was perhaps still under or around the plane where he couldn't be seen and for that reason neither one of us wanted to move the jet until all ground crew members were accounted for. Emphasize to the contractor that they need to follow proper procedures all the time for their own safety.
output: Rptr advises contract pushback crew fails to utilize air carrier pushback procs.

input: When trying to level off at 20;000 feet/foot the autopilot failed commanding down on the autopilot pitch trim at full down deflection beginning at 19;000 feet/foot the autopilot 'kicked' off at about 20;100 feet/foot it left the airplane in a trim-up position. I got the plane leveled and starting down at about 20;300 feet/foot and then leveled at 20;000 feet/foot with a lot of down force. Trying to re-trim the plane i found the trim wheel frozen. I hand flew for a few minutes in this condition and then finally forced the trim wheel loose. I re-engaged the autopilot with no further problems. Analysis: the plane flew through rain up to the freezing level (about 10;000 ft). I believe the trim tab assembly accumulated ice and froze; forcing the trim wheel broke it loose. I checked with the inspector who did the last plane inspection and he said the weep holes were clear.
output: A be90 pitched nose up at fl190 causing the autopilot to trip off. The pilot recovered at fl203 and with down elevator force regained aircraft control. The aircraft had flown through rain up to the freezing point and ice on the elevator trim tab was the apparent cause.

input: Received 3 resolution warnings to 'clb.' i disconnected the autoplt and began a climb from 11000'. At 11200' traffic alert and collision avoidance system stated 'conflict clr.' i advised dfw radar approach control of our evasion. Terminal radar approach control facility said only traffic in our area was at 10000'.
output: Acr has traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory responds.

input: Several maintenance write-ups going into zzz. Maintenance controller requested pilots to defer all with stickers; etc. Capt requested maintenance to perform maintenance action on all. Mechs came onboard and put deferral stickers on some; and fixed others; but no attempt to fix traffic alert and collision avoidance system capt called maintenance controller and requested maintenance controller attempt reset of traffic alert and collision avoidance system maintenance controller refused to attempt reset action for belief that system will just fail again on takeoff and it was time to get it fixed; however; they would not fix it unless capt refused aircraft faced with maintenance refusal to reset the traffic alert and collision avoidance system and maintenance controller insist that a reset attempt would not be appropriate and that a full repair was in order; capt took maintenance controller suggestion and refused aircraft the safety part of this is that maintenance controller apparently had no confidence in the traffic alert and collision avoidance system system making it to zzz1 in the first place. Maintenance controller asked capt intermediate fix he looked at log history -- apparently suggesting that capt knew the extent of the history of the traffic alert and collision avoidance system beyond what is rpted on the flight papers. The flight papers do not indicate a chronic history after the repair that would warrant no attempt to reset. Additionally; intermediate fix maintenance controller knew the unit would fail and that there was no maint/part in zzz1; maintenance controller should have taken action to not let the aircraft leave in that condition; or; to discuss the deferral options with the crew; or; to indicate a chronic item status after a unit replacement; and that the chronic status would be determined to be unable to reset. Resolution: the system needs parts at maintenance bases or within reach of all maintenance bases when a known chronic condition exists or is likely to exist. When a condition may occur when maintenance controller will refuse to reset a part or instrument because of chronic conditions; the log history will be listed as chronic in the paperwork as a flag to flight crew. A 'standard work' algorithm should be developed for maintenance that reflects changing market conditions for parts and parts held (or not held) in inventory. Pilots should not be asked to take a 'legal deferral' when at the same time; maintenance has no doubt of a defect/failure and significant history that a defect/failure cannot be repaired. Adding that; said defect should not be shown as operable intermediate fix there is no doubt that it is temporary in nature -- especially intermediate fix it is known or suspected that it will not remain operable for the duration of a flight segment.
output: A320 captain believes company maintenance is employing inappropriate documentation regarding the efficacy of maintenance performed in response to a logbook write-up of traffic alert and collision avoidance system system.

input: At the loading area; one jumper approached pilot door got my attention and signaled for a low/hop and pop jump for himself. During boarding i did notice a few solo jumpers (5 total). Thought to myself they were going to go to altitude with the tandem jumpers. Uneventful departure and climbout; and then i lined up for this low altitude jump about 2 plus miles out (from drop zone (dz)). I observed parachutes in the air; called other caravan; and he reported all chutes below 3k; so i communicated this back to jumpers to look for them. Approximately 1.5 miles before dz i heard the door open; we were passing through 4;000. I called unicom; jumpers in 1 minute. I am waiting for communication from the back of aircraft for course corrections and flaps (spotter calls flaps- is my queue to flaps 20 and power back ~300-700 pounds tq). About 10 seconds after door opens- i hear a jumper leave; i thought it was only the one going; but then; not sure but think i hear second one go; i then start to reduce power and to ask what's up to jumper in right seat. Then another jumper leaves and i feel the thump and same time i hear the yell from the back - 'someone just hit the tail.'i quickly think it better to lighten load for landing so; i tell remaining jumpers to prepare to exit if they want. They say ok they can jump. I redline up and about over the landing area; i get call - 'flaps' - flaps 20 and power back 500 pounds let them out about 6;000 feet/foot two jumpers stay in aircraft and land with me. Uneventful landing.i did find out there was a video; and after observing it i see that jumper that contacted the aircraft was 3rd out and a 4th jumper left the aircraft; too. I did not feel this or realize this till late the next day. Hearing/feeling a single jumper leave is not that noticeable on cg; and time between first guy out and last out is only 15-20 seconds.jumper that contacted the horizontal stabilizer landed under a reserve parachute in a field near the airport. Reserve was opened by automatic opening device.
output: Cessna 208 jump pilot reports a jumper hitting the horizontal stabilizer when a jump is initiated without informing the pilot. The flaps were up and the engine was at climb power. Apparently unconscious the jumpers reserve chute open automatically at low altitude.

input: While at cruise a left/right (directions) engine amber 'thrust reverser unlocked' annunciated. No other abnormal indications were noted. The quick reference handbook procedure states that intermediate fix no yaw; loss of airspd or buffet; operate engine normally. The capt chose to take a more conservative approach and to divert to zzz. Because air traffic control would not give us a clearance out of altitude without declaring an emergency one was declared and an uneventful landing was made.
output: Diversion by a b757-200 flight crew when the reverser annunciator warning alerts them to a possible unlocked condition.

input: On the departure from hnd i was incorrectly maintaining 481 feet per minute or better instead of 481 feet per mile. The controller asked for best rate and i corrected the problem quickly by asking for a brief shuttle climb which he approved but he still indicated he got an altitude alert. My terrain system never showed us below 1;000 feet above the terrain. However; i recognize i did not comply with the departure procedure. I have since reviewed this procedure with a flight instructor and the routing which i correctly had and never deviated from but i did repeatedly verify with the controllers that i was on the correct 080 radial and connected to the correct airway. When i was handed off to la center; the controller indicated he was told i had trouble with the routing but i never deviated. In the future i will make sure that i get the right climb rate based on the per mile not per minute which will lower the concern when arriving or departing a new busy airspace like las vegas allowing me to be more confident of the routing as well.
output: A c-182rg pilot departing hnd was given a terrain alert by air traffic control when he improperly maintained his climb rate at or above 481 feet per minute; rather than the 481 feet per mile as required for terrain clearance.

input: 20 mile se we (ltt x) were at an altitude of 10000 feet/foot we requested lower from air traffic control they informed us of a descent when clear of traffic off our left/right (directions) side. We then requested a visual flight rules descent 'on top.' air traffic control granted the request. As we progressed through 9500 feet/foot (dsnding 2000 fpm) in our descent air traffic control informed us of traffic y at 12 o'clock; 2 mile and 9000 feet/foot we rpted the traffic as 'not in sight.' no position rpt was given to the military aircraft y traffic from air traffic control with regard to our position we expedited our descent and within only secs; the military aircraft came into view at 1:30-2 o'clock; same altitude we executed evasive action and estimated the military to be within a 500 feet/foot of a collision course. The military never rpted us in sight. We believe the situation may have been avoided had we stayed instrument flight rules and had we received more definite traffic position rpting from air traffic control and had the other aircraft been alerted or informed of our pos.
output: Nmac.

input: We were cleared up to fl190 and an oncoming mlg was cleared to descend to fl200. We were flying an lgt; our climb being conducted in the flight level change mode. Passing through fl180; our climb rate was approximately 3000 feet per minute we got a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory at about fl184. At about the same time we got a 'clb; clb' resolution advisory with a commanded rate of climb of about 4000 feet per minute i performed a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii altitude deviation which climbed us up through the mlg's altitude with loss of separation. The reason for the alert was our rate of climb and the oncoming mlg's rate of descent the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii didn't know we were leveling at fl190; and i didn't know what the mlg was doing. Our company regulations contradict our operating manual in that our operating manual wants the aircraft to be flown with reference to the autopilot and flight director system commands which start a level off at 15 percent of the rate of climb which at 3000 feet per minute is 450 feet/foot before selected altitude however; the company regulations call for a 1000 feet per minute within 1000 feet/foot of selected altitude i suggest a reprogram of the autopilot and flight director system level off program.
output: An air carrier lgt climbed through another acft's altitude in response to a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii command.

input: Clred by ztl to descend from fl290 to what i (f/o) thought was fl240. I observed capt set what i thought was fl240 in altitude alert window and he began dsnt on autoplt. I then contacted company on non air traffic control radio for arrival, arrive questions; etc. When that was complete i again looked at our flight inertial navigation system and observed us descending through approximately fl233 for what was in the altitude alert window (230). I questioned the capt about 'weren't we just cleared to 240?' he thought fl230 was our clearance but said to confirm altitude cleared to with ztl (128.75 mhz). Center said it had been fl240. I advised center we were correcting. Altitude hold was pushed on flight control panel and i set fl240 back in altitude window. Aircraft descend (on autoplt) bottomed out at fl228 as capt corrected back toward fl240. At that time ztl told us to maintain fl230; which we did. Capt spoke to controller about misunderstanding as capt stated he thought we were cleared to fl230. Controller said; 'no prob.' no conflict observed by crew and none rpted by ztl. Supplemental information from acn 145559: as a final note; we suspect fl240 was dialed into our mode control panel but the selector switch was not seated in its detent and reverted to fl230 during our dsnt.
output: Alt deviation.

input: The flight was planned on a normal profile; but should have been planned unpressurized below 10000 feet/foot maintenance control from b737 desk at maintenance control advised that flight abc should have been planned unpressurized. I immediately sent an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message to the flight while i was typing the flight advised that they had lost pressurization and were diverting to zzzz1. I received an automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from the crew. The flight descended to below 10000 feet/foot and diverted to zzzz1. Ferry flight advisory as well as ferry permit should include information on known restrs such as unpressurized flight required. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter stated that this was a maintenance ferry; and was initially planned and filed at normal altitudes after the flight had departed; information was received from maintenance that the flight should be flown unpressurized below 10000 ft.
output: B737 is improperly dispatched at normal cruise altitudes but should have been planned for unpressurized flight flt diverted when aircraft became unpressurized.

input: Turb rpts were being received in the area from zab and other aircraft we asked for and climbed to fl380 (we were at cruise at fl360). The flight management computer indicated fl380 was below optimum. I looked ahead and saw lenticular clouds just before this incident. I had just seated the flight attendants about 30 seconds before using the public address right after seating the attendants; we incurred moderate turbulence and mountain wave at exactly the same time. The indicated airspd went from about .74 mach to the yellow indication on the masi with associated stick shaker warning in about a second or less. I reacted with emergency thrust and autoplt disengagement. We requested a lower flight level immediately and descended to fl340. During the descent we were able to increase the airspd and get out of the mountain wave and turbulence no emergency was declared and no air traffic control deviation occurred.
output: B737-700 encounters mountain wave and moderate turbulence at fl380. Mach deteriorates to stick shaker and descent must be made to regain airspd.

input: As capt of an e170 at fl360 and j149; i was en route approximately 20 mile westbound of geffs on j149; i was ordered by zdc to turn to heading 270 degrees immediately. There were 2 consecutive calls from zdc (i believe) both had the same instructions to turn to heading 270 degrees the first call was partially blocked. The 2 calls were within seconds of each other. As we began our turn to heading 270 degrees a b737 came within proximitypa and triggered a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory 'monitor vertical spd.' as the b737 flew directly under us i noticed on the traffic alert and collision avoidance system that they had only cleared us by 100 feet/foot on behalf of my aircraft and its crew; no deviations from any far's occurred to the best of my knowledge at this time.
output: Acr pilot described near midair collision at fl360 with zdc; federal aviation administration recorded operror.

input: According to automatic terminal information service the runways in use were arriving 4r instrument landing system and departures 4l. We prepared; programmed and briefed accordingly for [runway] 4l. After push from gate; i remember being informed of 20-minute taxi times by ramp; and therewith elected for single-engine taxi; as is customary to save fuel resources. Upon contacting ground at [taxiway] a; we were instructed to taxi b; hold at [taxiway] north approaching [taxiway] north we heard the aircraft in front receiving clearances and so started engine 1 in anticipation of a greatly truncated taxi time; it seemed we had been under way for maybe 3 minutes at this point. We were shortly after instructed to taxi via b; hold short [runway] 4l at celsius aircraft had been departing from [runway] 4l; so i was then confused as to which runway we were using. I asked the first officer to query ground. There was no response and a certain period of radio silence broken by other aircraft instructions. We were at that time approaching [runway] 4l at celsius running the after start check and transmitted a second time the question of which runway to expect. Ground abruptly told us he would tell us in 15 seconds; after which there was again a period of silence and some other aircraft instructions. We then were instructed to cross [runway] 4l and hold short of north on p; still without a runway to expect; but we were instinctively preparing for [runaway] 4r. (i thought there was a chance we would take [runway] 4l from the east). Being unfamiliar with the procedure of departing from the northbound outboard runway at kewr and being acutely aware of preventing an incursion on unfamiliar; complicated taxiways in inclement weather at night; i taxied slowly and tried to keep the first officer included eyes outside while juggling the runway change procedure and checklist. Ground urged us to contact tower; we complied. Tower told us to continue on p and line up/wait [runway] 4r. I was not comfortable with this clearance; still resolving the runway change with my first officer and in my own mind while paying attention to taxiing in unfamiliar territory. I asked the first officer to request 2 minutes delay to finalize our performance data and double; triple and quadruple check that we were absent error; omission or confusion on a procedure that could bring incursion; improper configuration or otherwise. The tower asked us if this a 'legit' timeframe to which i responded; 'yes it takes time to program our fms.' tower then informed us there was an 'obstacle free zone' in that area and could not accept our timeframe (i have seen no indication of this on the 10-9 airport diagram; 19-03; 10-7 or others; unless i overlooked something; so must take him at his word). Tower instructed us to cross [runway] 4l at v; left at d; hold at cc. I assumed we would switch back to [runway] 4l and we began reprogramming for the same upon setting the brake on taxiway d. Mindful of our fuel with both engines running; after a period of time; i asked tower what the plan was. Tower informed me he was waiting for us. I told him we were ready; again assuming [runway] 4l departure. Tower instead instructed a double right public address to v; hold short [runway] 4l. We again ran the runway change checklist; for the 3rd time; still nebulous of the runway assignment. Later; after crossing [runway] 4l we were instructed to taxi via p; cleared to depart [runway] 4r. Again confusion ensued as there is no p entry to runway [runway] 4r but p1. We then departed without further incident worthy of mention. There was no incursion or misconfiguration of the aircraft to my knowledge. Important to note; in my mind; is a total breakdown of cockpit resource management and the basic elements of communication between the tower and flight deck. Please let me say up front that i have high regard for kewr controllers and normally share good rapport; it is thereby bewildering why our flight encountered stonewalling to simple requests for normal information and incomplete phraseology. I am quite curious aboutthis. To the committee i wish to assert that airmanship dictates we communicate in a way that overcomes barriers rather than contribute thereto. I appreciate your tolerance in considering the following: requesting the departure runway during what was seemingly a fluid air traffic control situation; in inclement weather; at night; operating on unfamiliar taxi routes at an extremely busy airport while starting an engine and running checklists is little to ask; especially when it takes as much time to tell us what runway to expect as it does; 'i'll tell you in 15 seconds.' there is significant potential for human error in such high workload environments and i would hope in the future we are greeted with the same level of respect and consideration as a 777 bound for points far-flung and unknown.
output: Emb first officer reported ewr air traffic control issuing complicated taxi instructions and hesitance to provide expected departure runway led to confusion and distraction in the flight deck.

input: On departure from zzz; the nose gear unsafe (red) light illuminated when the gear handle was selected up. The 'gear door' light was also illuminated; but the nose gear indicator 'pin' was retracted. The loud noise from the nose gear area made it obvious that at the very least; the door had not closed properly. I selected the gear handle down; and subsequently we got 3 green and locked down indications. I directed the first officer to get vectors for runway(s) 27l; and declared an emergency as we would be landing overwt. The first officer made a beautiful landing at about 138000 pounds and minimal sink rate.
output: Md80 flight crew has a malfunctioning nose gear on takeoff declares emergency and diverts for lndg.

input: We departed aurora; il; on a cavu day to fly to ann arbor; mile to sell the aircraft the owner was flying and i flew coplt. In a space of about 20-25 minute(s) we were given about 7 altitude changes including being cleared to fl210 at one time. Also we were given second officer many heading changes to go over petty intersection (we filed over giper). We couldn't believe it and were annoyed with air traffic control after the controller cleared us to fl210 he later told us to maintain fl190. At fl190 i made a phone call to checked on arrangements at the other end while the pilot flew the airplane. Just as i was coming off the phone i heard something on the radio that sounded like 'fl210'. Started to climb again to fl210 as i acknowledged 'id leaving fl190 for fl210' the controller came back and said 'return to fl190' and that there was a military instrument flight rules traffic within 5 mile at fl200. We noted we had climbed to fl190; 250; and returned to fl190. The controller gave us a phone number to call when at ann arbor. That phone call told us they thought we went to fl190; 400 and were too close to the military acft.
output: Corp flight crew cleared to climb. Does climb. Told return to previous alt.

input: Crew arrived at aircraft at scheduled time and were met by mechanic and told all of what had been done in regards to the discrepancies from a previous flight on 10/thurs/04 involving an air turn back. After reviewing log book and waiting for last minute cargo offload; we pushed back and completed engine starts and taxi out for an uneventful takeoff on runway(s) 33r. On climb out an erratic temperature flux was noted on #1 acm gauge by selecting #3 temperature indicated steady. Before top of climb got zone one over temperature with temperature controller in automatic with maximum cold selected; since zone one trim valve indicated full heat selected manual temperature control and drove trim valve toward cool. Since zone one temperature remained high went to trim master off procedures selected zone two as master because #1 had seemed erratic. The acm temperature on #1 pack still erratic with fluctuations to higher temperatures #1 pack tripped as temperature fluctuated up to 185 degrees was able to reset first time; unable to reset on subsequent attempt; doors not positioning properly. Made attempt in manual but could not gain control because of previous history with this aircraft and extended over water flight planned made attempt to contact company for guidance with no luck; checkeded our position and elected to divert to zzzz1;fo. We jettisoned 60000 pounds of fuel and made a normal 585000 pound landing at zzzz1;fo. Due to one pack operation; aircraft depressurized in the descent at about 6000 feet/foot altitude when differential decreased to zero. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr was the flight engineer on this b747-100 that was involved in a previous diversion and fuel dump incident caused by the #3 pack air cycle machine failure. After repairs were made; the airplane was again dispatched over water and at top of climb the #1 pack air cycle machine displayed erratic temperatures the zone 1 control tripped for over temperature and then the #1 pack tripped off. Now operating with one pack on extended over water flight it was decided to divert. Fuel was dumped and the diversion station advised but landing was delayed. After a short wait; an uneventful landing was made. Maintenance replaced the #1 air cycle machine and the zone one trim air valve due to found failed open. Also replaced were several #1 pack sensors. While the above work was being done it was discovered the auxiliary power unit pneumatic ducting was cracked and the auxiliary power unit pneumatic check valve was found failed. These units were also replaced.
output: A b747-100 on climb diverted and dumped fuel due to #1 pack air cycle machine erratic; zone one temperature high and #1 pack tripped off over temp.

input: I landed on runway(s) 36r at tpa and on my rollout; i began braking and exchanged the tiller for my nosewheel steering. Upon doing second officer the aircraft veered sharply left/right (directions) (nosewheel had to have gone full l). I tried to regain control with the tiller; but it would not respond second officer i disengaged and using differential braking and rudder inputs i was able to get control only after the left/right (directions) main had gone off the runway(s) we were doing about 60 knot(s) when i engaged the tiller. After stopping; the steering seemed to work again; second officer i got back on the runway(s) and taxied to the ramp with neither ground nor tower saying anything. There was no aircraft or runway(s) damage. Also; no injuries were rpted. I grounded the aircraft and maintenance later found a problem with the nosegear feedback potentiometer. I submitted this rpt to document a potentially hazardous problem with the emb-120. We have another emb-120 that; as you taxi; the nosewheel for a split second at a time wants to turn left/right (directions) however; this has not yet caused any problems except gray hair. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information to use the nosewheel steering; the capt must first push the tiller down into a detent; then turn the tiller to the left/right (directions) or left/right (directions) the tiller has no function while in the 'up' position and can be moved to either side with no effect. In this incident; the aircraft immediately turned hard to the left/right (directions) as soon as the capt pushed the tiller into the detent but with no left/right (directions) turn commanded. The rptr's air carrier purchased or leased 2 brasilias from another air carrier both of these aircraft have had nose steering problems other aircraft in the fleet have had no such problems an interesting sidelight: the aircraft went off the side of the runway(s) in a cloud of dust and then back onto the runway(s) very quickly. The airport traffic control tower was not ware of this until the flight crew called it be telephone. Fortunately the aircraft did not need any help.
output: Rwy excursion.

input: Upon doing my preflight checks- i noticed that the orange patch on raft #2- in the overhead bin- had no mooring line cord under the patch at all. Upon investigation i found that the entire cord had either been pulled out or fallen out. There was no cord left under the orange patch. The pin it was attached to was also in a precarious position. Our current preflight- according to our manual - is only to verify it is present; not to check whether the mooring line is secure under the orange patch. This raft was within inches of inflating in the cabin had it been jostled or pushed in anyway. I have written about this before. I have attached pictures this time. My recommendation is that the preflight for the 10 person raft be changed to:verify that the raft is present in the last overhead. Add:that the mooring line is securely fastened underneath the orange patch in an ordered fashioned. If i would have had to access or use the 10 person raft on my flight; my success would have been low as the line would have most likely caught on something in the plane and deployed.
output: B737-800 flight attendant reported raft #2 in overhead bin missing mooring line and activation pin exposed posing a hazard of accidental inflation in the passenger cabin.

input: I was at el monte airport near arcadia; ca; flying my sma. I requested and received an instrument flight rules clearance to palomar airport at carlsbad at 9000 feet/foot my request had been for 5000 feet/foot i again requested the lower altitude but it was denied. Since my 43 yr old sma with only 185 hp and a full load was unable to get to 9000 feet/foot in the short distance specified; i cancelled the request and decided to make the flight visual flight rules after takeoff i climbed to a point about 1/2 way to the pomona vor and dme (co-located) leveled at about 2500 feet/foot to gain speed for a short distance; intending to climb at about a 120 degree heading to intercept a line connecting the pomona and oceanside vors; climbing to clear the santa ana area above 4400 feet/foot and then proceed over oceanside vor and dme (co-located) to land at palomar. However; when i started to climb i found that the electric propeller was stuck in high pitch. In working the manual control switch to try to reduce the pitch for climb i accidentally got the propeller against the high pitch stop. I then had very great difficulty juggling airspd and engine speed to get any climb at all. I tried to contact coast control but there were other xmissions on the frequencies and i had my hands full just flying the airplane at low speed trying to get 100 feet per minute climb in warm and turbulent air. The engine was laboring and vibrating and lugging at or below its minimum revolutions per minute i had to concentrate on getting above 4400 feet/foot second officer abandoned further attempts on the radio. I literally struggled to 4500 feet/foot and decided that was as much as i wanted to abuse the engine second officer stayed at 4500 feet/foot instead of 5500 feet/foot which i might not reach by the time of arrival, arrive over ocn anyway. On arrival, arrive at palomar; i found that a brush in the propeller pitch- change motor was not contacting the commutator. A short circuit had put a current through the brush spring and the spring had lost all strength due to high temperature i had spare brushes and was able to change to a new one but could not determine the cause of the short circuit. I ante meridiem not sure whether i may have failed to clear the edge of the area around the ont airport or the edge of the upper limit of the santa ana. I was second officer busy flying the airplane; trying to gain altitude trying to get the propeller working and trying to communicate by radio; that my course varied somewhat and i may have reached the edge of the santa ana area before reaching 4400 feet/foot i was too busy to determine those items accurately. In retrospect; it probably would have been better to turn around and return to el monte. I just could not think of everything and was worried about my predicament and possible engine damage; for it was taking a real beating.
output: Sma unable to comply with clearance altitude cancels instrument flight rules enters arsa.

input: Oceanic clearance delivery cpdlc late logon due to equipment glitch. [we] complied with b777 datalink comm guide as per reversion to voice procedures. Scottish [control] was upset we did not obtain our oceanic crossing clearance 30 minutes prior to coast out; which is not what the 15 minutes indicated on the form states. All issues were resolved and the crossing was otherwise uneventful.atc failure to communicated with the aircraft cpdlc systems on scheduled time.
output: When cpdlc communications failed a b777 crew reverted to voice comm to receive their oceanic clearance.

input: At fl410 we were issued a descent to fl300 95 nautical mile east of darby intersection. At the time we were about 145 nautical mile east of darby. We entered a 'place bearing distance' (pbd) into the flight management computer as 'darby/-95.' at this time the course line to the pbd shifted about 8 degrees to the left. The center controller (zid) noticed it immediately and told us that he thought we would fly south of darby if we remained on that course. The control display unit showed us direct to that pbd then darby. The flight management computer course line always shifts when a pbd is entered on a direct course. This time it was excessive. It is the first time air traffic control ever questioned me about it. Later on we were cleared to cross 35 nautical mile east of darby at fl240; this time the course shift was only 2 degrees. I believe the course line should not shift at all. If this shift is normal; could you please tell us how many degrees of shift we should expect and at what distances. This 8 degree course change was unexpected and was caught by a sharp controller almost at once. The airbus flight management computer always changes the course line. What's the best way to compensate for this anomaly?
output: A300 flight crew reports that the flight management computer will routinely place a down track fix off the direct course line; causing a track deviation. The error is normally small but in this case the deviation is noticed by zid.

input: Ifr flight we encountered severe turbulence at 3;000 feet/foot instrument meteorological conditions on a left downwind vector for instrument landing system runway xx; heading and altitude control were near impossible. The autopilot disengaged without command from pilot. This situation lasted approximately 50 seconds. After regaining control of aircraft; we proceeded with normal approach to landing.
output: A g-iv encountered severe turbulence on an instrument landing system final making aircraft control impossible for approximately 50 seconds. The approach and landing following the turbulence were normal.

input: Enrte to pick up a patient. Around lovelock; nv (lol); i started having the attitude indicator flag show itself. It would then retract. The a/i appeared to read correctly compared to the coplt's and standby attitude indicator. I was on top of a solid overcast this continued for several minute(s) and then the horizontal situation indicator heading flag started doing the same thing. I switched inverters and checkeded for circuit breakers out. No change and progressively worse. I elected to return to o43 as it was good visual meteorological conditions when i had left; but it has no weather rpting. I told zoa of my problems and started towards o43. The attitude indicator finally had a hard failure and i covered it up (sticky pads are great!). The horizontal situation indicator heading flag would stay retracted for a while and appeared correct compared to the coplt's directional gyro and magnetic compass. Nearing o43; i was still on top of an overcast center was vectoring me around for other traffic second officer i had a good look at the overcast i found a large hole and saw the airport cleared for the visual but i lost the airport and told center i wanted to go to rno. Direct to reno and descend now into instrument meteorological conditions everything is going ok albeit a lot of concentration and hard work. After a while; i ask for priority second officer i don't keep getting vectored. Shortly after mustang vor and dme (co-located) (fmg); i break out into visual meteorological conditions and see rno. Landing is uneventful. The first time in 20 yrs i have actually had to fly partial panel in instrument meteorological conditions a handful after yrs of glass and lots of redundancy in instruments crew and system there is a reason for all that redundancy and single pilot instrument flight rules with partial panel is truly a high workload i don't want to repeat any time soon! Training; training and practice truly make the difference! The instrument had a hard failure and was replaced later that day. It had been overhauled 3 times before.
output: Single pilot aboard ac690b has complete gyro failure enroute instrument flight rules diverts in instrument meteorological conditions to rno flying basic instruments.

input: Upon initiating approach into zzz; we were cleared to intercept the localizer x; reduce speed to 180 knot(s) and cleared for the instrument landing system x approach slowing through 200 knot(s) i called for flaps 8 degrees after which 'flaps fail' cas message illuminated. I xferred aircraft and radio control to the first officer and completed the quick reference handbook procedure for the cas message. We declared an emergency and after coordinating with approach returned to the final approach course and began the approach an uneventful flapless landing was performed on runway(s) x at zzz. We cleared the runway(s) and returned to the gate.
output: Crj200 capt reports flaps fail caution after selecting flaps 8. Quick reference handbook is consulted and uneventful flaps zero landing is accomplished.

input: We were en route to x51 and checked in with miami center. Center gave us a re-route that included the sscot1 area navigation arrival into x51. The problem is that there are no arrivals into x51. There are no arrivals in the flight management system or the efb for this airport. To access the sscot1 arrival in the flight management system we would have to change the destination airport to tmb. To view the sscot1 arrival on the efb we would have to select tmb. When i told the controller that we were unable to fly that arrival and that there were no arrivals into x51 he said that his computer showed that to be incorrect. The controller then assigned us fixes to fly. The next two center frequencies also tried to assign us arrivals into x51. The flight management system and approach plates do not match what air traffic control sees in their computers.
output: A citation 560xl flight crew was rerouted via the sscot1 area navigation standard terminal arrival route for their arrival into x51 (homestead general aviation) but discovered the arrival was in neither their flight management system database or their efb for use into their destination and so advised air traffic control miami center believed that to be incorrect but provided fix by fix clearances allowing the flight to continue to x51.

input: On the listed date and approximate time; i was conducting pattern work and landings. My wife was with me as the passenger and as i turned from left crosswind to left downwind for the runway my wife pointed out that aircraft y had crossed under my plane from my right and entered left downwind parallel to me and between my plane and the runway. It was at that time that the pilot made his very first radio transmission that he had entered the downwind; would take number one and 'had me in sight'. I asked him what he was doing and if he needed to get in front of me and he said that he would get in front of me to do a short approach for a touch and go and get out of my way. Prior to this radio transmission there was no radio contact with traffic in this pattern and certainly no attempt to communicate with planes or get into the normal pattern. The pilot simply flew under me; passed me between my plane and the runway; and took the number one spot. Had my wife not seen the plane and pointed it out; i would not have seen it before it gained altitude to get ahead of me.there was absolutely no reason for his action other than he had the ability to do so and obviously had no intent to use acceptable communication with other aircraft and or follow normal pattern flight for landing. No [priority handling was requested] and no warning was given as to why he was flying under me in a very maneuverable airplane; to overtake and pass my plane.this is not the first time i have observed this particular pilot display this type of flying behavior and i believe he poses a great risk to the many pilots; both experienced and student/inexperienced; that utilize this airport.
output: Pilot reported an near midair collision in the traffic pattern at a non-towered airport.

input: Departed kotzebue at approximately xa50 local on sep/fri/02. Departed visual flight rules with local traffic and weather advisory. Departed behind 2 other visual flight rules departures flew approximately 15 mile north of kotzebue and encountered marginal visual flight rules conditions. Returned to kotzebue and after contacting flight service station specialist found that the weather was below special visual flight rules conditions and dropping (visibility 3/4 mi). Could not get a special visual flight rules but could see the village at 3 mile did not have any place to land intermediate fix weather got worse. Could not find a place on the riverbank to land. I declared an emergency since i did not have instrument flight rules instruments and the situation was getting worse. Do not see how this could have been prevented with the rapidly changing weather in the artic part of alaska. In my judgement declaring an emergency was the safest thing to do. Landed with runway(s) in sight.
output: An airline transport pilot certificate pilot gets caught in a low visibility visual flight rules departure at a low altitude without 'imc' instruments declares an emergency returns and lands with three-fourths mile visibility at otz; ak.

input: Just after touchdown the aircraft started to drift slightly to the right. I believed this to have been caused by the 16 to 20 knot(s) crosswind coming from the north. I then applied left rudder to correct to center line. Then i received a steer inoperative engine indicating and crew alerting system message. At that point i continued to use rudder and differential braking to get the aircraft on center line. As we approached approximately 50 knot(s) the aircraft made an uncommanded violent break to the left and then immediately to the right. I did what i could to keep the aircraft on center line with aggressive rudder and differential braking. I was able to get the aircraft stopped on the runway. However; the aircraft was pointed approximately 20 to 30 degrees off of center line on a 070 heading. I immediately told tower that we were disabled on the runway and that i was not able to control the aircraft on the ground. The controller started sending aircraft around. I told tower that we will need to be towed back to the gate. Tower contacted port authority for assistance. We then ran aom procedures as best we could considering the fact that the aircraft was already stopped to ensure that we did not miss anything. We contacted dispatch and maintenance and told them of the problem. Maintenance started to request that i start pulling circuit breakers to other systems to attempt to restore the nose gear steering system and attempt to taxi it off the runway. I refused to do second officer i told him we have passengers on board an aircraft that was making violent random inputs to the nosewheel steering system. I will not voluntarily subject myself or the passengers to this unknown condition again. I demanded a tug. When the mechanic showed up he stated that the nose landing gear was pointed 55 degrees hard right and could not believe that the aircraft did not depart the runway. We got towed back to the gate uneventfully. When the mechanic called us back to give us an update on the status of the aircraft; he said that he sat there and watched the nose landing gear move continuously uncommanded left and right from center line and then violently go hard right and stay there. He stated that this is a hard fault. I know this has happened many other times to our pilots. What is being done to prevent this from happening again? Put out an ad for this defective system and have it reengineered before one goes in the dirt at high speed like my aircraft tried to do.callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information this is the second time that this reporter has experienced a nosewheel steering failure. The first instance occurred during taxi and the aircraft was towed back to the gate for repairs. He is also aware of several other failures that have occurred at his carrier and at others; and believes that it is time for the federal aviation administration to step in and require that the nosewheel steering system be redesigned.
output: Emb135 capt reports nosewheel steering failure during landing roll causing erratic steering inputs which he was able to overcome using differential braking. The aircraft did not experience a runway(s) excursion; and was towed to the gate.

input: To illustrate that the clear air turbulence iii status of the aircraft can be checkeded in cruise; i selected 'land' and the second autoplt on. The aircraft pitched down (at 2000 fpm). The first officer disconnected the autoplts and climbed to fl310. Altitude loss approximately 150 feet/foot air traffic control did not call us and we did not call atc.
output: Lgt freighter aircraft in cruise; rptr capt believes he can demonstrate clear air turbulence iii status of aircraft selects 'land' and #2 autoplt on. Aircraft pitches down at 2000 feet per minute pilot flying first officer disconnects autoplt and returns to assigned alt.

input: Filed from mtn via hvq then via the hvq transition on the ravnn5 to mtn. We were cleared as filed. Once enroute we were asked by center what part we were operating under. The question was ambiguous so i asked for clarification. Center replied and asked what part we were operating under and if we were authorized for the ravnn5. I replied that we were part 91 and we were capable of flying the arrival. At that time we pulled the standard terminal arrival route chart on the mfd and reviewed it. Upon examining the notes closely; i saw that note 5 stated 'all part 91; 101; 103; 105; 125; 133; 135 and 137 flight operations are prohibited on the beckley/charleston transition. As i was about to advise air traffic control that we needed different routing; they called us with a reroute via direct esl then mrb for the emi5 arrival. We reprogrammed the flight management system and continued the flight without event.there were several factors that i feel led to this: first; the note on the jeppesen standard terminal arrival route chart is very ambiguous and should say 'part 121 operators only on beckley/charleston transitions' . Also; the note should be near the route on the chart. Air traffic control should have been more clear in their query about our route. Asking 'what part are you?' is not clear. Lastly; we (the crew) should have reviewed the standard terminal arrival route chart prior to departure rather than rely on past experience with this procedure. We fly the ravnn5 routinely; although this was the first time we had flown it from this direction. Because we had flown the arrival many times; we didn't review the notes; only the route and altitudes.
output: A part 91 corporate jet crew filed to mtn on the ravnn5 hqv transition but they were informed by zid that only part 121 aircraft are permitted on that transition and so refilled the flight esl; mrb and the emi5 arrival.

input: Aircraft came in with a standby pitot heat inoperative and lgcu 2 fault. Standby pitot heat was deferred and number 2 lgcu was replaced and checked ok. On takeoff; the gear was raised and the nose wheel sounded like it would not stop spinning. An electronic centralized aircraft monitoring gear uplock not locked came on. We complied with electronic centralized aircraft monitoring by lowering the gear and raising it up again. We also received an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring for the standby pitot heat. The gear appeared to retract normally. We discussed the situation and decided to lower and raise the gear again. The gear lowered and did not raise. We informed air traffic control that we were returning. I sent a message to dispatch telling him we were returning because the gear would not come up. The flight attendants were told of the situation and no preparation was ordered. I informed the passengers and we landed without incident and taxied to the gate.
output: An a320 flight crew had landing gear problems after takeoff and decided to return to departure airport.

input: Climbing out of zzz in moderate rain and passing through about 18;000 feet; with the first officer flying; we got an airspeed disagree and altitude disagree on our displays; a master caution for engine; autopilot (b) kicked off; and vertical navigation disappeared all within a few seconds. We compared instruments and determined that the standby and captain's displays matched with airspeed at 280 and close to the same altitude still climbing. We transferred aircraft control and ran the airspeed unreliable checklist/altitude unreliable checklist. After reporting our difficulties with air traffic control we leveled at fl250; to finish checklist and run checklist for eec alternate mode. At that time the first officer instruments showed an airspeed of 130 knots indicated airspeed and 25;500 feet. It took a while to get through checklist; but we were able to get autopilot-a back. We talked about the bad weather at zzz and decided to continue to zzz1 due to visual meteorological conditions conditions there. On descent passing through 15;500 feet; first officer instrumentation appeared to recover. Approach and landing were uneventful. Priority handling was requested to ensure air traffic control was aware of our indication problems.
output: B737-700 captain reported a loss of reliable airspeed and altitude on the fo's side during climbout. The captain's instruments were functioning properly; so the crew decided to continue to destination due to it having better weather conditions than their departure airport.

input: I was on an instrument flight rules flight plan from elp to fzz via v198 sso v94 totec v16 pxr. I had received a weather briefing by phone in el paso and was told the only local thunderstorm call was east of deming vor and tacan (co-located) and moving east i departed and found very threatening thunderstorms near columbus vor and tacan (co-located) to the nw; north and ne. I requested a deviation to the sw which was granted. The thunderstorms started to appear to the westbound with lightning and rainshowers. The controller asked me to turn north to avoid the tombstone b military operating area which was apparently 'hot' -- i declined on account of strong thunderstorms and told the controller i was willing to make a 180 degree turn and return to elp. He then told me to climb to 11000 feet/foot and cleared me to continue on my present swestern heading the next controller could not receive my transmission and used a airlines flight as a relay station. He told me to deviate to the north to avoid the tombstone military operating area b and i again declined and volunteered to turn around to el paso. After several more calls i was told to continue on the present heading and i asked for a new route to douglas (dug) vor and tacan (co-located) v66 to tucson; then to phoenix which was granted. I was aware that i had penetrated the military operating area tombstone b airspace. I feel this was not well coordinated by zab controllers and placed me in an uncomfortable dilemma between complying with controllers who wanted me to fly into thunderstorms and my flight to avoid them and turn around intermediate fix necessary. Also the weather briefer admitted he had no radar coverage of my flight route second officer he relied on local observations.
output: Smt enters 'hot' military operating area while deviating wx.

input: The missed approach procedure for the instrument landing system 14 (21-1) in aex is incomplete or very confusing at best. The missed approach procedure states 'climb to 2000 direct to the vor.' when queried; many pilots think since there is a holding pattern depicted at gugem; the correct procedure is to climb to the vor and dme (co-located) then proceed to gugem and hold! When asking polk approach for the correct procedure or at least what they 'expect' a no radio aircraft to do; they responded; 'it has been brought to our attention before; our upper management knows about it and hasn't addressed it yet. Would you like alternate missed approach instructions?' (the controller didn't even know what course of action an aircraft executing a missed approach would take). I feel this needs to be addressed with commercial chart provider and corrected immediately.
output: A pilot commented that the missed approach procedure for aex is not specified beyond aex and pilots incorrectly assume that a holding pattern depicted is for missed approach holding. Reporter suggests chart makers need to build a proper missed approach procedure.

input: Due to fog; visibility from tower was restrict, restricted, restriction we were holding short of runway(s) 6r. An air carrier was cleared for takeoff we were air carrier x cleared into position and hold runway(s) 6r and read back. Like all previous aircraft we expected to be cleared to 5000/050 on the heading before switched to departure control then tower came on and said 'acr x; maintain 5000; turn left/right (directions) 050; contact dep...break air carrier y...rwy 6r; cleared for tkof' (in between we had spooled up and tried to confirm our takeoff clrnc). Capt said; 'twr; air carrier x confirmed cleared for takeoff we are rolling runway(s) 6r; 5000 and 250 on the hdg.' after a short confused pause (we had to go; since he had cleared an air carrier y for tkof). Tower came on and said; 'acr y cancel takeoff clearance hold short runway(s) 6r.' by that time we were airborne ready to switch to departure and encountered partial radio failure on the capt's side. No further action was required.
output: Acr x non adherence to air traffic control clearance instructed to hold in position made unauthorized takeoff pltdev.

input: We were on v2 (hnl r-110) climbing to 13000 feet/foot after contacting center he instructed us to fly a 095 degree heading for traffic and told us to climb to fl230. After a short while; center cleared us to the koa vor and dme (co-located) we were climbing through 14000 feet/foot and proceeding direct to the koa vor and dme (co-located) when center instructed us to maintain 13000 feet/foot at which point i noticed we were already climbing through 14400 feet/foot and my first officer questioned center by saying; 'we're climbing through 14400 feet/foot and you want us to descend to 13000 ft?' i noticed on the readout that we had +4 or 400 feet/foot vertical separation and felt that intermediate fix we descended we would be in the conflicting tfc's path. The traffic alert and collision avoidance system then instructed us not to descend and we got a visual on the b717 at our 11 o'clock low position he passed directly under us at approximately 500 ft.
output: B737-200 flight crew has a traffic alert and collision avoidance system alert while climbing to alt.

input: During takeoff roll; at vfr military training routes just as the nose began to rotate; a bang was heard below the fo's seat. At the same exact instant the bang occurred; the control yoke deflected abruptly to the left/right (directions) approximately 15 degrees both left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) main wheels were still on the ground both engine indications remained normal throughout the flight all system fluid levels; pressures; synoptics and flight characteristics also were normal throughout the flight dispatch informed us an aircraft departing after us; rpted some debris on the runway(s) dispatch also initially advised an md80 departed before me and may have had a tire problem considering all of our indications remained normal; and fluid levels were stable; i believed the most likely cause of the noise and control deflection was the result of some type of foreign object debris on the runway(s) possibly from the preceding md80. I contacted dispatch over satcom; i asked them to keep me updated with the status of the md80 upon landing much later into the flight dispatch informed me tire tread was found on the runway(s) again; all of our indications remained normal and tire pressures were also stable/normal. Upon landing and as a precautionary measure since we still were not certain where the foreign object debris originated from; i asked for the arff equipment to be alerted and standing by during our landing rollout. After parking the aircraft the crew went outside to observe the exterior of the aircraft #10 main landing wheel had tread separation. I realize it was likely and possible for some of the tire tread to strike one of the control surfaces displacing the control from its normal position however; anytime a control moves without crew input it is suspect and something to be very concerned about. Fortunately; the control deflection occurred while both main gear were still firmly on the runway(s) had the main gear been slightly off the runway(s) and the control deflected abruptly as it did; my concern is a wingtip or engine pod contacting/scraping the ground i have 2 questions: first; i would like to determine what caused the abrupt control deflection; and secondly; is there a simulator scenario that can duplicate tire tread separation just after both main gear lift off? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information reporter stated that the inboard left flap had sustained some damage. This was discovered after the return flight with flaps extended for inspection. It is assumed that the damage was done concurrent with the tread separation. To date there is no explanation for the deflection of the yoke to the right. One could speculate that damage to any flight control surface could cause a corresponding yoke movement; but the #10 tire is located on the left main gear and an impact from the tread would most likely create a roll to the left.
output: On rotation; b777 flight crew experienced a loud bang in the cockpit accompanied by control yoke roll deflection. It was discovered after landing that a main gear tire had blown.

input: Acr x instrument flight rules in cirrus at fl330; received traffic advisory from aircraft y at 11 o'clock and 7 mile descending treat at + 500 feet/foot altitude delta. Zla gave 20 degree left/right (directions) turn at 5 mile to traffic advisory at 3 mile to traffic advisory - resolution advisory of 'dsnd'. Followed resolution advisory while continuing 20 degree left/right (directions) turn given by air traffic control 'clr of conflict' and bottomed out at fl316. Climbed and maintained fl330. Never obtained visual contact.
output: Acft y descent through occupied altitude had less than standard separation from air carrier x traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory resolution advisory system error.

input: Sna tower cleared our aircraft into position and hold with another aircraft clearing down the runway(s) and another aircraft on final for runway(s) 29r. As we were going into position sna tower told us to 'pwr up' and be ready for immediate takeoff when aircraft downfield was clear we received takeoff clearance as we were still going into position on the runway(s) our operating procedures require at sna that we will not release brakes for takeoff until both engine epr is at least 1.25 epr with engs stabilized. Just after the capt released the brakes for takeoff sna tower told us to 'cancel takeoff clrnc' and taxi off the runway(s) due to landing traffic behind us. After receiving these instructions our aircraft was on takeoff roll with maximum thrust applied to our engs. I (fo) was pilot monitoring (not flying). The capt told me to tell him (the ctlr) unable. I relayed the message to the sna tower controller we were unable to comply since we had already started our takeoff roll. The controller then issued instructions for the aircraft behind us on final to execute a go around i ante meridiem not sure intermediate fix the sna tower controller was aware that we are prohibited from making a 'rolling tkof' at sna from runway(s) 29r.
output: Md90 flight crew has takeoff clearance canceled after starting takeoff roll at sna.

input: We pushed back from the gate on our own. The ramp area is not controlled. We taxied to taxiway h4 and held short of taxiway g and attempted to contact ground control for taxi. We tried several times to make contact; but he was busy with another aircraft. While holding short; a large 4 engine widebody airbus was taxiing south on taxiway g approaching taxiway h4. Neither ground control nor the airbus saw that the right wing on airbus was approaching our cockpit. My captain on ground frequency announced 'ground tell airbus to stop; airbus stop; airbus stop.' his wing was about 50 feet/foot from hitting us when he stopped quickly. I question our position about possibly being over the hold short line at taxiway h4. Either way; we should have held well short of taxiway h4. I know with his large wing span; the wing extends well past the taxiway h4 hold short line. It should be moved back or ground control should have control over the ramp area.
output: A b767-400 flight crew holding short of taxiway g on h4 at mco was forced to announce on ground control frequency that an oncoming airbus taxiing on g must stop to avoid a collision.

input: Atc did not mention anything about this so i'm not sure if this is an issue; but usage of the ipad is involved so i wanted to report. Captain was flying; descending via tyssn 3 arrival into las... Captain said it was his first leg into las after many years.... Descending in vertical navigation between cejay and kaddy; aircraft started to get high on the profile after transition altitude; which i called out. At some point the captain switched to level change to catch up. I dialed in 12;000 in the altitude alert window; the next restriction. We both were using ipads per new procedures; though i did have paper charts out as backup. While this was going on; captain's ipad auto locked; blanking his chart screen. I called out that we needed to level at 12;000. It started to overshoot and we may have gone up to two hundred feet below 12;000 (11;800) and returned to 12;000 in only seconds. The rest of the flight was uneventful. The la center controller did not mention it and subsequently switched us to approach.while late night flying and the captain's first trip into las may have been contributing factors; his ipad blanking at just the right time seemed to unsettle him a bit as he mentioned in later discussion. Better awareness among the pilots about ways to prevent the ipad from doing this may help the ipad transition to be more successful. If the ipad requires a passcode to show the charts again; it can be nearly impossible to quickly bring the screen back up; especially in turbulence. That segment of the star doesn't allow a lot of room for error due to a 'get down and slow down' requirement. I felt like i was aware of what was going on and thought 12;000 would be captured without overshoot; but we did go slightly below.
output: B737-800 flight crew momentarily descended 200 feet/foot below altitude restriction on las arrival while in level change mode. Loss of chart display on captain's ipad cited as a factor.

input: An evening call was received for an aircraft from maintenance control; flight crew reported '2-l arming levers get stuck when arming'. I was assigned to the gate call and i went to the aircraft. When i arrived at the aircraft there was nobody onboard so i referred to the logbook to see the exact discrepancy reported which was '2-l arming levers get stuck when arming' i approached the l-2 door and started to inspect the door mechanisms. I opened the door and noticed that the arming levers where indeed getting stuck; both while opening and closing; arming and disarming the l-2 door. I inspected the mechanisms inside the door lining and found no visible indication of what could've been causing the door handles to be getting stuck. I also visibly checked the girt bar engagement to the floor and all was operating normally. After closing the door one more time i 'armed' the door; then 'disarmed' the door with the handles being rough to disarm. While lifting the main handle to open the door i saw the escape slide starting to deploy and i let go of the door and the slide deployed completely. After the slide deployed i verified again; the position of the disarming levers and they were in the 'disarmed' position. Door might of been misrigged or worn down; causing handles to be getting stuck and mechanism within the door not disengaging properly. Evening.
output: A line aircraft maintenance technician (amt) reports an escape slide at passenger door 2-left on an erj-170 aircraft had deployed with the door slide lever in the up and 'disarm' position. Technician had been troubleshooting a flight crew squawk that the 'arming levers get stuck when arming door.'

input: I was flying my ultralight aircraft in moderate mid-day conditions and light winds. After approximately 30 minutes of uneventful flying i set up to land at my home field. Normal approach and set for landing on runway 13. Everything was normal until the last 10-20 feet/foot above ground level when a strong thermal or bit of turbulence that picked up one wing so hard and so fast that i was unable to correct. The ultralight rolled over and landed on its side with me still in the aircraft.local pilots arrived immediately and assisted in securing the aircraft. I did not immediately file a national aeronautics and space administration report since; as best i can tell; i did not deviate from any regulations or rules. When i spoke briefly with the local federal aviation administration a week ago they indicated that i might not even need to report this further. Just to clarify; this was a part 103 flight with a fully compliant ultralight. I was flying solo and for personal reasons. I have since been in contact with the federal aviation administration and they have asked to come inspect the ultralight to ensure part 103 compliance.
output: An ultralight aircraft was upset by a wind gust during approach at about 10 -20 feet/foot and landed on its side with pilot apparently uninjured; still in it.

input: This report is meant to provide information regarding the notice to airmen / of air missions system. As it stands now; the amount of information is excessive but my point of this report is with regards to the notams for mci. I'm making an assumption but it is my belief that the majority of air carriers are operating aircraft with advanced navigation systems which include global positioning system inertial reference system/unit inertial reference system/unit etc. The fact that these notams prevent the use of an airport as an alternate or an operating instrument approach to derive alternate minimums is unnecessary as these advanced aircraft are capable of area navigation or global positioning system substituting the inoperative vors in these notams. I want to point out that there is no standardization when it comes to notams such as one airport will completely exclude perfectly good approaches (mci) while other airports do not. In the case of [other airports]; they allow for area navigation subbing the inoperative components.
output: Air carrier dispatcher reported some notams for inoperative airport systems preclude use as an alternate airport while others do not.

input: On right downwind vector to runway(s) 14r at oma while descending from 4000 feet/foot and approaching 3000 feet/foot first officer (pilot monitoring) alerted captain (pilot flying) of traffic alert and collision avoidance system target closing and climbing quickly 600 ft below. At 400 ft below; captain exercised emergency authority and performed evasive climb. Target came within 300 feet and 1/2 mile. Target was never visually acquired. First officer notified air traffic control that we were climbing; and air traffic control responded with traffic call indicating target was a cessna and that he was within one half mile and had visual contact with us. Once clear of traffic; we were cleared for a visual approach to runway(s) 14r for uneventful landing. After landing captain elected to have a conversation with air traffic control where we learned that the cessna had departed an uncontrolled airfield visual flight rules enroute to oma and that air traffic control was surprised by the pop-up traffic. Although traffic alert and collision avoidance system provided basic target info; it never gave us either a visual or oral 'traffic' alert or 'ra'. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system was written up for maintenance evaluation. It appears that the approach pattern used by oma approach comes dangerously close to a nearby uncontrolled airfield with aircraft departing and arriving visual flight rules and without the knowledge or control of air traffic control suggest review of oma arrival patterns / altitudes to include possibility of conflicts with other airfields.
output: Air carrier captain reported an airborne conflict in the vicinity of oma with a corporate jet that had departed from a nearby non-towered airport.
