The rptr stated on checkeding the remainder of the lavatory sinks; all were found in the same condition except business class which was filled to overflowing and on takeoff spilled onto the counter and floor. The rptr said business class lavatories were blocked off. When asked by the analyst intermediate fix she was aware of any other incidents of this nature she said she had heard of two others but with no details.
output: A b777 flight attendant in charge rpts; prior to takeoff all lavatory sinks filled to the top with urine and fecal matter. Cockpit advised.

input: I was giving dual to an instrument/commercial student. Construction was in progress at the airport and we were given a taxi clearance to runway 9 to takeoff from the runway 5 intersection. After confirming our taxi instructions and runway feet available we taxied to the hold short line on runway 5 and completed our run-up. My student can read; write and understand the english language but it is not his native language. Because of this possible translation problem i asked for progressive taxi instructions to our holding position. I had an airport facility directory taxi diagram onboard the aircraft; but after the incursion i found that a larger printed version of an airport diagram would have helped my situational awareness. We were cleared for takeoff; and we taxied to the centerline and set full power. I checked the compass reading as we were rolling into position and it appeared to show proper indication. Because we were making a rolling start; these instruments were not giving the most accurate indications. By the time i realized we were on the wrong runway the aircraft reached rotation of 55 knots indicated airspeed and we were on the up-wind for runway 13. Air traffic control advised me that we departed off the incorrect runway and said; 'that is ok it is (runway 13) an active runway. We could contact departure.' after the incursion happened i reviewed the items that would have helped prevent it. 1. I will always have a blown up printed version of an airport taxi diagram. 2. The taxi route will be drawn out and reviewed before the aircraft is moved. 3. I should have let the compass stabilize before applying power and beginning the takeoff roll.
output: A flight instructor and his student had a runway incursion citing lack of situational awareness.

input: On the subject flight; we were cleared by the ord tower controller for takeoff on runway 28r from intersection ee. We performed the takeoff as per standard operating procedure with no issues. Just after clearing us for takeoff; i heard the controller instruct the aircraft behind us to; 'line up and wait'.during our takeoff roll; while we were still on the runway; and i would estimate about 20 knots below v1; i heard the tower controller clear the flight behind us to takeoff and the flight acknowledge the clearance. I remember thinking; 'boy; i hope we don't have to abort.'  being below v1 would have meant we would still be on the runway and another flight approaching takeoff speed coming at us on the runway. Hopefully they would be able to abort before hitting us. Fortunately our takeoff proceeded normally and nothing occurred.i am not completely familiar with air traffic control procedures. I don't know when the earliest time a controller is permitted to clear another aircraft to takeoff behind another departure. What i did know was that we were still about another three seconds from when the other flight read back the clearance until i called v1. If anything happened; (remote of course); standard operating procedure would have us stopping on the runway. Though the weather was clear; it was nighttime and i don't think the following aircraft would see us until it was way too late. Not to mention; if an abort was required there very well could have been debris left on the runway for the other plane to ingest. This would also depend on how fast i would be able to radio tower about the problem and the other aircrew to realize they were going to have to abort.overall; as i said; everyone may have been completely in the right and conformed to procedures. But from where i was sitting; i thought the takeoff clearance for the next flight was too soon and could been a disaster if something we always train in the simulator for (aborts); occurred.
output: Pilot is cleared for takeoff and is approaching v1 when he hears tower clear another aircraft for takeoff on the same runway. Pilot wonders what would happen if his aircraft had to abort; and also wonders what type of separation is required by air traffic control to have two aircraft on the same runway.

input: When taxiing into assigned gate parking position ground taxi director directed a stop (using light signal) about 4-6 feet/foot short of normal gate position very shortly thereafter (about 20 seconds) a green light indicated continue taxi. After moving only about 1 feet/foot the aircraft contacted something and aircraft was stopped and chocked. Subsequent investigation indicated that a fuel truck had moved into position forward of the left/right (directions) wing when the aircraft stopped the first time. The leading edge of the left/right (directions) wing was contacted by the fuel truck as the aircraft moved forward into final position the incident was apparently caused by an unnecessary and unintentional stop signal short of the intended stop point and poor coordination between the taxi director and other ground personnel svcing the aircraft supplemental information from acn 222876: the agent in the jetway indicated we were short of the gate and the parking lights went off. After a 15- 20 second pause; we received a green light. We added power to pull up to the final parking location and felt a bump.
output: Acr mlg wing tip strike on fuel truck when parking at gate.

input: We are at a summer camp. A group of kids and counselors saw a light and heard an extremely loud sound for about 5 seconds and saw it hit a tree. When we went to investigate what had happened; there were pieces of ice the size of a soccer ball and other smaller pieces of ice around the area where the noise had been heard. We believe that it was a megacryometeor; and have put some pieces in our freezer to preserve it should further investigation be necessary.
output: Observer reported ground strike from meteor.

input: Pushed off gate with 2 other aircraft pushing simultaneously [nearby] - all of us - tail north onto foxtrot. After 'before taxi/taxi' checklist we were cleared (by ramp) to 'follow the rj ahead on foxtrot to runway xxl'. I looked over just as a rj went past us on bravo (enroute to runway xxl); asked if we were clear right and pulled onto bravo to follow the rj. (ramp meant for us to follow the rj that pushed off other gate). The first officer caught the mistake immediately and contacted ground to tell them we were entering bravo. The controller politely informed us that we shouldn't enter an active taxiway without permission; and we continued down bravo to runway xxl without incident.i believe the following items contributed to my incorrect decision:1. A ramp clearance that included a runway lead my thinking to the runway rather than the ramp taxiway 'foxtrot' (which ends at 'bravo' near the end of runway xxl).2. An rj coincidentally crossing in front of us on bravo just as we received the clearance.
output: A b737-800 crew pushed back then was issued a ramp control clearance to follow a regional jet to the runway. The captain thinking the air traffic control clearance was issued to the runway; began taxiing and incurred a taxiway before contacting ground.

input: I piloted from bloomington; in (bmg) to [my destination on a 070 heading.] in the direct line of flight were the restricted areas r-3401b (west side) and r-3401a (east side).i approached restricted area b at 7;500 feet. I used information from my garmin 430w (jeppeson database; expired) and the sectional provided by flyq (current) to determine the altitudes for the -b restricted area were from 14;000 feet-17;999 feet (moa) and class east from 1;200-9;999 feet.on approaching r-3401a; i consulted the references to find the restricted area r-3401a extended from the surface to 14;000 feet. Prior to entering the r-3401a i turned and proceeded north until north of r-3401a; then resumed a direct heading to [my destination].my only contact with air traffic control was with the tower on departure from bmg. Throughout the flight i was monitoring 121.5; with the exception of getting the automatic terminal information service on arrival at [my destination].on landing i was greeted by the airport manager and asked to call columbus approach. They forwarded a message to me to call indianapolis [center] where i spoke with [someone who] informed me that i had violated restricted airspace in r-3401b (not r-3401a); which he said extended to 1;200 feet. I admitted i had flown through the area at what i believed was a permitted altitude. He noted that i was not monitoring center frequency. I was monitoring 121.5. He seemed surprised that i would be monitoring 121.5 (which is a pilot requirement) and admitted they had made no attempt to contact me on guard frequency. He also said i was in the middle of the r-3401b overlay before they noticed. I understand that airspace is the pilot's responsibility.i'm not sure what the corrective actions would be. Assuming r-3401b does extend to 1;200 feet as the center suggests; i can find no way to extract that information for r-3401b from the electronic sources. R-3401a does appear to report correctly.
output: Ga pilot reported air traffic control advised him of an airspace incursion that he stated did not display properly on his garmin 430w.

input: Enrte den-lax left/right (directions) side bleed trip would not reset. Abnormal procedures complied with; minimum equipment list procedures reviewed; and company maintenance control and dispatch notified. Approval to continue to lax was granted based on optimum cruise at fl250; left/right (directions) pack only operational; and flight management computer computations (fl250 input to crz page) for landing at lax with 4900 pounds fuel. Since company minimum planning fuel is 4000 pounds and we were visual flight rules at landing at lax; we decided to continue flight to lax. At 300 plus nautical mile from lax; air traffic control slowed us to 250 knot(s) with the new airspd of 250 knots indicated airspeed in the flight management computer 'crz' and 'des' pages; the landing fuel at lax was 4300 pounds the lower fuel computation at this point may have been due to higher than forecast headwinds. At about 150 plus nautical mile out of lax; air traffic control issued an amended clearance to pmd for the sadde 6 arrival, arrive i manually computed this route to be well north of lax; then westbound over the pacific; and then 180 degrees of vectors back around for a westbound landing on lax runway(s) 24 or 25. We input this into the flight management computer it confirmed my concern by showing lax fuel at 3900 pounds i then notified air traffic control that their new clearance would make us minimum fuel at lax. They then gave me my old direct clearance to lax of the civet 1 arrival, arrive our new flight management computer fuel was now about 4200 pounds at lax. During the approach at about 50 plus nautical mile lax approach control gave me an 's-vector' for sequencing; and asked me intermediate fix i could accept off-course vectoring due to our fuel. I stated that i could only accept a short vector; but our fuel was good for now. After the first vector; our flight management computer landing fuel was 4100 pounds he gave us one more 's-vector' for sequencing before clearing us to intercept runway(s) 25l final to follow a 'hvy' aircraft for landing i do not remember the fuel at touchdown; but our taxi-in fuel was 3700 pounds i and my first officer made sound and appropriate pilot decisions during this entire flight i complied with air traffic control at every opportunity; second officer longitude as it did not degrade the safety of our flight when a new air traffic control clearance did not give us minimum fuel; i appropriately notified air traffic control i would have thought absolutely nothing of this; other than we did a good job and it was a good example of what excessive air traffic control slow downs and vectoring can do to take what appears to be an acceptable fuel state and push that fuel state to the limits of acceptability. Unfortunately; i found out that an federal aviation administration inspector was on the jump seat of another air carrier heard that i was 'minimum fuel' (which i was not); and was investigating. Thus; i decided this rpt was appropriate for me; and to notify you of what i thought was excessive slow downs and clrncs/vectors on arrival, arrive into lax. Crews with less experience; and in aircraft without as good of on-board computers as the b737-300; might have accepted additional clrncs and vectors leading to a critical fuel state.
output: An air carrier flight crew with one air-conditioning pressurization system failed; decided to fly at 25000 feet/foot and this caused a higher than normal fuel burn.

input: [we] reported to aircraft on time. Inbound captain reported to me that the aircraft (b-767-300er) had 9 previous write-ups for the hpsov (high pressure shut-off valve) and engine bld (engine bleed) messages coming on 3-5 hours into the flight and had occurred again on his inbound leg. In addition it had write-ups for engine indicating and crew alerting system indications flickering on the same side and engine fire loop number 2 overheat warnings in the previous 3 days. I talked to maintenance control and they said that they replaced the hp valve and even the engine but could not get the problem resolved; so they believed it was a problem in the warning system or annunciator lights and since the valves was manually closed and placarded they could go with it. Meanwhile contract maintenance did not like the fact that this was a chronic unresolved problem and would not endorse it as airworthy. Complicating matters was the fact that when you get this warning the quick reference handbook commands you to shut down the corresponding air conditioning / alternating current pack rendering the aircraft un-airworthy for extended range twin operations  maintenance control said to change out the engine indicating and crew alerting system card but maintenance was not convinced this would do anything useful. Card was changed and then maintenance control told them to do a run-up. Supervisor mechanic was summoned to do the run-up and evaluation. Run-up was accomplished but he was only given 15 minutes on the runway to complete the task. [he] could not duplicate problem. He came back and said that this only occurs 3-5 hours into the flight according to the write-up information; that a 15 minute run-up was not a realistic test. [we] called maintenance control again. After going over the history of the problem; its chronic condition; problems with extended range twin operations operations; contributing discrepancies; i presented the question to maintenance control again and he said that he suspected a short circuit occurring in the wiring bundles in the engine pylon and that it needed a specialist to inspect it and troubleshoot. Based on this analysis none of the local mechanics would endorse the aircraft as airworthy including the supervisor mechanic who performed the run-up as they felt it would be compromising safety and i could only agree with their assessment. They then deferred the decision to maintenance control who also would not endorse the aircraft in its present condition. With everyone's reluctance to endorse the airplane as airworthy i could only turn the aircraft over to the station and maintenance control. Flight was canceled.
output: A b767-300 aircraft was rejected because the cause of repeat hpsov and engine bld engine indicating and crew alerting system alerts could not be isolated and repaired so the aircraft was not acceptable for extended range twin operations operations. In addition the aircraft had engine fire loop #2 overheat warnings.

input: While working south local control (lndg runway(s) 14r and departing runway(s) 28) i was alerted by the amass safety logic function that runway(s) 14r was occupied. I looked at the first arrival, arrive to ensure that wasn't the factor. It was not as that aircraft was clear of the runway(s) without looking any further and not knowing what the conflict was; i sent the next arrival, arrive around. After i sent the arrival, arrive around i noticed that the aircraft had touched its main gear on the runway(s) and pwred up and took off. After reviewing the amass data i was told that the arrival, arrive aircraft generated the alert on itself. Second officer there was no conflict as indicated by the amass. By luck i did not have a runway(s) 28 departure at the time as this false alert would have had the potential to cause a midair; the very thing this equipment is supposed to aid in preventing.
output: Ord controller described amass alarm event; allegedly caused by an arrival, arrive aircraft alarming on itself.

input: Encountered heavy traffic while holding. Decided to divert to land and wait for better traffic conditions. Automatic weather observing/reporting system reported 8 knot crosswind with some gusting. At roundout for landing sensed increasing sink rate. Applied full power to slow sink rate but experienced hard landing. At touchdown; the right main wheel assembly departed the aircraft. Aircraft veered to the right off the runway into soft ground and stopped. Two passengers and the pilot exited the aircraft through the right and left doors. No one was injured. In light of the high traffic and hot and humid weather conditions; flying a longer downwind leg would have given me more time to adjust to flight conditions and make a better landing. On inspecting the right main gear assembly; two days post event; there were signs of corrosion and what appeared to be fatigue fractures at the end of the gear strut. I believe the hard landing probably precipitated an already impending failure.
output: C182 pilot reported the right main wheel departed the aircraft after a hard landing in crosswind conditions.

input: Acr x cleared as filed (cha tys shine shine 1 clt at 15000'). We were approximately 30 nautical mile east of tys on the tys transition to the shine 1 arrival, arrive into clt at 15000' mean sea level we received a clearance from ztl to cross 10 east of snowbird at 11000' (which is not on the arr). The capt questioned the clearance of a snowbird fix--the dsnt to 11000' was not considered unusual. The controller explained about turboprop arrival, arrive gates into clt--'they want you off of snowbird at 13000'. Contact the shine sector on freq...' we contacted the next sector. By now we had descended out of 15000' to cross 10 east of snowbird at 11000'. We were now passing through 13000 for 11000'. We contacted center and rpted out of 13000 for 11000'; 10 mile east of snowbird. Center asked us to say altitude again; and called air carrier y at 12 o'clock at 12000'. We rpted we were at 12700' and he ordered an immediate climb back up to 13000'. We climbed back to 13000' and nothing else was said. It was unusual to receive a clearance other than the shine arrival, arrive and one sector had cleared us to an altitude the next sector had traffic in. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: rptr stated air carrier y was an mountain daylight time the flight crew reviewed the wrong altitude assignment with the receiving controller and they had been assigned 11000'. Rptr estimated they were 5 mile from air carrier y when they were back at 13000'. Routing over snowbird at 13000' was a new procedure that had been started that day.
output: Acr x was descended to 11000' should have been assigned 13000'. Operational deviation.

input: On a flight plan; i believe we were filed for the baset 3 arrival, arrive into lax; then at about trtle intersection socal changed arrival, arrive to the 'seavu 1' and assigned runway(s) 25r as the landing runway(s) the arrival, arrive and runway(s) were programmed into the flight management computer during reviewing of procedure air traffic control began issuing a series of speed reductions; which 160 knot(s) was the last. At about luvyn intersection we began to slow accordingly. We were using commercial chart #1 charts and i failed to see the notations on the inset for crossing altitudes from krain intersection to musik intersection and subsequently did not notify air traffic control of pending inability to meet restrs. My first officer began telling me 'you've got to get down' and he set a vertical speed descent of a significant amount. I readjusted the mode control panel for the speed requested by air traffic control and asked my first officer where and what the restrs were. I then did my best to meet the restrs at the speed requested. We executed the instrument landing system to and landed on runway(s) 25r without further incident. Air traffic control never questioned us. I believe the commercial chart #1 seavu 1 chart is too complex to be assigned without adequate time to review all the small notations. My recent lack of experience; degraded avionics and unfamiliarity with lax all contributed to some degree.
output: Inbound to lax; a late change in standard terminal arrival route assignment to seavu results in cockpit confusion and a possible altdev.

input: Winds were reported as gusting to around 30 down the runway on the day of the incident. Nearby taf's were forecasting windshear; and winds were varying from left to right crosswind. Upon touchdown; my student (private pilot certificate holder) put in proper crosswind input for a left crosswind; but winds shifted to a right crosswind; and it prevented the right wheel from touching down. Meanwhile; the aircraft drifted left; and we were unable to correct the aircraft to track centerline. Aircraft then departed the runway to the left; and stopped in the grass on the left of the runway. No injury or damage to the passengers or aircraft were noted. Air traffic control closed the runway until aircraft was removed from the grass.
output: Pa-28 flight instructor reported the pilot in training lost control during landing; resulting in a runway excursion.

input: We were assigned 9000 feet/foot and an intercept from the east for runway(s) 34 localizer vor and dme (co-located) (backcourse) in rno. Headed approximately at wagge. Night visual conditions with a few scattered clouds. With airport and runway(s) in sight level at 9000 approximately 17 vor and dme (co-located) on intercept heading (fo flying with missed approach point displayed; i had raw data displayed and localizer in manual mode). We had discussed the terrain prior to and again once we were in the descent at this time we received a terrain warning. We told approach we were getting the warning and would like to climb to silence the warning. We visually had the terrain but since it was night i was not comfortable with the situation. The warning changed as i was asking for altitude relief. I commanded the first officer to start a climb at 9350 feet/foot the warning ceased we were then cleared for localizer vor and dme (co-located) 34 bc/visual approach rest of apch/lndg uneventful. When i told approach control that we were climbing that i could not ignore my cockpit warnings; he indicated that 'that was too bad' that it was 'probably the twrs' that set off the warning. He did not indicate that our climbing to 9350 was a problem.
output: Acr on localizer vor and dme (co-located) backcourse approach at night has ground proximity warning system alert. Clbs.

input: Islip (isp); ny; class celsius airspace. The arpt/facilities directory lists effective hours for the part time operations(s) of the tower and effective hours for the part time class celsius services these hours are the same. The arpt/facilities directory does not state what class airspace is in effect in the following 2 sits: 1) during the time of normal tower operations(s) and class celsius services are suspended (for reasons of communications or radar probs). 2) during the time when islip tower is not operating and class celsius services are not provided. The january 6; 1994 aeronautical information manual paragraph 3-13f note 4 implies that class celsius airspace is in effect at all times: 'some facilities provide class celsius services only during published hours at other times; terminal instrument flight rules radar service will be provided. It is important to note that the communicationss requirements for entry into the airspace and transponder mode celsius requirements are in effect at all times.' the aeronautical information manual statement and the lack of information in the airport facilities directory lead to confusion. Functionally (if not legally) class celsius airspace at islip becomes class d airspace during situation 1) and class east airspace during situation 2). There seems to be an agreement between approach control and islip tower but it is not published. Entry procedures would be clear intermediate fix the airport facilities directory stated the following: when class celsius services are suspended and the tower is operating; class celsius airspace becomes class d airspace. When class celsius services are not provided and the tower is not operating; class celsius airspace becomes class east airspace. The airport facilities directory and aeronautical information manual should address these issues clrly second officer that pilots can know what the rules are. Keep in mind; clarity was the purpose of the airspace reclassification. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information n90 procedures specialist stated that the airspace goes away when the tower is closed and they treat the airspace as class east airspace. Pps said the aeronautical information manual was unclr.
output: Arpt facilities directory and aeronautical information manual are confusing as to isp class celsius airspace and communications requirements.

input: Dsnding from zdc airspace to roa airspace; watching for crossing traffic dash 8 had passed under us and was well clear to our left/right (directions) center advised we showed 200 feet/foot low. Altimeter read 60 feet/foot low which i rpted; altimeter setting change added 10 feet/foot we were waiting for altitude capture to take effect and it did not engage at 13000 feet/foot our assigned leveloff. We corrected manually but overshot 60 feet/foot neither pilot totally familiar with this autoplt system and were experimenting with it. Ctr's call of 100 feet/foot more than we indicate off is the second occasion where mode celsius not agree with altimeter. Plan to checked with several ctrs as to mode celsius readout and intermediate fix it is off; plan to have it adjusted.
output: Ltt aircraft in descent was advised by center controller that their altitude readout was 200 feet/foot low. Altimeter was misset; but also rptr capt says the aircraft mode celsius was in error.

input: Taxiing to takeoff position we heard a bang. Some passenber expressed concern second officer we turned off the runway(s) and had the aircraft checkeded out by air carrier mechs. It was determined that we lost the left/right (directions) nosewheel due to the axle failing.
output: B737-300 crew heard a 'thunk' when the nose gear axle broke and one of the nosewheels fell off the acft.

input: The navtech chart depiction of the meril7.meril is disconnected and gives the visual impression it is like the new half vector; half area navigation departures in clt. The departure is a area navigation off the runway standard instrument departure this has poor human factors design strictly for basis of space on a plate and small size. Poor design is complicated by the small screen area of the app further complicated by the small screen area of the ipad mini.
output: Regional jet captain reported the navtech meril7 standard instrument departure chart is poorly designed and does not depict well on the ipad mini.

input: Lndg on empty lot; pilot misjudged speed and rate of descent landed short of power line ahead of empty lot and balloon envelope draped over wires. Removed by power company. No damage to balloon; wires or other property. No injuries to personnel. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr was flying a piccard skysailer of 90000 cubic feet/foot volume. Another pilot was with him who had been flying the balloon; but gave it over to the rptr for landing the balloon was flying on the westbound side of the rio grande; near the river where there is cold air that drops to the surface. The rptr found a lot for landing and was forced into it by the falling air. The balloon envelope was slightly draped on a power line; not over it; after the deflation panel was operated. The crew of two jumped well clear of the basket. There was no arcing. A gentle tug by the power company got the envelope off of the wires with no damage. The rptr was taking prozac as prescribed by his doctor. As he does not have to take an federal aviation administration physical; he does not know intermediate fix this drug is not allowed for use by flight crew members. He will search this out. The rptr has heard nothing from the federal aviation administration on this.
output: A hot air balloon pilot's envelope draped over a power line. There were no injuries; property damage; or balloon damage. Weather factors down falling air that forced pilot into the ground before he was ready. Piccard skysailer 90.

input: Fss briefing prior to departure indicated ceilings in the area forecast to be 2500 feet/foot with 6 mile or greater visibility. Current conditions were lower than forecast. In fact; during initial departure from 3i7 en route to i23; ceiling was 300 feet/foot above ground level with 1 mile visibility. My mission was to fly one of our c172 aircraft to i23 where my boss had become stranded due to poor instrument flight rules weather he would then fly myself and himself back home. Unfortunately; upon arrival, arrive at the missed approach on the nondirectional radio beacon runway(s) 22 approach to i23; i did not break out of the clouds. As i announced on common traffic advisory frequency my intention to go missed; the boss got on the radio and unicom and a conversation ensued whereby i was told -- encouraged to descend below minimums. Not wishing to do this; i went missed; contacted cmh approach on the missed; and requested another approach knowing full well that i had no chance of finding the runway(s) at the minimum descent altitude but; i figured this would be good practice and it may help appease the boss. At least this way even though i refused to descend below minimums; at least i came back for a second approach as i contacted i23 on common traffic advisory frequency the boss once again told me how nice the weather was on the ground with excellent visibility. And i was told there was nothing down there except corn stalks; second officer it's 'safe' to 'come on down and have a look.' once again i proceeded down to the minimum descent altitude and no lower. After all; there must be some reason why the minimum descent altitude exists at that altitude intermediate fix it was 'safe' to go lower; then the approach would say second officer i announced the missed on common traffic advisory frequency and once again a conversation ensued; this time concerning where i should meet the boss. It was decided i would land at sgh and await his arrival, arrive the weather at sgh was 300 feet/foot overcast with 1 mile visibility. I shot the instrument landing system runway(s) 24 and landed. When the boss arrived; we took off with him as pilot in command and me as passenber at the destination 3i7; he proceeded to go below minimum descent altitude and scud run to the airport the point here is not to ram air turbine/ram air temperature on the boss; but to express some frustration about how some folks blatantly and willfully and repeatedly plan to deviate from procedures that were established to protect the safety of those in the aircraft as well as those on the ground intermediate fix a situation evolves whereby i end up in a questionable situation or a regulation is bent or broken; the first thing i do is situation down and analyze how the situation evolved; where were mistakes made; and how can a recurrence be prevented. As it happened on that day; when it came time to execute the missed; i did not promptly notify cmh approach and the flying of the missed approach procedure itself was sloppy because my attention was diverted to the common traffic advisory frequency -- unicom conversations with the boss on the ground while i refused the pressure to descend below minimum descent altitude i still slipped on applying the very old and very wise saying; 'aviate; navigate, navigation communicate.'
output: C172 making non precision approach i23 is pressured by boss on the ground to descend below minimum descent altitude rptr elects to make a go around for second approach same results and is told by boss to proceed to sgh where he will meet him. Because of distraction on the radio was late in advising approach control of the missed apch.

input: Entered hold at ketar and told to expect 2 turns in pattern. Expect further clearance (efc) then extended 20 minutes. After 3rd turn declared minimum fuel and was given clearance to next fix vepox. Then told to hold at vepox for 1 hour. We had now 50 minutes of fuel. Replied twice with 'unable'. Air traffic control reiterated one hour efc then asked if we were declaring minimum fuel. We replied affirmative and were given vectors to instrument landing system 16r at rjaa. At 1000 feet above ground level encounter reactive wind shear alert. Performed wind shear escape maneuver leveled at 4000 feet and requested and were given vectors to our alternate. Landed at our alternate without further incident. Fuel at touchdown approximately 10;000 pounds block in fuel 8800.
output: B777 captain encountered wind shear at 1000 feet during approach; with minimum fuel and went around. Flight diverted to a nearby alternate and landed with approximately 10000 pounds of fuel.

input: I had 2 instrument students aboard in an sma. One of the students had been practicing vor and dme (co-located) tracking with course reversals for about 30 minute(s) at sgd vor and dme (co-located) i broke off the exercise to proceed to sonoma skypark for landing with intention to change student pilots we had no sooner left the vor and dme (co-located) when the student passenber expressed a pressing need for the bathroom. At age 69 i ante meridiem very much aware of how pressing this need can become. I immediately diverted to sonoma valley. It had been raining in our area the night before and i was uncertain as to the condition of the dirt/gravel runway(s) 27/9 second officer i opted for what i knew as runway(s) 34; a paved strip. Because of my sense of urgency by what i considered a potential cockpit catastrophe i executed a power off short approach to what i had known for yrs to be runway(s) 34. The runway(s) was not runway(s) 34 but a ramp i do not know how recent the change but because of my passenber physical needs i chose to land. I used less than 1/2 of the existing runway(s) executed a 180 degree turn and deplaned my passenber when he returned to the aircraft we departed via runway(s) 9 which i determined to be damp but suitable.
output: Unauth landing on ramp instead of rwy.

input: A nonconservative margin of safety calculation has been used on components for the [fleet of aircraft] at the zzz location of the [company]. The calculation of margin of safety; ms; compares ultimate tensile strength ftu to stress s:ms = ftu/s - 1a positive ms is wanted to prevent overload failure. The maximum principal stress s1 was sometimes used at [company] in the ms calculation; i.e.; s = s1. This calculation is non-conservative; specifically when the stress state includes a compressive principal stress; s2. In the two-dimensional case; the tresca failure criterion stress is:stresca = s1 - s2because s2 < 0; i.e.; compressive; stresca is larger than the maximum principal stress; s1.using stresca in the ms formula therefore predicts failure at lower load levels than using s1.for ductile metals such as aerospace aluminum alloys; the tresca criterion matches observed failure behavior; as described in dowling's text mechanical behavior of materials. The first principal stress criterion applies only to brittle materials such as gray cast iron.an example calculation shows the possibility of generating a specious positive margin of safety. The ms1 calculated with first principal stress indicates positive margin (predicts no overload failure):s1 = 70 ksis2 = -50 ksiftu = 100 ksims1 = 100/70 - 1 = 0.42but the margin mstresca calculated with stresca predicts failure:mstresca = ftu/(s1 - s2) - 1 = 100/[70 - (-50)] - 1 = 100/120 - 1 = -0.17      an explanation of the stress tensor and its expression in terms of principal stresses can also be found in dowling's text.
output: Design engineer reported that nonconservative structural margin analysis/calculations were used on aircraft fuel tanks and fuel system components.

input: During our instrument landing system prm 10c ord approach while monitoring approach control and tower; the prm monitor frequency was being consistently used to control aircraft traffic on ord ground and airspace. I realized the voice was ord tower when we were switched to tower frequency. I advised both approach and tower of the simulcasting confusion by doing that. The condition continued. While in ord ops; i spoke with several pilots that had the same experience.the situation of monitoring two frequencies; while one is procedurally trained to be used for breakouts only; is not only confusing; it increases workload; leads to heavy conversation in the cockpit for coordination; and i expect to miss the potential breakout call from whoever is supposed to be monitoring our spacing between runway arrival lanes.
output: Air carrier captain reported that during an ord instrument landing system 10c prm approach; ord prm frequency was used operationally by terminal radar approach control facility tower; and ground control which potentially interferes with breakout commands. This caused confusion and increased pilot workload.

input: On jul/xx/97 i was assigned to the aircraft i had taken the job of replacing the vscf (backup generator) due to the failure of the oil quantity switch. I went and printed copies of the removal and installation maintenance manual and received the part from stores that had been ordered for the aircraft by either maintenance or one of our material distributors and placed in stash. At this point; i ante meridiem not 100% sure intermediate fix the part was a svcable unit or a robbed unit from another aircraft the part number that was on the deferral was correct but the part received was not for the aircraft confign. Following the procedures in the maintenance manual i removed and started installation of the unit. At this point i was removed from the job and asked to run an airplane for another maintenance crew. Other members of the crew completed installation of the unit for me. Approximately 3 weeks later; our materials records department found that the wrong confign unit had been installed on the aircraft the unit was then checkeded and replaced by another station without incident. I feel that my complacency of others ordering my parts for me had caused me to not verify that it was the correct part. Also; my over eagerness to work on this type may have also been a contributing factor in my judgement. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated that the maintenance manual was not specific enough on the 2 types of variable speed constant frequency air conditioning / alternating current backup power units for the 2 models of b777 aircraft however; the illustrated parts catalog clrly noted the 2 types. The rptr advised that the unit was ordered by another company maintenance organization and was on the job when work started. Operational checked was ok after installation. The rptr stated the federal aviation administration has made no contact.
output: A b777 was dispatched with the incorrect left/right (directions) engine variable speed constant frequency air conditioning / alternating current backup generator installed.

input: After push back and disconnect in lax; i attempted to taxi the aircraft but could not get aircraft to move despite using the most power allowed per procedure. Apparently there is a hole or depression in the asphalt that is well known to the ramp tower but perhaps not our push crews. This is dangerous as a crew unfamiliar or distracted could use too much power and damage equipment or seriously injure someone. This needs to be repaired or a disconnect spot painted on the ramp.
output: Air carrier flight crew reports a depression in the c9 alley way near spot 2 at lax; that traps a stationary aircraft preventing it from moving with maximum allowable congested area thrust.

input: Trying to turn panel lighting off when smoke erupted from knob that was being turned. Light smoke with electrical smell was visible about 1 minute after occurrence and elected to proceed back to the ramp. No other smoke was indicated on the 3 minute taxi back to the ramp. Aircraft engine was shut down and aircraft parked with no fire or burnt wire being noted. Fire trucks were standing by. What caused the problem i believe was the knob not being used in years and the switch being overworked. To prevent a recurrence would be to not move the knob as well as having the knob and electrical wiring repaired and to working order. Also; to use the checklist and to evacuate if the need arises.
output: A c150 panel light knob emitted smoke as it was turned so an emergency was declared; the pilot returned to parking and secured the aircraft.

input: During landing as i sat in my jumpseat near the 1l/1r doors; i noticed a distinctive odor coming from the airplane cabin. It smelled sweet and of sweaty gym socks. I could smell it through my face mask. I briefly brought my mask below my nose in order to further evaluate the odor. I did this a few times because i wanted to determine if it would dissipate or linger; it lingered. I then called the flight attendants in the back of the plane to ask them if they also smelled this odor. They did; and they told me 'it was really bad;' that it was quite strong in the back of the plane where they sat at their jumpseats. I then broke sterile cockpit and called the captain to alert him of the situation because i was concerned that we were having a toxic fume event. He told me he was busy with landing; but that he could turn the heat up to dissipate it some; and that he'd write it up on landing. The fumes never dissipated. For the rest of landing; we smelled this distinctive odor. Upon arriving at the gate; the captain wrote up the odor in the log book for maintenance. No flight service manager (fsm) met the plane. I noticed a little bit of a burning sensation in my nasal passages; throat; and lungs. When i got in the fresh air later; walking to my car; i felt a slight burning; tingling sensation in my eyes. When i got home; i then received a call from a flight service manager. The fsm wanted to know how i felt; and i told her that i just got home and was still monitoring my symptoms. I am still monitoring myself for any latent or delayed effects and reactions. Please note: due to the covid-19 pandemic and the new rules that go with it; unless i am having a life or death emergency or suspect i have covid-19; i was not able to go to the emergency room within x hours of this fume event to have my blood tested; which is standard operating procedure under normal circumstances.pilot should have called a medic and a flight service manager to meet the flight to evaluate crew's health and wellbeing.
output: "a321 flight attendant crew reported a dirty socks"" fumes event of varying intensity during initial climb and lasting until arrival at destination gate."""

input: When cleared to taxi into position and hold on runway(s) 24l at lax. The nose baggage door opened and a carry on bag fell out and nicked the propeller this event went undetected until the plane landed in palmdale and we noticed the bag missing and a nick in the propeller normal procedure is for the ramper to checked and secure the door and for the coplt to double-chk it before departure in our case; neither the ramper nor the coplt noticed a broken latch when checkeding the door. I cannot speak for the ramper but i know the coplt and i had flown together subsequent to the accident and we were both tired from having flown numerous days in a row with multiple lndgs in adverse weather over unfamiliar rtes.
output: Commuter has propeller damage due to open baggage door.

input: The main xmitter on frequency 126.77 failed to work. I changed to stand-by xmitter. The stand-by worked well. I changed back to the main xmitter -- it worked fine. This has happened numerous times. The xmitter appeared to be intermittent. I have been told it is a software problem what do we have to do to make our equipment reliable? Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr advised that he has incurred this problem a few times in the past. He was advised a 'couple of times' that the problem was associated with the incorrect operations(s) of the voice switching and control system the rptr wants the equipment to operate in an 'easier' format sequence.
output: Ztl controller concerned about intermittent frequency (127 pt 77) activation and usability.

input: Following a stabilized auto-coupled approach to runway(s) 35r in moderate rain and apparently steady wind; the autoplt was disconnected at 100' above ground level at that time it was noted that airspd was on target; sink rate steady 700 feet per minute engs spooled up and on g/s (as throughout the apch). Within approximately 3 secs after autoplt disconnect; the sink rate increased sharply w/o and perceptible change in attitude or power the capt increased thrust. Both the f/o and s/o noted and announced the high sink rate and the capt continued increasing thrust. A bounce ensued and the capt continued to track the centerline and adjust power and pitch. A second bounce followed; which struck the tail skid. Flight conditions required the use of engine anti-ice; however; no structural icing was evident. The radar reflected nothing other than scattered areas of light precipitation; even though the rain intensity appeared to increase during the event. Because the sink rate appeared to increase in only the last 50-60'; there was little time to react. Although a more aggressive application of thrust may not have; in this case; enabled us to cushion the initial t/d; it may have provided us with enough energy to more successfully have recovered (a flatter angle) from the bounce (given ample rwy); or accomplished a gar.
output: Tail skid strike on touchdown.

input: On taxi out the 'a' flight attendant called the flight deck and asked if we heard a 'siren' or 'alarm' sound. We assumed she meant an emergency vehicle outside the aircraft. We did not; but asked her to keep us informed. Just as we were taking the runway she called again. This time she was expressing concern over the sound; as were some of the passengers. She thought the sound was coming from an overhead bin. We declined taking off and cleared the runway. Air traffic control eventually had us taxi to a vacant area to the far west of the airport. Once we arrived in the remote area the flight attendant asked the passengers in the vicinity of the sound if they could explain the sound. None could. She then had them retrieve their bags from the overhead to 'make sure.' no explanation was forthcoming; which began to raise my suspicions. To be clear: the first officer and i did not ask for assistance; nor did we at any time use the words: 'bomb'; 'security'; or 'suspicious' on the radio frequency. As we were sorting this out several police cars gathered around us and blocked our forward progress. After some discussion with the first officer and the police we decided the best course of action would be to deplane the passengers and inspect the aircraft. The aircraft was inspected by police dogs; police; and company maintenance personnel. Nothing suspicious was found. During the event i was in contact (by phone) with dispatch maintenance control and the chief pilot. There were also detectives and station managers on the scene. The detective ran a search on the passenger manifest; which did not turn up anything. After discussion with my crew we decided we wanted to continue the flight. None of our 99 passengers opted to remain behind (all continued on with us).i have not heard the official explanation but the police suspected the noise was coming from a credit card scanner in the overhead that the flight attendants use for on board purchases.
output: Emb190 captain is informed by the a flight attendant of a siren-like noise in the cabin. The aircraft is taxied to a remote area where the passengers are deplaned and the aircraft throughly inspected by security; dogs; and company maintenance personnel. Nothing is found and the flight departs with all passengers on board.

input: Visual approach to runway(s) 13. After normal landing we turned off the runway(s) at taxiway x. I called for taxi clearance to gate. After receiving taxi clearance capt called for 'flaps up after landing chk.' after doing my 'after landing flow'; up to the point to turning on the auxiliary power unity master switch - waiting the 20 seconds for the 'flap open light' - i looked left/right (directions) to make sure the outer taxiway was clear and i noticed a small amount of smoke or a puff of smoke. Before i could say anything to the capt; the cabin interphone buzzer went off. The aft flight attendant told us 'the cabin was filling up with smoke.' about 2 seconds later the lead flight attendant opened the cockpit door and told us 'there is smoke in the cabin.' the capt brought the aircraft to a stop and told me to get up and take a look back. I saw smoke in the mid to rear cabin. The smoke was second officer dense that i could not see all the way to the rear of the cabin. I told the capt that 'there is a lot of smoke in the cabin.' there were no indications on the electronic centralized aircraft monitoring or any smell in the cockpit. At that moment the lead flight attendant asked the capt 'we need to evacuate/evacuation is it all right?' the capt said yes evacuate/evacuation i immediately called ground control and told them we have smoke in the cabin we are going to evacuate/evacuation get the fire trucks out here. Then i called on the company frequency and told them 'we have cabin smoke; we are going to evac.' then i got out the evacuate/evacuation chklist. The lead flight attendant had started the evacuate/evacuation as soon as the capt had said yes to her question. I read the evacuate/evacuation chklist; then grabbed my flashlight; and went to the forward cabin. To my surprise; almost everyone was off the aircraft i helped an older lady onto the slide then exited the aircraft myself out the front left/right (directions) door. There were mechs baggage handlers at the slide helping people. They did a great job of crowd control they had almost all of the people away from the aircraft and heading towards the terminal. After making sure everyone was away from the aircraft i walked around the rear of the aircraft and could not find any indications of smoke or anything abnormal. Supplemental information from acn 202579: the thing that should have been done different is i should have told the flight attendant over the p.a. To evacuate/evacuation as soon as i told the lead flight attendant to evacuate/evacuation the door came open and the slides out and the aft flight attendants were left/right (directions) in the dark for a few seconds before they started the evacuate/evacuation the first thing i did was shut the engs off because the forward slides deployed in front of the engs. After the engs are shut down there is a 7 second delay before i could have used the p.a. Again. All 123 people and crew of 7 were evacuated in a very short time; only one flight attendant was taken to the hospital with a cut on her head. This evacuate/evacuation happened close to our ramp and the agents helped the people as they came down the slides. All and all everything went pretty smooth.
output: Acr taxiing after landing has cabin fill with smoke. Evacuated acft.

input: While performing a left/right (directions) engine cfm fan blade root inspection job card on a b737-800 during a 'c' checked maintenance visit; the computer mapping task; which incorporates sending blade wt/moment data to engineering; was signed for but not accomplished due to an interpretation error of the job card. No fan blades were replaced on the #1 engine during the visit and the fan blade vibration history indicated that the vibration levels of the blades were within customer satisfactory levels. It was erroneously interped that a new blade mapping was not required because no blades were replaced. Therefore; no weights or moments were changed. The job card; however; states that during 'c' checked level or higher maintenance visits; fan blade mapping is required. The acft's #1 engine passed the operator's vibration survey maintenance manual task and no rebalance was required. Making revisions to the job card to give more direct guidance of operator's processes and procedures when third party maintenance is being performed; would greatly help reduce the likelihood of this error recurring.
output: A b737-800 inspector rpts that during a contract facility 'c' checked a #1 engine required fan blade weight rpt was signed off as accomplished but was not done.

input: The first officer/pilot monitoring noticed the turn coordinator was unstable and was giving us incorrect indications. After observing erratic indications and taking into consideration the weather that was at our destination; we decided to return to zzz. We were visual meteorological conditions and we were halfway to zzz1 when the decision to turn back was made. The weather in zzz1 was low visibility and so we elected to turn back and remain in visual meteorological conditions we contacted air traffic control and got a clearance back to zzz. We ended up cancelling a few minutes later. Then; we let [operations control] know what the issue and plan was.
output: C402 captain reported returning to the departure airport due to a malfunctioning turn coordinator.

input: We departed teb on an instrument flight rules flight. During preflight planning and flight management system programming; runway 6-24 was closed by notice to airmen / of air missions our passengers were delayed by almost an hour. The timing was such; that when we requested our instrument flight rules clearance; we expected runway 19. As we boarded the airplane for departure; runway 6-24 had re-opened. After engine start; when ready for taxi; we were instructed to taxi to runway 24 via papa; lima; hold short of runway 19 on lima. As we preceded northeast bound on papa; i remarked that the runway had re-opened and we were going to depart runway 24. My co-captain did not acknowledge my comment; even though he heard and acknowledged my checklist challenges. As we reached lima to hold short of runway 19; we were immediately cleared to cross 19 and enter the apron to hold short of runway 24. As we crossed the runway; he did a left u-turn into the apron; pulling up abeam the western edge of the pavement; closest to the approach end of runway 19. The tower controller advised us that we needed to move to the other side; (closest to runway 24); as we would be departing on 24. As we moved over to the east side of the apron; we were advised that they had our release; and asked if we were ready. We told him it would be just a minute; and we quickly re-programmed the flight management system for runway 24. Then we were cleared for departure off [runway] 24.the flight management system clearly portrayed the heading change upon reaching 1;500 mean sea level it also portrayed the teb 4.5 nautical mile arc; upon reaching we were ok to climb to 2;000 mean sea level we were handed off to new york departure; and as we checked in we were just about level at 2;000 mean sea level he advised us that we climbed too quickly and we were restricted to 1;500 until passing the 4.5 nautical mile arc. We pulled back on thrust to drift back down; but the controller said it was not necessary as we were now past the arc. He also informed us of an airbus inbound to ewr; and that this was the reason for the climb restriction. We never saw the airbus; and there was no traffic alert and collision avoidance system warning or advisory and no evasive maneuvering by us or the airbus. We had; however; encroached upon the minimum separation standards. We were subsequently cleared to climb and handed off. Other than runway 24; all other teb departures via the teb 8 specify an unrestricted climb to 2;000 mean sea level from runway 24; there is the restriction to cross the 4.5 nautical mile vor and dme (co-located) arc at 1;500; then climb and maintain 2;000. As a flight crew; we did not brief that important difference; because we honestly expected that runway to be closed at our departure time. The fact that my co-captain was still thinking of runway 19 became apparent to me as soon as he made the left u-turn into the apron. The tower controller also became aware of it at that time since he advised us to move closer to runway 24. As he acquired our release and cleared us for take-off; it would have been nice of him to remind us of that climb restriction; even though he has no obligation to do so. This restriction applies very quickly to a jet; and it is the major difference in the flying of this departure; compared to all the other runways. This altitude deviation happened as a result of several human errors. The assumption that runway 24 would remain closed was the first. As a crew; both pilots need to be familiar with the differences in the procedure from each possible runway. Prior to taxi; the automatic terminal information service was our first clue that runway 24 was re-opened and to be expected. The taxi clearance was our second chance to get that message. We taxied out with the wrong runway programmed into our flight management system our release came more quickly than expected; and since we were already delayed by our passenger's late arrival; we were anxious to get things underway. After all; the weather was excellent. What could be the problem? We do not get into teb often. Not even once a year do we use this airport. Due to its proximity to much high volume traffic; it definitely requires some homework prior to going in there. The teb 8 departure (for runway 24) could be simplified by just stating maintain 1;500. Let new york departure tell you when it is ok to climb. I have no idea how many jet airplanes fail to comply with that 4.5 nautical mile climb restriction; but i would be surprised if it is not a common occurrence.
output: A lj60 crew was prepared for a teb runway 19 departure; so when cleared for runway 24 teb 8 they did not re-brief the departure and the aircraft was climbed directly to 2;000 feet/foot bypassing the 1;500 feet/foot constraint.

input: I just happened to look up and saw the auxiliary power unity low oil pressure light illuminated. I reached up and moved the auxiliary power unity switch to 'off.' about 4 seconds later we got an auxiliary power unity fire warning indication but it was unusual in that it was weak and intermittent. I told the first officer to declare an emergency and roll the trucks while i proceeded to use the override button to pull the auxiliary power unity fire handle then rotated the handle to blow the bottle. We got a bottle discharge light and about 5 seconds later there was no more indication of fire. The first officer had a lot of difficulty getting a word to the tower there was a stuck microphone blocking their normal frequency we were on a backup frequency in all the excitement when the first officer did get through to tower he forgot to declare an emergency but did advise them of our situation and requested any information they could see on our situation and to get the fire trucks to us. Tower and many aircraft around us could not see anything unusual. The fire truck probably got to us in about 3 minute(s) and quickly confirmed all appeared normal. During this 3 minute(s) we also called the cabin crew to advise them of what had happened and to get their input as to what was going on in the cabin. They rpted an exhaust type of smell but other than that all was normal.
output: A boeing 737-200 received an intermittent auxiliary power unity fire warning and discharged the auxiliary power unity fire bottle at dfw.

input: Due to miscom between flight crew and cabin crew; 5 half weights (children) were entered on the weight and balance manifest. Whether those 5 passenber should have been counted as half weights or adults was later questioned. This discrepancy would have resulted in an overwt landing of approximately 400 pounds the maximum landing weight of the aft is 41226 pounds the flight was otherwise normal and uneventful. This event occurred because of a breakdown in cockpit resource management during a very busy; quick turnaround of a flight that was already 1 1/2 hours delayed. The lesson to be learned is that in busy; high workload environments; it is especially important to have clear communications and take the time to verify critical info.
output: Emb145 crew and flight attendants had 5 children weights counted instead of adult weights in the weight and balance computations. This was detected 7 days after the event occurred.

input: We have had an ongoing problem with our icss system the pos's fail at random. Sometimes they can be reset in the cabin attendant and at other times they have to be reset in the equipment room 3 floors down. This is an unsafe condition and could lead to an incident or accident intermediate fix they should fail at a critical time. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr stated the problem was found to be in the mother board of the system and this has been replaced.
output: Atc equipment problem communications icss position failed. Ongoing prob.

input: I calculated our weight and balance numbers using a greater quantity of fuel than actual. Once we realized the error; i corrected the calculations using the onboard paperwork and contacted the agent at the station where our flight originated and had them correct the paperwork for me. This error was due to the difference between the amount of fuel we had originally discussed as being desirable and what we left with. The error was primarily due to fatigue. Flts made during certain times of the day force a pilot to turn his or her regular sleep schedule upside down. This results in obvious oversights such as this one. A good solution would be better duty time regulations for example; one of our trips has a period of 36 hours with only 9 hours restrict, restricted, restriction this is perfectly legal; but pushes the crew too hard.
output: An error made in calculating weight and balance is attributed to fatigue brought on by legal but tiring scheduling that does not account for a normal sleep schedule.

input: I was the captain operating aircraft x. Climbing out of approximately fl280 we received the right engine bleed warning message (first officer flying pilot). I took the flight controls and stopped the climb. The bleed air closed before the bleed source could be selected to non-affected engine source. Initially; i did attempt to complete the procedure; however it did not work. The bleeds closed automatically leaving us with no air. We immediately put on our oxygen masks; i notified air traffic control and asked for a descent to 15;000. After the descent was initiated. I inquired air traffic control about 10;000 and terrain clearance. After reviewing terrain clearance and verification with air traffic control we continued to 10;000. The first officer completed both the descent checklist and the left/right (directions) bleed duct warning check list while in initial descent. During the descent the oxygen masks deployed as both the cabin altitude and then cabin warning messages were received. The masks deployed automatically. At 15;000 the auxiliary power unity was started. Initially the auxiliary power unity would not supply air. After a second attempt to go to manual auxiliary power unity we obtained air on the aircraft. The flight attendants were contacted and an announcement was made to the passengers. The company was notified via acars.the fire trucks were requested due to the nature of the situation; initially i was very concerned about the extreme heat in zzz and the passengers health without air conditioning. The flight returned to zzz without further incident landing runway x. The flight attendants reported all the passengers were ok and did not need assistance. I made an announcement once we were able to take the masks off at 10;000. I explained the reason for the return to zzz. In addition once at the gate another announcement was made apologizing for the inconvenience. Dispatch was contacted by telephone once at the gate. 2 maintenance write ups were completed at the gate: 1. Left/right (directions) eng bleed warning. 2. Pax oxygen masks deployed auto. After a delay we received another aircraft and the flight was completed to zzz1.
output: Crj-900 flight crew reported an aircraft bleed system malfunction during climbout. Flight crew diverted to nearest suitable airport.

input: We were on a visual approach to runway 27 and while slowing from 210 to 190; we selected flaps to one and then flaps to 5. We noticed the zipper was not lowering and then noticed the flaps were indicating up. We had no engine indicating and crew alerting system warning. We accelerated back to 210; and tried to cycle the flaps. Again; flaps did not indicate any movement and no icas warnings. Fuel was at about 7;400 pounds we asked for radar vectors to the north to troubleshoot and set up for possible approach to [the longest runway]. At this time i noticed we had a status message slat/flap elec. Again; with no engine indicating and crew alerting system message; i opted to set up for an all flaps up landing. We ran the landing with all flaps up checklist in the quick reference handbook flew an uneventful flaps up monitored approach to landing without requiring further assistance. When clear of the runway; we checked the brake cooling chart in the quick reference handbook before taxiing back to park. [we] landed at 167 knot(s) at about 163;000 pounds with auto brakes 4.
output: B757-200 captain reports failure of the flaps to move to the selected position during approach with no engine indicating and crew alerting system warnings; but with a status message indicating slat/flap elec. A zero flap landing ensues at a landing weight of 163;000 lbs.

input: During taxi out to runway(s) 32r at o'hare; a f/a came up to ask intermediate fix i could check the left (aft) service door for security. When i came back to the cockpit; we were very close to being cleared for takeoff and had not started our 3rd engine or completed taxi checks. Although rushed; we smartly started the engine and completed the after start check. As we were starting the taxi check; tower either cleared us for takeoff or on to hold. We finished the taxi check and began with the before takeoff checks; when the capt asked the f/o intermediate fix we were cleared for takeoff f/o replied yes; second officer we finished the check and began our roll (f/o flying). About 200' into the roll (very low airspeed; 20 kts); tower said 'you're not cleared for tkof!' at that time a wdb y flew just in front of us (just beginning his flare for landing on cross runway(s) 27r). We stopped immediately and tower then quickly cleared us for takeoff the capt recalled hearing only 'clred on to hold'; the f/o distinctly remembered tower clearing us for takeoff and i ante meridiem not sure since i was reading checklists. I do know thee was a lot of urgency. There was another similar call sign holding with us which possibly added to the confusion. The capt said that tower made a comment that we were out there together after they had answered for us or vice versa. Although all checklist items were complete; the capt was uncertain about our clearance but the f/o was 'sure' the tower had cleared us. Maybe a quick check with tower (even during this urgency) would have been best especially when there was a difference of opinions.
output: Airliner beginning takeoff is told to abort by tower controller confusion whether controller issued clearance or intermediate fix flight crew was in error.

input: I had both air carrier xxxx and air carrier xxyx on frequency inbound to ord. I was unaware of similar call signs at the time i issued a descent clearance to air carrier xxxx to fl250. After the clearance was issued and read back by air carrier xxyx; air carrier xxxx questioned the clearance and advised i had similar call signs on frequency. I tried to get air carrier xxyx to maintain altitude but he had already started his descent in cleveland centers airspace. I called the zob sector to advise what happened and then got the aircraft on frequency to the appropriate altitudes. Recommendation; similar call signs are always a risk. I am not sure why i didn't realize they were both on frequency but i didn't. Even when questioned by the correct pilot; and i realized the mix up; i still didn't hear clearly the correct call sign. Our frequencies are not always crystal clear and the voice inflections of pilots and controllers can easily make air carrier xxxx sound like air carrier xxyx. We will always have similar call signs in this business; i guess the best recommendation would be to be as alert to this possibility as one could be so it doesn't bite you.
output: Zau controller described similar call sign event that resulted in an uncoordinated descent into an adjacent sector's airspace.

input: On a flight from teb to mman. We received numerous updates regarding the weather via afis communications the conditions were visual flight rules before descent we briefed the approach in anticipation of a full vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) #1 to runway(s) 20. This approach entailed a teardrop course reversal; which had an 8 mile outbound and an 8 mile inbound leg. We briefed the rising terrain and selected egpws on our displays. After being handed off to monterrey approach control we started experiencing difficulty understanding the controller he initially spoke to us in spanish. The automatic terminal information service frequency was not working second officer we were given the automatic terminal information service verbally. Close in on the approach we were issued a heading to intercept the final approach course to vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) #3; runway(s) 20; a different approach than we had briefed and programmed. This necessitated reprogramming the flight management system and expediting the descent this new approach was a radar vectored approach to the final approach course. Therefore; we did not have the extra 16 miles to descend as stated earlier; for the original expected approach at the missed approach point we executed a missed approach in my flying experience i had never encountered a missed approach procedure which referred you to another 'apch plate' to view the missed approach procedure for the approach you were currently executing. (mman vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) #3 to runway(s) 20 refers you to vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) #1 runway(s) 20 for the missed approach alt). We were recleared onto the original approach vor and dme (co-located) vor and dme (co-located) #3 to runway(s) 20 and landed at mman. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr emphasized that the problem was more the result of planning for one specific approach and then being cleared for a technically much different one when it was really too late to prepare properly. Had the language problem not existed; he feels they would have instead refused the approach and requested a delay to prepare. The underlying problem in either case was the unusual situation regarding the missed approach point procedure being depicted on a different chart and the multiple versions of the vor and dme (co-located) approach to runway(s) 20. From previous investigation it is known that flight management system databases are restricted to only a single approach of a given type to a particular runway(s) the result is a discrepancy between the terminology on the approach charts (ie runway(s) 20 vor and dme (co-located) 1 and runway(s) 20 vor and dme (co-located) 3) and that which is presented to the flight crew by the flight management system therein the basic 'vor' approach to runway(s) 20 must be customized by the proper selection of transitions and maps. The ability to accurately do second officer under duress of severely limited time is highly questionable.
output: Language barriers with approach control confusing and unorthodox chartage; and flight management system database complexities conspire to force f2th flight crew to execute missed approach on vor and dme (co-located) approach to mman. Missed approach point turns out to be equally confusing.

input: I understand that the sim is not the airplane. However; the check airman showed us something i think could be serious. He put us at the marker configured for landing single engine gear down; flaps 20; rudder adjusted properly. He failed the auxiliary power unity second officer we were down to 1 electrical source. During the approach the aircraft became uncontrollable. We tried it again and put out the ram air turbine/ram air temperature this time; to a happy ending. Intermediate fix the sim is similar to the aircraft this could be a serious problem and should be in the book that in case of auxiliary power unity not start (or placarded inop) to put out the ram air turbine/ram air temperature it is not there now; and a serious accident could take place without warning. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr discussed the ramifications of an engine failure on the electrical and hydraulic systems of the b757. Among other system anomalies; one of the two electric pumps for the center hydraulic system (one of three systems) is shut down. The simulator demonstration showed a loss of both rudder and aileron authority to the point of loss of aircraft control the check airman demonstrated that deploying the 'rat' (ram air turbine [air driven hydraulic pump]) would provide ample additional hydraulic authority to return normal control response. He strongly noted that ram air turbine/ram air temperature deployment is 'not' part of any engine fail procedure checklist. Rptr did acknowledge the apparent dichotomy of the lack of any such simulator flight control problems during engine failure at takeoff procedures which are routinely flown to 1500 feet/foot or more before any checklist procedure is initiated. The requirement to start the auxiliary power unity (noted as 'if available') is not part of the immediate action steps of such a procedure and is only part of 'time permitting' or 'reference action' steps. Thus; the starting of the auxiliary power unity could well not be initiated until several minutes after the engine failure.
output: A b757 capt rpts that company training check airmen are demonstrating a loss of aileron and rudder control authority on apches when an engine fails and the auxiliary power unity is not available to allow full electric center hydraulic system capability. This demonstration is done in the simulator and authorized by the company. Nonetheless; his company dispatches these aircraft with inoperative apu's and with no federal aviation administration approved procedure to compensate for this shortcoming.

input: Lost power at approximately 1;000 feet toward end of climbout to remain in pattern for touch and go's was probably 1/4 to 1/2 mile beyond end of runway; turned back to runway and informed tower i had lost power and needed to land. I checked for any remedial problems and saw none; but noticed my prop was not turning. I proceeded to land back on runway and coast to a stop on the taxiway. I was able to hand push the plane to the fuel pumps and added fuel and the plane then restarted. The puzzle being the plane only took approximately 26 gallons when the tank holds 36; though only 32 usable; so i think there is some chance i might have had a vacuum created in the fuel tank. I do run un-vented fuel caps per a notice regarding the aeronca sedans because with vented caps there had been some incidents of planes running out of power attributed to the wing at higher pitch up creating a vacuum at the tank. The aeronca sedan has a belly vent that faces forward to pressurize the fuel tanks; or i could just have not realized how low the fuel was and it lost power because of the pitch up for climb then couldn't restart because the prop stopped turning i.e. I didn't pitch down aggressively enough.
output: Aeronca pilot reported the engine lost power during initial climb. The pilot was unable to restart the engine and returned to the runway to a successful landing. Post flight; the pilot conjectured that the engine failure could be due to inadequate fuel or a vacuum in the tanks.

input: The weather was forecast cavok and didn't see a cloud in the sky. Aircraft no comm. Made decision to proceed; thinking we would get automatic communications addressing & reporting system back after push. Captain spent the entire time until taxi out with dispatch; verifying and collecting data. Dispatch couldn't (wouldn't?) send performance data to captain; but relayed verbally. After actual push stayed no comm (until climbing through 27k). Made decision to continue with flight after push when we realized we were no comm based on weather; familiarity with airports; and no other traffic on ground. Took us 27 minutes to verify everything. Made trip uneventfully. Several thoughts:*we had to trust dispatch was passing valid numbers. They seemed reasonable; but i wasn't in the phone loop; so it could have been the winning lottery numbers for all i knew.*no way to communicate to dispatch without using cell phone. *no way to verify any of the info on the takeoff checklist; other than give it a sanity check.*dispatch couldn't send performance data to captain's cell phone; but kept sending the flight plan. After getting automatic communications addressing & reporting system back we got lots of takeoff data messages (sending to aircraft printer?)*there is no checklist for automatic communications addressing & reporting system inop/no comm for the a320; but there should be.*searched fom and frequency modulation for no comm and automatic communications addressing & reporting system inoperative nothing useful found.
