Aircraft was in zzz for a mvi post meridiem service checked during the walkaround #4 main tire was worn beyond limits and needed to be changed. I assisted mr y with the tire replacement. He installed the hub civil air patrol and safetied the mount attach bolts and then put his tools away and returned the tire cart while i finished the installation by putting the fairing on. No discrepancies were noted upon completion. How the fairing came off i have no idea. It was a routine tire change that was replaced per maintenance manual.
output: A b737-500 had #4 main tire and wheel assembly replaced per the maintenance manual. First downline station rpts #4 main hubcap fairing missing.

input: During boarding; this passenber kept going back and forth to the lavatory. Due to frozen oxygen pipes; we were 1 hour late departing second officer people were a little restless. By the third time this passenber went to the lavatory - within a 1/2 hour period -- i began to get a bit suspicious; especially since he was carrying his suitcase in the lavatory with him. After he came out; i checkeded the lavatory and then informed the capt of my suspicions. The passenber and his wife were originally in row xx; but asked to move back xz. Passenber insisted on keeping his carry-on suitcase near him (later found out there was a bottle of vodka inside). The passenber went in and out of lavatory several more times before we left the gate. He told me his wife had kidney problems the lavatory light smoke detector went off 3 times; but i never found any signs of 'evidence' (smoke; butts; etc). As we taxied out; they both acted strange. He would seem to get angry and she would comfort him; then she would start crying and angry and he'd hug her. Both the #4 flight attendant and i thought they were a bit 'odd.' during takeoff the passenber was 'bracing;' holding his ankles and yelling. His wife calmed him down and he seemed fine. As i rolled the carts up the aisle to start the service the passenber followed me up and asked me when he could have a drink. He went back to his seat then just started screaming 'help me; help me.' i asked his wife intermediate fix he was ok and again she calmed him down. He started yelling again and ran down the aisle to the lavatory. He was screaming and pounding in the lavatory. At that point; i called the capt and explained the situation and told him i wasn't feeling comfortable with this pax's behavior. He told me to keep an eye on him and 'call back intermediate fix there's any more problems -- we can land intermediate fix necessary.' within 5 minute(s) the passenber was crawling on the floor; yelling; and wouldn't settle down. Capt turned the seatbelt sign on. Passenber complied; but still continued to yell and swing his arms; growling and moaning. He stood up again and screamed 'help me; help me.' at that time; lots of other passenber were looking back. I called the capt; explained what was happening and requested to land and get him off. I felt threatened; i know other passenber felt the same. The passenber was asked to put on his seatbelt. He asked me intermediate fix we were going to crash. He again started screaming 'help me; get me out' and ran off to the lavatory. He was screaming and banging in the lavatory. I then asked his wife intermediate fix he was going to be ok and intermediate fix he'd ever been in an airline 'incident' since he seemed second officer afraid of flying and staying in a seatbelt. She said he'd never been in a crash or incident and had flown quite often. He was screaming and crying at the top of his lungs in the lavatory; second officer i asked the wife to go assist him. Also informed her that we'd be landing in detroit to let them off since he was threatening to and scaring both crew and passenber she apologized and complied. On final descent i checkeded the cabin and noticed passenber didn't have his seatbelt on. I asked him to buckle up and he started crying and cowering like a little boy. He buckled up for about 10 seconds then got angry and got up out of his seat yelling. Since we were minute(s) from landing i grabbed him as he started running up the aisle; but he pushed me out of his way. The #4 flight attendant then went after him; pulling on his clothes to get him to stop. He continued up the aisle; yelling to 'get me off; i want out.' i then called the capt to let him know the passenber was coming up front and was irate. The passenber made it to first class and then fell to the floor. The capt asked intermediate fix we needed help and the #7 flight attendant and i both said we needed help. The capt came out and the #4 flight attendant ended up restraining him.
output: A passenber acts strange during a ground delay. The condition escalates after departure until restraint of the passenber and diversion to an en route airport is required.

input: While on radar vectors for a visual approach we were flying an assigned heading and speed of 210 degrees and 210 knot(s) controller stated we had taken a wrong turn and advised us to turn left/right (directions) to 170 degrees immediately. We all agreed we had heard 210 degrees and i ante meridiem positive the pilot not flying read back heading and speed 210 degrees 210 knot(s) the controller said nothing further. There was obviously a communications breakdown of some type. Unfortunately; i don't know where the error of multiple errors occurred; but i assume safety was not compromised. Vigilance may be the only answer. We are human after all.
output: B727 flight crew turn to heading that is same as assigned airspd. P50 controller advises they took wrong hdg.

input: 'fly-by' over sql. On jan/xx/97; a 'v' formation of 3 high fixed wing aircraft made a low pass over runway(s) 30 at sql. This was a practice 'fly-by.' on jan/xx/97; a 'v' formation of 5 high fixed wing aircraft performed a 'fly-by' over runway(s) 30 at sql as part of a formal memorial service on both occasions; the altitude over the airport was 200 feet/foot followed by a slow climb along the ctrline of runway(s) 30 for about 2 mile then a slow climbing left/right (directions) turn along belmont slough to a sunken ship in mid-bay and south of san mateo bridge where the formation broke up and returned to sql. On both occasions; contact was maintained with sql tower and the flts were cleared for the low pass. While there are no known complaints; it is possible that occupants of residences and office buildings along the ctrline of runway(s) 30 and to the north may lodge noise complaints; leading to an examination of a possible violation of federal aviation regulation 91.119 (minimum safe alts). In the opinion of the rptr (the lead plane in both formations); the 'fly-by' at pattern altitude (800 ft) would have been simply inappropriate and would have destroyed the desired effect. On both occasions; the formations initiated a slow climb at the end of runway(s) 30 in order to maintain the integrity of the formations. Had the climb been any more abrupt; the participating aircraft probably would have scattered; a highly undesirable result given the occasion. It is estimated that at the end of the clear zone beyond and along the ctrline of runway(s) 30; the formation were at 350-400 feet/foot and clbing.
output: Sma aircraft rptr pilot was lead pilot in a 5 plane low fly-by. Low fly-by was coordinated with the tower but rptr was not certain about the occupants of office buildings and residences concerns for the low flying.

input: Acft #2 was cleared via navigational aid radial to intercept airway south of course. Descending aircraft #1 on course to parallel aircraft #2 to accommodate descent aircraft #1 was given descent clearance from fl370 to fl310. Aircraft #2 was observed not on radial vector and converging with aircraft #1. Aircraft #2 was turned 30 degrees left/right (directions) of course to maintain separation. Aircraft #1 was mistakenly turned 30 degrees left/right (directions) in error -- should have been 30 degrees left/right (directions) to maintain separation.
output: Artcc controller mistakenly turned 1 of 2 descending aircraft the wrong way for separation resulting in loss of legal separation.

input: During approach and completing mechanical checklist crew became aware flap handle selected for flaps 30 but flap indicator showed flaps set at 25 and a green light. Captain ordered a go around and maintained configuration while i handled the radio and checklist. This event occurred after a long two leg all night flight and the conditions were nighttime windy and moderate turbulence at low altitude. We completed the checklist and returned to runway xxl. On short final we received a; 'too low flaps'; and 'terrain terrain' ground proximity warning system warning because i misread the non-normal checklist item calling for flap inhibit to be engaged. I attribute this misread to several factors. I was tired; this was a brutal trip assignment; it was turbulent and i was dividing my attention between the checklist and monitoring the aircraft status i.e. Airspeed control radio and other set up functions.
output: B737 first officer reported a flap malfunction on final approach.

input: Landed and dropped off passenger. After getting automatic terminal information service code called ground and got clearance to taxi. I thought the active runway was the one i had landed on before dropping off my passenger; but it had changed. I thought the controller's instructions were to 'taxi across the runway to 23.' instead he may have said 'taxi across runway 23.' the ground controller told me i had taxied across the active runway. Not all the taxiways are labeled correctly.
output: A pilot misunderstood air traffic control instructions and taxied across an active fdk runway.

input: I was inbound to centennial airport for landing from the southeast. I called centennial tower and advised of my intentions approximately 10 miles southeast. Centennial tower cleared me to enter a midfield left downwind runway 17l. I requested runway 28 and was denied due to a high wing tail dragger aircraft doing touch and goes on runway 10. I entered my mid field left downwind for runway 17l. I was issued a traffic alert by the tower for the high wing aircraft doing touch and goes on 10. I was unable to locate the traffic and advised tower of this. My traffic alerter system in my aircraft advised me of the traffic climbing into me from the right but i could not locate this traffic. About 5 seconds later this aircraft crossed my nose at the same altitude within 200'. I turned to the right to avoid a collision. I advised tower that i now had the traffic and almost collided. Tower informed me that he had another aircraft coming from right to left in front of me on a left base leg and i was to follow that traffic for 17l. Tower cleared me number 2 to land behind the second aircraft (second aircraft was a high wing white cessna 172). I turned final behind the traffic and slowed to approach speed. I observed that i had plenty of room for landing behind the aircraft. Once the aircraft touched down in front of me the tower cleared it to exit the runway to the left on the reverse high speed taxiway. I observed the aircraft to be beyond this taxiway he was cleared for. Moments later the aircraft stopped on the runway then proceeded to make a wide left turn to almost face me. Tower issued me a go around clearance. I was now trying to climb over the runway traffic on 17l because the high wing tail dragger was on a 'crazy' left base for runway 10 over the ramp to the left of runway 17l. There was touch and go traffic on my parallel runway 17r; so i could not go right. I informed tower when i could not go straight without hitting the traffic on my runway that i was going to have to go right. As i continued my climb out tower cleared me for a left downwind runway 17l again. I informed tower that i would not accept 17l left downwind again due to the high wing tail dragger doing touch and goes on 10. Tower informed me that the tail dragger had made a full stop on runway 10. At this time i observed the tail dragger exit the runway as i was turning crosswind. I requested runway 28 for a full stop. Tower cleared me for the full stop. After landing i requested the tower phone number. After securing my aircraft i contacted the tower at the number given. The tower supervisor answered the phone. I asked the tower supervisor why i had been given the clearance for the left downwind runway 17l with conflicting cross traffic for another runway. Supervisor stated he did not know other than the controller did not expect me to be where i was. I asked if my downwind was flown different than expected. The supervisor stated that i had not; and the controller should have issued me a clearance to fly a downwind beyond the conflicting traffic. I asked the supervisor why the controller cleared the traffic that landed ahead of me for a taxiway that was already past causing it to stop and reverse on the runway in front of me. The supervisor stated that airplane stopped for a reason not known to them; and that it was beyond his control. I asked the supervisor why the tail dragger was doing touch and go landings on a cross runway while landings on the main runways where in use. The tower supervisor stated that is what they let this particular pilot fly in case he loses his engine. I asked how many times he flies thinking he is going to lose his engine; because this was about the 20th flight i had seen. The tower supervisor did not have an answer.
output: Cessna pilot reports a near midair collision in the traffic pattern at apa requiring evasive action. The traffic landing ahead of the reporter does not clear the runway after landing requiring a go-around. The traffic on the runway; the traffic for the parallel runway and the traffic for the crossing runway were all cited as conflicts during the go-around.

input: The tower local control positions were de-combined. Traffic was easterly operations. I was monitoring local north. A visual flight rules b350 was awaiting departure. I received a point out of a flight of two h60s that were transitioning from west to east that would definitely effect any north field traffic. I also anticipated the helicopters to be traffic for any departures on the northside. The local north controller issued traffic to the b350 that had departed referenced the h60s and a cherokee. The b350 reported the helicopter traffic in sight. Once i heard that the conflict appeared to be resolved; i resumed to assigning duties for the position rotation. The controller switched the b350 and advised terminal radar approach control facility that they were looking for the traffic.i was not aware of a cessna inbound. The c172 was on the south local controller frequency. At the time; the atm (air traffic manager) was in the cab talking to other controllers about other things; and during the occurrence he was standing directly behind the two controllers on position watching them work; obstructing my view. If he saw something peculiar; he could have brought it to the attention of any one of us at the time. After the fact; the atm discussed with me that the b350 did not have the cessna in sight. I assume this was after he reviewed the audio. I explained to him that i was not aware of the c172 until after the audio and falcon replay. Prior to this revelation; the north controller had called the cessna a cherokee but did give the traffic call. I heard the collision alert; which alarmed well after the b350 was switched to the sector. I heard externally the south controller give traffic alerts to a cessna that appeared to be not answering. The controller was making transmissions to provide the traffic. The controllers (and i am not sure if they did; you cannot hear from my distance) could have coordinated the cessna and b350 intentions. If i had known in time about the cessna; i could have suggested to the local south controller to give a suggested visual flight rules heading i.e. (for more positive control) vice the 'turn southbound' instruction. I would recommend a group review of the situation with all parties involved to discuss; learn and prevent any possible future re-occurrence.having an atm in the cab and talking to other controllers; and then literally standing behind the local controllers watching them; while they were working traffic during that event; may have been a contributing human factor to their performance. Especially when they are working [non]- standard operation.
output: Atc tower supervisor and local controller reported a nmac.

input: We were on downwind being vectored with new york approach to runway 4r in ewr. Air traffic control called out traffic at our 11 o'clock at 4;500 feet/foot (we were at 5;000 ft) doing aerial survey work and were advised that the traffic was under their control. The weather was clear and we searched for the traffic. Traffic showed on our traffic alert and collision avoidance system screen as closing but only 200 feet/foot below not the 500 feet/foot reported by the controller. We were on the latest and current ewr altimeter setting. We then were issued a traffic advisory by the traffic alert and collision avoidance system system. Shortly after we were issued a resolution advisory traffic alert and collision avoidance system climb. Almost simultaneously air traffic control recommended a climb to 5;500 feet/foot i used the tcs button to override the autopilot and commence the traffic alert and collision avoidance system climb of about 2;000 ft/minute as directed by the vsi. We advised air traffic control that we were in a traffic alert and collision avoidance system climb. The resolution advisory ended near 5;500 feet/foot and the flight continued normally.it is possible that the survey traffic either was not on the current altimeter setting or was not maintaining 4;500 feet/foot as directed by air traffic control atc said that the traffic was under their control but we never heard them issue any instructions to that traffic to avoid us or to even point us out to them.
output: Air carrier first officer is advised by air traffic control of visual flight rules traffic ahead maintaining a 500 feet/foot lower altitude. Traffic alert and collision avoidance system indicates a 200 feet/foot separation and issues a climb resolution advisory which is complied with.

input: During boarding at the gate in seattle; the left/right (directions) air conditioning pack tripped off due to a momentary overheat. It was written up in the aircraft logbook; and a mechanic signed it as a maintenance carry-over. On taxi out; we were able to reset pack to normal operations(s) (for best safety/redundancy of sys); and took off with all system operating normally. During cruise; we accepted fl370. However; because the pack was technically inoperative on paper; the minimum equipment list dispatch altitude is a maximum of fl350. We were advised of this by our dispatcher; and we immediately requested a lower altitude of fl330 for the duration of cruise. Safety of flight was never compromised; but this is a technicality of being dispatched for flight with something originally inoperative even though it works for the duration of the day.
output: The air carrier flight crew of an lgt reset the left/right (directions) air conditioning system during taxi out and it returns to normal operations(s) this system had been mel'ed and the aircraft had been restrict, restricted, restriction to a maximum altitude of fl35o on the dispatch release. The flight crew climbed to fl370 in violation of the release since the air conditioning and pressurization system now worked normally.

input: While researching the center of gravity (cg) limits for our flight we discovered the following anomaly for weight and balance calculations. I was very impressed with how close the adjusted weights method gets to the computer. But; and here is the rub; the adjusted weights cg is out when compared to an exact same load computed on the computer. I think that the cg envelope in the aom is wrong. It just does not move for the adjusted weights method like the other aircraft do. All the other aircraft have a reduced cg envelope when you do a manual weight and balance which in my mind makes for a safer procedure because doing so allows for a safe margin in case of computational errors. I have brought this up to management and have gotten the standard brick wall and dumb stare. Next step in my opinion is a safety report.
output: A b767 captain believes some computed weight and balance calculations in their aom are inaccurate.

input: During descent into atl from 25 nw rmg to rmg. Encountered moderate turbulence there had been no pilot rpts about chop and there were no echoes on radar indicating moderate or heavy precipitation. The flight attendants were picking up trays in preparation for landing and aircraft was descending from fl250 to 160. Flight attendants x and y were injured when they contacted the ceiling during the turbulence we notified the paramedics and they met the aircraft at the gate both flight attendants expressed their intention of seeing physicians within the next several days.
output: 2 flight attendants were hurt in turb.

input: I never thought it could happen to me. I was instructed to 'taxi into position and hold' (or second officer i thought) and i repeated that clearance when previously landed traffic cleared the runway(s) i was given an immediate departure and was told that my instructions had been to 'hold short.' i'm reminded of the simon and garfunkel lyric 'a man hears what he wants to hear and disregards the rest...' i believe that's what happened to me. I wanted to hear 'pos and hold;' and darnit; i did. I will not make this mistake again.
output: A c182 commercial pilot taxied into position and hold after being told to hold short of the runway(s) at ash; nh.

input: Scheduled air carrier deviating around thunderstorms given permission by zjx to enter warning area w-122. Permission then revoked and told turn 270 degree unable due to thunderstorms squawked xxxx and exercised emergency authority. Entered w-122 for 5 minute(s) no aircraft conflict. Flight at fl330. Military aircraft at fl310 holding. Controling agency needs to be a little more flexible when weather and scheduled air carrier flight crew. Could have restrict, restricted, restriction the military aircraft to fl310 and below and worked both concerns.
output: Acr attempting to avoid weather was denied permission to enter warning area. Squawked 7700 and diverted through warning area.

input: I refused the aircraft for an inoperative auxiliary power unity based on enroute terrain considerations as well as forecasted weather conditions in zzz1 at the expected time of arrival. The safest course of action was to have an aircraft with an operative auxiliary power unity at a minimum having either (preferably both) a backup pneumatic and/or electric component provided by the auxiliary power unity is always the safest course of action in any sense.
output: An a320 pilot refused an aircraft with an inoperative auxiliary power unity because of terrain and weather considerations.

input: During global positioning system runway(s) 3 approach into sbm; encountered severe turbulence in thunderstorm on approach not sure intermediate fix given approach clearance and unable to communicate with air traffic control decided to continue approach and deal with it on the ground successful landing flight plan canceled on the ground through another acft.
output: Cpr pilot encounters severe turbulence on approach to sbm and lands without clrnc.

input: Received the airplane with deferred minimum equipment list 21-xx-xx rh pack. Followed minimum equipment list procedure before pushing off the gate. Started the right engine conducted after start; combined with taxi checklist; then taxied. As we got closer to the runway first officer performed delayed before start followed by before takeoff [checklists]. Then we got cleared for takeoff. I was pilot monitoring. Conducted after takeoff checklist [in accordance with] minimum equipment list 21-xx-xx then continued climbing. Got to cruise fl250 everything seemed normal; then couple minutes after lh pack hi temperature combined with lh pack hi press caution messages appeared; which was mentioned in the minimum equipment list referenced minimum equipment list 21-xx-xx; ran quick reference handbook for messages appeared; then pack tripped off and cabin altitude started climbing rapidly. [advised] air traffic control and started the descent. On the descent cabin altitude caution message followed by cabin altitude warning. Preformed immediate action followed by quick reference handbook which directed us to land at the nearest suitable airport; advise company; air traffic control flight attendants; and passengers. Diverted to [nearby alternate]. Passenger oxygen didn't deploy.maintenance checked the aircraft and signed it off. We took off again. Message didn't reoccur; but we got l14th duct warning message! Not sure if that means lh pack needs to be rechecked because it's not supplying enough for the a/c demands while single pack; or it was just a high load?
output: Crj-200 captain reported that one a/c pack was deferred and the other a/c pack tripped off during cruise.

input: Once we finished the safety demo flight attendant x informed me that [passenger in] x1 was not wearing his mask and that during the safety demo she had to ask him twice to put on his mask. He was on a phone call after door closure. I went over and asked him to wear his mask properly as it was not covering his nose. I preceded to give him a warning. We; the crew; agreed that this aggressive behavior would not be tolerated as we did not want anything to escalate once in the air.
output: Flight attendant reported a passenger did not comply with the face mask policy.

input: Departed zzz as scheduled. During clbout fo's flight instruments failed. All flags appeared. Autoplt disengaged; flight instruments returned to normal and then failed again starting a cycle of this pattern. Ir 2 failed then appeared to come back. We decided to return to zzz; requested xxr. As we were vectored back for the approach in zzz various annunciator lights came on then would extinguish. (no bus off lights ever illuminated.) lights: automatic brake inoperative left/right (directions) pitot static; forward cargo/aft cargo; #2 electric hydraulic low pressure; left/right (directions) forward/aft left/right (directions) fuel pump low pressure. Equipment electric trim was inoperative #2 communications inoperative landed uneventfully; tr2 and tr3 had popped respective breakers. Weather was visual flight rules landing weight was 120.5 lbs.
output: B737 first officer reports numerous electrical malfunctions on departure which correct themselves then reappear. Flight crew returns to departure arpt.

input: The temperature was between 98 an 100 degrees local terrain was approximately 700' mean sea level during preflt i observed that fuel tanks were full and oil was 6 qts in the sma. The student and i flew to the nw of ftw to do commercial maneuvers. We did these for 2 hours then landed at feet/foot worth alliance airport (11 mile ne) to rest due to the heat. We departed alliance and flew to the nw and performed commercial maneuvers for 1 hour we were at 1900' mean sea level over the saginaw airport and cleared to land on runway(s) 16l at meacham when the engine started to run rough and the rpms went from 2200 down to 1000-1300. I advised ftw tower i had a rough engine and requested runway(s) 16r as it was closer. I was cleared to land on runway(s) 16r. Ten secs later the engine vibrated even more; second officer i advised tower i would be unable to make it to meacham and would be landing at the saginaw airport and would advise them after i landed intermediate fix we were ok. I landed the airplane (i took command of the plane at the first sign of a prob) and on short final pulled both the mixture and fuel valve handles to the off position to prevent a fire. Upon landing i rolled off the runway(s) onto the turnaround area at the end of the runway(s) i inspected the aircraft and noticed the left/right (directions) fuel tank empty and between one and two inches of fuel in the left/right (directions) fuel tank. Oil was 5 qts. After 30 minute(s) of waiting the mechanic came and w/o adding fuel; started the engine and did a full power static runup for a couple of minute(s) he then taxied the plane approximately 1/2 mile and parked it. He stated it had a bad left/right (directions) magneto and that a valve may have gotten hot and stuck; causing the loss of power this is the probable cause of the problem i also feel that performing commercial maneuvers for 3 hours in 100 degree heat with the mixture full rich and nearly 3000' density altitude may have caused the engine to burn much more fuel then expected. The flight lasted 3.1 hours with approximately 4 hours of fuel aboard. Even with fuel in the left/right (directions) wing and a gravity fed system the fuel could become 'positional' when low and not flow down to the engine in certain flight attitudes. (ours was straight and level when the problem occurred). Solution. Before ever flying an aircraft anywhere near the maximum endurance time be sure you know the actual fuel flow or the proc/maneuver you'll be doing. Don't ever assume the values given in the operating handbook are correct. Also; don't just add an extra gallon per hour 'just to be safe' either...your plane may burn an extra 2 or 3 gallons per hour intermediate fix it does; where will that leave you? Maybe in saginaw; tx.
output: Ga sma developes rough engine in traffic to ftw. Instructor pilot diverts to f04. Reporter suspects low fuel but ground crew indicates it could have been a sticking valve caused by high temperature plus a bad mag.

input: Enrte on a ferry flight from mdw-grr; first officer and i only members on board. Good weather daylight visual meteorological conditions clear accomplished normal takeoff no abnormal indications until approximately 4000 feet/foot on clbout -- door warning caption light illuminated. Requested leveloff at 5000 feet/foot to investigate problem ran emergency chklist. Sent first officer to back to see intermediate fix any abnormal indications are visible on door indicators -- in order to determine intermediate fix flight was able to continue to grr; our maintenance headquarters. Possibly just a faulty light -- aircraft door caption light can be deferred. First officer returns and says door handle is up; but does not look in secure position we discuss options. I tell him not to touch door because it is possibly unsafe and it is not plug type. He cautiously returns to checked other indicators (door pin visual indicators) and apparently door departed the aircraft at that time. First officer returns to cockpit and advises me. Emergency declared; we return to mdw airport vectors by zau. Prior to landing fly-by tower is initiated to see intermediate fix door is still hanging down which may adversely affect airplane during landing mdw tower says they see no door -- no obstructions. Visual; normal landing made without further incident. Do not know why we got initial door caption. I was last crew member to shut door; but apparently while i was in cockpit with my first officer a ramp agent had opened and reclosed the door for unknown reason. I'm not certain intermediate fix there was a mechanical problem with the door causing the door warning caption to come on; or intermediate fix door was not shut securely. However; on ground during engine start; on taxi; and during takeoff roll; no abnormal door indications existed. Door is presumed to be missing in lake michigan. No destruction to person or property on ground since it was a part 91 ferry flight no passenber on board. Both (2) required crew members safe. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the main cabin door has 6 small hash mark colored indicators which are aligned when the door is locked. The rptr said he closed and locked the door and checkeded the alignment of the windows and all were ok; but just minute(s) before departure a ramp agent opened the door and asked intermediate fix they were ready to go. The rptr stated the ramp agent then closed the door and the door warning light went out and the flight departed. The rptr said the aircraft was pressurized and doesn't believe the first officer could have moved the door handle when checkeding for being locked. The rptr stated the door did not damage any other structure when it departed. The rptr states the federal aviation administration has opened an investigation on the door incident.
output: A bae jetstream 3100 in climb at 4000 feet/foot had the cabin door warning light come on and leveled off at 5000 feet/foot when the door departed the acft.

input: Received revised closeout on approach into austin. Cargo weight increased from 2067 pounds to 3942 lbs.
output: Md80 flight crew on approach to aus receive an amended cargo weight closeout change from 2067 pounds to 3942 lbs.

input: We were approaching the final approach fix the gear handle was put in the down position by the capt and received a gear unsafe indication. We then consulted the abnormal chklist and performed the failure of 1 or more landing gear indicator chklist. This resulted in a normal indication; followed by a normal landing note: the chklist was accomplished after a go around and leveloff at 4000 feet/foot was accomplished. The operations(s) was done in a safe and efficient manner with good crew coordination callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr first officer said that he was not certain intermediate fix the gear was down or not during the approach into ewr -- he was too busy flying the aircraft he hadn't felt anything 'special' that would indicate that the gear had actually been up during the unsafe gear indication. He stated that they had reviewed the emergency gear extension chklist but did not use it since the capt simply recycled the gear and it came down in a normal fashion. The aircraft malfunction was written up in the logbook after landing at ewr.
output: A be1900 be02 first officer rpt on a problem with extending the gear by normal means while making an approach to ewr. Initially; it was thought that the gear would have to be extended through the use of the abnormal chklist.

input: We were landing in st thomas; vi; on runway(s) 10. There were thunderstorms on the localizer behind us and a few mile north of the localizer all the way to the airport but it was not yet raining at the airport the runway(s) was dry. The runway(s) at stt is 5000 feet/foot the wind was 180 degree at 12 knot(s) i touched down at about 1200 feet/foot past the threshold. I was about 5-10 above bug to allow for the thunderstorms and the direct xwinds. I used moderate to heavy braking along with engine reversing to stop. According to the tower (faa) at about 500 feet/foot from the last turnoff on runway(s) 10; a lot of smoke came out from under the landing gear. As it turned out; it was caused by the fact that wheel mains #1 and #3 momentarily skidded or locked and several layers of cord were rubbed off. However; the wheels (#1 and #3) remained completely inflated. Other than causing a momentary concern; all was well. We taxied to the gate on 4 fully inflated tires and parked at the gate. The problem was; that for what ever the reason; the anti-skid system did not release or correct for the impending skid that came about. Why i don't know. The system did not show any fault lights at the time.
output: Acr has brakes lock on landing rollout.

input: Faa inspector unable to ride cockpit jump seat because seatbelt was too small to fit him. Jump seat was put on minimum equipment list federal aviation administration said he was comfortable sitting in the back. Follow-up of the problem is being addressed by maintenance and the federal aviation administration callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated the aircraft was a dc9 and the cockpit jump seat harness did not fit the federal aviation administration inspector. The inspector was a large man but the harness lap belt did not reach across to the buckle. The rptr stated maintenance suspects the wrong jump seat harness was installed. The rptr said the inspector agreed to ride in the cabin and the jump seat was deferred as inoperative and not to be used.
output: A dc9 incurred a delay caused by a cockpit jump seat harness lap belt found to be too short. Suspect wrong type harness installed.

input: Aircraft x departed zzz; and i re-routed them to 'fghrn; then direct fah; then as filed.'  the company filed zzz1..fah.madii1.kord. They flew the ernny2 arrival instead. That is the way the company filed; the pilot never had to read back the arrival name. They weren't required to. When zmp passed the flight plan to zzz tower; the controller would normally say; 'cleared to ord via zzz1; then as filed.'  so the pilot/aircraft/fms flew the ernny2 standard terminal arrival route instead; which mke approach was not expecting.there is no safety in this plan. Two stars; the madii1 and the ernny2; are built right on top of each other; with similar fixes; so unless we ask the pilot every time; we have no way to know which arrival is programmed in the flight management system  additionally; the pilot; when programming; could see the first fix (zzz1 or fghrn) and push that button prematurely; without verifying the entire arrival.this situation is unsafe; and needs to be changed as soon as possible  they need to have one standard terminal arrival route here; with different transition way-points instead of two stars built on top of each other.
output: Zmp controller reports of confusion of two stars that go to one airport with similar fixes. Controllers do not know what standard terminal arrival route the pilots are actually flying until reporting in or questioned.

input: Acft slid backwards while parked at gate. The nose wheel was chocked and the brakes were released as per procedure i was signing the aircraft log book when i heard a noise from the cabin. Looking up; i noticed movement of the jetway. Actually; the jetway wasn't moving; the aircraft was sliding rearward. The brakes were applied by both myself and the f/o. The aircraft stopped; brakes were set. The aircraft was towed back to original parking spot and the remaining passenber deplaned. Luckily; no passenber were hurt and the aircraft sustained no damage. Large credit is due to the f/a's quick reaction in stopping the passenber from deplaning. I recommend 3 corrective actions in order to avoid such future incidents: chock main gear when only one is to be chocked; have ramp chocking area cleared of ice and snow or sanded as appropriate; and leave parking brakes set until all passenber have deplaned. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following: ramp was covered with sleet and the rptr said it was reasonable level. Nose chock had been placed tight against the nose wheel both front and back. F/o was the first to notice movement of the aircraft and set the parking brake. Company has investigated the incident and has changed the procedure to leave the parking brake on during winter months. Should solve the prob.
output: Acft parked at gate; brakes off per company procedure slides back; no damage.

input: Arrived in rno as scheduled. Performed a flaps 3 degree landing on runway(s) 16r per a320 standard operating procedure and runway(s) data from automatic communications addressing & reporting system used medium autobrakes and reverse thrust. Exit off of runway(s) 16r at taxiway p -- normal operations(s) standard taxi in and parking. Brake temperatures at gate average 650 degrees with the outboard left/right (directions) tire at 705 degrees maximum observed. Outside air temperature 31 degrees celsius rno ground used fans on wheels upon arrival, arrive bake temperatures were decreasing below 600 degrees by time we left cockpit. Briefed outbound crew and went to hotel. Capt was called by maintenance about 2 hours later and informed that 1 tire went flat on the next flt's pushback and that the other 3 needed replacement.
output: Following a flaps 3 landing in rno; a capt reports that on the next push back one tire deflated and the remaining three had to be replaced.

input: I was working local control position. Aircraft x departed enroute. I entered a center flight plan for the aircraft to receive continued flight following beyond terminal radar approach control facility airspace to his final destination. When nearing the boundary of terminal radar approach control facility airspace; the terminal radar approach control facility controller terminated radar services instead of handing the aircraft off to center. This creates a potentially dangerous situation in which an aircraft which had requested flight following is not being provided with those services.as a matter of standard practice; terminal radar approach control facility terminates radar services to visual flight rules aircraft when they near the boundary instead of handing the aircraft off to terminal radar approach control facility this occurs even when tower has done the extra work of entering a center flight plan; alleviating that work from tracon.unless an aircraft requests termination of flight following; hand-offs should be performed for all aircraft so they are not denied the visual flight rules flight following services they request. Services should be provided in accordance with f.a.a jo 7110.65 7-6-1.
output: An mri tower controller observed the terminal radar approach control facility controller terminate visual flight rules services to an aircraft instead of handing off the aircraft to the center.

input: Loud pop and deviation in egt gauge #1 engine which returned to normal -- suspected blown tire or compressor stall #1 engine coordinated with company and approach facilities diverted from fll direct mco (flt was scheduled fll direct bdl). Accomplished 2 low approachs runway(s) 17 at mco; second officer air carrier maintenance could look at landing gear and tires. Accomplished uneventful landing at runway(s) 18l mco. Xferred passenber to another aircraft and maintenance found remnants of a bird in the engine inlet.
output: A b727-200 on takeoff just at rotation incurred a bird strike to #1 engine flight diverted to mco.

input: Possible navigate, navigation track deviation on takeoff selected lateral navigation on mode control panel (confirmed on attitude direction indicator fma); first officer was pilot flying continued to hand fly the aircraft as per the pratt & whitney procedures on commercial chart 1 for zzzz departures at 1500 feet/foot above ground level vertical navigation was selected on mode control panel (confirmed on attitude direction indicator fma). Shortly after autoplt was engaged; the autoplt began a steady pitch up to well above the flight director pitch command causing a rapid decrease to near v2. Autoplt was disconnected; a proper pitch attitude was established and the departure was continued. In the course of the pitch-up distraction autoplt disconnect and re-establishment of proper pitch attitude; we overshot our first turn on the departure -- by how much i don't know. We re-established ourselves on the proper track as quickly as possible and continued the departure with no comments or complaints from departure ctl.
output: A b757 flying a demanding standard instrument departure had a track deviation after the ap pitched up when engaged requiring attention to the rapidly decreasing speed and not the track.

input: Originally assigned to fl310 then told to stop at fl290; frequency change and told to fly 270 degrees for ape vor and dme (co-located) told controller we were /india equipped; (normally filed /a) and could go direct ape. Controller said no; just fly 270 degree heading for now. We were just beginning to level at fl290 when i became unsure intermediate fix i had the correct altitude in the window and asked controller 'say assigned altitude for air carrier x.' controller responded 'fl310' which i read back 'roger fl310.' set this altitude in the window; and continued climb to fl310. At about fl306; controller said 'acr x; i thought you asked me filed altitude not assigned altitude descend to fl280.' we then descended to fl280. There were no conflicts rpted by the controller or traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii or visual.
output: Dc9 crew confirmed their cleared altitude the air route traffic control center radar controller thought they were asking about their filed altitude instead.

input: B747 was switched to low altitude sector upon reaching fl240. B727 came on frequency climbing through fl226 for fl230. B747 came on frequency high; and i thought low altitude sector would continue his descent to comply with an approach control crossing restrict, restricted, restriction i climbed b727 to fl260; but saw b747 mode celsius still indicating fl240. I tried to stop b727 at fl230; but pilot did not respond. I asked low altitude controller intermediate fix he was descending b747. Controller said he wasn't there. Controller issued descent to b747. Pilot complied; had been waiting for a break in radio congestion? B727 was issued 20 degree left/right (directions) turn and traffic issued; and advised traffic was descending to fl230. B727 rpted responding to an resolution advisory and he was descending to fl230.
output: A controller rpt on loss of separation between a b747 level at fl240 and a b727 climbing from fl230 to fl260 15 mile north of shb; in.

input: Entered the clouds at fl270 and after 15 minute(s) the manifold pressure dropped and we couldn't hold altitude informed center (zlc) and got lower assignment; which the power wouldn't hold. Finally declared an emergency and informed center that i would have to continue descent and land in sun valley without power upon reaching 8500 feet/foot we broke out and became visual. The engine had full power but no manifold pressure indication. I decided at that point to continue flight because i thought it was an instrument failure. We flew on to burley; identification and landed because of deteriorating weather at lower level. After landing i determined that i had a magneto failure and the static buildup on the air frame in the clouds affected the electronic ignition.
output: Lancair 4p engine failure. A continental tsio 550b with an electronic ignition system fails when pilot enters clouds at fl270. After a power off descent to 8500 feet/foot engine restarts and is normal to lndg.

input: The flight plan was planned further south; over nat a; that is normal for this direction and route. We had a cost index of 289; a flight time of 11:04 (+06); and a total burn of 257;542 pounds. After reviewing the upper winds i called the dispatcher to consider another route of flight that may save both time and fuel. My conversation with the dispatcher revealed a more northerly route; with less wind; total flight time of 10:58 (on time); a cost index of 54 and a total burn of 245;300 lbs. Basically this flight would have saved 12;000 pounds of fuel had it been optimized on the route i suggested.the reasoning given by the dispatcher for not filing the more efficient route was the complexity of validating with european air traffic control i was informed it would require him to 'piece' the 'validation' together taking more time than he had available. He repeated the route we got was 'validated' and it was a 'good one.' for the purpose of discussion turbulence avoidance was not a factor on this day's operation.these were the 'red flags' my crew and i noticed during the flight planning and review process:*an abnormal routing for this flight; a more southerly routing.*a cost index (ci) of 289 (normal ci is approximately 40 - 90).*total flight time 11:04 (six minutes over scheduled)*the upper winds chart indicated we were flying for a much greater time with a headwind over the planned route when compared to a more normal northerly route.*no significant turbulence forecast for the planned or alternative route possibilities.things for consideration:*it is unacceptable; except for mitigating air traffic control or other requirements; to burn 12;000 pounds of additional fuel when it is clearly not needed.*if the dispatcher staffing is so short the individuals cannot properly flight plan and monitor the flights assigned to them then questions of both safety and economy should be asked and answered.*[our airline] recently spent millions of dollars training pilots; dispatchers and other personnel about the need and practice of saving fuel. The cost of burning 12;000 pounds of extra fuel is estimated to be approximately $3;500. Considering this unneeded expense; was the effectiveness of the operational efficiency course (oet) course achieved and is there truly a commitment by upper united management to implement the needed processes and manpower required to achieve the fuel savings goals?to summarize:i personally realize it is often difficult to achieve optimum results in every operation; flight and effort made. However; it is unacceptable to accept such obvious inefficiencies when they can be avoided. The members of my crew expressed their feelings of antipathy as we left eddf operations with a flight plan; which needlessly burned 12;000 extra pounds of fuel; and that may be the real cost of today's flight.
output: A b747 air crew; after receiving a dispatch release from their dispatcher; asked the dispatcher if a more northerly route would save time and fuel. It would have but the dispatcher stated that the process of changing the routing would have taken more time than he had available.

input: This rpt pertains to 2 incidents -- both under the same flight number; but on different legs. The first incident involves takeoff performance data. The second involves an unanticipated delay on the first of a 3 leg flight between 2 fueling points. No damage was involved in either incident. During both incidents i used the same judgement as my colleagues and predecessors have used. But; these are also known as 'gray areas.' i ante meridiem new to turbine engine captaincy. And; given the special circumstances which are often unique to alaska; i have written this rpt in hopes of shedding light on the gray. I should have said 'i've been drinking.' it was a sunday. I wasn't scheduled. But; the statilon manager called with a problem our t-1040 had just completed the first of 2 charters for the school in shishmareff (shh). The temperature in shh was minus 40 degrees fahrenheit unbeknownst to miss a; who was flying the t-1040; a micro switch had frozen and the flaps would not retract. She had called our base in nome (ome) to consult with maintenance and they decided to send a mechanic and an airplane. I was to take the chieftain; drop the mechanic at shh; go empty to st. Michael's (smk); pick up 8 kids and 1 coach; drop them in shh; then return ome. As usual; plans changed. While preflting the chieftain; i received a rpt that the temperature in shh was minus 40 degrees fahrenheit company policy requires permission from maintenance to operate the chieftain in anything less than minus 35 degrees fahrenheit i asked the mechanic on duty to get permission. Permission was not granted and further instruction were issued to take the beechcraft c99 airliner. Meanwhile; the t-1040's flaps have thawed out and retracted. And; miss a is en route to ome. Intermediate fix we take the beech 99; miss a will fly coplt. The new routing will be ome-smk-shh-ome. When she arrived at ome. I received a pilot report directly from her. She indicated that the weather was real good and that there was lots of wind; 15- 20 knot(s) right down the runway(s) temperature 5 degrees fahrenheit unalakleet (unk) automatic weather observing/reporting system 30 nautical mile ne; was indicating similar observations. The wind was gusting to 30 knot(s) very favorable conditions. This leads us to the first issue at hand -- takeoff performance. With the projected load; required fuel; and in a confign with 10 passenber seats installed. We should weight about 10000 pounds on departure from smk. Smk is is 2318 feet/foot gravel surface runway(s) (today it's packed snow and gravel). There is about 100 feet/foot of undeclared overrun at each end. There are no buildings; trees or obstacles at either end. The only limiting performance chart for this flight is the 'accelerate-slow' chart. This chart indicates the length of runway(s) required to abort prior to v1 and go off the end of the runway(s) at 35 knot(s) given the atmospheric conditions for the day; a 10000 pound takeoff gross weight would require approximately 2300 feet/foot in addition; the beginning of the performance section states that federal aviation regulation 135 regulations permit an overrun. After the fact; my colleagues have stated they have been told that overrun is not permitted by the federal aviation administration intermediate fix second officer why has not an amended page been added to the aircraft pilots operating handbook (arpt facility manual)? After quizzing; my colleagues have unanimously said this was a sound operations(s) yet; i have received severe chastising from my chief pilot he has estimated that i was as much as 2000 pounds overwt. He has stated that i did not add an adequate safety margin. He has not stated how to determine a safety margin for contaminated surfaces. And; i'm sure that topic was not covered in training; because we spent less than 5 minute(s) on performance. Perhaps our training program is missing something. En route ome-smk; pedestrians were observed transiting runway(s) area during an overhead inspection of runway(s) conditions and wind at smk. One additional circuit was required to alert the pedestrians of our intentions. This activity resulted in several additional minute(s) of en route time. The entire flight was planned ome-smk-shh-ome. Intermediate stops at smk and shh. Fuel is only available at ome. Smk and shh are remote bush villages and do not have fueling facilities. Departure weight at smk was tobe minimum in order to comply with the 'accelerate-slow flaps 30 percent' performance requirement. Initial flight planning at ome did not consider time overhead for pedestrians at smk. Therefore; i departed shh-ome with approximately 1/10 of an hour short of the required fuel reserves for night visual flight rules the fuel gauges of this aircraft indicate by the 100 pounds and have a little mark every 50 pounds fuel observed on gauges departing shh was approximately 800 pounds fuel on paper; shh-ome is 750 pounds and was determined in conformance with company procedure company procedure is not written. I have flown with; and observed; every senior capt; 2 assistant chief pilots and 2 chief pilots at this company. After establishing fuel required for flight a 600 lb/hr fuel burn is used against flight time. This is a generic number and no consideration is applied to fuel burned during start and taxi. Everyone here uses the same procedure i landed at ome; cavu and excellent forecasts; with approximately 38 minute(s) fuel remaining on paper. Gauges are not the most reliable dials in these airplanes. The only way to know what you've really got is to see it. The big question here is: in what instances is fuel reserve to be used? After an extra 6 minutes overhead smk and know 6 minute(s) into my projected visual flight rules night fuel reserve; with 2 legs to go; and now knowing that i will return to ome short of the required night fuel reserve should i have interrupted my planned flight between 2 fueling facilities. Flown out of my way to pump on 15 gallons; on a night with very favorable forecasts? Most of my colleagues in western alaska believe that reserve is there for just such contingencies; and they do not believe i acted outside of the bounds of the regulations nor reasonableness. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information unable to discuss this matter with the rptr since only telephone contact revealed that he did no longer work for the part 135 operator in nome; ak; which prompted his questions.
output: Capt of a part 135 commuter took off overwt for the length of the runway(s) and complains that he is not properly trained and is expected to fly regardless of the weather and airport runway(s) conditions.

input: Aircraft y departed zzz1 airport instrument flight rules to the southeast out of the airspace; and aircraft x was inbound landing zzz. Aircraft x was cleared to the initial approach fix for runway x at zzz and descended to 060. Aircraft y was cleared to destination and climbed to 070. 2 additional aircraft departed zzz1 after aircraft y; and required more direct handling than aircraft y. Aircraft x mentioned that they were picking up traffic to their northwest; and by the time i looked; aircraft y was leaving 061; and aircraft x was at 072. They were separated by 2.62 miles and 900 feet vertically. During with dealing with the other departure's climbing out behind aircraft y; i lost the aircraft y's rate of climb reference the descending jet traffic. I immediately stopped aircraft x 's descent; and stopped aircraft y's climb and descended aircraft y. Due to covid protocol; this occurred while staffed with 4 cpcs and 1 supervisor to work the facility until xa:00 local time.better staffing to alleviate controller fatigue. Our staffing has been tight; and time on position has been increased at the facility for a while; resulting in long work sessions and short breaks sometimes to produce coverage to work the traffic; which has resumed close to 90% of pre-covid numbers.
output: Tracon controller reported a loss of separation between an air carrier and a small aircraft and cited staffing issues as a contributing factor.

input: I operated as the captain and pilot monitoring on the flight. Prior to leaving the hotel; we were contacted by crew scheduling. Crew scheduling notified us about the flight being delayed from its original scheduled departure time due to maintenance. The anticipated delay was six hours. We arrived at the aircraft and started our normal preflight duties. Several items were deferred: minimum equipment list 28-22-1-2-1 #2 left aft main tank pumps (tank 2 aft auto mode) and minimum equipment list 31-65-1 multifunction control display unit (dcu) #3. During preflight; we received a level 1 'tr 3 fail' alert and a subsequent flight management computer #2 fail. I entered the items into the logbook in accordance with fom flight crew handling of aircraft discrepancies and notified local maintenance. Three maintenance personnel arrived at the aircraft and we left the flight deck in order for maintenance to work on the problems. Maintenance cleared the level 1 'tr 3 fail' and deferred flight management computer #2. I requested and received amended release #1 adding minimum equipment list 34-63-1; #2 flight management computer inoperative - no rnp 4 operations. The crew reviewed minimum equipment list 34-63-1 operations procedures and operational limitations. Furthermore; we discussed the ramifications of one flight management computer operation and two (of three) mcdu's. The flight blocked out and shortly after departure; we received a level 1 'tr 3 fail' alert. Du 4; 5; 6 and mcdu #2 lost brief power approximately every seven to 10 minutes causing all three display units and mcdu #2 to blink off and then on. This event required the first officer to reselect flight management computer #1 on mcdu #2. We cross checked all displays and no errors were noted between the first officer's displays and my side. We discussed the problem and determined the first officer would continue to be the pilot flying unless we had a longer display failure. I continued to monitor the situation as pilot monitoring and discussed that we would contact maintenance control at the top of the climb. We selected and utilized autopilot 1 (ap1) for climb out and cruise. Upon leveling at fl310; we continued to observe a level 1 'tr 3 fail' alert. Du 4; 5; 6 and mcdu #2 lost power with increased frequency. Vfr low altitude training routes 3 showed a load of 0.03-0.04. We also; received level 1 'fire det 2 fault' alert. I asked the first officer to continue to fly and monitor air traffic control along with the international relief officer i contacted our dispatcher; maintenance; and requested to speak with a systems maintenance expert via sat phone. Up until this point; we felt there were no flight safety concerns to operating the aircraft on the intended flight. We did not feel that a complete failure of mcdu #2 was imminent. Also; we believed the power interruptions to du 4; 5; 6; and mcdu#2 were due to the opening and closing of the vfr low altitude training routes #3 relay. After discussing the situation with dispatch; the maintenance expert; and the crew; we elected to perform an air turn back to dispatch requested departure airport. I requested and received amended release #2 to change our destination to the dispatch requested destination. We were given a nearby airport as the alternate. Later; we received an amended release #3 changing destination alternate due to changing weather conditions at the destination. In consultation with dispatch; the crew did not feel the need to declare an emergency. We coordinated with air traffic control and dumped approximately 15;000 pounds of fuel to reduce to below max landing weight. Fuel dump was completed. Du 4; 5; 6 and mcdu #2 continued to blink off and on more frequently. During the descent; du 4 began to intermittently display a red x during the power cycle. We discussed the increased frequency of cycle times; and landing weather and i decided it would be best for me to assume the pilot flying duties. A positive transfer of aircraft control was performed and the first officer assumed the pilot monitoring duties for the remainder of the flight. During descent; du 4; 5; 6 and mcdu #2 continued to briefly lose power (blink off/on) approximately every 30 seconds. On final approach; mcdu #2 failed. A normal landing was made. Again; in consultation with dispatch; the crew did not feel the need to declare an emergency. The crew did not feel the safety of the flight was ever compromised nor did we need to deviate from an air traffic control clearance to safely complete the air turn back.
output: An md-11 departed with several mel's and shortly after takeoff a level 1 vfr low altitude training routes 3 fail alerted which resulted in du's 4; 5; 6 and mcdu #2 power loss. The flight returned to land at an alternate airport without declaring an emergency.

input: After a thorough preflt we departed dfw en route to cll. The capt was flying and i was the pilot not flying after completing the after takeoff chklist; the capt noted to me that the plane was not performing normally. We then heard noise from the left/right (directions) engine and saw that the cowling was coming loose. He slowed the aircraft we declared an emergency and returned to land at dfw without further incident. I think the problem was caused by worn fasteners on the engine cowling and this problem could have been avoided with using newer equipment than that of the emb-100. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information after the aircraft had returned to dfw; the first question the mechs asked the first officer was; 'did you checked the cowling on the preflt?' the answer was; 'of course i did.' the rptr stated that a new cowling was required; second officer he did not stay around for the installation of that. The next day; he talked to the crew who had flown the same aircraft and they told him that; after arriving at their destination airport 1 of the 6 fasteners had come loose. The fasteners are the snap-to-flush-close position type. Very hard to miss being open on a preflt. Rptr blames incident on aircraft age; aircraft being an emb-110.
output: Emer declared in a return land incident.

input: While departing from mgw; we were cleared for takeoff; on course; and maintain 3;000 feet/foot as we taxied onto the runway; the first officer and i looked at each other with a question on our faces as he read back the takeoff instructions and reached up to the altitude preselector and dialed it from 8;000 down to 3;000 feet/foot morgantown tower did not correct him; so we performed a normal takeoff with a left turn on course and a climb up to 3;000 feet/foot after the switch over to the departure frequency; and while leveling off at 3;000 feet/foot the ground proximity warning system activated with a 'terrain' warning. The first officer immediately checked in and requested higher. The controller responded with 'climb and maintain 8;000 ft.' after i initiated the climb; there were no subsequent ground proximity warning system hits and the flight continued uneventfully.
output: Flight crew departing mgw in visual meteorological conditions reports being instructed to climb on course and maintain 3;000 feet/foot leveling at 3;000 feet/foot a terrain warning is annunciated and the first officer quickly requests a higher altitude and is cleared to 8;000 ft.

input: For about 8 months i have noticed that phoenix vor and dme (co-located) has had an anomaly in the ne quadrant. Coming in on the fossl 2 arrival, arrive the course deviation indicators for both navigate, navigation receivers have fluctuated plus or minus 5 degrees this occurs from 30-60 nautical mile out and from fl250 and below. This has happened in different aircraft and to both navigate, navigation receivers second officer i don't think it is a problem on the airplanes. I know that it happens in the mornings; although recently on an afternoon arrival, arrive the vor and dme (co-located) seemed to work normally. This anomaly has caused my aircraft to start to turn in before reaching the pxr 015 degrees radial when using the autoplt vor/loc feature to capture the course. Intermediate fix it hadn't been visual flight rules and we weren't familiar with the geographic position of the radial we would have turned to a heading of 195 degrees about 8 mile too soon. Even intermediate fix the crew doesn't use the vor/loc feature of the autoplt or flight director system having the course deviation indicator jump inward could mislead a crew into turning in prior to the actual course. I don't know intermediate fix this anomaly has caused any traffic problems i have mentioned it to zab and phoenix terminal radar approach control facility and they don't seem to have had any other comments about it. The initial course deviation indicator movements are erratic second officer most pilots probably recognize that the needle movements are erroneous. However; as i mentioned before; intermediate fix the crew uses the autoplt vor/loc feature to capture the pxr 015 degree radial the aircraft will start to turn to a heading of 195 degrees too soon.
output: Atc navigate, navigation aid problem erratic vor.

input: A major road construction project is underway on and adjacent to airport property. Construction workers cut all telephone lines to the control tower at approximately xa00. This resulted in a total loss of stars interface and tdw (radar display); automatic terminal information service frequency all interphone communicationss with other facilities (particularly orlando international tower and terminal radar approach control facility mco); fdio; and the 'crash phone' to local fire departure and 911 operations(s) center phone lines were restored approximately xf30. This was the third time in less than a month that this construction crew had cut our phone lines; power lines; or both. After the previous time a cell phone was placed in the tower cabin attendant to be used to contact mco terminal radar approach control facility for necessary coords. We established procedures for all arrs to be placed on localizer back course to active runway(s) 25 and switch communicationss at 7 vor and dme (co-located) practice instrument approachs and pattern work (a significant portion of our business) were denied. A locally-based traffic rpting aircraft was told to remain outside class d airspace for the duration of his evening traffic rpts; which limited the information he could provide to local news affiliates. After the lines were repaired; i spoke with one of the phone company technicians. He said that intermediate fix the phone company could show negligence on the part of the construction company or the subcontractor that was supposed to mark buried cables; they would bill them for the cost of repairs. He conceded that such costs are not very high; and many construction companies find it most cost-effective to dig blindly and pay for any repairs that may be required than to pay a subcontractor to mark buried cables. The construction companies in question obviously don't get it. Until the federal aviation administration starts fining them for each and every service interruption they cause; this 'jeopardization' of safety will continue unabated. I figure $50000 per incident would get the message across effectively.
output: Twr controller feels construction company's repeated damage to telephone lines svcing the tower and its equipment should be compensated for; and the company fined for each instance of such loss to make it more expensive to pay for such damages than to avoid doing so.

input: While flying an smt single pilot on 12/fri/88 at approximately xa20; inversion was discovered at 7000' mean sea level while on instrument flight rules radar vectors to uca. Temperature was +10 degrees celsius at 70 and automatic terminal information service rpted uca temperature of 27 degrees fahrenheit griffis approach control cleared me to 3000'. While passing through 4300' mean sea level broke out of cloud bases; rpted uca in sight and was cleared for a visibility approach to runway(s) 15. Automatic terminal information service rpted ice pellets and light freezing rain. Expected some ice accumulation; second officer i then activated engine intake heat; propeller de-ice (electric) and boot automatic cycle for wings and horizontal and vertical stabilizers. Passing through 2700' mean sea level temperature went to -1 degree celsius and ice began to accumulate on windshield. I then activated windshield alcohol in 'auto on mode.' by this time i was in the downwind leg; had gear extended; and ice really started to accumulate (severe). Switched to uca tower and was cleared to land on 15. Began base leg and on roll out alcohol would not keep windshield clear of ice. Advised tower i was starting missed approach was instructed to fly runway(s) heading and climb to 3000'. (i had been in similar situations before and simply climbed to higher altitude to let ice melt off.) i would then make fairly steep approach to airport (to spend as little time in icing conditions as possible). I then gave the aircraft 100% torque to takeoff thrust; pitched up 10 degrees and aircraft didn't climb at this point i was still on base leg passing the final approach course. I waited about 5 secs to verify intermediate fix aircraft would not climb decided i then had a problem and would deploy flaps and make a blind approach to uca by slipping aircraft into final and using side window for visibility reference aircraft was high at this point; second officer i put flap indicator to the 5 degree position and aircraft yawed violently to the right. Felt like asymmetrical deployment of flaps. Quickly reset flap indicator to 0 degrees i was sinking at about 800 feet per minute now; and well past final approach to uca. Tried to turn with yoke (acft has spoilerons) to uca final. Aircraft would not respond and began to sink even faster. Looked out left window and saw rme air force base runway(s) 33. Immediately switched back to griffiss approach and advised them of problem and that i was going to land. Rme then cleared me to land on 33. Tried to turn left with spoilerons--no response. Began using rudder to maneuver aircraft toward final. Could not turn quickly enough. I then decided to make a gradual turn to final on 15. At this time sink rate was 1200 feet per minute asked for 15 and controller cleared me to land. Controller then exclaimed they had trucks on runway(s) had to slow descent rate somehow; second officer i cycled gear up and increased power to 110 degrees thrust--sink rate slowed to 800 feet per minute i then proceeded to use rudder and even differential thrust to maneuver aircraft to final. About 1/2 mile out at about 1 45 degree angle to final; controller advised trucks were still on runway(s) asked intermediate fix i could enter downwind to runway(s) 33. I was busy flying aircraft and wasn't sure intermediate fix i could even make 15. I then responded; 'sir; i can't do it right now.' he then said; 'ok; understand. You're cleared to land on 15; just be careful!' i said; 'roger.' after transmission i cycled gear to down position and was at 50' above ground level side window had now become iced over; second officer visibility landing was impossible. Wasn't sure intermediate fix i would make the runway(s) or not; but knew it would be close. I then began the flare and saw the glow of one runway(s) light through the front window. Wasn't sure intermediate fix it was the left or right side. Noticed i was approaching light directly head on; second officer i kicked hard right rudder to parallel my course to the light. Then i pulled the power to flight idle. Just then the controller exclaimed; 'trucks are clear of the runway(s) you are cleared to land.' i didn't respond to transmission aircraft then settled on runway(s) centerline about 500' down runway(s) occurrence was caused by severe icing and by alcohol windshield. An smt y shot the same approach behind me and made it. He had electric windshield heat. I've flown other aircraft with alcohol windshields and even in light icing conditions they are not very efficient. I think all aircraft certified for flight into icing conditions should have electric de-ice windshields. They seem to work thebest. Intermediate fix i could have seen out the windshield a normal approach and landing could have been accomplished to uca and occurrence would have been avoided.
output: Atx smt encounters heavy icing on approach which causes partial loss of control and vision problem. Unable to make destination airport makes emergency landing at close proximitypa military arpt.

input: On mar/xx/95; at xa13; upon landing at mcallen miller international airport after completion of the localizer back course runway(s) 31 approach on rollout; the nose gear collapsed and the aircraft skidded to a stop on the runway(s) the main gear remained down and locked. Tower and company were notified and the aircraft was evacuated and towed from the runway(s) after inspection; it was determined that the nose gear locking mechanism broke causing the gear to collapse. It was not any fault of the plt.
output: Acft equipment problem malfunction during a night operations(s) landing nose gear collapses on atx acft.

input: Aircraft x departed on an instrument flight rules flight plan. The aircraft was issued an instruction to fly runway heading for radar vectors and to climb and maintain three thousand. Per local standard operating procedure these are standard instructions for our runway configuration and for the type of instrument flight rules clearance that was filed by the pilot. The aircraft was cleared for takeoff and acknowledged a frequency change from the tower controller to contact departure; fly runway heading and climb to 3;000 feet and leveled off. Aircraft x  did not check in with departure until he was approximately 18 miles west of the airport. By this time he had entered a 3;800 feet. Minimum vectoring altitude (mva). Many methods were used in an effort to gain communications with the aircraft. I made multiple calls on several frequencies to include guard frequency. Tower was advised and attempted to contact the aircraft with no luck.at 18 miles when communications resumed; i advised the aircraft that he was in a higher minimum vector altitude and started his climb to 8;000 feet. He advised that he was still runway heading. I told him that i was aware of this but i needed him to climb above the minimum vector altitude before i would issue him a turn on course. He climbed to 8;000 feet and was issued a turn of 140 when he was above 3;800 feet. I asked the pilot if he was experiencing communication issues with the aircraft. He responded in the negative. I advised him several calls were made to him on multiple frequencies and guard. He stated that he never got switched to departure. Further review of the audio of the event illustrated that the pilot was given a frequency change from tower to departure; which he acknowledged. No other aircraft were having issues hearing the departure frequencies.my role in the event was that of the departure controller. I do not know what led to the event or why it happened. We advised the aircraft to expect final altitude 10 minutes after departure on instrument flight rules clearances. We used to issue 5 minutes after departure. Perhaps we may want to go back to 5 minutes after departure. This may get no radio aircraft climbing sooner so minimum vector altitude violations don't become as much of a factor.
output: Sba departure controller reported an aircraft did not contact them in a timely manner and flew below the minimum vectoring altitude.

input: After being cleared direct to mitoe and cleared for the visual approach to runway 29 in oak; we were descending from 3300 feet/foot to 2500 feet/foot mean sea level at approximately 2800-2700 feet/foot mean sea level the egpws warning activated and i initiated the recovery procedure. About 2 seconds later; the terrain warning terminated and the visual approach and landing to runway 29 were completed without further incident.
output: A b757 received an egpws alert at 2;800 feet/foot descending over the hayward hills on a visual approach for oak runway 29.

input: The flight was an ambulance flight that had originated in zzz; stopped in zzz1 for fuel and inbound customs and continued on to the drop-off airport of zzz2. The flight from zzz to zzz1 was uneventful for the first 95% of the flight aside from a couple minor generator problems it was planned to be 2 hours 30 minute(s) with the acft's range of about 3 hours and 30 minute(s) weather in zzz2 was forecast to be ok with some snow showers and lower visibility in the vicinity and a strong gusty nw wind; typical winter weather about 150 mile south of zzz1; i picked up the zzz2 automatic terminal information service to get an idea of the weather at zzz1 which has a weak automatic terminal information service and you have to be within 100 mile at times to be able to hear it. They were calling 3 mile snow and mist with 1500 feet/foot ceilings and tower visibility of 5 mile close to the forecast. When i picked up the zzz1 weather it was actually a little better than zzz2 and they were doing the instrument landing system to runway(s) 24r. The zzz1 winds; however; were 350 degrees and 26 knot(s) gusting to 37 knot(s) nearly a direct crosswind near the airplane's limitation. Knowing that it had been snowing all night in the area; i asked zzz2 approach intermediate fix there were any braking action rpts at zzz1 to plan on our landing distance data to see intermediate fix we could land there.
