No rpts were available when he called the zzz1 tower although they said there was blowing snow on all surfaces. The capt and i decided that we would shoot the instrument landing system to zzz1 and since the visibility was more than 3 mile we would take a look at the runway(s) surface and decide on what we would do. We broke out on the instrument landing system to zzz1; a good 5 mile out; and as we got closer the capt advised me to tell tower we were going to go around and land at zzz2. We performed the missed approach and missed approach chklist and checkeded on with zzz2 approach on a north heading at 3000 feet/foot we advised that we wanted to do the instrument landing system to runway(s) 24l or runway(s) 24r. They gave us a south heading and told us to expect runway(s) 24l. At about this time the low fuel light had come on steady meaning there was less than 600 pounds in either or both wings meaning less than 30 minute(s) of low altitude flying. We were given a heading to join the localizer and advised that the runway(s) 24l runway visual range was 1400 feet/foot a federal aviation regulation cry from the 5 mile that had been rpted approximately 20-25 mile earlier; and asked our intentions. We advised we would continue the approach both of us agreeing there wasn't any other option due to the fuel situation and lack of the weather knowledge at nearby airports that we could have used. The required runway visual range for runway(s) 24l is 3200 runway visual range or 300 feet/foot ceilings and 5/8 mile visibility. We had none of these. I had ground contact about 6 mile out and was just hoping that maybe it was a passing squall that would be over by the time we got to the airport i later checkeded the weather for the time of landing and it was 1/4 mile visibility; vv100 and a fairly steady 40 knot(s) crosswind just about the worst conditions you could ask for. The hand flown approach was done with great accuracy despite the windshear of +/-10 knot(s) all the way in from 5 mile and strong crosswind as we neared decision height it became apparent that we were not going to break out. The capt advised me that in addition to giving him track information that after decision height i was to call out height above touchdown zone elevation. We both caught the approach lights at about 150 feet/foot and continued to 100 feet/foot above touchdown zone and then 50 feet/foot and i called 50 feet/foot steady a couple of times as the capt tracked the localizer the visibility was terrible with the blowing snow and i did not see any landmarks as i ante meridiem very familiar with the airport as soon as we passed the threshold lights and were in between the runway(s) edge lights; the power was pulled to idle and we landed without incident. Tower asked us for the flight conditions on approach and i advised +/-10 knot(s) on approach and that we had the approach lights at minimums; a slight stretch in the truth. Nothing else was asked of us and we were handed off to ground for the taxi to the fixed-base operator 15 minute(s) later; visibility was greater than 5 mile with a 3000 feet/foot scattered ceiling with occasional snow squalls dropping visibility down to 1000 feet/foot or less as i sat with the medical crew and patient as the capt had gone inside to make a couple phone calls to company. As federal aviation regulation as preventing this from happening again; i ante meridiem not sure what to say. The weather had gone from forecast marginal visual flight rules to below approach minimums without warning to us. In a way; i feel it was out of our hands and with the lack of fuel we could not have easily found an airport close enough with weather that we knew was going to be steady enough for us to get in. The only thing that we could have done to remedy this situation would be to have made a fuel stop en route but since the weather was forecast to be ok; we just wanted to get the patient to their destination as quickly as possible. I think a contributing factor was crew fatigue. We had both been up approximately 24 hours and on duty for about 13 hours with about 8.5 hours of flight time at the time of the approach into zzz1. Flying for a large part 135 company; we do a lot of longitude days and nights and as much as you'd like to think you are used to it; you never are. The same goes for the weather both the capt and i have lived and flown in the area our entire lives and we both know now more than ever that the weather can never be expected to stay as predicted. I guess from here on out i will try and look at weather trends to get a better idea of what could happen in addition to what is expected. I will also think twice about doing longitude legs into areas with questionable weather and to carry extra fuel when possible to help with decision making. The only other way to get more rest at a part 135 company is not to fly for a part 135 company. Unfortunately; with the way the charter industry has been allowed to get; pilots will always be exploited to the full extent of their duty day without regard to natural sleep habits and good rest.
output: An lr25 medical flight encountered non forecast destination weather and winds. The crew diverted to a nearby airport and landed fatigued with low fuel in a 100 feet/foot ceiling.

input: While at fl340 the cabin altitude warning light illuminated; an emergency was declared and we began a descent to 12;000 feet/foot we put on our oxygen masks;established communication and backed it up with the rapid decompression emergency checklist. Cabin pressurization was restored at 12;000 and we continued to our destination. After pressurization was restored we no longer needed emergency handling.
output: A cessna citation lost control of pressurization at fl340; declared an emergency and descended to 12;000 mean sea level where they were able to regain control of cabin altitude and continued to their destination.

input: While [we were] being vectored for the approach the controller told us to fly heading 360. We told him we could not fly 360; but we could fly 330 because there was a thunderstorm in our path. He told us twice more to fly 360 for traffic and we told him we were unable due to a thunderstorm. Finally after the third time he told us to fly 360; we told him that we were declaring an emergency and that we would only be able to fly 330. We saw the traffic on traffic alert and collision avoidance system at 2.5 miles and we never received an advisory or an resolution advisory from traffic alert and collision avoidance system the controller said okay for the 330 and we requested a different runway to avoid more thunderstorms. We landed uneventful. Controllers should not vector airplanes into thunderstorms.
output: Md80 flight crew declared an emergency with approach control in order to fly the heading of their choice to avoid a thunderstorm. An uneventful landing ensued on a runway not aligned with thunderstorms.

input: Our shift hours were changed when the federal aviation administration forced their new work rules on us. They make us start our shift at xb45 now. That means that when the rest of my family is trying to go to bed i should be getting ready for work. However; i just go to work at xa00 and wait 1 hour and 45 minute(s) to start my shift to keep from keeping my family awake. Then i have to stay and work until xj45 when i ante meridiem dead tired and drive home after that! We need 3 people on the shift in order to safely rotate for relief periods. The management at this facility is going to continue operating these dangerous shifts until somebody dies.
output: Mci controller expressed concern regarding mgmnt's change of shift hours and staffing numbers.

input: Making loupe departure sjc. After turn to 120 degree heading first officer put aircraft on autoplt. Used performance mode (advanced cockpit). We had previously been cleared to maintain 250 knot(s) until further advised. Out of 10000 feet/foot aircraft in performance mode began to accelerate to normal performance climb speed performance mode had not been programmed for 250 knot(s) climb speed i caught airspd going through 275 knot(s) disconnected performance mode and the rest of the climb and departure was made at 250 knot(s) in indicated air speed mode. As the new fo's come out of training they use the advanced cockpit modes almost exclusively. (this is because of federal aviation administration insistence in training.) a little experience in plain ole' flying and airplane would be very helpful. Too much reliance on automatic system is going to burn you sooner or later.
output: Airspd deviation on standard instrument departure dep.

input: Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information rptr states he does not understand why he did not have enough fuel for his trip. There were no headwinds; just light winds. He planned to arrive at the airport in about 6 minute(s) when the engine sputtered. He immediately headed for the highway since he knew the area and located it right away even though it was night. He had planned for 3.9 flight hours and ran out of fuel at 3.3 hours he does not use the gauges; just time as his measure. His landing was good and no damage to the aircraft a passing motorist had a cell phone; he called the airport and they brought fuel to him. It took 24.1 gals which is the usable fuel for the c152. The federal aviation administration noticed that his bi-annual flight review had expired just a few days before; second officer he was flying in violation. They indicated they will probably suspend his certificate for 30 days but it will be 6 months before they can get the paperwork completed.
output: Pvt pilot of c152 runs out of fuel during night flight lands on hwy.

input: Pwr was advanced to 'stand-up' (approx 40 percent of n1). Aft cargo door light came on. Power was retarded and we return to the ramp. Door was confirmed locked. Speed of aircraft did not reach over 60 knot(s) no brakes were used to stop the acft.
output: An air carrier mlg crew aborted their takeoff due to a cargo door warning.

input: After landing at zzz ground control directed us to wait on taxiway b short of q1; then turn and stop on taxiway a to wait for our gate. While stopped at the taxiway a location pointing east; with throttles in idle thrust awaiting our gate to open; a loosely wadded roll of clear plastic approximately 15 feet in width and 3 feet in diameter driven by the wind tumbled and rolled (reported surface winds were 290/19) toward the aircraft from our 1 o'clock position across our nose (about 50 feet in front of the nose) toward the left wing. As it passed in front of the aircraft nose; i asked the captain; 'does it look like that foreign object debris will go in the engine?' radio chatter prevented a timely verbal reply; and seconds later; as the captain turned his head to look at the left engine nacelle; the number 1 engine (left nacelle) shuddered and stopped with an amber 'engine fail' indication on the center display panel. The captain remarked that the plastic had just entered the engine intake. The captain then directed me to cut off the number one engine after transferring the electrical bus to the auxiliary power unity which was already running. No fire warnings or high egt indications happened. The engine shuddered and stopped abruptly. While we were executing the engine failure checklist in the quick reference handbook a regional jet behind us reported small flames at the bottom back section of our left engine on ground control radio frequency. We then coordinated with responding fire department; maintenance; operations; and ground control to 1) verify the fire was out; 2) that the jet was safe to move to the gate; and 3) that no evacuation was needed. After getting the needed approval by the fire department and maintenance representatives; we then taxied into parking and deplaned the passengers without further incident. We also pointed out other multiple similar pieces of nearby drifting rubbish to field operations personnel and request that they clean them up before they created another similar hazard.
output: B737 first officer reported the left engine shut down abruptly after ingesting a large piece of plastic foreign object debris while waiting for their gate on a taxiway.

input: We were cleared for takeoff and a turn to a heading of 210 degrees from runway(s) 24l. The first officer was flying. Accelerating through 60 knot(s) i; the capt; noticed an aircraft on a perpendicular taxiway approximately 5000 feet/foot down the runway(s) begin to taxi onto our runway(s) i took control of the aircraft and initiated an abort while announcing to tower we were aborting for an aircraft on our runway(s) we quickly slowed to taxi speed and turned off the runway(s) prior to where the other aircraft was crossing our runway(s) tower was quite apologetic about the situation and insisted they had instructed the other aircraft to hold short of our runway(s) we ran our chklists and the opc; spoke to the passenber and flight attendants; then departed uneventfully for las vegas. Lesson learned; always be vigilant; especially during critical phases of flight humans make mistakes.
output: B737 departure from lax aborts takeoff after observing aircraft crossing downfield.

input: We had been experiencing continuous light turbulence during our descent on the gibbz2 arrival to washington dulles. Air traffic control gave us an initial heads-up that we could expect occasional moderate turbulence. I called the flight attendants and told them to take their jumpseats and that they would have about 5-10 minutes prior to the turbulence beginning. I followed up with a p/a to the passengers and then the turbulence began soon after. We were approximately 1 hour out from iad. The turbulence never let up; so i called the flight attendants and informed them that it did not appear we would be getting a smooth ride the rest of the way in so they should remain at their jumpseats for the duration of the flight. We sent dispatch a message for the moderate turbulence and they concurred that they had already had several reports of turbulence from other aircraft. We had the radar on and we were actively using both the auto mode and manual to get the best picture of the weather we were dealing with. For the most part we were looking at heavy rain. We were following another [company] aircraft on the arrival that was approximately 20 miles in front of us. At 6000 feet we heard a [company] aircraft state they were experiencing hail. Air traffic control never informed us or any of the other aircraft on the radio where that aircraft was. We were actively trying to figure out where the weather that was causing the hail was. The radar was getting a lot of attenuation due to the heavy rain showers. We saw the heavy rain showers about 10 miles ahead and got a turn from air traffic control but we still experienced severe turbulence +/- 200 feet and +/- 40kts and we were also in light hail for a short time. We informed air traffic control and they got us turned onto final approach a short time later. We checked with the flight attendants to make sure they were ok in the back and they reported no injuries; everyone was ok. After arriving at the gate we informed maintenance of the severe turbulence and the encounter with hail. There appeared to be no damage to the aircraft but i left before the technician had completed all of their inspections. I also spoke with dispatch on the phone to give a verbal report of the encounter with severe turbulence.
output: B737 captain reported encountering severe turbulence and hail during arrival into iad.

input: Botched departure out of madrid. After departing runway(s) 36l at mad we did not make the left/right (directions) turn to intercept the 008 degree radial as indicated by page 10-3d. We did parallel the outbound course and at 12 vor and dme (co-located) made the left/right (directions) turn to cnr. We realized our error after the departure when finding the fine print on page 10-3l. Page 10-3l has a note that states for initial clbout procedures refer to charts 10-3 to 10-3d. Page 10-3d had the notes for intercepting the 008 degree radial. I believe this is the only standard instrument departure that i have flown that has referenced another standard instrument departure page. Fatigue also played a part in my overlooking of this note. The night before was spent in a substandard hotel. Around xa00 ante meridiem my room temperature went from around 68 degrees fahrenheit to 90 degrees fahrenheit with the window open my room cooled to 80 degrees fahrenheit the trade off was that now street noise kept me up most of the night. My first officer had the same problem with room temperature many other cabin crew complained of the same problem 2 problems were directly related to our error. One is the small print of the note to refer to another chart. Sleeping conditions. Had we all had a good night's sleep and the fine print printed in bold; i believe this error would not have happened. Please reprint this note in bold on the 10-3l page and change hotel in madrid.
output: B767 crew had track deviation departing lemd.

input: Just prior to touchdown at hto (pwr was at idle and i would place us no more than 5 feet/foot above ground level prior to main gear touchdown). At this point we were committed to land on the 4200 feet/foot length runway(s) from the left/right (directions) corner of my eye; i spotted an object that i had only had enough time to recognize the shape and color as a deer. As quickly as it appeared; it was gone. I was unable to judge the distance of the deer from the aircraft due to the limited time i was given and the need for my attention with the landing rollout on the shorter runway(s) the aircraft showed no ctlability degradation. Because of this; i was uncertain intermediate fix we did in fact contact the deer. The rollout was uneventful and normal. The aircraft after landing chklists were accomplished and all system appeared normal. Our passenber was disembarked and we then inspected for signs of impact. Impact was made with the deer. The contact points were the left/right (directions) main landing gear outboard wheel; left/right (directions) main landing gear door; and left/right (directions) inboard flap fairing. No other contact was observed upon inspection that night or the following morning on the aircraft we then drove to the runway(s) to determine the locale of the deer. The body was found resting approximately 2000 feet/foot down runway(s) 28; left/right (directions) of ctrline approximately 15 feet/foot markings on the animal showed contact on the upper left/right (directions) hindquarter traveling longitudinally along the left/right (directions) side approximately 3/4 of its length. The animal's left/right (directions) rear leg was severed and the body was cut open from the left/right (directions) rear lower inside leg joint to the chest cavity. The leg was later found approximately 200 feet/foot further down runway(s) 28. Isp flight service station specialist and new york approach control were notified of the animal on the runway(s) they subsequently issued a notice to airmen / of air missions for the runway(s) closure. Isp flight service station specialist then notified the airport manager who promptly arrived to remove the carcass from the runway(s) no other restrs to the airport were noted and operations(s) were able to resume thereafter.
output: F900 flight crew strikes deer during touchdown at hto.

input: Accepted a road trip to travel to zzz (a non [company] city with no [company] ops) to replace 4 pobs (portable oxygen bottle) and 1 imk [inflight medical kit]. The replacement parts and my tools were loaded in zzz1 by stores/ramp. I was briefed to go through security and meet the crew at the airplane that was a rescue flight -no revenue passengers. After talking to crew; i was told they were waiting for clearance with a hazmat release to depart zzz1. Upon arrival in zzz; i was greeted by contract maintenance and we retrieved the replacement 4 pobs and imk from the fwd cargo hold. We loaded the parts into the contract maintenance vehicle and he drove me to ramp area where aircraft x was waiting. I replaced and secured the 4 pobs and 1 imk. The pobs and imk were made unserviceable and we packaged the unserviceable parts back into the original packaging and i signed off the write up in the log book and proceeded back to aircraft x (the rescue flight aircraft). The contract mx vendor and i loaded the old parts back into the fwd cargo hold. Aircraft x went on to perform a revenue flight to zzz2 and i was to return on aircraft x reposition with the flight that was stranded in zzz for the previous day's medical emergency diversion. While the captain was performing his pre-flight checks; i informed the captain that the spent pobs and possibly imk in fwd cargo hold are hazmat because of the clearance we had to get when departing zzz1 and that he may need to call and get the same clearance to depart zzz. The captain acknowledged me and said 'thanks; that's good information.' i took my seat in the back and we flew to zzz1 with no interruptions. I was made aware that there was a concern with the way the parts were brought back on [date]. Cause: the pilot in command should have called for the necessary clearance/documentation if there was a need. I assumed that because the pilot continued the flight; there was no issue or that he received the proper clearance. The captain was made aware of the hazmat parts before the entry door was closed and the air stairs pulled from the aircraft. Suggestions: mx is not trained on hazmat requirements; there should be some awareness or training for mx to know what is required. I wasn't sure; so i made sure the pilot was informed - because we had to have clearance when we left zzz1.
output: Technician reported the need of maintenance shipping/handling training when dealing with hazmat requirements.

input: Dsnded to cross 10 mile east of hli at 10000 feet/foot as per atc's restrict, restricted, restriction while leveling at 10000 feet/foot air traffic control inquired intermediate fix we had been cleared to 10000 or 12000 feet/foot we replied; 10000 ft.
output: Questionable assigned alt.

input: After initial taxi from our pushback position facing north; we had to make an abrupt stop to avoid getting too close to an rj taxiing on bravo from our left. The stop resulted in the purser and one other flight attendant getting injured. We were very conscious on our initial taxi of the aircraft parked to our right. Our speed was slow due to concern for jet blast directed back at the concourse. The rj approached from our blind spot on taxiway b from our left. Our initial taxi clearance was 'after the rj on your left; taxi to 32l t10 via alpha; alpha 7; tango.' we had an rj to our left on alpha in sight. The traffic; apparently; was the rj on bravo. The relief pilot saw the threat rj first and alerted 'stop! Stop!' my first thought was that we were going to run over someone or something imminently. The captain stopped the aircraft.
output: B777 first officer describes a near collision with a rj during initial taxi out of the gate. The brakes are applied vigorously by the captain; resulting in two flight attendant injuries.

input: The flight was en route from buffalo to utica. Upon arrival, arrive in the griffis terminal radar service area i was informed that utica was rpting 3/16 or 1/4 mile visibility. However; when i was 10 mile from the airport i didn't see any obstruction to visibility. I asked griffis approach to vector me over the airport about 3 mile out i had visual contact with the landing runway(s) (9/27) even though visibility was still rpted as 1/4 or 3/16. Utica tower was closed; but weather rpting was available. I told griffis that i had the airport and runway(s) in sight. He then cleared me for the contact approach i landed without incident.
output: Plt of an smt atx made a contact approach and landed when the latest weather rpt indicated that the visibility was below instrument flight rules landing minimums.

input: I continue to have very in depth conversations with local maintenance personnel concerning b737-800 thrust reverser problems. This plane had the same thrust reverser (tr) problem as others in our fleet. I requested in the log entry that the item not be signed off until proven the reverser was properly repaired. I explained in detail how this malfunction can be reproduced; as in advancing the throttles without vfr low altitude training routes activation. Bottom line; we have an endemic issue throughout the fleet on; in my estimation; about 10% of our planes in regards to the 737 thrust reversers. I will say again; as i said in my previous report; same problem; same plane. The 737 vfr low altitude training routes system requires 'multiple malfunctions' to allow vfr low altitude training routes deployment in flight. Vfr low altitude training routes deployment in flight i might add; will most likely result in a hull loss. The above described issue is one of the 'required multiple malfunctions' necessary for an in-flight deployment. We are being forced to fly potentially unsafe planes since corporate maintenance managers fail to heed warnings and recommendations by one of their maintenance rated captains.
output: B737-800 captain reports chronic issues with thrust reversers in some aircraft in his company's fleet. The thrust reverser fault light can be made to illuminate and remain so by advancing the thrust lever toward the takeoff position then retarding it to idle.

input: The inbound aircraft arrived with an minimum equipment list on the cockpit door. Our outbound paperwork was prepared with the minimum equipment list for our outbound leg. Maintenance showed up and fixed the door and correctly filled out the logbook removing the minimum equipment list  i was handed back the log book seconds before the gate agent was ready to close the main cabin door. I reviewed the logbook; but forgot the minimum equipment list was still on the dispatch release. We departed and it wasn't till i was reading the paper work for the next leg i realized my mistake of not talking with the dispatcher and removing the minimum equipment list from the release.the procedure of throwing everything at the captain and seeing what he can catch was in place. I missed this paper work mistake.all divisions of this company operate independently. It is up the captain to hunt down and find each 'easter egg' hidden by each independent division of the company. Dispatch/operations/maintenance should work together. After all; it is their airplane all day long. I get it handed to me and have 5 minutes to track each peculiarity.
output: Inter department coordination is cited as contributing to an air carrier departure with inaccurate dispatch papers by a pilot who received his maintenance log in the last minutes before departure.

input: Upon normal landing turbulence caused the plane to bounce causing a propeller strike and other related damage. An air carrier mlg y had just landed and air traffic control sequenced me right in. He was calling my base and final. There was another jet behind me; on final; runway(s) 21l and i think air traffic control rushed me in. I misjudged his (mlg y) touchdown point and got right into the turbulence.
output: Sma suffers propeller strike upon encountering wake turbulence at dtw.

input: I called for a weather briefing and filed an instrument flight rules flight plan at xa00. I drove to the airport and performed a preflt inspection and found no abnormalities. I received automatic terminal information service got my clearance taxied to the run-up area; performed the before takeoff chklist and found no abnormalities. I was cleared for takeoff clbout was very turbulent but smoothed out with altitude i raised the gear after liftoff and then the flaps. There were no abnormalities. During cruise there were no abnormalities. I received automatic terminal information service and was cleared for descent 5 mile out from myr i slowed to 130 knot(s) and extended the gear and verified it was in locked position by looking at the green light on the panel and the indicator on the floor between the seats. 1 mile from the threshold i did my gump checked and verified that the gear was in locked position i slowed the aircraft to 100 knot(s) and then lowered the flaps to full down position over the threshold i slowed the aircraft to 75 knot(s) and i touched down very softly. As soon as the wheels were on the ground the nose dropped abruptly and the aircraft slid to a stop. Tower control asked what had happened and intermediate fix i was ok. I told her i thought the nose gear had collapsed and that i was ok. I turned off the main switch; the strobes; the electric trim switch and i climbed out of the aircraft when i looked back i saw that the entire gear had collapsed and the aircraft was on its belly. The mains were dropping to the ground and the nose gear was in its well and the gear doors closed. The rescue team arrived and i verified the fuel lever was off and the gear switch was down.
output: An sma on landing experienced nose gear and main gear failure. All landing gear indications and warning system were normal prior to touchdown.

input: Prior to departure we called santa monica ground and said we would like to go south over lax. He gave us instructions through the visual flight rules corridor. After our run-up we called smo tower and said we were ready to go; she gave us instructions that seemed to be clrer at the time. Our instruction was to fly to the 'shoreline' and do a left/right (directions) 280 degree turn; etc. We interpreted her instructions to mean we were to follow the shoreline south past lax. While in the 280 degree turn we asked smo tower for a frequency change to approach she said to stay with her that it would be better. Second officer we stayed on smo tower frequency until south of hawthorn. Then asked for a frequency change again. Granted. We contacted socal approach and were told of a possible 'airspace violation.' upon reaching san diego we called the controller and were told we were 200 feet/foot too low and too federal aviation regulation westbound my opinion: the controllers at smo need to be clearer with their departure instructions; especially with people who may not be familiar with the airspace. The clearance should sound the same whether from ground or tower since tower asked us to stay with her; why did she not say we were approaching or in the wrong airspace. We should have not accepted and departed with instructions that we were not 100% sure of. We should have studied our charts better.
output: C182 misunderstood air traffic control clearance and followed the shoreline through the lax terminal control area rather than follow the shoreline route depicted on the chart. Further; rptr gives no indication he was aware of any altitude assignment.

input: Typed in regge intersection instead of reggy. Intxns are within 15-20 miles of each other and along the route of flight even when checkeding the flight plan with the flight management system the names sound alike; are along the route of flight and only adds 20 miles to the flight plan. (the difference seemed acceptable given the variation in arrs and the new arrival, arrive procedures in dca. Dca had instrument meteorological conditions conditions and a south landing was planned.)
output: B757 first officer rpts confusion over similar sounding fix names; regge and reggy; in zob airspace.

input: I accomplished a preflight inspection on the aircraft. I drained fuel out of the three peacock valves; one for each tank. I walked around the aircraft and inspected the aircraft in accordance with a normal preflight inspection. I started the aircraft and called for taxi clearance. I taxied to the run-up area adjacent to runway 13r. I did my pre-take off checks as follows:controls-were all free and correctinstruments were all set for take off.fuel was on and the transfer pump was running.all three tanks were full.trim was set to mid travel.run up was then accomplished. Magneto check showed about 50 revolutions per minute drop at 1700 rpm.accomplished a full throttle check.all checks were satisfactory.since this was my first flight in this airplane; i spent more time than i normally would making a full power check and a second magneto check. When i felt comfortable with the engines performance; i informed the tower i was ready for takeoff. The tower cleared me for take off on runway 13r. I taxied into position and applied about half throttle maybe 1;800 revolutions per minute i l the speed build to get used to the handling of the aircraft. When i was comfortable; i applied full throttle and continued the take off. At 70 mph indicated air speed i pulled back and made a positive break from the ground. The aircraft climbed normally and maintained 70 mph with little back pressure on the yoke. Between 300 and 400 feet i experienced my first power loss. The engine reduced in power to idle with no roughness or backfire. My hand was on the throttle. I reached to the right of the throttle and pushed in the mixture. It was all the way in. I reached to the left and pushed the carb heat in about 1/2 of an inch. The engine immediately regained power; approximately 2-3 seconds after the initial power loss. I thought that had fixed the problem but the engine lost power again. I reported to the tower that i had an engine failure. The tower cleared me to land on any runway. While i was communicating with the tower; i was moving the throttle trying to find a position that the engine would continue to run. The engine would regain power and loose power in 1 to 2 second increments. I also attempted to find a position with the mixture and carb heat that would keep the engine running at a steady revolutions per minute at this point; i prepared for a forced landing. I chose a strip of land to my left as my emergency landing spot but was unsure if i could make a landing there. As i lined up on the field; i evaluated my altitude and position. Still having enough altitude and airspeed; i made the decision to land on the airport property. As i got closer to the airport the closest possible landing was runway 31r. I avoided the barricades on the runway and landed without incident. The engine continued to run after i came to a stop. I taxied the aircraft to the hangar under its own power.
output: The pilot of an ercoupe 415 experienced a loss of engine power after takeoff. He was able to perform a landing on a closed runway with intermittent engine power available.

input: Inbound flight attendants informed us a heroin addict had urinated; vomited; and defecated all in the back galley and aft lavatory. They had deviated to zzz enroute to remove passenger. I am not sure how much clean-up was done by flight attendants and/or staff in zzz. When we got the plane; the cleaners were just finishing up. I don't think they were informed that the bathrooms needed a thorough cleaning and that it was bodily fluid. This is a hazard to their health and our health as well; as it doesn't ensure proper clean-up. We had to call them back to clean floor in galley. We weren't satisfied with clean-up but knew air carrier would do nothing about it. So we were forced to go ahead with the boarding. We personally did not use the facilities in the aft galley. I would like to know if there is a specific procedure for clean-up of feces; vomit; and urine. Shouldn't some sort of hazmat crew be dispatched?
output: Cabin attendant reports inadequate cleaning of bodily fluids left on board by a passenger from the previous flight.

input: During taxi before takeoff the left/right (directions) eec light illuminated with associated engine indicating and crew alerting system message. The capt and i complied with the procedure and turned off both eec's. As i monitored tower frequency the capt; relief pilot and i consulted the minimum equipment list mel 73-1a gave the capt 1 of 2 options: to continue the flight and he elected that option. We placarded the eec according to company procedures despite the provision in that minimum equipment list that no prior notification to dispatch was required; the capt chose to inform dispatch as an added precaution. Through zzz operations(s) we passed a message to dispatch with the details of the capt's decision. The message passed back to us from dispatch through zzz operations(s) was that the dispatcher agreed with the capt's decision and that; although the dispatcher appreciated the message; there was no requirement to have notified dispatch. We proceeded to zzz1 without incident. Once at zzz1; operations(s) informed us that maintenance had decided that the return flight would be canceled and that we would ferry the airplane back to zzz under federal aviation regulation part 91.
output: A b757-200 was dispatched overwater in non compliance with the left/right (directions) eec inoperative and deferred.

input: Being vectored to final approach runway(s) 12l msp at 4000 feet/foot received a final vector to intercept runway(s) 12l localizer and maintain 4000 feet/foot until established; then cleared for the instrument landing system runway(s) 12l msp. Capt engaged the instrument landing system guidance portion of the instrument landing system by arming the approach with the approach button. The engs immediately spooled up and climbed to 5000 feet/foot before he could turn off the autoplt and manually maneuver back to 4000 feet/foot we advised air traffic control that the aircraft had momentarily climbed to 5000 feet/foot approach controller said 'no prob.' we debriefed afterwards and concluded that the flight guidance unit was trying to capture the glideslope from below by flying up to it to intercept. We are further investigating to find out why it did this. This is not normal. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr indicated that this is a known problem with the software; and that his company has issued a bulletin to correct with a new procedure the procedure recommends that the approach not be armed until inside 18 mile from the runway(s) his company is working with the manufacturer; in the meantime; to see intermediate fix the software can be corrected.
output: An airbus a319 intercepting the glideslope from below left/right (directions) assigned altitude climbing 1000 feet/foot when autoflt was armed for the apch.

input: Several hours after takeoff from fco dispatch informed me that the aircraft was over maximum ramp weight and exceeded maximum takeoff weight due to an error in calculating weight of cargo. Load closeout showed weight slightly under plan and cargo weight slightly under plan; making actual takeoff weight shown on load closeout to be approximately 10000 pounds under maximum takeoff weight based on information provided en route aircraft weighed 12320 pounds more than the load closeout showed; exceeding maximum takeoff weight by 2545 pounds and exceeding maximum ramp weight by 2995 pounds i requested an off-load audit at ord. This meant that identify numbers on cargo containers were verified against what was supposed to be on the aircraft position of containers within the cargo compartments was also verified. I ante meridiem not totally sure intermediate fix we were actually overwt or not. Obviously somebody has to be correct and somebody made an error on the weight calculation; but load closeout numbers were close to those on the plan. What i would like to know is: how much did the cargo actually weigh?
output: A b767 flight crew receive word from dispatch while en route that the takeoff was overwt due to a calculation error.

input: I was the pilot flying doing the bankr2 standard terminal arrival route into clt. Because of the very steep descent profile and little distance to make altitude restrictions; the aircraft increased speed beyond published speed restriction of 250 knots after debbt. In trying to make restriction; i did not inform the pilot not flying to tell air traffic control of our inability to do both; slow and make altitude restriction. The bankr2 standard terminal arrival route is poorly designed and very difficult for aircraft to fly as published in vertical navigation the altitude restrictions are too many and varied; short distances between waypoints and unrealistic speed restrictions. We were given a more achievable standard terminal arrival route initially and then offered the bankr2. I should have looked at it carefully and seen the possibility of difficulty making the restrictions. Won't do this standard terminal arrival route again in its present form.
output: B737 pilot reported their aircraft was unable to meet altitude and speed restrictions published on the clt bankr2 star.

input: During preflt at bwi one morning i noticed the aircraft was covered with snow on wings; fuselage; and engine i coordinated with operations(s) for deice and was told that 'due to manpower shortages they would deice at the gate and not in the pad as usual.' after the passenber were loaded and door shut i noticed the ground personnel working with the deice truck. This went on for approximately 10 minute(s) as we were now past departure time i called operations(s) and inquired only to be told 'they were having probs.' i later noticed the truck was gone and assumed they had started deicing which they had with no communications with the cockpit to confirm configured for deice which is required by standard operating procedure after approximately 10 minute(s) they finally made contact saying you're all done. Type of solution; mix and start time. I had noticed that they had not done any of the fuselage because i had heard no sound or seen fluid running over the cockpit. I asked intermediate fix he had done the fuselage and he said no. I asked intermediate fix there was snow on it and he said yes but it looks like it's starting to melt. I then stated that they were not all done as he said and the whole airplane needed to be free of all adhering snow. All i got was ok. I then called operations(s) to inquire about the quality of the deicing to which he stated he would have to call the crew back to the plane. I did not even know they left. I then stated that this deice job was in clear violation of far's; company standard operating procedure and dangerous. I also stated i would require the jetway returned and the end of deice to confirm the airplane free of snow as i did not the recreational uas safety test the quality of the crew as they had already tried to give me a plane covered in frozen snow. When the deice was completed i did go and visually checked the status of the plane and determined it to be free of snow. I talked to the on duty supervisor and explained the situation and how dangerous it was to tell us a plane is clean when indeed it is not. I also explained it was in clear violation of federal aviation regulations and standard operating procedure he stated he would look into it and assured it would never happen again. I ante meridiem concerned about the quality of training of ground personnel responsible for passing me vital information of a plane which is incorrect and flat out dangerous.
output: Deicing procedures cause a b757 capt to call for a redo as well as make a personal inspection of the aircraft to make sure his aircraft was ready for flt.

input: During climb after leveling at fl290; zoa cleared us to climb to fl330. We put fl330 in the altitude window; both pilots confirmed it. The first officer checkeded the vertical navigation page to confirm that our weight was compatible with fl330. Pilot flying pressed the button and we climbed to fl330. We were given a frequency change to 134.450 (freqs may be reversed). We checkeded in and after a few seconds the controller questioned our altitude we told him we were at fl330 and had been cleared to go there. He said we should have been at fl290 and gave us a turn and a descent we said the previous controller had cleared us to fl330. He said the previous controller had cleared us to fl290. At this point the controller seemed a little uncomfortable and gave us a climb to fl330. We were heavy (approx 600000 lbs) and the climb was understandably slow. He asked us to increase our climb rate twice (i think). We told him we were heavy and were doing the best we could. We returned to fl330 and that was the end of it. I immediately sent a message to dispatch and asked the air traffic control coordinator to checked with oakland to see what happened. Dispatch sent us a message saying that there had been no loss of separation or any alarms. I don't believe this was our problem we didn't just dream up a clearance to fl330. There was no cockpit conversation going on at this point; no distractions whatsoever. All procedures were followed perfectly; it's just that both of us feel strongly that we heard and read back fl330.
output: A b777 flight crew thought they received a clearance to fl330; but air route traffic control center thought it was only to fl290.

input: This is an operator/paperwork issue. The outer pane of the aircraft was discovered to have cracked. A bombardier engineer was dispatched to the aircraft and applied 'speed tape' to the affected area for flight to the aircraft's home base for repair. The aircraft was flown at 250 knot(s) 26;000 feet/foot with a higher cabin to lower the pressure. Both inner and middle pane was intact and 100%. The windshield heat was functional. The engineer; director of maintenance; and operator all stated that the outer pane is not structural; not affected by the minimum equipment list in any way; shape or form (only inner and middle panes) and flyable with [speed] tape to the home base for repair. I asked if a ferry permit was needed and told without question that it was definitely not. The director of the company also stated that the designated airworthiness representative (dar) assigned as oversight to the operation in our departure airport; stated no [ferry] permit was required.being that it was a weekend; i tried to ascertain as much information as possible to verify this. I know the bombardier challenger series have windshield issues similar to the global express bd-700 series aircraft and therefore understood the reasoning and similarity considering the manufacturer. The director of maintenance (dom) has extensive experience with challenger and global express aircraft and therefore i have little doubt in his knowledge. My problem as a pilot and not an airframe and powerplant (a&p) technician; is that not all information is available either online; hotline; or elsewhere to assist a pilot in situations like this. I put my trust in those who do specialize in this area; but sometimes get the feeling that they are not being truthful with myself in this case; or the crews to generalize. Deliberately placing me or a crew in harms way would be reckless on his part.
output: First officer reports that pilots do not have any place or resource to go to get unbiased information about airworthiness concerns of their aircraft. An outer pane of a captain's forward windshield was found cracked on their bbd-700 aircraft; speed tape was applied. An engineer; the director of maintenance (dom); director of operations and designated airworthiness representative (dar) ok'd the aircraft to be flown to home base without any technical data.

input: We were instructed to turn left to 090 and climb and maintain 3000. Upon reaching 3000 departure informed us we were at 3300 feet/foot in the meridian there are three drains on the pilot side and two drains on the co-pilot side near the floor. These must be drained before every flight on the ground. In doing so a foreign object entered one or more of the drains. As we pressurized; it caused an error of 180 ft+/-;and a 40kt+/- error in indicated air speed we used the stand-by altimeter to continue the flight. We took the aircraft to a maintenance facility who corrected the problem. I don't know how to prevent this; the service center said it is a problem with some meridians. I suppose it is piper's problem. I am just glad there is a stand-by system.
output: A pa46t pilot reported erroneous airspeed and altimeter readings apparently caused by a foreign object in the pitot drain.

input: I had a flight to take 6 people to view bears at frazer lake. There is a fish weir there; and bears congregate by it to catch salmon. This lake is in the kodiak national wildlife refuge. Prior to the flight i looked for information on flying in the refuge; and found none in the alaska supplement or aeronautical information manual i had been told by the owner of the air carrier that i fly for that 'they' (alaska fish and game; who have fish biologists stationed at the weir) like pilots to stay 1000 feet/foot mean sea level above the weir intermediate fix fltseeing. When i got to the lake; the wind was blowing directly towards the river about 15 knot(s) it was gusty and white capping. I made an approach on a downwind about 1500 feet/foot mean sea level over the weir (the lake is about 400 feet/foot msl). Due to the winds and my load (6 passenber -- the beaver holds 7 passenber total); i elected to land into the wind; second officer my final approach was over the weir and river. After i landed and offloaded my passenber i started wondering intermediate fix it had actually been ok to come in over the river for the landing i had not found anything in writing that said it wasn't; and had seen the owner of the company i fly for make the same type of approach and landing the day before. I asked one of the fish biologists intermediate fix it was ok to make that type of approach when the wind was blowing from that direction; and did it bother the bears? He said yes; it was ok to land like that; and that it wouldn't bother the bears. At this point; i'm not sure intermediate fix there was anything inappropriate about landing over the river; but at the time with the conditions at the lake; it seemed like the safest thing to do. It might be nice intermediate fix the alaska supplement addressed the kodiak national wildlife refuge; as it does address other wildlife refuges in the state. There was no information about staying above 2000 feet/foot in wildlife areas; but nothing about landing in the areas; except you had to land in rivers; lakes; and airstrips that were approved.
output: Plt of a dehavilland beaver dhc2 on floats made visual approach over the weir during landing on frazer lake inside the kodiak national wildlife refuge. Rptr was concerned that it may not have been in compliance with the special wildlife refuge rules to not go lower than 1000 feet/foot over the weir when sightseeing.

input: I was training on local control. Aircraft x landed; i told them to turn left on a taxiway and contact ground. Aircraft y was cleared to land and on a short final for an intersecting runway. Ground control asked for a crossing. I said hold short. Ground told aircraft x to cross the runway. My trainer reacted quickly and yelled hold short to ground control. At this time aircraft y had touched down and there was no way to send him around. Ground quickly told aircraft x to stop and hold short of the runway. Aircraft x continued his crossing until realizing he needed to get off the runway. He made a 180 degree turn back; to hold short of 21 at the taxiway.
output: A tower controller reported the ground controller allowed an aircraft to enter a runway at the same time another aircraft was landing.

input: My direction of travel was sw (vfr). I was cleared for takeoff with left/right (directions) turn out approved. No traffic was provided by tower after turning crosswind at about 300 feet/foot above ground level and then continuing turn toward my sw heading i saw a cessna almost directly overhead on a north heading and about 250 feet/foot above me. I leveled out and then after clearing the other aircraft began to resume climb just as i was about to inform the tower the other aircraft rpted the event to tower stating that the diamond (me) passed within '50 yds.' tower then asked me intermediate fix i had the cessna traffic which of course i then had. I rpted back that i had the traffic i continued monitoring the tower frequency and a couple of minute(s) later the cessna made a further comment to the tower that 'that was too close.' the tower rpted back to him that the diamond had the traffic although true after the event; it was not true at the time of the event.
output: A da40 pilot reported having an near midair collision with a cessna shortly after takeoff from ryy.

input: Oakland center had just given us clearance to descend to 11000 feet/foot slow to 250 knot(s) after slowing we descended and leveled at 11000. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii alert traffic tfc followed by descend dsnd. A quick glance at the cathode ray tube showed an aircraft superimposing itself on us. A flick of the autoplt and a push on the yoke started our descent the coplt called approach and told them we were descending on a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory approach said maintain 11000. Aircraft 12 o'clock 3 mile opposite direction. Approach also told us of an aircraft passing 1000 feet/foot above us on the same arrival, arrive going to sjc; an mlg. The aircraft spotted at this time passing us 1000 feet/foot above at about 300 plus knot(s) an ease back to 11000 feet/foot was simultaneously made. While all of this was transpiring total loss of altitude 60-100 feet/foot estimated. It appears that the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii did its job but not in the manner it is programmed to do. The mlg was fast descending from altitude to 12000 in accordance with his clearance his speed was not slowed as ours was in view of the fact that he was going to an airport 30 mile further away. His rate of descent and speed triggered our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii to interpret a threat to us. Company written policy is to obey the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii this could have caused a mid air intermediate fix weather had been instrument flight rules the aircraft at 12 o'clock 3 mile would have been the unsuspecting recipient of a wind screen full of wdb. Traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii is a step in the right direction but not reliable enough to be blindly obeyed. Situational awareness is a must. The mark 8 mode 1 eyeball/brain is still the best mid air prevention.
output: Flc of wdb had traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii resolution advisory descend and started descent advising approach controller who instructed to maintain altitude account traffic 1000 feet/foot below opposite direction. Intruder was high descent mlg to 1000 feet/foot above the wdb flt.

input: Plt failure to follow air traffic control instruction. Flying at fl350 following several air traffic control vectors for climb from mdw; we leveled at fl350. A line of thunderstorms were along and north of our route and our vision was obstructed by cirrus and some 'blow-off' from thunderstorms south of our route we asked for climb to fl390. Center gave us a 'turn left/right (directions) 10 degrees climb to fl390; contact chicago on 1xx.xx.' coplt read back 'r turn 10 degs;' and the balance i set in a 10 degree left/right (directions) turn (s of track). When coplt contacted next controller he said; 'acft x leaving fl350 for fl390 heading 275 degs.' new controller said 'what? What is your heading?' coplt replied we set in wrong heading. I began turning 20 degrees left/right (directions) (n of track). Controller turned an air carrier y flight 10 degrees left/right (directions) and canceled his descent clearance then confirmed our new heading and added additional 10 degrees left/right (directions) then changed our climb limit to fl370. After air carrier y passed 8-10 mile south of us we were cleared to fl390. This was my first trip with one of our newly hired pilots and was the third leg of a 2 day trip. He thought i had heard something other than he had; but had read back the left/right (directions) turn; and i had heard 'r turn 10 degs' and had wanted to be south of course; because of weather second officer 10 degrees left/right (directions) became 10 degrees south away from weather he was also just about to question me when the controller asked 'what...' the cl604 operates on 1/2 bank function above fl315/fl320 by default; thus heading changes are slower than expected by the controller (supposition on my part) and result in a delay in course/track change. I believe my actions would have been challenged earlier with an established crew member; however my newer coplt was formulating a tactful questioning of my error.
output: Cl60 crew had a track deviation in zau class a.

input: While parking we noticed foreign object debris in the gate safety zone. We had an airplane swap; and when we went to that gate we noticed lots of foreign object debris in and around the safety zone. While observing the activities on the flight line; we observed that ramp agents did not conduct a foreign object debris walkdown before the departing aircraft was pushed off the gate; nor did the ramp agents conduct a foreign object debris walkdown before our new aircraft pulled in. I noticed foreign object debris scattered throughout the safety zone; so i entered the safety zone after the aircraft pulled out and before the next aircraft pulled in and picked up as much foreign object debris as i could in about 60 seconds. I picked up the following foreign object debris as the ramp agents stood around watching me: 1 zipper pull with nylon strap; 3 zipper pulls; 2 baggage emblems; 1 metal paper clip; 1 baggage key; 1 metal washer; 3 black pieces of plastic; 3 red stir sticks; and 3 paper baggage tags. Among the las ramp agents; there seemed to be no interest or any sense of urgency to pick up any of the foreign object debris in the safety zone or the large amount of trash around the safety zone. I observed at least one individual sitting with his feet propped up on the baggage tug dashboard while listening to his mp3 or cell phone while i was out picking up foreign object debris and trash. The station manager needs to take responsibility for ensuring a foreign object debris free environment on the flight line. Please help us to prevent ingesting foreign object debris in our engines by giving the foreign object debris program some additional emphasis.
output: Air carrier captain laments the large amount of foreign object debris found under and around his aircraft during preflight.

input: Inbnd push for ord. All traffic from westbound rted over bdf. Flow control nonexistent. Supervisor was constantly and loudly intervening in traffic situation. Weather had closed off the bdf 1 arrival, arrive route 1 aircraft was not given holding instructions. This was missed by handoff radar and manual controller aircraft entered adjacent sector w/o pointout. The handoff controller had cancelled the data block. The radar failed to notice it. Corrective action should require the handoff not to cancel data block until holding instructions are given!
output: Acr entered adjacent controller airspace without handoff.

input: Apparent inaccurate position rpting on the part of the conflicting aircraft to spn tower also; i suspect that the conflicting acft's transponder was inappropriately armed in order to affect traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii detection by our aircraft conflicting aircraft was asked its position by spn tower '5.8 dme' was the reply; as i recall. We were arriving at 6 vor and dme (co-located) my first officer then was the first of us to get a visual on other aircraft the second officer was next to get a visual on him. Conflicting aircraft was at co-alt and converging. A left/right (directions) turn away from the convergence was initiated by our flight i was trying to get traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii advisory of the conflicting aircraft our traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii was properly armed in ta/ra mode. Weather radar was being used by us. I did get a primary target on the screen without an resolution advisory or a traffic advisory by this time i had a good visual contact with converging aircraft a diverging condition had by this time been established. Our approach landing and parking was then routinely completed. Conflicting aircraft made a r-hand 360 degree turn in order to complete his approach and landing as #2. Our flight was properly cleared for an instrument apch.
output: On instrument approach air carrier has ltss.

input: The flight to cyhm was turbulent and we never made it to the planned cruising altitude due to turbulence. The arrival weather was approximately a 300 ft ceiling and around 4000 meters visibility and winds gusting from 25-30 knots at approximately 80-90 degrees off of runway heading. I was sitting in the jumpseat as an additional crewmember for the flight. The conditions in the cockpit were loud and i was unable to hear much of what was being said between the pilot flying and the pilot monitoring. I knew the planned approach was the instrument landing system to runway 12. I did not hear much of the brief due to the noise in the aircraft. As we proceeded into the terminal area; we were cleared to the apgom fix and cleared for the instrument landing system again; i did not hear much of what was being said cross-cockpit between the post meridiem and the pilot flying when given the approach clearance. I did catch that the pilot flying wanted to make sure that the aircraft was stable for the approach as early as possible. I wholly agreed with this philosophy due to conditions at the field. The approach was flown to a successful landing. After the fact i was informed by the line check airman that the aircraft descended to 2200 ft (the min altitude for the no-pt (no procedure turn) routing) when it should have been at 2700 ft (the minimum safe altitude for the sector we approached from and/or the minimum altitude for the procedure turn routing). The no-pt routing minimum altitude of 2200 ft is confusing when the minimum safe altitude is 2700 ft. Additionally; the apgom fix is depicted on the plan view of the approach plate; but not the profile view; making it difficult to determine what the minimum altitude is for that fix when cleared direct versus given the no-pt routing. The cat-ii instrument landing system plate shows a no-pt routing from the same fix; but with a minimum altitude of 2700 ft. The approach plate is ambiguous for what altitude should be maintained when cleared to the apgom fix and the approach.
output: Air carrier relief pilot reported descending to 2200 feet after being cleared for the cyhm instrument landing system runway 12 direct apgom. Pilot cited confusion as to the allowable minimum no procedure turn (nopt) altitude and noted a disparity between the instrument landing system runway 12 nopt (2200 feet) and instrument landing system clear air turbulence ii runway 12 nopt (2700 feet) altitudes.

input: I was relieving the radar controller at the gea sector. The situation included deviating aircraft in the vicinity of aco-cxr vor's. At the time i was sitting down; aircraft x was already given a temporary altitude of fl360 and was requesting fl370. Aircraft x had in his fourth line of the data block dr/slt and i was told that he was deviating right; and slt when able; and that i would be able to climb him shortly because he had traffic at fl370 off his left going direct hoxie; which should result in divergence. At that time i was also receiving a hand off from the fkl sector on an aircraft at fl360 that was head-on with aircraft x. Now here is where the problem came in; aircraft x was actually deviating left of direct slt and i was unable to climb him because of the fl370 traffic off to his left. So i asked that traffic if it could turn to the left and it could not due to weather. I also questioned aircraft x about why he was going left when he had told the previous controller that he was deviating right. In the mean time; i had my d-side point-out aircraft x to the lor sector; down to fl350. At this stage; aircraft x explained to me that when he first started to deviate to the right his route was djb-cxr-slt and that the previous controller had given him approval and slt when able. His deviating right of djb was actually left of going direct slt which ended up putting him on a converging path with the aircraft at fl370 instead of diverging. Now i had fl350 and i issue it to aircraft x and go about taking care of some things because there are a few other aircraft on frequency that are deviating and wanting higher. When i got back to aircraft x he was only out of fl358 and i told him to expedite to fl250; realizing what i was saying; i came back and correct myself and stated fl350. He responded that he was descending and would remain on that heading. I took care of a few other things and came back to aircraft x and told him to go direct slt and contact cle center. Shortly after it was brought to my attention that aircraft x was going through fl350; at that time the fkl controller was calling me about something else and i said make sure that aircraft x was stopping at fl350 and not going to fl250. They where able to stop him and he ended up leveling at fl310. Recommendation: there is a communication problem here that needs to be clarified on the part of the controller; when it comes to deviating aircraft. In most situations; when a aircraft deviates and then is given direct further downstream there is not a issue because the deviating will be in the same direction; but in this case it was not right of direct slt but left of direct slt. I can see two solutions; one is to enter that the aircraft is deviating and not whether it is left or right. Another would be for the controller to question the pilot as to how far the deviating is going to be when giving direct. Asking the pilot why he was left of course instead of right did take up time and could of been resolved later; the information was helpful for later situations but was not needed at that time. This situation could have had a tracker; at least for a little while; but we haven't been using trackers as much as in the past and this was unusual situation. The confusion led to the miscommunication of the altitude and thus the airspace violation.
output: Zob controller described an airspace infraction during multiple weather deviation events and less than clear communications with adjacent sectors.

input: We had a maintenance discrepancy at the gate involving the emergency brake system. Maintenance said that the system was normal after consulting with their manual. Even though the discrepancy was signed off and we were legal to depart; our system knowledge made us feel that a problem still existed. When we arrived at our destination the captain advised the new crew of our write-up. They contacted maintenance for a consultation and it was subsequently determined that a problem did in fact exist and remedial action was taken. Even though we were in doubt about the initial maintenance determination; we trusted their interpretation of their manual and the sign-off of the discrepancy. The possibility certainly existed that there was something we didn't fully understand that their manual covered. Additionally; we were aware that some pilots had been disciplined by the company regarding write-ups; which the company felt were frivolous. I personally think that this could have been in the back of our minds since we had already taken a delay and going against maintenance and investigating further would have significantly increased the delay and; if we were wrong; subjected us to possibly the same fate.
output: A b737-700 first officer reported departing on a flight with a mechanical issue that had been improperly documented by maintenance.

input: This center of gravity violation occurred; i believe; as a result of basic confusion. The general consensus is that the acft's out of center of gravity condition resulted when ground personnel confused load ctl's initial instruction to move 1 passenber forward; and communicated this to the cabin crew as needing to move 1 passenber aft. The flight crew discovered that the flight was tail heavy when rotation occurred with uncharacteristically light control pressures. I became aware of this particular flight almost before our turnover had been completed. The pilot in command was on the radio; asking for a verification of his fuel load. I had to look this up; as his release had been prepared by the dispatcher i was relieving. Shortly after that; the pilot in command called again; informing me something to the effect he had no passenber in zone 1; and 6 passenber in zone 2. I wrote this down; and gave the slip to the load controller responsible for the flight who was swamped with other loading issues at that time. Another dispatcher pointed out to me that the flight was airborne; adding a whole additional dimension to the urgency of this situation on advice of load control i instructed the flight crew to recount the passenber on board; row by row; and get the result back to us. Initially; it didn't match the 'final' numbers we had in our computer. The crew only rpted to row 10; second officer we needed to prompt them to rpt the passenber seated in row 11. Initially; they had rpted 2 people in that zone; but there was an infant in a child seat; which we count as a 1/2 weight in our federal aviation administration approved loading procedure load control using company-supplied software; determined that moving one of the adults from row 11 to row 1 would resolve the out-of-bal condition. The aircraft landed without incident; and a bag audit revealed a further loading discrepancy: the load manifest documentation was off by 2 bags. Copies of the original bag card; computer display; cabin count; and audit results were faxed to operations(s) assembled; and handed over to the duty manager while this incident was itself resolved without any particularly adverse consequences; during and immediately after its occurrence; a number of concerns emerged: 1) a conflict was revealed between acceptable mac % numbers as generated by our weight and balance software; and the limitations cited in the aom (a control document). 2) only the takeoff mac % is calculated or displayed by the computer -- not the landing mac %. The sf340 can burn out of center of gravity en route 3) no one seemed to be able to account for the differences between computed mac % limits and the aom's limits; or seemed to know which would take precedence: not the chief pilot on duty; nor either dispatch supervisor nor the duty manager nor any of the personnel on duty in maintenance control 4) no one seemed to be confident regarding any procedure for documenting this occurrence; or where a prescribed procedure might be found. 5) both the pilot in command and i became fixated; for a period of time during which the aircraft was still aloft; with the 'bureaucratic' issues raised by the out of center of gravity condition and had to be 'coached' to concentrate on flying the airplane. 6) our company's new fuel policy -- with its emphasis on carrying only the fuel strictly necessary for regulatory compliance -- appears to heighten flight crew anxiety; even in sits where the actual fuel on board is quite sufficient for extensive holding or flight to distant alternates (and; as a result; clear focus on incipient emergencies may be harder to achieve). 7) fear of being 'violated' may motivate some flight crew members to become preoccupied with potential disciplinary consequences when the appropriate concern should be with getting the aircraft safely on the ground 8) crm/drm can break down in the face of conflicts among flight crew agendas; company policies; goals; and objectives; and safety of flight i believe i was deficient in failing to recognize that the aircraft was aloft from the outset. All i would have had to do was point and click on a couple of menus; and i could have 'located' the flight almost instantly. A heightened awareness of the acft's phase of flight fuel on board (in mins); and the current conditions (including crash fire rescue equipment status) at the destination airport would have undoubtedly contributed to a more rational (and appropriate) prioritization of effort on my part. No one would deliberately risk a replay of the earlier aft center of gravity accident; and yet these 'near miss' weight and balance problems continue to plague our op.
output: Dispatcher of sf340 learns a flight is airborne with an illegal center of gravity and is concerned that repeated weight and balance anomalies at his air carrier may prove hazardous.

input: Preflted aircraft normally for first flight of the day. Station was late with paperwork; there was a catering issue; and we were hurrying to push on time. During pushback as we started engine #1; received an electronic centralized aircraft monitoring -- brake: antiskid nosewheel steering fault with the action 'brakes; limit to 1000 psi.' by this time we had reached the taxiway and the tug driver asked us to set brakes. Capt set brakes and advised the driver to remain on the headset. I checkeded the quick reference handbook abnormal and emergency procedures noted nothing pertinent. Capt suggested i checked the computer reset section; which i did. Located a small box simply called 'bscu' with a reference to fom. Looked up this section; it instructed us to reset the antiskid nosewheel switch. We did this; with no effect. There is a note in this flight manual section regarding circuit breakers; but the message this note referenced was not the message we had. It mentions 'brake: bscu 1(2) fault or system 1(2) fault' only. Our message did not match this; second officer i told the capt there was nothing else to do. We were blocking an active taxiway with an aircraft behind us; and the capt elected to have the tug pull us back in to the gate. A mechanic met the aircraft and; after conferring with maintenance control discovered 4 circuit breakers out on the aft breaker panel. Row mach number above the jumpseat. They were labeled 'brake system #1 and system #2 indicator and control.' once the breakers were reset; the fault cleared and the bite tests were good. Mechanic signed the book; and we departed; rest of flight was normal. Because maintenance was performed on the aircraft overnight; it seems likely that the mechanic who did the daily checked left these 4 breakers in the pulled position. I do not believe they 'popped.' this means that both the capt and i must have missed them during our cockpit preparation. Although not any excuse; there were a couple of factors that 'helped' this to occur. 1) the paper was late to the aircraft and we were feeling rushed. In addition; a few minute(s) prior to scheduled push; the flight attendant informed us of a catering issue; second officer we waited for that to be resolved before pushing a few minute(s) late. During this time we were working quickly and probably did not pay close enough attention to the circuit breaker panel on preflt. 2) the 4 circuit breakers in question are grouped together on the bottom row of the aft panel. There is a collared breaker immediately to the left/right (directions) and very close to the left/right (directions) of these breakers. There are additional collared breakers in the vicinity. Most of the collars on these breakers are white; which makes it difficult to see the white band on the pulled breakers -- especially in the dark; surrounded by other breakers. 3) the bscu reset procedure is incomplete; and difficult to find. You have to figure out it is a bscu problem find it in the quick reference handbook then refer to the flight manual which doesn't reference the exact message we had displayed. It then says that you 'can' try resetting breakers in certain cases; but doesn't say how to do that; which breakers to reset; or where they are. Obviously; we need to be more careful and pay more attention while preflting the circuit breaker panels. Beyond that; i suggest we change the color of the large collars on unused breakers to black. Thus; any white bands on popped or pulled breakers would be the only white on the panel; and would be very obvious -- even in the dark. That aft breaker panel is a mish-mash of pulled breakers; collars; empty spots; and other stuff; and can be difficult to properly preflt. In addition; the section on bscu resets could be modified to contain a more complete list of messages that could be generated by this fault; and where the breakers are to reset it.
output: A320 crew receives ecam--brake: anti skid national weather service fault during push back. Maintenance discovers 4 circuit breakers in a row had been left out by mechanics doing routine maintenance.

input: The unmanned aerial vehicle began a transit toward its home base due to rapidly deteriorating weather conditions in the vicinity of airport. I requested and was cleared into the adjacent operating areas at fl230 while transiting westbound. Crossing from adjacent areas; i requested clearance into the restricted area from center. Center stated that they would advise approach of our intentions. We remained with center while we transited into and loitered in the operating area. The recovery aircrew at the destination advised us that they would be unable to talk to center from their ground control station and requested we switch to destination airport approach so they could regain control of the aircraft. At that time i requested a handover to approach from center; on the same frequency i previously requested clearance into the restricted area; and was cleared to switch to approach from center. At that time we immediately switched to approach and checked in. The controller asked our intentions and i stated that the destination airport controllers would be regaining control of the unmanned aerial vehicle and that they would be requesting a recovery to its home base. Immediately following that call i passed the aircraft control over to the destination flight crew and they checked in with approach; who was querying the destination flight crew about our handover from center. Following the flight i spoke with a tower controller via telephone and relayed the above events.
output: A mq-9 pilot reported communications difficulties while attempting to transfer air traffic control control of the unmanned aerial vehicle to the final approach crew.

input: The airport arrival, arrive rate at las was decided to be 45 degrees based on 2 airlines telling the terminal radar approach control facility that their aircraft would land on runway(s) 1r (6000 ft) based on nw wind. Our big arrival, arrive push is always at xa00. When we started our push; we had aircraft taking runway(s) 1r with no problems after 20 minute(s) or second officer we had aircraft refusing to land on runway(s) 1r; which called for a glideslope and put zla into holding (all fixes). When the final controller is busy; he/she can't play 20 questions with every aircraft and safely move air traffic i believe the situation would've gotten out of control very fast intermediate fix not for the ground stop and holding. Airlines want the airport arrival, arrive rate high; then don't want to hold when things go bad. We stayed very busy for 2 hours and it didn't have to be complicated.
