As a traffic management coordinator; i can only base an airport arrival, arrive rate on information at hand and what aircraft tell me what they will or won't do. Changing the game plan in the middle of an arrival, arrive rush is bad for everyone and can be dangerous.
output: L30 traffic management coordinator expressed frustration regarding the differences between company commitments and pilot preferences in runway(s) acceptance practices.

input: Atl approach's to practice of 'voluntary' follow the preceding traffic visual approachs is once again reaching an obsessive level. In marginal conditions due to virga and sun angle; air traffic control was nearly demanding aircraft call preceding traffic in sight. In our case; they vectored us on a 90 degree angle to final and kept calling out traffic for us to call in sight second officer they could give us the visual. Conditions were marginal to call traffic but ok to call field; which we did. Air traffic control would not clear us for visual approach calling field in sight. He then sarcastically said; 'you can't see that aircraft 3 mile ahead?' as we passed through the ctrline and toward parallel traffic on approachs to runway(s) 27l. We again called field and; visibility getting better; called traffic finally cleared for visual. Kicked off autoplt; manually maneuvered aircraft back to ctrline. When air traffic control asked us about overshooting and we told him he didn't clear us to intercept; he told us he thought he had. Intermediate fix the wake turbulence doesn't kill us; the obsession to call traffic almost light emitting diode to a midair.
output: B757 pilot is concerned with visual approach applications by a80 ctlrs.

input: Ladd aaf changed their runway(s) numbers; but the published approachs will not be updated until several days later. 3 approachs are impacted. Controllers have been directed to continue clearing aircraft for the approachs as published and to the old rwy.
output: Fai terminal radar approach control facility controller voiced concern regarding runway(s) number change at ladd military aaf; alleging charting delay.

input: I am filing report due to the inadequate training i have received regarding the new quick reference handbook i have not used the new quick reference handbook in a training situation where i feel comfortable using the new procedural guide in an emergency situation.
output: B757 flight crew finds the online training received regarding the new quick reference handbook to be completely inadequate. The taxi is delayed after pushback to study the new quick reference handbook as an advance copy had not been made available to the pilots.

input: Maint allegedly fixed an item that was written in our aircraft logbook. They signed it off and we then flew the aircraft for 4 legs (tkof/lndgs). On the last leg we discovered that the 'fixed' item was again malfunctioning. We wrote it up again only to later find out that they never repaired the item. They said they did...but they lied. This aircraft was an lgt. Engineers at tulsa authority/authorized it to fly with this 'no go' item broken from srq to dfw. Maintenance performed the wrong checked on the landing gear warning system and then signed it off the maintenance item as fixed. When the item showed it was not fixed (4 legs later); then tulsa engineers grounded the aircraft we were lied to and therefore flew this aircraft in violation of federal aviation regulations and in violation of our own minimum equipment list recommend company mechs be checkeded for their legality.
output: Flt crew of lgt type aircraft noted a maintenance item written off as repaired. Aircraft had been flown several days with the item inoperative.

input: Location: gate at ont. After aircraft parked at the gate; parking brakes set; left/right (directions) and left/right (directions) engs shut down; and parking chklist complete; jetbridge pushed the aircraft approximately 1 feet/foot from parked position after jetbridge was pulled away from aircraft the nose slid back to original parked position request maintenance inspection of fuselage for sideload damage. Main wheels did not move from parked position during this event.
output: Acft struck by jetbridge after arrival, arrive at gate.

input: Cabin pressure loss at 35000'; rapid dsnt made to 26000' where manual pressure was able to maintain cabin pressure at 5000'. While finishing procedures air safety inspector gave f/a his identify wanting to come to the cockpit. Being distracted;i missed turning on the seat belt sign. I also had no idea he was on board. On deplaning; he informed me the seat belt sign was not on. I informed him jokingly that it was his fault; he distracted me during the time we were finishing our procs.
output: Pressurization problem at fl350 dictated emergency descent. Capt advised by aci he forgot the seat belt sign.

input: We had pack 2 overload and fail at fl250 with pack 1 already on minimum equipment list causing the cabin to rise rapidly. We [advised atc] to get air traffic control priority to 10;000 ft. We ran the associated checklists and decided zzz was the closest suitable airport. Landed in zzz.pack 2 overload with pack 1 on mel.
output: Emb-145 flight crew reported a loss of cabin pressure due to a pack 2 failure with pack 1 on mel.

input: After takeoff the lo hydraulic level annunciator illuminated. The appropriate checklist was run and the company was contacted for instructions; whether to continue to our destination or return to the departure airport. It was decided to continue due to long runways and better maintenance facilities (checklist list called for landing as soon as practical). Enroute all checklists were reviewed associated with a lo hydraulic level annunciator (i.e. No flap landing and manual gear extension). A crossing restriction was given by air traffic control during the briefing of the possible issue; the aircraft suddenly started an un-commanded turn to the right. The pilot flying used the heading mode and corrected back towards the assigned course during which air traffic control queried us as to what our heading was. This led the pilot flying to disconnect the autopilot and increase the rate of bank and descent rate to comply with the assigned crossing restriction. As pilot not flying i was heads down operating flight management system to put us back on course. I glanced up to check our position and noticed we were descending through 13000. I made the call to the pilot flying and he stated he was correcting. The altitude deviation was approximately 200 feet/foot it is unknown to both crewmembers as to why the flight management system commanded the turn. The pilot flying stated he was too involved with solving the flight management system issues as well as the lo hydraulic level problem which distracted him from the basic scan. The pilot monitoring was heads down solving the flight management system issue and did not keep a frequent scan of the aircraft. It is important to maintain the basic concept of a crew and the division of duties.
output: Cessna excel flight crew received lo hydraulic level annunciator after takeoff. They continue to their destination where a distraction caused by an flight management computer problem resulted in an overshoot of their cleared descend to altitude.

input: After landing on runway(s) 27l at cve the tower told us to roll through crossing runway(s) 18 w/o delay. The capt did not hear this instruction and applied brakes to stop aircraft to get off runway(s) 27l before crossing runway(s) 18. I told the capt to 'roll through' the intersecting runway(s) since i believed he had not heard the towers instructions. The tower then came back very angrily and told us to toll through runway(s) 18. The capt added power but the aircraft was slow to accelerate. As we were crossing runway(s) 18 another aircraft was in the landing flare on runway(s) 18. We xed runway(s) 18 w/o incident.
output: Potential conflict between two landing aircraft using multiple runway(s) operation intersecting rwys.

input: We were cleared to descend via the gibbz area navigation standard terminal arrival route to iad. We started the arrival in vertical navigation path allowing the flight management computer to calculate our vertical navigation. The airplane started down on vertical navigation path; however after looking at our distance and altitude we were going to cross jimve intersection very high; probably 2;000 feet/foot high. I disconnected the autopilot and immediately started a steeper descent with speed brakes deployed. Despite our effort we crossed jimve 600 feet/foot high.the same occurred at the next waypoint on the arrival; vertical navigation path was calculating a high crossing again. We discontinued vertical navigation and reverted to manual vertical navigation. The flight management computer had been programmed correctly and wind information input. We had flown this same aircraft on a previous leg that same day and no problems occurred on a previous area navigation arrival. The remainder of the flight was normal.
output: When their autoflight system; operating in vertical navigation path mode; failed to comply with the first two altitude constraints on the gibbz area navigation standard terminal arrival route to iad the flight crew of a b757-200 reverted to manual control on their descent path. The standard terminal arrival route had been properly programmed including descent wind forecasts and the autoflight system had conducted a previous area navigation standard terminal arrival route descent without incident.

input: Atc instructions were as follows: cleared to exit first available left/right (directions) turn. Runway(s) 14/32 closed. Not plowed. Blowing snow from left/right (directions) of runway(s) 23 obliterated taxiway exit signs. Snow drifted onto runway(s) could not definitely find taxiway as soon as i turned left/right (directions) i realized that i did not enter taxiway but a snow ridge alongside runway(s) shut down engs and was pushed back onto runway(s) followed fbo's truck to ramp. Parallel taxiway was also covered with ridges of blowing snow. Suggest buf airport install snow fences on airport property to prevent or at least decrease snow ridges. No damage to acft.
output: Arpt problem runway(s) and taxiway edge not fully plowed.

input: We were descending into the nashville terminal area. We had some warning of chop at 16000 feet/foot the seat belt sign was turned on in anticipation of chop. Once through 16000 feet/foot the chop stopped. We picked up light turbulence at 12000 feet/foot and the capt made a public address for flight attendants to be seated. We finally descended to 3000 feet/foot to leave turbulence #1 flight attendant advised us that she was injured along with one other passenber nashville operations(s) was advised that we would be needing medical assistance at our arrival, arrive gate. We were met by local police (qualified emt). All 3 flight attendants were injured along with 1 passenber #1 flight attendant and passenber were transported to local hospital.
output: The flight crew descended through turbulence with the seat belt sign on. 3 flight attendants and 1 passenber were injured.

input: On noise abatement climb out of lgb and cleared to 4000 feet/foot we noticed cessna on traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii we stopped climb and cessna overflew us at 3500 feet/foot we asked socal intermediate fix they noticed the cessna and they said 'no; but do now on mode c.'
output: B737 crew used traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic advisory to avoid an near midair collision in sct class b.

input: I departed my home airport and landed at zzz full stop and taxied back for a takeoff. Engine making full power at 60 knots added slight back pressure on yoke; plane became light on mains but with no rotation; checked airspeed passing 70 knots. Applied full back to yoke; still no rotation. Pulled throttle to idle; plane settled back onto runway. Began max breaking. Pulled mixture; slowed before running off end of pavement; past 200 feet of grass overrun and down a 20 feet ravine. Came to a stop in brush; with no injury to pilot. I checked the movement of yoke; free and clear but the elevator was not moving. I looked through baggage area into tail section and found the up elevator cable broken at the turnbuckle. The break was at the section where threaded section meets the barrel.
output: Pa28 pilot reports failure of his aircraft to rotate during takeoff even with full aft elevator input. The takeoff is rejected resulting in a runway excursion and damage to the aircraft but no injuries. A failed elevator control cable turnbuckle was discovered during post incident inspection.

input: Aircraft x was a seattle departure. S46 departure controller issued 'direct arrie' which is on his route; and a very common fix for direct. The pilot (non-native english speaking) read back arrie; and even pronounced 'arrie' when asked; but on further questioning had spelled it 'arrue' which was also on his flight plan. This put him in direct conflict with the marnr and jawbn arrivals. I gave him a heading of 250 while we figured out what was going on. At that time; the departure controller called to tell me it didn't look like aircraft x was going to arrie; and i informed him that i'd already turned him. Both arrie and arrue are on j523. I don't know if aircraft have qwerty keyboards; but for similar fixes to have only one letter different that are adjacent to each other on the keyboard may be a contributing factor. Rename either the arrie or arrue fix to something that is not similar to another fix on the airway.
output: Zse controller reported of an aircraft that went to an incorrect fix causing conflict with arrivals. The fix names were almost identical and off by one letter.

input: Thirty five minutes after departure and level at fl330; observed numerous level 1 and 2 alerts as well as loss of all flight management system navigation and way points. All system quantities and numeric values had x's displayed and all systems with left/right (directions) sides (not any engine indications) indicated that the left side had failed. Advised air traffic control of our loss of primary navigation and continued our present heading via air traffic control instructions. We took the next several minutes to assess the alerts and figure out what had actually failed and what was a false indication. Having figured out that several indicated failures were incorrect and assessing that what had failed had a functioning back up system or wouldn't affect us either way with our airport/runway landing choice; with visual meteorological conditions conditions existing from our current position all the way to our destination and with several items to still address and communications to make. Our filed destination was the closest; safest airport in point of time. Given our current status we declared emergency and received clearance via radar vectors (while the #2 vor and dme (co-located) was available for enroute navigation; given the task saturation we were experiencing; i elected to request vectors all the way in for the visual approach). We notified dispatch via automatic communications addressing & reporting system and spoke with maintenance control. We asked for any guidance for our given condition and was told to follow our via fail checklist (that doesn't exist). One piece of information maintenance did provide when asked was that the landing gear console lights 'should' illuminate indicating a down and locked condition (they were right/had 3 green for landing). We felt that the flaps/slats and landing gear would operate normally but wouldn't have any indication (pseu fault). With that in mind we requested a visual approach to 27r and to have the fire trucks standing by. In speaking with the flight attendants: i informed them of our status and that we would have the safety equipment standing by but to expect a normal landing and that i would let them know if anything changed. I made a public address to the passengers as well with the same message. We had to use the quick reference handbook performance section to figure vref/app speeds as that function of the ms didn't work. Since the first officer could manually tune the loc/course we decided he would fly the approach and i would make the landing. Having made a visual approach to a landing and with no irregularities noted by us; tower or the fire trucks; we taxied to the gate where we were met by maintenance personnel.it was determined that via 1 fail and according to the mechanic another internal failure that had yet to be identified when i left the aircraft.
output: A b717 via (versatile integrated avionics) 1 failed in flight resulting in the loss of critical flight information so an emergency was declared and the flight continued to its filed destination.

input: We were near the end of completing rvsm trailing cone engineering flight testing/data collection at 5000 feet/foot and the low level fuel annunciators began to flicker. The boost pumps were turned on per the abnormal procedures we completed the last condition. Initially we thought we had an annunciator problem with approximately 1600 pounds of fuel showing on the gauges; and because of the excellent reliability i have experienced on citation jets fuel quantity system also; the flight test engineer discussed having this discrepancy on the previous 2 flts. I was on vacation for 2 weeks prior to this flight takeoff fuel was indicating 2100 pounds then the annunciators came on steady (+/-185 15 pounds per design). I did not like the condition of the aircraft and decided to stop testing and return to ict (35 nautical mile nw of ict). Wichita approach control assigned heading 100 degrees and 4500 feet/foot vector for sequencing to runway(s) 19l. En route to ict; the left/right (directions) engine flamed out. Wichita approach control was advised. I was indicating approximately 195 knot(s) i was preparing myself and the aircraft for the left/right (directions) engine to flame out; and it did approximately 30 seconds after the left/right (directions) an emergency was declared. A speed of approximately 180 knot(s) was used to glide. The k-96 highway appeared to be the best place to land the aircraft considering wind and the fact that the fields had been soaked with heavy rains for the past 2 days. I aligned the aircraft with the roadway and tried to figure a way to fit into the flow of traffic i lowered the landing gear; and it came down and locked; with the windmilling engs driving the hydraulic pumps. Zero flaps was utilized to try and touch down beyond a set of power lines; and before another set of power lines. As the landing point was drawing near; i realized that i was going to land on a vehicle. This was the only traffic that i had concern for. The roadway ahead of this vehicle was clear i flew the aircraft over the median to avoid the vehicle and figuring that the operator would see me and slow or stop. I reasoned; once i passed the vehicle; she would stop. Once past that vehicle; i maneuvered the aircraft to align with the roadway. I touched down at stick shaker; with a lateral acceleration to the left/right (directions) i got the aircraft lateral acceleration stopped; but i was off the roadway to the left/right (directions) side. I maneuvered the aircraft back up and left/right (directions) onto the roadway. There was a culvert and a bridge approaching very quickly; directly ahead of the aircraft while i was off the roadway. I struck three side road delineator markers (reflectors) during the time i was off the roadway. I cleared the obstructions on the culvert/bridge area; ctred on the roadway; and slowly brought the aircraft to a stop. To avoid being hit from behind; i slowly brought the aircraft to a stop under normal braking. From the initial touchdown to the stop was approximately 1 mile i inadvertently got the left/right (directions) main landing gear off the roadway; trying to keep from blocking the entire sebound lanes of k-96. The fuel quantity indicated about 500-550 pounds in each fuel tank; 1000-1100 pounds total fuel at rest on the highway minimal damage was sustained to the aircraft nose radome and left/right (directions) wing leading edge; from the road delineators. A small amount of dirt/mud was thrown into the left/right (directions) engine inlet. The fuel gauging system was inaccurate. The system was an experimental fuel gauging system without the means to annunciate system diagnostic faults. A production aircraft would have annunciated the faults. 3 fuel quantity probes were found to be faulted; post incident investigation. I was not briefed of the fuel anomaly; nor was the conflicting annunciations written up by the previous crews for 2 flts. I would be more than happy to discuss this; for the purposes of enhancing aircraft safety. One conclusion is that you must the recreational uas safety test the worst indication/annunciator; when conflicting information is being presented in the cockpit.
output: Flc of citation 525 on a test flight has low level fuel annunciators flicker. Heading back to the airport the left/right (directions) engine flames out; then the left/right (directions) off airport landing is made on a hwy.

input: Location: 35 mile se pjg vor and dme (co-located) after being handed off from miq center to curacao; we were given the clearance to climb to and maintain fl350 to be level by 20 mile se of pjg. We computed the climb required and determined the aircraft could comply. We verified 20 mile controller agreed. The aircraft could comply with 10 mile to spare. At 35 mile from pjg on a310; climbing we got a traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii traffic alert. We noted that the aircraft was 2200 feet/foot above us and descending i told curacao control that we had the traffic in sight; even though we were not advised the controller said that that aircraft (y) was supposed to be at fl370; and was talking to miq center we ended up passing within 7 mile and 800 feet/foot vertical from aircraft y. I contacted miq center and found out that aircraft y was cleared from fl370 to fl130. I told the miq controller that he had violated his separation required. Aircraft y defended the action and said; we had you on the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii and varied their descent to avoid the direct conflict. I told aircraft y on the frequency that just because a controller gives you a clearance you are obligated to adjust as necessary intermediate fix the clearance was given in error. He said he had been cleared direct to an arrival, arrive point just nw of miq. The controller admitted he made an error.
output: Operror near pjg; fo.

input: I inadvertently oversvced the #2 integrated drive generator -- while pressure-filling; no oil overflowed. Shortly thereafter; i went into scheduled computer training. It was my intention to investigate why oil did not overflow. I just plain forgot. Plane had to return to the blocks. About 1 1/2 hours of delay. Callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the rptr stated when filling the integrated drive generator a dark bottle was used to monitor the overflow and it appeared to have at least a quart from the overflow port. The rptr said he had svced these integrated drive generator units numerous times and never experienced any trouble in svcing or replacement. The rptr stated the dark plastic bottle being used; combined with nighttime conditions; were contributing factors.
output: A b757-200 returned to the gate due to #2 integrated drive generator high oil temperature caused by oversvcing.

input: Fo (rptr) was pilot flying on high left/right (directions) downwind to runway(s) 27l at atl; we were 9 mile east of the runway(s) when i thought i heard the capt accept the clearance 'acr zyx; turn left/right (directions) heading 360 degs.' this would have been a base turn; and was what we were both expecting (our assigned heading prior to this was 090 degs). I was hand flying and began a turn to the left/right (directions) to 360 degrees after approximately 10 seconds on the heading 360 degrees the approach controller said; 'acr zyx; your heading should be 090 degrees turn left/right (directions) heading 100 degrees descend and maintain 3500 ft.' i quickly initiated the turn back to the left/right (directions) no conflict resulted; and the traffic alert and collision avoidance systemii never issued any traffic warnings. Both the capt and i thought we had heard our call sign; but the controller said he had been talking to a 'yzx;' not 'zyx.' we have both encountered and been subject to this type of audio-dyslexia before. However; in this case; we think the controller had misspoke. Contributing factors were: 1) this was the last leg of a 4 day trip; and both the capt and first officer had tight connecting flight times to commute back to their homes. Both were in a hurry to get to atl. 2) it was the usual place for a base turn to occur. 3) the frequency was very busy; and when the capt acknowledged the clearance he could have been stepped on by the proper aircraft acknowledging the clearance 4) similar call signs on same frequency without either crew being told. In the future; we will pay closer attention when other aircraft with similar call signs are on the same frequency sometimes the controllers will bring this to our attention other times they will not.
output: Dc9 crew accepted clearance for other acft.

input: I was the pilot in command of a piper cheyenne ii flying from bishop; ca; to reno; nv. I was approaching rno. Since tower was calling winds at 250 degrees at 15 knot(s) gusting to 20 knot(s) i asked for and was cleared to land on runway(s) 25. Gusty wind conditions were observed on final and on landing i touched the airplane down gently; put the propellers into reverse; and then began applying brakes. At some point during the landing roll; the left/right (directions) main tire went flat; but did not adversely affect directional control until the aircraft was below 40 knot(s) the aircraft was stopped on the runway(s) and towed to parking.
output: Air taxi pilot of a piper cheyenne ii has a flat tire on rollout after landing aircraft is towed off the rwy.

input: We were enroute to lax and beginning our descent on the standard terminal arrival route when we encountered wake turbulence from an airbus 380; 16 miles ahead of us. I was the pilot flying (pf). I immediately maintained control of the aircraft while disengaging automation and reducing aoa and thrust. Roll was unstable until we descended below the wake; where we stabilized the roll and recovered to the desired flight path. I don't recall how much aob we encountered but at least 20 degrees. We split up our duties and the pilot monitoring (first officer) reported the encounter to air traffic control and then talked with the flight attendants (f/a's) and informed the passengers as to what had happened. The b f/a said she 'may have' scraped her knee; the a and celsius were fine. After landing and passenger deplaning; we spoke with them to determine if she was hurt. She said she was fine; she looked fine and both the first officer and i looked at her and her knees and there was nothing; they went on to their next flight. My biggest concern was if she was injured but she insisted she was ok; and wanted to operate the next flight. I think she was ok; or else i would have taken a different course of action with her. Air traffic control did not inform us that we were following an a380; they had vectored us off course and slowed us but did not say why. Had we known; we would have sat the f/a's down.
output: B737 captain reported a flight attendant was slightly injured during a wake turbulence encounter on arrival into lax following an a380.

input: I was the flying pilot; performing reduced thrust; flaps 5; international civil aviation organization procedure takeoff. We had minimal spacing for takeoff behind an a320. Winds straight down the runway. During normal international civil aviation organization encountered mild wake turbulence from preceding aircraft. Retracted gear at the normal point. Approaching 1;300 feet/foot above ground level received master caution aural warning. I remained fully engaged flying the aircraft on the international civil aviation organization climb schedule; dealing with wake turbulence and the altitude restriction. A quick glance provided a gear door light with all three gear lights indicating black; not down and locked; which matched the handle position. I noted the need to monitor speed for gear door limits. While i flew; the captain and [relief pilot] commented the condition and the captain put the gear handle down noting the gear door indication. Upon normal cycling time the gear indicated 3 green gear lights with no other warnings or indications of problems. The captain then raised the gear handle; a normal retraction occurred. We referenced the associated checklists; determined we were in a normal condition; continued on to destination.
output: A b767-300 first officer reported encountering wake turbulence shortly after takeoff at their international departure airport; complicated by an abnormal gear door indication. Cycling the gear solved the indication problem and they continued.

input: Immediately after vfr military training routes and prior to gear retraction; aircraft incurred multiple seagull strikes from hundreds of seagulls rising up from departure end of runway(s) both engs had compressor stalls; aircraft had rapid deterioration of performance and 'some' smoke entered cabin through the air conditioning system neither engine 'flamed out' and after engs stabilized; there was a noticeable vibration of undetermined source of aircraft acft returned to msy for inspection. A normal instrument landing system and landing was completed on runway(s) 28. Aircraft required both engs changed plus worked on fuselage and wings. Smoke in cabin dissipated before landing there was no mention on automatic terminal information service of the seagulls on the runway(s) an updated automatic terminal information service from ground control was given during push back with no mention of the seagulls. His was/is an airport in an area of known seagull activity. My feeling is that this incident (which very easily could of been a disaster) could have been prevented with a more vigorous program of runway(s) protection on days and times when seagull activity is likely to occur.
output: Bird strike just after liftoff. Return land.

input: We did an air turnback because the aircraft would not pressurize in automatic standby; or manual modes. When we pulled back into the gate; the first officer pulled his seat forward and we found 5 circuit breakers out. Maintenance had brought the aircraft from the hangar and we did what we thought was a normal preflt; which according to our procedures includes 2 checkeds of the circuit breaker panels. After we were airborne and the aircraft did not pressurize; we leveled at 1000 feet/foot and i engaged the autoplt; gave the quick reference handbook to the first officer who went through all the procedures as we were climbing the first thing i thought about was circuit breakers since the pressurization panel did not appear to have any power to it. While the first officer went through the quick reference handbook i pulled his left/right (directions) armrest forward to checked the circuit breaker panel behind him. Just as i was doing this; air traffic control gave us a vector heading and a descent i looked at the circuit breakers and acknowledged air traffic control began the turn and descent and we ran our chklists and made a normal landing 3 times we checkeded the circuit breaker panels and 3 times we apparently missed 5 circuit breakers out. Supplemental information from acn 387267: i learned the aircraft had been in maintenance but no logbook write-up concerning pressurization. The fo's oxygen hose blocked the 4 circuit breakers; and i accidentally missed those breakers during the preflt.
output: A b737-200 returned to the field due to unable to pressurize the aircraft in any mode caused by all pressurization system circuit breakers open.

input: Climbing out of houston we were handed off from houston departure to houston center. No mention of a traffic conflict was given on either frequency. We received a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory for traffic 12 o'clock and 3-4 miles. The captain asked air traffic control about the traffic. Air traffic control responded very casually about the traffic and said something to effect of 'oh yeah; they didn't tell you about him.' he made it seem like it wasn't a conflict and in my mind i let my guard down slightly. A few seconds later we received a traffic alert and collision avoidance system resolution advisory at this point we were climbing through 13;000 feet/foot or so. I believe the traffic was descending to 12;500 feet/foot the captain was mostly talking to air traffic control on the radio.i hesitated a second or two to respond to the resolution advisory (due to my guard being down by atc's casual response to the traffic) and then i followed the 'descend; descend' resolution advisory a few seconds after initiating the descent i visually acquired the traffic (a beech baron) and informed the captain that he was in sight. At this point; i knew that the traffic was not going to be a collision hazard and shallowed my descent. I don't believe the captain heard that i had the traffic in sight and was wondering why i wasn't still descending at the recommended resolution advisory vertical speed. The traffic then passed off of our right wing; probably 200-300 feet/foot horizontally and 400-600 feet/foot vertically. At this point the captain visually acquired the aircraft. We climbed uneventfully after the incident. Air traffic control gave no indication that anything wrong had happened. 300-400 miles down the road to our destination; we were later contacted by a later center asking about the incident. The event occurred because air traffic control failed to separate traffic for us. I still don't know exactly why or how it happened but my belief is that we were handed off my houston departure too early and before we were properly separated by the conflicting traffic. Upon checking in with houston center; we were at that point still below his airspace and thus he wasn't really looking out for conflicting traffic. I think everyone made some mistakes in this incident. Air traffic control obviously failed to properly separate traffic. I personally failed in responding to the resolution advisory immediately. I believe the captain failed in his response to the traffic advisory and resolution advisory by calling air traffic control first --- and not looking for the traffic first. With air traffic control being the first 'link' in the chain being broken; the captain first called the one person who should have avoided the entire situation to begin with. Atc's response to the captain's inquiry was also a failure. By his responding casually and almost indicating that the traffic wasn't an issue; i believe both the captain and i lowered our guards.
output: A crj-200 experienced a traffic alert and collision avoidance system traffic advisory and resolution advisory with respect to a be58 while climbing through about 13;000 departing from iah.

input: Rudder oscillations that required us to turn off yaw damper and powered rudder. Referred to communications (cockpit operating manual) and performed appropriate procedure discussed situation with dispatcher and company maintenance continued flight as scheduled without further problems discussed event with head of safety department and base chief pilot callback conversation with rptr revealed the following information the capt was flying a dc9-30 when the rudder moved unexpectedly. The aft cabin attendant rpted the movement as the crew started through their uncommanded control movement chklist. Later she came to the flight station and told them of other movement when the crew was following some troubleshooting suggestions from their maintenance control personnel and had turned on the yaw damper and rudder hydraulic power the unusual movement stopped when the crew turned off the yaw damper and the hydraulic power to the rudder. They informed the dispatcher; maintenance control and air route traffic control center and continued to destination using manual rudder control a large group of company and emergency personnel met the aircraft after they arrived and at that time they discovered that the controller had declared an emergency for them. The maintenance personnel could not say what specific failure caused the movement; they were sure that it was a yaw damper component.
output: An air carrier dc9 flight crew experienced uncommanded rudder movement that; apparently; originated from the yaw damper.

input: Cos airport traffic control tower is an atc-8 facility. We have a great mix of air carrier general aviation and military style traffic we received an updated radar system (asr-11) late last yr. Unfortunately our displays and software were not updated to enable us to easily display all the weather information we now have the capability of displaying. When thunderstorms are in the area and we have the asr-11 weather radar showing that there is all 6 levels of weather information available we can only display 2 levels of weather information at a time. Second officer basically what this does is make the controller have to try and extrapolate where the other levels of weather are located and try not to turn aircraft into them. In other words; it will display the 2 levels of weather data you set up to display; but the rest of the display is blank as intermediate fix there was no other weather in the area. The only way for this issue to be resolved is for the federal aviation administration to update our radar displays and software to be able to fully utilize the information that the asr-11 is capable of providing. This would include newer digital displays capable of displaying multiple levels of weather information software capable of deciphering this enhanced weather information without these updates/enhancements the aircraft carrying the thousands upon thousands of flyers flying into and out of the colorado springs area are at risk.
output: Cos controller expressed concern regarding weather display limitation on newly operational asr-11 equip.

input: We were advised early on the downwind leg that we would receive a short approach the first officer was flying. On base leg; we were cleared for a visual approach i don't remember intermediate fix we were also told to contact tower at the outer marker as is usually the case. I presume we were. As we overheaded the outer marker we were high and fast. The first officer called for final flaps 15 knot(s) above the structural limit. I told him to level off until we were slow enough to extend final flaps which he did. We were stabilized on glide path and speed between 800-1000 feet/foot above ground level with landing chklist complete except for the flight attendants notifying us that they were out of the lower galley. (we would have to make a go around intermediate fix notification not received.) after stabilizing on glide path; i concentrated on the flight instruments airspd and runway(s) environment for the rest of the approach there was a lot of talk on the frequency but i never hear our call sign used again. The first officer was concerned about the galley status and asked the second officer 2 or 3 times intermediate fix the galley was clear the notification came via interphone about 20 seconds before landing after clearing the runway(s) and taxiing inbound i commented that we hadn't received any taxi instructions. I glanced down at the radio and was shocked to see that i was still on approach control frequency possible factors: not being stabilized on approach sooner. Being preoccupied with speed and flaps at the outer marker where i normally would checked in with tower the concern or focus on the flight attendants in the lower galley requiring us to contemplate a go around at the last moment. Corrective action: maybe put 'lndg clrnc' on chklist; intermediate fix not; 'think landing clrnc' after chklist complete.
output: Unauth landing lndg without clrnc.

input: I took over this flight from morning dispatcher while the aircraft was out of service due to return to field with landing gear issue. We decided to delay the flight out until maintenance announces aircraft is airworthy for our scheduled flight. After a few tests from maintenance; they were unable to fix the problem; requested us route the aircraft to zzz in order to fix it and we complied. We canceled the scheduled flight and rescheduled the aircraft to go directly to zzz as a maintenance ferry. I started to flight planning after the decision of ferry has been made. In the process; i found out that e145 lr2 performance was not available and i could not continue my flight plan without it. So i stopped and asked coordinator for extra assistance. He notified dispatch manager and operations system support and we delayed the flight out furthermore. Few hours after; we were finally able to get e145 lr2 gear down performance data loaded into our data system with limitation of flying at 8000 feet/foot i observed and followed the airplane manual for flight with landing gear down to ensure the flight may be operated safely. I sent the release over and coordinator faxed flight with landing gear down supplement to station after all operation limitations were met. The captain and i discussed about the limitations and weather conditions over the phone and we both agreed it is safe to conduct the plan. The flight finally departed msy heading zzz. I received a radio call not long after they passed mei (meridian vortac) from the crew stating they have a higher fuel burn than planned. The crew advised me they are using more fuel than planned and their burn rate is about 4;000 pounds per hour with fuel on board of 7;400 pounds i advised the crew to stand by and i will work on the fuel numbers for them again. I calculated from vxv (volunteer vortac) to zzz with the route planned will take about 3;000 pounds of fuel. On top of that i need to add the reserve fuel which makes our minimum fuel at 4;900 pounds from vxv (about 320 nautical mile away). After that calculation; i started to look for alternate airports nearby just in case we won't have enough fuel when cross vxv. Weather was good all around the country that night. I found tys; sdf; gsp; atl; bna; are all reporting and forecasting visual flight rules weather suitable for listing as alternate. The crew called again to check on the progress and alternate plan. They were informed about the plan of the possibility of diverting to alternate. When i asked them about their current fuel on board they told me 5;500 pounds i looked on the flight explore and measured vxv is still about 150 nautical mile away. At speed of 250 knots indicated airspeed with distance 150 nautical mile i came to realize; we don't have enough fuel to continue to zzz. So i advised the crew to divert to bna and they did. Comparing the actual burn number and the planned burn number; our actual fuel usage was about 1;000 pounds more than planned when the crew first called me and at the second radio call our actual fuel usage was about 1;300 pounds more than planned. The plan i provided to crew had a very low accuracy on fuel planning. We ended up short on fuel and had to divert. Have a step by step training manual for gear down ferry like we had for medical emergency on all type and variations. Have a second person check the performance data we received.
output: Flight planning data for a gear down ferry flight of an e145 provided inaccurate fuel burn numbers and the flight must divert due to insufficient fuel.

input: Aircraft x was a mci departure enroute [westbound] and the aircraft was slightly off route. I asked the pilot what fix they were navigating towards and they told me they were issued direct catts. There was a pause and the pilot spelled the fix and said katts. The flight plan had both fixes; catts which is on the standard departure out of mci and used daily and the other fix katts which was much further down in the flight plan. The issue was resolved quickly and without incident. Recommend maybe a little more clarification from the pilot when two identical sounding fixes are in the flight plan to ensure that everyone is on the same page. Or a slight change in the spelling of fixes that are sounding identical.
output: Zkc controller reported a departure on the chief7 standard instrument departure navigating to katts instead of the published standard instrument departure fix of catts. Both fixes are phonetically identical and very similar spelling.

input: On this day; c152 called for taxi. He was issued taxi to runway(s) 27r at 'r' intersection the left/right (directions) side of taxiway b. Pilot read back instructions correctly. For some reason; pilot turned left/right (directions) on b1; then left/right (directions) onto departure end of runway(s) 27r. Unfortunately; a pa44 was on a touch and go. The pa44 had just started his departure saw the cessna; aborted and turned off the runway(s) at taxiway left/right (directions) supplemental information from acn 597870: i called ground he gave me the taxi clearance 'taxi to runway(s) 27r at taxiway left/right (directions) r side of taxiway b.' after i read it back; i started to taxi. Because i thought i'm second officer familiar with airport i didn't pay attention during taxiing. I then taxied across taxi b; turned left/right (directions) on runway(s) 9l (believing this was taxiway b). Ground didn't stop me during my taxiing. During my turn to the runway(s) i saw the runway(s) white ctrline; and i also saw traffic at the beginning of the runway(s) which was taking off. I stopped immediately and the other aircraft also started to slow down. Then i added power to get clear of runway(s) as fast as possible and then contacted ground it's my responsibility to pay attention during every phase of flight but i didn't.
output: C152 taxiing for departure at sfb turned onto active runway(s) with traffic on touch and go departure roll.

input: No notification of hazmat on board; 17 minute(s) after takeoff received automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from load planning 'just informed by operations(s) that you have 3 different types of hazmat on board -- 1) rry -- radio active; 2) rmd -- combat; 3) rng -- non/flammable gas.' my response; that that information is insufficient. Next automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from load planning; 'that's what the sector lead informed me over the phone...that they still had your hazmat forms in their hand.' my response; i need that person's name. Next automatic communications addressing & reporting system message from load planning; 'copy on your message. Contacted operations(s) manager we will get you additional information asap.' next automatic communications addressing & reporting system message was from dispatcher with information on all 3 items including imp code; quantity; index number; destination and class number.
output: A b757-200 flight crew after takeoff was notified by dispatch they had undocumented hazmat on board. They got the required information over the radio and continued.

input: Received electronic centralized aircraft monitoring smoke lavatory message. Rang flight attendants to find source of smoke/fire. Response was that a male passenger was using aerosol hairspray in aft left lavatory. Once lavatory door was opened; alarm went off (ceased).
